It remains to construct a morphism \(\varphi:C\to\operatorname{im}(f)\) in that category. Apply the right-hand version of Lemma reference to \(X\stackrel q\twoheadrightarrow C\stackrel g\hookrightarrow Y\). It supplies a \(\varphi\) making the right half of \[\text{Diagram chapter1-unit-010-d009}\] commute. Lemma reference then shows that the whole diagram commutes.

Inferring that a subdiagram commutes from the commutativity of its outer frame is a standard technique that will be used repeatedly.

Additive Categories: Kernels and Cokernels

This section uses the notion of a functor preserving \(\varinjlim\) or \(\varprojlim\). This is basic category theory; see [Li1] or the brief review in Section 1.5. We first recall \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ab}}\)-categories and additive categories; see [Li1].

  • A category \(\mathcal C\) is an \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ab}}\)-category, or a preadditive category, if every \(\operatorname{Hom}(X,Y)\) is an abelian group, written additively (equivalently, a \(\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\)-module), and every composition map \(\operatorname{Hom}(Y,Z)\times\operatorname{Hom}(X,Y)\to\operatorname{Hom}(X,Z)\) is \(\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\)-bilinear. One may therefore speak of the morphism \(0\in\operatorname{Hom}(X,Y)\). An \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ab}}\)-category may have \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ab}}\)-subcategories; every full subcategory is automatically one.

  • If \(\mathcal C_1,\mathcal C_2\) are \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ab}}\)-categories, a functor \(F:\mathcal C_1\to\mathcal C_2\) is additive if the induced maps on \(\operatorname{Hom}\) sets are group homomorphisms. Equivalences of \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ab}}\)-categories and their quasi-inverses are always understood to be additive.

We shall need the following elementary but fundamental observation. By convention, a linear map of \(\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\)-modules means a module homomorphism.

Proposition. Let \(\mathcal C\) and \(\mathcal C'\) be \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ab}}\)-categories.

  1. Given adjoint functors \[\text{Diagram chapter1-unit-011-diagram-001},\] with \(F,G\) additive, the adjunction isomorphism \(\varphi:\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal C'}(F(\cdot),\cdot)\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal C}(\cdot,G(\cdot))\) is linear.

  2. For any \(\alpha:I\to\mathcal C\), the isomorphism in the universal property \[\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}}\left( \varinjlim \alpha, T \right) \simeq \varprojlim_{i \in \operatorname{Ob}(I)} \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}}(\alpha(i), T), \quad T \in \operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{C})\] is linear whenever the colimit exists. The analogous assertion holds for \(\varprojlim\).

Proof. For (i), the discussion following [Li1] says that \(\varphi\) is determined by the unit \(\eta\) and counit \(\varepsilon\): \[\varphi(f) = Gf \circ \eta_X, \quad \varphi^{-1}(g) = \varepsilon_Y \circ Fg, \quad f \in \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}'}(FX, Y), \; g \in \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}}(X, GY);\] bilinearity of composition makes \(\varphi\) linear. For (ii), the isomorphism is described by composition with \(\iota_i:\alpha(i)\to\varinjlim\alpha\), so it too is linear.

In an \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ab}}\)-category, \(X_1\times X_2\) exists if and only if \(X_1\sqcup X_2\) exists, and then there is a canonical isomorphism \(X_1\sqcup X_2\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}X_1\times X_2\). This structure is called a biproduct; see [Li1]. More generally, a biproduct of \(X_1,\ldots,X_n\) is an object \(Z\) with morphisms \(\text{Diagram chapter1-unit-011-d001}\), \(i=1,\ldots,n\), satisfying \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:biproduct-identities}{}\begin{gathered} p_i \iota_j = \begin{cases} \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}, & i=j \\ 0, & i \neq j \end{cases} \qquad \sum_{i=1}^n \iota_i p_i = \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{Z}. \end{gathered} \end{equation}\] Then the families \(\iota_i:X_i\to Z\) and \(p_i:Z\to X_i\) induce isomorphisms \[\coprod_{i=1}^n X_i \ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}Z \ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}\prod_{i=1}^n X_i.\] By convention, the biproduct for \(n=0\) is a zero object. If an \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ab}}\)-category \(\mathcal C\) has a zero object, [Li1] ensures that the zero morphism between any \(X,Y\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal C)\) agrees with \(0\in\operatorname{Hom}(X,Y)\). Moreover, the preceding \(\coprod_iX_i\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}\prod_iX_i\) is precisely the morphism \(\delta\) of equation; this follows directly from equation.

Convention. Write the \(n\)-fold biproduct \(Z\) as \(X_1\oplus\cdots\oplus X_n\). If binary biproducts exist, all \(n\)-fold biproducts for \(n\geq1\) can be formed iteratively using the canonical isomorphism \(X_1\oplus X_2\oplus X_3\simeq(X_1\oplus X_2)\oplus X_3\). Also set \[X^{\oplus n} := \underbracket{X \oplus \cdots \oplus X}_{n\; \text{terms}}.\] The product diagonal \(\delta_X:X\to X^{\oplus n}\) and the coproduct codiagonal \(\check\delta_X:X^{\oplus n}\to X\) are characterized by \(p_i\delta_X=\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_X=\check\delta_X\iota_i\) for \(1\leq i\leq n\). Explicitly, \(\delta_X=\sum_{i=1}^n\iota_i\) and \(\check\delta_X=\sum_{i=1}^np_i\).

Definition (Additive category). An \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ab}}\)-category \(\mathcal C\) is additive if:

  • it has a zero object \(0\);

  • every two objects \(X,Y\) have a biproduct \(X\oplus Y\).

An \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ab}}\)-subcategory of an additive category that is itself additive is an additive subcategory. Every finite family \(X_1,\ldots,X_n\) in an additive category has a biproduct \(X_1\oplus\cdots\oplus X_n\), also called their direct sum; the \(X_i\) are its direct summands.

An additive functor \(F:\mathcal C_1\to\mathcal C_2\) between additive categories preserves all finite products and coproducts, because:

  • \(F\) preserves biproducts; see [Li1];

  • \(F\) preserves zero objects, since \(F(\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_X)=\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{FX}\) and a zero object is characterized by \(\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}=0\); see [Li1].

If \(\mathcal C\) is an \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ab}}\)-category (respectively additive category), then \(\mathcal C^{\operatorname{op}}\) is naturally one as well, with \(f\mapsto f^{\operatorname{op}}\) an isomorphism \(\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal C^{\operatorname{op}}}(Y,X)\to\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal C}(X,Y)\) of groups. Henceforth, without ambiguity, \(0\) denotes both zero objects and zero morphisms in additive categories. A family \(f_i:X_i\to X'_i\), \(i=1,\ldots,n\), naturally induces \(f_1\oplus\cdots\oplus f_n:\bigoplus_iX_i\to\bigoplus_iX'_i\), explicitly \(\sum_{i=1}^n\iota'_if_ip_i\).

Example. The category \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ab}}\) is additive: addition on \(\operatorname{Hom}\) sets is pointwise, \((f+g)(x)=f(x)+g(x)\); the zero object is the zero group; and biproducts are the usual direct sums. Similarly, \(R\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\) is additive for any ring \(R\), and the forgetful functor \(R\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ab}}\) is additive. The category \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ban}}_{\ensuremath{\mathbb{C}}}\) of complex Banach spaces and continuous linear maps is also additive. Addition is again pointwise and the zero object is the zero space. For Banach spaces \((X_i,\|\cdot\|_i)\), \(i=1,2\), the biproduct may be taken to be the vector-space direct sum \(X_1\oplus X_2\) equipped with the norm \(\|(x_1,x_2)\|:=\max\{\|x_1\|_1,\|x_2\|_2\}\), where \(x_i\in X_i\).

Proposition. For morphisms \(f,g:X\to Y\) in an additive category \(\mathcal C\), \(f+g\) is the composite along the top row of the following commutative diagram: \[\text{Diagram chapter1-unit-011-d002}\] where \(f\times g\) comes from functoriality of products, and \(Y\times Y\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}Y\sqcup Y\) is the inverse of \(\delta\) in equation.

Proof. Write the biproduct maps as \(\iota_i^X,\iota_i^Y,p_i^X,p_i^Y\), \(i=1,2\). Expressing \(\delta_X\) and \(\check\delta_Y\) through them verifies the two triangles. Since \(f\oplus g=\iota_1^Yfp_1^X+\iota_2^Ygp_2^X\), \[\begin{equation} \check{\delta}_Y (f \oplus g) \delta_X = \check{\delta}_Y \iota_1^Y f p^X_1 \delta_X + \check{\delta}_Y \iota_2^Y g p^X_2 \delta_X = f + g. \end{equation}\] Identifying the biproducts with coproducts, commutativity of the square becomes \[\text{Diagram chapter1-unit-011-d003}\] which is precisely functoriality of \(\delta\) in equation.

Corollary. Let \(\mathcal C,\mathcal C'\) be additive categories and \(F:\mathcal C\to\mathcal C'\) a functor.

  1. \(F\) preserves finite products if and only if it preserves finite coproducts.

  2. If \(F\) preserves finite products, equivalently finite coproducts, then it is additive.

  3. If \(F\) preserves zero objects and biproducts, then it is additive.

  4. If \(F\) is an equivalence, then \(F\) and its quasi-inverse are additive.

  5. If \[\text{Diagram chapter1-unit-011-d004}\] is an adjoint pair, then \(F,G\) are additive; Proposition reference therefore applies.

Proof. For (i), a zero object is both the empty product and empty coproduct, so it remains only to consider the product and coproduct of \(X,Y\). The canonical isomorphism \(\delta:FX\sqcup FY\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}FX\times FY\) factors as \[FX \sqcup FY \to F(X \sqcup Y) \ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}F(X \times Y) \to FX \times FY .\] For (ii), the composite in Proposition reference along

Diagram chapter1-unit-011-d005

does not use addition on \(\operatorname{Hom}\) sets, only finite products and coproducts, the zero object, and their canonical maps. For (iii), all finite products or coproducts are built from zero objects and binary biproducts. Finally, a left adjoint preserves \(\varinjlim\), a right adjoint preserves \(\varprojlim\) ([Li1]), and equivalences preserve all limits. Thus (iv) and (v) follow from (ii).

In fact, Proposition reference shows that “additivity” is a property of the underlying category \(\mathcal C\), not additional structure.

Definition. Let \(\mathcal C\) be an \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ab}}\)-category with a zero object, and \(f:X\to Y\) a morphism.

  • If the equalizer \(\operatorname{ker}(f,0)\) exists, then \(\operatorname{ker}(f):=\operatorname{ker}(f,0)\) together with \(\operatorname{ker}(f)\hookrightarrow X\) is the kernel of \(f\).

  • If the coequalizer \(\operatorname{coker}(f,0)\) exists, then \(\operatorname{coker}(f):=\operatorname{coker}(f,0)\) together with \(Y\twoheadrightarrow\operatorname{coker}(f)\) is the cokernel of \(f\).

Thus the composites \(\operatorname{ker}(f)\to X\to Y\) and \(X\to Y\to\operatorname{coker}(f)\) are both \(0\).

Kernels and cokernels admit several complementary viewpoints.

  • For a morphism \(g:T\to X\) satisfying \(fg=0\),1 the universal property of \(\operatorname{ker}(f)=\operatorname{ker}(f,0)\) is the commutative diagram \[\text{Diagram chapter1-unit-011-d006}\]

  • For a morphism \(h:Y\to T\) satisfying \(hf=0\), the universal property of \(\operatorname{coker}(f)=\operatorname{coker}(f,0)\) is \[\text{Diagram chapter1-unit-011-d007}\]

  • The constructions are dual: \(\operatorname{coker}(f)=\operatorname{ker}(f^{\operatorname{op}})\) and \(\operatorname{ker}(f)=\operatorname{coker}(f^{\operatorname{op}})\).

Since precisely the zero morphisms factor through a zero object, the universal properties are also characterized by the pullback and pushout diagrams \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:Ker-Coker-triangles}{} \text{Diagram chapter1-unit-011-d008} \qquad \text{Diagram chapter1-unit-011-d009} \end{equation}\]

Remark. An arbitrary equalizer reduces to a kernel. For \[\text{Diagram chapter1-unit-011-d010},\] the condition \(fh=gh\) is equivalent to \((f-g)h=0\), hence \(\operatorname{ker}(f,g)=\operatorname{ker}(f-g,0)=:\operatorname{ker}(f-g)\). Dually, \(\operatorname{coker}(f,g)=\operatorname{coker}(f-g,0)=:\operatorname{coker}(f-g)\).

From now on, \(\mathcal C\) will mainly be additive.

Proposition. For morphisms \(X\xrightarrow{f}Y\xrightarrow{g}Z\) in an additive category \(\mathcal C\), there are commutative diagrams \[\text{Diagram chapter1-unit-011-d011} \quad \text{Diagram chapter1-unit-011-d012}\] where \(X\ensuremath{\underset{Y}{\times}}\operatorname{ker}(g)\to X\) (respectively \(Z\to Z\ensuremath{\underset{Y}{\sqcup}}\operatorname{coker}(f)\)) is the canonical morphism of the fiber product (respectively fiber coproduct),2 provided all indicated kernels, cokernels, and limits exist.

Proof. By equation, iterated fiber products give canonical isomorphisms \(\operatorname{ker}(gf)\simeq X\ensuremath{\underset{Z}{\times}}0\simeq X\ensuremath{\underset{Y}{\times}}(Y\ensuremath{\underset{Z}{\times}}0)\simeq X\ensuremath{\underset{Y}{\times}}\operatorname{ker}(g)\). Duality gives the cokernel statement.

Functoriality of equalizers and coequalizers induces functoriality of kernels and cokernels, characterized by \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:Ker-Coker-functoriality}{}\text{Diagram chapter1-unit-011-d013} \qquad \text{Diagram chapter1-unit-011-d014} \end{equation}\] The next result says that pullback preserves kernels and pushout preserves cokernels.

Proposition. If \[\text{Diagram chapter1-unit-011-d015}\] is a pullback (respectively pushout) square in an additive category, then the morphism \(\operatorname{ker}(f)\to\operatorname{ker}(g)\) (respectively \(\operatorname{coker}(f)\to\operatorname{coker}(g)\)) of equation is an isomorphism, provided the indicated objects exist.

Proof. By duality it suffices to treat pullbacks. For every \(T\), the universal properties give canonical isomorphisms \[\begin{align*} \operatorname{Hom}(T, \operatorname{ker}(f)) & \simeq \operatorname{ker}\left[ \operatorname{Hom}(T, X) \to \operatorname{Hom}(T, Y) \right] \\ & \simeq \operatorname{ker}\left[ \operatorname{Hom}(T, Y) \ensuremath{\underset{\operatorname{Hom}(T, Y')}{\times}} \operatorname{Hom}(T, X') \to \operatorname{Hom}(T, Y) \right] \\ & = \operatorname{ker}\left[ \operatorname{Hom}(T, X') \to \operatorname{Hom}(T, Y') \right] \simeq \operatorname{Hom}(T, \operatorname{ker}(g)), \end{align*}\] and the Yoneda lemma gives \(\operatorname{ker}(f)\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}\operatorname{ker}(g)\); see Theorem A.1.1.

Lemma. Let \(\mathcal C\) be additive and \(f:X\to Y\) a morphism.

  1. \(f\) is monic (respectively epic) if and only if \(\operatorname{ker}(f)=0\) (respectively \(\operatorname{coker}(f)=0\)).

  2. \(f\) is zero if and only if \(\operatorname{ker}(f)\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}X\), equivalently \(Y\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}\operatorname{coker}(f)\).

  3. Given \(k:Y\to Z\) (respectively \(k':W\to X\)), there is a unique morphism making the corresponding diagram commute: \[\text{Diagram chapter1-unit-011-d016} \quad \text{or} \quad \text{Diagram chapter1-unit-011-d017}\] provided the indicated kernels or cokernels exist. If \(k\) is monic (respectively \(k'\) is epic), then \(\operatorname{ker}(f)\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}\operatorname{ker}(kf)\) (respectively \(\operatorname{coker}(fk')\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}\operatorname{coker}(f)\)).

Proof. For (i), by duality consider only monomorphisms. By definition, \(f\) is monic precisely when \(f(g_1-g_2)=0\iff g_1-g_2=0\) for every \(g_1,g_2:T\to X\). Equivalently, every \(g:T\to X\) with \(fg=0\) factors through \(T\to0\to X\), exactly the universal property of \(\operatorname{ker}(f)=0\). For (ii), \(f=0\iff\operatorname{ker}(f,0)\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}X\) follows from the definition of an equalizer. For (iii), use \[\text{Diagram chapter1-unit-011-d018}\] The top inclusion is equality when \(k\) is monic. Apply the Yoneda lemma.

In an additive category, the image and coimage of Definition reference have simple descriptions.

Proposition. For \(f:X\to Y\) in an additive category \(\mathcal C\), there are canonical isomorphisms \[\begin{align*} \operatorname{im}(f) & \simeq \operatorname{ker}\left[ Y \to \operatorname{coker}(f) \right] \hookrightarrow Y, \\ \operatorname{coim}(f) & \simeq \operatorname{coker}\left[ \operatorname{ker}(f) \to X \right] \twoheadleftarrow X ; \end{align*}\] provided the indicated kernels and cokernels exist.

Proof. By duality consider only \(\operatorname{im}(f)\). Let \(i_1,i_2:Y\to Y\ensuremath{\underset{X}{\sqcup}}Y\) be canonical. By Yoneda it suffices to verify, for every \(T\), \[\begin{multline*} \operatorname{Hom}\left( T, \operatorname{im}(f) \right) = \left\{ h: T \to Y \;\middle|\; i_1 h = i_2 h \right\} \\ = \left\{ \begin{array}{r|l} h: T \to Y & \forall S \in \operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{C}),\; \forall s_1, s_2: Y \to S, \\ & s_1 f = s_2 f \implies s_1 h = s_2 h \end{array}\right\} \\ \xlongequal{s := s_1 - s_2} \left\{ \begin{array}{r|l} h: T \to Y & \forall S \in \operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{C}),\; \forall s: Y \to S, \\ & s f = 0 \implies sh = 0 \end{array}\right\} \\ = \left\{ \begin{array}{r|l} h: T \to Y & T \xrightarrow{h} Y \twoheadrightarrow \operatorname{coker}(f) \\ & \text{has composite}\; 0 \end{array}\right\} \ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\leftarrow}}\operatorname{Hom}\left( T, \operatorname{ker}\left[ Y \to \operatorname{coker}(f) \right] \right). \end{multline*}\] The first equality is \(\operatorname{im}(f):=\operatorname{ker}(i_1,i_2)\). For the second, rewrite the condition as \(s'i_1h=s'i_2h\) for every \(s':Y\ensuremath{\underset{X}{\sqcup}}Y\to S\) and use \[\begin{align*} \operatorname{Hom}\left( Y \ensuremath{\underset{X}{\sqcup}} Y, S \right) & \xrightarrow{1:1} \operatorname{Hom}(Y,S) \ensuremath{\underset{\operatorname{Hom}(X,S)}{\times}} \operatorname{Hom}(Y,S) \\ s' & \longmapsto \left( s' i_1, s' i_2 \right) =: (s_1, s_2). \end{align*}\] The fourth equality follows from the cokernel’s universal property, reducing to \(S=\operatorname{coker}(f)\).

If \(f=0\), Lemma reference(ii) gives the simplest example: \(\operatorname{im}(f)=0=\operatorname{coim}(f)\).

Example. Continuing Example reference, consider \(R\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\). A module homomorphism \(f:A\to B\) always has \(\operatorname{ker}(f)=f^{-1}(0)\) and \(\operatorname{coker}(f)=B/\{f(a):a\in A\}\). Its \(\operatorname{im}(f)\) is the set-theoretic image, \(\operatorname{coim}(f)=A/\operatorname{ker}(f)\), and the comparison in equation is the canonical module isomorphism \(A/\operatorname{ker}(f)\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}\operatorname{im}(f)\). Thus every morphism in \(R\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\) is strict.

Next consider the additive category \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ban}}_{\ensuremath{\mathbb{C}}}\) from Example reference. A continuous linear map \(f:X\to Y\) has the usual kernel \(\operatorname{ker}(f)=f^{-1}(0)\), which is again a Banach space, while \(\operatorname{coker}(f)=Y/\overline{\{f(x):x\in X\}}\) carries the quotient norm. The comparison morphism in equation becomes \[\text{Diagram chapter1-unit-011-d019}\] where the right side has the topology induced from \(Y\) and the left the quotient topology from \(X\). If \(f:X\to Y\) is a continuous injective linear map of Banach spaces with dense, non-surjective image, then \(\operatorname{coim}(f)=X\to Y=\operatorname{im}(f)\) is not an isomorphism. Hence \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ban}}_{\ensuremath{\mathbb{C}}}\) has non-strict morphisms.

  1. Translator’s note: the source says “for every morphism” without including the condition \(fg=0\), or dually \(hf=0\). These conditions have been restored because they are precisely the equalizer and coequalizer hypotheses; see correction O014-C006.↩︎

  2. Translator’s note: the source says “coproduct,” but the displayed object is the fiber coproduct \(Z\ensuremath{\underset{Y}{\sqcup}}\operatorname{coker}(f)\) and the proof uses duality with the fiber product; see correction O014-C005.↩︎

Generalization: Linear Categories over a Commutative Ring

The \(\operatorname{Hom}\) sets of an additive category have the structure of abelian groups. In many situations they also carry scalar multiplication by some commutative ring \(\Bbbk\). For example, every \(\operatorname{Hom}\) set in \(\Bbbk\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\) is naturally a \(\Bbbk\)-module, and composition of morphisms is \(\Bbbk\)-bilinear.

Definition. Let \(\Bbbk\) be a commutative ring. Suppose that every \(\operatorname{Hom}\) set in a category \(\mathcal{A}\) is equipped with a \(\Bbbk\)-module structure such that composition of morphisms \(\operatorname{Hom}(Y, Z) \times \operatorname{Hom}(X, Y) \to \operatorname{Hom}(X, Z)\) is a \(\Bbbk\)-bilinear map for all objects \(X,Y,Z\); in other words, the following diagram commutes: \[\text{Diagram chapter1-unit-012-d001}\] With these data, \(\mathcal{A}\) is called a \(\Bbbk\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\)-category.

Let \(F: \mathcal{A} \to \mathcal{A}'\) be a functor between \(\Bbbk\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\)-categories. If the map \(\operatorname{Hom}(X,Y) \to \operatorname{Hom}(FX,FY)\) is a \(\Bbbk\)-module homomorphism for every \(X,Y \in \operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{A})\), then \(F\) is called a \(\Bbbk\)-linear functor.

Observe that \(\Bbbk\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\) is a monoidal category under the tensor product \(\otimes := \ensuremath{\underset{\Bbbk}{\otimes}}\). Thus the term “\(\Bbbk\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\)-category” agrees with the terminology for enriched categories in [Li1]. The \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ab}}\)-categories introduced earlier are precisely the \(\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\)-categories. Conversely, forgetting scalar multiplication on a \(\Bbbk\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\)-category leaves an \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ab}}\)-category.

Example. A \(\Bbbk\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\)-category with a single object is nothing but a \(\Bbbk\)-algebra. The correspondence is given by \(\mathcal{A} \mapsto \operatorname{End}_{\mathcal{A}}(\star)\), where \(\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{A}) = \{\star\}\).

The argument of Proposition reference carries over verbatim and gives the following result.

Proposition. Let \(\mathcal{A}\) and \(\mathcal{A}'\) be \(\Bbbk\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\)-categories.

  1. Given a pair of adjoint functors

    \[\text{Diagram chapter1-unit-012-d002},\] with both \(F\) and \(G\) \(\Bbbk\)-linear, the adjunction isomorphism \(\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{A}'}(F(\cdot),\cdot) \ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}} \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{A}}(\cdot,G(\cdot))\) is \(\Bbbk\)-linear.

  2. For every \(\alpha: I \to \mathcal{A}\), the bijection \[\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{A}}\left(\varinjlim \alpha,T\right) \simeq \varprojlim_{i \in \operatorname{Ob}(I)} \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{A}}(\alpha(i),T), \quad T \in \operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{A})\] is \(\Bbbk\)-linear whenever \(\varinjlim \alpha\) exists. The same statement holds for \(\varprojlim\).

Unless otherwise specified, all functors and equivalences between \(\Bbbk\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\)-categories will henceforth be understood to be \(\Bbbk\)-linear.

Definition. If an additive category \(\mathcal{A}\) is equipped with a \(\Bbbk\)-linear structure compatible with its existing \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ab}}\)-category structure, then \(\mathcal{A}\) together with these data is called a \(\Bbbk\)-linear category.

This amounts to replacing the \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ab}}\)-category by a \(\Bbbk\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\)-category in the discussion of §reference. Most results about additive categories in this chapter extend to the \(\Bbbk\)-linear setting by exactly the same arguments. The sole exception concerns Corollary reference: in an additive category, addition on the \(\operatorname{Hom}\) sets can be characterized by properties of the category itself, but this is not true of scalar multiplication by \(\Bbbk\). Consequently, functors—and even equivalences—between \(\Bbbk\)-linear categories are not automatically \(\Bbbk\)-linear. We next collect a few results concerning \(\Bbbk\)-linearity. Recall that the center of a category \(\mathcal{A}\) is defined by \(Z(\mathcal{A}) := \operatorname{End}(\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{\mathcal{A}})\). Its elements are endomorphisms of the identity functor \(\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{\mathcal{A}}\), written as \((a_X)_{X \in \operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{A})}\) with \(a_X \in \operatorname{End}_{\mathcal{A}}(X)\). Composition makes the center a commutative monoid; see [Li1]. If \(\mathcal{A}\) is an \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ab}}\)-category, then \(Z(\mathcal{A})\) becomes a commutative ring under composition and addition \((a_X)_X + (b_X)_X := (a_X+b_X)_X\).

Proposition. Let \(\mathcal{A}\) be an \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ab}}\)-category. Then there is a bijection \[\left\{\text{$\Bbbk\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}$-category structures on $\mathcal{A}$}\right\} \stackrel{1:1}{\longleftrightarrow} \operatorname{Hom}_{\text{rings}}(\Bbbk,Z(\mathcal{A})).\] The map is given as follows. If a \(\Bbbk\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\)-category structure on \(\mathcal{A}\) has been fixed, define, for every \(a \in \Bbbk\) and \(X \in \operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{A})\), \(a_X := a \cdot \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_X \in \operatorname{End}_{\mathcal{A}}(X)\). Then \(a \mapsto (a_X)_{X \in \operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{A})} \in Z(\mathcal{A})\) is a ring homomorphism. Conversely, given a ring homomorphism on the right, \(a \mapsto (a_X)_{X \in \operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{A})}\), define a \(\Bbbk\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\)-category structure on \(\mathcal{A}\) by \(a \cdot f := f \circ a_X = a_Y \circ f\), for \(f \in \operatorname{Hom}(X,Y)\).

Proof. The condition for \((a_X)_{X \in \operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{A})}\) to belong to \(Z(\mathcal{A})\) is precisely \(f \circ a_X = a_Y \circ f\) for every \(f \in \operatorname{Hom}(X,Y)\). If \(\mathcal{A}\) is equipped with a \(\Bbbk\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\)-category structure, define \(a_X := a \cdot \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_X\). Bilinearity gives \[f \circ a_X = f \circ (a \cdot \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_X) = (a f) \circ \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_X = (a \cdot \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_Y) \circ f = a_Y \circ f,\] so \((a_X)_{X \in \operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{A})} \in Z(\mathcal{A})\). The remaining verifications are immediate.

Consequently, the \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ab}}\)-category \(\mathcal{A}\) is naturally a \(Z(\mathcal{A})\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\)-category.

Viewing Limits through Functors

There are two broad kinds of question about the relationship between a functor \(F: \mathcal{C} \to \mathcal{D}\) and limits. Taking \(\varinjlim\) as an example, let \(\alpha: I \to \mathcal{C}\) be a functor. One may ask:

  • Suppose \(\varinjlim \alpha\) exists. Does its image \(F\left(\varinjlim \alpha\right)\) yield \(\varinjlim (F\alpha)\)?

  • Suppose \(\varinjlim F\alpha\) exists. Can this limit be “lifted” to \(\mathcal{C}\)? In what sense is such a lift unique?

We focus on the case of \(\varinjlim\). These results of course have corresponding versions for \(\varprojlim\); by duality, there is no need to repeat the details. We organize the discussion of \(\varinjlim\) in terms of cocones and the category \((\alpha/\Delta)\).

Convention. For a fixed functor \(\alpha: I \to \mathcal{C}\), a collection of data \((L, (f_i)_{i \in \operatorname{Ob}(I)})\) in \(\mathcal{C}\) satisfying the following conditions is called a cocone with base \(\alpha\) and vertex \(L\):

  • \(L\) is an object of \(\mathcal{C}\);

  • each \(f_i : \alpha(i) \to L\) is a morphism in \(\mathcal{C}\) and satisfies the compatibility condition \(f_j \circ \alpha(i \to j) = f_i\), as \([i \to j]\) ranges over \(\mathrm{Mor}(I)\).

In the terminology of [Li1], these cocones form a category1 \((\alpha / \Delta)\). Concretely, once the base \(\alpha\) is fixed, a morphism from a cocone \((L, (f_i)_i)\) to a cocone \((M, (g_i)_i)\) is a commutative diagram \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:injlim-diagram}{}\text{Diagram chapter1-unit-013-d001} \end{equation}\] as \(i \to j\) ranges over \(\operatorname{Mor}(I)\); composition of morphisms is defined in the usual way. By definition, \(\varinjlim \alpha\), together with its family of canonical morphisms \(\iota_i: \alpha(i) \to \varinjlim \alpha\), is an initial object of \((\alpha / \Delta)\). In the evident way, the functor \(F\) induces a functor \((\alpha/\Delta) \to (F\alpha / \Delta)\) that takes a cocone \((L, (f_i)_i)\) to \((FL, (Ff_i)_i)\). Suppose \(\varinjlim \alpha\) exists. If \(\varinjlim F\alpha\) also exists, there is a unique morphism in \((F\alpha / \Delta)\) \[\varinjlim F\alpha \to F(\varinjlim \alpha),\] and this morphism is an isomorphism if and only if \(\left( F(\varinjlim \alpha), (F\iota_i)_i \right)\) gives \(\varinjlim F\alpha\). Dually, \(\varprojlim \alpha\) is characterized as a terminal object of \((\Delta/\alpha)\). Assuming that both projective limits under discussion exist, there is a unique morphism in \((\Delta/F\alpha)\) \[F\varprojlim \alpha \to \varprojlim F\alpha.\]

Definition. Given \(F: \mathcal{C} \to \mathcal{D}\) and a functor \(\alpha: I \to \mathcal{C}\), consider the induced functor between cocone categories \((\alpha/\Delta) \to (F\alpha/\Delta)\).

  • The functor \(F\) is said to preserve this \(\varinjlim\) if \((\alpha/\Delta) \to (F\alpha/\Delta)\) takes an initial object, when one exists, to an initial object.

  • The functor \(F\) is said to reflect this \(\varinjlim\) if any object of \((\alpha/\Delta)\) whose image is an initial object of \((F\alpha/\Delta)\) is itself an initial object.

  • The functor \(F\) is said to create this \(\varinjlim\) if, whenever \(\varinjlim F\alpha\) exists, \(\varinjlim \alpha\) also exists, and in this situation \(F\) preserves this \(\varinjlim\) and also reflects this \(\varinjlim\).

There are corresponding notions for \(\varprojlim\). The notions for \(\varinjlim\) and \(\varprojlim\) are obtained from one another by replacing \(\mathcal{C}\) and \(\mathcal{D}\) with \(\mathcal{C}^{\operatorname{op}}\) and \(\mathcal{D}^{\operatorname{op}}\).

Notice that these notions depend on the particular \(\alpha\) under consideration. For example, \(F\) may well preserve every finite \(\varinjlim\) without preserving \(\varinjlim\) in general. For a fixed \(\alpha\), saying that a functor creates \(\varinjlim\) (or \(\varprojlim\)) means that the cocone (or cone) in \(\mathcal{D}\) defining the limit can be lifted uniquely to \(\mathcal{C}\), and that the lifted cocone (or cone) gives the corresponding limit in \(\mathcal{C}\). This uniqueness comes from the condition in the definition concerning reflection of \(\varinjlim\) (or \(\varprojlim\)). This point of view will be evident in Example reference and Proposition reference below.

Proposition. Every fully faithful functor reflects every \(\varinjlim\) and every \(\varprojlim\).

Proof. It suffices to consider \(\varinjlim\). If \(F\) is fully faithful, the universal property of an initial object of \((\alpha/\Delta)\) can be checked, after applying \(F\), in \((F\alpha/\Delta)\).

We shall also use the following notion.

Definition. A functor \(F\) is called conservative if it satisfies the following condition: a morphism \(f \in \operatorname{Mor}(\mathcal{C})\) is an isomorphism if and only if \(Ff \in \operatorname{Mor}(\mathcal{D})\) is an isomorphism.

Remark. Suppose \(F\) is a conservative functor. If \(\varinjlim \alpha\) exists and \(F\) preserves this \(\varinjlim\), the functor \(F\) must also reflect it. Indeed, suppose \(L \in \operatorname{Ob}((\alpha/\Delta))\) is mapped to an initial object of \((F\alpha/\Delta)\). Consider the unique morphism \(\varinjlim \alpha \to L\) in \((\alpha/\Delta)\). Since \(F\) preserves this \(\varinjlim\), the image of that morphism under \(F\) must be an isomorphism. Conservativity then ensures that \(\varinjlim \alpha \to L\) is also an isomorphism.

Under these hypotheses, the condition that \(F\) reflect \(\varinjlim\) may be omitted from the definition of what it means for \(F\) to create \(\varinjlim\).

Example. We verify that the forgetful functor \(U\) from the category of groups \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Grp}}\) to the category of sets \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Set}}\) creates all small \(\varprojlim\).

This follows from the concrete constructions of \(\varprojlim\) in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Grp}}\) and \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Set}}\); see [Li1]. More explicitly, take a small category \(I\) and a functor \(\beta: I^{\operatorname{op}} \to \ensuremath{\mathsf{Grp}}\). As a set, \[\varprojlim U\beta = \left\{\begin{array}{r|l} (x_i)_i \in \prod_{i \in \operatorname{Ob}(I)} U\beta(i) & \forall [i \to j] \in \mathrm{Mor}(I), \\ & \beta(i \to j)(x_j) = x_i \end{array}\right\},\] and the projection \(p_i: \varprojlim U\beta \to U\beta(i)\) maps \((x_j)_j\) to \(x_i\). Our task is now to:

  1. equip \(\varprojlim U\beta\) with a group structure such that every \(p_i\) is a group homomorphism, and show that this group structure is unique;

  2. verify the universal property of \(\varprojlim \beta\) for this group together with the family of projection homomorphisms \((p_i)_i\).

Clearly, \(\varprojlim U\beta\) is a subgroup of the direct product \(\prod_i \beta(i)\). Regard this subgroup as \(\varprojlim \beta \in \operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Grp}})\); this is the unique group structure making every \(p_i\) a group homomorphism. This completes the first task.

We next verify the universal property of the cone \(\left( \varprojlim \beta, (p_i)_i\right)\). Consider any cone \((L, (q_i)_i)\) in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Grp}}\), with \(q_i: L \to \beta(i)\). The universal property gives a unique map \(\varphi: UL \to \varprojlim U\beta\) such that \(p_i \varphi = q_i\) for every \(i\). Concretely, \(\varphi\) is in fact given by \(y \mapsto (q_i(y))_{i \in \operatorname{Ob}(I)}\), so this map is a group homomorphism \(L \to \varprojlim \beta\).2 The verification is complete.

By an entirely similar argument, one can show that the forgetful functor from the category of compact Hausdorff spaces \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{CHaus}}\) to \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Set}}\) also creates all small \(\varprojlim\). The corresponding verification is left as an exercise in this chapter. The next result concerns a functor category of the form \(\mathcal{C}^J\) (which may be a “large” category, but this causes no problem). We need two preparatory steps.

  • Let \(J\) be a set. The product of \(J\) copies of \(\mathcal{C}\), namely \(\mathcal{C}^J\), is defined by \(\operatorname{Ob}\left(\mathcal{C}^J\right) = \operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{C})^J\) and \(\mathrm{Mor}\left(\mathcal{C}^J \right) = \mathrm{Mor}(\mathcal{C})^J\). For every \(j \in J\) there is an evident projection functor \(p_j: \mathcal{C}^J \to \mathcal{C}\).

    Given a category \(I\) and a functor \(\alpha: I \to \mathcal{C}^J\), if \(\varinjlim (p_j \alpha)\) exists for every \(j\), then \(\varinjlim \alpha\) also exists. It is constructed by taking colimits “pointwise” or “objectwise”: \(\varinjlim \alpha = \left( \varinjlim (p_j \alpha) \right)_{j \in J}\).

  • Let \(J\) be a category. We may consider the functor category \(\mathcal{C}^J\). For each \(j \in \operatorname{Ob}(J)\) there is an evaluation functor \(\mathrm{ev}_j: \mathcal{C}^J \to \mathcal{C}\), which maps an object \(F\) to \(Fj\) and a morphism \(\varphi = (\varphi_{j'})_{j' \in \operatorname{Ob}(J)}\) to \(\varphi_j\). We shall later consider functors of the form \(\alpha: I \to \mathcal{C}^J\) and their \(\varinjlim\). Observe that \(\alpha\) can be viewed as a functor \(I \times J \to \mathcal{C}\), whose value is denoted \(\alpha(i, j)\).

The two systems of notation are compatible. If \(J\) is a discrete category and is viewed as a set, then \(\mathcal{C}^J\) is simply the product discussed above. For a general \(J\), the forgetful functor \(\mathcal{F}: \mathcal{C}^J \to \mathcal{C}^{\operatorname{Ob}(J)}\) maps an object \(F\) to \((Fj)_{j \in \operatorname{Ob}(J)}\) and a morphism \(\varphi\) to \((\varphi_j)_{j \in \operatorname{Ob}(J)}\). Thus \(\mathrm{ev}_j = p_j \mathcal{F}\).

Proposition. Let \(J\) and \(\mathcal{C}\) be categories.

  1. The forgetful functor \(\mathcal{F}: \mathcal{C}^J \to \mathcal{C}^{\operatorname{Ob}(J)}\) creates \(\varinjlim\) and \(\varprojlim\).

  2. Let \(I\) be a category and suppose every functor \(I \to \mathcal{C}\) has a \(\varinjlim\) (or \(\varprojlim\)). Then all functors of the form \(I \to \mathcal{C}^J\) also have a \(\varinjlim\) (or \(\varprojlim\)) in \(\mathcal{C}^J\).

  3. Under the assumption in (ii), for every \(j \in \operatorname{Ob}(J)\) the evaluation functor \(\mathrm{ev}_j: \mathcal{C}^J \to \mathcal{C}\) preserves \(\varinjlim\) (or \(\varprojlim\)) for diagrams of shape \(I\). In other words, limits in \(\mathcal{C}^J\) are likewise defined “pointwise” or “objectwise.”

Proof. It suffices to consider \(\varinjlim\). For (i), let \(\alpha: I \to \mathcal{C}^J\) and suppose \(\varinjlim \mathcal{F}\alpha\) exists and is given by the cocone \[\left( (X(j))_{j \in \operatorname{Ob}(J)}, \; \left( \iota_i = (\iota_{i, j})_{j \in \operatorname{Ob}(J)} \right)_{i \in \operatorname{Ob}(I)} \right)\] with \(\iota_{i,j}: \alpha(i, j) \to X(j)\). We wish to lift it to a cocone in \(\mathcal{C}^J\) that gives \(\varinjlim \alpha\).

First observe that \(X(j) = \varinjlim \alpha(\cdot, j)\) for every \(j\). For each morphism \(j \to j'\), functoriality of colimits (see [Li1]) gives a unique morphism \(X(j \to j'): X(j) \to X(j')\) making the following diagram commute: \[\text{Diagram chapter1-unit-013-d002} \quad i \in \operatorname{Ob}(I).\] In this way, \(j \mapsto X(j)\) extends to a functor \(X: J \to \mathcal{C}\), while \(\iota_i: \alpha(i, \cdot) \to X\) are morphisms in \(\mathcal{C}^J\). It is immediate that \((X, (\iota_i)_i) \in \operatorname{Ob}(\alpha/\Delta)\); we next prove that this object is initial. Since the functor \(\mathcal{F}\) is conservative, reflection of \(\varinjlim\) need not be checked separately.

Given \((L, (f_i)_i) \in \operatorname{Ob}(\alpha/\Delta)\), the universal property of \(\varinjlim \mathcal{F}\alpha\) determines a unique morphism \(\varphi = (\varphi_j)_j : \mathcal{F}X \to \mathcal{F}L\) such that the triangular part of the following diagram commutes for every \((i, j)\): \[\text{Diagram chapter1-unit-013-d003}\] It remains to show that the square commutes for every \(j \to j'\), after which the family of components \(\varphi\) forms a morphism \(X \to L\). The outer frame is already known to commute, so \[\varphi_{j'} X(j \to j') \iota_{i, j} = L(j \to j') f_{i, j} = L(j \to j') \varphi_j \iota_{i, j}\] for every \(i\). Morphisms with domain \(X(j)\) are determined by their composites with all the \(\iota_{i,j}\), so the square commutes.

For (ii), consider a functor \(\alpha: I \to \mathcal{C}^J\). By the preceding discussion, \(\mathcal{F}\alpha: I \to \mathcal{C}^{\operatorname{Ob}(J)}\) has a \(\varinjlim\), defined objectwise. By (i), \(\mathcal{F}\) creates \(\varinjlim \alpha\) in \(\mathcal{C}^J\),3 while the assertion in (iii) that \(\mathrm{ev}_j\) preserves this \(\varinjlim\) follows immediately from the construction.

  1. More precisely, \(\Delta\) here denotes the diagonal functor \(\mathcal{C} \to \mathcal{C}^I\); see Example 1.6.3. The notation \(\Delta\) was chosen from the initial letter of the pinyin word duìjiǎo (“diagonal”). By a pictorial analogy, however, one may just as well picture \(\Delta\) as a “cocone”; see diagram equation.↩︎

  2. Translator’s note: the source writes \(L \to \varinjlim \beta\); the target corrects this to \(L \to \varprojlim \beta\), in accordance with the projective limit being proved (O014-C007).↩︎

  3. Translator’s note: the source writes \(\mathcal{C}\) here. The target corrects this to \(\mathcal{C}^J\), the domain of the forgetful functor \(\mathcal{F}\) and the category containing the newly constructed functor \(X: J \to \mathcal{C}\); see correction O014-C009.↩︎

Filtered Inductive Limits

A familiar fact from mathematical analysis is that, when a sequence converges, its limit may be computed from any subsequence. In category theory, this idea is embodied by cofinality. We begin with connectedness.

Definition. Let \(I\) be a category. If \(\operatorname{Ob}(I) \neq \emptyset\) and, for every \(i, i' \in \operatorname{Ob}(I)\), there exist \(n \geq 1\) and morphisms \[i = i_0 \leftarrow i_1 \to i_2 \leftarrow i_3 \to i_4 \leftarrow \cdots \to i_{2n} = i' ,\] then \(I\) is called connected.

We introduce an auxiliary concept that will be used repeatedly in the next several sections.

Definition (Comma category; see [Li1).] Given categories \(I\), \(J\), and a functor \(H: J \to I\), let \(i \in \operatorname{Ob}(I)\).

  • By definition, the objects of the comma category \((i/H)\) (or \((H/i)\)) are data \((j, i \to Hj)\) (or \((j, Hj \to i)\)), where \(j \in \operatorname{Ob}(J)\) and \(i \to Hj\) (or \(Hj \to i\)) is a morphism in \(I\). A morphism from \((j, i \to Hj)\) to \((j', i \to Hj')\) (or from \((j, Hj \to i)\) to \((j', Hj' \to i)\)) is a morphism \(f: j \to j'\) in \(J\) making the following diagram commute: \[\text{Diagram chapter1-unit-014-d001} \quad \text{or} \quad \text{Diagram chapter1-unit-014-d002}\] Composition and identity morphisms are defined in the usual way.

  • The two categories above come respectively with projection functors \(\Pi_{i/}: (i/H) \to J\) and \(\Pi_{/i}: (H/i) \to J\), taking an object \((j, i \to Hj)\) (or \((j, Hj \to i)\)) to \(j\) and a morphism \(f\) to \(f\).

  • Every morphism \(i \to i'\) in \(I\) naturally induces functors \((i'/H) \to (i/H)\) and \((H/i) \to (H/i')\), making the following diagrams commute: \[\text{Diagram chapter1-unit-014-d003} \quad \text{Diagram chapter1-unit-014-d004}\]

Example. Regard a functor \(\alpha: I \to \mathcal{C}\) as an object of \(\mathcal{C}^I\), and consider the diagonal functor \(\Delta: \mathcal{C} \to \mathcal{C}^I\) taking every object to the corresponding constant functor. By Definition reference, \((\alpha/\Delta)\) is precisely the category of “cocones” introduced in Convention reference, while the functor \(\Pi_{\alpha/}\) maps each cocone to its vertex.

Definition. For a functor \(H: J \to I\), if \((i/H)\) is connected for every \(i \in \operatorname{Ob}(I)\), then \(H\) is called cofinal; if \(H\) is the inclusion functor of a subcategory, the subcategory \(J\) is called cofinal.

It is easy to verify that if \(I \to J\) and \(J \to K\) are both cofinal, then the composite functor \(I \to K\) is also cofinal. The verification is left to the reader as an exercise. The next result shows that a limit may be computed by restricting the diagram along a cofinal functor. Recall that \(H\) induces \(H^{\operatorname{op}}: J^{\operatorname{op}} \to I^{\operatorname{op}}\).

Proposition. If \(H: J \to I\) is cofinal, then:

  • for a given functor \(\alpha: I \to \mathcal{C}\), \(\varinjlim \alpha\) exists if and only if \(\varinjlim \alpha H\) exists; in that case there is a canonical isomorphism \(\varinjlim \alpha H \simeq \varinjlim \alpha\);

  • dually, for a given functor \(\beta: I^{\operatorname{op}} \to \mathcal{C}\), \(\varprojlim \beta\) exists if and only if \(\varprojlim \beta H^{\operatorname{op}}\) exists; in that case there is a canonical isomorphism \(\varprojlim \beta H^{\operatorname{op}} \simeq \varprojlim \beta\).

Proof. We discuss only \(\varinjlim\). In the language of §reference, it suffices to prove that the functor \((\alpha/\Delta) \to (\alpha H / \Delta)\) is an equivalence. It takes a cocone with base \(\alpha\), namely \((L, (f_i)_i)\), to the cocone with base \(\alpha H\), namely \((L, (f_{Hj})_j)\).

We first prove that this functor is essentially surjective. Consider \(L \in \operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{C})\) and a family of morphisms \((g_j: \alpha H(j) \to L)_{j \in \operatorname{Ob}(J)}\) satisfying the compatibility condition \(g_{j'} \circ \alpha H(j \to j') = g_j\). For every \(i \in \operatorname{Ob}(I)\), since \((i/H)\) is nonempty, we may choose \(j\) and a morphism \(i \to H(j)\). Define \(f_i := g_j \circ \alpha(i \to H(j))\). This definition is independent of the choice of comma object \((j,i \to H(j))\): indeed, if there are morphisms in \((i/H)\) as in the diagram \[\text{Diagram chapter1-unit-014-d005}\] then the construction immediately gives \[g_j \circ \alpha(i\to H(j)) = g_{j''} \circ \alpha(i\to H(j'')) = g_{j'} \circ \alpha(i\to H(j')).\] Since \((i/H)\) is connected, this suffices to show that \(f_i\) is well-defined. The preceding discussion also implies that \((f_i)_i\) satisfies the compatibility condition \(f_i=f_{i'}\circ\alpha(i\to i')\): for every \(i \to i'\) and \(i' \to H(j')\), we may compute \(f_i\) using the comma object \((j',i \to i' \to H(j'))\). Hence \((L, (f_i)_i) \in \operatorname{Ob}((\alpha/\Delta))\) maps to \((L, (g_j)_j)\).

We next show that the functor is full and faithful. Giving a morphism in \((\alpha/\Delta)\), namely \((L, (f_i)_i) \to (L', (f'_i)_i)\), is equivalent to giving a morphism \(\theta: L \to L'\) in \(\mathcal{C}\) such that \(\theta f_i = f'_i\) for every \(i\). It suffices to check this condition on the objects \(H(j)\) in the cofinal image of \(H\): for every \(i\), choose \(j \in \operatorname{Ob}(J)\) and \(i \to H(j)\); the condition then becomes \(\theta f_{H(j)} = f'_{H(j)}\), which says precisely that \(\theta\) is a morphism in \((\alpha H / \Delta)\).

Definition. Following [Li1], a category \(I\) with \(\operatorname{Ob}(I)\neq\emptyset\) satisfying the following conditions is called filtered1.

  • For every \(i, j \in \operatorname{Ob}(I)\), there is an object \(k \in \operatorname{Ob}(I)\) together with morphisms \(i \rightarrow k\) and \(j \rightarrow k\).

  • For every pair of morphisms \(f, g: i \to j\) in \(I\), there is an object \(k \in \operatorname{Ob}(I)\) and a morphism \(h: j \to k\) such that \(hf = hg\).

If \(I\) is a filtered category and \(\alpha: I \to \mathcal{C}\) is a functor, the corresponding \(\varinjlim \alpha\) is called a filtered inductive limit.

Example. One common class of filtered categories comes from filtered partially ordered sets2. Every partially ordered set \((P, \leq)\) determines a corresponding category \(\mathcal{P}\) such that \(x \leq y \iff \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{P}}(x, y) \neq \emptyset\). If \(\mathcal{P}\) is a filtered category, then \((P, \leq)\) is called a filtered partially ordered set. A partially ordered set is filtered if and only if it is nonempty and every pair of elements \(i, j\) has a common upper bound \(k\). Every nonempty totally ordered set is plainly filtered.

Proposition. Let \(I\) be a filtered category. A full subcategory \(J\subset I\) is cofinal if and only if, for every \(i \in \operatorname{Ob}(I)\), there are \(j \in \operatorname{Ob}(J)\) and a morphism \(i \to j\); in that case \(J\) is also filtered.

Proof. The “only if” direction is clear. For the converse, given \(j \leftarrow i \to j'\), with \(j, j' \in \operatorname{Ob}(J)\), filteredness of \(I\) together with the hypothesis ensures the existence of a commutative diagram \[\text{Diagram chapter1-unit-014-d006}\] with \(k \in \operatorname{Ob}(J)\). This shows that \(J\) is cofinal.

To prove that \(J\) is filtered, take arbitrary \(i, j \in \operatorname{Ob}(J)\). Since \(I\) is filtered, there are \(k_0 \in \operatorname{Ob}(I)\) and morphisms \(i\to k_0\) and \(j\to k_0\); also choose \(k \in \operatorname{Ob}(J)\) and a morphism \(k_0 \to k\). Composing these morphisms yields morphisms \(i \rightarrow k \leftarrow j\) in \(J\).3 This proves the first condition for a filtered category. The second is proved by the same idea.

Example. Define \(\mathrm{OFin}_I := \left\{ \text{full subcategories}\; J \subset I: \operatorname{Ob}(J) \;\text{is finite} \right\}\). Ordered by \(\subset\), this is a filtered partially ordered set: for any \(J, K \in \mathrm{OFin}_I\), the subcategory obtained by taking the union of their sets of objects is a common upper bound for \(J\) and \(K\).

To see the usefulness of this construction, consider an arbitrary functor \(\alpha: I \to \mathcal{C}\) (or \(\beta: I^{\operatorname{op}} \to \mathcal{C}\)). Its restriction to a full subcategory \(J\) gives \(\alpha|_J\) (or \(\beta|_{J^{\operatorname{op}}}\)). If \(J \subset K\), there is a natural morphism \(\varinjlim \alpha|_J \to \varinjlim \alpha|_K\) (or \(\varprojlim \beta|_{K^{\operatorname{op}}} \to \varprojlim \beta|_{J^{\operatorname{op}}}\)), provided these limits exist. The next result explains how an arbitrary limit can be approximated “in a filtered manner” by limits over subcategories having only finitely many objects.

Proposition. In the situation above, there is a canonical isomorphism \[\varinjlim_{\substack{J \in \mathrm{OFin}_I \\ \subset}} \varinjlim \alpha|_J \ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}\varinjlim \alpha\] (or \(\varprojlim \beta \ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}} \varprojlim_{J \in \mathrm{OFin}_I^{\operatorname{op}}} \varprojlim \beta|_{J^{\operatorname{op}}}\)), provided that the iterated limit on the left (or on the right) exists.4

Proof. Consider the case of \(\varinjlim\). The universal property gives canonical bijections \[\begin{aligned} \operatorname{Hom}\left( \varinjlim_{J\in\mathrm{OFin}_I} \varinjlim \alpha|_J, S \right) &\simeq \varprojlim_{J\in\mathrm{OFin}_I^{\operatorname{op}}} \operatorname{Hom}\left( \varinjlim \alpha|_J, S \right) \\ &\simeq \varprojlim_{J\in\mathrm{OFin}_I^{\operatorname{op}}} \varprojlim \operatorname{Hom}(\alpha|_J, S) . \end{aligned}\] for arbitrary \(S \in \operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{C})\), while the right-hand side is an iterated \(\varprojlim\) of sets. It remains to check that, for a family of sets \((X_i)_{i \in \operatorname{Ob}(I)}\) together with a compatible family of maps \(\left( f_{i \to j}: X_j \to X_i \right)_{[i \to j] \in \operatorname{Mor}(I)}\), there is a bijection \[\text{Diagram chapter1-unit-014-d007}\]

For every \(J\), the concrete construction of the \(\varprojlim\) of sets is \[\varprojlim_{j \in \operatorname{Ob}(J)} X_j = \left\{ (x_j)_j \in \prod_{j \in \operatorname{Ob}(J)} X_j : \forall [i \to j] \in \operatorname{Mor}(J), \; f_{i \to j}(x_j) = x_i \right\},\] so the bijection is clear: every piece of data defining \(\varprojlim_i X_i\), whether a coordinate \(x_i\) or a compatibility condition \(f_{i \to j}(x_j) = x_i\), is contained in some \(J \in \mathrm{OFin}_I\).

Recall that the category \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Set}}\) has all small \(\varinjlim\) and \(\varprojlim\). Small filtered inductive limits have a particularly simple description.

Proposition. Let \(I\) be a small filtered category and \(\alpha: I \to \ensuremath{\mathsf{Set}}\) a functor. Define the following binary relation on the set \(\bigsqcup_{i \in \operatorname{Ob}(I)} \alpha(i)\): for \(x \in \alpha(i)\) and \(y \in \alpha(j)\), the relation \(x \sim y\) means that there is an object \(k\in\operatorname{Ob}(I)\) together with morphisms \(i\rightarrow k\) and \(j\rightarrow k\) such that \(\alpha(i \to k)(x) = \alpha(j \to k)(y)\). Then \(\sim\) is an equivalence relation, and \[\varinjlim \alpha = \left( \bigsqcup_{i \in \operatorname{Ob}(I)} \alpha(i) \right) \big/ \sim .\]

Proof. See the discussion following [Li1].

An element of the preceding \(\varinjlim \alpha\) will henceforth be written \([x_{i_0}]\), where \(i_0 \in \operatorname{Ob}(I)\) and \([x_{i_0}]\) is the equivalence class containing \(x_{i_0} \in \alpha(i_0)\). On the other hand, for a general small category \(J\) and functor \(\beta: J^{\operatorname{op}} \to \ensuremath{\mathsf{Set}}\), we write an element of \(\varprojlim \beta\) as \((y_j)_{j \in \operatorname{Ob}(J)}\), where \(y_j \in \beta(j)\) satisfies the compatibility condition \(\beta(j' \to j)(y_j) = y_{j'}\). Next consider a functor of the form \(\alpha: I \times J^{\operatorname{op}} \to \ensuremath{\mathsf{Set}}\), with \(I, J\) small categories; one may take \(\varinjlim\) and \(\varprojlim\) in the variables \(I\) and \(J\), respectively. For every \((i_0, j_0) \in \operatorname{Ob}(I \times J)\), there is a composite of natural maps \[\varprojlim_j \alpha(i_0, j) \to \alpha(i_0, j_0) \to \varinjlim_i \alpha(i, j_0);\] this composite is natural in \(i_0\) and \(j_0\). Varying \(j_0\) gives a canonical map \(\varprojlim_j \alpha(i_0, j) \to \varprojlim_j \varinjlim_i \alpha(i, j)\); then varying \(i_0\) gives a canonical map \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:filtered-finite-exchange}{} e: \varinjlim_i \varprojlim_j \alpha(i, j) \to \varprojlim_j \varinjlim_i \alpha(i, j). \end{equation}\] In terms of representatives, \(e\) maps \(\left[ (x_{i_0, j})_j \right]\) to \(\left( [ x_{i_0, j}] \right)_j\). If \(\operatorname{Mor}(J)\) is a finite set, the category \(J\) is called finite; equivalently, its object set is finite and every morphism set between two objects is finite. The next result will be used in §1.9.

Proposition. Let \(I\) be a small filtered category, \(J\) a finite category, and \(\alpha: I \times J^{\operatorname{op}} \to \ensuremath{\mathsf{Set}}\) a functor. Then the map \(e\) in equation is a bijection.

Proof. We first show that \(e\) is surjective. Given \((b_j)_{j \in \operatorname{Ob}(J)} \in \varprojlim_j \varinjlim_i \alpha(i, j)\), write each \(b_j\) as \([x_{i_j, j}]\). Since \(I\) is filtered and \(J\) is finite, we may choose a common target object \(i\in\operatorname{Ob}(I)\) for all \(i_j\), and replace each representative by its image along a morphism \(i_j\to i\). Thus all representatives may be written \(x_{i,j}\) with the same index \(i\). For every morphism \(j \to j'\) in \(J\), we have \[\left[ \alpha(i, j \to j') (x_{i, j'}) \right] = \left[ x_{i, j} \right].\] Since \(\operatorname{Mor}(J)\) is finite and \(I\) is filtered, we may choose one morphism \(i\to i_1\) that equalizes all these pairs, replace all representatives by their images at index \(i_1\), and then rename \(i_1\) as \(i\). Thus \(\alpha(i, j \to j') (x_{i, j'}) = x_{i, j}\) holds for every \([j \to j'] \in \operatorname{Mor}(J)\). Consequently, \(e\left( [(x_{i, j})_j] \right) = (b_j)_j\).

We next show that \(e\) is injective. Suppose \(e(x) = e(y)\). Since \(I\) is filtered, we may replace representatives of \(x\) and \(y\) by their images at one common index \(i\in\operatorname{Ob}(I)\), so that they have representatives \((x_{i,j})_j\) and \((y_{i,j})_j\). Thus \([x_{i,j}]=[y_{i,j}]\) for every \(j \in \operatorname{Ob}(J)\). Since \(I\) is filtered and \(J\) is finite, we may choose one common later index, replace all components by their images there, and rename it \(i\), so that \(x_{i,j}=y_{i,j}\) for every \(j\). Hence \(x=y\).

  1. Translator’s note: the source does not state the condition \(\operatorname{Ob}(I)\neq\emptyset\), so the empty category would satisfy both items vacuously; in the second item, the source also calls \(k\in\operatorname{Ob}(I)\) a morphism. The target adds the nonemptiness condition and corrects the type of \(k\) to an object (O014-C010 and O014-C011).↩︎

  2. When used to index limits, a filtered category can often be replaced by a filtered partially ordered set; see Remark A.2.3 and the explanations for the exercises in Appendix A.↩︎

  3. Translator’s note: the source calls \(i\rightarrow k_0\leftarrow j\) morphisms in \(J\), although \(k_0\) is only known to lie in \(I\). The target uses the composites into \(k\in\operatorname{Ob}(J)\) (O014-C012).↩︎

  4. Translator’s note: in the dual formula, the source writes an outer inductive limit. For \(J\subset K\), however, the transition morphism goes from the \(K\)-term to the \(J\)-term, so the terms form a diagram on \(\mathrm{OFin}_I^{\operatorname{op}}\) and the outer construction is a projective limit (O014-C013).↩︎

Kan Extensions

This section begins with the problem of extending a functor. Consider categories \(\mathcal{C}\), \(\mathcal{D}\), \(\mathcal{E}\) and functors \(K\) and \(F\) as in the following diagram: \[\text{Diagram chapter1-unit-015-d001}\] In the basic spirit of category theory, we would like to find a functor \(L\) indicated by the dashed arrow, together with a natural isomorphism \(F \simeq LK\). This problem generally has no solution: for example, there may be \(f \in \operatorname{Mor}(\mathcal{C})\) such that \(Kf\) is an isomorphism while \(Ff\) is not. Failing that, we may at least ask whether there is a best approximation. The answer is characterized by a universal property, with left and right versions.

Definition (D. Kan). Consider categories \(\mathcal{C}\), \(\mathcal{D}\), \(\mathcal{E}\) and functors \(K: \mathcal{C} \to \mathcal{D}\) and \(F: \mathcal{C} \to \mathcal{E}\).

  • A left Kan extension of the functor \(F\) along \(K\) is the following data \((\operatorname{Lan}_K F, \eta)\):

    • \(\operatorname{Lan}_K F: \mathcal{D} \to \mathcal{E}\) is a functor;

    • \(\eta: F \to (\operatorname{Lan}_K F) K\) is a natural transformation.

    These data must satisfy the following universal property: for every \(L: \mathcal{D} \to \mathcal{E}\) and \(\xi: F \to LK\), there is a unique natural transformation \(\chi: \operatorname{Lan}_K F \to L\) such that \(\xi = (\chi K) \eta\) (using vertical and horizontal composition of natural transformations), or, in \(2\)-cell diagrams: \[\text{Diagram chapter1-unit-015-d002} = \text{Diagram chapter1-unit-015-d003}.\]

  • A right Kan extension of the functor \(F\) along \(K\) is the following data \((\operatorname{Ran}_K F, \varepsilon)\):

    • \(\operatorname{Ran}_K F: \mathcal{D} \to \mathcal{E}\) is a functor;

    • \(\varepsilon: (\operatorname{Ran}_K F)K \to F\) is a natural transformation.

    These data must satisfy the following universal property: for every \(R: \mathcal{D} \to \mathcal{E}\) and \(\delta: RK \to F\), there is a unique natural transformation \(\theta: R \to \operatorname{Ran}_K F\) such that \(\delta = \varepsilon (\theta K)\), or, in \(2\)-cell diagrams: \[\text{Diagram chapter1-unit-015-d004} = \text{Diagram chapter1-unit-015-d005}.\]

If \(\mathcal{C}\), \(\mathcal{D}\), and \(\mathcal{E}\) in the definition are replaced respectively by \(\mathcal{C}^{\operatorname{op}}\), \(\mathcal{D}^{\operatorname{op}}\), and \(\mathcal{E}^{\operatorname{op}}\), the pattern of directions of the functors remains the same, while the natural transformations reverse direction. Thus left and right Kan extensions are dual notions. Using the functor categories \(\mathcal{E}^{\mathcal{C}}\) and \(\mathcal{E}^{\mathcal{D}}\), the universal properties of left and right Kan extensions state, respectively, the bijections \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:Kan-univ}{}\begin{aligned} \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{E}^{\mathcal{D}}}\left( \operatorname{Lan}_K F, L \right) & \xrightarrow{1:1} \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{E}^{\mathcal{C}}}\left( F, LK \right) \\ \chi & \longmapsto (\chi K)\eta , \\ \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{E}^{\mathcal{D}}}\left( R, \operatorname{Ran}_K F \right) & \xrightarrow{1:1} \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{E}^{\mathcal{C}}}\left( RK, F \right) \\ \theta & \longmapsto \varepsilon (\theta K); \end{aligned} \end{equation}\] their inverses are the maps \((L, \xi) \mapsto \chi\) and \((R, \delta) \mapsto \theta\), respectively, from Definition reference.

Proposition. Given categories \(\mathcal{C}\), \(\mathcal{D}\), \(\mathcal{E}\) and functors \(K: \mathcal{C} \to \mathcal{D}\) and \(F: \mathcal{C} \to \mathcal{E}\), consider the pullback (that is, precomposition) functor \(K^*: \mathcal{E}^{\mathcal{D}} \to \mathcal{E}^{\mathcal{C}}\) between the functor categories.

  1. If it exists, a left Kan extension \((\operatorname{Lan}_K F, \eta)\) is unique up to a unique isomorphism in \(\mathcal{E}^{\mathcal{D}}\); the same holds for a right Kan extension.

  2. If the left Kan extension (or right Kan extension) along \(K\) exists for every \(F\), these extensions assemble into a left adjoint to \(K^*\), \(\operatorname{Lan}_K: \mathcal{E}^{\mathcal{C}} \to \mathcal{E}^{\mathcal{D}}\) (or a right adjoint \(\operatorname{Ran}_K: \mathcal{E}^{\mathcal{C}} \to \mathcal{E}^{\mathcal{D}}\)); the family of natural transformations assembled from \(\eta\) (or \(\varepsilon\)) in Definition reference is exactly the unit (or counit) of this adjunction.

Proof. For (i), simply apply the universal property in Definition reference in the usual way.

For (ii), observe that \(LK = K^*(L)\) and \(RK = K^*(R)\); the desired adjunction is precisely the content of equation. The assertion about the unit or counit follows similarly; see [Li1].

By convention, the data \(\eta\) or \(\varepsilon\) in a Kan extension are often omitted from the notation. If the left Kan extension (or right Kan extension) along \(K\) exists for every \(F\), the functor \(\operatorname{Lan}_K\) (or \(\operatorname{Ran}_K\)) obtained in (ii) also has the corresponding uniqueness property, by uniqueness of adjoints [Li1].

Remark. Since the definition of a Kan extension involves only composition of \(2\)-cells, it extends to general \(2\)-categories; the present situation is the special case of the \(2\)-category \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Cat}}\). See [Li1] for details.

For every category \(\mathcal{C}\), denote the unique functor \(\mathcal{C} \to \mathbf{1}\) by \(!\); specifying a functor \(\mathbf{1} \to \mathcal{C}\) is equivalent to specifying an object of \(\mathcal{C}\). For every category \(\mathcal{E}\) and object \(X\) in it, write \(\Delta(X): \mathcal{C} \to \mathcal{E}\) for the composite \(\mathcal{C} \xrightarrow{!} \mathbf{1} \xrightarrow{\text{constant}\; X} \mathcal{E}\); this is the constant functor that sends every object to \(X\) and every morphism to \(\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_X\).

Example (Limits as Kan extensions). Let \(F: \mathcal{C} \to \mathcal{E}\) be a functor. Consider the diagram \[\text{Diagram chapter1-unit-015-d006}\] Then \(\operatorname{Lan}_! F\) (or \(\operatorname{Ran}_! F\)) exists if and only if \(\varinjlim F\) (or \(\varprojlim F\)) exists in \(\mathcal{E}\), and in that case the Kan extension is precisely the limit in question.

For example, consider \((\operatorname{Lan}_! F, \eta)\). The functor \(\operatorname{Lan}_! F: \mathbf{1} \to \mathcal{E}\) may be viewed as an object of \(\mathcal{E}\), while \(\eta\) is a natural transformation \(F \to \Delta(\operatorname{Lan}_! F)\) in \(\mathcal{E}^{\mathcal{C}}\). Its universal property is equivalent to the assertion that the data \((\operatorname{Lan}_! F, \eta)\) give an initial object of the category \((F/\Delta)\); this is precisely the description of \(\varinjlim F\) in §reference.

Example (Adjunctions as Kan extensions). Consider a pair of functors: \[\text{Diagram chapter1-unit-015-d007}\] If \((F, G)\) is equipped with the structure of an adjunction with unit \(\eta: \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{\mathcal{C}} \to GF\) and counit \(\varepsilon: FG \to \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{\mathcal{D}}\), then \((G, \eta)\) gives \(\operatorname{Lan}_F (\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{\mathcal{C}})\) and \((F, \varepsilon)\) gives \(\operatorname{Ran}_G (\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{\mathcal{D}})\).

To explain this, first we show that the following pullback functors \[\text{Diagram chapter1-unit-015-d008}\] themselves form a natural adjoint pair. Observe that \(\eta\) induces \(\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{\mathcal{C}}^* = \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{\mathcal{C}^{\mathcal{C}}} \to F^* G^* = (GF)^*\), and similarly \(\varepsilon\) induces \(G^* F^* \to \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{\mathcal{C}^{\mathcal{D}}}\); we continue to denote both by \(\eta\) and \(\varepsilon\). We must check the triangle identities characterizing the adjunction \((G^*, F^*, \eta, \varepsilon)\). In brief, these identities follow formally by applying pullback \((-)^*\) in functor categories to the triangle identities for \((F, G, \eta, \varepsilon)\); the details are left to the reader.

This adjunction gives a canonical bijection \(\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}^{\mathcal{D}}}(\underbracket{G^* \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{\mathcal{C}}}_{= G}, L) \ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}^{\mathcal{C}}}(\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{\mathcal{C}} , \underbracket{F^* L}_{=LF})\), for arbitrary \(L: \mathcal{D} \to \mathcal{C}\); when \(L = G\), \(\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_G\) maps to \(\eta\). Writing the universal property of \(\operatorname{Lan}_F (\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{\mathcal{C}})\) as the bijection in equation, one sees at once that \((G, \eta)\) gives \(\operatorname{Lan}_F (\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{\mathcal{C}})\). The argument for \(\operatorname{Ran}_G (\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{\mathcal{D}})\) is entirely similar.1

In practice, some situations require a further strengthening of the notion of Kan extension2, especially in the later treatment of derived functors.

Definition. Consider categories \(\mathcal{C}\), \(\mathcal{D}\), \(\mathcal{E}\), \(\mathcal{F}\) and functors \(K: \mathcal{C} \to \mathcal{D}\) and \(F: \mathcal{C} \to \mathcal{E}\).3

  • Suppose the right Kan extension \((\operatorname{Ran}_K F, \varepsilon)\) exists. A functor \(M: \mathcal{E} \to \mathcal{F}\) is said to preserve \(\operatorname{Ran}_K F\) if the composite \(2\)-cell \[\text{Diagram chapter1-unit-015-d009} =: \text{Diagram chapter1-unit-015-d010}\] gives a right Kan extension of \(MF\) along \(K\).

  • Suppose the left Kan extension \((\operatorname{Lan}_K F, \eta)\) exists. A functor \(M: \mathcal{E} \to \mathcal{F}\) is said to preserve \(\operatorname{Lan}_K F\) if the composite \(2\)-cell \[\text{Diagram chapter1-unit-015-d011} =: \text{Diagram chapter1-unit-015-d012}\] gives a left Kan extension of \(MF\) along \(K\).

  • If a left Kan extension \((\operatorname{Lan}_K F, \eta)\) (or a right Kan extension \((\operatorname{Ran}_K F, \varepsilon)\)) is preserved by every functor whose domain is \(\mathcal{E}\), the Kan extension is called absolute.

The next step is to explain the relationship between adjunctions and absolute Kan extensions. The result is extremely useful in the later study of derived functors; studying its proof also helps one become accustomed to Kan extensions and the manipulation of \(2\)-cells. Consider a pair of adjoint functors \(\text{Diagram chapter1-unit-015-diagram-013}\), specified by a unit \(\eta: \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{\mathcal{C}} \to GF\) and a counit \(\varepsilon: FG \to \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{\mathcal{C}'}\). Also given are functors \[K: \mathcal{C} \to \mathcal{D}, \quad K': \mathcal{C}' \to \mathcal{D}'.\] We shall now use \(2\)-cell diagrams systematically to represent functors, natural transformations between them, and their composites, making the argument more concise. In manipulating \(2\)-cells, we interchange vertical and horizontal composition without further comment; this is valid, as explained in [Li1].

Theorem (G. Maltsiniotis [Ma07).] Suppose \(K'F\) has an absolute right Kan extension along \(K\), denoted \(\mathrm{L}F\), while \(KG\) has an absolute left Kan extension along \(K'\), denoted \(\mathrm{R}G\). The associated data are displayed in the following diagrams: \[\text{Diagram chapter1-unit-015-d013} \quad \text{Diagram chapter1-unit-015-d014}\] In this situation, there are unique transformations \(\underline{\eta}: \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{\mathcal{D}} \to \mathrm{R}G \circ \mathrm{L}F\) and \(\underline{\varepsilon}: \mathrm{L}F \circ \mathrm{R}G \to \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{\mathcal{D}'}\) such that the following equations of composite \(2\)-cells hold: \[\begin{equation*} \begin{gathered} \hypertarget{o014.li2.chapter1.kan-extensions.g016}{} \text{Diagram chapter1-unit-015-d015} = \text{Diagram chapter1-unit-015-d016} \\ \hypertarget{o014.li2.chapter1.kan-extensions.g018}{} \text{Diagram chapter1-unit-015-d017} = \text{Diagram chapter1-unit-015-d018} \end{gathered} \end{equation*}\] Moreover, \(\underline{\eta}\) and \(\underline{\varepsilon}\) make \((\mathrm{L}F, \mathrm{R}G)\) an adjunction.

Proof.

The first task is to prove the existence and uniqueness of \(\underline{\eta}\) and \(\underline{\varepsilon}\). Since \(\mathrm{R}G\) is an absolute left Kan extension, the \(2\)-cell \[\text{Diagram chapter1-unit-015-d019} = (\mathrm{L}F)\beta : \mathrm{L}F \circ K \circ G \to \mathrm{L}F \circ \mathrm{R}G \circ K'\] makes \(\mathrm{L}F \circ \mathrm{R}G\) a left Kan extension of \(\mathrm{L}F \circ K \circ G\) along \(K'\). On the other hand, we also have \[\text{Diagram chapter1-unit-015-d020} = \varepsilon(\alpha G) : \mathrm{L}F \circ K \circ G \to K' \circ \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{\mathcal{C}'} = K' .\] Thus the universal property of the left Kan extension determines a unique \(\underline{\varepsilon}\) satisfying the equation of composite \(2\)-cells in the statement of the theorem.

The case of \(\underline{\eta}\) is dual. It suffices to observe that \((\mathrm{R}G)\alpha: \mathrm{R}G \circ \mathrm{L}F \circ K \to \mathrm{R}G \circ K' \circ F\) also makes \(\mathrm{R}G \circ \mathrm{L}F\) a right Kan extension, because \(\mathrm{L}F\) is an absolute right Kan extension.

It remains to verify the triangle identities for the unit \(\underline{\eta}\) and counit \(\underline{\varepsilon}\), namely the following equations of composite \(2\)-cells: \[\begin{equation*} \begin{gathered} \hypertarget{o014.li2.chapter1.kan-extensions.g022}{} \text{Diagram chapter1-unit-015-d021} = \text{Diagram chapter1-unit-015-d022} , \quad \hypertarget{o014.li2.chapter1.kan-extensions.g024}{} \text{Diagram chapter1-unit-015-d023} = \text{Diagram chapter1-unit-015-d024}, \end{gathered} \end{equation*}\] where unambiguous arrow labels have been omitted. We prove the first equation. By the universal property of \((\mathrm{R}G, \beta)\) as a left Kan extension, it suffices to show that the \(2\)-cells obtained by composing both sides with \(\beta\) are equal. For the left side of the first equation, begin with \[\text{Diagram chapter1-unit-015-d025} = \text{Diagram chapter1-unit-015-d026}\] where we used the characterization of \(\underline{\varepsilon}\). Next, using the characterization of \(\underline{\eta}\) and the triangle identities satisfied by \(\eta\) and \(\varepsilon\), the right-hand side above becomes \[\text{Diagram chapter1-unit-015-d027} = \text{Diagram chapter1-unit-015-d028} = \text{Diagram chapter1-unit-015-d029}\] This is the first triangle identity. The proof of the second is dual.

  1. Translator’s note: the source writes \(\operatorname{Ran}_F(\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{\mathcal{C}})\) in the final sentence, contrary to the preceding assertion concerning \((F,\varepsilon)\). The target corrects this to \(\operatorname{Ran}_G(\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{\mathcal{D}})\) (O014-C014).↩︎

  2. One common strengthening is called a pointwise Kan extension; it is not discussed here.↩︎

  3. Translator’s note: the source does not include the category \(\mathcal{F}\) in the initial list, even though it is used as the codomain of \(M\). The target adds it (O014-C015).↩︎

Constructing Kan Extensions by Limits

As in §reference, throughout this section we continue to consider functors \(K: \mathcal{C} \to \mathcal{D}\) and \(F: \mathcal{C} \to \mathcal{E}\), with the aim of studying the existence of \(\operatorname{Lan}_K F\) and \(\operatorname{Ran}_K F\). Recall the discussion at the beginning of §reference. The motivation for Kan extensions is to seek a functor \(G: \mathcal{D} \to \mathcal{E}\) such that \(F \simeq GK\), or at least to find the best approximation to one. How should \(Gd\) be defined for \(d \in \operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{D})\)? The only clue is that when \(d=Kc\), the object \(Gd\) ought to be \(Fc\), up to isomorphism. This suggests approximating \(Gd\) by a colimit \(\varinjlim\) (or a limit \(\varprojlim\)) of the objects \(Fc\), indexed by all \(c \in \operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{C})\) and morphisms \(Kc \to d\) (or \(d \to Kc\)). These two constructions have dual universal properties. We now make the construction precise. Given \(d \in \operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{D})\), define the categories \((K/d)\) and \((d/K)\) as in Definition reference, together with the projection functors \[\Pi_{/d}: (K/d) \to \mathcal{C}, \quad \Pi_{d/}: (d/K) \to \mathcal{C}.\] Our focus will be on the composite functors \(F\Pi_{/d}: (K/d) \to \mathcal{E}\) and \(F\Pi_{d/}: (d/K) \to \mathcal{E}\), which send the objects \((c,Kc \to d)\) and \((c,d \to Kc)\), respectively, to \(Fc\). Assuming that the limits under discussion exist, we first record a few observations.

  • Every morphism \(d \to d'\) induces a canonical morphism \(\varinjlim F\Pi_{/d} \to \varinjlim F\Pi_{/d'}\); it is characterized by requiring the diagram \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:Kan-limit-aux-0}{} \hypertarget{o014.li2.chapter1.kan-extensions-as-limits.g001}{} \text{Diagram chapter1-unit-016-d001} \end{equation}\] to commute for every \((c,Kc \to d) \in \operatorname{Ob}((K/d))\) (which induces an object \((c,Kc \to d') \in \operatorname{Ob}((K/d'))\)), where the vertical arrows are the structure morphisms of the colimits. This is an instance of the functoriality of colimits; see [Li1]1 and its proof.

  • Considering \((c,Kc \xrightarrow{\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}} Kc) \in \operatorname{Ob}(K/Kc)\) gives a canonical morphism \(\eta_c: Fc \to \varinjlim F\Pi_{/Kc}\).

  • Every morphism \(c \to c'\) induces a canonical morphism \(\varinjlim F\Pi_{/Kc} \to \varinjlim F\Pi_{/Kc'}\) that makes the following diagram commute: \[\text{Diagram chapter1-unit-016-d002}\]

By duality, \(\varprojlim F\Pi_{d/}\) has the corresponding properties, including a canonical morphism \(\varepsilon_c: \varprojlim F\Pi_{Kc/} \to Fc\). The next theorem is based on this functoriality.

Theorem. Consider functors \(K: \mathcal{C} \to \mathcal{D}\) and \(F: \mathcal{C} \to \mathcal{E}\).

  1. Suppose that for every \(d \in \operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{D})\), the colimit \(\varinjlim(F\Pi_{/d})\) exists in \(\mathcal{E}\). Then \((\operatorname{Lan}_K F)(d) := \varinjlim(F\Pi_{/d})\), together with the functoriality given by equation, determines the left Kan extension \(\operatorname{Lan}_K F: \mathcal{D} \to \mathcal{E}\). The associated natural transformation \(\eta: F \to (\operatorname{Lan}_K F)\circ K\) comes from the family \((\eta_c)_{c\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{C})}\) discussed above.

  2. Suppose that for every \(d \in \operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{D})\), the limit \(\varprojlim(F\Pi_{d/})\) exists in \(\mathcal{E}\). Then \((\operatorname{Ran}_K F)(d) := \varprojlim(F\Pi_{d/})\), together with the dual of equation, determines the right Kan extension \(\operatorname{Ran}_K F: \mathcal{D} \to \mathcal{E}\). The associated natural transformation \(\varepsilon: (\operatorname{Ran}_K F)\circ K \to F\) comes from the family \((\varepsilon_c)_{c\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{C})}\) discussed above.

  3. If \(K: \mathcal{C} \to \mathcal{D}\) is fully faithful, then the \(\eta\) constructed in (i) (or the \(\varepsilon\) constructed in (ii)) is an isomorphism.

Proof. By duality, we treat only the case of \(\operatorname{Lan}_K F\). For (i), we verify the universal property in Definition reference step by step. Let \(L: \mathcal{D} \to \mathcal{E}\) be a functor and let \(\xi: F \to LK\). For every \(d \in \operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{D})\), every object \((c,Kc \to d)\) of \((K/d)\), and every morphism in \((K/d)\) determined by \(f:c\to c'\), namely \((c,Kc\to d)\to(c',Kc'\to d)\), there is a commutative diagram \[\text{Diagram chapter1-unit-016-d003}\] The universal property of \(\varinjlim\) therefore gives \(\chi_d:(\operatorname{Lan}_K F)(d)\to Ld\), characterized by requiring the diagram \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:Kan-limit-aux-1}{} \hypertarget{o014.li2.chapter1.kan-extensions-as-limits.g004}{} \text{Diagram chapter1-unit-016-d004} \end{equation}\] to commute for all \((c,Kc\to d)\in\operatorname{Ob}((K/d))\); the arrow in the first row is the structure morphism of the colimit. We now prove that \((\chi_d)_{d\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{D})}\) defines a natural transformation \(\chi:\operatorname{Lan}_K F\to L\). Given \(d\to d'\), take \((c,Kc\to d)\) and its image \((c,Kc\to d')\). Comparing equation with equation, the question reduces to proving that the diagram \[\text{Diagram chapter1-unit-016-d005}\] commutes, which is immediate. The next step is to verify \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:Kan-limit-aux-2}{} \forall c \in \operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{C}), \quad \xi_c = \chi_{Kc} \eta_c: Fc \to LKc. \end{equation}\] Since \(\eta_c\) is the canonical morphism from \(Fc=F\Pi_{/Kc}(c,Kc\xrightarrow{\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}}Kc)\) to \((\operatorname{Lan}_K F)(Kc)\), equation equation is simply a special case of equation. Finally, we show that a natural transformation \(\chi:\operatorname{Lan}_K F\to L\) satisfying equation is unique. Fix \(d\) and consider any object \((c,Kc\to d)\) of \((K/d)\) and the associated diagram \[\text{Diagram chapter1-unit-016-d006}\] where \(Fc\to(\operatorname{Lan}_K F)(d)\) is the morphism appearing in equation. The square commutes by the naturality of \(\chi\), while the triangle commutes by equation. Since \(\chi_{Kc}\eta_c=\xi_c\), the composite \(Fc\to(\operatorname{Lan}_K F)(d)\xrightarrow{\chi_d}Ld\) equals \(L(Kc\to d)\xi_c\). As \((c,Kc\to d)\) varies, this family of equalities uniquely determines \(\chi_d\). Thus \(\left(\operatorname{Lan}_K F,\eta\right)\) is indeed a left Kan extension. Now consider (iii), and fix \(c\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{C})\). Since \(K\) is fully faithful, it is easy to see that \((K/Kc)\) has the terminal object \((c,Kc\xrightarrow{\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}}Kc)\). The morphism \(\eta_c:Fc\to\varinjlim F\Pi_{/Kc}\) comes from this terminal object and is therefore an isomorphism.

Remark. If \(\mathcal{C}\) is a small category, then \((K/d)\) and \((d/K)\) are also small categories for every \(d\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{D})\). Consequently, when \(\mathcal{E}\) is cocomplete (or complete), Theorem reference and Proposition reference show that \(K^*: \mathcal{E}^{\mathcal{D}} \to \mathcal{E}^{\mathcal{C}}\) has a left adjoint \(\operatorname{Lan}_K\) (or a right adjoint \(\operatorname{Ran}_K\)).

Example (Inverse image of presheaves). Take \(\mathcal{E}:=\ensuremath{\mathsf{Set}}\), which is both complete and cocomplete. Let \(f:X\to Y\) be a continuous map of topological spaces. Let \(\mathcal{C}:=\ensuremath{\mathsf{Open}}_Y\) be the category whose objects are the open subsets of \(Y\) and whose morphisms are inclusions of open subsets; similarly, let \(\mathcal{D}:=\ensuremath{\mathsf{Open}}_X\). Now define a functor \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Open}}_Y\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{Open}}_X\) that sends an open subset \(V\subset Y\) to \(f^{-1}V\), and regard it below as a functor \(K:\ensuremath{\mathsf{Open}}_Y^{\operatorname{op}}\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{Open}}_X^{\operatorname{op}}\). Readers familiar with sheaf theory will recognize that the objects of \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Open}}_Y^\wedge:=\ensuremath{\mathsf{Set}}^{\ensuremath{\mathsf{Open}}_Y^{\operatorname{op}}}\) are, by definition, precisely the presheaves on \(Y\), while \(K^*:\ensuremath{\mathsf{Open}}_X^\wedge\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{Open}}_Y^\wedge\) is the direct-image functor between the presheaf categories: it sends a presheaf \(\mathcal{F}\) on \(X\) to the presheaf on \(Y\) given by \(V\mapsto\mathcal{F}(f^{-1}V)\).
