In this situation, the left adjoint of the direct image is \(\operatorname{Lan}_K\), given by Theorem reference; it sends a presheaf \(\mathcal{G}\) on \(Y\) to \[\begin{gather*} U \mapsto \varinjlim_{\substack{V \subset Y: \text{open subset} \\ \text{such that}\; U \subset f^{-1} V }} \mathcal{G}(V), \quad U \subset X: \text{open subset}, \\ U \subset f^{-1}V \;\xleftrightarrow{\text{corresponds to}}\; \text{a morphism}\; K(V) \to U \;\text{in}\; \ensuremath{\mathsf{Open}}_X^{\operatorname{op}}. \end{gather*}\] Unsurprisingly, this is precisely the inverse image of \(\mathcal{G}\) in sheaf theory.

  1. Translator’s note: the source gives the locator as Lemma 2.7,4; it has been corrected to Lemma 2.7.4 here (O014-C016).↩︎

Gabriel–Zisman Localization

Gabriel–Zisman localization, henceforth simply called localization, is the most economical way to adjoin inverses to a family of morphisms in a category. The theory originates in [GZ67] and is characterized by a universal property.

Definition (P. Gabriel, M. Zisman). Let \(\mathcal{C}\) be a category and let \(S\) be a subset of \(\operatorname{Mor}(\mathcal{C})\) that contains all identity morphisms and is closed under composition. A localization of \(\mathcal{C}\) at \(S\) means a category \(\mathcal{C}[S^{-1}]\) (which may be a “large” category), together with a functor \(Q:\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{C}[S^{-1}]\), called the localization functor, satisfying the following conditions.

  • For every \(s\in S\), its image \(Q(s)\) is an isomorphism in \(\mathcal{C}[S^{-1}]\).

  • For every category \(\mathcal{D}\) (again possibly “large”) and functor \(F:\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{D}\), if \(F\) sends every morphism in \(S\) to an isomorphism, then there is a unique functor \(F[S^{-1}]:\mathcal{C}[S^{-1}]\to\mathcal{D}\) such that \(F=F[S^{-1}]Q\).

By convention, we often omit \(Q\) from the data. Some sources, such as [KS06], give a somewhat weaker universal property for localization1. We next show that localization is unique up to a unique isomorphism.

Proposition. If \((\mathcal{C}[S^{-1}],Q)\) and \((\mathcal{C}[S^{-1}]',Q')\) are both localizations of \(\mathcal{C}\) at \(S\), then there is a unique pair of functors \(\text{Diagram chapter1-unit-017-diagram-001}\) such that \(GQ=Q'\), \(G'Q'=Q\), and \(G'G=\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{\mathcal{C}[S^{-1}]}\), \(GG'=\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{\mathcal{C}[S^{-1}]'}\).

Proof. Since \(Q'\) sends \(S\) to isomorphisms, the universal property gives a unique \(G\) such that \(GQ=Q'\). Similarly, there is a unique \(G'\) such that \(G'Q'=Q\). Since \(G'GQ=Q\), taking \(\mathcal{D}=\mathcal{C}[S^{-1}]\) and \(F=Q\) in the universal property gives \(G'G=\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{\mathcal{C}[S^{-1}]}\). Likewise, \(GG'=\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{\mathcal{C}[S^{-1}]'}\)2.

Proposition. Suppose that the localization \((\mathcal{C}[S^{-1}],Q)\) exists. Let \(S^{\operatorname{op}}\) denote the corresponding image of \(S\) in \(\operatorname{Mor}(\mathcal{C}^{\operatorname{op}})\). Then there is an equivalence of categories, compatible with \(Q\), \(\mathcal{C}[S^{-1}]^{\operatorname{op}}\leftrightarrows \mathcal{C}^{\operatorname{op}}[(S^{\operatorname{op}})^{-1}]\).

Proof. By the uniqueness of localization, it suffices to apply \((-)^{\operatorname{op}}\) to all the categories and functors in Definition reference, since this operation does not reverse the direction of a functor.

The problem is thus reduced to the existence and construction of localization. For general \(\mathcal{C}\) and \(S\), one can construct \(\mathcal{C}[S^{-1}]\) by formally adjoining inverses to \(\mathcal{C}\), much as in the construction of a free group. More concretely, \(\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{C}[S^{-1}])=\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{C})\), while morphisms in \(\mathcal{C}[S^{-1}]\) are represented formally by finite zigzags \[\cdots b t^{-1} a s^{-1} \cdots = \left( \text{Diagram chapter1-unit-017-d001}\right)\] with \(a,b,\ldots\in\operatorname{Mor}(\mathcal{C})\) and \(s,t,\ldots\in S\). Composition and \(Q\) are defined in the evident way, but one must quotient by the equivalence relation generated by \[s^{-1}t^{-1}=(ts)^{-1}, \quad ss^{-1}=\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}, \quad s^{-1}s=\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}\] and so on; see the sketch in [GZ67]. Localization may therefore be viewed as a kind of calculus of fractions for morphisms. This construction is completely general, but its drawbacks are equally clear, chiefly because the equivalence relation is hard to work with. For example, it is difficult to characterize those \(f,g\in\operatorname{Mor}(\mathcal{C})\) for which \(Qf=Qg\). Fortunately, in practice \(S\) is often a left (or right) multiplicative system, to be introduced in Definition reference. In that case the description of \(\mathcal{C}[S^{-1}]\) can be simplified: the zigzags above can be straightened, so that every morphism can be written in the form \(as^{-1}\) (or \(s^{-1}a\)). Before introducing multiplicative systems, we record a simple property of the construction above.

Proposition. The localization functor \(Q:\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{C}[S^{-1}]\) is essentially surjective. Moreover, for every category \(\mathcal{D}\) and functors \(A,B:\mathcal{C}[S^{-1}]\to\mathcal{D}\), the evident map \[\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{D}^{\mathcal{C}[S^{-1}]}}(A,B) \to \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{D}^{\mathcal{C}}}\left(AQ,BQ\right)\] is a bijection. In other words, \(Q^*:\mathcal{D}^{\mathcal{C}[S^{-1}]}\to\mathcal{D}^{\mathcal{C}}\) is a fully faithful functor.

Proof. We may realize the localization concretely as above. Write the map induced by \(Q\) on objects as \(X\mapsto\underline{X}\). It is a bijection, hence \(Q\) is essentially surjective. It follows at once that the map \(\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{D}^{\mathcal{C}[S^{-1}]}}(A,B)\to \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{D}^{\mathcal{C}}}(AQ,BQ)\) is injective.

For surjectivity, let \(\varphi=(\varphi_X)_{X\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{C})}\in \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{D}^{\mathcal{C}}}(AQ,BQ)\). For each \(\underline{X}=QX\), define a morphism \(\tilde{\varphi}_{\underline{X}}:A\underline{X}\to B\underline{X}\) in \(\mathcal{D}\) to be \(\varphi_X\). It remains to show that \(\tilde{\varphi}:=(\tilde{\varphi}_{\underline{X}})_{\underline{X}}\) lies in \(\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{D}^{\mathcal{C}[S^{-1}]}}(A,B)\). In other words, for every morphism \(f:\underline{X}\to\underline{Y}\) in \(\mathcal{C}[S^{-1}]\), we must verify that the following diagram commutes in \(\mathcal{D}\): \[\text{Diagram chapter1-unit-017-d002}\] By the zigzag construction of morphisms, \(f\) decomposes into a string of morphisms of the form \(Qa\) or \((Qs)^{-1}\), with \(a\in\operatorname{Mor}(\mathcal{C})\) and \(s\in S\). The commutativity of the diagram therefore reduces to the corresponding property of \(\varphi\).

Definition. A subset \(S\subset\operatorname{Mor}(\mathcal{C})\) satisfying the following properties is called a left multiplicative system in \(\mathcal{C}\).

  1. For every \(X\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{C})\), one has \(\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_X\in S\).

  2. For all \(f,g\in S\), if the composite \(gf\) is defined, then \(gf\in S\).

  3. Given morphisms \(X\xrightarrow{s\in S}Z\xleftarrow{f}Y\), there are morphisms in \(\mathcal{C}\), \(X\xleftarrow{f'}W\xrightarrow{s'\in S}Y\), such that \(sf'=fs'\), depicted by the commutative diagram \[\text{Diagram chapter1-unit-017-diagram-004} \quad \text{commutative}.\]

  4. Let \(f,g:X\to Y\) be morphisms in \(\mathcal{C}\) and let \(s:Y\to W\) belong to \(S\). If \(sf=sg\), then there is a morphism \(t:Z\to X\) in \(S\) such that \(ft=gt\). Diagrammatically, \[\text{Diagram chapter1-unit-017-d003}\]

The dashed parts of these diagrams are the morphisms whose existence is asserted.

If the image \(S^{\operatorname{op}}\) of \(S\) in \(\operatorname{Mor}(\mathcal{C}^{\operatorname{op}})\) is a left multiplicative system, then \(S\) is called a right multiplicative system in \(\mathcal{C}\). Equivalently, reverse all arrows in conditions (S3) and (S4). A subset \(S\) that is both a left and a right multiplicative system is called a multiplicative system in \(\mathcal{C}\).

Convention. For a given left or right multiplicative system \(S\), from now on arrows belonging to \(S\) will always be drawn as \(\rightarrowtail\) in commutative diagrams, to distinguish them from the other arrows.

Fix \(X\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{C})\). In accordance with this convention, define the category \(S_{/X}\) (or \(S_{X/}\)) for a left (or right) multiplicative system \(S\) as follows. \[\begin{align*} \operatorname{Ob}\left(S_{/X}\right) &:= \left\{\text{morphisms}\;X\leftarrowtail Z\right\}, & \operatorname{Mor}(S_{/X}) &:= \left\{\text{commutative diagrams}\; \hypertarget{o014.li2.chapter1.gabriel-zisman-localization.g006}{} {\text{Diagram chapter1-unit-017-d004}}\right\}, \\ \operatorname{Ob}\left(S_{X/}\right) &:= \left\{\text{morphisms}\;X\rightarrowtail Z\right\}, & \operatorname{Mor}(S_{X/}) &:= \left\{\text{commutative diagrams}\; \hypertarget{o014.li2.chapter1.gabriel-zisman-localization.g007}{} {\text{Diagram chapter1-unit-017-d005}}\right\}. \end{align*}\] Note that if \(S\) is a left multiplicative system, then \(\left(S^{\operatorname{op}}\right)_{X/}=(S_{/X})^{\operatorname{op}}\).

Lemma. If \(S\) is a left (or right) multiplicative system, then \(S_{/X}^{\operatorname{op}}\) (or \(S_{X/}\)) is a filtered category.

Proof. By the duality observed above, we need only discuss the case of a right multiplicative system. For any objects \(i:X\to Z\) and \(j:X\to Z'\) of \(S_{X/}\), use the corresponding version of (S3) to construct a commutative diagram \[\text{Diagram chapter1-unit-017-d006}\] Then \(k:=i'j\in S\) gives an object of \(S_{X/}\), together with morphisms \(i\xrightarrow{j'}k\xleftarrow{i'}j\) in \(S_{X/}\).

Let \(i,j\) be as above. For any pair of morphisms in \(S_{X/}\), \(\text{Diagram chapter1-unit-017-d007}\) (a commutative diagram), the corresponding version of (S4) gives \(h:Z'\rightarrowtail W\) such that \(hf=hg\). Put \(k:=hj:X\rightarrowtail W\) and regard this as an object of \(S_{X/}\). We then obtain the commutative diagram in \(S_{X/}\) \(\text{Diagram chapter1-unit-017-diagram-010}\). These are exactly the defining conditions for a filtered category.

Let \(X,Y\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{C})\). We now define sets \(M_{X,Y}^l\) and \(M_{X,Y}^r\) for left and right multiplicative systems, respectively. Note that they need not be small sets.

  • Let \(S\) be a left multiplicative system. Abbreviate a diagram in \(\mathcal{C}\) of the form \[\text{Diagram chapter1-unit-017-diagram-011}\] by \((Z;s,a)\). These data form the set \(M_{X,Y}^l\).

  • Let \(S\) be a right multiplicative system. Abbreviate a diagram in \(\mathcal{C}\) of the form \[\text{Diagram chapter1-unit-017-diagram-012}\] by \((Z;a,s)\). These data form the set \(M_{X,Y}^r\).

Define a binary relation \(\sim\) as follows: \((Z;s,a)\sim(Z';s',a')\) (or \((Z;a,s)\sim(Z';a',s')\)) if and only if there is a commutative diagram of the form \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:localization-sim}{} \begin{array}{cc} \hypertarget{o014.li2.chapter1.gabriel-zisman-localization.g013}{} \text{Diagram chapter1-unit-017-d008} & \hypertarget{o014.li2.chapter1.gabriel-zisman-localization.g014}{} \text{Diagram chapter1-unit-017-d009} \\ \text{(left multiplicative system)} & \text{(right multiplicative system)} \end{array} \end{equation}\] For every \(f:X\to Y\), condition (S1) implies \((X;\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_X,f)\in M_{X,Y}^l\) and \((X;f,\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_Y)\in M_{X,Y}^r\). The two definitions are plainly dual.

Lemma. For a left (or right) multiplicative system \(S\) and arbitrary \(X,Y\), the relation \(\sim\) defined above is an equivalence relation on \(M_{X,Y}^l\) (or \(M_{X,Y}^r\)). In fact, there are bijections \[\text{Diagram chapter1-unit-017-d010} \quad \hypertarget{o014.li2.chapter1.gabriel-zisman-localization.g016}{} \text{Diagram chapter1-unit-017-d011}\] where \([Z;s,a]\) (or \([Z;a,s]\)) denotes the equivalence class containing \((Z;s,a)\) (or \((Z;a,s)\)).

Proof. Consider the functor \(\alpha:S_{/X}^{\operatorname{op}}\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{Set}}\) sending an object \(X\leftarrowtail Z\) to \(\operatorname{Hom}(Z,Y)\). By definition, \[M_{X, Y}^l = \bigsqcup_{X \leftarrowtail Z} \alpha(X \leftarrowtail Z),\] and since \(S_{/X}^{\operatorname{op}}\) is filtered (Lemma reference), it is easy to check that the binary relation \(\sim\) on \(M_{X,Y}^l\) arising from equation translates into the equivalence relation in Proposition reference. This also proves the bijection with \(\varinjlim\). The argument for the \(M_{X,Y}^r\) version is identical.

When discussing filtered colimits of sets, §reference assumes that the indexing category is small, so that the resulting colimit still lies in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Set}}\). Here \(S_{/X}\) and \(S_{Y/}\) need not be small categories. The assertion itself, however, does not depend on set size, and the argument can be formulated so as not to depend on a choice of Grothendieck universe.

The equivalence class \([Z;s,a]\) (or \([Z;a,s]\)) should be understood as the morphism \(as^{-1}\) (or \(s^{-1}a\)) in the category \(\mathcal{C}[S^{-1}]\) to be constructed.

Definition–Proposition. Let \(S\) be a left multiplicative system, let \(X,Y\) be arbitrary, and take \((U;s,a)\in M_{X,Y}^l\) and \((V;t,b)\in M_{Y,Z}^l\). Use (S3) to extend them to the following commutative diagram: \[\text{Diagram chapter1-unit-017-d012}\] Then \([V;t,b]\circ[U;s,a]:=[W;sr,bc]\in M_{X,Z}^l/\sim\) depends only on \([U;s,a]\) and \([V;t,b]\). The dual statement holds for right multiplicative systems.

Proof. First fix \((V;t,b)\) and vary \((U;s,a)\) within its equivalence class. In view of equation, it suffices, for a commutative diagram \[\text{Diagram chapter1-unit-017-d013}\] to prove \((W;sr,bc)\sim(W';s'r',bc')\). Apply (S3) to obtain an object \(Q\) and morphisms \(q,k\) such that \[\text{Diagram chapter1-unit-017-d014} \quad \text{commutes}.\]

Combining this with the preceding diagram gives \(tc'k=a'r'k=axr'k=arq=tcq\). By (S4), there is a \(w:P\rightarrowtail Q\) such that \(c'kw=cqw\). It is then easy to verify that \[\text{Diagram chapter1-unit-017-d015} \quad \text{commutes, that is,}\; (W;sr,bc)\sim(W';s'r',bc').\]

The case in which \((U;s,a)\) is fixed and \((V;t,b)\) varies within its equivalence class is similar.

Definition–Theorem. Let \(S\) be a left multiplicative system in a category \(\mathcal{C}\).

  1. There is a category \(\mathcal{C}[S^{-1}]^l\) (possibly a large category) whose object set is \(\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{C})\) and whose \(\operatorname{Hom}\) set between two objects \(X,Y\) is \(M_{X,Y}^l/\sim\). The identity morphism of \(X\) is \([X;\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_X,\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_X]\), and composition is given by the binary operation in Definition–Proposition reference.

  2. There is a functor \(Q^l:\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{C}[S^{-1}]^l\) that is the identity on objects and sends a morphism \(f:X\to Y\) to \([X;\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_X,f]\).

The dual statement holds for a right multiplicative system \(S\); the corresponding data are denoted \(Q^r:\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{C}[S^{-1}]^r\).

Proof. By duality, we need only consider a left multiplicative system.

For (i), it suffices to verify the properties of composition in \(\mathcal{C}[S^{-1}]^l\). The operation in Definition–Proposition reference plainly makes \([X;\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_X,\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_X]\) an identity morphism, so only associativity remains. Take \((A;s,a)\in M_{X,Y}^l\), \((B;t,b)\in M_{Y,Z}^l\), and \((C;u,c)\in M_{Z,W}^l\). Applying (S3) three times gives the commutative diagram \[\text{Diagram chapter1-unit-017-d016}\] The whole diagram gives an element of \(M_{X,W}^l\); its lower-left part gives a representative of \([B;t,b]\circ[A;s,a]\), and its lower-right part gives a representative of \([C;u,c]\circ[B;t,b]\). This proves associativity: \[[C;u,c]\circ([B;t,b]\circ[A;s,a])=([C;u,c]\circ[B;t,b])\circ[A;s,a].\]

For (ii), it remains to check that \(Q^l\) respects identities and composition. It preserves identities because \([X;\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_X,\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_X]\) has the required identity property. Now consider morphisms \(X\xrightarrow{f}Y\xrightarrow{g}Z\) in \(\mathcal{C}\). The diagram \[\text{Diagram chapter1-unit-017-d017}\] shows that \(Q^l(gf)=Q^l(g)Q^l(f)\).

Theorem (P. Gabriel, M. Zisman). Let \(S\) be a left (or right) multiplicative system in \(\mathcal{C}\). Then \(\left(\mathcal{C}[S^{-1}]^l,Q^l\right)\) (or \(\left(\mathcal{C}[S^{-1}]^r,Q^r\right)\)) is a localization of \(\mathcal{C}\) at \(S\).

Proof. By duality, we only verify the conditions of Definition reference for a left multiplicative system. Write \(Q=Q^l\). If \(f:X\to Y\) belongs to \(S\), the diagram \[\text{Diagram chapter1-unit-017-d018}\] shows that \([X;f,f]=[Y;\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_Y,\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_Y]\). Hence the following diagrams show that \([X;f,\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_X]=[X;\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_X,f]^{-1}\): \[\text{Diagram chapter1-unit-017-d019} \quad \hypertarget{o014.li2.chapter1.gabriel-zisman-localization.g025}{} \text{Diagram chapter1-unit-017-d020}\] Thus \(Q\) does send the elements of \(S\) to isomorphisms.

Now let \(F:\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{D}\) be a functor sending \(S\) to isomorphisms. Define \(F[S^{-1}]:\mathcal{C}[S^{-1}]^l\to\mathcal{D}\) as follows: on objects it sends \(X\) to \(FX\), and on morphisms it sends \([U;s,a]\in\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}[S^{-1}]^l}(X,Y)\) to \((Fa)(Fs)^{-1}\in\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{D}}(FX,FY)\)3. Clearly, \(F[S^{-1}]\) sends identity morphisms in \(\mathcal{C}[S^{-1}]^l\) to identity morphisms in \(\mathcal{D}\). Apply \(F\) to the diagram in Definition–Proposition reference and invert the arrows in \(F(S)\); it follows at once that \(F[S^{-1}]\) preserves composition. The equality \(F[S^{-1}]Q=F\) is also clear. Since every morphism in \(\mathcal{C}[S^{-1}]^l\) has the form \((Qa)(Qs)^{-1}\), no other definition of \(F[S^{-1}]\) is possible.

Convention. If \(S\) is a multiplicative system, Proposition reference shows that the two localizations can be identified; we write the resulting functor as \(Q:\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{C}[S^{-1}]\).

Corollary. Let \(S\) be a left (or right) multiplicative system in \(\mathcal{C}\). Morphisms \(f,g:X\to Y\) in \(\mathcal{C}\) satisfy \(Q^lf=Q^lg\) (or \(Q^rf=Q^rg\)) if and only if there exists \(s\in S\) such that \(fs=gs\) (or \(sf=sg\)).

Proof. It suffices to check the “only if” direction for a left multiplicative system \(S\). If \(Q^lf=Q^lg\), the construction of \(\mathcal{C}[S^{-1}]^l\) gives a commutative diagram \[\text{Diagram chapter1-unit-017-d021}\] from which \(fs=a=gs\).

Corollary. Let \(S\) be a left (or right) multiplicative system in \(\mathcal{C}\). Then \(Q^l\) (or \(Q^r\)) sends monomorphisms to monomorphisms (or epimorphisms to epimorphisms).

Proof. We prove only the case of a left multiplicative system. Let \(f:X\to Y\) be a monomorphism in \(\mathcal{C}\). Take \(\alpha,\beta:Q^lW\rightrightarrows Q^lX\) such that \((Q^lf)\alpha=(Q^lf)\beta\). Conditions (S2) and (S3) allow us to represent \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) by elements \((U;s,a)\) and \((U;s,b)\), respectively, of \(M^l_{W,X}\); the details are left to the reader as an exercise. The given equality then implies \(Q^l(fa)=Q^l(fb)\). By Corollary reference, there is a \(t\in S\) such that \(fat=fbt\). Hence \(at=bt\), and therefore \(\alpha=\beta\).

Remark. In the basic operations of category theory, we want to avoid large categories whenever possible. Definition–Theorem reference says that \(\mathcal{C}[S^{-1}]^l\) (or \(\mathcal{C}[S^{-1}]^r\)) may be a large category. The reason is that the \(\varinjlim\) in Lemma reference need not be small, so its value need not lie in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Set}}\). This is a somewhat delicate issue.

If \(S\) satisfies the following condition, however, then \(\mathcal{C}[S^{-1}]^l\) (or \(\mathcal{C}[S^{-1}]^r\)) is not large: assume that \(S_{/X}^{\operatorname{op}}\) (or \(S_{X/}\)) has a small cofinal subcategory (Definition reference) for every \(X\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{C})\). By Proposition reference, the colimit in question may be restricted to that subcategory, yielding an object of \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Set}}\). If \(\mathcal{C}\) itself is small, this condition holds automatically.

Lemma. Let \(S\) be a left (or right) multiplicative system in \(\mathcal{C}\). Then the localization functor \(Q^l\) (or \(Q^r\)) preserves finite \(\varprojlim\) (or finite \(\varinjlim\)).

Proof. We discuss only the case of a left multiplicative system. Let \(J\) be a finite category, and suppose that the limit associated with a functor \(\beta:J^{\operatorname{op}}\to\mathcal{C}\) exists. By Lemma reference, for every \(X\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{C})\) there are canonical bijections \[\begin{multline*} \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}[S^{-1}]^l}\left(Q^lX,Q^l\varprojlim\beta\right) \simeq \varinjlim_{X\leftarrowtail Z}\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}}\left(Z,\varprojlim\beta\right) \\ \simeq \varinjlim_{X\leftarrowtail Z}\varprojlim_{j\in\operatorname{Ob}(J)} \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}}\left(Z,\beta(j)\right). \end{multline*}\]

Applying Lemma reference and Proposition reference to the last term transforms it further into \[\varprojlim_{j \in \operatorname{Ob}(J)} \varinjlim_{X \leftarrowtail Z} \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}}\left( Z, \beta(j) \right) \simeq \varprojlim_{j \in \operatorname{Ob}(J)} \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}[S^{-1}]^l} \left(Q^l X, Q^l \beta(j) \right).\] Strictly speaking, §reference works in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Set}}\), whereas the \(\operatorname{Hom}\) sets here need not lie in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Set}}\). This is only a minor technical issue; see the related discussion in the proof of Lemma reference.

Theorem. Let \(\mathcal{C}\) be an \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ab}}\)-category and let \(S\) be a left (or right) multiplicative system in it.

  1. The category \(\mathcal{C}[S^{-1}]^l\) (or \(\mathcal{C}[S^{-1}]^r\)) has a canonical \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ab}}\)-category structure making \(Q^l\) (or \(Q^r\)) an additive, essentially surjective functor.

  2. If \(\mathcal{C}\) is an additive category and \(S\) is a multiplicative system, then \(\mathcal{C}[S^{-1}]\) is also an additive category.

  3. The preceding statements remain true if \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ab}}\)-categories are replaced by \(\Bbbk\)-linear categories, where \(\Bbbk\) is a commutative ring. If \(F\) in the universal property of Definition reference is \(\Bbbk\)-linear, then so is the associated functor \(F[S^{-1}]\).

Proof. For (i), it suffices to treat a left multiplicative system. We must define addition on the morphism sets of \(\mathcal{C}[S^{-1}]\). Let \[f,g\in\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}[S^{-1}]^l}(X,Y).\] Since \(S_{/X}^{\operatorname{op}}\) is filtered (Lemma reference), there are a morphism \(s:U\rightarrowtail X\) and morphisms \(a_1,a_2:U\to Y\) in \(\mathcal{C}\) such that \(f=[U;s,a_1]\) and \(g=[U;s,a_2]\). Define \[f+g:=[U;s,a_1+a_2]\in\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}[S^{-1}]}(X,Y).\] In particular, a zero morphism can be written \([U;s,0]\), and \(-[U;s,a]=[U;s,-a]\). One must still prove that \(f+g\) is independent of the choice of representatives; this too follows from the filteredness of \(S_{/X}^{\operatorname{op}}\), and the routine details are omitted. Once this operation is known to be well defined, the axioms for an \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ab}}\)-category and the additivity of \(Q\) are easy to verify.

Statement (ii) follows from (i), the definition of an additive category (Definition reference), and Lemma reference.

For (iii), if \(\mathcal{C}\) is \(\Bbbk\)-linear, define scalar multiplication on \(\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}[S^{-1}]}\) by \(t\cdot[U;s,a]=[U;s,ta]\) for \(t\in\Bbbk\). The required properties are immediate.

Example (Localization of rings). Giving a ring \(R\) is equivalent to giving an \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ab}}\)-category \(\mathcal{C}\) with a single object \(\star\) such that \(R=\operatorname{End}_{\mathcal{C}}(\star)\). If \(R\) is commutative, the conditions that \(S\subset R=\operatorname{Mor}(\mathcal{C})\) be a left or a right multiplicative system coincide. In this case, the ring corresponding to the \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ab}}\)-category \(\mathcal{C}[S^{-1}]\) is precisely the localization \(R[S^{-1}]\) of \(R\); see [Li1]. For a general ring \(R\), the theory in this section provides a construction of noncommutative localizations. The related theory is also a branch of noncommutative ring theory; see [Lam99] for a detailed account.

Example (Central localization). Write the center of an additive category \(\mathcal{C}\) as \(Z(\mathcal{C})\); this is a commutative ring. See the discussion preceding Proposition reference. For any multiplicative subset \(S\) of \(Z(\mathcal{C})\), it is easy to check that the set of morphisms \[\{s_X \in \operatorname{End}_{\mathcal{C}}(X): s \in S, \; X \in \operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{C}) \}\] is a multiplicative system. The corresponding category \(\mathcal{C}[S^{-1}]\) can of course be constructed using the calculus of fractions above, but a shorter construction is \[\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{C}[S^{-1}]) := \operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{C}), \quad \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}[S^{-1}]}(X, Y) := \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}}(X, Y) \ensuremath{\underset{Z(\mathcal{C})}{\otimes}} Z(\mathcal{C})[S^{-1}],\] with composition defined in the usual way. The relevant checks are left as an exercise for this chapter.

Remark. For general \(\mathcal{C}\) and \(S\), the case in which the localization functor \(Q:\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{C}[S^{-1}]\) has a fully faithful right adjoint is especially interesting and important. A localization with this property is called a reflective localization. The Gabriel–Popescu theorem to be introduced in Appendix § A.3 is a typical example.

Remark (Localization of product categories). Finally, let \(\mathcal{C}_i\) be categories equipped with left (or right) multiplicative systems \(S_i\), for \(i=1,2\), and write their localization functors as \(Q_i:\mathcal{C}_i\to\mathcal{C}_i[S_i^{-1}]\). Clearly, \(S_1\times S_2\) is also a left (or right) multiplicative system in \(\mathcal{C}_1\times\mathcal{C}_2\). From the construction in Definition–Theorem reference, one readily checks that \[(Q_1, Q_2): \mathcal{C}_1 \times \mathcal{C}_2 \to \mathcal{C}_1[S_1^{-1}] \times \mathcal{C}_2[S_2^{-1}]\] is the corresponding localization. This statement generalizes to products of arbitrary families of categories.

  1. From the perspective of \(2\)-categories, the more natural universal property is this: for every \(\mathcal{D}\), the functor \(Q^*:\mathcal{D}^{\mathcal{C}[S^{-1}]}\to\mathcal{D}^{\mathcal{C}}\) is fully faithful, and \(G\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{D}^{\mathcal{C}})\) is isomorphic to some \(Q^*(F)=FQ\) if and only if \(G\) sends the elements of \(S\) to isomorphisms. The functor \(Q\) in Definition reference automatically has this property—the fully faithful part is Proposition reference, and the rest is easy.↩︎

  2. Translator’s note: the source has \(\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{\mathcal{C}[S^{-1}]}\) for this last identity. Since \(GG'\) is an endofunctor of \(\mathcal{C}[S^{-1}]'\), the prime has been added to the target localization here (O014-C017).↩︎

  3. Translator’s note: the source has \(\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{D}}(X,Y)\). Since \((Fa)(Fs)^{-1}:FX\to FY\), the source and target objects have been corrected to \(FX\) and \(FY\) here (O014-C018).↩︎

Kan Extensions Along Localization

Suppose that the localization of \(\mathcal{C}\) at \(S\subset\operatorname{Mor}(\mathcal{C})\), namely \(Q:\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{C}[S^{-1}]\), exists. This section investigates the problem of extending functors: given a category \(\mathcal{E}\) and a functor \(F:\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{E}\), can one obtain the following commutative diagram? \[\text{Diagram chapter1-unit-018-d001}\] Since \(F\) need not send the morphisms in \(S\) to isomorphisms, the functor indicated by the dashed arrow need not exist. Nevertheless, we may still seek the best possible approximations to such an extension: the left Kan extension \((\operatorname{Lan}_QF,\eta)\) and the right Kan extension \((\operatorname{Ran}_QF,\varepsilon)\). We will omit \(\eta\) and \(\varepsilon\) from the notation from now on. The aim of this section is to give sufficient conditions, for fixed \(\mathcal{C}\), \(S\), and \(F\), under which \(\operatorname{Lan}_QF\) and \(\operatorname{Ran}_QF\) exist; once they do, Proposition reference guarantees their uniqueness. These results will be used in the study of derived functors; see § 4.6. The idea is to choose a suitable subcategory of \(\mathcal{C}\). We retain the convention of §reference: morphisms belonging to \(S\) are marked by \(\rightarrowtail\). The arguments in this section make no assumptions about set size.

Proposition. Let \(\mathcal{I}\) be a full subcategory of \(\mathcal{C}\), let \(S\subset\operatorname{Mor}(\mathcal{C})\) be a left (or right) multiplicative system, and set \(T:=S\cap\operatorname{Mor}(\mathcal{I})\).

  1. If \(T\) is assumed to be a left (or right) multiplicative system in \(\mathcal{I}\), these data induce a functor \(\mathcal{I}[T^{-1}]^l\to\mathcal{C}[S^{-1}]^l\) (or \(\mathcal{I}[T^{-1}]^r\to\mathcal{C}[S^{-1}]^r\)1).

  2. Assume the following condition: for every morphism \(s:W\to Y\) (or \(s:Y\to W\)) in \(S\) with \(Y\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{I})\), there is a morphism \(g:V\to W\) such that \(sg\in T\) (or \(g:W\to V\) such that \(gs\in T\)). Then \(T\) is a left (or right) multiplicative system, and the functor in (i) is fully faithful.

Proof. By duality, it suffices to consider a left multiplicative system. The functor in (i) comes from the universal property of localization; on morphisms it sends every equivalence class \([U;s,a]\) relative to \(T\) to the same class \([U;s,a]\) relative to \(S\).

For (ii), first verify that \(T\) is a left multiplicative system. Conditions (S1) and (S2) of Definition reference are immediate. For (S3), given \(X\stackrel{t}{\rightarrowtail}Z\stackrel{f}{\leftarrow}Y\), construct in \(\mathcal{C}\) the diagram \[\text{Diagram chapter1-unit-018-d002}\] then choose \(g:V\to W\) such that \(s'g\in T\). The morphisms \(s'g\) and \(f'g\) meet the requirements of (S3). The argument for (S4) is the same.

Let \(X,Y\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{I})\). For a morphism in \(\mathcal{C}[S^{-1}]^l\) represented by \(X\leftarrowtail U\to Y\), the condition allows us to choose \(V\to U\) so that the composite \(V\to U\to X\) belongs to \(T\). Thus \(\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{I}[T^{-1}]^l}(X,Y)\to \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}[S^{-1}]^l}(X,Y)\) is surjective. A similar argument shows that every equivalence \(\sim\) in \(M_{X,Y}^l\) can be realized inside \(\mathcal{I}\), proving that the same map is injective.

The following lemma is stated only for a right multiplicative system \(S\); the case of a left multiplicative system is dual.

Lemma. Let \(S\subset\operatorname{Mor}(\mathcal{C})\) be a right multiplicative system. For a given \(\underline{X}:=QX\in \operatorname{Ob}\left(\mathcal{C}[S^{-1}]\right)\), define the category \((Q/\underline{X})\) as in Definition reference. We shall represent an object \((Y,QY\to\underline{X})\) of \((Q/\underline{X})\), nonuniquely, by a diagram \(Y\xrightarrow{a}U\stackrel{s}{\leftarrowtail}X\) in \(\mathcal{C}\).

Define \(S_{X/}\) as in §reference. The functor \(S_{X/}\to(Q/\underline{X})\) that sends an object \([X\stackrel{t}{\rightarrowtail}V]\) to the diagram \(V=V\stackrel{t}{\leftarrowtail}X\), which determines \((V,QV\to\underline{X})\), is cofinal (Definition reference).

Proof. For \([X\stackrel{t}{\rightarrowtail}V]\) as in the statement, specifying a morphism from \((Y,QY\to\underline{X})\) to the corresponding \((V,QV\to\underline{X})\) amounts to specifying a morphism \(b:Y\to V\) in \(\mathcal{C}\) such that the diagram \(Y\xrightarrow{b}V\stackrel{t}{\leftarrowtail}X\) represents the morphism \(QY\to\underline{X}\) in \(\mathcal{C}[S^{-1}]\).

Given \(Y\xrightarrow{a}U\stackrel{s}{\leftarrowtail}X\), the following diagram maps \((Y,QY\to\underline{X})\) to an object coming from \(S_{X/}\): \[\begin{equation*} \text{Diagram chapter1-unit-018-d003} \end{equation*}\]

Next, consider objects \([X\stackrel{t_i}{\rightarrowtail}V_i]\) of \(S_{X/}\) and morphisms from \((Y,QY\to\underline{X})\) to their images, determined by \(b_i:Y\to V_i\) for \(i=1,2\). Using the right-hand diagram in equation, choose a commutative diagram \[\text{Diagram chapter1-unit-018-d004}\] Thus \(u_i:[X\rightarrowtail V_i]\to [X\stackrel{u}{\rightarrowtail}W]\), while \(b\) also determines a morphism from \((Y,QY\to\underline{X})\) to the object \((W,QW\to\underline{X})\) corresponding to \(u\). All the conditions needed for cofinality now follow readily.

Proposition. Let \(\mathcal{I}\) be a full subcategory of \(\mathcal{C}\), let \(S\subset\operatorname{Mor}(\mathcal{C})\) be a left (or right) multiplicative system, and put \(T:=S\cap\operatorname{Mor}(\mathcal{I})\). Assume the following “resolution condition”: for every \(X\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{C})\), there is a morphism \(s:U\to X\) (or \(s:X\to U\)), where \(U\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{I})\) and \(s\in S\).

  1. Then \(T\subset\operatorname{Mor}(\mathcal{I})\) is a left (or right) multiplicative system, and \(\mathcal{I}[T^{-1}]\to\mathcal{C}[S^{-1}]\) is an equivalence.

  2. Suppose further that a functor \(F:\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{E}\) sends the elements of \(T\) to isomorphisms. Then \(\operatorname{Ran}_QF\) (or \(\operatorname{Lan}_QF\)) exists, and the following diagram commutes up to isomorphism: \[\text{Diagram chapter1-unit-018-d005}\] Here \(\mathcal{I}[T^{-1}]\to\mathcal{E}\) is determined by the universal property of localization.

  3. For \(X\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{C})\), define the categories \(S_{/X}\) and \(S_{X/}\) as in §reference. Under the assumptions of (ii), there are canonical isomorphisms2 \[\begin{align*} \left(\operatorname{Ran}_Q F\right)(QX) &\simeq \varprojlim_{[X \leftarrowtail Y] \in \operatorname{Ob}(S_{/X}^{\operatorname{op}})} FY, \\ \left(\operatorname{Lan}_Q F\right)(QX) &\simeq \varinjlim_{[X \rightarrowtail Y] \in \operatorname{Ob}(S_{X/})} FY. \end{align*}\]

The canonical morphism of the Kan extension \(\varepsilon:(\operatorname{Ran}_QF)Q\to F\) (or \(\eta:F\to(\operatorname{Lan}_QF)Q\)) is, in the situation of (iii), determined by the term \(FX\) corresponding to \(\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_X\in\operatorname{Ob}(S_{/X}^{\operatorname{op}})\) (or \(\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_X\in\operatorname{Ob}(S_{X/})\)).

Proof. It suffices to discuss a right multiplicative system. The condition in Proposition reference(ii) plainly holds, so \(T\) is a right multiplicative system. Denote its localization by \(Q':\mathcal{I}\to\mathcal{I}[T^{-1}]\), and denote the fully faithful functor \(\mathcal{I}[T^{-1}]\to\mathcal{C}[S^{-1}]\) of Proposition reference(ii) by \(\iota_Q\). The resolution condition also ensures that \(\iota_Q\) is essentially surjective, hence an equivalence. This proves (i).

Now consider (ii). Write \(\iota:\mathcal{I}\to\mathcal{C}\) for the inclusion functor. By the universal property, there is a functor \(F':\mathcal{I}[T^{-1}]\to\mathcal{E}\) making the following diagram commute: \[\text{Diagram chapter1-unit-018-d006}\]

Choose any quasi-inverse \(\iota_Q^{-1}\) to \(\iota_Q\). We will show that \(F'\circ\iota_Q^{-1}\) gives the left Kan extension \(\operatorname{Lan}_QF\); equivalently, \(\operatorname{Lan}_QF\) exists and \(F'\simeq(\operatorname{Lan}_QF)\circ\iota_Q\).

To prove the existence of \(\operatorname{Lan}_QF\), define \(\Pi_{/\underline{X}}:(Q/\underline{X})\to\mathcal{C}\) as in Definition reference, where \(\underline{X}:=QX\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{C}[S^{-1}])\). In view of Theorem reference(i), it is enough to show that \(\varinjlim F\Pi_{/\underline{X}}\) exists for every \(\underline{X}\).

Apply the cofinal functor \(S_{X/}\to(Q/\underline{X})\) of Lemma reference and Proposition reference. This reduces \(\varinjlim F\Pi_{/\underline{X}}\) to \(\varinjlim_{[X\rightarrowtail U]}FU\), with the colimit taken over \(S_{X/}\).

Since \(S_{X/}\) is filtered (Lemma reference), the resolution condition together with Proposition reference ensures that the objects \([X\rightarrowtail U]\) with \(U\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{I})\) form a cofinal full subcategory of \(S_{X/}\). Another application of Proposition reference therefore lets us restrict the colimit to \(U\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{I})\).

We seek to prove that \(\varinjlim F\Pi_{/\underline{X}}\), or equivalently \(\varinjlim_{[X\rightarrowtail U]}FU\), exists. The original problem depends only on the isomorphism class of \(\underline{X}\), so (i) reduces it to the case \(X\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{I})\). But the following diagram gives a morphism in \(S_{X/}\): \[\begin{equation*} \text{Diagram chapter1-unit-018-d007} \quad \text{where} \quad U \in \operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{I}) \end{equation*}\] All arrows marked \(\rightarrowtail\) become isomorphisms under \(F\). Thus in this case \(\varinjlim FU\) not only exists but is isomorphic to \(FX\). This also proves \(F'\simeq(\operatorname{Lan}_QF)\circ\iota_Q\). Statement (ii) follows.

Finally consider (iii). For \(X\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{C})\), the preceding argument shows that \(\varinjlim_{[X\rightarrowtail Y]\in\operatorname{Ob}(S_{X/})}FY\) exists and gives \((\operatorname{Lan}_QF)(QX)\). Under this correspondence, the canonical morphism \(\eta_X\) of the left Kan extension is naturally determined by the term corresponding to \([X\stackrel{\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}}{\rightarrowtail}X]\); see the construction in §reference.

Proposition. Under the hypotheses of Proposition reference, \(\operatorname{Ran}_QF\) (or \(\operatorname{Lan}_QF\)) is the absolute right (or left) Kan extension of \(F\) along \(Q\); see Definition reference.

Proof. The first condition in Proposition reference concerns only the left (or right) multiplicative system \(S\) in \(\mathcal{C}\) and the subcategory \(\mathcal{I}\), not \(F\); the second only requires \(F\) to send \(T:=S\cap\operatorname{Mor}(\mathcal{I})\) to isomorphisms. In particular, for any functor \(M:\mathcal{E}\to\mathcal{F}\), the condition on \(F\) is inherited at once by \(MF:\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{F}\).

We discuss only \(\operatorname{Lan}_QF\). With the notation from the proof of Proposition reference, \(\operatorname{Lan}_QF\) is concretely taken to be the composite \[\mathcal{C}[S^{-1}] \xrightarrow{\iota_Q^{-1}} \mathcal{I}[T^{-1}] \xrightarrow{F'} \mathcal{E}\] Here \(\iota_Q\) and \(F'\) both come from the universal property of localization. Hence \(M(\operatorname{Lan}_QF)=MF'\iota_Q^{-1}\). The commutative diagram \[\text{Diagram chapter1-unit-018-d008}\] shows that \(MF'\) is also induced by the universal property of localization. Apply the construction of Proposition reference to \(\mathcal{C}\xrightarrow{MF}\mathcal{F}\); it yields \(\operatorname{Lan}_Q(MF)=MF'\iota_Q^{-1}\). In other words, \(\operatorname{Lan}_QF\) is preserved by \(M\).

  1. Translator’s note: in the right-hand case, the source gives the target as \(\mathcal{C}[T^{-1}]^r\). It has been corrected to \(\mathcal{C}[S^{-1}]^r\), since \(T\subset\operatorname{Mor}(\mathcal{I})\) whereas \(S\subset\operatorname{Mor}(\mathcal{C})\) (O014-C019).↩︎

  2. The limit in the first formula is indexed by \(\operatorname{Ob}(S_{/X}^{\operatorname{op}})\) because we use \(\varprojlim_i\beta(i)\) to denote the limit of a functor \(\beta:I^{\operatorname{op}}\to\mathcal{C}\).↩︎

Adjoint Functor Theorems

Functors often occur in adjoint pairs. Consider categories \(\mathcal{C}\) and \(\mathcal{D}\) and a pair of functors \[\text{Diagram chapter1-unit-019-d001}\] such that \((F,G)\) is an adjoint pair. Then \(F\) preserves \(\varinjlim\) and \(G\) preserves \(\varprojlim\), whenever the limits in question exist. Conversely, one naturally asks: if \(F:\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{D}\) preserves colimits, what ensures that it has a right adjoint? If \(G:\mathcal{D}\to\mathcal{C}\) preserves limits, what ensures that it has a left adjoint? In many cases the adjoint can be written down explicitly, but sometimes an abstract existence result is needed. Such results are collectively called adjoint functor theorems. Their hypotheses fall roughly into two classes. First, to use preservation of colimits (or limits), one assumes that \(\mathcal{C}\) (or \(\mathcal{D}\)) is cocomplete (or complete). Second, one needs conditions closely related to set size. Our first task is to reformulate the existence of an adjoint appropriately. By duality, we state only the case of a left adjoint. For a functor \(G:\mathcal{D}\to\mathcal{C}\) and \(c\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{C})\), Definition reference gives a category \((c/G)\) whose objects are data \((d,c\xrightarrow{f}Gd)\).

Lemma. A functor \(G:\mathcal{D}\to\mathcal{C}\) has a left adjoint if and only if \((c/G)\) has an initial object for every \(c\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{C})\).

Proof. Fix \(c\). Specifying a morphism \((d_0,c\xrightarrow{\beta_0}Gd_0)\to(d,c\xrightarrow{\beta}Gd)\) in \((c/G)\) amounts to specifying \(\alpha:d_0\to d\) such that \[\text{Diagram chapter1-unit-019-d002}\] commutes. Thus \((d_0,\beta_0)\) is initial in \((c/G)\) if and only if \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:adjoint-vs-comma-aux}{} \hypertarget{o014.li2.chapter1.adjoint-functor-theorem.g003}{} \text{Diagram chapter1-unit-019-d003} \end{equation}\] is a bijection for every \(d\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{D})\). This is the basis of the argument.

Suppose that \(G\) has a left adjoint \(F\), and let \(c\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{C})\). We claim that \(Fc\), together with the unit \(\eta_c:c\to G(Fc)\), is initial in \((c/G)\). For any \((d,c\xrightarrow{\beta}Gd)\), the map in equation, \(\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{D}}(Fc,d)\to\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}}(c,Gd)\), sends \(\alpha\) to \((G\alpha)\eta_c\). This is exactly the bijection on \(\operatorname{Hom}\) sets supplied by the adjunction, so \((Fc,\eta_c)\) is initial.

Conversely, suppose that \((c/G)\) has an initial object for every \(c\), and write it as \((Fc,\eta_c:c\to G(Fc))\). Since initial objects are unique up to unique isomorphism, these objects form a functor \(F:\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{D}\), and \((\eta_c)_{c\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{C})}\) gives \(\eta:\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{\mathcal{C}}\to GF\). For every \((c,d)\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{C})\times\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{D})\), define the bijection from equation: \[\begin{align*} \varphi_{c, d}: \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{D}}(Fc, d) & \to \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}}(c, Gd) \\ \alpha & \mapsto (G\alpha) \eta_c. \end{align*}\] These bijections are plainly functorial in \(c\) and \(d\). Hence \((F,G,\varphi)\) is an adjoint pair with unit \(\eta\).

Definition. Let \(\mathcal{E}\) be a category. A nonempty small subset \(\Gamma\) of \(\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{E})\) is called a weakly initial family if, for every \(e'\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{E})\), there is an \(e\in\Gamma\) such that \(\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{E}}(e,e')\) is nonempty.1 If \(e\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{E})\) and \(\{e\}\) is weakly initial, then \(e\) itself is called a weakly initial object.

Every initial object is weakly initial. Weakly terminal families and weakly terminal objects are defined similarly.

Lemma. If \(\Gamma\) is a weakly initial family in \(\mathcal{E}\) and \(e:=\prod_{x\in\Gamma}x\) exists, then \(e\) is weakly initial.

Proof. For every \(e'\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{E})\), there are \(y\in\Gamma\) and a morphism \(y\to e'\). Take the composite \(e\xrightarrow{\text{projection}}y\to e'\).

Return to adjoint functor theorems. To apply Lemma reference, we must study the projection functor \(\Pi_{c/}:(c/G)\to\mathcal{D}\) from Definition reference.

Proposition. Let \(\mathcal{D}\) be complete, let \(G:\mathcal{D}\to\mathcal{C}\) preserve all small limits, and fix \(c\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{C})\).

  1. The functor \(\Pi_{c/}\) is conservative (Definition reference) and creates all small limits (Definition reference).

  2. The category \((c/G)\) is complete.

  3. The functor \(\Pi_{c/}\) sends monomorphisms to monomorphisms.

Proof. For (i), conservativity is clear. The key point is that, given \(\beta:J\to(c/G)\) sending \(j\in\operatorname{Ob}(J)\) to \((d_j,c\xrightarrow{f_j}Gd_j)\), one can lift \(\varprojlim_jd_j\) and its projection morphisms to \((\varprojlim_jd_j,c\xrightarrow{f}G(\varprojlim_jd_j))\) and show that it is \(\varprojlim\beta\). Explicitly, take \(f\) to be the composite in the first row of the commutative diagram \[\text{Diagram chapter1-unit-019-d004} \quad j' \in \operatorname{Ob}(J).\] The remaining checks are routine and are omitted; compare the examples in §reference.

Statement (ii) follows from the completeness of \(\mathcal{D}\) and (i).

For (iii), first observe that for every morphism \(f:a\to b\) in any category, a direct manipulation of the definitions gives \[f \;\text{is monic} \iff \text{Diagram chapter1-unit-019-d005} \;\text{is a pullback diagram}.\]

Now consider a monomorphism in \((c/G)\) from \((d',c\to Gd')\) to \((d,c\to Gd)\), determined by \(\iota:d'\to d\) in \(\mathcal{D}\). By (i), \[(d', c \to Gd') \ensuremath{\underset{(d, c \to Gd)}{\times}} (d', c \to Gd') = \left( d' \ensuremath{\underset{d}{\times}} d' , \; c \to G\left( d' \ensuremath{\underset{d}{\times}} d' \right) \right) .\] The left-hand side identifies with \((d',c\to Gd')\), with both projections corresponding to \(\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{d'}\). Thus \(d'\ensuremath{\underset{d}{\times}}d'\) identifies with \(d'\) in the same way. In other words, \(\iota\) is monic.

Lemma. If a complete category \(\mathcal{E}\) has a weakly initial family \(\Gamma\), then \(\mathcal{E}\) has an initial object.

Proof. Completeness and Lemma reference ensure that \(\mathcal{E}\) has a weakly initial object \(e\). Let \(I\) be the full subcategory of \(\mathcal{E}\) with \(\operatorname{Ob}(I)=\{e\}\); it is small. Completeness gives a limit \(x\) of the inclusion \(I\to\mathcal{E}\), with canonical morphism \(i:x\to e\). Its universal property says \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:jointly-weak-initial-obj-aux}{} \hypertarget{o014.li2.chapter1.adjoint-functor-theorem.g006}{} \text{Diagram chapter1-unit-019-d006} \end{equation}\] for arbitrary \(t\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{E})\). This immediately shows that \(i\) is monic.

We show that \(x\) is initial. Given \(y\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{E})\), choose any morphism \(e\to y\) and call the composite \(x\xrightarrow{i}e\to y\) by \(f\). For any \(g:x\to y\), consider the equalizer \(j:\operatorname{ker}(f,g)\hookrightarrow x\). There is a morphism \(k:e\to\operatorname{ker}(f,g)\), hence \(ijk:e\to e\). Taking \(\psi=\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_x\) in equation gives \((ijk)i=(\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_e)i=i\). Cancelling the monomorphism \(i\) on the left gives \(jki=\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_x\), and consequently \(f=fjki=gjki=g\). This proves the claim.

The following result is due to P. Freyd and is also known as the General Adjoint Functor Theorem.

Theorem (P. Freyd’s Adjoint Functor Theorem). Let \(\mathcal{C}\) and \(\mathcal{D}\) be categories.

  1. Let \(\mathcal{D}\) be complete and let \(G:\mathcal{D}\to\mathcal{C}\) preserve all small limits. Then \(G\) has a left adjoint if and only if the following solution set condition holds: for every \(c\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{C})\), there is a family of morphisms \((f_i:c\to Gd_i)_{i\in I}\), indexed by a small set \(I\), such that for every \(f:c\to Gd\) there are \(i\in I\) and \(\alpha:d_i\to d\) for which \(f\) factors as \(c\xrightarrow{f_i}Gd_i\xrightarrow{G\alpha}Gd\).

  2. Let \(\mathcal{C}\) be cocomplete and let \(F:\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{D}\) preserve all small colimits. Then \(F\) has a right adjoint if and only if the following cosolution set condition holds: for every \(d\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{D})\), there is a family of morphisms \((g_i:Fc_i\to d)_{i\in I}\), indexed by a small set \(I\), such that for every \(g:Fc\to d\) there are \(i\in I\) and \(\beta:c\to c_i\) for which \(g\) factors as \(Fc\xrightarrow{F\beta}Fc_i\xrightarrow{g_i}d\).

Proof. We prove only (i). Fix \(c\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{C})\). By Lemma reference, \(G\) has a left adjoint if and only if \((c/G)\) has an initial object. The solution set condition says exactly that \((c/G)\) has the weakly initial family \(\{(d_i,c\to Gd_i):i\in I\}\), where \(I\) is small. Since every initial object is weakly initial, the “only if” direction is clear. In the other direction, Lemma reference reduces the problem to the completeness of \((c/G)\), which is precisely Proposition reference(ii).

Example. Consider the category of groups \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Grp}}\) and the forgetful functor \(U:\ensuremath{\mathsf{Grp}}\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{Set}}\). The category \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Grp}}\) is complete and \(U\) preserves all small limits. To deduce from Theorem reference that \(U\) has the left adjoint \(\mathrm{F}:\ensuremath{\mathsf{Set}}\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{Grp}}\), which constructs the free group on a set, the key is to verify the solution set condition for every small set \(c\).

Take any \(d\in\operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Grp}})\) and map \(f:c\to Ud\). Factor \(f\) as \(c\to Us\xrightarrow{U\iota}Ud\), where \(s\) is the subgroup of \(d\) generated by \(f(c)\) and \(\iota:s\to d\) is the inclusion. Presenting \(s\) by the generating set \(f(c)\) and relations shows that the isomorphism classes of all such data \((s,c\to Us)\) form a small set \(I\). This establishes the solution set condition.

The same procedure works for other algebraic structures, such as \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ab}}\) and \(R\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\), again giving left adjoints to the forgetful functors; see the latter part of [ML98]. Likewise, for any commutative ring \(\Bbbk\), taking the multiplicative monoid of a \(\Bbbk\)-algebra gives a forgetful functor \(U:\Bbbk\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Alg}}\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{Mon}}\). The same technique shows that \(U\) has a left adjoint sending a monoid \(M\) to \(\Bbbk[M]\); see [Li1].

The approach through the Adjoint Functor Theorem reference not only applies uniformly to many algebraic structures; in the free-group case it is also shorter than the classical construction in [Li1].

The Special Adjoint Functor Theorem reference, to be introduced shortly, replaces the solution set condition by conditions on generators and subobjects. We pause to define generators and cogenerators in a category; these notions will also be used in the later section on Grothendieck categories, among other places.

Definition. Let \(\mathcal{E}\) be a category and let \(\Sigma\) be a nonempty small subset of \(\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{E})\).

  • The set \(\Sigma\) is called a generating family if the following holds: given any pair \(f,g:x\to y\) in \(\mathcal{E}\), if \(f\epsilon=g\epsilon\) for every \(s\in\Sigma\) and every \(\epsilon:s\to x\), then \(f=g\). If \(\{s\}\) is a generating family for \(\mathcal{E}\), then \(s\) is called a generator of \(\mathcal{E}\).

  • The set \(\Sigma\) is called a cogenerating family if the following holds: given any pair \(f,g:x\to y\) in \(\mathcal{E}\), if \(\delta f=\delta g\) for every \(s\in\Sigma\) and every \(\delta:y\to s\), then \(f=g\). If \(\{s\}\) is a cogenerating family for \(\mathcal{E}\), then \(s\) is called a cogenerator of \(\mathcal{E}\).

The two notions are plainly dual.

Lemma. Let \(\Sigma\) be a small subset of \(\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{C})\). If every object of \(\mathcal{C}\) can be expressed as a colimit (or limit) of elements of \(\Sigma\), then \(\Sigma\) is a generating (or cogenerating) family.

Proof. For colimits, a morphism \(\varinjlim\alpha=:x\to y\) is uniquely determined by its composites with all \(\alpha(i)\xrightarrow{\iota_i}\varinjlim\alpha\).

Example. Here are some basic examples of generators and cogenerators.

  • In \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Set}}\), the singleton \(\{\mathrm{pt}\}\) is a generator: for maps \(f,g:X\to Y\), specifying \(\epsilon:\{\mathrm{pt}\}\to X\) amounts to specifying \(x\in X\), so \(f\epsilon=g\epsilon\) for every \(\epsilon\) is equivalent to pointwise equality of \(f\) and \(g\). The set \(\{0,1\}\) is a cogenerator, because if \(f(x)\ne g(x)\) for some \(x\in X\), one can choose \(\delta:Y\to\{0,1\}\) such that \(\delta(f(x))\ne\delta(g(x))\).

  • Let \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{CHaus}}\) be the category of compact Hausdorff spaces and continuous maps. The singleton \(\{\mathrm{pt}\}\) is again a generator, while \([0,1]\) is a cogenerator: for every compact Hausdorff space \(Y\) and distinct \(a,b\in Y\), Urysohn’s lemma [Xiong] gives a continuous map \(\delta:Y\to[0,1]\) with \(\delta(a)=0\) and \(\delta(b)=1\).

  • Let \(R\) be a ring. In \(R\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\), the module \(R\) is a generator because specifying an \(R\)-module homomorphism \(R\to M\) amounts to specifying an element of \(M\). Taking coproducts shows that every nonzero free \(R\)-module is also a generator.

  • Consider the Yoneda embedding \(h_{\mathcal{E}}:\mathcal{E}\to\mathcal{E}^\wedge\) of a small category \(\mathcal{E}\). Then \(h_{\mathcal{E}}(\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{E}))\) is a generating family for \(\mathcal{E}^\wedge\). This follows immediately from the density theorem for the Yoneda embedding in Appendix § A.1 and Lemma reference.

The Special Adjoint Functor Theorem involves one more set-theoretic notion. Recall the posets \((\mathrm{Sub}_e,\subset)\) and \((\mathrm{Quot}_e,\twoheadleftarrow)\) introduced in Definition reference, where \(e\) is an object of a category \(\mathcal{E}\).

Definition. A category \(\mathcal{E}\) is called well-powered (or well-copowered) if \(\mathrm{Sub}_e\) (or \(\mathrm{Quot}_e\)) is a small set for every \(e\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{E})\).

In this section, well-poweredness will be paired with completeness. Choose a representative \(s\hookrightarrow e\) of every element of \(\mathrm{Sub}_e\). Thus for any subset \(S\subset\mathrm{Sub}_e\) it makes sense, independently of the representatives chosen, to ask whether the fiber product \(\prod_{s\in S}(s\hookrightarrow e)\) exists. Dually, for a subset \(S\subset\mathrm{Quot}_e\), one may ask whether the fiber coproduct \(\coprod_{s\in S}(e\twoheadrightarrow s)\) exists.

  • If \(\mathcal{E}\) is complete, then well-poweredness implies that for every \(e\), all subsets \(S\subset\mathrm{Sub}_e\) have fiber products.

  • If \(\mathcal{E}\) is cocomplete, then well-copoweredness implies that for every \(e\), all subsets \(S\subset\mathrm{Quot}_e\) have fiber coproducts.

Lemma. Let \(\mathcal{E}\) be complete and well-powered. If there is a cogenerating family \(\Sigma\subset\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{E})\), then \(\mathcal{E}\) has an initial object.

Proof. Take \(e:=\prod_{s\in\Sigma}s\), and let \(x\) be the fiber product of all elements of \(\mathrm{Sub}_e\); only here is well-poweredness used. We show that \(x\) is initial in \(\mathcal{E}\).

By construction, \(x\hookrightarrow e\) is the infimum of the poset \((\mathrm{Sub}_e,\subset)\); in particular, \(\mathrm{Sub}_x=\{x\}\). For any object \(y\) and \(f,g\in\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{E}}(x,y)\), the equalizer \(\operatorname{ker}(f,g)\) must therefore be \(x\) itself, so \(f=g\). It remains to show that \(\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{E}}(x,y)\) is nonempty for every \(y\).

Form in \(\mathcal{E}\) the product \(\prod_{s\in\Sigma}s^{\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{E}}(y,s)}\). Define \(i:y\to\prod_{s\in\Sigma}s^{\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{E}}(y,s)}\) so that its projection onto the component corresponding to \(s\in\Sigma\) and \(\delta\in\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{E}}(y,s)\) is exactly \(\delta\). Since \(\Sigma\) is cogenerating, \(i\) is easily seen to be monic. For every \(s\in\Sigma\), take the diagonal morphism \(d_s:s\to s^{\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{E}}(y,s)}\), and form the pullback \[\text{Diagram chapter1-unit-019-d007}\] Lemma reference ensures that \(j\) is also monic, giving a subobject of \(e\). Since \(x\) is the infimum of \(\mathrm{Sub}_e\), there is a morphism \(x\hookrightarrow z\). The composite \(x\hookrightarrow z\to y\) is the required morphism.

Theorem (Special Adjoint Functor Theorem). Let \(\mathcal{C}\) and \(\mathcal{D}\) be categories.

  1. A functor \(G:\mathcal{D}\to\mathcal{C}\) has a left adjoint if it satisfies the following conditions.

    • \(\mathcal{D}\) is complete and well-powered, and \(G\) preserves all small limits;

    • there is a cogenerating family \(\Sigma\subset\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{D})\).

  2. A functor \(F:\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{D}\) has a right adjoint if it satisfies the following conditions.

    • \(\mathcal{C}\) is cocomplete and well-copowered, and \(F\) preserves all small colimits;

    • there is a generating family \(\Sigma\subset\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{C})\).

Proof. By duality, it suffices to prove (i). Lemma reference again reduces the problem to showing that \((c/G)\) has an initial object for \(c\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{C})\); the strategy is to apply Lemma reference.

Proposition reference(ii) shows that \((c/G)\) is complete. Moreover, Definition reference and the definition of \((c/G)\) show at once that all data \((d,c\to Gd)\) with \(d\in\Sigma\) form a cogenerating family for \((c/G)\). Since \(\Sigma\) is small, this is a small set.

Let \(e=(d,c\to Gd)\in\operatorname{Ob}((c/G))\). Subobjects are isomorphism classes of monomorphisms. By Proposition reference, the projection \(\Pi_{c/}:(c/G)\to\mathcal{D}\) is conservative and preserves monomorphisms, so it induces an order-preserving embedding \(\mathrm{Sub}_e\hookrightarrow\mathrm{Sub}_d\). Thus \((c/G)\) is well-powered.

Corollary. If a complete well-powered category \(\mathcal{D}\) has a cogenerating family \(\Sigma\), then \(\mathcal{D}\) is cocomplete.

Dually, if a cocomplete well-copowered category \(\mathcal{C}\) has a generating family \(\Sigma\), then \(\mathcal{C}\) is complete.

Proof. It suffices to prove the assertion for \(\mathcal{D}\). Let \(I\) be a small category. By Example reference, it is enough to show that \((\alpha/\Delta)\) has an initial object for every \(\alpha:I\to\mathcal{D}\). By Lemma reference, this is equivalent to saying that the diagonal functor \(\Delta\) has a left adjoint. Clearly \(\Delta\) preserves all small limits and colimits, so Theorem reference applies.

Example. Let \(\iota:\ensuremath{\mathsf{CHaus}}\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{Top}}\) be the inclusion of compact Hausdorff spaces into topological spaces. Example reference showed that \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{CHaus}}\) has the cogenerator \([0,1]\). By the Tychonoff theorem [Xiong], \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{CHaus}}\) is readily seen to be complete, and \(\iota\) preserves all small limits; details are left to the reader. Furthermore, the power set of a small set is small, so \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{CHaus}}\) is well-powered. Theorem reference(i) therefore gives a left adjoint \(C:\ensuremath{\mathsf{Top}}\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{CHaus}}\) to \(\iota\). In point-set topology, \(C(X)\) is called the Stone–Čech compactification of \(X\); the unit gives a canonical morphism \(\eta_X:X\to\iota C(X)\). The constructions in Lemma reference and Theorem reference agree with the classical construction of the Stone–Čech compactification.

Adjoint functor theorems provide sufficient conditions for representability. For representable functors, see [Li1] or the definition of a representable functor in Appendix § A.1. The key observation is this: if \(G:\mathcal{D}\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{Set}}\) has a left adjoint \(F\), then \(G\) is representable. Indeed, consider the singleton \(\{\mathrm{pt}\}\) and put \(r_G:=F(\{\mathrm{pt}\})\). The canonical bijections \[\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{D}}\left( r_G, d \right) \simeq \operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{Set}}}\left( \{\mathrm{pt}\}, Gd \right) \simeq Gd , \quad d \in \operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{D})\] imply \(G\simeq\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{D}}(r_G,\cdot)\).

Corollary. If a complete well-powered category \(\mathcal{D}\) has a cogenerating family \(\Sigma\), then a functor \(G:\mathcal{D}\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{Set}}\) is representable if and only if it preserves all small limits.

Proof. The “only if” direction is a general property of representable functors. For the converse, Theorem reference ensures that \(G\) has a left adjoint \(F:\ensuremath{\mathsf{Set}}\to\mathcal{D}\); now apply the observation above.

Exercises

Consider the category of groups \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Grp}}\). Prove that a group homomorphism \(\varphi:H\to G\) is a monomorphism (or epimorphism) in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Grp}}\) if and only if its underlying map is injective (or surjective). Some references, including [Li1], do not adequately explain this fact. Hint. It suffices to prove the “only if” direction. For monomorphisms, consider homomorphisms from \(\operatorname{ker}\varphi\) to \(H\). For epimorphisms, one must show that if \(\varphi(H)\ne G\), then there are distinct group homomorphisms \(f,g:G\rightrightarrows K\) whose restrictions to \(\varphi(H)\) agree. One approach is to take \(K\) to be the amalgamated free product defined by two copies of the embedding \(\varphi(H)\hookrightarrow G\) in [Li1], and to take \(f\) and \(g\) as the embeddings of \(G\) into the two copies. Uniqueness of reduced expressions [Li1] implies \(f\ne g\).

Show that in the category \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Top}}\), the image of \(f:X\to Y\) is \(f(X)\) with the subspace topology from \(Y\), while its coimage is \(f(X)\) with the quotient topology from \(X\). Give the corresponding topological interpretations of strict monomorphisms and strict epimorphisms.

Let \(\mathcal{C}\) have finite limits and finite colimits. Prove that the following statements about a morphism \(f:X\to Y\) are equivalent.

  1. The morphism \(f\) is a strict epimorphism.

  2. The canonical morphism \(\operatorname{coim}(f)\to Y\) is an isomorphism.

  3. \(X\ensuremath{\underset{Y}{\times}}X\rightrightarrows X\xrightarrow{f}Y\) is a coequalizer diagram.

  4. The morphism \(f:X\to Y\) is the coequalizer of some pair \(a,b:W\rightrightarrows X\).

Hint. Recall that being epic is equivalent to \(\operatorname{im}(f)\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}Y\) (Lemma reference), and use Proposition reference. It is easy to prove (i) \(\iff\) (ii) \(\iff\) (iii) \(\implies\) (iv). For (iv) \(\implies\) (ii), consider the solid part of the commutative diagram \[\text{Diagram chapter1-unit-019-diagram-008}\] The universal property of the coequalizer gives the dashed arrow and shows that it and \(\operatorname{coim}(f)\to Y\) are inverse to each other.

Let \(\mathcal{C}\) have finite limits and finite colimits. Prove that if a morphism \(f\) has a right inverse (or left inverse), then \(f\) is a strict epimorphism (or strict monomorphism). Hint. If \(fg=\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_Y\), then \(f\) is the coequalizer of \(gf\) and \(\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_X\).

Prove that an additive-category structure on any category, if it exists, is unique. Hint. Apply Proposition reference.

Compare Example reference. Let \(U\) be the forgetful functor from compact Hausdorff spaces \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{CHaus}}\) to sets \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Set}}\). Prove that \(U\) creates all small limits. Show that it does not create all small colimits.

Let \(\mathcal{I}\) be the category of all finite sets and surjective maps. Prove that \(\mathcal{I}^{\operatorname{op}}\) is not filtered in the sense of §reference.

In Definition reference, prove that every morphism \(F\to F'\) induces canonical morphisms \(\operatorname{Lan}_KF\to\operatorname{Lan}_KF'\) and \(\operatorname{Ran}_KF\to\operatorname{Ran}_KF'\), provided these Kan extensions exist. Characterize the induced morphisms.

Let \(K\) and \(F\) be as in §reference. Prove that if \(M:\mathcal{E}\to\mathcal{F}\) has a left adjoint (or right adjoint), then \(M\) preserves \(\operatorname{Ran}_KF\) (or \(\operatorname{Lan}_KF\)). Hint. By duality, suppose that \(M\) has a right adjoint \(N\), with unit \(\eta':\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}\to NM\) and counit \(\varepsilon':MN\to\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}\). For any functor \(L:\mathcal{D}\to\mathcal{F}\), there are canonical bijections \[\begin{multline*} \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{F}^{\mathcal{D}}} \left( M (\operatorname{Lan}_K F) , L \right) \simeq \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{E}^{\mathcal{D}}} \left( \operatorname{Lan}_K F, N L \right) \\ \stackrel{\text{\href{#eqn:Kan-univ}{equation}}}{\simeq} \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{E}^{\mathcal{C}}} \left( F, NLK \right) \simeq \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{F}^{\mathcal{C}}} \left( MF, LK \right). \end{multline*}\]

Using the general properties of \(\eta'\) and \(\varepsilon'\), verify that when \(L=M(\operatorname{Lan}_KF)\) this bijection sends \(\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}\) to \(M\eta\), where \(\eta\) is the morphism belonging to \(\operatorname{Lan}_KF\).

For general \(L\), use the familiar technique from the proof of the Yoneda lemma to verify that an arbitrary morphism \[\varphi:M(\operatorname{Lan}_KF)\to L\] corresponds to the composite \[\begin{aligned} (\varphi K)(M\eta):\quad MF &\xrightarrow{M\eta} M(\operatorname{Lan}_K F)K, \\ M(\operatorname{Lan}_K F)K &\xrightarrow{\varphi K} LK . \end{aligned}\]

Consider the diagram of functors \[\text{Diagram chapter1-unit-019-d008}\] where \(EF\) is left adjoint to \(G\), with counit \(\varepsilon:EFG\to\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{\mathcal{D}'}\). Prove that if, for every category \(\mathcal{X}\), the functor \(F^*:\mathcal{X}^{\mathcal{D}}\to\mathcal{X}^{\mathcal{C}}\) is fully faithful, then \(E\) can also be realized as a left adjoint to \(FG\), with the same counit \(\varepsilon\). Hint. The following argument is from [GZ67]. Let \(\eta:\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{\mathcal{C}}\to GEF\) be the unit of \((EF,G)\). Taking \(\mathcal{X}=\mathcal{D}\) gives \(\eta':\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{\mathcal{D}}\to FGE\) such that \(\eta'F=F\eta\). Check the triangle identities for \((E,FG)\) with \(\eta'\) and \(\varepsilon\). First, \((FG\varepsilon)(\eta'FG)=(FG\varepsilon)(F\eta G)=\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{FG}\). On the other hand, taking \(\mathcal{X}=\mathcal{D}'\) shows that \((\varepsilon E)(E\eta')=\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_E\) is equivalent to \((\varepsilon EF)(E\eta'F)=\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{EF}\); but \((\varepsilon EF)(E\eta'F)=(\varepsilon EF)(EF\eta)=\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{EF}\).

Consider an adjoint pair \(\text{Diagram chapter1-unit-019-d009}\), and put \[S := \left\{ s \in \operatorname{Mor}(\mathcal{C}): Fs \;\text{is invertible} \right\};\] this factors \(F\) uniquely as \(\mathcal{C}\xrightarrow{Q}\mathcal{C}[S^{-1}]\xrightarrow{H}\mathcal{D}\). Prove that the following statements are equivalent.

  1. The functor \(G\) is fully faithful.

  2. The counit \(\varepsilon:FG\to\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{\mathcal{D}}\) is an isomorphism.

  3. The functor \(H\) is an equivalence of categories, with \(QG\) as a quasi-inverse.

  4. For every category \(\mathcal{X}\), the functor \(F^*:\mathcal{X}^{\mathcal{D}}\to\mathcal{X}^{\mathcal{C}}\) is fully faithful.

Also state the dual version of this result. Hint. The following argument is from [GZ67]. First, (i) \(\iff\) (ii) is fairly easy; see the hint in [Li1].

For (ii) \(\implies\) (iii), one must prove \(QGH\simeq\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{\mathcal{C}[S^{-1}]}\). Proposition reference reduces this to \(QGHQ\simeq Q\). Consider the unit \(\eta:\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{\mathcal{C}}\to GF\). Since \((\varepsilon F)(F\eta)=\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_F\), the morphism \(F\eta\) is an isomorphism, hence \(Q\eta:Q\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}QGF=QGHQ\).

For (iii) \(\implies\) (iv), the fact that \(H\) is an equivalence implies that \(H^*\) is fully faithful, while Proposition reference applies to \(Q^*\).

For (iv) \(\implies\) (ii), put \(E=\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{\mathcal{D}}\) in the preceding exercise. Then \(FG\) is a right adjoint to \(\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{\mathcal{D}}\), with counit \(\varepsilon\). Since right adjoints to \(\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{\mathcal{D}}\) are unique up to isomorphism, \(\varepsilon\) is an isomorphism.

Let \(S\) be a left multiplicative system in \(\mathcal{C}\). Prove that every commutative diagram in \(\mathcal{C}[S^{-1}]^l\) of the form \[\text{Diagram chapter1-unit-019-d010}\]

arises from a commutative diagram in \(\mathcal{C}\) of the form

\[\text{Diagram chapter1-unit-019-d011}\] where \(f,g\in\operatorname{Mor}(\mathcal{C})\) are given and, as usual, \(\rightarrowtail\) denotes a morphism in \(S\). State the corresponding version for a right multiplicative system. Hint. Represent \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) by \((U^\dagger;s,a)\) and \((U';t,b)\), respectively. Apply (S3) to obtain \(W,h,r\) and a commutative diagram in \(\mathcal{C}\) \[\text{Diagram chapter1-unit-019-d012}\] This shows that the upper square in the following diagram commutes: \[\text{Diagram chapter1-unit-019-d013}\] For the lower square, first show that it commutes after applying \(Q^l\); then use Corollary reference to choose \(U\rightarrowtail W\) and adjust it to the required commutative diagram.

Verify the details of central localization in Example reference. Prove that the category \(\mathcal{C}[S^{-1}]\) defined there and the localization supplied by Theorem reference are equivalent as \(Z(\mathcal{C})[S^{-1}]\)-linear categories.

Complete the details in the proof of Proposition reference(i).

Use the Adjoint Functor Theorem reference to construct the free product \(G\star H\) of any two groups \(G\) and \(H\); see [Li1].

Let \(\mathrm{F}(X)\) be the free group on a set \(X\). Prove that the canonical map \(\iota:X\to U(\mathrm{F}(X))\) is injective, where \(U\) is the forgetful functor from groups to sets. Hint. For distinct \(x,y\in X\), there is a group \(H\) and a map of sets \(f:X\to U(H)\) such that \(f(x)\ne f(y)\).

(P. Freyd) Let \(\mathcal{D}\) be complete and let \(G:\mathcal{D}\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{Set}}\) preserve all small limits and satisfy the following solution set condition: there is a small subset \(\Gamma\subset\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{D})\) such that for every \(d\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{D})\) and \(p\in Gd\), there are \(x\in\Gamma\), \(q\in Gx\), and \(f:x\to d\) with \((Gf)(q)=p\). Prove that \(G\) is representable. Hint. Write an object of \(\left(\{\mathrm{pt}\}/G\right)\) as \((d,p)\), where \(d\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{D})\) and \(p\in Gd\). The condition says exactly that \(\Gamma^\natural:=\{(x,q):x\in\Gamma,\;q\in Gx\}\) is a weakly initial family for \(\left(\{\mathrm{pt}\}/G\right)\). Show that this category has an initial object \((r_G,u_G)\). Following the argument for equation, show that for every \(d\) there is a bijection \[\text{Diagram chapter1-unit-019-d014}\]

  1. Translator’s note: the source has the subscript \(\mathcal{C}\); it has been corrected to \(\mathcal{E}\), the category introduced in this definition (O014-C020).↩︎

Abelian Categories

An abelian category is an additive category with kernels and cokernels in which every morphism is strict. Abelian categories generalize the category \(R\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\) of left modules or \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}\text{-}}R\) of right modules over a ring \(R\), and support the study of such notions as injective and projective objects, complexes, homology and cohomology, and exact sequences. Module categories are the prototype of abelian categories, but do not exhaust their substance. There are two reasons for this.

  1. In a general abelian category, objects have no elements and morphisms are not maps. Diagram-chasing methods from module categories are therefore no longer available; the most basic exact sequences must instead be derived by operations on objects and functors. Prominent examples are the snake lemma and the five lemma discussed in §reference, whose proofs use a substitute for diagram chasing (Lemma reference). Even so, the arguments are considerably more involved than their module-category counterparts.

  2. Even when one starts with a module category or one of its abelian subcategories, abstract abelian categories arise when studying functor categories, localizations, or Serre quotients. In geometry and topology, sheaf theory naturally leads to such constructions.

The Freyd–Mitchell embedding theorem reference states that every small abelian category admits a fully faithful embedding into some \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}\text{-}}R\), and that the embedding functor preserves exact sequences. Once this result is accepted, many assertions about exact sequences reduce readily to the case of \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}\text{-}}R\). This reduction keeps diagram chasing available, but its chief benefit may be psychological reassurance: on the one hand it sidesteps the essence of abelian categories, and on the other hand any proof of the embedding theorem must still establish several core facts about abelian categories from scratch. This chapter does not depend on the embedding theorem, nor logically on module theory, but readers are expected to have a basic knowledge of homological algebra in module categories. Diagram-chasing skills remain useful and may even be indispensable in the natural order of study; readers are encouraged to consult [Li1] or the relevant parts of another textbook. Appendix §reference derives the embedding theorem as an application of the Ind construction. A cocomplete abelian category with a generator in which filtered small colimits are exact is called a Grothendieck category. Such categories are the subject of the final section, §reference; these conditions are directly related to assumptions on set size. Grothendieck categories occur frequently in geometry and enjoy better properties, such as completeness (Corollary reference) and the existence of canonical injective resolutions (Theorem reference). They are a closer analogue of module categories than general abelian categories; the precise meaning of this statement is explained by the Gabriel–Popescu theorem reference in the appendix. The basic isomorphism theorems of module theory remain valid for general abelian categories. The same is true of such fundamental notions as subobjects, quotient objects, direct-sum decompositions, indecomposable objects, simple objects, and composition series, all central concerns of algebra. They will be treated in §§reference— reference. For example, the Krull–Remak–Schmidt theorem on direct-sum decompositions has an abstract generalization (Theorem reference). The language of lattice theory is useful here; see §reference. It should be stressed that statements involving infinite direct sums often hold only in Grothendieck categories. Section reference begins with the definition and characterization of abelian subcategories, and then introduces quotients of an abelian category by a certain kind of abelian subcategory, called a Serre subcategory; the result is a Serre quotient. These quotients are characterized by a universal property and can be constructed by the localization introduced in §reference. The section also introduces the group \(\mathrm{K}_0\) of an abelian category and its basic properties, including the Euler–Poincaré principle (Theorem reference) and the exact sequence for \(\mathrm{K}_0\) of a Serre quotient (Proposition reference). These techniques are common in applications. The construction of \(\mathrm{K}_0\) applies to a broader class of structures than abelian categories, called exact categories; see [Bu10] for the theory. Moreover, \(\mathrm{K}_0\) is only the beginning of a sequence of abelian groups \(\mathrm{K}_n\) for \(n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}_{\geq0}\). A satisfactory interpretation of the higher K-groups requires homotopy-theoretic ideas, especially the notion of a “spectrum”, and lies beyond the scope of this book.

Reading Guide. As noted above, readers should have some familiarity with concrete operations in module categories. For the basic theory of complexes and their cohomology, the material in §§reference—reference is essential. Apart from the treatment of abelian subcategories, the material in §reference is used less often later, but it remains standard knowledge and is related to several definitions in the discussion of derived categories. Section reference on Grothendieck categories is supplementary; it requires relatively involved arguments and material from the appendices, and may be skipped on a first reading.

A complex written as data \((X^n,d^n)_n\), where \(d^n:X^n\to X^{n+1}\), is also called a cochain complex. If instead one uses subscripts, writing \((X_n,d_n)_n\) with \(d_n:X_n\to X_{n-1}\), it is called a chain complex. Except in Chapter 8, this book primarily uses cochain notation.

Definition of an Abelian Category

Section reference introduced \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ab}}\)-categories and additive categories. The abelian categories studied in this chapter form a special class of additive categories.

Definition (Abelian category). Let \(\mathcal{A}\) be an additive category. If every morphism in \(\mathcal{A}\) has a kernel and a cokernel, and every morphism is strict (Definition reference), then \(\mathcal{A}\) is called an abelian category.

If \(\mathcal{A}\) is also a \(\Bbbk\)-linear category (Definition reference), it is called a \(\Bbbk\)-linear abelian category.

Remark. An abelian category has all finite limits and colimits. Indeed, finite products and coproducts exist (both are biproducts), as do equalizers and coequalizers (Remark reference); these suffice to construct all finite limits and colimits. See [Li1].

By Example reference, \(R\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\) is an abelian category for every ring \(R\). Replacing \(R\) by \(R^{\text{op}}\) shows the same for the category \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}\text{-}}R\) of right modules; the special case \(R=\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\) shows that \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ab}}\) is abelian. By contrast, the category \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ban}}_{\ensuremath{\mathbb{C}}}\) from the same example is not abelian, since it has nonstrict morphisms.

Proposition. If an additive category \(\mathcal{A}\) is abelian, then so is \(\mathcal{A}^{\operatorname{op}}\).

Proof. Kernels and cokernels are dual, while Remark reference shows that the morphism \(\operatorname{coim}(f)\to\operatorname{im}(f)\) in \(\mathcal{A}\) is exactly the morphism \(\operatorname{coim}(f^{\operatorname{op}})\to\operatorname{im}(f^{\operatorname{op}})\) in \(\mathcal{A}^{\operatorname{op}}\).

One abstract way to construct new abelian categories from existing ones is to form functor categories. First note that if \(\mathcal{A}\) is an \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ab}}\)-category, then for every category \(I\)1, the functor category \(\mathcal{A}^I\) is naturally an \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ab}}\)-category: for functors \(F,G:I\rightrightarrows\mathcal{A}\), addition in \(\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{A}^I}(F,G)\) is defined objectwise by \((\varphi_i)_i+(\psi_i)_i:=(\varphi_i+\psi_i)_i\).

Proposition. If \(\mathcal{A}\) is an abelian category, then \(\mathcal{A}^I\) is an abelian category for every category \(I\).
