Proof. By Proposition reference, finite products and coproducts, and kernels and cokernels, are constructed objectwise in \(\mathcal{A}^I\). The image and coimage of a morphism, and hence the canonical morphism \(\operatorname{coim}\to\operatorname{im}\), are likewise constructed objectwise. Thus every abelian category axiom for \(\mathcal{A}^I\) reduces to the corresponding axiom for \(\mathcal{A}\).

Every morphism \(f:X\to Y\) in an abelian category has a unique epi–mono factorization (Proposition reference), concretely \(X\twoheadrightarrow(\operatorname{coim}(f)\simeq\operatorname{im}(f))\hookrightarrow Y\). Lemma reference(iii) therefore gives immediately \[\operatorname{ker}(f) = \operatorname{ker}[X \to \operatorname{im}(f)], \quad \operatorname{coker}(f) = \operatorname{coker}[\operatorname{im}(f) \to Y].\]

Remark. For morphisms \(X\xrightarrow{f}Z\xleftarrow{g}Y\) in an abelian category, the construction of the fiber product (see Remark reference) shows that \(X\ensuremath{\underset{Z}{\times}}Y\) is the equalizer of \(\text{Diagram chapter2-unit-021-diagram-001}\), that is, \(\operatorname{ker}[X\oplus Y\xrightarrow{(f,-g)}Z]\). The morphisms \(X\leftarrow X\ensuremath{\underset{Z}{\times}}Y\rightarrow Y\) carried by the fiber product come from the projections \(X\xleftarrow{p_1}X\oplus Y\xrightarrow{p_2}Y\).

For \(X'\xleftarrow{f'}Z'\xrightarrow{g'}Y'\), the fiber coproduct construction realizes \(X'\ensuremath{\underset{Z'}{\sqcup}}Y'\) as \(\operatorname{coker}[Z'\xrightarrow{(-f',g')}X'\oplus Y']\), and the morphisms \(X'\rightarrow X'\ensuremath{\underset{Z'}{\sqcup}}Y'\leftarrow Y'\) come from \(X'\xrightarrow{\iota_1}X'\oplus Y'\xleftarrow{\iota_2}Y'\). These properties are of course evident for modules.

The following result will be used repeatedly.

Proposition. Suppose that a diagram in an abelian category \(\mathcal{A}\) \[\text{Diagram chapter2-unit-021-d001}\] is a pullback (or pushout), and that \(g\) is epic (or \(f\) is monic). Then the diagram is also a pushout (or pullback), and \(f\) is epic (or \(g\) is monic).

Proof. It suffices to treat the pullback case. We claim that

  • \(X\xrightarrow{(a,f)}X'\oplus Y\) gives \(\operatorname{ker}[X'\oplus Y\xrightarrow{(g,-b)}Y']\);

  • \((g,-b):X'\oplus Y\to Y'\) is epic.

The assertion about the kernel follows from the description of \(X\simeq X'\ensuremath{\underset{Y'}{\times}}Y\) as a kernel in Remark reference. Since \(g=(g,-b)\iota_1\), the fact that \(g\) is epic implies that \((g,-b)\) is epic as well.

Consequently, \(Y'=\operatorname{im}((g,-b))\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\leftarrow}}\operatorname{coker}[X\xrightarrow{(a,f)}X'\oplus Y]\). Viewing this from the other direction and applying the description of a fiber coproduct as a cokernel in Remark reference shows at once that \[\text{Diagram chapter2-unit-021-d002}\] is a pushout. Composing the two columns with the automorphisms \(-\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_X\) and \(-\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_Y\), respectively, recovers the original diagram, which is therefore also a pushout. In the pushout case we already know that \(\operatorname{coker}(f)\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}\operatorname{coker}(g)\) (Proposition reference); hence \(f\) is epic (Lemma reference).

Corollary. A subquotient in an abelian category can equivalently be defined as a quotient object of a subobject or as a subobject of a quotient object.

Proof. Proposition reference shows that Proposition reference applies to every abelian category.

For the category \(R\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\) of left modules over any ring \(R\), all the results above are of course familiar; the same holds for right modules.

  1. If one does not want \(\mathcal{A}^I\) to be large, one should assume that \(I\) is small. This does not affect the substance here.↩︎

A First Look at Complexes

The starting point of this section is a pair of morphisms in an abelian category satisfying \(gf=0\), namely \(X \xrightarrow{f} Y \xrightarrow{g} Z\). The composite \(\operatorname{ker}(g) \hookrightarrow Y \twoheadrightarrow \operatorname{coker}(f)\) gives a morphism \(\operatorname{ker}(g) \to \operatorname{coker}(f)\); what interests us is its epi–mono factorization. There are two mutually dual points of view.

Lemma. Let \(f:X\to Y\) and \(g:Y\to Z\) be morphisms in an abelian category \(\mathcal{A}\) such that \(gf=0\).

  1. There are unique morphisms \(\varphi\) and \(\psi\) that make the following diagrams commute: \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:cplx-transition}{} \hypertarget{o014.li2.chapter2.first-look-at-complexes.g001}{} \text{Diagram chapter2-unit-022-d001} \qquad \hypertarget{o014.li2.chapter2.first-look-at-complexes.g002}{} \text{Diagram chapter2-unit-022-d002} \end{equation}\] Moreover, \(\varphi\) is a monomorphism and \(\psi\) is an epimorphism.

  2. The morphism \(\operatorname{ker}(g)\to\operatorname{coker}(f)\) has the two epi–mono factorizations displayed in the following diagram; they are connected by a unique isomorphism \(\operatorname{coker}(\varphi)\simeq\operatorname{ker}(\psi)\): \[\text{Diagram chapter2-unit-022-d003}\]

Proof. First consider (i). The two diagrams are dual to one another (Remark reference and Proposition reference): the diagram on the right is equivalent to considering in \(\mathcal{A}^{\operatorname{op}}\) the sequence \(Z \xrightarrow{g^{\operatorname{op}}} Y \xrightarrow{f^{\operatorname{op}}} X\). Thus, for equation, it suffices to consider \(\varphi\).

The condition \(gf=0\) says precisely that \(f\) factors through \(\operatorname{ker}(g)\hookrightarrow Y\). Applying Lemma reference on coimages to this factorization gives \(\varphi\). Next, because \(X\to\operatorname{coim}(f)\) is an epimorphism, the factorization of \(f\) as \(X \twoheadrightarrow \operatorname{coim}(f) \xrightarrow{\overline{f}} Y\) is unique. Here \(\overline{f}\) may be taken either as the composite \(\operatorname{coim}(f) \xrightarrow{\varphi} \operatorname{ker}(g) \hookrightarrow Y\) or as the composite \(\operatorname{coim}(f) \ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}\operatorname{im}(f) \hookrightarrow Y\). The latter composite is a monomorphism, and hence so is \(\varphi\).

To obtain (ii), we show that there is a unique monomorphism \(\operatorname{coker}(\varphi)\hookrightarrow\operatorname{coker}(f)\) (or epimorphism \(\operatorname{ker}(g)\twoheadrightarrow\operatorname{ker}(\psi)\)) that makes the following diagram commute: \[\hypertarget{o014.li2.chapter2.first-look-at-complexes.g004}{} \text{Diagram chapter2-unit-022-d004} \quad \hypertarget{o014.li2.chapter2.first-look-at-complexes.g005}{} \text{Diagram chapter2-unit-022-d005}\] Once this is proved, the two epi–mono factorizations in (ii) can be read directly from the outer frames of the diagrams. The isomorphism along the middle path is then uniquely determined by Proposition reference.

It remains to construct the diagrams above. Since the two diagrams are dual, it suffices to discuss the one on the left. Lemma reference (iii) shows that \(\operatorname{coker}(\varphi)\) can also be identified with the cokernel of the composite \(X\to\operatorname{ker}(g)\). The desired morphism therefore comes from the functoriality of cokernels and is characterized by equation. Why is this morphism a monomorphism? Proposition reference expresses the cokernel of a composite morphism as the pushout of the original cokernel; explicitly, the diagram is \[\text{Diagram chapter2-unit-022-d006} \quad \text{(pushout diagram)}\] with all morphisms canonical. Proposition reference then shows that the morphism in the second row is a monomorphism.

In the situation of Lemma reference, write \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:homology-3}{}\begin{aligned} \operatorname{H}\left[ X \xrightarrow{f} Y \xrightarrow{g} Z \right] & := \operatorname{coker}\left[ \operatorname{im}(f) \xrightarrow{\varphi} \operatorname{ker}(g) \right] \\ & \simeq \operatorname{ker}\left[ \operatorname{coker}(f) \xrightarrow{\psi} \operatorname{im}(g) \right] ; \end{aligned} \end{equation}\] this object can also be characterized as the middle term in the epi–mono factorization of \(\operatorname{ker}(g)\to\operatorname{coker}(f)\). As expected, equation is functorial.

Proposition. Given a commutative diagram in an abelian category \[\text{Diagram chapter2-unit-022-d007} \qquad g'f' = 0, \quad gf = 0,\] there is a unique morphism \(\Phi: \operatorname{H}[X \to Y \to Z] \to \operatorname{H}[X' \to Y' \to Z']\) that makes the following diagram commute: \[\text{Diagram chapter2-unit-022-d008}\] The two outer vertical arrows come from the functoriality of kernels and cokernels, while the horizontal arrows are those of Lemma reference.

Proof. As in the argument of Lemma reference, if \(\Phi\) exists then it is unique, and it suffices to check that \(\Phi\) makes the right-hand square commute. Here is the construction. Since \(\operatorname{im}(g)=\operatorname{ker}[Z\to\operatorname{coker}(g)]\) and \(\operatorname{im}(g')=\operatorname{ker}[Z'\to\operatorname{coker}(g')]\), the functoriality of kernels gives a unique morphism \(\operatorname{im}(g)\to\operatorname{im}(g')\) that makes the right half of the following diagram commute: \[\text{Diagram chapter2-unit-022-d009}\] The pattern of Lemma reference shows that the left half also commutes. The morphism \(\operatorname{ker}(\psi)\to\operatorname{ker}(\psi')\) induced by it is the desired morphism.

Proposition. Given morphisms satisfying \(gf=0\) and \(g'f'=0\), there is a canonical isomorphism \[\begin{multline*} \operatorname{H}\left[ X \xrightarrow{f} Y \xrightarrow{g} Z \right] \oplus \operatorname{H}\left[ X' \xrightarrow{f'} Y' \xrightarrow{g'} Z' \right] \\ \simeq \operatorname{H}\left[ X \oplus X' \xrightarrow{f \oplus f'} Y \oplus Y' \xrightarrow{g \oplus g'} Z \oplus Z' \right]. \end{multline*}\]

Proof. Use the morphisms \(\iota\), \(p\), and so forth associated with biproducts, as in equation. By the functoriality in Proposition reference, these morphisms also induce \[\text{Diagram chapter2-unit-022-d010}\]

The characterization of the induced morphism \(\Phi\) in Proposition reference also tells us that \((a,b,c)\mapsto\Phi\) is compatible with composition, preserves addition, sends \(0\) to \(0\), and sends \(\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}\) to \(\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}\). Hence the morphisms induced at the level of \(\operatorname{H}[\cdots]\) also satisfy the biproduct identities equation.

Notice that the preceding statement need not hold for infinite coproducts or infinite products in a general abelian category.

Definition (Complexes). Let \(\mathcal{A}\) be an additive category. Consider a sequence of morphisms in \(\mathcal{A}\) \[\cdots \to X^n \xrightarrow{d^n} X^{n+1} \xrightarrow{d^{n+1}} X^{n+2} \to \cdots.\] The sequence may have finitely many terms, extend infinitely in one or both directions, or form a cycle. If \(d^{n+1}d^n=0\) for every \(n\), the data \((X^n,d^n)_n\) are called a complex; the customary notation is \((X^\bullet,d^\bullet)\), \(X^\bullet\), or \(X\). The term \(X^n\) is conventionally called the degree-\(n\) term of the complex \(X\).

This chapter is chiefly concerned with abelian categories, where the cohomology and exactness of complexes can be studied.

Definition (Cohomology and exact sequences). Let \(\mathcal{A}\) be an abelian category.

  • For a complex \(X\), in accordance with equation, its cohomology at any non-end term \(X^n\) is defined by \[\operatorname{H}^n(X) = \operatorname{H}^n(X^\bullet, d^\bullet) := \operatorname{H}\left[ X^{n-1} \xrightarrow{d^{n-1}} X^n \xrightarrow{d^n} X^{n+1} \right].\]

  • If \(\operatorname{H}^n(X)=0\), the complex \(X\) is said to be exact at \(X^n\); this is equivalent to \(\operatorname{im}(d^{n-1})=\operatorname{ker}(d^n)\). A complex that is exact at every term is called an exact sequence; an exact complex is also called acyclic.

The properties of cohomology are one of the main themes of this book and will be studied further in §reference.

Remark (Homology of chain complexes). In Definition reference, choose decreasing indices and use subscripts, namely \[\cdots \to X_n \xrightarrow{d_n} X_{n-1} \to \cdots, \quad d_{n-1} d_n = 0,\] and all the preceding definitions apply unchanged. By conventions originating in topology, the version with increasing indices \((X^\bullet,d^\bullet)\) is usually called a cochain complex, while the version with decreasing indices \((X_\bullet,d_\bullet)\) is called a chain complex. For a chain complex \(X\) in an abelian category, the homology object at \(X_n\) is defined as the following object of \(\mathcal{A}\): \[\operatorname{H}_n(X) = \operatorname{H}_n(X_\bullet, d_\bullet) := \operatorname{H}\left[ X_{n+1} \xrightarrow{d_{n+1}} X_n \xrightarrow{d_n} X_{n-1} \right].\]

In algebra, complexes (that is, cochain complexes) and chain complexes differ only in notation, and passing between them is straightforward. For an additive category \(\mathcal{A}\), one way to remain entirely within the same category is to reflect the indices by setting \[X^n := X_{-n}, \quad d^n := d_{-n}.\] Another way is to reverse the arrows, which involves the opposite category. If a complex in \(\mathcal{A}\) \[\cdots \to X^n \xrightarrow{d^n} X^{n+1} \to \cdots\] is viewed in \(\mathcal{A}^{\operatorname{op}}\), it becomes the chain complex \[\begin{gather*} \cdots \leftarrow X_n \xleftarrow{d_{n+1}} X_{n+1} \leftarrow \cdots, \\ X_n := X^n, \quad d_{n+1} := d^{n, \operatorname{op}}. \end{gather*}\]

If \(\mathcal{A}\) is an abelian category and the chain complex \((X_\bullet,d_\bullet)\) in \(\mathcal{A}^{\operatorname{op}}\) is defined by reversing the arrows, there is a canonical isomorphism \(\operatorname{H}^n(X^\bullet)\simeq\operatorname{H}_n(X_\bullet)\). In particular, \(X^\bullet\) is exact if and only if \(X_\bullet\) is exact. To see this, it suffices to note that \(\operatorname{H}[X \xrightarrow{f} Y \xrightarrow{g} Z]\) can be characterized as the middle term in the epi–mono factorization of \(\operatorname{ker}(g)\to\operatorname{coker}(f)\). Viewed in \(\mathcal{A}^{\operatorname{op}}\), the same object is also the middle term in the epi–mono factorization of \(\operatorname{ker}(f^{\operatorname{op}})\to\operatorname{coker}(g^{\operatorname{op}})\).

Exactness of a complex can be checked term by term. The following standard forms will henceforth be used without further explanation.

  • Monomorphism.The complex \(0\to X'\xrightarrow{f}X\) is exact if and only if \(\operatorname{ker}(f)=0\), that is, if and only if \(f\) is a monomorphism (Lemma reference). This is also equivalent to \(X'\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}\operatorname{coim}(f)\) (Lemma reference).

  • Epimorphism.Dually, the complex \(X\xrightarrow{g}X''\to0\) is exact if and only if \(g\) is an epimorphism, and this is also equivalent to \(\operatorname{im}(g)\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}X''\).

  • Kernel.Consider the complex \(0\to X'\xrightarrow{f}X\xrightarrow{g}X''\). In accordance with equation, factor \(f\) through \(X'\twoheadrightarrow\operatorname{im}(f)\hookrightarrow\operatorname{ker}(g)\). The claim is that \(0\to X'\to X\to X''\) is exact if and only if \(X'\to\operatorname{ker}(g)\) is an isomorphism. In other words, up to isomorphism, an exact sequence of this form is always \(0\to\operatorname{ker}(g)\to X\xrightarrow{g}X''\) and is given by the kernel of a morphism.

    The argument is easy. Consider equation. The complex is exact at \(X\) if and only if \(\operatorname{im}(f)\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}\operatorname{ker}(g)\), while exactness at \(X'\) is equivalent to \(X'\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}\operatorname{im}(f)\). Now apply Proposition reference to \(X'\twoheadrightarrow\operatorname{im}(f)\hookrightarrow\operatorname{ker}(g)\).

  • Cokernel.Dually, the complex \(X'\xrightarrow{f}X\xrightarrow{g}X''\to0\) induces a morphism \(\operatorname{coker}(f)\to X''\) through equation. This complex is exact if and only if \(\operatorname{coker}(f)\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}X''\). Thus, up to isomorphism, an exact sequence of this form arises from a cokernel.

  • Short exact sequence.An exact sequence of the form \(0\to X'\to X\to X''\to0\) is called a short exact sequence. The two preceding items together give two equivalent, mutually dual characterizations of exactness:

    • \(X'\to X\) is a monomorphism and \(X''=\operatorname{coker}[X'\hookrightarrow X]\);

    • \(X\to X''\) is an epimorphism and \(X'=\operatorname{ker}[X\twoheadrightarrow X'']\).

As an application, every morphism \(f:X\to Y\) gives short exact sequences \[0 \to \operatorname{ker}(f) \to X \to \operatorname{im}(f) \to 0, \quad 0 \to \operatorname{im}(f) \to Y \to \operatorname{coker}(f) \to 0,\] which can be spliced into the exact sequence \(0\to\operatorname{ker}(f)\to X\xrightarrow{f}Y\to\operatorname{coker}(f)\to0\). Next, suppose that \(f\) can be embedded in an exact sequence of the form \[L' \xrightarrow{\lambda} L \to X \xrightarrow{f} Y \to R \xrightarrow{\rho} R''\] with both \(\lambda\) and \(\rho\) isomorphisms. Exactness then forces both \(L\to X\) and \(Y\to R\) to be zero, so \(\operatorname{ker}(f)=0\) and \(\operatorname{im}(f)=Y\); in other words, \(f\) is an isomorphism. This is a commonly used technique for testing whether a morphism is an isomorphism. The biproducts considered in §reference give a very simple class of short exact sequences; Proposition reference will characterize them.

Proposition. Let \(X_1,X_2\) be objects of an abelian category \(\mathcal{A}\). Then \(0\to X_1\xrightarrow{\iota_1}X_1\oplus X_2\xrightarrow{p_2}X_2\to0\) is a short exact sequence.

Proof. Take the short exact sequences \(0\to X_1\xrightarrow{\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}}X_1\to0\to0\) and \(0\to0\to X_2\xrightarrow{\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}}X_2\to0\). Proposition reference shows that their direct sum is still exact.

Some Diagram Lemmas

The arguments in this section follow [KS06]. We begin with a criterion for exactness that may be viewed as a substitute for diagram chasing [Li1] in general abelian categories. Throughout this section, fix an abelian category \(\mathcal{A}\).

Lemma. Let \(X'\xrightarrow{f}X\xrightarrow{g}X''\) be a complex. This complex is exact if and only if, for every morphism \(S\xrightarrow{h}X\) satisfying \(gh=0\), there are a morphism \(S'\to X'\) and an epimorphism \(S'\twoheadrightarrow S\) that make the following diagram commute: \[\text{Diagram chapter2-unit-023-d001}\]

Proof. First consider the “only if” direction. The morphisms \(f\) and \(h\) both factor through \(\operatorname{ker}(g)\). On the basis of these factorizations, take \(S':=S\ensuremath{\underset{\operatorname{ker}(g)}{\times}}X'\), and take \(S'\to S\) and \(S'\to X'\) to be the natural morphisms from the fiber product. Exactness implies that \(X'\twoheadrightarrow\operatorname{ker}(g)\), so Proposition reference implies that \(S'\to S\) is also an epimorphism.

Now consider the “if” direction. For \(S:=\operatorname{ker}(g)\) with its natural morphism \(h:S\hookrightarrow X\), the hypothesis supplies the solid part of the following diagram: \[\text{Diagram chapter2-unit-023-d002}\] The dashed part, namely \(\alpha\), comes from the factorization of \(f\) given by \(gf=0\). We show that the diagram commutes. The outer frame and the lower-right triangle are already known to commute. Thus the two morphisms in the upper-left triangle become equal after composition with \(h\). Since \(h\) is a monomorphism, the upper-left triangle also commutes, proving the claim. Finally, the diagram shows that the composite \(S'\to X'\xrightarrow{\alpha}S\) is an epimorphism, and hence \(\alpha\) is an epimorphism. Thus \(f\) has an epi–mono factorization \(X'\twoheadrightarrow\operatorname{ker}(g)\hookrightarrow X\), which gives \(\operatorname{im}(f)=\operatorname{ker}(g)\). The complex is therefore exact.

For another approach that replaces diagram chasing in general abelian categories, see [stacks]. We now discuss the Snake Lemma, which is indispensable in applications. Consider the diagram \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:snake}{} \hypertarget{o014.li2.chapter2.diagram-lemmas.g003}{} \text{Diagram chapter2-unit-023-d003} \end{equation}\] subject to the following assumptions:

  • \(X'\xrightarrow{f}X\xrightarrow{g}X''\to0\) and \(0\to Y'\xrightarrow{u}Y\xrightarrow{v}Y''\) are given exact sequences;

  • \(\operatorname{ker}':=\operatorname{ker}[X'\to Y']\hookrightarrow X'\), with \(\operatorname{ker}\) and \(\operatorname{ker}''\) defined in the same way;

  • \(Y'\twoheadrightarrow\operatorname{coker}':=\operatorname{coker}[X'\to Y']\), with \(\operatorname{coker}\) and \(\operatorname{coker}''\) defined in the same way;

  • the morphisms \(\operatorname{ker}'\to\operatorname{ker}\), \(\operatorname{coker}'\to\operatorname{coker}\), and so forth come from the functoriality of kernels and cokernels in equation.

Thus equation is a commutative diagram; every column and both middle rows are exact. We now explain how to construct the dashed connecting morphism \(\delta:\operatorname{ker}''\to\operatorname{coker}'\). The first step is to derive the following commutative diagram from equation; all its rows are exact: \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:snake-conn}{} \hypertarget{o014.li2.chapter2.diagram-lemmas.g004}{} \text{Diagram chapter2-unit-023-d004} \end{equation}\] Here the following points apply:

  • \(\Box\) and \(\boxplus\) indicate that the corresponding squares are, respectively, a pullback and a pushout diagram. Pullbacks preserve kernels, while pushouts preserve cokernels; this explains the upper-left and lower-right squares in the diagram;

  • Proposition reference applies to the \(\Box\) and \(\boxplus\) parts of equation. This explains why \(X\ensuremath{\underset{X''}{\times}}\operatorname{ker}''\to\operatorname{ker}''\) is an epimorphism and \(\operatorname{coker}'\to\operatorname{coker}'\ensuremath{\underset{Y'}{\sqcup}}Y\) is a monomorphism;

  • the dashed arrow \(\operatorname{ker}(g)\dashrightarrow Y'\) is none other than the natural morphism \(\operatorname{ker}(g)\to\operatorname{ker}(v)\) coming from the functoriality of kernels in equation;

  • similarly, the functoriality of cokernels gives the dashed arrow \(X''\simeq\operatorname{coker}(f)\to\operatorname{coker}(u)\).

Notice that the composite \(\operatorname{ker}(g)\dashrightarrow Y'\to\operatorname{coker}'\) in equation is zero, because it becomes zero after precomposition with \(X'\twoheadrightarrow\operatorname{im}(f)\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}\operatorname{ker}(g)\). Similarly, the composite \(\operatorname{ker}''\to X''\dashrightarrow\operatorname{coker}(u)\) is zero, because its further composite with \(\operatorname{coker}(u)\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}\operatorname{im}(v)\hookrightarrow Y''\) is zero. Denote the composite along the middle path in equation by \(\delta_0:X\ensuremath{\underset{X''}{\times}}\operatorname{ker}''\to\operatorname{coker}'\ensuremath{\underset{Y'}{\sqcup}}Y\). The preceding observation immediately gives \[\delta_0 s = 0, \quad t \delta_0 = 0.\] Consequently, \(\delta_0\) has a unique factorization \[X \ensuremath{\underset{X''}{\times}} \operatorname{ker}'' \twoheadrightarrow \operatorname{coker}(s) \xrightarrow{\exists!} \operatorname{ker}(t) \hookrightarrow \operatorname{coker}' \ensuremath{\underset{Y'}{\sqcup}} Y .\]

The horizontal morphisms in the upper-right and lower-left corners of equation are known to be an epimorphism and a monomorphism, respectively. Hence \(\operatorname{coker}(s)\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}\operatorname{ker}''\) and \(\operatorname{coker}'\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}\operatorname{ker}(t)\). We have therefore obtained the desired canonical morphism \(\delta:\operatorname{ker}''\to\operatorname{coker}'\).

Remark. The canonical nature of the connecting morphism can be stated more explicitly as follows. Consider the commutative diagram \[\text{Diagram chapter2-unit-023-d005}\] with every row exact. The diagram gives rise to \(\operatorname{ker}'\), \(\underline{\operatorname{ker}'}\), and so forth. The corresponding connecting morphisms \(\delta\) and \(\underline{\delta}\) fit into the commutative diagram \[\text{Diagram chapter2-unit-023-d006}\] By definition, to prove this it suffices to show that \(\delta_0\) and \(\underline{\delta_0}\) also fit into the corresponding commutative square. Everything follows from the functoriality of kernels, cokernels, products, and coproducts. The details are left to the reader.

The following two observations will be used in the proof below.

  • The construction of the connecting morphism is self-dual: when equation is viewed in \(\mathcal{A}^{\operatorname{op}}\), all arrows are reversed, while the roles of \(\operatorname{ker}'\) and \(\operatorname{coker}'\), and so forth, are interchanged. The resulting diagram in \(\mathcal{A}^{\operatorname{op}}\) still resembles equation, except that it is rotated through half a turn. When the corresponding connecting morphism is viewed back in \(\mathcal{A}\), it still runs from \(\operatorname{ker}''\) to \(\operatorname{coker}'\), and it agrees with the \(\delta\) constructed above.

  • The morphism \(\operatorname{ker}\to\operatorname{ker}''\) factors as \(\operatorname{ker}\to X\ensuremath{\underset{X''}{\times}}\operatorname{ker}''\to\operatorname{ker}''\). Inspection of equation shows that the two composites \[\operatorname{ker}\to \operatorname{ker}'' \xrightarrow{\delta} \operatorname{coker}' \hookrightarrow \operatorname{coker}' \ensuremath{\underset{Y'}{\sqcup}} Y, \qquad \operatorname{ker}\to X \ensuremath{\underset{X''}{\times}} \operatorname{ker}'' \xrightarrow{\delta_0} \operatorname{coker}' \ensuremath{\underset{Y'}{\sqcup}} Y\] are equal. But the second composite is also equal to \(\operatorname{ker}\to X\to Y\to\operatorname{coker}'\ensuremath{\underset{Y'}{\sqcup}}Y\), which is zero. We therefore obtain \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:snake-conn-complex}{} \operatorname{ker}\to \operatorname{ker}'' \xrightarrow{\delta} \operatorname{coker}' \quad \text{has composite}\; 0. \end{equation}\]

Theorem (Snake Lemma). Consider diagram equation in an abelian category \(\mathcal{A}\). Then \(\operatorname{ker}'\to\operatorname{ker}\to\operatorname{ker}''\xrightarrow{\delta}\operatorname{coker}'\to\operatorname{coker}\to\operatorname{coker}''\) is an exact sequence. If \(f:X'\to X\) in the diagram is a monomorphism (or \(v:Y\to Y''\) is an epimorphism), then \(\operatorname{ker}'\to\operatorname{ker}\) is also a monomorphism (or \(\operatorname{coker}\to\operatorname{coker}''\) is also an epimorphism).

Proof. The last assertion is easy to prove: if \(f\) is a monomorphism, then the composite \(\operatorname{ker}'\hookrightarrow X'\xrightarrow{f}X\) is also a monomorphism. Since equation commutes, this implies that \(\operatorname{ker}'\to\operatorname{ker}\) is a monomorphism. The case in which \(v\) is an epimorphism is obtained by reversing all arrows.

The main part of the proof is the exactness of the first sequence. By the duality observed above, it suffices to prove that \(\operatorname{ker}'\to\operatorname{ker}\to\operatorname{ker}''\to\operatorname{coker}'\) is exact.

First, \(\operatorname{ker}'\to\operatorname{ker}\to\operatorname{ker}''\) is a complex. Indeed, it is induced by \(X'\to X\to X''\), whose composite is zero. We now use Lemma reference to prove exactness. Suppose that a morphism \(\psi:S\to\operatorname{ker}\) makes the composite \(S\xrightarrow{\psi}\operatorname{ker}\to\operatorname{ker}''\) zero. We must construct a commutative diagram \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:snake-lemma-aux-1}{} \hypertarget{o014.li2.chapter2.diagram-lemmas.g007}{} \text{Diagram chapter2-unit-023-diagram-007} \end{equation}\] where \(\operatorname{ker}'\leftarrow S'\xrightarrow{h}S\) remains to be constructed. To do so, first apply Lemma reference to the composite \(S\xrightarrow{\psi}\operatorname{ker}\to X\) to obtain the commutative diagram \[\text{Diagram chapter2-unit-023-d007}\] Thus the composite \(S'\to X'\to Y'\xrightarrow{u}Y\) is equal to the composite \(S'\xrightarrow{\psi h}\operatorname{ker}\to X\to Y\), namely zero. Since \(u\) is a monomorphism, the composite \(S'\to X'\to Y'\) is also zero. Hence \(S'\to X'\) factors through \(\operatorname{ker}'\), giving all the arrows in equation.

Now consider the left part of equation: the outer frame and the lower square commute. The familiar Lemma reference shows that the upper square also commutes. Therefore \(\operatorname{ker}'\to\operatorname{ker}\to\operatorname{ker}''\) is exact.

Next consider \(\operatorname{ker}\to\operatorname{ker}''\xrightarrow{\delta}\operatorname{coker}'\). Equation equation first shows that this sequence is a complex. To prove its exactness, we again use Lemma reference. Suppose that a morphism \(\psi:S\to\operatorname{ker}''\) satisfies \(\delta\psi=0\). We must construct a commutative diagram of the form \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:snake-lemma-aux-2}{} \hypertarget{o014.li2.chapter2.diagram-lemmas.g009}{} \text{Diagram chapter2-unit-023-d008} \end{equation}\] The construction of \(\delta\) showed that \(X\ensuremath{\underset{X''}{\times}}\operatorname{ker}''\to\operatorname{ker}''\to0\) is exact. Hence there is a commutative diagram \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:snake-lemma-aux-3}{} \hypertarget{o014.li2.chapter2.diagram-lemmas.g010}{} \text{Diagram chapter2-unit-023-d009} \end{equation}\]

Consider the composite \(S_1\to X\ensuremath{\underset{X''}{\times}}\operatorname{ker}''\to X\to Y\xrightarrow{v}Y''\). Comparing the diagram above with equation and equation, we see that this composite is zero. Hence \(S_1\to X\ensuremath{\underset{X''}{\times}}\operatorname{ker}''\to X\to Y\) factors as \(S_1\xrightarrow{\xi}Y'\xrightarrow{u}Y\). We now prove that the composite \(S_1\xrightarrow{\xi}Y'\to\operatorname{coker}'\) is zero. Begin with the commutative diagram \[\text{Diagram chapter2-unit-023-d010}\]

The composite along the first row is \(\delta\psi=0\), so the composite along the second row is also zero. Consequently, the composite \(S_1\xrightarrow{\xi}Y'\xrightarrow{u}Y\to\operatorname{coker}'\ensuremath{\underset{Y'}{\sqcup}}Y\) is zero. On the other hand, the composite \(Y'\xrightarrow{u}Y\to\operatorname{coker}'\ensuremath{\underset{Y'}{\sqcup}}Y\) equals \(Y'\to\operatorname{coker}'\to\operatorname{coker}'\ensuremath{\underset{Y'}{\sqcup}}Y\). In the construction of \(\delta\) we proved that \(\operatorname{coker}'\to\operatorname{coker}'\ensuremath{\underset{Y'}{\sqcup}}Y\) is a monomorphism. Thus the composite \(S_1\xrightarrow{\xi}Y'\to\operatorname{coker}'\) is indeed zero.

The next step is to apply Lemma reference to the exact sequence \(X'\to Y'\to\operatorname{coker}'\). This gives a commutative diagram \[\text{Diagram chapter2-unit-023-d011}\]

Write \(\lambda\) for the composite \(S_0\twoheadrightarrow S_1\to X\ensuremath{\underset{X''}{\times}}\operatorname{ker}''\to X\). Also write the morphisms \(X'\to Y'\) and \(X\to Y\) as \(a\) and \(b\), respectively. The preceding discussion gives the commutative diagram \[\text{Diagram chapter2-unit-023-d012}\] Both squares in this diagram are known to commute; commutativity of the triangle comes from the definition of \(\lambda\), while commutativity of the trapezoid on the right comes from the preceding discussion of \(\xi\).

It follows at once that \(b\lambda=bfk\), so \(\lambda-fk:S_0\to X\) factors through \(\operatorname{ker}=\operatorname{ker}(b)\hookrightarrow X\). Finally, consider the diagram \[\text{Diagram chapter2-unit-023-d013}\] To obtain the diagram in equation, it suffices to show that its upper square commutes. The lower square and the curved part are known to commute; the usual argument reduces the problem to commutativity of the outer frame. Since \(g(\lambda-fk)=g\lambda\), this in turn reduces to the known commutative diagram (see equation): \[\text{Diagram chapter2-unit-023-d014}\] All the required conditions are therefore satisfied.

The connecting homomorphism \(\delta\) and Theorem reference are much simpler in the category \(R\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\) of \(R\)-modules; see [Li1].

Proposition (Five Lemma). Consider a commutative diagram with exact rows in an abelian category \(\mathcal{A}\): \[\text{Diagram chapter2-unit-023-d015}\]

  1. If \(f_1\) is an epimorphism and \(f_2,f_4\) are monomorphisms, then \(f_3\) is a monomorphism (only the first four columns are involved);

  2. if \(f_5\) is a monomorphism and \(f_2,f_4\) are epimorphisms, then \(f_3\) is an epimorphism (only the last four columns are involved);

  3. if \(f_1\) is an epimorphism, \(f_5\) is a monomorphism, and \(f_2,f_4\) are both isomorphisms, then \(f_3\) is an isomorphism.

Proof. Clearly (i) and (ii) are dual to each other, while (iii) follows from (i)–(ii) and Proposition reference. It therefore suffices to prove (i).

Suppose that a morphism \(h:S\to X_3\) satisfies \(f_3h=0\); we must prove that \(h=0\). The composite \(S\xrightarrow{h}X_3\to X_4\xrightarrow{f_4}Y_4\) is zero, and therefore so is \(S\xrightarrow{h}X_3\to X_4\). Applying Lemma reference to the exact sequence \(X_2\to X_3\to X_4\) gives a commutative diagram \[\text{Diagram chapter2-unit-023-d016}\]

We now construct a commutative diagram \[\text{Diagram chapter2-unit-023-diagram-018}\] Here is how. Since \(f_3h=0\), the composite \(S'\to X_2\xrightarrow{f_2}Y_2\to Y_3\) is zero. Applying Lemma reference to \(S'\to Y_2\) and the exact sequence \(Y_1\to Y_2\to Y_3\) gives the right-hand part of the diagram. Applying Lemma reference to \(S''\to Y_1\) and the exact sequence \(X_1\xrightarrow{f_1}Y_1\to0\) gives the left-hand part.

Take the composite \(S'''\to S'\) and consider the following diagram: \[\text{Diagram chapter2-unit-023-d017}\] We show that this diagram commutes. The only issue is the upper-left square. Compose the two paths

Diagram chapter2-unit-023-d018

and

Diagram chapter2-unit-023-d019

in that square with \(f_2\) on the right. Since the two squares \(\text{Diagram chapter2-unit-023-d020}\) and \(\text{Diagram chapter2-unit-023-d021}\) commute and \(f_2\) is a monomorphism, the upper-left square also commutes.

Thus the composite \(S'''\twoheadrightarrow S'\twoheadrightarrow S\xrightarrow{h}X_3\) is zero, and hence \(h=0\). This proves the result.

This section has introduced only two of the most commonly used diagram lemmas. Using the language of double complexes, G. Bergman found the comprehensive Salamander Lemma, which subsumes the Snake Lemma and several classical diagram lemmas of homological algebra. Interested readers may consult [Be12].

A Glimpse of Lattice Theory

This section gives a brief introduction to a class of partially ordered structures called lattices. The discussion will help clarify the structure of abelian categories. Throughout this section we consider various partially ordered sets \((P,\leq)\); the corresponding category is denoted by \(\mathcal{P}\). For every subset \(S\) of a partially ordered set \((P,\leq)\), there are notions of upper and lower bounds, a supremum \(\sup S\), and an infimum \(\inf S\). A subset \(S\subset P\) has a supremum (or infimum) if and only if the coproduct (or product) of all the objects in \(S\) exists in the category \(\mathcal{P}\); in that case the supremum (or infimum) is precisely that coproduct (or product).

Definition. If every two elements \(a,b\) of a partially ordered set \((P,\leq)\) have a supremum \(a\vee b\) and an infimum \(a\wedge b\), then \((P,\leq)\) is called a lattice. If, in addition, \((P,\leq)\) itself has an upper bound and a lower bound, they are both unique and are denoted by \(1\) and \(0\), respectively; in this case \(P\) is called a bounded lattice.

If \(a,b\) are elements of a partially ordered set \((P,\leq)\) and \(a\leq b\), then \([a,b]:=\left\{x\in P:a\leq x\leq b\right\}\) is also a partially ordered set under \(\leq\) and is called the interval determined by \(a,b\).

If \(P\) is a lattice, every interval in \(P\) is closed under \(\vee\) and \(\wedge\) and is a bounded lattice. If \(P\) is a bounded lattice, then \(P=[0,1]\), and for every \(x\in P\) one has \(x\wedge0=0\), \(x\vee0=x=x\wedge1\), and \(x\vee1=1\). From the categorical point of view, \(a\wedge b\), \(a\vee b\), \(1\), and \(0\) correspond, respectively, to the product of two objects, the coproduct of two objects, a terminal object (that is, an empty product), and an initial object (that is, an empty coproduct) in the category; this can be checked directly. As an illustration of the operations \(\wedge\) and \(\vee\), prove the following fact. If \(a^\flat,a,b\in P\) satisfy \(a^\flat\leq a\), then \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:modular-inequality}{} a^\flat \vee (a \wedge b) \leq (a^\flat \vee b) \wedge a. \end{equation}\] By the definition of a supremum, it first suffices to prove \(a^\flat\leq(a^\flat\vee b)\wedge a\) and \((a\wedge b)\leq(a^\flat\vee b)\wedge a\). By the definition of an infimum, it then suffices to prove, respectively, the inequalities \[a^\flat \leq a^\flat \vee b, \quad a^\flat \leq a, \quad a \wedge b \leq a^\flat \vee b, \quad a \wedge b \leq a;\] the third follows from \(a\wedge b\leq b\leq a^\flat\vee b\), and the others are clear.

Definition. Let \(P\) be a lattice.

  • \(P\) is called a modular lattice if the following property holds: whenever \(a^\flat,a,b\in P\) satisfy \(a^\flat\leq a\), then \[a^\flat \vee (a \wedge b) = (a^\flat \vee b) \wedge a.\]

  • Suppose that \(P\) is a bounded lattice. If \(x,c\in P\) satisfy \(x\vee c=1\) and \(x\wedge c=0\), then \(c\) is called a complement of \(x\) in \(P\).

We now consider some basic examples of lattices.

  • The set of positive integers \(\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}_{\geq1}\) is a lattice under divisibility (\(x\mid y\iff x\leq y\)): \(x\vee y=\mathrm{lcm}(x,y)\) and \(x\wedge y=\mathrm{gcd}(x,y)\). The reader can check that this lattice is modular, has lower bound \(1\), but has no upper bound.

  • Let \(R\) be a ring and \(M\) a left \(R\)-module. Its set of submodules \(\mathrm{Sub}_M\) is a bounded modular lattice under \(\subset\): \(x\vee y=x+y\) and \(x\wedge y=x\cap y\); its upper bound is \(M\) and its lower bound is \(\{0\}\). This is the origin of the term “modular lattice.”

  • All closed subspaces of a Hilbert space \(H\) form a bounded lattice under \(\subset\): \(x\vee y:=\overline{x+y}\) and \(x\wedge y=x\cap y\). One can prove that this lattice is not modular when \(H\) is infinite-dimensional (Birkhoff–von Neumann).

Remark. The definition of a lattice also contains a duality. Given the partial order \(\leq\) on a set \(P\), we may consider the opposite partial order \(\leq^{\operatorname{op}}\): \(x\leq^{\operatorname{op}}y\iff x\geq y\); this is equivalent to replacing \(\mathcal{P}\) by \(\mathcal{P}^{\operatorname{op}}\). If \((P,\leq)\) is a lattice (or a bounded lattice), then so is \((P,\leq^{\operatorname{op}})\). Moreover, \(\wedge,\vee,0,1\) in \((P,\leq)\) correspond, respectively, to \(\vee,\wedge,1,0\) in \((P,\leq^{\operatorname{op}})\).

Lemma. Let \(P\) be a lattice. Then \(P\) is modular if and only if the following property holds for every interval \(I\) in \(P\): if \(c^\flat,c\) are both complements of \(x\in I\) in \(I\) and \(c^\flat\leq c\), then \(c^\flat=c\).

Proof. If \(P\) is a modular lattice, then every interval \(I\) is also a modular lattice. Without loss of generality, assume \(I=P\); for the \(x,c^\flat,c\) in the statement, we have \[c = c \wedge 1 = c \wedge (x \vee c^\flat) = c^\flat \vee (x \wedge c) = c^\flat \vee 0 = c^\flat .\]

Conversely, assume that the condition on complements holds for every interval. Let \(a^\flat,a,b\in P\) satisfy \(a^\flat\leq a\). Set \[b \wedge a \leq c_1 := a^\flat \vee (b \wedge a) \underset{\because \href{#eqn:modular-inequality}{equation}}{\leq} a \wedge (b \vee a^\flat) =: c_2 \leq b \vee a^\flat.\] We prove that \(c_1,c_2\) are both complements of \(b\) in \(\left[b\wedge a,\;b\vee a^\flat\right]\), so that \(c_1=c_2\). First, the definition immediately gives \(c_1\leq a\); therefore \[b \wedge a \geq b \wedge c_1 = (a^\flat \vee (b \wedge a)) \wedge b \underset{\because \href{#eqn:modular-inequality}{equation}}{\geq} (a^\flat \wedge b) \vee (b \wedge a) = b \wedge a ,\] so \(b\wedge c_1=b\wedge a\). On the other hand, \(b\vee c_1=a^\flat\vee(b\wedge a)\vee b=a^\flat\vee b\). Thus \(c_1\) is indeed a complement of \(b\) in \(\left[b\wedge a,\;b\vee a^\flat\right]\).

Lattice duality (Remark reference) reverses the order relation between \(a^\flat,a\), interchanges \(\wedge\) and \(\vee\), and interchanges the roles of \(c_1\) and \(c_2\). Thus the preceding argument, carried out in \((P,\leq^{\operatorname{op}})\), shows that \(c_2\) is a complement of \(b\) in \(\left[b\wedge a,\;b\vee a^\flat\right]\).

Proposition. Let \(a,b\) be elements of a modular lattice \((P,\leq)\). Then there is an isomorphism of partially ordered sets \[\text{Diagram chapter2-unit-024-d001}\] called the standard isomorphism.

Proof. The two maps are clearly well defined and order-preserving. For \(x\in[a\wedge b,a]\), the definition of a modular lattice gives \((x\vee b)\wedge a=(a\wedge b)\vee x\), whose right-hand side is \(x\). Dually, \(y\in[b,a\vee b]\) implies \((y\wedge a)\vee b=y\) (Remark reference); thus the two maps are mutually inverse.

The Zassenhaus lemma of elementary algebra (see [Li1], especially its module-theoretic version) and its consequences can be distilled using lattice theory.

Theorem (Zassenhaus Lemma for Modular Lattices). Let \((P,\leq)\) be a modular lattice. For given elements \(u^\flat\leq u\) and \(v^\flat\leq v\), there is a diagram \[\text{Diagram chapter2-unit-024-d002}\] meaning that its elements satisfy the following patterns: \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:Zassenhaus-cases}{} \hypertarget{o014.li2.chapter2.glimpse-of-lattice-theory.g003}{} \text{Diagram chapter2-unit-024-d003} \qquad \hypertarget{o014.li2.chapter2.glimpse-of-lattice-theory.g004}{} \text{Diagram chapter2-unit-024-d004} \quad \hypertarget{o014.li2.chapter2.glimpse-of-lattice-theory.g005}{} \text{Diagram chapter2-unit-024-d005} . \end{equation}\] Moreover, there are standard isomorphisms between the intervals \[\begin{multline*} \left[ u^\flat \vee (u \wedge v^\flat), \; u^\flat \vee (u \wedge v) \right] \ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\leftarrow}}\left[ (u^\flat \wedge v) \vee (u \wedge v^\flat), \; u \wedge v \right] \\ \ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}\left[ (u^\flat \wedge v) \vee v^\flat, \; (u \wedge v) \vee v^\flat \right], \end{multline*}\] realized by the maps \(x\vee u^\flat\vee(u\wedge v^\flat)\mapsfrom x\mapsto x\vee(u^\flat\wedge v)\vee v^\flat\) in Proposition reference.

Proof. The isomorphisms in the last part are obtained by applying Proposition reference to the two parallelograms in the diagram; what remains to be checked are the relations in equation. Notice that the diagram is left–right symmetric under \(u\leftrightarrow v\) and \(u^\flat\leftrightarrow v^\flat\); it therefore suffices to check its left half. The partial-order relations among its elements are immediate. For the \(\wedge\) case, the definition of a modular lattice gives \[\begin{equation*} \left( u^\flat \vee (u \wedge v^\flat)\right) \wedge (u \wedge v) = \left( u^\flat \wedge (u \wedge v) \right) \vee (u \wedge v^\flat) = (u^\flat \wedge v) \vee (u \wedge v^\flat). \end{equation*}\] For the \(\vee\) case, the inequality \(u\wedge v^\flat\leq u\wedge v\) immediately gives \[\begin{equation*} u^\flat \vee (u \wedge v^\flat) \vee (u \wedge v) = u^\flat \vee (u \wedge v). \end{equation*}\] This proves equation.

Next consider a finite descending chain in a lattice, written \(x_0\geq x_1\geq\cdots\geq x_r\) (\(r\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}_{\geq0}\)). A descending chain obtained by inserting finitely many intermediate elements is called a refinement of the original descending chain; if the inserted elements include some \(y\notin\{x_0,\ldots,x_r\}\), it is called a proper refinement.

Definition. Two descending chains of the same length in a modular lattice, \(x_0\geq\cdots\geq x_r\) and \(x'_0\geq\cdots\geq x'_r\), are called equivalent if the following condition holds: there is a bijection \(\sigma\) from \(\{0,\ldots,r-1\}\) to itself (that is, a permutation)1 such that, for every \(0\leq i<r\), there is an isomorphism of partially ordered sets \[\tau_i: \left[ x_{i+1}, x_i \right] \simeq \left[ x'_{\sigma(i) + 1}, x'_{\sigma(i)} \right],\] and \(\tau_i\) decomposes into a finite composite of standard isomorphisms (Proposition reference) or their inverses.

Theorem (Schreier Refinement Theorem for Modular Lattices).

Consider descending chains \[x_0 \geq \cdots \geq x_r, \quad y_0 \geq \cdots \geq y_s,\] in a modular lattice \((P,\leq)\) such that \(x_0=y_0\) and \(x_r=y_s\), with \(r,s\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}_{\geq0}\). Then each chain has a refinement, and the two refinements are equivalent.

Proof. The argument is the same as in the case of groups [Li1]; both are based on Theorem reference. We give the outline. Define \[x_{i, j} := x_{i+1} \vee (x_i \wedge y_j), \quad y_{j, i} := (x_i \wedge y_j) \vee y_{j+1},\] with \(0\leq i<r\) and \(0\leq j\leq s\) for \(x_{i,j}\), and with \(0\leq i\leq r\) and \(0\leq j<s\) for \(y_{j,i}\). Then \(x_{i,j+1}\leq x_{i,j}\), \(x_{i,0}=x_i\), and \(x_{i,s}=x_{i+1}\), so \(\left(x_{i,j}\right)_{i,j}\), in that order, refines \(x_0\geq\cdots\geq x_r\). Similarly, \(\left(y_{j,i}\right)_{j,i}\) refines \(y_0\geq\cdots\geq y_s\). Taking \(u^\flat=x_{i+1}\), \(u=x_i\), \(v^\flat=y_{j+1}\), and \(v=y_j\) in Theorem reference, we obtain \[\left[ x_{i, j+1}, x_{i,j} \right] \simeq \left[ y_{j, i+1}, y_{j, i} \right],\] and this isomorphism decomposes into standard isomorphisms and their inverses. The assertion follows.

From now on, we consider only strictly ascending or strictly descending chains.

Definition. Fix a partially ordered set \(P\) and elements \(a\leq b\) in it.2 If a descending chain \(b=x_0>\cdots>x_r=a\) in \(P\) has no proper refinement, it is called a composition series of \([a,b]\).

The length of this composition series is defined to be \(r\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}_{\geq0}\); notice that \(r=0\) if and only if \(a=b\).

Theorem (Jordan–Hölder Theorem for Modular Lattices). Let \(a<b\) be elements of a modular lattice \((P,\leq)\). Then any two composition series of \([a,b]\) have the same length and are equivalent in the sense of Definition reference.

Proof. This follows immediately from Theorem reference.

The next important question is to determine which intervals in a partially ordered set have composition series. As in the familiar theory of modules, their existence can be guaranteed by ascending- and descending-chain conditions.

Definition. Let \((P,\leq)\) be a partially ordered set. If there is no infinite ascending chain \(x_1<x_2<x_3<\cdots\) in \(P\), then \(P\) is called Noetherian; if there is no infinite descending chain \(x_1>x_2>x_3>\cdots\), then \(P\) is called Artinian. A partially ordered set that is both Artinian and Noetherian is said to have finite length.

If \((P,\leq)\) is Noetherian (or Artinian, or of finite length), then every subset of it has the same property. It is easy to prove that the Noetherian (or Artinian) condition is equivalent to the assertion that every nonempty subset of \(P\) has a maximal (or minimal) element with respect to \(\leq\). In this chapter these notions will be applied chiefly to partially ordered sets of subobjects; see Definition reference.

Definition. Fix a category \(\mathcal{C}\). An object \(X\) of \(\mathcal{C}\) is called Noetherian (or Artinian, or of finite length) if its partially ordered set of subobjects \((\mathrm{Sub}_X,\subset)\) is Noetherian (or Artinian, or of finite length).

We now return to general partially ordered sets.

Lemma. Let \(a\leq b\) be elements of a partially ordered set \((P,\leq)\).

  1. If \([a,b]\) has finite length, then every chain in it can be refined to a composition series; in particular, \([a,b]\) has a composition series.

  2. If \([a,b]\) is a modular lattice and has a composition series, then \([a,b]\) has finite length.

Proof. Without loss of generality, assume \(a<b\). For (i), given a chain \(y_0>\cdots>y_r\), it suffices to show that every \([y_{i+1},y_i]\) has a composition series.3 Without loss of generality, assume \(y_{i+1}=a\) and \(y_i=b\). The Artinian condition guarantees a minimal element \(x^0\in[a,b]\) with \(x^0>a\). Similarly, if \(x^0\neq b\), there is a minimal element \(x^1\in[a,b]\) with \(x^1>x^0\), and so on. By the Noetherian condition, this process must stop after finitely many steps, producing a chain \(b>\cdots>x^0>a\) with no proper refinement.

For (ii), choose a composition series \(b=x_0>\cdots>x_r=a\). Theorem reference shows that every finite chain \(\cdots>y_i>y_{i+1}>\cdots\) has a refinement equivalent to the composition series above; hence the length of that chain cannot exceed the length of the composition series. Thus \([a,b]\) is a partially ordered set of finite length.

Definition. Let \((P,\leq)\) be a bounded modular lattice of finite length. Choose any composition series \(1=x_0>\cdots>x_r=0\) of \(P\). The number \(r\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}_{\geq0}\) is called the length of \((P,\leq)\).

Theorem reference shows that this length is well defined and does not depend on the chosen composition series; the length of \((P,\leq)\) is \(0\) if and only if \(P\) is a one-point set.

  1. Translator’s note (O014-C021): the source has \(\{0,\ldots,r\}\), but the successive factors being paired are indexed by \(0\leq i<r\); the index \(i=r\) would leave \(x_{i+1}\) undefined.↩︎

  2. Translator’s note (O014-C022): the source has \(a<b\), but the next sentence explicitly includes the case \(a=b\) and \(r=0\); the target uses the weaker hypothesis consistent with that case.↩︎

  3. Translator’s note (O014-C023): the source has \([y_i,y_{i+1}]\) and then sets \(y_i=a\), \(y_{i+1}=b\). Since \(y_i>y_{i+1}\), both orders are reversed; the target uses the interval \([y_{i+1},y_i]\) and the well-typed assignment.↩︎

Direct-Sum Decompositions

We begin by discussing how morphisms between direct sums are represented by matrices. The argument is exactly the same as in the module-theoretic case [Li1]; only a brief review is given here. Fix an additive category \(\mathcal{A}\). Consider objects \(X_1,\ldots,X_n\) and \(X'_1,\ldots,X'_m\) of \(\mathcal{A}\). The direct sum \(\bigoplus_{i=1}^nX_i\) introduced in Definition reference comes with a family of morphisms \(X_j\xrightarrow{\iota_j}\bigoplus_{i=1}^nX_i\xrightarrow{p_j}X_j\). Likewise, \(\bigoplus_{i=1}^mX'_i\) has morphisms \(p'_j,\iota'_j\), and so on. The universal properties of products and coproducts give \[\begin{align*} \operatorname{Hom}\left( \bigoplus_{j=1}^n X_j, \bigoplus_{i=1}^m X'_i \right) & \xrightarrow[\sim]{\phi \mapsto (p'_i \phi)_i } \prod_{i=1}^m \operatorname{Hom}\left(\bigoplus_{j=1}^n X_j , X'_i \right) \\ & \xrightarrow[\sim]{(p'_i \phi)_i \mapsto (p'_i \phi \iota_j)_{i, j}} \prod_{j=1}^n \prod_{i=1}^m \operatorname{Hom}(X_j, X'_i). \end{align*}\] Thus every morphism \(\phi:\bigoplus_{j=1}^nX_j\to\bigoplus_{i=1}^mX'_i\) corresponds to the matrix \[\mathcal{M}(\phi) = (\phi_{ij})_{\substack{1 \leq i \leq m \\ 1 \leq j \leq n}} = \begin{pmatrix} \phi_{11} & \cdots & \phi_{1n} \\ \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\ \phi_{m1} & \cdots & \phi_{mn} \end{pmatrix}, \quad \phi_{ij} := p'_i \phi \iota_j: X_j \to X'_i.\] Conversely, every matrix \(\mathcal{M}=(\phi_{ij})_{\substack{1\leq i\leq m\\1\leq j\leq n}}\) formed from morphisms \(\phi_{ij}:X_j\to X'_i\) uniquely determines a morphism \(\phi\) such that \(\mathcal{M}=\mathcal{M}(\phi)\). Composition of morphisms agrees with matrix multiplication: \[\mathcal{M}(\psi\phi) = \mathcal{M}(\psi) \mathcal{M}(\phi)\] where multiplication of matrix entries is given by composition \(\operatorname{Hom}(X'_j,X''_i)\times\operatorname{Hom}(X_k,X'_j)\to\operatorname{Hom}(X_k,X''_i)\).

Lemma. Given a family of morphisms \(\phi_i:X_i\to X'_i\) in \(\mathcal{A}\), \(i=1,\ldots,n\), set \(\phi:=(\phi_1,\ldots,\phi_n):\bigoplus_{i=1}^nX_i\to \bigoplus_{i=1}^nX'_i\). Then \(\phi\) is an isomorphism if and only if each \(\phi_i\) is an isomorphism.

Proof. The implication \(\impliedby\) is clear. For \(\implies\), write write the matrix \(\mathcal{M}(\phi^{-1})\) as \((\psi_{ij})_{i,j}\). Then \[\mathcal{M}(\phi^{-1}) \mathcal{M}(\phi) = \begin{pmatrix} \psi_{11} \phi_1 & \cdots & \psi_{1n} \phi_n \\ \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\ \psi_{n1} \phi_1 & \cdots & \psi_{nn} \phi_n \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{X_1} & & \\ & \ddots & \\ & & \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{X_n} \end{pmatrix}\] so \(\phi_1,\ldots,\phi_n\) all have left inverses. The same argument shows that they all have right inverses.

Continue to consider a direct-sum decomposition \(X\simeq\bigoplus_{i=1}^nX_i\), where \(n\geq1\) and \(X_i\neq0\) for every \(i\). It gives morphisms \(\iota_i:X_i\to X\) and \(p_i:X\to X_i\). For each \(1\leq i\leq n\), set \(e_i:=\iota_ip_i\in\operatorname{End}(X)\). These morphisms have the following properties. Recall that an idempotent in the ring \(\operatorname{End}(X)\) is an element \(e\in\operatorname{End}(X)\) satisfying \(e^2=e\); when no confusion can arise, we also call \(e\) an idempotent in \(\mathcal{A}\).

  1. Every \(e_i\) is idempotent: \(e_i^2=(\iota_ip_i)(\iota_ip_i)=\iota_i(p_i\iota_i)p_i=\iota_ip_i\).

  2. Orthogonality: \(i\neq j\implies e_ie_j=\iota_ip_i\iota_jp_j=0\).

  3. The equality \(\sum_{i=1}^ne_i=1\) holds in the ring \(\operatorname{End}(X)\).

From now on we regard the direct summands \(X_i\) as subobjects of \(X\) and write the decomposition as an equality \(X=\bigoplus_{i=1}^nX_i\). Conversely, if \(\mathcal{A}\) is abelian, a family of idempotents \(e_1,\ldots,e_n\in\operatorname{End}(X)\) satisfying (E1)–(E3) determines subobjects of \(X\) by \[X_i := \operatorname{ker}\left( \sum_{j \neq i} e_j \right) = \operatorname{im}(e_i), \quad i=1, \ldots, n.\] On the one hand they come with monomorphisms \(X_i\xrightarrow{\iota_i}X\); on the other, \(e_i:X\to X\) factors uniquely as \(X\xrightarrow{p_i}X_i\xrightarrow{\iota_i}X\). This is precisely the data required for a direct sum. Passing from the idempotents \(e_1,\ldots,e_n\) to the direct summands \(X_1,\ldots,X_n\) does not require all the properties of an abelian category. It is enough to assume that \(\mathcal{A}\) is an \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ab}}\)-category with a zero object in which every idempotent has a kernel. Such a category is called a Karoubian category or a pseudo-abelian category. The exercises of this chapter discuss this further.

Proposition. Let \(X\neq0\) be an object of an abelian category (or, more generally, a Karoubian category) \(\mathcal{A}\), and let \(n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}_{\geq1}\). The constructions above give a bijection \[\text{Diagram chapter2-unit-025-d001}\] Reordering the direct summands \(X_1,\ldots,X_n\) corresponds to reordering the idempotents \(e_1,\ldots,e_n\).

Proof. See [Li1].

In the special case \(n=2\), direct-sum decompositions are related to a special class of short exact sequences, called split short exact sequences.

Proposition. For a short exact sequence \(0\to X'\xrightarrow{f}X\xrightarrow{g}X''\to0\) in an abelian category, the following statements are equivalent.

  1. There is an \(s:X''\to X\) such that \(gs=\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{X''}\).

  2. There is an \(r:X\to X'\) such that \(rf=\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{X'}\).

  3. There is a diagram \(\text{Diagram chapter2-unit-025-diagram-002}\) for which \(X\simeq X'\oplus X''\); see the review of biproducts in §reference.

  4. The map \(g_*:\operatorname{Hom}(S,X)\to\operatorname{Hom}(S,X'')\), sending \(\varphi\) to \(g\varphi\), is surjective for every object \(S\).

  5. The map \(f^*:\operatorname{Hom}(X,S)\to\operatorname{Hom}(X',S)\), sending \(\psi\) to \(\psi f\), is surjective for every object \(S\).

If any of these conditions holds, the short exact sequence \(0\to X'\to X\to X''\to0\) is called split. The morphism \(s:X''\to X\) in (i), the morphism \(r:X\to X'\) in (ii), 1 and the isomorphism \(X\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}X'\oplus X''\) in (iii), denoted by \(\Phi\), correspond as follows:

  • from \(\Phi\) to \(s\), take the composite \(X''\xrightarrow{\iota_2}X'\oplus X''\xrightarrow{\Phi^{-1}}X\);

  • from \(s\) to \(r\), factor \(\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_X-sg:X\to X\) uniquely as \(X\xrightarrow{r}X'\xrightarrow{f}X\); this is the desired \(r\);

  • from \(r\) to \(\Phi\), take \((r,g):X\to X'\oplus X''\), which is an isomorphism.

Moreover, for a given \(s\) or its corresponding \(r\), the orthogonal idempotents corresponding to the direct-sum decomposition in (iii) are \[e' := fr = \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_X - sg, \quad e'' := sg = \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_X - fr.\]

Proof. For modules, see [Li1]. Its proof uses only algebraic operations in \(\operatorname{Hom}\) sets and the characterization of biproducts, all of which also hold in an abelian category, so the argument carries over without change. We omit the details.

In the setting of Proposition reference, given \(f:X'\to X\) and \(g:X\to X''\), an \(s\) satisfying \(gs=\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{X''}\) is called a section of \(g\), while an \(r\) satisfying \(rf=\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{X'}\) is called a retraction of \(f\); these terms come from topology. The existence of a section or retraction implies, respectively, that \(g\) is an epimorphism or \(f\) is a monomorphism, but the converses do not hold. Notice also that the five statements (i)–(v) of the proposition are collectively self-dual.

Definition. Let \(S\) be a nonzero object of an abelian category \(\mathcal{A}\). If \(S=S'\oplus S''\) implies \(S'=0\) or \(S''=0\), then \(S\) is called indecomposable.

Corollary. A nonzero object \(X\) of an abelian category is indecomposable if and only if \[\forall e \in \operatorname{End}(X), \quad e^2 = e \iff (e = 0 \;\vee\; e = 1).\]

Proof. Apply Proposition reference.

We wish to study decompositions \(X=X_1\oplus\cdots\oplus X_n\), where \(X\neq0\) and every \(X_i\) is indecomposable. There are two questions: existence and uniqueness. For modules this is the content of the Krull–Remak–Schmidt theorem; see [Li1]. For a general abelian category, some preparation is needed. We follow the approach of [Kr15].

Definition. Let \(\mathcal{A}\) be any category. A bi-chain in \(\mathcal{A}\) is data \((X_n,\alpha_n,\beta_n)_{n=0}^\infty\), where the \(X_n\) are objects and \(\text{Diagram chapter2-unit-025-diagram-003}\) are morphisms between them, with \(\alpha_n\) an epimorphism and \(\beta_n\) a monomorphism for \(n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}_{\geq0}\). An object \(X\) of \(\mathcal{A}\) is said to satisfy the bi-chain condition if, for every bi-chain \((X_n,\alpha_n,\beta_n)_{n=0}^\infty\) with \(X_0=X\), both \(\alpha_n\) and \(\beta_n\) are isomorphisms for \(n\gg0\).

The following result generalizes [Li1].

Lemma (Fitting’s lemma in an abelian category). Let \(\mathcal{A}\) be an abelian category, let \(X\) be a nonzero object satisfying the bi-chain condition, and let \(f\in\operatorname{End}(X)\).

  1. For \(n\gg0\), \(\operatorname{ker}(f^n)\) and \(\operatorname{im}(f^n)\) are independent of \(n\); denote them by \(\operatorname{ker}(f^\infty)\) and \(\operatorname{im}(f^\infty)\), respectively. Then \(X=\operatorname{ker}(f^\infty)\oplus\operatorname{im}(f^\infty)\).

  2. If \(X\) is indecomposable, then \(f\) is either invertible or nilpotent in the ring \(\operatorname{End}(X)\).

Proof. For \(n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}_{\geq0}\), define \(X_n:=\operatorname{im}(f^n)\), so \(X_0=X\). Proposition reference and \(\operatorname{coim}\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}\operatorname{im}\) give an epimorphism \(\alpha_n:X_n\to X_{n+1}\) induced by \(f\) and a monomorphism \(\beta_n:X_{n+1}\to X_n\). Thus we obtain a bi-chain \((X_n,\alpha_n,\beta_n)_{n=0}^\infty\).

For \(n\gg0\), \(\alpha_n\) and \(\beta_n\) are isomorphisms. Hence the subobject \(\operatorname{im}(f^\infty):=\operatorname{im}(f^n)\) of \(X\), for \(n\gg0\), is well defined; write its monomorphism as \(\iota:\operatorname{im}(f^\infty)\hookrightarrow X\). Likewise, \(\operatorname{ker}(f^n)=\operatorname{ker}[X\to\operatorname{im}(f^n)]\) is a subobject \(\operatorname{ker}(f^\infty)\) independent of \(n\) for \(n\gg0\).

For \(n\gg0\), the morphism \(\alpha_{2n-1}\cdots\alpha_n:X_n\to X_{2n}\) is invertible. Denote its inverse by \(\psi:\operatorname{im}(f^\infty)\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}\operatorname{im}(f^\infty)\) and set \[p := \psi f^n: X \to \operatorname{im}(f^\infty), \quad \operatorname{ker}(p) = \operatorname{ker}(f^\infty) \qquad (n \gg 0).\] Since \(p\iota=\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{\operatorname{im}(f^\infty)}\), the endomorphism \(e:=\iota p\in\operatorname{End}(X)\) is idempotent, with \(\operatorname{im}(e)=\operatorname{im}(f^\infty)\) and \(\operatorname{ker}(e)=\operatorname{ker}(f^\infty)\). Proposition reference gives the decomposition in (i).

If \(X\) is indecomposable, then either \(\operatorname{im}(f^\infty)=0\) and \(\operatorname{ker}(f^\infty)=X\), in which case \(f\) is nilpotent, or \(\operatorname{im}(f^\infty)=X\) and \(\operatorname{ker}(f^\infty)=0\), in which case \(f\) is invertible. This proves (ii).

Recall from [Li1] that if \(S\) is a ring and \(S\smallsetminus S^\times\) is a two-sided ideal, then \(S\) is called local.

Corollary. Let \(X\) be a nonzero object in an abelian category satisfying the bi-chain condition. Then \(X\) is indecomposable if and only if \(\operatorname{End}(X)\) is a local ring.

Proof. Lemma reference shows that if \(X\) is indecomposable, every element of \(\operatorname{End}(X)\) is either nilpotent or invertible. The remainder of the argument concerns only the ring structure of \(\operatorname{End}(X)\) and is the same as [Li1].

We can now state the version of the Krull–Remak–Schmidt theorem for abelian categories.

Theorem (M. Atiyah). Let \(X\) be a nonzero object of an abelian category.

  1. If \(X\) satisfies the bi-chain condition, then there exist \(n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}_{\geq1}\) and indecomposable subobjects \(X_1,\ldots,X_n\) such that \(X=\bigoplus_{i=1}^nX_i\), and every \(\operatorname{End}(X_i)\) is a local ring.

  2. Suppose that \(X\) has decompositions \(\bigoplus_{i=1}^nX_i\) and \(\bigoplus_{j=1}^mX'_j\), where every \(X_i\) and \(X'_j\) is indecomposable and every \(\operatorname{End}(X_i)\) and \(\operatorname{End}(X'_j)\) is local. Then \(n=m\), and there is a bijection \(\sigma\) of \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\) such that \(X_i\simeq X'_{\sigma(i)}\) for every \(i\).

Proof. The main point is to prove that an \(X\) satisfying the bi-chain condition has a decomposition as in (i). Everything else involves only algebraic operations in the rings \(\operatorname{End}\) and is the same as [Li1]. We therefore assume the bi-chain condition in what follows.

If \(X=Y\oplus Z\) with \(Y\neq0\), then \(Y\) also satisfies the bi-chain condition. Indeed, given a bi-chain \((Y_n,\alpha_n,\beta_n)_{n=0}^\infty\) with \(Y_0=Y\), take \(X_n:=Y_n\oplus Z\), \(\tilde{\alpha}_n:=\alpha_n\oplus\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_Z\), and \(\tilde{\beta}_n:=\beta_n\oplus\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_Z\). This gives a bi-chain with \(X_0=X\), while Lemma reference shows that \(\tilde{\alpha}_n\) (or \(\tilde{\beta}_n\)) is an isomorphism if and only if \(\alpha_n\) (or \(\beta_n\)) is.

If \(X\) is already indecomposable, Corollary reference shows that \(\operatorname{End}(X)\) is local, proving (i). If (i) were false for \(X\), there would be nonzero subobjects \(X_1,Y_1\) such that \(X=X_1\oplus Y_1\) and (i) remained false for \(X_1\). Repeating the process on \(X_1\) gives \(X_1=X_2\oplus Y_2\), and iteration produces a bi-chain \((X_n,\alpha_n,\beta_n)_{n=0}^\infty\), where \(\alpha_n:X_n\twoheadrightarrow X_{n+1}\) and \(\beta_n:X_{n+1}\hookrightarrow X_n\) arise from \(X_n=X_{n+1}\oplus Y_{n+1}\). None is an isomorphism, and \(X_0:=X\), contradicting the bi-chain condition. This proves the assertion.

In applications, the key issue is knowing when the bi-chain condition holds. Here is one sufficient condition.

Proposition. Let \(X\) be an object of finite length in an abelian category (Definition reference). Then \(X\) satisfies the bi-chain condition.

Proof. Let \((X_n,\alpha_n,\beta_n)_{n=0}^\infty\) be a bi-chain with \(X_0=X\). Then \[\left(\operatorname{im}(\beta_0\cdots\beta_n)\right)_{n=0}^\infty\] is a descending chain in the partially ordered set \(\mathrm{Sub}_X\). Since all \(\beta_n\) are monomorphisms, for \(n\gg0\) the Artinian condition gives a commutative diagram \[\text{Diagram chapter2-unit-025-d002}\] and \(\beta_n\) is an isomorphism. Similarly, apply the Noetherian condition to the ascending chain \(\left(\operatorname{ker}(\alpha_n\cdots\alpha_0)\right)_{n=0}^\infty\) and use the fact that every \(\alpha_n\) is an epimorphism. For \(n\gg0\) this gives a commutative diagram with exact rows \[\text{Diagram chapter2-unit-025-d003}\] and \(\alpha_n\) is an isomorphism.

The exercises introduce further ways to deduce the bi-chain condition.

  1. Editorial correction (O014-C024): the source writes \(r:X'\to X\) here, but (ii), the equality \(rf=\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{X'}\), and the subsequent construction all require \(r:X\to X'\). The type-correct direction is used here.↩︎

Subobjects and the Isomorphism Theorems

Throughout this section, let \(\mathcal{A}\) be an abelian category. For every object \(X\) of \(\mathcal{A}\), the partially ordered set of its subobjects is denoted by \((\mathrm{Sub}_X,\subset)\), following the convention of §reference. The results of this section are familiar when \(\mathcal{A}=R\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\), where \(R\) is any ring, but different arguments are required for an abelian category.

Definition. Let \(X\) be an object of \(\mathcal{A}\).

  • For a subobject \(X'\) of \(X\), the corresponding quotient is defined by \(X/X':=\operatorname{coker}[X'\to X]\); it is naturally a quotient object of \(X\). Every epimorphism \(f:X\twoheadrightarrow X''\) may be viewed as the quotient of \(X\) by \(\operatorname{ker}(f)\).

  • For subobjects \(X_1,\ldots,X_n\) of \(X\), their intersection and sum are respectively defined by \[\begin{align*} X_1 \cap \cdots \cap X_n & := X_1 \ensuremath{\underset{X}{\times}} \cdots \ensuremath{\underset{X}{\times}} X_n, \\ X_1 + \cdots + X_n & := \operatorname{im}\left[ X_1 \oplus \cdots \oplus X_n \xrightarrow{\sigma} X \right]. \end{align*}\] Here \(\sigma\) is induced by the morphisms \(X_i\hookrightarrow X\) and may be viewed as summation. Both are naturally subobjects of \(X\): the case of \(X_1\cap\cdots\cap X_n\) follows from Lemma reference, while the case of \(X_1+\cdots+X_n\) follows directly from the definition.

For example, the definition of cohomology can be rewritten using a quotient: \[\operatorname{H}^n(X) := \operatorname{ker}(d_X^n)/\operatorname{im}(d_X^{n-1}).\] More generally, let \(I\) be any set and let \((X_i)_{i\in I}\) be a family of subobjects of \(X\). The same method gives a well-defined \(\bigcap_{i\in I}X_i\) (respectively, \(\sum_{i\in I}X_i\)), provided that their fiber product over \(X\) (respectively, their coproduct \(\bigsqcup_{i\in I}X_i\) in \(\mathcal{A}\)) exists. The role of this definition is clarified by the following fact.

Proposition. Let \((X_i)_{i\in I}\) be a family of subobjects of \(X\). If their fiber product over \(X\) (respectively, their coproduct \(\bigsqcup\) in \(\mathcal{A}\)) exists, it gives the infimum (respectively, supremum) of \((X_i)_{i\in I}\) in the partially ordered set \((\mathrm{Sub}_X,\subset)\).

Proof. By construction, \(\bigcap_{j\in I}X_j\subset X_i\subset\sum_{j\in I}X_j\) for every \(i\).

Now consider a subobject \(Y\hookrightarrow X\). For the intersection, suppose that \(\forall i\in I,\;Y\subset X_i\), that is, that there is a family of commutative diagrams \(\text{Diagram chapter2-unit-026-diagram-001}\). The universal property of the fiber product gives a morphism \(Y\to\bigcap_{i\in I}X_i\), and hence \(Y\subset\bigcap_{i\in I}X_i\). For the sum, suppose instead that \(\forall i\in I,\;X_i\subset Y\). The universal property of the coproduct gives a commutative diagram \[\text{Diagram chapter2-unit-026-d001}\]

By Lemma reference, the morphism \(\bigsqcup_{i\in I}X_i\to Y\) factors uniquely through \(\operatorname{coim}(\sigma)\simeq\operatorname{im}(\sigma)\), compatibly with the morphism to \(X\). Thus \(\sum_{i\in I}X_i:=\operatorname{im}(\sigma)\subset Y\).

Convention. In view of Proposition reference, we may also dispense with fiber products or coproducts and define the intersection \(\bigcap_iX_i\) (respectively, the sum \(\sum_iX_i\)) of a family of subobjects \((X_i)_{i\in I}\) directly as their infimum (respectively, supremum) in \(\mathrm{Sub}_X\), whenever it exists. The indexing set \(I\) is always assumed to be small. If \(I\) has a filtered partial order and \(i\leq j\implies X_i\subset X_j\), the supremum \(\sum_{i\in I}X_i\) may equally well be denoted by the increasing union \(\bigcup_{i\in I}X_i\).

Corollary. For every object \(X\), the partially ordered set \((\mathrm{Sub}_X,\subset)\) is a bounded lattice in the sense of Definition reference.

Proof. The supremum of two subobjects \(Y,Z\) is \(Y+Z\), and their infimum is \(Y\cap Z\); the greatest element of \(\mathrm{Sub}_X\) is \(X\), and the least is \(0\).

This section focuses on \((\mathrm{Sub}_X,\subset)\), but the version in terms of quotient objects \((\mathrm{Quot}_X,\twoheadleftarrow)\) is entirely equivalent. Indeed, there is an evident order-reversing bijection \(\mathrm{Sub}_X\simeq\mathrm{Quot}_X\): a subobject \(X'\) and a quotient object \(X''\) correspond if and only if they can be placed in a short exact sequence \(0\to X'\to X\to X''\to0\). We shall therefore not discuss the quotient version separately.

Definition. Given a morphism \(f:X\to Y\) and subobjects \(X'\hookrightarrow X\) and \(Y'\hookrightarrow Y\), write \[f^{-1}(Y') := X \ensuremath{\underset{Y}{\times}} Y', \quad f(X') := \operatorname{im}\left[ X' \hookrightarrow X \xrightarrow{f} Y \right];\] the first is the preimage of \(Y'\) and a subobject of \(X\), while the second is the image of \(X'\) and a subobject of \(Y\). These constructions give order-preserving maps in both directions: \(\text{Diagram chapter2-unit-026-diagram-003}\).

Lemma. Let \(f:X\to Y\) be as above.

  1. For every \(X'\in\mathrm{Sub}_X\) and \(Y'\in\mathrm{Sub}_Y\), \[X' \subset f^{-1}(Y') \iff f(X') \subset Y'.\]

  2. For a family \((X'_i)_{i\in I}\) in \(\mathrm{Sub}_X\) (respectively, \((Y'_i)_{i\in I}\) in \(\mathrm{Sub}_Y\)), 1 we have \[f\left( \sum_{i \in I} X'_i \right) = \sum_{i \in I} f(X'_i), \quad f^{-1}\left( \bigcap_{i \in I} Y'_i \right) = \bigcap_{i \in I} f^{-1}(Y'_i),\] provided the intersections and sums in question exist.

Proof. For (i), by definition \(X'\subset f^{-1}(Y')\) is equivalent to the existence of a commutative diagram \[\text{Diagram chapter2-unit-026-d002}\] Since \(f(X')\) is the image of \(X'\hookrightarrow X\xrightarrow{f}Y\), 2 Lemma reference shows that such diagrams correspond bijectively to \[\text{Diagram chapter2-unit-026-d003}\] which proves (i). If the partially ordered sets are regarded as categories \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Sub}}_X\), and so on, (i) says that \(f(\cdot):\ensuremath{\mathsf{Sub}}_X\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{Sub}}_Y\) is left adjoint to \(f^{-1}(\cdot):\ensuremath{\mathsf{Sub}}_Y\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{Sub}}_X\). Since products (respectively, coproducts) correspond to infima (respectively, suprema), (ii) follows from [Li1].

Proposition. Consider subobjects \(i:A\hookrightarrow X\) and \(j:B\hookrightarrow X\). The morphism \((i,j):A\oplus B\to X\) is an isomorphism if and only if \[A \cap B = 0, \quad A + B = X.\] Moreover, the commutative diagram \[\text{Diagram chapter2-unit-026-d004}\] is both a pushout and a pullback; here \(\delta_1\) and \(\delta_2\) are the canonical morphisms.

Proof. Define the diagonal morphism \(\Delta:A\cap B\to A\oplus B\) by \(p_i\Delta=\delta_i\) for \(i=1,2\). Also define the antidiagonal morphism \(\Delta^-:A\cap B\to A\oplus B\) by \(p_1\Delta^-=-\delta_1\) and \(p_2\Delta^-=\delta_2\).

Remark reference says that \(\Delta\) gives an isomorphism \(A\cap B:=A\ensuremath{\underset{X}{\times}}B\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}} \operatorname{ker}\left[A\oplus B\xrightarrow{(i,-j)}X\right]\). Replacing \((i,-j)\) by \((i,j)\) leaves the image of \(A\oplus B\to X\) equal to \(A+B\), while the kernel morphism changes from \(\Delta\) to \(\Delta^-\). We therefore obtain a commutative diagram with an exact row \[\text{Diagram chapter2-unit-026-d005}\] Thus \((i,j):A\oplus B\to X\) is an isomorphism if and only if \(A+B=X\) and \(A\cap B=0\).

Remark reference also identifies \(A\ensuremath{\underset{A\cap B}{\sqcup}}B\) with \((A\oplus B)/\operatorname{im}(\Delta^-)\). Hence we have a commutative diagram \[\text{Diagram chapter2-unit-026-d006}\] whose upper-left square is a pushout; its outer frame is therefore also a pushout. Since \(\delta_1\) is a monomorphism, Proposition reference shows that the outer frame is also a pullback.

In other words, \(B\) is a complement of \(A\) in the lattice \(\mathrm{Sub}_X\) (Definition reference) if and only if \((i,j):A\oplus B\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}X\); the latter is often written as \(A\oplus B=X\). Starting from this fact, one can recursively use lattice-theoretic language to determine whether \(X\) is a direct sum of finitely many prescribed subobjects \(X_1,\ldots,X_n\); the result is analogous to the module case. For an infinite family of subobjects one generally needs to work in a Grothendieck category; see r@sec:Grothendieck-cat§reference§2.10. The related material is left to the exercises. Module theory rests on several basic isomorphism theorems; see [Li1]. We now extend them to an arbitrary abelian category \(\mathcal{A}\).

Theorem. Fix an object \(X\).

  1. For every morphism \(f:X\to Y\), there is a canonical isomorphism \(X/\operatorname{ker}(f)\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}\operatorname{im}(f)\) making the diagram \[\text{Diagram chapter2-unit-026-d007} \quad \text{commutative}.\]

  2. Fix a subobject \(Z\hookrightarrow X\), and denote the natural morphism \(X\twoheadrightarrow\overline{X}:=X/Z\) by \(\pi\). There is an order-preserving bijection \[\text{Diagram chapter2-unit-026-d008}\] with notation as in Definition reference. If \(Y\supset Z\), there is a canonical isomorphism \(X/Y\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}\overline{X}/\overline{Y}\) making the diagram \[\text{Diagram chapter2-unit-026-d009}\] commutative. Moreover, \(\overline{Y_1\cap Y_2}=\overline{Y_1}\cap\overline{Y_2}\) and \(\overline{Y_1+Y_2}=\overline{Y_1}+\overline{Y_2}\).

  3. For \(Y,Z\in\mathrm{Sub}_X\), there is a canonical isomorphism \(Y/(Y\cap Z)\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}(Y+Z)/Z\) making the diagram \[\text{Diagram chapter2-unit-026-d010} \quad \text{commutative}.\]

Proof. In view of the short exact sequence \(0\to\operatorname{ker}(f)\to X\to\operatorname{im}(f)\to0\), assertion (i) merely restates the definition.

For (ii), given \(Y\), first form the following commutative diagram with exact rows: \[\text{Diagram chapter2-unit-026-d011}\] The dashed arrow comes from functoriality of cokernels equation. Theorem reference immediately gives \(\operatorname{ker}[Y/Z\to\overline{X}]=0\) and \(X/Y\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}\operatorname{coker}[Y/Z\to\overline{X}]\). In particular, \[Y/Z = \operatorname{im}[Y \to \overline{X}] = \pi(Y) \;\in \mathrm{Sub}_{\overline{X}}, \quad X/Y \simeq \overline{X}/\pi(Y).\]

We have already observed that both maps in (ii) preserve order. We now show that they are inverse. Given \(Y\), the monomorphism \(\overline{Y}\hookrightarrow\overline{X}\) is the kernel of \(\overline{X}\to\overline{X}/\overline{Y}\). Hence Proposition reference says that \(\pi^{-1}(\overline{Y}):=X\ensuremath{\underset{\overline{X}}{\times}}\overline{Y}\hookrightarrow X\) is the kernel of the composite \(X\to\overline{X}\to\overline{X}/\overline{Y}\). By the preceding isomorphism, this is also the kernel of \(X\to X/Y\), identifying \(\pi^{-1}(\overline{Y})\) with \(Y\).

Conversely, given \(\overline{Y}\), set \(Y:=X\ensuremath{\underset{\overline{X}}{\times}}\overline{Y}=\pi^{-1}(\overline{Y})\) and consider the pullback diagram \[\text{Diagram chapter2-unit-026-d012}\] Since \(\pi\) in the lower row is an epimorphism, Proposition reference says that the morphism in the upper row is also an epimorphism. Thus \(\overline{Y}=\pi(Y)\).

Finally, the equalities \(\overline{Y_1\cap Y_2}=\overline{Y_1}\cap\overline{Y_2}\) and \(\overline{Y_1+Y_2}=\overline{Y_1}+\overline{Y_2}\) follow immediately from the order-preserving bijection \(Y\leftrightarrow\overline{Y}\).

For (iii), consider the commutative diagram with exact rows \[\text{Diagram chapter2-unit-026-d013}\] where \(\theta\) comes from functoriality of cokernels. Proposition reference says that the left square is a pushout. Pushouts preserve cokernels (Proposition reference), so \(\theta\) is an isomorphism.

Corollary. Consider a commutative diagram \[\text{Diagram chapter2-unit-026-d014}\] where \(k,c\) are the morphisms characterized by functoriality equation. If the middle square is a pullback (respectively, a pushout), then \(c\) is a monomorphism (respectively, \(k\) is an epimorphism).

Proof. It is enough to handle the pullback case. Since pullback along \(f\) can be performed in stages, it suffices to consider two cases: \(f\) is an epimorphism or \(f\) is a monomorphism. If \(f\) is an epimorphism, Proposition reference says that the middle square is also a pushout, and then \(c\) is an isomorphism. If \(f\) is a monomorphism, factor the pullback along \(g\) into stages as \[\text{Diagram chapter2-unit-026-d015}\] Proposition reference says that \(W\to\operatorname{im}(g)\ensuremath{\underset{Z}{\times}}Y\) is an epimorphism, so \(\operatorname{coker}(g')=\operatorname{coker}(g'')\). It remains to consider the case in which both \(f\) and \(g\) are monomorphisms. Then \(W=Y\cap X\), and \(c\) factors as \(Y/(Y\cap X)\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}(Y+X)/X\hookrightarrow Z/X\).

Theorem. For every object \(X\), the partially ordered set \((\mathrm{Sub}_X,\subset)\) is a bounded modular lattice in the sense of Definition reference.

Proof. We already know that \((\mathrm{Sub}_X,\subset)\) is a bounded lattice. Consider any interval \([Y_1,Y_2]\) in \(\mathrm{Sub}_X\). Lemma reference reduces the problem to the following assertion: for all \(A,B,C\in[Y_1,Y_2]\), \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:Abel-cat-interval-complement}{} \left( A, B \;\text{are both complements of}\; C, \; A \subset B \right) \implies A = B. \end{equation}\]

First, the order-preserving bijection in Theorem reference(ii) reduces equation to the case \(Y_1=0\) and \(Y_2=X\). By Proposition reference, the hypothesis about complements becomes \(A\oplus C\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}X\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\leftarrow}}B\oplus C\), where the two isomorphisms are induced by the monomorphisms \(\iota_A,\iota_B,\iota_C\) from \(A,B,C\) to \(X\).
