By hypothesis, there is an \(\alpha:A\to B\) such that \(\iota_A=\iota_B\alpha\). Hence the diagram \[\text{Diagram chapter2-unit-026-d016}\] is commutative. Thus \((\alpha,\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_C)\) is an isomorphism, and Lemma reference then implies that \(\alpha\) is an isomorphism. This proves equation.

Modularity of the subobject lattice is an important bridge for transporting standard arguments from module theory to abelian categories.

  1. Editorial correction (O014-C025): the source introduces the families \((X_i)\) and \((Y_i)\) without primes, while the two formulas that follow use \(X'_i\) and \(Y'_i\). Primes are added to the declaration to match the formulas.↩︎

  2. Editorial correction (O014-C026): the source calls \(f(X')\) the coimage, but Definition reference defines it as \(\operatorname{im}[X'\to X\to Y]\), namely the image and a subobject of \(Y\). The term consistent with that object is used here.↩︎

Simple and Semisimple Objects

Throughout this section, let \(\mathcal{A}\) be an abelian category.

Convention. By convention, the coproduct \(\coprod_{i \in I} X_i\) of a family of objects \((X_i)_{i \in I}\) in an abelian category, whenever it exists, is written \(\bigoplus_{i \in I} X_i\) and called their direct sum. If \(I\) is finite, all the conventions of Definition reference apply.

Definition. A nonzero object \(X\) of \(\mathcal{A}\) is called simple if \(\mathrm{Sub}_X=\left\{0,X\right\}\).

Simplicity of \(X\) means that for every short exact sequence \(0\to X'\to X\to X''\to0\), exactly one of \(X'=0\) and \(X'\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}X\) holds; equivalently, exactly one of \(X\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}X''\) and \(X''=0\) holds. Consequently, \(X\) is simple in \(\mathcal{A}\) if and only if it is simple in \(\mathcal{A}^{\operatorname{op}}\). Notice that \(X\neq0\) if and only if \(\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_X\neq0\), and this is also equivalent to \(\operatorname{End}(X)\) being a nonzero ring.

Lemma (Schur’s lemma). Let \(X,Y\) be objects. If \(X\) (respectively, \(Y\)) is simple, then every nonzero morphism in \(\operatorname{Hom}(X,Y)\) is a monomorphism (respectively, an epimorphism). Consequently, if \(X\) is simple, then \(\operatorname{End}(X)\) is a division ring.

Proof. Suppose that \(X\) is simple and that \(f:X\to Y\) is nonzero. Then necessarily \(\operatorname{ker}(f)=0\). The case in which \(Y\) is simple follows by duality. A morphism that is both a monomorphism and an epimorphism is an isomorphism (Proposition reference); taking \(X=Y\) therefore shows that \(\operatorname{End}(X)\) is a division ring.

We know that \(\mathrm{Sub}_X\) is a bounded modular lattice (Theorem reference). Lemma reference shows that \(X\) has finite length if and only if the partially ordered set \([0,X]\) has a composition series; such a series is also called a composition series of \(X\). For an object \(X\) of finite length, its length is defined by \[\ell(X) := \text{the length of }\mathrm{Sub}_X\;\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}_{\geq0};\] see Definition reference. Notice that \(\ell(X)=0\iff X=0\). By convention, \(Y\subsetneq Z\) means \(Y\subset Z\) and \(Y\neq Z\).

Definition–Theorem (Jordan–Hölder theorem). Let \(X\) be an object of finite length, and choose a composition series \(X=X_0\supsetneq\cdots\supsetneq X_r=0\). The objects \(X_i/X_{i+1}\), considered up to isomorphism, are called the composition factors of \(X\). They are simple. Their multiset, with multiplicities, is denoted \(\mathrm{JH}(X)\) and is independent of the chosen composition series.

Proof. The composition factors must be simple, for otherwise \(X_0\supsetneq\cdots\supsetneq X_r\) would admit a proper refinement. Let \(X=X'_0\supsetneq\cdots\supsetneq X'_s\) be another composition series. Theorem reference says that it is equivalent to \(X_0\supsetneq\cdots\supsetneq X_r\). In particular, there is a bijection \(i\leftrightarrow j\) between their index sets such that the intervals \(\left[X_{i+1},X_i\right]\) and \(\left[X'_{j+1},X'_j\right]\) can be linked by standard isomorphisms \([a\wedge b,a]\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}[b,a\vee b]\) in a modular lattice; see Proposition reference.

So far everything has been phrased in lattice-theoretic language. However, Theorem reference(iii) shows that such interval isomorphisms correspond to isomorphisms of quotient objects in \(\mathcal{A}\), \[X_i/X_{i+1} \simeq X'_j/X'_{j+1}.\] As \(i\leftrightarrow j\) varies, this proves that the composition factors are independent of the chosen composition series, up to isomorphism and reordering.

The number of elements of \(\mathrm{JH}(X)\), counted with multiplicity, is exactly \(\ell(X)\). Multisets also have a union operation, which adds multiplicities; it will again be denoted by \(\cup\).

Lemma. Given a short exact sequence \(0\to X'\to X\to X''\to0\), the object \(X\) has finite length if and only if both \(X'\) and \(X''\) do. In that case, \(\mathrm{JH}(X)=\mathrm{JH}(X')\cup\mathrm{JH}(X'')\), and hence \(\ell(X)=\ell(X')+\ell(X'')\).

Proof. Theorem reference(ii) identifies \(\mathrm{Sub}_{X'}\) and \(\mathrm{Sub}_{X''}\) with the intervals \([0,X']\) and \([X',X]\) in \(\mathrm{Sub}_X\), respectively. Thus finite length of \(X\) implies finite length of \(X'\) and \(X''\). Conversely, suppose that \(X'\) and \(X''\) have finite length, and choose composition series \[X'=X'_0\supsetneq\cdots\supsetneq X'_r=0,\quad X''=X''_0\supsetneq\cdots\supsetneq X''_s=0.\] By Theorem reference(ii), lift every \(X''_i\) to a subobject \(Y_i\) of \(X\) satisfying \(Y_i\supset X'\). In particular, \(Y_0=X\) and \(Y_s=X'\), so \[X=Y_0\supsetneq\cdots\supsetneq Y_s\supsetneq X'_1\supsetneq\cdots \supsetneq X'_r=0\] is a composition series whose subquotients form \(\mathrm{JH}(X')\cup\mathrm{JH}(X'')\).

Definition. An object \(X\) is called

  • semisimple if \(X=\bigoplus_{i\in I}X_i\) for some family of simple objects \((X_i)_{i\in I}\);

  • split if every short exact sequence \(0\to X'\to X\to X''\to0\) splits.

If every object of \(\mathcal{A}\) is semisimple (respectively, split), then \(\mathcal{A}\) is called a semisimple (respectively, split) abelian category.1

Many sources require \(I\) to be finite in the definition of a semisimple object.

Lemma. If \(X=\bigoplus_{i=1}^nX_i\), where \(X_1,\ldots,X_n\) are simple, then \(X\) has finite length, \(\mathrm{JH}(X)=\left\{X_1,\ldots,X_n\right\}\), counted with multiplicity, and \(\ell(X)=n\).

Proof. Consider the composition series \(\bigoplus_{i=1}^nX_i\supsetneq\bigoplus_{i=1}^{n-1}X_i\supsetneq\cdots \supsetneq0\).

Remark. For a general semisimple object \(X=\bigoplus_{i\in I}X_i\), the Noetherian, Artinian, and finite-length properties of \(X\) are all equivalent to finiteness of \(I\). Indeed, by adding (or removing) direct summands indexed by \(I\), one can readily construct a strictly ascending (or strictly descending) chain in \(\mathrm{Sub}_X\).

We wish to understand the relation between split and semisimple objects. The argument is similar to the module case [Li1].

Proposition. Let \(X\) be a split object. Then every subobject and every quotient object of \(X\) is split. If, in addition, \(X\) is Artinian, then \(X\) is a semisimple object of finite length.

Proof. Given a short exact sequence \(0\to X'\to X\to X''\to0\), the hypothesis implies \(X\simeq X'\oplus X''\), so \(X''\) embeds as a subobject of \(X\). It is therefore enough to show that every subobject \(X'\) of \(X\) is split. Given \(X'_0\subset X'\), there is a \(Y\subset X\) such that \(X=X'_0\oplus Y\). It remains to prove \[X'=X'_0\oplus(Y\cap X').\] This follows from Proposition reference. On the one hand, \(X'_0\cap(Y\cap X')\subset X'_0\cap Y=0\). On the other hand, \(\mathrm{Sub}_X\) is modular, and hence \(X'_0+(Y\cap X')=X'\cap(Y+X'_0)=X'\cap X=X'\). This proves the displayed decomposition.

Now suppose also that \(X\) is Artinian. If \(X\neq0\), it has a minimal nonzero subobject \(X_1\), which must be simple, and there is a direct-sum decomposition \(X=X_1\oplus Y_1\). The object \(Y_1\) is still Artinian and split. If \(Y_1\neq0\), continue by writing \(Y_1=X_2\oplus Y_2\), and so on. The Artinian condition ensures that the strictly descending chain \(X\supsetneq Y_1\supsetneq Y_2\cdots\) terminates after finitely many steps, giving the required decomposition \(X=X_1\oplus\cdots\oplus X_n\).

We may ask conversely whether semisimple objects are split. For a general abelian category, a finiteness assumption is again needed.

Proposition. For an object \(X\), consider the following properties.

  1. \(X=\sum_{Y\in\mathcal{F}}Y\), where \(\mathcal{F}\) is a finite subset of \(\mathrm{Sub}_X\) and every \(Y\in\mathcal{F}\) is simple;

  2. \(X=\bigoplus_{Y\in\mathcal{F}}Y\), where \(\mathcal{F}\) is a finite subset of \(\mathrm{Sub}_X\) and every \(Y\in\mathcal{F}\) is simple;

  3. \(X\) is split.

Then (i) \(\implies\) (ii) \(\implies\) (iii).

Proof. Repeat the proof of (i) \(\implies\) (ii) \(\implies\) (iii) in [Li1].

Remark. To extend Proposition reference to an infinite subset \(\mathcal{F}\subset\mathrm{Sub}_X\), one must require \(\mathcal{A}\) to be a Grothendieck category, as introduced in § 2.10. Every semisimple object in a Grothendieck category is then split, and every semisimple Grothendieck category is automatically split. Once the relevant definitions are in place, the argument is similar to the module case and is left as an exercise in this chapter.

  1. Terminology in the literature is not uniform; some authors call what is termed a split abelian category here a semisimple abelian category.↩︎

Exact Functors, Injective Objects, and Projective Objects

Given a functor \(F: \mathcal{A} \to \mathcal{B}\), one may ask whether it preserves \(\varinjlim\) or \(\varprojlim\); see [Li1] or the discussion in §reference. This section focuses on the case in which \(\mathcal{A}\) and \(\mathcal{B}\) are abelian categories and \(F\) is an additive functor. Taking the special instances of \(\varprojlim\) (or \(\varinjlim\)) given by \(\operatorname{ker}\) (or \(\operatorname{coker}\)), every morphism \(f:X\to Y\) in \(\mathcal{A}\) yields a canonical morphism \(F\operatorname{ker}(f)\to\operatorname{ker}F(f)\) and its dual \(\operatorname{coker}F(f)\to F\operatorname{coker}(f)\); they make the following diagrams commute. \[\text{Diagram chapter2-unit-028-d001} \quad \text{Diagram chapter2-unit-028-d002}\]

  • If \(F\operatorname{ker}(f)\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}\operatorname{ker}F(f)\) for every \(f\), we say that \(F\) preserves kernels;

  • if \(\operatorname{coker}F(f)\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}F\operatorname{coker}(f)\) for every \(f\), we say that \(F\) preserves cokernels.

If \((X^\bullet,d^\bullet)\) is a complex in an abelian category, then \((FX^\bullet,Fd^\bullet)\) is also a complex; the issue to be examined is exactness.

Proposition. For an additive functor \(F:\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{B}\) between abelian categories, the following statements are equivalent:

  1. \(F\) preserves kernels;

  2. if \(0\to X'\xrightarrow{f}X\xrightarrow{g}X''\) is exact in \(\mathcal{A}\), then \(0\to F(X')\xrightarrow{Ff}F(X)\xrightarrow{Fg}F(X'')\) is exact in \(\mathcal{B}\);

  3. \(F\) preserves all finite \(\varprojlim\).

Dually, the following statements are also equivalent:

  1. \(F\) preserves cokernels;

  2. if \(X'\xrightarrow{f}X\xrightarrow{g}X''\to0\) is exact in \(\mathcal{A}\), then \(F(X')\xrightarrow{Ff}F(X)\xrightarrow{Fg}F(X'')\to0\) is exact in \(\mathcal{B}\);

  3. \(F\) preserves all finite \(\varinjlim\).

Proof. By duality, it suffices to discuss (L1)–(L3).

(L1) \(\implies\) (L2). An exact sequence of the form \(0\to\bullet\to\bullet\to\bullet\) is precisely a kernel diagram of a morphism; see the explanation at the end of §reference.

(L2) \(\implies\) (L3). Every finite \(\varprojlim\) can be constructed from finite products and equalizers. We already know that additive functors preserve biproducts; since \(F\) preserves \(\operatorname{ker}\), it preserves all equalizers (Remark reference). Thus \(F\) preserves all finite \(\varprojlim\).

(L3) \(\implies\) (L1) is immediate.

For an additive functor \(F\) as above, if every exact sequence \((X^\bullet,d^\bullet)\) gives an exact sequence \((FX^\bullet,Fd^\bullet)\), we say that \(F\) preserves exact sequences. Likewise, one may ask whether \(F\) preserves short exact sequences; these two properties turn out to be equivalent.

Proposition. For an additive functor \(F:\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{B}\) between abelian categories, the following statements are equivalent:

  1. \(F\) preserves short exact sequences;

  2. \(F\) preserves exact sequences;

  3. \(F\) preserves all finite \(\varprojlim\) and finite \(\varinjlim\).

Proof. (E1) \(\implies\) (E2). Take an exact sequence \((X^\bullet,d^\bullet)\) in \(\mathcal{A}\) and decompose the complex into short exact sequences \[\text{Diagram chapter2-unit-028-d003}\] where the morphism \(\mathbf{d}^n\) is characterized by \(d^n=\iota^{n+1}\mathbf{d}^n\); the index \(n\) may be arbitrary, except that \(X^n\) cannot be the rightmost term of the exact sequence.

By assumption, the sequence \(0\to F(\operatorname{ker}(d^n))\xrightarrow{F\iota^n}F(X^n) \xrightarrow{F\mathbf{d}^n}F(\operatorname{ker}(d^{n+1}))\to0\) remains exact, and \(Fd^n=F\iota^{n+1}F\mathbf{d}^n\). The short exact sequences can therefore be reassembled into the exact sequence \((FX^\bullet,Fd^\bullet)\) in \(\mathcal{B}\).

(E2) \(\implies\) (E3). If \(F\) preserves exact sequences, it satisfies conditions (L2) and (R2) of Proposition reference.

(E3) \(\implies\) (E1). Suppose that \(0\to X'\to X\to X''\to0\) is exact in \(\mathcal{A}\). Applying Proposition reference once more, we see that \(0\to F(X')\to F(X)\to F(X'')\) and \(F(X')\to F(X)\to F(X'')\to0\) are both exact; hence \(0\to F(X')\to F(X)\to F(X'')\to0\) is exact.

Notice that (E3) \(\iff\) (L3) \(\wedge\) (R3).

Definition (Exact functors). For an additive functor \(F:\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{B}\) between abelian categories, consider conditions (L1)–(L3), (R1)–(R3) of Proposition reference, and conditions (E1)–(E3) of Proposition reference.

  • If any of (L1)–(L3) holds, then \(F\) is called left exact.

  • If any of (R1)–(R3) holds, then \(F\) is called right exact.

  • If any of (E1)–(E3) holds, then \(F\) is called exact; this is equivalent to saying that \(F\) is both left exact and right exact.

For example, every equivalence between abelian categories is of course an exact functor. Another extreme example is the zero functor: it sends every object to a zero object and every morphism to a zero morphism; this functor is also exact. By Lemma reference, a left exact functor preserves monomorphisms, while a right exact functor preserves epimorphisms.

Remark. In view of (E1), if \(F\) is known to be left exact (or right exact), then \(F\) is exact if and only if \(F\) preserves epimorphisms (or monomorphisms).

A standard way to check left or right exactness is by means of adjoint functors.

Theorem. Consider a pair of additive functors between abelian categories \(\mathcal{A}\) and \(\mathcal{B}\): \[\text{Diagram chapter2-unit-028-d004}\] Suppose that \(F\) and \(G\) can be equipped as an adjoint pair \((F,G,\varphi)\). Then \(F\) is right exact and \(G\) is left exact; indeed, \(F\) preserves \(\varinjlim\) and \(G\) preserves \(\varprojlim\).

Proof. Apply [Li1] and conditions (L3), (R3) of Proposition reference.

Example (Left/right exactness of limits). Let \(\mathcal{A}\) be an abelian category, let \(I\) be any category, and suppose that every functor \(\alpha:I\to\mathcal{A}\) has a \(\varinjlim\) (or a \(\varprojlim\)). Endow \(\mathcal{A}^I\) with the abelian-category structure of Proposition reference. We shall show that the functor \(\varinjlim:\mathcal{A}^I\to\mathcal{A}\) (or \(\varprojlim\)) is right exact (or left exact).

It suffices to discuss \(\varinjlim\). By Theorem reference, one strategy is to show that \(\varinjlim\) has a right adjoint. Define the diagonal functor \(\Delta:\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{A}^I\), which sends \(L\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{A})\) to the constant functor \(\operatorname{Ob}(I)\ni i\mapsto L\). We have an adjoint pair \[\text{Diagram chapter2-unit-028-d005}\] This follows immediately from the universal property of \(\varinjlim\): in \(\mathcal{A}^I\), giving a morphism from a functor \(\alpha:I\to\mathcal{A}\) to \(\Delta(L)\) is equivalent to giving a compatible family of morphisms \(f_i:\alpha(i)\to L\); in other words, a cone with base \(\alpha\) and vertex \(L\). See the related review in §reference.

Example. Let \(f:R\to S\) be a ring homomorphism. Consider the following functors between categories of left modules: \[\text{Diagram chapter2-unit-028-d006}\] Here the forgetful functor \({}_{R\to S}\mathcal{F}\) is simply the operation of regarding an \(S\)-module as an \(R\)-module via \(f\). The functors \(S\ensuremath{\underset{R}{\otimes}}(\cdot)\) and \(\operatorname{Hom}_R({}_R S,\cdot)\) are discussed in [Li1]; here \({}_R S\) means \(S\) regarded as a left \(R\)-module. According to [Li1], \[\left(S\ensuremath{\underset{R}{\otimes}}-,\;{}_{R\to S}\mathcal{F}\right) \quad\text{and}\quad \left({}_{R\to S}\mathcal{F},\;\operatorname{Hom}_R({}_R S,-)\right)\] are adjoint pairs. Theorem reference then implies \[S\ensuremath{\underset{R}{\otimes}}(\cdot)\ \text{is right exact},\quad \operatorname{Hom}({}_R S,\cdot)\ \text{is left exact},\quad {}_{R\to S}\mathcal{F}\ \text{is exact}.\] This exactness can also be checked directly by algebraic means. For example, for the forgetful functor \({}_{R\to S}\mathcal{F}\), whether a sequence of module homomorphisms \(\cdots\to M^n\xrightarrow{d^n}M^{n+1}\to\cdots\) is a complex (that is, \(d^{n+1}d^n=0\)), or is exact (that is, \(\operatorname{im}(d^n)=\operatorname{ker}(d^{n+1})\)), depends only on the additive-group structure of \(M^n\), not on multiplication in \(R\) or \(S\). In other words, \({}_{\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\to S}\mathcal{F}:S\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ab}}\) is already an exact functor. Alternatively, one can check directly that \({}_{R\to S}\mathcal{F}\) preserves all limits; this follows directly from the construction in [Li1].

An exact functor automatically preserves the \(\operatorname{im}\simeq\operatorname{coim}\) of a morphism (Definition reference, Proposition reference); it also preserves cohomology.

Proposition. Let \(F:\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{B}\) be an exact functor between abelian categories. For every complex \((X^\bullet,d^\bullet)\) in \(\mathcal{A}\), there is a canonical isomorphism in \(\mathcal{B}\) \[F\operatorname{H}^n(X^\bullet,d^\bullet)\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}} \operatorname{H}^n(FX^\bullet,Fd^\bullet),\qquad n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}.\]

Proof. It suffices to consider a three-term complex \(X'\xrightarrow{f}X\xrightarrow{g}X''\). Returning to definition equation, \[\begin{multline*} F\left(\operatorname{H}\left[X'\xrightarrow{f}X\xrightarrow{g}X''\right]\right) =F\operatorname{coker}\left[\operatorname{im}(f)\to\operatorname{ker}(g)\right]\\ \simeq\operatorname{coker}\left[F\operatorname{im}(f)\to F\operatorname{ker}(g)\right]\\ \simeq\operatorname{coker}\left[\operatorname{im}(Ff)\to\operatorname{ker}(Fg)\right] =\operatorname{H}\left[FX'\xrightarrow{Ff}FX\xrightarrow{Fg}FX''\right], \end{multline*}\] and all the isomorphisms that occur are canonical.

Faithful exact functors have particularly useful properties.

Proposition. For an additive functor \(F:\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{B}\) between abelian categories, the following statements are equivalent:

  1. \(F\) is exact and faithful;

  2. \(F\) is exact, and \(FX=0\iff X=0\) for every \(X\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{A})\);

  3. \(X'\to X\to X''\) is exact in \(\mathcal{A}\) if and only if \(FX'\to FX\to FX''\) is exact in \(\mathcal{B}\).

Proof. (i) \(\implies\) (ii): If \(FX=0\), then \(F(\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_X)=\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{FX}=0\), whence \(\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_X=0\) and \(X=0\).

(ii) \(\implies\) (iii): Apply Proposition reference to the cohomology.

(iii) \(\implies\) (i): This condition immediately implies that \(F\) is exact. Suppose that \(u:X\to Y\) satisfies \(Fu=0\). Since \[X\xrightarrow{\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}}X\xrightarrow{u}Y\xrightarrow{\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}}Y,\] the image of this sequence under \(F\) is exact; hence the sequence itself is exact and \(u=0\).

Localization (see §reference) provides an important example of an exact functor.

Proposition (Exactness of localization). Let \(\mathcal{A}\) be an abelian category and let \(S\subset\operatorname{Mor}(\mathcal{A})\) be a multiplicative family (Definition reference). Then the category \(\mathcal{A}[S^{-1}]\) supplied by Theorem reference has a canonical abelian-category structure, and the localization functor \(Q:\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{A}[S^{-1}]\) is exact.

Proof. Theorem reference gives \(\mathcal{A}[S^{-1}]\) a canonical additive-category structure under which \(Q\) is an additive functor. We shall show that every morphism \(f\) in \(\mathcal{A}[S^{-1}]\) has a kernel and cokernel and is strict. By the construction of \(\mathcal{A}[S^{-1}]\), after composing \(f\) with an isomorphism from \(S\), we may assume that \(f\) is the image under \(Q\) of a morphism in \(\mathcal{A}\); this does not change the property to be proved. Lemma reference says that \(Q\) preserves all finite \(\varinjlim\) and \(\varprojlim\). In particular, \(Q\) sends \(\operatorname{ker}\), \(\operatorname{coker}\), \(\operatorname{im}\), and \(\operatorname{coim}\) in \(\mathcal{A}\) to the corresponding constructions in \(\mathcal{A}[S^{-1}]\), and therefore also preserves diagram equation. This shows that \(\mathcal{A}[S^{-1}]\) is an abelian category; condition (E3) of Proposition reference shows that \(Q\) is exact.

If, in addition, \(\mathcal{A}\) is a \(\Bbbk\)-linear abelian category, where \(\Bbbk\) is a commutative ring, then \(Q\) is a functor between \(\Bbbk\)-linear abelian categories. This too is part of Theorem reference. Another extremely important example is the \(\operatorname{Hom}\) functor. If \(T\) is an object of an abelian category \(\mathcal{A}\), then \(\operatorname{Hom}(T,\cdot)\) defines a functor \(\mathcal{A}\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ab}}\), while \(\operatorname{Hom}(\cdot,T)\) defines a functor \(\mathcal{A}^{\operatorname{op}}\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ab}}\); on morphisms, they send \(f:X\to Y\) to \(f_*\) and \(f^*\) on \(\operatorname{Hom}\), respectively. Both are plainly additive functors. If \(\mathcal{A}\) is a \(\Bbbk\)-linear abelian category, the \(\operatorname{Hom}\) functors may take values in \(\Bbbk\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\) and become \(\Bbbk\)-linear. This extension has little effect on the discussion below, so we do not treat it separately.

Proposition (Left exactness of \(\operatorname{Hom}\)). Let \(\mathcal{A}\) be an abelian category and let \(T\) be an object of \(\mathcal{A}\). Then \(\operatorname{Hom}(T,\cdot):\mathcal{A}\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ab}}\) and \(\operatorname{Hom}(\cdot,T):\mathcal{A}^{\operatorname{op}}\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ab}}\) are both left exact functors.

Proof. By duality (replacing \(\mathcal{A}\) by \(\mathcal{A}^{\operatorname{op}}\)), it suffices to treat \(\operatorname{Hom}(T,\cdot)\). The point is to show that \(\operatorname{Hom}(T,\cdot)\) preserves \(\operatorname{ker}\). Since \(\operatorname{ker}\) in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ab}}\) is simply the kernel from group theory, this follows immediately from the universal property of \(\operatorname{ker}\).

Definition. Let \(X\) be an object of an abelian category \(\mathcal{A}\). If \(\operatorname{Hom}(X,\cdot):\mathcal{A}\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ab}}\) is an exact functor, then \(X\) is called a projective object; if \(\operatorname{Hom}(\cdot,X):\mathcal{A}^{\operatorname{op}}\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ab}}\) is an exact functor, then \(X\) is called an injective object.

By Remark reference and Proposition reference, to decide whether an object \(X\) is projective (or injective), it suffices to check whether the functor \(\operatorname{Hom}(X,\cdot)\) (or \(\operatorname{Hom}(\cdot,X)\)) preserves epimorphisms. Consequently:

  • An object \(P\) is projective if and only if, for every exact sequence in \(\mathcal{A}\) of the form \(Y\xrightarrow{g}X\to0\) and every morphism \(P\to X\), there exists a \(P\to Y\) making the following diagram commute. \[\text{Diagram chapter2-unit-028-d007}\] (Equivalently, \(g_*:\operatorname{Hom}(P,Y)\to\operatorname{Hom}(P,X)\) is surjective.)

  • An object \(I\) is injective if and only if, for every exact sequence in \(\mathcal{A}\) of the form \(0\to X\xrightarrow{f}Y\) and every morphism \(X\to I\), there exists a \(Y\to I\) making the following diagram commute. \[\text{Diagram chapter2-unit-028-d008}\] (Equivalently, \(f^*:\operatorname{Hom}(Y,I)\to\operatorname{Hom}(X,I)\) is surjective.)

Lemma. Consider a short exact sequence \(0\to X'\xrightarrow{f}X\xrightarrow{g}X''\to0\) in an abelian category. If \(X'\) is injective or \(X''\) is projective, then this short exact sequence splits.

Proof. By duality, we may assume without loss of generality that \(X'\) is injective. Apply the characterization above to the commutative diagram \[\text{Diagram chapter2-unit-028-d009}\] The relation \(rf=\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{X'}\) then satisfies the condition of Proposition reference.

Lemma. Consider a family of objects \((X_i)_{i\in I}\) in an abelian category \(\mathcal{A}\). If the coproduct \(\coprod_{i\in I}X_i\) (or the product \(\prod_{i\in I}X_i\)) exists in \(\mathcal{A}\), then the coproduct is projective (or the product is injective) if and only if every \(X_i\) is so.

Proof. By duality, it suffices to consider the coproduct \(\coprod_{i\in I}X_i\). The universal property gives an isomorphism of functors \[\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{A}}\left(\coprod_{i\in I}X_i,-\right) \ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}\prod_{i\in I}\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{A}}\left(X_i,-\right): \mathcal{A}\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ab}}.\] It remains only to use the following elementary observation: for a family of maps \((f_i:A_i\to B_i)_{i\in I}\), where \(A_i,B_i\) are sets, the induced map \((f_i)_{i\in I}:\prod_{i\in I}A_i\to\prod_{i\in I}B_i\) is surjective if and only if every \(f_i\) is surjective.

For example, let \(R\) be a ring. Every free \(R\)-module is a projective object of \(R\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\). Indeed, it suffices to show that \(R\) itself is projective; but \(\operatorname{Hom}(R,\cdot):R\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ab}}\) is isomorphic to the forgetful functor \(\mathcal{F}:R\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ab}}\) via the isomorphism that sends a homomorphism \(\varphi:R\to X\) to \(\varphi(1)\in X\). Thus \(\operatorname{Hom}(R,\cdot)\) is exact. Free modules are also generators for \(R\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\); see Definition reference and Example reference. An injective object that is also a cogenerator (or a projective object that is also a generator) is very useful. Here is a simple characterization.

Proposition (Injective cogenerators and projective generators). In an abelian category \(\mathcal{A}\), an injective (or projective) object \(X\) is a cogenerator (or generator) if and only if \(\operatorname{Hom}(T,X)\neq0\) (or \(\operatorname{Hom}(X,T)\neq0\)) for every \(T\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{A})\) with \(T\neq0\).

Equivalently, \(\operatorname{Hom}(\cdot,X)\) (or \(\operatorname{Hom}(X,\cdot)\)) is a faithful exact functor.

Proof. We treat only the case in which \(X\) is injective. First suppose that \(X\) is a cogenerator. Apply the definition of cogenerator to \[\text{Diagram chapter2-unit-028-d010}\] There is then a \(\delta\in\operatorname{Hom}(T,X)\) such that \(\delta=\delta\circ\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_T\neq\delta\circ0=0\).

Conversely, we wish to show that if \(h:S\to T\) is nonzero, then there is a \(\delta\in\operatorname{Hom}(T,X)\) such that \(\delta h\neq0\). Observe that there is a \(\delta'\in\operatorname{Hom}(\operatorname{im}(h),X)\) with \(\delta'\neq0\). Since \(S\twoheadrightarrow\operatorname{im}(h)\) is an epimorphism, the composite \(S\twoheadrightarrow\operatorname{im}(h)\xrightarrow{\delta'}X\) is nonzero. Now use the injectivity of \(X\) (see the discussion following Definition reference) to extend \(\delta'\) to \(\delta:T\to X\).

The assertion about faithful exact functors is an immediate application of Proposition reference.

To do homological algebra in an abelian category, one often needs enough injective or projective objects.

Definition. Let \(\mathcal{A}\) be an abelian category.

  • If, for every \(X\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{A})\), there are an injective object \(I\) and a monomorphism \(X\hookrightarrow I\), then \(\mathcal{A}\) is said to have enough injectives.

  • If, for every \(X\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{A})\), there are a projective object \(P\) and an epimorphism \(P\twoheadrightarrow X\), then \(\mathcal{A}\) is said to have enough projectives.

These two notions are dual to each other. A standard way to construct injective or projective objects is to use adjoints of exact functors; here are the details.

Proposition. Consider a pair of functors between abelian categories \[\text{Diagram chapter2-unit-028-d011}\] and suppose that \(F\) is exact.

  • If \(G\) is a left adjoint of \(F\), then \(G\) sends projective objects in \(\mathcal{B}\) to projective objects in \(\mathcal{A}\);

  • if \(G\) is a right adjoint of \(F\), then \(G\) sends injective objects in \(\mathcal{B}\) to injective objects in \(\mathcal{A}\).

Proof. By duality, it suffices to consider the case in which \(G\) is a left adjoint. In this case \(G\) is necessarily additive (Corollary reference). Let \(P\) be a projective object of \(\mathcal{B}\). For every exact sequence \((X^\bullet,d^\bullet)\) in \(\mathcal{A}\), there is an isomorphism of complexes in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ab}}\) \[\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{A}}(GP,X^\bullet)\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}} \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{B}}(P,FX^\bullet).\] Since \(F\) is exact, \((FX^\bullet,Fd^\bullet)\) is an exact sequence, and hence the right-hand side is exact in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ab}}\). Therefore \(\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{A}}(GP,\cdot):\mathcal{A}\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ab}}\) is an exact functor.

For example, consider a ring \(R\) and the forgetful functor \(\mathcal{F}:R\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ab}}\). By Example reference, \(\mathcal{F}\) is exact and has the right adjoint \(G:=\operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ab}}}(R,\cdot)\). Proposition reference shows that \(G\) sends injective objects in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ab}}\) to injective objects in \(R\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\). Injective objects in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ab}}\) are easy to characterize: they are precisely the divisible \(\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\)-modules. This is the standard way to construct injective \(R\)-modules in module theory and to show that \(R\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\) has enough injectives; see [Li1]. On the other hand, \(R\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\) also has enough projectives: for every \(R\)-module \(X\), choose a set of generators \(A\subset X\); then \(R^{\oplus A}\twoheadrightarrow X\).

Example. The following combined exercise involves an abstract abelian category and will be used in §3.12 to study long exact sequences of derived functors. Let \(\mathcal{A}\) be an abelian category. Consider the category \(\mathbf{2}\) (whose diagram is \(0\to1\); see the book’s introduction on categories). The functor category \(\mathcal{A}^{\mathbf{2}}\) is again abelian (Proposition reference); it is the arrow category: its objects are morphisms \(X_0\to X_1\) in \(\mathcal{A}\), and its morphisms are commutative squares in \(\mathcal{A}\) \[\text{Diagram chapter2-unit-028-d012}\] For \(i\in\{0,1\}\), the evaluation functor \(\mathrm{ev}_i:\mathcal{A}^{\mathbf{2}}\to\mathcal{A}\) sends an object \(X_0\to X_1\) to \(X_i\). In addition, define additive functors from \(\mathcal{A}\) to \(\mathcal{A}^{\mathbf{2}}\) by 1 \[L_0:X\mapsto[X\to0],\quad L_1:X\mapsto[0\to X],\quad H:X\mapsto[X\xrightarrow{\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_X}X],\] for \(X\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{A})\); the definitions on morphisms are clear. We shall prove the following assertions.

  1. The functors \(\mathrm{ev}_0\) and \(\mathrm{ev}_1\) are both exact and both send injective (or projective) objects of \(\mathcal{A}^{\mathbf{2}}\) to injective (or projective) objects of \(\mathcal{A}\). Moreover, \(H\), \(L_0\), and \(L_1\) are all exact.

  2. The functors \(L_0,H\) (or \(H,L_1\)) send injective (or projective) objects of \(\mathcal{A}\) to injective (or projective) objects of \(\mathcal{A}^{\mathbf{2}}\).

  3. If \(\mathcal{A}\) has enough injectives (or projectives), then so does \(\mathcal{A}^{\mathbf{2}}\).

Since \(\varinjlim\) and \(\varprojlim\) in \(\mathcal{A}^{\mathbf{2}}\) are constructed objectwise, the functors \(\mathrm{ev}_0,\mathrm{ev}_1\) and \(H,L_0,L_1\) are indeed exact. The remainder of (i) and (ii) follows from the adjoint relations satisfied by \(\mathrm{ev}_i\); the diagrams are as follows, and verification is a simple exercise: \[\text{Diagram chapter2-unit-028-d013} \quad \text{Diagram chapter2-unit-028-d014}\] For (iii), first consider injective objects. Take an object \([X_0\xrightarrow{f}X_1]\) of \(\mathcal{A}^{\mathbf{2}}\), and choose monomorphisms \(\epsilon_i:X_i\hookrightarrow I_i\), where \(I_i\) is injective, \(i\in\{0,1\}\). These give two morphisms in \(\mathcal{A}^{\mathbf{2}}\), which may be written as the commutative diagrams \[\text{Diagram chapter2-unit-028-d015} \quad \text{and} \quad \text{Diagram chapter2-unit-028-d016}\] The two framed columns are \(L_0(I_0)\) and \(H(I_1)\), respectively. By (ii), both are injective objects in \(\mathcal{A}^{\mathbf{2}}\), and so is their direct sum (Lemma reference). Hence the commutative diagram \[\text{Diagram chapter2-unit-028-d017}\] embeds \([X_0\xrightarrow{f}X_1]\) into an injective object. For projective objects, use the functors \(H\) and \(L_1\).

The discussion in Example reference extends from \(\mathcal{A}^{\mathbf{2}}\) to a general functor category \(\mathcal{A}^{\mathcal{C}}\); the argument presents no essentially new difficulty. The exercises in this chapter give the details.

  1. Editorial correction (O014-C027): the source writes \(H:X\to[X\xrightarrow{\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_X}X]\), whereas the context defines the object map of the functor \(H\), in parallel with \(L_0\) and \(L_1\). The assignment arrow \(\mapsto\) is used here.↩︎

Serre Subcategories and \(\mathrm{K}_0\) Groups

A full subcategory of an abelian category automatically inherits the structure of an \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ab}}\)-category, so one may ask whether the full subcategory is an additive category or an abelian category.

Definition. If \(\mathcal{B}\) is a full subcategory of an abelian category \(\mathcal{A}\), \(\mathcal{B}\) is itself abelian, and the inclusion functor \(\iota:\mathcal{B}\to\mathcal{A}\) is exact (Definition reference), then \(\mathcal{B}\) is called an abelian subcategory of \(\mathcal{A}\).

Proposition. A full subcategory \(\mathcal{B}\) of an abelian category \(\mathcal{A}\) is an abelian subcategory if and only if the following conditions hold.

  • \(0\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{B})\);

  • if \(X,Y\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{B})\), then \(X\oplus Y\) may also be chosen as an object of \(\mathcal{B}\);

  • for every morphism \(f:X\to Y\), if \(X,Y\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{B})\), then \(\operatorname{ker}(f)\) and \(\operatorname{coker}(f)\) may also be chosen as objects of \(\mathcal{B}\).

Proof. Notice that these conditions are self-dual. The “only if” direction is clear. Now suppose that the conditions hold. Then \(\mathcal{B}\) is an additive category and \(\iota:\mathcal{B}\to\mathcal{A}\) is an additive functor. We next show that \(\iota\) preserves all finite \(\varprojlim\) and \(\varinjlim\). First, \(\iota\) preserves \(0\) and finite direct sums. Moreover, equalizers can be expressed as \(\operatorname{ker}\) (Remark reference), while the stated condition says that \(\mathcal{B}\) is closed under taking \(\operatorname{ker}\). Thus \(\iota\) preserves all finite \(\varprojlim\); the case of \(\varinjlim\) is dual.

Recalling the definitions of \(\operatorname{im}\) and \(\operatorname{coim}\) in Definition reference and using the preceding step, we see that \(\mathcal{B}\) is closed under both constructions. For every morphism \(f\) in \(\mathcal{B}\), the canonical morphism \(\operatorname{coim}(f)\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}\operatorname{im}(f)\) in diagram equation is an isomorphism in \(\mathcal{A}\), hence also in \(\mathcal{B}\). Therefore \(\mathcal{B}\) is an abelian subcategory.

Definition (J.-P. Serre). A full subcategory \(\mathcal{T}\) of an abelian category \(\mathcal{A}\) is called a Serre subcategory of \(\mathcal{A}\) if it satisfies the following conditions.

  • \(0\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{T})\);

  • for every short exact sequence \(0\to X'\to X\to X''\to0\) in \(\mathcal{A}\), one has \(X\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{T})\) if and only if \(X',X''\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{T})\).

If the last condition is weakened as follows: for every exact sequence in \(\mathcal{A}\) \[W\to X'\to X\to X''\to Y,\] if \(W,X',X'',Y\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{T})\), then \(X\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{T})\), then \(\mathcal{T}\) is called a weak Serre subcategory of \(\mathcal{A}\) 1.

For example, if \(R\) is a commutative ring, all Noetherian (or Artinian) modules form a Serre subcategory of \(R\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\). This is a standard fact in module theory [Li1]. If \(\mathcal{T}\) is a Serre subcategory (or weak Serre subcategory) of \(\mathcal{A}\), then \(\mathcal{T}^{\operatorname{op}}\) is a Serre subcategory (or weak Serre subcategory) of \(\mathcal{A}^{\operatorname{op}}\). A weak Serre subcategory \(\mathcal{T}\) has the following saturation property: if \(X\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{A})\) is isomorphic to an object of \(\mathcal{T}\), then \(X\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{T})\). This follows by applying the last condition to the exact sequence \(0\to0\to X\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}Y\to0\).

Corollary. If \(\mathcal{T}\) is a weak Serre subcategory of an abelian category \(\mathcal{A}\), then \(\mathcal{T}\) is an abelian subcategory of \(\mathcal{A}\).

Proof. It suffices to verify the conditions of Proposition reference. First, \(0\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{T})\). Next, insert the following exact sequences into the definition of a weak Serre subcategory: \[\begin{gather*} 0\to X\to X\oplus Y\to Y\to0 \quad\text{(Proposition~\href{#prop:biproduct-ses}{reference})},\\ 0\to0\to\operatorname{ker}(f)\to X\xrightarrow{f}Y,\quad X\xrightarrow{f}Y\to\operatorname{coker}(f)\to0\to0, \end{gather*}\] which shows that \(\mathcal{T}\) is closed under direct sums, \(\operatorname{ker}\), and \(\operatorname{coker}\).

Example. If \(F:\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{B}\) is an exact functor between abelian categories, then the objects satisfying \(FX=0\) form a Serre subcategory of \(\mathcal{A}\), denoted by \(\operatorname{ker}(F)\).

Theorem (Serre quotient). Let \(\mathcal{T}\) be a Serre subcategory of an abelian category \(\mathcal{A}\). Then there is an abelian category \(\mathcal{A}/\mathcal{T}\) (which may be a large category), together with an exact, essentially surjective functor \(Q:\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{A}/\mathcal{T}\), such that \(\operatorname{ker}(Q)=\mathcal{T}\) and with the following universal property: for every abelian category \(\mathcal{B}\) and every exact functor \(F:\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{B}\) with \(\operatorname{ker}(F)\supset\mathcal{T}\), there is a unique exact functor \(G:\mathcal{A}/\mathcal{T}\to\mathcal{B}\) such that \(F=GQ\).

In this universal property, \(G\) is faithful if and only if \(\operatorname{ker}(F)=\mathcal{T}\).

Proof. Define \(S:=\left\{f\in\operatorname{Mor}(\mathcal{A}):\operatorname{ker}(f),\operatorname{coker}(f)\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{T})\right\}\). We shall show that \(S\) is a multiplicative system in the sense of Definition reference.

Clearly \(S\) contains all identity morphisms, so (S1) holds. Let \(f:X\to Y\) and \(g:Y\to Z\) belong to \(S\). The mutually dual exact sequences \[\begin{gather*} 0\to\operatorname{ker}(f)\to\operatorname{ker}(gf)\xrightarrow{f}\operatorname{ker}(g),\\ \operatorname{coker}(f)\xrightarrow{g}\operatorname{coker}(gf)\to\operatorname{coker}(g)\to0, \end{gather*}\] immediately give \(gf\in S\), so (S2) holds. Next consider morphisms \(X\xrightarrow{s\in S}Z\xleftarrow{f}Y\). Define \(W:=X\ensuremath{\underset{Z}{\times}}Y\), with morphism \(s':W\to Y\). Observe that \(\operatorname{ker}(s')\simeq\operatorname{ker}(s)\) (Proposition reference), and \(f\) induces \(\operatorname{coker}(s')\hookrightarrow\operatorname{coker}(s)\) (Corollary reference); hence \(s'\in S\). Thus (S3) holds. Finally, consider morphisms \(\text{Diagram chapter2-unit-029-diagram-001}\), with \(sf=sg\). Since \(\operatorname{im}(f-g)\hookrightarrow\operatorname{ker}(s)\), we have \(\operatorname{im}(f-g)\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{T})\); therefore \(Z:=\operatorname{ker}(f-g)\hookrightarrow X\) is a morphism in \(S\), proving (S4).

Thus \(S\) is a left multiplicative system. All the conditions are self-dual, so \(S\) is also a right multiplicative system. Now take the localization functor \(Q:\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{A}/\mathcal{T}:=\mathcal{A}[S^{-1}]\). Proposition reference says that \(Q\) is essentially surjective (indeed, \(\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{A})=\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{A}/\mathcal{T})\)), while Proposition reference says that \(Q\) is an exact functor between abelian categories. Notice that \(\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{QX}=Q(\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_X)\) equals \(0\) if and only if there is a \(U\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{A})\) such that \(U\xrightarrow{0}X\) lies in \(S\) (this can be checked directly using Corollary reference); this implies \(X=\operatorname{coker}[U\xrightarrow{0}X]\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{T})\). Conversely, if \(X\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{T})\), we may take \(U=X\). Hence \(\operatorname{ker}(Q)=\mathcal{T}\).

We next verify the universal property. If \(\operatorname{ker}(F)\supset\mathcal{T}\), then the exact sequence \(\operatorname{ker}(s)\to X\xrightarrow{s\in S}Y\to\operatorname{coker}(s)\) shows that \(F\) sends every element of \(S\) to an isomorphism, and the universal property of localization determines the required \(G\).

It remains to verify that \(G\) is exact. Theorem reference first ensures that \(G\) is additive. Since every morphism in \(\mathcal{A}[S^{-1}]\) can, after composition with an isomorphism arising from \(S\), be represented by a morphism in \(\mathcal{A}\), checking that \(G\) preserves kernels reduces to the exactness of \(F\) and \(Q\). The same applies to cokernels. Since \(Q\) is essentially surjective and \(\operatorname{ker}(Q)=\mathcal{T}\), the characterization of faithfulness reduces to statement (ii) of Proposition reference.

Notice that \(\mathcal{A}/\mathcal{T}\) is constructed as a localization and may therefore be a “large category.” The exercises give another description of \(\mathcal{A}/\mathcal{T}\) that controls the size of the Serre quotient under the assumption that \(\mathcal{A}\) is a well-powered category (Definition reference).

Example. Let \(S\) be a multiplicative subset of a commutative ring \(R\). Define a full subcategory \(\mathcal{T}\) of \(R\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\) by declaring that \(M\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{T})\) if and only if, for every \(m\in M\), there is an \(s\in S\) such that \(sm=0\). It is easy to verify that \(\mathcal{T}\) is a Serre subcategory. We now show that \(R\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}/\mathcal{T}\) is equivalent to \(R[S^{-1}]\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\).

The assignment \(M\mapsto M[S^{-1}]:=M\ensuremath{\underset{R}{\otimes}}R[S^{-1}]\) defines an exact functor \(F:R\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\to R[S^{-1}]\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\) that sends \(\mathcal{T}\) to zero, so the universal property gives an exact functor \(G:R\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}/\mathcal{T}\to R[S^{-1}]\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\). Clearly \(\operatorname{ker}(F)=\mathcal{T}\), so \(G\) is faithful. Moreover, \(G\) is essentially surjective: regard any \(R[S^{-1}]\)-module \(N\) as an \(R\)-module; one checks directly that there is an isomorphism of \(R[S^{-1}]\)-modules \(N\ensuremath{\underset{R}{\otimes}}R[S^{-1}]\simeq N\).

It remains to prove that \(G\) is full and faithful. Given an \(R[S^{-1}]\)-module homomorphism \(\varphi:M_1[S^{-1}]\to M_2[S^{-1}]\), form the fiber product 2 \(M_0:=M_1\ensuremath{\underset{M_2[S^{-1}]}{\times}}M_2\), where the map \(M_1\to M_2[S^{-1}]\) is the composite \(M_1\to M_1[S^{-1}]\xrightarrow{\varphi}M_2[S^{-1}]\). Write its projections as \(p_1:M_0\to M_1\) and \(p_2:M_0\to M_2\). The kernel and cokernel of \(p_1\) are \(S\)-torsion modules, so \(p_1\) lies in the multiplicative system defining the Serre quotient. Hence the roof \(\text{Diagram chapter2-unit-029-diagram-002}\) defines a morphism in \(R\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}/\mathcal{T}\) that is sent to \(\varphi\). This proves the claim.

We now introduce an important construction closely related to Serre subcategories.

Definition. Let \(\mathcal{A}\) be an abelian category. Define the commutative group \(\mathrm{K}_0(\mathcal{A})\) as follows, writing the group operation additively. Take the free \(\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\)-module \(F\) with basis \(\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{A})\), and write the element corresponding to \(X\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{A})\) as \(\ensuremath{\left\langle X \right\rangle}\in F\). Let \(R\subset F\) be the submodule generated by the elements \[\ensuremath{\left\langle X \right\rangle}-\ensuremath{\left\langle X' \right\rangle}-\ensuremath{\left\langle X'' \right\rangle},\quad 0\to X'\to X\to X''\to0:\ \text{a short exact sequence in }\mathcal{A},\] and call \(\mathrm{K}_0(\mathcal{A}):=F/R\) the \(\mathrm{K}_0\) group of \(\mathcal{A}\). We henceforth denote the image of \(X\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{A})\) in \(\mathrm{K}_0(\mathcal{A})\) by \([X]\).

Lemma. For every abelian category \(\mathcal{A}\), the following equalities hold in \(\mathrm{K}_0(\mathcal{A})\).

  1. \([0]=0\);

  2. if \(X,Y\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{A})\) and \(X\simeq Y\), then \([X]=[Y]\);

  3. \([X\oplus Y]=[X]+[Y]\);

  4. if \(0\to X^1\xrightarrow{f^1}\cdots\xrightarrow{f^{n-1}}X^n\to0\) is an exact sequence in \(\mathcal{A}\), then \(\sum_{i=1}^{n}(-1)^i[X^i]=0\);

  5. in the notation of §reference, for a family of subobjects \(X=X_0\supset\cdots\supset X_r=0\), one has \[[X]=\sum_{i=0}^{r-1}[X_i/X_{i+1}].\]

Proof. Take the short exact sequence \(0\to0\to0\to0\to0\); this gives (i). If \(X\simeq Y\), then \(0\to X\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}Y\to0\to0\), together with (i), gives (ii). The short exact sequence of Proposition reference gives (iii).

For (iv), append zero terms and extend the exact sequence infinitely in both directions. Consider the short exact sequences \[0\to\operatorname{ker}(f^i)\to X^i\to\operatorname{im}(f^i)\to0,\quad i=1,\ldots,n.\] Then \(\left[X^i\right]=\left[\operatorname{ker}(f^i)\right]+\left[\operatorname{im}(f^i)\right] =\left[\operatorname{ker}(f^i)\right]+\left[\operatorname{ker}(f^{i+1})\right]\); now take the alternating sum.

Finally, (v) follows by induction on \(r\), using the short exact sequence \(0\to X_1\to X_0\to X_0/X_1\to0\).

Remark. Since this book requires groups to be realized on small sets, and in view of Lemma reference (ii), a fully precise formulation of \(\mathrm{K}_0(\mathcal{A})\) should require \(\mathcal{A}\) to have a small skeleton [Li1]. This issue has little effect here.

Theorem (Euler–Poincaré principle). Let \(\cdots\to X^i\xrightarrow{d_X^i}X^{i+1}\to\cdots\) be a complex in an abelian category \(\mathcal{A}\) with only finitely many nonzero terms. Then the equality \[\sum_i(-1)^i\left[\operatorname{H}^i(X)\right] =\sum_i(-1)^i\left[X^i\right],\quad \operatorname{H}^i(X):=\operatorname{H}\left[X^{i-1}\xrightarrow{d_X^{i-1}}X^i \xrightarrow{d_X^i}X^{i+1}\right]\] holds in \(\mathrm{K}_0(\mathcal{A})\).

Proof. For every \(i\) there is an exact sequence \[0\to\operatorname{ker}\left(d_X^{i-1}\right)\to X^{i-1} \xrightarrow{d_X^{i-1}}\operatorname{ker}\left(d_X^i\right) \to\operatorname{H}^i(X)\to0,\] and all terms are \(0\) for \(|i|\gg0\). Apply Lemma reference (iv) and sum in \(\mathrm{K}_0(\mathcal{A})\) to obtain \[\sum_i(-1)^i \left(\left[X^{i-1}\right]+\left[\operatorname{H}^i(X)\right]\right) =\sum_i(-1)^i \left(\left[\operatorname{ker}\left(d_X^{i-1}\right)\right] +\left[\operatorname{ker}\left(d_X^i\right)\right]\right).\] The terms on the right-hand side cancel in pairs; rearranging gives \(\sum_i(-1)^i[\operatorname{H}^i(X)]=\sum_i(-1)^i[X^i]\).

Example. Let \(\mathcal{A}\) be the abelian category of finite-dimensional vector spaces over a division ring \(D\). Since every vector space has a basis, \(\mathrm{K}_0(\mathcal{A})=\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\cdot[D]\). On the other hand, the assignment \([X]\mapsto\dim_D X\) defines a group homomorphism \(\dim:\mathrm{K}_0(\mathcal{A})\to\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\) sending \([D]\) to \(1\). Thus \(\dim:\mathrm{K}_0(\mathcal{A})\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\).

If infinite-dimensional vector spaces are allowed, the \(\mathrm{K}_0\) group becomes trivial. Indeed, for every \(D\)-vector space \(V\), a cardinality argument gives a \(D\)-vector space \(W\) such that \(V\oplus W\simeq W\) and \(\dim_D W=\max\{\dim_D V,\aleph_0\}\); consequently, \([V]=0\).

For an exact functor \(F:\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{B}\) between abelian categories, since \(F\) preserves short exact sequences, the assignment \([X]\mapsto[FX]\) defines a group homomorphism 3 \(\mathrm{K}_0(F):\mathrm{K}_0(\mathcal{A}) \to\mathrm{K}_0(\mathcal{B})\). Therefore, if \(\mathcal{A}\) is an abelian subcategory of \(\mathcal{B}\), there is a natural homomorphism \(\mathrm{K}_0(\mathcal{A})\to\mathrm{K}_0(\mathcal{B})\).

Proposition. Let \(\mathcal{T}\) be a Serre subcategory of an abelian category \(\mathcal{A}\), and write its Serre quotient as \(\mathcal{B}:=\mathcal{A}/\mathcal{T}\). Then the exact functors \(\mathcal{T}\to\mathcal{A}\xrightarrow{Q}\mathcal{B}\) induce an exact sequence of additive groups \[\mathrm{K}_0(\mathcal{T})\to\mathrm{K}_0(\mathcal{A}) \xrightarrow{\mathrm{K}_0(Q)}\mathrm{K}_0(\mathcal{B})\to0.\]

Proof. First, \(Q:\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{B}\) is essentially surjective, so \(\mathrm{K}_0(\mathcal{A})\to\mathrm{K}_0(\mathcal{B})\) is surjective. The composite \(\mathrm{K}_0(\mathcal{T})\to\mathrm{K}_0(\mathcal{A}) \to\mathrm{K}_0(\mathcal{B})\) is plainly \(0\). It remains to prove \(\operatorname{ker}(\mathrm{K}_0(Q))\subset \operatorname{im}\left[\mathrm{K}_0(\mathcal{T})\to \mathrm{K}_0(\mathcal{A})\right]\).

Let \(\sum_{i=1}^n a_i[X_i]\in\operatorname{ker}(\mathrm{K}_0(Q))\), where \(a_1,\ldots,a_n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\). This is equivalent to the existence of a family of short exact sequences in \(\mathcal{B}\), \(0\to Y'_j\xrightarrow{f_j}Y_j\xrightarrow{g_j}Y''_j\to0\), and integers \(b_j\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\) for \(j=1,\ldots,m\), such that \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:K0-exact-seq-aux-0}{} \sum_{i=1}^n a_i\ensuremath{\left\langle QX_i \right\rangle} =\sum_{j=1}^m b_j \left(\ensuremath{\left\langle Y_j \right\rangle}-\ensuremath{\left\langle Y'_j \right\rangle}-\ensuremath{\left\langle Y''_j \right\rangle}\right) \end{equation}\] in the free \(\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\)-module with basis \(\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{B})\). Since \(Q:\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{B}\) is constructed by localization in Theorem reference, that theorem together with §reference gives:

  • \(Q\) identifies \(\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{A})\) with \(\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{B})\), so equation gives the equality in \(\mathrm{K}_0(\mathcal{A})\) \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:K0-exact-seq-aux-1}{} \sum_{i=1}^n a_i[X_i] =\sum_{j=1}^m b_j\left([Y_j]-[Y'_j]-[Y''_j]\right); \end{equation}\]

  • moreover, after replacing \(Y_j\), \(Y'_j\), \(Y''_j\), and \(f_j\) and \(g_j\) by isomorphic objects and morphisms in \(\mathcal{B}\) arising from \(S\), we may arrange that there are morphisms \(u_j\) and \(v_j\) in \(\mathcal{A}\) such that \(f_j=Q(u_j)\) and \(g_j=Q(v_j)\). From \(Q(v_ju_j)=g_jf_j=0\) and Corollary reference, a further adjustment by members of \(S\) lets us arrange that \(v_ju_j=0\).

Thus, for every \(1\leq j\leq m\), there are exact sequences in \(\mathcal{A}\) \[\begin{gather*} 0\to\operatorname{ker}(v_j)\to Y_j\xrightarrow{v_j}Y''_j \to\operatorname{coker}(v_j)\to0,\\ 0\to\operatorname{ker}(u_j)\to Y'_j\xrightarrow{u_j}\operatorname{ker}(v_j) \to\frac{\operatorname{ker}(v_j)}{\operatorname{im}(u_j)}\to0. \end{gather*}\] Since \(Q\) is exact, \(\operatorname{coker}(v_j)\), \(\operatorname{ker}(u_j)\), and \(\frac{\operatorname{ker}(v_j)}{\operatorname{im}(u_j)}\) all belong to \(\mathcal{T}=\operatorname{ker}(Q)\). Therefore, in \(\mathrm{K}_0(\mathcal{A})\), \[[Y_j]-[Y'_j]-[Y''_j]\in \operatorname{im}\left[\mathrm{K}_0(\mathcal{T}) \to\mathrm{K}_0(\mathcal{A})\right].\] Substituting these relations into equation gives \(\operatorname{ker}(\mathrm{K}_0(Q))\subset \operatorname{im}\left[\mathrm{K}_0(\mathcal{T}) \to\mathrm{K}_0(\mathcal{A})\right]\).

For an exact sequence such as the one in Proposition reference, a strategy that invariably succeeds is to try to extend it to the left: seek a family of higher K-groups \(\mathrm{K}_i(\cdot)\) for \(i\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}_{\geq0}\) together with a canonical exact sequence \[\cdots\to\mathrm{K}_{i+1}(\mathcal{B}) \to\mathrm{K}_i(\mathcal{T})\to\mathrm{K}_i(\mathcal{A}) \to\mathrm{K}_i(\mathcal{B})\to\cdots\] One also hopes that the family \((\mathrm{K}_i(\mathcal{A}))_{i\geq0}\) contains deep information about \(\mathcal{A}\) and is, at least to some extent, computable. This is the subject of K-theory, whose applications also encompass exact categories, which are more general than abelian categories. Because the relevant constructions are based on the viewpoint of homotopy theory, this book cannot treat them in detail; interested readers may consult [Lai19], or the summary in [Bu10].

  1. This somewhat abrupt definition is designed specifically for derived categories; see §4.4.↩︎

  2. Editorial correction (O014-C029): the source defines \(M_0\) as the set of elements \(m\in M_1\) whose images “come from” \(M_2\), and then uses a restriction \(\varphi|_{M_0}:M_0\to M_2\). A preimage in \(M_2\) is not canonical when \(M_2\to M_2[S^{-1}]\) has an \(S\)-torsion kernel, so that morphism is not well-defined. We use instead the canonical fiber product and its two projections.↩︎

  3. Editorial correction (O014-C028): the source prints \(\mathrm{K}_0(f)\), but this homomorphism is induced by the functor \(F\); we use \(\mathrm{K}_0(F)\).↩︎

Grothendieck Categories

All the main statements in this section are formulated relative to a chosen Grothendieck universe, rather than in terms of unqualified “large” categories. Recall the notions of small limits, completeness, and generators (Definition reference).

Definition (Grothendieck category [Gr57).] Let \(\mathcal{A}\) be an abelian category. It is called a Grothendieck category if the following conditions hold.

  • \(\mathcal{A}\) is cocomplete; in other words, it has all small \(\varinjlim\);

  • \(\mathcal{A}\) has a generator;

  • for every small filtered category \(I\) (see §reference), the functor \(\varinjlim:\mathcal{A}^I\to\mathcal{A}\) is exact. Equivalently, for every diagram \(\alpha\to\beta\to\gamma\) in \(\mathcal{A}^I\), \[\begin{multline*} \forall i\in\operatorname{Ob}(I),\quad 0\to\alpha(i)\to\beta(i)\to\gamma(i)\to0 \quad\text{is exact} \\ \implies 0\to\varinjlim\alpha\to\varinjlim\beta \to\varinjlim\gamma\to0\quad\text{is exact}. \end{multline*}\]

Example reference has already shown that \(\varinjlim\) preserves cokernels. Therefore, by Remark reference, the last condition is also equivalent to saying that every small filtered \(\varinjlim\) preserves monomorphisms. The following argument illustrates the usefulness of this condition.

Proposition. Let \(\mathcal{A}\) be a Grothendieck category. For every small set \(I\), taking direct sums (that is, coproducts) gives an exact functor \(\bigoplus_I:\mathcal{A}^I\to\mathcal{A}\).

Proof. The finite case is clear, while Proposition reference expresses \(\bigoplus_I\) as a filtered \(\varinjlim\) of finite direct sums.

We next obtain a seemingly simple but very useful property; it too rests on the exactness of filtered \(\varinjlim\).

Proposition. Fix a small filtered partially ordered set \((I,\leq)\). Let \(\mathcal{A}\) be a Grothendieck category, or more generally suppose that \(\varinjlim:\mathcal{A}^{(I,\leq)}\to\mathcal{A}\) exists and is exact. For every

  • \(X\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{A})\) and subobject \(Y\subset X\),

  • family of subobjects \(\left(X_i\right)_{i\in I}\) of \(X\) satisfying \(i\leq j\implies X_i\subset X_j\),

with the notation of Convention reference, one has \[\begin{gather*} \varinjlim_{i\in I}X_i\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}\bigcup_{i\in I}X_i\subset X,\\ Y\cap\left(\bigcup_{i\in I}X_i\right) =\bigcup_{i\in I}(Y\cap X_i)\;\in\mathrm{Sub}_X. \end{gather*}\]

Proof. Since \(\varinjlim_i\) is exact, the canonical morphism \(\iota:\varinjlim_iX_i\to X\) determined by all the maps \(X_i\hookrightarrow X\) and the universal property of \(\varinjlim\) remains a monomorphism. If all \(X_i\hookrightarrow X\) factor through a subobject \(Z\subset X\), that universal property gives a factorization of \(\iota\) as \(\varinjlim_iX_i\to Z\subset X\). Thus \(\iota:\varinjlim_iX_i\hookrightarrow X\) indeed gives the supremum of \((X_i)_{i\in I}\) in \(\mathrm{Sub}_X\). This proves the first equality.

Next write the quotient morphism \(X\to X/Y\) as \(q\). Then \(Y=\operatorname{ker}(q)\) and \(Y\cap X_i=\operatorname{ker}(q|_{X_i})\). Consider the compatible family of morphisms \(q|_{X_i}:X_i\to X/Y\). Since taking \(\varinjlim_i\) preserves kernels, the preceding paragraph gives \(Y\cap\left(\bigcup_{i\in I}X_i\right)= \bigcup_{i\in I}(Y\cap X_i)\).

Example (Module categories). Let \(R\) be a ring. Then \(R\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\) is a Grothendieck category. Indeed, its cocompleteness is already known [Li1], while exactness of filtered \(\varinjlim\) is given by [Li1]. In the special case \(R=\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\), the category \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ab}}\) is a Grothendieck category.

To develop the theory further, we need some preparation concerning generators.

Definition. Let \(s\) be a generator of a category \(\mathcal{C}\). If, for every monomorphism \(i:S_1\hookrightarrow S_2\) in \(\mathcal{C}\), the associated map \(i_*:\operatorname{Hom}(s,S_1)\hookrightarrow\operatorname{Hom}(s,S_2)\) is bijective if and only if \(i\) is an isomorphism, then \(s\) is called a strong generator of \(\mathcal{C}\).

Proposition. Let \(s\) be a strong generator of a category \(\mathcal{C}\) and suppose that, for every object \(X\) and monomorphisms \(S_i\hookrightarrow X\) with \(i=1,2\), the fiber product \(S_1\cap S_2:=S_1\ensuremath{\underset{X}{\times}}S_2\) exists. If \(\kappa:=|\operatorname{Hom}(s,X)|\), then \(|\mathrm{Sub}_X|\leq2^\kappa\).

Proof. Let \(s\) be a strong generator and \(X\) any object. We shall show that \[\begin{align*} \mathrm{Sub}_X&\longrightarrow \left\{\text{subsets of }\operatorname{Hom}(s,X)\right\}\\ S&\longmapsto\operatorname{Hom}(s,S) \end{align*}\] is injective, which gives the desired inequality.

Take \(S_1,S_2\in\mathrm{Sub}_X\) such that \(\operatorname{Hom}(s,S_1)=\operatorname{Hom}(s,S_2)\). If \(S_1\subset S_2\), the definition of a strong generator immediately gives \(S_1=S_2\). In general, \(S_1\cap S_2\subset S_i\) for \(i=1,2\) (see Definition reference), and as subsets of \(\operatorname{Hom}(s,X)\), \[\operatorname{Hom}\left(s,S_1\cap S_2\right) =\operatorname{Hom}(s,S_1)\cap\operatorname{Hom}(s,S_2)=\operatorname{Hom}(s,S_i),\qquad i=1,2.\] The preceding step gives \(S_1=S_1\cap S_2=S_2\), as claimed.

Proposition. Every generator in an abelian category is automatically a strong generator.

Proof. Let \(\mathcal{A}\) be an abelian category and let \(s\) be a generator. Given a monomorphism \(i:S_1\hookrightarrow S_2\), consider the pair of morphisms \[\text{Diagram chapter2-unit-030-d001}\] If \(i\) is not an isomorphism, then \(q\neq0\). Thus, by the definition of a generator, there is an \(\epsilon\in\operatorname{Hom}(s,S_2)\) such that \(q\epsilon\neq0\epsilon=0\); this morphism \(\epsilon\) cannot factor through \(S_1=\operatorname{ker}(q)\).

Corollary. Every Grothendieck category is both well-powered and co-well-powered (Definition reference).

Proof. An abelian category has all finite fiber products, while every \(\operatorname{Hom}\) set is small by assumption. Thus well-poweredness follows from Proposition reference and Proposition reference. Moreover, in an abelian category \(\mathrm{Sub}_X\) and \(\mathrm{Quot}_X\) always have the same cardinality.

Corollary. Every Grothendieck category \(\mathcal{A}\) is complete; in other words, it has all small \(\varprojlim\).

Proof. The category \(\mathcal{A}\) is cocomplete and co-well-powered. Apply Corollary reference.

Thus a Grothendieck category has all small direct sums and small direct products. The exercises in this chapter show that the canonical morphism \(\delta:\bigoplus_{i\in I}X_i\to\prod_{i\in I}X_i\) in equation is a monomorphism; for module categories this is of course already clear.

Corollary. Let \(\mathcal{A}\) be a Grothendieck category. A functor \(G:\mathcal{A}^{\operatorname{op}}\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{Set}}\) is representable if and only if \(G\) preserves all small \(\varprojlim\); more concretely, \(G\) turns every small \(\varinjlim\) in \(\mathcal{A}\) into a small \(\varprojlim\) in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Set}}\).

Proof. Apply Corollary reference to \(\mathcal{A}^{\operatorname{op}}\).

Although the definition of a Grothendieck category is not self-dual, the dual version of the preceding result still holds; see Corollary reference. We shall now show that Grothendieck categories have enough injectives. In fact, not only does a monomorphism \(X\hookrightarrow I\) as in Definition reference exist, but \(I\) can also be chosen functorially in \(X\).

Lemma. Let \(\mathcal{A}\) be a Grothendieck category and let \(s\) be a generator. An object \(I\) is injective if and only if, for every monomorphism \(X\hookrightarrow s\), every morphism \(X\to I\) extends to a morphism \(s\to I\); in other words, the data can be completed to a commutative diagram \(\text{Diagram chapter2-unit-030-diagram-002}\).

Proof. Injectivity is equivalent to the following statement: for every monomorphism \(A\hookrightarrow B\), every morphism \(f:A\to I\) extends to a morphism \(B\to I\). Thus the “only if” direction is clear.

We now prove the converse. Recall that \(\mathcal{A}\) is well-powered. Given data \(I\xleftarrow{f}A\hookrightarrow B\) as above, consider the small set \[\mathcal{S}:=\left\{\begin{array}{r|l} (A',f')&A\subset A'\subset B\quad\text{(as subobjects)},\\ &f':A'\to I\quad\text{extends }f \end{array}\right\},\] partially ordered by extension. By exactness of filtered \(\varinjlim\), every totally ordered subset \(\mathcal{T}\) of \(\mathcal{S}\) has an upper bound \[\widetilde{A}:=\varinjlim_{(A',f')\in\mathcal{T}}A',\qquad \widetilde{f}:=\varinjlim_{(A',f')\in\mathcal{T}}f':\widetilde{A}\to I.\] Zorn’s lemma shows that \(\mathcal{S}\) has a maximal element \((A',f')\). We claim that \(A'=B\). Otherwise, because \(s\) is a strong generator, there is a \(g:s\to B\) that does not factor through \(A'\hookrightarrow B\). We shall show that \(f'\) extends to \(A'+g(s)\to I\), contradicting the maximality of \((A',f')\).

Set \(Y:=A'\cap g(s)\). Consider the solid part of the following commutative diagram: \[\text{Diagram chapter2-unit-030-d002}\] By assumption, a \(\varphi\) as shown by the dashed arrow exists and makes the triangular part commute. Since \(\varphi\) vanishes on \(\operatorname{ker}(g)\), there is also an \(f''\) as shown by the dashed arrow such that \(\varphi=f''g\). Pulling back along \(g^{-1}(Y)\twoheadrightarrow Y\) (an epimorphism by Proposition reference), we find that the restrictions of \(f'\) and \(f''\) to \(Y\) agree. By the universal property of the fibered coproduct, they can therefore be glued to a morphism \(A'+g(s)\to I\). This proves the claim.

We now introduce a variant of the so-called “small object argument.” The reader should briefly review Definition A.2.7 and the related discussion of regular cardinals; what follows uses their basic operations and properties.

Definition. Let \(\mathcal{C}\) be a category with all small filtered \(\varinjlim\), let \(I\subset\operatorname{Mor}(\mathcal{C})\) be a subset, and let \(\alpha\) be a small regular cardinal.

  1. An object \(X\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{C})\) is called \(\alpha\)-small relative to \(I\) if the following condition holds. Let \(\widetilde{\alpha}\) be a small regular cardinal with \(\widetilde{\alpha}\geq\alpha\). For every functor \(\beta\mapsto Y_\beta\) from the ordinal \(\widetilde{\alpha}\), regarded as a small filtered category, to \(\mathcal{C}\), if \(Y_\beta\to Y_{\beta'}\) belongs to \(I\) whenever \(\beta\leq\beta'\), then the canonical map \[\varinjlim_\beta\operatorname{Hom}\left(X,Y_\beta\right) \longrightarrow\operatorname{Hom}\left(X,\varinjlim_\beta Y_\beta\right)\] (see Equation A.2.1) is a bijection.

  2. If \(X\) is \(\alpha\)-small relative to \(\operatorname{Mor}(\mathcal{C})\), then \(X\) is called an \(\alpha\)-small object.

Relative to the chosen \(I\), if \(\alpha\leq\alpha'\), then \(\alpha\)-smallness implies \(\alpha'\)-smallness.

Lemma. Let \(\mathcal{A}\) be a Grothendieck category, let \(X\) be an object of \(\mathcal{A}\), and let \(\alpha\) be a small regular cardinal. If \(\alpha>\kappa:=|\mathrm{Sub}_X|\), then \(X\) is \(\alpha\)-small relative to all monomorphisms (Definition reference).

Proof. Consider data \(\beta\mapsto Y_\beta\) from Definition reference (i), with the condition that \(Y_\beta\to Y_{\beta'}\) is a monomorphism whenever \(\beta\leq\beta'\). We may take \(\alpha=\widetilde{\alpha}\) in that definition without loss of generality.

Since filtered \(\varinjlim\) in \(\mathcal{A}\) is exact, every \(Y_\beta\to\varinjlim_\gamma Y_\gamma\) remains a monomorphism. Exactness of filtered \(\varinjlim\) in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ab}}\) also implies that the map \[\varinjlim_{\gamma<\alpha}\operatorname{Hom}(X,Y_\gamma) \longrightarrow\operatorname{Hom}\left(X,\varinjlim_{\gamma<\alpha}Y_\gamma\right)\] is injective; it therefore remains to prove surjectivity. We henceforth regard each \(Y_\beta\) as a subobject of \(\varinjlim_\gamma Y_\gamma\).

For a morphism \(f:X\to\varinjlim_\gamma Y_\gamma\), every \(\beta<\alpha\) determines a subobject \(f^{-1}(Y_\beta)\) of \(X\). We may assume that \(f^{-1}(Y_\beta)\neq X\) for every \(\beta\), since otherwise there is nothing left to prove. Recall that \(f^{-1}\) is given by a fiber product. Using exactness of filtered \(\varinjlim\) once more, we obtain a natural isomorphism \[\varinjlim_\beta f^{-1}(Y_\beta) \simeq f^{-1}\left(\varinjlim_\beta Y_\beta\right)=X.\] There are at most \(\kappa\) subobjects \(f^{-1}(Y_\beta)\), so there is a subset \(S\) of \(\alpha\) with \(|S|\leq\kappa\) such that the left-hand side may be replaced by \(\varinjlim_{\beta\in S}\).

Consider the ordinal \(\sigma:=\sup S\leq\alpha\). We claim that \(\sigma<\alpha\). Otherwise, \(|S|\leq\kappa<\alpha\) and \(|S|\geq\mathrm{cf}(\alpha)\) (Proposition A.2.8 (ii)) would give \(\mathrm{cf}(\alpha)<\alpha\), contradicting the regularity of \(\alpha\). This claim ensures that \(f^{-1}(Y_\beta)\) is a subobject of \(f^{-1}(Y_\sigma)\) for every \(\beta\in S\). Consequently, \(f^{-1}(Y_\sigma)=X\), so \(f\) factors through \(Y_\sigma\).

Theorem (A. Grothendieck). Let \(\mathcal{A}\) be a Grothendieck category. Write \(\mathcal{I}\) for the full subcategory of \(\mathcal{A}\) consisting of injective objects, and write its inclusion functor as \(\iota:\mathcal{I}\to\mathcal{A}\). There are a functor \(F:\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{I}\) and a natural transformation \(\varphi:\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{\mathcal{A}}\to\iota F\) such that every \[\varphi_X:X\to F(X),\qquad X\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{A})\] is a monomorphism in \(\mathcal{A}\). In particular, \(\mathcal{A}\) has enough injectives.

Proof. Choose a generator \(s\). Let \(F_0\) be the identity functor \(\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{\mathcal{A}}\). The first step is to form, for every object \(X\), the pushout diagram \[\text{Diagram chapter2-unit-030-d003}\] Proposition reference ensures that \(\varphi(0,1)_X:X\to F_1(X)\) in this diagram is a monomorphism. As \(X\) varies, the assignment \(X\mapsto F_1(X)\) becomes an endofunctor of \(\mathcal{A}\), and \(\varphi(0,1):F_0\to F_1\) becomes a natural transformation.

More generally, for every small ordinal \(\alpha\) we shall construct a functor \(F_\alpha:\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{A}\) together with a family of natural transformations \(\varphi(\beta,\alpha):F_\beta\to F_\alpha\) for \(\beta\leq\alpha\), having the following properties.

  • \(\varphi(\alpha,\alpha)=\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{F_\alpha}\);

  • \(\varphi(\beta,\alpha)_X:F_\beta(X)\to F_\alpha(X)\) is a monomorphism for every \(X\);

  • if \(\gamma\leq\beta\leq\alpha\), then \(\varphi(\beta,\alpha)\varphi(\gamma,\beta)=\varphi(\gamma,\alpha)\).

The construction proceeds by transfinite recursion [Li1]. Starting with \(\alpha=0\), suppose that \(F_\beta\) and the family of transformations \(\varphi(\beta',\beta)\) have been defined for every ordinal \(\beta<\alpha\). Set \[F_\alpha(X) := \begin{cases} F_1(F_\beta(X)), & \alpha = \beta + 1:\ \text{a successor ordinal}, \\ \varinjlim_{\beta < \alpha} F_\beta(X), & \alpha: \text{a limit ordinal}, \end{cases}\] where the \(\varinjlim\) is formed with respect to \((\varphi(\beta',\beta))_{\beta'\leq\beta<\alpha}\). The properties of \(F_1\) and the fact that filtered \(\varinjlim\) preserves monomorphisms determine the evident choices of \(\varphi(\beta,\alpha)\).

By Lemma A.2.10, choose a small regular cardinal \(\alpha\) such that \(\alpha>|\mathrm{Sub}_s|\). We show that \(F_\alpha X\) is injective for every \(X\). Given \(Y\hookrightarrow s\) and \(f:Y\to F_\alpha X\), the definition of a regular cardinal A.2.7 implies that \(\alpha\) is a limit ordinal. The construction of \(F_\alpha\), the inclusion \(\mathrm{Sub}_Y\subset\mathrm{Sub}_s\), and Lemma reference show that \(f\) factors through some \(\varphi:Y\to F_\beta X\) with \(\beta+1<\alpha\). Consider the commutative diagram \[\text{Diagram chapter2-unit-030-d004}\] This diagram shows directly that \(f\) extends to a morphism \(s\to F_\alpha X\). Lemma reference then implies that \(F_\alpha X\) is injective. Finally, take \(F:=F_\alpha:\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{I}\) and \(\varphi:=\varphi(0,\alpha)\).

Corollary. Every Grothendieck category has an injective cogenerator.

Proof. Choose a generator \(s\) of the Grothendieck category \(\mathcal{A}\). The set \(\mathrm{Quot}_s\) is known to be small. Choose an injective object \(I\) and a monomorphism \(\bigoplus_{Q\in\mathrm{Quot}_s}Q\hookrightarrow I\). We use the criterion in Proposition reference to show that \(I\) is a cogenerator.

Let \(T\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{A})\) be nonzero. There is a nonzero morphism \(s\to T\), which factors as \(s\twoheadrightarrow Q'\hookrightarrow T\). Consequently there is a \[Q' \stackrel{\text{evident}}{\hookrightarrow} \bigoplus_{Q \in \mathrm{Quot}_s} Q \hookrightarrow I.\] By the definition of an injective object, this composite extends to a morphism \(T\to I\), and the extension is plainly nonzero. This proves the claim.

Corollary. Let \(\mathcal{A}\) be a Grothendieck category. A functor \(F:\mathcal{A}\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{Set}}\) is representable if and only if it preserves all small \(\varprojlim\).

Proof. The category \(\mathcal{A}\) has a cogenerator; apply Corollary reference.

Another characterization of Grothendieck categories is given by the Gabriel–Popescu–Kuhn theorem A.3.2 in the appendix to this book.

Exercises

Show that the full additive subcategory of \(\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\) formed by free \(\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\)-modules is not an abelian category.

Let \(X\) be an object of an abelian category and let \(Y,Z\in\mathrm{Sub}_X\). Consider the isomorphisms of partially ordered sets \[\text{Diagram chapter2-unit-030-d005}\] where the vertical arrows come from Theorem reference (ii), the lower horizontal arrow comes from the isomorphism \(Y/(Y\cap Z)\simeq(Y+Z)/Z\) in Theorem reference (iii), and the upper horizontal arrow is the map \(W\mapsto W+Z\) of Proposition reference. Show that the diagram commutes.

Let \(\Bbbk\) be a commutative ring and \(\mathcal{A}\) a \(\Bbbk\)-linear abelian category. Prove that if \(\operatorname{Hom}(X,X)\) is an Artinian \(\Bbbk\)-module for every \(X\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{A})\), then \(\mathcal{A}\) satisfies the bi-chain condition of Definition reference. Hint. For a bi-chain \((X_n,\alpha_n,\beta_n)_{n=0}^\infty\), the assignment \(f\mapsto\beta_n f\alpha_n\) defines a sequence of monomorphisms of \(\Bbbk\)-modules \(\operatorname{Hom}(X_{n+1},X_{n+1})\hookrightarrow\operatorname{Hom}(X_n,X_n)\). Show that this morphism is an isomorphism if and only if both \(\alpha_n\) and \(\beta_n\) are isomorphisms.

Let \(\mathcal{K}\) be an \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ab}}\)-category with a zero object. If \(\operatorname{ker}(e)\) exists for every \(X\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{K})\) and every idempotent \(e\in\operatorname{End}(X)\), then \(\mathcal{K}\) is called a Karoubian category.

  1. Prove that every idempotent \(e\) in a Karoubian category has a cokernel, and that there is a canonical isomorphism \(\operatorname{ker}(e)\simeq\operatorname{coker}(e)\).

  2. For every \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ab}}\)-category \(\mathcal{C}\) with a zero object, canonically construct a Karoubian category \(\mathrm{kar}(\mathcal{C})\) together with a fully faithful additive functor \(\varphi_{\mathcal{C}}:\mathcal{C}\to\mathrm{kar}(\mathcal{C})\) such that, for every Karoubian category \(\mathcal{K}\), the functor \[\varphi_{\mathcal{C}}^*: \mathcal{K}^{\mathrm{kar}(\mathcal{C})}\to \mathcal{K}^{\mathcal{C}},\quad F\mapsto F\varphi_{\mathcal{C}}\] is an equivalence. Here \(\mathcal{K}^{\mathcal{C}}\) denotes the functor category whose objects are all additive functors \(\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{K}\), and similarly for the other notation.

  3. If \(\Bbbk\) is a commutative ring and \(\mathcal{C}\) is \(\Bbbk\)-linear, then \(\mathrm{kar}(\mathcal{C})\) also carries a natural \(\Bbbk\)-linear structure.

The category \(\mathrm{kar}(\mathcal{C})\) is usually called the Karoubi envelope of \(\mathcal{C}\); it is obtained by formally adjoining all direct summands to \(\mathcal{C}\). Hint. Take the objects of \(\mathrm{kar}(\mathcal{C})\) to be pairs \((X,e)\), where \(X\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{C})\) and \(e\in\operatorname{End}(X)\) is idempotent. A morphism \((X,p)\to(Y,q)\) is a morphism \(f:X\to Y\) in \(\mathcal{C}\) satisfying \(qf=f=fp\), while \(\varphi_{\mathcal{C}}(X)=(X,\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_X)\).

For a ring \(R\), verify that all projective \(R\)-modules form a Karoubian category that is not abelian.

Let the abelian category \(\mathcal{A}\) have all small direct sums \(\bigoplus_{i\in I}\) (respectively, all small products \(\prod_{i\in I}\)). Prove that a small set \(\Sigma\subset\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{A})\) is a family of generators (respectively, a family of cogenerators) if and only if, for every \(X\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{A})\), there is a small direct sum (respectively, small product) \(S\) of members of \(\Sigma\), together with an epimorphism \(S\twoheadrightarrow X\) (respectively, a monomorphism \(X\hookrightarrow S\)). Hint. For a family of generators, the “if” direction is easy. For the “only if” direction, take the evident morphism \[f: \bigoplus_{s \in \Sigma} \bigoplus_{\varphi \in \operatorname{Hom}(s, X)} s \to X;\] every morphism \(\varphi\) factors through \(f\). Hence every composite \(s\xrightarrow{\varphi'}X\to\operatorname{coker}(f)\) is \(0\); conclude that \(\operatorname{coker}(f)=0\).

Let \(A,B,C\) be subobjects of an object \(X\) in an abelian category, and suppose that \(A\cap(B+C)=0=B\cap C\). Prove that \(A\cap B=0\) and \((A+B)\cap C=0\). Hint. Construct a monomorphism \((A+B)\cap C\to A\), then show that it factors through \(A\cap(B+C)\). You may first try the case of a module category.

Prove that the abelian category of finitely generated \(\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\)-modules has enough projective objects but does not have enough injective objects.

(Schanuel’s lemma) Let \(P,Q\) be projective objects in an abelian category and consider the short exact sequences \[\begin{gather*} 0 \to K \to P \xrightarrow{\phi} M \to 0, \\ 0 \to L \to Q \xrightarrow{\psi} M \to 0. \end{gather*}\] From these data, form the pullback diagram \[\text{Diagram chapter2-unit-030-d006}\] Show that there are short exact sequences \(0\to L\to X\xrightarrow{\psi'}P\to0\) and \(0\to K\to X\xrightarrow{\phi'}Q\to0\), and then prove that there is an isomorphism \(K\oplus Q\simeq L\oplus P\). Hint.Apply Propositions reference and reference.

Prove that \(\ensuremath{\mathbb{Q}}/\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\) is an injective cogenerator for \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ab}}\).

Verify in detail the adjunctions in Example reference.

Let \(\mathcal{C}\) be a nonempty category and \(\mathcal{A}\) an abelian category. For every \(c\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{C})\), the evaluation functor \(\mathrm{ev}_c:\mathcal{A}^{\mathcal{C}}\to\mathcal{A}\) sends \(F\) to \(Fc\).

  1. Suppose that \(\mathcal{A}\) has all direct sums of the forms \(\bigoplus_{c\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{C})}\) and \(\bigoplus_{f\in\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}}(c,c')}\). For every \(c\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{C})\), define a functor \(\mathcal{L}_c:\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{A}^{\mathcal{C}}\) on objects by \((\mathcal{L}_cX)(c')=\bigoplus_{\operatorname{Hom}(c,c')}X\). Complete its definition on morphisms so that \(\mathcal{L}_c\) is left adjoint to \(\mathrm{ev}_c\).

  2. Under the preceding assumptions, prove that if \(\mathcal{A}\) has enough projective objects, then so does \(\mathcal{A}^{\mathcal{C}}\).

  3. Investigate the dual version. Suppose that \(\mathcal{A}\) has all products of the forms \(\prod_{c\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{C})}\) and \(\prod_{f\in\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}}(c',c)}\). Define a functor \(\mathcal{R}_c:\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{A}^{\mathcal{C}}\) by \((\mathcal{R}_cX)(c')=\prod_{\operatorname{Hom}(c',c)}X\) that is right adjoint to \(\mathrm{ev}_c\). Then prove that if \(\mathcal{A}\) has enough injective objects, so does \(\mathcal{A}^{\mathcal{C}}\).

  4. Investigate the relation of these constructions to Example reference when \(\mathcal{C}=\mathbf{2}\).
