With the notation of the preceding exercise, let \(\mathcal{C}\) be a small category. Prove that if \(s\) is a generator (respectively, cogenerator) for \(\mathcal{A}\), then all the \(\mathcal{L}_c(s)\) (respectively, \(\mathcal{R}_c(s)\)), as \(c\) ranges over \(\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{C})\), form a family of generators (respectively, cogenerators) for \(\mathcal{A}^{\mathcal{C}}\), provided the required direct sums (respectively, direct products) exist. Hint. For the generator case, for every \(c\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{C})\) and every morphism \(f:X\to Y\) in \(\mathcal{A}^{\mathcal{C}}\) there is a commutative diagram \[\text{Diagram chapter2-unit-030-d007}\] The condition for a family to be a family of generators is equivalent to saying that, as \(c\) ranges over \(\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{C})\), all the maps \(f_*\) in the second column determine \(f\) uniquely.

(Direct construction of the Serre quotient) For a Serre subcategory \(\mathcal{T}\) of an abelian category \(\mathcal{A}\), define a new category whose set of objects is \(\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{A})\), and whose set of morphisms from \(X\) to \(Y\) is \[\varinjlim_{X' \subset X, Y' \subset Y} \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{A}}(X', Y/Y'), \quad \text{where}\; X/X',\;Y'\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{T}).\]

  1. Complete the definition of composition of morphisms and show that this category is equivalent to the Serre quotient \(\mathcal{A}/\mathcal{T}\) of Theorem reference. Hint.

    Verify that this category has the universal property stated in Theorem reference.

  2. Use this construction to show that if \(\mathcal{A}\) is well-powered (Definition reference), then \(\mathcal{A}/\mathcal{T}\) is also a \(\mathcal{U}\)-category, where \(\mathcal{U}\) is the chosen Grothendieck universe.

Let \(\mathcal{B}\) be an abelian subcategory of \(\mathcal{A}\), and suppose that for every \(X\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{A})\) there is a sequence of subobjects \(0=X_0\subset\cdots\subset X_n=X\) such that \(X_i/X_{i-1}\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{B})\). Prove that the inclusion functor \(\mathcal{B}\to\mathcal{A}\) induces an isomorphism of groups \(\mathrm{K}_0(\mathcal{B})\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}\mathrm{K}_0(\mathcal{A})\). Hint. Use the Schreier refinement theorem reference to show that \([X]\mapsto\sum_{i=1}^n[X_i/X_{i-1}]\) gives an inverse map independent of the choice of the sequence of subobjects.

Let \(\mathrm{isom}\) be the set of isomorphism classes of all objects in an additive category \(\mathcal{A}\). Write \(\ensuremath{\left\langle X \right\rangle}\) for the image of the isomorphism class of an object \(X\) in the free \(\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\)-module \(\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}^{\oplus\mathrm{isom}}\). Define the direct-sum version of the \(\mathrm{K}_0\) group by \[\mathrm{K}_{\oplus}(\mathcal{A}) := \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}^{\oplus \mathrm{isom}} \big/ \text{the submodule generated by all}\; \ensuremath{\left\langle X \oplus Y \right\rangle} - \ensuremath{\left\langle X \right\rangle} - \ensuremath{\left\langle Y \right\rangle}.\]

Let \(\mathrm{ind}\) be the set of isomorphism classes of indecomposable objects. Prove that if \(\mathcal{A}\) is Karoubian and every nonzero object has a finite direct-sum decomposition \(X\simeq X_1\oplus\cdots\oplus X_k\), with \(X_i\neq0\) and \(\operatorname{End}(X_i)\) a local ring (see the discussion before Corollary reference), then there is a canonical isomorphism \[\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}^{\oplus \mathrm{ind}} \ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}\mathrm{K}_{\oplus}(\mathcal{A}).\] Hint. Recall that if \(\operatorname{End}(X_i)\) is a local ring, then \(X_i\) is indecomposable; prove this directly or see [Li1]. Then use [Li1] to obtain uniqueness of the decomposition.

Let \(\mathcal{A}\) be a Grothendieck category and \((X_i)_{i\in I}\) a family of objects indexed by a small set \(I\). Prove that the canonical morphism \(\delta:\bigoplus_{i\in I}X_i\to\prod_{i\in I}X_i\) in equation is a monomorphism. Hint. For every finite subset \(F\subset I\), consider the commutative diagram \[\text{Diagram chapter2-unit-030-d008}\] Take the filtered \(\varinjlim\) of \(\iota_F\delta_F\) over all finite \(F\subset I\), and conclude that \(\delta\) is a monomorphism; see Proposition reference.

Prove that if \(\mathcal{A}\) is a Grothendieck category, then the category of complexes \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})\) (see §3.1) and the functor category \(\mathcal{A}^{\mathcal{C}}\) are both Grothendieck categories, where \(\mathcal{C}\) is any small category.

(Characterization of direct sums) Let \(\mathcal{A}\) be a Grothendieck category. Consider \(X\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{A})\) and a family of subobjects \((X_i)_{i\in I}\), where \(I\) is a small set. The restriction of the canonical morphism \(\bigoplus_{i\in I}X_i\to X\) to each \(X_i\) is the inclusion \(X_i\hookrightarrow X\). Prove that \(\bigoplus_{i\in I}X_i\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}X\) if and only if the following properties hold.

  1. \(X=\sum_{i\in I}X_i\);

  2. for every \(i\in I\) one has \(X_i\cap\sum_{\substack{j\in I\\j\neq i}}X_j=0\).

Observe that condition (ii) need only be checked on finite subsets of \(I\). If \(I\) itself is finite, the preceding statement holds in any abelian category. Hint. Property (i) is equivalent to the canonical morphism being an epimorphism, while (ii) is equivalent to its being a monomorphism. The first is immediate; for the second, use filtered \(\varinjlim\) to reduce to the case of finite \(I\).

Consider an object \(X\) in a Grothendieck category \(\mathcal{A}\).

  1. Supply a detailed proof of Remark reference. Hint. Use the preceding exercise to handle infinite direct sums.

  2. Under the following hypothesis, prove that if \(X\) is split, then \(X\) is semisimple: for every nonzero \(Y\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{A})\), there is a nonzero subobject \(Y_0\subset Y\) such that every chain in the partially ordered set \(\mathrm{Sub}_{Y_0}\smallsetminus\{Y_0\}\) has an upper bound. Verify this hypothesis for \(\mathcal{A}=R\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\). Hint. You may follow the implication (iii) \(\implies\) (i) in the proof of [Li1], together with the proof of [Li1].

Complexes

The notion of a complex was introduced briefly in § reference. For a complex \(X=(X^n,d^n)_n\) in an abelian category \(\mathcal{A}\), the cohomology \(\operatorname{H}^n(X):=\operatorname{ker}(d^n)/\operatorname{im}(d^{n-1})\) 1 extracts important invariants from \(X\). Conversely, 2 a complex whose cohomology vanishes in every degree is an exact sequence, also called an acyclic complex. Much of §§ 3.2– 3.5 does not involve cohomology and applies to an arbitrary additive category \(\mathcal{A}\). The category of complexes over \(\mathcal{A}\) is denoted by \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})\). Unless stated otherwise, all complexes in this chapter are cochain complexes in the sense of Remark reference; whenever \(\Bbbk\) occurs, it denotes an arbitrary commutative ring. For complexes \(X\) and \(Y\) over an additive category \(\mathcal{A}\), homotopy is an equivalence relation on \(\operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})}(X,Y)\). It can also be understood through the \(\operatorname{Hom}\) complex \(\operatorname{Hom}^\bullet(X,Y)\), studied in § 3.2. If \(\mathcal{A}\) is abelian, homotopic morphisms induce the same maps on cohomology. The mapping cone \(\operatorname{Cone}(f)\) introduced in § 3.3 will subsequently play a major role in the study of derived categories. Mapping cones are closely related to homotopy, and both have direct topological interpretations. A double complex \(X=(X^{p,q},\ensuremath{{}^\vartriangleright d}^{p,q},\ensuremath{{}^\vartriangle d}^{p,q})_{p,q}\) may be viewed as a complex with two independent directions, or equivalently as a “complex of complexes.” A double complex \(X\) can be flattened by direct sums (respectively, direct products) into a complex \(\operatorname{tot}_{\oplus}X\) (respectively, \(\operatorname{tot}_{\Pi}X\)), called a total complex of \(X\). The precise definitions involve several signs; these details are the subject of § 3.5. One of the basic techniques of homological algebra is to derive a long exact sequence in cohomology from a short exact sequence of complexes \(0\to X'\xrightarrow{f}X\xrightarrow{g}X''\to0\): \[\cdots \to \operatorname{H}^n(X') \xrightarrow{\operatorname{H}^n(f)} \operatorname{H}^n(X) \xrightarrow{\operatorname{H}^n(g)} \operatorname{H}^n(X'') \xrightarrow{\text{connecting morphism}} \operatorname{H}^{n+1}(X') \to \cdots .\] Long exact sequences can also be understood from the viewpoint of mapping cones, although this requires a nontrivial argument. These topics are treated in §§ 3.6– 3.7. To help the reader become familiar with the basic operations on complexes, § 3.8 offers an integrated exercise based on the Hochschild homology \(\operatorname{HH}_n(M)\) and Hochschild cohomology \(\operatorname{HH}^n(M)\) of an \((R,R)\)-bimodule \(M\). Hochschild homology and cohomology have many uses throughout mathematics. This chapter gives only a brief pedagogical introduction; both will reappear as examples in later chapters. Using the truncation functors introduced in § 3.9, we shall relate the vertical or horizontal cohomology of a double complex to the cohomology of its total complex in § 3.10. Certain boundedness conditions on the double complex are needed. Some textbooks treat these properties with spectral sequences; following [KS06], this book takes a somewhat indirect route and proves them directly. For an object \(X\) of an abelian category \(\mathcal{A}\), a resolution of \(X\) has left and right versions, concretely given by exact sequences 3 \[0\to X\to I^0\to I^1\to I^2\to\cdots \quad\text{or}\quad \cdots\to P_1\to P_0\to X\to0 .\] Equivalently, one replaces \(X\) by a complex with better properties through a quasi-isomorphism \(X\to I:=(I^n)_n\) or \(P:=(P_n)_n\to X\), where \(P\) is a chain complex. A quasi-isomorphism is a morphism inducing isomorphisms on cohomology or homology. If every \(I^n\) (respectively, \(P_n\)) is required to be injective (respectively, projective), the construction is called an injective (respectively, projective) resolution of \(X\). Resolutions are studied in depth in § 3.11. They are also functorial and unique up to homotopy in the following sense. For the injective version, suppose the solid part of the following diagram lies in \(\mathcal{A}\). \[\text{Diagram chapter3-unit-031-d001}\] Assume that both rows are exact and that every \((I')^n\) is injective. There are dashed arrows \(\beta^0,\beta^1,\ldots\) making the entire diagram commutative, and the morphism of complexes \(\beta:I\to I'\) is unique up to homotopy. This is a joint application of Theorem in § 3.11 and Lemma in § 3.11, both special cases of broader statements. In fact, § 3.11 treats not only resolutions of objects \(X\) of \(\mathcal{A}\), but also resolutions of complexes. Its results include the useful Cartan–Eilenberg resolution (Theorem in § 3.11). Some arguments for complexes inevitably become lengthy, even though their underlying idea remains clear. Replacing objects of \(\mathcal{A}\) by injective (respectively, projective) resolutions, applying a left exact (respectively, right exact) functor \(F:\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{B}\) termwise, and then taking \(\operatorname{H}^n\) (respectively, \(\operatorname{H}_n=\operatorname{H}^{-n}\)) leads to the classical definition of the right derived functors \(\mathrm{R}^nF\) (respectively, the left derived functors \(\mathrm{L}_nF\)). Short exact sequences in \(\mathcal{A}\) then induce long exact sequences of derived functors; see § 3.12. Resolutions of complexes also allow derived functors to be evaluated on bounded-below or bounded-above complexes; in the classical literature these constructions are called hyperderived functors. Right (respectively, left) derived functors and their long exact sequences naturally give rise to cohomological (respectively, homological) \(\delta\)-functors, among which derived functors are “universal.” Proposition in § 3.12 characterizes universal \(\delta\)-functors by the erasability (respectively, co-erasability) condition of Definition in § 3.12. This result is due to Grothendieck. The associated collection of techniques forms the core of classical homological algebra. Another important construction consists of the right (respectively, left) derived functors of a bifunctor \(F:\mathcal{A}_1\times\mathcal{A}_2\to\mathcal{B}\) such that \(F\) is left exact (respectively, right exact) in both variables. Standard examples are the \(\operatorname{Ext}\) and \(\operatorname{Tor}\) functors of § 3.14; the former necessarily involves complexes over an opposite category. Theorem in § 3.14 studies a class of bifunctors called balanced and shows that deriving in either variable gives the same result. Its proof rests on basic properties of the cohomology of double complexes. Suppose that \(\mathcal{A}\) has exact countable products. The construction \(\lim^1\) discussed in § 3.13 is another example of a right derived functor: it is the first right derived functor of \(\varprojlim\), while all higher right derived functors vanish (Theorem in § 3.13). To obtain practical criteria ensuring \(\lim^1=0\), we shall introduce the Mittag–Leffler condition in Definition in § 3.13. Finally, in § 3.15 we study K-injective and K-projective complexes and define K-injective and K-projective resolutions. These are natural generalizations of injective and projective resolutions to unbounded complexes. Because K-injectivity and K-projectivity are properties of an entire complex, their definitions are more concise and natural than the termwise definitions of injective and projective resolutions. They extend the definition of derived functors to unbounded complexes. The issue is existence: Theorems in § 3.15 and in § 3.15 give partial results. Their proofs are comparatively intricate and require some properties of \(\lim^1\).

  1. Editorial correction (O014-C032): the source prints \(\operatorname{im}(d^{n+1})\). Under the cochain convention \(X^{n-1}\xrightarrow{d^{n-1}}X^n\xrightarrow{d^n}X^{n+1}\), the subobject contained in \(\operatorname{ker}(d^n)\) is \(\operatorname{im}(d^{n-1})\); the corrected index agrees with the book’s earlier definition.↩︎

  2. Editorial correction (O014-C030): the source has a full stop followed by a stray character before the clause about the vanishing of all cohomology, leaving the transition ungrammatical. The context gives the converse direction, restored here without changing the mathematical claim.↩︎

  3. Editorial correction (O014-C031): the source prints \(0\to X\to I^0\to I^2\to\cdots\), omitting \(I^1\). The diagram immediately following uses \(I^0,I^1,I^2\) in order; the missing term \(I^1\) is restored here.↩︎

Complexes over Additive Categories

Definition reference briefly introduced complexes and their usual notation. Let \(\mathcal{A}\) be an additive category, and consider unbounded complexes over it, that is, complexes without endpoint terms, \(X=(X^n,d^n)_{n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}}\). The morphism \(d^n\) is often denoted by \(d_X^n\). For historical reasons, the morphisms \(d_X^n\) are also called “differentials.”

Definition. A morphism from a complex \(X\) to a complex \(Y\) is defined to be data \((f^n)_{n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}}\), also abbreviated to \(f\), where \(f^n\in\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{A}}(X^n,Y^n)\) satisfies \[d_Y^n f^n=f^{n+1}d_X^n,\quad n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}.\]

All complexes and their morphisms form a category \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})\). The identity morphism of a complex \(X\) is determined by \((\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_X)^n:=\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{X^n}\), and composition is defined by \((gf)^n=g^nf^n\). Addition \(f+g:=(f^n+g^n)_{n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}}\) makes \(\operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})}(X,Y)\) an abelian group.

If \(\mathcal{A}\) is a \(\Bbbk\)-linear category in the sense of Definition reference, for a fixed commutative ring \(\Bbbk\), then \(\operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})}(X,Y)\) is also a \(\Bbbk\)-module under termwise scalar multiplication. In every result of this section, “additive” may be replaced by the more general term “\(\Bbbk\)-linear.” For brevity, only the additive version will be stated. The key property in the definition of a complex is \(d^{n+1}d^n=0\). It can also be recast in the language of differential graded objects. 1

Definition (Graded objects). Let \(\mathcal{A}\) be an arbitrary category. Recall the construction of the product category \(\mathcal{A}^{\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}}\):

  • its objects are of the form \(X=(X^n)_{n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}}\), where \(X^n\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{A})\);

  • its morphisms are of the form \(f=(f^n:X^n\to Y^n)_{n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}}\), with no further condition, and composition is performed termwise (or degreewise), so that \((gf)^n=g^nf^n\);

  • define an automorphism \(T\) of \(\mathcal{A}^{\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}}\) by the following “shift” functor: \((TX)^n=X^{n+1}\) and \((Tf)^n=f^{n+1}\).

An object \(X=(X^n)_n\) is also called a \(\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\)-graded object over \(\mathcal{A}\), or simply a graded object.

More generally, objects of \(\mathcal{A}^{\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}^m}\) are called \(\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}^m\)-graded objects and are written \((X^{n_1,\ldots,n_m})_{n_1,\ldots,n_m}\); their morphisms are written \((f^{n_1,\ldots,n_m})_{n_1,\ldots,n_m}\). This category carries a family of mutually commuting shift functors \(T_1,\ldots,T_m\). The special case \(m=2\) is also called a bigraded object.

If \(\mathcal{A}\) is additive, then so is \(\mathcal{A}^{\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}^m}\): addition of morphisms, direct sums of objects, and all other operations are performed degreewise.

Definition (Differential graded objects). Let \(\mathcal{A}\) be an additive category. A differential graded object over \(\mathcal{A}\) is data \((X,d)\), where \(X\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{A}^{\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}})\) and \(d:X\to TX\) satisfies \((Td)d=0\). A morphism \((X,d_X)\to(Y,d_Y)\) is a morphism \(f\in\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{A}^{\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}}}(X,Y)\) satisfying \((Tf)d_X=d_Yf\).

Writing \(d\) in a differential graded object \((X,d)\) concretely as a family of morphisms \(d_X^n:X^n\to X^{n+1}\), the condition on \(d\) is \(d_X^{n+1}d_X^n=0\), while the condition on a morphism is \(f^{n+1}d_X^n=d_Y^nf^n\). We have thus recovered Definition reference. Hence the category of differential graded objects over \(\mathcal{A}\) is isomorphic to the category of complexes. We shall pass between these two viewpoints without further comment. The first step in studying complexes is to understand the various limits in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})\). The version for the product category \(\mathcal{A}^{\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}}\) is straightforward: limits can be formed at each \(n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\), that is, termwise or degreewise in \(\mathcal{A}\). We now explain how to lift this construction to \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})\). Write \(U:\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})\to\mathcal{A}^{\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}}\) for the forgetful functor sending a differential graded object \((X,d)\) to its underlying graded object \(X\).

Lemma (Termwise construction of limits). For any functor \(\alpha:I\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})\), write \(\overline{\alpha}:=U\alpha\). Suppose that \(\varinjlim\overline{\alpha}\) exists. It admits a unique structure as an object of \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})\) for which it is \(\varinjlim\alpha\). The corresponding statement holds for \(\varprojlim\).

In the language of Definition reference, this says that the forgetful functor \(U\) creates \(\varinjlim\) and \(\varprojlim\).

Proof. Suppose that \(\alpha:I\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})\) sends \(i\in\operatorname{Ob}(I)\) to the differential graded object \(\alpha(i)=(\overline{\alpha}(i),d_i)\). If \(\varinjlim\overline{\alpha}\) exists, the morphisms \(d_i\) determine \(d:\varinjlim\overline{\alpha}\to (T\varinjlim\overline{\alpha}\simeq \varinjlim T\overline{\alpha})\); here the automorphism \(T\) automatically preserves \(\varinjlim\). This morphism is characterized by the commutative diagram \[\text{Diagram chapter3-unit-032-d001} \qquad (i \in \operatorname{Ob}(I)) .\]

The relations \((Td_i)d_i=0\) imply \((Td)d=0\), so \((\varinjlim\overline{\alpha},d)\) is an object of \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})\). The diagram also shows that this is the unique choice making all maps \((\overline{\alpha}(i),d_i)\to (\varinjlim\overline{\alpha},d)\) morphisms.

We verify its universal property as \(\varinjlim\alpha\) in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})\). Suppose a compatible family of morphisms \(f_i:\alpha(i)\to L\) in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})\) is given. Forgetting the differentials gives \(f_i:\overline{\alpha}(i)\to U(L)\), which determines a unique \(f:\varinjlim\overline{\alpha}\to U(L)\). The key point is to show that \(f\) is a morphism in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})\). Although this is to be expected, we write the diagram explicitly: \[\text{Diagram chapter3-unit-032-d002} \qquad (i \in \operatorname{Ob}(I)).\] Commutativity of every part follows directly from the definitions or the construction. Thus the composites of \(d_Lf\) and \((Tf)d\) with every map \(\overline{\alpha}(i)\to\varinjlim\overline{\alpha}\) agree. Therefore \(d_Lf=(Tf)d\), as required.

Proposition. The category \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})\) is additive. If \(\mathcal{A}\) is complete (respectively, cocomplete), then \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})\) is also complete (respectively, cocomplete).

Proof. Use Lemma reference to reduce every required limit to a degreewise limit in \(\mathcal{A}\).

Definition (Translation functors). Let \(X\) be an object of \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})\) and let \(n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\). Define the complex \(X[n]\) as follows: 2 \[\left(X[n]\right)^k:=X^{k+n},\quad d_{X[n]}^k:=(-1)^nd_X^{k+n}.\] This construction gives an additive functor \([n]:\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})\). If \(f:X\to Y\) is a morphism of complexes, then \(f[n]:X[n]\to Y[n]\) is given by \(f[n]^k:=f^{n+k}\).

It is clear that \(X[n]\) is again a complex, so the functor is well defined. The following properties are also immediate.

  • \([0]=\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})}\).

  • \([n][m]=[n+m]\). Thus \([n]\) is an automorphism of \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})\), with inverse \([-n]\).

  • The family \((d_X^n)_{n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}}\) gives a morphism of complexes \(d_X:X\to X[1]\) (Hint: \(d_X^{n+1}d_X^n=0\)).

Convention. Every object \(S\) of \(\mathcal{A}\) may be regarded as a complex \((S^n,d_S^n)_{n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}}\) with \(S^0:=S\), every other term equal to \(0\), and every \(d_S^n\) the zero morphism. This identification gives a fully faithful additive functor \(\mathcal{A}\hookrightarrow\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})\). More generally, for every \(n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\), \(S[-n]\) is the complex concentrated in degree \(n\): it places \(S\) in degree \(n\) and \(0\) in every other degree.

The following result is immediate.

Proposition. For an additive functor \(F:\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{A}'\), the assignment \((X^n,d_X^n)_n\mapsto(FX^n,Fd_X^n)_n\) defines a functor \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}F:\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A}')\). It commutes with translation functors: \([m]\circ\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}F=\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}F\circ[m]\) for every \(m\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\).

Remark. Every result in this section also applies to the chain complexes \((X_\bullet,d_\bullet)\) mentioned in Remark reference. The translation functor on the category of chain complexes is defined by \[X[n]_k:=X_{k+n},\quad d^{X[n]}_k=(-1)^nd^X_{n+k}\] If one passes between the two conventions via \(X_n=X^{-n}\) and \(d_n=d^{-n}\), then the translation \([1]\) for chain complexes corresponds to the translation \([-1]\) for cochain complexes.

  1. The related discussion continues in § 5.2.↩︎

  2. Inserting \((-1)^n\) in the definition of \(d_{X[n]}\) is useful. This version is also isomorphic to the signless version \(X[n]^\circ:=\left(X^{n+k},d_X^{k+n}\right)_k\). For \(n=1\), define \(X[1]\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}X[1]^\circ\) using the sign pattern \(\cdots,+,-,+,\cdots\).↩︎

\(\operatorname{Hom}\) Complexes and Homotopy

We previously defined \(\operatorname{Hom}\) between two complexes. This section explains how to promote it to a complex and how to promote composition of morphisms to a kind of multiplication on complexes. We continue to let \(\mathcal{A}\) be an additive category. If \(\Bbbk\) is any commutative ring and \(\mathcal{A}\) is a \(\Bbbk\)-linear category, every statement in this section has an evident \(\Bbbk\)-linear version. Recall that taking \(\operatorname{Hom}\) sets gives a functor \(\operatorname{Hom}:\mathcal{A}^{\operatorname{op}}\times\mathcal{A}\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ab}}\). The notation \(\operatorname{Hom}\) without a superscript refers to the \(\operatorname{Hom}\) set in \(\mathcal{A}\) or in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})\); when necessary, a subscript distinguishes the category.

Definition (\(\operatorname{Hom}\) complex). Let \(X,Y\) be objects of \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})\). For every \(n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\), define \[\operatorname{Hom}^n\left(X, Y \right) := \prod_{k \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}} \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{A}}\left( X^k, Y^{k+n} \right);\] termwise composition of morphisms gives \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:Hom-cplx-multiplication}{}\begin{aligned} \operatorname{Hom}^n \left(Y, Z \right) \times \operatorname{Hom}^m\left( X, Y \right) & \longrightarrow \operatorname{Hom}^{n+m}\left(X , Z \right) \\ (g, f) & \longmapsto gf := \left( g^{k+m} f^k \right)_{k \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}}. \end{aligned} \end{equation}\] Notice that \(d_X=(d_X^k)_k\in\operatorname{Hom}^1(X,X)\), and similarly for \(d_Y\). Accordingly, define \[\begin{align*} d^n = d_{\operatorname{Hom}^\bullet(X, Y)}^n: \operatorname{Hom}^n\left(X, Y \right) & \longrightarrow \operatorname{Hom}^{n+1}\left(X, Y \right) \\ f & \longmapsto d_Y f - (-1)^n f d_X. \end{align*}\]

The operation equation is plainly associative and distributive over addition. Given morphisms \(u:\underline{X}\to X\) and \(v:Y\to\underline{Y}\) in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})\), regard them respectively as elements of \(\operatorname{Hom}^0(\underline{X},X)\) and \(\operatorname{Hom}^0(Y,\underline{Y})\). For every \(n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\) there is then a homomorphism \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:Hom-cplx-functoriality}{}\begin{aligned} \operatorname{Hom}^n(u, v): \operatorname{Hom}^n\left( X, Y\right) & \longrightarrow \operatorname{Hom}^n\left(\underline{X}, \underline{Y}\right) \\ f & \longmapsto vfu. \end{aligned} \end{equation}\]

Definition–Proposition. The data \(\left(\operatorname{Hom}^n(X,Y),d^n\right)_{n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}}\) above form an object of \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ab}})\), called the \(\operatorname{Hom}\) complex. As \(X\) and \(Y\) vary, this construction together with equation gives an additive functor \[\operatorname{Hom}^\bullet: \ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})^{\operatorname{op}} \times \ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A}) \to \ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ab}}).\]

Proof. First verify that \(d^{n+1}d^n=0\). Since \(d_Y^2=0=d_X^2\), a direct calculation gives \[\begin{align*} d^{n+1} \left( d^n f \right) & = d_Y \left( d_Y f - (-1)^n f d_X \right) - (-1)^{n+1} \left( d_Y f - (-1)^n f d_X \right) d_X \\ & = (-1)^{n+1} d_Y f d_X - (-1)^{n+1} d_Y f d_X = 0. \end{align*}\]

Next consider functoriality. Place the map \(\operatorname{Hom}^\bullet(u,v)\) defined in equation into the diagram 1 \[\text{Diagram chapter3-unit-033-d001}\] Because \(d_Xu=ud_{\underline{X}}\) and \(vd_Y=d_{\underline{Y}}v\), this diagram is plainly commutative.

The differential \(d_{\operatorname{Hom}^\bullet(X,Y)}\) is also compatible with shifts. Its proof is much easier than its statement.

Lemma. Let \(n,m\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\) and \(f\in\operatorname{Hom}^n(X,Y)\). Identify \(f\) with the element \(\underline{f}=(f^k)_k\) of \(\operatorname{Hom}^{n-m}(X,Y[m])\), or with the element \(\overline{f}=(f^{k-m})_k\) of \(\operatorname{Hom}^{n-m}(X[-m],Y)\). Then \[\begin{align*} d^{n-m}_{\operatorname{Hom}^\bullet(X, Y[m])} \underline{f} & \xlongequal{\text{under the identification}} (-1)^m d^n_{\operatorname{Hom}^\bullet(X, Y)} f, \\ d^{n-m}_{\operatorname{Hom}^\bullet(X[-m], Y)} \overline{f} & \xlongequal{\text{under the identification}} d^n_{\operatorname{Hom}^\bullet(X, Y)} f. \end{align*}\] Consequently, \(\operatorname{Hom}^\bullet(X,Y[m])=\operatorname{Hom}^\bullet(X,Y)[m]\simeq \operatorname{Hom}^\bullet(X[-m],Y)\).

Proof. For example, for the first equality, \[(d^{n-m}_{\operatorname{Hom}^\bullet(X, Y[m])} \underline{f})^k = d_{Y[m]}^{k+n-m} \underline{f}^k - (-1)^{n-m} \underline{f}^{k+1} d_X^k : X^k \to Y^{k+n+1},\] which also equals \((-1)^m\left(d_Y^{k+n}f^k-(-1)^nf^{k+1}d_X^k\right)\). The argument for \(\overline{f}\) is similar: although the case of \(\overline{f}\) has no factor \((-1)^m\), there is still an isomorphism of \(\operatorname{Hom}\) complexes; see the footnote to Definition reference.

The multiplication defined in equation also obeys the Leibniz rule.

Lemma. Let \(X,Y,Z\) be complexes and \((g,f)\in\operatorname{Hom}^n(Y,Z)\times\operatorname{Hom}^m(X,Y)\). With respect to the multiplication in equation, the following equality holds: \[\begin{aligned} d^{n+m}(gf) &= (d^n g)f \\ &\quad + (-1)^n g(d^m f) \end{aligned}\] in \(\operatorname{Hom}^{n+m+1}(X,Z)\).

Proof. This is a direct calculation, left to the reader.

Lemma. Let \(n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\) and \(f\in\operatorname{Hom}^n(X,Y)\). Then \(d^nf=0\) if and only if \(f\in\operatorname{Hom}(X,Y[n])\).

Proof. Via Lemma reference, identify \(f\) with an element of \(\operatorname{Hom}^0(X,Y[n])\), reducing the question to the case \(n=0\). Clearly, \(d^0f=0\iff d_Yf=fd_X\).

Definition. Let \(n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\). Regard \(\operatorname{Hom}(X,Y[n])\) as a subset of \(\operatorname{Hom}^n(X,Y)\).

  • If \(f,g\in\operatorname{Hom}(X,Y[n])\) and \(h\in\operatorname{Hom}^{n-1}(X,Y)\) (equivalently, \(h\in\operatorname{Hom}^{-1}(X,Y[n])\)) 2 satisfies \(g-f=d^{n-1}h\), then \(h\) is called a homotopy from \(f\) to \(g\).

  • For \(f,g\) as above, if there exists a homotopy from \(f\) to \(g\), then \(f\) and \(g\) are called homotopic. A morphism \(f\) homotopic to the zero morphism is called null-homotopic.

As the special case \(n=0\), a morphism \(f\in\operatorname{Hom}(X,Y)\) is null-homotopic if and only if there is a family of morphisms \(h^m:X^m\to Y^{m-1}\) such that \[\forall m \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}, \quad f^m = d_Y^{m-1} h^m + h^{m+1} d_X^m .\]

Homotopy is an equivalence relation. Lemma reference gives the key equality in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ab}}\) (or \(\Bbbk\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\)): \[\operatorname{H}^n\left(\operatorname{Hom}^\bullet(X, Y), d^\bullet \right) = \operatorname{Hom}\left(X, Y[n]\right) \big/ \{\text{null-homotopic morphisms} \}.\] The next result shows that null-homotopic morphisms are not merely closed under addition but form an ideal.

Lemma. Let \(X\xrightarrow{f}Y[m]\) and \(Y\xrightarrow{g}Z[n]\) be morphisms of complexes. If \(f\) or \(g\) is null-homotopic, then \(g[m]\circ f:X\to Z[n+m]\) is null-homotopic.

Proof. We suppress the superscripts on \(d\). Suppose \(f=dh\), where \(h\in\operatorname{Hom}^{-1}(X,Y[m])\). Interpreting composition inside \(\operatorname{Hom}^\bullet\), we may abbreviate \(g[m]\circ f\) as \(gf\). Lemma reference gives \(d(gh)=(dg)h+(-1)^ng(dh)=(-1)^ngf\), so \(gf\) is null-homotopic. The case \(g=dh\) is similar.

Suppressing the subscript on \(d_{\operatorname{Hom}^\bullet}\), Lemmas reference and reference show that the multiplication on \(\operatorname{Hom}^\bullet\) in equation induces \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:homotopy-cat-cmposition}{} \operatorname{H}^n\left(\operatorname{Hom}^\bullet(Y, Z) \right) \times \operatorname{H}^m\left(\operatorname{Hom}^\bullet(X, Y) \right) \to \operatorname{H}^{n+m}\left( \operatorname{Hom}^\bullet(X, Z) \right) , \end{equation}\] and the binary operation equation inherits associativity and distributivity over addition from equation.

Definition. Define the category \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{A})\) from \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})\) by setting \[\begin{align*} \operatorname{Ob}\left( \ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{A}) \right) & := \operatorname{Ob}\left( \ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A}) \right), \\ \operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{A})}\left( X, Y \right) & := \operatorname{H}^0\left( \operatorname{Hom}^\bullet\left( X, Y \right), d^\bullet_{\operatorname{Hom}} \right), \end{align*}\] with composition determined by equation for \(n=m=0\).

Observe that \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{A})\) is an additive category: addition on morphism sets is clear, the zero object comes from the zero object of \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})\), and the existence of products (or coproducts) follows from the more general property that there are natural isomorphisms \[\begin{align*} \operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{A})}\left( X, \prod_{i \in I} Y_i \right) & \simeq \prod_{i \in I} \operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{A})}(X, Y_i) \\ \text{or}\quad \operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{A})}\left( \coprod_{i \in I} X_i, Y \right) & \simeq \prod_{i \in I} \operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{A})}(X_i, Y), \end{align*}\] where \(I\) is any set, provided \(\prod_{i\in I}Y_i\) (or \(\coprod_iX_i\)) exists at the level of \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})\). Since taking products and taking \(\operatorname{H}^0\) commute in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ab}})\), everything reduces to the evident isomorphisms of \(\operatorname{Hom}\) complexes \[\begin{align*} \operatorname{Hom}^\bullet\left(X, \prod_i Y_i\right) & \simeq \prod_i \operatorname{Hom}^\bullet(X, Y_i) \\ \text{or}\quad \operatorname{Hom}^\bullet\left(\coprod_i X_i, Y\right) & \simeq \prod_i \operatorname{Hom}^\bullet(X_i, Y). \end{align*}\] The shift functor \([n]\) induces an automorphism of the additive category \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{A})\), still denoted by \([n]\). The additive functor \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{A})\) is the identity on objects and the quotient map on morphism sets. The following universal property is immediate.

Proposition. If \(\mathcal{B}\) is an \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ab}}\)-category and the additive functor \(F:\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})\to\mathcal{B}\) sends every null-homotopic morphism to the zero morphism, then \(F\) factors uniquely through \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{A})\).

The exercises in the next chapter will show that \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{A})\) is generally not an abelian category.

Remark. For chain complexes (Remark reference) there is a corresponding \(\operatorname{Hom}_\bullet\): \[\begin{gather*} \operatorname{Hom}_n(X, Y) := \prod_{k \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}} \operatorname{Hom}\left(X_k, Y_{k+n} \right), \\ d_n f = d_Y f - (-1)^n f d_X, \quad f \in \operatorname{Hom}_n(X, Y). \end{gather*}\] Indeed, use the convention in Remark reference, setting \(X^n=X_{-n}\), \(d^n=d_{-n}\), and so on. Then \(\left(\operatorname{Hom}_n(X,Y),d_n\right)_n\) is precisely the chain complex corresponding to \(\left(\operatorname{Hom}^n(X,Y),d^n\right)_n\): \[\begin{align*} \operatorname{Hom}_n\left(X, Y \right) & = \prod_{k \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}} \operatorname{Hom}\left( X_k, Y_{n+k} \right) \xlongequal{h = -k} \prod_{h \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}} \operatorname{Hom}\left(X^h, Y^{h-n} \right) \\ & = \operatorname{Hom}^{-n} \left(X, Y\right), \end{align*}\] and the relation between \(d_n\) and \(d^{-n}\) is similar. Of course, chain complexes have a corresponding version of \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{A})\) as well.

Given an additive functor \(F:\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{B}\) between additive categories and any \(X,Y\in\operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A}))\), applying \(F\) termwise gives a morphism in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ab}})\) \[\begin{align*} \operatorname{Hom}^\bullet\left(X, Y\right) & \to \operatorname{Hom}^\bullet\left(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}F(X), \ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}F(Y) \right) \\ (f^k)_{k \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}}\in\operatorname{Hom}^r(X,Y) & \mapsto (F(f^k))_{k \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}}\in \operatorname{Hom}^r\left(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}F(X),\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}F(Y)\right) \qquad (r\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}). \end{align*}\] Taking \(\operatorname{H}^0\) on both sides gives \[\operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{A})}(X,Y)\longrightarrow \operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{B})} \bigl(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}F(X),\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}F(Y)\bigr).\] Thus we obtain a functor \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}F:\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{A})\to \ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{B})\) that makes the following diagram commute: \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:KF}{}\text{Diagram chapter3-unit-033-diagram-002} \end{equation}\] The top row is the functor in Proposition reference. These constructions are compatible with adjoint pairs.

Proposition. Consider an adjoint pair \((F,G,\varphi)\), where \(\text{Diagram chapter3-unit-033-d002}\) are additive functors between additive categories. Then \[\text{Diagram chapter3-unit-033-d003}\] naturally forms an adjoint pair as well.

Proof. The adjunction data \(\varphi\) are a family of bijections \(\varphi_{A,B}:\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{B}}(FA,B)\simeq \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{A}}(A,GB)\), functorial in \(A\) and \(B\). Proposition reference ensures that these bijections are linear, and hence they induce a canonical isomorphism of complexes \[\operatorname{Hom}^\bullet\left( \ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}F(X), Y \right) \simeq \operatorname{Hom}^\bullet\left( X, \ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}G(Y) \right).\] In degree \(r\), this isomorphism sends \[(f^k)_{k\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}}\in\operatorname{Hom}^r(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}F(X),Y) \longmapsto (\varphi_{X^k,Y^{k+r}}(f^k))_{k\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}} \in\operatorname{Hom}^r(X,\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}G(Y)).\] 3 By equation, taking \(\operatorname{H}^0\) on both sides makes \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}F\) left adjoint to \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}G\).

  1. Translator’s note (O014-C033): the source labels both horizontal arrows \(\operatorname{Hom}^{n+1}(u,v)\). Since the upper arrow connects terms of degree \(n\), this translation restores its label to \(\operatorname{Hom}^n(u,v)\); the lower arrow retains the label \(\operatorname{Hom}^{n+1}(u,v)\).↩︎

  2. Translator’s note (O014-C034): the source does not state the degree of \(h\), although \(d^{n-1}h\) requires \(h\in\operatorname{Hom}^{n-1}(X,Y)\). This translation makes its type explicit.↩︎

  3. Translator’s note (O014-C035): the source writes the component as \(\varphi_{A,B}(f^n)\) without tying \(A\) and \(B\) to the source and target of the relevant graded component. This translation uses \(r\) for the complex degree and \(k\) for the family index, so the component is typed as \(\varphi_{X^k,Y^{k+r}}(f^k)\).↩︎

Mapping Cones

We continue to let \(\mathcal{A}\) be an additive category, with its associated category of complexes \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})\).

Definition. Given a morphism \(f:X\to Y\) in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})\), its mapping cone \(\operatorname{Cone}(f)\) is defined to be the following complex: \[\begin{align*} \operatorname{Cone}(f)^n & := X^{n+1} \oplus Y^n, \\ d^n_{\operatorname{Cone}(f)} & := \;\text{in matrix notation}\; \par\textbf{Diagram chapter3-unit-034-d001}\par \\ & : X^{n+1} \oplus Y^n \to X^{n+2} \oplus Y^{n+1} , \end{align*}\] for \(n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\). Since \(d_{X[1]}^n=-d_X^{n+1}\), there is also the more concise notation \[\operatorname{Cone}(f) := \left( X[1] \oplus Y , \; \begin{pmatrix} d_{X[1]} & 0 \\ f[1] & d_Y \end{pmatrix} \right) .\]

It is easy to prove that \(\operatorname{Cone}(f)\) is indeed a complex, as the following matrix calculation shows: \[\begin{pmatrix} -d_X^{n+1} & 0 \\ f^{n+1} & d_Y^n \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} -d_X^n & 0 \\ f^n & d_Y^{n-1} \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} d_X^{n+1} d_X^n & 0 \\ - f^{n+1} d_X^n + d_Y^n f^n & d_Y^n d_Y^{n-1} \end{pmatrix}.\]

Example. Let \(f:X\to Y\) be a morphism in \(\mathcal{A}\). Regard \(X,Y\) as objects of \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})\) concentrated in degree \(0\). Then \(\operatorname{Cone}(f)\) is precisely the complex \([X\xrightarrow{f}Y]\), in degrees \(-1,0\), with all other terms equal to \(0\).

The following two functoriality properties follow immediately from the definition.

Proposition. Given a commutative diagram in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})\) \[\text{Diagram chapter3-unit-034-d002}\] the matrix \(\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix} \varphi[1] & 0 \\ 0 & \psi \end{smallmatrix}\bigr)\) defines a morphism \(\operatorname{Cone}(f)\to\operatorname{Cone}(f')\).

Proposition. Let \(F:\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{A}'\) be an additive functor and let \(f:X\to Y\) be a morphism in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})\). The associated functor \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}F:\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})\to \ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A}')\) satisfies the following canonical isomorphism in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A}')\): \[(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}F)(\operatorname{Cone}(f)) \simeq \operatorname{Cone}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}F(f)).\]

The mapping cone can be placed in the following “triangle,” which underlies all the theory to come.

Definition. Consider a morphism \(f:X\to Y\) in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})\). It gives the following canonical morphisms in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})\): \[Y \xrightarrow{\alpha(f)} \operatorname{Cone}(f) \xrightarrow{\beta(f)} X[1] ,\] explicitly expressed in matrix notation as \[\begin{align*} \alpha(f)^n & := \text{inclusion}\; \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{Y^n} \end{pmatrix}: Y^n \to X[1]^n \oplus Y^n , \\ \beta(f)^n & := \text{projection}\; \begin{pmatrix} \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{X[1]^n} & 0 \end{pmatrix}: X[1]^n \oplus Y^n \to X[1]^n . \end{align*}\] It is clear that these are indeed morphisms in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})\).

We next collect several homotopy properties of mapping cones. First we show that a mapping cone may be regarded as a “homotopy cokernel” or a “homotopy kernel” of a morphism. This is the realization, at the level of complexes, of a basic idea in homotopy theory.

Proposition. Let \(f:X\to Y\) be a morphism in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})\). There are canonical bijections \[\text{Diagram chapter3-unit-034-d003}\] where \(T\) is any object of \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})\) and \(\operatorname{Hom}:=\operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})}\). More explicitly,

  • the image \((u,h)\) of \(\tilde{u}:\operatorname{Cone}(f)\to T\) satisfies \(u=\tilde{u}\circ\alpha(f)\);

  • the image \((v,k)\) of \(\tilde{v}:T\to\operatorname{Cone}(f)[-1]\) satisfies \(v=\beta(f)[-1]\circ\tilde{v}\).

Proof. First consider \(\operatorname{Hom}(\operatorname{Cone}(f),T)\). A morphism \(\tilde{u}:\operatorname{Cone}(f)\to T\) is equivalent to families of morphisms in \(\mathcal{A}\), \(h^n:X^{n+1}\to T^n\) and \(u^n:Y^n\to T^n\), for \(n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\), satisfying the matrix equation \[\begin{pmatrix} h^{n+1} & u^{n+1} \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} -d_X^{n+1} & 0 \\ f^{n+1} & d_Y^n \end{pmatrix} = d_T^n \begin{pmatrix} h^n & u^n \end{pmatrix}.\] Expanding it shows that this equation is equivalent to saying that \(u=(u^n)_n:Y\to T\) is a morphism in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})\) and that \(h:=(h^{n-1})_n\) satisfies \(d_{\operatorname{Hom}^\bullet(X,T)}^{-1}h=uf\). This is the required bijection; the equality \(u=\tilde{u}\circ\alpha(f)\) follows immediately from the definition of \(\alpha(f)\).

Next consider a morphism \(\tilde{v}:T\to\operatorname{Cone}(f)[-1]\). It is equivalent to families of morphisms in \(\mathcal{A}\), \(v^n:T^n\to X^n\) and \(\underline{k}^n:T^n\to Y^{n-1}\), satisfying \[\begin{pmatrix} d_X^n & 0 \\ -f^n & -d_Y^{n-1} \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} v^n \\ \underline{k}^n \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} v^{n+1} \\ \underline{k}^{n+1} \end{pmatrix} d_T^n \quad (n \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}).\] This equation is equivalent to saying that \(v=(v^n)_n:T\to X\) is a morphism in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})\) and that \(k:=(-\underline{k}^n)_n\) satisfies \(d_{\operatorname{Hom}^\bullet(T,Y)}^{-1}k=fv\). The equality \(v=\beta(f)[-1]\circ\tilde{v}\) also follows immediately from the definition of \(\beta(f)\).

Remark (Homotopy cokernel and homotopy kernel). Proposition reference shows that a morphism \(u:Y\to T\) (or \(v:T\to X\)) has \(uf\) (or \(fv\)) null-homotopic if and only if it factors through \(\alpha(f):Y\to\operatorname{Cone}(f)\) (or through \(\beta(f)[-1]:\operatorname{Cone}(f)[-1]\to X\)). This naturally recalls the universal property of a cokernel (or kernel), with the following differences:

  • the requirement that \(uf\) (or \(fv\)) be null-homotopic replaces the strict equality \(=0\);

  • the factorization \(\tilde{u}\) (or \(\tilde{v}\)) supplied by the proposition not only witnesses the fact that \(uf\) (or \(fv\)) is null-homotopic but also records how it is homotoped to \(0\); this is data one level higher.

These properties cannot simply be handled in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})\) or \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{A})\) using elementary category-theoretic notions; in fact, kernels and cokernels seldom exist in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{A})\). For this reason, \(Y\to\operatorname{Cone}(f)\) is also called the homotopy cokernel of \(f\), while \(\beta(f)[-1]:\operatorname{Cone}(f)[-1]\to X\) is called the homotopy kernel of \(f\). Remarkably, the mapping cone \(\operatorname{Cone}(f)\) and its shifts play both the “cokernel” and “kernel” roles in this sense.

A morphism \(f\) in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})\) is said to be canonically homotopic to \(g\) if there is a canonical \(h\) such that \(g-f=d^{-1}h\); if \(f\) is canonically homotopic to \(0\), it is called canonically null-homotopic.

Proposition. Let \(\mathcal{A}\) be an additive category.

  1. If \(f:X\to Y\) is an isomorphism in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})\), then \(\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{\operatorname{Cone}(f)}\) is canonically null-homotopic.

  2. For any morphism \(f:X\to Y\) in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})\), the morphisms in Definition reference satisfy \[\beta(f) \circ \alpha(f) = 0,\] while \(\alpha(f)\circ f\) and \(f[1]\circ\beta(f)\) are both canonically null-homotopic.

Proof. First consider (i). By functoriality of mapping cones (Proposition reference), it suffices to consider \(f=\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_X\). Define \[s^n := \begin{pmatrix} 0 & \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{X^n} \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix} : X^{n+1} \oplus X^n \to X^n \oplus X^{n-1}, \quad n \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}.\] A direct calculation gives \[\begin{multline*} d^{n-1}_{\operatorname{Cone}(\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_X)} s^n + s^{n+1} d^n_{\operatorname{Cone}(\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_X)} = \\ \begin{pmatrix} -d_X^n & 0 \\ \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{X^n} & d_X^{n-1} \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} 0 & \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{X^n} \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix} + \begin{pmatrix} 0 & \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{X^{n+1}} \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} -d_X^{n+1} & 0 \\ \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{X^{n+1}} & d_X^n \end{pmatrix} = \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{X^{n+1} \oplus X^n}, \end{multline*}\] so \(s=(s^n)_{n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}}\) makes \(\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{\operatorname{Cone}(\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_X)}\) null-homotopic.

Next consider (ii). Clearly \(\beta(f)\circ\alpha(f)=0\). The remaining homotopies come from Proposition reference: take \(T=\operatorname{Cone}(f)\), so that \(\tilde{u}:=\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{\operatorname{Cone}(f)}\in\operatorname{Hom}(\operatorname{Cone}(f),T)\) makes \(\alpha(f)\circ f\) null-homotopic; take \(T=\operatorname{Cone}(f)[-1]\), so that \(\tilde{v}:=\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{\operatorname{Cone}(f)[-1]}\in\operatorname{Hom}(T,\operatorname{Cone}(f)[-1])\) makes \(f\circ\beta(f)[-1]\) null-homotopic, and hence also makes \(f[1]\circ\beta(f)\) null-homotopic.

Definition reference produces two new morphisms \(\alpha(f)\) and \(\beta(f)\) from \(f\). Up to homotopy, the mapping cones of these two morphisms produce no new objects. We begin with \(\operatorname{Cone}(\alpha(f))\). First observe that \[\operatorname{Cone}(\alpha(f))^n = Y^{n+1} \oplus \operatorname{Cone}(f)^n = Y^{n+1} \oplus X^{n+1} \oplus Y^n.\] In matrix notation, \[\begin{align*} \alpha(\alpha(f)) & = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{X[1]} & 0 \\ 0 & \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_Y \end{pmatrix} : \operatorname{Cone}(f) \to \operatorname{Cone}(\alpha(f)) , \\ \beta(\alpha(f)) & = \begin{pmatrix} \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{Y[1]} & 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix} : \operatorname{Cone}(\alpha(f)) \to Y[1]. \end{align*}\]

Lemma. For a morphism \(f:X\to Y\) in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})\), matrix notation defines a pair of morphisms \[\begin{pmatrix} -f[1] \\ \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{X[1]} \\ 0 \end{pmatrix} : \text{Diagram chapter3-unit-034-d004} : \begin{pmatrix} 0 & \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{X[1]} & 0 \end{pmatrix}.\] They satisfy \(\psi\circ\phi=\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{X[1]}\) and make the following diagram commute in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{A})\): \[\text{Diagram chapter3-unit-034-d005}\] Moreover, \(\phi\) and \(\psi\) are inverse to each other in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{A})\).

Proof. By the preceding description of \(\operatorname{Cone}(\alpha(f))\), its differential \(d_{\operatorname{Cone}(\alpha(f))}^n\) is, in matrix notation, \[\begin{pmatrix} -d_Y^{n+1} & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -d_X^{n+1} & 0 \\ \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{Y^{n+1}} & f^{n+1} & d_Y^n \end{pmatrix} : Y^{n+1} \oplus X^{n+1} \oplus Y^n \to Y^{n+2} \oplus X^{n+2} \oplus Y^{n+1}.\] It suffices to verify the following statements in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})\):

  • \(\phi:=(\phi^n)_{n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}}\) and \(\psi:=(\psi^n)_{n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}}\) are both morphisms of complexes;

  • \(\psi\circ\phi=\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{X[1]}\);

  • \(\psi\circ\alpha(\alpha(f))=\beta(f)\);

  • \(\beta(\alpha(f))\circ\phi=-f[1]\);

  • there is an \(s=(s^n)_{n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}}\in\operatorname{Hom}^{-1}\left(\operatorname{Cone}(\alpha(f)), \operatorname{Cone}(\alpha(f))\right)\) such that \(\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{\operatorname{Cone}(\alpha(f))}-\phi\circ\psi =d^{-1}_{\operatorname{Hom}^\bullet}(s)\).

The first four statements are elementary. For the last, take, in matrix notation, \[s^n := \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 0 & \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{Y^n} \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}: \operatorname{Cone}(\alpha(f))^n \to \operatorname{Cone}(\alpha(f))^{n-1}\] and verify it directly.

For the case of \(\beta(f)\), we make a slight modification and consider the mapping cone of \(-\beta(f)[-1]:\operatorname{Cone}(f)[-1]\to X\).

Definition. For a morphism \(f:X\to Y\) in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})\), its mapping cylinder is defined by \[\operatorname{Cyl}(f) := \operatorname{Cone}\left( \operatorname{Cone}(f)[-1] \xrightarrow{-\beta(f)[-1]} X \right).\] It is equipped with canonical morphisms \(X\to\operatorname{Cyl}(f)\to\operatorname{Cone}(f)\).

The mapping cylinder has functoriality of the same form as that of the mapping cone (Proposition reference). In view of Remark reference, \(\operatorname{Cyl}(f)\) can be compared with a coimage in an additive category—roughly speaking, it is a “cokernel of a kernel” (Proposition reference)—and may therefore be viewed as the homotopy coimage of \(f\). More explicitly, \(\operatorname{Cyl}(f)^n=\operatorname{Cone}(f)^n\oplus X^n=X^{n+1}\oplus Y^n\oplus X^n\). The morphism \(X\to\mathrm{Cyl}(f)\) (or \(\mathrm{Cyl}(f)\to\operatorname{Cone}(f)\)) is the inclusion into the third direct summand (or the projection onto the first two), and \[d_{\operatorname{Cyl}(f)}^n = \begin{pmatrix} d_{\operatorname{Cone}(f)}^n & 0 \\ -\beta(f)^n & d_X^n \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} -d_X^{n+1} & 0 & 0 \\ f^{n+1} & d_Y^n & 0 \\ -\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{X^{n+1}} & 0 & d_X^n \end{pmatrix} .\]

Lemma. For a morphism \(f:X\to Y\) in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})\), one can define a pair of morphisms \[\begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_Y \\ 0 \end{pmatrix} : \text{Diagram chapter3-unit-034-d006} : \begin{pmatrix} 0 & \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_Y & f \end{pmatrix}.\] They satisfy \(\psi\circ\phi=\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_Y\) and make the following diagram commute in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{A})\): \[\text{Diagram chapter3-unit-034-d007}\] Moreover, \(\phi\) and \(\psi\) are inverse to each other in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{A})\). In addition, \(f\) factors as the composite \(X\to\operatorname{Cyl}(f)\xrightarrow{\psi}Y\).

Proof. The reader may verify directly from the definition that \(\phi\) and \(\psi\) are morphisms of complexes. Then \(\psi\circ\phi=\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_Y\) is immediate. To prove that \(\phi\) and \(\psi\) are inverse in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{A})\), as in Lemma reference, take \[\begin{align*} s^n & := \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 0 & -\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{X^n} \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}: X^{n+1} \oplus Y^n \oplus X^n \to X^n \oplus Y^{n-1} \oplus X^{n-1}, \\ s & := (s^n)_{n \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}}, \end{align*}\] and verify \(\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{\operatorname{Cyl}(f)}-\phi\circ\psi=d^{-1}_{\operatorname{Hom}^\bullet}(s)\).

The right-hand square in the diagram already commutes in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})\). For the left-hand square, simply observe that the composite \(X\to\mathrm{Cyl}(f)\xrightarrow{\psi}Y\) equals \(f\).

Lemmas reference and reference show that, up to isomorphism in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{A})\), any morphism \(f:X\to Y\) can be replaced by the much simpler projection \(\operatorname{Cone}(\alpha(f))[-1]\to Y\) (or by the inclusion \(X\to\operatorname{Cyl}(f)\)), and this construction is functorial in \(f\). This is an important idea in homological algebra and homotopy theory. The special case \(f=\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_X\) of the mapping cylinder has another use: it can be used to interpret homotopy. For readers familiar with homology theory, all of this has a topological interpretation, but here we discuss only the algebraic version.

Proposition. Let \(X\) be an object of \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})\) and set \(\mathrm{Cyl}_X:=\mathrm{Cyl}(\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_X)\). Notice that \(\mathrm{Cyl}_X^n=X^{n+1}\oplus X^n\oplus X^n\).

  1. In \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})\) there are morphisms \(\text{Diagram chapter3-unit-034-diagram-008}\), defined in matrix notation, for every \(n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\), by \[\begin{equation*} i_0^n := \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \\ \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{X^n} \end{pmatrix} , \quad i_1^n := \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{X^n} \\ 0 \end{pmatrix} , \quad j^n := \begin{pmatrix} 0 & \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{X^n} & \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{X^n} \end{pmatrix}. \end{equation*}\] These morphisms satisfy \(ji_0=\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_X=ji_1\), and the image of \(j\) in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{A})\) is an isomorphism.

  2. For every object \(Y\) of \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})\), there is a bijection \[\begin{align*} \left\{\begin{array}{r|l} (f, g, h) & f, g \in \operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})}(X, Y) \\ & h \in \operatorname{Hom}^{-1}(X, Y) \\ & g - f = d^{-1}_{\operatorname{Hom}^\bullet(X, Y)} h \end{array}\right\} & \xrightarrow{1:1} \operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})}\left( \mathrm{Cyl}_X, Y \right) \\ (f, g, h) & \longmapsto \tilde{h} = (\tilde{h}^n)_{n \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}}, \; \tilde{h}^n := \begin{pmatrix} h^n & g^n & f^n \end{pmatrix}. \end{align*}\] In particular, \(f=\tilde{h}i_0\) and \(g=\tilde{h}i_1\).

Proof. For (i), note that \(i_0\) is precisely the canonical morphism \(X\to\mathrm{Cyl}(\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_X)\) in Definition reference, while \(i_1\) is the morphism \(\phi:X\to\mathrm{Cyl}(\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_X)\) in Lemma reference. The commutative diagram in Lemma reference shows that they give the same isomorphism in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{A})\).

For \(j\), it is easy to verify that \(j^{n+1}d_{\operatorname{Cyl}_X}^n=\bigl(0\;d_X^n\;d_X^n\bigr)=d_X^nj^n\). Thus \(j\) is indeed a morphism, while \(ji_0=\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_X=ji_1\) is immediate. Since \(i_0\) and \(i_1\) are isomorphisms in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{A})\), so is \(j\).

For (ii), write any element \(\tilde{h}\) of \(\operatorname{Hom}^0(\mathrm{Cyl}_X,Y)\) as \[\tilde{h}=\left((h^n,g^n,f^n)\right)_{n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}},\] where \[h^n: X^{n+1} \to Y^n, \quad f^n: X^n \to Y^n, \quad g^n: X^n \to Y^n\] are morphisms in \(\mathcal{A}\). Suppressing superscripts and using matrix notation, calculate \[\begin{align*} \tilde{h} \; d_{\mathrm{Cyl}_X} & = \begin{pmatrix} h & g & f \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} -d_X & 0 & 0 \\ \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_X & d_X & 0 \\ -\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_X & 0 & d_X \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} -hd_X + g - f & g d_X & f d_X \end{pmatrix} , \\ d_Y \; \tilde{h} & = \begin{pmatrix} d_Y h & d_Y g & d_Y f \end{pmatrix}. \end{align*}\] Therefore \(\tilde{h}\) is a morphism of complexes if and only if \(f,g\in\operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})}(X,Y)\) and \(g-f=hd_X+d_Yh\).

Remark. Mapping cones and mapping cylinders of course have versions for chain complexes (see Remark reference). Given a morphism of chain complexes \(f:X\to Y\), define \[\begin{array}{rlrl} \operatorname{Cone}(f)_n & :=(X[-1] \oplus Y)_n, & \operatorname{Cyl}(f)_n & := (X[-1] \oplus Y \oplus X)_n, \\ d_{\operatorname{Cone}(f)} & := \begin{pmatrix} d_{X[-1]} & 0 \\ f[-1] & d_Y \end{pmatrix}, & d_{\operatorname{Cyl}(f)} & := \begin{pmatrix} d_{X[-1]} & 0 & 0 \\ f[-1] & d_Y & 0 \\ -\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{X[-1]} & 0 & d_X \end{pmatrix}. \end{array}\]

Every statement in this section carries over to chain complexes. In particular, there are canonical morphisms \[X \xrightarrow{f} Y \xrightarrow{\alpha(f)} \operatorname{Cone}(f) \xrightarrow{\beta(f)} X[-1], \quad X \to \operatorname{Cyl}(f) \to \operatorname{Cone}(f).\]

Complexes on the Opposite Category

Let \(\mathcal{A}\) be an additive category. This section relates complexes on \(\mathcal{A}\) and on \(\mathcal{A}^{\operatorname{op}}\). Since functors involving \(\mathcal{A}^{\operatorname{op}}\), such as the \(\operatorname{Hom}\) functor, occur frequently, this procedure is simple but necessary; some of the signs involved also require a little care. Beginning readers are advised to skip this section or merely skim it on a first reading. The discussion has three aspects: complexes, homotopy, and mapping cones. The derived-category version considered later (Proposition in the later discussion of derived categories) is a direct application of these results. Recall that if \(f:X\to Y\) is a morphism in \(\mathcal{A}\), then \(f^{\operatorname{op}}\) denotes the corresponding morphism \(Y\to X\) in \(\mathcal{A}^{\operatorname{op}}\).

Definition–Proposition. The isomorphism of additive categories \(\sigma:\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A}^{\operatorname{op}})\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})^{\operatorname{op}}\) is defined as follows. For an object \(X\) of \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A}^{\operatorname{op}})\), define in \(\mathcal{A}\) \[(\sigma X)^n := X^{-n}, \quad d_{\sigma X}^n = (-1)^{n+1} \left[ d_X^{-n-1, \operatorname{op}}: (\sigma X)^n \to (\sigma X)^{n+1} \right], \quad n \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}.\] For a morphism \(f=\left(f^n:X^n\to Y^n\right)_n\) in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A}^{\operatorname{op}})\), take its image \(\sigma f\) to be the following morphism in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})\): \[(\sigma f)^n := \left(f^{-n} \right)^{\operatorname{op}} : (\sigma Y)^n \to (\sigma X)^n,\] that is, a morphism \(\sigma X\to\sigma Y\) in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})^{\operatorname{op}}\). For every \(m\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\), there is a natural isomorphism \[s_m: \sigma \circ [m] \ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}[-m] \circ \sigma,\] where \([-m]\) is regarded as a functor from \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})^{\operatorname{op}}\) to itself (strictly speaking, it should be written \([-m]^{\operatorname{op}}\)).

Proof. The general case of \(s_m\) reduces step by step to the case \(m=1\). Define \(s_1=(s_{1,X})_X\) as follows. For every \(n\), take \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:sigma-s}{}\text{Diagram chapter3-unit-035-d001} \end{equation}\] The entire verification reduces to \(s_{1, X}^{n+1} d^n_{\sigma(X[1])} = -d_{X[1]}^{-n-1, \operatorname{op}} = d_X^{-n, \operatorname{op}} = (-1)^n d_{\sigma X}^{n-1} = d^n_{(\sigma X)[-1]} s_{1,X}^n\).

If the construction \(\sigma\) with coefficient \((-1)^{n+1}\) is applied in both directions, \(\sigma^2X\) is naturally isomorphic to \(X\) through the isomorphism whose degree-\(n\) component is \((-1)^n\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{X^n}\). To obtain an inverse, define the reverse construction by the same formulas on objects and morphisms, but use the coefficient \((-1)^n\) on the differential. The composites in both orders are then exactly the identity functor, so \(\sigma\) is indeed an isomorphism of categories. 1

Remark. If \(\mathcal{A}\) is an abelian category, the signs on \(d_{\sigma X}^\bullet\) do not change the cohomology introduced in Definition reference; thus \(\operatorname{H}^{-n}(\sigma X)\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{A})\) corresponds to \(\operatorname{H}^n(X)\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{A}^{\operatorname{op}})\).

We next examine the relation between \(\sigma\) and homotopy.

Proposition. The functor \(\sigma\) defined above induces an equivalence of additive categories \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{A}^{\operatorname{op}})\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{A})^{\operatorname{op}}\).

Proof. Let \(X,Y\) be objects of \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A}^{\operatorname{op}})\). For \(f=(f^k)_k\in\operatorname{Hom}^{-1}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A}^{\operatorname{op}})}(X,Y)\), use the following table to define the corresponding \(\sigma f\in\operatorname{Hom}^{-1}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})}(\sigma Y,\sigma X)\) in \(\mathcal{A}\): \[\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|} \hline \text{Category} & \multicolumn{3}{c|}{\text{Morphism}} \\ \hline \mathcal{A}^{\operatorname{op}} & X^k \xrightarrow{(-1)^{k+1} f^k} Y^{k-1} & d_Y^{k-1} f^k + f^{k+1} d_X^k & (d^{-1}f)^k \\ \mathcal{A} & (\sigma Y)^{-k+1} \xrightarrow{(\sigma f)^{-k+1}} (\sigma X)^{-k} & (\sigma f)^{-k+1} d_{\sigma Y}^{-k} + d_{\sigma X}^{-k-1} (\sigma f)^{-k} & d^{-1} (\sigma f)^{-k} \\ \hline \end{array}\] This suffices to show \[\begin{aligned} \operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{A}^{\operatorname{op}})}(X, Y) &\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}\operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{A})}(\sigma Y, \sigma X) \\ &= \operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{A})^{\operatorname{op}}}(\sigma X, \sigma Y). \end{aligned}\]

Finally, using \(\sigma\) and the family of isomorphisms \((s_m)_m\) constructed above, we compare mapping cones in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})\) and \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A}^{\operatorname{op}})\). The details are somewhat routine.

Proposition. For every morphism \(f:X\to Y\) in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A}^{\operatorname{op}})\), there is a commutative diagram in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})\) 2: \[\text{Diagram chapter3-unit-035-d002}\] where \(\theta\) is a canonical isomorphism and \(s_{1,X}\) is the isomorphism supplied by Definition–Proposition reference.

Proof. If \(\operatorname{Cone}(f)\) were replaced by \(X[1]\oplus Y\), the statement would be easy and the required isomorphism would simply be \((s_{1,X},\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{\sigma Y})\). The complication is that the matrix \(d_{\operatorname{Cone}(f)}\) has the off-diagonal entry \(f[1]\). Nevertheless, we follow the same method: using equation, for every \(n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\) define the isomorphism \[\begin{multline*} \theta^n: \sigma\left(\operatorname{Cone}(f)\right)^n = \sigma\left(X[1]\right)^n \oplus (\sigma Y)^n \\ \xrightarrow[\sim]{(s_{1,X}, \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}})^n = ((-1)^{n-1} \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}, \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}) } (\sigma X)[-1]^n \oplus (\sigma Y)^n \xlongequal{\text{interchange}} \left( (\sigma Y) \oplus (\sigma X)[-1] \right)^n . \end{multline*}\] Under this identification, the morphism \(d_{\sigma(\operatorname{Cone}(f))}^n\) in \(\mathcal{A}\) corresponds to \[\begin{pmatrix} d_{\sigma Y}^n & 0 \\ * & d_{(\sigma X)[-1]}^n \end{pmatrix} : \left( (\sigma Y) \oplus (\sigma X)[-1] \right)^n \to \left( (\sigma Y) \oplus (\sigma X)[-1] \right)^{n+1} .\] As noted at the start of the proof, the diagonal entries pose no problem; we need only determine the lower-left entry. By Definition–Proposition reference, this entry is \((-1)^{n+1}\) times the following composite in \(\mathcal{A}\): \[\text{Diagram chapter3-unit-035-d003}\] Thus the result is \(-\sigma(f)^n\). It follows that \[\theta := (\theta^n)_{n \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}}: \sigma(\operatorname{Cone}(f)) \ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}\operatorname{Cone}(\sigma(f))[-1]\] is indeed an isomorphism in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})\). Once this is established, verifying commutativity presents no essential difficulty.

Of course, the results of this section also apply to chain complexes and extend to the case in which \(\mathcal{A}\) is a \(\Bbbk\)-linear category.

  1. Translator’s note (O014-C036): arguing from \(n(n+1)\equiv0\pmod{2}\), the source states that applying \(\sigma\) twice returns \(X\) strictly. Using the same formula in both directions instead gives the differential \(-d_X\), not \(d_X\). The signed natural isomorphism and the corrected inverse construction are recorded above.↩︎

  2. Here \(\alpha(\cdot)\) and \(\beta(\cdot)\) are both defined relative to \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})\). If the diagram is viewed in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})^{\operatorname{op}}\), all its arrows must be reversed.↩︎

Double Complexes

Throughout this section, \(\mathcal{A}\) remains an additive category. Roughly speaking, a double complex may be thought of as a two-dimensional version of a complex, with differentials in the horizontal and vertical directions.

Definition (Double complex). A double complex on an additive category \(\mathcal{A}\) consists of a family of objects \(\left(X^{p,q}\right)_{(p,q)\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}^2}\) of \(\mathcal{A}\), together with morphisms \(\ensuremath{{}^\vartriangleright d}^{p,q}:X^{p,q}\to X^{p+1,q}\) and \(\ensuremath{{}^\vartriangle d}^{p,q}:X^{p,q}\to X^{p,q+1}\) satisfying \[\ensuremath{{}^\vartriangleright d}^{p+1,q} \ensuremath{{}^\vartriangleright d}^{p,q} = 0, \quad \ensuremath{{}^\vartriangle d}^{p, q+1} \ensuremath{{}^\vartriangle d}^{p,q} = 0, \quad \ensuremath{{}^\vartriangleright d}^{p, q+1} \ensuremath{{}^\vartriangle d}^{p,q} = \ensuremath{{}^\vartriangle d}^{p+1, q} \ensuremath{{}^\vartriangleright d}^{p,q}.\] These data are usually abbreviated as \((X^{\bullet,\bullet},\ensuremath{{}^\vartriangleright d},\ensuremath{{}^\vartriangle d})\), \(X^{\bullet,\bullet}\), or \(X\).

The conditions on \(\ensuremath{{}^\vartriangleright d},\ensuremath{{}^\vartriangle d}\) may be abbreviated as \[\ensuremath{{}^\vartriangleright d}^2 = 0, \quad \ensuremath{{}^\vartriangle d}^2 = 0, \quad \ensuremath{{}^\vartriangleright d}\ensuremath{{}^\vartriangle d}= \ensuremath{{}^\vartriangle d}\ensuremath{{}^\vartriangleright d}.\]

Definition. Given an additive category \(\mathcal{A}\), a morphism from a double complex \(X\) to a double complex \(Y\) is a family of morphisms \[f = \left( f^{p,q}: X^{p, q} \to Y^{p, q} \right)_{(p, q) \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}^2},\] such that, for all \(p,q\), \[\ensuremath{{}^\vartriangleright d}_Y^{p, q} f^{p, q} = f^{p+1, q} \ensuremath{{}^\vartriangleright d}_X^{p, q}, \quad \ensuremath{{}^\vartriangle d}_Y^{p, q} f^{p, q} = f^{p, q+1} \ensuremath{{}^\vartriangle d}_X^{p, q}.\] These relations may be abbreviated as \(\ensuremath{{}^\vartriangleright d}_Yf=f\ensuremath{{}^\vartriangleright d}_X\) and \(\ensuremath{{}^\vartriangle d}_Yf=f\ensuremath{{}^\vartriangle d}_X\).

As in Proposition reference, these definitions make all double complexes on \(\mathcal{A}\) into an additive category \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}^2(\mathcal{A})\). Visually, a double complex \(X\) is displayed as \[\text{Diagram chapter3-unit-036-d001}\] Every row \(\left(X^{\bullet,q},d^{\bullet,q}\right)\) and every column \(\left(X^{p,\bullet},d^{p,\bullet}\right)\) is a complex. Thus a double complex can be assembled by columns or by rows.

Definition. Define the additive functor \(F_{\mathrm{I}}:\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}^2(\mathcal{A})\to \ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A}))\) as follows: for a double complex \(X\), set \((F_{\mathrm{I}}X)^p=X^{p,\bullet}\) and \(d_{F_{\mathrm{I}}X}^p=\ensuremath{{}^\vartriangleright d}^{p,\bullet}:(F_{\mathrm{I}}X)^p\to (F_{\mathrm{I}}X)^{p+1}\). Similarly, the formulas \((F_{\mathrm{II}}X)^q=X^{\bullet,q}\) and \(d_{F_{\mathrm{II}}X}^q=\ensuremath{{}^\vartriangle d}^{\bullet,q}\) define an additive functor \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}^2(\mathcal{A})\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A}))\). Here \(p,q\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\).

Definition reference implies that both \(F_{\mathrm{I}}\) and \(F_{\mathrm{II}}\) are isomorphisms of additive categories. This is depicted as follows: \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:bicplx-diagram}{}\text{Diagram chapter3-unit-036-d002} \end{equation}\]

Definition (Total complex). Suppose that \(\mathcal{A}\) has countable coproducts, denoted by the direct sum symbol \(\bigoplus\), and let \(X\) be an object of \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}^2(\mathcal{A})\). Define a complex \(\operatorname{tot}_{\oplus}(X)\) on \(\mathcal{A}\) as follows:

  • \(\operatorname{tot}_{\oplus}(X)^n := \bigoplus_{p+q=n} X^{p, q}\);

  • the restriction of \(d^n:\operatorname{tot}_{\oplus}(X)^n\to \operatorname{tot}_{\oplus}(X)^{n+1}\) to the summand \(X^{p,q}\) is \(\ensuremath{{}^\vartriangleright d}^{p,q}+(-1)^p\ensuremath{{}^\vartriangle d}^{p,q}\).

Suppressing superscripts, writing out \(d^2:X^{p,q}\to X^{p+2,q}\oplus X^{p+1,q+1}\oplus X^{p,q+2}\) gives \[d^2 = \left( \ensuremath{{}^\vartriangleright d}^2, \; (-1)^p \ensuremath{{}^\vartriangleright d}\ensuremath{{}^\vartriangle d}+ (-1)^{p+1} \ensuremath{{}^\vartriangle d}\ensuremath{{}^\vartriangleright d}, \; \ensuremath{{}^\vartriangle d}^2 \right) = (0, 0, 0).\] Replacing coproducts in the construction of \(\operatorname{tot}_{\oplus}\) by products \(\prod\) similarly gives \(\operatorname{tot}_{\Pi}X\in\operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A}))\), provided the required products exist. The definition of \(d^n:\operatorname{tot}_{\Pi}(X)^n\to\operatorname{tot}_{\Pi}(X)^{n+1}\) is analogous to the \(\operatorname{tot}_{\oplus}\) case: require that the projection of \(d^{n-1}\) to \(X^{p,q}\) be the composite \[\operatorname{tot}_{\Pi}^{n-1}(X) \xrightarrow{\text{projection}} X^{p-1, q} \oplus X^{p,q-1} \xrightarrow{(\ensuremath{{}^\vartriangleright d}^{p-1, q}, (-1)^p \ensuremath{{}^\vartriangle d}^{p, q-1})} X^{p, q};\] the same reasoning gives \(d^2=0\). When there is no danger of confusion, both \(\operatorname{tot}_{\oplus}X\) and \(\operatorname{tot}_{\Pi}X\) are called the total complex of \(X\). The following property should be clear.

Proposition. Under the respective hypotheses, \(\operatorname{tot}_{\oplus}\) and \(\operatorname{tot}_{\Pi}\) are both additive functors from \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}^2(\mathcal{A})\) to \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})\).

In the definition of the total complex, the superscripts \(p\) and \(q\) may at first appear asymmetric. To dispel this impression, define an additive automorphism \(\mathrm{swap}\) of \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}^2(\mathcal{A})\) such that \(\mathrm{swap}(X)^{p,q}=X^{q,p}\) and \(\ensuremath{{}^\vartriangleright d}\) and \(\ensuremath{{}^\vartriangle d}\) are interchanged. The accompanying sign \((-1)^{pq}\) is essentially the same mechanism as the Koszul sign rule in [Li1].

Proposition. For every \((p,q)\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}^2\) and every object \(X\) of \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}^2(\mathcal{A})\), define a family of isomorphisms \[r^{p, q}_X := (-1)^{pq} \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{X^{p,q}} : X^{p, q} \to \mathrm{swap}(X)^{q,p} .\]

  • If \(\mathcal{A}\) has countable coproducts, then \((r_X^{p,q})_{(p,q)\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}^2}\) induces an isomorphism \(r_X:\operatorname{tot}_{\oplus}(X)\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}\operatorname{tot}_{\oplus}(\mathrm{swap}(X))\).

  • If \(\mathcal{A}\) has countable products, then \((r_X^{p,q})_{(p,q)\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}^2}\) induces an isomorphism \(r_X:\operatorname{tot}_{\Pi}(X)\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}\operatorname{tot}_{\Pi}(\mathrm{swap}(X))\).

Proof. For every \((p,q)\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}^2\), the diagram \[\text{Diagram chapter3-unit-036-d003}\] commutes, so \(r_X\) is indeed a morphism of complexes.

The requirement that countable coproducts (or countable products) exist in the definition of \(\operatorname{tot}_{\oplus}X\) (or \(\operatorname{tot}_{\Pi}X\)) can be weakened. If, for each \(n\), only finitely many pairs \((p,q)\) satisfy \(p+q=n\) and \(X^{p,q}\neq0\), then the coproduct (or product) in the definition of the total complex becomes a finite direct sum. In this case, both total complexes may be denoted uniformly by \(\operatorname{tot}(X)\). There will be further discussion after Definition in § 3.10.

Remark. By the same idea, for every \(k\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}_{\geq1}\) one can define a \(k\)-fold complex as data \[\left( X^{p_1, \ldots, p_k} \in \operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{A}) \right)_{p_1, \ldots, p_k \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}}, \quad {}^1 d, \ldots, {}^k d,\] where \({}^i d^{p_1,\ldots,p_k}:X^{p_1,\ldots,p_k}\to X^{p_1,\ldots,p_i+1,\ldots,p_k}\) and \[{}^i d^2 = 0, \quad {}^i d {}^j d = {}^j d {}^i d \quad \text{(superscripts suppressed)}.\] All \(k\)-fold complexes form an additive category \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}^k(\mathcal{A})\). Following Definition reference, one can also define a family of additive functors \(F_i:\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}^k(\mathcal{A})\to \ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}^{k-1}(\mathcal{A}))\) such that every \(F_i\) is an equivalence of categories (\(k\geq2\) and \(i=1,\ldots,k\)).

In this setting, if \(\mathcal{A}\) has countable coproducts or products, the total-complex functor may be defined in the same way: \[\operatorname{tot}_{\oplus} \; \text{or} \; \operatorname{tot}_{\Pi}: \ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}^k(\mathcal{A}) \to \ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A}).\] The details are the same as for double complexes and need not be repeated.

Define isomorphisms from \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}^2(\mathcal{A})\) to itself by \([m]_{\mathrm{I}}:=F_{\mathrm{I}}^{-1}\circ[m]\circ F_{\mathrm{I}}\) and \([m]_{\mathrm{II}}:=F_{\mathrm{II}}^{-1}\circ[m]\circ F_{\mathrm{II}}\), corresponding respectively to horizontal and vertical shifts of double complexes. For all \(a,b\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\), \([a]_{\mathrm{I}}[b]_{\mathrm{II}}=[b]_{\mathrm{II}}[a]_{\mathrm{I}}\). We now examine the effect of these functors on total complexes and their relation to the automorphism \(\mathrm{swap}\).

Proposition. For all \(X\in\operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}^2(\mathcal{A}))\) and \((p,q)\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}^2\), denote the standard embedding \(X^{p,q}\hookrightarrow \mathrm{tot}_{\oplus}(X)^{p+q}\) by \(\iota_{p,q}\). For every \(n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\), define

  • \(\theta_X^n:\operatorname{tot}_{\oplus}\left(X[1]_{\mathrm{I}}\right)^n\to \operatorname{tot}_{\oplus}(X)[1]^n\) so that its restriction to \(X[1]_{\mathrm{I}}^{p,q}=X^{p+1,q}\) is \(\iota_{p+1,q}\);

  • \((\theta'_X)^n:\operatorname{tot}_{\oplus}\left(X[1]_{\mathrm{II}}\right)^n \to\operatorname{tot}_{\oplus}(X)[1]^n\) so that its restriction to \(X[1]_{\mathrm{II}}^{p,q}=X^{p,q+1}\) is \((-1)^p\iota_{p,q+1}\).

These define canonical isomorphisms in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})\): \[\begin{align*} \theta_X & = (\theta_X^n)_n: \operatorname{tot}_{\oplus} \left( X[1]_{\mathrm{I}} \right) \ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}\operatorname{tot}_{\oplus} \left(X\right)[1], \\ \theta'_X & = ((\theta'_X)^n)_n: \operatorname{tot}_{\oplus} \left( X[1]_{\mathrm{II}} \right) \ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}\operatorname{tot}_{\oplus} \left(X\right)[1], \end{align*}\] together with the anticommutative diagram (that is, its two composites differ by a minus sign) \[\text{Diagram chapter3-unit-036-d004}\] and the commutative diagram \[\text{Diagram chapter3-unit-036-d005}\] where \(r\) is as defined in Proposition reference. If \(\operatorname{tot}_{\oplus}\) is replaced by \(\operatorname{tot}_{\Pi}\), one obtains the same \(\theta_X,\theta'_X\) and the corresponding anticommutative diagram.

Proof. Direct verification from the definition of the total complex (Definition reference) and the definition of the shift functor (Definition reference) shows that \(\theta_X\) and \(\theta'_X\) are morphisms of complexes; the details are lengthy but not difficult. Anticommutativity reduces to the observation that the diagram \[\text{Diagram chapter3-unit-036-d006}\] is anticommutative.

Now consider the assertion about the commutative diagram. Let \((p,q)\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}^2\) and compare the restrictions of the two composites to \((X[1]_{\mathrm{I}}[1]_{\mathrm{II}})^{p,q}\). As explained above, \(\theta\) followed by \(\theta'\) (for \(X\)) and \(\theta'\) followed by \(\theta\) (for \(\mathrm{swap}(X)\)) give respectively \[(-1)^{p+1}, \; (-1)^q \; \in \operatorname{Aut}(X^{p+1, q+1}) \quad \text{($\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}$ suppressed)}.\] On the other hand, the restrictions of \(r_{X[1]_{\mathrm{I}}[1]_{\mathrm{II}}}\) and \(r_X[2]\) to \(X^{p+1,q+1}\) are respectively \((-1)^{pq}\) and \((-1)^{(p+1)(q+1)}\). But \((p+1)(q+1)-pq\equiv(p+1)-q\pmod{2}\). This proves the claim.
