As a simple generalization of the anticommutative diagram above, the reader is asked to prove that, for all \(a,b\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\), the two morphisms \[\operatorname{tot}_{\oplus}(X[a]_{\mathrm{I}}[b]_{\mathrm{II}}) \rightrightarrows \operatorname{tot}_{\oplus}(X)[a+b]\] defined in the two orders (\(\theta\) then \(\theta'\), and \(\theta'\) then \(\theta\)) differ by the sign \((-1)^{ab}\); on the other hand, the commutative diagram above remains valid for \(X[a]_{\mathrm{I}}[b]_{\mathrm{II}}\). The same statements hold with \(\operatorname{tot}_{\Pi}\) in place of \(\operatorname{tot}_{\oplus}\). One of the main uses of double complexes is the study of bifunctors. What is a bifunctor?

Convention. A functor of the form \(F:\mathcal{A}_1\times\mathcal{A}_2\to\mathcal{B}\) is called a bifunctor. Once objects \(X_i\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{A}_i)\) are fixed, we obtain one-variable functors \(F(X_1,\cdot):\mathcal{A}_2\to\mathcal{B}\) and \(F(\cdot,X_2):\mathcal{A}_1\to\mathcal{B}\). We can therefore discuss additivity, exactness, and many other notions in each variable of \(F\).

Definition–Proposition. Let \(\mathcal{A}_1,\mathcal{A}_2,\mathcal{B}\) be additive categories and let \(F:\mathcal{A}_1\times\mathcal{A}_2\to\mathcal{B}\) be a bifunctor additive in each variable. There is an associated functor \[\text{Diagram chapter3-unit-036-d007}\]

Consequently, if \(\mathcal{B}\) has countable coproducts or countable products, one can define respectively \[\begin{gather*} \ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}_{\oplus} F := \operatorname{tot}_{\oplus} \circ \ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}^2 F: \ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A}_1) \times \ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A}_2) \to \ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{B}), \\ \ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}_{\Pi} F := \operatorname{tot}_{\Pi} \circ \ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}^2 F: \ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A}_1) \times \ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A}_2) \to \ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{B}). \end{gather*}\] If the totalizations under discussion involve only finite direct sums, then \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}_{\oplus}F=\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}_{\Pi}F\). 1

Proof. The double-complex condition \(\ensuremath{{}^\vartriangleright d}\ensuremath{{}^\vartriangle d}=\ensuremath{{}^\vartriangle d}\ensuremath{{}^\vartriangleright d}\) follows directly from the definition of a bifunctor; the rest is clear.

The category of double complexes also has a notion of homotopy. Let \(f,g:X\to Y\) be morphisms in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}^2(\mathcal{A})\). A homotopy from \(f\) to \(g\) is a pair of families of morphisms satisfying the following conditions. \[\begin{equation*} \begin{gathered} \hypertarget{o014.li2.chapter3.double-complexes.g008}{} \text{Diagram chapter3-unit-036-d008} \qquad (p,q) \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}^2 , \\ \ensuremath{{}^\vartriangle d}^{p-1, q} h^{p, q} = h^{p, q+1} \ensuremath{{}^\vartriangle d}^{p, q}, \qquad \ensuremath{{}^\vartriangleright d}^{p, q-1} k^{p,q} = k^{p+1, q} \ensuremath{{}^\vartriangleright d}^{p,q}, \\ g^{p,q} - f^{p, q} = \ensuremath{{}^\vartriangleright d}^{p-1, q} h^{p,q} + h^{p+1, q} \ensuremath{{}^\vartriangleright d}^{p,q} + \ensuremath{{}^\vartriangle d}^{p, q-1} k^{p,q} + k^{p, q+1} \ensuremath{{}^\vartriangle d}^{p,q}. \end{gathered} \end{equation*}\] This is reasonable: from \(\ensuremath{{}^\vartriangle d}h=h\ensuremath{{}^\vartriangle d}\), \(\ensuremath{{}^\vartriangleright d}k=k\ensuremath{{}^\vartriangleright d}\), and the definition of a double complex, it is easy to check that \(\ensuremath{{}^\vartriangleright d}h+h\ensuremath{{}^\vartriangleright d}+\ensuremath{{}^\vartriangle d}k+k\ensuremath{{}^\vartriangle d}\) always defines a morphism in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}^2(\mathcal{A})\). Homotopies of double complexes are reflected by total complexes. More precisely, given \((h^{p,q},k^{p,q})_{p,q\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}}\), one can define \(\hat{h}\in\operatorname{Hom}^{-1}\left(\operatorname{tot}_{\oplus}(X),\operatorname{tot}_{\oplus}(Y)\right)\) so that the restriction of \(\hat{h}\) to the direct summand \(X^{p,q}\) is \[\left( h^{p,q}, (-1)^p k^{p,q} \right): X^{p,q} \to Y^{p-1, q} \oplus Y^{p, q-1},\] which makes \(\operatorname{tot}_{\oplus}(g)-\operatorname{tot}_{\oplus}(f)=d^{-1}\hat{h}\); the case of \(\operatorname{tot}_{\Pi}\) is handled in the same way. Thus the homotopy relation on double complexes defines \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}^2(\mathcal{A})\) together with a functor \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}^2(\mathcal{A})\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}^2(\mathcal{A})\). If countable coproducts (or products) exist, the functor \(\operatorname{tot}_{\oplus}\) (or \(\operatorname{tot}_{\Pi}\)) descends to a functor \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}^2(\mathcal{A})\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{A})\). Return to a bifunctor \(F:\mathcal{A}_1\times\mathcal{A}_2\to\mathcal{B}\) between additive categories, assumed additive in each variable. The following is the bifunctor version of equation.

Proposition. Let \(F\) be as above. Then \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}^2F\) factors through \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}^2F:\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{A}_1)\times\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{A}_2)\to \ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}^2(\mathcal{B})\).

Similarly, \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}_{\oplus}F\) or \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}_{\Pi}F\) factors through \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{A}_1)\times\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{A}_2)\to \ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{B})\) and is denoted respectively by \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}_{\oplus}F\) or \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}_{\Pi}F\), provided the functor \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}_{\oplus}F\) or \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}_{\Pi}F\) is defined.

Proof. Take \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}_{\oplus}F\) as an example. We must show that, for a null-homotopic morphism \(f_1=d^{-1}g:X_1\to Y_1\) in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A}_1)\) and an arbitrary morphism \(f_2:X_2\to Y_2\) in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A}_2)\), the corresponding morphism \((\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}^2F)(f_1,f_2):\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}^2F(X_1,X_2)\to \ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}^2F(Y_1,Y_2)\) is null-homotopic. The evident choice is \(h^{p,q}:=F(g^p,f_2^q)\) and \(k^{p,q}:=0\). Since \(f_2\) is a morphism, \(h\) indeed commutes with \(\ensuremath{{}^\vartriangle d}=F(\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}},d)\). The second variable is handled similarly.

Proposition reference gives canonical isomorphisms \[\begin{gather*} \ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}_{\oplus} F(X[1], Y) \simeq \ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}_{\oplus}F(X, Y)[1] \simeq \ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}_{\oplus}F(X, Y[1]), \\ \ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}_{\oplus} F(X[1], Y) \simeq \ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}_{\oplus}F(X, Y)[1] \simeq \ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}_{\oplus}F(X, Y[1]). \end{gather*}\] The same statements hold with \(\Pi\) in place of \(\oplus\).

Example (\(\operatorname{Hom}\) double complex). Consider the bifunctor \(\operatorname{Hom}(\cdot,\cdot):\mathcal{A}^{\operatorname{op}}\times\mathcal{A}\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ab}}\), which sends a pair of objects \((S,T)\) to \(\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{A}}(S,T)\). We will show that the \(\operatorname{Hom}\) complex \(\operatorname{Hom}^\bullet(X,Y)\) is canonically isomorphic to the value at \((X,Y)\) of the composite functor \[\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})^{\operatorname{op}} \times \ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A}) \xrightarrow{(\sigma^{-1}, \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}})} \ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A}^{\operatorname{op}}) \times \ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A}) \xrightarrow{\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}_{\Pi} \operatorname{Hom}(\cdot, \cdot)} \ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ab}}),\] where \(\sigma\) is as in Definition–Proposition reference.

To this end, first consider the bifunctor \(F:\mathcal{A}\times\mathcal{A}^{\operatorname{op}}\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ab}}\) defined by \(F(T,S)=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{A}}(S,T)\), and the composite functor \[\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A}) \times \ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})^{\operatorname{op}} \xrightarrow{(\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}, \sigma^{-1})} \ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A}) \times \ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A}^{\operatorname{op}}) \xrightarrow{\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}^2 F} \ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}^2(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ab}}).\] Let \(X,Y\in\operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A}))\). The image of \((Y,X)\) under the composite functor above is called the \(\operatorname{Hom}\) double complex and is denoted by \(\operatorname{Hom}^{\bullet,\bullet}(X,Y)\). In view of the evident commutative diagram \[\text{Diagram chapter3-unit-036-d009}\] and Proposition reference, it suffices to prove that there is a canonical isomorphism \[\operatorname{tot}_{\Pi}\operatorname{Hom}^{\bullet,\bullet}(X,Y) \ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}\operatorname{Hom}^\bullet(X,Y).\]

Inspecting the definitions gives \[\begin{equation*} \begin{aligned} \operatorname{Hom}^{p, q}(X, Y) & = \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{A}}\left( X^{-q}, Y^p \right), \\ \ensuremath{{}^\vartriangleright d}^{p, q} & = (d_Y^p)_* : \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{A}}\left( X^{-q}, Y^p \right) \to \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{A}}\left( X^{-q}, Y^{p+1} \right), \\ \ensuremath{{}^\vartriangle d}^{p, q} & = (-1)^q (d_X^{-q-1})^* : \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{A}}\left( X^{-q}, Y^p \right) \to \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{A}}\left( X^{-q-1}, Y^p \right). \end{aligned} \end{equation*}\] 2 Now determine \(\operatorname{tot}_{\Pi}\operatorname{Hom}^{\bullet,\bullet}(X,Y)\). First, \[\left(\operatorname{tot}_{\Pi} \operatorname{Hom}^{\bullet, \bullet}(X, Y)\right)^n = \prod_{p+q=n} \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{A}}\left( X^{-q}, Y^p \right) = \prod_{k \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}} \operatorname{Hom}\left( X^k, Y^{k+n} \right)\] under the substitution \(k=-q\), which is precisely \(\operatorname{Hom}^n(X,Y)\). Next describe \(d_{\operatorname{tot}_{\Pi}\operatorname{Hom}^{\bullet,\bullet}(X,Y)}^n\): its \((p,q)\)-coordinate in \(\operatorname{Hom}^{n+1}(X,Y)\), where \(p+q=n+1\), comes from \[\text{Diagram chapter3-unit-036-d010}\] The horizontal arrow is \((d_Y^{p-1})_*\), while the vertical arrow is \((-1)^{p+q-1}(d_X^{-q})^*=(-1)^n(d_X^{-q})^*\). The isomorphism that multiplies the factor \(\operatorname{Hom}^{p,q}(X,Y)\) by \((-1)^q\) changes the sign of the vertical term. Comparing with Definition reference gives the canonical isomorphism \(\operatorname{tot}_{\Pi}\operatorname{Hom}^{\bullet,\bullet}(X,Y)\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}\operatorname{Hom}^\bullet(X,Y)\), as required.

Finally, if \(\mathcal{A}\) is \(\Bbbk\)-linear, then \(\operatorname{Hom}^{\bullet,\bullet}(X,Y)\) naturally becomes a functor with values in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}^2(\Bbbk\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}})\).

  1. Translator’s note (O014-C038): the source omits \(F\) from this equality and from the rightmost term of each of the two isomorphisms below. Since the functors being defined are \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}_{\oplus}F\) and \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}_{\Pi}F\), this translation restores \(F\) in all three places.↩︎

  2. Translator’s note (O014-C039): the source uses the coefficient \((-1)^{q+1}\), which corresponds to reusing the formula for \(\sigma\) but not to the strict inverse \(\sigma^{-1}\) obtained from the sign correction in the preceding section. This translation uses the inverse coefficient \((-1)^q\); consequently, the totalization is identified with the \(\operatorname{Hom}\) complex by component signs \((-1)^q\), rather than by literal equality.↩︎

Complexes on an Abelian Category

In this section, \(\mathcal{A}\) is assumed to be an abelian category. As usual, all statements about additivity in this section also extend to the case in which \(\mathcal{A}\) is a \(\Bbbk\)-linear category. For a complex \(X\) on an abelian category, we can discuss its cohomology (Definition reference). Recall that \([n]\) not only shifts the superscripts of a complex but also multiplies \(d_X^\bullet\) by the sign \((-1)^n\). This sign change does not alter the kernel or image of any \(d_X\). Thus \[\operatorname{H}^k\left( X[n] \right) = \operatorname{H}^{n+k} \left(X \right), \quad k, n \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}.\] Proposition reference has already shown that \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})\) is an additive category. We now show that it is also abelian.

Proposition. The category \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})\) is abelian. More precisely, for all \(X,Y\in\operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A}))\), \(X \oplus Y = (X^n \oplus Y^n, (d_X^n, d_Y^n))_{n \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}}\), and for every morphism \(f:X\to Y\) one may take \[\begin{gather*} \operatorname{ker}(f) = \left( \operatorname{ker}(f^n) \right)_{n \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}}, \quad \operatorname{coker}(f) = \left( \operatorname{coker}(f^n) \right)_{n \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}}, \\ \operatorname{im}(f) = \left( \operatorname{im}(f^n) \right)_{n \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}}, \quad \operatorname{coim}(f) = \left( \operatorname{coim}(f^n) \right)_{n \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}}. \end{gather*}\] 1

Suppose morphisms \(f\) and \(g\) in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})\) are composable and \(gf=0\). Then \(H:=\operatorname{H}\left[X\xrightarrow{f}Y\xrightarrow{g}Z\right]\) is the following complex:

  • its degree-\(n\) term is \(H^n:=\operatorname{H}\left[X^n\xrightarrow{f^n}Y^n\xrightarrow{g^n}Z^n\right]\);

  • the morphism \(d_H^n:H^n\to H^{n+1}\) is determined by \(d_X^n\), \(d_Y^n\), and \(d_Z^n\), together with the functoriality of \(\operatorname{H}[\cdots]\) (Proposition reference). 2

Consequently, \(X\xrightarrow{f}Y\xrightarrow{g}Z\) is exact if and only if \(X^n\xrightarrow{f^n}Y^n\xrightarrow{g^n}Z^n\) is exact for every \(n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\).

Proof. Proposition reference explained how to use the forgetful functor from complexes to graded objects, \(U:\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})\to\mathcal{A}^{\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}}\), to reduce the required \(\varinjlim\) and \(\varprojlim\) to degreewise constructions in \(\mathcal{A}\). The point is that \(U\) creates \(\varinjlim\) and \(\varprojlim\) (Lemma reference). This gives degreewise constructions of \(X\oplus Y\), \(\operatorname{ker}(f)\), \(\operatorname{coker}(f)\), and so forth.

In particular, by the characterization equation, the canonical morphism \(\operatorname{coim}(f)\to\operatorname{im}(f)\) is given by the morphisms \(\operatorname{coim}(f^n)\to\operatorname{im}(f^n)\) in \(\mathcal{A}\). A degreewise isomorphism is an isomorphism of complexes. Thus every morphism in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})\) is strict. Therefore \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})\) is an abelian category. 3 The description of \(\operatorname{H}[X\to Y\to Z]\) follows in the same way.

Remark. The same method proves that the category of double complexes \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}^2(\mathcal{A})\), and even the category of \(k\)-fold complexes \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}^k(\mathcal{A})\), remains abelian for \(k\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}_{\geq1}\); see Remark reference.

Next consider a morphism \(f:X\to Y\) in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})\). For every \(n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\), Proposition reference uniquely determines \(\operatorname{H}^n(f):\operatorname{H}^n(X)\to\operatorname{H}^n(Y)\) so that the following diagram commutes: \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:induced-morphism-cohomology}{}\text{Diagram chapter3-unit-037-d001} \end{equation}\] For composable morphisms \(X\xrightarrow{f}Y\xrightarrow{g}Z\), this characterization immediately gives \(\operatorname{H}^n(gf)=\operatorname{H}^n(g)\operatorname{H}^n(f)\); moreover, \(\operatorname{H}^n(\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_X)=\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{\operatorname{H}^n(X)}\).

Proposition (Cohomology as a functor). For every \(n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\), the definition above gives an additive functor \(\operatorname{H}^n:\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})\to\mathcal{A}\).

Proof. The properties \(\operatorname{H}^n(gf)=\operatorname{H}^n(g)\operatorname{H}^n(f)\) and \(\operatorname{H}^n(\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}})=\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}\) follow directly from the characterization equation. In the same way one obtains \(\operatorname{H}^n(f_1+f_2)=\operatorname{H}^n(f_1)+\operatorname{H}^n(f_2)\) and \(\operatorname{H}^n(tf)=t\operatorname{H}^n(f)\) when \(\mathcal{A}\) is \(\Bbbk\)-linear and \(t\in\Bbbk\).

A short exact sequence of complexes automatically induces a long exact sequence in cohomology. This is the most elementary form of a long exact sequence in homology theory.

Proposition (A short exact sequence induces a long exact sequence). Let \(0\to X\xrightarrow{f}Y\xrightarrow{g}Z\to0\) be a short exact sequence in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})\). Then Theorem reference gives the following canonical exact sequence in \(\mathcal{A}\): \[\begin{equation*} \text{Diagram chapter3-unit-037-d002} \end{equation*}\]

This sequence has the following functoriality. If there is a commutative diagram in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})\) whose rows are exact, \[\text{Diagram chapter3-unit-037-d003}\] then one obtains a commutative diagram \[\text{Diagram chapter3-unit-037-d004}\]

Proof. For every \(n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\) there is an exact sequence \(\operatorname{coker}(d_X^{n-1})\to\operatorname{coker}(d_Y^{n-1})\to\operatorname{coker}(d_Z^{n-1})\to0\). Indeed, take the \(\operatorname{coker}\) part of the exact sequence in Theorem reference applied to the diagram \[\text{Diagram chapter3-unit-037-d005}\] 4 Similarly, there is an exact sequence \(0\to\operatorname{ker}(d_X^n)\to\operatorname{ker}(d_Y^n)\to\operatorname{ker}(d_Z^n)\). The two sequences fit into the following commutative diagram with exact rows: \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:long-exact-sequence-ses-aux}{}\text{Diagram chapter3-unit-037-d006} \end{equation}\] The vertical arrows are induced respectively by \(d_X^{n-1}\), \(d_Y^{n-1}\), and \(d_Z^{n-1}\) and have epi–mono factorizations of the form \(\operatorname{coker}(d^{n-2})\stackrel{d^{n-1}}{\twoheadrightarrow} \operatorname{im}(d^{n-1})\hookrightarrow\operatorname{ker}(d^n)\), with subscripts suppressed.

By Lemma reference (iii), the epimorphism \(\operatorname{coker}(d^{n-2})\twoheadrightarrow\operatorname{im}(d^{n-1})\) determines the kernels of the vertical arrows in equation; then equation gives in turn \(\operatorname{H}^{n-1}(X)\), \(\operatorname{H}^{n-1}(Y)\), and \(\operatorname{H}^{n-1}(Z)\). Likewise, the monomorphism \(\operatorname{im}(d^{n-1})\hookrightarrow\operatorname{ker}(d^n)\) determines their cokernels, giving in turn \(\operatorname{H}^n(X)\), \(\operatorname{H}^n(Y)\), and \(\operatorname{H}^n(Z)\). Applying Theorem reference now yields the connecting morphism \(\delta^{n-1}:\operatorname{H}^{n-1}(Z)\to\operatorname{H}^n(X)\) and the portion of the long exact sequence containing the terms \(\operatorname{H}^n\) and \(\operatorname{H}^{n-1}\). Its functoriality follows from Remark reference.

Definition (Quasi-isomorphism). Let \(f:X\to Y\) be a morphism in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})\). If \(\operatorname{H}^n(f)\) is an isomorphism for every \(n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\), then \(f\) is called a quasi-isomorphism.

Proposition. Let \(f:X\to Y\) be a morphism in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})\) and let \(n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\). If \(f\) is null-homotopic, then \(\operatorname{H}^n(f)=0\).

Proof. Choose \(h\in\operatorname{Hom}^{-1}(X,Y)\) such that \(f=d_Yh+hd_X\). The composite \(\operatorname{ker}(d_X^n)\hookrightarrow X^n\xrightarrow{h^{n+1}d_X^n}Y^n\) is zero. On the other hand, \(d_Y^{n-1}h^n\) factors through \(\operatorname{im}(d_Y^{n-1})\). Together these facts give \(\operatorname{H}^n(f)=0\).

Corollary. For every \(n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\), the cohomology functor \(\operatorname{H}^n:\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})\to\mathcal{A}\) factors uniquely through \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{A})\). The notion of quasi-isomorphism therefore extends to morphisms in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{A})\). If \(f:X\to Y\) is an isomorphism in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{A})\), then \(f\) is a quasi-isomorphism.

Proof. Combine Propositions reference and reference.

  1. Translator’s note (O014-C040): the source writes \(\operatorname{ker}(f)^n\), \(\operatorname{coker}(f)^n\), \(\operatorname{im}(f)^n\), and \(\operatorname{coim}(f)^n\) on the left but equates each with an entire family indexed by \(n\) on the right. This translation removes the superscript \(n\) on the left so that all four are identities of complexes; their degree-\(n\) components remain exactly those shown on the right.↩︎

  2. Translator’s note (O014-C041): the source mentions only \(d_X^n\) and \(d_Y^n\). This translation adds \(d_Z^n\), which is needed to give a morphism between the two three-term diagrams and hence to induce \(d_H^n\).↩︎

  3. Translator’s note (O014-C042): the closing sentence of the source names \(\mathcal{A}\), although that category was already assumed abelian; the category just proved abelian is \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})\). This translation corrects the category name.↩︎

  4. Translator’s note (O014-C043): the source states the sequence \(\operatorname{coker}(d_X^n)\to\operatorname{coker}(d_Y^n)\to\operatorname{coker}(d_Z^n)\to0\), while the vertical arrows in the diagram immediately following it are \(d_X^{n-1}\), \(d_Y^{n-1}\), and \(d_Z^{n-1}\). This translation aligns the cokernel indices with the diagram; renaming the index then gives the row indexed by \(n-2\) used below.↩︎

Mapping Cones and Long Exact Sequences

Long exact sequences are a principal tool of homological algebra. This section compares three ways of constructing a long exact sequence from a short exact sequence. Up to certain signs, all three give the same result. Throughout the section, \(\mathcal{A}\) is assumed to be an abelian category.

Proposition. Let \(f:X\to Y\) be a morphism in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})\). Take \(\alpha(f)\) and \(\beta(f)\) as in Definition reference. Then \[0 \to Y \xrightarrow{\alpha(f)} \operatorname{Cone}(f) \xrightarrow{\beta(f)} X[1] \to 0\] is an exact sequence in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})\).

Proof. Recall the definitions of \(\alpha(f)\) and \(\beta(f)\). Since exactness can be checked degreewise (Proposition reference), it suffices to prove the exactness of \[0 \to Y^n \xrightarrow{(0, \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}})} X^{n+1} \oplus Y^n \xrightarrow{\text{projection}} X^{n+1} \to 0,\] for every \(n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\). This is Proposition reference.

Given a morphism \(f:X\to Y\) in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})\), the short exact sequence in Proposition reference, together with Proposition reference, gives the following long exact sequence in \(\mathcal{A}\): \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:cone-long-exact-sequence}{} \cdots \to \operatorname{H}^n(Y) \xrightarrow{\operatorname{H}^n(\alpha(f))} \operatorname{H}^n(\operatorname{Cone}(f)) \xrightarrow{\operatorname{H}^n(\beta(f))} \underbracket{\operatorname{H}^n(X[1])}_{= \operatorname{H}^{n+1}(X)} \xrightarrow{\xi^n} \operatorname{H}^{n+1}(Y) \to \cdots \end{equation}\] The morphism labeled \(\xi^n\) is the connecting morphism induced by this short exact sequence. Corollary reference will prove that \(\xi^n\) is precisely \(\operatorname{H}^{n+1}(f):\operatorname{H}^{n+1}(X)\to\operatorname{H}^{n+1}(Y)\). Thus every part of the mapping-cone long exact sequence equation is explicit and comes from \(f\), \(\alpha(f)\), and \(\beta(f)\). The next result goes in the opposite direction: every short exact sequence in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})\) also has a natural relation with a mapping cone. This relation can be constructed in two ways.

Lemma. Given a short exact sequence \(0\to X\xrightarrow{f}Y\xrightarrow{g}Z\to0\) in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})\), the two morphisms \[\Phi := (0, g): \operatorname{Cone}(f) \to Z, \quad \Phi' := (f[1], 0): X[1] \to \operatorname{Cone}(g)\] are quasi-isomorphisms of complexes and have the following properties:

  1. \(\Phi \circ \alpha(f) = g\) and \(\beta(g) \circ \Phi' = f[1]\);

  2. \(\alpha(g)\Phi + \Phi'\beta(f):\operatorname{Cone}(f)\to\operatorname{Cone}(g)\) is canonically null-homotopic.

Proof. Consider the following commutative diagrams in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})\): \[\text{Diagram chapter3-unit-038-d001} \quad \text{Diagram chapter3-unit-038-d002}\] Every row is exact. Hence functoriality of mapping cones (Proposition reference) gives morphisms in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})\) arranged as \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:cone-qis-aux}{}\text{Diagram chapter3-unit-038-d003} \end{equation}\] Checking degree by degree and using the diagrams above and the definition of a mapping cone shows that both rows of equation are exact. It is also easy to see that \(\operatorname{Cone}(f)\to\operatorname{Cone}(0\to Z)\simeq Z\) (or \(X[1]\simeq\operatorname{Cone}(X\to0)\to\operatorname{Cone}(g)\)) is exactly \(\Phi\) (or \(\Phi'\)). Once they are known to be morphisms of complexes, the equalities in (i) are immediate.

Applying Proposition reference to equation gives, for every \(n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\), exact sequences \[\begin{gather*} \operatorname{H}^n\left( \operatorname{Cone}(\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_X) \right) \to \operatorname{H}^n \left( \operatorname{Cone}(f) \right) \xrightarrow{\operatorname{H}^n(\Phi)} \operatorname{H}^n(Z) \to \operatorname{H}^{n+1} \left( \operatorname{Cone}(\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_X) \right), \\ \operatorname{H}^{n-1}\left( \operatorname{Cone}(\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_Z) \right) \to \operatorname{H}^n(X[1]) \xrightarrow{\operatorname{H}^n(\Phi')} \operatorname{H}^n\left( \operatorname{Cone}(g) \right) \to \operatorname{H}^n\left( \operatorname{Cone}(\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_Z) \right). \end{gather*}\] Lemma reference (i) and Proposition reference show that the terms at both ends are all \(0\). Thus \(\Phi\) and \(\Phi'\) are quasi-isomorphisms.

Finally, verify (ii). Using \(\operatorname{Cone}(f)^n=X^{n+1}\oplus Y^n\) and \(\operatorname{Cone}(g)^n=Y^{n+1}\oplus Z^n\), write the morphisms as matrices: \[\begin{gather*} \text{Diagram chapter3-unit-038-d004}, \quad \alpha(g) \Phi + \Phi' \beta(f) = \begin{pmatrix} f[1] & 0 \\ 0 & g \end{pmatrix}. \end{gather*}\] On the other hand, take \(s=(s^n)_n\in\operatorname{Hom}^{-1}\left(\operatorname{Cone}(f),\operatorname{Cone}(g)\right)\) with \[s^n := \begin{pmatrix} 0 & \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{Y^n} \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}: X^{n+1} \oplus Y^n \to Y^n \oplus Z^{n-1} ,\] which is also the only natural choice. A direct matrix calculation shows that \(d_{\operatorname{Cone}(g)}^{n-1}s^n+s^{n+1}d_{\operatorname{Cone}(f)}^n\) equals \[\begin{pmatrix} -d_Y^n & 0 \\ g^n & d_Z^{n-1} \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} 0 & \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{Y^n} \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix} + \begin{pmatrix} 0 & \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{Y^{n+1}} \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} -d_X^{n+1} & 0 \\ f^{n+1} & d_Y^n \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} f^{n+1} & 0 \\ 0 & g^n \end{pmatrix}.\] Thus \(\alpha(g)\Phi+\Phi'\beta(f)\) is indeed null-homotopic.

In summary, a short exact sequence \(0\to X\xrightarrow{f}Y\xrightarrow{g}Z\to0\) in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})\) gives three ways to obtain the following long exact sequence in \(\mathcal{A}\): \[\text{Diagram chapter3-unit-038-d005}\]

  1. Applying Proposition reference directly gives the long exact sequence \[\text{Diagram chapter3-unit-038-d006}\]

  2. Use the quasi-isomorphism \(\Phi:\operatorname{Cone}(f)\to Z\) from Lemma reference together with equation to obtain the commutative diagram \[\text{Diagram chapter3-unit-038-d007}\] where

    • \(\eta^n := \operatorname{H}^n(\beta(f)) \operatorname{H}^n(\Phi)^{-1}\);

    • \(\xi^n\) is the connecting morphism in equation, of the form \[\operatorname{H}^{n+1}(X)=\operatorname{H}^n(X[1])\to\operatorname{H}^{n+1}(Y).\]

    Since the first row is known to be exact, the second is exact as well.

  3. Proceed similarly, now using the quasi-isomorphism \(\Phi':X[1]\to\operatorname{Cone}(g)\) from Lemma reference. This gives the commutative diagram \[\text{Diagram chapter3-unit-038-d008}\] where

    • \((\eta')^n := \operatorname{H}^n(\Phi')^{-1} \operatorname{H}^n(\alpha(g))\);

    • \((\xi')^n\) comes from the connecting morphism \(\operatorname{H}^{n+1}(Y)=\operatorname{H}^n(Y[1])\to\operatorname{H}^{n+1}(Z)\) in equation, with \(g\) in place of \(f\).

    Since the first row is known to be exact, the second is exact as well.

How are these three long exact sequences alike, and how do they differ? We first state the conclusions.

  • Constructions (A) and (B) differ only by certain minus signs: Proposition reference will show that \(\eta^n=-\delta^n\), while Corollary reference implies \(\xi^n=\operatorname{H}^{n+1}(f)\).

  • Constructions (A) and (C) give the same result: Corollary reference, based on the result for (B), will show that \((\eta')^n=\delta^n\), while Corollary reference implies \((\xi')^n=\operatorname{H}^{n+1}(g)\).

  • Thus (B) and (C) differ only by a sign in the connecting morphism \(\operatorname{H}^n(Z)\to\operatorname{H}^{n+1}(X)\). This can be explained by the rotation axiom (TR3) for triangulated categories; see Proposition in the discussion of derived categories in Chapter 4.

We now prove these relations.

Proposition. In the situation above, \(\eta^n=-\delta^n\) for every \(n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\).

Proof. The following argument is taken from [KS06]. Because it is rather intricate, readers are encouraged first to try the concrete case \(\mathcal{A}=R\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\), with \(R\) a ring; the diagram-chasing method of [Li1] gives a direct proof in that case.

For a general abelian category \(\mathcal{A}\), fix \(n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\) and take the fiber product \[S := \operatorname{coker}(d_Y^{n-1}) \ensuremath{\underset{\operatorname{coker}(d_Z^{n-1})}{\times}} \operatorname{H}^n(Z).\] How is the connecting morphism \(\delta^n\) constructed? It is obtained by applying equation to the diagram in equation, \[\text{Diagram chapter3-unit-038-d009}\] here rearranged into the form \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:connecting-eta-delta-0}{}\text{Diagram chapter3-unit-038-d010} \end{equation}\] All rows and columns here are exact. The arrow \(a\) is induced by \(d_Y^n\), the arrow \(b\) is induced by \(f^{n+1}\), and the existence and uniqueness of \(u\) follow because commutativity of the right-hand part implies \(cav=0\). Inspecting the construction in equation shows that the diagram \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:connecting-eta-delta-0.5}{}\text{Diagram chapter3-unit-038-d011} \quad \text{commutes}; \end{equation}\] since \(w\) is known to be an epimorphism, this diagram also uniquely determines \(\delta^n\).

To compare it with the mapping cone, verify directly from the definitions that the following diagram commutes: \[\text{Diagram chapter3-unit-038-d012}\] The definitions of the horizontal arrows should be clear. Since the fan-shaped part of equation commutes, the diagram above implies that the composite \[\begin{multlined} S \xrightarrow{(-u, v)} \operatorname{ker}\left( d_X^{n+1} \right) \oplus \operatorname{coker}\left( d_Y^{n-1} \right) \\ {}\xrightarrow[\text{top row}]{\text{of the diagram above}} \operatorname{coker}\left( d_{\operatorname{Cone}(f)}^{n-1} \right) \xrightarrow{d_{\operatorname{Cone}(f)}^n} \operatorname{ker}\left( d_{\operatorname{Cone}(f)}^{n+1} \right) \end{multlined}\] is \(0\). Therefore \(S \xrightarrow{(-u, v)} \operatorname{ker}\left( d_X^{n+1} \right) \oplus \operatorname{coker}\left( d_Y^{n-1} \right) \to \operatorname{coker}\left( d_{\operatorname{Cone}(f)}^{n-1} \right)\) factors uniquely as \(S \to \operatorname{H}^n(\operatorname{Cone}(f)) \hookrightarrow \operatorname{coker}\left( d_{\operatorname{Cone}(f)}^{n-1} \right)\). We claim that the following diagram commutes: \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:connecting-eta-delta-1}{}\text{Diagram chapter3-unit-038-d013} \end{equation}\] Indeed, commutativity of each square is routine to verify. By the upper-right square in equation and \(\Phi=(0,g)\), the part \[\text{Diagram chapter3-unit-038-d014}\] of diagram equation also commutes. Moreover, because \(\operatorname{H}^n(Z)\to\operatorname{coker}(d_Z^{n-1})\) is a monomorphism, composing with this arrow shows that the remaining curved left-hand part of equation commutes as well.

Notice that the two composites \[\begin{aligned} \operatorname{H}^n(\operatorname{Cone}(f)) &\hookrightarrow \operatorname{coker}\left( d_{\operatorname{Cone}(f)}^{n-1} \right) \to \operatorname{coker}(d_X^n), \\ \operatorname{H}^n(\operatorname{Cone}(f)) &\xrightarrow{\operatorname{H}^n(\beta(f))} \operatorname{H}^{n+1}(X) \hookrightarrow \operatorname{coker}(d_X^n) \end{aligned}\] are equal, since both are induced by projection onto \(X^{n+1}\). Hence equation gives the commutative diagram \[\text{Diagram chapter3-unit-038-d015}\] By equation, this implies that the composites \(S\xrightarrow{w}\operatorname{H}^n(Z)\xrightarrow{\delta^n}\operatorname{H}^{n+1}(X)\) and \(S\xrightarrow{w}\operatorname{H}^n(Z)\xrightarrow{\eta^n}\operatorname{H}^{n+1}(X)\) differ by a minus sign. Since \(w\) is an epimorphism, \(\eta^n=-\delta^n\), as required.

Corollary. In the situation above, \((\eta')^n=\delta^n\) for every \(n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\).

Proof. Use the notation of Lemma reference. By Proposition reference, it suffices to prove that \((\eta')^n+\eta^n=0\). This equality follows immediately from the fact that \(\alpha(g)\Phi+\Phi'\beta(f):\operatorname{Cone}(f)\to\operatorname{Cone}(g)\) is null-homotopic (Lemma reference (ii)).

Corollary. For any morphism \(f:X\to Y\) in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})\), the connecting morphism \(\xi^n:\operatorname{H}^{n+1}(X)\simeq\operatorname{H}^n(X[1])\to\operatorname{H}^{n+1}(Y)\) in the long exact sequence equation equals \(\operatorname{H}^{n+1}(f)\).

Proof. Apply Lemma reference to the short exact sequence \(0\to Y\to\operatorname{Cone}(f)\to X[1]\to0\). This gives the quasi-isomorphism \((0,\beta(f))\) and the following commutative diagram with exact rows: \[\text{Diagram chapter3-unit-038-d016}\] The morphism \(\psi:\operatorname{Cone}(\alpha(f))\to X[1]\) discussed in Lemma reference is precisely \((0,\beta(f))\) here: its degree-\(n\) component is the projection from \(Y^{n+1}\oplus\operatorname{Cone}(f)^n=Y^{n+1}\oplus X^{n+1}\oplus Y^n\) onto \(X^{n+1}\). The commutative diagram in that lemma therefore gives \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:cone-connecting-aux}{} \text{in $\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{A})$} \quad f[1] \circ (0, \beta(f)) + \beta(\alpha(f)) = 0 . \end{equation}\]

Now recall that \[\xi^n:\operatorname{H}^n(X[1])\to\operatorname{H}^{n+1}(Y)\] is the connecting morphism of the short exact sequence \[0 \to Y \xrightarrow{\alpha(f)} \operatorname{Cone}(f) \xrightarrow{\beta(f)} X[1] \to 0,\] and applying Proposition reference to this sequence shows immediately that the composite \[\operatorname{H}^n(\operatorname{Cone}(\alpha(f))) \xrightarrow[\sim]{\operatorname{H}^n((0, \beta(f)))} \operatorname{H}^n(X[1]) \xrightarrow{\xi^n} \operatorname{H}^{n+1}(Y)\] equals \(-\operatorname{H}^n(\beta(\alpha(f)))\). But equation implies \(\operatorname{H}^n(\beta(\alpha(f)))=-\operatorname{H}^n(f[1])\circ \operatorname{H}^n((0,\beta(f)))\). Thus \(\xi^n=\operatorname{H}^n(f[1])=\operatorname{H}^{n+1}(f)\).

Corollary. With the notation above, \(f\) is a quasi-isomorphism if and only if \(\operatorname{H}^n(\operatorname{Cone}(f))=0\) for every \(n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\).

Proof. Substitute Corollary reference into the long exact sequence equation; the conclusion follows at once.

Exercises: Hochschild Homology and Cohomology

This section returns to concrete mathematics. Let \(\Bbbk\) be a commutative ring. Tensor products \(\ensuremath{\underset{\Bbbk}{\otimes}}\) of \(\Bbbk\)-modules will be abbreviated to \(\otimes\), the \(n\)-th tensor power of a \(\Bbbk\)-module \(M\) will be written \(M^{\otimes n}\), and we set \(M^{\otimes 0}:=\Bbbk\). For a \(\Bbbk\)-algebra \(R\), as usual, the left and right actions of \(\Bbbk\) on every \((R,R)\)-bimodule are assumed to agree. Thus an \((R,R)\)-bimodule is also identified with a left \(R\otimes R^{\operatorname{op}}\)-module.

Definition (Bar complex). Let \(R\) be a \(\Bbbk\)-algebra. For every \(n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}_{\geq 0}\), define the \((R,R)\)-bimodule \[\begin{gather*} \mathsf{B}_n R := R \otimes R^{\otimes n} \otimes R = R^{\otimes (n+2)}, \\ r(r_0 \otimes \cdots \otimes r_{n+1})r' = rr_0 \otimes \cdots \otimes r_{n+1} r', \end{gather*}\] where \(r,r',r_0,\ldots,r_{n+1}\in R\). For every \(n\geq1\), define the bimodule homomorphism \[\begin{equation*} \begin{split} b_n: \mathsf{B}_n R & \to \mathsf{B}_{n-1} R, \\ b_n \left( r_0 \otimes \cdots \otimes r_{n+1} \right) & := \sum_{k=0}^n (-1)^k \cdots \otimes r_k r_{k+1} \otimes \cdots . \end{split} \end{equation*}\] We call \(\mathsf{B}R:=\left(\mathsf{B}_nR,b_n\right)_{n\geq0}\) the bar complex of \(R\); it is a chain complex in the sense of Remark reference.

The classical notation for \(r_0\otimes\cdots\otimes r_{n+1}\in\mathsf{B}_nR\) is \((r_0|\cdots|r_{n+1})\); this is the origin of the name “bar.” The homomorphism \(b\) acts by deleting one separator in every possible way and then summing the results with alternating signs. From this it is easy to see that \(b^2=0\). Indeed, \(b^2(r_0|\cdots|r_{n+1})\) is a linear combination of elements of the form \[\begin{gather*} (\cdots |r_{h-1} r_h| \cdots |r_{k-1} r_k| \cdots ) \quad \text{or} \quad ( \cdots | r_{h-1} r_h r_{h+1} | \cdots ). \end{gather*}\] There are exactly two ways to obtain any such term from \((\cdots|r_{h-1}|\cdots|r_k|\cdots)\) by deleting separators, and their signs cancel. Thus \(\mathsf{B}R\) is indeed a chain complex. Now augment the bar complex as in the following diagram and denote the result by \(\mathsf{B}'R\). The morphism \(b_0\) in the diagram is also called the augmentation homomorphism. \[\text{Diagram chapter3-unit-039-d001}\]

Lemma. The augmented chain complex \(\mathsf{B}'R\) is exact. More precisely, if \(\mathsf{B}'R\) is regarded as a chain complex of \(\Bbbk\)-modules, then \(\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{\mathsf{B}'R}\) is null-homotopic.

Proof. We construct a family of \(\Bbbk\)-module homomorphisms \(h_n:\mathsf{B}'_nR\to\mathsf{B}'_{n+1}R\), for \(n\geq-1\), such that \(b_{n+1}h_n+h_{n-1}b_n=\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{\mathsf{B}'_nR}\) (with, of course, the conventions \(h_{-2}=0\) and \(b_{-1}=0\)). This will prove that \(\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{\mathsf{B}'R}\) is null-homotopic. Concretely, take \[h_n(r_0 | \cdots | r_{n+1}) = (1_R | r_0 | \cdots | r_{n+1}),\] and extend linearly on \(\mathsf{B}'_nR\). For every \(n\geq0\) and \(r_0,\ldots,r_{n+1}\in R\), we obtain \[\begin{align*} b_{n+1} h_n \left(r_0 | \cdots | r_{n+1} \right) & = (r_0 | \cdots | r_{n+1}) + \sum_{k=0}^n (-1)^{k+1} (1_R | \cdots | r_k r_{k+1} | \cdots), \\ h_{n-1} b_n \left(r_0 | \cdots | r_{n+1} \right) & = \sum_{k=0}^n (-1)^k (1_R | \cdots | r_k r_{k+1} | \cdots). \end{align*}\] It follows immediately that \[(b_{n+1} h_n + h_{n-1} b_n)(r_0 | \cdots | r_{n+1}) = (r_0 | \cdots | r_{n+1}).\] Since \(b_0h_{-1}(r)=b_0(1_R|r)=r\), the equality also holds directly for \(n=-1\).

At first sight, the definitions of \(\mathsf{B}R\) and \(\mathsf{B}'R\) may seem like unexpected inventions. Example in the discussion of Chapter 8 will later view these chain complexes from the perspective of comonads and give a natural explanation.

Convention. Define \(R^e:=R\otimes R^{\operatorname{op}}\). For every \((R,R)\)-bimodule \(M\), including the special case \(M=R\), henceforth:

  • regard \(M\) as a left \(R^e\)-module through \((r\otimes r')m=rmr'\);

  • regard \(M\) as a right \(R^e\)-module through \(m(r\otimes r'):=r'mr\).

With this convention, for every \(M\) we can define the chain complex of \(\Bbbk\)-modules \(M\ensuremath{\underset{R^e}{\otimes}}\mathsf{B}R\) and the complex \(\operatorname{Hom}_{R^e}\left(\mathsf{B}R,M\right)\).

Definition (G. Hochschild). For every \(n\), define the \(\Bbbk\)-linear functors \(\operatorname{HH}_n,\operatorname{HH}^n:(R,R)\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\rightrightarrows\Bbbk\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\) as follows: \[\begin{array}{cl} \text{Hochschild homology} & \operatorname{HH}_n(M) := \operatorname{H}_n\left(M\ensuremath{\underset{R^e}{\otimes}}\mathsf{B}R\right), \\ \text{Hochschild cohomology} & \operatorname{HH}^n(M) := \operatorname{H}^n\left(\operatorname{Hom}_{R^e}(\mathsf{B}R,M)\right). \end{array}\] In the special case \(M=R\), these objects are called respectively the Hochschild homology \(\operatorname{HH}_n(R)\) and Hochschild cohomology \(\operatorname{HH}^n(R)\) of \(R\).

To simplify the descriptions of \(\operatorname{HH}_n(M)\) and \(\operatorname{HH}^n(M)\), introduce the following two Hochschild complexes: \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:HH-cplx}{}\begin{aligned} \index[sym1]{CRM@$C_\bullet(R, M)$, $C^\bullet(R, M)$} C_\bullet(R,M) & := \left[ \cdots \to M \otimes R^{\otimes n} \xrightarrow{d_n} \cdots \xrightarrow{d_2} M \otimes R \xrightarrow{d_1} M \right], \\ C^\bullet(R,M) & := \left[ M \xrightarrow{d^0} \operatorname{Hom}_{\Bbbk}(R, M) \xrightarrow{d^1} \cdots \to \operatorname{Hom}_{\Bbbk}(R^{\otimes n}, M) \xrightarrow{d^n} \cdots \right]. \end{aligned} \end{equation}\] Their degrees are respectively \(\ldots,2,1,0\) and \(0,1,2,\ldots\); all other terms are set equal to \(0\). The homomorphisms \(d_n\) and \(d^n\) are defined as follows.

  1. In bar notation, continue to write an element \(m\otimes r_1\otimes\cdots\otimes r_n\) of \(M\otimes R^{\otimes n}\) as \((m|r_1|\cdots|r_n)\). Define \[\begin{multline} \hypertarget{eqn:HH-cplx-d}{} d_n(m|r_1|\cdots|r_n)=\\ \underbracket{(mr_1|r_2|\cdots|r_n) +\sum_{k=1}^{n-1}(-1)^k (m|\cdots|r_kr_{k+1}|\cdots)}_{=:d'_n(m|r_1|\cdots|r_n)} +(-1)^n(r_nm|r_1|\cdots|r_{n-1}). \end{multline}\]

  2. Identify an element of \(\operatorname{Hom}_{\Bbbk}(R^{\otimes n},M)\) with a \(\Bbbk\)-multilinear map \(R^n\to M\) (see [Li1]). Define \[\begin{multline*} (d^nf)(r_1,\ldots,r_{n+1})=\\ r_1f(r_2,\ldots,r_{n+1}) +\sum_{k=1}^n(-1)^kf(\ldots,r_kr_{k+1},\ldots) +(-1)^{n+1}f(r_1,\ldots,r_n)r_{n+1}. \end{multline*}\]

For every \(n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}_{\geq0}\), there are isomorphisms \[\text{Diagram chapter3-unit-039-d002}\] 1 and \[\text{Diagram chapter3-unit-039-d003}\] A short calculation shows that, through these isomorphisms, \(\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_M\otimes b_n\) corresponds to \(d_n\), while \(b_{n+1}^*\) corresponds to \(d^n\).2 Thus the isomorphisms above are isomorphisms of complexes and give the following result. To display the parameter \(R\) explicitly once again, write \(\operatorname{HH}_n(R,M):=\operatorname{HH}_n(M)\) and \(\operatorname{HH}^n(R,M):=\operatorname{HH}^n(M)\). 3 With this notation, \[\operatorname{HH}^n(R, M) \simeq \operatorname{H}^n(C^\bullet(R, M)), \quad \operatorname{HH}_n(R, M) \simeq \operatorname{H}_n(C_\bullet(R, M)).\] Readers new to the subject are encouraged to check the calculation in detail.

Remark. Suppose that \(R\) is commutative. Every \(R\)-module \(M\) becomes an \((R,R)\)-bimodule by \(rmr':=rr'm\). In this case, the complex \(C_\bullet(R,M)\) (or \(C^\bullet(R,M)\))4 is a complex of \(R\)-modules if we set \[r\cdot(m|r_1|\cdots|r_n)=(rm|r_1|\cdots|r_n) \quad\text{or}\quad (r\cdot f)(r_1,\ldots,r_n)=rf(r_1,\ldots,r_n).\] Consequently, \(\operatorname{HH}_n(M)\) and \(\operatorname{HH}^n(M)\) both acquire \(R\)-module structures. This can of course also be proved at the level of the bar complex.

Example. Take \(M=R=\Bbbk\). It follows immediately from the construction above that \(d_1,d_2,\ldots\) are successively \(0,\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}},0,\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}},\ldots\). Thus \(\operatorname{HH}_0(\Bbbk)=\Bbbk\) and \(\operatorname{HH}_{\geq1}(\Bbbk)=0\). A similar argument gives \(\operatorname{HH}^0(\Bbbk)=\Bbbk\) and \(\operatorname{HH}^{\geq1}(\Bbbk)=0\).

In higher degrees \(n\), computing \(\operatorname{HH}^n(M)\) and \(\operatorname{HH}_n(M)\) from the original definition is generally difficult. Example in § 3.14 and in § 3.14 will later show respectively that \[\operatorname{HH}_n(M) \simeq \operatorname{Tor}^{R^e}_n(M, R), \quad \operatorname{HH}^n(M) \simeq \operatorname{Ext}_{R^e}^n(R, M),\] provided that \(R\), as a \(\Bbbk\)-module, is respectively flat and projective. At that point, some special cases of \(\operatorname{HH}_n\) and \(\operatorname{HH}^n\) can be computed with simpler complexes. For general \(R\), in the exercises of Chapter 8 we will explain \(\operatorname{HH}_n\) and \(\operatorname{HH}^n\) as relative \(\operatorname{Tor}\) and relative \(\operatorname{Ext}\).

Example (Degree zero: center and cocenter). First consider \(\operatorname{HH}^0(M)\). By definition, \(d^0:M=C^0(R,M)\to C^1(R,M)=\operatorname{Hom}_{\Bbbk}(R,M)\) maps \(m\) to \([r\mapsto rm-mr]\). Therefore \[\operatorname{HH}^0(M)=\left\{m\in M:\forall r\in R,\;rm=mr\right\}.\] The right-hand side may naturally be called the center of \(M\); when \(M=R\), this is precisely the center in the sense of ring theory.

Next consider \(\operatorname{HH}_0(M)\). Write \([M,R]\) for the \(\Bbbk\)-submodule of \(M\) generated by all elements of the form \(mr-rm\), with \(m\in M\) and \(r\in R\). Since \(d_1(m|r)=mr-rm\), we obtain \[\operatorname{im}\left[d_1:M\otimes R\to M\right]=[M,R], \quad \operatorname{HH}_0(M)=M/[M,R].\] In particular, the case \(M=R\) gives the submodule \([R,R]\) of \(R\) generated by all \([r',r]:=r'r-rr'\). The corresponding \(\Bbbk\)-module \(R/[R,R]\) is called the cocenter of \(R\). Every \(\Bbbk\)-module homomorphism \(\varphi:R\to N\) satisfying \(\varphi(rr')=\varphi(r'r)\), that is, having a “trace-like” property, factors uniquely through \(R/[R,R]=\operatorname{HH}_0(R)\).

Example (Degree one: derivations). Now consider \(\operatorname{HH}^1(M)\). Write \([r,m]:=rm-mr\). Then \[\begin{align*} \operatorname{ker}(d^1) &=\left\{D\in\operatorname{Hom}_{\Bbbk}(R,M): \forall r_1,r_2\in R,\; r_1D(r_2)-D(r_1r_2)+D(r_1)r_2=0\right\},\\ \operatorname{im}(d^0) &=\left\{[\mathord{\cdot},m]\in\operatorname{Hom}_{\Bbbk}(R,M):m\in M\right\}. \end{align*}\] The condition defining \(\operatorname{ker}(d^1)\) may be rewritten as the Leibniz rule \(D(r_1r_2)=r_1D(r_2)+D(r_1)r_2\). A \(\Bbbk\)-module homomorphism \(D\) with this property is regarded as a derivation on \(R\) with values in \(M\). The \(\Bbbk\)-module formed by these homomorphisms is denoted by \(\operatorname{Der}_{\Bbbk}(R,M)\), while the elements of the form \([\mathord{\cdot},m]\) form the submodule \(\mathrm{Inn}_{\Bbbk}(R,M)\). Thus the quotient module \[\operatorname{HH}^1(M)=\operatorname{Der}_{\Bbbk}(R,M)/\mathrm{Inn}_{\Bbbk}(R,M)\] classifies all derivations on \(R\) with values in \(M\), modulo \(\mathrm{Inn}_{\Bbbk}(R,M)\).

Now suppose that \(R\) is commutative, in order to interpret \(\operatorname{HH}_1(M)\). We need a little preparation. Define the free \(R\)-module \(\bigoplus_{r\in R}R\widetilde{\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}r}\) with basis the symbols \(\widetilde{\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}r}\), and define the submodule \(N\) generated by the following elements: \[\widetilde{\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}(r+r')}-\widetilde{\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}r}-\widetilde{\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}r'}, \quad \widetilde{\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}tr}-t\widetilde{\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}r}, \quad \widetilde{\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}rr'}-r\widetilde{\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}r'}-r'\widetilde{\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}r},\] where \(r,r'\in R\) and \(t\in\Bbbk\). Thus define the \(R\)-module \[\begin{align*} \Omega_{R|\Bbbk} &:=\bigoplus_{r\in R}R\widetilde{\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}r}\bigg/N\\ &=\sum_{r\in R}R\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}r,\qquad \mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}r:=\text{the image of }\widetilde{\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}r}. \end{align*}\] This is called the module of Kähler differentials of the \(\Bbbk\)-algebra \(R\) and is characterized by the following universal property: \[\text{Diagram chapter3-unit-039-d004} \qquad M:\text{an $R$-module}.\] The reader is asked to verify this directly. This isomorphism shows that \(R\to\Omega_{R|\Bbbk}\) given by \(r\mapsto\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}r\) (corresponding to \(\varphi=\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}\)) is a “universal derivation.” Topics related to this properly belong to the theory of commutative rings; we merely record the result here.

Return to \(\operatorname{HH}_1(M)\), still assuming that \(R\) is commutative. Let \(M\) be an \(R\)-module made into an \((R,R)\)-bimodule by \(rmr':=(rr')m\). It is immediate that \(d_1:M\otimes R\to M\) is \(0\), while the image of \(d_2:M\otimes R^{\otimes2}\to M\otimes R\) is generated by elements of the form \((rm|r')-(m|rr')+(r'm|r)\). We therefore obtain homomorphisms of \(\Bbbk\)-modules in both directions \[\text{Diagram chapter3-unit-039-d005}\] From the descriptions of \(\operatorname{im}(d_2)\) and \(\Omega_{R|\Bbbk}\), a routine check shows that these homomorphisms are well defined and mutually inverse. In fact, both are isomorphisms of \(R\)-modules. Thus, when \(R\) is commutative, we obtain \(\operatorname{HH}_1(M)\simeq M\ensuremath{\underset{R}{\otimes}}\Omega_{R|\Bbbk}\). In particular, \(\operatorname{HH}_1(R)\simeq\Omega_{R|\Bbbk}\).

Hochschild homology and cohomology contain a wealth of information; their connection with derivations and differential forms is no accident. The exercises will give further interpretations of Hochschild cohomology. Return to the Hochschild chain complex. Keeping the actions of \(R^e\) on \(\mathsf{B}_nR\) and on \(M\) in mind, the intuitive idea is to arrange an element \((m|r_1|\cdots|r_n)\) of \(C_n(R,M)\) in a circle:

Diagram chapter3-unit-039-d006

Thus \(d_n(m|r_1|\cdots|r_n)\) is obtained by deleting a separator in \(n+1\) ways and summing the results with alternating signs. In the special case \(M=R\), the picture has an evident rotational symmetry. Algebraically, for every \(n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}_{\geq0}\) define the \(\Bbbk\)-module homomorphism \[\text{Diagram chapter3-unit-039-d007}\] then \(t_n^{n+1}=\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}\). This homomorphism realizes the symmetry. Rotational symmetry leads to the theory of cyclic homology. Historically, there have been at least two motivations for studying cyclic homology. The first is to seek an analogue of de Rham theory in the noncommutative setting. The second is to study and apply K-theory, including various generalizations of the index theorem. This section uses Hochschild homology and cohomology and cyclic homology only as a light vehicle for familiarizing the reader with operations on complexes; the treatment is merely introductory. Readers wishing to go further may consult monographs such as [Lo98, Wi19]. All complexes (or double complexes) mentioned below are understood to be chain complexes (or chain double complexes). For every \(n\geq0\), define \(N_n:=\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}+t_n+\cdots+(t_n)^n \in\operatorname{End}_{\Bbbk}(R^{\otimes(n+1)})\). Define the cyclic double complex \(\mathrm{CC}(R)=(\mathrm{CC}(R)_{p,q})_{(p,q)\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}^2}\) to be the following double complex. \[\text{Diagram chapter3-unit-039-d008}\] All its terms are \(\Bbbk\)-modules, and all terms with \(q<0\) are defined to be \(0\). The morphisms \(d_q\) and \(d'_q\) are defined in equation. Notice that:

  • the even columns are the Hochschild chain complex \(C_\bullet(R,R)\) of equation;

  • it is easy to prove that the odd columns are the augmented bar complex \(\mathsf{B}'R\), with the indices shifted so that it begins in degree \(0\). Hence Lemma reference implies that all odd columns are exact; in fact, they are \(0\) in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\Bbbk\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}})\).

To show that \(\mathrm{CC}(R)\) is indeed a double complex, we need the following observation. Its proof is elementary and interesting, with no essential difficulty, so it is left as an exercise in this chapter.

Lemma. Let \(R\) be a \(\Bbbk\)-algebra. For every \(q\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}_{\geq1}\), the following equalities hold in \(\operatorname{Hom}_{\Bbbk}\left(R^{\otimes(q+1)},R^{\otimes q}\right)\): \[d_q(\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}-t_q)=(\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}-t_{q-1})d'_q, \quad d'_qN_q=N_{q-1}d_q.\]

For every double complex \(C=(C_{i,j})_{(i,j)\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}^2}\) and \(m\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\), define its horizontal shift5 \(C_{\mathrm{I}}[m]\) to be the double complex \((C_{m+i,j})_{i,j}\). For every \(p\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\), define the horizontal brutal truncation functor \(\sigma_{\mathrm{I},\leq p}C\) (or \(\sigma_{\mathrm{I},\geq p}C\)) by replacing with \(0\) every \(C_{i,j}\) for which \(i>p\) (or \(i<p\)) and leaving all other terms unchanged. This gives a short exact sequence of double complexes (note the order): \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:homology-I-brute-truncation}{} 0 \to \sigma_{\mathrm{I}, \leq p} C \to C \to \sigma_{\mathrm{I}, \geq p+1} C \to 0. \end{equation}\] Moreover, for every \(a\leq b\), define \(\sigma_{\mathrm{I},[a,b]}:= \sigma_{\mathrm{I},\leq b}\sigma_{\mathrm{I},\geq a} =\sigma_{\mathrm{I},\geq a}\sigma_{\mathrm{I},\leq b}\). Apply these functors to \(\mathrm{CC}(R)\) and then take the total complex \(\operatorname{tot}_{\Pi}\) (Definition reference); this leads to the following definition.

Definition (B. Feigin, B. Tsygan; A. Connes). For a \(\Bbbk\)-algebra \(R\) and every \(n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\), define \[\begin{align*} \mathrm{HP}_n(R) &:=\operatorname{H}_n\left(\operatorname{tot}_{\Pi}(\mathrm{CC}(R))\right) &\text{(periodic cyclic homology)},\\ \mathrm{HC}_n(R) &:=\operatorname{H}_n\left( \operatorname{tot}\left(\sigma_{\mathrm{I},\geq0}\mathrm{CC}(R)\right)\right) &\text{(cyclic homology)}. \end{align*}\] Both are functors \(\Bbbk\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Alg}}\to\Bbbk\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\).

Since \(\sigma_{\mathrm{I},\geq0}\mathrm{CC}(R)\) lies in the first quadrant, its total complex involves only the finite direct sums \(\bigoplus_{\substack{p+q=n\\p,q\geq0}}\mathrm{CC}_{p,q}(R)\). The subscript on \(\operatorname{tot}\) is therefore unnecessary. The definition immediately gives \(\mathrm{HC}_{<0}(R)=0\), while \(\mathrm{HC}_0(R)\) is the quotient of \(R\) by \(\operatorname{im}[d_1:R^{\otimes2}\to R]\) and \(\operatorname{im}[\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}-t_0]=0\), namely \(R/[R,R]\). The exercises will give computations in more special cases. The cyclic complex has the periodicity \(\mathrm{CC}(R)=\mathrm{CC}(R)_{\mathrm{I}}[-2]\), which yields an isomorphism \(\mathrm{HP}_n(R)\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}\mathrm{HP}_{n-2}(R)\). For cyclic homology, the corresponding construction is the epimorphism “shift two columns to the left” \[\begin{align*} \sigma_{\mathrm{I},\geq0}\mathrm{CC}(R) &\to\left(\sigma_{\mathrm{I},\geq0}\mathrm{CC}(R)\right)_{\mathrm{I}}[-2]\\ \mathrm{CC}(R)_{p,q} &\to\begin{cases} \mathrm{CC}(R)_{p-2,q}\;\text{(identity)},&p\geq2,\\ 0,&0\leq p<2. \end{cases} \end{align*}\] Its kernel is given by columns \(0\) and \(1\) of \(\mathrm{CC}(R)\), namely the sub-double-complex \(\sigma_{\mathrm{I},[0,1]}\mathrm{CC}(R)\). This defines Connes’s periodicity operator \(S:\mathrm{HC}_n(R)\to\mathrm{HC}_{n-2}(R)\) on cyclic homology.

Theorem (A. Connes). Let \(R\) be a \(\Bbbk\)-algebra. There is a canonical long exact sequence \[\cdots \xrightarrow{S} \mathrm{HC}_{n-1}(R) \xrightarrow{B} \operatorname{HH}_n(R) \xrightarrow{I} \mathrm{HC}_n(R) \xrightarrow{S} \mathrm{HC}_{n-2}(R) \to \cdots,\] where \(S\) is Connes’s periodicity operator and \(I\) is induced by the inclusion \[C_\bullet(R,R)\xrightarrow{\text{column $0$}} \sigma_{\mathrm{I},\geq0}\mathrm{CC}(R).\] The map \(B\) is the corresponding connecting homomorphism.

Proof. The first step is to apply equation to obtain the short exact sequence of double complexes \[\text{Diagram chapter3-unit-039-d009}\] Taking total complexes involves only finite direct sums. Checking degree by degree shows that the result remains a short exact sequence \[\text{Diagram chapter3-unit-039-d010}\] We already know that \(\mathsf{B}'R\) is exact. Applying the long exact sequence of Proposition reference shows that \(C_\bullet(R,R)\to \operatorname{tot}\left(\sigma_{\mathrm{I},[0,1]}\mathrm{CC}(R)\right)\) is a quasi-isomorphism of complexes.

Next consider the short exact sequence mentioned when defining \(S\): \[\text{Diagram chapter3-unit-039-d011}\] After taking total complexes, this remains a short exact sequence. By the preceding step, the degree-\(n\) homology groups of the three total complexes are identified respectively with \(\operatorname{HH}_n(R)\), \(\mathrm{HC}_n(R)\), and \(\mathrm{HC}_{n-2}(R)\).6 This proves the theorem.

Remark. Define the cyclic double complex in the cochain sense, \(\mathrm{CC}'(R)\), by \(\mathrm{CC}'(R)^{p,q}:= \operatorname{Hom}_{\Bbbk}\left(\mathrm{CC}(R)_{p,q},\Bbbk\right)\). In analogy with Definition reference, define \[\begin{align*} \mathrm{HP}^n(R) &:=\operatorname{H}^n\left(\operatorname{tot}_{\oplus}(\mathrm{CC}'(R))\right) &\text{(periodic cyclic cohomology)},\\ \mathrm{HC}^n(R) &:=\operatorname{H}^n\left( \operatorname{tot}\left(\sigma_{\mathrm{I}}^{\geq0}\mathrm{CC}'(R)\right)\right) &\text{(cyclic cohomology)} \end{align*}\] and so forth, where \(\sigma_{\mathrm{I}}^{\geq0}\) still denotes the horizontal brutal-truncation functor.

Write \(R^\vee:=\operatorname{Hom}_{\Bbbk}(R,\Bbbk)\) and make it an \((R,R)\)-bimodule by \[(r\varphi r')(x):=\varphi(r'xr).\] By currying, the \(\Bbbk\)-linear dual of the Hochschild column is identified with \(C^\bullet(R,R^\vee)\); this identification requires no finiteness hypothesis. Consequently, the long exact sequence in Theorem reference has a cohomological version \[\cdots \xrightarrow{S} \mathrm{HC}^{n+1}(R) \xrightarrow{I} \operatorname{HH}^{n+1}(R,R^\vee) \xrightarrow{B} \mathrm{HC}^n(R) \xrightarrow{S} \mathrm{HC}^{n+2}(R) \to \cdots.\] 7 The corresponding Connes periodicity operator \(S\) comes from the monomorphism “shift two columns to the right,” namely \[\sigma_{\mathrm{I}}^{\geq0}\mathrm{CC}'(R) \to\left(\sigma_{\mathrm{I}}^{\geq0}\mathrm{CC}'(R)\right)_{\mathrm{I}}[2].\]

As our toolkit grows, we will return repeatedly to Hochschild homology and cohomology and to cyclic homology and cohomology.

  2. Translator’s note (O014-C045): the source writes \(b_n^*\), which starts at \(\operatorname{Hom}_{R^e}(\mathsf{B}_{n-1}R,M)\); the degree-\(n\) differential comes from \(b_{n+1}:\mathsf{B}_{n+1}R\to\mathsf{B}_nR\).↩︎

However, the \(\Bbbk\)-linear dual of \(C_\bullet(R,R)\) has coefficients in \(R^\vee\), not in the regular bimodule \(R\), unless an additional identification \(R^\vee\simeq R\) is supplied.↩︎

Truncation Functors

At the beginning of this section, let \(\mathcal{A}\) be an additive category.

Definition. For a complex \(X \in \operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A}))\), use the following terms and corresponding full subcategories:

Term bounded bounded below bounded above
Condition \(|n| \gg 0 \implies X^n = 0\) \(n \ll 0 \implies X^n = 0\) \(n \gg 0 \implies X^n = 0\)
Full subcategory \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}^{\ensuremath{\mathrm{b}}}(\mathcal{A})\) \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}^+(\mathcal{A})\) \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}^-(\mathcal{A})\)

More generally, for \(-\infty \leq s \leq t \leq +\infty\), let \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}^{[s,t]}(\mathcal{A})\) denote the full subcategory consisting of complexes satisfying \(n \notin [s, t] \implies X^n = 0\), and define \[\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}^{\geq s}(\mathcal{A}) := \ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}^{[s, +\infty]}(\mathcal{A}), \quad \ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}^{\leq t}(\mathcal{A}) := \ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}^{[-\infty, t]}(\mathcal{A}).\]

All these full subcategories are additive categories. If \(\mathcal{A}\) is an abelian category, then \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}^+(\mathcal{A})\), \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}^-(\mathcal{A})\), and \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}^{\ensuremath{\mathrm{b}}}(\mathcal{A}) = \ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}^+(\mathcal{A}) \cap \ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}^-(\mathcal{A})\) are abelian subcategories.1 The shift functor \([n]\) preserves \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}^+(\mathcal{A})\), \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}^-(\mathcal{A})\), and \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}^{\ensuremath{\mathrm{b}}}(\mathcal{A})\), but maps \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}^{[a,b]}(\mathcal{A})\) to \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}^{[a-n, b-n]}(\mathcal{A})\). Moreover, \(\mathcal{A}\) is naturally identified with \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}^{\geq 0}(\mathcal{A}) \cap \ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}^{\leq 0}(\mathcal{A})\). For every \(\star \in \{+, -, \ensuremath{\mathrm{b}}\}\), the notion of homotopy between morphisms (Definition reference) restricts to \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}^{\star}(\mathcal{A})\). Thus Definition reference has the following variant.

Definition. For \(\star \in \{+, -, \ensuremath{\mathrm{b}}\}\), \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{A})\) has a full additive subcategory \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}^\star(\mathcal{A})\) that is closed under the shift functors.

From now on, we require \(\mathcal{A}\) to be an abelian category. We study how to truncate the part of a complex \(X\) in degrees \(<n\) (or \(>n\)). The naive idea is to replace every term in that part by \(0\). Although simple, this disrupts cohomology, so we introduce a more refined version.

Definition (Truncation functors). Let \(\mathcal{A}\) be an abelian category and let \(n \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\). For a complex \(X\), define \[\text{Diagram chapter3-unit-040-d001}\] The omitted terms are clear, and in the vertical direction only morphisms other than \(\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}\) and \(0\) are marked. We thus obtain morphisms between the complexes listed on the left; in this notation, every \(\operatorname{coim}(d^i)\) is identified with \(\operatorname{im}(d^i)\) through the canonical comparison isomorphism.

It is clear that \(\tau^{\leq n}\), \(\tilde{\tau}^{\leq n}\), \(\tau^{\geq n}\), and \(\tilde{\tau}^{\geq n}\) are all additive functors. We have \(\tau^{\leq n} = [-n] \circ \tau^{\leq 0} \circ [n]\); the same holds for \(\tilde{\tau}^{\leq n}\), \(\tau^{\geq n}\), and \(\tilde{\tau}^{\geq n}\). Moreover, if \(m \leq n\), there are evident epimorphisms \(\tau^{\geq m} X \twoheadrightarrow \tau^{\geq n} X\) and \(\tilde{\tau}^{\geq m} X \twoheadrightarrow \tilde{\tau}^{\geq n} X\), and evident monomorphisms \(\tau^{\leq m} X \hookrightarrow \tau^{\leq n} X\) and \(\tilde{\tau}^{\leq m} X \hookrightarrow \tilde{\tau}^{\leq n} X\).

Lemma. For every \(k \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\), the comparison morphisms \(\tau^{\leq n}X \to \tilde{\tau}^{\leq n}X\) and \(\tilde{\tau}^{\geq n}X \to \tau^{\geq n}X\) in the diagram above induce the following isomorphisms in \(\mathcal{A}\)2 \[\begin{align*} \operatorname{H}^k\left( \tau^{\leq n} X\right) & \ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}\operatorname{H}^k\left( \tilde{\tau}^{\leq n} X\right) \simeq \begin{cases} \operatorname{H}^k(X), & k \leq n \\ 0, & k > n \end{cases}, \\ \operatorname{H}^k\left( \tilde{\tau}^{\geq n} X\right) & \ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}\operatorname{H}^k\left( \tau^{\geq n} X\right) \simeq \begin{cases} \operatorname{H}^k(X), & k \geq n \\ 0, & k < n \end{cases}, \end{align*}\] and the following short exact sequences in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})\): \[\begin{equation*} \begin{gathered} 0 \to \tilde{\tau}^{\leq n-1} X \to \tau^{\leq n} X \to \operatorname{H}^n(X)[-n] \to 0, \\ 0 \to \operatorname{H}^n(X)[-n] \to \tau^{\geq n} X \to \tilde{\tau}^{\geq n+1} X \to 0, \\ 0 \to \tau^{\leq n} X \to X \to \tilde{\tau}^{\geq n+1} X \to 0, \\ 0 \to \tilde{\tau}^{\leq n-1} X \to X \to \tau^{\geq n} X \to 0, \\ 0 \to \tau^{\leq n} X \to \tilde{\tau}^{\leq n} X \to \operatorname{Cone}\left(\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{\operatorname{im}(d_X^n) [-n-1]} \right) \to 0. \end{gathered} \end{equation*}\] Here \(\operatorname{H}^n(X)[-n]\) is understood according to Convention reference. All these morphisms are functorial in \(X\).

Proof. The degree-\(n\) component of the morphism \(\tilde{\tau}^{\leq n-1} X \to \tau^{\leq n} X\) is \(\operatorname{coim}(d^{n-1}) \xrightarrow{\sim} \operatorname{im}(d^{n-1}) \hookrightarrow \operatorname{ker}(d^n)\),3 and every other component is \(\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}\). The degree-\(n\) component of the morphism \(\tau^{\leq n} X \to \operatorname{H}^n(X)[-n]\) is \[\operatorname{ker}(d^n) \twoheadrightarrow \operatorname{ker}(d^n)/\operatorname{im}(d^{n-1}) = \operatorname{H}^n(X).\]

The degree-\(n\) component of the morphism \(\tau^{\geq n} X \to \tilde{\tau}^{\geq n+1} X\) is the epimorphism induced by \(d^n\), \(\operatorname{coker}(d^{n-1}) \twoheadrightarrow \operatorname{im}(d^n)\), and every other component is \(\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}\). The degree-\(n\) component of the morphism \(\operatorname{H}^n(X)[-n] \to \tau^{\geq n} X\) is \[\operatorname{ker}(d^n)/\operatorname{im}(d^{n-1}) \hookrightarrow X^n/\operatorname{im}(d^{n-1}) = \operatorname{coker}(d^{n-1}).\]

All remaining verifications are routine and are left to the reader as exercises.

Thus \(\tau^{\leq n}\) and \(\tilde{\tau}^{\leq n}\) (or \(\tau^{\geq n}\) and \(\tilde{\tau}^{\geq n}\)) do indeed truncate cohomology in degrees \(>n\) (or \(<n\)).

Remark. For a complex \(X \in \operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A}))\), applying the functor \(\sigma\) of Definition–Proposition reference gives \[\sigma X \in \operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A}^{\operatorname{op}})) = \operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A}^{\operatorname{op}})^{\operatorname{op}}).\] Ignoring some \(\pm\) signs that have no effect in this context, this operation amounts to reversing the arrows in the complex and then reversing the degree indices. By the duality between \(\operatorname{ker}\) and \(\operatorname{coker}\), under this operation \(\tau^{\geq n}(X)\) corresponds to \(\tau^{\leq -n}(\sigma X) \in \operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A}^{\operatorname{op}}))\), and so forth. Similarly, because \(\operatorname{im}\) and \(\operatorname{coim}\) are dual to each other, \(\tilde{\tau}^{\geq n}(X) \in \operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A}))\) corresponds to \(\tilde{\tau}^{\leq -n}(\sigma X) \in \operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A}^{\operatorname{op}}))\).

Compared with \(\tilde{\tau}^{\leq n}\) and \(\tilde{\tau}^{\geq n}\), the functors \(\tau^{\leq n}\) and \(\tau^{\geq n}\) have some properties that are easier to use. The first is adjunction.

Proposition. For every \(n \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\), there are the following adjunctions: \[\begin{gather*} \operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})}(X, Y) \simeq \operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}^{\leq n}(\mathcal{A})}\left(X, \tau^{\leq n} Y \right), \quad X \in \operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}^{\leq n}(\mathcal{A})) \\ \operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})}(X, Y) \simeq \operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}^{\geq n}(\mathcal{A})}\left(\tau^{\geq n} X, Y \right), \quad Y \in \operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}^{\geq n}(\mathcal{A})). \end{gather*}\]

Proof. This is clear from the definition of truncation. The reader may write down the corresponding unit and counit morphisms: they are the morphisms shown in Definition reference, or \(\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}\).

Next, \(\tau^{\leq n}\) and \(\tau^{\geq n}\) descend to \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{A})\).

Definition–Proposition. For every \(n \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\), the functor \(\tau^{\leq n}\) (or \(\tau^{\geq n}\)) naturally induces a functor from \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{A})\) to itself, still denoted by \(\tau^{\leq n}\) (or \(\tau^{\geq n}\)).

Proof. Let \(h \in \operatorname{Hom}^{-1}(X, Y)\). For the case of \(\tau^{\leq n}\), define \(\overline{h}^n := h^n \circ \bigl(\operatorname{ker}(d_X^n) \hookrightarrow X^n\bigr)\). Define \(\overline{h} \in \operatorname{Hom}^{-1}\left( \tau^{\leq n} X, \tau^{\leq n} Y \right)\) by the following diagram: \[\text{Diagram chapter3-unit-040-d002}\] It is easy to see that \(\tau^{\leq n}\left( d^{-1} h \right) = d^{-1} \overline{h}\).

For the case of \(\tau^{\geq n}\), instead define \(\underline{h}^{n+1} := \bigl(Y^n \twoheadrightarrow \operatorname{coker}(d_Y^{n-1})\bigr) \circ h^{n+1}\) and use this to define \(\underline{h} \in \operatorname{Hom}^{-1}\left( \tau^{\geq n} X, \tau^{\geq n} Y \right)\); the remainder is similar. The two cases are of course dual.

The following simple but important property follows immediately from Definition reference.

Proposition. For all integers \(a<b\) and \(n\), and \(X \in \operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A}))\), we have4 \[\begin{gather*} \tau^{\leq a} \tau^{\geq b}(X) = 0 = \tau^{\geq b} \tau^{\leq a}(X), \\ \tau^{\leq n }\tau^{\geq n}(X) \simeq \operatorname{H}^n(X)[-n] \simeq \tau^{\geq n} \tau^{\leq n}(X) \quad \text{(canonical isomorphisms).} \end{gather*}\]

  1. Translator’s note (O014-C050): the source states the second assertion without requiring \(\mathcal{A}\) to be abelian, although at this point \(\mathcal{A}\) has only been assumed additive. The assertion is made conditional here.↩︎

  2. Translator’s note (O014-C051): the source refers to “the morphisms above,” which could be read as the transition morphisms for \(m\leq n\) in the immediately preceding paragraph; only the two comparison morphisms displayed here induce these cohomology isomorphisms.↩︎

  3. Translator’s note (O014-C052): the source writes \(\operatorname{im}(d^{n-1})\) directly as the degree-\(n\) term of \(\tilde{\tau}^{\leq n-1}X\); that term is actually \(\operatorname{coim}(d^{n-1})\), canonically identified with its image.↩︎

  4. Translator’s note (O014-C053): the source writes \(X \in \operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{A})\), but the truncation functors and \(\operatorname{H}^n\) in this proposition act on complexes.↩︎

Cohomology of double complexes

This section examines the cohomology of a double complex \(X\) in the horizontal and vertical directions, and its relationship with the cohomology of the total complex. The results will be used to study derived functors of bifunctors; the argument follows [KS06]. Let \(\mathcal{A}\) be an abelian category. As always, when \(\mathcal{A}\) is a \(\Bbbk\)-linear abelian category, all the results have corresponding generalizations. Recall that Definition reference (or the more explicit diagram equation) introduced a pair of invertible additive functors \[\text{Diagram chapter3-unit-041-d001}\] Using them, define for every double complex \(X\) (with \(p,q,n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\) below) \[\begin{align*} \operatorname{H}_{\mathrm{I}}^p(X) & := (\operatorname{H}^p \circ F_{\mathrm{I}})(X) = \text{the complex}\; \left[ \text{Diagram chapter3-unit-041-d002}\right] \quad \text{(see Proposition~\href{#prop:abelian-cat-cplx}{reference})}, \\ \operatorname{H}_{\mathrm{II}}^q(X) & := (\operatorname{H}^q \circ F_{\mathrm{II}})(X) \\ & = \text{the complex}\; \left[ \cdots \xrightarrow{\ensuremath{{}^\vartriangleright d}} \operatorname{H}^q(X^{p, \bullet}, \ensuremath{{}^\vartriangle d}) \xrightarrow{\ensuremath{{}^\vartriangleright d}} \operatorname{H}^q(X^{p+1, \bullet}, \ensuremath{{}^\vartriangle d}) \xrightarrow{\ensuremath{{}^\vartriangleright d}} \cdots \right] , \\ \tau_{\mathrm{I}}^{\leq n} & := (F_{\mathrm{I}})^{-1} \circ \tau^{\leq n} \circ F_{\mathrm{I}}, \\ \tau_{\mathrm{II}}^{\leq n} & := (F_{\mathrm{II}})^{-1} \circ \tau^{\leq n} \circ F_{\mathrm{II}}, \end{align*}\] 1 There are likewise functors \(\tilde{\tau}_{\mathrm{I}}^{\leq n}\), \(\tau_{\mathrm{I}}^{\geq n}\), \(\tilde{\tau}_{\mathrm{I}}^{\geq n}\) and \(\tilde{\tau}_{\mathrm{II}}^{\leq n}\), \(\tau_{\mathrm{II}}^{\geq n}\), \(\tilde{\tau}_{\mathrm{II}}^{\geq n}\). Thus there are still morphisms of functors \[\begin{gather*} \tau_{\mathrm{I}}^{\leq n} \to \tilde{\tau}_{\mathrm{I}}^{\leq n} \to \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}^2(\mathcal{A})} \to \tilde{\tau}_{\mathrm{I}}^{\geq n} \to \tau_{\mathrm{I}}^{\geq n}, \\ \tau_{\mathrm{II}}^{\leq n} \to \tilde{\tau}_{\mathrm{II}}^{\leq n} \to \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}^2(\mathcal{A})} \to \tilde{\tau}_{\mathrm{II}}^{\geq n} \to \tau_{\mathrm{II}}^{\geq n}. \end{gather*}\]

Definition. For a double complex \(X\), write \(\operatorname{Supp}(X) := \left\{ (p,q) \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}^2 : X^{p,q} \neq 0 \right\}\). Let \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}^2_f(\mathcal{A})\) be the full subcategory consisting of those objects \(X\) of \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}^2(\mathcal{A})\) for which the set \(\{(p,q)\in\operatorname{Supp}(X):p+q=n\}\) is finite for every \(n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\).

Example. If \(\operatorname{Supp}(X)\subset\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}_{\geq 0}^2\) (the first quadrant), if \(\operatorname{Supp}(X)\subset\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}_{\leq 0}^2\) (the third quadrant), or if \(\operatorname{Supp}(X)\) is the union of finitely many rows or columns, then \(X\) is an object of \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}^2_f(\mathcal{A})\).

The total complexes \(\operatorname{tot}_{\oplus}(X)\) and \(\operatorname{tot}_{\Pi}(X)\) are defined for every object \(X\) of \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}^2_f(\mathcal{A})\), with no additional assumption on \(\mathcal{A}\). Moreover, \(\operatorname{tot}_{\oplus}(X)=\operatorname{tot}_{\Pi}(X)\) in this case. We therefore obtain an additive functor \(\operatorname{tot}:\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}^2_f(\mathcal{A})\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})\). We now make a simple but necessary observation. Given an object \(X\) of \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}^2_f(\mathcal{A})\) and \(n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\), there is a finite subset \(S\subset\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}^2\) such that \(\operatorname{H}^n(\operatorname{tot}(X))\) is completely determined by the data \(\left(X^{p,q},\ensuremath{{}^\vartriangleright d}^{p,q},\ensuremath{{}^\vartriangle d}^{p,q}\right)_{(p,q)\in S}\).

Lemma. The total-complex functor \(\operatorname{tot}:\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}^2_f(\mathcal{A})\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})\) is exact (Definition reference).

Proof. Let \(X\xrightarrow{f}Y\xrightarrow{g}Z\) be an exact sequence in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}^2_f(\mathcal{A})\). Recalling the relevant definitions, such as Proposition reference, it suffices to show that for every \(n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\) the sequence \[\bigoplus_{p+q=n} X^{p,q} \xrightarrow{\bigoplus_{p+q=n} f^{p,q}} \bigoplus_{p+q=n} Y^{p,q} \xrightarrow{\bigoplus_{p+q=n} g^{p,q}} \bigoplus_{p+q=n} Z^{p,q}\] is exact in \(\mathcal{A}\). Since these direct sums are finite, this reduces to the exactness of \(X^{p,q}\xrightarrow{f^{p,q}}Y^{p,q}\xrightarrow{g^{p,q}}Z^{p,q}\).

Although the next lemma may look complicated, it is merely an exercise in the definitions and applies to every additive category \(\mathcal{A}\).

Lemma. Let \(h\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\) and let \(Y\) be an object of \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})\). Form

  • the object \(Y[-h]\) of \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})\);

  • the object \(Y_{\mathrm{I}}[-h]\) of \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A}))\), whose term in degree \(h\) is \(Y\) and whose other terms are \(0\).

There are then canonical isomorphisms in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})\) \[\begin{gather*} (\operatorname{tot}\circ F_{\mathrm{I}}^{-1}) \operatorname{Cone}\left( \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{Y_{\mathrm{I}}[-h]} \right) \simeq \operatorname{Cone}\left( \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{Y[-h]} \right), \\ (\operatorname{tot}\circ F_{\mathrm{I}}^{-1}) \left( Y_{\mathrm{I}}[-h] \right) \simeq Y[-h]. \end{gather*}\]

Proof. By definition, \(\operatorname{Cone}\left(\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{Y_{\mathrm{I}}[-h]}\right)\) is the object \(Y\xrightarrow{\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_Y}Y\) of \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}^{[h-1,h]}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A}))\), concentrated in degrees \(h-1\) and \(h\). Hence \(Z:=F_{\mathrm{I}}^{-1}\operatorname{Cone}\left(\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{Y_{\mathrm{I}}[-h]}\right)\) is the double complex shown below: \[\text{Diagram chapter3-unit-041-d003}\] All columns corresponding to \(p\notin\{h-1,h\}\) are zero. The definition of the total complex (Definition reference) now gives at once \[\begin{align*} \operatorname{tot}(Z)^n & = Y^{n-h+1} \oplus Y^{n-h} = Y[-h]^{n+1} \oplus Y[-h]^n \\ & = \operatorname{Cone}\left( \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{Y[-h]} \right)^n , \\ d_{\operatorname{tot}(Z)}^n & = \begin{pmatrix} (-1)^{h-1} d_Y^{n-h+1} & 0 \\ \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{Y^{n-h+1}} & (-1)^{h} d_Y^{n-h} \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} - d_{Y[-h]}^{n+1} & 0 \\ \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{Y[-h]^{n+1}} & d_{Y[-h]}^n \end{pmatrix} \\ & = d_{\operatorname{Cone}\left( \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{Y[-h]} \right)}^n . \end{align*}\] The second isomorphism can be checked similarly, but more easily, and is left to the reader.

Lemma. Let \(X\) be an object of \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}^2_f(\mathcal{A})\) and let \(q\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\).

  1. The natural morphism \(\operatorname{tot}\left(\tau_{\mathrm{I}}^{\leq q}X\right)\to \operatorname{tot}\left(\tilde{\tau}_{\mathrm{I}}^{\leq q}X\right)\) is a quasi-isomorphism.

  2. There is a canonical short exact sequence \[0 \to \operatorname{tot}\left( \tilde{\tau}_{\mathrm{I}}^{\leq q-1} (X) \right) \to \operatorname{tot}\left( \tau_{\mathrm{I}}^{\leq q}(X) \right) \to \operatorname{H}_{\mathrm{I}}^q(X)[-q] \to 0.\]

Proof. Apply Lemma reference in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A}))\) to obtain the short exact sequences \[\begin{gather*} 0 \to \tau^{\leq q} F_{\mathrm{I}} (X) \to \tilde{\tau}^{\leq q} F_{\mathrm{I}} (X) \to \operatorname{Cone}\left( \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{\operatorname{im}\left( d^q_{F_{\mathrm{I}} X} \right)_{\mathrm{I}} [-q-1]} \right) \to 0, \\ 0 \to \tilde{\tau}^{\leq q-1} F_{\mathrm{I}}(X) \to \tau^{\leq q} F_{\mathrm{I}}(X) \to \operatorname{H}^q_{\mathrm{I}}(X)_{\mathrm{I}}[-q] \to 0. \end{gather*}\] The notation \((\cdots)_{\mathrm{I}}[\cdots]\) has the meaning specified in Lemma reference. Apply \(\operatorname{tot}\circ F_{\mathrm{I}}^{-1}\) to these short exact sequences. Lemma reference says that \(\operatorname{tot}\) is exact, and \(F_{\mathrm{I}}^{-1}\) is of course exact as well. Substitution from Lemma reference gives short exact sequences in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})\) \[\begin{gather*} 0 \to \operatorname{tot}\left(\tau_{\mathrm{I}}^{\leq q} X\right) \to \operatorname{tot}\left( \tilde{\tau}_{\mathrm{I}}^{\leq q} X \right) \to \operatorname{Cone}\left( \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{\operatorname{im}( d_{F_{\mathrm{I}} X}^q )[-q-1]} \right) \to 0, \\ 0 \to \operatorname{tot}\left( \tilde{\tau}_{\mathrm{I}}^{\leq q-1} X \right) \to \operatorname{tot}\left( \tau_{\mathrm{I}}^{\leq q}X \right) \to \operatorname{H}_{\mathrm{I}}^q(X)[-q] \to 0. \end{gather*}\] The second is precisely (ii). Part (i) follows from the first together with Propositions reference and reference (i).
