For any object \(X\) of \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}^2(\mathcal{A})\), let \(\operatorname{H}_{\mathrm{I}}(X)\) and \(\operatorname{H}_{\mathrm{II}}(X)\) denote the following double complexes (\(p,q\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\)): \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:HIHII}{}\begin{aligned} \left( \operatorname{H}_{\mathrm{I}}(X)^{p, \bullet}, \ensuremath{{}^\vartriangle d}_{\operatorname{H}_{\mathrm{I}}(X)}^{p, \bullet} \right) & := \operatorname{H}_{\mathrm{I}}^p(X), & \ensuremath{{}^\vartriangleright d}_{\operatorname{H}_{\mathrm{I}}(X)}^{\bullet, \bullet} := 0, \\ \left( \operatorname{H}_{\mathrm{II}}(X)^{\bullet, q}, \ensuremath{{}^\vartriangleright d}_{\operatorname{H}_{\mathrm{II}}(X)}^{\bullet, q} \right) & := \operatorname{H}_{\mathrm{II}}^q(X), & \ensuremath{{}^\vartriangle d}_{\operatorname{H}_{\mathrm{II}}(X)}^{\bullet, \bullet} := 0, \end{aligned} \end{equation}\] In other words, \(\operatorname{H}_{\mathrm{I}}(X)\) (respectively \(\operatorname{H}_{\mathrm{II}}(X)\)) is obtained by taking the cohomology of \(X\) in the \(\ensuremath{{}^\vartriangleright d}\)-direction (respectively the \(\ensuremath{{}^\vartriangle d}\)-direction). Both are endofunctors of \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}^2(\mathcal{A})\). We may then define \(\operatorname{H}_{\mathrm{II}}\operatorname{H}_{\mathrm{I}}(X)\) and \(\operatorname{H}_{\mathrm{I}}\operatorname{H}_{\mathrm{II}}(X)\); both satisfy \(\ensuremath{{}^\vartriangleright d}=0=\ensuremath{{}^\vartriangle d}\).

Theorem. Let \(f:X\to Y\) be a morphism in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}^2_f(\mathcal{A})\). If the induced morphism \(\operatorname{H}_{\mathrm{II}}\operatorname{H}_{\mathrm{I}}(X)\to \operatorname{H}_{\mathrm{II}}\operatorname{H}_{\mathrm{I}}(Y)\) is an isomorphism, then \(\operatorname{tot}(f):\operatorname{tot}(X)\to\operatorname{tot}(Y)\) is a quasi-isomorphism.

The same conclusion holds if instead the induced morphism \(\operatorname{H}_{\mathrm{I}}\operatorname{H}_{\mathrm{II}}(X)\to \operatorname{H}_{\mathrm{I}}\operatorname{H}_{\mathrm{II}}(Y)\) is assumed to be an isomorphism.

Proof. The condition is equivalent to saying that the morphism \(\operatorname{H}_{\mathrm{I}}^n(f):\operatorname{H}_{\mathrm{I}}^n(X)\to \operatorname{H}_{\mathrm{I}}^n(Y)\) in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})\) is a quasi-isomorphism for every \(n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\). The first step is to reduce to the case in which \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:double-cplx-tot-aux}{} q \ll 0 \implies \tilde{\tau}_{\mathrm{I}}^{\leq q}(X) = 0 = \tilde{\tau}_{\mathrm{I}}^{\leq q}(Y). \end{equation}\] Indeed, let \(r\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\). Functorial truncation as in Lemma reference shows that the original condition implies that \(\operatorname{H}_{\mathrm{I}}^n(\tau_{\mathrm{I}}^{\geq r}f): \operatorname{H}_{\mathrm{I}}^n(\tau_{\mathrm{I}}^{\geq r}X)\to \operatorname{H}_{\mathrm{I}}^n(\tau_{\mathrm{I}}^{\geq r}Y)\) is also a quasi-isomorphism for every \(n\). For a fixed \(n\), however, the definition of \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}^2_f(\mathcal{A})\) shows that when \(r\ll0\) there is a commutative diagram \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:double-cplx-tot-aux2}{}\text{Diagram chapter3-unit-041-d004} \end{equation}\] The double complexes in the second row satisfy equation. We may therefore replace \(f\) by \(\tau_{\mathrm{I}}^{\geq r}f\) from now on and assume equation. Our goal is to prove that \(\operatorname{H}^n(\operatorname{tot}(f))\) is an isomorphism for the chosen \(n\).

For every \(q\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\), Lemma reference (ii) gives a commutative diagram with exact rows \[\text{Diagram chapter3-unit-041-d005}\] 2 The right-hand vertical arrow is a quasi-isomorphism, and all the vertical arrows come from \(f\). We shall prove that both \(\alpha_q\) and \(\beta_q\) are quasi-isomorphisms. If \(\alpha_{q-1}\) is a quasi-isomorphism, then functoriality of the associated long exact sequences (Proposition reference), together with Proposition reference, implies that \(\beta_q\) is also a quasi-isomorphism. On the other hand, Lemma reference (i) gives the commutative diagram \[\text{Diagram chapter3-unit-041-d006}\] Thus, if \(\beta_q\) is a quasi-isomorphism, then so is \(\alpha_q\). Since \(\alpha_q\) is simply \(0\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}0\) when \(q\ll0\), recursion shows that \(\alpha_q\) and \(\beta_q\) are quasi-isomorphisms for all \(q\).

Recall that \(n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\) has been fixed. By an argument similar to that for equation, when \(q\gg0\) there is a commutative diagram \[\text{Diagram chapter3-unit-041-d007}\] Hence \(\operatorname{H}^n(\operatorname{tot}(f))\) is indeed an isomorphism.

Finally, the same argument applies when \(\operatorname{H}_{\mathrm{I}}\operatorname{H}_{\mathrm{II}}(X)\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}} \operatorname{H}_{\mathrm{I}}\operatorname{H}_{\mathrm{II}}(Y)\). Alternatively, one may use Proposition reference to interchange \(\operatorname{H}_{\mathrm{I}}\) and \(\operatorname{H}_{\mathrm{II}}\).

The proof above is rather involved. Example in § 5.6 will give another proof based on spectral sequences.

Corollary. Let \(X\) be an object of \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}_f^2(\mathcal{A})\). If \(X\) is row-exact, that is, if \(\left(X^{\bullet,q},\ensuremath{{}^\vartriangleright d}\right)\) is exact for every \(q\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\), then \(\operatorname{tot}(X)\) is exact. Likewise, if \(X\) is column-exact, then \(\operatorname{tot}(X)\) is exact.

Proof. If \(X\) is row-exact, then \(\operatorname{H}_{\mathrm{II}}\operatorname{H}_{\mathrm{I}}(X)=0\). Theorem reference therefore implies that \(\operatorname{tot}(X)\to\operatorname{tot}(0)=0\) is a quasi-isomorphism; in other words, \(\operatorname{tot}(X)\) is exact.

The argument in the column-exact case is identical. Alternatively, the two cases can be deduced from one another by Proposition reference.

  1. Translator’s note (O014-C054): in the first two definitions the source prints only the composite functors \(\operatorname{H}^p\circ F_{\mathrm{I}}\) and \(\operatorname{H}^q\circ F_{\mathrm{II}}\) on the right, although the left-hand sides are their values on the double complex \(X\). The argument \(X\) has been restored.↩︎

  2. Translator’s note (O014-C055): the source labels the right-hand vertical arrow only by \(\simeq\). The theorem’s hypothesis says that this morphism is the quasi-isomorphism \(\operatorname{H}_{\mathrm{I}}^q(f)[-q]\), not necessarily an isomorphism of complexes; the morphism has therefore been named and its precise property stated.↩︎

Resolutions

Let \(\mathcal{A}\) be an abelian category, and consider a complex \(X\in\operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A}))\). If \(X^n\) is an injective object (respectively a projective object) of \(\mathcal{A}\) for every \(n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\), we say that \(X\) consists of injective objects (respectively projective objects). Recall the trivial fact that \(0\) is both injective and projective.

Definition. Let \(X\in\operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A}))\).

  • If \(X\to I\) is a quasi-isomorphism in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})\), where \(I\in\operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}^+(\mathcal{A}))\) consists of injective objects, then \(X\to I\) is called an injective resolution of \(X\).

  • If \(P\to X\) is a quasi-isomorphism in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})\), where \(P\in\operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}^-(\mathcal{A}))\) consists of projective objects, then \(P\to X\) is called a projective resolution of \(X\).

Replacing \(\mathcal{A}\) by \(\mathcal{A}^{\operatorname{op}}\), that is, reversing all arrows, shows that injective and projective resolutions are dual notions.

Example. As the most elementary and classical special case, consider an injective resolution \(X\to I\) of \(X\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{A})\). The definition requires only \(I\in\operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}^+(\mathcal{A}))\), but we would like to take \(I\in\operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}^{\geq0}(\mathcal{A}))\). This is possible: use the truncation \[X \to I \to \tau^{\geq 0} I .\] To see that the composite is an injective resolution, two properties must be checked. First, Lemma reference shows that it remains a quasi-isomorphism. Second, \(\tau^{\geq0}I\) still consists of injective objects. Indeed, consider the short exact sequence \(0\to\operatorname{im}(d_I^{n-1})\to I^n\to\operatorname{coker}(d_I^{n-1})\to0\). Since \(d_I^{n-1}=0\) when \(n\ll0\), while \(\operatorname{coker}(d_I^{n-1})\simeq\operatorname{im}(d_I^n)\) when \(n<0\), Lemmas reference and reference show recursively that for \(n\leq0\) \[I^n \simeq \operatorname{im}\left(d_I^{n-1} \right) \oplus \operatorname{coker}\left( d_I^{n-1} \right) , \quad \text{and hence}\; \operatorname{coker}\left(d_I^{n-1} \right) \;\text{is injective};\] the recursion starts at \(n\ll0\), where this formula becomes \(0=0\oplus0\). Taking \(n=0\) shows that \(\operatorname{coker}(d_I^{-1})\) is injective, so \(\tau^{\geq0}I\) consists of injective objects.

In practice one is interested in resolutions that extend sufficiently far. The observation above shows that we may replace \(X\to I\) by \(X\to\tau^{\geq0}I\), so that the injective resolution has the form \[\text{Diagram chapter3-unit-042-d001}\] This can also be flattened and viewed as the exact sequence in \(\mathcal{A}\) \[0 \to X \to I^0 \to I^1 \to \cdots, \quad \text{every $I^n$ is injective, $n \geq 0$}.\]

Similarly, for a projective resolution \(P\to X\), replace it by the composite \(\tau^{\leq0}P\to P\to X\). We may thus assume that it comes from the exact sequence in \(\mathcal{A}\) \[\cdots \to P^{-1} \to P^0 \to X \to 0, \quad \text{every $P^n$ is projective, $n \leq 0$.}\] This is usually written in chain-complex notation as \(\cdots\to P_1\to P_0\to X\to0\), where \(P_n:=P^{-n}\).

The question is whether injective or projective resolutions exist. By duality, it is enough to discuss the construction of injective resolutions first. The simplest case is again \(X\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{A})\). Assume that \(\mathcal{A}\) has enough injectives; see Definition reference. Choose a monomorphism \(X\to I^0\) with \(I^0\) injective. Suppose recursively that an exact sequence \[0 \to X \to I^0 \to \cdots \to I^n, \quad n \geq 0,\] has been constructed with \(I^0,\ldots,I^n\) injective. At the initial step \(n=0\), use the cokernel \(\operatorname{coker}[X\to I^0]\); for \(n\geq1\), use \(\operatorname{coker}[I^{n-1}\to I^n]\). In either case choose an injective object \(I^{n+1}\) and a monomorphism from that cokernel to \(I^{n+1}\). Composition gives \(I^n\to I^{n+1}\) such that \(0\to X\to\cdots\to I^{n+1}\) is still exact. Repeating the construction yields an injective resolution of \(X\). 1 If \(\mathcal{A}\) has enough projectives, the construction of a projective resolution \(\cdots\to P^0\to X\to0\) for \(X\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{A})\) is entirely dual. These constructions extend to complexes, subject to boundedness conditions, as follows.

Theorem. Let \(\mathcal{A}^\flat\) be an additive full subcategory of \(\mathcal{A}\), and suppose that for every object \(A\) of \(\mathcal{A}\) there is a monomorphism \(A\hookrightarrow B\) (respectively an epimorphism \(B\twoheadrightarrow A\)) with \(B\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{A}^\flat)\). Then:

  1. For every object \(X\) of \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}^+(\mathcal{A})\) (respectively \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}^-(\mathcal{A})\)), there is a quasi-isomorphism \[f: X \to I \quad \text{(respectively $f: P \to X$)},\] where \(f\) is a monomorphism (respectively an epimorphism), and \(I\in\operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}^+(\mathcal{A}^\flat))\) (respectively \(P\in\operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}^-(\mathcal{A}^\flat))\)).

  2. More precisely, if \(m\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\) and \(X\in\operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}^{\geq m}(\mathcal{A}))\) (respectively \(X\in\operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}^{\leq m}(\mathcal{A}))\)), then one may take \(I\in\operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}^{\geq m}(\mathcal{A}))\) (respectively \(P\in\operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}^{\leq m}(\mathcal{A}))\)).

Consequently, if \(\mathcal{A}\) has enough injectives (respectively enough projectives), then every such \(X\) has an injective resolution \(X\hookrightarrow I\) (respectively a projective resolution \(P\twoheadrightarrow X\)).

Proof. By duality, we treat only the version in which \(X\) belongs to \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}^+(\mathcal{A})\). For (i), suppose recursively that we have a commutative diagram \[\text{Diagram chapter3-unit-042-d002}\] where the second row is a complex of objects of \(\mathcal{A}^\flat\), \(m\ll0\implies I^m=0\), every \(f^m\) is a monomorphism for \(m\leq n\), and for \(m\leq n-1\) the morphism \(f^m\) induces an isomorphism \(\operatorname{ker}(d_X^m)/\operatorname{im}(d_X^{m-1})\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}} \operatorname{ker}(d_I^m)/\operatorname{im}(d_I^{m-1})\).

We wish to extend the second row to the right. First suppose that \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:resolution-existence-aux0}{} f^n\left( \operatorname{im}\left(d_X^{n-1} \right) \right) = \operatorname{im}\left( d^{n-1}_I \right) \cap f^n\left( \operatorname{ker}\left( d_X^n \right) \right) = \operatorname{im}\left( d^{n-1}_I \right) \cap f^n(X^n) ; \end{equation}\] note that the inclusions \(\cdots\subset\cdots\subset\cdots\) always hold. The pushout construction gives the diagram \[\begin{equation*} \text{Diagram chapter3-unit-042-d003} \end{equation*}\] Since \(f^n\) is a monomorphism and equation implies \[\begin{multline*} \left( f^n\left( \operatorname{ker}\left( d_X^n \right) \right) + \operatorname{im}\left( d_I^{n-1}\right) \right) \cap f^n(X^n) \\ \xlongequal{\text{Theorem \href{#prop:subobject-modularity}{reference}}} f^n\left( \operatorname{ker}\left( d_X^n \right) \right) + \left( \operatorname{im}\left( d_I^{n-1}\right) \cap f^n(X^n) \right) \\ = f^n\left( \operatorname{ker}\left( d_X^n \right) \right) + f^n\left(\operatorname{im}\left(d_X^{n-1} \right) \right) = f^n\left( \operatorname{ker}\left( d_X^n \right) \right), \end{multline*}\] the basic operations discussed in §reference show that \(\alpha\) is also a monomorphism.

Applying Proposition reference twice shows that \(\beta\) and \(\eta\) in the pushout diagram are monomorphisms as well. Choose a monomorphism \(T\hookrightarrow I^{n+1}\) with \(I^{n+1}\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{A}^\flat)\). This gives the composite morphisms \[\begin{gather*} d_I^n: I^n \twoheadrightarrow I^n / \left( f^n \left( \operatorname{ker}\left( d_X^n \right) \right) + \operatorname{im}\left( d_I^{n-1}\right) \right) \xrightarrow{\eta} T \hookrightarrow I^{n+1}, \\ f^{n+1}: X^{n+1} \xrightarrow{\beta} T \hookrightarrow I^{n+1}. \end{gather*}\] Clearly \(d_I^nd_I^{n-1}=0\), \(f^{n+1}\) is a monomorphism, and \(d_I^nf^n=f^{n+1}d_X^n\). On cohomology, the monomorphism \(f^n\) induces \[\begin{align*} \frac{\operatorname{ker}\left( d_X^n \right)}{\operatorname{im}\left( d_X^{n-1} \right)} \longrightarrow \frac{\operatorname{ker}\left( d_I^n \right)}{\operatorname{im}\left( d_I^{n-1} \right)} & = \frac{ f^n\left(\operatorname{ker}d_X^n \right) + \operatorname{im}\left( d_I^{n-1} \right)}{ \operatorname{im}\left(d_I^{n-1}\right) } \\ \text{($\because$ Theorem \href{#prop:Abel-cat-isom-thm}{reference} (iii))} \quad & \simeq \frac{ f^n\left(\operatorname{ker}d_X^n \right) }{ f^n\left(\operatorname{ker}d_X^n \right) \cap \operatorname{im}\left(d_I^{n-1}\right) }; \end{align*}\] by equation and the monicity of \(f^n\), this is plainly an isomorphism. The extension to the right is complete.

We now explain how, in general, to modify \(I^n\) so as to reduce to the case where equation holds. Consider the canonical morphisms \[\text{Diagram chapter3-unit-042-d004}\] Choose \(J\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{A}^\flat)\) and a monomorphism \(j:I^n\oplus(X^n/\operatorname{im}(d_X^{n-1}))\hookrightarrow J\). Define the composite morphisms \[\begin{gather*} f' : X^n \xrightarrow{(f^n, q)} I^n \oplus \left( X^n / \operatorname{im}\left( d_X^{n-1} \right) \right) \xrightarrow{j} J, \\ d': I^{n-1} \xrightarrow{d_I^{n-1}} I^n \xrightarrow{\iota_1} I^n \oplus \left( X^n / \operatorname{im}\left( d_X^{n-1} \right) \right) \xrightarrow{j} J. \end{gather*}\] It is easy to see that \(f'\) is a monomorphism, \(\operatorname{ker}(d')=\operatorname{ker}(d_I^{n-1})\), and \(f'd_X^{n-1}=d'f^{n-1}\).

Moreover, working in \(I^n\oplus(X^n/\operatorname{im}(d_X^{n-1}))\) shows that \[f'(X^n) \cap \operatorname{im}(d') = f'\left( \operatorname{im}\left( d_X^{n-1} \right) \right).\] Thus replacing \(d_I^{n-1}:I^{n-1}\to I^n\) (respectively \(f^n:X^n\to I^n\)) by \(d':I^{n-1}\to J\) (respectively \(f':X^n\to J\)) ensures equation.

Finally consider (ii). In the construction above set \(\cdots=I^{m-2}=I^{m-1}=0\). Equation equation plainly holds for \(n=m-1\) (all its terms are zero), so extending the diagram to the right produces no nonzero terms in degrees below \(m\). This proves the claim.

Corollary. Suppose that \(\mathcal{A}\) has enough injectives (respectively enough projectives). Then \(X\in\operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A}))\) has an injective resolution \(X\to I\) (respectively a projective resolution \(P\to X\)) if and only if \(\operatorname{H}^n(X)=0\) for \(n\ll0\) (respectively \(n\gg0\)).

Proof. Consider the injective case. The quasi-isomorphism condition in the definition of a resolution gives the “only if” direction. Conversely, for \(m\ll0\) the truncation functor gives a quasi-isomorphism \(X\to\tau^{\geq m}X\in\operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}^+(\mathcal{A}))\), reducing the “if” direction to Proposition reference.

The theoretical value of injective and projective resolutions is illustrated by the following fundamental result, which also implies their uniqueness up to homotopy.

Theorem. Fix a quasi-isomorphism \(\alpha:X\to Y\) in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})\).

  • Given a morphism \(\gamma:X\to I\), where \(I\) is an object of \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}^+(\mathcal{A})\) consisting of injective objects, there is a unique morphism \(\beta\) in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{A})\) making the diagram commute: \[\text{Diagram chapter3-unit-042-d005}\]

  • Given a morphism \(\gamma:P\to Y\), where \(P\) is an object of \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}^-(\mathcal{A})\) consisting of projective objects, there is a unique morphism \(\beta\) in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{A})\) making the diagram commute: \[\text{Diagram chapter3-unit-042-d006}\]

The two assertions are of course dual. A concise treatment will be given after Theorem reference. When \(\alpha\) is a monomorphism (respectively an epimorphism), one can moreover choose \(\beta\) so that the first (respectively second) diagram commutes already in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})\); this is the content of Lemma reference below and its dual. In fact, the exercises for this chapter give a direct proof of Theorem reference based on that lemma, with a hint, and the reader is encouraged to try it. Whichever approach one takes, the following property is indispensable.

Lemma. Let \(X\) be an acyclic object of \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})\).

  • If an object \(I\) of \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}^+(\mathcal{A})\) consists of injective objects, then \(\operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{A})}(X,I)=0\).

  • If an object \(P\) of \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}^-(\mathcal{A})\) consists of projective objects, then \(\operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{A})}(P,X)=0\).

Proof. It is enough to treat the case of \(I\). Fix \(\alpha\in\operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})}(X,I)\). We seek morphisms \(h^n:X^n\to I^{n-1}\) such that \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:alpha-homotopy-aux}{} \alpha^n = d_I^{n-1} h^n + h^{n+1} d_X^n , \quad n \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}. \end{equation}\]

Suppose recursively that \(\ldots,h^{n-1},h^n\) have been found so that equation holds for \(\ldots,\alpha^{n-2},\alpha^{n-1}\). This is legitimate because all these \(h\)’s may be taken to be zero when \(n\ll0\). We seek the dashed morphisms \[\text{Diagram chapter3-unit-042-d007}\] 2 that make the whole diagram commute. First, \[\left( \alpha^n - d_I^{n-1} h^n \right) d_X^{n-1} = d_I^{n-1} \alpha^{n-1} - d_I^{n-1} \left( \alpha^{n-1} - d_I^{n-2} h^{n-1} \right) = 0.\] Since \(X\) is acyclic, this induces the displayed morphism \(\beta\). Since \(I^n\) is injective, \(\beta\) extends to a morphism \(h^{n+1}:X^{n+1}\to I^n\), as required.

From the perspective of derived categories, Theorems reference and reference already provide enough information to begin studying derived functors. The kinds of resolutions introduced next are better suited for use with spectral sequences; see §reference. We state the injective versions and first make some preparations.

Lemma. Let \(\alpha:X\to Y\) be a quasi-isomorphism and a monomorphism in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})\). Given a morphism \(\gamma:X\to I\) in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})\), where \(I\in\operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}^+(\mathcal{A}))\) consists of injective objects, there is a morphism \(\beta:Y\to I\) in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})\) such that \(\gamma=\beta\alpha\).

Proof. Using \(\alpha^n\), regard each \(X^n\) as a subobject of \(Y^n\), and omit \(\alpha^n\) from the notation. We construct \(\beta^n\) step by step, taking \(\beta^n=0\) when \(n\ll0\). Suppose suitable morphisms \(\ldots,\beta^{n-2},\beta^{n-1}\) have been found. The desired morphism \(\beta^n:Y^n\to I^n\) can and must be defined on the subobjects \(X^n\) and \(\operatorname{im}(d_Y^{n-1})\) as follows.

  • On \(X^n\), the morphism \(\beta^n\) equals \(\gamma^n\).

  • On \(\operatorname{im}(d_Y^{n-1})\), it is induced by the composite \(Y^{n-1}\xrightarrow{\beta^{n-1}}I^{n-1} \xrightarrow{d_I^{n-1}}I^n\). For this to make sense, we claim that \(d_I^{n-1}\beta^{n-1}\) restricts to zero on \(\operatorname{ker}(d_Y^{n-1})\). Consider the commutative diagram \[\text{Diagram chapter3-unit-042-d008}\] The inductive hypothesis on \(\ldots,\beta^{n-2},\beta^{n-1}\) and the equality \(d_I^{n-1}d_I^{n-2}=0\) show that the composite along the second row is zero. Since \(\gamma\) is a morphism of complexes, the composite \(\operatorname{ker}(d_X^{n-1})\to\cdots\to I^n\) is also zero. We obtain a commutative diagram \[\text{Diagram chapter3-unit-042-d009}\] But the quasi-isomorphism condition says \(\operatorname{H}^{n-1}(X)\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}\operatorname{H}^{n-1}(Y)\), proving the claim.

If we can prove the equality of subobjects \[X^n \cap \operatorname{im}\left(d_Y^{n-1} \right) = \operatorname{im}\left( d_X^{n-1} \right),\] then the pushout diagram of Proposition reference and the universal property of the pushout extend the morphism to \(X^n+\operatorname{im}(d_Y^{n-1})\); injectivity of \(I^n\) then extends it to \(\beta^n:Y^n\to I^n\). The inclusion \(\supset\) is clear.

The point is to show that any morphism \(\phi:T\to Y^n\) in \(\mathcal{A}\) which factors through \(X^n\cap\operatorname{im}(d_Y^{n-1})\) automatically factors through \(\operatorname{im}(d_X^{n-1})\). Such a \(\phi\) induces a morphism \(T\to\operatorname{ker}(d_X^n)=X^n\cap\operatorname{ker}(d_Y^n)\). Composing along the second row of the commutative diagram \[\text{Diagram chapter3-unit-042-d010}\] gives zero. Since \(\operatorname{H}^n(X)\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}\operatorname{H}^n(Y)\), the composite along the first row is zero as well. Thus \(\phi\) factors through \(\operatorname{im}(d_X^{n-1})\).

By construction, \(\beta=(\beta^n)_n\) is a morphism \(Y\to I\), and \(\gamma=\beta\alpha\) follows from the construction too.

Lemma. Let \(A,C\in\operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A}))\). For every \(n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\), define \(B^n:=A^n\oplus C^n\), with its evident morphisms \(A^n\xrightarrow{i^n}B^n\xrightarrow{p^n}C^n\). There is a bijection \[\operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})}(C, A[1]) \xrightarrow{1:1} \left\{\begin{array}{r|l} \text{families of morphisms}\; (d_B^n)_{n \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}} & \text{such that}\; (B^n, d_B^n)_n \;\text{is a complex and} \\ & 0 \to A \xrightarrow{(i^n)_n} B \xrightarrow{(p^n)_n} C \to 0 \;\text{is exact} \end{array}\right\},\] explicitly sending \(\delta:C\to A[1]\) to the differential given in matrix form by \[d_B^n = \begin{pmatrix} d_A^n & \delta^n \\ 0 & d_C^n \end{pmatrix}: B^n \to B^{n+1}.\]

Proof. Once \((B^n,d_B^n)_n\) is known to be a complex and \((i^n)_n\) and \((p^n)_n\) are morphisms of complexes, exactness of \(0\to A\to B\to C\to0\) follows by checking it termwise.

The equalities \(d_B^ni^n=i^{n+1}d_A^n\) and \(d_C^np^n=p^{n+1}d_B^n\) hold for all \(n\) if and only if there are morphisms \(\delta^n:C^n\to A^{n+1}\) for which \(d_B^n\) has the upper-triangular matrix in the statement. It remains to characterize the families \((\delta^n)_n\) for which \(d_B^{n+1}d_B^n=0\). A routine calculation gives the necessary and sufficient condition \(d_A^{n+1}\delta^n+\delta^{n+1}d_C^n=0\), equivalently \(d_{A[1]}^n\delta^n=\delta^{n+1}d_C^n\).

Proposition (Horseshoe Lemma). Let \(0\to A\to B\to C\to0\) be a short exact sequence in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})\), with \(A,B,C\in\operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}^+(\mathcal{A}))\). Choose injective resolutions \(\epsilon:A\to I\) and \(\eta:C\to K\) with the properties stated in Theorem reference. These data extend to a commutative diagram with exact rows in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}^+(\mathcal{A})\) \[\text{Diagram chapter3-unit-042-d011}\] such that \(\kappa:B\to J\) is also an injective resolution and is a monomorphism.

The reader may wish to give a relatively simple proof of the special case \(A,B,C\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{A})\).

Proof. Construct the pushout diagram in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})\) \[\text{Diagram chapter3-unit-042-d012}\] Here we use two facts:

  • a pushout preserves the cokernel \(C\);

  • Proposition reference and monicity of \(A\to B\) imply that \(I\to L\) is also a monomorphism.

Thus the diagram still has exact rows, and \(L\in\operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}^+(\mathcal{A}))\). Another application of Proposition reference, now using the monicity of \(\epsilon\), shows that \(B\to L\) is a monomorphism too.

Because \(I^n\) is injective, Lemma reference implies that \(0\to I^n\to L^n\to C^n\to0\) splits for every \(n\), giving an isomorphism \(\Phi^n:L^n\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}I^n\oplus C^n\). Lemma reference then determines \(\delta:C\to I[1]\) so that \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:horseshoe-aux}{}\text{Diagram chapter3-unit-042-d013} \quad \text{always commutes, where}\; e^n := \begin{pmatrix} d_I^n & \delta^n \\ 0 & d_C^n \end{pmatrix}. \end{equation}\]

Likewise, Lemma reference constructs from any \(\theta:K\to I[1]\) a complex \(J\) such that \[J^n := I^n \oplus K^n, \quad d_J^n := \begin{pmatrix} d_I^n & \theta^n \\ 0 & d_K^n \end{pmatrix}, \quad 0 \to I \to J \to K \to 0 \;\text{is exact}.\] We want to choose \(\theta\) so that the composite \(L^n\xrightarrow[\sim]{\Phi^n}I^n\oplus C^n \xrightarrow{(\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}},\eta^n)}J^n\) defines a morphism \(L\to J\). If it does, then \(L\to J\) is a monomorphism. Let \(\kappa\) be the composite \(B\to L\to J\); it remains a monomorphism, and the diagram in the statement is readily checked to commute. Since \(\epsilon\) and \(\eta\) are quasi-isomorphisms, functoriality of the long exact sequences in Proposition reference, together with the Five Lemma (Proposition reference), shows that \(\kappa\) is a quasi-isomorphism as well, and hence is the desired injective resolution.

How should \(\theta\) be chosen? By equation, the displayed maps \(L^n\to J^n\) form a morphism of complexes if and only if \[\begin{pmatrix} \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{I^{n+1}} & 0 \\ 0 & \eta^{n+1} \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} d_I^n & \delta^n \\ 0 & d_C^n \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} d_I^n & \theta^n \\ 0 & d_K^n \\ \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{I^n} & 0 \\ 0 & \eta^n \end{pmatrix}, \quad n \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}};\] 3 in other words, \(\delta=\theta\eta\). Since the quasi-isomorphism \(\eta\) is a monomorphism in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})\) and \(I[1]\) consists of injective objects, Lemma reference gives such a \(\theta:K\to I[1]\).

To state the next result, for a given complex \(X\) and every \(p\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\) define \[B^p := \operatorname{im}\left( d_X^{p-1} \right), \quad Z^p := \operatorname{ker}\left( d_X^p \right), \quad H^p := Z^p/B^p = \operatorname{H}^p(X) ,\] thereby decomposing \(X\) into the short exact sequences \[0 \to Z^p \to X^p \xrightarrow{d_X^p} B^{p+1} \to 0, \quad 0 \to B^p \to Z^p \to H^p \to 0.\] The Cartan–Eilenberg resolution introduced next may be viewed as a simultaneous resolution of these short exact sequences.

Theorem (H. Cartan, S. Eilenberg). Suppose that \(\mathcal{A}\) has enough injectives. For every object \(X\) of \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}^+(\mathcal{A})\), there is a double complex \(I\) satisfying the following conditions, together with a morphism \(\epsilon:X\to(I^{\bullet,0},\ensuremath{{}^\vartriangleright d}^{\bullet,0})\) in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})\), where \(\ensuremath{{}^\vartriangleright d}\) and \(\ensuremath{{}^\vartriangle d}\) come from the double-complex structure on \(I\) (Definition reference):

  1. For all \((p,q)\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}^2\), one has \(q<0\implies I^{p,q}=0\).

  2. Choose \(N\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\) such that \(n<N\implies X^n=0\). Then, for all \((p,q)\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}^2\), one has \(p<N\implies I^{p,q}=0\).

  3. For every \(p\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\), there is an injective resolution of \(X^p\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{A})\) \[0 \to X^p \xrightarrow{\epsilon^p} I^{p, 0} \xrightarrow{\ensuremath{{}^\vartriangle d}^{p, 0}} I^{p, 1} \xrightarrow{\ensuremath{{}^\vartriangle d}^{p,1}} \cdots .\]

  4. The preceding morphisms induce an injective resolution of \(Z^p:=\operatorname{ker}(d_X^p)\) \[0 \to \operatorname{ker}\left( d_X^p \right) \to \operatorname{ker}\left( \ensuremath{{}^\vartriangleright d}^{p, 0} \right) \to \operatorname{ker}\left( \ensuremath{{}^\vartriangleright d}^{p, 1} \right) \to \cdots .\]

  5. Likewise, \(B^{p+1}:=\operatorname{im}(d_X^p)\) has an injective resolution \[0 \to \operatorname{im}\left( d_X^p \right) \to \operatorname{im}\left( \ensuremath{{}^\vartriangleright d}^{p, 0} \right) \to \operatorname{im}\left( \ensuremath{{}^\vartriangleright d}^{p, 1} \right) \to \cdots .\]

  6. Likewise, \(H^p:=\operatorname{H}^p(X)\) has an injective resolution \[0 \to \operatorname{H}^p\left(X\right) \to \underbracket{\operatorname{H}^p\left( I^{\bullet, 0}, \ensuremath{{}^\vartriangleright d}\right) \to \operatorname{H}^p\left( I^{\bullet, 1}, \ensuremath{{}^\vartriangleright d}\right) \to \cdots}_{= \operatorname{H}^p_{\mathrm{I}}\left( I \right), \;\text{see \S\href{#sec:double-cplx-coh}{reference}} } .\]

Data \((I,\epsilon)\) with these properties are called a Cartan–Eilenberg resolution of \(X\).

Proof. Choose \(N\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\) such that \(n<N\implies X^n=0\). We have already defined the short exact sequences \[\begin{align*} 0 \to Z^N \to X^N \to B^{N+1} \to 0, & & 0 \to B^{N+1} \to Z^{N+1} \to H^{N+1} \to 0, \\ 0 \to Z^{N+1} \to X^{N+1} \to B^{N+2} \to 0, & & 0 \to B^{N+2} \to Z^{N+2} \to H^{N+2} \to 0, \\ \vdots & & \end{align*}\] For every \(H^n\) (respectively \(B^n\)), choose an injective resolution as in Example reference; when \(n<N\) (respectively \(n\leq N\)), take it to be \(0\to0\).

  • Note that \(Z^N=H^N\). Proposition reference extends the injective resolutions of \(Z^N\) and \(B^{N+1}\) simultaneously to an injective resolution \(I^{N,\bullet}\) of \(X^N\), compatible with the first short exact sequence.

  • Next use Proposition reference to extend the injective resolutions of \(B^{N+1}\) and \(H^{N+1}\) simultaneously to an injective resolution of \(Z^{N+1}\), compatible with the second short exact sequence.

  • Repeat the same operation to obtain an injective resolution \(I^{N+1,\bullet}\) of \(X^{N+1}\) together with an injective resolution of \(Z^{N+2}\), compatible with the third and fourth short exact sequences, respectively.

Continuing in this way gives, for every \(n\), an injective resolution \(X^n\to I^{n,0}\to I^{n,1}\to\cdots\); put \(I^{n,\bullet}:=0\) when \(n<N\). The construction also specifies maps \(I^{n,m}\to I^{n+1,m}\) so as to form a double complex \((I,\ensuremath{{}^\vartriangleright d},\ensuremath{{}^\vartriangle d})\). One must check \(\ensuremath{{}^\vartriangleright d}^2=0\), but there is no substantive difficulty. 4

One may also regard \(\epsilon\) as a morphism of double complexes \(X\to I\), provided \(X\) is identified with the double complex concentrated in row \(0\) (the horizontal axis \(q=0\)).

Remark. For all \(p,q\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\), consider the short exact sequences occurring in the Cartan–Eilenberg resolution \[\begin{gather*} 0 \to \operatorname{ker}\left( \ensuremath{{}^\vartriangleright d}^{p,q} \right) \to I^{p,q} \xrightarrow{\ensuremath{{}^\vartriangleright d}^{p,q}} \operatorname{im}\left( \ensuremath{{}^\vartriangleright d}^{p,q} \right) \to 0, \\ 0 \to \operatorname{im}\left( \ensuremath{{}^\vartriangleright d}^{p-1,q} \right) \to \operatorname{ker}\left( \ensuremath{{}^\vartriangleright d}^{p,q} \right) \to \underbracket{\operatorname{H}^p\left( I^{\bullet, q}, \ensuremath{{}^\vartriangleright d}\right)}_{=: \operatorname{H}_{\mathrm{I}}(I)^{p,q}} \to 0, \\ 0 \to \operatorname{im}\left( \ensuremath{{}^\vartriangleright d}^{p-1,q} \right) \to I^{p, q} \to \operatorname{coker}\left( \ensuremath{{}^\vartriangleright d}^{p-1,q} \right) \to 0. \end{gather*}\] Their leftmost terms are all injective, so Lemma reference implies that they split. Recall that every additive functor \(F:\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{B}\) preserves split short exact sequences. For fixed \(q\), the images of the displayed sequences under \(F\) give the corresponding decompositions of the complex \((F(I^{\bullet,q}),F(\ensuremath{{}^\vartriangleright d}))\). In particular, \[F\operatorname{H}^p\left( I^{\bullet, q}, \ensuremath{{}^\vartriangleright d}\right) \simeq \operatorname{H}^p\left( F(I^{\bullet, q}), F(\ensuremath{{}^\vartriangleright d}) \right).\] In other words, \(F\) preserves horizontal cohomology in a Cartan–Eilenberg resolution.

Remark. A Cartan–Eilenberg resolution gives another, indirect way to construct an injective resolution of \(X\in\operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}^+(\mathcal{A}))\). First regard \(X\) as a double complex concentrated in row \(0\). It is easy to see that \(\epsilon:X\to I\) is a morphism in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}^2_f(\mathcal{A})\). In the notation of §reference, first take vertical cohomology \(\operatorname{H}_{\mathrm{II}}\) of \(X\) and \(I\), and then horizontal cohomology \(\operatorname{H}_{\mathrm{I}}\). The induced morphism \(\operatorname{H}_{\mathrm{I}}\operatorname{H}_{\mathrm{II}}(X)\to \operatorname{H}_{\mathrm{I}}\operatorname{H}_{\mathrm{II}}(I)\) is an isomorphism. Hence Theorem reference shows that \[\operatorname{tot}(\epsilon): X = \operatorname{tot}(X) \to \operatorname{tot}(I)\] is a quasi-isomorphism in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}^+(\mathcal{A})\). For every \(n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\), \(\operatorname{tot}^n(I)\) is a finite direct sum of injective objects. We have therefore obtained an injective resolution \(X\to\operatorname{tot}(I)\).

  1. Translator’s note (O014-C056): the source applies the formula \(\operatorname{coker}[I^{n-1}\to I^n]\) also when \(n=0\), introducing an undefined \(I^{-1}\). The initial step has been written with \(\operatorname{coker}[X\to I^0]\), and the printed formula restricted to \(n\geq1\).↩︎

  2. Translator’s note (O014-C057): the lower-left node is printed as \(X\) in the source, although \(d_X^n\), \(\alpha^n\), and \(h^n\) all have domain \(X^n\). The node has been restored to \(X^n\).↩︎

  3. Translator’s note (O014-C058): the lower-right entry of the left-hand inner matrix is printed as \(d_K^n\) in the source. For the composition to be well typed on \(I^n\oplus C^n\) and yield the displayed equality, it has been restored to \(d_C^n\).↩︎

  4. Translator’s note (O014-C059): where the horizontal differential is being constructed, the source repeats the vertical map \(I^{n,m}\to I^{n,m+1}\). The following check of \(\ensuremath{{}^\vartriangleright d}^2=0\) determines the intended direction, \(I^{n,m}\to I^{n+1,m}\), which has been restored.↩︎

Classical derived functors

The purpose of this section is to explain, without using the language of derived categories, how to study right derived functors (respectively left derived functors) for abelian categories with enough injectives (respectively projectives). This already encompasses many cohomology theories commonly encountered in applications. The definitions use the injective resolutions (respectively projective resolutions) introduced in §reference.

Definition. Let \(F:\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{B}\) be an additive functor between abelian categories.

  • Suppose that \(\mathcal{A}\) has enough injectives. For every \(X\in\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}^+(\mathcal{A})\), choose an injective resolution \(X\to I\). For each \(n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\), define the value at \(X\) of the \(n\)-th right derived functor \(\mathrm{R}^nF\) by \[\mathrm{R}^n F(X) := \operatorname{H}^n(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}F(I)).\]

  • Suppose that \(\mathcal{A}\) has enough projectives. For every \(X\in\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}^-(\mathcal{A})\), choose a projective resolution \(P\to X\). For each \(n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\), define the value at \(X\) of the \(n\)-th left derived functor \(\mathrm{L}_nF\) by \[\mathrm{L}_n F(X) := \operatorname{H}^{-n}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}F(P)).\]

These functors all take values in \(\mathcal{B}\). By construction, they come with canonical families of morphisms \(\operatorname{H}^n(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}F(X))\to\mathrm{R}^nF(X)\) and \(\mathrm{L}_nF(X)\to\operatorname{H}^{-n}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}F(X))\).

This formulation leaves several questions. In what sense do these objects depend on the chosen resolutions? And how does one promote a definition on objects to a functor? Right and left derived functors are plainly dual, so we discuss only right derived functors below. We begin with the second question, encapsulating the basic tool in a lemma.

Lemma. Consider the solid part of the following diagram in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}^+(\mathcal{A})\): \[\text{Diagram chapter3-unit-043-d001} \qquad \begin{array}{rl} X \to I: & \text{a quasi-isomorphism}, \\ Y \to J: & \text{an injective resolution}, \\ f: & \text{an arbitrary morphism}. \end{array}\] There is a unique morphism \(\beta\) in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{A})\) for which the diagram commutes in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{A})\).

Proof. Apply Theorem reference to \(X\to I\) and to the composite \(X\xrightarrow{f}Y\to J\).

Reversing arrows gives the projective-resolution version in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}^-(\mathcal{A})\). In fact, the exercises for this chapter show that when \(X\hookrightarrow I\), one may choose \(\beta\) so that the diagram commutes in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})\). Since this section uses only \(\operatorname{H}^n(\beta)\), the version in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{A})\) suffices. Return to derived functors. Let \(f:X\to Y\) be a morphism in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}^+(\mathcal{A})\), and choose injective resolutions \(X\to I\) and \(Y\to J\). Lemma reference shows that, for every \(n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\), the morphism \[\mathrm{R}^n F(f) := \operatorname{H}^n(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}F\beta): \; \operatorname{H}^n(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}F(I)) \to \operatorname{H}^n(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}F(J))\] depends only on \(f\) and the resolutions \(X\to I\), \(Y\to J\). Once the resolutions are fixed, one has \[\begin{gather*} \mathrm{R}^n F(f_1 + f_2) = \mathrm{R}^n F(f_1) + \mathrm{R}^n F(f_2), \\ \mathrm{R}^n F(gf) = \mathrm{R}^n F(g) \; \mathrm{R}^n F(f), \quad \mathrm{R}^n F(\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}) = \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}. \end{gather*}\] Taking \(X=Y\) and \(f=\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_X\) also shows that different injective resolutions give the same \((\mathrm{R}^nF)(X)\) up to a unique isomorphism. Thus, like objects characterized by universal properties throughout category theory, \(\mathrm{R}^nF(X)\) is independent of its auxiliary data (the injective resolution) up to canonical isomorphism, and \(\mathrm{R}^nF:\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}^+(\mathcal{A})\to\mathcal{B}\) is an additive functor. By construction, if \(F,G:\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{B}\) are additive functors, every morphism \(F\to G\) canonically induces \(\mathrm{R}^nF\to\mathrm{R}^nG\) for all \(n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\). Once an injective resolution \(X\to I\) is fixed, the morphism \(\mathrm{R}^nF(X)\to\mathrm{R}^nG(X)\) is concretely determined by \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}F(I)\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}G(I)\). Similarly, it induces \(\mathrm{L}_nF\to\mathrm{L}_nG\).

Convention. Whenever we speak below of right derived functors (respectively left derived functors) of an additive functor \(F:\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{B}\), we implicitly assume that \(\mathcal{A}\) has enough injectives (respectively enough projectives).

Theorem (Long exact sequence of derived functors). Let \(F:\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{B}\) be an additive functor between abelian categories, and consider a short exact sequence \(0\to X\to Y\to Z\to0\) in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})\).

  • If \(X,Y,Z\in\operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}^+(\mathcal{A}))\), there are canonical morphisms \(\delta^n=\delta^n_{X,Y,Z}:\mathrm{R}^nF(Z)\to \mathrm{R}^{n+1}F(X)\) for \(n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\), and an exact sequence \[\cdots \to \mathrm{R}^{n-1} F(Z) \xrightarrow{\delta^{n-1}} \mathrm{R}^n F(X) \to \mathrm{R}^n F(Y) \to \mathrm{R}^n F(Z) \xrightarrow{\delta^n} \mathrm{R}^{n+1} F(X) \to \cdots .\]

  • If \(X,Y,Z\in\operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}^-(\mathcal{A}))\), there are canonical morphisms \(\partial_n=\partial_n^{X,Y,Z}:\mathrm{L}_nF(Z)\to \mathrm{L}_{n-1}F(X)\) for \(n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\), and an exact sequence \[\cdots \to \mathrm{L}_{n+1} F(Z) \xrightarrow{\partial_{n+1}} \mathrm{L}_n F(X) \to \mathrm{L}_n F(Y) \to \mathrm{L}_n F(Z) \xrightarrow{\partial_n} \mathrm{L}_{n-1} F(X) \to \cdots .\]

The connecting morphisms \(\delta^n\) and \(\partial_n\) are functorial as follows. If \[\text{Diagram chapter3-unit-043-d002}\] is a commutative diagram with exact rows, then, in the respective cases, the two diagrams \[\text{Diagram chapter3-unit-043-d003} \quad \text{and} \quad \hypertarget{o014.li2.chapter3.classical-derived-functors.g004}{} \text{Diagram chapter3-unit-043-d004}\] commute for every \(n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\).

Proof. We treat only \(\mathrm{R}^nF\). Apply Proposition reference to \(0\to X\to Y\to Z\to0\) to obtain a commutative diagram with exact rows \[\text{Diagram chapter3-unit-043-d005}\] in which every column is an injective resolution. Lemma reference ensures that \(0\to I^n\to J^n\to K^n\to0\) splits. Its image under \(F\) is therefore still a split short exact sequence, so \(0\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}F(I)\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}F(J)\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}F(K)\to0\) remains exact. Proposition reference now gives the morphisms \(\delta^n\) and the long exact sequence \[\cdots \to \mathrm{R}^{n-1} F(Z) \xrightarrow{\delta^{n-1}} \mathrm{R}^n F(X) \to \mathrm{R}^n F(Y) \to \mathrm{R}^n F(Z) \xrightarrow{\delta^n} \cdots\]

Functoriality of \(\delta^n\) is more involved. We use the abelian category \(\mathcal{A}^{\mathbf{2}}\) of Example reference. First express the given commutative diagram with exact rows as the short exact sequence in \(\mathcal{A}^{\mathbf{2}}\) \[0 \to [X \xrightarrow{\alpha} X'] \to [Y \xrightarrow{\beta} Y'] \to [Z \xrightarrow{\gamma} Z'] \to 0.\] Example reference says that \(\mathcal{A}^{\mathbf{2}}\) has enough injectives. Choose injective resolutions \([X\to X']\hookrightarrow\mathcal{I}\) and \([Z\to Z']\hookrightarrow\mathcal{K}\), and use Proposition reference to extend them to a commutative diagram with exact rows in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A}^{\mathbf{2}})\): \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:long-exact-sequence-primer-aux}{}\text{Diagram chapter3-unit-043-d006} \end{equation}\] such that \([Y\to Y']\to\mathcal{J}\) is also an injective resolution. Write \(\mathcal{J}^n=[J^n\to(J')^n]\), and similarly for the other terms. The evaluation functors \(\mathrm{ev}_0\) and \(\mathrm{ev}_1\) from Example reference show that \(J^n\), \((J')^n\), and the corresponding terms are injective objects of \(\mathcal{A}\), while \(Y\to J\), \(Y'\to J'\), and the corresponding maps are injective resolutions in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})\). Thus compatible injective resolutions have been erected above the original diagram.

Now expand the first row of equation as the following commutative diagram with exact rows in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})\): \[\text{Diagram chapter3-unit-043-d007}\] For every \(n\), both rows split because \(I^n\) and \((I')^n\) are injective. Applying \(F\) degreewise therefore preserves their exactness. Functoriality of \(\delta^n\) now reduces to the corresponding assertion of Proposition reference.

In the classical setting, one is mainly interested in the restrictions of \(\mathrm{R}^nF\) and \(\mathrm{L}_nF\) to \(\mathcal{A}\), still written \(\mathrm{R}^nF(X)\) and \(\mathrm{L}_nF(X)\) for \(X\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{A})\). They are computed by flattening an injective resolution to an exact sequence \(0\to X\to I^0\to I^1\to\cdots\) (or a projective resolution to \(\cdots\to P^1\to P^0\to X\to0\)); see Example reference. Derived functors defined on complexes were called hyper-derived functors in the early literature and are more naturally treated using derived categories or spectral sequences. We therefore focus below on the classical case \(X\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{A})\). The first step is to distill the long exact sequence of Theorem reference into the notion of a \(\delta\)-functor.

Definition. Let \(\mathcal{A}\) and \(\mathcal{B}\) be abelian categories. A cohomological \(\delta\)-functor from \(\mathcal{A}\) to \(\mathcal{B}\) consists of the following data:

  • additive functors \(F^n:\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{B}\) for \(n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}_{\geq0}\);

  • for each short exact sequence \(0\to X\to Y\to Z\to0\) in \(\mathcal{A}\), specified morphisms \(\delta^n:F^nZ\to F^{n+1}X\), called connecting morphisms, for \(n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}_{\geq0}\). They are functorial in morphisms of short exact sequences and yield an exact sequence \[\begin{equation*} \text{Diagram chapter3-unit-043-d008} \end{equation*}\]

A morphism from a cohomological \(\delta\)-functor \((F^n,\delta^n)_{n\geq0}\) to \((G^n,\eta^n)_{n\geq0}\) is a family of morphisms \(\varphi^n:F^n\to G^n\) compatible with the connecting morphisms of short exact sequences. In other words, the diagram \[\text{Diagram chapter3-unit-043-d009}\] 1 must commute for all \(n\geq1\) and every short exact sequence \(0\to X\to Y\to Z\to0\).

Dually, a homological \(\delta\)-functor from \(\mathcal{A}\) to \(\mathcal{B}\) consists of the following data:

  • additive functors \(F_n:\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{B}\) for \(n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}_{\geq0}\);

  • for each short exact sequence \(0\to X\to Y\to Z\to0\) in \(\mathcal{A}\), specified connecting morphisms \(\partial_n:F_nZ\to F_{n-1}X\) for \(n\geq1\), functorial in morphisms of short exact sequences and yielding an exact sequence \[\begin{equation*} \text{Diagram chapter3-unit-043-d010} \end{equation*}\]

Morphisms of homological \(\delta\)-functors are defined analogously, with compatibility with connecting morphisms.

The long exact sequences in the definition automatically imply that \(F^0\) is left exact and \(F_0\) is right exact. We now return to derived functors.

Proposition. Let \(F:\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{B}\) be an additive functor between abelian categories. If \(\mathcal{A}\) has enough injectives, then:

  • \(n<0\implies\mathrm{R}^nF=0\);

  • if \(I\) is injective in \(\mathcal{A}\), then \(n>0\implies\mathrm{R}^nF(I)=0\);

  • \((\mathrm{R}^nF,\delta^n)_{n\geq0}\) is a cohomological \(\delta\)-functor;

  • if \(F\) is left exact, there is a canonical isomorphism \(F\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}\mathrm{R}^0F\).

Dually, if \(\mathcal{A}\) has enough projectives, then:

  • \(n<0\implies\mathrm{L}_nF=0\);

  • if \(P\) is projective in \(\mathcal{A}\), then \(n>0\implies\mathrm{L}_nF(P)=0\);

  • \((\mathrm{L}_nF,\partial_n)_{n\geq0}\) is a homological \(\delta\)-functor;

  • if \(F\) is right exact, there is a canonical isomorphism \(\mathrm{L}_0F\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}F\).

Proof. By duality, it suffices to treat \(\mathrm{R}^nF\). Choose an injective resolution \(0\to X\to I^0\to I^1\to\cdots\) of \(X\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{A})\). Then \[\mathrm{R}^n F(X) = \operatorname{H}^n ( \cdots \to 0 \to 0 \to \underbracket{FI^0}_{\text{term in degree $0$}} \to \underbracket{FI^1}_{\text{term in degree $1$}} \to \cdots ).\] This immediately gives \(\mathrm{R}^nF(X)=0\) when \(n<0\). If \(X=I\) is injective, take the resolution \(0\to I\xrightarrow{\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}}I\to0\to \cdots\), which gives \(\mathrm{R}^nF(I)=0\) for \(n>0\).

In view of this, the assertion about cohomological \(\delta\)-functors is just a restatement of Theorem reference.

Finally suppose that \(F\) is left exact. Since \(X\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}\operatorname{ker}[I^0\to I^1]\) and a left exact functor preserves kernels, \(\mathrm{R}^0F(X)=\operatorname{ker}[FI^0\to FI^1]\) is canonically isomorphic to \(FX\).

In general, one considers right derived functors only for left exact functors, and left derived functors only for right exact functors. Why? An elementary explanation comes from the problem of extending exact sequences. For example, if \(F\) is left exact and \(0\to X\to Y\to Z\to0\) is a short exact sequence in \(\mathcal{A}\), we would like to extend the exact sequence \(0\to FX\to FY\to FZ\) as far as possible to the right. Right derived functors do exactly this. For \(n\geq1\), the functors \(\mathrm{R}^nF\) and \(\mathrm{L}_nF\) are customarily called the higher derived functors of \(F\), with domain understood to be the objects of \(\mathcal{A}\) rather than complexes. As an application of extending an exact sequence, the following corollary says that higher derived functors are precisely the obstructions to exactness.

Corollary. For a left exact (respectively right exact) additive functor \(F:\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{B}\), the following are equivalent.

  1. \(F:\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{B}\) is exact.

  2. For every \(X\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{A})\) and \(n>0\), \(\mathrm{R}^nF(X)=0\) (respectively \(\mathrm{L}_nF(X)=0\)).

  3. For every \(X\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{A})\), \(\mathrm{R}^1F(X)=0\) (respectively \(\mathrm{L}_1F(X)=0\)).

Proof. Consider the left exact case. For (i) \(\implies\) (ii), the complex \(I^0\to I^1\to\cdots\) used to compute the derived functors is exact away from its zeroth term, and therefore so is its image under \(F\). The implication (ii) \(\implies\) (iii) is trivial. For (iii) \(\implies\) (i), use \(\mathrm{R}^0F\simeq F\) and apply the exact sequence \[0 \to FX \to FY \to FZ \to \mathrm{R}^1 F(X)\] to each short exact sequence \(0\to X\to Y\to Z\to0\) in \(\mathcal{A}\).

Convention. Let \(F:\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{B}\) be a left exact (respectively right exact) additive functor. An object \(A\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{A})\) is called \(F\)-acyclic if all its higher right derived functors (respectively left derived functors) under \(F\) vanish. For example, when \(F\) is left exact (respectively right exact), Proposition reference implies that every injective (respectively projective) object is \(F\)-acyclic.

The following classical technique, called dimension shifting, is often used in recursive arguments with derived functors.

Proposition (Dimension shifting). Let \(F:\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{B}\) be a left exact (respectively right exact) additive functor, and suppose that \(\mathcal{A}\) has enough injectives (respectively enough projectives). Let \[0 \to X \to A \to B \to 0, \quad (\text{respectively}\; 0 \to B \to A \to X \to 0 ),\] be a short exact sequence in \(\mathcal{A}\), with \(A\) \(F\)-acyclic. Then for \(n\geq1\) there are natural isomorphisms \[\mathrm{R}^n F(X) \simeq \begin{cases} \mathrm{R}^{n-1} F(B), & n \geq 2, \\ \operatorname{coker}\left[FA \to FB \right], & n = 1, \end{cases}\] respectively \[\mathrm{L}_n F(X) \simeq \begin{cases} \mathrm{L}_{n-1} F(B), & n \geq 2, \\ \operatorname{ker}\left[ FB \to FA \right], & n = 1. \end{cases}\]

Proof. By duality, prove only the assertion about \(\mathrm{R}^nF(X)\). Inspect the corresponding long exact sequence \[\mathrm{R}^{n-1} F(A) \to \mathrm{R}^{n-1} F(B) \to \mathrm{R}^n F(X) \to \underbracket{\mathrm{R}^n F(A)}_{= 0}, \quad n \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}_{\geq 1},\] and use \(\mathrm{R}^0F(A)\simeq FA\) and \(\mathrm{R}^0F(B)=FB\).

The next key result shows that \(F\)-acyclic objects may also be used to compute derived functors.

Corollary. Let \(F:\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{B}\) be left exact (respectively right exact), and suppose there is an exact sequence in \(\mathcal{A}\) \[0 \to X \to A^0 \to A^1 \to \cdots \quad (\text{respectively}\; \cdots \to A_1 \to A_0 \to X \to 0 ),\] where every \(A^n\) (respectively \(A_n\)) is \(F\)-acyclic for \(n\geq0\). In addition, set \(A^{-n}=0\) (respectively \(A_{-n}=0\)) for every \(n\geq1\).2 Then, for every \(n\geq0\), there are natural isomorphisms \[\mathrm{R}^n F(X) \simeq \operatorname{H}^n\left( FA^\bullet \right) \quad \text{or}\quad \mathrm{L}_n F(X) \simeq \operatorname{H}_n\left(FA_\bullet\right).\]

Proof. We prove only the assertion about \(\mathrm{R}^nF(X)\). For \(m\geq1\), put \[B^m := \operatorname{im}\left[ A^{m-1} \to A^m \right] = \operatorname{ker}\left[ A^m \to A^{m+1} \right];\] also put \(B^0:=X\). The original exact sequence then decomposes into \[0 \to B^m \to A^m \to B^{m+1} \to 0, \quad m \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}_{\geq 0}.\] When \(n=0\), the claim reduces to preservation of kernels: \(FX\simeq\operatorname{ker}[FA^0\to FA^1]\). For \(n\geq1\), repeated dimension shifting using Proposition reference gives natural isomorphisms \[\mathrm{R}^n F(X) = \mathrm{R}^n F(B^0) \simeq \cdots \simeq \mathrm{R}^1 F(B^{n-1}) \simeq \operatorname{coker}\left[ FA^{n-1} \to FB^n \right];\] and because \(F\) preserves kernels, the definition of \(B^n\) identifies \(FB^n\) with \(\operatorname{ker}[FA^n\to FA^{n+1}]\). Thus, for \(n\geq1\), \[\mathrm{R}^n F(X) \simeq \frac{\operatorname{ker}\left[ FA^n \to FA^{n+1} \right]}{\operatorname{im}\left[ FA^{n-1} \to FA^n \right]}.\]

The preceding argument relies mainly on the long exact sequence and hardly at all on the definition of derived functors. This suggests characterizing the derived functors of \(F\) among general cohomological (respectively homological) \(\delta\)-functors. The key requirement is that their positive-degree terms be effaceable (respectively co-effaceable).

Definition (A. Grothendieck). Let \(E:\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{B}\) be an additive functor between abelian categories. It is called effaceable (respectively co-effaceable) if for every \(X\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{A})\) there is a monomorphism \(a:X\hookrightarrow Y\) (respectively an epimorphism \(a:Y\twoheadrightarrow X\)) such that \(Ea=0\).

We shall derive the following universal property from effaceability.

Definition. Let \((R^n,\delta^n)_{n\geq0}\) be a cohomological \(\delta\)-functor from \(\mathcal{A}\) to \(\mathcal{B}\). It is called a universal cohomological \(\delta\)-functor if, for every cohomological \(\delta\)-functor \((F^n,\delta_F^n)_{n\geq0}\) from \(\mathcal{A}\) to \(\mathcal{B}\), every morphism \(\varphi^0:R^0\to F^0\) extends uniquely to a morphism \((\varphi^n)_{n\geq0}\) of \(\delta\)-functors.

Dually, let \((L_n,\partial_n)_{n\geq0}\) be a homological \(\delta\)-functor with the following property: for every homological \(\delta\)-functor \((F_n,\partial_n^F)_{n\geq0}\), every morphism \(\varphi_0:F_0\to L_0\) extends uniquely to \((\varphi_n)_{n\geq0}\). Then \((L_n,\partial_n)_{n\geq0}\) is called a universal homological \(\delta\)-functor.

Our goal is to show that, for a left exact (respectively right exact) functor \(F:\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{B}\), a universal cohomological \(\delta\)-functor with \(R^0=F\) (respectively a universal homological \(\delta\)-functor with \(L_0=F\)), if it exists, is unique up to a unique isomorphism.

Lemma. Let \(E:\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{B}\) be effaceable, let \(0\to X\xrightarrow{u}I\xrightarrow{v}B\to0\) be a short exact sequence in \(\mathcal{A}\), and let \(f:X\to Y\) be any morphism. There is a commutative diagram with exact rows \[\begin{equation*} \text{Diagram chapter3-unit-043-d011} \end{equation*}\] such that \(E\iota=0\).

Proof. Choose a monomorphism \(h:Y\hookrightarrow J_0\) such that \(Eh=0\), and form the pushout diagram \[\text{Diagram chapter3-unit-043-d012}\] where \(k\) is a monomorphism by Proposition reference. Set \(\iota=kh:Y\to J\) and \(C:=\operatorname{coker}(\iota)\). This gives the left-hand square of the required diagram; functoriality of cokernels gives the right-hand square.

Proposition. Let \((R^n,\delta^n)_{n\geq0}\) be a cohomological \(\delta\)-functor from \(\mathcal{A}\) to \(\mathcal{B}\). If \(R^n\) is effaceable for every \(n>0\), then \((R^n,\delta^n)_{n\geq0}\) is universal.

Dually, a homological \(\delta\)-functor whose positive-degree parts are co-effaceable is universal.

Proof. We prove only the cohomological version. Let \((F^n,\delta_F^n)_{n\geq0}\) be another cohomological \(\delta\)-functor from \(\mathcal{A}\) to \(\mathcal{B}\), and fix \(\varphi^0:R^0\to F^0\). We construct \(\varphi^n\) recursively for \(n\geq1\). Given \(X\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{A})\), the hypothesis supplies a short exact sequence \[0 \to X \to I \to B \to 0\] such that \(R^n(X\to I)=0\). The corresponding long exact sequences give the solid part of a commutative diagram with exact rows \[\text{Diagram chapter3-unit-043-d013}\] Exactness of the rows and the universal property of the cokernel give a unique dashed arrow \(\varphi_X^n\) making the whole diagram commute. This characterizes \(\varphi_X^n\), although it still appears to depend on the choice of \(X\hookrightarrow I\).

Given any morphism \(f:X\to Y\), we claim there is a commutative diagram with exact rows \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:erasable-univ-delta}{}\text{Diagram chapter3-unit-043-d014} \end{equation}\] such that both \(R^n(X\to I)\) and \(R^n(Y\to J)\) are zero. Indeed, first choose \(X\hookrightarrow I\), then apply Lemma reference. Substituting this into the constructions of \(\varphi_X^n\) and \(\varphi_Y^n\) yields \[\text{Diagram chapter3-unit-043-d015}\] Every face except the right one commutes by construction, definition, or the induction hypothesis. Since \(R^{n-1}B\to R^nX\) is an epimorphism, the usual argument shows that the right face commutes too.

This simultaneously proves that \(\varphi_X^n\) is independent of the choice of \(X\hookrightarrow I\) (take \(f=\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_X\) and observe from the proof of Lemma reference that any two maps \(X\hookrightarrow I_i\) can be sent by pushouts into a common \(X\hookrightarrow J\)) and that it is functorial in \(X\) (take arbitrary \(f\)). This recursively completes the construction of \(\varphi^n\).

It remains to show that \((\varphi^n)_{n\geq0}\) is compatible with the connecting morphisms. Given a short exact sequence \(0\to X\to Y\to Z\to0\), use Lemma reference to choose a commutative diagram with exact rows \[\text{Diagram chapter3-unit-043-d016}\] such that \(R^n(X\to I)=0\). For each \(n\geq1\), form the diagram \[\text{Diagram chapter3-unit-043-d017}\] 3 By the preceding commutative diagram and the axioms of a cohomological \(\delta\)-functor, the composites along the two rows are the connecting morphisms \(F^{n-1}Z\to F^nX\) and \(R^{n-1}Z\to R^nX\) whose compatibility is at issue. The left square commutes by functoriality of \(\varphi^{n-1}\), and the right square by the construction of \(\varphi_X^n\).

Corollary (Characterization of derived functors). Let \(F:\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{B}\) be left exact and suppose that \(\mathcal{A}\) has enough injectives. Then \((\mathrm{R}^nF,\delta^n)_{n\geq0}\) is the universal cohomological \(\delta\)-functor satisfying \(\mathrm{R}^0F\simeq F\).

Dually, if \(F\) is right exact and \(\mathcal{A}\) has enough projectives, then \((\mathrm{L}_nF,\partial_n)_{n\geq0}\) is the universal homological \(\delta\)-functor satisfying \(\mathrm{L}_0F\simeq F\).

Proof. It is enough to discuss the left exact case. For \(n>0\), the functor \(\mathrm{R}^nF\) is effaceable: every \(X\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{A})\) embeds into an injective object \(I\), and Proposition reference gives \(\mathrm{R}^nF(I)=0\). The same proposition gives \(\mathrm{R}^0F\simeq F\). Apply Proposition reference.

For a short exact sequence \(0\to X\to Y\to Z\to0\), the connecting morphisms \(\delta^{n-1}\) and \(\eta^{n-1}\) have domains \(F^{n-1}(Z)\) and \(G^{n-1}(Z)\), respectively, and codomains \(F^n(X)\) and \(G^n(X)\). Both left-hand objects have therefore been restored to \(Z\).↩︎

If it were applied also at \(n=0\), it would force \(A^0=0\) (respectively \(A_0=0\)), contradicting the resolution term just introduced. The intended range \(n\geq1\) has been made explicit.↩︎

Since their domains are \(F^{n-1}B\) and \(R^{n-1}B\), and their codomains are \(F^nX\) and \(R^nX\), the well-typed indices are \(n-1\); the labels have been restored to \(\delta_F^{n-1}\) and \(\delta^{n-1}\).↩︎

Example: \(\lim\nolimits^1\)

Our first example of derived functors comes from a common class of inverse limits. Regard \(\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}_{\geq0}\) as a category under its usual total order; then \(\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}_{\geq0}^{\operatorname{op}}\) may be displayed as \(\cdots\to2\to1\to0\). For any category \(\mathcal{A}\), consider the functor category \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:InvSys}{} \index[sym1]{InvSys@$\ensuremath{\mathsf{InvSys}}$} \ensuremath{\mathsf{InvSys}}(\mathcal{A}) := \mathcal{A}^{\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}_{\geq 0}^{\operatorname{op}}}. \end{equation}\] Its objects may be identified with data \((A_n,f_n)_{n\geq0}\), where \(A_n\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{A})\) and \(f_n\in\operatorname{Hom}(A_{n+1},A_n)\). Such data are also called inverse systems in \(\mathcal{A}\). Using derived functors, this section studies their inverse limits when \(\mathcal{A}\) is abelian.

Convention. An abelian category \(\mathcal{A}\) is said to have exact countable products (respectively exact countable coproducts) if it has countable products (respectively countable coproducts, or direct sums) and the product functor \(\prod:\mathcal{A}^{\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}_{\geq0}}\to\mathcal{A}\) (respectively the direct-sum functor \(\oplus:\mathcal{A}^{\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}_{\geq0}}\to\mathcal{A}\)) is exact.

The product functor is always left exact. Thus, assuming countable products exist, its exactness is equivalent to preservation of epimorphisms: for every family of epimorphisms \((g_n:A_n\to B_n)_{n\geq0}\), the corresponding map \(\prod_{n\geq0}g_n:\prod_{n\geq0}A_n\to\prod_{n\geq0}B_n\) must also be an epimorphism. The assertion for countable coproducts is dual.

Hypothesis. Throughout this section, the abelian category \(\mathcal{A}\) is assumed to have exact countable products.

The category \(R\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\) of modules over any ring \(R\) has this property.

Definition. Given an object \(A=(A_n,f_n)_n\) of \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{InvSys}}(\mathcal{A})\), define the shift morphism \(T_A:\prod_{n\geq0}A_n\to\prod_{n\geq0}A_n\) as follows. When \(\mathcal{A}=\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ab}}\), \(T_A((a_n)_{n\geq0}):=(f_n(a_{n+1}))_{n\geq0}\); the general definition is analogous. Define further the canonical morphism \[\Delta_A := T_A - \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}: \prod_{n \geq 0} A_n \to \prod_{n \geq 0} A_n.\] As \(A\) varies, these maps give endomorphisms \(T\) and \(\Delta=T-\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}\) of the product functor \(\prod_{n\geq0}\).

Notice that this definition requires only that \(\mathcal{A}\) be an \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ab}}\)-category with countable products. Recall that inverse limits are generally constructed from equalizers and products. Here \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{InvSys}}(\mathcal{A})\) is naturally an abelian category (Proposition reference), so the construction reduces to \(\varprojlim A=\operatorname{ker}[\Delta_A:\prod_nA_n\to\prod_nA_n]\). Moreover, \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{InvSys}}(\mathcal{A})\) also has exact countable products, since limits in a functor category are constructed pointwise; see §reference.

Lemma. The construction above gives a left exact additive functor \(\varprojlim:\ensuremath{\mathsf{InvSys}}(\mathcal{A})\to\mathcal{A}\). On the other hand, the product functor \(\prod_{n\geq0}:\ensuremath{\mathsf{InvSys}}(\mathcal{A})\to\mathcal{A}\) is exact.

Proof. Both functors are plainly additive, and left exactness follows from Example reference. By hypothesis, the functor \(\prod_{n\geq0}:(A_n,f_n)_n\mapsto\prod_nA_n\) also preserves epimorphisms, since it does so pointwise. Remark reference therefore shows that it is exact.

Definition. Define additive functors \(\lim^n:\ensuremath{\mathsf{InvSys}}(\mathcal{A})\to\mathcal{A}\) by \[\begin{align*} \lim\nolimits^0 & := \varprojlim = \operatorname{ker}\Delta: \; A \mapsto \operatorname{ker}\Delta_A, \\ \lim\nolimits^1 & := \operatorname{coker}\Delta: \; A \mapsto \operatorname{coker}\Delta_A , \\ \lim\nolimits^n & := 0, \quad n \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}_{\geq 2}. \end{align*}\]

Let \(0\to X\to Y\to Z\to0\) be a short exact sequence in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{InvSys}}(\mathcal{A})\); equivalently, it is exact pointwise. Applying the exact functor \(\prod_{n\geq0}\) and its endomorphism \(\Delta\) gives the commutative diagram with exact rows \[\text{Diagram chapter3-unit-044-d001}\] The Snake Lemma (Theorem reference) gives the long exact sequence \[0 \to \lim\nolimits^0 X \to \lim\nolimits^0 Y \to \lim\nolimits^0 Z \xrightarrow[\text{connecting morphism}]{\delta^0} \lim\nolimits^1 X \to \lim\nolimits^1 Y \to \lim\nolimits^1 Z \to 0 ;\] it is functorial in short exact sequences. For \(n>0\), set \(\delta^n:=0\). We summarize this as follows.

Lemma. The data \((\lim^n,\delta^n)_{n\geq0}\) form a cohomological \(\delta\)-functor from \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{InvSys}}(\mathcal{A})\) to \(\mathcal{A}\) (Definition reference), with \(\lim^0=\varprojlim\).

We now turn to the right derived functors of \(\varprojlim\). If \(\mathcal{A}\) has enough injectives, then so does \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{InvSys}}(\mathcal{A})\). Indeed, the exercises in already discuss the general functor category \(\mathcal{A}^{\mathcal{C}}\); here \(\mathcal{C}=\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}_{\geq0}^{\operatorname{op}}\). We give a direct proof of the following slightly more precise result.

[Translator’s clarification: the following results are under the standing assumption that \(\mathcal{A}\) has enough injective objects.]

Lemma. Under Hypothesis reference, define the additive full subcategory \(\mathcal{R}\) of \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{InvSys}}(\mathcal{A})\) by \[\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{R}) = \left\{\begin{array}{l|l} R = (R_k, r_k)_{k \geq 0} & R \;\text{is injective}, \; \Delta_R \; \text{is an epimorphism}, \\ \; \in \operatorname{Ob}\left( \ensuremath{\mathsf{InvSys}}(\mathcal{A}) \right) & \forall k, \; R_k \;\text{is injective in $\mathcal{A}$} \end{array}\right\}.\] For every \(A\in\operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{InvSys}}(\mathcal{A}))\), there are an object \(R\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{R})\) and a monomorphism \(A\hookrightarrow R\).

Proof. For every \(m\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}_{\geq0}\), define a functor \(\mathcal{R}_m:\mathcal{A}\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{InvSys}}(\mathcal{A})\) by sending an object \(X\) to \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:Rm-construction}{}\text{Diagram chapter3-unit-044-d002} \end{equation}\] This is plainly right adjoint to \(\mathrm{ev}_m:(A_n,f_n)_{n\geq0}\mapsto A_m\), and hence preserves injective objects (Proposition reference). It is also straightforward to check that \(\Delta_{\mathcal{R}_mX}\) is an epimorphism; one can write down a right inverse explicitly.

Given \(A=(A_n,f_n)_{n\geq0}\), choose for each \(m\) an injective object \(I_m\) of \(\mathcal{A}\) and a monomorphism \(A_m\hookrightarrow I_m\). Then \(A\hookrightarrow\prod_{m\geq0}\mathcal{R}_m(I_m)=:R\). By Lemma reference, the object on the right is still injective; in fact, by construction every \(R_k\) is injective in \(\mathcal{A}\). Since \(\prod_m\) is exact, \(\Delta_R=\prod_m\Delta_{\mathcal{R}_m(I_m)}\) remains an epimorphism. Thus \(R\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{R})\).

We may therefore discuss \(\mathrm{R}^n\varprojlim\) for \(n\geq0\). Recall that the right derived functors of \(\varprojlim\) are characterized as a universal cohomological \(\delta\)-functor (Corollary reference).

Theorem (S. Eilenberg). Under Hypothesis reference, \(\lim\nolimits^n\) is effaceable in the sense of Definition reference for every \(n>0\). Consequently there is a canonical isomorphism \(\mathrm{R}^1\varprojlim\simeq\lim^1\), while \(\mathrm{R}^n\varprojlim=0\) for \(n\notin\{0,1\}\).

Proof. Lemma reference shows that \(\lim^1\) is effaceable. Hence \((\lim^n)_{n\geq0}\) is a universal \(\delta\)-functor by Proposition reference.

Having identified \(\lim^1\) as the obstruction to exactness of \(\varprojlim\), we now study conditions that ensure \(\lim^1=0\).

Example. If an object \(A\) of \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{InvSys}}(\mathcal{A})\) satisfies \(\lim^1A=0\), then \(\lim^1Q=0\) for every quotient object \(Q\) of \(A\). Indeed, the long exact sequence induced by \(0\to K\to A\to Q\to0\) ends with \(\lim^1A\to\lim^1Q\to0\).

Example. If every \(f_n:A_{n+1}\to A_n\) has a section (a right inverse) \(s_n\), then \(\Delta_A\) also has a section \(\Sigma_A:\prod_nA_n\to\prod_nA_n\), and hence \(\Delta_A\) is an epimorphism. In element notation, one may recursively define \(\Sigma_A((b_n)_n)=(a_n)_n\) by \(a_0=0\) and \(a_{n+1}:=s_n(a_n+b_n)\). The general case is analogous.

Definition (Mittag-Leffler condition). Suppose that every morphism in a category \(\mathcal{C}\) has an image (Definition reference), and let \(X=(X_k,f_k)_{k\geq0}\) be an object of \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{InvSys}}(\mathcal{C})\). For \(b\geq a\), let \(f_a^b:X_b\to X_a\) be the composite \(f_a\cdots f_{b-1}\), with \(f_a^a=\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}\). The inverse system \(X\) is called Mittag-Leffler if \[\forall k \geq 0, \; \exists N \geq k, \quad n \geq N \implies \operatorname{im}f^n_k = \operatorname{im}f^N_k.\]

For example, if every \(f_k\) is an epimorphism, then \((X_k,f_k)_{k\geq0}\) is automatically Mittag-Leffler. For a Mittag-Leffler system \((X_k,f_k)_{k\geq0}\), each \(X_k\) has a well-defined subobject \(X_k^\flat:=\operatorname{im}f_k^N\) for \(N\gg k\). It is easy to see that every morphism \[\cdots \to X^\flat_2 \xrightarrow{f^\flat_1} X^\flat_1 \xrightarrow{f^\flat_0} X^\flat_0\] in the resulting inverse system, where \(f_k^\flat:=f_k|_{X_{k+1}^\flat}\), is an epimorphism.

Lemma. Let \(\mathcal{C}\) be \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Set}}\) or \(R\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\) for an arbitrary ring \(R\), and suppose that an object \((X_n,f_n)_{n\geq0}\) of \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{InvSys}}(\mathcal{C})\) is Mittag-Leffler.

  1. The inclusions \(X_n^\flat\hookrightarrow X_n\) induce a canonical isomorphism \(\varprojlim_nX_n^\flat\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}\varprojlim_nX_n\).

  2. If \(\mathcal{C}=\ensuremath{\mathsf{Set}}\) and every \(X_n\) is nonempty, then \(\varprojlim_nX_n\neq\emptyset\).

Proof. For (i), write down the explicit construction of the inverse limit in these categories: \[\varprojlim_n X_n = \left\{ (x_n)_{n \geq 0} \in \prod_{n \geq 0} X_n : \forall n \geq 0,\; f_n(x_{n+1}) = x_n \right\};\] every \(x_n\) in this expression automatically belongs to \(\bigcap_{N\geq n}\operatorname{im}(f_n^N)\), which immediately gives \(\varprojlim_nX_n=\varprojlim_nX_n^\flat\).

For (ii), the definition shows that every \(X_n^\flat\) is nonempty. By (i), the problem reduces to the case where every \(f_n\) is surjective, when the claim is clear.

Proposition. Let \(R\) be a ring and \(\mathcal{A}:=R\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\). If an object \(A=(A_n,f_n)_{n\geq0}\) of \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{InvSys}}(\mathcal{A})\) is Mittag-Leffler, then \(\lim^1A=0\). Equivalently, for every short exact sequence \(0\to A\to B\to C\to0\) in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{InvSys}}(\mathcal{A})\), the sequence \(0\to\varprojlim A\to\varprojlim B\to\varprojlim C\to0\) is exact.

Proof. First prove the equivalence of the two assertions. Let \(A\in\ensuremath{\mathsf{InvSys}}(\mathcal{A})\). If \(\lim^1A=0\), exactness of \(0\to\varprojlim A\to\varprojlim B\to\varprojlim C\to0\) follows immediately from the long exact sequence. Conversely, suppose this sequence is always exact. Choose a monomorphism \(A\hookrightarrow B\) with \(B\) injective in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{InvSys}}(\mathcal{A})\). Dimension shifting (Proposition reference) gives \(\mathrm{R}^1\varprojlim A=0\), and Theorem reference then gives \(\lim^1A=0\).

Now prove the main assertion. Suppose that \(A\) is Mittag-Leffler in the short exact sequence \(0\to\underbracket{(A_n,f_n)_n}_{=A}\xrightarrow{\varphi} \underbracket{(B_n,g_n)_n}_{=B}\xrightarrow{\psi} \underbracket{(C_n,h_n)_n}_{=C}\to0\). 1 We must show that \(\varprojlim\psi\) is an epimorphism. By Lemma reference (ii), it is enough to show, for every \(c=(c_n)_{n\geq0}\in\varprojlim C\), that the inverse system of nonempty sets \[\cdots \to \psi_2^{-1}(c_2) \xrightarrow{g_1} \psi_1^{-1}(c_1) \xrightarrow{g_0} \psi_0^{-1}(c_0)\] is Mittag-Leffler, since this makes \((\varprojlim\psi)^{-1}(c)\) nonempty.

Given \(k\geq0\), choose \(N\geq k\) large enough that \(\operatorname{im}f_k^n=\operatorname{im}f_k^N\) for all \(n\geq N\). Fix \(b_N\in\psi_N^{-1}(c_N)\). To verify the Mittag-Leffler condition, we show that for every \(n\geq N\) there is a \(b_n\in\psi_n^{-1}(c_n)\) such that \(g_k^n(b_n)=g_k^N(b_N)\).

Choose any \(b_n'\in\psi_n^{-1}(c_n)\). Then \(\psi_N(g_N^n(b_n'))=c_N=\psi_N(b_N)\), so there is an \(a_N\) such that \(g_N^n(b_n')-b_N=\varphi_N(a_N)\). Choose \(a_n\) with \(f_k^n(a_n)=f_k^N(a_N)\). Then \(b_n:=b_n'-\varphi_n(a_n)\) has the required properties.

For a general abelian category \(\mathcal{A}\) satisfying Hypothesis reference, there are counterexamples in which the Mittag-Leffler condition does not imply \(\lim^1=0\); see [Roo06] for a detailed discussion. The following elementary exercise will be used in §reference.

Corollary. Suppose that \(\mathcal{A}\) satisfies Hypothesis reference, and let \(A\to B\to C\to D\) be an exact sequence in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{InvSys}}(\mathcal{A})\). If \(\lim^1A=0\), then \[\varprojlim B \to \varprojlim C \to \varprojlim D\] is exact in \(\mathcal{A}\).

Proof. Put \(H:=\operatorname{ker}[C\to D]\) and \(X:=\operatorname{im}[A\to B]\). Since \(\varprojlim\) is left exact, there is a canonical isomorphism \[\operatorname{ker}\left[ \varprojlim C \to \varprojlim D\right] \simeq \varprojlim H .\] The morphism \(B\to C\) factors as \(B\twoheadrightarrow H\hookrightarrow C\), so it remains to prove that \(\varprojlim B\to\varprojlim H\) is an epimorphism. Example reference gives \(\lim^1X=0\). Applying \(\varprojlim\) to \(0\to X\to B\to H\to0\) then shows that \(\varprojlim B\to\varprojlim H\) is an epimorphism.

  1. Translator’s note (O014-C063): under the brace for \(C\), the source writes the inverse system as \((C_n,h_n)\) without its indexing subscript. Since \(C\) is an object of \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{InvSys}}(\mathcal{A})\), the notation has been restored to \((C_n,h_n)_n\).↩︎

Example: \(\operatorname{Ext}\) and \(\operatorname{Tor}\)

We shall study the derived functors of \(\operatorname{Hom}\) and \(\otimes\). It is useful to introduce a few auxiliary concepts first.

Definition. Let \(\mathcal{A}_1\), \(\mathcal{A}_2\), and \(\mathcal{B}\) be abelian categories, and let the bifunctor \(F:\mathcal{A}_1\times\mathcal{A}_2\to\mathcal{B}\) (Convention reference) be left exact in both variables. If, for every injective object \(I_i\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{A}_i)\) (\(i=1,2\)), both functors \[F(I_1,\cdot):\mathcal{A}_2\to\mathcal{B}\quad\text{and}\quad F(\cdot,I_2):\mathcal{A}_1\to\mathcal{B}\] are exact, then \(F\) is called balanced.

Dually, if \(F\) is right exact in both variables, and if for every projective object \(P_i\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{A}_i)\) the functors \(F(P_1,\cdot)\) and \(F(\cdot,P_2)\) are both exact, then \(F\) is again called balanced.

By duality, the following theorem is stated only for bifunctors that are left exact in both variables.

Theorem. Let \(\mathcal{A}_1\), \(\mathcal{A}_2\), and \(\mathcal{B}\) be abelian categories, and suppose that \(\mathcal{A}_1\) and \(\mathcal{A}_2\) have enough injective objects. Let the bifunctor \(F:\mathcal{A}_1\times\mathcal{A}_2\to\mathcal{B}\) be left exact in both variables. We may therefore take right derived functors in either variable. For fixed \(X_i\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{A}_i)\), \(i=1,2\), write \[\mathrm{R}_{\mathrm{I}}^n F(\cdot,X_2):\mathcal{A}_1\to\mathcal{B},\qquad \mathrm{R}_{\mathrm{II}}^n F(X_1,\cdot):\mathcal{A}_2\to\mathcal{B}.\] If \(F\) is balanced, then there is a canonical isomorphism of bifunctors \[\mathrm{R}_{\mathrm{I}}^nF(X_1,X_2)\simeq \mathrm{R}_{\mathrm{II}}^nF(X_1,X_2).\]

Proof. The following argument relies on the theory of double complexes; see §reference and §reference. For \(i=1,2\), choose an injective resolution \(0\to X_i\to I_i^0\to I_i^1\to\cdots\); define \(I_i^n:=0\) for \(n<0\). This defines the double complex \(F(I_1^\bullet,I_2^\bullet)\).

On the other hand, form the complexes \(F(X_1,I_2^\bullet)\) and \(F(I_1^\bullet,X_2)\). Regard them as double complexes concentrated, respectively, on the vertical axis \((0,\bullet)\) and the horizontal axis \((\bullet,0)\). Since \(X_i\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}\operatorname{ker}[I_i^0\to I_i^1]\hookrightarrow I_i^0\), there are morphisms in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}^2_f(\mathcal{B})\) \[F(X_1,I_2^\bullet)\xrightarrow{\lambda} F(I_1^\bullet,I_2^\bullet)\xleftarrow{\rho} F(I_1^\bullet,X_2).\] We shall show that \(\operatorname{tot}(\lambda)\) and \(\operatorname{tot}(\rho)\) are quasi-isomorphisms.

First consider \(\lambda\). Take horizontal cohomology \(\operatorname{H}_{\mathrm{I}}\) on both sides; this leaves \(F(X_1,I_2^\bullet)\), which lies on the vertical axis, unchanged.
