Since \(F(\cdot,I_2^q)\) is exact for every \(q\), we obtain \[\left(\operatorname{H}_{\mathrm{I}}F(I_1^\bullet,I_2^\bullet)\right)^{p,q} =\begin{cases} 0,&p\neq0,\\ \operatorname{ker}\left[F(I_1^0,I_2^q)\to F(I_1^1,I_2^q)\right] =F(X_1,I_2^q),&p=0. \end{cases}\] Thus \(\operatorname{H}_{\mathrm{I}}(\lambda)\) is an isomorphism from \(\operatorname{H}_{\mathrm{I}}F(X_1,I_2^\bullet)\) to \(\operatorname{H}_{\mathrm{I}}F(I_1^\bullet,I_2^\bullet)\), so \(\operatorname{H}_{\mathrm{II}}\operatorname{H}_{\mathrm{I}}(\lambda)\) is also an isomorphism. Theorem reference now shows that \(\operatorname{tot}(\lambda)\) is a quasi-isomorphism.

For \(\rho\), the same argument shows that \(\operatorname{H}_{\mathrm{I}}\operatorname{H}_{\mathrm{II}}(\rho)\) is an isomorphism; Theorem reference then implies that \(\operatorname{tot}(\rho)\) is also a quasi-isomorphism.

The total complex of \(F(X_1,I_2^\bullet)\) is still that complex itself, and taking \(\operatorname{H}^n\) gives \(\mathrm{R}_{\mathrm{II}}^nF(X_1,X_2)\). Likewise, taking \(\operatorname{H}^n\) of \(F(I_1^\bullet,X_2)\), or of its total complex, gives \(\mathrm{R}_{\mathrm{I}}^nF(X_1,X_2)\). Using \(\operatorname{tot}(F(I_1^\bullet,I_2^\bullet))\) as an intermediary yields \[\mathrm{R}_{\mathrm{I}}^nF(X_1,X_2)\simeq \mathrm{R}_{\mathrm{II}}^nF(X_1,X_2).\] Because every morphism \(X_i\to Y_i\) lifts to a morphism between injective resolutions, uniquely up to homotopy, what we have obtained is in fact an isomorphism of bifunctors \(\mathrm{R}_{\mathrm{I}}^nF\simeq\mathrm{R}_{\mathrm{II}}^nF\).

Remark. The argument actually gives a method for resolving both variables simultaneously and then deriving \(F\) in a balanced way by means of the total complex of the double complex \(F(I_1^\bullet,I_2^\bullet)\).

Now let \(\mathcal{A}\) be an abelian category and consider the bifunctor \(\operatorname{Hom}=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{A}}:\mathcal{A}^{\operatorname{op}}\times\mathcal{A}\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ab}}\). Proposition reference says that \(\operatorname{Hom}\) is left exact in both variables. For every \(n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\), make the following definitions.

  • If \(\mathcal{A}\) has enough projective objects, define \(\operatorname{Ext}^n_{\mathcal{A},\mathrm{I}}(X,Y):=\mathrm{R}^n_{\mathrm{I}}\operatorname{Hom}(X,Y)\), computed using a projective resolution of \(X\) in \(\mathcal{A}\).

  • If \(\mathcal{A}\) has enough injective objects, define \(\operatorname{Ext}^n_{\mathcal{A},\mathrm{II}}(X,Y):=\mathrm{R}^n_{\mathrm{II}}\operatorname{Hom}(X,Y)\), computed using an injective resolution of \(Y\) in \(\mathcal{A}\).

Definition–Proposition (The \(\operatorname{Ext}\) functor). The bifunctor \(\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{A}}\) is balanced. Consequently, whenever the abelian category \(\mathcal{A}\) has enough injective and projective objects, there is, for every \(n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\), a bifunctor \[\operatorname{Ext}^n=\operatorname{Ext}^n_{\mathcal{A}}:\mathcal{A}^{\operatorname{op}}\times\mathcal{A}\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ab}}\] such that \(\operatorname{Ext}^n_{\mathcal{A}}(X,Y):=\operatorname{Ext}^n_{\mathrm{I}}(X,Y)\simeq \operatorname{Ext}^n_{\mathrm{II}}(X,Y)\) (canonically).

Proof. Balancedness is an immediate consequence of the definitions of injective and projective objects, so Theorem reference applies.

If \(R\) is a ring and \(\mathcal{A}=R\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\) or \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}\text{-}}R\), we write \(\operatorname{Ext}^n_{\mathcal{A}}\) as \(\operatorname{Ext}^n_R\). Observe that \(\operatorname{Ext}^0=\operatorname{Hom}\), while \((\operatorname{Ext}^n)_{n\geq0}\) has, in the variables \(X\) and \(Y\) respectively, long exact sequences of the form \[\begin{gather*} \cdots\to\operatorname{Ext}^{n-1}(X',Y)\xrightarrow{\delta^{n-1}}\operatorname{Ext}^n(X'',Y)\to \operatorname{Ext}^n(X,Y)\to\operatorname{Ext}^n(X',Y)\to\cdots,\\ \cdots\to\operatorname{Ext}^{n-1}(X,Y'')\xrightarrow{\delta^{n-1}}\operatorname{Ext}^n(X,Y')\to \operatorname{Ext}^n(X,Y)\to\operatorname{Ext}^n(X,Y'')\to\cdots, \end{gather*}\] where \(0\to X'\to X\to X''\to0\) and \(0\to Y'\to Y\to Y''\to0\) are given short exact sequences. If \(\mathcal{A}\) is a \(\Bbbk\)-linear abelian category, the values of \(\operatorname{Ext}^n\) may naturally be regarded as objects of \(\Bbbk\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\).

Remark. The symbol \(\operatorname{Ext}\) stands for “extension,” because the elements of \(\operatorname{Ext}^1(X,Y)\) correspond bijectively to the isomorphism classes of extensions \(0\to Y\to E\to X\to0\) (that is, short exact sequences); the higher \(\operatorname{Ext}^n\) have a similar interpretation. This fact is best understood through the derived category; see §4.5.

The characterization of exact functors in Corollary reference immediately gives the following.

  • An object \(I\) is injective \(\iff \operatorname{Ext}^1(\cdot,I)=0\iff \operatorname{Ext}^{\geq1}(\cdot,I)=0\).

  • An object \(P\) is projective \(\iff \operatorname{Ext}^1(P,\cdot)=0\iff \operatorname{Ext}^{\geq1}(P,\cdot)=0\).

Example (\(\operatorname{HH}^n\) as \(\operatorname{Ext}^n\)). Return to the basic setting for Hochschild homology and cohomology from §reference: \(\Bbbk\) is a commutative ring and \(R\) is a \(\Bbbk\)-algebra; now assume in addition that \(R\) is projective as a \(\Bbbk\)-module. Write \(\otimes:=\otimes_{\Bbbk}\). Since projective modules are direct summands of free modules, \(R^{\otimes n}\) is still projective as a \(\Bbbk\)-module. 1 Regard \(R\otimes R^{\otimes n}\otimes R\) as a left \(R^e\)-module, where \(R^e:=R\otimes R^{\operatorname{op}}\). Since \(R\otimes(\cdot)\otimes R:\Bbbk\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\to R^e\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\) is left adjoint to the forgetful functor [Li1], it carries projective objects to projective objects (Proposition reference). Thus Lemma reference shows that the bar complex \(\mathsf{B}R\) gives a projective resolution of \(R\) as a left \(R^e\)-module, \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:bar-proj-resolution}{} \cdots\to\mathsf{B}_1R\to\mathsf{B}_0R\to R\to0. \end{equation}\] Now let \(M\) be an \((R,R)\)-bimodule. Substituting the original definition of Hochschild cohomology from Definition reference gives \[\operatorname{HH}^n(M)=\operatorname{H}^n\left(\operatorname{Hom}_{R^e}(\mathsf{B}R,M)\right) =\operatorname{Ext}^n_{R^e}(R,M).\]

We next turn to the \(\operatorname{Tor}\) functor. Let \(R\) be a ring. The module categories \(R\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\) (and \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}\text{-}}R\)) have enough projective objects2. The tensor product gives a bifunctor \[\otimes_R:\ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}\text{-}}R\times R\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ab}},\] which is right exact in either variable (see [Li1]). Apply the right-exact version of the preceding theory to define the left derived functors in both variables, \(\mathrm{L}_{\mathrm{I},n}\otimes_R\) and \(\mathrm{L}_{\mathrm{II},n}\otimes_R\); these can be nonzero only for \(n\geq0\). Recall also the definition of a flat module [Li1].

Definition–Proposition (The \(\operatorname{Tor}\) functor). For every ring \(R\), the bifunctor \(\otimes_R\) is balanced. Hence, for every \(n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\), one may define a bifunctor \[\operatorname{Tor}_n=\operatorname{Tor}_n^R:\ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}\text{-}}R\times R\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ab}}\] by \(\operatorname{Tor}_n^R(X,Y):=(\mathrm{L}_{\mathrm{I},n}\otimes_R)(X,Y)\simeq (\mathrm{L}_{\mathrm{II},n}\otimes_R)(X,Y)\) (canonically).

Proof. Balancedness follows from the fact that every projective module is flat [Li1]. Apply the left-derived-functor version of Theorem reference.

We have \(\operatorname{Tor}^R_0(X,Y)=X\ensuremath{\underset{R}{\otimes}}Y\), while \((\operatorname{Tor}_n)_{n\geq0}\) has the following long exact sequences: \[\begin{gather*} \cdots\to\operatorname{Tor}^R_{n+1}(X'',Y)\xrightarrow{\partial_{n+1}}\operatorname{Tor}^R_n(X',Y)\to \operatorname{Tor}^R_n(X,Y)\to\operatorname{Tor}^R_n(X'',Y)\to\cdots,\\ \cdots\to\operatorname{Tor}^R_{n+1}(X,Y'')\xrightarrow{\partial_{n+1}}\operatorname{Tor}^R_n(X,Y')\to \operatorname{Tor}^R_n(X,Y)\to\operatorname{Tor}^R_n(X,Y'')\to\cdots, \end{gather*}\] where \(0\to X'\to X\to X''\to0\) and \(0\to Y'\to Y\to Y''\to0\) are given short exact sequences. As in the case of \(\operatorname{Ext}\), we obtain the following characterizations.

  • A right \(R\)-module \(M\) is flat \(\iff \operatorname{Tor}^R_1(M,\cdot)=0\iff \operatorname{Tor}^R_{\geq1}(M,\cdot)=0\).

  • A left \(R\)-module \(N\) is flat \(\iff \operatorname{Tor}^R_1(\cdot,N)=0\iff \operatorname{Tor}^R_{\geq1}(\cdot,N)=0\).

Let \(M\) be an \(R\)-module. In analogy with the definition of a projective resolution, a flat resolution of \(M\) is an exact sequence of the form \[\cdots\to F^2\to F^1\to F^0\to M\to0,\qquad \text{each $F^n$ is a flat $R$-module}.\] By Corollary reference and the preceding observation, \(\operatorname{Tor}^R_n(X,Y)\) can also be computed using a flat resolution of \(X\) or \(Y\). This is the practical technique for computing \(\operatorname{Tor}\), whereas projective resolutions play a chiefly theoretical role. Such computations can naturally be balanced as well. Choose arbitrary flat resolutions \(\cdots\to P_1\to P_0\to X\to0\) and \(\cdots\to Q_1\to Q_0\to Y\to0\). Form the double complex, in the sense of chain complexes, \(P_\bullet\ensuremath{\underset{R}{\otimes}}Q_\bullet\), and denote its total complex by \(P\otimes Q\). The homological version of Remark reference gives \(\operatorname{Tor}_n^R(X,Y)\simeq\operatorname{H}_n(P\otimes Q)\); the only properties needed are the exactness of \(P_p\ensuremath{\underset{R}{\otimes}}(\cdot)\) and \((\cdot)\ensuremath{\underset{R}{\otimes}}Q_q\), precisely the properties guaranteed by flatness.

Remark (Bimodule structure). Let \(A\) and \(B\) be rings, let \(X\) be an \((A,R)\)-bimodule, and let \(Y\) be an \((R,B)\)-bimodule. Since \(\operatorname{Tor}_n^R\) is a bifunctor, \(\operatorname{Tor}_n^R(X,Y)\) carries a canonical \((A,B)\)-bimodule structure. For example, consider left multiplication by \(A\): every \(a\in A\) gives an endomorphism of \(X\) as a right \(R\)-module and hence induces an endomorphism \(L_a\) of \(\operatorname{Tor}_n^R(X,Y)\); one has \(L_aL_{a'}=L_{aa'}\) and \(L_1=\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}\). Right multiplication by \(B\) is handled similarly in the second variable. For \(n=0\), this recovers the natural bimodule structure on \(X\ensuremath{\underset{R}{\otimes}}Y\).

If \(Y\), as a left \(R\)-module, is supplied with a flat resolution \(\cdots\to P_0\to Y\to0\), the left \(A\)-action can be read directly from the complex \(X\ensuremath{\underset{R}{\otimes}}P_\bullet\): it comes from left multiplication by \(A\) on \(X\). Right multiplication is treated in the same way.

As a special case, if a ring homomorphism \(R\to S\) is fixed, then \(\operatorname{Tor}_n^R(\cdot,S)\) (or \(\operatorname{Tor}_n^R(S,\cdot)\)) naturally becomes a functor \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}\text{-}}R\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}\text{-}}S\) (or \(R\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\to S\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\)).

A similar argument shows that, when \(X\) is an \((R,A)\)-bimodule and \(Y\) is an \((R,B)\)-bimodule, every \(\operatorname{Ext}_R^n(X,Y)\) naturally carries an \((A,B)\)-bimodule structure.

For a commutative ring \(R\), there is no need to distinguish left from right \(R\)-modules; the corresponding category is denoted by \(R\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\). Every \(R\)-module is then naturally an \((R,R)\)-bimodule, so \(\operatorname{Tor}_n^R\) becomes a bifunctor \((R\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}})^2\to R\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\).

Proposition. For a commutative ring \(R\), there is a canonical isomorphism of bifunctors \[\operatorname{Tor}_n^R(X,Y)\simeq\operatorname{Tor}_n^R(Y,X)\] for every \(n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\).

Proof. Choose flat resolutions \(P_\bullet\) and \(Q_\bullet\) of \(X\) and \(Y\), respectively. Write \(P\otimes Q\) for the total complex of the double complex \(P_\bullet\ensuremath{\underset{R}{\otimes}}Q_\bullet\), and define \(Q\otimes P\) similarly. The symmetry constraint for the tensor product [Li1] gives canonical isomorphisms \[P_p\ensuremath{\underset{R}{\otimes}}Q_q\simeq Q_q\ensuremath{\underset{R}{\otimes}}P_p,\qquad p,q\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}.\] In other words, \(P_\bullet\ensuremath{\underset{R}{\otimes}}Q_\bullet\simeq \mathrm{swap}(Q_\bullet\ensuremath{\underset{R}{\otimes}}P_\bullet)\). Apply Proposition reference to obtain a canonical isomorphism of total complexes \(P\otimes Q\simeq Q\otimes P\). This proves the assertion.

Remark. The symbol \(\operatorname{Tor}\) stands for “torsion,” as suggested by the following example. Let \(\mathfrak{a}\) be a left ideal of a ring \(R\), and let \(X\) be any right \(R\)-module. Since the free left module \(R\) is flat, apply Proposition reference to \(0\to\mathfrak{a}\to R\to R/\mathfrak{a}\to0\) to shift dimensions. This gives \[\begin{align*} \operatorname{Tor}^R_1(X,R/\mathfrak{a}) &\simeq \operatorname{ker}\left[ X\ensuremath{\underset{R}{\otimes}}\mathfrak{a}\to X\ensuremath{\underset{R}{\otimes}}R\simeq X\right]\\ &\simeq \left\{\sum_i x_i\otimes a_i\in X\ensuremath{\underset{R}{\otimes}}\mathfrak{a}: \sum_i x_i a_i=0\right\},\\ \operatorname{Tor}^R_n(X,R/\mathfrak{a})&\simeq\operatorname{Tor}^R_{n-1}(X,\mathfrak{a}),\qquad(n>1). \end{align*}\] If, moreover, \(t\in R\) is not a right zero divisor and we take \(\mathfrak{a}:=Rt\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\leftarrow}}R\) (mapping \(r\) to \(rt\)), then \(\operatorname{Tor}^R_1(X,R/Rt)\simeq\{x\in X:xt=0\}\), the \(t\)-torsion submodule of \(X\); for \(n>1\), \(\operatorname{Tor}^R_n(X,R/Rt)=0\).

Example (\(\operatorname{HH}_n\) as \(\operatorname{Tor}_n\)). Continue from the opening setup of Example reference, but weaken the condition on \(R\) by requiring only that \(R\) be flat as a \(\Bbbk\)-module. Then \(R^{\otimes n}\) is flat as well. The associativity constraint \((\cdot)\ensuremath{\underset{R^e}{\otimes}}(R\otimes R^{\otimes n}\otimes R)\simeq (\cdot)\otimes R^{\otimes n}\) shows that \(R\otimes R^{\otimes n}\otimes R\) is a flat left \(R^e\)-module. Thus \(\mathsf{B}R\) is a flat resolution of \(R\) as a left \(R^e\)-module, as in equation.

For every \((R,R)\)-bimodule \(M\), the original definition of Hochschild homology from Definition reference gives \[\operatorname{HH}_n(M)=\operatorname{H}_n\left(M\ensuremath{\underset{R^e}{\otimes}}\mathsf{B}R\right) =\operatorname{Tor}_n^{R^e}(M,R).\]

We can now combine Examples reference and reference to compute further examples of Hochschild homology and cohomology. First take the polynomial algebra \(R=\Bbbk[t]\) and identify \(R^e=R\otimes R^{\operatorname{op}}\) with \(\Bbbk[x,y]\). The scalar action on \(R\) as an \(R^e\)-module is \(h(x,y)\cdot f(t)=h(t,t)f(t)\), and \(R\) has the free resolution \[0\to R^e\xrightarrow{\text{multiplication by }x-y}R^e \xrightarrow{f\mapsto f(t,t)}R\to0.\] Computing \(\operatorname{Ext}^n_{R^e}(R,\cdot)\) and \(\operatorname{Tor}_n^{R^e}(\cdot,R)\) from this resolution immediately gives \(\operatorname{HH}_n(R)\simeq R\simeq\operatorname{HH}^n(R)\) for \(n\in\{0,1\}\), while \(\operatorname{HH}_n(R)=0=\operatorname{HH}^n(R)\) for \(n>1\). Next take \(R=\Bbbk[t]/(t^2)\), so that \(R^e=\Bbbk[x,y]/(x^2,y^2)\). As an \(R^e\)-module, \(R\) has a free resolution of period \(2\), \[\cdots\xrightarrow{x+y}R^e\xrightarrow{x-y}R^e\xrightarrow{x+y}R^e \xrightarrow{\text{multiplication by }x-y}R^e\xrightarrow{f\mapsto f(t,t)}R\to0,\] whose exactness is left to the reader to verify directly. For every \(R\)-module \(M\), applying \(M\ensuremath{\underset{R^e}{\otimes}}(\cdot)\) and \(\operatorname{Hom}_{R^e}(\cdot,M)\) gives, respectively, \[\begin{gather*} \cdots\xrightarrow{2t}M\xrightarrow{0}M\xrightarrow{2t}M\xrightarrow{0}M \to M\ensuremath{\underset{R^e}{\otimes}}R\to0,\\ 0\to\operatorname{Hom}_{R^e}(R,M)\to M\xrightarrow{0}M\xrightarrow{2t}M \xrightarrow{0}M\xrightarrow{2t}\cdots. \end{gather*}\] Thus \(\operatorname{HH}_k(M)\) and \(\operatorname{HH}^k(M)\) depend only on \(k\bmod2\); this periodicity might be difficult to see from the definitions alone.

If \(\Bbbk\) is a field, \(\operatorname{HH}_n(M)\) and \(\operatorname{HH}^n(M)\) can be read off from these complexes, but the answer depends on \(\mathrm{char}(\Bbbk)\). The exercises will treat the general case \(R=\Bbbk[t]/(t^n)\). The following result is often used in algebraic topology and also provides a small check on the preceding material; it concerns chain complexes and their homology (Remark reference). Let \(C=(C_\bullet,d^C_\bullet)\) (respectively, \(D=(D_\bullet,d^D_\bullet)\)) be a chain complex of right \(R\)-modules (respectively, left \(R\)-modules). Form the double chain complex \(C_\bullet\otimes D_\bullet\) and denote its total complex by \[C\otimes D:=\operatorname{tot}_{\oplus}\left(C_\bullet\otimes D_\bullet\right);\] the subscript \(R\) on the tensor product is omitted. Concretely, the degree-\(n\) term of the total complex \(C\otimes D\) is \(\bigoplus_{p+q=n}C_p\otimes D_q\), while the restriction of \(d_n\) to \(C_p\otimes D_q\) is \(d^C_p\otimes\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}+(-1)^p\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}\otimes d^D_q\). This gives a canonical homomorphism \[\kappa:\bigoplus_{p+q=n}\operatorname{H}_p(C)\otimes\operatorname{H}_q(D)\to \operatorname{H}_n(C\otimes D).\]

Theorem (Künneth theorem for homology). Let \(C,D\) be chain complexes as above. If every \(C_p\) and every \(\operatorname{im}(d^C_p)\) is a flat right \(R\)-module, then there is a canonical short exact sequence \[\text{Diagram chapter3-unit-045-d001}\]

Proof. For every \(p\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\), define submodules of \(C_p\) by \(B_p:=\operatorname{im}(d^C_{p+1})\) and \(Z_p:=\operatorname{ker}(d^C_p)\). Regard these as chain complexes \(Z=Z_\bullet\) and \(B=B_\bullet\) by setting \(d^Z=d^B:=0\). There is then a short exact sequence of chain complexes \[\text{Diagram chapter3-unit-045-d002}\]

The short exact sequence \(0\to Z_p\to C_p\xrightarrow{d^C_p}B_{p-1}\to0\) and the long exact sequence for \(\operatorname{Tor}\) imply that \(Z_p\) is also flat. Since \(B_{p-1}\) is flat, the sequence \[0\to Z_p\otimes D_q\to C_p\otimes D_q\to B_{p-1}\otimes D_q\to0\] remains exact. Since direct sums of modules, including infinite direct sums, preserve exactness, we obtain a short exact sequence of chain complexes \(0\to Z\otimes D\to C\otimes D\xrightarrow{d^C\otimes\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_D} B[-1]\otimes D\to0\).

Because \(d^Z=d^{B[-1]}=0\), the associated long exact sequence in homology simplifies, by flatness, to \[\begin{multline*} \overbracket{\displaystyle\bigoplus_{p+q=n+1}B_{p-1}\otimes\operatorname{H}_q(D)}^{= \bigoplus_{p+q=n}B_p\otimes\operatorname{H}_q(D)}\xrightarrow{\partial_{n+1}} \displaystyle\bigoplus_{p+q=n}Z_p\otimes\operatorname{H}_q(D)\to\operatorname{H}_n(C\otimes D)\\ \to\underbracket{\displaystyle\bigoplus_{p+q=n}B_{p-1}\otimes\operatorname{H}_q(D)}_{= \bigoplus_{p+q=n-1}B_p\otimes\operatorname{H}_q(D)}\xrightarrow{\partial_n} \displaystyle\bigoplus_{p+q=n-1}Z_p\otimes\operatorname{H}_q(D). \end{multline*}\] It remains only to explain the connecting morphisms \(\partial_{n+1}\) and \(\partial_n\). Up to possible signs, they arise from the inclusions \(B_p\hookrightarrow Z_p\). To see this, return to the explicit construction of the long exact sequence, namely the homological version of Proposition reference; here one can use a diagram chase, as in the discussion preceding [Li1]. The details are left to the reader.

It follows that \(\operatorname{coker}(\partial_{n+1})\) may be identified with \(\bigoplus_{p+q=n}\operatorname{H}_p(C)\otimes\operatorname{H}_q(D)\), and the induced monomorphism to \(\operatorname{H}_n(C\otimes D)\) is \(\kappa\).

Finally, \(0\to B_p\to Z_p\to\operatorname{H}_p(C)\to0\) is a flat resolution of \(\operatorname{H}_p(C)\). Hence \(\operatorname{ker}(\partial_n)\simeq \bigoplus_{p+q=n-1}\operatorname{Tor}_1^R(\operatorname{H}_p(C),\operatorname{H}_q(D))\). This gives the asserted short exact sequence.

Notice that if \(R\) is a division ring, then \(\kappa\) is necessarily an isomorphism. Because \(D\) plays the role of homology coefficients in topology, the special case of Theorem reference in which \(D\) is concentrated in degree zero is also called the universal coefficient theorem. Results of this kind have many variants. Moreover, the ring structure supplies operations on \(\operatorname{Tor}\) that are absent for other derived bifunctors. These structures are better formulated in the language of derived categories or spectral sequences.

  1. Alternatively, use the tensor adjunction [Li1].↩︎

  2. Indeed, free modules are always projective; see [Li1].↩︎

K-injective and K-projective complexes

Injective and projective resolutions of complexes supplied the initial definition of derived functors in §reference. That construction requires bounded-below or bounded-above complexes, whereas applications involving unbounded complexes and their derived categories require a broader class of resolutions. The theory of K-injective and K-projective resolutions originates with [Spa88]. This section provides some preparation for that theory; the arguments follow [stacks], and the reader may also consult [KS06] or [BN93].

Definition (N. Spaltenstein). Let \(\mathcal{A}\) be an abelian category.

  • A complex \(I\in\operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A}))\) is called a K-injective complex1 if, for every acyclic complex \(X\in\operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A}))\), the complex \(\operatorname{Hom}^\bullet(X,I)\) is also acyclic.

    If \(f:A\to I\) is a quasi-isomorphism in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})\) and \(I\) is K-injective, then \(f\) is called a K-injective resolution of \(A\).

  • A complex \(P\in\operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A}))\) is called a K-projective complex if, for every acyclic complex \(X\in\operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A}))\), the complex \(\operatorname{Hom}^\bullet(P,X)\) is also acyclic.

    If \(f:P\to A\) is a quasi-isomorphism in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})\) and \(P\) is K-projective, then \(f\) is called a K-projective resolution of \(A\).

If every object of \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})\) has a K-injective resolution (respectively, a K-projective resolution), then \(\mathcal{A}\) is said to have enough K-injective complexes (respectively, enough K-projective complexes).

The two sets of definitions are plainly dual. In practice, the following criterion is often easier to use.

Lemma. A complex \(I\) (respectively, \(P\)) is K-injective (respectively, K-projective) if and only if, for every acyclic complex \(X\), \(\operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{A})}(X,I)=0\) (respectively, \(\operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{A})}(P,X)=0\)).

Proof. Let \(n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\). Lemma reference gives \[\operatorname{H}^n \operatorname{Hom}^\bullet(X, I) \simeq \operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{A})}(X[-n], I), \quad \operatorname{H}^n \operatorname{Hom}^\bullet(P, X) \simeq \operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{A})}(P, X[n]);\] but \(X\) is acyclic if and only if \(X[-n]\) is acyclic, and this is also equivalent to \(X[n]\) being acyclic.

Example. Lemma reference can immediately be restated as follows.

  • If \(I\in\operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}^+(\mathcal{A}))\) consists of injective objects, then \(I\) is K-injective.

  • If \(P\in\operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}^-(\mathcal{A}))\) consists of projective objects, then \(P\) is K-projective.

Thus an injective (respectively, projective) resolution is a special case of a K-injective (respectively, K-projective) resolution.

Example (A. Dold). The one-sided boundedness condition in Example reference is essential. For example, take \(\mathcal{A}=\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}/4\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\) and consider the acyclic complex \(Q\) in it: \[\cdots \xrightarrow{2} \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}/4\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\xrightarrow{2} \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}/4\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}} \xrightarrow{2} \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}/4\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\xrightarrow{2} \cdots.\] Every term is a free module. On the other hand, the termwise tensor product \(Q\ensuremath{\underset{\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}/4\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}}{\otimes}}\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}/2\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\) is the complex \[\cdots \xrightarrow{0} \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}/2\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\xrightarrow{0} \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}/2\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}} \xrightarrow{0} \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}/2\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\xrightarrow{0} \cdots.\] Therefore \(Q\) is not K-projective. Indeed, if \(Q\) were K-projective, then \(\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_Q\) would be homotopic to \(0\), and hence so would \(\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{Q\otimes\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}/2\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}}\), contradicting \(\operatorname{H}^n(Q\ensuremath{\underset{\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}/4\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}}{\otimes}}\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}/2\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}})=\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}/2\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\).

From another point of view, this example also shows that an unbounded complex consisting of projective objects need not be an appropriate resolution: \(0\to Q\) and \(0\to0\) are both quasi-isomorphisms, but the preceding paragraph shows that \(\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_Q\) is not homotopic to \(0\). Thus \(Q\) and \(0\) are not isomorphic in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{A})\), and Theorem reference cannot simply be extended to the unbounded case.

The following result is the natural generalization of Theorem reference; its proof is likewise postponed until the discussion following Theorem in § 4.4.

Theorem. Let \(\alpha:X\to Y\) be a quasi-isomorphism in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})\).

  • Given a morphism \(\gamma:X\to I\), where \(I\) is a K-injective complex, there is a commutative diagram in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{A})\) \[\text{Diagram chapter3-unit-046-d001}\]

  • Given a morphism \(\gamma:P\to Y\), where \(P\) is a K-projective complex, there is a commutative diagram in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{A})\) \[\text{Diagram chapter3-unit-046-d002}\]

In both cases, \(\beta\) is unique as a morphism in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{A})\).

Proposition. The equivalence \(\sigma\) of Definition–Proposition reference has the following property: \(X\in\operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A}^{\operatorname{op}}))\) is K-injective (respectively, K-projective) if and only if \(\sigma X\in\operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})^{\operatorname{op}}) =\operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A}))\) is K-projective (respectively, K-injective).

Proof. The functor \(\sigma\) preserves acyclic complexes and induces \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{A}^{\operatorname{op}})\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}} \ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{A})^{\operatorname{op}}\) (Proposition reference); hence \(\sigma\) preserves the criterion of Lemma reference.

Next consider adjoint functors. Proposition reference has a corresponding version in this setting.

Proposition. Consider a pair of functors between abelian categories \(\text{Diagram chapter3-unit-046-diagram-003}\), and suppose that \(F\) is exact.

  • If \(G\) is left adjoint to \(F\), then \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}G:\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{B})\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{A})\) carries K-projective complexes to K-projective complexes.

  • If \(G\) is right adjoint to \(F\), then \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}G:\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{B})\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{A})\) carries K-injective complexes to K-injective complexes.

Proof. By duality it suffices to consider the case in which \(G\) is a left adjoint. In this case \(G\) is automatically additive (Corollary reference). Let \(P\in\operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{B}))\) be K-projective. For every acyclic complex \(X\in\operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A}))\), Proposition reference gives an isomorphism \[\operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{A})}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}G(P), X) \simeq \operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{B})}(P, \ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}F(X)).\] Since \(F\) is exact, \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}F(X)\) is acyclic, so the right-hand side is \(0\). Apply Lemma reference.

The next task in this section is to investigate the existence of K-injective or K-projective resolutions. The argument is somewhat intricate; we begin with the K-injective case.

Lemma. Consider a sequence of complexes over \(\mathcal{A}\), \(\cdots\to I_2\to I_1\to I_0\). Suppose that:

  • every \(I_k\) is K-injective;

  • for every \(k\) and \(n\), the morphism \(I_{k+1}^n\to I_k^n\) is an epimorphism admitting a section (in other words, it has a right inverse; see the discussion after Proposition reference);

  • for every \(n\), the object \(I^n:=\varprojlim_k I_k^n\) exists in \(\mathcal{A}\).

Then the induced differentials \(d_I^n:=\varprojlim_k d_{I_k}^n:I^n\to I^{n+1}\) make \(I:=(I^n,d_I^n)_n\) a K-injective complex.

Proof. Let \(X\in\operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A}))\) be acyclic. For each \(k\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}_{\geq0}\), take the following portion of the complex \(\operatorname{Hom}^\bullet(X,I_k)\): \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:K-injective-projlimit-aux}{}\text{Diagram chapter3-unit-046-d003} \end{equation}\] This sequence is exact because \(I_k\) is K-injective. Now consider the homomorphism induced by \(I_{k+1}\to I_k\), \[\operatorname{Hom}\left(X^n,I_{k+1}^{n-2}\right)\to \operatorname{Hom}\left(X^n,I_k^{n-2}\right).\] Since there is a section \(I_k^{n-2}\to I_{k+1}^{n-2}\), this homomorphism is an epimorphism. The same remains true after taking \(\prod_n\). Thus, as \(k\) varies, the leftmost term in equation satisfies the Mittag–Leffler condition (Definition reference).

Now let \(k\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}_{\geq0}\) vary in equation. Corollary reference gives an exact sequence \[\text{Diagram chapter3-unit-046-d004}\] Interchanging \(\varprojlim_k\) and \(\prod_n\) now gives an exact sequence2 \[\text{Diagram chapter3-unit-046-d005}\] This too is a portion of \(\operatorname{Hom}^\bullet(X,I)\), and its cohomology at the middle term is precisely \(\operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{A})}(X,I)\). Hence \(\operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{A})}(X,I)=0\). Apply Lemma reference to finish the proof.

Lemma. Suppose that \(\mathcal{A}\) has enough injective objects. For every \(A\in\operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A}))\), there is a commutative diagram in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})\) \[\text{Diagram chapter3-unit-046-d006}\] with \(\tau^{\geq k}A\) and the arrows between them as in Definition reference, such that:

  • every \(I_k\) is an object of \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}^+(\mathcal{A})\) consisting of injective objects;

  • every vertical arrow \(f_k\) is both a monomorphism and a quasi-isomorphism;

  • for every \(k\) and \(n\), the morphism \(I_{k+1}^n\to I_k^n\) is an epimorphism admitting a section.

Proof. We construct the diagram from right to left. All injective resolutions discussed below are implicitly monomorphisms.

First apply Theorem reference to \(\tau^{\geq0}A\in\operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}^+(\mathcal{A}))\) to obtain an injective resolution \(f_0:\tau^{\geq0}A\to I_0\).

Next, the definitions directly show that \(\tau^{\geq-k-1}A\to\tau^{\geq-k}A\) is an epimorphism in every degree, and hence an epimorphism in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}^+(\mathcal{A})\). Suppose that the required quasi-isomorphisms \[\tau^{\geq0}A\xrightarrow{f_0}I_0,\quad\ldots,\quad \tau^{\geq-k}A\xrightarrow{f_k}I_k\] and the corresponding commutative diagram have been constructed. Choose an injective resolution \(H\xrightarrow{g}J\) of \(H:=\operatorname{ker}[\tau^{\geq-k-1}A\to\tau^{\geq-k}A]\) by Theorem reference. The Horseshoe Lemma, Proposition reference, then gives a commutative diagram with exact rows in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})\): \[\text{Diagram chapter3-unit-046-d007}\] such that \(f_{k+1}\) is an injective resolution. Exactness of the first row is equivalent to exactness of \(0\to J^n\to I_{k+1}^n\to I_k^n\to0\) for every \(n\). Since all its terms are injective objects of \(\mathcal{A}\), Lemma reference shows that \(I_{k+1}^n\to I_k^n\) admits a section. This proves the result.

The following discussion uses notation from §reference. Take \(A\) as above. As \(k\geq0\) varies, the complexes \(\tau^{\geq-k}A\) form an object of \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{InvSys}}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A}))\), which we denote by \(\tau A\). The definition of the truncation functors gives a family of canonical morphisms \(A\to\tau^{\geq-k}A\). Considering the complexes \(\tau^{\geq-k}A\) degree by degree shows that their \(\varprojlim_k\) exists and that these canonical morphisms induce an isomorphism \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:A-lim-truncation}{} A \ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}\varprojlim_{k \geq 0} \left( \tau^{\geq -k} A \right). \end{equation}\] Now consider the \(I_k\). Suppose that \(\mathcal{A}\) has countable products; then \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})\) also has countable products, constructed degree by degree. For \(A\in\operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A}))\), consider the diagram in Lemma reference. It follows that \[I:=\varprojlim_k I_k \quad \text{exists}.\] More concretely, Definition reference and the discussion following it place \(I\) and \(A\) in exact sequences \[\begin{gather*} 0 \to I \to \prod_k I_k \xrightarrow{\Delta_I} \prod_k I_k, \\ 0 \to A \to \prod_k \tau^{\geq -k} A \xrightarrow{\Delta_{\tau A}} \prod_k \tau^{\geq -k} A, \end{gather*}\] where \(\Delta_I\) and \(\Delta_{\tau A}\) are as in that definition. We obtain commutative diagrams \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:K-injective-diagonal}{}\text{Diagram chapter3-unit-046-d008} \quad \text{Diagram chapter3-unit-046-d009} \end{equation}\] The two vertical arrows are defined by inclusion into the first coordinate of the mapping cone; the reader may check this directly. Another explanation, though more elaborate than necessary, can be given using the universal property of the homotopy kernel (Proposition reference). On the other hand, \((f_k)_{k\geq0}\) and the universal property of \(\varprojlim\) give a morphism \[f:A\simeq\varprojlim_k(\tau^{\geq-k}A)\to\varprojlim_k I_k=I,\] which makes the following diagram commute: \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:K-injective-A-I}{}\text{Diagram chapter3-unit-046-d010} \end{equation}\] Lemmas reference and reference show that \(I\) is a K-injective complex. If \(f\) is a quasi-isomorphism, then \(f\) is a K-injective resolution of \(A\). This last step requires an additional hypothesis.

Lemma. In the situation above, suppose in addition that \(\mathcal{A}\) has exact countable products (Convention reference). Then \(f\) is a quasi-isomorphism if and only if \(A\to\operatorname{Cone}(\Delta_{\tau A})[-1]\) is a quasi-isomorphism.

Proof. Consider the natural commutative diagram3 \[\text{Diagram chapter3-unit-046-d011}\] Taking the long exact sequences of the mapping cones equation gives a commutative diagram with exact rows: \[\text{Diagram chapter3-unit-046-d012}\] Every \(f_k\) is a quasi-isomorphism, and exactness of countable products ensures that \(\prod_k f_k\) remains a quasi-isomorphism. Applying Proposition reference shows that \(\operatorname{Cone}(\Delta_{\tau A})\to\operatorname{Cone}(\Delta_I)\)4 is also a quasi-isomorphism.

Next we prove that \(I\to\operatorname{Cone}(\Delta_I)[-1]\) is a quasi-isomorphism. First, \(\Delta_I\) is an epimorphism; this can be checked degree by degree. Indeed, \(\Delta_{I^n}:\prod_k I_k^n\to\prod_k I_k^n\) is an epimorphism because \(I_{k+1}^n\to I_k^n\) admits a section; see Example reference. Compare the short exact sequence \(0\to I\to\prod_k I_k\xrightarrow{\Delta_I}\prod_k I_k\to0\) with Lemma reference. It follows that the previously defined morphism \(I\to\operatorname{Cone}(\Delta_I)[-1]\) is indeed a quasi-isomorphism.

Insert these results into the commutative diagram equation and then take cohomology. This gives the desired necessary and sufficient condition.

Theorem. An abelian category \(\mathcal{A}\) satisfying the following two conditions has enough K-injective complexes:

  • \(\mathcal{A}\) has exact countable products;

  • \(\mathcal{A}\) has enough injective objects.

Proof. Lemma reference shows that it suffices to prove that \(A\to\operatorname{Cone}(\Delta_{\tau A})[-1]\) is a quasi-isomorphism for every \(A\in\operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A}))\). Let \(n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\). Since countable products are exact, Lemma reference gives canonical isomorphisms \[\operatorname{H}^n\left( \prod_k \tau^{\geq -k} A \right) \simeq \prod_k \operatorname{H}^n\left( \tau^{\geq -k} A \right) \simeq \prod_{k \geq -n} \operatorname{H}^n(A).\] If elementwise reasoning is available in \(\mathcal{A}\), then after taking \(\operatorname{H}^n\), the morphism \(\Delta_{\tau A}\) has the form \[\text{Diagram chapter3-unit-046-d013}\] Clearly \(\nabla^n\) is an epimorphism (a section can be written down explicitly), while \(\operatorname{ker}(\nabla^n)=\{(a)_{k\geq-n}:a\in\operatorname{H}^n(A)\}\) is the diagonal subobject. This argument readily translates to a general category \(\mathcal{A}\). Now consider the long exact sequence of the mapping cone \[\cdots \to \operatorname{H}^n \operatorname{Cone}(\Delta_{\tau A})[-1] \to \prod_{k \geq -n} \operatorname{H}^n(A) \xrightarrow[\text{epi}]{\nabla^n} \prod_{k \geq -n} \operatorname{H}^n(A) \to \operatorname{H}^n \operatorname{Cone}(\Delta_{\tau A}) \cdots\] This sequence identifies the morphism \(\operatorname{H}^n\operatorname{Cone}(\Delta_{\tau A})[-1]\to \prod_{k\geq-n}\operatorname{H}^n(A)\) with the inclusion of \(\operatorname{ker}(\nabla^n)\). Moreover, equation gives a commutative diagram \[\text{Diagram chapter3-unit-046-d014}\] Thus, for every \(n\), the morphism \(\operatorname{H}^n(A)\to\operatorname{H}^n(\operatorname{Cone}(\Delta_{\tau A})[-1])\) is an isomorphism.

Reversing the arrows by means of Proposition reference gives the dual version of Theorem reference.

Theorem. An abelian category \(\mathcal{A}\) satisfying the following two conditions has enough K-projective complexes:

  • \(\mathcal{A}\) has exact countable coproducts;

  • \(\mathcal{A}\) has enough projective objects.

Corollary. If \(\mathcal{A}\) is a Grothendieck category with enough projective objects (Definition reference), then \(\mathcal{A}\) also has enough K-projective complexes.

Proof. By definition, a Grothendieck category \(\mathcal{A}\) has countable coproducts. Proposition reference says that those countable coproducts are exact. Apply Theorem reference.

Example. Let \(R\) be a ring. Theorem reference and Corollary reference show that \(R\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\) has enough K-injective and K-projective complexes.

In fact, every complex in a Grothendieck category has a K-injective resolution, and these K-injective resolutions can be made functorial, as in Theorem reference. This is the main theorem of [Serp03]; see also [stacks]. That result covers many situations arising in geometry that are not covered by Theorem reference.

  1. A perhaps more natural term would be homotopically injective complex, and similarly homotopically projective complex.↩︎

  2. Translator’s note (O014-C064): in the third term the source omits the subscript \(k\) on \(\varprojlim_k\). This sentence explicitly interchanges \(\varprojlim_k\) with \(\prod_n\), and the vertical isomorphism below identifies the limit with \(I^{n+1}\), so the target restores that subscript.↩︎

  3. Translator’s note (O014-C065): in the source, the first lower horizontal arrow is labelled \(\Delta_A\). The lower row belongs to the inverse system \(\tau A\), and the right side of that row already uses \(\alpha(\Delta_{\tau A})\) and \(\operatorname{Cone}(\Delta_{\tau A})\); the target therefore restores the label \(\Delta_{\tau A}\).↩︎

  4. Translator’s note (O014-C066): the source writes \(\Delta_{\tau_A}\) at this occurrence, although the inverse-system object that was defined is \(\tau A\) and all surrounding notation uses \(\Delta_{\tau A}\). The target makes this consistent with the defined notation.↩︎

Exercises

Let \(\Bbbk\) be a commutative ring. Thus \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\Bbbk\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}})\) and \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\Bbbk\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}})\) are naturally \(\Bbbk\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\)-categories in the sense of Definition reference. Prove that, for every \(n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\) and every object \(X\) of \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\Bbbk\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}})\), there are canonical isomorphisms of \(\Bbbk\)-modules \[\operatorname{H}^n(X) \simeq \operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\Bbbk\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}})}(\Bbbk,X[n]) \simeq \operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\Bbbk\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}})}(\Bbbk[-n],X).\] On the right, \(\Bbbk\) is regarded as a complex concentrated in degree \(0\).

This exercise relates homotopies between morphisms to isomorphisms between their mapping cones. Let \(\mathcal{A}\) be an additive category and take any pair of morphisms \(f,g\in\operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})}(X,Y)\). Construct a bijection \[\left\{ \begin{array}{c} s\in\operatorname{Hom}^{-1}(X,Y): \\ d^{-1}_{\operatorname{Hom}^\bullet(X,Y)}(s)=f-g \end{array} \right\} \xrightarrow{1:1} \left\{ \begin{array}{c} h:\operatorname{Cone}(f)\to\operatorname{Cone}(g),\\ \text{a morphism of complexes making}\\ \text{the following diagram commute} \end{array} \right\},\] \[\begin{equation*} \text{Diagram chapter3-unit-047-d001} \end{equation*}\] and prove that every such morphism \(h\) is an isomorphism of complexes. In particular, \(f\) and \(g\) are homotopic if and only if such an \(h\) exists. Hint. Commutativity of the diagram in degree \(n\) is equivalent to the matrix equation \[h^n= \begin{pmatrix} \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{X^{n+1}}&0\\ s^{n+1}&\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{Y^n} \end{pmatrix}, \quad\text{where}\quad s^{n+1}:X^{n+1}\to Y^n.\]

(Split exactness) Let \(\mathcal{A}\) be an Abelian category and \(X\) a complex over it. Prove that the following statements are equivalent.

  1. \(X\) is equal to \(0\) in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{A})\);

  2. \(\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_X\) is null-homotopic;

  3. \(X\) is acyclic and there exists \((s^n)_n\in\operatorname{Hom}^{-1}(X,X)\) such that \(d^ns^{n+1}d^n=d^n\) for every \(n\);

  4. there is a family of objects \((Y^n)_n\) in \(\mathcal{A}\) and an isomorphism of complexes \(\Phi:X\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}(Y^n\oplus Y^{n+1},\overline d^{\,n})_n\), where \(\overline d\) is represented by the matrix \(\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}0&1\\0&0\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)\).

A complex satisfying any of these conditions is also called split exact.1 For \(X=[\cdots\,0\to A\to B\to C\to0\,\cdots]\), prove that this condition is equivalent to \(X\) being a split short exact sequence. Hint. It suffices to prove (iii) \(\implies\) (iv). The condition implies that \(d^{n-1}s^n\in\operatorname{End}_{\mathcal{A}}(X^n)\) is idempotent. This gives a decomposition \(X^n=Y^n\oplus Z^n\) with \(Y^n=\operatorname{im}(d^{n-1}s^n)\). Prove that \(Y^n=\operatorname{im}(d^{n-1})\) and that the restriction of \(d^n\) gives an isomorphism \(Z^n\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}\operatorname{im}(d^n)\); then take \(\Phi\) corresponding to \(\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}ds\\d\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)\).

Let \(\mathcal{A}\) be an Abelian category. Prove that \(X\) is an injective object of \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})\) if and only if every term of \(X\) is injective in \(\mathcal{A}\) and \(X\) is equal to \(0\) in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{A})\). State the version for projective objects. Hint. For the only-if direction, observe that the short exact sequence in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})\) \(0\to X\to\operatorname{Cone}(\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_X)\to X[1]\to0\) splits. Proposition reference then shows that \(X\) is acyclic. Choose a section \(X[1]\to\operatorname{Cone}(\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_X)\) and write it as \(\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}1\\-\theta\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)\), where \(\theta^n:X^{n+1}\to X^n\). Verify that \(d_X^{n-1}\theta^{n-1}+\theta^nd_X^n=\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{X^n}\) to prove that \(\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_X\) is null-homotopic.

Fix \(n\). By the preceding exercise, decompose \(X^n=Y^n\oplus Y^{n+1}\); it remains to prove that \(Y^n\) is injective. For any morphism \(f:A\to Y^n\) and monomorphism \(g:A\hookrightarrow B\) in \(\mathcal{A}\), consider the commutative diagram with exact row in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})\) \[\text{Diagram chapter3-unit-047-d002}\] where \(\Psi^n=\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}f\\0\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)\). Use this diagram to verify the injectivity criterion for \(Y^n\).

For the if direction, again write \(X^n=Y^n\oplus Y^{n+1}\) and describe explicitly all possible morphisms \(f:Z\to X\).

Let \(\Bbbk\) be a commutative ring and let \(R\) be a unital \(\Bbbk\)-algebra, in accordance with the convention of this book. Write down the canonical isomorphisms \(\operatorname{HH}_0(M_n(R))\simeq\operatorname{HH}_0(R)\) and \(\operatorname{HH}^0(M_n(R))\simeq\operatorname{HH}^0(R)\), where \(M_n(R)\) is the \(\Bbbk\)-algebra of \(n\times n\) matrices over \(R\). In fact, analogous isomorphisms hold in every degree \(m\), for both \(\operatorname{HH}_m\) and \(\operatorname{HH}^m\); see [Lo98].

In the setting of §reference, define the sub-bimodule \(\mathrm{Triv}_nR\) of \(\mathsf{B}_nR\), for every \(n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}_{\geq0}\), by \[\begin{align*} \mathrm{Triv}_nR &:=\sum_{h=1}^n R\otimes (\cdots\otimes \underbracket{\;\Bbbk\;}_{\text{$h$-th factor}} \otimes\cdots)\otimes R, \qquad \mathrm{Triv}_0R=0. \end{align*}\]

  1. Verify that this defines a subcomplex \(\mathrm{Triv}R\) of \(\mathsf{B}R\), and that \(\mathrm{Triv}R\) is exact. Hint. Restrict \((h^n)_n\) from the proof of Lemma reference to \(\mathrm{Triv}R\).

  2. Write \(\overline R:=R/\Bbbk\) as a \(\Bbbk\)-module and define the reduced bar complex of \(R\) to be the quotient \[\overline{\mathsf{B}}R :=\mathsf{B}R/\mathrm{Triv}R =\left(R\otimes\overline R^{\otimes n}\otimes R,b_n\right)_{n\geq0}.\] Following the pattern of equation, simplify \(M\ensuremath{\underset{R^e}{\otimes}}\overline{\mathsf{B}}R\) and \(\operatorname{Hom}_{R^e}(\overline{\mathsf{B}}R,M)\).

  3. Give canonical isomorphisms \(\operatorname{H}_n(M\ensuremath{\underset{R^e}{\otimes}}\overline{\mathsf{B}}R)\simeq\operatorname{HH}_n(M)\) and \(\operatorname{H}^n(\operatorname{Hom}_{R^e}(\overline{\mathsf{B}}R,M))\simeq\operatorname{HH}^n(M)\). Hint. In general, this follows from the theorem on normalized complexes in the Dold–Kan correspondence, in § 8.5, provided that \(\mathsf{B}R\) is understood from the viewpoint of the Example in § 8.7.

Let \(\Bbbk\) be a commutative ring, and let \(\widetilde R\) and \(R\) be unital \(\Bbbk\)-algebras, in accordance with the convention of this book. Suppose there is a split short exact sequence of \(\Bbbk\)-modules \[\text{Diagram chapter3-unit-047-d003}\] where \(M\) is a two-sided ideal of \(\widetilde R\), \(ps=\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_R\), and \(M^2=\{0\}\). Use \(s\) to identify \(\widetilde R\) with \(R\oplus M\).

  1. For \(m\in M\) and \(r\in R\), choose any \(\widetilde r\in p^{-1}(r)\). Prove that \(\widetilde rm\) and \(m\widetilde r\) depend only on \(m\) and \(r\), and that these operations make \(M\) an \((R,R)\)-bimodule.

  2. Prove that there is a bilinear map \(f:R^2\to M\) such that multiplication in \(\widetilde R\) is given by \[(r_1,m_1)(r_2,m_2) =(r_1r_2,r_1m_2+m_1r_2+f(r_1,r_2)), \quad r_1,r_2\in R,\quad m_1,m_2\in M.\]

  3. Such data \((R,\widetilde R,M)\) are called a square-zero extension of \(R\) by \(M\). Prove that, up to the appropriate notion of isomorphism, square-zero extensions are classified by \(\operatorname{HH}^2(M)\), with the zero element corresponding to the trivial extension \(R\times M\). Hint. Compute \(\operatorname{HH}^2(M)\) using the reduced bar complex from the preceding exercise.

Complete the proof of Lemma reference.

In the setting of Definition reference, verify for the special case \(R=\Bbbk\) that:

  1. if \(n\) is odd, then \(\mathrm{HP}_n(\Bbbk)=\mathrm{HC}_n(\Bbbk)=0\);

  2. if \(n\) is even (or nonnegative even), then \(\mathrm{HP}_n(\Bbbk)\) (or \(\mathrm{HC}_n(\Bbbk)\)) is isomorphic to \(\Bbbk\).

In the setting of Definition reference and Theorem reference, take the polynomial ring \(R=\Bbbk[t]\).

  1. Prove that \(\Omega_{R\mid\Bbbk}\) in Example reference is a free \(R\)-module of rank \(1\), with basis \(\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}t\).

  2. Describe the connecting morphism \(B:\mathrm{HC}_0(R)\to\mathrm{HH}_1(R)\); note that both sides are isomorphic to \(R\).

  3. Describe all the \(\mathrm{HC}_n(R)\) as explicitly as possible. For \(\Bbbk=\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\), prove that \(\mathrm{HC}_1(\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}[t])=\bigoplus_{n\geq2}\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}/n\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\).

Hint. Use the long exact sequence of Theorem reference and the calculation of \(\operatorname{HH}_n(\Bbbk[t])\) in high degrees in Example reference.

Let \(\mathcal{A}\) be an Abelian category and let \(0\to X\to I^0\to I^1\to\cdots\) be an exact sequence in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})\). Regard \(I=[I^0\to I^1\to\cdots]\) as a double complex, with \(I^{p,q}:=(I^p)^q\). Assuming that \(I\in\operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}^2_f(\mathcal{A}))\), prove that the evident morphism \(X\to\operatorname{tot}(I)\) is a quasi-isomorphism.

Let \(X\in\operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}^2_f(\mathcal{A}))\), where \(\mathcal{A}\) is an Abelian category. Prove that, if the \(i\)-th column \(\left(X^{i,\bullet},\ensuremath{{}^\vartriangle d}\right)\) and the \(j\)-th row \(\left(X^{\bullet,j},\ensuremath{{}^\vartriangleright d}\right)\) are exact for every \(i,j\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\smallsetminus\{0\}\), then for every \(n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\) there is a canonical isomorphism \(\operatorname{H}^n(X^{0,\bullet},\ensuremath{{}^\vartriangle d})\simeq \operatorname{H}^n(X^{\bullet,0},\ensuremath{{}^\vartriangleright d})\). Hint. Define the brutal truncation functor \(\sigma_{\mathrm{I}}^{\leq n}\) (respectively \(\sigma_{\mathrm{I}}^{\geq n}\)) from \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}^2(\mathcal{A})\) to itself by replacing the terms \((X^{i,j})_{(i,j)\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}^2}\) for \(i>n\) (respectively \(i<n\)) by \(0\) and leaving all other terms unchanged. Use Theorem reference to prove that both morphisms in \[\text{$0$-th column} =\sigma_{\mathrm{I}}^{\leq0}\sigma_{\mathrm{I}}^{\geq0}(X) \twoheadleftarrow \sigma_{\mathrm{I}}^{\geq0}X \hookrightarrow X\] induce quasi-isomorphisms on total complexes. Do the same after interchanging the roles of rows and columns.

Use Lemma reference to prove the existence part for \(\beta\) in Theorem reference. Hint. It suffices to treat the first case. The mapping-cylinder lemma, reference, factors \(X\xrightarrow{\alpha}Y\) as \(X\xrightarrow{\alpha'}\operatorname{Cyl}(\alpha)\xrightarrow{\psi}Y\), where \(\alpha'\) is a monomorphism and \(\psi\) is invertible in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{A})\).

With the notation of the preceding exercise, prove the uniqueness part for \(\beta\) in Theorem reference. Hint. It suffices to treat the first case. Use the mapping cylinder again to reduce to the case in which every \(\alpha^n:X^n\hookrightarrow Y^n\) is the inclusion of a direct summand. Suppose the morphisms \(\beta_i:Y\to I\) in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})\), for \(i=1,2\), satisfy \(\gamma-\beta_i\alpha=d^{-1}_{\operatorname{Hom}^\bullet(X,I)}h_i\), where \(h_i\in\operatorname{Hom}^{-1}(X,I)\). Let \(C:=\operatorname{coker}(\alpha)\) be the acyclic complex and define \(h^n:Y^n\simeq X^n\oplus C^n\to I^{n-1}\) so that its restriction to \(X^n\) (respectively \(C^n\)) is \(h_1^n-h_2^n\) (respectively \(0\)). Verify that \[\beta_1-\beta_2-d^{-1}_{\operatorname{Hom}^\bullet(Y,I)}h:Y\to I\] becomes \(0\) after composition with \(\alpha\). Thus, up to homotopy, \(\beta_1-\beta_2\) factors as \(Y\twoheadrightarrow C\to I\); apply Lemma reference to the second morphism.

Let \(\mathcal{A}\) be an Abelian category. Prove that \((\operatorname{H}^n)_{n\geq0}\) is a universal cohomological \(\delta\)-functor from the Abelian category \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}^{\geq0}(\mathcal{A})\) (see Definition reference) to \(\mathcal{A}\). Hint. To show that \(\operatorname{H}^n\) is effaceable when \(n>0\), take \(\alpha(\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_X):X\hookrightarrow\operatorname{Cone}(\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_X)\). This morphism factors through the brutal truncation \(\sigma^{\geq0}\operatorname{Cone}(\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_X)\). Use Proposition reference (i).

(Complex version of the Milnor exact sequence) Let \(R\) be any ring and let \((X_k,f_k)_{k\geq0}\) be an object of \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{InvSys}}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(R\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}))\). Suppose \((X_k^n,f_k^n)_{k\geq0}\) satisfies the Mittag–Leffler condition for every \(n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\). The notation \(f_k\) will henceforth be suppressed. Follow these steps to construct a short exact sequence \[0\to\lim\nolimits^1_k\operatorname{H}^{n-1}(X_k) \to\operatorname{H}^n(\varprojlim_kX_k) \to\varprojlim_k\operatorname{H}^n(X_k)\to0.\]

  1. As in Theorem reference, define \(B_k^n\subset Z_k^n\subset X_k^n\) and \(H_k^n\), and make \(B_k\subset Z_k\subset X_k\) and \(H_k\) complexes with \(d_{B_k}=d_{Z_k}=d_{H_k}=0\). Prove that \((B_k^n)_{k\geq0}\) satisfies the Mittag–Leffler condition for every \(n\).

  2. Prove that \(0\to\varprojlim_kZ_k\to\varprojlim_kX_k \xrightarrow{d}(\varprojlim_kX_k)[1]\) is exact.

  3. Define \(B^n:=\operatorname{im}(d^{n-1}:\varprojlim_kX_k^{n-1}\to \varprojlim_kX_k^n)\)2, and make \(B\) a complex with \(d_B=0\). Prove that there is a short exact sequence \(0\to B[1]\to\varprojlim_kB_k[1]\to\lim\nolimits^1_kZ_k\to0\). Hint. Use the short exact sequence \(0\to Z_k\to X_k\xrightarrow{d}B_k[1]\to0\) and the Mittag–Leffler condition on \((X_k^n)_{k\geq0}\).

  4. Deduce the isomorphism \(\lim\nolimits^1_kZ_k\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}\lim\nolimits^1_kH_k\) and the short exact sequence \(0\to\varprojlim_kB_k\to\varprojlim_kZ_k \to\varprojlim_kH_k\to0\). Hint. Use the short exact sequence \(0\to B_k\to Z_k\to H_k\to0\) and the Mittag–Leffler condition on \((B_k^n)_{k\geq0}\).

  5. Take the appropriate inclusions \(B\subset\varprojlim_kB_k\subset\varprojlim_kZ_k\) and consider the corresponding quotients to obtain the required short exact sequence.

Let \(\Bbbk\) be a field. Define objects \(A\) and \(B\) of \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{InvSys}}(\Bbbk\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}})\) by \(A_k:=X^k\Bbbk\llbracket X\rrbracket\) and \(B_k:=X^k\Bbbk[X]\), taking the transition morphisms to be the inclusions. Neither satisfies the Mittag–Leffler condition. Prove that \(\lim\nolimits^1A=0\), whereas \(\lim\nolimits^1B\simeq \Bbbk\llbracket X\rrbracket/\Bbbk[X]\). Hint. Embed these systems of ideals into systems of rings, and use the dimension-shifting technique of Proposition reference to compute \(\lim\nolimits^1\).

Let \(D\) be a division ring. Prove that \(\operatorname{Ext}_D^n\) and \(\operatorname{Tor}_n^D\) vanish for \(n>0\).

For every ring \(R\), formulate precisely and prove the canonical isomorphism \(\operatorname{Tor}_n^R(X,Y)\simeq\operatorname{Tor}_n^{R^{\operatorname{op}}}(Y,X)\).

Let the integral domain \(R\) be a principal ideal domain. For all finitely generated \(R\)-modules \(M,N\) and every \(n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}_{\geq0}\), describe \(\operatorname{Ext}_R^n(M,N)\) and \(\operatorname{Tor}_n^R(M,N)\) explicitly.

Let \(M\) be a \(\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\)-module. Prove that \(\operatorname{Tor}_1^\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}(\ensuremath{\mathbb{Q}}/\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}},M)\) is the subgroup of \(M\) consisting of all its torsion elements.

(Universal coefficient theorem for cohomology) Let \(R\) be a ring and let \(C=(C_\bullet,d^C_\bullet)\) be a chain complex of left \(R\)-modules. For any left \(R\)-module \(M\), applying \(\operatorname{Hom}_R(\cdot,M)\) termwise gives a cochain complex \(C^\bullet:=\operatorname{Hom}(C_\bullet,M)\); denote its degree-\(n\) cohomology by \(\operatorname{H}^n(C,M)\). Suppose that \(B_n:=\operatorname{im}(d_{n+1})\) and \(Z_n:=\operatorname{ker}(d_n)\) are projective modules for every \(n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\), and define \(H_n:=Z_n/B_n=\operatorname{H}_n(C)\). Prove that, for every \(n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\), there is a canonical short exact sequence \[0\to\operatorname{Ext}_R^1(\operatorname{H}_{n-1}(C),M) \to\operatorname{H}^n(C,M) \to\operatorname{Hom}_R(\operatorname{H}_n(C),M)\to0.\] Prove also that, if \(R\) is a principal ideal domain and every \(C_n\) is free, then these hypotheses always hold. Hint. Define the functor \(D(\cdot):=\operatorname{Hom}_R(\cdot,M)\) from \((R\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}})^{\operatorname{op}}\) to \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ab}}\). Use the short exact sequence \(0\to H_n\to C_n/B_n\to B_{n-1}\to0\) and the hypotheses to obtain a commutative diagram with exact rows \[\text{Diagram chapter3-unit-047-d004}\] Prove that \(d_{D(C)}^{n-1}\) factors as \(D(C_{n-1})\twoheadrightarrow D(Z_{n-1}) \xrightarrow{D(d^C_n)}D(C_n/B_n)\hookrightarrow D(C_n)\) and that \(D(C_n/B_n)\simeq\operatorname{ker}(d_C^n)\). Thus the cokernel of the middle morphism in the diagram is \(\operatorname{H}^n(C,M)\). On the other hand, the sequence \(0\to B_{n-1}\to Z_{n-1}\to H_{n-1}\to0\) shows that the cokernel of the left morphism is \(\operatorname{Ext}_R^1(\operatorname{H}_{n-1}(C),M)\). Apply the snake lemma, Theorem reference.

In the setting of §reference, take \(R=\Bbbk[t]/(t^n)\), where \(t\) is a polynomial variable and \(n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}_{\geq1}\), so that \(R^e=\Bbbk[x,y]/(x^n,y^n)\).3

  1. Prove that the following chain complex is exact: \[\cdots\xrightarrow{v}R^e\xrightarrow{u}R^e \xrightarrow{v}R^e\xrightarrow{u}R^e\to R\to0,\] where \(R^e\to R\) maps \(f(x,y)\) to \(f(t,t)\) and \[u:=x-y,\qquad v:=\sum_{\substack{a+b=n-1\\a,b\geq0}}x^ay^b.\] Deduce that, for every \(R\)-module \(M\), \(\operatorname{HH}_{k+2}(M)\simeq\operatorname{HH}_k(M)\) and \(\operatorname{HH}^{k+2}(M)\simeq\operatorname{HH}^k(M)\).

  2. Let \(\Bbbk\) be a field. Describe \(\operatorname{HH}_k(M)\) and \(\operatorname{HH}^k(M)\), distinguishing the cases \(k\geq1\) and whether \(\mathrm{char}(\Bbbk)\) is relatively prime to \(n\).

For any ring \(R\) and \(n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}_{\geq0}\), prove that \(\operatorname{Tor}_n^R\) commutes with small filtered inductive limits; that is, \[\operatorname{Tor}_n^R(\varinjlim_iX_i,Y) \simeq\varinjlim_i\operatorname{Tor}_n^R(X_i,Y), \qquad \operatorname{Tor}_n^R(X,\varinjlim_iY_i) \simeq\varinjlim_i\operatorname{Tor}_n^R(X,Y_i).\] Discuss whether there is an analogous statement for the \(\operatorname{Ext}\) functors.

Prove that an object \(I\) of an Abelian category \(\mathcal{A}\) is injective if and only if, regarded as a complex, \(I\) is K-injective. State the dual version. Hint. One direction follows from Example reference. For the converse, regard a short exact sequence \(0\to A\to B\to C\to0\) in \(\mathcal{A}\) as an acyclic complex, and construct a morphism from that complex to \(I\) from the given morphism \(A\to I\).

(N. Nitsure) Let \(F:\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{B}\) be a left exact functor between Abelian categories. Suppose \(\mathcal{A}\) has enough injective objects and \(X\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{A})\). Take an injective resolution \(0\to X\to I^0\to I^1\to\cdots\) and an \(F\)-acyclic resolution \(0\to X\to A^0\to A^1\to\cdots\). Write \[I=[\cdots\to0\to I^0\to I^1\to\cdots], \qquad A=[\cdots\to0\to A^0\to A^1\to\cdots].\]

  • Lemma reference determines a unique morphism \(\beta:A\to I\) in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{A})\) compatible with \(A\leftarrow X\rightarrow I\). After applying \(F\), this morphism gives4 \[c^n:=\operatorname{H}^n(F(\beta)): \operatorname{H}^n(F(A))\to\operatorname{H}^n(F(I))=\mathrm{R}^nF(X).\]

  • On the other hand, Corollary reference gives, by dimension shifting, an isomorphism \[d^n:\operatorname{H}^n(F(A))\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}\mathrm{R}^nF(X).\]

Prove that \(d^n=(-1)^{n(n+1)/2}c^n\) for every \(n\geq0\). Hint. This is the content of [Ni09].

  1. More generally, let \(X\) be a complex over an additive category \(\mathcal{A}\). If there are two families of objects \((Y^n)_n\) and \((H^n)_n\) such that \(X^n\simeq Y^n\oplus H^n\oplus Y^{n+1}\) and \(d\) is identified with \(\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}0&0&1\\0&0&0\\0&0&0\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)\), then \(X\) is called split.↩︎

  2. Translator’s note (O014-C067): the source omits the subscript \(k\) from the limit in the codomain, even though the domain, the system under discussion, and the subsequent exact sequence all use \(\varprojlim_k\). The target restores that subscript.↩︎

  3. Translator’s note (O014-C068): the source gives the coefficient ring as \(R[x,y]\). However, for \(R=\Bbbk[t]/(t^n)\), the ring \(R^e=R\otimes_{\Bbbk}R^{\operatorname{op}}\) is canonically \(\Bbbk[x,y]/(x^n,y^n)\). The target restores the required coefficient ring \(\Bbbk\).↩︎

  4. Translator’s note (O014-C069): the source writes \(\operatorname{H}^n(\beta):\operatorname{H}^n(A)\to\operatorname{H}^n(I)\) and, in the following item, \(\operatorname{H}^n(A)\). Since \(F\)-acyclicity is being used to compute the derived functors of \(F\), the morphism and complexes whose cohomology must be taken are \(F(\beta)\), \(F(A)\), and \(F(I)\). The target restores the application of \(F\).↩︎

Triangulated Categories and Derived Categories

Derived categories were pioneered by A. Grothendieck and J.-L. Verdier in the 1960s to study duality theorems in algebraic geometry. Subsequent developments have shown that they provide a convenient and powerful language in geometry, topology, and representation theory alike. The information recorded by the derived category \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}(\mathcal{A})\) of an Abelian category \(\mathcal{A}\) lies between a complex and its cohomology. It is expressed precisely in the language of triangulated categories introduced in §§ 4.1– 4.2: \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}(\mathcal{A})\) is equipped with the translation autoequivalence \(X\mapsto X[1]\) and a class of sequences of morphisms called distinguished triangles (also called exact triangles), \[X \xrightarrow{f} Y \xrightarrow{g} Z \xrightarrow{h} X[1], \quad \text{or, for short,}\quad X\to Y\to Z\xrightarrow{+1} .\] These triangles satisfy axioms (TR0)–(TR5). For example, a distinguished triangle can be rotated into \[Y \xrightarrow{g} Z \xrightarrow{h} X[1] \xrightarrow{-f[1]} Y[1] \quad\text{or}\quad Z[-1] \xrightarrow{-h[-1]} X \xrightarrow{f} Y \xrightarrow{g} Z .\] Distinguished triangles replace short exact sequences in the category of complexes \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})\), though the more accurate analogy is with cofiber sequences in homotopy theory. Cohomological functors from a triangulated category to an Abelian category provide a mechanism for producing long exact sequences from distinguished triangles. The passage from \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})\) to \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}(\mathcal{A})\) is the subject of § 4.4 and proceeds in two steps.

  1. The first step passes from \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})\) to \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{A})\). The latter is equipped with the translation functor \(X\mapsto X[1]\) and the structure of a triangulated category. For every morphism \(f:X\to Y\), its mapping cone together with the canonical morphisms \[X \xrightarrow{f} Y \xrightarrow{\alpha(f)} \operatorname{Cone}(f) \xrightarrow{\beta(f)} X[1]\] forms the corresponding distinguished triangle, up to isomorphism. The tools needed for this step were prepared in the first half of .

  2. The second step formally adjoins inverses to all quasi-isomorphisms, or equivalently, formally makes every acyclic complex zero, by localization. The result is \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}(\mathcal{A})\), which has the same collection of objects as \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})\) and inherits its triangulated structure from \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{A})\). This step rests on the general theory of Verdier localization in § 4.3. It is here that the octahedral axiom (TR5), the most intricate axiom in the definition of a triangulated category, plays its role.

Taking cohomology of complexes gives the cohomological functor \(\operatorname{H}^0:\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}(\mathcal{A})\to\mathcal{A}\) at the level of the derived category, with \(\operatorname{H}^n(X):=\operatorname{H}^0(X[n])\). Starting instead from the category of bounded-below (or bounded-above, or bounded) complexes, the same procedure gives the triangulated category \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^+(\mathcal{A})\) (or \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^-(\mathcal{A})\), or \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^{\ensuremath{\mathrm{b}}}(\mathcal{A})\)). These may also be regarded as full triangulated subcategories of \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}(\mathcal{A})\), characterized respectively by \(n\ll0\) (or \(n\gg0\), or \(|n|\gg0\)) \(\implies\operatorname{H}^n(X)=0\). More generally, cohomology-vanishing conditions can be used to define the full subcategories \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^{\geq0}(\mathcal{A})\) and \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^{\leq0}(\mathcal{A})\) of \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}(\mathcal{A})\), and the truncation functors on complexes can still be defined on the derived category. The canonical functor \(\mathcal{A}\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}(\mathcal{A})\) is fully faithful and identifies \(\mathcal{A}\) with \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^{\leq0}(\mathcal{A})\cap\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^{\geq0}(\mathcal{A})\). If \(\mathcal{A}\) has enough injective or projective objects, then \(\operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}(\mathcal{A})}(X,Y[n])\simeq \operatorname{Ext}^n_{\mathcal{A}}(X,Y)\), where \(X\) and \(Y\) are objects of \(\mathcal{A}\) viewed as complexes concentrated in degree zero. 1 The definition of \(\operatorname{Ext}^n_{\mathcal{A}}\) is given in § reference, and all these matters are treated in § 4.5. For a left exact functor \(F:\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{A}'\), its classical right derived functor is realized at the level of bounded-below derived categories as \(\mathrm{R}F:\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^+(\mathcal{A})\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^+(\mathcal{A}')\). It can be characterized as a left Kan extension; the relevant data are expressed by the following \(2\)-cell diagram. \[\text{Diagram chapter4-unit-048-d001}\]

Here \(Q\) and \(Q'\) denote the localization functors, while \(\mathrm{R}F\) must also be equipped with a triangulated-functor structure. The classical \(\mathrm{R}^nF\) is obtained by restricting \(\mathrm{R}F\) to \(\mathcal{A}\) and then taking \(\operatorname{H}^n\). If instead \(F\) is right exact, the lift of the classical left derived functor \(\mathrm{L}_nF\) is represented as follows. 2 \[\text{Diagram chapter4-unit-048-d002}\] As in the classical theory, the existence of derived functors and the detailed structure of derived categories depend on resolutions of complexes. Resolutions provide the scaffolding needed to work concretely with derived categories. Details appear in §§ 4.6– 4.8. The unbounded version \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}(\mathcal{A})\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}(\mathcal{A}')\) has a similar formulation and will be discussed in § 4.11. By considering the amplitude of a derived functor, that is, the “shift” it produces at the level of cohomology, one can discuss the dimension of a derived functor (Definition–Proposition in § 4.7). Under suitable conditions, taking derived functors is also compatible with composition (Theorem in § 4.8). This provides a uniform explanation for several spectral sequences in the classical theory, called Grothendieck spectral sequences and described in Theorem in § 4.8. The general theory of spectral sequences is deferred to Chapter 5. All these constructions can be formulated for general triangulated categories and their Verdier localizations. It is worth noting that applications often involve triangulated categories that do not arise directly from Abelian categories, or cohomological functors other than \(\operatorname{H}^n\). In this general setting, the roles of truncation functors and of \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^{\leq0}\) and \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^{\geq0}\) are taken by a \(t\)-structure on the triangulated category, but this book does not treat that topic. The derived functors discussed concretely in this chapter are limited to examples arising in algebra. The first is the functor \(\operatorname{RHom}\) in § 4.9. This is the derived-category version of the \(\operatorname{Ext}\) functor and involves the theory of derived bifunctors. Several adjunctions will also be lifted to derived categories, following the principle of replacing \(\operatorname{Hom}\) by \(\operatorname{RHom}\). Next, § 4.10 treats products and coproducts in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}(\mathcal{A})\) and then introduces the lift of \(\lim^n\), denoted \(\mathrm{R}\lim\). Like \(\lim^n\), this functor has a concise description in terms of the homotopy limit (Definition in § 4.10), though at the level of derived categories the description can only be given in a coarse form. Then § 4.12 introduces the derived-category version of the \(\operatorname{Tor}\) functor, namely the derived tensor product \(\ensuremath{\underset{}{\overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes}}}\), a triangulated bifunctor. That section also proves many facts, including the associativity constraint (Proposition in § 4.12) and the \(\operatorname{RHom}\) version of the adjunction (Theorem in § 4.12). As in the classical theory, \(\operatorname{RHom}\) and \(\ensuremath{\underset{}{\overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes}}}\) are the two fundamental examples of derived functors. A complete and clean description requires unbounded derived categories and the derived functors between them. This in turn requires the theory of § 4.11, especially the notions of K-projective and K-flat resolutions. In the module-theoretic setting considered here, the existence of these resolutions poses no problem. Finally, several shortcomings of the derived category \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}(\mathcal{A})\) should be noted.

  1. Among the axioms of a triangulated category, (TR2) says that every morphism can be placed in a distinguished triangle. Such a triangle is unique up to isomorphism, but not “up to unique isomorphism” in the sense familiar from algebra.

  2. Triangulated categories usually have neither kernels nor cokernels, making the operations \(\varinjlim\) and \(\varprojlim\) extremely difficult to carry out. Mapping cones provide substitutes in the homotopical sense, but, as already noted, their uniqueness in the derived category is problematic.

  3. Although derived functors at the level of derived categories have a clear definition, unlike universal cohomological \(\delta\)-functors they are difficult to characterize simply by effaceability; see Proposition reference.

The root of the problem is that the homotopy relation is erased too crudely when \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}(\mathcal{A})\) is constructed. These shortcomings must be remedied by a construction that is higher than the derived category and perhaps also more natural; the derived category should be only the shadow cast by that construction.

  1. Translator’s note (O014-C071): the source describes \(X\) and \(Y\) as complexes over \(\mathcal{A}\). The fully faithful embedding \(\mathcal{A}\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}(\mathcal{A})\) in the preceding sentence and the definition of \(\operatorname{Ext}^n_{\mathcal{A}}\) in § reference, however, give this formula for objects of \(\mathcal{A}\) viewed as degree-zero complexes; the intended scope has been restored here.↩︎

  2. Translator’s note (O014-C070): in the following diagram, the source labels the right vertical arrow \(Q\), even though its source and target are \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}^-(\mathcal{A}')\) and \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^-(\mathcal{A}')\), respectively. In accord with the preceding diagram and the names used in the prose, the label \(Q'\) has been restored here.↩︎

Definition of a Triangulated Category

A triangulated category is an additive category with translation, equipped with a class of distinguished triangles. We begin by explaining what a category with translation is.

Definition. A category with translation is data \((\mathcal{D},T)\) consisting of a category \(\mathcal{D}\) and an equivalence \(T:\mathcal{D}\to\mathcal{D}\). 1 The equivalence \(T\) is called the translation functor of \(\mathcal{D}\). In addition, choose a quasi-inverse \(T^{-1}\) of \(T\) and isomorphisms \(T^{-1}T\simeq\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{\mathcal D}\simeq TT^{-1}\) so that these data form an adjoint equivalence in the sense of [Li1].

  • A functor from \((\mathcal{D},T)\) to \((\mathcal{D}',T')\) is a functor \(F:\mathcal{D}\to\mathcal{D}'\) together with a chosen isomorphism \(FT\simeq T'F\). By convention, the isomorphism is suppressed and these data are abbreviated as \(F:(\mathcal{D},T)\to(\mathcal{D}',T')\).

  • A morphism between two functors \(\text{Diagram chapter4-unit-049-diagram-001}\) is a morphism \(\varphi:F\to F'\) that makes the following diagram commute: \[\text{Diagram chapter4-unit-049-d001}\]

  • A subcategory of a category with translation \((\mathcal{D},T)\) is a subcategory \(\mathcal{D}'\) of \(\mathcal{D}\) that is closed under \(T\) and for which \(T':=T|_{\mathcal{D}'}\) makes \((\mathcal{D}',T')\) a category with translation.

If \(\mathcal{D}\) is additive and \(T\) is an additive functor (as it is automatically; see Corollary reference), then \((\mathcal{D},T)\) is called an additive category with translation; functors between such categories are also required to be additive. After fixing a commutative ring \(\Bbbk\), the same definition applies in the \(\Bbbk\)-linear setting.

If \((\mathcal{D},T)\) is a category with translation, then so is \((\mathcal{D}^{\operatorname{op}},T^{-1})\). By convention, the data \((\mathcal{D},T)\) are often abbreviated to \(\mathcal{D}\). The following notion is particularly useful.

Definition (Morphisms with degree). A morphism of degree \(m\) in a category with translation \((\mathcal{D},T)\) is a morphism of the form \(f:X\to T^mY\), also written \(f:X\xrightarrow{+m}Y\). Given \(X\xrightarrow[f]{+m}Y\xrightarrow[g]{+n}Z\), their composite \(gf\) is defined to be the morphism of degree \(m+n\) given by \(T^m(g)f\). Commutative diagrams can likewise be considered for morphisms of this kind.

In the multivariable setting, suppose that \(\mathcal{D}\) is equipped with strictly commuting automorphisms \(T_1,\ldots,T_n\), so that \(T_iT_j=T_jT_i\). A morphism of degree \((m_1,\ldots,m_n)\) is defined to be a morphism of the form \(X\to T_1^{m_1}\cdots T_n^{m_n}Y\). It is written \(X\xrightarrow{+(m_1,\ldots,m_n)}Y\).

For example, given a category \(\mathcal{A}\), the category \((\mathcal{A}^{\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}},T)\) of graded objects from Definition reference is a category with translation. More generally, one can consider the category \(\mathcal{A}^{\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}^n}\) of \(\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}^n\)-graded objects, together with a translation functor \(T_1,\ldots,T_n\) in each variable, and then discuss morphisms with degree between \(\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}^n\)-graded objects. The multivariable case, however, is not a focus of this chapter.

Example. The category of complexes \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})\) over an additive category \(\mathcal{A}\), together with the translation functor \(T:X\mapsto X[1]\) from Definition reference, is an additive category with translation. The category \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{A})\) from Definition reference inherits the translation functor from \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})\), which is still denoted by \(T\). The canonical functor \(F:\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{A})\) plainly satisfies \(FT=TF\). The same applies, for every \(\star\in\{+,-,\ensuremath{\mathrm{b}}\}\), to the categories \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}^{\star}(\mathcal{A})\) (or \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}^{\star}(\mathcal{A})\)) introduced in Definition reference (or Definition reference).

In this chapter we mainly consider additive categories with translation.

Definition. Let \((\mathcal{D},T)\) be an additive category with translation. A triangle in it is a sequence of morphisms in \(\mathcal{D}\) of the form \[X\xrightarrow{f}Y\xrightarrow{g}Z\xrightarrow{h}TX.\] A morphism between two triangles is a commutative diagram of the form \[\text{Diagram chapter4-unit-049-d002}\] The two rows are the given triangles. Such a morphism is also abbreviated to \((X,Y,Z)\to(X',Y',Z')\). Isomorphisms between triangles are defined in the same way. The same notion is available if the additive category is replaced by a more general \(\Bbbk\)-linear category, where \(\Bbbk\) is any commutative ring.

Clearly, triangles in \((\mathcal{D},T)\) are the same as triangles in \((\mathcal{D}^{\operatorname{op}},T^{-1})\).

Remark. Consider a triangle \(X\xrightarrow{f}Y\xrightarrow{g}Z\xrightarrow{h}TX\) in a \(\Bbbk\)-linear category with translation \((\mathcal{D},T)\), and let \(\epsilon,\zeta,\eta\in\Bbbk^\times\). If \(\epsilon\zeta\eta=1\), then the original triangle is isomorphic to \(X\xrightarrow{\epsilon f}Y\xrightarrow{\zeta g}Z \xrightarrow{\eta h}TX\), as shown by the commutative diagram \[\text{Diagram chapter4-unit-049-d003}\]

In the notation of Definition reference, a triangle can also be written \(X\to Y\to Z\xrightarrow{+1}\), or more pictorially as \(\text{Diagram chapter4-unit-049-diagram-005}\). Thus a triangle may be pictured as an upward-spiraling chain, while a morphism between triangles resembles the structure of deoxyribonucleic acid: the arrows \(\alpha\), \(\beta\), \(\gamma\), and so forth can be compared to the hydrogen bonds between bases.

Definition ( and ). A triangulated category is an additive category with translation \((\mathcal{D},T)\) equipped with a class \(\mathcal{H}\) of triangles, called distinguished triangles, satisfying the following axioms.

  1. Every triangle isomorphic to a distinguished triangle is distinguished.

  2. For every \(X\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{D})\), the triangle \(X\xrightarrow{\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_X}X\to0\to TX\) is distinguished.

  3. Every morphism \(f:X\to Y\) can be extended to a distinguished triangle of the form \(X\xrightarrow{f}Y\to Z\to TX\), where \(Z\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{D})\).

  4. A triangle \(X\xrightarrow{f}Y\xrightarrow{g}Z\xrightarrow{h}TX\) is distinguished if and only if its “counterclockwise rotation” \[Y\xrightarrow{g}Z\xrightarrow{h}TX\xrightarrow{-Tf}TY\] is distinguished. The sign pattern may equivalently be chosen as \((-++)\), \((+-+)\), or \((---)\); see Remark reference.

  5.
