Suppose the solid part of the following diagram is commutative: \[\text{Diagram chapter4-unit-049-d004}\] If both rows are distinguished triangles, there exists a morphism \(\gamma:Z\to Z'\) as indicated by the dashed arrow such that the whole diagram containing \(\alpha\), \(\beta\), \(\gamma\), and \(T\alpha\) commutes. Thus one obtains a morphism of triangles.

  6. Suppose that distinguished triangles \[\begin{gather*} X\xrightarrow{f}Y\xrightarrow{h}Z'\to TX,\\ Y\xrightarrow{g}Z\xrightarrow{k}X'\to TY,\\ X\xrightarrow{gf}Z\xrightarrow{m}Y'\to TX \end{gather*}\] are given. There exists a distinguished triangle \[Z'\xrightarrow{u}Y'\xrightarrow{v}X'\xrightarrow{w}TZ'\] such that the following diagram commutes: \[\text{Diagram chapter4-unit-049-d005}\]

Data \((\mathcal{D},T,\mathcal{H})\) satisfying only (TR0)–(TR4) are called a pretriangulated category. The data \(T\) and \(\mathcal{H}\) are often omitted from the notation. A triangulated functor from \(\mathcal{D}\) to \(\mathcal{D}'\) is a functor \(F:\mathcal{D}\to\mathcal{D}'\) between additive categories with translation that maps distinguished triangles to distinguished triangles. Morphisms between triangulated functors are the same as the morphisms in Definition reference; this also defines a quasi-inverse of a triangulated functor. If two triangulated functors \(\text{Diagram chapter4-unit-049-diagram-008}\) are quasi-inverse to one another, they are said to form an equivalence between \(\mathcal{D}\) and \(\mathcal{D}'\).

If \((\mathcal{D},T)\) is \(\Bbbk\)-linear, all the definitions above have corresponding extensions.

Remark. In the notation of Definition reference, axiom (TR5) can be rewritten as the diagram \[\text{Diagram chapter4-unit-049-d006}\] The dashed part represents the morphisms whose existence is asserted by the axiom. Four faces of this octahedron are distinguished triangles, and the other four faces are commutative; the details are left to the reader. For this reason, (TR5) is also called the octahedral axiom.

Remark (Duality). Let \((\mathcal{D},T,\mathcal{H})\) be a pretriangulated (or triangulated) category. Regard \(T^{-1}\) as an endofunctor of \(\mathcal{D}^{\operatorname{op}}\) and denote it by \(S\). Define a class of triangles \(\mathcal{K}\) on \((\mathcal{D}^{\operatorname{op}},S)\) as follows. If \[[X\xrightarrow{f}Y\xrightarrow{g}Z\xrightarrow{h}TX] \;\in\mathcal{H},\] then its clockwise rotation \([T^{-1}Z\xrightarrow{-T^{-1}h}X\xrightarrow{f}Y\xrightarrow{g}Z] \in\mathcal{H}\) may be regarded as the following triangle in \(\mathcal{D}^{\operatorname{op}}\): \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:op-triangle}{} Z\xrightarrow{g^{\operatorname{op}}}Y\xrightarrow{f^{\operatorname{op}}}X \xrightarrow{-(T^{-1}h)^{\operatorname{op}}}SZ. \end{equation}\] Define \(\mathcal{K}\) to be the class of all triangles of the form equation. It is straightforward to verify that \((\mathcal{D}^{\operatorname{op}},S,\mathcal{K})\) is a pretriangulated (or triangulated) category. It is also clear that applying this procedure twice recovers the original \((\mathcal{D},T,\mathcal{H})\).

The notions of pretriangulated subcategory and triangulated subcategory will be introduced in Definition–Proposition in § 4.2; we postpone their discussion until then.

  1. Many references require \(T\) to be an automorphism. In that case one may choose an inverse functor \(T^{-1}\) satisfying \(T^{-1}T=\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{\mathcal D}=TT^{-1}\). This condition covers every situation treated in this book and avoids possible subtleties from \(2\)-category theory, so the reader may harmlessly make the same assumption. The study of stable model categories or stable \(\infty\)-categories, however, cannot avoid the case in which the equivalence is not an isomorphism, especially in topology.↩︎

Lemma. If \(X \xrightarrow{f} Y \xrightarrow{g} Z \xrightarrow{+1}\) is a distinguished triangle in a pretriangulated category, then \(gf=0\).

Proof. Axioms (TR1) and (TR4) give the commutative diagram \[\text{Diagram chapter4-unit-050-d001}\] from which \(gf=0\) is immediate.

Definition (Cohomological functor). Let \(\mathcal{D}\) be a pretriangulated category and \(\mathcal{A}\) an Abelian category. An additive functor \(H: \mathcal{D} \to \mathcal{A}\) is called a cohomological functor if it has the following property: for every distinguished triangle \(X \to Y \to Z \xrightarrow{+1}\) in \(\mathcal{D}\), the corresponding sequence \(HX \to HY \to HZ\) is exact in \(\mathcal{A}\).

Remark (Long exact sequence of a cohomological functor). For a cohomological functor \(H\) and any distinguished triangle \(X \to Y \to Z \xrightarrow{+1}\) in \(\mathcal{D}\), repeated rotation by (TR3) extends the exact sequence in Definition reference to the long exact sequence \[\cdots \to HT^{-1}Z \to HX \to HY \to HZ \to HTX \to HTY \to \cdots .\] Rotating the triangle introduces some minus signs, but these do not affect the exactness of the sequence above.

The basic examples of cohomological functors are the \(\operatorname{Hom}\) functors.

Proposition. Let \(\mathcal{D}\) be a pretriangulated category and let \(S\) be an object of \(\mathcal{D}\). Then both \(\operatorname{Hom}(S, \cdot): \mathcal{D} \to \ensuremath{\mathsf{Ab}}\) and \(\operatorname{Hom}(\cdot, S): \mathcal{D}^{\operatorname{op}} \to \ensuremath{\mathsf{Ab}}\) are cohomological functors.

If \((\mathcal{D}, T)\) is \(\Bbbk\)-linear, the corresponding assertion holds with \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ab}}\) replaced by \(\Bbbk\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\).

Proof. By duality it suffices to prove the assertion for \(\operatorname{Hom}(S, \cdot)\). Consider a distinguished triangle \(X \xrightarrow{f} Y \xrightarrow{g} Z \xrightarrow{+1}\) and the corresponding sequence \[\operatorname{Hom}(S, X) \xrightarrow{f_*} \operatorname{Hom}(S, Y) \xrightarrow{g_*} \operatorname{Hom}(S, Z).\] Lemma reference implies \(g_* f_* = (gf)_* = 0\). Conversely, suppose that \(h \in \operatorname{Hom}(S, Y)\) satisfies \(g_*(h) = gh = 0\), and consider the following diagram, whose solid part is commutative. 1 \[\text{Diagram chapter4-unit-050-d002}\] If a morphism \(k: S \to X\) can be found as indicated by the dashed arrow so that the entire diagram commutes, then \(f_*(k) = h\). Axiom (TR1) ensures that both rows are distinguished triangles. After applying suitable rotations (TR3), the existence of \(k\) follows from (TR4).

Corollary. In a pretriangulated category, if a triangle has the form \(X \xrightarrow{f} Y \to 0 \xrightarrow{+1}\), then \(f\) must be an isomorphism.

Proof. For every object \(S\), Proposition reference gives an exact sequence in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ab}}\) \[\underbracket{\operatorname{Hom}(S, T^{-1} 0)}_{= 0} \to \operatorname{Hom}(S, X) \xrightarrow{f_*} \operatorname{Hom}(S, Y) \to \underbracket{\operatorname{Hom}(S, 0)}_{= 0},\] so \(f_*\) is an isomorphism. Since \(S\) is arbitrary, \(f\) is an isomorphism.

  1. Translator’s note (O014-C072): at the vertex \(TS\), the source draws two coincident dashed arrows to \(TX\), one unlabeled and one labeled \(Tk\). A morphism of triangles has only the single component \(Tk\) in this position; the redundant unlabeled arrow has been removed here.↩︎

Basic Properties

The preceding section gave only the definitions and initial properties of triangulated categories and cohomological functors. This section develops their structure further.

Proposition. Consider the following commutative diagram in a pretriangulated category \(\mathcal{D}\): \[\text{Diagram chapter4-unit-051-d001}\] If each row is a distinguished triangle and any two of \(\alpha\), \(\beta\), and \(\gamma\) are isomorphisms, then the remaining morphism is also an isomorphism.

Proof. After suitable rotations (TR3), we may assume without loss of generality that \(\alpha\) and \(\gamma\) are isomorphisms. To show that \(\beta\) is an isomorphism, it suffices to prove, for every object \(S\), that \(\operatorname{Hom}(S, Y) \xrightarrow{\beta_*} \operatorname{Hom}(S, Y')\) is an isomorphism. Proposition reference gives the following commutative diagram with exact rows: \[\text{Diagram chapter4-unit-051-d002}\] Now apply Proposition reference.

In the argument above, \(\operatorname{Hom}(S, \cdot)\) may also be replaced by \(\operatorname{Hom}(\cdot, S)\).

Remark. For the moment, call a triangle \(X \to Y \to Z \xrightarrow{+1}\) a special triangle (or a cospecial triangle) if, for every \(S \in \operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{D})\), the sequence \[\cdots \to \operatorname{Hom}(S, X) \to \operatorname{Hom}(S, Y) \to \operatorname{Hom}(S, Z) \to \operatorname{Hom}(S, TX) \to \cdots\] (or the corresponding version with \(\operatorname{Hom}(\cdot, S)\)) is exact. If \(X_i \to Y_i \to Z_i \xrightarrow{+1}\) is a family of distinguished triangles (\(i \in I\)), then \(\prod_i X_i \to \prod_i Y_i \to \prod_i Z_i \xrightarrow{+1}\) (or \(\coprod_i X_i \to \coprod_i Y_i \to \coprod_i Z_i \xrightarrow{+1}\)) is a special triangle (or a cospecial triangle), provided the products (or coproducts) in question exist. This follows simply from the universal properties of products and coproducts together with [Li1]. Notice that because \(T: \mathcal{D} \to \mathcal{D}\) is an equivalence, it necessarily preserves products and coproducts. Proposition reference extends to the case in which both rows are special (or cospecial) triangles.

Corollary. For every morphism \(f: X \to Y\) in a pretriangulated category \(\mathcal{D}\), the distinguished triangle \(X \xrightarrow{f} Y \to Z \xrightarrow{+1}\) in axiom (TR2) is unique up to isomorphism.

Proof. Given distinguished triangles \(X \xrightarrow{f} Y \to Z \xrightarrow{+1}\) and \(X \xrightarrow{f} Y \to Z' \xrightarrow{+1}\), axiom (TR4) gives a morphism \(\gamma\) that makes the diagram \[\text{Diagram chapter4-unit-051-d003}\] commute. Proposition reference then implies that \(\gamma\) is an isomorphism.

It must be emphasized that the isomorphism in Corollary reference is not canonical.

Lemma. Let \(\mathcal{D}\) be a pretriangulated category and let \(X_i \xrightarrow{f_i} Y_i \xrightarrow{g_i} Z_i \xrightarrow{h_i} TX_i\) be a family of distinguished triangles. Suppose that \(\prod_i X_i\), \(\prod_i Y_i\), and \(\prod_i Z_i\) all exist. Then \[\prod_{i \in I} X_i \xrightarrow{\prod_i f_i } \prod_{i \in I} Y_i \xrightarrow{\prod_i g_i} \prod_{i \in I} Z_i \xrightarrow{\prod_i h_i} \underbracket{\prod_{i \in I} TX_i}_{\simeq T(\prod_{i \in I} X_i)}\] is also a distinguished triangle. The corresponding assertion holds with \(\prod_{i \in I}\) replaced by \(\coprod_{i \in I}\).

Proof. By duality, we need only treat the case of \(\prod_{i \in I}\). From now on we always identify \(\prod_i TX_i\) with \(T(\prod_i X_i)\). By (TR2), choose a distinguished triangle \(\prod_i X_i \xrightarrow{\prod_i f_i} \prod_i Y_i \to Q \xrightarrow{h} \prod_i TX_i\). For every \(i \in I\), apply (TR4) to obtain a commutative diagram \[\text{Diagram chapter4-unit-051-d004}\] in which all vertical morphisms other than \(\gamma_i\) are the canonical projections. The universal property of the product then gives a commutative diagram \[\text{Diagram chapter4-unit-051-d005}\] The second row is a special triangle in the sense of Remark reference. The extended version of Proposition reference now implies that \(\prod_{i \in I} \gamma_i\) is an isomorphism.

Corollary. In every pretriangulated category, a triangle of the form \(X \xrightarrow{\iota_1} X \oplus Y \xrightarrow{p_2} Y \xrightarrow{0} TX\) is always distinguished; here \(\iota_i\) and \(p_j\) are defined as in §reference.

Proof. Apply Lemma reference to the distinguished triangles \(X \xrightarrow{\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_X} X \to 0 \to TX\) and \(0 \to Y \xrightarrow{\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_Y} Y \to 0\).

Conversely, if one morphism in a distinguished triangle is \(0\), then the triangle comes from a direct sum. This fact can be verified by rotating the triangle into the following form.

Proposition. In every pretriangulated category, a distinguished triangle of the form \(X \to M \to Y \xrightarrow{0} TX\) must be isomorphic to the triangle \(X \to X \oplus Y \to Y \xrightarrow{0} TX\) from Corollary reference.

Proof. A suitably rotated version of (TR4) shows that there is a morphism \(\alpha: X \oplus Y \to M\) such that the following diagram is a morphism of distinguished triangles: \[\text{Diagram chapter4-unit-051-d006}\] Proposition reference implies that \(\alpha\) is an isomorphism.

The next result shows that additivity in the definition of a triangulated functor is actually redundant.

Corollary. Let \(\mathcal{D}\) and \(\mathcal{D}'\) be pretriangulated categories, with both translation functors denoted by \(T\). Let \(F: (\mathcal{D}, T) \to (\mathcal{D}', T)\) be a functor between categories with translation. If \(F\) maps distinguished triangles to distinguished triangles, then \(F\) is additive and hence is automatically a triangulated functor.

Proof. The distinguished triangle \(0 \xrightarrow{\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}} 0 \xrightarrow{\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}} 0 \xrightarrow{\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}} 0\) in \(\mathcal{D}\) gives the distinguished triangle \(F(0) \xrightarrow{\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}} F(0) \xrightarrow{\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}} F(0) \xrightarrow{\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}} F(0)\) in \(\mathcal{D}'\). Lemma reference then gives \(\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{F(0)} = \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{F(0)} \circ \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{F(0)} = 0\), so \(F(0) \simeq 0\). This also implies that \(F\) maps zero morphisms to zero morphisms.

Next consider the distinguished triangle in \(\mathcal{D}\) supplied by Corollary reference, namely \(X \xrightarrow{\iota_1} X \oplus Y \xrightarrow{p_2} Y \xrightarrow{0} TX\). The corresponding triangle \[FX \xrightarrow{F\iota_1} F(X \oplus Y) \xrightarrow{Fp_2} FY \xrightarrow{0} TFX\] is distinguished in \(\mathcal{D}'\). Take \(M := F(X \oplus Y)\) in Proposition reference. The morphism \(\alpha\) in the proof of that proposition can clearly be taken to be the canonical morphism \(FX \oplus FY \to F(X \oplus Y)\) determined by the universal property of the direct sum. Thus \(\alpha\) is an isomorphism. By Corollary reference (iii), \(F\) is additive.

The next two results show that, in an equivalence of pretriangulated categories (Definition reference), it is enough to assume that the functor in one direction is triangulated. This is another application of Proposition reference.

Proposition. Let \(\mathcal{D}\) and \(\mathcal{D}'\) be pretriangulated categories, and consider functors \(\text{Diagram chapter4-unit-051-diagram-007}\) such that \((F, G)\) is an adjunction. Then \(F\) is a triangulated functor if and only if \(G\) is a triangulated functor. In this case the unit \(\eta: \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{\mathcal{D}} \to GF\) and counit \(\varepsilon: FG \to \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{\mathcal{D}'}\) of the adjunction are compatible with the translation functors; see Definition reference.

Proof. By duality, it suffices to consider the case in which \(F\) is a triangulated functor. Corollary reference shows that \(G\) is additive. Denote both translation functors on \(\mathcal{D}\) and \(\mathcal{D}'\) by \(T\). Transporting the structure gives a new adjunction \[\hat{F} := T F T^{-1}, \quad \hat{G} := T G T^{-1}, \quad \hat{\eta} := T\eta T^{-1}, \quad \hat{\varepsilon} := T \varepsilon T^{-1}.\] Since \(\hat{F} \simeq F\), uniqueness of right adjoints [Li1] gives a corresponding isomorphism \(\hat{G} \simeq G\) and commutative diagrams \[\text{Diagram chapter4-unit-051-d007} \quad \text{Diagram chapter4-unit-051-d008}\] In particular, \(GT \simeq TG\) and \(FGT \simeq FTG \simeq TFG\). After composing the commutative diagram for \(\hat{\varepsilon}\) and \(\varepsilon\) on the right with \(T\), it can be rewritten as \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:adjoint-triangulated-aux0}{}\text{Diagram chapter4-unit-051-d009} \end{equation}\] This equation and its dual version for \(\eta\) show that \(\eta\) and \(\varepsilon\) are compatible with the translation functors.

We now show that \(G\) preserves distinguished triangles. Consider a distinguished triangle \(X \xrightarrow{f} Y \xrightarrow{g} Z \xrightarrow{+1}\) in \(\mathcal{D}'\). Choose a distinguished triangle \(GX \xrightarrow{Gf} GY \xrightarrow{h} A \xrightarrow{+1}\) in \(\mathcal{D}\), apply \(F\) to it, and then use (TR3) to obtain the commutative diagram \[\begin{equation*} \text{Diagram chapter4-unit-051-d010} \end{equation*}\]

Apply the adjunction to this diagram, and adjust the rightmost square using equation and \(GT \simeq TG\). One readily obtains a commutative diagram \[\text{Diagram chapter4-unit-051-d011}\] whose first row is a distinguished triangle. For every \(B \in \operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{D})\), apply \(\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{D}}(B, \cdot)\) to obtain a commutative diagram \[\text{Diagram chapter4-unit-051-d012}\] Proposition reference shows that the first row is exact. On the other hand, by \(TG \simeq GT\) and the adjunction, the second row is isomorphic to the sequence induced by the distinguished triangle \(X \xrightarrow{f} Y \xrightarrow{g} Z \xrightarrow{+1}\), namely \[\text{Diagram chapter4-unit-051-d013}\] and hence is also exact. Since \(B\) is arbitrary, Proposition reference implies that \(A \to GZ\) is an isomorphism. Thus \(GX \xrightarrow{Gf} GY \xrightarrow{Gg} GZ \to TGX\) is indeed a distinguished triangle in \(\mathcal{D}\).

Corollary. Let \(\mathcal{D}\) and \(\mathcal{D}'\) be pretriangulated categories and let the functors \(\text{Diagram chapter4-unit-051-diagram-015}\) be quasi-inverse to one another. Then:

  1. \(F\) is a triangulated functor if and only if \(G\) is a triangulated functor;

  2. if \(F\) is a triangulated functor, then \(F\) and \(G\) give an equivalence of the pretriangulated categories.

Proof. Use [Li1] to realize \((F, G)\) and \((G, F)\) as adjunctions, and then apply Proposition reference.

Definition–Proposition (Pretriangulated subcategories). Let \(\mathcal{D}'\) be a full additive subcategory of a pretriangulated category \(\mathcal{D}\) that is closed under the translation functor \(T\). Denote the inclusion functor by \(\iota: \mathcal{D}' \to \mathcal{D}\).

  1. If a pretriangulated structure on \(\mathcal{D}'\) making \(\iota\) a triangulated functor exists, it is unique. In this case, a triangle \(X \to Y \to Z \xrightarrow{+1}\) in \(\mathcal{D}'\) is distinguished if and only if it is distinguished in \(\mathcal{D}\).

  2. This pretriangulated structure exists if and only if the following condition holds: whenever \(X \to Y \to Z \xrightarrow{+1}\) is a distinguished triangle in \(\mathcal{D}\) and any two of its terms belong to \(\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{D}')\), the remaining term is isomorphic to an object of \(\mathcal{D}'\).

  3. If, in addition, \(\mathcal{D}\) is assumed to be triangulated, then \(\mathcal{D}'\) is also triangulated.

Such a pretriangulated (or triangulated) category \(\mathcal{D}'\) is called a pretriangulated subcategory (or triangulated subcategory) of \(\mathcal{D}\).

Proof. First consider (i). Suppose that \(\iota\) is triangulated. Every distinguished triangle in \(\mathcal{D}'\) is of course distinguished in \(\mathcal{D}\). Conversely, suppose that a distinguished triangle \(X \xrightarrow{f} Y \to Z \xrightarrow{+1}\) in \(\mathcal{D}\) satisfies \(X, Y, Z \in \operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{D}')\). Choose any distinguished triangle \(X \xrightarrow{f} Y \to Z' \xrightarrow{+1}\) in \(\mathcal{D}'\). Applying Corollary reference in \(\mathcal{D}\) shows that the two triangles are isomorphic. Since \(\mathcal{D}'\) is full, (TR0) implies that \(X \xrightarrow{f} Y \to Z \xrightarrow{+1}\) is also distinguished in \(\mathcal{D}'\). This is precisely the pretriangulated structure asserted in (i).

If this pretriangulated structure exists, then Corollary reference shows that the condition in (ii) is necessary, since after rotation we may always assume that \(X, Y \in \operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{D}')\). Conversely, assume the condition in (ii) and define the distinguished triangles in \(\mathcal{D}'\) as stated in (i). Axioms (TR0), (TR1), (TR3), and (TR4) for \(\mathcal{D}'\) are inherited directly from \(\mathcal{D}\). For (TR2), given a morphism \(f: X \to Y\) in \(\mathcal{D}'\), choose a distinguished triangle \(X \xrightarrow{f} Y \to Z \xrightarrow{+1}\) in \(\mathcal{D}\). The condition says that \(Z\) is isomorphic to an object of \(\mathcal{D}'\); we may therefore assume that \(Z \in \operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{D}')\) and thus obtain a distinguished triangle in \(\mathcal{D}'\). This proves that \(\mathcal{D}'\) is pretriangulated and establishes sufficiency.

For (iii), the point is to verify (TR5) for \(\mathcal{D}'\). Indeed, the triangle \(Z' \to Y' \to X' \xrightarrow{+1}\) obtained by applying (TR5) in \(\mathcal{D}\) is automatically distinguished in \(\mathcal{D}'\) by (i).

Convention. Fix a category \(\mathcal{C}\). A subcategory \(\mathcal{C}'\) is called a saturated subcategory if it is closed under isomorphisms, that is, \[\forall X \in \operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{C}'), \; \forall Y \in \operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{C}), \quad X \simeq Y \implies Y \in \operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{C}') .\] For every nonempty family of full subcategories \((\mathcal{C}_i)_{i \in I}\), their intersection \(\bigcap_{i \in I} \mathcal{C}_i\) is by definition the full subcategory of \(\mathcal{C}\) satisfying \(\operatorname{Ob}\left( \bigcap_{i \in I} \mathcal{C}_i \right) = \bigcap_{i \in I} \operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{C}_i)\).

Proposition. Let \(\mathcal{D}\) be a pretriangulated (or triangulated) category, and let \((\mathcal{D}_i)_{i \in I}\) be a family of saturated pretriangulated (or saturated triangulated) subcategories, with \(I \neq \emptyset\). Then \(\bigcap_{i \in I} \mathcal{D}_i\) is also a saturated pretriangulated (or saturated triangulated) subcategory.

Proof. An intersection of saturated subcategories plainly preserves the condition in Definition–Proposition reference (ii).

A common technique is to cut out a saturated pretriangulated (or triangulated) subcategory using a cohomological functor.

Proposition. Let \(\mathcal{D}\) be a pretriangulated (or triangulated) category, \(H: \mathcal{D} \to \mathcal{A}\) a cohomological functor, and \(\mathcal{T}\) a weak Serre subcategory of \(\mathcal{A}\) (Definition reference). Define a full subcategory \(\mathcal{D}_{H, \mathcal{T}}\) of \(\mathcal{D}\) by \[X \in \operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{D}_{H, \mathcal{T}}) \iff \forall n \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}, \; H(T^n X) \in \operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{T}).\] Then \(\mathcal{D}_{H, \mathcal{T}}\) is a saturated pretriangulated (or saturated triangulated) subcategory of \(\mathcal{D}\).

Proof. It suffices to verify the condition in Definition–Proposition reference (ii). Recall that a weak Serre subcategory is saturated. Hence saturation and \(T\)-invariance of \(\mathcal{D}_{H, \mathcal{T}}\) are clear. Now consider a distinguished triangle \(X \to Y \to Z \xrightarrow{+1}\) in \(\mathcal{D}\), two of whose terms lie in \(\mathcal{D}_{H, \mathcal{T}}\). After rotation, we may assume without loss of generality that \(X, Z \in \operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{D}_{H, \mathcal{T}})\). For every \(n \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\), there is an exact sequence \[H(T^{n-1} Z) \to H(T^n X) \to H(T^n Y) \to H(T^n Z) \to H(T^{n+1} X).\] The definition of a weak Serre subcategory immediately gives \(H(T^n Y) \in \operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{T})\).

Example. Let \(\mathcal{D}\) be a pretriangulated (or triangulated) category and let \(H: \mathcal{D} \to \mathcal{A}\) be a cohomological functor. Define \(\mathcal{N}_H\) to be the full subcategory whose objects satisfy \(H(T^n X) = 0\) for every \(n \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\). This is the case of Proposition reference in which \(\mathcal{T}\) is the subcategory consisting of zero objects. Thus \(\mathcal{N}_H\) is a pretriangulated (or triangulated) subcategory.

The following technical result will be used later in § 4.3; it depends on the octahedral axiom (TR5).

Lemma (J.-L. Verdier). Every commutative diagram in a triangulated category \(\mathcal{D}\) \[\text{Diagram chapter4-unit-051-d014}\] can be extended to a diagram \[\text{Diagram chapter4-unit-051-d015}\] such that every row and column is a distinguished triangle, the square marked \(\star\) is anticommutative (that is, \((To) h'' = -(Th') q\)), and every other square is commutative.

Proof. We construct the required distinguished triangles step by step and then prove their commutativity and anticommutativity properties. First apply (TR2) separately to \(u\), \(v\), \(f\), and \(f'\) to obtain the portion \[\text{Diagram chapter4-unit-051-d016}\] of the diagram, with every row and column distinguished. Next apply (TR2) to \(fu = vf' : X' \to Y\) to obtain a distinguished triangle \(X' \to Y \xrightarrow{m} A \xrightarrow{n} TX'\). The following construction is based on (TR5).

  1. Apply (TR5) to the three distinguished triangles containing \(f'\), \(v\), and \(vf'\) to obtain the following morphism of distinguished triangles: \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:triangulated-9-diag-aux-0}{}\text{Diagram chapter4-unit-051-d017} \end{equation}\] The last row is a newly constructed distinguished triangle.

  2. Apply (TR5) to the three distinguished triangles containing \(u\), \(f\), and \(fu\) to obtain the following morphism of distinguished triangles: \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:triangulated-9-diag-aux-1}{}\text{Diagram chapter4-unit-051-d018} \end{equation}\] The last row is a newly constructed distinguished triangle.

  3. Apply (TR2) to \(f'' := ja: X'' \to Y''\) to obtain a distinguished triangle \(X'' \xrightarrow{f''} Y'' \xrightarrow{g''} Z'' \xrightarrow{h''} TX''\).

  4. Consider the following distinguished triangles obtained from the preceding steps and rotations (TR3): \[\begin{gather*} X'' \xrightarrow{a} A \xrightarrow{b} Z \xrightarrow{c} TX'', \quad A \xrightarrow{j} Y'' \xrightarrow{k} TZ' \xrightarrow{-Ti} TA, \\ X'' \xrightarrow{f'' = ja} Y'' \xrightarrow{g''} Z'' \xrightarrow{h''} TX'' . \end{gather*}\] Applying (TR5) then gives a morphism of distinguished triangles \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:triangulated-9-diag-aux-2}{}\text{Diagram chapter4-unit-051-d019} \end{equation}\] The last row is a newly constructed distinguished triangle. Set \(w := bi\). Commutativity of equation implies \(l = -Tw\); rotation therefore gives the distinguished triangle \[Z' \xrightarrow{w} Z \xrightarrow{t} Z'' \xrightarrow{q} TZ' .\]

The operations above give the second row and third column of the required diagram. The remaining first row (or fourth column) is obtained by rotating the fourth row (or first column) according to (TR3), and is therefore also a distinguished triangle (see Remark reference).

We now verify the commutativity and anticommutativity properties. From \(w = bi\) and \(s = jm\), as implied by equation, it follows that \((u, v, w)\) and \((r, s, t)\) are respectively the composites \[\begin{gather*} (X', Y', Z') \xrightarrow[\href{#eqn:triangulated-9-diag-aux-0}{equation}]{(\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}, v, i)} (X', Y, A) \xrightarrow[\href{#eqn:triangulated-9-diag-aux-1}{equation}]{(u, \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}, b)} (X, Y, Z), \\ (X, Y, Z) \xrightarrow[\href{#eqn:triangulated-9-diag-aux-1}{equation}]{(r, m, \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}})} (X'', A, Z) \xrightarrow[\href{#eqn:triangulated-9-diag-aux-2}{equation}]{(\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}, j, t)} (X'', Y'', Z''), \end{gather*}\] so both are morphisms of triangles. Finally, consider the morphism \((o, p, q, -To)\) in the diagram. It remains to prove that the following diagram is commutative: \[\text{Diagram chapter4-unit-051-d020}\] Indeed, equation implies \(o = na\), so both wings commute. Since the three squares on the right of equation commute, the upper part also commutes; commutativity of the lower part follows from equation. This proves the assertion.

Except for Proposition reference, every assertion in this section also holds for \(\Bbbk\)-linear categories, where \(\Bbbk\) is a commutative ring.

Remark. Generators and compact objects in triangulated categories are important topics not treated in this book. Although the ideas resemble the versions in Definition reference and A.2.2, these notions require different definitions in a triangulated category. This leads to an important form of the Brown Representability Theorem for triangulated categories: if \(\mathcal{D}\) is a “compactly generated” triangulated category with small \(\coprod\), and a cohomological functor \(H: \mathcal{D}^{\operatorname{op}} \to \ensuremath{\mathsf{Ab}}\) maps small \(\coprod\) in \(\mathcal{D}\) to \(\prod\) in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ab}}\), then \(H\) is representable. Readers who need this result are advised to consult [stacks].

Notice the family resemblance between the Brown Representability Theorem and the various representability and adjoint-functor theorems in §reference, §reference, and § A.2.

Localization of Triangulated Categories

This section examines the relation between triangulated categories and Gabriel–Zisman localization. More precisely,

  • the construction of categorical localization in §reference formally adjoins inverses to the morphisms in a multiplicative system, and our first task is to show that this construction preserves the (pre)triangulated structure;

  • for a triangulated category, localization can also be viewed as formally making a triangulated subcategory zero; this idea is analogous to the construction of Serre quotients in §reference.

Throughout what follows, \((\mathcal{D}, T)\) is assumed to be a pretriangulated category. If one passes from additive categories to the \(\Bbbk\)-linear setting, where \(\Bbbk\) is any commutative ring, every result in this section has a corresponding generalization; we omit the details.

Definition. Let \(S \subset \operatorname{Mor}(\mathcal{D})\) be a multiplicative system as in Definition reference. We say that \(S\) is compatible with triangulation if the following conditions hold.

  1. For \(s \in \operatorname{Mor}(\mathcal{D})\), one has \(s \in S\) if and only if \(Ts \in S\).

  2. Consider the following diagram, in which the solid part is given: \[\text{Diagram chapter4-unit-052-d001}\] If \(\alpha, \beta \in S\), then there is a morphism \(\gamma\), as indicated by the dashed arrow, such that the entire diagram commutes and \(\gamma \in S\).

Notice that (ST2) is a strengthening of (TR4) for \(S\).

Proposition. Let \(S \subset \operatorname{Mor}(\mathcal{D})\) be a multiplicative system compatible with triangulation. Then the localization \(\mathcal{D}[S^{-1}]\) has a unique pretriangulated-category structure for which \(Q: \mathcal{D} \to \mathcal{D}[S^{-1}]\) is a triangulated functor. Up to isomorphism, the distinguished triangles in \(\mathcal{D}[S^{-1}]\) are precisely the images of distinguished triangles in \(\mathcal{D}\). If \(\mathcal{D}\) is triangulated, then so is \(\mathcal{D}[S^{-1}]\).

Proof. Theorem reference shows that \(\mathcal{D}[S^{-1}]\) is an additive category. Moreover, (ST1) and the universal property of localization give a unique pair of endofunctors of \(\mathcal{D}[S^{-1}]\) that make the following diagram commute: \[\text{Diagram chapter4-unit-052-d002}\] The universal property also shows that the two functors in the second row are mutually inverse. To simplify notation, we continue to write them as \(\text{Diagram chapter4-unit-052-diagram-003}\). Thus \((\mathcal{D}[S^{-1}], T)\) is an additive category with translation.

We first prove uniqueness of the pretriangulated structure. By definition, the triangulated functor \(Q\) must preserve distinguished triangles. Conversely, let \(X \xrightarrow{f} Y \to Z \xrightarrow{+1}\) be a distinguished triangle in \(\mathcal{D}[S^{-1}]\). After replacing it by an isomorphic triangle, we may assume that \(f: X \to Y\) comes from a morphism in \(\mathcal{D}\), which we denote by \(f_0: X_0 \to Y_0\) to avoid ambiguity. By (TR2), extend \(f_0\) to a distinguished triangle \(X_0 \xrightarrow{f_0} Y_0 \to Z_0 \xrightarrow{+1}\). Corollary reference then guarantees that its image under \(Q\) is isomorphic to the original triangle.

We now prove existence of the pretriangulated structure. Define the distinguished triangles in \(\mathcal{D}[S^{-1}]\) as stated in the proposition. Axiom (TR0) is immediate, while (TR1) and (TR3) are inherited directly from \(\mathcal{D}\). For (TR2), consider a morphism \(f: X \to Y\) in \(\mathcal{D}[S^{-1}]\). As usual, after replacing its objects by isomorphic ones using morphisms from \(S\), we may assume that \(f\) comes from \(\mathcal{D}\); thus (TR2) reduces to the assertion in \(\mathcal{D}\).

For (TR4), consider the following commutative diagram in \(\mathcal{D}[S^{-1}]\); the dashed part will be dealt with below. \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:localization-triangulated-aux}{}\text{Diagram chapter4-unit-052-d003} \end{equation}\] Here each row is a distinguished triangle and all horizontal arrows come from \(\mathcal{D}\). From the construction in §reference, one can show that there are objects \(A, B \in \operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{D})\), a morphism \([A \to B] \in \operatorname{Mor}(\mathcal{D})\), and \(s, t \in S\) such that \(\alpha = as^{-1}\) and \(\beta = bt^{-1}\) in \(\mathcal{D}[S^{-1}]\), and such that the solid part of the following diagram commutes in \(\mathcal{D}\). The dashed part and the object \(C\) will be discussed presently. \[\text{Diagram chapter4-unit-052-d004}\] The explicit construction is somewhat cumbersome and appears as a guided exercise in .

Apply (TR2) to \(A \to B\) in \(\mathcal{D}\) to obtain a distinguished triangle \(A \to B \to C \xrightarrow{+1}\) as the second row. Then apply (ST2) to obtain \(C \xrightarrow{u \in S} Z\), and apply (TR4) to obtain \(C \xrightarrow{c} Z'\), so that the entire diagram commutes in \(\mathcal{D}\). In \(\mathcal{D}[S^{-1}]\), set \(\gamma := c u^{-1}\). With this choice the whole diagram equation commutes. This verifies (TR4).

If \(\mathcal{D}\) is triangulated, verification of (TR5) for \(\mathcal{D}[S^{-1}]\) likewise reduces to verification in \(\mathcal{D}\).

Proposition. Let \(\mathcal{N}\) be a saturated triangulated subcategory of a triangulated category \(\mathcal{D}\) (Definition–Proposition reference, Convention reference). Then \[S\mathcal{N} := \left\{\begin{array}{r|l} s \in \operatorname{Mor}(\mathcal{D}) & \exists \;\text{a distinguished triangle}\; X \xrightarrow{s} Y \to Z \xrightarrow{+1} \\ & \text{such that}\; Z \in \operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{N}) \end{array}\right\}\] is a multiplicative system compatible with triangulation.

Proof. Since \(\mathcal{N}\) is closed under translation, rotating triangles shows that \(S\mathcal{N}\) satisfies (ST1). Next consider the commutative diagram in (ST2), and suppose that \(\alpha, \beta \in S\mathcal{N}\). Lemma reference gives a diagram \[\text{Diagram chapter4-unit-053-d001}\] in which every row and column is a distinguished triangle, all squares commute, and \((\alpha, \beta, \gamma)\) is a morphism of triangles. Using the saturation of \(\mathcal{N}\), the fact that \(\alpha, \beta \in S\), and Corollary reference, we see that \(X'', Y'' \in \operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{N})\). The definition of a saturated triangulated subcategory then implies \(Z'' \in \operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{N})\), hence \(\gamma \in S\). This verifies (ST2).

We next verify the axioms for a multiplicative system (Definition reference). Since \(0 \in \operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{N})\), axiom (S1) follows from (TR1).

To verify (S2), let \(f, g \in S\mathcal{N}\). Choose distinguished triangles \(X \xrightarrow{f} Y \to Z' \xrightarrow{+1}\) and \(Y \xrightarrow{g} Z \to X' \xrightarrow{+1}\) with \(Z', X' \in \operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{N})\), and use (TR2) to choose a distinguished triangle \(X \xrightarrow{gf} Z \to Y' \xrightarrow{+1}\). Applying (TR5) gives a distinguished triangle \(Z' \to Y' \to X' \xrightarrow{+1}\). The saturated triangulated-subcategory property therefore implies \(Y' \in \operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{N})\), that is, \(gf \in S\mathcal{N}\).

To verify (S3), consider morphisms \(X \xrightarrow{s \in S\mathcal{N}} Z \xleftarrow{f} Y\). Choose a distinguished triangle \(X \xrightarrow{s} Z \xrightarrow{h} N \xrightarrow{+1}\) with \(N \in \operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{N})\), and use (TR2) to choose a triangle \(Y \xrightarrow{hf} N \to U \xrightarrow{+1}\). Apply (TR4) to the solid part of the diagram \[\text{Diagram chapter4-unit-053-d002}\] to obtain the morphisms indicated by the dashed arrows, and hence a morphism of distinguished triangles. After rotation, this yields an element \(s': W := T^{-1} U \to Y\) of \(S\mathcal{N}\), a corresponding morphism \(f': W \to X\), and the commutative diagram required in (S3): \[\text{Diagram chapter4-unit-053-d003}\]

To verify (S4), replace \((f, g)\) in that axiom by \((f-g, 0)\). It suffices to prove the following assertion: for a morphism \(f: X \to Y\), if there is an \(s: Y \to W\) with \(s \in S\mathcal{N}\) and \(sf = 0\), then there is a \(t: Z \to X\) with \(t \in S\mathcal{N}\) and \(ft = 0\). To prove this, choose a distinguished triangle \(N \to Y \xrightarrow{s} W \xrightarrow{+1}\) with \(N \in \operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{N})\). Since \(\operatorname{Hom}(X, \cdot)\) is cohomological and \(sf=0\), there is an \(h \in \operatorname{Hom}(X, N)\) such that \(f\) factors as \(X \xrightarrow{h} N \to Y\). Choose a distinguished triangle \(Z \xrightarrow{t} X \xrightarrow{h} N \xrightarrow{+1}\); then \(t \in S\mathcal{N}\). On the other hand, \(ht=0\) (Lemma reference) implies \(ft = 0\). Thus (S4) holds.

The arguments for the dual versions of (S3) and (S4) are identical.

Theorem (Verdier localization). Let \(\mathcal{N}\) be a saturated triangulated subcategory of \(\mathcal{D}\). Define \(\mathcal{D}/\mathcal{N} := \mathcal{D}\left[ (S\mathcal{N})^{-1}\right]\) (which is allowed to be a “large” category), equipped with the triangulated structure from Proposition reference. Then the localization functor \(Q: \mathcal{D} \to \mathcal{D}/\mathcal{N}\) has the following properties.

  1. For every morphism \(f: X \to Y\) in \(\mathcal{D}\), one has \(Qf = 0\) if and only if \(f\) factors as \(X \to N \to Y\) with \(N \in \operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{N})\); in particular, \(Q\) maps \(\mathcal{N}\) to \(0\).

  2. For every pretriangulated category \(\mathcal{E}\) and every triangulated functor \(F: \mathcal{D} \to \mathcal{E}\), if \(F\) maps \(\mathcal{N}\) to \(0\), then \(F\) factors uniquely as \(\mathcal{D} \xrightarrow{Q} \mathcal{D}/\mathcal{N} \xrightarrow{\overline{F}} \mathcal{E}\), where \(\overline{F}\) is a triangulated functor.

  3. For every Abelian category \(\mathcal{A}\) and every cohomological functor \(H: \mathcal{D} \to \mathcal{A}\), if \(H\) maps \(\mathcal{N}\) to \(0\), then \(H\) factors uniquely as \(\mathcal{D} \xrightarrow{Q} \mathcal{D}/\mathcal{N} \xrightarrow{\overline{H}} \mathcal{A}\), where \(\overline{H}\) is a cohomological functor.

Proof. For (i), if \(f\) factors as \(X \to N \to Y\), then \(Qf = 0\). Indeed, the rotation \(N \to 0 \to TN \xrightarrow{+1}\) of the distinguished triangle \(N \xrightarrow{\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_N} N \to 0 \xrightarrow{+1}\) shows that \(N \to 0\) is mapped to an isomorphism in \(\mathcal{D}/\mathcal{N}\). Conversely, if \(Qf = 0\), there is a morphism \(s: M \to X\) with \(s \in S\mathcal{N}\) and \(fs = 0\) (Corollary reference). By the definition of \(S\mathcal{N}\), there is a commutative diagram whose rows are distinguished triangles (the solid part): \[\text{Diagram chapter4-unit-053-d004} \quad (N \in \operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{N})),\] By (TR4), the morphisms indicated by the dashed arrows can be supplied so that the entire diagram commutes. This diagram factors \(f\) as \(X \to N \to Y\).

Consider the situation in (ii). Put \(s \in S\mathcal{N}\) into a distinguished triangle \(X \xrightarrow{s} Y \to N \xrightarrow{+1}\) with \(N \in \operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{N})\). Then \(FX \xrightarrow{Fs} FY \to 0 \xrightarrow{+1}\) is a distinguished triangle in \(\mathcal{E}\). Corollary reference shows that \(Fs\) is an isomorphism. The universal property then gives a unique factorization \(H = \overline{F} \circ Q\), where \(\overline{F}\) is an additive functor. In view of the description of the triangulated structure on \(\mathcal{D}/\mathcal{N}\) (Proposition reference), it is straightforward to verify that \(\overline{F}\) preserves translations and triangles; the details are left to the reader.

Consider the situation in (iii). Again put \(s \in S\mathcal{N}\) into a distinguished triangle \(X \xrightarrow{s} Y \to N \xrightarrow{+1}\). Applying \(H\) gives the exact sequence \(\underbracket{HT^{-1} N}_{=0} \to HX \xrightarrow{Hs} HY \to \underbracket{HN}_{=0}\), so \(Hs\) is an isomorphism. The universal property then gives a unique factorization \(H = \overline{H} \circ Q\), where \(\overline{H}\) is additive. To verify that \(\overline{H}\) is cohomological, recall that the distinguished triangles in \(\mathcal{D}/\mathcal{N}\) are isomorphic to images of distinguished triangles in \(\mathcal{D}\).

Example. Cohomological functors give an important class of multiplicative systems compatible with triangulation. Let \(H: \mathcal{D} \to \mathcal{A}\) be a cohomological functor. A morphism \(f: X \to Y\) in \(\mathcal{D}\) is called an \(H\)-quasi-isomorphism if \(H(T^n f)\) is an isomorphism in \(\mathcal{A}\) for every \(n \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\). All \(H\)-quasi-isomorphisms form a subset \(S_H \subset \operatorname{Mor}(\mathcal{D})\). It plainly satisfies (ST1), while (ST2) follows from the long exact sequence of a cohomological functor (Remark reference) together with Proposition reference.

On the other hand, define \(\mathcal{N}_H\) as in Example reference. It is a saturated triangulated subcategory, so \(S\mathcal{N}_H\) is defined. The two are related as follows.

Proposition. Let \(H: \mathcal{D} \to \mathcal{A}\) be a cohomological functor. Then \(S\mathcal{N}_H = S_H\).

Proof. Let \(f: X \to Y\) be a morphism in \(\mathcal{D}\). Extend \(f\) to a distinguished triangle \(X \xrightarrow{f} Y \to N \xrightarrow{+1}\). Recall that \(N\) is unique up to isomorphism. The long exact sequence of a cohomological functor therefore implies \[f \;\text{is an $H$-quasi-isomorphism} \iff \forall n, \; H(T^n N) = 0,\] and the right-hand side is equivalent to \(N \in \operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{N}_H)\). This proves the assertion.

Thus there are at least two ways to localize at \(S_H\): adjoin inverses to the elements of \(S_H\), or make \(\mathcal{N}_H\) zero. These give two universal properties of the Verdier localization \(Q: \mathcal{D} \to \mathcal{D}/\mathcal{N}_H = \mathcal{D}[S_H^{-1}]\). Finally, we discuss the relation between localization and subcategories. Let \(\mathcal{N}\) and \(\mathcal{I}\) be triangulated subcategories of a triangulated category \(\mathcal{D}\), with \(\mathcal{N}\) saturated. Then \(\mathcal{N} \cap \mathcal{I}\) is also a saturated triangulated subcategory of \(\mathcal{I}\). The universal property of Verdier localization determines a triangulated functor \(i: \mathcal{I}/(\mathcal{N} \cap \mathcal{I}) \to \mathcal{D}/\mathcal{N}\). Note the following simple fact. The system \(S(\mathcal{N} \cap \mathcal{I})\), defined relative to \(\mathcal{N} \cap \mathcal{I} \subset \mathcal{I}\), satisfies \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:S-N-D}{} S(\mathcal{N} \cap \mathcal{I}) = S\mathcal{N} \cap \operatorname{Mor}(\mathcal{I}). \end{equation}\] The inclusion \(\subset\) is clear. For \(\supset\), suppose that a morphism \(f: X \to Y\) in \(\mathcal{I}\) can be placed in a distinguished triangle \(X \xrightarrow{f} Y \to N \xrightarrow{+1}\) in \(\mathcal{D}\) with \(N \in \operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{N})\). Corollary reference shows that \(N\) is isomorphic to an object in \(\mathcal{I}\). Since \(\mathcal{N}\) is saturated, we may take \(N \in \operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{N} \cap \mathcal{I})\), and hence \(f \in S(\mathcal{N} \cap \mathcal{I})\).

Proposition. Let \(\mathcal{N}\), \(\mathcal{D}\), and \(\mathcal{I}\) be as above, and assume the following “resolution condition”: for every \(X \in \operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{D})\), there exist \(U \in \operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{I})\) and a morphism \(U \to X\) belonging to \(S\mathcal{N}\). Then \(i: \mathcal{I}/(\mathcal{N} \cap \mathcal{I}) \to \mathcal{D}/\mathcal{N}\) is an equivalence of triangulated categories.

The same conclusion holds if the resolution condition is replaced by: for every \(X \in \operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{D})\), there exist \(U \in \operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{I})\) and a morphism \(X \to U\) belonging to \(S\mathcal{N}\).

Proof. Proposition reference implies that \(i\) is an equivalence, and Corollary reference shows that the equivalence is triangulated.

The result above will be used in the study of derived functors.

Derived Categories

The first half of this section considers an additive category \(\mathcal{A}\); when derived categories are defined later, \(\mathcal{A}\) will be required to be Abelian. Example reference has already shown that \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})\) and \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{A})\) are additive categories with translation; the translation functor in both is denoted by \(X \mapsto X[1]\). Consider a morphism \(f: X \to Y\) in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})\) and its mapping cone \(\operatorname{Cone}(f)\). Definition reference gives the following triangle in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})\): \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:Cone-triangle}{} \text{Diagram chapter4-unit-054-d001} \end{equation}\] Passing to the quotient gives a triangle in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{A})\).

Theorem. Regard \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{A})\) as an additive category with translation \(T: X \mapsto X[1]\). Call a triangle \(X \to Y \to Z \xrightarrow{+1}\) in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{A})\) distinguished if it is isomorphic to a triangle of the form equation. These distinguished triangles form a set \(\mathcal{H}\) for which \((\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{A}), T, \mathcal{H})\) is a triangulated category.

Proof. We verify the axioms in Definition reference one by one. Axioms (TR0) and (TR2) are immediate from the definition, while (TR3) follows from the commutative diagram in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{A})\) supplied by Lemma reference: \[\text{Diagram chapter4-unit-054-d002}\]

For (TR1), given \(X \in \operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{A}))\), consider the mapping-cone triangle of the zero morphism \(0 \to X \to X \xrightarrow{+1}\). Rotating it by (TR3) gives the distinguished triangle \(X \xrightarrow{\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_X} X \to 0 \xrightarrow{+1}\).

For (TR4), consider the following commutative diagram in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{A})\) (the solid part): \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:cplx-triangulated-aux-0}{}\text{Diagram chapter4-unit-054-d003} \end{equation}\] Commutativity of the left square is equivalent to the existence of a family of morphisms in \(\mathcal{A}\), \(h^n: X^n \to (Y')^{n-1}\), such that \[\beta^n f^n - (f')^n \alpha^n = h^{n+1} d_X^n + d_{Y'}^{n-1} h^n , \quad n \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}.\] In matrix notation, define for every \(n \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\) the morphism \[\gamma^n = \begin{pmatrix} \alpha^{n+1} & 0 \\ h^{n+1} & \beta^n \end{pmatrix} : X^{n+1} \oplus Y^n \to (X')^{n+1} \oplus (Y')^n .\] Check that \[\begin{pmatrix} \alpha^{n+1} & 0 \\ h^{n+1} & \beta^n \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} -d_X^n & 0 \\ f^n & d_Y^{n-1} \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} -d_{X'}^n & 0 \\ (f')^n & d_{Y'}^{n-1} \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} \alpha^n & 0 \\ h^n & \beta^{n-1} \end{pmatrix},\] so these matrices determine a morphism \(\gamma: \operatorname{Cone}(f) \to \operatorname{Cone}(f')\). It is clear that the two right-hand squares in equation commute in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})\). Notice that the homotopy \((h^n)_{n \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}}\) can be chosen in several ways, so \(\gamma\) is not unique.

It remains to verify (TR5). In the statement of that axiom, without loss of generality take \(Z' = \operatorname{Cone}(f)\), \(X' = \operatorname{Cone}(g)\), and \(Y' = \operatorname{Cone}(gf)\), while \(h\), \(k\), and \(m\) are respectively \(\alpha(f)\), \(\alpha(g)\), and \(\alpha(gf)\); the corresponding morphisms of degree \(+1\) have the form \(\beta(\cdot)\). Functoriality of the mapping cone (Proposition reference), or a direct check, gives morphisms \[\text{Diagram chapter4-unit-054-d004}\] By functoriality of the mapping cone, every square in diagram (TR5) not involving \(w\) commutes. For the remaining part, namely the lower-right square in (TR5), to commute as well, the morphism \(w: X' \to TZ'\) must, and can only, be the composite \[X' \xrightarrow{\beta(g)} TY \xrightarrow{T(\alpha(f))} T Z' .\]

It therefore remains to prove that \(Z' \xrightarrow{u} Y' \xrightarrow{v} X' \xrightarrow{w} TZ'\) is a distinguished triangle. Notice that for every \(n \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\), \[\begin{align*} \operatorname{Cone}(u)^n & = \operatorname{Cone}(f)^{n+1} \oplus \operatorname{Cone}(gf)^n = X^{n+2} \oplus Y^{n+1} \oplus X^{n+1} \oplus Z^n , \\ (X')^n & = \operatorname{Cone}(g)^n = Y^{n+1} \oplus Z^n . \end{align*}\] In matrix notation, define \[\begin{align*} \varphi^n & := \begin{pmatrix} 0 & \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{Y^{n+1}} & f^{n+1} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{Z^n} \end{pmatrix} : \operatorname{Cone}(u)^n \to (X')^n , \\ \psi^n & := \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{Y^{n+1}} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \\ 0 & \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{Z^n} \end{pmatrix} : (X')^n \to \operatorname{Cone}(u)^n . \end{align*}\] A direct check shows that these define morphisms \(\varphi: \operatorname{Cone}(u) \leftrightarrows X' : \psi\) in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})\) satisfying \(\varphi \circ \psi = \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{X'}\), as well as \(\varphi \circ \alpha(u) = v\) and \(\beta(u) \circ \psi = w\). Next consider the diagram \[\text{Diagram chapter4-unit-054-d005}\] It suffices to show that this diagram commutes in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{A})\) and that \(\psi\) and \(\varphi\) are inverse in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{A})\). The only point still to be proved is that \(\psi \circ \varphi\) is homotopic to \(\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{\operatorname{Cone}(u)}\). Let \(h^n : \operatorname{Cone}(u)^n \to \operatorname{Cone}(u)^{n-1}\) be the evident composite \[X^{n+2} \oplus Y^{n+1} \oplus X^{n+1} \oplus Z^n \twoheadrightarrow X^{n+1} \hookrightarrow X^{n+1} \oplus Y^n \oplus X^n \oplus Z^{n-1}.\] A routine verification gives \(\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{\operatorname{Cone}(u)^n} - \psi^n \varphi^n = h^{n+1} d_{\operatorname{Cone}(u)}^n + d_{\operatorname{Cone}(u)}^{n-1} h^n\). This proves the assertion.

Homotopy equivalence is indispensable in the proof. If one works at the level of \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})\), mapping cones cannot produce a triangulated category.

Proof (Proof of Theorems reference and reference). We can now complete the previously deferred part of the proof of Theorem reference. By duality, it suffices to consider the situation \(Y \xleftarrow{\alpha} X \xrightarrow{\gamma} I\), where \(\alpha\) is a quasi-isomorphism and \(I \in \operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}^+(\mathcal{A}))\) consists of injective objects. The cohomological functor \(\operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{A})}(\cdot, I)\) (Proposition reference) gives a long exact sequence \[\begin{multline*} \operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{A})}\left( \operatorname{Cone}(\alpha), I \right) \to \operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{A})}(Y, I) \\ \xrightarrow{\alpha^*} \operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{A})}(X, I) \to \operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{A})}(\operatorname{Cone}(\alpha)[-1], I); \end{multline*}\] but \(\operatorname{Cone}(\alpha)\) is acyclic (Corollary reference), so Lemma reference implies that \(\alpha^*\) is an isomorphism.

The argument for Theorem reference, concerning K-injective or K-projective complexes, is entirely similar.

Corollary. For \(\star \in \{+, -, \ensuremath{\mathrm{b}}\}\), the category \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}^\star(\mathcal{A})\) introduced in Definition reference is a triangulated subcategory of \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{A})\) (Definition–Proposition reference).

Proof. Clearly \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}^\star(\mathcal{A})\) is closed under the translation functor. Moreover, for a mapping-cone triangle \(X \xrightarrow{f} Y \to \operatorname{Cone}(f) \xrightarrow{+1}\), it is clear that \(X,Y\) belong to \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}^\star(\mathcal{A})\) if and only if \(\operatorname{Cone}(f) \in \ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}^\star(\mathcal{A})\). This proves that condition (ii) in Definition–Proposition reference holds.

Proposition. Let \(F: \mathcal{A}_1 \to \mathcal{A}_2\) be an additive functor between additive categories. Then \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}F: \ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{A}_1) \to \ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{A}_2)\) is a triangulated functor. The same assertion holds with \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}^\star(\cdot)\) in place of \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\cdot)\), for \(\star \in \{+, -, \ensuremath{\mathrm{b}}\}\).

Proof. This follows from Proposition reference (for translation) and Proposition reference (for mapping cones).

Corollary. Let \(\mathcal{A}'\) be a full additive subcategory of \(\mathcal{A}\). Then \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{A}')\) embeds as a triangulated subcategory of \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{A})\). The same assertion holds with \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}^\star(\cdot)\) in place of \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\cdot)\), for \(\star \in \{+, -, \ensuremath{\mathrm{b}}\}\).

Proposition. Let \(\mathcal{A}\) be an Abelian category. For every \(n \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\), the functor \(\operatorname{H}^n: \ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{A}) \to \mathcal{A}\) is cohomological in the sense of Definition reference. The same assertion holds with \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}^\star(\mathcal{A})\) in place of \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{A})\), for \(\star \in \{+, -, \ensuremath{\mathrm{b}}\}\).

Proof. Consider the distinguished mapping-cone triangle in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{A})\), \(X \xrightarrow{f} Y \xrightarrow{\alpha(f)} \operatorname{Cone}(f) \xrightarrow{+1}\). By the long exact sequence equation and Corollary reference (the heart of §reference), the sequence \[\operatorname{H}^n(X) \xrightarrow{\operatorname{H}^n(f)} \operatorname{H}^n(Y) \xrightarrow{\operatorname{H}^n(\alpha(f))} \operatorname{H}^n(\operatorname{Cone}(f))\] is indeed exact.

The definition of the derived category will involve Verdier localization. In the notation of Example reference, the cohomological functor \(\operatorname{H}^0: \ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{A}) \to \mathcal{A}\) determines a multiplicative system compatible with triangulation, \[\mathrm{qis} := S_{\operatorname{H}^0} \subset \operatorname{Mor}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{A})),\] whose elements are precisely the quasi-isomorphisms. Another way to understand \(\mathrm{qis}\) is to consider the saturated triangulated subcategory \(\mathcal{N} := \mathcal{N}_{\operatorname{H}^0}\) of \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{A})\), consisting of the acyclic complexes. Proposition reference implies \(S\mathcal{N} = \mathrm{qis}\). For \(\star \in \{+, -, \ensuremath{\mathrm{b}}\}\), we similarly define the multiplicative system compatible with triangulation \(\mathrm{qis}^\star := \mathrm{qis} \cap \operatorname{Mor}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}^\star(\mathcal{A}))\) and the subcategory \(\mathcal{N}^\star := \mathcal{N} \cap \ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}^\star(\mathcal{A})\); they still satisfy \(S\mathcal{N}^\star = \mathrm{qis}^\star\).

Definition. The derived category of an Abelian category \(\mathcal{A}\) is defined to be the triangulated category \[\begin{align*} \ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}(\mathcal{A}) & := \ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{A})\left[ \mathrm{qis}^{-1} \right] \\ & = \ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{A})/\mathcal{N}. \end{align*}\] Likewise, for \(\star \in \{+, -, \ensuremath{\mathrm{b}}\}\), define the triangulated category \[\begin{align*} \ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^\star(\mathcal{A}) & := \ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}^\star(\mathcal{A})\left[ (\mathrm{qis}^\star)^{-1} \right] \\ & = \ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}^\star(\mathcal{A})/\mathcal{N}^\star . \end{align*}\] We call \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^+(\mathcal{A})\) (respectively, \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^-(\mathcal{A})\) and \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^\ensuremath{\mathrm{b}}(\mathcal{A})\)) the bounded-below (respectively, bounded-above and bounded) derived category of \(\mathcal{A}\).

An issue that is difficult to avoid is controlling the size of a derived category in the set-theoretic sense, since we do not want \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}(\mathcal{A})\) to be a “large” category; see the related discussion in Remark reference. We defer this issue until Corollary reference.

Proposition. Every short exact sequence \(0 \to X \xrightarrow{f} Y \xrightarrow{g} Z \to 0\) in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})\) extends canonically to a distinguished triangle \(X \to Y \to Z \xrightarrow{+1}\) in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}(\mathcal{A})\). More precisely, there is a canonical commutative diagram in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{A})\) \[\text{Diagram chapter4-unit-054-d006}\] in which the first and third rows are distinguished triangles, and both \(\Phi\) and \(\Phi'\) are quasi-isomorphisms.

Proof. The commutative diagram is simply a restatement of Lemma reference. The first row is the distinguished mapping-cone triangle of \(f\), while the third row is a rotation of the mapping-cone triangle of \(g\).

Thus short exact sequences in the category of complexes are reflected in the triangulated structure on the derived category. Conversely, it is very rare for an Abelian category \(\mathcal{A}\) to have the property that \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}(\mathcal{A})\) is Abelian; the exercises in this chapter will characterize such categories. The exercises in this chapter will also introduce the group \(\mathrm{K}_0(\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^{\ensuremath{\mathrm{b}}}(\mathcal{A}))\) and relate it to \(\mathrm{K}_0(\mathcal{A})\) from Definition reference; the reader is encouraged to work this out. By the characterization of \(\mathcal{N}\) and Theorem reference, the cohomological functor \(\operatorname{H}^n: \ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{A}) \to \mathcal{A}\) factors through the derived category as \[\begin{equation*} \index[sym1]{Hn} \operatorname{H}^n: \ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}(\mathcal{A}) \to \mathcal{A}, \quad \operatorname{H}^n(X) = \operatorname{H}^0(X[n]), \end{equation*}\] where \(n \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\). The same applies to \(\star \in \{+, -, \ensuremath{\mathrm{b}}\}\) and \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^{\star}(\mathcal{A})\). The universal property determines triangulated functors \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^{\ensuremath{\mathrm{b}}}(\mathcal{A}) \to \ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^{\pm}(\mathcal{A}) \to \ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}(\mathcal{A})\) that commute with the cohomology functor \(\operatorname{H}^0\). We want to regard these functors as embeddings of triangulated subcategories; for this we need the following abstract result.

Lemma. Let \(\mathcal{N}\) and \(\mathcal{I}\) be triangulated subcategories of a triangulated category \(\mathcal{D}\), with \(\mathcal{N}\) saturated. If either of the following conditions holds in \(\mathcal{D}\), then the functor \(i: \mathcal{I}/(\mathcal{N} \cap \mathcal{I}) \to \mathcal{D}/\mathcal{N}\) is fully faithful:

  1. every morphism \(Y \to N\) factors as \(Y \to Y' \to N\);

  2. every morphism \(N \to Y\) factors as \(N \to Y' \to Y\);

here \(Y \in \operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{I})\) and \(N \in \operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{N})\) are given, and \(Y' \in \operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{N} \cap \mathcal{I})\).

Proof. By duality, it suffices to consider the case in which (i) holds. Recall that equation guarantees \(S(\mathcal{N} \cap \mathcal{I}) = S\mathcal{N} \cap \operatorname{Mor}(\mathcal{I})\). We wish to apply the criterion in Proposition reference (ii). Thus it suffices to prove the following: suppose \(s: W \to Y\) belongs to the multiplicative system \(S\mathcal{N}\) and \(Y \in \operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{I})\). Then there is a \(g: V \to W\) such that \(V \in \operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{I})\) and \(sg \in S\mathcal{N}\).

There is clearly a distinguished triangle \(W \xrightarrow{-s} Y \to N \xrightarrow{+1}\) with \(N \in \operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{N})\). Factor \(Y \to N\) as \(Y \xrightarrow{\alpha} Y' \xrightarrow{\beta} N\), with \(Y' \in \operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{N} \cap \mathcal{I})\). Extend \(\alpha\) to a distinguished triangle \(V \to Y \xrightarrow{\alpha} Y' \xrightarrow{+1}\) in \(\mathcal{I}\) to obtain the following diagram, whose solid part is determined: \[\text{Diagram chapter4-unit-054-d007}\] each row being a distinguished triangle. Use (TR4) to choose \(Tg: TV \to TW\) so that the entire diagram commutes. Notice that \(V \in \operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{I})\) and \(TV \to TY\) belongs to \(S\mathcal{N}\); therefore \(sg: V \to Y\) also belongs to \(S\mathcal{N}\). This proves the assertion.

Proposition. For every \(\star \in \{+, -, \ensuremath{\mathrm{b}}\}\), the functor \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^{\star}(\mathcal{A}) \to \ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}(\mathcal{A})\) is fully faithful. For every \(X \in \operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}(\mathcal{A}))\), the object \(X\) is isomorphic to an object of \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^{+}(\mathcal{A})\) (respectively, \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^{-}(\mathcal{A})\) and \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^{\ensuremath{\mathrm{b}}}(\mathcal{A})\)) if and only if \(n \ll 0\) (respectively, \(n \gg 0\) and \(|n| \gg 0\)) implies \(\operatorname{H}^n(X) = 0\).

Proof. The first assertion is an application of Lemma reference: take \(\mathcal{D} = \ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{A})\), \(\mathcal{I} = \ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}^\star(\mathcal{A})\), and \(\mathcal{N} = \mathcal{N}_{\operatorname{H}^0}\). For example, when \(\star = +\), we must show that for every \(Y \in \operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}^+(\mathcal{A}))\), \(N \in \operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{N})\), and morphism \(N \to Y\), there is a factorization \[N \to Y' \to Y, \quad Y' \in \operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{N}^+).\] This holds because, for \(n \ll 0\), the morphism \(N \to Y\) naturally factors as \(N \to \tau^{\geq n} N \to \tau^{\geq n} Y = Y\), where \(\tau^{\geq n}\) is the truncation functor from Definition reference and \(\tau^{\geq n} N \in \operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{N}^+)\).

Next, if \(X \in \operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A}))\) satisfies \(n \ll 0 \implies \operatorname{H}^n(X) = 0\), then for \(n \ll 0\) the morphism \(X \to \tau^{\geq n} X\) is a quasi-isomorphism and hence an isomorphism in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}(\mathcal{A})\). This characterizes, up to isomorphism, the image of \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^+(\mathcal{A}) \to \ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}(\mathcal{A})\).

The argument for \(\star = -\) is dual. In the same way, \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}^{\ensuremath{\mathrm{b}}}(\mathcal{A}) \to \ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}^\pm(\mathcal{A})\) induces a fully faithful functor \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^{\ensuremath{\mathrm{b}}}(\mathcal{A}) \to \ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^\pm(\mathcal{A})\), whose image is also characterized by \(\operatorname{H}^n\). This gives the case of \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^{\ensuremath{\mathrm{b}}}(\mathcal{A}) \to \ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}(\mathcal{A})\).

Corollary. Every functor in the sequence \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^{\ensuremath{\mathrm{b}}}(\mathcal{A}) \to \ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^{\pm}(\mathcal{A}) \to \ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}(\mathcal{A})\) is an embedding of a triangulated subcategory.

Proof. Use the long exact sequence of \(\operatorname{H}^n\) to verify, for \(\star \in \{+, -, \ensuremath{\mathrm{b}}\}\), that \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^\star(\mathcal{A})\), as a full additive subcategory of \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}(\mathcal{A})\), satisfies condition (ii) in Definition–Proposition reference. It is therefore a triangulated subcategory; the case \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^{\ensuremath{\mathrm{b}}}(\mathcal{A}) \to \ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^{\pm}(\mathcal{A})\) is also clear.

Definition. For \(-\infty \leq s \leq t \leq +\infty\), let \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^{[s,t]}(\mathcal{A})\) (or \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}^{[s, t]}(\mathcal{A})\)) denote the full subcategory of \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}(\mathcal{A})\) (or \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{A})\)) defined by the condition \[n \notin [s, t] \implies \operatorname{H}^n(X) = 0 .\] In addition, set \[\begin{align*} \ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^{\geq s}(\mathcal{A}) & := \ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^{[s, +\infty]}(\mathcal{A}), & \ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^{\leq t}(\mathcal{A}) & := \ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^{[-\infty, t]}(\mathcal{A}), \\ \ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}^{\geq s}(\mathcal{A}) & := \ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}^{[s, +\infty]}(\mathcal{A}), & \ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}^{\leq t}(\mathcal{A}) & := \ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}^{[-\infty, t]}(\mathcal{A}). \end{align*}\]

There are natural additive functors \(\mathcal{A} \to \ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A}) \to \ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}(\mathcal{A})\) that regard each object as a complex concentrated in degree zero. Theorem reference will show that under this identification \(\mathcal{A}\) is equivalent to \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^{\leq 0}(\mathcal{A}) \cap \ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^{\geq 0}(\mathcal{A})\).

Remark. If \(\mathcal{A}\) is \(\Bbbk\)-linear, where \(\Bbbk\) is a commutative ring, then \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}(\mathcal{A})\), \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^{\ensuremath{\mathrm{b}}}(\mathcal{A})\), and so on, as well as the embeddings between them, are also \(\Bbbk\)-linear; see Theorem reference (iii).

Since the truncation functors \(\tau^{\leq n}\) and \(\tau^{\geq n}\) from Definition–Proposition reference preserve acyclic complexes, they induce functors \(\tau^{\leq n}: \ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}(\mathcal{A}) \to \ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^{\leq n}(\mathcal{A})\) and \(\tau^{\geq n}: \ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}(\mathcal{A}) \to \ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^{\geq n}(\mathcal{A})\).

Proposition. For every \(n \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\), there are canonical adjoint pairs and a distinguished triangle \[\begin{equation*} \begin{gathered}\text{Diagram chapter4-unit-054-d008} \\ \text{Diagram chapter4-unit-054-d009} \\ \tau^{\leq n} X \to X \to \tau^{\geq n+1} X \xrightarrow{+1}, \quad X \in \operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}(\mathcal{A})). \end{gathered} \end{equation*}\]

Proof. It suffices to discuss the first adjoint pair. Let \(X \in \operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^{\leq n}(\mathcal{A}))\) and \(Y \in \operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}(\mathcal{A}))\). The unit and counit of the proposed adjunction are respectively \(\eta_X: X \to \tau^{\leq n} X\) and \(\varepsilon_Y: \tau^{\leq n} Y \to Y\). The morphism \(\varepsilon_Y\) is the canonical morphism already defined at the level of complexes, while \(\eta_X\) is the inverse of the quasi-isomorphism \(\tau^{\leq n} X \to X\). It remains to verify the triangle identities. After truncating at the level of complexes, it suffices to check them when \(X\) comes from \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}^{\leq n}(\mathcal{A})\); in that case \(\eta_X = \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_X\). The required triangle identities then follow from the complex-level version in Proposition reference.

For the distinguished triangle, recall that at the level of \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})\) there is a short exact sequence \(0 \to \tau^{\leq n} X \to X \to \tilde{\tau}^{\geq n+1} X \to 0\) and a quasi-isomorphism \(\tilde{\tau}^{\geq n+1} X \to \tau^{\geq n+1} X\) (Lemma reference).

Remark (Direct construction of the derived category). Let \(\mathrm{Qis} \subset \operatorname{Mor}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A}))\) denote the set of all quasi-isomorphisms. Suppose that, in defining \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}(\mathcal{A})\), instead of first passing to \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{A})\), we directly adjoin inverses to quasi-isomorphisms to obtain \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})[\mathrm{Qis}^{-1}]\). Is the result equivalent to \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}(\mathcal{A})\)? The answer is yes. A little thought about the universal property shows that the key is to verify the following property for every category \(\mathcal{D}\) and functor \(G: \ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A}) \to \mathcal{D}\): suppose \(G\) maps \(\mathrm{Qis}\) to isomorphisms and \(f, g \in \operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})}(X, Y)\) are homotopic. Then \(Gf = Gg\).

The key is to use the mapping cylinder. Let \(h\) be a homotopy from \(f\) to \(g\). As in Proposition reference (ii), this homotopy determines a morphism \(\tilde{h}: \operatorname{Cyl}_X \to Y\) such that \(f = \tilde{h} i_0\) and \(g = \tilde{h} i_1\). Part (i) of that proposition, however, states that \(j i_0 = j i_1\), where \(j: \operatorname{Cyl}_X \to X\) is a quasi-isomorphism. Hence \(Gj\) is an isomorphism, which in turn implies \(G i_0 = G i_1\). This proves the property.

Although \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}(\mathcal{A})\) can be constructed directly as \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})[\mathrm{Qis}^{-1}]\), the advantage of passing through \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{A})\) is that the latter has a triangulated structure; another reason is that \(\mathrm{Qis}\) is not a multiplicative system. The same assertion holds for \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^\star(\mathcal{A})\), with \(\star \in \{+, -, \ensuremath{\mathrm{b}}\}\).

Another important kind of triangulated subcategory is one defined by cohomology.

Definition (Triangulated subcategories defined by cohomology). Let \(\mathcal{T}\) be a weak Serre subcategory of \(\mathcal{A}\) (Definition reference). Define the full subcategory \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}_{\mathcal{T}}(\mathcal{A})\) of \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}(\mathcal{A})\) by \[X \in \operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}_{\mathcal{T}}(\mathcal{A})) \iff \forall n \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}, \; \operatorname{H}^n(X) \in \operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{T}).\] By Proposition reference, this is a saturated triangulated subcategory of \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}(\mathcal{A})\).

For \(\star \in \{+, -, \ensuremath{\mathrm{b}}\}\), define the saturated triangulated subcategory \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^\star_{\mathcal{T}}(\mathcal{A}) := \ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}_{\mathcal{T}}(\mathcal{A}) \cap \ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^\star(\mathcal{A})\).

Finally, there is a simple relation between the derived categories of \(\mathcal{A}\) and \(\mathcal{A}^{\operatorname{op}}\). Equip the opposite of a triangulated category with the triangulated structure described in Remark reference.

Proposition. The equivalence \(\sigma: \ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A}^{\operatorname{op}}) \ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}} \ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})^{\operatorname{op}}\) from Definition–Proposition reference induces equivalences of triangulated categories \[\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}(\mathcal{A}^{\operatorname{op}}) \simeq \ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}(\mathcal{A})^{\operatorname{op}}, \quad \ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^\pm(\mathcal{A}^{\operatorname{op}}) \simeq \ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^\mp(\mathcal{A})^{\operatorname{op}}, \quad \ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^{\ensuremath{\mathrm{b}}}(\mathcal{A}^{\operatorname{op}}) \simeq \ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^{\ensuremath{\mathrm{b}}}(\mathcal{A})^{\operatorname{op}}.\] Moreover, for every \(n \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\), \(\tau^{\leq n} \circ \sigma = \sigma \circ \tau^{\geq -n}\) and \(\tau^{\geq n} \circ \sigma = \sigma \circ \tau^{\leq -n}\).

Proof. Proposition reference shows that \(\sigma\) induces \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{A}^{\operatorname{op}}) \simeq \ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{A})^{\operatorname{op}}\). This functor preserves distinguished triangles (compare carefully the diagram in Proposition reference with Remark reference: after reversing the first row of the former diagram, it is the image of a distinguished triangle; the second row is distinguished in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{A})\) and, after reversal, becomes distinguished in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{A})^{\operatorname{op}}\)). It also preserves cohomology (Remark reference), and therefore induces \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}(\mathcal{A}^{\operatorname{op}}) \ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}} \ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}(\mathcal{A})^{\operatorname{op}}\). The assertions about the truncation functors follow from Remark reference.

Morphisms and Extensions

Throughout this section, \(\mathcal{A}\) is an Abelian category. Without further comment, we identify \(\operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A}))\), \(\operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{A}))\), and \(\operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}(\mathcal{A}))\); when necessary, we distinguish the morphism sets in these categories by writing \(\operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}(\mathcal{A})}\), \(\operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{A})}\), \(\operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})}\), and \(\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{A}}\). Readers not yet familiar with K-injective and K-projective complexes may skip the statements concerning them.

Proposition. Suppose \(X \in \operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}^+(\mathcal{A}))\) consists of injective objects, or, more generally, suppose \(X \in \operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A}))\) is a K-injective complex as in Definition reference. Then \(\operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{A})}(\cdot, X) \simeq \operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}(\mathcal{A})}(\cdot, X)\).

Dually, suppose \(X \in \operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}^-(\mathcal{A}))\) consists of projective objects, or suppose \(X \in \operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A}))\) is a K-projective complex. Then \(\operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{A})}(X, \cdot) \simeq \operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}(\mathcal{A})}(X, \cdot)\).

Proof. By duality, it suffices to treat \(\operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}(\mathcal{A})}(\cdot, X)\). Lemma reference gives \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:Hom-D-injective-aux}{} \operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}(\mathcal{A})}(T, X) \simeq \varinjlim_{\substack{\alpha: S \to T \\ \text{quasi-isomorphism in }\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{A})}} \operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{A})}(S, X), \quad T \in \operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{A})). \end{equation}\]

Suppose \(X \in \operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}^+(\mathcal{A}))\) consists of injective objects. For a quasi-isomorphism \(\alpha \in \operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{A})}(S, T)\), Theorem reference shows that \(\alpha^*: \operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{A})}(T, X) \ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}} \operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{A})}(S, X)\). Hence the \(\varinjlim\) in equation is equal to \(\operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{A})}(T, X)\).

If \(X \in \operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A}))\) is K-injective, use Theorem reference instead.

One immediate application of the preceding proposition is to control the size of a derived category. Here we again use the chosen Grothendieck universe \(\mathcal{U}\), together with the terminology of \(\mathcal{U}\)-categories (that is, “categories” in the standard convention of this book) and small \(\mathcal{U}\)-categories.

Corollary. Use the notation above. Let \(\mathcal{A}\) be a \(\mathcal{U}\)-category.

  1. If \(\mathcal{A}\) has enough injective objects (respectively projective objects), then \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^+(\mathcal{A})\) (respectively \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^-(\mathcal{A})\)) is also a \(\mathcal{U}\)-category.

  2. If \(\mathcal{A}\) has enough K-injective or K-projective complexes (Definition reference), then \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}(\mathcal{A})\) is also a \(\mathcal{U}\)-category.

  3. If \(\mathcal{A}\) is a small \(\mathcal{U}\)-category, then so is \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}(\mathcal{A})\).

Proof. It suffices to verify that \(\operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}(\mathcal{A})}(X,Y)\) is a small \(\mathcal{U}\)-set. Notice that the \(\operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{A})}\) version is easy to handle, since it is straightforward to prove that \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})\) is a \(\mathcal{U}\)-category.

Suppose \(\mathcal{A}\) has enough injective objects and \(X \in \operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^+(\mathcal{A}))\). Without loss of generality, we may assume that \(X \in \operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}^+(\mathcal{A}))\) consists of injective objects; (i) then follows from Proposition reference. If \(X\) has a K-injective resolution (respectively \(Y\) has a K-projective resolution), without loss of generality we may assume that \(X\) is K-injective (respectively \(Y\) is K-projective); the same argument gives (ii).

For (iii), observe that \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{A})\) is then a small \(\mathcal{U}\)-category. Apply this observation to Remark reference.

Proposition (Orthogonality). Let \(a,b,n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\), with \(a<b\).

  1. If \(X \in \operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^{\leq a}(\mathcal{A}))\) and \(Y \in \operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^{\geq b}(\mathcal{A}))\), then \(\operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}(\mathcal{A})}(X,Y)=0\).

  2. If \(X \in \operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^{\leq n}(\mathcal{A}))\) and \(Y \in \operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^{\geq n}(\mathcal{A}))\), then \(\operatorname{H}^n\) induces a canonical isomorphism \[\operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}(\mathcal{A})}(X, Y) \ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{A}}\left( \operatorname{H}^n(X), \operatorname{H}^n(Y) \right).\]

Proof. Let \(a\leq b\). Represent a morphism \(f\in\operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}(\mathcal{A})}(X,Y)\) by a diagram \(X\xleftarrow{s}Z\xrightarrow{g}Y\) in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{A})\), where \(s\) is a quasi-isomorphism. Replacing \(f\) by \(g\), we may reduce to the case in which \(f\) comes from \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})\). Next replace \(f\) by the composite \(\tau^{\leq a}X\to X\xrightarrow{f}Y\to\tau^{\geq b}Y\) in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})\). The two morphisms at the ends of this composite are quasi-isomorphisms. We may therefore reduce further to the case \(X\in\operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}^{\leq a}(\mathcal{A}))\) and \(Y\in\operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}^{\geq b}(\mathcal{A}))\).

If \(a<b\), every morphism \(X\to Y\) in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})\) must be zero. This proves (i).

Now take \(X\) and \(Y\) as above, but set \(a=n=b\) to treat (ii).
