Consider the canonical morphisms \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:derived-cat-orthogonality-aux}{} \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{A}}\left( \operatorname{H}^n(X), \operatorname{H}^n(Y) \right) \xleftarrow{\operatorname{H}^n} \operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})}(X, Y) \to \operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{A})}(X, Y) \to \operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}(\mathcal{A})}(X, Y). \end{equation}\]

  • The first morphism \(\operatorname{H}^n\) is an isomorphism: because \(X\in\operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}^{\leq n}(\mathcal{A}))\) and \(Y\in\operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}^{\geq n}(\mathcal{A}))\), any \(f\in\operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})}(X,Y)\) can be nonzero only in degree \(n\), and the only conditions on \(f^n\) are \[f^n\left( \operatorname{im}(d_X^{n-1}) \right) = 0 , \quad f\left(X^n\right) \subset \operatorname{ker}\left( d_Y^n \right).\] But \(X^n/\operatorname{im}(d_X^{n-1})=\operatorname{H}^n(X)\) and \(\operatorname{ker}(d_Y^n)=\operatorname{H}^n(Y)\).

  • The second morphism is also an isomorphism, since the conditions on \(X,Y\) imply \(\operatorname{Hom}^{-1}(X,Y)=\{0\}\).

Thus, to prove (ii), it remains to show that the last morphism in equation is an isomorphism. Applying Lemma reference gives \[\operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}(\mathcal{A})}(X, Y) \simeq \varinjlim_{[Y \rightarrowtail Z] \in \operatorname{Ob}(\mathrm{qis}_{Y/}) } \operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{A})}(X, Z).\] If \(Y\to Z\) is a quasi-isomorphism, then both morphisms in \(Y\to Z\to\tau^{\geq n}Z\) are quasi-isomorphisms in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{A})\). This shows that the quasi-isomorphisms \(Y\to Z\) with \(Z\) coming from \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}^{\geq n}(\mathcal{A})\) form a cofinal full subcategory of the filtered category \(\mathrm{qis}_{Y/}\) (Definition reference and Proposition reference). By Proposition reference, we may henceforth restrict the \(\varinjlim\) to this subcategory.

We already know that the first two morphisms in equation are canonical isomorphisms. Take \(Y\to Z\) as above. This gives the commutative diagram \[\text{Diagram chapter4-unit-055-d001}\] which shows that \(\operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{A})}(X,Y)\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}} \operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{A})}(X,Z)\). Hence the preceding \(\varinjlim\) is constant with value \(\operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{A})}(X,Y)\). The last morphism in equation is therefore an isomorphism.

Theorem. Regarding the objects of \(\mathcal{A}\) as complexes concentrated in degree zero gives an equivalence of additive categories \(\mathcal{A}\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^{\leq0}(\mathcal{A})\cap \ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^{\geq0}(\mathcal{A})\), with quasi-inverse given by \(\operatorname{H}^0\).

Proof. It is clear that the objects of \(\mathcal{A}\) give objects of \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^{\leq0}(\mathcal{A})\cap\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^{\geq0}(\mathcal{A})\). Thus we obtain an additive functor \(\Phi:\mathcal{A}\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^{\leq0}(\mathcal{A})\cap \ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^{\geq0}(\mathcal{A})\). Proposition reference (ii) implies that \(\Phi\) is fully faithful.

We next show that \(\Phi\) is essentially surjective. Let \(X\) be an object of \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^{\leq0}(\mathcal{A})\cap\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^{\geq0}(\mathcal{A})\). Applying the truncation functors to the complex \(X\) in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})\), we see that every morphism in \(X\to\tau^{\geq0}X\leftarrow\tau^{\leq0}\tau^{\geq0}X\) is a quasi-isomorphism, while Proposition reference gives \(\tau^{\leq0}\tau^{\geq0}X\simeq\operatorname{H}^0(X)\). Hence \(\Phi\) is an equivalence and \(\operatorname{H}^0\) is its quasi-inverse.

More generally, for every \(n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\), the functor \(S\mapsto S[-n]\) gives an additive equivalence from \(\mathcal{A}\) to \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^{\geq n}(\mathcal{A})\cap\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^{\leq n}(\mathcal{A})\), with \(\operatorname{H}^n\) as quasi-inverse. This is simply the shifted version of the result above. Henceforth, without further comment, we identify \(\mathcal{A}\) with the full additive subcategory \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^{\geq0}(\mathcal{A})\cap\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^{\leq0}(\mathcal{A})\) of \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^{\ensuremath{\mathrm{b}}}(\mathcal{A})\).

Definition. Let \(\star\in\{+,-,\ensuremath{\mathrm{b}},\hspace{0.8em}\}\) (where \(\star=\hspace{0.8em}\) means that there is no superscript), and let \(\mathcal{A}\) and \(\mathcal{A}'\) be Abelian categories. If a triangulated functor \(R:\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^\star(\mathcal{A})\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^\star(\mathcal{A}')\) restricts to \(\mathcal{A}\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^{[a,b]}(\mathcal{A}')\), where \(-\infty\leq a\leq b\leq+\infty\), then \(R\) is said to have amplitude contained in \([a,b]\).

Here is a simple observation: if \(X'\to X\to X''\xrightarrow{+1}\) is a distinguished triangle in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}(\mathcal{A})\) and \(X',X''\in\operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^{[a,b]}(\mathcal{A}))\), then \(X\in\operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^{[a,b]}(\mathcal{A}))\). This follows immediately from the long exact sequence for \(\operatorname{H}^n\).

Lemma. If the amplitude of \(R\) is contained in \([a,b]\), then for every \(-\infty<c\leq d<+\infty\) one has \[R\;\text{restricts to}\;\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^{[c,d]}(\mathcal{A})\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^{[c+a,d+b]}(\mathcal{A}').\]

Proof. The case \(c=d\) is immediate. If \(c<d\), then for every \(X\in\operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^{[c,d]}(\mathcal{A}))\), take the distinguished triangle from Proposition reference \[\tau^{\leq d-1}X\to X\to\tau^{\geq d}X\xrightarrow{+1},\quad \tau^{\geq d}X\simeq\operatorname{H}^d(X)[-d]\] and apply the preceding observation to its image under \(R\) to carry out the induction.

Consequently, if \(R\) has finite amplitude, then it restricts to \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^{\ensuremath{\mathrm{b}}}(\mathcal{A})\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^{\ensuremath{\mathrm{b}}}(\mathcal{A}')\). We next give a related result explaining how a triangulated functor is determined by its values on \(\mathcal{A}\).

Proposition (Way-out Lemma [Har66).] Let \(\mathcal{T}\) be a weak Serre subcategory of \(\mathcal{A}\) and let \(\star\in\{\hspace{0.8em},+,\ensuremath{\mathrm{b}}\}\). Consider triangulated functors \(F,G:\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^{\star}_{\mathcal{T}}(\mathcal{A})\to \ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}(\mathcal{A}')\) and a morphism \(\eta:F\to G\) between them such that \(\eta_X:FX\to GX\) is an isomorphism for every \(X\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{T})\). Then \(\eta\) is also an isomorphism if one of the following conditions holds:

  1. \(\star=\ensuremath{\mathrm{b}}\);

  2. \(\star=+\), and there exists \(k\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\) such that \(F,G\) restrict to \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^{\geq0}_{\mathcal{T}}(\mathcal{A})\to \ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^{\geq k}(\mathcal{A}')\);

  3. \(\star=\hspace{0.8em}\), and there exist \(k,\ell\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\) such that \(F,G\) respectively restrict to \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^{\geq0}_{\mathcal{T}}(\mathcal{A})\to \ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^{\geq k}(\mathcal{A}')\) and \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^{\leq0}_{\mathcal{T}}(\mathcal{A})\to \ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^{\leq\ell}(\mathcal{A}')\).

In addition, let \(\mathfrak{I}\) be a subset of \(\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{T})\) such that for every \(X\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{T})\) there exist \(I\in\mathfrak{I}\) and a monomorphism \(X\hookrightarrow I\). If the condition on \(\eta_X\) is replaced by the condition that \(\eta_I\) be an isomorphism for every \(I\in\mathfrak{I}\), then \(\eta\) is still an isomorphism under assumption (i) or (ii).

Of course, (ii) also has a dual version for \(\star=-\), which we do not write out.

Proof. For (i), simply repeat the argument of Lemma reference; use the distinguished triangle \(\tau^{\leq d}X\to X\to\tau^{\geq d+1}X\xrightarrow{+1}\) and Proposition reference inductively to reduce to the case \(X\simeq\operatorname{H}^{d+1}(X)[-d-1]\).

For (ii), the goal is to prove that \(\operatorname{H}^j(FX)\to\operatorname{H}^j(GX)\) is an isomorphism for every \(X\in\operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^+_{\mathcal{T}}(\mathcal{A}))\) and \(j\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\). Consider the distinguished triangle above once more, but take \(d\gg0\) so that \(F\tau^{\geq d+1}X\) and \(G\tau^{\geq d+1}X\) both lie in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^{\geq j+1}(\mathcal{A}')\). We obtain a commutative diagram with exact rows \[\text{Diagram chapter4-unit-055-d002}\] But \(\tau^{\leq d}X\in \operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^{\ensuremath{\mathrm{b}}}_{\mathcal{T}}(\mathcal{A}))\), so this case follows from (i).

For (iii), choose any \(d\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\). Using \(\tau^{\leq d}X\to X\to\tau^{\geq d+1}X\xrightarrow{+1}\) and Proposition reference, this case follows from (ii) and its dual.

Now consider the final assertion. Since (ii) has been proved, it suffices to show that \(\eta_X\) is an isomorphism for every \(X\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{T})\). Take an exact sequence \(0\to X\to I^0\to I^1\to\cdots\) with every \(I^n\in\mathfrak{I}\). Write this sequence as a quasi-isomorphism of complexes \(X\to I\); it remains to prove that \(\eta_I\) is an isomorphism. To do this, define the brutal truncation \(\sigma^{\leq d}I\) of the complex, which agrees with \(I\) in degrees \(\leq d\) and has zero terms in all other degrees; define \(\sigma^{\geq d+1}I\) similarly. We can now follow the arguments for (i) and (ii), using instead the canonical short exact sequence in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})\) \[0\to\sigma^{\geq d+1}I\to I\to\sigma^{\leq d}I\to0\] and its corresponding distinguished triangle. The details are left to the reader.

Recall Theorem reference. Its key ingredient is the full faithfulness \(\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{A}}(X,Y)\simeq\operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}(\mathcal{A})}(X,Y)\). What information do we obtain when the degrees of \(X\) and \(Y\) are shifted relative to one another? This is our next topic.

Definition (\(\operatorname{Ext}\) functors: General case). For \(X,Y\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{A})\) and \(n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\), define \(\operatorname{Ext}^n_{\mathcal{A}}(X,Y):= \operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}(\mathcal{A})}\left(X,Y[n]\right)\). The functor \(\operatorname{Ext}^n_{\mathcal{A}}:\mathcal{A}^{\operatorname{op}}\times\mathcal{A}\to \ensuremath{\mathsf{Ab}}\) is additive in each variable.

The notation \(\operatorname{Ext}^n_{\mathcal{A}}(X,Y)\) already appeared in Definition–Proposition reference. The discussion of \(\operatorname{RHom}\) will reconcile the two definitions; see Corollary reference. Here we do not assume that \(\mathcal{A}\) has enough injective or projective objects. As for \(\operatorname{Hom}\), functoriality of \(\operatorname{Ext}^n\) in its two variables is still called pullback and pushout, respectively. When no confusion can arise, \(\operatorname{Ext}^n_{\mathcal{A}}\) is also abbreviated to \(\operatorname{Ext}^n\). We now show that its properties resemble those of the \(\operatorname{Ext}^n\) defined in §reference.

Proposition. Below, \(X,Y\) are arbitrary objects of \(\mathcal{A}\). The family of bifunctors \((\operatorname{Ext}^n)_{n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}}\) has the following properties.

  1. If \(n<0\), then \(\operatorname{Ext}^n(X,Y)=0\).

  2. There is a canonical isomorphism \(\operatorname{Ext}^0(X,Y)\simeq\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{A}}(X,Y)\).

  3. Short exact sequences \(0\to X'\to X\to X''\to0\) and \(0\to Y'\to Y\to Y''\to0\) in \(\mathcal{A}\) induce the respective long exact sequences \[\begin{gather*} \cdots \to \operatorname{Ext}^{n-1}(X', Y) \xrightarrow{\delta^{n-1}} \operatorname{Ext}^n(X'', Y) \to \operatorname{Ext}^n(X, Y) \to \operatorname{Ext}^n(X', Y) \to \cdots , \\ \cdots \to \operatorname{Ext}^{n-1}(X, Y'') \xrightarrow{\delta^{n-1}} \operatorname{Ext}^n(X, Y') \to \operatorname{Ext}^n(X, Y) \to \operatorname{Ext}^n(X, Y'') \to \cdots , \end{gather*}\] with every connecting morphism \(\delta^n\) functorial in the short exact sequence.

  4. If \(\operatorname{Ext}^1(X,\cdot)=0\) (respectively \(\operatorname{Ext}^1(\cdot,Y)=0\)), then \(X\) (respectively \(Y\)) is a projective (respectively injective) object of \(\mathcal{A}\).

Proof. Assertions (i) and (ii) follow immediately from Proposition reference.

For (iii), first use Proposition reference to turn the short exact sequences canonically into distinguished triangles \(X'\to X\to X''\xrightarrow{+1}\) and \(Y'\to Y\to Y''\xrightarrow{+1}\) in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}(\mathcal{A})\). Then use the fact that \(\operatorname{Hom}\) is a cohomological functor in each variable (Proposition reference).

Finally, (iv) follows by applying (i) and (ii) to the long exact sequences in (iii).

Since \(\operatorname{Ext}^n\) is given by \(\operatorname{Hom}\) in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}(\mathcal{A})\), for \(f\in\operatorname{Ext}^n(X,Y)\) and \(g\in\operatorname{Ext}^n(X',Y')\) there is an evident direct sum \(f\oplus g\in\operatorname{Ext}^n(X\oplus X',Y\oplus Y')\). On the other hand, \(\operatorname{Ext}\) has a composition operation, \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:Ext-composition}{}\text{Diagram chapter4-unit-055-d003} \end{equation}\] where \(m,n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\). It is easy to see that this operation is associative and bilinear. Consequently, the Abelian group \[\operatorname{Ext}(X):=\bigoplus_{n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}}\operatorname{Ext}^n(X,X)\] has a natural ring structure, with \(\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_A\in\operatorname{End}_{\mathcal{A}}(A)\) as multiplicative identity, while \(\operatorname{Ext}(X,Y):=\bigoplus_{n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}}\operatorname{Ext}^n(X,Y)\) becomes an \((\operatorname{Ext}(Y),\operatorname{Ext}(X))\)-bimodule. More generally, if \(\mathcal{A}\) is \(\Bbbk\)-linear, where \(\Bbbk\) is a commutative ring, then the functors \(\operatorname{Ext}^n\) take values in \(\Bbbk\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\), while \(\operatorname{Ext}(X)\) becomes a \(\Bbbk\)-algebra. The definition of multiplication in equation shows that \(\operatorname{Ext}(X)\) is in fact a graded \(\Bbbk\)-algebra; see [Li1]. Such constructions are extremely useful in representation theory.

Definition. Let \(X\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{A})\). The graded algebra \(\operatorname{Ext}(X)\) defined above is called the \(\operatorname{Ext}\)-algebra of the object \(X\).

The notation \(\operatorname{Ext}\) abbreviates “extension.” To explain the concrete connection, we first define what an extension means.

Definition. Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be objects of \(\mathcal{A}\) and let \(n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}_{\geq1}\). An exact sequence in \(\mathcal{A}\) of the form \[\mathcal{E}:\quad 0\to Y\to E^1\to\cdots\to E^n\to X\to0\] is called an \(n\)-extension of \(X\) by \(Y\). For fixed \(X,Y\), consider the following binary relation on the set of all \(n\)-extensions: \[\begin{multline*} \mathcal{E} \sim_0 \mathcal{E}' \iff \text{there is a commutative diagram} \\ \text{Diagram chapter4-unit-055-d004} \end{multline*}\] This binary relation generates an equivalence relation \(\sim\).1 The equivalence classes of \(n\)-extensions form the set \(\operatorname{Ext}^{n,\text{Yoneda}}(X,Y)\).

Proposition reference implies that equivalence of \(1\)-extensions is the same as isomorphism of short exact sequences \[\text{Diagram chapter4-unit-055-d005}\]

Convention. Henceforth a \(1\)-extension is simply called an extension, and equivalence between such extensions is called isomorphism. A split short exact sequence (Proposition reference) is also called a split extension; all such extensions are isomorphic.

The following operations are available on \(n\)-extensions.

  • Composition.For \([\mathcal{E}_1]\in\operatorname{Ext}^{n,\text{Yoneda}}(Y,Z)\) and \([\mathcal{E}_2]\in\operatorname{Ext}^{m,\text{Yoneda}}(X,Y)\), define \([\mathcal{E}_1]\circ[\mathcal{E}_2]\in \operatorname{Ext}^{n+m,\text{Yoneda}}(X,Z)\) by splicing the two exact sequences end-to-end at \(Y\). This operation is also called the Yoneda product.

  • Pullback.For a morphism \(f:X'\to X\), the corresponding map \(f^*:\operatorname{Ext}^{n,\text{Yoneda}}(X,Y)\to \operatorname{Ext}^{n,\text{Yoneda}}(X',Y)\) is obtained as follows. Given \([\mathcal{E}]\in\operatorname{Ext}^{n,\text{Yoneda}}(X,Y)\), consider the commutative diagram \[\text{Diagram chapter4-unit-055-d006}\] The square marked \(\Box\) is a pullback square, while \(E^{n-1}\to E^n\ensuremath{\underset{X}{\times}}X'\) is determined by \(E^{n-1}\to E^n\) and \(E^{n-1}\xrightarrow{0}X'\). Pullback preserves kernels, and \(E^n\ensuremath{\underset{X}{\times}}X'\to X'\) is still an epimorphism (Proposition reference); from this one checks that the first row remains exact. Its equivalence class is \(f^*[\mathcal{E}]\).

  • Pushout.For a morphism \(g:Y\to Y'\), the corresponding map \(g_*:\operatorname{Ext}^{n,\text{Yoneda}}(X,Y)\to \operatorname{Ext}^{n,\text{Yoneda}}(X,Y')\) is obtained as follows. Given \([\mathcal{E}]\in\operatorname{Ext}^{n,\text{Yoneda}}(X,Y)\), pushout gives the commutative diagram \[\text{Diagram chapter4-unit-055-d007}\] Here \(E^1\ensuremath{\underset{Y}{\sqcup}}Y'\to E^2\) is determined by \(E^1\to E^2\) and \(Y'\xrightarrow{0}E^2\). Dually, one checks that the second row remains exact. Its equivalence class is \(g_*[\mathcal{E}]\).

  • Direct sum.Take the termwise direct sum of two extensions, \(\mathcal{E}\oplus\mathcal{E}'\), and then take its equivalence class. This gives a map \[\text{Diagram chapter4-unit-055-d008}\]

  • Baer sum.This is the following map: \[\text{Diagram chapter4-unit-055-d009}\] It is defined by pulling \([\mathcal{E}_1]\oplus[\mathcal{E}_2]\) back along \(X\hookrightarrow X\times X\), then pushing it out along \(Y\oplus Y\twoheadrightarrow Y\) (these morphisms come from Convention reference). The result is \([\mathcal{E}_1]\dot{+}[\mathcal{E}_2]\in \operatorname{Ext}^{n,\text{Yoneda}}(X,Y)\).

One checks that pullback and pushout commute: \(g_*f^*=f^*g_*\), while the Baer sum \(\dot{+}\) is commutative. These properties also follow from those of \(\operatorname{Ext}^n\) by the following theorem.

Theorem (Nobuo Yoneda). For all \(X,Y\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{A})\) and \(n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}_{\geq1}\), there is a canonical bijection \[\operatorname{Ext}^{n,\text{Yoneda}}(X,Y) \xrightarrow{1:1} \operatorname{Ext}^n(X,Y),\] which sends the equivalence class of an \(n\)-extension \(0\to Y\to E^1\to\cdots\to E^n\to X\to0\) to \(as^{-1}\in\operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}(\mathcal{A})}(X,Y[n])\), where \[\text{Diagram chapter4-unit-055-d010}\] and all omitted terms are zero. Under this bijection, composition, direct sum, pullback, and pushout of \(n\)-extensions correspond to the respective operations on \(\operatorname{Ext}^n\), while the Baer sum \(\dot{+}\) corresponds to the additive group law on \(\operatorname{Ext}^n(X,Y)\).

Proof. An equivalence of extensions \(\mathcal{E}\sim\mathcal{E}'\) is reflected by a quasi-isomorphism between the corresponding complexes \(Z\) and \(Z'\). Thus the displayed map is well defined. It remains to prove that it is surjective and injective. We begin with surjectivity.

Every \(f\in\operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}(\mathcal{A})}(X,Y[n])\) is represented by a diagram \(X\xleftarrow{s}Z\xrightarrow{a}Y[n]\) in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})\), where \(s\) is a quasi-isomorphism. After precomposing with the quasi-isomorphism \(\tau^{\leq0}Z\to Z\), we may assume that \(Z\in\operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}^{\leq0}(\mathcal{A}))\). Next, the adjunction in Proposition reference factors \(s\) and \(a\) through the quasi-isomorphism \(Z\twoheadrightarrow\tau^{\geq-n}Z\). Hence we may assume that \(Z\in\operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}^{[-n,0]}(\mathcal{A}))\).

Since \(Z\) is exact outside degree \(0\), imitate the definition of the pushout of an extension above and define a complex \(Z'\) to be the second row of the following diagram: \[\text{Diagram chapter4-unit-055-d011}\] The vertical morphisms give a quasi-isomorphism \(Z\to Z'\), and \(a\) factors as \(Z\to Z'\xrightarrow{a'}Y[n]\).

Moreover, \(Z\xrightarrow{s}X\) also factors canonically as \(Z\to Z'\xrightarrow{s'}X\). This is immediate when \(n>1\); when \(n=1\), the morphism \((s')^0:Z^0\ensuremath{\underset{Z^{-1}}{\sqcup}}Y\to X\) is determined by \(s^0:Z^0\to X\) and \(Y\xrightarrow{0}X\).

In short, we have reduced to the case in which \(X\xleftarrow{s}Z\xrightarrow{a}Y[n]\) has the form \[\text{Diagram chapter4-unit-055-d012}\] Flattening this diagram, however, gives the \(n\)-extension \(0\to Y\to Z^{-n+1}\to\cdots\to Z^0\to X\to0\). This proves surjectivity.

We now prove injectivity. In view of equation, the starting point is a commutative diagram in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{A})\) \[\text{Diagram chapter4-unit-055-d013} \quad \begin{array}{l} W \in \operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})), \quad s_i, t: \;\text{quasi-isomorphisms}, \\ (Z_i; s_i, a_i) \;\text{has the reduced form above and corresponds to an $n$-extension},\\ (i = 1, 2) . \end{array}\] We wish to show that this diagram gives an equivalence of \(n\)-extensions. As before, first precompose with \(\tau^{\leq0}W\to W\) to reduce to \(W\in\operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}^{\leq0}(\mathcal{A}))\). Next, use the truncation adjunction to factor all the morphisms in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})\) through \(W\twoheadrightarrow\tau^{\geq-n}W\). Let \(K\) be the kernel of \(W\twoheadrightarrow\tau^{\geq-n}W\). Since \(\operatorname{Hom}^{-1}(K,V)=0\) for every \(V\in\operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}^{[-n,0]}(\mathcal{A}))\), the homotopies between these morphisms factor in the same way. This operation therefore does not change the commutativity of the diagram in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{A})\). We have reduced to the case \(W\in\operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}^{[-n,0]}(\mathcal{A}))\).

Similarly, \(\operatorname{Hom}^{-1}(W,X)=0\), so the left half of the diagram already commutes in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})\). For the right half, since \(a_i^{-n}=\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_Y\), we may modify the morphisms \(W\to Z_i\) by suitable homotopies so that the right half also commutes in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})\). Now repeat the pushout operation from the surjectivity proof to reduce to \(W^{-n}=Y\) and \(b^{-n}=\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_Y\), without changing the commutativity of the left half, as one verifies directly. Thus \((W;t,b)\) also corresponds to an \(n\)-extension, and the commutative diagram witnesses the equivalence relation \(\sim\) in Definition reference. This proves injectivity.

Compatibility of composition, direct sum, pullback, and pushout with this bijection is a routine verification. For the Baer sum \(\dot{+}\), Proposition reference realizes the sum \(f+g\) in \(\operatorname{Ext}^n(X,Y):=\operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}(\mathcal{A})}(X,Y[n])\) as the composite \(X\to X\oplus X\xrightarrow{f\oplus g}(Y\oplus Y)[n]\to Y[n]\), which agrees exactly with the definition of \(\dot{+}\).

Dually, an element of \(\operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}(\mathcal{A})}(X,Y[n])\) can also be represented by a diagram of the form \(X\xrightarrow{b}Z\xleftarrow{t}Y[n]\) in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})\), where \(t\) is a quasi-isomorphism. The exercises for this chapter compare these two constructions.

Proposition. Consider an extension \(0\to Y\xrightarrow{f}E\xrightarrow{g}X\to0\). In the exact sequence from Proposition reference (iii), \[\begin{gather*} \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{A}}(X,E) \xrightarrow{g_*} \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{A}}(X,X) \to \operatorname{Ext}^1(X,Y), \end{gather*}\] the element of \(\operatorname{Ext}^1(X,Y)\) determined by this extension is the image of \(\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_X\).

Proof. The connecting homomorphism \(\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{A}}(X,X)\to\operatorname{Ext}^1(X,Y)\) is precisely \(e_*\), where \(e\in\operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}(\mathcal{A})}(X,Y[1])\) is determined by the diagram in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})\) \[\text{Diagram chapter4-unit-055-d014}\] as in Proposition reference. But \(\operatorname{Cone}(f)\) is the complex \(Y\xrightarrow{f}E\) concentrated in degrees \(-1\) and \(0\). Comparison with Theorem reference immediately shows that \(e\) comes from the extension \(0\to Y\xrightarrow{f}E\xrightarrow{g}X\to0\).

Proposition. The zero element of the additive group \(\left(\operatorname{Ext}^{n,\text{Yoneda}}(X,Y),\dot{+}\right)\) is represented by the following extensions:

\(n = 1\) The split extension \(0 \to Y \to X \oplus Y \to X \to 0\)
\(n = 2\) \(0 \to Y \xrightarrow{\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_Y} Y \xrightarrow{0} X \xrightarrow{\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_X} X \to 0\)
\(n \geq 3\) \(0 \to Y \xrightarrow{\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_Y} Y \to 0 \to \cdots \to 0 \to X \xrightarrow{\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_X} X \to 0\) .

Proof. For \(n=1\), suppose that the short exact sequence \(0\to Y\xrightarrow{f}E\xrightarrow{g}X\to0\) corresponds to the zero element. The exact sequence in Proposition reference shows that there is an \(s\in\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{A}}(X,E)\) such that \(gs=\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_X\); hence the short exact sequence splits.

Next consider \(n=2\). Both \(\operatorname{Ext}^1(0,Y)\) and \(\operatorname{Ext}^1(X,0)\) are plainly zero groups; corresponding extensions may be taken to be \(0\to Y\xrightarrow{\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}}Y\to0\to0\) and \(0\to0\to X\xrightarrow{\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}}X\to0\). Since \(\operatorname{Ext}^1\times\operatorname{Ext}^1\to\operatorname{Ext}^2\) is bilinear, splicing these two extensions gives the zero element of \(\operatorname{Ext}^2(X,Y)\). For \(n\geq3\), consider the \((n-1)\)-extension \(0\to\cdots\to0\to X\xrightarrow{\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}}X\to0\); the same argument gives the zero element of \(\operatorname{Ext}^n(X,Y)\).

  1. In other words, \(\mathcal{E}_1\sim\mathcal{E}_2\) if and only if they can be connected by a chain of commutative diagrams of this kind.↩︎

Triangulated Functors and Localization

Fix a triangulated category \(\mathcal{D}\) and a saturated triangulated subcategory \(\mathcal{N}\), and denote the corresponding Verdier localization by \(Q: \mathcal{D} \to \mathcal{D}/\mathcal{N}\). Likewise, consider a triangulated category \(\mathcal{D}'\) and \(Q': \mathcal{D}' \to \mathcal{D}'/\mathcal{N}'\). Let \(F: \mathcal{D} \to \mathcal{D}'\) be a triangulated functor. Consider the diagram whose solid part is given: \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:derived-situation}{}\text{Diagram chapter4-unit-056-d001} \end{equation}\] The naive hope is to complete the dashed part so that the entire diagram commutes. If \(F\left(\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{N})\right) \subset \operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{N}')\), then \(Q'F\) annihilates \(\mathcal{N}\), and the universal property in Theorem reference induces the dashed functor. In practice, however, \(F\) rarely has this property. We therefore settle for less and turn to the Kan extensions introduced in §reference.

Definition (Derived functors of a triangulated functor). Let \(F: \mathcal{D} \to \mathcal{D}'\) be as above.

  • If \(\operatorname{Lan}_Q(Q' F)\) exists and is a triangulated functor, denote it by \(\mathrm{R}^{\mathcal{N}'}_{\mathcal{N}} F: \mathcal{D}/\mathcal{N} \to \mathcal{D}'/\mathcal{N}'\);

  • if \(\operatorname{Ran}_Q(Q' F)\) exists and is a triangulated functor, denote it by \(\mathrm{L}^{\mathcal{N}'}_{\mathcal{N}} F: \mathcal{D}/\mathcal{N} \to \mathcal{D}'/\mathcal{N}'\).

We call \(\mathrm{R}^{\mathcal{N}'}_{\mathcal{N}} F\) (respectively, \(\mathrm{L}^{\mathcal{N}'}_{\mathcal{N}} F\)) the right derived functor (respectively, left derived functor) of the triangulated functor \(F\). Its uniqueness up to unique isomorphism follows from the uniqueness of Kan extensions.

By Definition reference of Kan extensions, these data fit into the \(2\)-cell diagrams \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:derived-can-morphism}{}\text{Diagram chapter4-unit-056-d002} \quad \text{Diagram chapter4-unit-056-d003} \end{equation}\] The universal property says that every way of filling equation with a \(2\)-cell is obtained uniquely by “pushing out” the diagram for \(\mathrm{R}^{\mathcal{N}'}_{\mathcal{N}}F\), or uniquely by “pulling into” the diagram for \(\mathrm{L}^{\mathcal{N}'}_{\mathcal{N}}F\), according to the direction of the filling. As an illustration, we explain how the universal property of the \(2\)-cell derives a canonical morphism \(\mathrm{R}^{\mathcal{N}'}_{\mathcal{N}}F \to \mathrm{R}^{\mathcal{N}'}_{\mathcal{N}}G\) from a morphism of functors \(F \to G\), assuming that these derived functors exist. Examine the diagram on the left: \[\text{Diagram chapter4-unit-056-d004} \xlongequal{\text{vertical composition}} \text{Diagram chapter4-unit-056-d005}\] By the universal property of equation, the vertical composite in the left-hand diagram is uniquely the pushout of the diagram corresponding to \(\mathrm{R}^{\mathcal{N}'}_{\mathcal{N}}F\), as shown on the right. This “push” is the desired canonical morphism. The case of left derived functors is of course dual. The next remark shows that these canonical morphisms are compatible with translation.

Remark. Suppose that \(\mathrm{R}^{\mathcal{N}'}_{\mathcal{N}}F\) (respectively, \(\mathrm{L}^{\mathcal{N}'}_{\mathcal{N}}F\)) exists. If \((L,\xi)\) (respectively, \((R,\delta)\)) in the universal property of the Kan extension is taken to consist of a triangulated functor and a morphism compatible with translation (see Definition reference), then the determined morphism \(\chi: \mathrm{R}^{\mathcal{N}'}_{\mathcal{N}}F \to L\) (respectively, \(\theta: R \to \mathrm{L}^{\mathcal{N}'}_{\mathcal{N}}F\)) is automatically compatible with translation as well. This follows immediately from uniqueness.

Definition reference raises two questions. First, how can the existence of \(\mathrm{R}^{\mathcal{N}'}_{\mathcal{N}}F\) (or \(\mathrm{L}^{\mathcal{N}'}_{\mathcal{N}}F\)) be guaranteed? Second, how do these functors relate to composition of functors? We address the two questions in order.

Definition. Let \(\mathcal{N}\), \(\mathcal{N}'\), and \(F: \mathcal{D} \to \mathcal{D}'\) be as above, and let \(\mathcal{I}\) be a triangulated subcategory of \(\mathcal{D}\). If the following conditions hold,

  • Resolution condition.for every \(X \in \operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{D})\) there is a morphism \(X \to Y\) (respectively, \(Y \to X\)) in \(S\mathcal{N}\) with \(Y \in \operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{I})\);

  • \(\mathcal{N}\)-preservation condition. \(F\left(\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{N}\cap\mathcal{I})\right) \subset \operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{N}')\),

then \(\mathcal{I}\) is called \(F\)-injective (respectively, \(F\)-projective).

For example, if \(F\left(\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{N})\right) \subset \operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{N}')\), then \(\mathcal{D}\) itself is both \(F\)-injective and \(F\)-projective. The condition \(F\left(\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{N}\cap\mathcal{I})\right)\subset\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{N}')\), together with the universal property of Verdier localization, gives a triangulated functor \(F^\flat: \mathcal{I}/(\mathcal{I}\cap\mathcal{N}) \to \mathcal{D}'/\mathcal{N}'\).

Proposition. If \(\mathcal{I}\) is an \(F\)-injective (respectively, \(F\)-projective) triangulated subcategory, then \(\mathrm{R}^{\mathcal{N}'}_{\mathcal{N}}F\) (respectively, \(\mathrm{L}^{\mathcal{N}'}_{\mathcal{N}}F\)) exists, and the following diagram commutes up to isomorphism: \[\text{Diagram chapter4-unit-056-d006}\]

Proof. Consider the case of \(\mathrm{R}^{\mathcal{N}'}_{\mathcal{N}}F\). The existence of the left Kan extension \(\operatorname{Lan}_Q(Q'F)\) follows from Proposition reference (ii). The only point requiring verification is that \(Q'F\) sends \(S\mathcal{N}\cap\operatorname{Mor}(\mathcal{I}) \xlongequal{\href{#eqn:S-N-D}{equation}}S(\mathcal{N}\cap\mathcal{I})\) to isomorphisms. Take \(f:A\to B\) in this set and complete it to a distinguished triangle \(A\xrightarrow{f}B\to C\xrightarrow{+1}\), where \(C\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{N}\cap\mathcal{I})\). Then the distinguished triangle \(FA\xrightarrow{Ff}FB\to FC\xrightarrow{+1}\) has \(FC\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{N}')\), ensuring that \((Q'F)(f)\) is an isomorphism.

Proposition reference implies that \(i\) has a triangulated quasi-inverse \(i^{-1}\). Consequently, \(\mathrm{R}^{\mathcal{N}'}_{\mathcal{N}}F:=F^\flat\circ i^{-1}\) gives \(\operatorname{Lan}_Q(Q'F)\) and is at the same time a triangulated functor.

Theorem. Consider triangulated categories \(\mathcal{D}\), \(\mathcal{D}'\), and \(\mathcal{D}''\), with saturated triangulated subcategories \(\mathcal{N}\), \(\mathcal{N}'\), and \(\mathcal{N}''\). Let triangulated functors \(\mathcal{D}\xrightarrow{F}\mathcal{D}'\xrightarrow{F'}\mathcal{D}''\) be given.

  1. Suppose that the right derived functors \(\mathrm{R}^{\mathcal{N}'}_{\mathcal{N}}F\), \(\mathrm{R}^{\mathcal{N}''}_{\mathcal{N}'}F'\), and \(\mathrm{R}^{\mathcal{N}''}_{\mathcal{N}}(F'F)\) exist. There is then a corresponding canonical morphism \[\mathrm{R}^{\mathcal{N}''}_{\mathcal{N}} (F' F) \to \left( \mathrm{R}^{\mathcal{N}''}_{\mathcal{N}'} F' \right) \left( \mathrm{R}^{\mathcal{N}'}_{\mathcal{N}} F \right).\]

  2. The analogous statement holds for left derived functors, with the corresponding canonical morphism \[\left( \mathrm{L}^{\mathcal{N}''}_{\mathcal{N'}} F' \right) \left( \mathrm{L}^{\mathcal{N}'}_{\mathcal{N}} F \right) \to \mathrm{L}^{\mathcal{N}''}_{\mathcal{N}} (F' F).\]

  3. Fix a triangulated subcategory \(\mathcal{I}\) of \(\mathcal{D}\) (and a triangulated subcategory \(\mathcal{I}'\) of \(\mathcal{D}'\)). If \(\mathcal{I}\) is \(F\)-injective, \(\mathcal{I}'\) is \(F'\)-injective, and \(F(\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{I}))\subset\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{I}')\), then \(\mathcal{I}\) is \(F'F\)-injective and the canonical morphism in (i) is an isomorphism.

  4. The analogous statement holds with “injective” replaced by “projective.” In this case, \(\mathcal{I}\) is \(F'F\)-projective and the canonical morphism in (ii) is an isomorphism.

Proof. Clearly, (i), (iii) are respectively dual to (ii), (iv), so it suffices to consider the former pair.

For (i), write \(R:=\mathrm{R}^{\mathcal{N}'}_{\mathcal{N}}F\) and \(R':=\mathrm{R}^{\mathcal{N}''}_{\mathcal{N}'}F'\). Consider the \(2\)-cell diagram \[\text{Diagram chapter4-unit-056-d007}\] The universal property of the left Kan extension gives \(\mathrm{R}^{\mathcal{N}''}_{\mathcal{N}}(F'F)\to R'R\), characterized by \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:R-composite-aux}{}\text{Diagram chapter4-unit-056-d008} \;\text{composed with}\; = \text{Diagram chapter4-unit-056-d009} \end{equation}\]

For (iii), the fact that \(\mathcal{I}\) is \(F'F\)-injective follows directly from Definition reference and the condition \(F(\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{I}))\subset\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{I}')\). Let \(Y\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{I})\). The construction in Proposition reference gives \[\begin{gather*} RQY = Q'FY \in \operatorname{Ob}\left(\mathcal{I}'/(\mathcal{N}'\cap\mathcal{I}')\right), \\ (R'R)QY = R'(Q'FY) = Q'' F'FY = \mathrm{R}^{\mathcal{N}''}_{\mathcal{N}} (F' F)(QY). \end{gather*}\]

For a general object \(QX\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{D}/\mathcal{N})\), with \(X\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{D})\), there is a morphism \(X\to Y\) in \(S\mathcal{N}\) with \(Y\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{I})\), so that \(QX\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}QY\). Applying the preceding step yields an isomorphism \(\mathrm{R}^{\mathcal{N}''}_{\mathcal{N}}(F'F)(QX)\simeq R'R(QX)\). The interested reader may check that these isomorphisms are indeed compatible with the morphism \(\mathrm{R}^{\mathcal{N}''}_{\mathcal{N}}(F'F)\to R'R\) characterized by equation.

Remark (P. Deligne’s definition). By Proposition reference (iii), under the hypotheses of Proposition reference, the derived functors can be written as \[\begin{align*} (\mathrm{R}_{\mathcal{N}}^{\mathcal{N}'} F)(QX) & \simeq \varinjlim_{(X \to Y) \in \operatorname{Ob}(S\mathcal{N}_{X/})} (Q'F)Y, \\ (\mathrm{L}_{\mathcal{N}}^{\mathcal{N}'} F)(QX) & \simeq \varprojlim_{(Y \to X) \in \operatorname{Ob}(S\mathcal{N}_{/X}^{\operatorname{op}})} (Q'F)Y. \end{align*}\] These isomorphisms are canonical and, by means of resolutions, each limit is attained by some \(Y\). In [SGA4-3], Deligne defines \((\mathrm{R}F_{\mathcal{N}}^{\mathcal{N}'} F)(QX)\) and \((\mathrm{L}_{\mathcal{N}}^{\mathcal{N}'} F)(QX)\) respectively as the above limits, provided that the limit in question is actually attained by some \(Y\). One advantage of this definition is that it can be applied to a single object \(X\), and hence can be made “partial.”

The formulas above also describe the morphisms that come with the derived functors as Kan extensions, \(Q'F\to(\mathrm{R}^{\mathcal{N}'}_{\mathcal{N}}F)Q\) and \((\mathrm{L}^{\mathcal{N}'}_{\mathcal{N}}F)Q\to Q'F\). They correspond, respectively, to the terms \(Y=X\) in \(\varinjlim\) and \(\varprojlim\).

We now turn to bifunctors. Let \(\mathcal{D}_1\), \(\mathcal{D}_2\), and \(\mathcal{D}'\) be triangulated categories, with translation functors \(T_1\), \(T_2\), and \(T'\), respectively.

Definition. A triangulated bifunctor from \(\mathcal{D}_1\times\mathcal{D}_2\) to \(\mathcal{D}'\) consists of the following data.

  • A bifunctor \(F:\mathcal{D}_1\times\mathcal{D}_2\to\mathcal{D}'\) endowed with the structure of a triangulated functor in each variable.

  • For all \(X\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{D}_1)\) and \(Y\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{D}_2)\), the following diagram is anticommutative (that is, its two composites differ by a minus sign)1 \[\text{Diagram chapter4-unit-056-d010}\] The arrows come from the triangulated-functor structures of \(F\) in the two variables.

In the situation above, take \(\mathcal{N}_1\), \(\mathcal{N}_2\), and \(\mathcal{N}'\) to be saturated triangulated subcategories of \(\mathcal{D}_1\), \(\mathcal{D}_2\), and \(\mathcal{D}'\), respectively. Denote the corresponding localization functors by \(Q_i:\mathcal{D}_i\to\mathcal{D}_i/\mathcal{N}_i\) (\(i=1,2\)) and \(Q':\mathcal{D}'\to\mathcal{D}'/\mathcal{N}'\). Now fix a triangulated bifunctor \(F:\mathcal{D}_1\times\mathcal{D}_2\to\mathcal{D}'\). For this bifunctor we may study the functor-extension problem in the diagram \[\text{Diagram chapter4-unit-056-d011}\] Since \((Q_1,Q_2)\) is the localization at the multiplicative system \(S\mathcal{N}_1\times S\mathcal{N}_2\) (Remark reference), we can still speak of the two Kan extensions of \(Q'F\) along \((Q_1,Q_2)\).

Definition (Derived functors of a triangulated bifunctor). For the data above, if \[\operatorname{Lan}_{(Q_1, Q_2)} (Q' F), \quad \text{(respectively, $\operatorname{Ran}_{(Q_1, Q_2)}(Q' F)$)}\] exists and is a triangulated bifunctor, denote it by \(\mathrm{R}^{\mathcal{N}'}_{\mathcal{N}_1\times\mathcal{N}_2}F\) (respectively, \(\mathrm{L}^{\mathcal{N}'}_{\mathcal{N}_1\times\mathcal{N}_2}F\)) and call it the right derived bifunctor (respectively, left derived bifunctor) of \(F\).

Definition. Consider a triangulated bifunctor \(F:\mathcal{D}_1\times\mathcal{D}_2\to\mathcal{D}'\), together with \(\mathcal{N}_1\), \(\mathcal{N}_2\), and \(\mathcal{N}'\) as above. Let \(\mathcal{I}_i\) be a triangulated subcategory of \(\mathcal{D}_i\). We call \((\mathcal{I}_1,\mathcal{I}_2)\) \(F\)-injective (respectively, \(F\)-projective) if the following properties hold simultaneously:

  • for every \(X_1\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{I}_1)\), the subcategory \(\mathcal{I}_2\) is \(F(X_1,\cdot)\)-injective (respectively, projective);

  • for every \(X_2\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{I}_2)\), the subcategory \(\mathcal{I}_1\) is \(F(\cdot,X_2)\)-injective (respectively, projective).

For \(\mathcal{I}_j\) as above (\(j=1,2\)), the universal property of Verdier localization gives \(i_j:\mathcal{I}_j/(\mathcal{I}_j\cap\mathcal{N}_j) \to\mathcal{D}_j/\mathcal{N}_j\). The following is the counterpart of Proposition reference.

Proposition. Suppose that \((\mathcal{I}_1,\mathcal{I}_2)\) is \(F\)-injective.

  1. The right derived bifunctor \(\mathrm{R}F:=\mathrm{R}^{\mathcal{N}'}_{\mathcal{N}_1\times\mathcal{N}_2}F\) exists, and the following diagram commutes up to isomorphism: \[\text{Diagram chapter4-unit-056-d012}\] where \(F^\flat\) is determined by the universal property of localization.

  2. For \(X_1\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{I}_1)\) and \(X_2\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{I}_2)\), there are canonical isomorphisms \[(\mathrm{R}F)(Q_1 X_1, \cdot) \simeq \mathrm{R}^{\mathcal{N}'}_{\mathcal{N}_2} F(X_1, \cdot), \quad (\mathrm{R}F)(\cdot, Q_2 X_2) \simeq \mathrm{R}^{\mathcal{N}'}_{\mathcal{N}_1} F(\cdot, X_2).\]

The corresponding statements remain valid if \(F\)-injective is replaced by \(F\)-projective and \(\mathrm{R}F\) by \(\mathrm{L}F\).

Proof. It suffices to treat the \(F\)-injective case. First, Proposition reference (i) implies that \(i\) is an equivalence. The hypotheses show that \(Q'F\) sends \(S\mathcal{N}_1\cap\operatorname{Mor}(\mathcal{I}_1)\times S\mathcal{N}_2\cap\operatorname{Mor}(\mathcal{I}_2)\) to isomorphisms; this need only be checked in each variable separately. Proposition reference (ii) implies that \(Q'F\) has a left Kan extension along \((Q_1,Q_2)\), namely \(\mathrm{R}F\), which makes the diagram above commute up to isomorphism.

We next show that \(\mathrm{R}F\) is a triangulated bifunctor. By Proposition reference, the relevant properties can be transported along the equivalence \(i\) and checked for \(F\) on \(\mathcal{I}_1\times\mathcal{I}_2\). This proves (i).

For (ii), by symmetry it suffices to fix \(X_1\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{I}_1)\). In this case \(F^\flat(Q_1X_1,\cdot): \mathcal{I}_2/(\mathcal{I}_2\cap\mathcal{N}_2) \to\mathcal{D}'/\mathcal{N}'\) is determined from \(Q'F(X_1,\cdot)\) by the universal property of localization, and the following diagram of functors commutes up to isomorphism: \[\text{Diagram chapter4-unit-056-d013}\] Since \(\mathcal{I}_2\) is \(F(X_1,\cdot)\)-injective, comparison with the construction in Proposition reference shows that \((\mathrm{R}F)(Q_1X_1,\cdot)\) is precisely \(\mathrm{R}^{\mathcal{N}'}_{\mathcal{N}_2}F(X_1,\cdot)\).

Once \(F\)-injective (respectively, \(F\)-projective) data \((\mathcal{I}_1,\mathcal{I}_2)\) are available, the limit formulas in Remark reference also apply to the left (respectively, right) derived bifunctor of \(F\).

  1. Compare Proposition reference.↩︎

General Theory of Derived Functors

Let \(\mathcal{A}\) and \(\mathcal{A}'\) be abelian categories, and fix an additive functor \(F:\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{A}'\). We now apply the theory of §reference, and in particular the setting of equation, to \[\begin{equation*} \text{Diagram chapter4-unit-057-d001} \qquad (\star \in \{+, -, \hspace{0.8em}\}) \end{equation*}\] Here \(Q\) and \(Q'\) are localization functors of triangulated categories, and \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}^\star F\) is a triangulated functor (Proposition reference). The blank superscript \(\star=\hspace{0.8em}\) corresponds to the case of \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{A})\) and \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}(\mathcal{A})\). Recall that \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^{\star}(\mathcal{A})=\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}^{\star}(\mathcal{A})/\mathcal{N}^{\star}\), where \(\mathcal{N}^{\star}\) is the saturated triangulated subcategory of acyclic complexes; likewise for \(\mathcal{A}'\). Unless \(F\) is exact, in general there is no triangulated functor \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^{\star}(\mathcal{A})\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^{\star}(\mathcal{A}')\) that makes the diagram above commute. The natural approach is to study the right and left derived functors in the sense of Definition reference, using the two kinds of Kan extension respectively.

Definition (Derived functors between derived categories). For \(\star\in\{+,-,\hspace{0.8em}\}\), if \[\begin{align*} {}^\star \mathrm{R}F: \ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^\star(\mathcal{A}) & \to \ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^\star(\mathcal{A}'): \quad \text{the right derived functor of $\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}^\star F$}, \quad \text{or} \\ {}^\star \mathrm{L}F: \ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^\star(\mathcal{A}) & \to \ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^\star(\mathcal{A}'): \quad \text{the left derived functor of $\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}^\star F$} \end{align*}\] exists, it is called the right derived functor (respectively, left derived functor) of \(F:\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{A}'\). When the derived functor exists, define, for every \(n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\), \[\begin{gather*} {}^\star \mathrm{R}^n F := \operatorname{H}^n \circ {}^\star \mathrm{R}F, \\ {}^\star \mathrm{L}_n F := \operatorname{H}^{-n} \circ {}^\star \mathrm{L}F. \end{gather*}\] Both are functors with values in \(\mathcal{A}'\). The subscript \(n\) is used to agree with the customary notation for chain complexes when studying left derived functors. The left superscript \(\star\) is often omitted when no confusion can arise.

Example (Deriving an exact functor). The simplest case is that in which \(F\) is exact. For every \(\star\in\{+,-,\hspace{0.8em}\}\), the derived functors \({}^\star\mathrm{R}F\) and \({}^\star\mathrm{L}F\) always exist. Indeed, \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}^\star F\) preserves acyclic complexes, so its derived functor is determined directly by the universal property of localization.

Theorem (Long exact sequence of derived functors). Fix \(\star\in\{+,-,\hspace{0.8em}\}\). If \({}^\star\mathrm{R}F\) or \({}^\star\mathrm{L}F\) exists, then every distinguished triangle \(X\to Y\to Z\xrightarrow{+1}\) in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^\star(\mathcal{A})\) gives rise to a canonical long exact sequence \[\begin{gather*} \cdots \to {}^\star \mathrm{R}^{n-1} F(Z) \to {}^\star \mathrm{R}^n F(X) \to {}^\star \mathrm{R}^n F(Y) \to {}^\star \mathrm{R}^n F(Z) \to {}^\star \mathrm{R}^{n+1} F(X) \to \cdots , \\ \cdots \to {}^\star \mathrm{L}_{n+1} F(Z) \to {}^\star \mathrm{L}_n F(X) \to {}^\star \mathrm{L}_n F(Y) \to {}^\star \mathrm{L}_n F(Z) \to {}^\star \mathrm{L}_{n-1} F(X) \to \cdots . \end{gather*}\]

Proof. By definition, both \({}^\star\mathrm{R}F\) and \({}^\star\mathrm{L}F\) are triangulated functors. Now apply the cohomology functor \(\operatorname{H}^0\).

How do we ensure that derived functors exist, and how do we compute them? Proposition reference already contains the general idea. For \(\star\in\{+,-,\hspace{0.8em}\}\), take \(\mathcal{N}^\star\) as in Definition reference. We seek a triangulated subcategory \(\mathcal{I}\) of \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}^\star(\mathcal{A})\) such that \({}^\star\mathrm{R}F\) or \({}^\star\mathrm{L}F\) can be defined as the composite in the diagram of functors \[\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^\star(\mathcal{A}) = \ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}^\star(\mathcal{A})/\mathcal{N}^\star \xleftarrow{\text{equivalence}} \mathcal{I}/\mathcal{I} \cap \mathcal{N}^\star \xrightarrow{\text{universal property of localization}} \ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}^\star(\mathcal{A}')/\mathcal{N}^\star = \ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^\star(\mathcal{A}') .\] How should \(\mathcal{I}\) be chosen? It should be \(F\)-injective (respectively, \(F\)-projective) in the following sense.

Convention. Fix \(\star\). If a triangulated subcategory \(\mathcal{I}\) of \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}^\star(\mathcal{A})\) is a \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}^\star F\)-injective (respectively, \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}^\star F\)-projective) triangulated subcategory in the sense of Definition reference, we call \(\mathcal{I}\) an \(F\)-injective (respectively, \(F\)-projective) subcategory for short.

If \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}^\star(\mathcal{A})\) has an \(F\)-injective (respectively, \(F\)-projective) subcategory \(\mathcal{I}\), Proposition reference guarantees the existence of \({}^\star\mathrm{R}F\) (respectively, \({}^\star\mathrm{L}F\)). Its restriction to \(\mathcal{I}\) is isomorphic to \(Q'\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}^\star F\), while the limit formulas in Remark reference make explicit the canonical morphism that accompanies the derived functor as a Kan extension: \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:L-R-can}{} Q' \ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}^\star F \to ({}^\star \mathrm{R}F)Q \quad \text{or} \quad ({}^\star \mathrm{L}F)Q \to Q' (\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}^\star F). \end{equation}\] The entire general theory developed in §reference applies directly. For example, consider additive functors between abelian categories \[\mathcal{A} \xrightarrow{F} \mathcal{A}' \xrightarrow{F'} \mathcal{A}'' .\] Provided the derived functors in question exist, there are canonical morphisms \[{}^\star \mathrm{R}(F'F) \to ({}^* \mathrm{R}F')({}^* \mathrm{R}F), \quad \left( {}^\star \mathrm{L}F' \right) \left( {}^\star \mathrm{L}F \right) \to {}^\star \mathrm{L}(F' F),\] and Theorem reference gives sufficient conditions for these morphisms to be isomorphisms. There is also the following compatibility.

Lemma. If \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{A})\) and \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}^+(\mathcal{A})\) each have an \(F\)-injective subcategory, then the restriction of \(\mathrm{R}F\) to \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^+(\mathcal{A})\) is \({}^+\mathrm{R}F\).

The corresponding statement also holds for \(F\)-projective subcategories, \(\mathrm{L}F\), and \({}^-\mathrm{L}F\).

Proof. We first consider \(\mathrm{R}F\). Let \(X\in\operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}^+(\mathcal{A}))\). Write \(\mathrm{qis}_{X/}\) for the category of all quasi-isomorphisms \(X\to Y\) in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{A})\), and \(\mathrm{qis}^+_{X/}\) for its version in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}^+(\mathcal{A})\). Remark reference gives a canonical isomorphism \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:derived-as-limit}{}\begin{aligned} \mathrm{R}F(QX) \simeq \varinjlim_{[X \to Y] \in \operatorname{Ob}(\mathrm{qis}_{X/})} (Q' \ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}F)(Y). \end{aligned} \end{equation}\]

For every object \(X\to Y\) of \(\mathrm{qis}_{X/}\), if \(m\ll0\) (depending only on \(X\)), then \(X\to Y\to\tau^{\geq m}Y\) is an object of \(\mathrm{qis}^+_{X/}\). Lemma reference ensures that \(\mathrm{qis}_{X/}\) is filtered, so Proposition reference ensures that the full subcategory \(\mathrm{qis}^+_{X/}\) is cofinal in it. Thus the \(\varinjlim\) in equation may be taken over \(\mathrm{qis}^+_{X/}\) (Proposition reference), and its value is precisely \({}^+\mathrm{R}F(QX)\).

For \(\mathrm{L}F\), use the left-derived-functor version of Remark reference and truncate in the opposite direction.

We next discuss the bifunctors introduced in Convention reference. The corresponding theory has also been prepared in §reference. Let \(\mathcal{A}_1\), \(\mathcal{A}_2\), and \(\mathcal{B}\) be abelian categories, and let \(F:\mathcal{A}_1\times\mathcal{A}_2\to\mathcal{B}\) be additive in each variable. As in Definition–Proposition reference, define \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:totCF}{}\begin{aligned} \ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}_{\oplus} F & := \operatorname{tot}_{\oplus} \circ \ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}^2 F \quad \text{(if $\mathcal{B}$ has countable coproducts)}, \\ \ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}_{\Pi} F & := \operatorname{tot}_{\Pi} \circ \ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}^2 F \quad \text{(if $\mathcal{B}$ has countable products)}. \end{aligned} \end{equation}\] By Proposition reference, both factor through functors at the level of \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\cdot)\), denoted by \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}_{\oplus}F\) and \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}_{\Pi}F\).

Proposition. The functors \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}_{\Pi}F,\;\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}_{\oplus}F: \ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}^\star(\mathcal{A}_1)\times\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}^\star(\mathcal{A}_2) \to\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}^\star(\mathcal{B})\) above are triangulated bifunctors in the sense of Definition reference.

Proof. Take \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}_{\Pi}F\) as an example (assuming that \(\mathcal{B}\) has countable products). The discussion following Proposition reference shows that this functor is compatible with translation in each variable, while Proposition reference gives the anticommutative diagram required in the definition of a triangulated bifunctor. It remains to prove that \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}_{\Pi}F\) preserves mapping cones in each variable. For the first variable, take a morphism \(f:X_1\to X'_1\) in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A}_1)\) and an object \(X_2\) of \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A}_2)\). There are canonical isomorphisms in \(\mathcal{B}\) \[\begin{align*} \ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}_{\Pi}F(\operatorname{Cone}(f), X_2)^n & \simeq \prod_{p+q=n} F(X_1^{p+1}, X_2^q ) \times F( (X'_1)^p, X_2^q ) \\ & \simeq \prod_{p+q=n+1} F( X_1^p, X_2^q ) \times \prod_{p+q=n} F( (X'_1)^p, X_2^q ) \\ & \simeq \operatorname{Cone}\left(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}_{\Pi}(f, \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{X_2}) \right)^n , \quad n \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}. \end{align*}\] It remains to verify that these isomorphisms form an isomorphism of complexes and are compatible with the morphisms \(\alpha(\cdot)\) and \(\beta(\cdot)\) accompanying the mapping cones. There is no essential difficulty, and the details are left to the reader.

Next, let \(Q_i:\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{A}_i)\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}(\mathcal{A}_i)\) and \(Q:\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{B})\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}(\mathcal{B})\) be the localization functors (\(i=1,2\)). Place these data in the framework of Definition reference, taking \(\mathcal{D}_1\), \(\mathcal{D}_2\), and \(\mathcal{D}'\) to be, respectively, \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}^\star(\mathcal{A}_1)\), \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}^\star(\mathcal{A}_2)\), and \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}^\star(\mathcal{B})\), while the acyclic complexes form \(\mathcal{N}_1^\star\), \(\mathcal{N}_2^\star\), and \((\mathcal{N}')^\star\).

Definition (Derived bifunctors). Fix \(\star\in\{+,-,\hspace{0.8em}\}\) and consider an additive bifunctor \(F:\mathcal{A}_1\times\mathcal{A}_2\to\mathcal{B}\).

  • Suppose that \(\mathcal{B}\) has countable products. If the right derived bifunctor of \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}_{\Pi}F\) in the sense of Definition reference, \[\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^\star(\mathcal{A}_1)\times\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^\star(\mathcal{A}_2) \to\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^\star(\mathcal{B}),\] exists, it is called the right derived bifunctor of \(F\) and is denoted by \({}^\star\mathrm{R}F\).

  • Suppose that \(\mathcal{B}\) has countable coproducts. If the left derived bifunctor of \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}_{\oplus}F\), \[\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^\star(\mathcal{A}_1)\times\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^\star(\mathcal{A}_2) \to\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^\star(\mathcal{B}),\] exists, it is called the left derived bifunctor of \(F\) and is denoted by \({}^\star\mathrm{L}F\).

We continue to write \({}^\star\mathrm{R}^nF:=\operatorname{H}^n\circ{}^\star\mathrm{R}F\) and \({}^\star\mathrm{L}_nF:=\operatorname{H}^{-n}\circ{}^\star\mathrm{L}F\).

Fix \(\star\in\{+,-,\hspace{0.8em}\}\), and let \(\mathcal{I}_i\) be a triangulated subcategory of \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}^\star(\mathcal{A}_i)\), \(i=1,2\). As usual, if \((\mathcal{I}_1,\mathcal{I}_2)\) is a pair of \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}^\star F\)-injective (respectively, projective) subcategories in the sense of Definition reference, we call the pair \(F\)-injective (respectively, \(F\)-projective). Proposition reference immediately gives the following conclusions, and all the isomorphisms are canonical.

  • If \((\mathcal{I}_1,\mathcal{I}_2)\) is \(F\)-injective, then \({}^\star\mathrm{R}F\) exists and \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:derived-bifunctor-1}{} (X_1, X_2) \in \operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{I}_1) \times \operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{I}_2) \implies {}^\star \mathrm{R}F(Q_1 X_1, Q_2 X_2) \simeq Q \ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}_{\Pi}F(X_1, X_2). \end{equation}\]

  • If \((\mathcal{P}_1,\mathcal{P}_2)\) is \(F\)-projective, then \({}^*\mathrm{L}F\) exists and \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:derived-bifunctor-2}{} (X_1, X_2) \in \operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{P}_1) \times \operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{P}_2) \implies {}^\star \mathrm{L}F(Q_1 X_1, Q_2 X_2) \simeq Q \ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}_{\oplus}F(X_1, X_2). \end{equation}\]

We next discuss a product on derived bifunctors. We begin with its version at the level of complexes. Keep the notation above, but now assume that \(F\) is right exact in each variable. For every complex \(X\), write \(Z^n(X):=\operatorname{ker}(d_X^n)\) and \(B^n(X):=\operatorname{im}(d_X^{n-1})\). For every \((p,q)\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}^2\), there is a natural morphism \[F\left( Z^p(X_1), Z^q(X_2) \right) \to Z^{p+q}\left( \ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}_{\oplus}F(X_1, X_2) \right).\] This morphism sends the images of \(F(B^p(X_1),Z^q(X_2))\) and \(F(Z^p(X_1),B^q(X_2))\) into \(B^{p+q}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}_{\oplus}F(X_1,X_2))\). Taking quotients and using the right exactness of \(F\) gives a canonical morphism \[\kappa: F\left(\operatorname{H}^p(X_1), \operatorname{H}^q(X_2)\right) \to \operatorname{H}^{p+q}\left( \ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}_{\oplus} F(X_1, X_2) \right).\] The discussion preceding the Künneth theorem for homology, Theorem reference, is the special case of this construction with \(F=\otimes_R\). Now change the hypothesis: let \(F\) be left exact in each variable. Dualizing the construction above gives a canonical morphism \[\lambda: \operatorname{H}^{p+q}\left( \ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}_{\Pi} F(X_1, X_2) \right) \to F\left( \operatorname{H}^p(X_1), \operatorname{H}^q(X_2) \right).\] The existence of the countable \(\oplus\) or \(\prod\) under discussion is still assumed. Since only cohomology matters here, \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}\) may also be replaced by \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}\).

Proposition. Suppose that \(F\) is right exact (respectively, left exact) in each variable, that \(\star\in\{+,-,\hspace{0.8em}\}\), and that there is an \(F\)-projective pair \((\mathcal{P}_1,\mathcal{P}_2)\) (respectively, an \(F\)-injective pair \((\mathcal{I}_1,\mathcal{I}_2)\)). Then there is a canonical morphism \[F\left(\operatorname{H}^p(\cdot), \operatorname{H}^q(\cdot) \right) \to \operatorname{H}^{p+q} {}^\star \mathrm{L}F \quad \text{or} \quad \operatorname{H}^{p+q} {}^\star \mathrm{R}F \to F\left(\operatorname{H}^p(\cdot), \operatorname{H}^q(\cdot) \right),\] where both sides are functors from \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^\star(\mathcal{A}_1)\times\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^\star(\mathcal{A}_2)\) to \(\mathcal{B}\). These morphisms are characterized by the commutative diagram \[\begin{equation*} \text{Diagram chapter4-unit-057-d002} \end{equation*}\] or by \[\begin{equation*} \text{Diagram chapter4-unit-057-d003} \end{equation*}\] where \(X_i\in\operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}^\star(\mathcal{A}_i))\). The arrows labeled \(\mathrm{can}\) are the canonical morphisms accompanying the derived functors as Kan extensions (after applying \(\operatorname{H}^{p+q}\)); see equation for the one-variable case.

Proof. By duality, it suffices to discuss the case involving \(\kappa\). Observe that, apart from \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}_{\oplus}F(X_1,X_2)\), the other two vertices in the diagram depend only on \(Q_1X_1\) and \(Q_2X_2\).

Fix the pair \((\mathcal{P}_1,\mathcal{P}_2)\). Since all morphisms in the diagram are functorial and \(\mathcal{P}_i/(\mathcal{P}_i\cap\mathcal{N}^\star_i)\) is equivalent to \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^\star(\mathcal{A}_i)\), it suffices to determine the desired morphism for \(X_i\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{P}_i)\); this can be checked by drawing a diagram. In this case, however, \({}^\star\mathrm{L}F(Q_1X_1,Q_2X_2)=\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}_{\oplus}F(X_1,X_2)\), so the claim is immediate.

In short, everything can be computed by taking resolutions, and the final result is independent of the choice of resolutions.

Bounded Derived Functors

This section explains how to study \({}^+\mathrm{R}F\) and \({}^-\mathrm{L}F\) by means of injective and projective resolutions. The case of unbounded derived categories is deferred to §reference.

Convention. This section focuses on \(\star\in\{+,-\}\) and adopts the following conventions.

  • For right derived functors we always take \(\star=+\) and use the abbreviation \(\mathrm{R}F:={}^+\mathrm{R}F: \ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^+(\mathcal{A})\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^+(\mathcal{A}')\).

  • For left derived functors we always take \(\star=-\) and use the abbreviation \(\mathrm{L}F:={}^-\mathrm{L}F: \ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^-(\mathcal{A})\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^-(\mathcal{A}')\).

In view of Lemma reference, these conventions cause no confusion.

Definition–Proposition. Let \(\mathcal{A}^\flat\) be a full additive subcategory of \(\mathcal{A}\). We call \(\mathcal{A}^\flat\) of type I relative to \(F\) if the following conditions hold; in this case \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}^+(\mathcal{A}^\flat)\) is an \(F\)-injective subcategory of \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}^+(\mathcal{A})\):

  1. for every \(X\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{A})\), there is a monomorphism \(X\hookrightarrow I\) with \(I\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{A}^\flat)\);

  2. if \(0\to X'\to X\to X''\to0\) is a short exact sequence in \(\mathcal{A}\) and \(X',X\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{A}^\flat)\), then \(X''\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{A}^\flat)\) and \(0\to FX'\to FX\to FX''\to0\) is exact.

Dually, we call \(\mathcal{A}^\flat\) of type P relative to \(F\) if the following conditions hold; in this case \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}^-(\mathcal{A}^\flat)\) is an \(F\)-projective subcategory of \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}^-(\mathcal{A})\):

  1. for every \(X\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{A})\), there is an epimorphism \(P\twoheadrightarrow X\) with \(P\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{A}^\flat)\);

  2. if \(0\to X'\to X\to X''\to0\) is a short exact sequence in \(\mathcal{A}\) and \(X,X''\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{A}^\flat)\), then \(X'\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{A}^\flat)\) and \(0\to FX'\to FX\to FX''\to0\) is exact.

Proof. It suffices to treat the type-I version. First, \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}^+(\mathcal{A}^\flat)\) is a triangulated subcategory of \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}^+(\mathcal{A})\) (Corollary reference). Theorem reference shows that for every \(X\in\operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}^+(\mathcal{A}))\) there is a quasi-isomorphism \(X\to I\) with \(I\in\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}^+(\mathcal{A}^\flat)\). This is the resolution condition for an \(F\)-injective subcategory. It remains to prove that if \(X\in\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}^+(\mathcal{A}^\flat)\) is acyclic, then \(FX\) is also acyclic.

For every \(n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\), there is a short exact sequence \(0\to\operatorname{ker}(d^n)\to X^n\xrightarrow{d^n}\operatorname{ker}(d^{n+1})\to0\). If \(n\ll0\), then \(\operatorname{ker}(d^n)=X^n=0\). Applying (I2) recursively for all \(n\) gives \(\operatorname{ker}(d^n)\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{A}^\flat)\) together with short exact sequences in \(\mathcal{A}'\) \[0 \to F\operatorname{ker}(d^n) \to FX^n \xrightarrow{Fd^n} F\operatorname{ker}(d^{n+1}) \to 0.\] Splicing these short exact sequences shows that \(FX\) is acyclic.

The terms type I and type P are merely convenient labels. There is a complete characterization of the subcategories \(\mathcal{A}^\flat\) that give \(F\)-injective or \(F\)-projective subcategories; see [KS06]. The next result shows that derived functors can be computed by taking resolutions in a full subcategory of type I or P.

Theorem. Suppose that \(\mathcal{A}\) has a full additive subcategory \(\mathcal{A}^\flat\) of type I (respectively, type P) relative to the additive functor \(F:\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{A}'\). Then the derived functor \(\mathrm{R}F\) (respectively, \(\mathrm{L}F\)) exists. More precisely:

  1. for every \(X\in\operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}^+(\mathcal{A}))\) (respectively, \(X\in\operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}^-(\mathcal{A}))\)), there is a quasi-isomorphism \(X\to I\) (respectively, \(P\to X\)) with \(I\in\operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}^+(\mathcal{A}^\flat))\) (respectively, \(P\in\operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}^-(\mathcal{A}^\flat))\));

  2. for the quasi-isomorphism in (i), the morphism in equation gives \[\mathrm{R}F(QX) \ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}\mathrm{R}F(QI) \ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\leftarrow}}Q' \ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}^+ F(I), \quad \mathrm{L}F(QX) \ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\leftarrow}}\mathrm{L}F(QP) \ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}Q' \ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}^- F(P);\]

  3. \(\mathrm{R}F\) restricts to \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^{\geq0}(\mathcal{A})\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^{\geq0}(\mathcal{A}')\) (respectively, \(\mathrm{L}F\) restricts to \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^{\leq0}(\mathcal{A})\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^{\leq0}(\mathcal{A}')\));

  4. suppose that \(F\) is left exact (respectively, right exact). If \(X\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{A})\), the morphism in equation gives an isomorphism \(FX\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}\mathrm{R}^0F(QX)\) (respectively, \(FX\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\leftarrow}}\mathrm{L}_0F(QX)\));

  5. if \(X\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{A}^\flat)\), then, for \(n>0\), \(\mathrm{R}^nF(X)=0\) (respectively, \(\mathrm{L}_nF(X)=0\)).

Proof. It suffices to consider \(\mathrm{R}F\). Since \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}^+(\mathcal{A}^\flat)\) is \(F\)-injective, a quasi-isomorphism \(X\to I\) always exists. The existence of \(\mathrm{R}F\) and the isomorphism \(\mathrm{R}F(QX)\simeq Q'\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}^+F(I)\) merely restate Proposition reference. This proves (i) and (ii).

For (iii), if \(X\in\operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^{\geq0}(\mathcal{A}))\), we may assume that \(X\) comes from an object of \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}^{\geq0}(\mathcal{A})\). Theorem reference allows us to choose a quasi-isomorphism \(X\to I\) with \(I\in\operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}^{\geq0}(\mathcal{A}^\flat))\). Hence \[\mathrm{R}F(QX) \simeq Q' \ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}^+ F(I) \in \operatorname{Ob}\left( \ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^{\geq 0}(\mathcal{A}')\right).\] If, in addition, \(X\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{A}^\flat)\), the quasi-isomorphism \(X\to I\) may be taken to be \(\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_X\). In that case \(\mathrm{R}F(QX)=Q'\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}^+F(X)=Q'FX\) is concentrated in degree zero. This also proves (v).

Finally, consider (iv). Suppose that \(F\) is left exact. For \(X\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{A})\), choose an exact sequence \(0\to X\to I^0\to I^1\to\cdots\), with every \(I^n\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{A}^\flat)\). Put \(I=[I^0\to I^1\to\cdots]\). By (ii) and left exactness, \(FX\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}\operatorname{ker}[Fd_I^0:F(I^0)\to F(I^1)] \simeq\mathrm{R}^0F(X)\), as desired.

Example (Injective and projective objects). Suppose that \(\mathcal{A}\) has enough injective objects, and let \(\mathcal{A}^\flat\) be the full additive subcategory of injective objects. It is of type I relative to every \(F\): condition (I1) holds by assumption, while for (I2), Lemma reference shows that the short exact sequence in that condition splits. Thus \(X'\oplus X''\) is injective, and Lemma reference implies that \(X''\) is injective as well.

Dually, if \(\mathcal{A}\) has enough projective objects, the full additive subcategory consisting of those objects is of type P relative to every \(F\).

Example reference connects this discussion with the classical definition of derived functors in §reference. Suppose that \(\mathcal{A}\) has enough injective objects. Consider the restriction \(\mathrm{R}^nF|_{\mathcal{A}}\) of the right derived functor. Since a short exact sequence in \(\mathcal{A}\) extends canonically to a distinguished triangle (Proposition reference), the long exact sequence immediately makes \((\mathrm{R}^nF|_{\mathcal{A}})_{n\geq0}\) a cohomological \(\delta\)-functor in the sense of Definition reference. Dually, the left derived functors form the homological \(\delta\)-functor \((\mathrm{L}_nF|_{\mathcal{A}})_{n\geq0}\).

Proposition. Suppose that \(F\) is left exact (respectively, right exact) and that \(\mathcal{A}\) has enough injective (respectively, projective) objects. Then \(\mathrm{R}^nF:\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}^+(\mathcal{A})\to\mathcal{A}'\) (respectively, \(\mathrm{L}_nF:\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}^-(\mathcal{A})\to\mathcal{A}'\)) agrees with the version previously defined in Definition reference.

More generally, if there is a subcategory \(\mathcal{A}^\flat\) of type I (respectively, type P), as in Definition–Proposition reference, then \((\mathrm{R}^nF|_{\mathcal{A}})_{n\geq0}\) (respectively, \((\mathrm{L}_nF|_{\mathcal{A}})_{n\geq0}\)) is a universal \(\delta\)-functor in the sense of Definition reference.

Proof. It suffices to treat the left-exact case. For \(X\in\operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}^+(\mathcal{A}))\), choose an injective resolution \(X\to I\). Theorem reference (ii) gives canonical isomorphisms \(\mathrm{R}^nF(QX)\simeq\operatorname{H}^n\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}^+F(I)\) for every \(n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\). The right-hand side is precisely the version of the derived functor from Definition reference.

More generally, suppose that \(\mathcal{A}^\flat\) is of type I relative to \(F\). To prove the universality of \((\mathrm{R}^nF|_{\mathcal{A}})_{n\geq0}\), by Proposition reference it suffices to show that \(\mathrm{R}^nF|_{\mathcal{A}}\) is effaceable for \(n>0\). This follows directly from condition (I1) in Definition–Proposition reference and Theorem reference (v).

To derive a composite of functors, one often needs a larger class of objects for resolutions. We need the following concept.

Definition. Suppose that \(\mathrm{R}F\) (respectively, \(\mathrm{L}F\)) exists. An object \(X\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{A})\) is called \(F\)-acyclic if \(\mathrm{R}F(X)\) (respectively, \(\mathrm{L}F(X)\)) is an object of \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^{\geq0}(\mathcal{A}')\cap\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^{\leq0}(\mathcal{A}') \simeq\mathcal{A}'\).

The next result shows that derived functors can be computed using \(F\)-acyclic resolutions; compare Corollary reference.

Corollary. Let \(\mathcal{A}^\flat\) be a full additive subcategory of \(\mathcal{A}\) of type I (respectively, type P) relative to \(F\). Define \(\mathcal{A}^\natural\) to be the full additive subcategory consisting of all \(F\)-acyclic objects of \(\mathcal{A}\). Then:

  1. \(\mathcal{A}^\natural\supset\mathcal{A}^\flat\);

  2. \(\mathcal{A}^\natural\) is also of type I (respectively, type P);

  3. for every quasi-isomorphism \(X\to I\) (respectively, \(P\to X\)), with \(I\in\operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}^+(\mathcal{A}^\natural))\) (respectively, \(P\in\operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}^-(\mathcal{A}^\natural))\)), the morphism in equation gives \[\mathrm{R}F(QX) \ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}\mathrm{R}F(QI) \ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\leftarrow}}Q' \ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}^+ F(I), \quad \mathrm{L}F(QX) \ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\leftarrow}}\mathrm{L}F(QP) \ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}Q' \ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}^- F(P).\]

Proof. Theorem reference (v) implies (i), so condition (I1) or (P1) also holds for \(\mathcal{A}^\natural\). For (I2), suppose that \(0\to X'\to X\to X''\to0\) is a short exact sequence in \(\mathcal{A}\) and that \(X',X\) are \(F\)-acyclic. The long exact sequence from Theorem reference gives exact sequences \[\underbracket{\mathrm{R}^n F(X)}_{= 0} \to \mathrm{R}^n F(X'') \to \underbracket{\mathrm{R}^{n+1}F(X')}_{= 0}, \quad n \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}_{\geq 1} ,\] so \(X''\) is \(F\)-acyclic. On the other hand, the \(n=0\) portion of the long exact sequence, together with \(\mathrm{R}^1F(X')=0\), shows that \(0\to FX'\to FX\to FX''\to0\) is exact. The proof of (P2) is dual. This proves (ii).

Finally, (iii) follows by applying Theorem reference (ii) to \(\mathcal{A}^\natural\).

We now discuss deriving a composite of functors. The basic tool is Theorem reference.

Theorem (Deriving a composite of functors). Consider additive functors between abelian categories \[\mathcal{A} \xrightarrow{F} \mathcal{A}' \xrightarrow{F'} \mathcal{A}''.\] Suppose that there are full subcategories \(\mathcal{A}^\flat\) of \(\mathcal{A}\) and \((\mathcal{A}')^\flat\) of \(\mathcal{A}'\), of type I relative to \(F\) and \(F'\), respectively, in the sense of Definition–Proposition reference. If \(F\) sends the objects of \(\mathcal{A}^\flat\) to \(F'\)-acyclic objects of \(\mathcal{A}'\), then the canonical morphism \(\mathrm{R}(F'F)\to(\mathrm{R}F')(\mathrm{R}F)\) is an isomorphism.

There is a corresponding version for the left derived functors \(\mathrm{L}F\), \(\mathrm{L}F'\), and the canonical morphism \((\mathrm{L}F')(\mathrm{L}F)\to\mathrm{L}(F'F)\), using subcategories of type P.

Proof. It suffices to treat right derived functors. Let \((\mathcal{A}')^\natural\) be the full additive subcategory of \(F'\)-acyclic objects in \(\mathcal{A}'\). Corollary reference, together with Definition–Proposition reference, shows that \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}^+(\mathcal{A}^\flat)\) and \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}^+((\mathcal{A}')^\natural)\) are, respectively, \(F\)-injective and \(F'\)-injective subcategories of \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}^+(\mathcal{A})\) and \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}^+(\mathcal{A}')\). Apply Theorem reference.

Using the amplitude from Definition reference, we can define the dimensions of the right and left derived functors of \(F\).

Definition–Proposition. Suppose that \(F:\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{A}'\) is left exact (respectively, right exact), and that the derived functor \(\mathrm{R}F\) (respectively, \(\mathrm{L}F\)) exists and is determined as in Theorem reference. There is a \(d\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}_{\geq0}\sqcup\{+\infty\}\) such that the amplitude of the derived functor is contained in \([0,d]\) (respectively, \([-d,0]\)). The infimum of all such \(d\) is called the dimension of \(\mathrm{R}F\) (respectively, \(\mathrm{L}F\)).

Proof. It suffices to treat the left-exact case. Theorem reference implies that \(\mathrm{R}F\) restricts to \(\mathcal{A}\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^{\geq0}(\mathcal{A}')\), so its amplitude is contained in an interval \([0,d]\).

Consequently, if \(\mathrm{R}F\) (respectively, \(\mathrm{L}F\)) exists and has finite dimension, it restricts to \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^{\ensuremath{\mathrm{b}}}(\mathcal{A})\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^{\ensuremath{\mathrm{b}}}(\mathcal{A}')\).

Example (\(\operatorname{Tor}\)-dimension). Let \(R\) be a ring and \(X\) a right \(R\)-module. Consider the right-exact functor from \(R\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\) to \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ab}}\) that sends \(Y\mapsto X\otimes Y:=X\ensuremath{\underset{R}{\otimes}}Y\). Since \(R\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\) has enough projective objects, \(\mathrm{L}(X\otimes\cdot)\) exists, and \(\mathrm{L}_n(X\otimes\cdot)\) is precisely \(\operatorname{Tor}^R_n(X,\cdot)\) from Definition–Proposition reference. The dimension of \(\mathrm{L}(X\otimes\cdot)\) is called the \(\operatorname{Tor}\)-dimension of \(X\). A similar definition applies to left \(R\)-modules, and Proposition reference implies that the two agree when \(R\) is commutative. The derived tensor-product functor is discussed further in §reference.

Now fix abelian categories \(\mathcal{A}_1\), \(\mathcal{A}_2\), and \(\mathcal{B}\), and an additive bifunctor \[F: \mathcal{A}_1 \times \mathcal{A}_2 \to \mathcal{B}.\] We do not require \(\mathcal{B}\) to have countable coproducts or products, because \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}^2F\) restricts to \[\begin{gather*} \ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}^2 F: \ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}^{\pm}(\mathcal{A}_1) \times \ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}^{\pm} (\mathcal{A}_2) \to \ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}^2_f(\mathcal{B}). \end{gather*}\] On \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}^2_f(\mathcal{B})\), the total-complex functor \(\operatorname{tot}_{\oplus}=\operatorname{tot}_{\Pi}\) is always defined; denote this functor by \(\operatorname{tot}\). Likewise, denote \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}_{\oplus}F=\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}_{\Pi}F\) by \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}F\), and \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}_{\oplus}F=\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}_{\Pi}F\) by \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}F\). To study the derived bifunctors of Definition reference, we consider triangulated subcategories \(\mathcal{I}_i\) (respectively, \(\mathcal{P}_i\)) of \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}^+(\mathcal{A}_i)\) (respectively, \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}^-(\mathcal{A}_i)\)). As usual, the sign is determined by whether we are considering the right or left derived bifunctor, and \(i=1,2\). How should we choose the pair \((\mathcal{I}_1,\mathcal{I}_2)\) or \((\mathcal{P}_1,\mathcal{P}_2)\)? Definition–Proposition reference and the techniques of §reference give the following answer.

Lemma. Let \(\mathcal{A}_i^\flat\subset\mathcal{A}_i\) be full additive subcategories, \(i=1,2\). If the following conditions hold simultaneously, then the pair \(\bigl(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}^+(\mathcal{A}_1^\flat), \ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}^+(\mathcal{A}_2^\flat)\bigr)\) (respectively, \(\bigl(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}^-(\mathcal{A}_1^\flat), \ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}^-(\mathcal{A}_2^\flat)\bigr)\)) is \(F\)-injective (respectively, \(F\)-projective) in the sense of Definition reference:

  • for fixed \(X_1\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{A}_1^\flat)\), \(\mathcal{A}_2^\flat\) is of type I (respectively, type P) relative to \(F(X_1,\cdot)\);

  • for fixed \(X_2\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{A}_2^\flat)\), \(\mathcal{A}_1^\flat\) is of type I (respectively, type P) relative to \(F(\cdot,X_2)\).

In particular, if \(\mathcal{A}_1\) and \(\mathcal{A}_2\) each have enough injective (respectively, projective) objects, then \(\mathrm{R}F\) (respectively, \(\mathrm{L}F\)) exists.

Proof. Set \(\mathcal{I}_i:=\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}^+(\mathcal{A}_i^\flat)\), \(i=1,2\). The only point to prove is that, for every \(X_1\in\operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}^+(\mathcal{A}_1^\flat))\), the functor \((\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}F)(X_1,\cdot):\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}^+(\mathcal{A}_2^\flat) \to\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}^+(\mathcal{B})\) sends acyclic complexes to acyclic complexes; the same statement holds after interchanging the indices \(1\) and \(2\). The existence of \(\mathrm{R}F\) (respectively, \(\mathrm{L}F\)) then follows directly from Proposition reference.

Take \(Y\in\operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}^+(\mathcal{A}_2^\flat))\). Then \((\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}^2F)(X_1,Y)\) belongs to \(\operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}^2_f(\mathcal{B}))\). By condition (I2), each column \(F(X_1^p,Y^\bullet)\) is acyclic. Therefore Corollary reference implies that \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}F(X_1,Y):=\operatorname{tot}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}^2F(X_1,Y))\) is exact, as desired.

If \(F\)-injective (respectively, \(F\)-projective) subcategories are available, the functor \(\mathrm{R}F\) (respectively, \(\mathrm{L}F\)) can be determined by equation (respectively, equation).

Example: \(\operatorname{RHom}\)

Throughout this section, \(\mathcal{A}\) remains an abelian category. If \(\mathcal{A}\) is moreover \(\Bbbk\)-linear, where \(\Bbbk\) is a commutative ring, every statement in this section can be strengthened by replacing \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ab}}\) with \(\Bbbk\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\). The bifunctor \(\operatorname{Hom}:=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{A}}:\mathcal{A}^{\operatorname{op}}\times\mathcal{A}\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ab}}\) is left exact in each variable. To study its derived bifunctor in the sense of Definition reference, we need some preparation.
