First, the general theory of §reference gives \[\begin{align*} \ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}\operatorname{Hom}: \ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}^+(\mathcal{A}^{\operatorname{op}}) \times \ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}^+(\mathcal{A}) & \to \ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}^+(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ab}}), \\ \ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}\operatorname{Hom}: \ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}^+(\mathcal{A}^{\operatorname{op}}) \times \ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}^+(\mathcal{A}) & \to \ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}^+(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ab}}). \end{align*}\] Denote all localization functors by \(Q\). Recall the isomorphism \(\sigma:\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}^\pm(\mathcal{A}^{\operatorname{op}})\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}} \ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}^{\mp}(\mathcal{A})^{\operatorname{op}}\) of Definition–Proposition reference. The isomorphisms it induces at the level of the triangulated categories \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}^\pm\) and \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^\pm\) are also denoted by \(\sigma\) (Propositions reference and reference).

Definition. If the right derived bifunctor of \(\operatorname{Hom}\) in the sense of Definition reference exists, denote it by \(\operatorname{RHom}=\operatorname{RHom}_{\mathcal{A}}\). It is a functor from \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^+(\mathcal{A}^{\operatorname{op}})\times\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^+(\mathcal{A})\) to \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^+(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ab}})\) and, by means of \(\sigma:\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^{\pm}(\mathcal{A}^{\operatorname{op}})\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}} \ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^{\mp}(\mathcal{A})^{\operatorname{op}}\), can also be regarded as a functor \[\operatorname{RHom}: \ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^-(\mathcal{A})^{\operatorname{op}} \times \ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^+(\mathcal{A}) \to \ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^+(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ab}}).\]

Lemma. Write \(\mathcal{I}_{\mathcal{A}}\) (respectively, \(\mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{A}}\)) for the full subcategory of injective (respectively, projective) objects of \(\mathcal{A}\).

  • If \(\mathcal{A}\) has enough injective objects, then \((\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}^+(\mathcal{A}^{\operatorname{op}}), \ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}^+(\mathcal{I}_{\mathcal{A}}))\) is \(\operatorname{Hom}\)-injective.

  • If \(\mathcal{A}\) has enough projective objects, then \((\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}^+(\mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{A}}^{\operatorname{op}}), \ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}^+(\mathcal{A}))\) is \(\operatorname{Hom}\)-injective.

Proof. It suffices to treat the case of enough injectives; the projective case is entirely similar. We verify the conditions of Lemma reference.

First, fix \(X_1\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{A})\). Recall that \(\mathcal{I}_{\mathcal{A}}\) is of type I for every additive functor \(F:\mathcal{A}\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ab}}\) (Example reference); take the special case \(F=\operatorname{Hom}(X_1,\cdot)\).

Second, fix \(X_2\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{I}_{\mathcal{A}})\). To verify that \(\mathcal{A}^{\operatorname{op}}\) is of type I relative to \(\operatorname{Hom}(\cdot,X_2)\), observe that the resolution condition (I1) holds trivially. For (I2), it suffices to show that \(\operatorname{Hom}(\cdot,X_2):\mathcal{A}^{\operatorname{op}}\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ab}}\) is exact; this is precisely the characterization of \(X_2\) as an injective object.

The following result involves the \(\operatorname{Hom}\) complex of Definition reference, denoted by \(\operatorname{Hom}^\bullet\).

Theorem. Suppose that \(\mathcal{A}\) has enough injective objects or enough projective objects.

  1. The right derived bifunctor \(\operatorname{RHom}\) exists.

  2. If \(\mathcal{A}\) has enough injective objects and \(X_2\to I_2\) is an injective resolution, then it induces an isomorphism \[\operatorname{RHom}(QX_1, QX_2) \ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}Q \operatorname{Hom}^\bullet(X_1, I_2).\] In particular, if \(X_1\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{A})\), then \(\operatorname{RHom}(QX_1,\cdot)\simeq\mathrm{R}(\operatorname{Hom}(X_1,\cdot)): \ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^+(\mathcal{A})\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^+(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ab}})\).

  3. If \(\mathcal{A}\) has enough projective objects and \(P_1\to X_1\) is a projective resolution, then it induces an isomorphism \[\operatorname{RHom}(QX_1, QX_2) \ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}Q \operatorname{Hom}^\bullet(P_1, X_2).\] In particular, if \(X_2\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{A})\), then \(\operatorname{RHom}(\cdot,QX_2)\simeq\mathrm{R}(\operatorname{Hom}(\cdot,X_2)): \ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^-(\mathcal{A})^{\operatorname{op}}\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^+(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ab}})\).

  4. There is a canonical isomorphism \(\operatorname{H}^n\operatorname{RHom}(X,Y)\simeq \operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}(\mathcal{A})}(X,Y[n])\), where \(X\in\operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^-(\mathcal{A}))\) and \(Y\in\operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^+(\mathcal{A}))\). If \(X,Y\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{A})\), the right-hand side is precisely \(\operatorname{Ext}^n(X,Y)\) from Definition reference.

Proof. By Lemma reference and the following observations, statements (i)–(iii) all follow by applying Lemma reference:

  • at the level of complexes, Example reference gives a canonical isomorphism \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}\operatorname{Hom}(\sigma^{-1}(X_1),X_2)\simeq\operatorname{Hom}^\bullet(X_1,X_2)\);

  • \(P_1\to X_1\) is a projective resolution in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}^-(\mathcal{A})\) if and only if the corresponding morphism \(\sigma^{-1}(X_1)\to\sigma^{-1}(P_1)\) is an injective resolution in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}^+(\mathcal{A}^{\operatorname{op}})\).

For (iv), first suppose that \(\mathcal{A}\) has enough injective objects. We may assume that \(Y\in\operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}^+(\mathcal{A}))\) consists of injective objects. Identifying the objects of \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{A})\) and \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}(\mathcal{A})\), Proposition reference gives \[\operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}(\mathcal{A})}(X, Y[n]) \simeq \operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{A})}(X, Y[n]) \simeq \operatorname{H}^n \operatorname{Hom}^\bullet(X, Y) \xrightarrow[\sim]{\text{(ii)}} \operatorname{H}^n \operatorname{RHom}(X, Y).\] If \(\mathcal{A}\) has enough projective objects, the argument is entirely similar.

Corollary. Let \(X,Y\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{A})\). If \(\mathcal{A}\) has enough injective (respectively, projective) objects, then \(\operatorname{Ext}^n(X,Y)\) from Definition reference is canonically isomorphic to \(\operatorname{Ext}^n_{\mathcal{A},\mathrm{II}}(X,Y)\) (respectively, \(\operatorname{Ext}^n_{\mathcal{A},\mathrm{I}}(X,Y)\)) as defined in §reference.

Proof. Apply Theorem reference (ii) and (iii) directly.

Definition. Let \(X\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{A})\). The following dimensions are dimensions of right derived functors in the sense of Definition–Proposition reference.

  • If \(\mathcal{A}\) has enough injective objects, the dimension of \(\mathrm{R}(\operatorname{Hom}(\cdot,X)): \ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^-(\mathcal{A})^{\operatorname{op}}\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^+(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ab}})\) is called the injective dimension of \(X\) and is denoted by \(\mathrm{inj.dim}(X)\).

  • If \(\mathcal{A}\) has enough projective objects, the dimension of \(\mathrm{R}(\operatorname{Hom}(X,\cdot)): \ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^+(\mathcal{A})\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^+(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ab}})\) is called the projective dimension of \(X\) and is denoted by \(\mathrm{proj.dim}(X)\).

For \(X\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{A})\) and \(n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}_{\geq0}\sqcup\{\infty\}\), an injective resolution \(0\to X\to I^0\to I^1\to\cdots\) is said to have length \(\leq n\) if \(k>n\Rightarrow I^k=0\); projective resolutions are treated in the same way. The notation \(\operatorname{Ext}^{\geq m}(Y,X)=0\) means that \(k\geq m\Rightarrow\operatorname{Ext}^k(Y,X)=0\), and similarly in the other cases.

Proposition. Let \(n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}_{\geq0}\). If \(\mathcal{A}\) has enough injective objects, then \[\begin{align*} \mathrm{inj.dim}(X) \leq n & \iff \operatorname{Ext}^{\geq n+1}(\cdot, X) = 0 \\ & \iff \operatorname{Ext}^{n+1}(\cdot, X) = 0 \iff X\;\text{has an injective resolution of length $\leq n$}. \end{align*}\]

If \(\mathcal{A}\) has enough projective objects, then \[\begin{align*} \mathrm{proj.dim}(X) \leq n & \iff \operatorname{Ext}^{\geq n+1}(X, \cdot) = 0 \\ & \iff \operatorname{Ext}^{n+1}(X, \cdot) = 0 \iff X\;\text{has a projective resolution of length $\leq n$}. \end{align*}\]

Proof. It suffices to discuss injective resolutions. Suppose that \(\mathrm{inj.dim}(X)\leq n\). The definition of dimension implies that, for every \(Y\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{A})\), \(\bigl(\mathrm{R}\operatorname{Hom}(\cdot,X)\bigr)(Y)\) lies in \(\operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^{[0,n]}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ab}}))\), and hence \(\operatorname{Ext}^{\geq n+1}(Y,X)=0\).

Now suppose that \(\operatorname{Ext}^{n+1}(\cdot,X)=0\). Take an injective resolution \(0\to X\to I^0\xrightarrow{d^0}\cdots\). Repeatedly applying dimension shifting from Proposition reference to the short exact sequences \[0 \to X \to I^0 \to \operatorname{im}\left(d_I^0 \right) \to 0, \quad 0 \to \operatorname{im}\left( d_I^{k-2}\right) \to I^{k-1} \to \operatorname{im}\left(d_I^{k-1} \right) \to 0\] for \(1<k\leq n\) gives \[\operatorname{Ext}^1\left(\cdot, \operatorname{im}\left(d_I^{n-1}\right) \right) \simeq \cdots \simeq \operatorname{Ext}^{n+1}\left(\cdot, X \right) = 0.\] Thus \(\operatorname{im}(d_I^{n-1})\) is injective (Corollary reference). Replacing \(I^n\) by this object gives an injective resolution of length \(\leq n\).

If \(X\) has an injective resolution of length \(\leq n\), computing the derived functor with this resolution shows that, for every \(Y\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{A})\), \(\bigl(\mathrm{R}\operatorname{Hom}(\cdot,X)\bigr)(Y)\) lies in \(\operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^{[0,n]}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ab}}))\).

In keeping with Example reference, injective and projective dimension may also be viewed as two kinds of “\(\operatorname{Ext}\)-dimension,” although this terminology is not standard.

Definition–Proposition (Global dimension). Suppose that \(\mathcal{A}\) has enough injective and projective objects. Then \[\text{Diagram chapter4-unit-059-d001}\] This value is denoted by \(\mathrm{gl.dim}(\mathcal{A})\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}_{\geq0}\sqcup\{\infty\}\) and is called the global dimension, or global homological dimension, of \(\mathcal{A}\).

Proof. For every \(n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}_{\geq0}\), Proposition reference shows that \(n\geq\sup_X\mathrm{inj.dim}(X)\) is equivalent to \(\operatorname{Ext}^{\geq n+1}(\cdot,\cdot)=0\). Take the infimum over all \(n\) satisfying this condition. The case of \(\mathrm{proj.dim}\) is exactly the same, and the vertical equality is immediate.

For example, if \(R\) is a principal ideal domain, every submodule of a free \(R\)-module is again free [Li1]. Thus every \(R\)-module, say \(M\), has a free resolution of the form \(0\to F_1\to F_0\to M\to0\), which shows that \(\mathrm{gl.dim}(R\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}})\leq1\). Global dimension is an upper bound for the dimensions of all derived functors.

Corollary. Let \(F:\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{A}'\) be a left-exact (respectively, right-exact) functor between abelian categories, and suppose that \(\mathcal{A}\) has enough injective and projective objects. Then the dimension of \(\mathrm{R}F\) (respectively, \(\mathrm{L}F\)) is at most \(\mathrm{gl.dim}(\mathcal{A})\).

Proof. The definition of dimension involves the amplitude of \(\mathrm{R}F\) (respectively, \(\mathrm{L}F\)); see Definition reference. To control the amplitude, for every \(X\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{A})\) use Proposition reference to choose an injective (respectively, projective) resolution of length at most \(\mathrm{gl.dim}(\mathcal{A})\), and compute \(\mathrm{R}F(X)\) (respectively, \(\mathrm{L}F(X)\)) using that resolution.

We conclude this section with a result of adjunction type.

Theorem. Consider an adjoint pair of additive functors between abelian categories \(\text{Diagram chapter4-unit-059-diagram-002}\). Suppose that \(\mathcal{A}\) has enough projective objects and \(\mathcal{A}'\) has enough injective objects. Then there is a canonical isomorphism in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^+(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ab}})\) \[\operatorname{RHom}_{\mathcal{A'}}\left(\mathrm{L}F(X), Y\right) \simeq \operatorname{RHom}_{\mathcal{A}}\left(X, \mathrm{R}G(Y) \right),\] where \(X\in\operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^-(\mathcal{A}))\) and \(Y\in\operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^+(\mathcal{A}'))\). Consequently, there is a canonical isomorphism in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ab}}\) \[\operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}(\mathcal{A'})}\left(\mathrm{L}F(X), Y\right) \simeq \operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}(\mathcal{A})}\left(X, \mathrm{R}G(Y) \right).\]

Proof. Choose a projective resolution \(P\to X\) and an injective resolution \(Y\to I\). Applying Theorem reference gives \[\operatorname{RHom}_{\mathcal{A}}(\mathrm{L}F(QX), QY) \simeq Q\operatorname{Hom}^\bullet\left( \ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}F(P), I \right).\] But \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}F(P)\) is obtained by applying \(F\) degree by degree to the complex. From the definition of the \(\operatorname{Hom}\) complex and the adjunction, the right-hand side is isomorphic to \(Q\operatorname{Hom}^\bullet(P,\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}G(I))\), which is precisely \(\operatorname{RHom}_{\mathcal{A}}(QX,\mathrm{R}G(QY))\).

Theorem reference shows that a projective resolution of \(X\) is unique up to unique isomorphism in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}^-(\mathcal{A})\), and every morphism in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^-(\mathcal{A})\) lifts uniquely to projective resolutions (Proposition reference). The same holds for injective resolutions of \(Y\). This suffices to show that the isomorphism constructed above is functorial in \((X,Y)\).

The final assertion follows by applying \(\operatorname{H}^0\) to both sides.

Here \(\mathrm{L}F\) and \(\mathrm{R}G\) are not adjoint functors in the strict sense: the former is a functor between \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^-\) categories, whereas the latter is a functor between \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^+\) categories. The version for unbounded derived categories in §reference will remove this discrepancy.

Example: \(\mathrm{R}\lim\) as a Homotopy Limit

This section continues the discussion of §reference. Let \(\mathcal{A}\) be an abelian category.

Lemma. Suppose that \(\mathcal{A}\) has exact countable products (respectively, exact countable coproducts); see Convention reference. Then every functor in the sequence \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{A})\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}(\mathcal{A})\) preserves countable products (respectively, countable coproducts). In this case, there are canonical isomorphisms \(\operatorname{H}^n(\prod_kX_k)\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}\prod_k\operatorname{H}^n(X_k)\) (respectively, \(\operatorname{H}^n(\bigoplus_kX_k)\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}\bigoplus_k\operatorname{H}^n(X_k)\)).

Proof. It suffices to prove the product case. Exactness of countable products directly gives \(\operatorname{H}^n(\prod_kX_k)\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}\prod_k\operatorname{H}^n(X_k)\).

For every complex \(Y\), the definition shows that \(\operatorname{Hom}^\bullet(Y,\prod_kX_k)\) is isomorphic to the product of the \(\operatorname{Hom}^\bullet(Y,X_k)\) formed degree by degree in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ab}})\). Apply exactness of countable products when taking \(\operatorname{H}^0\) to obtain a canonical isomorphism \(\operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{A})}(Y,\prod_kX_k)\simeq \prod_k\operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{A})}(Y,X_k)\). Thus \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{A})\) preserves \(\prod_k\).

We now prove that \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{A})\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}(\mathcal{A})\) preserves \(\prod_k\); the localization functor \(Q\) is suppressed. Suppose we are given a family of morphisms \(f_k:Y\to X_k\) in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}(\mathcal{A})\). We wish to prove that there is a unique \(f\in\operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}(\mathcal{A})}(Y,\prod_kX_k)\) satisfying \(p_hf=f_h\) for every \(h\), where \(p_h:\prod_kX_k\to X_h\) is the canonical projection in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{A})\). We may assume that each \(f_k\) is represented by a diagram in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{A})\) \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:D-countable-product-aux0}{} Y \xrightarrow{b_k} Z_k \xleftarrow{s_k} X_k, \quad s_k:\; \text{a quasi-isomorphism}. \end{equation}\] The morphism \(s:=\prod_ks_k:\prod_kX_k\to\prod_kZ_k\) remains a quasi-isomorphism. The diagram \[Y \xrightarrow{b := (b_k)_k} \prod_k Z_k \xleftarrow{s} \prod_k X_k\] determines \(f\in\operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}(\mathcal{A})}(Y,\prod_kX_k)\). Notice that \(f\) depends only on \((f_k)_k\), not on the choices made in equation. The commutativity of the following diagram implies that \(p_hf=f_h\) for every \(h\): \[\text{Diagram chapter4-unit-060-d001}\]

If \(g\in\operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}(\mathcal{A})}(Y,\prod_kX_k)\) also satisfies \(p_hg=f_h\) for every \(h\), there is a commutative diagram in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{A})\) \[\text{Diagram chapter4-unit-060-d002} \quad \begin{array}{l} h \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}, \\ t, t_h:\;\text{quasi-isomorphisms}, \\ u := (r_k)_k t = \prod_k t_k , \end{array}\] such that the second row represents \(g\), while the \(\par\textbf{Diagram chapter4-unit-060-diagram-003}\par\) part represents \(f_h\). The square is constructed using the version of condition (S3) in Definition reference for a right multiplicative system, while commutativity of the lower part is immediate.

Exactness of \(\prod_k\) shows that \(u\) is a quasi-isomorphism. Consequently, \(g\) is also represented by the \(\par\textbf{Diagram chapter4-unit-060-diagram-004}\par\) part of the diagram. But \(Y\xrightarrow{c_k}M_k\xleftarrow{t_k}X_k\) represents \(f_k\). Comparing this with the construction of \(f\) above gives \(f=g\).

Remark. If the indexing set for the product (respectively, coproduct) is replaced by an arbitrary small set \(I\), the corresponding statement remains valid.

Let \(\mathcal{D}\) be an \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ab}}\)-category. Consider the category \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{InvSys}}(\mathcal{D}):=\mathcal{D}^{\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}_{\geq0}^{\operatorname{op}}}\) from equation. Its objects are data \(X=(X_k,f_k)_{k\geq0}\), where \(X_k\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{D})\) and \(f_k\in\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{D}}(X_{k+1},X_k)\). If \(\mathcal{D}\) has countable products, define the canonical morphism as in Definition reference: \[\Delta_X := T_X - \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}: \prod_k X_k \to \prod_k X_k.\] Dually, an object of the category \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{DirSys}}(\mathcal{D}):=\mathcal{D}^{\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}_{\geq0}}\) consists of data \(X=(X_k,g_k)_{k\geq0}\)1, where \(X_k\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{D})\) and \(g_k\in\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{D}}(X_k,X_{k+1})\). Similarly, define \(\nabla_X:=T_X-\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}:\bigoplus_kX_k\to\bigoplus_kX_k\), assuming that \(\mathcal{D}\) has countable coproducts; \(T_X\) is again the analogous shift morphism. If \(\operatorname{ker}(\Delta_X)\) or \(\operatorname{coker}(\nabla_X)\) exists, there are canonical isomorphisms \[\begin{align*} X \in \operatorname{Ob}\left( \ensuremath{\mathsf{InvSys}}(\mathcal{D}) \right) & \implies \varprojlim_k X_k \simeq \operatorname{ker}(\Delta_X), \\ X \in \operatorname{Ob}\left( \ensuremath{\mathsf{DirSys}}(\mathcal{D}) \right) & \implies \varinjlim_k X_k \simeq \operatorname{coker}(\nabla_X). \end{align*}\] The naive hope is to apply this to \(\mathcal{D}=\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}(\mathcal{A})\). Derived categories are rarely abelian categories. Nevertheless, Remark reference shows that mapping cones can serve as homotopical versions of kernels and cokernels. Roughly speaking, the analogous construction in a triangulated category is a distinguished triangle.

Definition (M. Bökstedt, A. Neeman [BN93).] Let \(\mathcal{D}\) be a triangulated category.

  • If \(\mathcal{D}\) has countable products, a homotopy limit (or homotopy \(\varprojlim\)) of an object \(X\in\operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{InvSys}}(\mathcal{D}))\) means a distinguished triangle \[\operatorname{holim}(X) \to \prod_k X_k \xrightarrow{\Delta_X} \prod_k X_k \xrightarrow{+1} .\]

  • If \(\mathcal{D}\) has countable coproducts, a homotopy colimit (or homotopy \(\varinjlim\)) of an object \(X\in\operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{DirSys}}(\mathcal{D}))\) means a distinguished triangle \[\bigoplus_k X_k \xrightarrow{\nabla_X} \bigoplus_k X_k \to \operatorname{hocolim}(X) \xrightarrow{+1} .\]

The distinguished triangles occurring in this definition are isomorphic to one another (Corollary reference), but the isomorphisms are not canonical. Return to complexes. Observe that \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{InvSys}}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A}))= \ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{InvSys}}(\mathcal{A}))\); the objects of both categories are the same commutative diagrams \[\text{Diagram chapter4-unit-060-d003} \quad \text{with each row a complex}.\] Morphisms in the two categories are likewise the same two-level commutative diagrams. Thus, in \(\mathcal{D}:=\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}(\mathcal{A})\), we can compare \(\operatorname{holim}(X)\) with the right derived functor \(\mathrm{R}\lim(X)\) of \(\varprojlim\), provided that both exist. Also observe that the cohomology \(\operatorname{H}^m\) of an object \(X\in\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{InvSys}}(\mathcal{A}))\) is \((\operatorname{H}^m(X_k),\operatorname{H}^m(f_k))_{k\geq0}\). Thus \(X\to Y\) is a quasi-isomorphism if and only if every \(X_k\to Y_k\) is a quasi-isomorphism in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})\).

Theorem. Suppose that \(\mathcal{A}\) is an abelian category with exact countable products and enough injective objects.

  1. The right derived functor of the left-exact functor \(\varprojlim:\ensuremath{\mathsf{InvSys}}(\mathcal{A})\to\mathcal{A}\) exists and is written \[\mathrm{R}\lim : \ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^+\left(\ensuremath{\mathsf{InvSys}}(\mathcal{A})\right) \to \ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^+(\mathcal{A}) .\]

  2. For every object \(X=(X_k,f_k)_{k\geq0}\) of \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}^+(\ensuremath{\mathsf{InvSys}}(\mathcal{A}))\), there is a distinguished triangle in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}(\mathcal{A})\) \[\mathrm{R}\lim(X) \to \prod_k X_k \xrightarrow{\Delta_X} \prod_k X_k \xrightarrow{+1}.\] In particular, \(\mathrm{R}\lim(X)\simeq\operatorname{holim}(X)\).

  3. The dimension of \(\mathrm{R}\lim\) in the sense of Definition–Proposition reference is at most \(1\).

Proof. Since \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{InvSys}}(\mathcal{A})\) has enough injective objects, (i) holds. More precisely, take the category \(\mathcal{R}\) from Lemma reference and apply Theorem reference to \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{InvSys}}(\mathcal{A})\) and \(\mathcal{R}\). For every \(X=(X_k,f_k)_{k\geq0}\) in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}^+(\ensuremath{\mathsf{InvSys}}(\mathcal{A}))\), there is a quasi-isomorphism \(X\to Y\) with \(Y\in\operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}^+(\mathcal{R}))\). Then \(\mathrm{R}\lim(X)=\varprojlim Y\). The definition of \(\mathcal{R}\) ensures that \(\Delta_Y\) is surjective degree by degree, so there is a short exact sequence in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}^+(\mathcal{A})\) \[0 \to \varprojlim Y \to \prod_{k \geq 0} Y_k \xrightarrow{\Delta_Y} \prod_{k \geq 0} Y_k \to 0.\] Furthermore, every \(X_k\to Y_k\) is a quasi-isomorphism, so \(\prod_{k\geq0}X_k\to\prod_{k\geq0}Y_k\) is also a quasi-isomorphism. This gives the distinguished triangle in (ii): \[\mathrm{R}\lim(X) \to \prod_{k \geq 0} X_k \xrightarrow{\Delta_X} \prod_{k \geq 0} X_k \xrightarrow{+1} .\]

For (iii), if \(X\in\operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{InvSys}}(\mathcal{A}))\), then \(\Delta_X\) is a morphism in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{InvSys}}(\mathcal{A})\), and \(\operatorname{holim}(X)\simeq\operatorname{Cone}(\Delta_X)[-1]\) lies in \(\operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^{[0,1]}(\mathcal{A}))\). This is also a restatement of Theorem reference.

There is a dual version of Theorem reference for \(\varinjlim:\ensuremath{\mathsf{DirSys}}(\mathcal{A})\to\mathcal{A}\); we do not repeat the details. Example reference will show how to obtain \(\mathrm{R}\lim\) on the unbounded derived category so that Theorem reference (ii) remains valid.

  1. Such data are also called a direct system in \(\mathcal{D}\).↩︎

Unbounded Derived Functors

Consider an additive functor \(F:\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{A}'\) between abelian categories. This section returns to Definition reference and focuses on the versions of derived functors for unbounded derived categories, \[\mathrm{R}F, \; \mathrm{L}F: \ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}(\mathcal{A}) \to \ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}(\mathcal{A}').\] To guarantee the existence of \(\mathrm{R}F\) or \(\mathrm{L}F\) and to compute with it, we need the notions of K-injective and K-projective complexes from Definition reference, together with the corresponding resolutions.

Lemma. Let \(\mathcal{A}\) be an abelian category. If \(Z\in\operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{A}))\) is both K-injective (respectively, K-projective) and acyclic, then \(Z=0\).

Proof. Lemma reference implies that \(\operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{A})}(Z,Z)=0\).

We first state a general result. Fix triangulated categories \(\mathcal{D}_1\), \(\mathcal{D}_2\), and \(\mathcal{D}'\), together with their saturated triangulated subcategories \(\mathcal{N}_1\), \(\mathcal{N}_2\), and \(\mathcal{N}'\).

Lemma. Given a triangulated bifunctor \(G:\mathcal{D}_1\times\mathcal{D}_2\to\mathcal{D}'\), define a full subcategory \(\mathcal{K}_2^G\) of \(\mathcal{D}_2\) by \[\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{K}_2^G) = \left\{ X_2 \in \operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{D}_2) : X_1 \in \operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{N}_1) \implies G(X_1, X_2) \in \operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{N}') \right\}.\] Then \(\mathcal{K}_2^G\) is a saturated triangulated subcategory. After interchanging the two variables, the corresponding statement holds for \(\mathcal{K}_1^G\subset\mathcal{D}_1\).

Proof. The isomorphism \(G(X_1,X_2[1])\simeq G(X_1,X_2)[1]\) shows that \(\mathcal{K}_2^G\) is closed under translation. Similarly, suppose that \(I\to J\to K\xrightarrow{+1}\) is a distinguished triangle with \(I,K\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{K}_2^G)\). From the distinguished triangle \[G(X_1, I) \to G(X_1, J) \to G(X_1, K) \xrightarrow{+1}\] it follows immediately that \(X_1\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{N}_1)\implies G(X_1,J)\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{N}')\). Saturation is clear.

This result can be applied to \(\operatorname{Hom}:\mathcal{A}^{\operatorname{op}}\times\mathcal{A}\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ab}}\) and the corresponding triangulated bifunctor \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}_{\Pi}\operatorname{Hom}\). Example reference has shown that the latter bifunctor is essentially the \(\operatorname{Hom}\) complex: \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:CPiHom}{}\begin{gathered} (\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}_{\Pi} \operatorname{Hom})(\sigma^{-1} X_1, X_2) \simeq \operatorname{Hom}^\bullet\left( X_1, X_2 \right), \\ (\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}_\Pi \operatorname{Hom})(\sigma^{-1} X_1, X_2) \simeq \operatorname{Hom}^\bullet\left( X_1, X_2 \right)\; \text{viewed in $\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ab}})$}, \end{gathered} \end{equation}\] where \(\sigma:\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A}^{\operatorname{op}})\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}} \ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})^{\operatorname{op}}\) and \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{A}^{\operatorname{op}})\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{A})^{\operatorname{op}}\) are the isomorphisms from Definition–Proposition reference and Proposition reference. We shall later need the corresponding version for derived categories.

Proposition. All K-injective (respectively, K-projective) complexes form a saturated triangulated subcategory \(\mathcal{I}\) (respectively, \(\mathcal{P}\)) of \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{A})\). If \(\mathcal{A}\) has enough K-injective (respectively, K-projective) complexes, then for every additive functor \(F:\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{A}'\), the subcategory \(\mathcal{I}\) (respectively, \(\mathcal{P}\)) is \(F\)-injective (respectively, \(F\)-projective).

Proof. It suffices to treat the K-injective case. The first assertion follows by applying Lemma reference to \(G=\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}_{\Pi}\operatorname{Hom}\), using the definition of K-injective complexes in Definition reference and equation: the subcategory \(\mathcal{K}_2^G\) there is precisely \(\mathcal{I}\) here.

Suppose that \(\mathcal{A}\) has enough K-injective complexes. If \(I\) is an acyclic K-injective complex, Lemma reference implies that \(I=0\), so \((\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}F)I\) is certainly acyclic. Thus all the conditions in Definition reference for an \(F\)-injective triangulated subcategory are satisfied.

Write \(Q:\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{A})\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}(\mathcal{A})\) and \(Q':\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{A}')\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}(\mathcal{A}')\) for the localization functors.

Corollary. If \(\mathcal{A}\) has enough K-injective complexes, then \(F\) has a right derived functor \(\mathrm{R}F:\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}(\mathcal{A})\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}(\mathcal{A}')\), such that \(\mathrm{R}F(QX)\simeq Q'\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}F(X)\) whenever \(X\) is K-injective.

Dually, if \(\mathcal{A}\) has enough K-projective complexes, then \(F\) has a left derived functor \(\mathrm{L}F:\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}(\mathcal{A})\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}(\mathcal{A}')\), such that \(\mathrm{L}F(QX)\simeq Q'\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}F(X)\) whenever \(X\) is K-projective.

Proof. Apply Proposition reference in the general framework of Proposition reference.

Now fix abelian categories \(\mathcal{A}_1\), \(\mathcal{A}_2\), and \(\mathcal{B}\). For an additive bifunctor \(F:\mathcal{A}_1\times\mathcal{A}_2\to\mathcal{B}\), consider the unbounded version of the derived bifunctor \(\mathrm{R}F\) (respectively, \(\mathrm{L}F\)) from Definition reference. From now on, we always assume that \(\mathcal{B}\) has countable products (respectively, countable coproducts). Concretely, we wish to determine \(\mathrm{R}F\) (respectively, \(\mathrm{L}F\)) using the subcategories \(\mathcal{I}_1\), \(\mathcal{I}_2\) (respectively, \(\mathcal{P}_1\), \(\mathcal{P}_2\)) above.

Lemma. For \(i=1,2\), take the triangulated subcategory \(\mathcal{I}_i\) (respectively, \(\mathcal{P}_i\)) of \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{A}_i)\) from Proposition reference.

  • If \(\mathcal{A}_1\) and \(\mathcal{A}_2\) have enough K-injective complexes, then \(\mathcal{I}_1\times\mathcal{I}_2\) is \(F\)-injective.

  • If \(\mathcal{A}_1\) and \(\mathcal{A}_2\) have enough K-projective complexes, then \(\mathcal{P}_1\times\mathcal{P}_2\) is \(F\)-projective.

Proof. It suffices to treat the K-injective case. The key is to show that if \(X_1\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{I}_1)\), then \((\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}_{\Pi}F)(X_1,\cdot)\) sends every acyclic object \(Z\) of \(\mathcal{I}_2\) to an acyclic object of \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{B})\). But Lemma reference gives \(Z=0\), and \((\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}_{\Pi}F)(X_1,\cdot)\) is additive, so the assertion follows immediately. The corresponding result follows after interchanging the indices \(1\) and \(2\).

Write \(Q:\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{B})\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}(\mathcal{B})\) and \(Q_i:\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{A}_i)\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}(\mathcal{A}_i)\) for the localization functors (\(i=1,2\)).

Proposition. For \(F:\mathcal{A}_1\times\mathcal{A}_2\to\mathcal{B}\), suppose that \(\mathcal{A}_1\) and \(\mathcal{A}_2\) both have enough K-injective (respectively, K-projective) complexes. Then the derived bifunctor \(\mathrm{R}F\) (respectively, \(\mathrm{L}F\)) exists. If \(X_i\in\operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{A}))\) is K-injective (respectively, K-projective) for \(i=1,2\), then there is a canonical isomorphism \[\mathrm{R}F(Q_1 X_1, Q_2 X_2) \simeq Q (\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}_{\Pi} F)(X_1, X_2) \quad \text{(respectively, $\mathrm{L}F(Q_1 X_1, Q_2 X_2) \simeq Q (\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}_{\oplus} F)(X_1, X_2)$) }.\]

Proof. Apply Lemma reference directly to Proposition reference.

For a particular bifunctor \(F\), one can often choose \(F\)-injective (respectively, \(F\)-projective) subcategories larger than the subcategories of K-injective (respectively, K-projective) complexes. The \(\operatorname{RHom}\) functor to be discussed next is one example.

Theorem (Unbounded \(\operatorname{RHom}\)). Suppose that the abelian category \(\mathcal{A}\) has enough K-injective or enough K-projective complexes. For simplicity, denote every localization functor by \(Q\).

  1. The bifunctor \(\operatorname{Hom}=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{A}}:\mathcal{A}^{\operatorname{op}}\times\mathcal{A} \to\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ab}}\) has a right derived bifunctor \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}(\mathcal{A}^{\operatorname{op}})\times\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}(\mathcal{A}) \to\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ab}})\). Via the equivalence \(\sigma\) of Proposition reference, it can also be written as \[\operatorname{RHom}: \ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}(\mathcal{A})^{\operatorname{op}} \times \ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}(\mathcal{A}) \to \ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ab}}).\] Moreover, if \(\mathcal{A}\) has enough K-injective (respectively, K-projective) complexes, then \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{A})^{\operatorname{op}}\times\mathcal{I}\) (respectively, \(\mathcal{P}^{\operatorname{op}}\times\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{A})\)) is \(\operatorname{Hom}\)-injective.

  2. Suppose that \(\mathcal{A}\) has enough K-injective complexes and that \(X_2\to I_2\) is a K-injective resolution. This resolution induces \[\operatorname{RHom}(Q X_1, Q X_2) \ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}Q \operatorname{Hom}^\bullet(X_1, I_2).\] In particular, \(\operatorname{RHom}(QX_1,\cdot)\simeq \mathrm{R}\left(\operatorname{Hom}(X_1,\cdot)\right)\).

  3. Suppose that \(\mathcal{A}\) has enough K-projective complexes and that \(P_1\to X_1\) is a K-projective resolution. This resolution induces \[\operatorname{RHom}(Q X_1, Q X_2) \ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}Q \operatorname{Hom}^\bullet(P_1, X_2).\] In particular, \(\operatorname{RHom}(\cdot,QX_2)\simeq \mathrm{R}\left(\operatorname{Hom}(\cdot,X_2)\right)\).

  4. There is a canonical isomorphism \(\operatorname{H}^n\operatorname{RHom}(X,Y)\simeq \operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}(\mathcal{A})}(X,Y[n])=: \operatorname{Ext}^n(X,Y)\) (Definition reference).

Proof. The argument is nearly identical to that for Theorem reference. For example, suppose that \(\mathcal{A}\) has enough K-injective complexes. The key is to show that \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{A})^{\operatorname{op}}\times\mathcal{I}\) is \(\operatorname{Hom}\)-injective.

  • Fix a complex \(X_1\). The functor \((\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}_\Pi\operatorname{Hom})(X_1,\cdot)\) sends every acyclic K-injective complex \(X_2\) to an acyclic complex, because \(X_2\) is \(0\) in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{A})\) (Lemma reference).

  • Fix a K-injective complex \(X_2\). If \(X_1\) is acyclic, the definition of a K-injective complex implies that \(\operatorname{Hom}^\bullet\left(X_1,X_2\right)\) is acyclic. By equation, \((\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}_\Pi\operatorname{Hom})(X_1,X_2)\) is therefore acyclic as well.

Thus the acyclicity conditions required for the \(\operatorname{Hom}\)-injective property have been verified, while the resolution conditions hold directly.

Theorem. Consider an adjoint pair of additive functors between abelian categories \(\text{Diagram chapter4-unit-061-diagram-001}\). Suppose that \(\mathcal{A}\) has enough K-projective complexes and \(\mathcal{A}'\) has enough K-injective complexes. Then there is a canonical isomorphism in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ab}})\) \[\operatorname{RHom}_{\mathcal{A'}}\left(\mathrm{L}F(X), Y\right) \simeq \operatorname{RHom}_{\mathcal{A}}\left(X, \mathrm{R}G(Y) \right),\] where \(X\in\operatorname{Ob}\left(\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}(\mathcal{A})\right)\) and \(Y\in\operatorname{Ob}\left(\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}(\mathcal{A}')\right)\).

Proof. The argument is the same as for Theorem reference. The only difference is that injective (respectively, projective) resolutions are replaced by K-injective (respectively, K-projective) resolutions, and Theorem reference replaces Theorem reference in the discussion of uniqueness of resolutions.

Remark. Applying \(\operatorname{H}^0\) to both sides of Theorem reference gives the adjunction \[\operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}(\mathcal{A'})}\left(\mathrm{L}F(X), Y\right) \simeq \operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}(\mathcal{A})}\left(X, \mathrm{R}G(Y) \right).\]

Since derived functors obtained through resolutions are always absolute Kan extensions in the sense of Definition reference (Proposition reference), Theorem reference also says that \((\mathrm{L}F,\mathrm{R}G)\) is an adjoint pair. The two approaches give the same adjunction isomorphism. Why? It suffices to consider the case in which \(X\) is K-projective and \(Y\) is K-injective. In this case, the adjunction isomorphism of Theorem reference is realized concretely by the unit \(\eta\) and counit \(\varepsilon\) at the level of \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\cdot)\) as \[\begin{align*} \operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{A}')}\left( \ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}F(X), Y\right) \simeq \operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{A})}\left( X, \ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}G(Y) \right). \end{align*}\] On the other hand, Theorem reference determines \(\underline{\eta}\) and \(\underline{\varepsilon}\) at the level of derived categories. The characterization given there suffices to show that they are compatible with \(\eta\) and \(\varepsilon\). The details are left to the interested reader.

Finally, another set of sufficient conditions for the existence of unbounded derived functors is based on finite dimension (Definition–Proposition reference). Although the proof technique does not go beyond the scope of this book, we state the result without proof to avoid a digression; see [stacks]. The starting point is the construction of bounded derived functors in Theorem reference.

Proposition. Let \(F:\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{A}'\) be a left-exact (respectively, right-exact) functor between abelian categories. Assume that

  • relative to \(F\), there is a full additive subcategory \(\mathcal{A}^\flat\) of \(\mathcal{A}\) of type I (respectively, type P), as in Definition–Proposition reference;

  • the corresponding bounded derived functor \({}^+\mathrm{R}F\) (respectively, \({}^-\mathrm{L}F\)) has finite dimension.

Then \(\mathrm{R}F\) (respectively, \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{L}}F\)): \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}(\mathcal{A})\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}(\mathcal{A}')\) exists. Moreover, \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{A}^\flat)\) is an \(F\)-injective (respectively, \(F\)-projective) subcategory of \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{A})\).

Example. Suppose that \(\mathcal{A}\) has exact countable products and enough injective objects. Take the left-exact functor \(F\) to be \(\varprojlim:\ensuremath{\mathsf{InvSys}}(\mathcal{A})\to\mathcal{A}\). Theorem reference (iii) shows that the bounded version of \(\mathrm{R}\lim\) has dimension at most \(1\), while the subcategory \(\mathcal{R}\subset\ensuremath{\mathsf{InvSys}}(\mathcal{A})\) is of type I relative to \(\varprojlim\). The preceding result therefore gives the unbounded derived functor \[\mathrm{R}\lim: \ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{InvSys}}(\mathcal{A})) \to \ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}(\mathcal{A}).\]

As in Theorem reference (ii), for every object \(X\) of \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{InvSys}}(\mathcal{A}))\) there is a distinguished triangle in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}(\mathcal{A})\) \[\mathrm{R}\lim(X) \to \prod_k X_k \xrightarrow{\Delta_X} \prod_k X_k \xrightarrow{+1} .\] In particular, \(\mathrm{R}\lim(X)\simeq\operatorname{holim}(X)\). By Proposition reference, the original proof applies with no other changes: simply replace every \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}^+(\cdots)\) by \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\cdots)\).

Example: K-Flat Complexes and \(\ensuremath{\underset{}{\overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes}}}\)

Throughout this section, \(\Bbbk\) is a commutative ring.

Convention. Let \(R\) and \(S\) be \(\Bbbk\)-algebras. By the convention of this book, every \((R,S)\)-bimodule \(M\) is tacitly assumed to satisfy \(tm=mt\) for \(t\in\Bbbk\) and \(m\in M\). In other words, \((R,S)\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\simeq(R\ensuremath{\underset{\Bbbk}{\otimes}}S^{\operatorname{op}})\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\). When \(\Bbbk=\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\), this condition is redundant.

From now on, the forgetful functor \((R,S)\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\to R\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\) (respectively, \((R,S)\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}\text{-}}S\)) is written \(M\mapsto{}_RM\) (respectively, \(M\mapsto M_S\)); the same notation applies to complexes. These forgetful functors are exact, and the triangulated functors they induce between derived categories are denoted in the same way.

Notice that, for every complex \(M\) of \((R,S)\)-bimodules, one has \[M_S \;\text{acyclic} \iff M \;\text{acyclic} \iff {}_R M \;\text{acyclic}.\] From now on, let \(R\), \(A\), and \(B\) be \(\Bbbk\)-algebras. Our starting point is the bifunctor given by the tensor product, \[\otimes_R: (A, R)\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}} \times (R, B)\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}} \to (A, B)\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}},\] which is right exact in each variable. The simplest case is \(A=\Bbbk=B\); the corresponding bifunctor becomes \(\otimes_R:\ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}\text{-}}R\times R\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{\Bbbk}}\). For convenience, if \(X\) is a complex of \((A,R)\)-bimodules and \(Y\) is a complex of \((R,B)\)-bimodules, we henceforth write the bicomplex obtained by taking tensor products term by term as \(X^\bullet\ensuremath{\underset{R}{\otimes}}Y^\bullet\), and write its total complex as \[X \ensuremath{\underset{R}{\otimes}} Y := \operatorname{tot}_{\oplus} \left( X^\bullet \ensuremath{\underset{R}{\otimes}} Y^\bullet \right).\] Categories of bimodules have enough K-projective complexes (apply Example reference); hence Proposition reference ensures the existence of the unbounded left derived bifunctor.

Definition. Denote the left derived bifunctor \(\mathrm{L}\left(\cdot\ensuremath{\underset{R}{\otimes}}\cdot\right)\) of \(\otimes_R\) by \[\ensuremath{\underset{R}{\overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes}}} : \ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}((A, R)\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}) \times \ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}((R, B)\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}) \to \ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}((A, B)\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}).\] When no confusion can arise, \(X\ensuremath{\underset{R}{\overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes}}}Y\) is also abbreviated to \(X\ensuremath{\underset{}{\overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes}}}Y\).

The abstract definition above is straightforward, but to study \(\otimes_R\) further we still need to introduce a class of quasi-isomorphisms called K-flat resolutions. The reasons include the following:

  • the definition of a K-flat resolution is directly related to the tensor product and is more useful for establishing important properties and making concrete computations, as already seen in §reference;

  • in geometric settings such as sheaf theory, K-injective resolutions may be available while K-projective resolutions are not; in that situation, K-flat resolutions are the only means of studying the derived tensor product.

Definition (N. Spaltenstein [Spa88).] Let \(X\) be a complex of right \(R\)-modules. If, for every complex \(Y\) of left \(R\)-modules, \[Y \;\text{acyclic} \implies X \ensuremath{\underset{R}{\otimes}} Y\;\text{acyclic},\] then \(X\) is called K-flat1; this property depends only on the isomorphism class of \(X\) in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}\text{-}}R)\). K-flatness is defined similarly for complexes of left \(R\)-modules.

For bounded-above complexes, K-flatness follows from the familiar notion of flatness in module theory.

Proposition. Let \(X\) be an object of \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}^-(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}\text{-}}R)\), and suppose that every \(X^n\) is flat. Then \(X\) is K-flat. The same statement holds for objects of \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}^-(R\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}})\).

Proof. Let \(Y\) be an acyclic complex of left \(R\)-modules; we shall prove that \(X\ensuremath{\underset{R}{\otimes}}Y\) is acyclic. Using truncation functors, write \(Y\) as \(\varinjlim_m\tau^{\leq m}Y\). Degree by degree, \(\varinjlim_m\) commutes both with tensor products [Li1] and with \(\bigoplus\); it therefore suffices to consider the case in which \(Y\) is bounded above. Then \(X^\bullet\ensuremath{\underset{R}{\otimes}}Y^\bullet\) belongs to the category \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}^2_f(\Bbbk\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}})\) of Definition reference. Since \(X^p\ensuremath{\underset{R}{\otimes}}Y^\bullet\) is acyclic for every \(p\), Corollary reference ensures that \(X\ensuremath{\underset{R}{\otimes}}Y\) is acyclic.

In view of this result, if the reader is interested only in bounded-above derived categories, every K-flat complex appearing in this section may be replaced by a bounded-above complex of flat modules.

Definition. If \(P\to X\) is a quasi-isomorphism in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}((A,R)\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}})\) and \(P_R\) is K-flat, then this morphism is called a K-flat resolution of \(X\) relative to \(R\). If every \(X\in\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}((A,R)\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}})\) has a K-flat resolution relative to \(R\), then \((A,R)\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\) is said to have enough K-flat complexes relative to \(R\).

A K-flat resolution relative to \(R\) is defined similarly for \(X\in\operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}((R,B)\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}))\).

A natural question is how to guarantee that a category of bimodules has enough K-flat complexes relative to \(R\). What is the relation between K-flat and K-projective complexes? As expected, the bridge comes from the classical adjunction between \(\otimes\) and \(\operatorname{Hom}\) [Li1]. The first step is to lift that adjunction to the level of complexes. If \(Y\) is an object of \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}((R,B)\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}})\) and \(Z\) is an object of \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}((A,B)\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}})\), the \(\operatorname{Hom}\) complex \(\operatorname{Hom}^\bullet(Y_B,Z_B)\) can be endowed degree by degree with an \((A,R)\)-bimodule structure, making it an object of \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}((A,R)\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}})\).

Proposition (\(\operatorname{Hom}\)–\(\otimes\) adjunction: complex version). Let \(X\) be an object of \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}((A,R)\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}})\), let \(Y\) be an object of \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}((R,B)\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}})\), and let \(Z\) be an object of \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}((A,B)\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}})\). There are canonical isomorphisms in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\Bbbk\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}})\) \[\begin{align*} \operatorname{Hom}^\bullet\left( X \ensuremath{\underset{R}{\otimes}} Y, \; Z \right) & \simeq \operatorname{Hom}^\bullet\left( X, \operatorname{Hom}^\bullet(Y_B, Z_B) \right) \\ & \simeq \operatorname{Hom}^\bullet\left( Y, \operatorname{Hom}^\bullet({}_A X, {}_A Z) \right). \end{align*}\]

Consequently, taking \(\operatorname{ker}(d^0)\) gives isomorphisms of \(\Bbbk\)-modules \[\begin{align*} \operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}((A, B)\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}})}\left( X \ensuremath{\underset{R}{\otimes}} Y, \; Z \right) & \simeq \operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}((A, R)\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}})}\left( X, \operatorname{Hom}^\bullet(Y_B, Z_B) \right) \\ & \simeq \operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}((R, B)\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}})}\left( Y, \operatorname{Hom}^\bullet({}_A X, {}_A Z) \right). \end{align*}\]

Proof. It suffices to treat the first isomorphism. To simplify notation, write \(Y\) and \(Z\) for \(Y_B\) and \(Z_B\) below, and omit the subscript on \(\operatorname{Hom}\). Fix \(n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\). The degree-\(n\) term on the left-hand side is \[\begin{multline} \hypertarget{eqn:tensor-Hom-cplx-aux}{} \prod_k \operatorname{Hom}\left( (X \ensuremath{\underset{R}{\otimes}} Y)^k, Z^{k+n}\right) \simeq \prod_k \prod_{p+q=k} \operatorname{Hom}\left(X^p \ensuremath{\underset{R}{\otimes}} Y^q, Z^{k+n}\right) \\ = \prod_{p, q} \operatorname{Hom}\left( X^p \ensuremath{\underset{R}{\otimes}} Y^q, Z^{p+q+n} \right) \simeq \prod_p \prod_q \operatorname{Hom}\left( X^p, \operatorname{Hom}\left(Y^q, Z^{p+q+n}\right) \right) \\ \simeq \prod_p \operatorname{Hom}\left( X^p, \operatorname{Hom}^{p+n}(Y, Z) \right), \end{multline}\] and the last term is precisely the degree-\(n\) term on the right-hand side. Concretely, under the second isomorphism \(\simeq\), the homomorphism of \((A,B)\)-bimodules \(\varphi^{p,q}:X^p\ensuremath{\underset{R}{\otimes}}Y^q\to Z^{p+q+n}\) corresponds to \[\left[ x \mapsto [y \mapsto \varphi^{p,q}(x \otimes y)] \right] \; \in \operatorname{Hom}\left( X^p, \operatorname{Hom}\left(Y^q, Z^{p+q+n}\right) \right).\] It remains only to verify that equation determines an isomorphism of complexes.

Take an element of the degree-\(n\) term on the left and write it as \((\varphi^{p,q})_{p,q\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}}\). The \((p,q)\)-component of its image under \(d_{\operatorname{Hom}^\bullet(X\otimes Y,Z)}\) sends \(x\otimes y\in X^p\ensuremath{\underset{R}{\otimes}}Y^q\) to \[d_Z \varphi^{p,q}(x \otimes y) - (-1)^n \left( \varphi^{p+1, q}(d_X x \otimes y) + (-1)^p \varphi^{p, q+1}(x \otimes d_Y y) \right).\]

For the corresponding element of degree \(n\) on the right, the \(p\)-component of its image under \(d_{\operatorname{Hom}^\bullet(X,\operatorname{Hom}^\bullet(Y,Z))}\) sends \(x\in X^p\) to \[d_{\operatorname{Hom}^\bullet(Y, Z)}\left[ y \mapsto \varphi^{p,q}(x \otimes y) \right]_{q \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}} - (-1)^n \left[ y \mapsto \varphi^{p+1, q}(d_X x \otimes y) \right]_{q \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}};\] expanding the definition of \(d^{p+n}_{\operatorname{Hom}^\bullet(Y,Z)}\) further, for the fixed pair \((p,q)\) this becomes \[y \mapsto d_Z \varphi^{p,q}(x \otimes y) - (-1)^{p+n} \varphi^{p, q+1}(x \otimes d_Y y) - (-1)^n \varphi^{p+1, q}(d_X x \otimes y).\] This proves the assertion.

We now return to the relation between K-projective and K-flat complexes.

Lemma. Let \(X\) be a K-projective complex of \((A,R)\)-bimodules. If \(A\) is flat as a \(\Bbbk\)-module, then \(X_R\) is K-flat.

Let \(Y\) be a K-projective complex of \((R,B)\)-bimodules. If \(B\) is flat as a \(\Bbbk\)-module, then \({}_RY\) is K-flat.

Proof. It suffices to prove the first assertion. Take an acyclic complex \(Y\) of left \(R\)-modules. Regard every left \(A\)-module \(I\) (that is, every \((A,\Bbbk)\)-bimodule) as a complex concentrated in degree zero. Proposition reference, with \(B=\Bbbk\), gives \[\operatorname{Hom}^\bullet\left(X \ensuremath{\underset{R}{\otimes}} Y, \; I\right) \simeq \operatorname{Hom}^\bullet\left(X, \operatorname{Hom}^\bullet(Y_{\Bbbk}, I_{\Bbbk}) \right).\]

Suppose that \(I\) is an injective left \(A\)-module. Then \(I_{\Bbbk}\) is an injective \(\Bbbk\)-module, because the forgetful functor \(A\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\to\Bbbk\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\) has the exact left adjoint \(A\ensuremath{\underset{\Bbbk}{\otimes}}(\cdot)\); see Proposition reference and [Li1]. Hence the complex of \(\Bbbk\)-modules \(\operatorname{Hom}^\bullet(Y_{\Bbbk},I_{\Bbbk})\) is acyclic. It remains acyclic as a complex of \((A,R)\)-bimodules, so the K-projectivity of \(X\) implies that \(\operatorname{Hom}^\bullet(X\ensuremath{\underset{R}{\otimes}}Y,I)\) is acyclic.

Because \(I\) is injective, it is easy to see that, for every \(n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\), \[\operatorname{Hom}\left( \operatorname{H}^n\left( X \ensuremath{\underset{R}{\otimes}} Y \right), I\right) \simeq \operatorname{H}^{-n} \operatorname{Hom}^\bullet\left( X \ensuremath{\underset{R}{\otimes}} Y, \; I \right) = 0.\]

Since every left \(A\)-module embeds into an injective module, \(X\ensuremath{\underset{R}{\otimes}}Y\) must be acyclic. This proves the assertion.

If the reader is interested only in tensor products over commutative rings, that is, in the special case \(A=R=B=\Bbbk\), or only in the case where \(\Bbbk\) is a field, all the flatness assumptions on \(A\) or \(B\) above are automatically satisfied.

Corollary. If \(A\) (respectively, \(B\)) is flat as a \(\Bbbk\)-module, then \((A,R)\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\) (respectively, \((R,B)\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\)) has enough K-flat complexes relative to \(R\).

Taking \(A=\Bbbk\) (respectively, \(B=\Bbbk\)) further shows that K-projective complexes of right (respectively, left) \(R\)-modules are always K-flat relative to \(R\), and that \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}\text{-}}R\) (respectively, \(R\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\)) has enough K-flat complexes. We now explain how to determine the derived functor of \(\otimes_R\) by means of K-flat resolutions. To simplify notation, all localization functors \(Q\) will henceforth be suppressed.

Proposition. Define the full subcategory \(\mathcal{F}_{A,R}\) of \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}((A,R)\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}})\) by \[\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{F}_{A,R}) = \{ X: X_R \;\text{K-flat} \};\] and define \(\mathcal{F}_{R,B}\) similarly. Both are saturated triangulated subcategories. We now determine subcategories of \[\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}((A,R)\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}) \times \ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}((R,B)\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}) \quad \text{that are $\otimes_R$-projective}.\]

  1. Suppose that \((A,R)\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\) has enough K-flat complexes relative to \(R\). Then \(\left(\mathcal{F}_{A,R},\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}((R,B)\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}})\right)\) is an \(\otimes_R\)-projective subcategory. Consequently, if \(Y\) is a complex of \((R,B)\)-bimodules, then \(\cdot\ensuremath{\underset{R}{\overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes}}}Y\) is the left derived functor of \(\cdot\ensuremath{\underset{R}{\otimes}}Y\) and can be computed using K-flat resolutions.

  2. Suppose that \((R,B)\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\) has enough K-flat complexes relative to \(R\). Then \((\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}((A,R)\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}),\mathcal{F}_{R,B})\) is an \(\otimes_R\)-projective subcategory. Consequently, if \(X\) is a complex of \((A,R)\)-bimodules, then \(X\ensuremath{\underset{R}{\overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes}}}\cdot\) is the left derived functor of \(X\ensuremath{\underset{R}{\otimes}}\cdot\) and can be computed using K-flat resolutions.

Proof. Lemma reference shows that \(\mathcal{F}_{A,R}\) and \(\mathcal{F}_{R,B}\) are saturated triangulated subcategories. For the remaining assertions, it suffices to treat (i). Recalling the relevant definitions in §reference, the key is to verify the following properties:

  • for a complex \(X\) in \(\mathcal{F}_{A,R}\), if \(Y\) is acyclic, then \(X\ensuremath{\underset{R}{\otimes}}Y\) is acyclic;

  • for a fixed \(Y\), if \(X\) is an acyclic complex in \(\mathcal{F}_{A,R}\), then \(X\ensuremath{\underset{R}{\otimes}}Y\) is acyclic.

The first property follows directly from the definition of K-flatness. Now consider the second. Since \(X\ensuremath{\underset{R}{\otimes}}Y\) uses only the left \(R\)-action on \(Y\), we may assume that \(B=\Bbbk\). In this case, Corollary reference ensures the existence of a K-flat resolution \(Q\to Y\) in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(R\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}})\). We thus obtain \[\begin{gather*} \text{a distinguished triangle in }\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(R\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}) \quad Q \to Y \to N \xrightarrow{+1}, \quad N: \text{an acyclic complex}, \\ \text{a distinguished triangle in }\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(A\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}) \quad X \ensuremath{\underset{R}{\otimes}} Q \to X \ensuremath{\underset{R}{\otimes}} Y \to X \ensuremath{\underset{R}{\otimes}} N \xrightarrow{+1}. \end{gather*}\] Since \(X\) is acyclic and \(Q\) is K-flat, \(X\ensuremath{\underset{R}{\otimes}}Q\) is acyclic. On the other hand, since \(N\) is acyclic and \(X\) is K-flat relative to \(R\), \(X\ensuremath{\underset{R}{\otimes}}N\) is acyclic. Thus \(X\ensuremath{\underset{R}{\otimes}}Y\) is acyclic as well.

Finally, the assertion about \(\ensuremath{\underset{R}{\overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes}}}\) is simply a direct application of Proposition reference (ii).

Example (Change of rings and \(\ensuremath{\underset{}{\overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes}}}\)). For a homomorphism \(R\to S\) of \(\Bbbk\)-algebras, regard \(S\) as an \((S,R)\)-bimodule. Following [Li1], consider the right-exact additive functor \[\begin{equation*} {}_{R \to S} P := S \ensuremath{\underset{R}{\otimes}} (\cdot): R\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}} \to S\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}} . \end{equation*}\] This functor has a left derived functor \(\mathrm{L}{}_{R\to S}P\). Taking \(A=S\) and \(B=\Bbbk\) in Corollary reference and Proposition reference (ii) shows that flatness causes no difficulty here and that \[\mathrm{L}{}_{R \to S} P \simeq S \ensuremath{\underset{R}{\overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes}}} (\cdot) .\]

Change of rings is also transitive: given homomorphisms \(R\to S\to T\), there is a canonical isomorphism \[\mathrm{L} {}_{S \to T} P \circ \mathrm{L} {}_{R \to S} P \ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}\mathrm{L} {}_{R \to T} P.\] Indeed, the displayed morphism comes from Theorem reference on deriving a composite of functors. Moreover, since \[X \ensuremath{\underset{S}{\otimes}} (S \ensuremath{\underset{R}{\otimes}} Y) \simeq X_R \ensuremath{\underset{R}{\otimes}} Y, \quad X \in \operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}\text{-}}S)), \; Y \in \operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(R\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}})),\] the functor \({}_{R\to S}P\) preserves K-flat complexes. This ensures that the canonical morphism is an isomorphism.

In exactly the same way, one can define the left derived functor \(\mathrm{L}P_{R\to S}\) of \(P_{R\to S}=(\cdot)\ensuremath{\underset{R}{\otimes}}S:\ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}\text{-}}R\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}\text{-}}S\), which is given by \((\cdot)\ensuremath{\underset{R}{\overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes}}}S\).

Proposition. If \(A\) or \(B\) is flat as a \(\Bbbk\)-module, there is a canonical \(2\)-cell diagram \[\text{Diagram chapter4-unit-062-d001}\]

Proof. Properties of this kind are usually proved with the aid of resolutions. In brief, let \(X\) be a complex of \((A,R)\)-bimodules and \(Y\) a complex of \((R,B)\)-bimodules. By Proposition reference, we may assume that \(X_R\) (respectively, \({}_RY\)) is K-flat. Then \(X\ensuremath{\underset{R}{\otimes}}Y\) computes \(\ensuremath{\underset{R}{\overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes}}}\) in both the first and second rows, giving the isomorphism \(\Rightarrow\), which we provisionally denote by \(\alpha\).

To characterize \(\alpha\) abstractly, one may take the following viewpoint. Add another layer above the diagram under consideration, written schematically as \[\text{Diagram chapter4-unit-062-diagram-002}\] All vertical arrows here are localization functors. We wish to fill the bottom face with \(\text{Diagram chapter4-unit-062-d002}\). The other faces of the cube are easy to handle: by the definition of a left derived bifunctor, the front and back faces have such fillings; by the universal property of localization, the left and right faces commute up to isomorphism; and the top face commutes by the definition of the tensor product. Tracing these faces gives a morphism between composite functors \[\par\textbf{Diagram chapter4-unit-062-d003}\par \;\Rightarrow \cdots \Rightarrow\; \par\textbf{Diagram chapter4-unit-062-d004}\par \; =: \beth.\]

Recall that \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}(\cdots)\times\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}(\cdots)\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}(\cdots)\) is absolute as a right Kan extension (Proposition reference). Therefore the composite \[\begin{equation*} \begin{gathered} \par\textbf{Diagram chapter4-unit-062-d005}\par \quad \text{is the right Kan extension of $\beth$ along} \quad \par\textbf{Diagram chapter4-unit-062-d006}\par. \end{gathered} \end{equation*}\] Applying the morphism into \(\beth\) and the universal property of the right Kan extension (Definition reference) gives the desired \(\alpha\).

Once the existence of \(\alpha\) has been established, take K-flat complexes as in the first paragraph of the proof and compute all the functors in the upper layer. This proves that \(\alpha\) is an isomorphism.

From now on, arguments of this kind based on universal properties will often be omitted; instead, we shall verify statements directly using resolutions.

  1. A more reasonable name might be a homotopy-flat complex.↩︎

Corollary. The functor \(\ensuremath{\underset{R}{\overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes}}}\) of Definition reference, under the assumption that \(A\) or \(B\) is flat as a \(\Bbbk\)-module, satisfies the canonical isomorphism \[\operatorname{H}^{-n}\left( X \ensuremath{\underset{R}{\overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes}}} Y \right) \simeq \operatorname{Tor}^R_n(X, Y), \quad n \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}},\] where \(X\) is an \((A,R)\)-bimodule, \(Y\) is an \((R,B)\)-bimodule, and \(\operatorname{Tor}^R_n\) is as in Definition–Proposition reference.

Proof. The left-hand side is obtained by composing the diagram of Proposition reference in the direction

Diagram chapter4-unit-063-d001

whereas the right-hand side is obtained by composing it in the direction

Diagram chapter4-unit-063-d002

.

Proposition (Associativity constraint). Let \(A\), \(B\), \(R\), and \(S\) be \(\Bbbk\)-algebras. Consider the following two functors: \[\begin{gather*} \ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}((A,R)\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}) \times \ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}((R,S)\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}) \times \ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}((S,B)\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}) \to \ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}((A,B)\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}), \\ (X, Y, Z) \mapsto (X \ensuremath{\underset{R}{\overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes}}} Y) \ensuremath{\underset{S}{\overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes}}} Z, \\ (X, Y, Z) \mapsto X \ensuremath{\underset{R}{\overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes}}} (Y \ensuremath{\underset{S}{\overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes}}} Z). \end{gather*}\] If \(A\) and \(B\) are both flat as \(\Bbbk\)-modules, there is a canonical isomorphism \[a(X,Y,Z): (X \ensuremath{\underset{R}{\overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes}}} Y) \ensuremath{\underset{S}{\overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes}}} Z \ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}X \ensuremath{\underset{R}{\overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes}}} (Y \ensuremath{\underset{S}{\overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes}}} Z).\]

Proof. Fix \(Y\). By Proposition reference, we may assume that \(X_R\) and \({}_R Z\) are K-flat. Then every \(\ensuremath{\underset{R}{\overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes}}}\) can be computed at the level of complexes, and the assertion reduces to the associativity constraint for tensor products [Li1].

Under these flatness assumptions, taking \(\ensuremath{\underset{}{\overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes}}}\) of three or more objects in different orders yields results that are mutually isomorphic through the associativity constraint. These isomorphisms also satisfy coherence, which can be formulated by imitating the pentagon axiom for monoidal categories; see [Li1]. Again, one takes K-flat resolutions and checks the assertion at the level of complexes. To keep the discussion brief, this book presents only the special case of a commutative ring.

Example (\(\ensuremath{\underset{}{\overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes}}}\) over a commutative ring). Let \(R\) be a commutative ring. In the definition \(\ensuremath{\underset{}{\overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes}}}:=\ensuremath{\underset{R}{\overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes}}}\), take every ring to be \(R\), in particular \(\Bbbk=R\). Then \((R,R)\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}=R\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\), and all the preceding flatness assumptions are automatically satisfied. Consequently, \(\operatorname{H}^{-n}(X\ensuremath{\underset{}{\overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes}}}Y)\simeq\operatorname{Tor}^R_n(X,Y)\) for all \(R\)-modules \(X\) and \(Y\).

This makes \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}(R\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}})\) a monoidal category with respect to \(\ensuremath{\underset{}{\overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes}}}\) in the sense of [Li1]. Its unit object is \(R\) itself, and its associativity constraint comes from \(a=(a(X,Y,Z))_{X,Y,Z}\) in Proposition reference. Since \(R\) is a flat \(R\)-module, it is K-flat (Proposition reference); hence both \(R\ensuremath{\underset{}{\overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes}}}(\cdot)\) and \((\cdot)\ensuremath{\underset{}{\overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes}}}R\) can be computed at the level of complexes, making all the monoidal-category axioms easy to prove. Furthermore, \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}(R\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}})\) is a symmetric monoidal category in the sense of [Li1]. Its braiding (or commutativity constraint) \(c(X,Y):X\ensuremath{\underset{}{\overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes}}}Y\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}Y\ensuremath{\underset{}{\overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes}}}X\) comes from the commutativity constraint at the level of complexes, and its axioms are also checked there. In view of Proposition reference, swapping the superscripts in the total complex causes no difficulty here.

Example (\(\operatorname{Tor}\)-algebra). Continue with the setting of Example reference, with \(R\) commutative. Identify the complexes of \(R\)-modules \(X,Y,Z,W\) with their images in the derived category. For every \((p,q)\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}^2\), there is a canonical morphism \[\begin{multline*} \operatorname{H}^{-p}\left( X \ensuremath{\underset{}{\overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes}}}Y \right) \otimes \operatorname{H}^{-q}\left( Z \ensuremath{\underset{}{\overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes}}}W \right) \to \operatorname{H}^{-p-q}\left( (X \ensuremath{\underset{}{\overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes}}}Y) \ensuremath{\underset{}{\overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes}}}(Z \ensuremath{\underset{}{\overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes}}}W) \right) \\ \simeq \operatorname{H}^{-p-q}\left( (X \ensuremath{\underset{}{\overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes}}}Z) \ensuremath{\underset{}{\overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes}}}(Y \ensuremath{\underset{}{\overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes}}}W) \right) \to \operatorname{H}^{-p-q} \left( (X \otimes Z) \ensuremath{\underset{}{\overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes}}}(Y \otimes W) \right), \end{multline*}\] where the first part applies Proposition reference (take \(F=\otimes\)), the second uses the associativity and commutativity constraints on \((\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}(R\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}),\ensuremath{\underset{}{\overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes}}})\), and the third comes from the canonical morphism accompanying \(\ensuremath{\underset{}{\overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes}}}\) as a left derived bifunctor: \[QX_1 \ensuremath{\underset{}{\overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes}}}QX_2 \to Q(X_1 \otimes X_2), \quad X_1, X_2 \in \operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(R\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}})),\] For precision, the localization functor \(Q:\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(R\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}})\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}(R\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}})\) has been written explicitly again here.

  • The composite of the three canonical morphisms above gives an “external product” for the \(\operatorname{Tor}\) functor: \[\operatorname{Tor}^R_p(X, Y) \otimes \operatorname{Tor}^R_q(Z, W) \to \operatorname{Tor}^R_{p+q}(X \otimes Z, Y \otimes W).\]

  • Take \(Z=X\) and \(W=Y\) to be \(R\)-algebras (concentrated in degree \(0\)). Their multiplications give homomorphisms of \(R\)-modules \(X\otimes X\to X\) and \(Y\otimes Y\to Y\). Composing the external product with these homomorphisms gives \[\operatorname{Tor}^R_p(X, Y) \otimes \operatorname{Tor}^R_q(X, Y) \to \operatorname{Tor}^R_{p+q}(X,Y),\] called the “internal product” for the \(\operatorname{Tor}\) functor. This makes \(\bigoplus_{n \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}} \operatorname{Tor}^R_n(X, Y)\) a \(\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\)-graded \(R\)-algebra in the sense of [Li1], called the \(\operatorname{Tor}\)-algebra. It has nonzero components only in nonnegative degrees, and its degree-zero component is the subalgebra \(\operatorname{Tor}^R_0(X,Y)=X\otimes Y\), whose definition may be found in [Li1]. The associativity required for the product can be verified by reducing it to the associativity constraint for \(\ensuremath{\underset{}{\overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes}}}\) and to the associativity of multiplication on \(X\) and \(Y\) separately.

  • Suppose further that \(X\) and \(Y\) are commutative \(R\)-algebras. In this case, the \(\operatorname{Tor}\)-algebra is also an “anticommutative” \(\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\)-graded algebra in the sense of [Li1]1: for all \(p,q\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\), \[a \in \operatorname{Tor}^R_p(X, Y), \; b \in \operatorname{Tor}^R_q(X, Y) \implies ab = (-1)^{pq} ba.\] Since both \(X\otimes X\to X\) and \(Y\otimes Y\to Y\) are commutative, where does the sign come from? Its source is the definition of the external product. Let \(C_1\) and \(C_2\) be two copies of \(X\ensuremath{\underset{}{\overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes}}}Y\). Then \(ab\) and \(ba\) differ through the isomorphism \(C_1\ensuremath{\underset{}{\overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes}}}C_2\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}C_2\ensuremath{\underset{}{\overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes}}}C_1\), namely the commutativity constraint for \(\ensuremath{\underset{}{\overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes}}}\). If \(C_1\) and \(C_2\) are represented by K-flat complexes, this isomorphism of total complexes is exactly the isomorphism \(r_{C_1^\bullet \otimes C_2^\bullet}\) of Proposition reference; on the component of bidegree \((p,q)\), it produces the sign \((-1)^{pq}\).

Return to general \(\Bbbk\)-algebras. To discuss the adjunction between \(\ensuremath{\underset{}{\overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes}}}\) and \(\operatorname{RHom}\), one more lemma is needed. Below, \(\operatorname{RHom}_{(A,B)}\) denotes \(\operatorname{RHom}\) in \((A,B)\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\); analogous notation is used for other categories of bimodules (or of left or right modules).

Lemma. Fix \(\Bbbk\)-algebras \(A\), \(B\), and \(R\). Suppose that \(B\) is flat as a \(\Bbbk\)-module. Then the forgetful functor from \((A,B)\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\) to \(A\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\) preserves K-injective complexes, and \(\operatorname{RHom}_A\) has a canonical lift to a functor \[\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}\left((A,R)\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\right)^{\operatorname{op}} \times \ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}\left((A,B)\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\right) \to \ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}\left((R,B)\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\right),\] in other words, there is a canonical \(2\)-cell diagram \[\text{Diagram chapter4-unit-063-d003}\]

Likewise, if \(A\) is flat as a \(\Bbbk\)-module, then \(\operatorname{RHom}_B\) has an analogous lift.

Proof. Because \(B\) is a flat \(\Bbbk\)-module, the functor \(Y\mapsto{}_A Y\) has the exact left adjoint \((\cdot)\ensuremath{\underset{\Bbbk}{\otimes}}B\), and therefore preserves K-injective complexes.

Next take \(X\in\operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}((A,R)\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}))\) and \(Y\in\operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(A,B)\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}})\), with \(Y\) K-injective. By the preceding step, \(\operatorname{Hom}^\bullet\left({}_A X,{}_A Y\right)\) computes \(\operatorname{RHom}_A({}_A X,{}_A Y)\), while at the same time it is a complex of \((R,B)\)-bimodules. This completes the lift.

Theorem (Adjunction between \(\operatorname{RHom}\) and \(\ensuremath{\underset{}{\overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes}}}\)). Let \(A\), \(B\), and \(R\) be \(\Bbbk\)-algebras. Below, \(X\), \(Y\), and \(Z\) denote objects of \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}((A,R)\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}})\), \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}((R,B)\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}})\), and \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}((A,B)\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}})\), respectively. Suppose that \(B\) is flat as a \(\Bbbk\)-module. Then there is a canonical isomorphism in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}(\Bbbk\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}})\) \[\begin{equation*} \operatorname{RHom}_{(A,B)} \left( X \ensuremath{\underset{R}{\overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes}}} Y, Z \right) \ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}\operatorname{RHom}_{(R,B)}\left( Y, \operatorname{RHom}_A \left( {}_A X, {}_A Z \right) \right). \end{equation*}\]

If instead \(A\) is assumed flat as a \(\Bbbk\)-module, there is a canonical isomorphism in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}(\Bbbk\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}})\) \[\begin{equation*} \operatorname{RHom}_{(A,B)}\left( X \ensuremath{\underset{R}{\overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes}}} Y, Z \right) \ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}\operatorname{RHom}_{(A,R)}\left( X, \operatorname{RHom}_B\left( Y_B , Z_B \right) \right). \end{equation*}\]

Proof. Consider the first equality. Suppose that \(Y\) is K-projective and \(Z\) is K-injective. Lemma reference ensures that \({}_R Y\) is K-flat, while Lemma reference ensures that \({}_A Z\) remains K-injective. Every displayed \(\operatorname{RHom}\) and \(\ensuremath{\underset{R}{\overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes}}}\) can therefore be computed at the level of complexes. The desired isomorphism then follows from Proposition reference.

Example (Adjunction for change of rings). In the setting of Example reference (take a homomorphism \(R\to S\) of \(\Bbbk\)-algebras, \(A=S\), \(B=\Bbbk\), and \(X=S\)), the first equality in Theorem reference becomes the canonical isomorphism \[\begin{gather*} \operatorname{RHom}_S\left( \mathrm{L} {}_{R \to S} P(Y), Z \right) \simeq \operatorname{RHom}_R\left( Y, {}_R Z \right), \\ Y \in \operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}(R\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}})), \quad Z \in \operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}(S\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}})). \end{gather*}\] The only point still requiring explanation is \(\operatorname{RHom}_S({}_S S,{}_S Z)\simeq{}_R Z\), which follows immediately from the isomorphism at the level of complexes \[\operatorname{Hom}^\bullet\left({}_S S, \cdot\right) \simeq {}_R (\cdot) : \ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(S\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}) \to \ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(R\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}).\]

If, furthermore, both \(R\) and \(S\) are commutative rings and \(\Bbbk:=R\), then \(\operatorname{RHom}_S\) (respectively, \(\operatorname{RHom}_R\)) takes values in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}(S\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}})\) (respectively, \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}(R\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}})\)). The adjunction isomorphism can then be written as the canonical isomorphism in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}(R\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}})\): \[{}_R \operatorname{RHom}_S\left( \mathrm{L} {}_{R \to S} P(Y), Z \right) \simeq \operatorname{RHom}_R\left( Y, {}_R Z \right) .\] Everything can be verified at the level of complexes by taking K-injective and K-projective resolutions. The case of right modules is similar.

Exercises

Let \((\mathcal{D}, T, \mathcal{H})\) be a pretriangulated category (respectively, a triangulated category). Define a new family of triangles \(\mathcal{H}^-\) by \[[X \xrightarrow{f} Y \xrightarrow{g} Z \xrightarrow{h} TX] \in \mathcal{H} \iff [X \xrightarrow{f} Y \xrightarrow{g} Z \xrightarrow{-h} TX] \in \mathcal{H}^- .\]

  1. Prove that \((\mathcal{D},T,\mathcal{H}^-)\) is also a pretriangulated category (respectively, a triangulated category).

  2. Prove that \((\mathcal{D},T,\mathcal{H})\) and \((\mathcal{D},T,\mathcal{H}^-)\) are equivalent as pretriangulated categories.

Let \((\mathcal{D},T,\mathcal{H})\) be a pretriangulated category. Prove that every monomorphism (respectively, epimorphism) \(u:X\to Y\) in \(\mathcal{D}\) has a left inverse (respectively, a right inverse). Use this to show that a pretriangulated category that is also abelian must be split (Definition reference). Hint. Place the monomorphism \(u\) in a distinguished triangle \(X\xrightarrow{u}Y\xrightarrow{v}Z\xrightarrow{w}TX\). From \(u\circ T^{-1}w=0\), deduce that \(w=0\), and then apply Proposition reference.

Apply the preceding exercise to give an example of an abelian category \(\mathcal{A}\) for which neither \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{A})\) nor \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}(\mathcal{A})\) is an abelian category. Hint. Consider the morphism \(f:\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}/p^2\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\twoheadrightarrow\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}/p\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\) in \(\mathcal{A}=\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ab}}\), where \(p\) is prime. If \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{A})\) were abelian, consider the epi–mono factorizations of \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}f\) and \(\operatorname{H}^0(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}f)\), then express both as projections onto direct summands and inclusion morphisms to obtain a contradiction.

Let \(\mathcal{A}\) be an abelian category. Prove that \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}(\mathcal{A})\) is an abelian category if and only if \(\mathcal{A}\) is split. Hint. For the “only if” direction, embed \(\mathcal{A}\) in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}(\mathcal{A})\) and apply the preceding exercises. For the “if” direction, show that when \(\mathcal{A}\) is split, taking cohomology gives an equivalence from \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}(\mathcal{A})\) to \(\mathcal{A}^{\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}}\).

It is often said that the octahedral axiom (TR5) for a triangulated category replaces the isomorphism theorem \(\dfrac{X/Z}{Y/Z}\simeq X/Y\) in an abelian category, where \(X\supset Y\supset Z\) (Theorem reference (ii)). Explain explicitly what this statement means.

(\(\mathrm{K}_0\) of a pretriangulated category) For every pretriangulated category \((\mathcal{D},T,\mathcal{H})\), define \(\mathrm{K}_0(\mathcal{D})\) to be the quotient of the free \(\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\)-module generated by \(\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{D})\) by the relations \[\text{there is a distinguished triangle}\; X \to Y \to Z \xrightarrow{+1} \implies [X] - [Y] + [Z] = 0,\] where \([X]\in\mathrm{K}_0(\mathcal{D})\) denotes the equivalence class containing \(X\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{D})\).

  1. Prove that \([0]=0\), \([TX]=-[X]\), and \([X\oplus Y]=[X]+[Y]\).

  2. Show that every triangulated functor \(F:\mathcal{D}\to\mathcal{D}'\) induces a canonical homomorphism \(\mathrm{K}_0(\mathcal{D})\to\mathrm{K}_0(\mathcal{D}')\).

  3. Consider a cohomological functor \(H:\mathcal{D}\to\mathcal{A}\), where \(\mathcal{A}\) is an abelian category. Suppose that, for every \(X\), \(|n|\gg_X0\implies H(T^nX)=0\). Define a natural homomorphism \(\mathrm{K}_0(\mathcal{D})\to\mathrm{K}_0(\mathcal{A})\). Hint. Send \([X]\) to \(\sum_n(-1)^n[H(T^nX)]\). Apply Lemma reference (iv).
