  4. Consider the special case \(\mathcal{D}:=\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^{\ensuremath{\mathrm{b}}}(\mathcal{A})\). Give mutually inverse homomorphisms \[\text{Diagram chapter4-unit-063-d004}\] where \(A\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{A})\), also regarded as a complex concentrated in degree \(0\). Hint. One composite is plainly the identity; the other requires truncating the complex.

Let \(X\in\operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}(\mathcal{A}))\). Prove that \[\begin{gather*} X \in \ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^{\leq 0}(\mathcal{A}) \iff \forall Z \in \operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^{\geq 1}(\mathcal{A})), \; \operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}(\mathcal{A})}(X, Z) = 0, \\ X \in \ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^{\geq 0}(\mathcal{A}) \iff \forall Z \in \operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^{\leq -1}(\mathcal{A})), \; \operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}(\mathcal{A})}(Z, X) = 0. \end{gather*}\] Hint. Apply Proposition reference (i), together with the adjoint pairs and distinguished triangle in Proposition reference.

In the setting of Theorem reference, suppose that \(F'\) satisfies \(F'(\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{N}'))\subset\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{N}'')\) (regard this as a kind of “exactness”). If \(\mathcal{D}\) has an \(F\)-injective or an \(F\)-projective subcategory, prove that the canonical morphism \[\mathrm{R}^{\mathcal{N}''}_{\mathcal{N}} (F' F) \to \left( \mathrm{R}^{\mathcal{N}''}_{\mathcal{N}'} F' \right) \left( \mathrm{R}^{\mathcal{N}'}_{\mathcal{N}} F \right)\] or \[\left( \mathrm{L}^{\mathcal{N}''}_{\mathcal{N'}} F' \right) \left( \mathrm{L}^{\mathcal{N}'}_{\mathcal{N}} F \right) \to \mathrm{L}^{\mathcal{N}''}_{\mathcal{N}} (F' F)\] is an isomorphism.

In the setting of Theorem reference, show that the following diagrams of functors and morphisms between them commute (the notation \(\mathcal{N}\) and so forth is suppressed): \[\text{Diagram chapter4-unit-063-d005} \quad \text{Diagram chapter4-unit-063-d006}\]

For \(F=\operatorname{Hom}\), express explicitly the canonical morphism of Proposition reference in the form \(\operatorname{Ext}^{q-p}(X,Y)\to\operatorname{Hom}\left(\operatorname{H}^p(X),\operatorname{H}^q(Y)\right)\).

Reformulate the bijection in Theorem reference as follows. From an \(n\)-extension \(0\to Y\to E^1\to\cdots\to E^n\to X\to0\), construct \(t^{-1}b\in\operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}(\mathcal{A})}(X,Y[n])\) as follows: \[\text{Diagram chapter4-unit-063-d007}\] This gives \(t^{-1}b\in\operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}(\mathcal{A})}(X,Y[n])\). Prove that this bijection differs by the factor \((-1)^n\) from the original bijection based on \(as^{-1}\). In the special case \(n=1\), use the \(t^{-1}b\) version to derive the corresponding version of Proposition reference (the one involving the image of \(\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_Y\)). Hint. Prove that \(ta+(-1)^{n-1}bs:Z\to W\) is canonically null-homotopic. For the second part, note the minus sign in Proposition reference.

Suppose that all objects \(S,T\) in an abelian category \(\mathcal{A}\) satisfy \(\operatorname{Ext}^2_{\mathcal{A}}(S,T)=0\). Prove that every \(X\in\operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^{\ensuremath{\mathrm{b}}}(\mathcal{A}))\) is isomorphic to \(\bigoplus_n\operatorname{H}^n(X)[-n]\). Show that \(\mathcal{A}:=\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\) satisfies this condition. Hint. We may assume that \(X\) is a bounded complex. Begin with \(n\gg0\). Apply Theorem reference and Proposition reference to the \(2\)-extension \(0\to\operatorname{ker}(d^n)\to X^n\xrightarrow{d^n}X^{n+1}\to\operatorname{coker}(d^n)\to0\), then modify \(X\) step by step until \(d^\bullet=0\), throughout up to isomorphism.

Prove that if \(\mathcal{A}\) has enough injective objects, \(F:\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{A}'\) is a left-exact additive functor, and \(\mathrm{R}F\) has finite dimension, then the homomorphism \(\mathrm{K}_0(\mathcal{A})\simeq\mathrm{K}_0(\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^{\ensuremath{\mathrm{b}}}(\mathcal{A})) \to\mathrm{K}_0(\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^{\ensuremath{\mathrm{b}}}(\mathcal{A}'))\simeq \mathrm{K}_0(\mathcal{A}')\) induced by the triangulated functor \(\mathrm{R}F\) is determined by \[[A] \mapsto \sum_n (-1)^n \left[\mathrm{R}^n F(A)\right], \quad A \in \operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{A}).\]

Let \(R\) be a ring. Prove that a filtered direct limit \(\varinjlim\) of K-flat complexes in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(R\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}})\) is again K-flat.

Let \(R\) be a ring. If a complex \(P\) of \(R\)-modules is K-flat and every \(P^n\) is a flat \(R\)-module, then \(P\) is called strongly K-flat.

  1. Prove that for every \(X\in\operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(R\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}))\) there is a strongly K-flat complex \(P\) together with a quasi-isomorphism \(P\to X\). Hint. Use the dual of the argument for the existence of K-injective resolutions; see §reference.

  2. Write \(\mathcal{SF}\) for the full subcategory of \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(R\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}})\) formed by the strongly K-flat complexes. Express \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}(R\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}})\) as the localization of \(\mathcal{SF}\) at the quasi-isomorphisms.

(P. Berthelot, A. Ogus) Let \(f\) be a non-zero-divisor in a commutative ring \(R\). For every \(R\)-module \(M\), write \(M[f]:=\{m\in M:fm=0\}\). A module \(M\) with \(M[f]=0\) is called \(f\)-torsion-free. First show that an \(f\)-torsion-free \(M\) can be embedded as a submodule of \(M[\frac{1}{f}]=M\ensuremath{\underset{R}{\otimes}}R[\frac{1}{f}]\). Thus \(f^mM\) makes sense for every \(m\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\).

Let \(X\) be a complex of \(f\)-torsion-free \(R\)-modules. Using the observation above, define a subcomplex \(\eta_fX\) of \(X^\bullet\ensuremath{\underset{R}{\otimes}}R[\frac{1}{f}]\) by \[(\eta_f X)^n := \left\{ x \in f^n X^n : d_X^n(x) \in f^{n+1} X^{n+1} \right\}, \quad n \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}.\]

  1. Prove that multiplication degree by degree by \(f\) gives an isomorphism \(\eta_f(X[1])\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}(\eta_fX)[1]\).

  2. Show that if \(f,g\in R\) are both non-zero-divisors and every \(X^n\) is \(fg\)-torsion-free, then \(\eta_f\eta_gX=\eta_{fg}X\).

  3. Give a canonical isomorphism \(\operatorname{H}^n(X)/\operatorname{H}^n(X)[f]\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}\operatorname{H}^n(\eta_fX)\); thus the effect of \(\eta_f\) is to correct \(f\)-torsion. Deduce that if \(X\) and \(Y\) are complexes of \(f\)-torsion-free \(R\)-modules and \(\alpha:X\to Y\) is a quasi-isomorphism, then \(\alpha\) induces a quasi-isomorphism \(\eta_f(\alpha):\eta_fX\to\eta_fY\).

  4. Prove that in this way \(\eta_f\) induces an additive functor \(\mathrm{L}\eta_f:\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}(R\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}})\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}(R\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}})\) whose restriction to \(\mathcal{SF}\) from the preceding exercise equals \(\eta_f\).

  5. Show that \(\mathrm{L}\eta_f\) is not a triangulated functor. Thus it is not a left derived functor in the sense of Definition reference, although it remains a right Kan extension. Hint. Take \(R=\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\) and \(f=p\) prime. Verify that \(\mathrm{L}\eta_p(\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}/p\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}})=0\), whereas \(\mathrm{L}\eta_p(\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}/p^2\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}})\simeq\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}/p\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\).

Continuing the preceding exercise, give a canonical morphism \(\mathrm{L}\eta_f X \ensuremath{\underset{R}{\overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes}}} \mathrm{L}\eta_f Y \to \mathrm{L}\eta_f\left( X \ensuremath{\underset{R}{\overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes}}} Y \right)\) and show that this morphism is symmetric in \(X\) and \(Y\) in the appropriate sense. In the language of [Li1], \(\mathrm{L}\eta_f\) is in fact a right-lax monoidal functor with respect to \(\ensuremath{\underset{R}{\overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes}}}\).

  1. The literal term is somewhat misleading, because this property is a natural manifestation of commutativity. Graded-commutative is more appropriate, as in Example reference.↩︎

Spectral Sequences

Spectral sequences are classical algebraic tools that continually find new uses, and their roots in topology run especially deep. Some textbooks and lecture notes even use them as a basic tool of homological algebra to establish some of the fundamental properties in and . Spectral sequences were introduced by J. Leray in the 1940s and gradually assumed their modern form through the work of J.-L. Koszul, H. Cartan, and others. Their chief motivation was the study of the homology groups of fiber bundles. In algebraic terms, the original problem amounts to understanding the homology (or cohomology) of a chain complex (or complex) \(X\). Let us take the case of a complex as our example. Although \(X\) itself may be difficult to grasp, it can be studied through a suitable filtration \(\cdots\supset\mathrm{F}^pX\supset\mathrm{F}^{p+1}X\supset\cdots\). The filtration \(\mathrm{F}^\bullet X\) induces a filtration on every \(\operatorname{H}^n(X)\). Information about \(\mathrm{F}^\bullet X\) and its subquotients can then be used to approximate, step by step, each subquotient \(\operatorname{gr}^p\operatorname{H}^n(X)\) of the filtered cohomology. Spectral sequences are the art of organizing such successive approximations. A complex may also be generalized to a differential object \((X,d)\) in an abelian category (Definition reference), leading to the abstract definition of a spectral sequence in Definition reference. A spectral sequence is a sequence of differential objects \(\mathscr{E}=(E_r,d_r)_r\) such that the cohomology of each “page,” \(\operatorname{H}(E_r,d_r)\), is the next page \(E_{r+1}\). Adding a grading and allowing the differential \(d\) to have a degree gives the notions of graded spectral sequences \(E_r^p\) and bigraded spectral sequences \(E_r^{p,q}\) (Definition reference). Concretely, the differentials in a bigraded spectral sequence have the form \[\begin{gather*} d_r^{p, q}: E_r^{p, q} \to E_r^{p+r, q-r+1}, \\ E_r = (E_r^{p, q})_{(p, q) \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}^2}, \quad d_r = (d_r^{p, q})_{(p, q) \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}^2}. \end{gather*}\] A filtered complex gives a filtered differential object and hence naturally produces a bigraded spectral sequence. This is the form of spectral sequence that occurs most often in applications. Every notion has a corresponding version for chain complexes and their homology. This chapter begins with W. Massey’s theory of exact couples. Exact couples are another device for producing spectral sequences, and their scope is wider than that of filtered differential objects. After introducing filtrations and graded structures in §reference, we give the general definition of a spectral sequence in §reference, together with its graded and bigraded versions and such basic terminology as degeneration, boundedness, and the limiting page. At the end of that section, Remark reference explains how to read exact sequences from the edges of a spectral sequence, an important technique. Exact couples are defined in §reference. Next, §reference explains how an exact couple produces a graded spectral sequence from a filtered differential object, and §reference goes on to explain how a filtered complex produces a bigraded spectral sequence. That section also treats the central notion of convergence and the Classical Convergence Theorem reference. Some of the verifications are slightly technical, but there is no fundamental difficulty. Readers may first work in a concrete abelian category such as \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ab}}\) to simplify the arguments. A double complex gives rise to a filtered complex in two ways, according as the total complex is filtered by the horizontal or the vertical coordinate. The corresponding spectral sequences are denoted by \(\mathscr{E}_{\mathrm{I}}\) and \(\mathscr{E}_{\mathrm{II}}\), respectively. Their details are the subject of §reference. We also give standard applications, including the derivation of balanced bifunctors (Example reference), the spectral sequence of hyperderived functors (Example reference), and the Grothendieck spectral sequence (Theorem reference). The Cartan–Eilenberg resolutions introduced earlier (Theorem reference) play a role here. The Grothendieck spectral sequence concerns the derivation of a composite of functors and is particularly common in geometry. As an example involving right derived functors, consider left-exact additive functors between abelian categories \(\mathcal{A}\xrightarrow{F}\mathcal{A}'\xrightarrow{F'}\mathcal{A}''\), where \(\mathcal{A}\) and \(\mathcal{A}'\) have enough injective objects. If \(F\) sends injective objects to \(F'\)-acyclic objects (Convention reference), there is a canonical strongly convergent bigraded spectral sequence \[E_2^{p, q} = (\mathrm{R}^p F') (\mathrm{R}^q F)(X) \Rightarrow \mathrm{R}^{p+q}(F' F)(X), \quad X \in \operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{A}).\] The derivation of composite functors can also be handled at the level of derived categories; see Theorem reference. Besides being formally elementary and easy to compute, the spectral-sequence version can provide additional information in concrete situations, such as exact sequences in low degrees. The final section of the chapter, §reference, briefly introduces multiplicative structures on spectral sequences. This aspect has received attention since the earliest history of spectral sequences. Proposition reference shows that a filtered differential graded algebra gives rise to a spectral sequence with a canonical multiplicative structure; a deeper treatment is left to specialized monographs. As an exercise in applications, the Lyndon–Hochschild–Serre spectral sequence, which is fundamental in group cohomology, can be obtained both as an application of the Grothendieck spectral sequence and concretely from a filtered complex. The latter approach also equips it with a canonical multiplicative structure. This topic will be discussed in §reference in the future.

Filtrations and Graded Structures

We encountered graded objects in Definition reference. A \(\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\)-graded object in an arbitrary category \(\mathcal{A}\) is simply called a graded object; by definition, these are the objects \((X^p)_{p\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}}\) of \(\mathcal{A}^{\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}}\). A \(\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}^2\)-graded object is simply called a bigraded object; by definition, these are the objects \((X^{p,q})_{(p,q)\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}^2}\) of \(\mathcal{A}^{\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\times\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}}\). Morphisms between graded (or bigraded) objects are written as \((f^p)_p\) (or \((f^{p,q})_{p,q}\)), as usual, and are composed degree by degree. If \(\mathcal{A}\) is an abelian category, then \(\mathcal{A}^{\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}}\) and \(\mathcal{A}^{\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\times\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}}\) are also abelian categories; kernels, cokernels, and all other operations are computed degree by degree. The category \(\mathcal{A}^{\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}}\) has a shift autoequivalence \(T\) determined by \((TX)^p=X^{p+1}\) and \((Tf)^p=f^{p+1}\). More generally, \(\mathcal{A}^{\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}^n}\) has a family of shift autoequivalences \(T_1,\ldots,T_n\) corresponding to shifts along the \(n\) coordinates. These shifts commute strictly: \(T_iT_j=T_jT_i\). Within the framework of this chapter, graded structures arise primarily from filtrations.

Definition. Let \(X\) be an object of an additive category \(\mathcal{A}\).

  • A decreasing filtration \(\mathrm{F}^\bullet X\) is a sequence of subobjects \[\cdots \supset \mathrm{F}^p X \supset \mathrm{F}^{p+1} X \supset \cdots \quad (p \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}).\]

  • If there exist \(a\leq b\) such that \(\mathrm{F}^aX=X\) and \(\mathrm{F}^bX=0\), the filtration is called finite.

  • Increasing filtrations \(\mathrm{F}_\bullet X\) and their finiteness are defined similarly.

Decreasing and increasing filtrations can be distinguished by the position of the index \(p\). When no confusion is likely, both are simply called filtrations. Decreasing filtrations are customary in the study of complexes and cohomology, whereas increasing filtrations are customary for chain complexes and homology. This chapter mainly uses decreasing filtrations. All filtered objects \((X,\mathrm{F}^\bullet X)\) form a category \(\mathrm{Fil}^\bullet(\mathcal{A})\). A morphism \(f:(X,\mathrm{F}^\bullet X)\to(Y,\mathrm{F}^\bullet Y)\) is a morphism \(f:X\to Y\) that preserves the filtrations; that is, for every \(p\), it restricts to a morphism \(\mathrm{F}^pX\to\mathrm{F}^pY\). The category \(\mathrm{Fil}_\bullet(\mathcal{A})\) is defined similarly. For every \(X\), a decreasing filtration \(\mathrm{F}^\bullet X\) (or increasing filtration \(\mathrm{F}_\bullet X\)) gives a graded object \((\mathrm{F}^pX)_{p\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}}\) (or \((\mathrm{F}_pX)_{p\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}}\)). This defines a functor \(\mathrm{Fil}^\bullet(\mathcal{A})\to\mathcal{A}^{\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}}\) (or \(\mathrm{Fil}_\bullet(\mathcal{A})\to\mathcal{A}^{\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}}\)), called the Rees construction. If \(\mathcal{A}\) is an abelian category, there is another way to construct a graded object from a filtration.

Definition. Let \(\mathcal{A}\) be an abelian category, and consider a filtration \(\mathrm{F}^\bullet X\) (or \(\mathrm{F}_\bullet X\)) on an object \(X\). Define the graded object \(\operatorname{gr}X\) by \[\operatorname{gr}^p X := \mathrm{F}^p X / \mathrm{F}^{p+1} X \quad (\text{or} \quad \operatorname{gr}_p X := \mathrm{F}_p X / \mathrm{F}_{p-1} X).\] This defines a functor \(\operatorname{gr}:\mathrm{Fil}^\bullet(\mathcal{A})\to\mathcal{A}^{\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}}\) (or \(\operatorname{gr}:\mathrm{Fil}_\bullet(\mathcal{A})\to\mathcal{A}^{\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}}\)).

To extract information about \(X\) from \((\operatorname{gr}^pX)_p\), we need at least \(\bigcup_p\mathrm{F}^pX=X\) and \(\bigcap_p\mathrm{F}^pX=0\), using the notation of Convention reference. To make the first condition meaningful and useful, we also want \(\varinjlim_{p\to-\infty}\) to be exact in \(\mathcal{A}\), or else we may simply require that there be an \(M\) such that \(\mathrm{F}^MX=X\). We begin with some related notions.

Definition. Let \(\mathcal{A}\) be an abelian category and let \(X\) be an object with a filtration \(\mathrm{F}^\bullet X\).

  • If \(\bigcap_p\mathrm{F}^pX=0\), the filtration is called separated.

  • If \(\bigcup_p\mathrm{F}^pX=X\) and either of the following conditions holds, the filtration is called exhaustive:

    1. \(\mathcal{A}\) has exact countable filtered direct limits \(\varinjlim\); more precisely, \(\varinjlim:\mathcal{A}^{(\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}_{\geq0},\leq)}\to\mathcal{A}\) exists and is exact1;

    2. there is an \(M\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\) such that \(\mathrm{F}^MX=X\).

  • If the family of canonical morphisms \(X\twoheadrightarrow X/\mathrm{F}^pX\) induces an isomorphism \(X\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}\varprojlim_pX/\mathrm{F}^pX\), the filtration is called complete.

Increasing filtrations \(\mathrm{F}_\bullet X\) are treated in the same way.

The notion of completeness is inspired by the case of topological groups; see [Li1]. A finite filtration is automatically separated, exhaustive, and complete; this is the principal case needed in this chapter. Observe that if there is an \(N\) such that \(\mathrm{F}^NX=0\), then \(\mathrm{F}^\bullet X\) is separated and complete. Moreover, since the kernel of \(X\to\varprojlim_pX/\mathrm{F}^pX\) is \(\bigcap_p\mathrm{F}^pX\), completeness implies separatedness. The image of an exhaustive filtration is still exhaustive; this follows by interpreting \(\bigcup_p\) as \(\sum_p\) and then applying Lemma reference (ii). Moreover, an exhaustive filtration satisfies \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:exhaustion-intersection}{}\begin{gathered} \varinjlim_{p \to -\infty} \mathrm{F}^p X \ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}\bigcup_p \mathrm{F}^p X = X, \\ K = K \cap \left( \bigcup_p \mathrm{F}^p X \right) = \bigcup_p \left( K \cap \mathrm{F}^p X \right), \end{gathered} \end{equation}\] where \(K\) is any subobject of \(X\). Under condition (a) for an exhaustive filtration, these assertions follow readily from Proposition reference; under condition (b), they are immediate.

Proposition. Let \(\mathcal{A}\) be an abelian category, and let \(f:(X,\mathrm{F}^\bullet X)\to(Y,\mathrm{F}^\bullet Y)\) be a morphism in \(\mathrm{Fil}^\bullet(\mathcal{A})\).

  1. Suppose that \(\mathrm{F}^\bullet X\) is separated and exhaustive. If \(\operatorname{gr}(f)\) is a monomorphism, then \(f\) is a monomorphism.

  2. Suppose that \(\mathrm{F}^\bullet X\) is complete and exhaustive, while \(\mathrm{F}^\bullet Y\) is separated and exhaustive. If \(\operatorname{gr}(f)\) is an isomorphism, then \(f\) is also an isomorphism, and in this case \(\mathrm{F}^\bullet Y\) is complete as well.

The corresponding statements hold for increasing filtrations.

Proof. For each \(p\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\), consider the following commutative diagram with exact rows: \[\text{Diagram chapter5-unit-064-d001}\] Write \(K^p\) and \(C^p\) for the kernel and cokernel of \(\mathrm{F}^pX\xrightarrow{f}\mathrm{F}^pY\).

For (i), apply Theorem reference to the diagram above. This gives \(K^{p+1}=K^p\). In particular, \(K^p\subset\bigcap_{\ell\geq p}\mathrm{F}^\ell X=0\), so the restriction of \(f\) to every \(\mathrm{F}^pX\) is a monomorphism. To prove that \(f\) itself is a monomorphism, it remains only to use \[\operatorname{ker}(f) \xlongequal{\because\; \text{\href{#eqn:exhaustion-intersection}{equation}}} \bigcup_p \left( \operatorname{ker}(f) \cap \mathrm{F}^p X \right) = 0.\]

For (ii), the diagram gives both \(K^{p+1}=K^p\) and \(C^{p+1}\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}C^p\). For each \(\ell>p\), consider the commutative diagram with exact rows \[\text{Diagram chapter5-unit-064-d002}\] Another application of Theorem reference gives the isomorphism induced by \(f\) \[\mathrm{F}^p X / \mathrm{F}^\ell X \ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}\mathrm{F}^p Y / \mathrm{F}^\ell Y.\]

Taking \(\varinjlim_{p:p<\ell}\) on both sides and using equation gives \(X/\mathrm{F}^\ell X\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}Y/\mathrm{F}^\ell Y\). Taking \(\varprojlim_\ell\) now gives the commutative diagram \[\text{Diagram chapter5-unit-064-d003}\] It follows that both \(f\) and \(Y\to\varprojlim_\ell Y/\mathrm{F}^\ell Y\) are isomorphisms.

  1. If \(\mathcal{A}\) is a Grothendieck category, then (a) holds automatically.↩︎

General definition of spectral sequences

We begin with the general definition of a differential object. This involves an additive category with translation \((\mathcal{A},T)\) as in Definition reference, as well as morphisms with degree as in Definition reference.

Definition. A differential object over an additive category with translation \((\mathcal{A},T)\) is data \((X,d)\), where \(X\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{A})\) and \(d:X\xrightarrow{+1}X\) satisfies \(d^2=0\).

  • A morphism from \((X,d)\) to \((X',d')\) is a morphism \(\alpha:X\to X'\) satisfying \(d'\alpha=\alpha d\).

  • All differential objects form a category \((\mathcal{A},T)_d\); we also write \(\mathcal{A}_d:=(\mathcal{A},\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{\mathcal{A}})_d\).

If \(\mathcal{A}\) is an \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ab}}\)-category (or a \(\Bbbk\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\)-category, where \(\Bbbk\) is a commutative ring), then so is \((\mathcal{A},T)_d\). The forgetful functor \((\mathcal{A},T)_d\to\mathcal{A}\) sends \((X,d)\) to \(X\).

Proposition. The forgetful functor \((\mathcal{A},T)_d\to\mathcal{A}\) creates all \(\varinjlim\) and \(\varprojlim\) (Definition reference).

Proof. Replay the proof of Lemma reference.

It follows that if \(\mathcal{A}\) is an Abelian category, then \((\mathcal{A},T)_d\) is also Abelian and \((\mathcal{A},T)_d\to\mathcal{A}\) is exact. In the case of an Abelian category, one distinguishing feature of a differential object is that it has homology or cohomology.

Definition. Let \(\mathcal{A}\) be an Abelian category. We define the additive functor \[\operatorname{H}:(\mathcal{A},T)_d\to\mathcal{A},\qquad \operatorname{H}(X,d):=\operatorname{ker}(d)/\operatorname{im}(T^{-1}d).\]

We call a triangular diagram in an Abelian category \(\mathcal{A}\) \(\text{Diagram chapter5-unit-065-diagram-001}\) exact if \[\cdots T^{k-m}C\to T^kA\to T^kB\to T^kC\to T^{k+m}A\cdots\] is an exact sequence extending infinitely in both directions. More general triangular diagrams with degrees are treated in the same way.

Lemma. Let \((\mathcal{A},T)\) be an Abelian category with translation. If \(0\to(X',d')\to(X,d)\to(X'',d'')\to0\) is a short exact sequence in \((\mathcal{A},T)_d\), then the following diagram is exact at every vertex: \[\text{Diagram chapter5-unit-065-d001}\]

Proof. In \(\mathcal{A}\), consider the sequence of complexes \[0\to(T^nX',T^nd')_n\to(T^nX,T^nd)_n \to(T^nX'',T^nd'')_n\to0.\] It is exact degree by degree, hence is a short exact sequence. Apply Proposition reference to it.

Example (Complexes as differential objects). For an additive category \(\mathcal{A}\), consider \(\mathcal{A}^{\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}}\) together with the translation functor \(T:(X^n)_n\mapsto(X^{n+1})_n\). By the discussion in §reference, objects of \((\mathcal{A}^{\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}},T)_d\) are also called differential graded objects, and there is an isomorphism of categories \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})\simeq(\mathcal{A}^{\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}},T)_d\). If \(\mathcal{A}\) is Abelian, then plainly \[\operatorname{H}(X,d)=\left(\operatorname{H}^p(X)\right)_{p\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}}.\]

We can now give the definition of a spectral sequence. To simplify the discussion, we first consider the case without translation, or equivalently the case of morphisms without degree; in other words, we take \(T=\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}\).

Definition (J. Leray, J.-L. Koszul). Let \(\mathcal{A}\) be an Abelian category and \(a\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\). A spectral sequence starting at \(a\) is data \(\mathscr{E}=(E_r,d_r)_{r\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}_{\geq a}}\) together with \((t_r)_{r\geq a+1}\), where

  • \((E_r,d_r)\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{A}_d)\);

  • \(t_r:\operatorname{H}(E_{r-1},d_{r-1})\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}E_r\) for \(r\geq a+1\).

The data \(a\) and \((t_r)_r\) are often omitted from the notation.

A morphism of spectral sequences \(\mathscr{E}\to\mathscr{E}'\) is a family of morphisms in \(\mathcal{A}_d\) \(\varphi_r:(E_r,d_r)\to(E'_r,d'_r)\) satisfying \(t_r\operatorname{H}(\varphi_{r-1})=\varphi_rt_r\) for \(r\geq a+1\).

The pair \((E_r,d_r)\) is customarily called the \(r\)-th page of the spectral sequence \(\mathscr{E}\); computing \(E_{r+1}\) from \(E_r\) amounts to turning the page. Abstractly, the precise page at which a spectral sequence starts is immaterial, but in applications it depends on the particular context. If \(d_r\) in a spectral sequence is viewed as a morphism \(\operatorname{H}(E_{r-1},d_{r-1})\to\operatorname{H}(E_{r-1},d_{r-1})\), then both \(\operatorname{ker}(d_r)\) and \(\operatorname{im}(d_r)\) correspond to subobjects of \(\operatorname{ker}(d_{r-1})\) that contain \(\operatorname{im}(d_{r-1})\). For simplicity, suppose the spectral sequence starts at \(a=0\). Define \(Z_1\) (respectively \(B_1\)) to be \(\operatorname{ker}(d_0)\) (respectively \(\operatorname{im}(d_0)\)), then define \(Z_2\) (respectively \(B_2\)) as the inverse image of \(\operatorname{ker}(d_1)\) (respectively \(\operatorname{im}(d_1)\)) under \(E_0\supset Z_1\twoheadrightarrow E_1\), and so on. Iteration yields \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:spectral-sequence-Z-B}{}\begin{gathered} 0=:B_0\subset B_1\subset B_2\subset\cdots\subset Z_2\subset Z_1 \subset Z_0=:E_0, \\ Z_r\leftrightarrow\operatorname{ker}(d_{r-1}),\quad B_r\leftrightarrow\operatorname{im}(d_{r-1}),\quad Z_r/B_r\simeq E_r. \end{gathered} \end{equation}\]

  • If \(Z_\infty:=\bigcap_rZ_r\) and \(B_\infty:=\bigcup_rB_r\) exist, the limit of the spectral sequence \(\mathscr{E}\) is defined to be \(E_\infty:=Z_\infty/B_\infty\).

  • If there is an \(r\) such that \(r'\geq r\implies d_{r'}=0\), then \(\mathscr{E}\) is said to degenerate at the \(E_r\) page. In this case clearly \(Z_r=Z_{r+1}=\cdots\) and \(B_r=B_{r+1}=\cdots\), so \(Z_r=Z_\infty\) and \(B_r=B_\infty\); consequently, \(E_r=E_\infty\).

When discussing homologically graded spectral sequences, we shall instead use the notation \((E^r,d^r)_r\) and \(B^r,Z^r\).

Proposition. Let \(\varphi_r:\mathscr{E}\to\mathscr{E}'\) be a morphism of spectral sequences. If \(\varphi_r\) is an isomorphism, then \(\varphi_s\) is also an isomorphism for \(s\geq r\); if the limits exist, then \(\varphi_\infty:E_\infty\to E'_\infty\) is also an isomorphism.

Proof. The isomorphism \(\varphi_r\) induces an isomorphism \(\operatorname{H}(E_r,d_r)\to\operatorname{H}(E'_r,d'_r)\), which is precisely \(\varphi_{r+1}\). Without loss of generality, suppose that the spectral sequences start at \(r\). Then \((\varphi_s)_{s\geq r}\) is an isomorphism of spectral sequences, and the assertion concerning \(\varphi_\infty\) is immediate.

More generally, for an Abelian category with translation \((\mathcal{A},T)\), the definition of a spectral sequence extends to the case \((E_r,d_r)\in\operatorname{Ob}((\mathcal{A},T^{a_r})_d)\), where \(a_1,a_2,\ldots\) is a sequence of integers. The definitions of \(\operatorname{H}(E_r,d_r)\) and \(B_r,Z_r\) above remain unchanged. In the generalization we shall need later, we may go even further and equip \(\mathcal{A}\) with a family of mutually commuting automorphisms \(T_1,\ldots,T_n\), with \[d_r:E_r\xrightarrow{+\vec{a}_r}E_r,\qquad \vec{a}_r=(a_{r,1},\ldots,a_{r,n})\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}^n.\] Following this idea, we introduce the two most commonly used versions, both of which involve graded structures.

Definition (Spectral sequences: graded and bigraded versions). Let \(\mathcal{A}\) be an Abelian category. Cohomologically graded and cohomologically bigraded spectral sequences, both written \(\mathscr{E}=(E_r,d_r)_r\), are defined as follows. \[\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|} \hline \text{Version} & E_r & d_r & \text{Degree of morphism} \\ \hline \text{Graded} & (E_r^p)_{p\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}}\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{A}^{\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}}) & (d_r^p)_p & d_r^p:E_r^p\xrightarrow{+r}E_r^{p+r} \\ \text{Bigraded} & (E_r^{p,q})_{(p,q)\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}^2}\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{A}^{\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\times\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}}) & (d_r^{p,q})_{(p,q)} & d_r^{p,q}:E_r^{p,q}\xrightarrow{+(r,-r+1)}E_r^{p+r,q-r+1} \\ \hline \end{array}\] In both cases \((d_r)^2=0\) is required, with composition understood as the composition of morphisms with degrees, and the data include a specified isomorphism \(\operatorname{H}(E_{r-1},d_{r-1})\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}E_r\).

Dually, a homologically graded (or bigraded) spectral sequence is defined as the following data \((E^r,d^r)_{r\geq1}\), again with \((d^r)^2=0\) and a specified isomorphism \(\operatorname{H}(E^r,d^r)\simeq E^{r+1}\): \[\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|} \hline \text{Version} & E^r & d^r & \text{Degree of morphism} \\ \hline \text{Graded} & (E^r_p)_{p\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}}\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{A}^{\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}}) & (d^r_p)_p & d^r_p:E^r_p\xrightarrow{-r}E^r_{p-r} \\ \text{Bigraded} & (E^r_{p,q})_{(p,q)\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}^2}\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{A}^{\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\times\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}}) & (d^r_{p,q})_{(p,q)} & d^r_{p,q}:E^r_{p,q}\xrightarrow{+(-r,r-1)}E^r_{p-r,q+r-1} \\ \hline \end{array}\] Morphisms between these spectral sequences are defined in the usual way and must be compatible with the specified isomorphisms.

In \((p,q)\) coordinates, the directions of \(d_r\) and \(d^r\) in a bigraded spectral sequence are as follows.

Diagram chapter5-unit-065-d002

Diagram chapter5-unit-065-d003

In either version, following the preceding pattern, we may define the objects \(B_r^p\subset Z_r^p\), \(B_r^{p,q}\subset Z_r^{p,q}\), \(E_\infty^p\), \(E_\infty^{p,q}\), as well as \(B^r_p\subset Z^r_p\), \(B^r_{p,q}\subset Z^r_{p,q}\), \(E^\infty_p\), \(E^\infty_{p,q}\), and so forth.

Example (The finite-width case). In many common situations, the nonzero terms of a bigraded spectral sequence are concentrated in a horizontal (or vertical) strip of width \(s\), where \(s\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}_{\geq0}\), as in the following figure: \[\par\textbf{Diagram chapter5-unit-065-d004}\par \quad \text{or} \quad \par\textbf{Diagram chapter5-unit-065-d005}\par\] Inspection of the arrow directions shows that \(r>s\) (or \(r\geq s\)) implies \(d_r^{p,q}=0\) for all \(p,q\); in this case the spectral sequence degenerates at the \(E_r\) page. The homological case is similar.

Definition. Let \(\mathscr{E}\) be a cohomological (or homological) bigraded spectral sequence, and let \(r\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\). If for every \(n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\) there are at most finitely many \((p,q)\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}^2\) satisfying \(p+q=n\) and \(E_r^{p,q}\neq0\) (or \(E^r_{p,q}\neq0\)), then \(E_r\) (or \(E^r\)) is called bounded.

It follows from \(E_{r+1}\simeq\operatorname{H}(E_r,d_r)\) that \(E_r^{p,q}=0\implies E_{r+1}^{p,q}=0\). In particular, if \(E_r\) is bounded, then \(E_{r+1}\) is bounded. The homological case is similar.

Proposition. Let \(\mathscr{E}\) be a cohomological (or homological) bigraded spectral sequence for which \(E_r\) (or \(E^r\)) is bounded. For every \((p,q)\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}^2\), there is an \(r(p,q)\) such that, whenever \(r\geq r(p,q)\), one has \(E_r^{p,q}=E_{r+1}^{p,q}\) (or \(E^r_{p,q}=E^{r+1}_{p,q}\)). Consequently, the limit of \(\mathscr{E}\) exists and satisfies \(E_r^{p,q}=E_\infty^{p,q}\) (or \(E^r_{p,q}=E^\infty_{p,q}\)).

Proof. It suffices to discuss the case of \(E_r\). Fix \(n\). By boundedness, for all \((p,q)\) with \(p+q=n\) and all sufficiently large \(r\), we have \(E_r^{p-r,q+r-1}=0\), hence \(B_r^{p,q}=0\). Similarly, for sufficiently large \(r\), we have \(E_r^{p+r,q-r+1}=0\), hence \(Z_r^{p,q}=E_r^{p,q}\). This proves the assertion.

Definition. Let \(\mathscr{E}\) be a cohomological (or homological) bigraded spectral sequence, and let \(r\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\). If \(E_r^{p,q}\neq0\) (or \(E^r_{p,q}\neq0\)) implies \(p,q\geq0\), then \(E_r\) (or \(E^r\)) is said to lie in the first quadrant. The other quadrants are defined similarly.

An \(E_r\) lying in the first or third quadrant is clearly bounded. It follows from \(E_{r+1}\simeq\operatorname{H}(E_r,d_r)\) that if \(E_r\) lies in any given quadrant, then \(E_{r+1}\) lies in the same quadrant. The homological case is similar.

Remark (Edge calculations). Spectral sequences lying in the first quadrant occur especially often. For the cohomological version, the edge terms \(E_r^{\bullet,0}\) and \(E_r^{0,\bullet}\) have special properties. Fix \(p,q\geq1\). By carefully examining the direction of \(d_r\) and recalling that \(E_{r+1}\simeq\operatorname{H}(E_r,d_r)\), one verifies that \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:edge-ss-coh}{}\begin{array}{cc} E_2^{p,0}\twoheadrightarrow E_3^{p,0}\twoheadrightarrow\cdots \twoheadrightarrow E_{p+1}^{p,0}=E_\infty^{p,0} & \text{($\because$ all outgoing $d$ are $0$)}, \\ E_\infty^{0,q}=E_{q+2}^{0,q}\hookrightarrow E_{q+1}^{0,q} \hookrightarrow\cdots\hookrightarrow E_2^{0,q}\hookrightarrow E_1^{0,q} & \text{($\because$ all incoming $d$ are $0$)}. \end{array} \end{equation}\] A first-quadrant homological bigraded spectral sequence has the corresponding properties: \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:edge-ss-ho}{}\begin{array}{cc} E^\infty_{p,0}=E^{p+1}_{p,0}\hookrightarrow E^p_{p,0} \hookrightarrow\cdots\hookrightarrow E^3_{p,0}\hookrightarrow E^2_{p,0} & \text{($\because$ all incoming $d$ are $0$)}, \\ E^1_{0,q}\twoheadrightarrow E^2_{0,q}\twoheadrightarrow\cdots \twoheadrightarrow E^{q+2}_{0,q}=E^\infty_{0,q} & \text{($\because$ all outgoing $d$ are $0$)}. \end{array} \end{equation}\]

The morphisms arising from equation or equation are collectively called edge morphisms. The preceding discussion gives the following exact sequence (\(p\geq2\)): \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:low-exact-coh}{} 0\to E^{0,p-1}_\infty\to E^{0,p-1}_p\xrightarrow{d}E^{p,0}_p \to E^{p,0}_\infty\to0, \end{equation}\] in which every morphism except \(d\) is an edge morphism. There is also a homological version of this exact sequence (\(p\geq2\)): \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:low-exact-ho}{} 0\to E^\infty_{p,0}\to E^p_{p,0}\xrightarrow{d}E^p_{0,p-1} \to E^\infty_{0,p-1}\to0. \end{equation}\] Beginning readers should be sure to draw the directions of the morphisms \(d\) involving these terms, determine when they are \(0\), and thereby verify all the assertions above.

Exact couples

Several commonly used kinds of spectral sequence arise from exact couples, a discovery due to W. Massey. To grasp the essential idea, we first return to the case without degrees.

Definition (Exact couple). An exact couple over an Abelian category \(\mathcal{A}\) is an exact diagram in \(\mathcal{A}\) \[\text{Diagram chapter5-unit-066-d001}\] Morphisms between data \(\mathscr{C}:=(D,E,i,j,k)\) are defined in the evident way.

Given an exact couple \(\mathscr{C}=(D,E,i,j,k)\), set \(d:=jk:E\to E\). Then \(dj=jkj=0\) and \(kd=kjk=0\), whence \(d^2=0\). The exactness conditions readily give the following factorizations: \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:exact-couple-aux}{} \text{Diagram chapter5-unit-066-d002} \quad \text{Diagram chapter5-unit-066-d003} \end{equation}\] Also define \(E':=\operatorname{H}(E,d)\), \(D':=i(D)\), and \(i':=i|_{i(D)}:D'\to D'\).

Lemma. Given an exact couple \(\mathscr{C}=(D,E,i,j,k)\), the data constructed above, \[\mathscr{C}'=(D',E',i',j',k'):\quad \text{Diagram chapter5-unit-066-d004}\] also form an exact couple.

Proof. Examining equation and using the exactness conditions, one readily verifies that \[\begin{align*} \operatorname{ker}(i') &= i(D)\cap\operatorname{ker}(i)=\operatorname{ker}(j)\cap k(E) \\ &=\operatorname{im}\left[\operatorname{ker}(d)\xrightarrow{k}i(D)\right]=\operatorname{im}(k'), \\ \operatorname{ker}(j') &= i\left(j^{-1}(jk(E))\right) \\ &=i\left(k(E)+\operatorname{ker}(j)\right)=i\left(i(D)\right)=\operatorname{im}(i'), \\ \operatorname{ker}(k') &= (\operatorname{ker}(k)\cap\operatorname{ker}(d))/\operatorname{im}(d) =(j(D)\cap\operatorname{ker}(jk))/\operatorname{im}(d) \\ &=j(D)/\operatorname{im}(d)=\operatorname{im}(j'). \end{align*}\] Thus the new triangular diagram is still exact.

Iterating this procedure gives a sequence of exact couples \((\mathscr{C}_{(r)})_{r\geq1}\), with \(\mathscr{C}_{(1)}=\mathscr{C}\) and \(\mathscr{C}_{(r+1)}=\mathscr{C}_{(r)}'\) for \(r\geq1\). Writing \(\mathscr{C}_{(r)}=(D_r,E_r,i_r,j_r,k_r)\), the sequence \((E_r,d_r:=j_rk_r)_{r\geq1}\) is a spectral sequence.

Lemma. For the spectral sequence \((E_r,d_r)_{r\geq1}\) obtained from an exact couple \(\mathscr{C}=(D,E,i,j,k)\), define the family of subobjects \(\overline{B}_r\subset\overline{Z}_r\) of \(E=E_1\) according to equation. Bars are used because the indexing starts at \(r=1\); see Proposition reference below. For \(r\geq0\), \[\begin{gather*} \overline{B}_{r+1}=j\left(\operatorname{ker}(i^r)\right) \subset k^{-1}\left(\operatorname{im}(i^r)\right)=\overline{Z}_{r+1}; \\ \overline{B}_\infty=j\left(\bigcup_{r\geq2}\operatorname{ker}(i^r)\right) \subset k^{-1}\left(\bigcap_{r\geq2}\operatorname{im}(i^r)\right) =\overline{Z}_\infty, \end{gather*}\] provided that the relevant \(\bigcup_r\) and \(\bigcap_r\) exist. More precisely, the exact couple \(\mathscr{C}_{(r+1)}\) is canonically isomorphic to \[\text{Diagram chapter5-unit-066-d005}\] where \(\overline{k}_{r+1}\) is induced by \(k:E\to D\), while \(\overline{j}_{r+1}\) is characterized by the commutative diagram \[\text{Diagram chapter5-unit-066-d006}\]

Proof. The description of the exact couple \(\mathscr{C}_{(r+1)}\) can be proved recursively. The case \(r=0\) is trivial (\(i^0=\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}\)), and the descriptions of \(\overline{B}_{r+1}\) and \(\overline{Z}_{r+1}\) are immediate consequences. Since the details are somewhat routine, they are omitted. The assertion \(\overline{B}_\infty\subset\overline{Z}_\infty\) follows from Lemma reference (ii).

We next explain how to construct an exact couple from a differential object.

Proposition. Let \(\alpha:(D,d)\to(D,d)\) be a monomorphism in \(\mathcal{A}_d\), and write \(d_\alpha\) for the morphism induced by \(d\) on \(\operatorname{coker}(\alpha)\). Then there is an exact couple \[\text{Diagram chapter5-unit-066-d007}\] Take the inverse images of \(\overline{B}_{r+1}\subset\overline{Z}_{r+1}\) in \(E_0:=\operatorname{coker}(\alpha)\), and denote them by \[0=:B_0\subset B_1\subset B_2\subset\cdots\subset Z_2\subset Z_1 \subset Z_0:=\operatorname{coker}(\alpha).\] For every \(r\geq0\):

  • \(B_{r+1}\) is the image of \((\alpha^r)^{-1}(dD)\subset D\) in \(\operatorname{coker}(\alpha)\);

  • \(Z_{r+1}\) is the image of \(d^{-1}(\alpha^{r+1}D)\subset D\) in \(\operatorname{coker}(\alpha)\);

  • \(d_{r+1}\in\operatorname{End}(Z_{r+1}/B_{r+1})\) is induced by \(d^{-1}(\alpha^{r+1}D)\xrightarrow{d}\alpha^{r+1}D \xleftarrow[\sim]{\alpha^{r+1}}D\).

In particular, there are canonical isomorphisms \[E_{r+1}\simeq\dfrac{Z_{r+1}}{B_{r+1}} \simeq\dfrac{d^{-1}(\alpha^{r+1}D)+\alpha D} {(\alpha^r)^{-1}(dD)+\alpha D},\qquad r\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}_{\geq1}.\]

Proof. The exact couple is obtained by applying Lemma reference (with \(T=\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{\mathcal{A}}\)) to the short exact sequence in \(\mathcal{A}_d\) \[0\to(D,d)\xrightarrow{\alpha}(D,d) \to(\operatorname{coker}(\alpha),d_\alpha)\to0.\] In particular, \(j\) is induced by \(D\twoheadrightarrow\operatorname{coker}(\alpha)\), while \(k\) is essentially the connecting morphism in the long exact sequence. The description of \(B_{r+1}\) is simply the version of Lemma reference lifted to \(E_0\). For \(Z_{r+1}\), besides that lemma, the key point is the description of the connecting morphism \(k:\operatorname{H}(\operatorname{coker}(\alpha),d_\alpha)\to\operatorname{H}(D,d)\). A careful review of the constructions in equation and equation shows that this morphism is induced by the middle vertical morphism \(\overline{d}\) in the following commutative diagram with exact rows: \[\text{Diagram chapter5-unit-066-d008}\] and \(\overline{d}\) itself comes from \(d:D\to D\). The remaining verifications are lengthy but straightforward; the reader may begin with the case where \(\mathcal{A}\) is a category of modules.

Thus the spectral sequence provided by a differential object can be made to start at \(0\) by setting \(E_0:=\operatorname{coker}(\alpha)\) and \(d_0:=d_\alpha\). For an Abelian category with translation \((\mathcal{A},T)\), morphisms with degrees can still be composed and notions such as exactness remain available, so the theory of exact couples readily extends to the case in which \(i,j,k\) have degrees. For example, in the situation to be discussed in §reference, we can consider the exact couple \[\text{Diagram chapter5-unit-066-d009} \xlongequal{\text{unrolled}} \left[ \text{Diagram chapter5-unit-066-d010} \right].\] Denote this exact couple by \(\mathscr{C}\). The natural extension of Lemma reference to the case with degrees shows that \(\mathscr{C}_{(r)}\) has the form \(\text{Diagram chapter5-unit-066-diagram-011}\). Thus \(d_r=j_rk_r\) is a morphism of degree \(r\). The resulting spectral sequence is therefore graded.

The spectral sequence of a filtered differential object

Throughout this section, we work with an Abelian category with translation \((\mathcal{A},T)\).

Definition. An object \((X,d)\in\operatorname{Ob}((\mathcal{A},T)_d)\) equipped with a filtration \(\left(\mathrm{F}^\bullet X,d_{\mathrm{F}^\bullet X}\right)\) is called a filtered differential object over \((\mathcal{A},T)\). In this case, \(\operatorname{gr}^pX\) is also naturally equipped with \(\operatorname{gr}^pd:\operatorname{gr}^pX\to T\operatorname{gr}^pX\), so that \((\operatorname{gr}^pX,\operatorname{gr}^pd)\in\operatorname{Ob}((\mathcal{A},T)_d)\).

Since \(d_{\mathrm{F}^pX}\) on the subobject \(\mathrm{F}^pX\) is best understood as the restriction of \(d:X\to TX\), we continue to denote it by \(d\). A similar definition applies to increasing filtrations, with an entirely dual formulation. We return to spectral sequences. The preceding section explained how to construct an exact couple from a differential object. Now consider a filtered differential object \((X,d,\mathrm{F}^\bullet X)\) over \(\mathcal{A}\). Write \(S:(Y^p)_p\mapsto(Y^{p+1})_p\) for the standard translation functor on \(\mathcal{A}^{\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}}\); it plainly commutes with \(T\), acting on each \(Y^p\). Consequently, the morphisms considered below have two kinds of degree: the “filtration degree” corresponding to \(S\) and the “internal degree” corresponding to \(T\). For the moment we focus on the former. Since the filtration is decreasing, there is a monomorphism \[\alpha:\left(\mathrm{F}^{p+1}X,d\right)_{p\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}} \hookrightarrow S^{-1}\left(\mathrm{F}^{p+1}X,d\right)_{p\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}} =\left(\mathrm{F}^{p}X,d\right)_{p\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}}.\] Thus \(E_0:=\operatorname{coker}(\alpha)=\left(\operatorname{gr}^pX,\operatorname{gr}^pd\right)_{p\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}}\) and \(E_1^p=\operatorname{H}(\operatorname{gr}^pX,\operatorname{gr}^pd)\). Regard \(\alpha\) as a morphism of degree \(-1\) in \(\mathcal{A}^{\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}}\) (with respect to \(S\)). Applying Proposition reference gives the following exact couple with degrees over \(\mathcal{A}^{\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}}\): \[\mathscr{C}=\left[\text{Diagram chapter5-unit-067-d001}\right],\] where the \(\nwarrow\) arrow comes from the connecting morphism induced by the short exact sequence \(0\to(\mathrm{F}^{p+1}X,d)\to(\mathrm{F}^pX,d) \to(\operatorname{gr}^pX,\operatorname{gr}^pd)\to0\). The resulting sequence \(\mathscr{E}=(E_r^p,d_r^p)_{\substack{r\geq0\\p\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}}}\) is called the spectral sequence determined by \(\mathrm{F}^\bullet X\) in \(\mathcal{A}^{\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}}\). At the end of §reference we explained that \(d_r\) is a morphism of degree \(r\) with respect to \(S\), namely \[d_r=\left(d_r^p:E_r^p\to(S^rE_r)^p=E_r^{p+r}\right)_{p\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}};\] of course, the degree of \(d_r\) can also be read from the formula in Proposition reference. In other words, a filtered differential object \((X,d,\mathrm{F}^\bullet X)\) gives a cohomologically graded spectral sequence as in Definition reference. Notice that \(d_r^p\) here may also carry an internal degree (unless \(T=\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{\mathcal{A}}\)); this is suppressed from the notation and will be set out in detail in §reference. Following the pattern of equation, define subobjects of \(Z_0=(\operatorname{gr}^pX,\operatorname{gr}^pd)_p\) by \[B_r=(B_r^p)_p\subset(Z_r^p)_p=Z_r.\] To simplify notation, the statements below suppress the internal degree of \(d\); this amounts to considering the special case \(T=\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{\mathcal{A}}\). The extension to the general case is routine: translation functors need only be inserted appropriately wherever \(d^{-1}(\cdots)\) or \(d(\cdots)\) occurs, so that the expressions make strict sense.

Proposition. For a filtered differential object \((X,d,\mathrm{F}^\bullet X)\), the associated spectral sequence satisfies \[\begin{align*} Z_r^p&=\dfrac{\left(\mathrm{F}^pX\cap d^{-1}\mathrm{F}^{p+r}X\right) +\mathrm{F}^{p+1}X}{\mathrm{F}^{p+1}X}, \\ B_r^p&=\dfrac{\left(\mathrm{F}^pX\cap d\mathrm{F}^{p-r+1}X\right) +\mathrm{F}^{p+1}X}{\mathrm{F}^{p+1}X}, \end{align*}\] and \(d_r^p:E_r^p\to E_r^{p+r}\) is induced by the morphism \(d^{-1}\mathrm{F}^{p+r}X\xrightarrow{d} \mathrm{F}^{p+r}X\cap\operatorname{ker}(d)\).

Proof. Observe that the degree-\(p\) component of \(\alpha^r\) may be identified with the inclusion \(\mathrm{F}^pX\hookrightarrow\mathrm{F}^{p-r}X\) or \(\mathrm{F}^{p+r}X\hookrightarrow\mathrm{F}^pX\). The assertion reduces to the graded version of Proposition reference.

Since \(\varinjlim\) and \(\varprojlim\) in \(\mathcal{A}^{\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}}\) are taken degree by degree, \(E_\infty=(E_\infty^p)_{p\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}}\) can be written as \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:filtered-diff-infty}{} E_\infty^p=\dfrac{Z_\infty^p}{B_\infty^p} =\dfrac{\bigcap_r\left((\mathrm{F}^pX\cap d^{-1}\mathrm{F}^{p+r}X) +\mathrm{F}^{p+1}X\right)} {\bigcup_r\left((\mathrm{F}^pX\cap d\mathrm{F}^{p-r+1}X) +\mathrm{F}^{p+1}X\right)}, \end{equation}\] provided the displayed \(\bigcap\) and \(\bigcup\) exist for every \(p\).

Remark. Proposition reference on the spectral sequence of a filtered differential object is the foundation for the later discussions in this chapter. It is an application of exact couples, but we could equally regard the formulas in Proposition reference as direct definitions and verify from them all the properties required of a spectral sequence.

From the preceding description, the spectral sequence \(E_r^p\) of \((X,d,\mathrm{F}^\bullet X)\) can be viewed as a process of successively approximating \(\operatorname{H}(X,d)\). To make precise what “approximating” means, we need the following concept.

Definition (Induced filtration). For a filtered differential object \((X,d,\mathrm{F}^\bullet X)\) over \((\mathcal{A},T)\), the object \(\operatorname{H}(X,d)\) carries the induced filtration \[\mathrm{F}^p\operatorname{H}(X,d):= \operatorname{im}\left[\mathrm{F}^pX\cap\operatorname{ker}(d)\to\operatorname{H}(X,d)\right], \qquad p\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}.\]

Lemma. If there is an \(N\) with \(\mathrm{F}^NX=0\), then \(\mathrm{F}^N\operatorname{H}(X,d)=0\). If \(\mathrm{F}^\bullet X\) is an exhaustive filtration in the sense of Definition reference, then \(\mathrm{F}^\bullet\operatorname{H}(X,d)\) is exhaustive as well.

Proof. The first part is immediate; we prove the second. By Lemma reference (ii), \(\bigcup_p\mathrm{F}^p\operatorname{H}(X,d)\) is the image of \(\bigcup_p(\mathrm{F}^pX\cap\operatorname{ker}(d))\), while equation gives \[\bigcup_p\left(\mathrm{F}^pX\cap\operatorname{ker}(d)\right) =\left(\bigcup_p\mathrm{F}^pX\right)\cap\operatorname{ker}(d)=\operatorname{ker}(d).\] Moreover, if there is an \(M\) with \(\mathrm{F}^MX=X\), then of course \(\mathrm{F}^M\operatorname{H}(X,d)=\operatorname{H}(X,d)\).

We shall apply the graded version of these observations in §reference.

Lemma. For a filtered differential object \((X,d,\mathrm{F}^\bullet X)\) and every \(p\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\), there is a canonical isomorphism \[\operatorname{gr}^p\operatorname{H}(X,d)\simeq \dfrac{\mathrm{F}^pX\cap\operatorname{ker}(d)} {(\mathrm{F}^{p+1}X\cap\operatorname{ker}(d)) +(\mathrm{F}^pX\cap\operatorname{im}(T^{-1}d))}.\]

Proof. Expand the definition of \(\mathrm{F}^p\operatorname{H}(X,d)/\mathrm{F}^{p+1}\operatorname{H}(X,d)\) and use the standard isomorphism theorem for Abelian categories, Proposition reference, to obtain \[\begin{align*} \operatorname{gr}^p\operatorname{H}(X,d) &=\dfrac{(\mathrm{F}^pX\cap\operatorname{ker}(d))+\operatorname{im}(T^{-1}d)} {(\mathrm{F}^{p+1}X\cap\operatorname{ker}(d))+\operatorname{im}(T^{-1}d)} \\ &=\dfrac{(\mathrm{F}^pX\cap\operatorname{ker}(d)) +(\mathrm{F}^{p+1}X\cap\operatorname{ker}(d))+\operatorname{im}(T^{-1}d)} {(\mathrm{F}^{p+1}X\cap\operatorname{ker}(d))+\operatorname{im}(T^{-1}d)} \\ &\simeq\dfrac{\mathrm{F}^pX\cap\operatorname{ker}(d)} {((\mathrm{F}^{p+1}X\cap\operatorname{ker}(d))+\operatorname{im}(T^{-1}d)) \cap(\mathrm{F}^pX\cap\operatorname{ker}(d))} \\ &=\dfrac{\mathrm{F}^pX\cap\operatorname{ker}(d)} {(\mathrm{F}^{p+1}X\cap\operatorname{ker}(d)) +(\mathrm{F}^pX\cap\operatorname{im}(T^{-1}d))}. \end{align*}\] The last step uses the fact that \(\mathrm{Sub}_X\) is a modular lattice1 (Theorem reference), together with \(\mathrm{F}^{p+1}X\cap\operatorname{ker}(d)\subset\mathrm{F}^pX\cap\operatorname{ker}(d)\) and \(\operatorname{im}(T^{-1}d)\subset\operatorname{ker}(d)\). The remaining steps are standard.

Definition–Proposition. For a filtered differential object \((X,d,\mathrm{F}^\bullet X)\), construct the associated cohomologically graded spectral sequence \((E_r,d_r)_r\). If the \(\bigcap_r\) and \(\bigcup_r\) in equation exist, then the limit \(E_\infty\) exists, and the \(\operatorname{gr}\operatorname{H}(X,d)\) determined by the induced filtration can be canonically realized as a subquotient of \(E_\infty\).

  • If \(\operatorname{gr}\operatorname{H}(X,d)=E_\infty\), the spectral sequence \((E_r,d_r)_r\) is called weakly convergent.

  • If \((E_r,d_r)_r\) is weakly convergent and \(\mathrm{F}^\bullet\operatorname{H}(X,d)\) is exhaustive and complete, the spectral sequence \((E_r,d_r)_r\) is called strongly convergent.

Proof. Fix \(p\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\). In the expression for \(E_\infty^p\) in equation, the numerator contains \((\mathrm{F}^pX\cap\operatorname{ker}(d))+\mathrm{F}^{p+1}X\), while the denominator is contained in \((\mathrm{F}^pX\cap\operatorname{im}(T^{-1}d))+\mathrm{F}^{p+1}X\) (recall that \(d\) is a morphism \(X\to TX\)). This gives the following subquotient of \(E_\infty^p\): \[\begin{multline*} \dfrac{(\mathrm{F}^pX\cap\operatorname{ker}(d))+\mathrm{F}^{p+1}X} {(\mathrm{F}^pX\cap\operatorname{im}(T^{-1}d))+\mathrm{F}^{p+1}X} \\ \simeq\dfrac{\mathrm{F}^pX\cap\operatorname{ker}(d)} {((\mathrm{F}^pX\cap\operatorname{im}(T^{-1}d))+\mathrm{F}^{p+1}X) \cap(\mathrm{F}^pX\cap\operatorname{ker}(d))} \\ =\dfrac{\mathrm{F}^pX\cap\operatorname{ker}(d)} {(\mathrm{F}^pX\cap\operatorname{im}(T^{-1}d)) +(\mathrm{F}^{p+1}X\cap\operatorname{ker}(d))}. \end{multline*}\] The first isomorphism is standard. The following equality uses the fact that \(\mathrm{Sub}_X\) is a modular lattice, together with \(\mathrm{F}^pX\cap\operatorname{im}(T^{-1}d) \subset\mathrm{F}^pX\cap\operatorname{ker}(d)\) and \(\mathrm{F}^{p+1}X\subset\mathrm{F}^pX\). Now apply Lemma reference.

Definitions of convergence vary slightly among references. All the statements above have corresponding versions for differential objects with increasing filtrations \((X,d,\mathrm{F}_\bullet X)\) and the associated homologically graded spectral sequences.

  1. That is, for all subobjects \(A,A^\flat,B\subset X\) with \(A^\flat\subset A\), one has \(A^\flat+(A\cap B)=(A^\flat+B)\cap A\).↩︎

The spectral sequence of a filtered complex

We continue the line of thought from §reference, still with a fixed Abelian category \(\mathcal{A}\). The result of Proposition reference for filtered differential objects can be extended to allow the morphism \(d\) to have a degree. In particular, this theory applies to filtered complexes. Concretely, replace the previous \(\mathcal{A}\) by \(\mathcal{A}^{\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}}\) and denote its translation functor by \(T\). By Example reference, an object \((X,d)\) of \((\mathcal{A}^{\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}},T)_d\) can be identified with a complex \(X\in\operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A}))\). If we further take a decreasing filtration \((X,d,\mathrm{F}^\bullet X)\), then \[\begin{align*} \operatorname{H}(X,d)&=\left(\operatorname{H}^n(X)\right)_{n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}}, \\ \operatorname{H}\left(\mathrm{F}^pX,d\right) &=\left(\operatorname{H}^n\left(\mathrm{F}^pX\right)\right)_{n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}}, \\ \mathrm{F}^p\operatorname{H}^n(X)&:= \operatorname{im}\left[\mathrm{F}^pX^n\cap\operatorname{ker}(d_X^n)\to\operatorname{H}^n(X)\right] \quad\text{(Definition~\href{#def:induced-filtration-H}{reference}).} \end{align*}\] Thus the \(E_r\) in the spectral sequence \(\mathscr{E}\) constructed above in fact takes values in \(\mathcal{A}^{\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\times\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}}\) and is a bigraded object. Besides the filtration degree \(p\), there is an “internal degree” \(n\) coming from the complex structure; the corresponding translation functors \(S\) and \(T\) commute strictly. We already know that \(d_r\) has degree \(r\) with respect to \(S\); we now determine its degree with respect to \(T\).

  • In the exact couple \(\mathscr{C}_{(1)}\) used to construct \(\mathscr{E}\), the morphism \(\nwarrow\) has degree \(1\) with respect to \(T\), while the other morphisms have degree zero. Indeed, \(\nwarrow\) comes from the cohomological connecting morphism and hence has degree \(1\) with respect to \(T\), while the other arrows plainly have degree zero.

  • Using the description in Lemma reference, the same statement follows recursively for \(\mathscr{C}_{(r)}\) for every \(r\).

  • Consequently, both \(d_r\) and the \(d\) in \((X,d)\) are morphisms of degree \(1\) with respect to \(T\). This is also immediate from the description in Proposition reference.

For applications, the customary convention is to use the indices \(p\) and \(q:=n-p\). Thus \[\begin{gather*} E_r=(E_r^{p,q})_{(p,q)\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}^2} =\left(Z_r^{p,q}/B_r^{p,q}\right)_{(p,q)\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}^2}, \\ E_0^{p,q}=\left(\operatorname{gr}^pX\right)^{p+q}, \\ E_1^{p,q}=\operatorname{H}^{p+q}\left(\operatorname{gr}^pX,\operatorname{gr}^pd\right), \\ d_r=\left(d_r^{p,q}:E_r^{p,q}\to E_r^{p+r,q-r+1}\right)_{(p,q)\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}^2} :E_r\xrightarrow{(r,-r+1)}E_r. \end{gather*}\] In other words, a filtered complex gives a cohomological bigraded spectral sequence as in Definition reference. Dually, a chain complex with an increasing filtration gives a homological bigraded spectral sequence.

Example. Consider a filtered complex \((X,d,\mathrm{F}^\bullet X)\). If for every \(n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\) one has \(\mathrm{F}^0X^n=X^n\) and \(\mathrm{F}^{n+1}X^n=0\), then \(E_0\) lies in the first quadrant (Definition reference). This follows immediately from \(E_0^{p,q}=(\operatorname{gr}^pX)^{p+q}\).

Proposition. For a complex \(X\in\operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A}))\) with decreasing filtration \(\mathrm{F}^\bullet X\), the associated spectral sequence satisfies \[\begin{align*} Z_r^{p,q}&= \dfrac{\left(\mathrm{F}^pX^{p+q}\cap d^{-1}\mathrm{F}^{p+r}X^{p+q+1}\right)+\mathrm{F}^{p+1}X^{p+q}} {\mathrm{F}^{p+1}X^{p+q}}, \\ B_r^{p,q}&= \dfrac{\left(\mathrm{F}^pX^{p+q}\cap d\mathrm{F}^{p-r+1}X^{p+q-1}\right)+\mathrm{F}^{p+1}X^{p+q}} {\mathrm{F}^{p+1}X^{p+q}}, \end{align*}\] and \(d_r^{p,q}:E_r^{p,q}\to E_r^{p+r,q-r+1}\) is induced by \[d^{-1}\mathrm{F}^{p+r}X^{p+q+1}\xrightarrow{d} \mathrm{F}^{p+r}X^{p+q+1}\cap\operatorname{ker}(d).\]

Proof. In Proposition reference, include the complex degree \(n=p+q\) and observe that \(d\) has degree \(1\) with respect to the complex translation functor \(T\).

Similarly, equation has the bigraded version \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:filtered-cplx-infty}{} E_\infty^{p,q}=\dfrac{Z_\infty^{p,q}}{B_\infty^{p,q}} =\dfrac{\bigcap_r\left((\mathrm{F}^pX^{p+q}\cap d^{-1}\mathrm{F}^{p+r}X^{p+q+1})+\mathrm{F}^{p+1}X^{p+q}\right)} {\bigcup_r\left((\mathrm{F}^pX^{p+q}\cap d\mathrm{F}^{p-r+1}X^{p+q-1})+\mathrm{F}^{p+1}X^{p,q}\right)}, \end{equation}\] provided the displayed \(\bigcup\) and \(\bigcap\) exist. In this case \(E_\infty=(E_\infty^{p,q})_{(p,q)\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}^2}\). Definition–Proposition reference now becomes a bigraded statement: for all \(p,q\), the object \(\operatorname{gr}^p\operatorname{H}^{p+q}(X)\) can be canonically realized as a subquotient of \(E_\infty^{p,q}\). The convergence properties of the spectral sequence are correspondingly refined by the grading.

Definition. For a filtered complex \((X,d,\mathrm{F}^\bullet X)\) over \(\mathcal{A}\), construct the associated cohomologically graded spectral sequence \((E_r,d_r)_r\). If the \(\bigcap_r\) and \(\bigcup_r\) in equation exist, then \(\operatorname{gr}^p\operatorname{H}^{p+q}(X)\) can be canonically realized as a subquotient of \(E_\infty^{p,q}\).

  • If \(\operatorname{gr}^p\operatorname{H}^{p+q}(X)=E_\infty^{p,q}\) for every \((p,q)\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}^2\), then \((E_r,d_r)_r\) is called weakly convergent.

  • If the sequence is weakly convergent and, for every \(n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\), the filtration \(\mathrm{F}^\bullet\operatorname{H}^n(X)\) is exhaustive and complete, then \((E_r,d_r)_r\) is called strongly convergent.

Convention. Strong convergence of a spectral sequence is also denoted by \(E_r^{p,q}\Rightarrow\operatorname{H}^{p+q}(X)\). The subscript \(r\) is usually written concretely as \(1\), \(2\), and so on, depending on which page of the spectral sequence we wish to describe.

More generally, suppose we are given a cohomological bigraded spectral sequence \(\mathscr{E}\), a filtered graded object \((H,\mathrm{F}^\bullet H)\), and isomorphisms \(E_\infty^{p,q}\simeq\operatorname{gr}^pH^{p+q}\), with \(\mathrm{F}^\bullet H\) exhaustive and complete. We also denote this situation by \(E_r^{p,q}\Rightarrow H^{p+q}\). Homological bigraded spectral sequences are treated similarly; in particular, \(E^r_{p,q}\Rightarrow H_{p+q}\) entails \(E^\infty_{p,q}\simeq\operatorname{gr}_pH_{p+q}\).

The following classical convergence theorem is sufficient for initial applications. For more general convergence conditions, see [Boa99].

Theorem (Classical convergence theorem). Consider a filtered complex \((X,d,\mathrm{F}^\bullet X)\). Suppose that for every \(n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\),

  • the filtration \(\mathrm{F}^\bullet X^n\) is exhaustive (Definition reference),

  • there is an \(N=N(n)\) such that \(\mathrm{F}^NX^n=0\).

Then the associated spectral sequence is strongly convergent (Definition–Proposition reference).

If the hypotheses are strengthened so that the filtration on every \(X^n\) is finite (Definition reference), then the induced filtration on \(\operatorname{H}^n(X)\) is also finite. In this case the associated spectral sequence is bounded (Definition reference).

Proof. By the graded version of Lemma reference, the induced filtration \(\mathrm{F}^\bullet\operatorname{H}^n(X)\) is exhaustive and complete. It therefore remains to prove weak convergence.

We need to recall the proof of Definition–Proposition reference, which explains how to realize \(\operatorname{gr}^p\operatorname{H}^{p+q}(X)\) as a subquotient of \(E_\infty^{p,q}\) for each \((p,q)\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}^2\). The key point is \[\begin{equation*} \begin{split} \bigcap_r&\left(\left(\mathrm{F}^pX^{p+q}\cap d^{-1}\mathrm{F}^{p+r}X^{p+q+1}\right)+\mathrm{F}^{p+1}X^{p+q}\right) \\ &\supset(\mathrm{F}^pX^{p+q}\cap\operatorname{ker}(d))+\mathrm{F}^{p+1}X^{p+q},\\ \bigcup_r&\left(\left(\mathrm{F}^pX^{p+q}\cap d\mathrm{F}^{p-r+1}X^{p+q-1}\right)+\mathrm{F}^{p+1}X^{p+q}\right) \\ &\subset(\mathrm{F}^pX^{p+q}\cap\operatorname{im}(d))+\mathrm{F}^{p+1}X^{p+q}. \end{split} \end{equation*}\] Proving weak convergence is equivalent to strengthening both inclusions to equalities. But when \(r\gg0\) relative to \(p,q\), the expression inside \(\bigcap_r\) in the first line is simply \((\mathrm{F}^pX^{p+q}\cap\operatorname{ker}(d))+\mathrm{F}^{p+1}X^{p+q}\), so equality holds.

For the second line, the term \(+\mathrm{F}^{p+1}X^{p+q}\) can first be moved outside \(\bigcup_r\). Recall that \(d(\mathrm{F}^\bullet X^n)\) is an exhaustive filtration of \(d(X^n)\). Hence \[\begin{multline*} \bigcup_r\left(\mathrm{F}^pX^{p+q}\cap d\mathrm{F}^{p-r+1}X^{p+q-1}\right)\\ \xlongequal{\because\;\text{\href{#eqn:exhaustion-intersection}{equation}}} \mathrm{F}^pX^{p+q}\cap\bigcup_r d\mathrm{F}^{p-r+1}X^{p+q-1}\\ =\mathrm{F}^pX^{p+q}\cap d\bigcup_r \mathrm{F}^{p-r+1}X^{p+q-1} =\mathrm{F}^pX^{p+q}\cap\operatorname{im}(d). \end{multline*}\]

Finally, suppose the filtration on every \(X^n\) is finite. Then \(\mathrm{F}^\bullet\operatorname{H}^n(X)\) is naturally bounded. To show that the spectral sequence is bounded, fix \(r,n\) and take \(p+q=n\). By the description in Proposition reference, when \(p\gg0\) the numerator of \(Z_r^{p,q}\) is \(0\), while when \(p\ll0\) its denominator is \(X^n\). Thus only finitely many \((p,q)\) satisfy \(E_{r+1}^{p,q}\neq0\).

The dual version is clear and will not be repeated.

Corollary (Exact sequence of low-degree terms). Let the filtered complex \((X,d,\mathrm{F}^\bullet X)\) satisfy \[\mathrm{F}^0X^n=X^n,\qquad \mathrm{F}^{n+1}X^n=0, \qquad n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}},\] as in Example reference. The associated spectral sequence gives the canonical exact sequence \[0\to E_2^{1,0}\to\operatorname{H}^1(X)\to E_2^{0,1}\xrightarrow{d}E_2^{2,0} \to\operatorname{H}^2(X).\] Dually, for a chain complex \(X\) with increasing filtration, if \(\mathrm{F}_{-1}X=0\) and \(\mathrm{F}_nX=X\), there is a canonical exact sequence \[\operatorname{H}_2(X)\to E^2_{2,0}\xrightarrow{d}E^2_{0,1}\to\operatorname{H}_1(X) \to E^2_{1,0}\to0.\]

Proof. Substitute \(p=2\) into equation to obtain the exact sequence \[0\to E_\infty^{0,1}\to E_2^{0,1}\xrightarrow{d}E_2^{2,0} \to E_\infty^{2,0}\to0.\] By the classical convergence theorem reference, \(E_\infty^{0,1}\simeq\operatorname{gr}^0\operatorname{H}^1(X)\), \(E_\infty^{1,0}\simeq\operatorname{gr}^1\operatorname{H}^1(X)\), and \(E_\infty^{2,0}\simeq\operatorname{gr}^2\operatorname{H}^2(X)\). The hypotheses give \[\begin{gather*} \operatorname{gr}^2\operatorname{H}^2(X)=\mathrm{F}^2\operatorname{H}^2(X),\qquad \operatorname{gr}^1\operatorname{H}^1(X)=\mathrm{F}^1\operatorname{H}^1(X),\\ \operatorname{gr}^0\operatorname{H}^1(X)=\operatorname{H}^1(X)/\mathrm{F}^1\operatorname{H}^1(X) =\operatorname{H}^1(X)/E_\infty^{1,0}. \end{gather*}\] Moreover, substituting \(p=1\) into equation gives \(E_2^{1,0}=E_\infty^{1,0}\). Splicing these equalities together yields the asserted exact sequence. The homological version is analogous.

If \(E_r^{p,q}\) is strongly convergent, then once sufficiently many pages \((E_r,d_r)\) are known, in principle one can read \((\operatorname{gr}^p\operatorname{H}^{p+q}(X))_{p,q\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}}\) from \(E_\infty\). Passing from \((\operatorname{gr}^p\operatorname{H}^n(X))_p\) to \(\operatorname{H}^n(X)\), however, amounts to determining a series of extensions in \(\mathcal{A}\), which is generally difficult unless \(\operatorname{H}^n(X)\) splits. If we consider only coarser properties, a spectral sequence can sometimes provide a concise answer. The following example is essentially an application of the Euler–Poincaré principle.

Lemma. Let \(\mathscr{E}=(E_r,d_r)_{r\geq1}\) be a cohomological bigraded spectral sequence, and suppose there is an \(r\) such that \[\left\{(p,q)\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}^2:E_r^{p,q}\neq0\right\} \quad\text{is a finite set}.\] Then for \(r\gg0\), \(\mathscr{E}\) degenerates at the \(E_r\) page.

Proof. By the hypothesis, for sufficiently large \(r\) all nonzero terms of \(E_r\) are concentrated in a region of finite length and width. Apply Example reference.

Proposition. Let the cohomological bigraded spectral sequence \((E_r,d_r)_r\) satisfy the following conditions:

  • there is an \(r\) such that \(\{(p,q)\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}^2:E_r^{p,q}\neq0\}\) is a finite set;

  • there is strong convergence \(E_r^{p,q}\Rightarrow H^{p+q}\) in the sense of Convention reference.

Then in the group \(\mathrm{K}_0(\mathcal{A})\) of Definition reference, for \(r\gg0\) one has \[\sum_{n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}}(-1)^n[H^n] =\sum_{p,q\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}}(-1)^{p+q}[E_r^{p,q}],\] and both sides are finite sums.

Proof. For \(r\gg0\), only finitely many terms on the right are nonzero. Moreover, \[E_{r+1}^{p,q}\simeq\operatorname{H}\left[ E_r^{p-r,q+r-1}\xrightarrow{d}E_r^{p,q} \xrightarrow{d}E_r^{p+r,q-r+1}\right].\] If degree is counted by \(n:=p+q\), then \(d\) has degree \(1\). Take the alternating sum over \(n\) in \(\mathrm{K}_0(\mathcal{A})\) and apply Theorem reference to obtain \[\sum_{p,q\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}}(-1)^{p+q}[E_r^{p,q}] =\sum_{p,q\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}}(-1)^{p+q}[E_{r+1}^{p,q}].\]

Lemma reference shows that the spectral sequence eventually degenerates. Thus, for \(r\gg0\), \(E_r^{p,q}=E_\infty^{p,q}\) for every \((p,q)\). Consequently, \[\sum_{p,q}(-1)^{p+q}[E_r^{p,q}] =\sum_{p,q}(-1)^{p+q}[\operatorname{gr}^p\operatorname{H}^{p+q}(X)] =\sum_n(-1)^n\sum_p[\operatorname{gr}^pH^n],\] and the hypotheses ensure that all these sums are finite. By Lemma reference (v) and the properties of \(\mathrm{F}^\bullet H\), we also have \(\sum_p[\operatorname{gr}^pH^n(X)]=[\operatorname{H}^n(X)]\).

If \((E_r,d_r)_r\) comes from a filtered complex \((X,d,\mathrm{F}^\bullet)\) and the filtration \(\mathrm{F}^\bullet X^n\) on every \(X^n\) is finite, then Theorem reference ensures that the strong-convergence hypothesis \(E_r^{p,q}\Rightarrow\operatorname{H}^{p+q}(X)\) in Proposition reference holds automatically. The condition on \(\{(p,q):E_r^{p,q}\neq0\}\), however, is not automatic. Filtered complexes already suffice to produce some simple but useful spectral sequences; see the exercises for this chapter. Since algebra is the subject of this book, several of the best-known spectral sequences arise from bicomplexes. We therefore turn next to the bicomplex case.

Spectral sequences of bicomplexes and their applications

Throughout this section, we assume that the Abelian category \(\mathcal{A}\) has the countable direct sums or countable products under consideration. Let \(X\) be a bicomplex over \(\mathcal{A}\), written \(X\in\operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}^2(\mathcal{A}))\). The total complex \(\operatorname{tot}_{\oplus}X\) has two decreasing filtrations, \[\begin{align*} \mathrm{F}^p_{\mathrm{I}} (\operatorname{tot}_{\oplus} X)^n & = \bigoplus_{\substack{i+j=n \\ i \geq p}} X^{i, j}, \\ \mathrm{F}^q_{\mathrm{II}} (\operatorname{tot}_{\oplus} X)^n & = \bigoplus_{\substack{i+j=n \\ j \geq q}} X^{i, j} . \end{align*}\] Examining each \((i,j)\) component separately shows that \[\bigcap_p \mathrm{F}^p_{\mathrm{I}} = 0 = \bigcap_q \mathrm{F}^q_{\mathrm{II}}, \quad \bigcup_p \mathrm{F}^p_{\mathrm{I}} = \operatorname{tot}_{\oplus} X = \bigcup_q \mathrm{F}^q_{\mathrm{II}}.\] We thus obtain two filtered complexes. The corresponding spectral sequences are denoted respectively by \(\mathscr{E}_{\mathrm{I}}=\mathscr{E}_{\mathrm{I}}(X)\) and \(\mathscr{E}_{\mathrm{II}}=\mathscr{E}_{\mathrm{II}}(X)\), or more concretely by \(E_{\mathrm{I},r}^{p,q}\) and \(E_{\mathrm{II},r}^{p,q}\), where \(r\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}_{\geq0}\). If \(X^{p,q}\neq0\implies p,q\geq0\), we say that \(X\) lies in the first quadrant. In this case, for \(\star\in\{\mathrm{I},\mathrm{II}\}\), \[\mathrm{F}_\star^0 \left(\operatorname{tot}_{\oplus} X \right)^n = \left(\operatorname{tot}_{\oplus} X\right)^n, \quad \mathrm{F}_\star^{n+1} \left(\operatorname{tot}_{\oplus} X \right)^n = 0 ,\] so the corresponding spectral sequences also lie in the first quadrant. For a chain bicomplex \(X\), one similarly defines two increasing filtrations, \[\begin{align*} \mathrm{F}_{\mathrm{I}, p} \left( \operatorname{tot}_{\oplus} X \right)_n & = \bigoplus_{\substack{i+j=n \\ i \leq p}} X_{i, j}, \\ \mathrm{F}_{\mathrm{II}, q} \left( \operatorname{tot}_{\oplus} X \right)_n & = \bigoplus_{\substack{i+j=n \\ j \leq q}} X_{i, j}, \end{align*}\] together with the corresponding homological bigraded spectral sequences.

Proposition. For \(X\in\operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}^2(\mathcal{A}))\), the first few pages of its two spectral sequences and their corresponding morphisms \(d\) are described as follows: \[\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|c|} \hline & E_0^{p,q} & d_0^{p,q} & E_1^{p,q} & d_1^{p,q} & E_2^{p,q} \\ \hline \mathscr{E}_{\mathrm{I}} & X^{p,q} & (-1)^p \ensuremath{{}^\vartriangle d}^{p,q} & \operatorname{H}^q(X^{p, \bullet}, \ensuremath{{}^\vartriangle d}) & \operatorname{H}^q(\ensuremath{{}^\vartriangleright d}^{p, \bullet}) & \operatorname{H}_{\mathrm{I}}\operatorname{H}_{\mathrm{II}}(X)^{p,q} \\ \mathscr{E}_{\mathrm{II}} & X^{q,p} & \ensuremath{{}^\vartriangleright d}^{q,p} & \operatorname{H}^q(X^{\bullet, p}, \ensuremath{{}^\vartriangleright d}) & (-1)^q \operatorname{H}^q(\ensuremath{{}^\vartriangle d}^{\bullet, p}) & \operatorname{H}_{\mathrm{II}} \operatorname{H}_{\mathrm{I}}(X)^{q,p} \\ \hline \end{array}\] The functors \(\operatorname{H}_{\mathrm{I}},\operatorname{H}_{\mathrm{II}}:\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}^2(\mathcal{A}) \to\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}^2(\mathcal{A})\) are defined in §reference, especially in equation.

For chain complexes and their homology, the same method gives the following table. \[\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|c|} \hline & E^0_{p,q} & d^0_{p,q} & E^1_{p,q} & d^1_{p,q} & E^2_{p,q} \\ \hline \mathscr{E}_{\mathrm{I}} & X_{p,q} & (-1)^p \ensuremath{{}^\vartriangle d}_{p,q} & \operatorname{H}_q(X_{p, \bullet}, \ensuremath{{}^\vartriangle d}) & \operatorname{H}_q(\ensuremath{{}^\vartriangleright d}_{p, \bullet}) & \operatorname{H}_{\mathrm{I}}\operatorname{H}_{\mathrm{II}}(X)_{p,q} \\ \mathscr{E}_{\mathrm{II}} & X_{q,p} & \ensuremath{{}^\vartriangleright d}_{q,p} & \operatorname{H}_q(X_{\bullet, p}, \ensuremath{{}^\vartriangleright d}) & (-1)^q \operatorname{H}_q(\ensuremath{{}^\vartriangle d}_{\bullet, p}) & \operatorname{H}_{\mathrm{II}} \operatorname{H}_{\mathrm{I}}(X)_{q,p} \\ \hline \end{array}\]

Proof. This follows by a direct verification from the description in Proposition reference; the sign on \(\ensuremath{{}^\vartriangle d}\) comes from the definition of the total complex. We omit the details.

The same definitions and results apply to \(\operatorname{tot}_{\Pi}X\), with entirely similar properties. For \(X\in\operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}^2_f(\mathcal{A}))\) (Definition reference), its total complex involves only finite direct sums. Thus there is no need to distinguish the \(\oplus\) and \(\Pi\) versions; both are denoted uniformly by \(\operatorname{tot}X\).

Theorem. Let \(X\in\operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}^2_f(\mathcal{A}))\). The two corresponding spectral sequences \(\mathscr{E}_{\mathrm{I}}\) and \(\mathscr{E}_{\mathrm{II}}\) are bounded and strongly convergent, and the two corresponding induced filtrations on \(\operatorname{H}^n(\operatorname{tot}X)\) are finite for every \(n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\).

Proof. The definition of \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}^2_f(\mathcal{A})\) shows that \(\mathrm{F}_{\mathrm{I}}^\bullet\left(\operatorname{tot}X\right)^n\) and \(\mathrm{F}_{\mathrm{II}}^\bullet\left(\operatorname{tot}X\right)^n\) are finite filtrations for every \(n\). Apply Theorem reference.

We now present several representative applications. Since all the filtrations and spectral sequences involved are finite, these results apply to every Abelian category1.

Example. We now reprove Theorem reference using spectral sequences: if a morphism \(f:X\to Y\) in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}^2_f(\mathcal{A})\) induces \(\operatorname{H}_{\mathrm{II}}\operatorname{H}_{\mathrm{I}}(X)\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}} \operatorname{H}_{\mathrm{II}}\operatorname{H}_{\mathrm{I}}(Y)\) (or \(\operatorname{H}_{\mathrm{I}}\operatorname{H}_{\mathrm{II}}(X)\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}} \operatorname{H}_{\mathrm{I}}\operatorname{H}_{\mathrm{II}}(Y)\)), then \(\operatorname{tot}(f):\operatorname{tot}(X)\to\operatorname{tot}(Y)\) is a quasi-isomorphism.

First suppose that \(\operatorname{H}_{\mathrm{II}}\operatorname{H}_{\mathrm{I}}(X)\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}} \operatorname{H}_{\mathrm{II}}\operatorname{H}_{\mathrm{I}}(Y)\). The morphism \(f\) induces a morphism of spectral sequences \(\mathscr{E}_{\mathrm{II}}(X)\to\mathscr{E}_{\mathrm{II}}(Y)\). This is already an isomorphism on the \(E_2\) page and hence also gives an isomorphism on the limit page \(E_\infty\) (Proposition reference).

By the convergence guaranteed by Theorem reference, the morphism \(\operatorname{gr}^p\left(\operatorname{H}^n\operatorname{tot}(X)\right)\to \operatorname{gr}^p\left(\operatorname{H}^n\operatorname{tot}(Y)\right)\) induced by \(\operatorname{tot}(f)\) is an isomorphism for all \(p,n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\). The induced filtrations on \(\operatorname{H}^n\) are known to be finite. Therefore \(\operatorname{H}^n\operatorname{tot}(f):\operatorname{H}^n\operatorname{tot}(X)\to\operatorname{H}^n\operatorname{tot}(Y)\) is also an isomorphism (Proposition reference).

If instead we consider the spectral sequence \(\mathscr{E}_{\mathrm{I}}\), the analogous argument deduces that \(\operatorname{tot}(f)\) is a quasi-isomorphism from \(\operatorname{H}_{\mathrm{I}}\operatorname{H}_{\mathrm{II}}(X)\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}} \operatorname{H}_{\mathrm{I}}\operatorname{H}_{\mathrm{II}}(Y)\).

Example (Deriving a bifunctor). Let the Abelian categories \(\mathcal{A}_1\) and \(\mathcal{A}_2\) have enough injective objects (or projective objects), and let the bifunctor \(F:\mathcal{A}_1\times\mathcal{A}_2\to\mathcal{B}\) be left exact (or right exact) in each variable. We discuss the left-exact case. Take \(X_i\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{A}_i)\) and choose injective resolutions \(0\to X_i\to I_i^0\to\cdots\); define \(I_i^n:=0\) for \(n<0\) (\(i=1,2\)). These data form a first-quadrant bicomplex \[Y^{p, q} := F\left( I_1^p, I_2^q \right).\] The corresponding first-quadrant spectral sequence \(\mathscr{E}_{\mathrm{I}}\) therefore satisfies \[E_1^{p,q} = \operatorname{H}^q\left( F(I_1^p, I_2^\bullet) \right) \Rightarrow \operatorname{H}^{p+q}(\operatorname{tot}(Y)), \quad p,q \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}.\] The right-hand side \(\operatorname{H}^{p+q}(\operatorname{tot}Y)\) is the value of the right-derived bifunctor \(\mathrm{R}^{p+q}F(X_1,X_2)\); see Definition reference.

Now suppose in addition that \(F\) is balanced (Definition reference); then \(F(I_1^p,\cdot)\) is exact. This shows that \(q\neq0\implies E_1^{p,q}=0\), while \(E_1^{p,0}=F(I_1^p,X_2)\). Hence \(q\neq0\implies E_2^{p,q}=0\), and \[\begin{align*} E_2^{p,0} & = \operatorname{H}^p\left[ \cdots \to F(I_1^p, X_2) \to F(I_1^{p+1}, X_2) \to \cdots \right] \\ & = (\mathrm{R}_{\mathrm{I}}^p F)(X_1, X_2), \quad \text{with the notation of Theorem~\href{#prop:balanced-primer}{reference}}. \end{align*}\] In particular, the spectral sequence degenerates at the \(E_2\) page, so \[\begin{align*} E_2^{p,q} & = E_\infty^{p,q}, \\ E_\infty^{p,q} & = \operatorname{gr}^p \operatorname{H}^{p+q}\left(\operatorname{tot}(Y)\right) = 0, \quad \text{if}\; q \neq 0, \\ E_\infty^{p,0} & = \operatorname{H}^p\left(\operatorname{tot}(Y)\right) = \mathrm{R}^p F(X_1, X_2) . \end{align*}\] Thus \(\mathrm{R}^nF(X_1,X_2)\simeq (\mathrm{R}_{\mathrm{I}}^nF)(X_1,X_2)\). If instead we use \(\mathscr{E}_{\mathrm{II}}\), the same argument gives \(\mathrm{R}^nF(X_1,X_2)\simeq (\mathrm{R}_{\mathrm{II}}^nF)(X_1,X_2)\). Hence \(\mathrm{R}_{\mathrm{I}}F\simeq\mathrm{R}_{\mathrm{II}}F\), which is precisely the assertion of Theorem reference.

Example (The spectral sequence of hyperderived functors). Let \(\mathcal{A}\) and \(\mathcal{B}\) be Abelian categories, let \(\mathcal{A}\) have enough injective objects (or projective objects), and let \(F:\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{B}\) be a left-exact (or right-exact) additive functor. In the first half of §reference, for a complex \(X\in\operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}^+(\mathcal{A}))\) (or \(X\in\operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}^-(\mathcal{A}))\)), we defined the right-derived functors \(\mathrm{R}^nF(X)\) (or the left-derived functors \(\mathrm{L}_nF(X)\)), where \(n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\).
