Every element of \(C_1(G,\Bbbk)\) has a unique expression as a \(\Bbbk\)-linear combination of the elements \([g]:=(g)^\dagger\otimes1\) for \(g\in G\). Observe that \(C_0(G,\Bbbk)\simeq\Bbbk\) and \[\left( \partial'_1 \otimes \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{\Bbbk}\right)[g] = 1 - 1 = 0, \quad \left( \partial'_2 \otimes \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{\Bbbk}\right)((g_1 | g_2)^\dagger \otimes 1) = [g_2] - [g_1 g_2] + [g_1].\] Therefore \(\operatorname{H}_1(G,\Bbbk)\) is isomorphic to the quotient \(\Bbbk\)-module \[Q := \bigoplus_{g \in G} \Bbbk \cdot [g] \bigg/ \ensuremath{\left\langle [g_1 g_2] - [g_1] + [g_2] : g_1, g_2 \in G \right\rangle};\] The map \(g\mapsto[g]\) induces a group homomorphism \(a:G\to(Q,+)\). It has the following universal property: for every \(\Bbbk\)-module \(N\) and group homomorphism \(b:G\to(N,+)\), there is a unique \(\Bbbk\)-module homomorphism \(\varphi:Q\to N\) such that \(b=\varphi a\). The reader may quickly verify this universal property and deduce from it the canonical isomorphism of \(\Bbbk\)-modules \[\text{Diagram chapter6-unit-073-d004}\] where \(G_{\mathrm{ab}}:=G/G_{\mathrm{der}}\) is the abelianization of \(G\) and \(G_{\mathrm{der}}\) is its derived subgroup, as in [Li1]. Readers who know the topological background of group homology will recognize the connection with the Hurewicz theorem in homology theory.

It is natural also to ask for the composite of the isomorphism \(\operatorname{H}_1(G,\Bbbk)\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}\mathfrak{I}/\mathfrak{I}^2\) from Example reference with the isomorphism above. We claim that this composite is given explicitly by \[\text{Diagram chapter6-unit-073-d005}\]

Why is this so? The isomorphism in Example reference comes from the map \(\operatorname{H}_1(G,\Bbbk)\to\operatorname{H}_0(G,\mathfrak{I})\simeq \mathfrak{I}/\mathfrak{I}^2\) induced by the short exact sequence \(0\to\mathfrak{I}\to\Bbbk[G]\to\Bbbk\to0\). Write down the following commutative diagram with exact rows: \[\text{Diagram chapter6-unit-073-d006}\] The map \(\partial'_1\otimes\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{\Bbbk[G]}\) sends \((g)^\dagger\otimes1_{\Bbbk[G]}\) to \(1_G-g\in C_0(G,\mathfrak{I})=\mathfrak{I}\), thereby determining an element of \(\mathfrak{I}/\mathfrak{I}^2\simeq \operatorname{H}_0(G,\mathfrak{I})\).3 This is precisely the construction in the snake lemma.

Remark. The form of the standard cochain complex (respectively standard chain complex) shows that, as an additive group, \(\operatorname{H}^n(G,M)\) (respectively \(\operatorname{H}_n(G,M)\)) is completely determined by the additive structure of \(M\); multiplication by elements of \(\Bbbk\) only supplies its \(\Bbbk\)-module structure. Thus the case \(\Bbbk=\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\) already captures the essence of group cohomology (respectively homology), although allowing general coefficients causes no additional difficulty.

Remark (Normalized version). To compute \(\operatorname{H}^n(G,M)\) and \(\operatorname{H}_n(G,M)\), one may instead use the normalized free resolution \(\overline{\mathsf{L}}\to\Bbbk\) supplied by Proposition reference. Denote the corresponding cochain and chain complexes by \((\overline{C}^n(G,M))_n\) and \((\overline{C}_n(G,M))_n\), respectively, and call them the normalized standard cochain complex and normalized standard chain complex. They are, respectively, a subcomplex and a quotient complex of the original versions. For example, in the cohomological case, the description of \(\mathsf{L}_n\) in equation gives \[\overline{C}^n(G, M) = \left\{\begin{array}{r|l} f \in C^n(G, M) & \exists 1 \leq k \leq n, \; g_k = 1_G \\ & \implies f(g_1, \ldots, g_n) = 0 \end{array}\right\}.\]

  1. Translator’s correction: the source ends the argument list at \(g_n\), but \(d^nf\in C^{n+1}(G,M)\) and the calculation above uses \((g_1,\ldots,g_{n+1})\).↩︎

  2. Translator’s correction: the source prints \(\mathsf{L}^n\), whereas the chain complex and the basis in the same sentence use \(\mathsf{L}_n\).↩︎

  3. Translator’s correction: the source uses \(C^0\) and \(\operatorname{H}^0\), but the diagram and the connecting morphism being computed are homological, so the correct indices are \(C_0\) and \(\operatorname{H}_0\).↩︎

Low-degree cohomology: crossed homomorphisms and group extensions

This section aims to deepen our understanding of \(\operatorname{H}^1\) and \(\operatorname{H}^2\). Fix a group \(G\) and a commutative ring \(\Bbbk\). Given a \(G\)-module \(M\), define the following submodules of \(C^n(G,M)\) for the standard complex \(C(G,M)\) of Proposition reference: \[Z^n(G,M):=\operatorname{ker}(d^n)\supset\operatorname{im}(d^{n-1})=:B^n(G,M),\] and set \(B^0(G,M)=0\). We identify \[\begin{equation*} \operatorname{H}^n(G,M)\quad\text{with}\quad Z^n(G,M)/B^n(G,M). \end{equation*}\] In view of their topological origins, the elements of \(Z^n(G,M)\) are also called \(n\)-cocycles, while the elements of \(B^n(G,M)\) are called \(n\)-coboundaries. Recall that \(C^n(G,M)\) consists of all maps \(f:G^n\to M\). The low-degree part of the standard complex is \[\text{Diagram chapter6-unit-074-d001}\] In particular, \(Z^0(G,M)=M^G\). We next consider the case \(n=1\).

Definition (Crossed homomorphism). Let \(M\) be a \(G\)-module. The elements of \(Z^1(G,M)\) are also called crossed homomorphisms from \(G\) to \(M\); in other words, a crossed homomorphism is a map \(f:G\to M\) satisfying \[f(g_1g_2)=g_1f(g_2)+f(g_1),\qquad g_1,g_2\in G.\] For fixed \(\Bbbk\), they form a \(\Bbbk\)-module under pointwise operations.

Notice that the elements of \(B^1(G,M)\) are the crossed homomorphisms of the form \(f_m:g\mapsto gm-m\), where \(m\in M\). In general, every crossed homomorphism \(f\) satisfies \(f(1_G)=0\) (take \(g_1=g_2=1_G\)) and \(g^{-1}f(g)=-f(g^{-1})\) (take \(g_1=g^{-1}\) and \(g_2=g\)).

Example. If \(G\) acts trivially on \(M\), then the crossed homomorphisms are precisely the homomorphisms from \(G\) to the additive group \((M,+)\), and \(B^1(G,M)=\{0\}\). Thus in this case \[\operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{Grp}}}(G,M)\simeq\operatorname{H}^1(G,M).\]

Another way to understand crossed homomorphisms is through semidirect products. For a \(G\)-module \(M\), use the \(G\)-action to form the semidirect product \(M\rtimes G\). Its elements have the form \((m,g)\) with \(m\in M\) and \(g\in G\), and it has a projection homomorphism \(\pi:M\rtimes G\to G\) sending \((m,g)\) to \(g\).

Proposition.

Let \(M\) be a \(G\)-module. There is a canonical bijection \[Z^1(G,M)\xrightarrow{1:1} \left\{\text{group homomorphisms }\sigma:G\to M\rtimes G \;\middle|\;\pi\sigma=\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_G\right\}.\] A map \(\sigma\) on the right-hand side is also called a section of \(\pi\); the crossed homomorphism \(f\) corresponds to the section \(\sigma(g)=(f(g),g)\).

Proof. A map \(\sigma\) satisfying \(\pi\sigma=\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_G\) must have the form \(\sigma(g)=(f(g),g)\) for some map \(f:G\to M\). By the definition of the semidirect product, \(\sigma\) is a group homomorphism if and only if the following equality holds in \(M\): \[f(g_1)+g_1f(g_2)=f(g_1g_2),\qquad g_1,g_2\in G.\] This is exactly the definition of a crossed homomorphism.

Crossed homomorphisms are also related to the augmentation ideal \(\mathfrak{I}\subset\Bbbk[G]\) introduced in Remark reference.

Proposition. For every \(G\)-module \(M\), there is a canonical isomorphism \(\operatorname{Hom}_G(\mathfrak{I},M)\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}Z^1(G,M)\) sending a homomorphism \(\varphi\) to the crossed homomorphism \(f(g)=\varphi(g-1_G)\).

Proof. As a \(\Bbbk\)-module, \(\mathfrak{I}\) has basis \(\{g-1_G:g\in G,\;g\neq1_G\}\). Thus specifying a \(\Bbbk\)-module homomorphism \(\varphi:\mathfrak{I}\to M\) is equivalent to specifying a map \(f:G\to M\) satisfying \(f(1_G)=0\), with \(f(g)=\varphi(g-1_G)\). The condition that \(\varphi\) be a \(G\)-module homomorphism is \(\varphi(g_1(g_2-1_G))=g_1\varphi(g_2-1_G)\). But \[\text{left-hand side}=\varphi(g_1g_2-1_G-g_1+1_G) =f(g_1g_2)-f(g_1),\qquad \text{right-hand side}=g_1f(g_2).\] This is exactly the crossed-homomorphism condition.

For the next step, the case \(n=2\), we first recall the notion of a group extension. Take \(\Bbbk=\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\) and introduce some terminology.

Definition. Let \(A\) be a group. An extension of \(G\) by \(A\) is a short exact sequence of groups [Li1] \[0\to A\to E\xrightarrow{\pi}G\to1.\]

Henceforth we abbreviate the data of the group extension to \(E\). A group homomorphism \(s:G\to E\) satisfying \(\pi s=\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_G\) is called a splitting of the extension. In this case \(s\) embeds \(G\) as a subgroup of \(E\), thereby identifying \(E\) with the semidirect product \(A\rtimes G\). An extension possessing a splitting is called split. See [Li1] for details.

Broadly speaking, the theory of group extensions studies how to build a larger group from a normal subgroup and a quotient group. To relate this to the cohomology of \(G\)-modules, from now on write the group \(A\) above as \(M\), require it to be commutative, and write its group operation additively. Such a group extension determines a group homomorphism \[\alpha:G\to\operatorname{Aut}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{Grp}}}(M),\qquad \alpha(g)(x)=exe^{-1},\qquad e\in\pi^{-1}(g)\ \text{chosen arbitrarily}.\] Thus \(M\) becomes a \(G\)-module through \(\alpha\); this is the most basic invariant of a group extension. Given a \(G\)-module \(M\), we wish to classify all extensions of \(G\) by \(M\) whose associated \(\alpha\) is precisely the given \(G\)-module structure on \(M\), up to equivalence (or isomorphism) of extensions. An equivalence from an extension \(E\) to an extension \(E'\) is defined in the evident way as a commutative diagram of groups \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:group-ext-diagram}{}\text{Diagram chapter6-unit-074-d002} \end{equation}\] The reader is invited to verify that \(\varphi\) in this diagram is automatically a group isomorphism, and that an extension is split if and only if it is equivalent to the semidirect product \(M\rtimes G\).

Definition. Define the category \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ext}}(G,M)\) of all extensions of \(G\) by the given \(G\)-module \(M\); its morphisms are the commutative diagrams equation.

This category is a groupoid: all its morphisms are invertible. Classifying extensions amounts to describing \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ext}}(G,M)\) up to equivalence of categories. This divides into two subproblems:

  • describe \(\operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ext}}(G,M))/\simeq\), that is, the equivalence classes of extensions, and identify the split extensions among them;

  • describe the morphisms in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ext}}(G,M)\), that is, the isomorphisms between extensions.

We begin with the simpler second subproblem. First, an extension \(E\) has a simple class of automorphisms of the form \(\operatorname{Ad}_m:e\mapsto mem^{-1}\), where \(m\in M\) and the group operation in \(E\) is written multiplicatively; these are called inner automorphisms. For abstract reasons, the inner automorphisms form a normal subgroup of \(\operatorname{Aut}(E)\), and the corresponding quotient group is called the outer automorphism group of \(E\). To classify group extensions, we need to compute cohomology using the normalized standard complex \(\overline{C}(G,M)\) described in Remark reference. Accordingly, define \[\begin{gather*} \overline{C}^n(G,M)\supset\overline{Z}^n(G,M) \supset\overline{B}^n(G,M),\\ \operatorname{H}^n(G,M)\simeq\overline{Z}^n(G,M)/\overline{B}^n(G,M). \end{gather*}\] We have \(\overline{C}^0(G,M)=C^0(G,M)=M\). The preceding discussion of crossed homomorphisms has also shown that \(\overline{Z}^1(G,M)=Z^1(G,M)\).

Lemma. Let \(0\to M\to E\xrightarrow{\pi}G\to1\) be an object of \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ext}}(G,M)\). Its automorphism group is canonically isomorphic to \(\overline{Z}^1(G,M)\), while its outer automorphism group is canonically isomorphic to \(\operatorname{H}^1(G,M)\). More explicitly, an element \(z\in\overline{Z}^1(G,M)\) corresponds to the automorphism sending \(e\in E\) to \(z(\pi(e))e\).

Proof. For the moment, write the group operation on \(M\) multiplicatively. Take \(E'=E\) in the commutative diagram equation. For every \(e\in E\), there is a unique \(z(e)\in M\) such that \(\varphi(e)=z(e)e\). If \(m\in M\), then \(\varphi(me)=m\varphi(e)=mz(e)e=z(e)me\), so \(z(e)\) depends only on the image of \(e\) in \(G\); henceforth we write it as a map \(z:G\to M\). Conversely, every map \(z:G\to M\) determines a map \(\varphi:E\to E\) by \(\varphi(e)=z(\pi(e))e\), and equation commutes at the level of sets.

Consider a map \(z:G\to M\) and the corresponding \(\varphi\). Put \(g_i=\pi(e_i)\) for \(i=1,2\). Then \[\begin{align*} \varphi(e_1e_2)&=z(g_1g_2)e_1e_2,\\ \varphi(e_1)\varphi(e_2)&=z(g_1)e_1z(g_2)e_2\\ &=z(g_1)\underbracket{g_1\cdot z(g_2)}_{ \text{the $G$-module structure on $M$}}e_1e_2. \end{align*}\] Thus \(\varphi\) is a group homomorphism if and only if \(z\) is a crossed homomorphism. It is clear that composition of group homomorphisms corresponds to addition of crossed homomorphisms. Now take \(m\in M\). The corresponding inner automorphism is \(e\mapsto mem^{-1}=mem^{-1}e^{-1}e\). Clearly \(mem^{-1}e^{-1}\in M\), and in additive notation this element is \(m-\pi(e)m\). This proves the assertion.

Definition. The groupoid \(\tau^{\leq2}\overline{\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}}(G,M)\) is defined as follows: its set of objects is \(\overline{Z}^2(G,M)\), while its morphism sets are \[\operatorname{Hom}(f,f'):=\{w\in\overline{C}^1(G,M):f'=d^1w+f\}.\] Composition of morphisms is defined by addition in \(\overline{C}^1(G,M)\). Thus the isomorphism classes of objects correspond bijectively to the elements of \(\operatorname{H}^2(G,M)\).

The meaning of the notation is clear: \(\tau^{\leq2}\overline{\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}}(G,M)\) is the category determined by the truncated complex \(\tau^{\leq2}\overline{C}(G,M)\).

Theorem. Let \(M\) be a \(G\)-module. The category \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ext}}(G,M)\) is equivalent to \(\tau^{\leq2}\overline{\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}}(G,M)\). In particular, equivalence classes of extensions of \(G\) by \(M\) correspond bijectively to elements of \(\operatorname{H}^2(G,M)\), and the equivalence class of split extensions corresponds to \(0\in\operatorname{H}^2(G,M)\).

Proof. We first construct a functor \(\tau^{\leq2}\overline{\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}}(G,M)\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ext}}(G,M)\). Given a map \(f:G^2\to M\), define a binary operation on the set \(M\times G\) by \[(m_1,g_1)\cdot(m_2,g_2):= \left(m_1+g_1\cdot m_2+f(g_1,g_2),g_1g_2\right).\] Associativity is equivalent to the identity \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:grp-2-cocycle}{} f(g_1,g_2)+f(g_1g_2,g_3) =g_1\cdot f(g_2,g_3)+f(g_1,g_2g_3), \end{equation}\] that is, to \(f\in Z^2(G,M)\). Furthermore, \((0,1_G)\) is the identity if and only if \[f(g,1_G)=0=f(1_G,g),\] that is, if and only if \(f\in\overline{Z}^2(G,M)\). Taking \((g_1,g_2,g_3)=(g,g^{-1},g)\) in equation and using the last equality gives \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:grp-2-cocycle-inv}{} f(g,g^{-1})=g\cdot f(g^{-1},g). \end{equation}\]

Thus \(M\times G\) acquires a monoid structure from \(f\in\overline{Z}^2(G,M)\); denote this monoid by \(E\). It is automatically a group, since equation gives \[(0,g)^{-1}=\left(-f(g^{-1},g),g^{-1}\right),\qquad (m,1_G)^{-1}=(-m,1_G).\] It is easy to prove that the maps \(m\mapsto(m,1_G)\) and \((m,g)\mapsto g\) give a group extension \(0\to M\to E\to G\to1\) that induces precisely the original \(G\)-action on \(M\). Verify that \(f=0\) corresponds to the semidirect product \(E=M\rtimes G\).

If, moreover, \(w\in\overline{C}^1(G,M)\) and \(f':=d^1w+f\), denote the corresponding extension by \(E'\). The map \[(m,g)\mapsto(m-w(g),g)\] gives an isomorphism from \(E\) to \(E'\). Indeed, the condition that this map preserve multiplication is equivalent to the identity \[-w(g_1)-g_1\cdot w(g_2)+(d^1w)(g_1,g_2)=-w(g_1g_2),\] which is exactly the definition of \(d^1w\).

We have therefore obtained a functor \(\tau^{\leq2}\overline{\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}}(G,M)\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ext}}(G,M)\), and both categories are groupoids. Comparing automorphism groups of objects by Lemma reference shows that this functor is fully faithful. It remains to show that it is essentially surjective.

Let \(E\) be an object of \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ext}}(G,M)\). Choose an arbitrary section \(s:G\to E\) of the map \(\pi:E\to G\) in the extension data; that is, a map satisfying \(\pi s=\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_G\). This is equivalent to choosing a representative of every \(M\)-coset in \(E\). A section \(s\) is called normalized if \(s(1_G)=1_E\). For all \(g_1,g_2\in G\), the elements \(s(g_1g_2)\) and \(s(g_1)s(g_2)\) have the same image under \(\pi\). Hence there is a unique \(f(g_1,g_2)\in M\) such that \[s(g_1)s(g_2)=f(g_1,g_2)s(g_1g_2).\]

It is easy to prove that associativity, \((s(g_1)s(g_2))s(g_3)=s(g_1)(s(g_2)s(g_3))\), translates into equation, namely \(f\in Z^2(G,M)\). If \(s\) is normalized, then \(f(1_G,g)=0=f(g,1_G)\) for every \(g\), which is equivalent to \(f\in\overline{Z}^2(G,M)\).

For the chosen normalized section \(s\), give \(M\times G\) the group structure corresponding to \(f\). Consider the bijection \[M\times G\xrightarrow{1:1}E,\qquad(m,g)\mapsto ms(g).\] The preceding discussion shows immediately that this bijection preserves group multiplication and gives an isomorphism in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ext}}(G,M)\). This completes the proof of the equivalence.

In the final part of the essential-surjectivity argument, changing the section \(s\) is equivalent to choosing an arbitrary map \(h:G\to M\) and taking \(s'(g):=h(g)s(g)\). The corresponding map \(f':G^2\to M\) becomes \[\begin{align*} f'(g_1,g_2)&=\left(h(g_1)+g_1\cdot h(g_2)-h(g_1g_2)\right)+f(g_1,g_2)\\ &=(d^1h)(g_1,g_2)+f(g_1,g_2). \end{align*}\] If one also requires \(h(1_G)=0\), then \(d^1h\in\overline{B}^2(G,M)\). Historically, this observation was the starting point for the connection between extensions and \(\operatorname{H}^2(G,M)\); it also supplies a group-extension interpretation for the definitions of \(\overline{Z}^2(G,M)\) and \(\overline{B}^2(G,M)\), although this was left implicit in the proof.

Remark. Theorem reference says that the complex \(\tau^{\leq2}\overline{C}(G,M)\) is a linear incarnation of the category of group extensions \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ext}}(G,M)\): the term in degree \(2\) describes objects, the term in degree \(1\) describes morphisms, and the term in degree \(0\) remains to be interpreted. For \(m\in M=\overline{C}^0(G,M)\), there is an inner automorphism of the group extension \(\operatorname{Ad}_m:e\mapsto mem^{-1}\), which is trivial if and only if \(m\in M^G=\operatorname{H}^0(G,M)\). From the viewpoint of inner automorphisms, we may regard the elements of \(M\) as 2-morphisms in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ext}}(G,M)\): for \(m\in M\) and \(\varphi_1,\varphi_2\in\operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ext}}(G,M)}(E,E')\), \[\text{interpret the 2-cell diagram}\; \text{Diagram chapter6-unit-074-d003} \;\text{as}\;\varphi_2=\operatorname{Ad}_m\varphi_1.\]

Notice that \(\operatorname{Ad}_m\varphi_1=\varphi_1\operatorname{Ad}_m\) and \(\operatorname{Ad}_{m_1}\operatorname{Ad}_{m_2}=\operatorname{Ad}_{m_1+m_2}\). Thus \(\operatorname{H}^0(G,M)\) becomes the “2-automorphism group” of every morphism \(\varphi\). In this sense, the complex \(\tau^{\leq2}\overline{C}(G,M)\) may be called a linear incarnation of the 2-category \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ext}}(G,M)\). See [Li1] for the definition of a 2-category.

Other aspects of group extensions will be discussed in §reference. Before that, we need to introduce more operations on group homology and cohomology.

Induced modules

For a group homomorphism \(\varphi:H\to G\), Proposition reference gives the right adjoint \(\operatorname{Hom}_H(\Bbbk[G],\cdot)\) and the left adjoint \(\Bbbk[G]\ensuremath{\underset{\Bbbk[H]}{\otimes}}(\cdot)\) of \(\varphi^*\). This section focuses on the common case in which \(H\subset G\) is a subgroup and \(\varphi\) is the inclusion homomorphism. We begin by introducing notation.

Definition (Induced module). Let \(H\) be a subgroup of \(G\). For an \(H\)-module \(N\), define the \(G\)-modules \[\operatorname{Ind}^G_H(N):=\operatorname{Hom}_H(\Bbbk[G],N),\qquad \operatorname{ind}^G_H(N):=\Bbbk[G]\ensuremath{\underset{\Bbbk[H]}{\otimes}}N.\] As \(N\) varies, both constructions give functors \(H\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\to G\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\).

Both operations may be called induction from \(H\) to \(G\) in a broad sense. The functor \(\operatorname{ind}^G_H\) is also sometimes called induction with finite support; this terminology will be explained by Lemma reference below.

Proposition. The functors \(\operatorname{Res}^G_H:G\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\to H\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\) and \(\operatorname{Ind}^G_H,\operatorname{ind}^G_H:H\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\to G\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\) are all exact. The functor \(\operatorname{Ind}^G_H\) preserves injective objects, \(\operatorname{ind}^G_H\) preserves projective objects, and \(\operatorname{Res}^G_H\) preserves both.

Proof. We already know that \(\operatorname{Res}^G_H\) is exact. Choosing coset representatives shows that \(\Bbbk[G]\) is a free left \(\Bbbk[H]\)-module, so \(\operatorname{Hom}_{\Bbbk[H]}(\Bbbk[G],\cdot)\) is exact. Similarly, \(\Bbbk[G]\) is a free right \(\Bbbk[H]\)-module, so \(\Bbbk[G]\ensuremath{\underset{\Bbbk[H]}{\otimes}}(\cdot)\) is exact. By the adjunctions, the assertions about preserving injective and projective objects follow directly from Proposition reference.

Proposition reference provides a way to construct injective (or projective) resolutions in \(G\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\): take an injective (or projective) resolution of the given \(G\)-module \(M\) in \(\Bbbk\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\), and then induce that resolution to \(G\) using \(\operatorname{Ind}^G_{\{1\}}\) (or \(\operatorname{ind}^G_{\{1\}}\)). The following result is commonly called Shapiro’s lemma.

Theorem (B. Eckmann, D. K. Faddeev, A. Shapiro). Let \(H\) be a subgroup of \(G\). For every \(H\)-module \(N\) and \(n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\), there are canonical isomorphisms \[\operatorname{H}^n\left(G,\operatorname{Ind}^G_H(N)\right)\simeq\operatorname{H}^n(H,N),\qquad \operatorname{H}_n\left(G,\operatorname{ind}^G_H(N)\right)\simeq\operatorname{H}_n(H,N).\] The two sides of each isomorphism, viewed as functors in \(N\), have long exact sequences, and the isomorphisms are compatible with those sequences.

Proof. We give two methods. For cohomology, the first considers the functors \[A^n:=\operatorname{H}^n\left(G,\operatorname{Ind}^G_H(\cdot)\right).\] Since \(\operatorname{Ind}^G_H\) is exact, this family of functors has long exact sequences inherited from \(\operatorname{H}^n(G,\cdot)\) and hence is a cohomological \(\delta\)-functor in the sense of Definition reference. For \(n=0\), Corollary reference gives a canonical isomorphism \[A^0(N)=(\operatorname{Ind}^G_H(N))^G\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}N^H,\qquad \varphi\mapsto\varphi(1_G).\] To extend this canonically to an isomorphism of cohomological \(\delta\)-functors \(A^n\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}\operatorname{H}^n(H,\cdot)\), it suffices to prove that \(A^n\) is effaceable for \(n>0\) (Definition reference, Proposition reference). By Proposition reference, if \(N\) is embedded into an injective \(H\)-module \(I\), then \(\operatorname{Ind}^G_H(N)\hookrightarrow\operatorname{Ind}^G_H(I)\) and \(\operatorname{Ind}^G_H(I)\) is an injective \(G\)-module. Hence \(n>0\) implies \(\operatorname{H}^n(G,\operatorname{Ind}^G_H(I))=0\), proving effaceability.

The idea for homology is similar and uses the coeffaceability of homological \(\delta\)-functors. The required degree-zero isomorphism \(N_H\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}(\operatorname{ind}^G_H(N))_G\) also comes from Corollary reference.

The second method works in the derived category. For cohomology, we again start from the canonical isomorphism \[\underbracket{\operatorname{Hom}_G(\Bbbk,\operatorname{Ind}^G_H(\cdot))}_{ \simeq\operatorname{Ind}^G_H(\cdot)^G} \simeq \underbracket{\operatorname{Hom}_H(\Bbbk,\cdot)}_{\simeq(\cdot)^H} :H\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\to\Bbbk\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}.\] Both sides are left-exact functors. Since \(\operatorname{Ind}^G_H\) preserves injective objects, taking right-derived functors in Theorem reference (iii) gives \[\begin{equation*} \operatorname{RHom}_G(\Bbbk,\mathrm{R}\operatorname{Ind}^G_H(\cdot)) \simeq\operatorname{RHom}_H(\Bbbk,\cdot). \end{equation*}\]

But \(\operatorname{Ind}^G_H\) is exact, so \(\mathrm{R}\operatorname{Ind}^G_H(\cdot)\) is determined by the universal property of localization and may still be denoted by \(\operatorname{Ind}^G_H\). Thus at the level of derived categories there is an isomorphism of triangulated functors \[\operatorname{RHom}_G(\Bbbk,\operatorname{Ind}^G_H(\cdot)) \simeq\operatorname{RHom}_H(\Bbbk,\cdot).\] Taking \(\operatorname{H}^n\) on both sides gives the desired result.

The idea for homology is similar; the key is the isomorphism \[\Bbbk\ensuremath{\underset{{\Bbbk[G]}}{\overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes}}} \left(\Bbbk[G]\ensuremath{\underset{{\Bbbk[H]}}{\overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes}}}(\cdot)\right) \simeq\Bbbk\ensuremath{\underset{{\Bbbk[H]}}{\overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes}}}(\cdot).\] This is also a special case of Example reference or of Proposition reference on the associativity constraint. Since \(\operatorname{ind}^G_H\) is exact, \(\Bbbk[G]\ensuremath{\underset{{\Bbbk[H]}}{\overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes}}}(\cdot)\) may also be replaced by \(\Bbbk[G]\ensuremath{\underset{\Bbbk[H]}{\otimes}}(\cdot)\); the remaining steps are the same.

Notice that if \(\operatorname{Res}^G_H\) is interpreted as \(\Bbbk[G]\ensuremath{\underset{\Bbbk[G]}{\otimes}}(\cdot)\) according to equation, then, since \(\operatorname{Res}^G_H\Bbbk=\Bbbk\), the isomorphism \(\operatorname{RHom}_G(\Bbbk,\mathrm{R}\operatorname{Ind}^G_H(\cdot)) \simeq\operatorname{RHom}_H(\Bbbk,\cdot)\) reduces to the adjunction between \(\operatorname{RHom}\) and \(\ensuremath{\underset{}{\overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes}}}\) (Theorem reference). Group cohomology and homology can be described concretely through the standard complex and the standard chain complex of Propositions reference and reference. We want to make the isomorphisms in Theorem reference explicit in terms of these complexes. There is no essential difficulty. To distinguish the group, for every group \(H\) write the complex of \(H\)-modules \(\mathsf{L}\) from Definition reference as \(\mathsf{L}^H\); it gives a free resolution \(\mathsf{L}^H\to\Bbbk\).

Lemma. Let \(\varphi:H\to G\) be a group homomorphism. The corresponding homomorphism \(H^{n+1}\to G^{n+1}\) induces a quasi-isomorphism of complexes \(\mathsf{L}^H\to\varphi^*(\mathsf{L}^G)\) whose composite with \(\varphi^*(\mathsf{L}^G)\to\varphi^*\Bbbk=\Bbbk\) equals \(\mathsf{L}^H\to\Bbbk\).

In particular, if \(H\) is a subgroup of \(G\), there is a quasi-isomorphism \(\mathsf{L}^H\to\operatorname{Res}^G_H\mathsf{L}^G\) with the above composite property.

Proof. It follows directly from the definitions that \(\mathsf{L}^H\to\varphi^*(\mathsf{L}^G)\) is a morphism of complexes; the assertion about its composite is equally clear. Since \(\varphi^*\) is exact, while \(\mathsf{L}^G\to\Bbbk\) and \(\mathsf{L}^H\to\Bbbk\) are both quasi-isomorphisms, \(\mathsf{L}^H\to\varphi^*(\mathsf{L}^G)\) is a quasi-isomorphism as well.

Proposition. Let \(H\) be a subgroup of \(G\) and \(N\) an \(H\)-module. Identify \(\operatorname{H}^n(G,\operatorname{Ind}^G_H(N))\) (or \(\operatorname{H}^n(H,N)\)) with the \(\operatorname{H}^n\) of the standard complex \(C(G,\operatorname{Ind}^G_H(N))\) (or \(C(H,N)\)), as in Proposition reference. Then the isomorphism \[\operatorname{H}^n\left(G,\operatorname{Ind}^G_H(N)\right)\simeq\operatorname{H}^n(H,N), \qquad n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}_{\geq0},\] is induced by the morphism of complexes \[\begin{align*} C^m(G,\operatorname{Ind}^G_H(N))&\to C^m(H,N),\\ [f:G^m\to\operatorname{Ind}^G_H(N)]&\mapsto [(h_1,\ldots,h_m)\mapsto f(h_1,\ldots,h_m)(1_G)]\\ &\quad=(f|_{H^m})(\cdot)(1_G), \end{align*}\] where \(h_1,\ldots,h_m\in H\).

Proof. Again there are two methods. First, verify that the displayed maps \(C^m(G,\operatorname{Ind}^G_H(N))\to C^m(H,N)\) do indeed form a morphism of complexes. Because \(\operatorname{Ind}^G_H\) is exact, as \(N\) varies these maps induce a morphism between cohomological \(\delta\)-functors. In degree zero, this map is clearly the canonical isomorphism \(\operatorname{Ind}^G_H(N)^G\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}N^H\), \(\varphi\mapsto\varphi(1_G)\). We already know that \(\operatorname{H}^n(G,\operatorname{Ind}^G_H(\cdot))\) is a universal cohomological \(\delta\)-functor (Theorem reference). Thus the above morphism is unique and must agree with the isomorphism \(\operatorname{H}^n(G,\operatorname{Ind}^G_H(N))\simeq\operatorname{H}^n(H,N)\) in that theorem.

For the second method, let \(M\) (respectively, \(N\)) be a bounded-below complex of \(G\)-modules (respectively, \(H\)-modules). Extend the functors \(\operatorname{Ind}^G_H\) and \(\operatorname{Res}^G_H\) degreewise to complexes, keeping the same notation. The adjunction of Proposition reference lifts to \(\operatorname{Hom}\) complexes:

\[\operatorname{Hom}^\bullet_H(\operatorname{Res}^G_HM,N) \simeq\operatorname{Hom}^\bullet_G(M,\operatorname{Ind}^G_H(N)).\] A direct verification is not difficult; this can also be understood as the adjunction between \(\operatorname{Hom}^\bullet\) and \(\otimes\) described earlier (Proposition reference).

Now let \(N\) be an \(H\)-module and take an injective resolution \(\iota:N\to I\). Then \(\operatorname{Ind}^G_H(N)\to\operatorname{Ind}^G_H(I)\) is still an injective resolution, and naturality of the \(\operatorname{Hom}\) complexes gives the following commutative diagram of complexes (the solid part): \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:Shapiro-explicit-diagram}{} \text{Diagram chapter6-unit-075-d001} \end{equation}\] where \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) come from the morphism in Lemma reference. Thus \(\beta\alpha\) is the familiar map \(\operatorname{Hom}^\bullet_H(\Bbbk,I)\to\operatorname{Hom}^\bullet_H(\mathsf{L}^H,I)\). The solid horizontal isomorphisms come from the adjunction, and all vertical arrows are quasi-isomorphisms.

Recall the second proof of Theorem reference. The first row of equation gives the derived-category form of \[\operatorname{H}^n(H,N)\simeq\operatorname{H}^n(G,\operatorname{Ind}^G_H(N)),\qquad n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}.\] On the other hand, the substance of Proposition reference is the isomorphisms of complexes \[\operatorname{Hom}^\bullet_H(\mathsf{L}^H,N)\simeq C(H,N),\qquad \operatorname{Hom}^\bullet_G(\mathsf{L}^G,\operatorname{Ind}^G_H(N)) \simeq C(G,\operatorname{Ind}^G_H(N)).\] It therefore remains only to supply the arrow \(\gamma\) in equation so that the square commutes, and to describe it. Since \(\iota\) is monic, such a \(\gamma\), if it exists, is unique.

Take \(m\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}_{\geq0}\) and \(\phi\in\operatorname{Hom}^m_G(\mathsf{L}^G,\operatorname{Ind}^G_H(N))\). Inspecting the construction shows that the image of \(\phi\) in \(\operatorname{Hom}^m_H(\mathsf{L}^H,I)\) is \[(h_0,\ldots,h_m)\mapsto \iota\left(\phi(h_0,\ldots,h_m)(1_G)\right).\] Comparison with the isomorphism in the proof of Proposition reference immediately shows that \(\gamma\) can be defined as asserted.

We now state the homological version, using the notation for the standard chain complex from Proposition reference.

Proposition. Let \(H\) be a subgroup of \(G\) and \(N\) an \(H\)-module. Identify \(\operatorname{H}_n(G,\operatorname{ind}^G_H(N))\) (or \(\operatorname{H}_n(H,N)\)) with the \(\operatorname{H}_n\) of the standard chain complex \(C(G,\operatorname{ind}^G_H(N))\) (or \(C(H,N)\)), as in Proposition reference. Then the isomorphism

\[\operatorname{H}_n\left(G,\operatorname{ind}^G_H(N)\right)\simeq\operatorname{H}_n(H,N), \qquad n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}_{\geq0},\] is induced by the morphism of complexes \[\begin{align*} C_m(H,N)&\to C_m(G,\operatorname{ind}^G_H(N)),\\ (h_1|\cdots|h_m)^\dagger\otimes y &\mapsto(h_1|\cdots|h_m)^\dagger\otimes(1_G\otimes y), \end{align*}\] where \(h_1,\ldots,h_m\in H\) and \(y\in N\).

Proof. We explain only the derived-category approach. Take a projective resolution \(\pi:P\to N\) in \(H\)-modules. The commutative diagram equation from the proof of Proposition reference must be replaced by \[\text{Diagram chapter6-unit-075-d002}\] where the solid horizontal arrows come from the associativity constraint for tensor products at the level of complexes, while all vertical arrows are quasi-isomorphisms. Once again, it remains to describe \(\gamma\). The rest of the argument is similar to the cohomological version.

Change of groups

Consider a group homomorphism \(\varphi:H\to G\). In what follows, \(M\) denotes an arbitrary \(G\)-module and \(N\) an arbitrary \(H\)-module. Our first task in this section is to define two families of canonical homomorphisms \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:change-of-group-coh}{}\begin{aligned} \operatorname{H}^n(G, M) & \to \operatorname{H}^n(H, \varphi^* M), \\ \operatorname{H}_n(H, \varphi^* M) & \to \operatorname{H}_n(G, M), \end{aligned} \end{equation}\] where \(n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}_{\geq0}\). Since \(\varphi^*:G\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\to H\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\) is exact, the functors on both sides of these homomorphisms have long exact sequences; in other words, they are cohomological or homological \(\delta\)-functors. The homomorphisms above will be compatible with the long exact sequences. We present two constructions. For cohomology, the first method considers the family of functors \(B^n:=\operatorname{H}^n(H,\varphi^*(\cdot))\). There is a canonical homomorphism \[M^G \hookrightarrow M^{\varphi(H)} = (\varphi^* M)^H = B^0(M).\] Because \((\operatorname{H}^n(G,\cdot))_n\) is a universal cohomological \(\delta\)-functor, this homomorphism extends uniquely to a morphism of cohomological \(\delta\)-functors \(\operatorname{H}^n(G,\cdot)\to B^n\). The homology case is similar; the key is to use the canonical homomorphism \((\varphi^*M)_H=M_{\varphi(H)}\twoheadrightarrow M_G\). The second method works in the derived category. We introduce some related notation.

Convention. Write \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(G):=\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(G\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}})\), \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(G):=\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(G\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}})\), and \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}(G):=\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}(G\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}})\); use similar notation when one-sided or two-sided boundedness conditions are imposed. Likewise, write \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\Bbbk):=\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\Bbbk\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}})\), together with \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\Bbbk)\), \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}(\Bbbk)\), and so forth.

The functor on derived categories induced by the exact functor \(\varphi^*\) is still denoted \(\varphi^*:\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}(G)\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}(H)\). Use the customary notation \(\mathrm{R}\) and \(\mathrm{L}\) for right- and left-derived functors, respectively. We seek morphisms between triangulated functors \[\begin{align*} \mathrm{R}\left( (\cdot)^G \right) & \to \mathrm{R}\left( (\cdot)^H \right) \circ \varphi^* , \\ \mathrm{L}\left( (\cdot)_H \right) \circ \varphi^* & \to \mathrm{L}\left((\cdot)_G \right). \end{align*}\] The key is the universal property. In the cohomology case, lift the functors \((\cdot)^G\), \((\cdot)^H\), and so on to the level of complexes, with the same notation. Consider the following 2-cell diagram involving categories, functors, and morphisms of functors, all understood to be triangulated. \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:grp-pullback-2-cell}{} \text{Diagram chapter6-unit-076-d001} \end{equation}\] The \(\Rightarrow\) on the curved part comes from the previously used morphism \((\cdot)^G\to(\cdot)^H\circ\varphi^*\). The \(\stackrel{\sim}{\Rightarrow}\) on the left square comes from the exactness of \(\varphi^*\), while the \(\Rightarrow\) on the right square is part of the data of the right-derived functor \(\mathrm{R}((\cdot)^H)\). The superscript \(+\) is used here only for simplicity; the unbounded version requires the theory of §reference. Recall that 2-cell diagrams can be composed vertically, meaning that the morphisms \(\Rightarrow\) between functors are composed. By the universal property of right-derived functors (see Remark reference and the preceding discussion), there is a unique \(\Downarrow\) in the left-hand diagram below such that \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:change-of-groups-univ}{} \text{Diagram chapter6-unit-076-d002} \xlongequal{\text{vertical composite}} \;\text{the vertical composite of \href{#eqn:grp-pullback-2-cell}{equation}} \text{Diagram chapter6-unit-076-d003} \end{equation}\] The symbol in the left-hand diagram is part of the data of the right-derived functor \(\mathrm{R}\left((\cdot)^G\right)\). This uniquely determines the morphism \[\mathrm{R}\left( (\cdot)^G \right) \to \mathrm{R}\left((\cdot)^H \right) \circ \varphi^* .\] The method for homology is dual. It uses the universal property of left-derived functors and the previously used morphism \((\cdot)_H\circ\varphi^*\to(\cdot)_G\). We next give a more direct description.

Lemma. For every group homomorphism \(\varphi:H\to G\), the morphisms characterized above can be defined as follows.

  • In the cohomology case, take the composite \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:change-of-group-dec-1}{} \mathrm{R}\left( (\cdot)^G \right) \to \mathrm{R}\left( (\cdot)^H \circ \varphi^* \right) \to \mathrm{R}\left( (\cdot)^H \right) \circ \varphi^* . \end{equation}\] The first part comes from \((\cdot)^G\to(\cdot)^H\circ\varphi^*\), since a morphism of functors induces a morphism between their right-derived functors; the second part comes from Theorem reference (i).

  • The homology case is similar: take the composite \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:change-of-group-dec-2}{} \mathrm{L}\left( (\cdot)_H \right) \circ \varphi^* \to \mathrm{L} \left( (\cdot)_H \circ \varphi^* \right) \to \mathrm{L}\left( (\cdot)_G \right). \end{equation}\] The first part comes from Theorem reference (ii), and the second from \((\cdot)_H\circ\varphi^*\to(\cdot)_G\).

Proof. It suffices to discuss the cohomology case. First, for the morphisms in equation, check the following equalities of vertical composites: \[\text{Diagram chapter6-unit-076-d004} = \text{Diagram chapter6-unit-076-d005}\] and \[\text{Diagram chapter6-unit-076-d006} = \text{Diagram chapter6-unit-076-d007}\]

The first equality characterizes the induced morphism \(\mathrm{R}((\cdot)^G)\to \mathrm{R}((\cdot)^H\circ\varphi^*)\), while the second characterizes the canonical morphism in Theorem reference. Both arise from the universal property of right-derived functors; see the explanation at the beginning of §reference. Splicing these equalities together shows that the composite equation satisfies equation.

Remark. The first method, based on the universal cohomological \(\delta\)-functor property, can be combined with derived-category theory to give another concise construction for the cohomology case of equation. Recall that for every \(G\)-module \(M\) and every \(n\), there are canonical isomorphisms \[\operatorname{H}^n(G, M) \simeq \operatorname{Ext}^n_G(\Bbbk, M) \simeq \operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}(G)}(\Bbbk, M[n]), \quad \operatorname{Ext}^\bullet_G := \operatorname{Ext}^\bullet_{\Bbbk[G]};\] and likewise for \(H\)-modules. Since \(\varphi^*\Bbbk\simeq\Bbbk\) and \(\varphi^*\) is a triangulated functor, we assert that the desired canonical homomorphism is the composite \[\operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}(G)}(\Bbbk, M[n]) \xrightarrow{\text{functor} \;\varphi^*} \operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}(H)}\left( \varphi^* \Bbbk, \varphi^* (M[n])\right) \simeq \operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}(H)}\left(\Bbbk, (\varphi^* M)[n]\right).\]

To prove this, it suffices to note that when \(n=0\) the formula becomes the evident embedding \(M^G\hookrightarrow(\varphi^*M)^H\) (because \(\varphi^*\Bbbk\simeq\Bbbk\) sends \(1\) to \(1\)), and that every morphism in the composite above is compatible with the long exact sequence in the second variable of the \(\operatorname{Hom}\) functor in a triangulated category (Proposition reference).

Remark. If \(\varphi\) is the inclusion of a subgroup, then \(\varphi^*=\operatorname{Res}^G_H\) preserves injective and projective objects. By Theorem reference (iii) and (iv), the two morphisms in Lemma reference, \[\mathrm{R}\left( (\cdot)^H \circ \varphi^* \right) \to \mathrm{R}\left( (\cdot)^H \right) \circ \varphi^*, \quad \mathrm{L}\left( (\cdot)_H \right) \circ \varphi^* \to \mathrm{L} \left( (\cdot)_H \circ \varphi^* \right)\] are isomorphisms. The description of the canonical morphisms therefore simplifies further: take an injective resolution \(M\to I:=[I^0\to I^1\to\cdots]\). Then \(\operatorname{Res}^G_H(M)\to\operatorname{Res}^G_H(I)\) is also an injective resolution, and the action on \(M\) of the morphism \(\mathrm{R}\left((\cdot)^G\right)\to \mathrm{R}\left((\cdot)^H\right)\circ\operatorname{Res}^G_H\) is \[I^G \to \left( \operatorname{Res}^G_H(I)\right)^H, \quad I^G := \left[ I^{0, G} \to I^{1, G} \to \cdots \right], \;\text{and similarly}.\]

In the homology case, take a projective resolution \(P\to M\). The action on \(M\) of the morphism \(\mathrm{L}\left((\cdot)_H\right)\circ\operatorname{Res}^G_H \to\mathrm{L}\left((\cdot)_G\right)\) is \(\left(\operatorname{Res}^G_H(P)\right)_H\to P_G\).

Lemma. Let \(F\xleftarrow{\psi}G\xleftarrow{\varphi}H\) be group homomorphisms, \(L\) an \(F\)-module, and \(n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}_{\geq0}\). Then the composite \(\operatorname{H}^n(F,L)\to\operatorname{H}^n(G,\psi^*L)\to \operatorname{H}^n(H,\varphi^*\psi^*L)\) equals \(\operatorname{H}^n(F,L)\to\operatorname{H}^n(H,(\psi\varphi)^*L)\).

Likewise, the composite \(\operatorname{H}_n(H,\varphi^*\psi^*L)\to\operatorname{H}_n(G,\psi^*L)\to\operatorname{H}_n(F,L)\) equals \(\operatorname{H}_n(H,(\psi\varphi)^*L)\to\operatorname{H}_n(F,L)\).

Analogous equalities also hold at the level of derived categories.

Proof. The assertion about \(\operatorname{H}^n\) (or \(\operatorname{H}_n\)) is an immediate application of the universal cohomological (or homological) \(\delta\)-functor property and need only be checked for \(n=0\).

For the derived-category version, the assertion about \(\operatorname{H}^n\) is replaced by \[\left[ \mathrm{R}((\cdot)^F) \to \mathrm{R}((\cdot)^G) \circ \psi^* \to \mathrm{R}((\cdot)^H) \circ \varphi^* \circ \psi^* \right] \xlongequal{\text{composite}} \left[ \mathrm{R}((\cdot)^F) \to \mathrm{R}((\cdot)^H) \circ (\psi\varphi)^* \right].\] For this, it suffices to check the property equation for the left-hand side. This reduces to an interesting and straightforward exercise in the composition of 2-cells, which the reader is invited to try.

We now generalize the canonical homomorphisms equation further.

Definition. Let \(M\) be a \(G\)-module and \(N\) an \(H\)-module. Below, \(f\) is always a \(\Bbbk\)-module homomorphism and \(h\) is an arbitrary element of \(H\).

  • If \(f:M\to N\) satisfies \(f(\varphi(h)x)=hf(x)\) for \(x\in M\), then \(f\) is called \(\varphi\)-equivariant.

  • If \(f:N\to M\) satisfies \(f(hy)=\varphi(h)f(y)\) for \(y\in N\), then \(f\) is called \(\varphi\)-equivariant.

Equivariance is also equivalent to saying that \(f\) gives an \(H\)-module homomorphism \(\varphi^*M\to N\) or \(N\to\varphi^*M\). Moreover, \(\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_M:M\to\varphi^*M\) and \(\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_M:\varphi^*M\to M\) are both \(\varphi\)-equivariant.

Definition. If \(f:M\to N\) is \(\varphi\)-equivariant, define a family of canonical homomorphisms \[\operatorname{H}^n(f) := \left[ \operatorname{H}^n(G, M) \to \operatorname{H}^n(H, \varphi^* M) \to \operatorname{H}^n(H, N) \right] \;\text{as the composite};\] if \(f:N\to M\) is \(\varphi\)-equivariant, define a family of canonical homomorphisms \[\operatorname{H}_n(f) := \left[ \operatorname{H}_n(H, N) \to \operatorname{H}_n(H, \varphi^* M) \to \operatorname{H}_n(G, M) \right] \;\text{as the composite}.\]

Notice that \(f\) and \(\varphi\) point in opposite directions in the cohomology case and in the same direction in the homology case. The homomorphisms in Definition reference are compatible with long exact sequences. They include the functoriality of \(\operatorname{H}^n\) and \(\operatorname{H}_n\) (or the natural homomorphisms equation) as the special cases \(\varphi=\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_G\) (or \(f=\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_M\)). These homomorphisms also lift to the level of derived categories. Equivariant module homomorphisms can also be composed in tandem with group homomorphisms; the definition is evident.

Proposition (Functoriality with respect to equivariant homomorphisms). Consider group homomorphisms \(F\xleftarrow{\psi}G\xleftarrow{\varphi}H\) and equivariant module homomorphisms \(L\xrightarrow{g}M\xrightarrow{f}N\), where \(L\) is an \(F\)-module, \(M\) a \(G\)-module, and \(N\) an \(H\)-module. For every \(n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\), we have \(\operatorname{H}^n(fg)=\operatorname{H}^n(f)\operatorname{H}^n(g)\).

If instead the equivariant module homomorphisms point in the reverse direction, \(L\xleftarrow{g}M\xleftarrow{f}N\), then \(\operatorname{H}_n(gf)=\operatorname{H}_n(g)\operatorname{H}_n(f)\). Analogous composition equalities also hold at the level of derived categories.

Proof. It suffices to discuss the cohomology case. Fix \(n\). By Lemma reference, it is enough to prove that the diagram \[\text{Diagram chapter6-unit-076-d008}\] commutes. But each square commutes by the functoriality of equation. The derived-category version is entirely similar.

Example (Conjugation). Let \(H\lhd G\). Every \(t\in G\) induces an automorphism of \(H\), \(a_t:h\mapsto t^{-1}ht\). Now let \(M\) be a \(G\)-module and, to simplify notation, continue to write \(M\) for \(\operatorname{Res}^G_HM\). The homomorphism \(c_t:M\xrightarrow{x\mapsto tx}M\) is equivariant with respect to the oppositely directed group homomorphism \(H\xleftarrow{a_t}H\). The corresponding homomorphism \[\operatorname{H}^n(c_t): \operatorname{H}^n(H, M) \to \operatorname{H}^n(H, M),\] decomposes by definition as \(\operatorname{H}^n(H,M)\to\operatorname{H}^n(H,a_t^*M)\xrightarrow{c_t}\operatorname{H}^n(H,M)\); each part is a morphism between cohomological \(\delta\)-functors.

  • When \(n=0\), the first part is simply \(\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_M:M^H\to a_t^*(M)^H=M^H\).

  • When \(n=0\), the second part is \(c_t:M^H\to M^H\), which depends only on the coset \(tH\).

If an injective resolution \(M\to I\) of the \(G\)-module is chosen, applying \(c_t:I^{n,H}\to I^{n,H}\) termwise gives \(\operatorname{H}^n(c_t)\). When \(G=H\), the coset \(tG=G\), so \(\operatorname{H}^n(c_t)=\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}\).

The homology case is similar, but \(a_t\) must be replaced by the group automorphism \(b_t:h\mapsto tht^{-1}\), which points in the same direction as the homomorphism \(c_t\); the reader is invited to verify this.

Finally, we explain how to define the canonical homomorphisms of Definition reference explicitly using the standard complex (or standard chain complex) of Proposition reference (or Proposition reference). This makes all the operations concrete.

Proposition. Consider a group homomorphism \(\varphi:H\to G\). Let \(M\) be a \(G\)-module, \(N\) an \(H\)-module, and \(n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}_{\geq0}\). Identify \(\operatorname{H}^n(G,M)\) (or \(\operatorname{H}_n(G,M)\)) with the \(\operatorname{H}^n\) (or \(\operatorname{H}_n\)) of the standard complex \(C(G,M)\) (or chain complex \(C(G,M)\)); do the same after replacing \((G,M)\) by \((H,N)\).

  • Let the module homomorphism \(f:M\to N\) be \(\varphi\)-equivariant. Then \(\operatorname{H}^n(f)\) is induced by the morphism of complexes \[\text{Diagram chapter6-unit-076-d009}\]

  • Let the module homomorphism \(f:N\to M\) be \(\varphi\)-equivariant. Then \(\operatorname{H}_n(f)\) is induced by the morphism of chain complexes \[\text{Diagram chapter6-unit-076-d010}\]

In fact, these formulas give the morphism induced by \(f\) at the level of derived categories.

The result above also applies, with the same formulas, to the normalized standard complex \((\overline{C}^m(G,M))_m\) and normalized chain complex \((\overline{C}_m(G,M))_m\) introduced in Remark reference.

Proof. The problem divides into two parts: first the case \(f=\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_M\), which is an explicit description of the canonical homomorphisms equation, and second the case \(\varphi=\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}\). The latter is straightforward, so we discuss only the former.

Consider the cohomology case. Proposition reference gives a projective resolution of \(G\)-modules \(\mathsf{L}^G\to\Bbbk\) (or a projective resolution of \(H\)-modules \(\mathsf{L}^H\to\Bbbk\)). Now consider \[\operatorname{Hom}^\bullet_G \left( \mathsf{L}^G, \cdot\right) \xrightarrow{\varphi^*} \operatorname{Hom}^\bullet_H\left( \varphi^* (\mathsf{L}^G), \varphi^*(\cdot)\right) \to \operatorname{Hom}^\bullet_H\left(\mathsf{L}^H, \varphi^*(\cdot)\right),\] where the second part comes from the morphism \(\mathsf{L}^H\to\varphi^*(\mathsf{L}^G)\) (see Lemma reference). Denote its composite by \(\Theta\). The asserted morphism of complexes \(C(G,M)\to C(H,\varphi^*(M))\) corresponds to the action of \(\Theta\) on the \(G\)-module \(M\).

We now prove that this formula indeed gives the canonical homomorphism defined above. The first method returns to the definition equation, which comes from the universal cohomological \(\delta\)-functor property. It suffices to show that \(C(G,M)\to C(H,\varphi^*M)\) induces the embedding \(M^G\to(\varphi^*M)^H\) on \(\operatorname{H}^0\) and is compatible with long exact sequences. Details are left to the reader.

The second method works in the derived category. The functor \(\operatorname{Hom}^\bullet_H(\mathsf{L}^H,\cdot)\) preserves acyclic complexes, so it induces a functor \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^+(H)\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^+(\Bbbk)\) at the level of derived categories, with the same notation. This functor can be identified with \(\operatorname{RHom}_H(\Bbbk,\cdot)\). Thus verifying equation is equivalent to verifying the following equality of vertical composites: \[\begin{equation*} \text{Diagram chapter6-unit-076-d011} = \text{Diagram chapter6-unit-076-d012} \end{equation*}\] The symbols involving \(\operatorname{Hom}^\bullet\) come from \(\mathsf{L}^G\to\Bbbk\) and \(\mathsf{L}^H\to\Bbbk\). The complex-level version of the morphism \((\cdot)^G\to(\cdot)^H\circ\varphi^*\) is readily identified with \(\varphi^*:\operatorname{Hom}^\bullet_G(\Bbbk,\cdot)\to \operatorname{Hom}^\bullet_H(\varphi^*\Bbbk,\varphi^*(\cdot)) =\operatorname{Hom}^\bullet_H(\Bbbk,\varphi^*(\cdot))\). The desired equality therefore reduces to commutativity of the outer frame of the following diagram of complexes: \[\text{Diagram chapter6-unit-076-d013}\] It remains only to show that the curved lower part commutes, but this is exactly the content of Lemma reference. This proves the cohomology case. The homology case is similar.

Finally, the version for \(\overline{C}(G,M)\) is obtained by replacing \(\mathsf{L}^G\) and \(\mathsf{L}^H\) in the proof with \(\overline{\mathsf{L}}^G\) and \(\overline{\mathsf{L}}^H\), respectively; everything else is unchanged.

Once the explicit formulas of Proposition reference are available, the equalities \(\operatorname{H}^n(fg)=\operatorname{H}^n(f)\operatorname{H}^n(g)\) and \(\operatorname{H}_n(gf)=\operatorname{H}_n(g)\operatorname{H}_n(f)\) in Proposition reference, as well as their derived-category versions, are immediate at the level of complexes.

Group extensions revisited

To gain a more concrete understanding of the operations defined in §reference, and to continue the preliminary discussion in §reference of group extensions (Definition reference), we return to the relationship between group extensions and \(\operatorname{H}^2\). We begin from the viewpoint of group theory. In what follows, consider a \(G\)-module \(M\) and an extension \(0\to M\to E\xrightarrow{\pi}G\to1\). Such extensions have natural pullback, pushout, and addition operations, following ideas similar to those of §reference.

  • Pullback.Let \(\varphi:H\to G\) be a group homomorphism. Form the fiber product in the category of groups \[\varphi^*E:=E\ensuremath{\underset{G}{\times}}H =\{(e,h)\in E\times H:\pi(e)=\varphi(h)\}.\] The monomorphism \(M\to\varphi^*E\), \(x\mapsto(x,1_H)\), determines a group extension \(0\to M\to\varphi^*E\xrightarrow{\text{projection}}H\to1\). This gives a functor \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ext}}(G,M)\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ext}}(H,M)\). If \(\varphi\) is the inclusion of a subgroup \(H\), pullback along \(\varphi\) simply amounts to taking \(\pi^{-1}(H)\).

  • Pushout.Let \(\theta:M\to N\) be a homomorphism of \(G\)-modules. Form the fibered coproduct \[\theta_*E:=N\ensuremath{\underset{M}{\sqcup}}E =\frac{N\times E}{(y+\theta(x),e)\sim(y,xe)}, \qquad x\in M,\ y\in N,\ e\in E.\] Write \([y,e]\) for the image of \((y,e)\in N\times E\) in it. Its multiplication is \[[y_1,e_1][y_2,e_2] =[y_1+\pi(e_1)y_2,e_1e_2].\] There are natural homomorphisms \[N\xrightarrow{y\mapsto[y,1_E]}\theta_*E \xrightarrow{[y,e]\mapsto\pi(e)}G,\] which determine a group extension \(\theta_*E\). This gives a functor \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ext}}(G,M)\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ext}}(G,N)\).

  • Taking the inverse.As a special case, \(E\) can be pushed out along the \(G\)-module homomorphism \(M\xrightarrow{x\mapsto-x}M\); denote the resulting extension by \(-E\).

  • Direct sum.Given objects \(E_i\) of \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ext}}(G_i,M_i)\) for \(i=1,2\), there is an evident group extension \[0\to M_1\oplus M_2\to E_1\times E_2\to G_1\times G_2\to1,\] where \(G_1\times G_2\) acts on \(M_1\oplus M_2\) by \((g_1,g_2)(x_1,x_2)=(g_1x_1,g_2x_2)\). Denote this extension by \(E_1\oplus E_2\).

  • Baer sum.Now take objects \(E_1,E_2\) of \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ext}}(G,M)\) and form \(E_1\oplus E_2\). The addition map \(M\oplus M\to M\) is a \(G\)-module homomorphism for the action of the diagonal subgroup \(G\) of \(G\times G\). Thus first pull \(E_1\oplus E_2\) back along the diagonal inclusion \(G\hookrightarrow G\times G\), and then push out along the addition homomorphism \(M\oplus M\to M\). Denote the resulting object of \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ext}}(G,M)\) by \(E_1\dot{+}E_2\).

Pullback and pushout can be combined into a single operation. Let \(\varphi:H\to G\) be a group homomorphism and let the additive-group homomorphism \(\theta:M\to N\) be \(\varphi\)-equivariant (Definition reference). There is a corresponding functor \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ext}}(G,M)\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ext}}(H,N)\), defined by first pulling back along \(\varphi\) and then pushing out along \(\theta:\varphi^*M\to N\). The normalized standard complex \(\overline{C}(G,M)\) has parallel operations. Given \(\varphi\) and \(\theta\) as above, Proposition reference explicitly gives a morphism of complexes \(\overline{C}(G,M)\to\overline{C}(H,N)\); this defines the corresponding pullback, pushout, and inverse operations. The direct sum is defined by \[\begin{gather*} \oplus:\overline{C}^n(G_1,M_1)\oplus\overline{C}^n(G_2,M_2) \to\overline{C}^n(G_1\times G_2,M_1\oplus M_2),\\ f_1\oplus f_2:((g_{1,i},g_{2,i}))_{i=1}^n\mapsto \left(f_1(g_{1,1},\ldots,g_{1,n}), f_2(g_{2,1},\ldots,g_{2,n})\right). \end{gather*}\] As \(n\) varies, this gives a morphism of complexes \(\overline{C}(G_1,M_1)\oplus\overline{C}(G_2,M_2) \to\overline{C}(G_1\times G_2,M_1\oplus M_2)\). Following the same pattern, define the Baer sum on \(\overline{C}(G,M)\) using direct sum, pullback, and pushout. The result is simply addition in \(\overline{C}^n(G,M)\).

Proposition. Up to canonical isomorphism, pullback, pushout, taking inverses, direct sum, and Baer sum of group extensions correspond, under the equivalence of Theorem reference, to the respective operations on the complex \(\tau^{\leq2}\overline{C}(G,M)\) (or the category \(\tau^{\leq2}\overline{\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}}(G,M)\)).

Proof. Given a group extension \(0\to M\to E\to G\to1\), choose a normalized section \(s:G\to E\) and the corresponding \(f\in\overline{Z}^2(G,M)\) as in the proof of Theorem reference. Let \(\varphi:H\to G\) be a group homomorphism. A normalized section of \(\varphi^*E\) can be chosen as \[s':h\mapsto(s(\varphi(h)),h)\in E\ensuremath{\underset{G}{\times}}H.\] Then \(s'(h_1)s'(h_2)=f'(h_1,h_2)s'(h_1h_2)\), where \[f'(h_1,h_2):=f(\varphi(h_1),\varphi(h_2)),\qquad h_1,h_2\in H.\] This proves the pullback case. For pushout along a \(G\)-module homomorphism \(\theta:M\to N\), use the notation above and choose the normalized section of \(\theta_*E\) to be \[s'(g):=[0,s(g)]\in\theta_*E=N\ensuremath{\underset{M}{\sqcup}}E.\] Computing in \(\theta_*E\) gives \[\begin{align*} s'(g_1)s'(g_2)&=[0,s(g_1)][0,s(g_2)]=[0,s(g_1)s(g_2)]\\ &=[0,f(g_1,g_2)s(g_1g_2)] =[\theta f(g_1,g_2),s(g_1g_2)]\\ &=[\theta f(g_1,g_2),1_E]s'(g_1g_2). \end{align*}\] Thus the \(f'\) corresponding to \(s'\) is precisely \(\theta f\). This proves the pushout case.

The direct-sum case is checked in the same way, and the details are left to the reader. Taking inverses and forming Baer sums decompose into the operations above.

As a special case, up to canonical isomorphism, taking inverses and forming Baer sums of group extensions correspond respectively to inversion and addition in the group \(\operatorname{H}^2(G,M)\).

Definition. If \(A\) is a central subgroup of \(E\) in a group extension \(0\to A\to E\to G\to1\), the extension is called a central extension.

Given a central extension as above, suppose that for every central extension \(0\to B\to F\to G\to1\), there is a unique group homomorphism \(\varphi:E\to F\) making the following diagram commute: \[\text{Diagram chapter6-unit-077-d001}\] Then \(0\to A\to E\to G\to1\) is called a universal central extension of \(G\). If it exists, it is unique up to a unique isomorphism.

By definition, every inner automorphism of a central extension is trivial. For every additive group \(A\), define the corresponding category of central extensions by \[\ensuremath{\mathsf{CExt}}(G,A):=\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ext}}(G,A),\qquad \text{with $A$ regarded as a $G$-module with trivial action}.\]

Lemma. If a group \(G\) has a universal central extension \(0\to A\to E\xrightarrow{\pi}G\to1\), then \(G=G_{\mathrm{der}}\) and \(E=E_{\mathrm{der}}\).

Proof. Consider the split central extension \(0\to E_{\mathrm{ab}}\to E_{\mathrm{ab}}\times G\to G\to1\) of \(G\). There are homomorphisms \((0,\pi)\) and \((q,\pi)\) from the extension \(E\) to \(E_{\mathrm{ab}}\times G\), where \(q:E\to E_{\mathrm{ab}}\) is the quotient homomorphism. The uniqueness part of the universal property implies \(q=0\), that is, \(E=E_{\mathrm{der}}\). It follows at once that \(G=G_{\mathrm{der}}\).

Using the pushout construction, it is not difficult to prove that \(\varphi\) in Definition reference factors uniquely through \(E\to(\varphi|_A)_*E\). Thus the universal property can be rewritten as follows: for every central extension \(0\to B\to F\to G\to1\), there is a unique group homomorphism \(\theta:A\to B\) and a unique isomorphism \(\theta_*E\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}F\) in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{CExt}}(G,B)\). Under the assumption \(G=G_{\mathrm{der}}\), the category \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{CExt}}(G,B)\) has no nontrivial automorphisms. The definition of a universal central extension can therefore be reformulated once more: for every abelian group \(B\), there is a bijection \[\text{Diagram chapter6-unit-077-d002}\] The left-hand side is a functor of \(B\). The right-hand side likewise gives a functor \(\kappa:\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ab}}\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{Set}}\), whose functoriality in \(B\) is given by pushout of extensions. Thus the existence of a universal central extension becomes the question whether \(\kappa\) is representable.

Theorem. A group \(G\) has a universal central extension if and only if \(G=G_{\mathrm{der}}\). When this condition holds, the central subgroup \(A\) in a universal central extension is isomorphic to \(\operatorname{H}_2(G,\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}})\).

Proof. By Lemma reference, it suffices to prove the “if” direction. Consider the functor \(\kappa\) above. Theorem reference identifies \(\kappa(B)\) with \(\operatorname{H}^2(G,B)\), while Proposition reference shows that pushout corresponds to the respective operation on \(\operatorname{H}^2(G,\cdot)\). We know that \(\operatorname{H}_1(G,\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}})\simeq G_{\mathrm{ab}}=0\) (Example reference). Taking \(n=2\) in Proposition reference therefore gives \(\operatorname{H}^2(G,B)\simeq\operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ab}}}(\operatorname{H}_2(G,\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}),B)\), naturally in \(B\). Hence \(\kappa\) is representable.

The group \(\operatorname{H}_2(G,\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}})\) is also called the Schur multiplier of \(G\). Corollary reference below is useful for computing it. In practice, the crucial matter is often an explicit description of the universal central extension; the existence criterion above is only the first step. As another application of \(\operatorname{H}^2\), we derive a result in group theory.

Theorem (Schur–Zassenhaus).

Let \(1\to A\to E\xrightarrow{\pi}G\to1\) be a group extension in which \(A\) and \(G\) are finite groups of relatively prime orders. Then the extension splits.

Proof. The first step is to handle the case in which \(A\) is abelian. Give \(A\) the \(G\)-module structure arising from the group extension. It is enough to prove that \(\operatorname{H}^2(G,A)\) is trivial. Since \(|A|\) and \(|G|\) are relatively prime, it suffices to prove the following equalities for \(k=2\): \[k\geq1\implies |A|\cdot\operatorname{H}^k(G,A)=0 =|G|\cdot\operatorname{H}^k(G,A).\]

The first equality is easy. For every \(t\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\), the endomorphism \(A\to A\) given by multiplication by \(t\) induces on every \(\operatorname{H}^k(G,A)\) the endomorphism that is likewise multiplication by \(t\); this is a simple exercise in this chapter. The second equality is another exercise in this chapter; Corollary reference below will give a complete, though somewhat circuitous, proof.

For general \(A\), our next aim is to show that \(E\) has a subgroup \(H\) of order \(|G|\). This will imply \(H\cap A=\{1\}\) and make \(\pi|_H:H\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}G\) an isomorphism, whose inverse gives a splitting of the group extension. We argue by induction on \(|E|\). We may assume without loss of generality that \(|A|>1\).

Choose a prime \(p\) dividing \(|A|\), so that \(p\nmid|G|\), and take a Sylow \(p\)-subgroup \(P\) of \(A\). Then \(P\) is also a Sylow \(p\)-subgroup of \(E\). Since \(A\lhd E\) and all Sylow \(p\)-subgroups are conjugate, all of them are contained in \(A\). Counting the Sylow \(p\)-subgroups in \(A\) and \(E\), respectively, gives \((E:N_E(P))=(A:N_A(P))\), where \(N_E\) and \(N_A\) denote normalizers; rearranging, \[(N_E(P):N_A(P))=(E:A)=|G|.\]

We have \(N_A(P)\lhd N_E(P)\). The corresponding group extension \[1\to N_A(P)\to N_E(P)\to N_E(P)/N_A(P)\to1\] still satisfies the hypotheses of the theorem. If \(N_E(P)\neq E\), the induction hypothesis gives a subgroup \(H\) of \(N_E(P)\) with \(|H|=(N_E(P):N_A(P))=|G|\), proving the assertion.

We may therefore assume that \(P\lhd E\), hence \(P\lhd A\). Consider the group extension \[1\to A/P\to E/P\to G\to1.\] By induction, there is a subgroup \(H\) of \(E\) such that \(H\supset P\) and \(|H/P|=|G|\). A basic fact of group theory says that the center \(Z:=Z_P\) of \(P\) is nontrivial. We have \(Z\lhd H\) and \((H/Z:P/Z)=(H:P)=|G|\). Applying induction again, there is a subgroup \(K\) of \(H\) such that \(K\supset Z\) and \(|K/Z|=|G|\).

We now have a group extension \(1\to Z\to K\to K/Z\to1\). Since \(Z\) is a \(p\)-group, if \(K\neq E\), induction gives a subgroup of \(K\) of order \(|K/Z|=|G|\), proving the assertion. Henceforth assume \(K=E\). Then necessarily \(H=E\), so \((H:P)=|G|\) gives \(P=A\); in this case \(Z=Z_A\lhd E\).

Finally, consider the group extension \(1\to A/Z\to E/Z\to G\to1\). We obtain a subgroup \(Q\) of \(E\) such that \(Q\supset Z\) and \(|Q/Z|=|G|\). If \(A\) is nonabelian, then \(Z\neq A\) and \(Q\neq E\); considering the group extension \(1\to Z\to Q\to Q/Z\to1\) yields a subgroup of \(Q\) of order \(|G|\). If \(A\) is abelian, the problem was already solved at the beginning of the proof.

If \(A\) is abelian, all splittings of the extension \(E\) in Theorem reference are conjugate by \(A\). Indeed, specifying a splitting is equivalent to specifying an isomorphism of group extensions \(A\rtimes G\simeq E\), so any two splittings \(s,s':G\to E\) differ by an automorphism of \(E\). But Lemma reference or Theorem reference shows that the outer automorphism group of the extension is \(\operatorname{H}^1(G,A)\), and the first step in the proof of Theorem reference showed that this group is trivial. The conjugacy property of splittings extends to general \(A\), but its proof is more involved.

Examples: cyclic groups and free groups

For \(m\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}_{\geq1}\), in this section \(C_m\) denotes the cyclic group of order \(m\) with a chosen generator \(\sigma\), and its group operation is written multiplicatively. We begin with a general construction.

Definition–Proposition. Let \(\Bbbk\) be a commutative ring. If \(G\) is finite, define \[\nu=\nu^G:=\sum_{g\in G}g\in\Bbbk[G].\] If \(G\) acts on \(\Bbbk[G]\) by left multiplication, then \(\Bbbk[G]^G=\Bbbk\nu\). If \(G\) is infinite, then \(\Bbbk[G]^G=\{0\}\).

Proof. For \(e=\sum_{g\in G}a_gg\in\Bbbk[G]\), the condition \(e\in\Bbbk[G]^G\) is equivalent to all the coefficients \(a_g\) being equal.

Similarly, if \(G\) is finite, then \(\nu\) is also invariant under right multiplication by \(G\). It lies in the center of \(\Bbbk[G]\).

Convention. Let \(A\) be a \(G\)-module. For any \(e,e'\in\Bbbk[G]\), write \[A^{e=e'}:=\{a\in A:ea=e'a\}.\]

We now consider group cohomology with coefficients in \(\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\). The group algebra \(\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}[C_m]\) is commutative, and writing \(1:=1_{C_m}\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}[C_m]\) causes no confusion. Clearly \(A^{C_m}=A^{\sigma=1}\) for every \(C_m\)-module \(A\). In this case, \[\begin{equation*} \nu=1+\sigma+\cdots+\sigma^{m-1}\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}[C_m], \end{equation*}\] and the equality \((\sigma-1)\nu=\sigma^m-1=0\) in \(\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}[C_m]\) implies \[\nu A\subset A^{\sigma=1},\qquad (\sigma-1)A\subset A^{\nu=0}.\] We now show that, in the special case \(A=\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}[C_m]\), both inclusions above are equalities.

Lemma. Write \(\mathfrak{I}\subset\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}[C_m]\) for the augmentation ideal of Remark reference. We have \[\begin{align*} \nu\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}[C_m]&=\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}[C_m]^{\sigma=1}=\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\nu,\\ (\sigma-1)\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}[C_m]&=\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}[C_m]^{\nu=0}=\mathfrak{I}. \end{align*}\]

Proof. For the first part, we have already shown that \(\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}[C_m]^{\sigma=1}=\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}[C_m]^{C_m}=\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\nu\). Since \(\nu\sigma^k=\nu=\sigma^k\nu\) for every \(k\), we have \(\nu\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}[C_m]=\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\nu\).

For the second part, take \(e=\sum_{k\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}/m\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}}e_k\sigma^k\). Then \(\nu e=(\sum_{k\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}/m\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}}e_k)\nu\) is zero if and only if \(\sum_{k\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}/m\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}}e_k=0\), which is equivalent to \(e\in\mathfrak{I}\). This gives the second equality. Moreover, \(\sigma^k-1=(\sigma-1)(1+\cdots+\sigma^{k-1})\) implies \(\mathfrak{I}\subset(\sigma-1)\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}[C_m]\), so the first equality holds as well.

Lemma. The trivial \(C_m\)-module \(\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\) has a free resolution \[\cdots\xrightarrow{\nu}\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}[C_m]\xrightarrow{\sigma-1}\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}[C_m] \xrightarrow{\nu}\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}[C_m]\xrightarrow{\sigma-1}\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}[C_m] \to\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\to0,\] where \(\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}[C_m]\twoheadrightarrow\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\) is the augmentation homomorphism and the remaining arrows repeat with period \(2\).

Proof. Lemma reference gives short exact sequences \[\begin{gather*} 0\to\mathfrak{I}\to\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}[C_m]\xrightarrow{\nu}\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\nu\to0,\\ 0\to\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\nu\to\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}[C_m]\xrightarrow{\sigma-1}\mathfrak{I}\to0. \end{gather*}\] In addition, there is an isomorphism \(\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\nu\xrightarrow[\sim]{\nu\mapsto1}\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\). Splicing the two sequences alternately gives the asserted resolution.

Proposition.

Let \(A\) be a \(C_m\)-module and \(n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}_{\geq0}\). There are canonical isomorphisms \[\begin{align*} \operatorname{H}^n(C_m,A)&\simeq \begin{cases} A^{\sigma=1},&n=0,\\ A^{\nu=0}/(\sigma-1)A,&n>0\ \text{odd},\\ A^{\sigma=1}/\nu A,&n>0\ \text{even}, \end{cases}\\ \operatorname{H}_n(C_m,A)&\simeq \begin{cases} A/(\sigma-1)A,&n=0,\\ A^{\sigma=1}/\nu A,&n>0\ \text{odd},\\ A^{\nu=0}/(\sigma-1)A,&n>0\ \text{even}. \end{cases} \end{align*}\]

Proof. By Lemma reference, the cohomology and homology of \(A\) are computed, respectively, by the one-sided, 2-periodic cochain and chain complexes \[\begin{gather*} 0\to\underbracket{A}_{\text{degree }0} \xrightarrow{\sigma-1}\underbracket{A}_{\text{degree }1} \xrightarrow{\nu}A\xrightarrow{\sigma-1}\cdots,\\ \cdots\xrightarrow{\sigma-1}A\xrightarrow{\nu} \underbracket{A}_{\text{degree }1}\xrightarrow{\sigma-1} \underbracket{A}_{\text{degree }0}\to0. \end{gather*}\]

We next study the homology and cohomology of free groups [Li1], with the infinite cyclic group \(\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\) as the simplest special case. Write the free group on a set \(X\) as \(G:=\mathbf{F}(X)\). We first describe the structure of the augmentation ideal \(\mathfrak{I}\subset\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}[G]\).

Lemma. Let \(X\) be a set and \(G:=\mathbf{F}(X)\). Then \(\mathfrak{I}\) is the free left \(\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}[G]\)-module with basis \(\{x-1_G:x\in X\}\).

Proof. Write \(X-1_G:=\{x-1_G:x\in X\}\subset\mathfrak{I}\). We first show that this set generates the left \(\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}[G]\)-module \(\mathfrak{I}\). For every \(x\in X\), write \(G(x)\) (respectively, \(G(x^{-1})\)) for the set of elements of \(G\) whose reduced expression ends in \(x\) (respectively, \(x^{-1}\)). Then \(G\smallsetminus\{1_G\}\) is the disjoint union of all the \(G(x)\) and \(G(x^{-1})\) as \(x\) ranges over \(X\). We know that \(\{h-1_G:h\in G,\ h\neq1_G\}\) is a \(\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\)-basis of \(\mathfrak{I}\), and \[\begin{align*} gx\in G(x)&\implies gx-1_G=g(x-1_G)+(g-1_G),\\ &\ell(gx)=\ell(g)+1,\\ gx^{-1}\in G(x^{-1})&\implies gx^{-1}-1_G=-(gx^{-1})(x-1_G)+(g-1_G),\\ &\ell(gx^{-1})=\ell(g)+1. \end{align*}\] Induction on length shows that \(X-1_G\) generates \(\mathfrak{I}\).

To show that \(X-1_G\) is a basis, take an arbitrary \(G\)-module \(A\) and a map \(\varphi:X-1_G\to A\). We claim that there is a \(G\)-module homomorphism \(\widetilde{\varphi}:\mathfrak{I}\to A\) making the following diagram commute: \[\text{Diagram chapter6-unit-078-d001}\] Since \(X-1_G\) generates \(\mathfrak{I}\), the homomorphism \(\widetilde{\varphi}\) in this diagram is automatically unique. It therefore suffices to prove the universal property of the free module.

Use the \(G\)-module structure on \(A\) to form the semidirect product \(E:=A\rtimes G\). Consider the map of sets \(X\to E\) sending \(x\) to \((\varphi(x-1_G),x)\). The universal property of the free group extends this map uniquely to a group homomorphism \(\Phi:G\to E\). Looking at the second coordinate shows that the composite \(G\xrightarrow{\Phi}E\xrightarrow{\text{projection}}G\) is \(\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_G\). Hence Proposition reference gives a crossed homomorphism \(\psi:G\to A\) such that \(\Phi(g)=(\psi(g),g)\). By Proposition reference, the crossed homomorphism \(\psi\) corresponds to a \(G\)-module homomorphism \(\widetilde{\varphi}:\mathfrak{I}\to A\) satisfying \(\widetilde{\varphi}(g-1_G)=\psi(g)\). Therefore \[\widetilde{\varphi}(x-1_G)=\psi(x)=\varphi(x-1_G), \qquad x\in X.\] This proves the assertion.

Proposition. Let \(X\) be a set and \(G:=\mathbf{F}(X)\). The short exact sequence from the augmentation homomorphism, \(0\to\mathfrak{I}\to\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}[G]\to\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\to0\), is a free resolution of the trivial \(G\)-module \(\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\). Consequently:

  1. for every \(G\)-module \(A\), \[n\geq2\implies\operatorname{H}^n(G,A)=0=\operatorname{H}_n(G,A);\]

  2. if \(A\) is an abelian group with trivial \(G\)-action, then \(\operatorname{H}^1(G,A)\simeq A^X\) and \(\operatorname{H}_1(G,A)\simeq A^{\oplus X}\).

Proof. The first part and assertion (i) follow immediately from Lemma reference. Assertion (ii) can be read off from the free resolution and the description of \(\mathfrak{I}\) in Lemma reference; the reader is invited to verify it.

Definition. For a group \(G\), define the following elements of \(\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}_{\geq0}\sqcup\{\infty\}\): \[\begin{align*} \mathrm{cd}(G)&:=\sup\{n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}_{\geq0}:\exists M\in\operatorname{Ob}(G\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}), \ \operatorname{H}^n(G,M)\neq0\},\\ \mathrm{hd}(G)&:=\sup\{n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}_{\geq0}:\exists M\in\operatorname{Ob}(G\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}), \ \operatorname{H}_n(G,M)\neq0\}. \end{align*}\] The quantity \(\mathrm{cd}(G)\) (respectively, \(\mathrm{hd}(G)\)) is called the cohomological dimension (respectively, homological dimension) of \(G\).

By Proposition reference, the above \(\mathrm{cd}(G)\) (respectively, \(\mathrm{hd}(G)\)) also equals the projective dimension (respectively, \(\operatorname{Tor}\)-dimension) of the trivial \(G\)-module \(\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\). See Example reference and Proposition reference.

Corollary. If \(G\) is a nontrivial free group, then \(\mathrm{cd}(G)=\mathrm{hd}(G)=1\).

For cohomology, the converse of the result above also holds: \(\mathrm{cd}(G)=1\) implies that \(G\) is a free group. This is known as the Stallings–Swan theorem [Sw69].

Finite-index subgroups

In this section, with a commutative ring \(\Bbbk\) fixed, we consider a group \(G\) and its subgroup \(H\). Our aim is to discuss some special phenomena that occur when the index \((G:H)\) is finite. Definition reference defines the induced \(G\)-modules \(\operatorname{Ind}^G_H(N)\) and \(\operatorname{ind}^G_H(N)\) for every \(H\)-module \(N\). Our first step in this section is to realize them as certain spaces of maps; at this stage, \((G:H)\) need not be finite. For every \(\Bbbk\)-module \(V\), give the set of maps \(\{f:G\to V\}\) the following \(G\)-module structure. Its \(\Bbbk\)-module structure comes from pointwise operations on maps, while the \(G\)-action is \[(g f)(x) = f(xg), \quad f: G \to V, \; g, x \in G.\] For every map \(f:G\to V\), write \(\operatorname{Supp}(f):=\{x\in G:f(x)\neq0\}\). To make the statement convenient, choose representatives \((g_i)_{i\in I}\) for the coset decompositions such that 1 \[G = \bigsqcup_{i \in I} g_i H = \bigsqcup_{i \in I} Hg_i^{-1}.\]

Lemma (Induced modules as spaces of maps). There are canonical isomorphisms of \(G\)-modules as follows. \[\begin{equation*} \begin{gathered} \hypertarget{o014.li2.chapter6.finite-index-subgroups.g001}{} \text{Diagram chapter6-unit-079-d001} \\ \hypertarget{o014.li2.chapter6.finite-index-subgroups.g002}{} \text{Diagram chapter6-unit-079-d002} \end{gathered} \end{equation*}\] where \(g\in G\), \(y\in N\), and \(i\in I\). The right-hand sides of the isomorphisms are given the \(G\)-module structure discussed above. These maps do not depend on the choice of representatives \(g_i\).

Proof. Verify directly that all the maps are well-defined, \(G\)-equivariant, mutually inverse, and independent of the choice of representatives.

The isomorphisms of Proposition reference are easily rewritten using the spaces of maps above. For example, \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:Ind-as-mappings}{} \text{Diagram chapter6-unit-079-d003} \end{equation}\]

Corollary. For every \(H\)-module \(N\), \(\operatorname{ind}^G_H(N)\) embeds canonically as a \(G\)-submodule of \(\operatorname{Ind}^G_H(N)\). If \((G:H)\) is finite, the two are equal.

Proof. The \(G\)-modules on the right-hand sides of Lemma reference have an evident inclusion. If \((G:H)\) is finite, every map \(f:G\to N\) has \(H\backslash\operatorname{Supp}(f)\) finite.

We next define corestriction maps under the assumption that \((G:H)\) is finite. To simplify notation, for a \(G\)-module \(M\) we write the \(H\)-module \(\operatorname{Res}^G_H(M)\) simply as \(M\) below.

  • The family of canonical homomorphisms in equation, with \(\varphi\) taken to be the inclusion \(H\hookrightarrow G\), is called restriction and is denoted by \[\mathrm{res}^n: \operatorname{H}^n(G, M) \to \operatorname{H}^n(H, M), \quad n \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}_{\geq 0}.\]

  • Likewise, in the homology case there is a canonical homomorphism in the opposite direction, \[\mathrm{res}_n: \operatorname{H}_n(H, M) \to \operatorname{H}_n(G, M), \quad n \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}_{\geq 0}.\]

When \(\mathrm{res}^n\) is described through the standard cochain complex by Proposition reference, its effect is simply to restrict a map \(G^n\to M\) to \(H^n\), whence the name. Section reference has already lifted these operations to the derived category.

Definition. Assume \((G:H)\) is finite. For every \(G\)-module \(M\), define the following \(\Bbbk\)-module homomorphisms: \[\text{Diagram chapter6-unit-079-d004}\] where \(g\in G\) is any representative of the coset \(\bar g\). Both homomorphisms are functorial in \(M\).

In the first row of the definition, \(gx\) clearly depends only on the coset \(\bar g=gH\). The second row requires a little explanation. For a given \(x\in M\), the image of \(gx\) in \(M_H\) depends only on the coset \(Hg\). Therefore, for every coset \(t\in H\backslash G\), we can choose an arbitrary representative \(\theta(t)\in G\) and sum the images of \(\theta(t)x\) as \(t\) ranges over \(H\backslash G\). If \(x\) is replaced by \(g'x\), with \(g'\in G\), then \((\theta(t)g')_{t\in H\backslash G}\) is still a family of representatives ranging over \(H\backslash G\), and hence \[\sum_t (\theta(t) g' x\;\text{viewed in the quotient}) = \sum_t (\theta(t) x\;\text{viewed in the quotient}).\] Thus \(\nu_{G|H}\) is well-defined at the level of \(M_G\).

Definition–Proposition. Assume \((G:H)\) is finite and let \(M\) be a \(G\)-module.

  1. There is a family of canonical homomorphisms \[\mathrm{cor}^n: \operatorname{H}^n(H, M) \to \operatorname{H}^n(G, M), \quad n \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}_{\geq 0},\] compatible with long exact sequences and giving \(\nu^{G|H}:M^H\to M^G\) in degree \(0\).
