  2. Likewise, there is a family of canonical homomorphisms compatible with long exact sequences, \[\mathrm{cor}_n: \operatorname{H}_n(G, M) \to \operatorname{H}_n(H, M),\] giving \(\nu_{G|H}:M_G\to M_H\) in degree \(0\).

Both families of homomorphisms are called corestriction, since they point in the direction opposite to restriction2.

Proof. First consider cohomology. We give two explanations. For the first, \(\operatorname{Res}^G_H:G\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\to H\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\) is an exact functor preserving injective objects. Consequently, \(M\mapsto\operatorname{H}^n(H,M)\) is the \(n\)th right-derived functor of \(M\mapsto M^H\), for \(n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}_{\geq0}\). Functoriality of \(\nu^{G|H}\) therefore makes it induce a morphism of cohomological \(\delta\)-functors \(\operatorname{H}^n(H,\cdot)\to\operatorname{H}^n(G,\cdot)\).

The second explanation involves the derived category. The argument above is easily upgraded to the derived-category level, but here we give another viewpoint based on adjunction. First, we assert that the adjunction between \(\operatorname{ind}^G_H\) and \(\operatorname{Res}^G_H\) lifts to the \(\operatorname{RHom}\) level, giving \[\operatorname{RHom}_G\left(\operatorname{ind}^G_H(\Bbbk), M\right) \simeq \operatorname{RHom}_H(\Bbbk, M).\] A similar idea appeared in the proof of Theorem reference. The key is to interpret \(\operatorname{ind}^G_H\) as the change-of-rings functor \(\Bbbk[H]\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\to\Bbbk[G]\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\) induced by \(\Bbbk[H]\to\Bbbk[G]\), note that it is exact (Proposition reference), and then apply Example reference.

Furthermore, the assumption that \((G:H)\) is finite, together with Corollary reference, gives \[\operatorname{RHom}_G\left(\operatorname{ind}^G_H(\Bbbk), M\right) \simeq \operatorname{RHom}_G\left( \operatorname{Ind}^G_H(\Bbbk), M \right) \to \operatorname{RHom}_G(\Bbbk, M),\] where the last part comes from \(\Bbbk\to\operatorname{Ind}^G_H(\Bbbk)\). This is the unit of the adjoint pair \((\operatorname{Res}^G_H,\operatorname{Ind}^G_H)\) evaluated at \(\Bbbk\), and it can also be described more concretely using Lemma reference: an element \(t\in\Bbbk\) is sent to the corresponding constant map \(G\to\Bbbk\).

This yields a canonical morphism \(\operatorname{RHom}_H(\Bbbk,M)\to\operatorname{RHom}_G(\Bbbk,M)\). Taking \(\operatorname{H}^n\) on both sides gives the desired result. Determining its behavior for \(n=0\) amounts to replacing \(\operatorname{RHom}\) by \(\operatorname{Hom}\) in the operations above. More explicitly, if \(\operatorname{ind}^G_H\subset\operatorname{Ind}^G_H\) is realized as spaces of maps and the adjunction isomorphisms are described using equation, then \[\text{Diagram chapter6-unit-079-d005}\] 3 The composite above is plainly \(\nu^{G|H}:M^H\to M^G\). This proves the assertion.

Proposition. Assume \((G:H)\) is finite. For every \(G\)-module \(M\) and \(n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}_{\geq0}\), the composites of homomorphisms \[\begin{gather*} \operatorname{H}^n(G, M) \xrightarrow{\mathrm{res}^n} \operatorname{H}^n(H, M) \xrightarrow{\mathrm{cor}^n} \operatorname{H}^n(G, M), \\ \operatorname{H}_n(G, M) \xrightarrow{\mathrm{cor}_n} \operatorname{H}_n(H, M) \xrightarrow{\mathrm{res}_n} \operatorname{H}_n(G, M) \end{gather*}\] are both the endomorphism given by multiplication by \((G:H)\).

Proof. First consider the case \(n=0\). In cohomology the map is \(M^G\hookrightarrow M^H\xrightarrow{\nu^{G|H}}M^G\), which plainly sends \(x\in M^G\) to \((G:H)x\). In homology the map is \(M_G\xrightarrow{\nu_{G|H}}M_H\twoheadrightarrow M_G\); a direct check gives the same conclusion.

Now suppose \(n\geq1\). In the cohomology case, choose an embedding \(M\hookrightarrow I\) with \(I\) an injective \(G\)-module; then \(I\) is also an injective \(H\)-module. Write \(L:=I/M\). Functoriality of restriction and corestriction, together with the long exact sequences, gives a commutative diagram with exact columns: \[\text{Diagram chapter6-unit-079-d006}\] By induction, the composite in the first row is multiplication by \((G:H)\). Since all the vertical arrows are surjective, the same is true of the composite in the second row. The homology argument is similar: take an epimorphism \(P\twoheadrightarrow M\) with \(P\) a projective \(G\)-module.

Notice that the case \(n=0\) also lets us conclude at the derived-category level that the composite \(\operatorname{RHom}_G(\Bbbk,M)\to\operatorname{RHom}_H(\Bbbk,M)\to\operatorname{RHom}_G(\Bbbk,M)\) is \((G:H)\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}\). The homology case is analogous.

Corollary. Let \(|G|=m\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}_{\geq1}\). For every \(G\)-module \(M\), we have \[n \geq 1 \implies m \operatorname{H}^n(G, M) = m \operatorname{H}_n(G, M) = \{0\}.\]

Proof. In Proposition reference, take \(H=\{1\}\) and use the elementary fact that if \(n\geq1\), then \(\operatorname{H}^n(\{1\},M)\) and \(\operatorname{H}_n(\{1\},M)\) both vanish.

For the rest of the section, take \(\Bbbk=\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\) and regard \(\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\) as a trivial \(G\)-module. Example reference gives canonical isomorphisms \(\operatorname{H}_1(G,\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}})\simeq G_{\mathrm{ab}}\) and \(\operatorname{H}_1(H,\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}})\simeq H_{\mathrm{ab}}\). If \((G:H)\) is finite, then \(\mathrm{cor}_1:\operatorname{H}_1(G,\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}})\to\operatorname{H}_1(H,\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}})\) corresponds to the group homomorphism \[\begin{equation*} \mathrm{Ver}_{G|H}: G_{\mathrm{ab}} \to H_{\mathrm{ab}}, \end{equation*}\] called the transfer homomorphism from \(G\) to \(H\) (German: die Verlagerung). The key is to give a group-theoretic description of \(\mathrm{Ver}_{G|H}\). Recall that \(G\) acts on the right of \(H\backslash G\) by right multiplication.

Proposition. Assume \((G:H)\) is finite. Choose a representative in \(G\) for every coset in \(H\backslash G\), expressed as a map \(\theta:H\backslash G\to G\). For every \(s\in G\) and \(t\in H\backslash G\), there is a unique \(h_{t,s}\in H\) such that \[\theta(t)s = h_{t, s} \theta(ts).\] The transfer homomorphism defined above can be described by \[\mathrm{Ver}_{G|H}(\underbracket{s\;\text{as a class}}_{\in G_{\mathrm{ab}}}) = \prod_{t \in H \backslash G} \underbracket{h_{t, s}\;\text{as a class}}_{\in H_{\mathrm{ab}}}.\]

Proof. Take the short exact sequence of \(G\)-modules \(0\to\mathfrak{I}_G\to\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}[G]\to\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\to0\), where \(\mathfrak{I}_G\) is the augmentation ideal of \(\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}[G]\) (Example reference). The inclusion \(\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}[H]\subset\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}[G]\) gives an \(H\)-submodule \(\mathfrak{I}_H\subset\mathfrak{I}_G\). Since \(\mathrm{cor}_n\) is compatible with long exact sequences, and \(\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}[G]\) is projective both as a \(G\)-module and as an \(H\)-module, we obtain the commutative diagram \[\text{Diagram chapter6-unit-079-d007}\]

We check the required equality in \(\mathfrak{I}_G/\mathfrak{I}_H\mathfrak{I}_G\). The end of Example reference shows that the image of \(s\in G\) in \(G_{\mathrm{ab}}\) corresponds through the first row to the image of \(1_G-s\) in \(\mathfrak{I}_G/\mathfrak{I}_G^2\). Applying \(\nu_{G|H}\) to it gives \[\begin{align*} \sum_{t \in H \backslash G} \theta(t)(1_G - s) & = \sum_t (\theta(t) - \theta(t)s) = \sum_t (\theta(t) - h_{t, s}\theta(ts)) \\ & = \sum_t \theta(t) - \sum_t h_{t, s} \theta(ts) \\ & = \sum_t \theta(ts) - \sum_t h_{t, s} \theta(ts) \;\in \mathfrak{I}_G \end{align*}\] in \(\mathfrak{I}_G/\mathfrak{I}_H\mathfrak{I}_G\). The last equality holds because, as \(t\) varies, both \(t\) and \(ts\) range over \(H\backslash G\). The final expression is also equal to \(\sum_t(1_G-h_{t,s})\theta(ts)\).

Finally, observe that \((1_G-h_{t,s})\theta(ts)\equiv1_G-h_{t,s} \pmod{\mathfrak{I}_H\mathfrak{I}_G}\), while the right-hand side corresponds to the image of \(h_{t,s}\;\bmod\mathfrak{I}_H\) in \(\mathfrak{I}_H/\mathfrak{I}_H^2\) through the third row. This proves the assertion.

The map described above, \(s\bmod G_{\mathrm{der}}\mapsto\prod_t h_{t,s}\bmod H_{\mathrm{der}}\), is a classical construction in group theory. Having identified it with \(\mathrm{cor}_1\), we have also proved that it is independent of the choice of \(\theta\).

  1. Editorial correction: the Chinese source indexes the representatives by \(i\in H\), whereas the decompositions themselves are indexed by the set \(I\).↩︎

  2. With good reason, many sources call the corestriction homomorphism the “transfer.” This book uses the term transfer homomorphism in a narrower sense; see the discussion below.↩︎

  3. Editorial correction: the Chinese source writes \(\operatorname{Res}^G_M\) and \(\operatorname{Hom}_H(\operatorname{Ind}^G_H\Bbbk,M)\); the adjunction and module types require \(\operatorname{Res}^G_H\) and \(\operatorname{Hom}_G(\operatorname{Ind}^G_H\Bbbk,M)\), as displayed here.↩︎

The Lyndon–Hochschild–Serre spectral sequence

Throughout this section, fix a commutative ring \(\Bbbk\), a group \(G\), and a normal subgroup \(H\lhd G\). Recall the restriction functor \(\operatorname{Res}^G_H:G\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\to H\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\) and the inflation functor \(\mathrm{Infl}^G_{G/H}:G/H\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\to G\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\) from Definition reference. For every \(G\)-module \(M\), introduce the notation \[M^{H\lhd G}:=(\operatorname{Res}^G_HM)^H,\qquad M_{H\lhd G}:=(\operatorname{Res}^G_HM)_H.\] Notice that \(M^{H\lhd G}\) has an evident left \(G/H\)-action, \((gH)\cdot x:=gx\). Similarly, \(M_{H\lhd G}\) has an evident left \(G/H\)-action. This gives two functors \[(\cdot)^{H\lhd G},\ (\cdot)_{H\lhd G}: G\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\to G/H\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}.\]

Lemma. The functor \((\cdot)^{H\lhd G}\) is right adjoint to \(\mathrm{Infl}^G_{G/H}\), while \((\cdot)_{H\lhd G}\) is left adjoint to it.

Proof. This is a straightforward extension of Proposition reference; verification is left to the reader.

There are evident commutative diagrams of functors \[\text{Diagram chapter6-unit-080-d001}\quad\text{Diagram chapter6-unit-080-d002}\] The functor \((\cdot)^{H\lhd G}\) is left exact and preserves injective objects, since it has the exact left adjoint \(\mathrm{Infl}^G_{G/H}\). Similarly, \((\cdot)_{H\lhd G}\) is a right-exact functor that preserves projective objects. Theorem reference on deriving composite functors therefore gives canonical isomorphisms in the derived category \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}(\Bbbk\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}})\) (with appropriate parentheses omitted): \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:LHS-derived}{} \begin{gathered} \mathrm{R}(\cdot)^G\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}} \mathrm{R}(\cdot)^{G/H}\circ\mathrm{R}(\cdot)^{H\lhd G},\\ \mathrm{L}(\cdot)_G\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\leftarrow}} \mathrm{L}(\cdot)_{G/H}\circ\mathrm{L}(\cdot)_{H\lhd G}. \end{gathered} \end{equation}\] The derived functors \(\mathrm{R}(\cdot)^{H\lhd G}\) and \(\mathrm{L}(\cdot)_{H\lhd G}\) in these formulas are not new objects. For each of the commutative diagrams \[\text{Diagram chapter6-unit-080-d003}\quad\text{Diagram chapter6-unit-080-d004}\] derive both composites according to Theorem reference. Since \(\operatorname{Res}^G_H\) is exact and preserves both injective and projective objects (Proposition reference), while the forgetful functor is exact, that theorem gives \[\begin{gather*} \text{forgetful}\circ\mathrm{R}(\cdot)^{H\lhd G} \ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\leftarrow}}\mathrm{R}(\text{composite functor}) \ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}\mathrm{R}(\cdot)^H\circ\operatorname{Res}^G_H,\\ \text{forgetful}\circ\mathrm{L}(\cdot)_{H\lhd G} \ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}\mathrm{L}(\text{composite functor}) \ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\leftarrow}}\mathrm{L}(\cdot)_H\circ\operatorname{Res}^G_H. \end{gather*}\] In other words, after applying the forgetful functor, the right-derived functor \(\mathrm{R}(\cdot)^{H\lhd G}\) is the same as \(\mathrm{R}(\cdot)^H\), and the left-derived functor \(\mathrm{L}(\cdot)_{H\lhd G}\) is the same as \(\mathrm{L}(\cdot)_H\). It is therefore natural to write their cohomology and homology as \[\begin{align*} \mathrm{R}^n(\cdot)^{H\lhd G} &=\operatorname{H}^n(H,\cdot)\quad\text{with its $G/H$-action},\\ \mathrm{L}_n(\cdot)_{H\lhd G} &=\operatorname{H}_n(H,\cdot)\quad\text{with its $G/H$-action}. \end{align*}\] Notice that we have begun to omit the restriction functor \(\operatorname{Res}\) from the notation. These actions are easy to describe. For cohomology, let \(M\) be a \(G\)-module and \(n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}_{\geq0}\). There are at least three viewpoints on the \(G/H\)-action:

  1. Take an injective resolution \(0\to M\to I^0\to\cdots\). It is also an injective resolution of \(H\)-modules. The group \(G/H\) acts naturally on the complex \(\cdots\to I^{n,H}\to I^{n+1,H}\to\cdots\), and hence on \(\operatorname{H}^n(H,M)\). This description comes directly from the abstract construction above.

  2. The group \(G/H\) acts on the functor \((\cdot)^H:G\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\to\Bbbk\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\). The universal property of universal cohomological \(\delta\)-functors then makes it act on \(\operatorname{H}^n(H,M)\), compatibly with long exact sequences.

  3. In Example reference, every \(t\in G/H\) acts on \(\operatorname{H}^n(H,M)\) through \(\operatorname{H}^n(c_t)\).

The reader is invited to verify that these three descriptions agree. The key is to reduce their comparison to the case \(n=0\). The next important step is to extract more concrete information from equation. This involves the cohomological and homological bigraded spectral sequences of Definition reference, together with the following preparation.

Lemma. For every \(G\)-module \(M\) and every \(n\), the canonical homomorphism \(\operatorname{H}^n(G,M)\to\operatorname{H}^n(H,M)\) (see equation) factors through \(\operatorname{H}^n(H,M)^{G/H}\). The canonical homomorphism \(\operatorname{H}_n(H,M)\to\operatorname{H}_n(G,M)\) factors through \(\operatorname{H}_n(H,M)_{G/H}\).

Proof. We discuss cohomology. Take an injective resolution \(M\to I\), with \(I=[I^0\to I^1\to\cdots]\), and write \(I^H:=[I^{0,H}\to\cdots]\). Since \(I\) is also an injective resolution of \(M\) as an \(H\)-module, the inclusion \(I^G\hookrightarrow I^H\) induces \(\operatorname{H}^n(G,M)\to\operatorname{H}^n(H,M)\).

As expected, Remark reference ensures that this map is precisely the canonical homomorphism in question. Now compare it with the discussion of the \(G/H\)-action above.

Theorem (R. Lyndon, G. Hochschild–J.-P. Serre). Let \(M\) be a \(G\)-module and \(H\lhd G\).

  1. There are first-quadrant cohomological and homological spectral sequences \[\begin{align*} E_2^{p,q}&\simeq\operatorname{H}^p\left(G/H,\operatorname{H}^q(H,M)\right) \Rightarrow\operatorname{H}^{p+q}(G,M),\\ E^2_{p,q}&\simeq\operatorname{H}_p\left(G/H,\operatorname{H}_q(H,M)\right) \Rightarrow\operatorname{H}_{p+q}(G,M). \end{align*}\]

  2. Let \(n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}_{\geq1}\) and suppose that \(\operatorname{H}^i(H,M)=0\) for all \(1\leq i<n\) in the cohomological case, or \(\operatorname{H}_i(H,M)=0\) for all \(1\leq i<n\) in the homological case. Then there are, respectively, exact sequences \[\begin{equation*} \begin{split} 0\to\operatorname{H}^n(G/H,M^H)&\to\operatorname{H}^n(G,M)\to\operatorname{H}^n(H,M)^{G/H}\\ &\to\operatorname{H}^{n+1}(G/H,M^H)\to\operatorname{H}^{n+1}(G,M), \end{split} \end{equation*}\] and \[\begin{equation*} \begin{split} \operatorname{H}_{n+1}(G,M)&\to\operatorname{H}_{n+1}(G/H,M_H)\\ &\to\operatorname{H}_n(H,M)_{G/H}\to\operatorname{H}_n(G,M) \to\operatorname{H}_n(G/H,M_H)\to0. \end{split} \end{equation*}\] Notice that for \(n=1\) the hypothesis is vacuous.

  3. In the cohomological exact sequence above, every morphism other than \(\operatorname{H}^n(H,M)^{G/H}\to\operatorname{H}^{n+1}(G/H,M^H)\) comes from the equivariant homomorphism \(M^H\hookrightarrow M\) (relative to \(G/H\twoheadleftarrow G\); see Definition reference), the homomorphism \(M\xrightarrow{\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}}M\) (relative to \(G\hookleftarrow H\)), and the factorization in Lemma reference. The homological exact sequence is similar.

Proof. For (i), it suffices to express equation concretely through the Grothendieck spectral sequence of Theorem reference.

We now discuss (ii). If \(n=1\), the hypothesis is vacuous and the corresponding exact sequence is precisely the low-degree exact sequence in Theorem reference; its underlying principle is the edge computation in Remark reference. We next review and extend that argument to general \(n\). The idea is to exploit the zero terms in the spectral sequence.

It suffices to discuss the cohomological case. The hypothesis shows that the spectral sequence in (i) satisfies \[1\leq q<n\implies E_2^{p,q}=E_3^{p,q}=\cdots=E_\infty^{p,q}=0.\]

Recall that the direction of \(d_r\) is \(d_r^{p,q}:E_r^{p,q}\to E_r^{p+r,q-r+1}\) and that \(E_{r+1}^{p,q}\) is the cohomology of \(E_r^{p,q}\) with respect to \(d_r\). Every \(d\) leaving \(E_{n+1}^{n+1,0}\) (or entering \(E_{n+1}^{0,n}\)) is zero. We therefore obtain the horizontal exact sequence in the diagram \[\text{Diagram chapter6-unit-081-d001}\] The reason for the vertical isomorphisms is similar: once every \(d\) entering or leaving \(E_r^{p,q}\) is zero, there is an isomorphism \(E_r^{p,q}\simeq E_{r+1}^{p,q}\). In the same way one obtains \[\operatorname{H}^n(G/H,M^H)\simeq E_2^{n,0}\simeq\cdots \simeq E_\infty^{n,0}.\]

Next, recall that the target \(\operatorname{H}^{p+q}(G,M)\) of the spectral sequence has a finite decreasing filtration \(\cdots\supset\mathrm{F}^k\supset\mathrm{F}^{k+1}\supset\cdots\), with \(E_\infty^{p,q}\simeq\operatorname{gr}^p\operatorname{H}^{p+q}(G,M)\). At the edge of the first quadrant, this gives \[\begin{align*} E_\infty^{n+1,0}&\simeq\mathrm{F}^{n+1} \subset\operatorname{H}^{n+1}(G,M),\\ E_\infty^{0,n}&\simeq\operatorname{H}^n(G,M)/\mathrm{F}^1. \end{align*}\]

How can one determine \(\mathrm{F}^1\subset\operatorname{H}^n(G,M)\)? On the line \(p+q=n\), only \((n,0)\) and \((0,n)\) can possibly satisfy \(E_\infty^{p,q}\neq0\). Thus the filtration on \(\operatorname{H}^n(G,M)\) has the form \[0=\mathrm{F}^{n+1} \underbracket{\subset}_{E_\infty^{n,0}}\mathrm{F}^n =\cdots=\mathrm{F}^1 \underbracket{\subset}_{E_\infty^{0,n}}\mathrm{F}^0 =\operatorname{H}^n(G,M).\] Combining all the isomorphisms and exact sequences above gives the desired result.

Assertion (iii) is as expected, but the following argument is somewhat long and may be skipped. For brevity, we discuss only \(\operatorname{H}^n(G,M)\to\operatorname{H}^n(H,M)^{G/H}\); the other cases are similar or easy. Recall the construction in §reference. Take an injective resolution \(M\to I\), with \(I\) a complex of \(G\)-modules, and then take a Cartan–Eilenberg resolution \(J\) of the complex of \(G/H\)-modules \(I^H\) (Theorem reference). Regarding the complexes \(I^G\) and so forth as double complexes concentrated on the horizontal axis gives a commutative diagram of double complexes of \(\Bbbk\)-modules \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:LHS-SS-aux}{}\text{Diagram chapter6-unit-081-d002} \end{equation}\]

Following the convention of Proposition reference, write \(\operatorname{H}_{\mathrm{II}}\operatorname{H}_{\mathrm{I}}(\cdot)\) for the operation of first taking horizontal and then vertical cohomology of a double complex. Note the following points.

  • Since the horizontal cohomology \(\operatorname{H}_{\mathrm{I}}(J)\) of the Cartan–Eilenberg resolution gives an injective resolution of \(\operatorname{H}^p(I^H)\) in column \(p\) (\(p\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\)), the morphism \(I^H\to J\) induces the isomorphism \[\operatorname{H}^n(H,M)=\operatorname{H}^n(I^H) =\operatorname{H}_{\mathrm{II}}\operatorname{H}_{\mathrm{I}}(I^H)^{n,0} \ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}\operatorname{H}_{\mathrm{II}}\operatorname{H}_{\mathrm{I}}(J)^{n,0}.\]

  • Remark reference gives \(\operatorname{H}_{\mathrm{I}}(J^{G/H})\simeq\operatorname{H}_{\mathrm{I}}(J)^{G/H}\). Since \(\operatorname{H}_{\mathrm{I}}(J)\) vertically resolves each \(\operatorname{H}^p(H,M)\), while \((\cdot)^{G/H}\) is left exact, applying \(\operatorname{H}_{\mathrm{II}}\operatorname{H}_{\mathrm{I}}(\cdot)^{n,0}\) to \(J^{G/H}\hookrightarrow J\) corresponds to \[\text{the inclusion homomorphism}\qquad \operatorname{H}^n(H,M)^{G/H}\hookrightarrow\operatorname{H}^n(H,M).\]

  • We have shown that \(I^G\hookrightarrow I^H\) induces on \(\operatorname{H}^n\) (or, equivalently, on \(\operatorname{H}_{\mathrm{II}}\operatorname{H}_{\mathrm{I}}(\cdot)^{n,0}\)) the canonical homomorphism \(\operatorname{H}^n(G,M)\to\operatorname{H}^n(H,M)\).

Filter the first-quadrant double complex \(J^{G/H}\) decreasingly by the vertical coordinate (the \(p\)th step is the part with vertical coordinate \(\geq p\)). The corresponding spectral sequence is \((E_r^{p,q})_{p,q}\), where \(r=0,1,\ldots\). Write \(\operatorname{ker}(d^n)_{n,0}\) for the projection of \(\operatorname{ker}(d^n)\) in the total complex \(\operatorname{tot}(J^{G/H})\) onto the component \((n,0)\). The description of \(Z_r^{p,q}\) in Proposition reference, together with the observations above, gives \[\begin{multline} \hypertarget{eqn:LHS-SS-aux1}{} \operatorname{ker}(d^n)_{n,0}\simeq Z_\infty^{0,n} \subset\cdots\subset Z_2^{0,n}\\ \twoheadrightarrow E_2^{0,n} =\operatorname{H}_{\mathrm{II}}\operatorname{H}_{\mathrm{I}}(J^{G/H})^{n,0} \simeq\operatorname{H}^n(H,M)^{G/H}. \end{multline}\]

We now describe \(\operatorname{H}^n(G,M)\to\operatorname{H}^n(H,M)^{G/H}\). Choose a representative of an element of \(\operatorname{H}^n(G,M)\) in \(\operatorname{ker}[I^{n,G}\to I^{n+1,G}]\), map it through \(I^G\to J^{G/H}\) into \(\operatorname{ker}(d^n)_{n,0}\), and then follow equation to \(\operatorname{H}_{\mathrm{II}}\operatorname{H}_{\mathrm{I}}(J^{G/H})^{n,0}\). To take its image further in \(\operatorname{H}^n(H,M)\), apply \(\operatorname{H}_{\mathrm{II}}\operatorname{H}_{\mathrm{I}}(\cdot)^{n,0}\) to the whole diagram equation and compose along

Diagram chapter6-unit-081-d003

. If instead we follow

Diagram chapter6-unit-081-d004

and use the three observations above, the result is the canonical homomorphism \(\operatorname{H}^n(G,M)\to\operatorname{H}^n(H,M)\). This proves (iii).

Remark reference will give a canonical and perhaps more natural construction of the Lyndon–Hochschild–Serre spectral sequence. The cohomological exact sequence above is also called the inflation–restriction exact sequence, because the canonical homomorphism \(\operatorname{H}^n(G/H,M^H)\to\operatorname{H}^n(G,M)\) is commonly called the inflation homomorphism, while \(\operatorname{H}^n(G,M)\to\operatorname{H}^n(H,M)^{G/H}\) is called the restriction homomorphism. The more complicated morphisms are \[\operatorname{H}^n(H,M)^{G/H}\to\operatorname{H}^{n+1}(G/H,M^H),\qquad \operatorname{H}_{n+1}(G/H,M_H)\to\operatorname{H}_n(H,M)_{G/H}.\] They are both called transgression maps, in keeping with the transgression maps in the theory of characteristic classes. As an application, we briefly derive a formula of Hopf for computing \(\operatorname{H}_2(G,\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}})\) from a presentation of the group \(G\). Here we take \(\Bbbk=\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\) and give \(\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\) the trivial \(G\)-module structure.

Corollary (H. Hopf). Let \(G\) be a group and \(G\simeq F/R\), where \(F\) is a free group and \(R\lhd F\). Write \([F,R]\) for the subgroup of \(R\) generated by the elements \([f,r]:=frf^{-1}r^{-1}\), with \(f\in F\) and \(r\in R\). This subgroup is normal in \(R\) and \([F,R]\subset[F,F]:=F_{\mathrm{der}}\). There is an isomorphism \[\operatorname{H}_2(G,\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}})\simeq(R\cap[F,F])/[F,R].\]

Proof. Proposition reference gives \(\operatorname{H}_2(F,\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}})=0\). Thus the exact sequence in Theorem reference for \(n=1\) becomes \[0\to\operatorname{H}_2(G,\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}})\to\operatorname{H}_1(R,\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}})_G \to\operatorname{H}_1(F,\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}})\to\operatorname{H}_1(G,\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}})\to0.\] Interpreting \(\operatorname{H}_1\) through Example reference, we obtain \[0\to\operatorname{H}_2(G,\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}})\to\left(\frac{R}{[R,R]}\right)_G \to\frac{F}{[F,F]}\to\frac{G}{[G,G]}\to0.\]

The action of \(G\) on \(R/[R,R]\) is as follows. Choose a preimage \(f\in F\) of \(g\in G\); one can verify that the action of \(g\) comes from the conjugation action of \(f\) on \(R\) (exercise). For an arbitrary \(\bar r\in R/[R,R]\), choose a preimage \(r\in R\). Then \(g\bar r-\bar r\) (with the group operation written additively) is the image of \[frf^{-1}\cdot r^{-1}\in R \quad\text{(with the group operation written multiplicatively)}.\] As \(f\) and \(r\) vary, these elements generate \([F,R]\). Hence \((R/[R,R])_G\simeq R/[F,R]\); the rest is immediate.

Remark (Multiplicative structure of the Lyndon–Hochschild–Serre spectral sequence). In the cohomological case, write the spectral sequence of a \(G\)-module \(M\) as \(E_r^{p,q}(M)\). The cup-product operation to be introduced in §reference, applied to the cohomology of \(G/H\) and \(H\), equips the \(E_2\) term with a multiplicative structure \[\cup:E_2^{p_1,q_1}(M_1)\otimes E_2^{p_2,q_2}(M_2) \to E_2^{p_1+p_2,q_1+q_2}(M_1\otimes M_2),\] while the convergence target of the spectral sequence also has a cup product, applied to the group \(G\): \[\cup:\operatorname{H}^{n_1}(G,M_1)\otimes\operatorname{H}^{n_2}(G,M_2) \to\operatorname{H}^{n_1+n_2}(G,M_1\otimes M_2).\] The question is whether these structures can be defined on every page and whether \(d_r\) has good properties with respect to them, such as the Leibniz rule \[d_r(\alpha_1\cup\alpha_2) =d_r(\alpha_1)\cup\alpha_2 +(-1)^{p_1+q_1}\alpha_1\cup(d_r\alpha_2), \qquad \alpha_i\in E_r^{p_i,q_i}(M_i).\]

In their original work [HS53], Hochschild and Serre wrote down directly a canonical filtration on the normalized standard complex \(\overline{C}(G,M)\) that is compatible with the cup product defined at the level of \(\overline{C}(G,M)\). Consequently, every page inherits a multiplication with the properties above. Concretely, they use the decreasing filtration \(\overline{C}(G,M)=\mathrm{F}^0\supset\mathrm{F}^1\supset\cdots\). If \(p>n\), the degree-\(n\) term of the complex \(\mathrm{F}^p\) is \(0\); otherwise, the degree-\(n\) term of \(\mathrm{F}^p\) is \[\left\{\begin{array}{r|l} f\in\overline{C}^n(G,M) & (g_1,\ldots,g_n)\ \text{has at least }n-p+1\text{ entries in }H\\ &\implies f(g_1,\ldots,g_n)=0 \end{array}\right\}.\] The details are left as an exercise for this chapter; interested readers, or those who need them, may consult the original work.

In particular, \(\overline{C}(G,\Bbbk)\) becomes a filtered differential graded algebra, and the spectral sequence \(E_r^{p,q}(\Bbbk)\) has the corresponding multiplicative structure (Definition reference and Proposition reference). From the topological viewpoint, this is entirely unsurprising.

The cup-product operation

Let \(G\) be an arbitrary group. As usual, write \(\otimes=\otimes_{\Bbbk}\); this notation denotes both the tensor product of \(\Bbbk\)-modules and the tensor product of \(G\)-modules.

Convention. Write \(\operatorname{Ext}_G^\bullet:=\operatorname{Ext}_{\Bbbk[G]}^\bullet\) and \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}(G):=\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}(G\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}})\).

The aim of this section is to construct a cup-product operation on cohomology for arbitrary \(G\)-modules \(M_1\) and \(M_2\), \[\cup: \operatorname{H}^p(G, M_1) \otimes \operatorname{H}^q(G, M_2) \to \operatorname{H}^{p+q}(G, M_1 \otimes M_2), \quad p, q \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}_{\geq 0},\] which for \(p=q=0\) gives the evident morphism \(M_1^G\otimes M_2^G\to(M_1\otimes M_2)^G\). Reformulated in terms of \(\operatorname{Ext}_G^\bullet\), the aim is equivalently to define \[\cup: \operatorname{Ext}^p_G(\Bbbk, M_1) \otimes \operatorname{Ext}^q_G(\Bbbk, M_2) \to \operatorname{Ext}_G^{p+q}(\Bbbk, M_1 \otimes M_2).\] Recall that \(\operatorname{Ext}^p_G(\Bbbk,M_1)\simeq\operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}(G)}(\Bbbk,M_1[p])\). Our first viewpoint on the cup product is based on morphisms in the derived category. Readers interested only in concrete computations with complexes may proceed directly to Definition–Proposition reference.

Definition. Write the left-derived bifunctor of \(\otimes:G\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\times G\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\to G\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\) as \(\ensuremath{\underset{}{\overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes}}}\). This bifunctor gives \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^-(G)\) the structure of a symmetric monoidal category, with the trivial \(G\)-module \(\Bbbk\) as its unit object.

The tensor product \(\otimes\) of complexes is defined, as usual, by taking the total complex \(\operatorname{tot}_{\oplus}\). The commutativity constraint in the symmetric monoidal structure involves several signs; see Proposition reference for details. A projective \(G\)-module remains projective as a \(\Bbbk\)-module (Proposition reference, with \(H\) trivial), and is therefore also flat. If \(X\) and \(Y\) are bounded-above complexes of \(G\)-modules, and every term of \(X\) is flat as a \(\Bbbk\)-module, then \[X \otimes Y = X \ensuremath{\underset{}{\overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes}}}Y, \quad Y \otimes X = Y \ensuremath{\underset{}{\overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes}}}X;\] see Proposition reference. In particular, \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:G-mod-tensor-unit}{} \Bbbk \otimes Y = \Bbbk \ensuremath{\underset{}{\overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes}}}Y \simeq Y \simeq Y \ensuremath{\underset{}{\overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes}}}\Bbbk = Y \otimes \Bbbk. \end{equation}\]

Lemma. Let \(\varphi:H\to G\) be a group homomorphism. Continue to write the functor on derived categories induced by the exact functor \(\varphi^*\) as \(\varphi^*:\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^-(G)\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^-(H)\). Then \(\varphi^*\) is a monoidal functor with respect to \(\ensuremath{\underset{}{\overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes}}}\); see [Li1] and the remark following it. In other words, there are canonical isomorphisms satisfying all compatibility conditions, \[\varphi^*(\Bbbk) \simeq \Bbbk, \quad \varphi^* X_1 \ensuremath{\underset{}{\overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes}}}\varphi^* X_2 \simeq \varphi^* (X_1 \ensuremath{\underset{}{\overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes}}}X_2).\]

Proof. The isomorphism \(\varphi^*\Bbbk\simeq\Bbbk\) (indeed, an equality) and all its compatibilities are immediate. Furthermore, if a \(G\)-module \(M\) is flat as a \(\Bbbk\)-module, then so is \(\varphi^*M\). Since \(\ensuremath{\underset{}{\overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes}}}\) can be computed using resolutions that are flat over \(\Bbbk\), the canonical isomorphism \(\varphi^*X_1\ensuremath{\underset{}{\overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes}}}\varphi^*X_2\simeq\varphi^*(X_1\ensuremath{\underset{}{\overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes}}}X_2)\) is obtained by reducing to the case in which \(X_1\) and \(X_2\) are termwise flat over \(\Bbbk\).

We can now formulate a preliminary version of the cup product in the derived category; the operation simply reflects the tensor-product operation. For the moment, write the isomorphism \(\Bbbk\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}\Bbbk\otimes\Bbbk=\Bbbk\ensuremath{\underset{}{\overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes}}}\Bbbk\) given by equation as \(\delta\).

Definition. Let \(X_1\) and \(X_2\) be objects of \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^-(G)\). Define the \(\Bbbk\)-module homomorphism \[\overset{\mathrm{L}}{\cup}: \operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}(G)}(\Bbbk, X_1) \otimes \operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}(G)}(\Bbbk, X_2) \to \operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}(G)}\left(\Bbbk, X_1 \ensuremath{\underset{}{\overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes}}}X_2\right)\] as follows: \(\alpha\overset{\mathrm{L}}{\cup}\beta\) is the composite morphism \[\Bbbk \xrightarrow{\delta} \Bbbk \otimes \Bbbk = \Bbbk \ensuremath{\underset{}{\overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes}}}\Bbbk \xrightarrow{\alpha \ensuremath{\underset{}{\overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes}}}\beta} X_1 \ensuremath{\underset{}{\overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes}}}X_2.\]

Clearly, the map \((\alpha,\beta)\mapsto\alpha\overset{\mathrm{L}}{\cup}\beta\) is bilinear, so the definition is valid. The operation can also be understood as the composition of morphisms. Indeed, from the general properties of monoidal categories, it is easy to see that \(\alpha\overset{\mathrm{L}}{\cup}\beta\) is given by the following composite: \[\text{Diagram chapter6-unit-082-d001}\] The first part is based on equation, while the second is composition of morphisms in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}(G)\). The following properties are formal consequences of Definition reference, or of the reformulation above; throughout, \(X_i\) and \(X\) are objects of \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^-(G)\).

  • Functoriality.The operation \(\overset{\mathrm{L}}{\cup}\) is functorial in \(X_1\) and \(X_2\).

  • Unit.Under the isomorphisms in equation, both the left and the right action of \(\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}\in\operatorname{End}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}(G)}(\Bbbk)\) through \(\overset{\mathrm{L}}{\cup}\) on \(\operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}(G)}(\Bbbk,X)\) are the identity.

  • Associativity.Let \(\alpha_i\in\operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}(G)}(\Bbbk,X_i)\) for \(i=1,2,3\). Up to the associativity constraint for \(\ensuremath{\underset{}{\overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes}}}\), \[\alpha_1 \overset{\mathrm{L}}{\cup} (\alpha_2 \overset{\mathrm{L}}{\cup} \alpha_3) = (\alpha_1 \overset{\mathrm{L}}{\cup} \alpha_2) \overset{\mathrm{L}}{\cup} \alpha_3 .\]

  • Commutativity.Under the commutativity constraint \(X_1\ensuremath{\underset{}{\overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes}}}X_2\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}X_2\ensuremath{\underset{}{\overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes}}}X_1\), the element \(\alpha\overset{\mathrm{L}}{\cup}\beta\) is mapped to \(\beta\overset{\mathrm{L}}{\cup}\alpha\). To see this, it suffices to apply Definition reference and the following commutative diagram: \[\text{Diagram chapter6-unit-082-d002}\] All vertical arrows are commutativity constraints for \(\ensuremath{\underset{}{\overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes}}}\). This is a general fact about symmetric monoidal categories.

We next define the cup product at the level of cohomology of \(G\)-modules; several signs will be involved.

Definition (Cup product). Let \(M_1\) and \(M_2\) be \(G\)-modules and let \(p_1,p_2\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\). In Definition reference, take \(X_i=M_i[p_i]\), and then compose \(\overset{\mathrm{L}}{\cup}\) with the canonical morphisms \[\begin{align*} M_1[p_1] \ensuremath{\underset{}{\overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes}}}M_2[p_2] & \xrightarrow{\text{can}} M_1[p_1] \otimes M_2[p_2] \\ & \xrightarrow[\sim]{\theta'} (M_1[p_1] \otimes M_2) [p_2] \xrightarrow[\sim]{\theta} (M_1 \otimes M_2)[p_1 + p_2] \end{align*}\] in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}(G)\), where

  • \(\mathrm{can}\) is the canonical morphism associated with the left-derived bifunctor;

  • the canonical isomorphisms \(\theta\) and \(\theta'\) are defined as in Proposition reference.

This yields the cup product on cohomology, \[\cup: \operatorname{Ext}^{p_1}_G(\Bbbk, M_1) \otimes \operatorname{Ext}^{p_2}_G(\Bbbk, M_2) \to \operatorname{Ext}^{p_1 + p_2}_G(\Bbbk, M_1 \otimes M_2),\] or, in other notation, \(\cup:\operatorname{H}^{p_1}(G,M_1)\otimes\operatorname{H}^{p_2}(G,M_2) \to\operatorname{H}^{p_1+p_2}(G,M_1\otimes M_2)\).

If \(p_1=p_2=0\), the cup product is obtained by taking the tensor product of two morphisms \(\Bbbk\to M_1\) and \(\Bbbk\to M_2\) in \(G\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\), namely \(\Bbbk\simeq\Bbbk\otimes\Bbbk\to M_1\otimes M_2\). The result is precisely the evident map \((M_1)^G\otimes(M_2)^G\to(M_1\otimes M_2)^G\). Inspecting the definition, the isomorphism \(M_1[p_1]\otimes M_2[p_2]\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}(M_1\otimes M_2)[p_1+p_2]\) involved has the following concrete description: on its only nonzero term \(M_1[p_1]^{-p_1}\otimes M_2[p_2]^{-p_2}=M_1\otimes M_2\), it acts as \((-1)^{p_1p_2}\); the sign comes from \(\theta'\). In addition to the functoriality and unit law already formulated in the derived category, the cup product has the following properties.

  • Associativity.For \(\alpha_i\in\operatorname{H}^{p_i}(G,M_i)\) with \(i=1,2,3\), one has \[(\alpha_1 \cup \alpha_2) \cup \alpha_3 = \alpha_1 \cup (\alpha_2 \cup \alpha_3).\] This property follows easily from the associativity of \(\overset{\mathrm{L}}{\cup}\), but the sign mentioned above still needs to be taken into account. In fact, the sign on both sides is \((-1)^{p_1p_2+p_2p_3+p_1p_3}\).

  • Graded commutativity.Let \(c:M_1\otimes M_2\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}M_2\otimes M_1\) be the isomorphism determined by \(x\otimes y\mapsto y\otimes x\). For all \(\alpha\in\operatorname{H}^p(G,M_1)\) and \(\beta\in\operatorname{H}^q(G,M_2)\), one has \[\operatorname{H}^{p+q}(c)(\alpha \cup \beta) = (-1)^{pq} \beta \cup \alpha.\]

    Indeed, by the commutativity of \(\overset{\mathrm{L}}{\cup}\), it suffices to check that the following diagram commutes: \[\text{Diagram chapter6-unit-082-d003}\] The vertical arrows on the left and in the middle are the commutativity constraints for tensor products in the derived category or the category of complexes. The left square plainly commutes. For the right square, the last part of Proposition reference says that the following diagram commutes: \[\text{Diagram chapter6-unit-082-d004}\] However, by the anticommutative diagram in Proposition reference and its straightforward generalization, the isomorphism \(M_2[q]\otimes M_1[p]\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}(M_2\otimes M_1)[p+q]\) obtained by extracting \([q]\) first differs by \((-1)^{pq}\) from the one obtained by extracting \([p]\) first. This proves commutativity of the right square in the original diagram.

  • Cohomology algebra.In particular, \(\operatorname{H}^\bullet(G,\Bbbk):=\bigoplus_p\operatorname{H}^p(G,\Bbbk)\) becomes a graded \(\Bbbk\)-algebra under \(\cup\), and its multiplication satisfies the graded commutativity law above, \(\beta\cup\alpha=(-1)^{pq}\alpha\cup\beta\). In fact, one can prove that \(\operatorname{H}^\bullet(G,\Bbbk)\) is the same as the graded \(\Bbbk\)-algebra in Definition reference, \[\operatorname{Ext}_G(\Bbbk) := \bigoplus_p \operatorname{Ext}^p_G(\Bbbk, \Bbbk) = \bigoplus_p \operatorname{H}^p(G, \Bbbk).\]

  • Bimodule structure. Under the operation \(\cup\), \(\bigoplus_p\operatorname{H}^p(G,M)\) becomes a graded bimodule with left and right actions by \(\operatorname{H}^\bullet(G,\Bbbk)\).

A group homomorphism \(\varphi:H\to G\) induces a homomorphism of cohomology algebras \(\varphi^*:\operatorname{H}^\bullet(G,\Bbbk)\to\operatorname{H}^\bullet(H,\Bbbk)\). This is an immediate consequence of the following result.

Proposition (Change of groups). Use the notation of Definition reference. Let \(\varphi:H\to G\) be a group homomorphism. Write \(\varphi^*:\operatorname{H}^{p_i}(G,M_i)\to\operatorname{H}^{p_i}(H,\varphi^*M_i)\) for the canonical homomorphism in equation, for \(i=1,2\). Then \[\varphi^*(\alpha \cup \beta) = \varphi^* \alpha \cup \varphi^* \beta.\]

As a special case, if \(H\subset G\) is a subgroup, the restriction map \(\mathrm{res}^n:\operatorname{H}^n(G,M)\to\operatorname{H}^n(H,M)\) discussed in §reference preserves cup products.

Proof. Apply \(\varphi^*\) to every morphism in Definition reference, and then use the fact that \(\varphi^*\) is a monoidal functor (Lemma reference). In \(\operatorname{Ext}_H^{p_1+p_2}(\Bbbk,\varphi^*M_1\otimes\varphi^*M_2)\), this gives \[\begin{multline*} \varphi^*(\alpha \cup \beta) \xlongequal{\text{identified with}} \;\text{the composite morphism} \\ \left[ \Bbbk \xrightarrow{\delta} \Bbbk \ensuremath{\underset{}{\overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes}}}\Bbbk \xrightarrow{\varphi^* \alpha \ensuremath{\underset{}{\overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes}}}\varphi^* \beta} \varphi^* M_1[p_1] \ensuremath{\underset{}{\overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes}}}\varphi^* M_2[p_2] \to (\varphi^* M_1 \otimes \varphi^* M_2)[p_1 + p_2] \right]. \end{multline*}\] Here, \(\varphi^*\alpha\in\operatorname{Ext}_H^{p_1}(\Bbbk,\varphi^*M_1) \simeq\operatorname{Hom}_H(\varphi^*\Bbbk,\varphi^*M_1[p_1])\) is obtained by applying the functor \(\varphi^*\) to the morphism \(\alpha\). By Remark reference, however, this element is also the image of \(\alpha\) under the canonical homomorphism equation; the same applies to \(\varphi^*\beta\). The result is \(\varphi^*\alpha\cup\varphi^*\beta\).

Our next aim is to describe the cup product through the standard complex \(C(G,M)\) of Proposition reference. This description is not only more concrete; it also lifts the cup product canonically to the level of complexes. We begin with the definition. Later, Proposition reference will show that it agrees with the previous version.

Definition–Proposition (Cup product on the standard complex). Let \(M_1\) and \(M_2\) be \(G\)-modules. For all \(p_1,p_2\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\), define the homomorphisms \[\text{Diagram chapter6-unit-082-d005}\] where \(g_1,\ldots,g_{p_1+p_2}\in G\).

  1. These homomorphisms satisfy associativity (taking \(M_1\), \(M_2\), and \(M_3\) into account) and the Leibniz rule \[d(f_1 \cup f_2) = df_1 \cup f_2 + (-1)^{p_1} f_1 \cup d f_2;\] in particular, \(\cup\) gives a morphism of complexes \(\cup:C(G,M_1)\otimes C(G,M_2)\to C(G,M_1\otimes M_2)\).

  2. The normalized standard complex introduced in Remark reference is closed under \(\cup\), and hence there is a morphism \[\cup: \overline{C}(G, M_1) \otimes \overline{C}(G, M_2) \to \overline{C}(G, M_1 \otimes M_2).\]

Proof. Associativity follows immediately from the formula for \(\cup\), while the Leibniz rule is also easy to verify. Let \[\varphi \in C^p(G, M_1), \quad \psi \in C^q(G, M_2).\] In \[\begin{multline*} (d\varphi \cup \psi)(g_1, \ldots, g_{p+q+1}) = \\ \left( g_1 \varphi(g_2, \ldots, g_{p+1}) + \sum_{k=1}^p (-1)^k \varphi(\ldots, g_k g_{k+1}, \ldots) + (-1)^{p+1} \varphi(g_1, \ldots, g_p) \right) \\ \otimes (g_1 \cdots g_{p+1}) \psi(g_{p+2}, \ldots, g_{p+q+1}) \end{multline*}\] and \[\begin{multline*} (-1)^p (\varphi \cup d\psi)(g_1, \ldots, g_{p+q+1}) = \varphi(g_1, \ldots, g_p) \otimes \\ (g_1 \cdots g_p) \bigg( (-1)^p g_{p+1} \psi(g_{p+2}, \ldots, g_{p+q+1}) + \sum_{k=p+1}^{p+q} (-1)^k \psi(\ldots, g_k g_{k+1}, \ldots) \\ + (-1)^{p+q+1} \psi(g_{p+1}, \ldots, g_{p+q}) \bigg), \end{multline*}\] the term \(\varphi(g_1,\ldots,g_p)\otimes(g_1\cdots g_{p+1}) \psi(g_{p+2},\ldots)\) occurs respectively as the last and first term, and the two cancel. The sum of the two expressions is therefore \(d(\varphi\cup\psi)(g_1,\ldots,g_{p+q+1})\).

Notice that the Leibniz rule is equivalent to saying that, as \(p_1,p_2\) vary, \(\cup\) gives a morphism of complexes. This proves (i).

If both \(f_1\) and \(f_2\) belong to the normalized standard complex, the definition implies that \((f_1\cup f_2)(g_1,\ldots,g_{p_1+p_2})=0\) whenever one of \(g_1,\ldots,g_{p_1+p_2}\) equals \(1_G\). This also proves (ii).

Recall that the standard complex \(C(G,M)\) essentially computes \(\operatorname{RHom}_G(\Bbbk,M)=\operatorname{Hom}_G^\bullet(\mathsf{L},M)\) through the free resolution \(\mathsf{L}\to\Bbbk\), where \(M\) is a \(G\)-module. More precisely, for \(\mathsf{L}\) we use the chain complex \((\mathsf{L}_n,\partial_n)_n\) in Definition reference. By setting \(\mathsf{L}^n:=\mathsf{L}_{-n}\) while retaining the morphisms \(\partial_n\), \(\mathsf{L}\) may be regarded as a complex.

Lemma. Write the free resolution of Definition reference as \(\epsilon:\mathsf{L}\to\Bbbk\). Then:

  1. \(\epsilon\otimes\epsilon:\mathsf{L}\otimes\mathsf{L} \to\Bbbk\otimes\Bbbk\simeq\Bbbk\) is a projective resolution of the \(G\)-module \(\Bbbk\);

  2. one can define a morphism of complexes \(\Delta:\mathsf{L}\to\mathsf{L}\otimes\mathsf{L}\) whose degree-\(-n\) term is given by \[\text{Diagram chapter6-unit-082-d006}\] and which makes the following diagram commute: \[\text{Diagram chapter6-unit-082-d007}\]

Proof. For (i), notice that every term of \(\mathsf{L}\otimes\mathsf{L}\) remains a projective \(G\)-module; one may use Proposition reference. To prove that \(\epsilon\otimes\epsilon\) is a quasi-isomorphism, factor the morphism as \[\mathsf{L} \otimes \mathsf{L} \to \mathsf{L} \otimes \Bbbk \to \Bbbk \otimes \Bbbk.\] Since \(\mathsf{L}\) consists of flat \(\Bbbk\)-modules, both parts are quasi-isomorphisms.

For (ii), it is clear that every \(\Delta_n\) is a homomorphism of \(G\)-modules. A direct calculation, split into the various cases, verifies that \(\Delta\) is indeed a morphism of complexes. Commutativity of the diagram is immediate.

In comparison with the cup product in topology, \(\Delta\) here is analogous to the “diagonal embedding” of a space. This morphism can also be interpreted through the Alexander–Whitney map to be introduced in §reference; see the exercises in . Notice that, because \(\epsilon\otimes\epsilon\) is a quasi-isomorphism, the general theory of complexes guarantees the existence of a morphism \(\mathsf{L}\to\mathsf{L}\otimes\mathsf{L}\) that makes the diagram in (ii) commute, and this morphism is unique up to homotopy (Theorem reference). The value of Lemma reference (ii) lies in its explicit formula. Return to the description of \(\overset{\mathrm{L}}{\cup}\) in Definition reference. Represent the morphisms \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}(G)\) by morphisms of complexes \(\mathsf{L}\to X_1\) and \(\mathsf{L}\to X_2\), respectively, where the \(X_i\) are bounded-above complexes, and lift \(\delta\) to \(\Delta\) through Lemma reference. The composite of \(\alpha\overset{\mathrm{L}}{\cup}\beta \in\operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}(G)}(\Bbbk,X_1\ensuremath{\underset{}{\overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes}}}X_2)\) with the canonical morphism \(X_1\ensuremath{\underset{}{\overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes}}}X_2\xrightarrow{\text{can}}X_1\otimes X_2\) is given concretely by the composite of morphisms of complexes \[\text{Diagram chapter6-unit-082-d008}\] For \(G\)-modules \(M_i\) and \(p_i\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\), one has \(\operatorname{H}^{p_i}\operatorname{Hom}^\bullet(\mathsf{L},M_i)\simeq\operatorname{H}^{p_i}(G,M_i)\), for \(i=1,2\). We next interpret the cup product through \(\operatorname{Hom}\) complexes. For arbitrary complexes of \(G\)-modules \(X,Y,X',Y'\) and \(m,n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\), define the \(\Bbbk\)-module homomorphism \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:group-cup-3-aux}{} \mu^{m, n}: \operatorname{Hom}_G^m(X, Y) \otimes \operatorname{Hom}_G^n(X', Y') \to \operatorname{Hom}_G^{m+n}(X \otimes X', Y \otimes Y'), \end{equation}\] as follows. For an element \(f\otimes g\) on the left, define \[\begin{gather*} \mu^{m, n}(f \otimes g)(x \otimes x') := (-1)^{pn} f(x) \otimes g(x') \; \in Y^{p+m} \otimes (Y')^{q+n}, \\ x \otimes x' \in X^p \otimes (X')^q . \end{gather*}\] A direct verification shows that all the \(\mu^{m,n}\) give a morphism of complexes \[\mu: \operatorname{Hom}_G^\bullet(X, Y) \otimes \operatorname{Hom}_G^\bullet(X', Y') \to \operatorname{Hom}_G^\bullet(X \otimes X', Y \otimes Y'),\] or, in other words, that equation satisfies the Leibniz rule. The sign \((-1)^{pn}\) in the definition can be explained by the Koszul sign rule to be discussed in §reference and the exercises in , since the formula interchanges the positions of \(g\) and \(x\).

Lemma. Apply the operation above with \(X=X'=\mathsf{L}\), \(Y=M_1\), and \(Y'=M_2\). Then the morphism of complexes \[\begin{multline} \hypertarget{eqn:group-cup-3-aux1}{} \operatorname{Hom}^\bullet_G(\mathsf{L}, M_1) \otimes \operatorname{Hom}^\bullet_G(\mathsf{L}, M_2) \xrightarrow{\mu} \operatorname{Hom}^\bullet_G(\mathsf{L} \otimes \mathsf{L}, M_1 \otimes M_2) \\ \xrightarrow{\Delta^*} \operatorname{Hom}^\bullet(\mathsf{L}, M_1 \otimes M_2) \end{multline}\] induces on cohomology the cup product of Definition reference.

Proof. For \(i=1,2\), use Lemma reference to identify \(\operatorname{Hom}_G^{p_i}(\mathsf{L},M_i)\) with \(\operatorname{Hom}_G^0(\mathsf{L},M_i[p_i])\). Choose \(f_i\) in it satisfying \(d_{\operatorname{Hom}^\bullet}f_i=0\), and consider the image of \(f_1\otimes f_2\) under equation. Since \(f_i\) can be nonzero only on \(\mathsf{L}_{p_i}\), the sign in this image is \((-1)^{p_1p_2}\), exactly the sign in Definition reference. The remaining verification is immediate.

Recall that \(\operatorname{Hom}^\bullet(\mathsf{L},M_i)\simeq C(G,M_i)\), so that \(\operatorname{H}^{p_i}(G,M_i)\simeq\operatorname{H}^{p_i}(C(G,M_i))\). The concrete map is given in the proof of Proposition reference, for \(i=1,2\).

Proposition. The cup product in Definition reference is the same as the composite homomorphism \[\begin{multline*} \operatorname{H}^{p_1}(G, M_1) \otimes \operatorname{H}^{p_2}(G, M_2) \simeq \operatorname{H}^{p_1}(C(G, M_1)) \otimes \operatorname{H}^{p_2}(C(G, M_2)) \\ \xrightarrow{\kappa} \operatorname{H}^{p_1 + p_2}\left( C(G, M_1) \otimes C(G, M_2) \right) \\ \xrightarrow{\operatorname{H}^{p_1 + p_2}(\cup)} \operatorname{H}^{p_1 + p_2}(C(G, M_1 \otimes M_2)) \simeq \operatorname{H}^{p_1 + p_2}(G, M_1 \otimes M_2), \end{multline*}\] where the canonical morphism \(\kappa\) is as described immediately before Theorem reference. The conclusion is the same when the normalized standard complex is used.

Proof. Interpret the cup product as in Lemma reference. Take \(f_i\in C^{p_i}(G,M_i)\). For the bar notation in the display below, put \(p:=p_1\). For \(g_1,\ldots,g_{p_1+p_2}\in G\), the element \[(g_1 | \cdots | g_{p_1 + p_2}) := \left(1_G, g_{[1, 1]}, \ldots, g_{[1, p_1 + p_2]} \right) \in \mathsf{L}_{p_1 + p_2}\] has, after applying \(\Delta\), the following component in \(\mathsf{L}_{p_1}\otimes\mathsf{L}_{p_2}\): \[\begin{multline*} (-1)^{p_1 p_2} \left( 1_G, \ldots, g_{[1, p_1]}\right) \otimes \left(g_{[1, p_1]}, \ldots, g_{[1, p_1 + p_2]} \right) \\ = (-1)^{p_1 p_2} (g_1 | \cdots | g_p) \otimes g_1 \cdots g_{p_1} \left( g_{p_1 + 1} |\cdots| g_{p_1 + p_2} \right). \end{multline*}\]

Under \(\mu^{p_1,p_2}(f_1\otimes f_2)\) in equation, this element is mapped to \[f_1(g_1, \ldots, g_{p_1}) \otimes g_1 \cdots g_{p_1} f_2(g_{p_1 + 1}, \cdots, g_{p_1 + p_2}).\] Thus the operation in equation is indeed compatible with \(\cup\) on \(C(G,M)\). The version for the normalized standard complex is the same.

Notice that although the description of the cup product on the standard complex is direct and transparent, graded commutativity is difficult to derive directly from it; in the framework of the standard complex, a rather roundabout proof is required. This book does not take that route.

Remark. The structure exhibited by Definition–Proposition reference is genuinely richer than its cohomological version in Definition reference, because it equips the entire standard complex with a differential graded structure. Thus \(C(G,\Bbbk)\) under \(\cup\) becomes a differential graded algebra in the sense of Definition reference or reference; the same holds for \(\overline{C}(G,\Bbbk)\). The cohomological version of the cup product is obtained only after taking \(\operatorname{H}^\bullet\): it is graded, but not differential.

The cup product on the standard complex is functorial. Let \(\varphi:H\to G\) be a group homomorphism, let \(M_i\) (respectively, \(N_i\)) be \(G\)-modules (respectively, \(H\)-modules), and let \(f_i:M_i\to N_i\) be a homomorphism equivariant with respect to \(\varphi\), for \(i=1,2\); see Definition reference. Then the following diagram commutes: \[\text{Diagram chapter6-unit-082-d009}\] The vertical arrows come from the equivariant homomorphisms \(f_1\), \(f_2\), and \(f_1\otimes f_2\); see Proposition reference. The normalized standard complex inherits this property.

Corollary. Suppose there is a short exact sequence of \(G\)-modules \(0\to M'_1\xrightarrow{f}M_1\xrightarrow{g}M''_1\to0\) such that the corresponding sequence \[0 \to M'_1 \otimes M_2 \to M_1 \otimes M_2 \to M''_1 \otimes M_2 \to 0\] is also short exact. Write the connecting homomorphism on cohomology as \(\delta^p:\operatorname{H}^p(G,M''_1)\to\operatorname{H}^{p+1}(G,M'_1)\), and so forth. Then \[(\delta^p \alpha) \cup \beta = \delta^{p+q}(\alpha \cup \beta), \quad \alpha \in \operatorname{H}^p(G, M''_1), \; \beta \in \operatorname{H}^q(G, M_2).\]

If instead one takes a short exact sequence \(0\to M'_2\to M_2\to M''_2\to0\) such that \[0 \to M_1 \otimes M'_2 \to M_1 \otimes M_2 \to M_1 \otimes M''_2 \to 0\] remains exact, then \[\alpha \cup (\delta^q \beta) = (-1)^p \delta^{p+q} (\alpha \cup \beta).\]

Proof. Handle the first case using the cup product on the standard complex. Choose a representative \(a''\in C^p(G,M''_1)\) of \(\alpha\). Recall the concrete construction of \(\delta^p\alpha\) through the snake lemma: there is an \(a\in C^p(G,M_1)\) mapping to \(a''\), and \(da''=0\) implies that \(da\) comes from some \(a'\in C^{p+1}(G,M'_1)\); the cohomology class of the latter element is \(\delta^p\alpha\). Diagrammatically: \[\text{Diagram chapter6-unit-082-d010}\]

Next, choose a representative \(b\in C^q(G,M_2)\) of \(\beta\). From \(db=0\) and the Leibniz rule, one obtains \(d(a''\cup b)=0\) and \[\text{Diagram chapter6-unit-082-d011}\] This implies that the cohomology class of \(a'\cup b\) is \(\delta^{p+q}(\alpha\cup\beta)\).

The argument for the second case is similar, or it can be reduced to the first case by graded commutativity.

As an application, we now explain the relationship between the corestriction \(\mathrm{cor}^n\) of Definition–Proposition reference and the cup product.

Proposition (Projection formula). Let \(M_1\) and \(M_2\) be \(G\)-modules, let \(H\) be a subgroup of \(G\), and suppose \((G:H)\) is finite. For all \(\alpha\in\operatorname{H}^p(G,M_1)\) and \(\beta\in\operatorname{H}^q(H,M_2)\), the following equality holds in \(\operatorname{H}^{p+q}(G,M_1\otimes M_2)\): \[\begin{equation*} \mathrm{cor}^{p+q}(\mathrm{res}^p(\alpha) \cup \beta) = \alpha \cup \mathrm{cor}^q(\beta); \end{equation*}\] and likewise with the left and right positions interchanged.

Proof. First handle the case \(p=q=0\). Recall that \(\mathrm{cor}^0\) becomes \(\nu^{G|H}:M_i^H\to M_i^G\), which sends \(x\in M_i^H\) to \(\sum_{gH}gx\in M_i^G\). It therefore suffices to prove that the following diagram commutes: \[\text{Diagram chapter6-unit-082-d012}\]

This is immediate. If \(x\in M_1^G\) and \(y\in M_2^H\), then \(\nu^{G|H}(x\otimes y)=\sum_{gH}gx\otimes gy =\sum_{gH}x\otimes gy=x\otimes\nu^{G|H}(y)\).

For the case \(p\geq1\) or \(q\geq1\), we use dimension shifting and a recursive argument. For example, consider the case \(p\geq1\) and the short exact sequence of \(G\)-modules \[0 \to M_1 \to \operatorname{Ind}^G_{\{1\}} M_1 \to M'_1 \to 0,\] where the first morphism sends \(x\) to \([g\mapsto gx]\), for \(g\in G\). As a homomorphism of \(\Bbbk\)-modules, this morphism has the left inverse \(\varphi\mapsto\varphi(1_G)\); hence tensoring the short exact sequence with \(M_2\) preserves exactness. On the other hand, for \(n\geq1\), \(\operatorname{H}^n(G,\operatorname{Ind}^G_{\{1\}}(M_1))\simeq\operatorname{H}^n(\{1\},M_1)=0\) (Theorem reference). Thus the connecting homomorphism gives a surjection \[\delta_G^{p-1}: \operatorname{H}^{p-1}(G, M'_1) \twoheadrightarrow \operatorname{H}^p(G, M_1).\]

If this short exact sequence is restricted to \(H\), one still obtains a connecting homomorphism \(\delta_H^{p-1}:\operatorname{H}^{p-1}(H,M'_1)\to\operatorname{H}^p(H,M_1)\), and so forth. Notice that \(\operatorname{Res}^G_H\) commutes with the operation \(\otimes M_2\).

We may therefore suppose that \(\alpha=\delta_G^{p-1}(\alpha')\). Compatibility of \(\mathrm{res}\) and \(\mathrm{cor}\) with connecting homomorphisms gives \[\begin{multline*} \mathrm{cor}^{p+q}\left( \mathrm{res}^p(\delta_G^{p-1} \alpha') \cup \beta \right) = \mathrm{cor}^{p+q}\left( \delta_H^{p-1} (\mathrm{res}^{p-1} \alpha') \cup \beta \right) \\ \xlongequal{\text{Corollary \href{#prop:cup-ses}{reference}}} \mathrm{cor}^{p+q} \delta_H^{p+q-1} \left( (\mathrm{res}^{p-1} \alpha') \cup \beta \right) \\ = \delta^{p+q-1}_G \mathrm{cor}^{p+q-1} \left( (\mathrm{res}^{p-1} \alpha') \cup \beta \right) \xlongequal{\text{induction}} \delta^{p+q-1}_G \left(\alpha' \cup \mathrm{cor}^q \beta\right) \\ \xlongequal{\text{Corollary \href{#prop:cup-ses}{reference}}} (\delta^{p-1}_G \alpha') \cup \mathrm{cor}^q \beta . \end{multline*}\]

The induction on \(q\) is entirely similar. The version with the left and right positions interchanged follows from graded commutativity.

Example. Let \(C_m\) be a cyclic group of order \(m\), where \(m\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}_{\geq1}\). Take the coefficient ring \(\Bbbk=\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\). We explain how to understand, through the cup product, the periodic isomorphism \(\operatorname{H}^n(C_m,A)\simeq\operatorname{H}^{n+2}(C_m,A)\) implied by Proposition reference, where \(A\) is an arbitrary \(C_m\)-module and \(n\geq1\).

Choose any generator \(t\) of \(\operatorname{H}^2(C_m,\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}})\simeq\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}/m\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\). We claim that for \(n\geq1\), the cup product induces an isomorphism \[t \cup (\cdot): \operatorname{H}^n(C_m, A) \ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}\operatorname{H}^{n+2}(C_m, \Bbbk \otimes A) = \operatorname{H}^{n+2}(C_m, A).\]

Choose a generator \(\sigma\) of \(C_m\). There are short exact sequences \[\begin{array}{cc} 0 \to \mathfrak{I} \to \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}[C_m] \to \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\to 0, & 0 \to \mathfrak{I} \otimes A \to \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}[C_m] \otimes A \to A \to 0, \\ 0 \to \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\xrightarrow{\nu} \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}[C_m] \xrightarrow{\sigma - 1} \mathfrak{I} \to 0, & 0 \to A \xrightarrow{\nu \otimes \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}} \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}[C_m] \otimes A \xrightarrow{(\sigma-1) \otimes \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}} \mathfrak{I} \otimes A \to 0. \end{array}\] The sequences on the left come from Lemma reference. Each of their terms is a free \(\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\)-module, so the sequences on the right obtained by applying \(\otimes A\) are also exact. First, this gives \[\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}= \operatorname{H}^0(C_m, \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}) \twoheadrightarrow \operatorname{H}^1(C_m, \mathfrak{I}) \ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}\operatorname{H}^2(C_m, \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}) = \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}/m\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}},\] where both maps are connecting homomorphisms from the long exact sequences. Choose a preimage \(\tilde{t}\) of \(t\) in \(\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\); this integer must be relatively prime to \(m\). Corollary reference gives the commutative diagram \[\text{Diagram chapter6-unit-082-d013}\]

The exercises in this chapter will show that the composite in the first row is the periodic isomorphism. It therefore suffices to prove that \(\tilde{t}\cup(\cdot)\) is an isomorphism. This is clear: the operation is precisely multiplication by \(\tilde{t}\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\), while \(m\operatorname{H}^n(C_m,A)=\{0\}\) (Corollary reference). In fact, if \(t\) corresponds to \(1\bmod m\), take \(\tilde{t}=1\); it is then immediately clear that the periodic isomorphism is exactly \(t\cup(\cdot)\).

Remark (Cap product). As in topology, there is also an operation between group cohomology and group homology called the cap product, \[\cap: \operatorname{H}^p(G, M_1) \otimes \operatorname{H}_q(G, M_2) \to \operatorname{H}_{q-p}(G, M_1 \otimes M_2), \quad M_1, M_2: \text{$G$-modules}.\] Since this book does not use the cap product, we mention it only briefly. Regard an element \(\alpha\in\operatorname{H}^p(G,M_1)\) as a morphism \(\Bbbk\to M_1[p]\) in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}(G)\). This element induces the following morphism in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^-(G)\): \[\begin{multline*} \Bbbk \ensuremath{\underset{{\Bbbk[G]}}{\overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes}}} M_2 \ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}\Bbbk \ensuremath{\underset{{\Bbbk[G]}}{\overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes}}} (\Bbbk \ensuremath{\underset{}{\overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes}}}M_2) \xrightarrow{\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}\otimes \alpha \otimes \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}} \Bbbk \ensuremath{\underset{{\Bbbk[G]}}{\overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes}}} (M_1[p] \ensuremath{\underset{}{\overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes}}}M_2) \\ \xrightarrow{\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}\ensuremath{\underset{}{\overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes}}}\mathrm{can}} \Bbbk \ensuremath{\underset{{\Bbbk[G]}}{\overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes}}} (M_1[p] \otimes M_2) \xrightarrow{\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}\ensuremath{\underset{}{\overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes}}}\theta} \Bbbk \ensuremath{\underset{{\Bbbk[G]}}{\overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes}}} \left( (M_1 \otimes M_2)[p] \right) \xrightarrow{\theta'} \left(\Bbbk \ensuremath{\underset{{\Bbbk[G]}}{\overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes}}} (M_1 \otimes M_2)\right) [p]. \end{multline*}\] Finally, take \(\operatorname{H}^{-q}\) of this composite to obtain \[\alpha \cap (\cdot): \operatorname{H}_q(G, M_2) \to \operatorname{H}_{q-p}(G, M_1 \otimes M_2).\] In the special case \(p=q\), one obtains a pairing \[\ensuremath{\left\langle \cdot, \cdot \right\rangle}: \operatorname{H}^p(G, M_1) \otimes \operatorname{H}_p(G, M_2) \to \left( M_1 \otimes M_2 \right)_G .\]

Tate Cohomology

For a finite group \(G\) and a commutative ring \(\Bbbk\), Definition–Proposition reference introduced the element \(\nu = \sum_{g \in G} g\) of \(\Bbbk[G]^G\). It lies in the center of \(\Bbbk[G]\). Thus, for every \(G\)-module \(M\), multiplication \(x \mapsto \nu x\) gives a \(G\)-module homomorphism \(M \to M\), again denoted by \(\nu\). The identities \(\nu g = \nu = g \nu\) imply \(\nu M \subset M^G\) and \(\mathfrak{I}M \subset M^{\nu = 0}\), where \(\mathfrak{I}\) is the augmentation ideal of \(\Bbbk[G]\) and \(M^{\nu=0}\) is as in Convention reference. Consequently, \(\nu\) induces a \(\Bbbk\)-module homomorphism \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:nu-coinv-inv}{} \nu: M_G \to M^G . \end{equation}\] Since group homology (respectively, cohomology) can be regarded as a derived version of \(M_G\) (respectively, \(M^G\)), the canonical homomorphism \(M_G \to M^G\) suggests a bridge between homology and cohomology. Why not, for example, consider its cokernel in some derived sense1? We set this idea aside for the moment and define the corresponding cohomology in the classical way.

Definition (Tate cohomology). Let \(G\) be a finite group and \(M\) a \(G\)-module. For every \(n \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\), define \[\begin{align*} \ensuremath{\hat{\mathrm{H}}}^n(G, M) & := \operatorname{H}^n(G, M) \quad (n \geq 1), \\ \ensuremath{\hat{\mathrm{H}}}^0(G, M) & := M^G / \nu M \\ & = \operatorname{coker}\left[ \nu: M_G \to M^G \right] \twoheadleftarrow \operatorname{H}^0(G, M), \\ \ensuremath{\hat{\mathrm{H}}}^{-1}(G, M) & := M^{\nu=0} / \mathfrak{I} M \\ & = \operatorname{ker}\left[ \nu: M_G \to M^G \right] \hookrightarrow \operatorname{H}_0(G, M), \\ \ensuremath{\hat{\mathrm{H}}}^{-n}(G, M) & := \operatorname{H}_{n-1}(G, M) \quad (n \geq 2). \end{align*}\] All of these modules are functorial in \(M\).

Tate cohomology is often used in Galois theory and algebraic number theory; one example is the \(\ensuremath{\hat{\mathrm{H}}}^{-1}\) appearing in [Li1]. It is due to J. Tate. A useful cohomology theory generally has a long exact sequence, and Tate cohomology is no exception.

Theorem. Let \(0 \to M' \to M \to M'' \to 0\) be a short exact sequence of \(G\)-modules. There is then a long exact sequence \[\cdots \to \ensuremath{\hat{\mathrm{H}}}^n(G, M) \to \ensuremath{\hat{\mathrm{H}}}^n(G, M'') \xrightarrow{\delta^n} \ensuremath{\hat{\mathrm{H}}}^{n+1}(G, M') \to \ensuremath{\hat{\mathrm{H}}}^{n+1}(G, M) \to \cdots\] extending infinitely in both directions. The connecting homomorphisms \(\delta^n\) are functorial with respect to morphisms of short exact sequences, that is, with respect to commutative diagrams with exact rows \[\text{Diagram chapter6-unit-083-d001}\]

Proof. Splice the long exact sequences in homology and cohomology as follows: \[\text{Diagram chapter6-unit-083-d002}\] Here \(N_1,N_2,N_3\) are all the homomorphisms previously denoted by \(\nu\). The diagram above is commutative and its rows are exact. The only point requiring explanation is the commutativity of the two squares that touch \(0\). This can be checked explicitly using the standard complex and the chain complex, while recalling the connecting morphisms \(\operatorname{H}_1 \to \operatorname{H}_0\) and \(\operatorname{H}^0 \to \operatorname{H}^1\); the verification is left as an exercise.

The Snake Lemma now gives the exact sequence \[\text{Diagram chapter6-unit-083-d003}\] This is one part of the desired exact sequence, and the functoriality of the connecting homomorphism \(\delta^{-1}\) follows from the Snake Lemma. The remaining parts reduce to the long exact sequences in group homology and group cohomology, together with the commutative diagram with exact rows proved in the first step.

We next state the Tate-cohomology version of Shapiro’s Lemma (Theorem reference). Recall that if \(G\) is finite, then for every subgroup \(H\) the two induction functors \(\operatorname{Ind}^G_H,\operatorname{ind}^G_H:H\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\to G\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\) coincide; see Corollary reference. From now on both will be denoted by \(\operatorname{Ind}^G_H\).

Proposition. For a finite group \(G\), a subgroup \(H\), and an \(H\)-module \(N\), there is a canonical isomorphism \[\ensuremath{\hat{\mathrm{H}}}^n(H, N) \simeq \ensuremath{\hat{\mathrm{H}}}^n\left( G, \operatorname{Ind}^G_H(N)\right), \quad n \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}.\]

Proof. For \(n \geq 1\) or \(n \leq -2\), the assertion reduces to Theorem reference. We next handle the cases \(n=-1,0\). Realize \(\operatorname{Ind}^G_H(N)\) as a mapping space by Lemma reference. Write \(\nu^G\) (respectively, \(\nu^H\)) for the \(\nu\) corresponding to \(G\) (respectively, \(H\)). It remains to prove that the following diagram commutes: \[\text{Diagram chapter6-unit-083-d004}\] The vertical isomorphisms come from Corollary reference. Let \(y\in N\), and write \([y]\) for its image in \(N_H\). The image of \([y]\) in \(\operatorname{Ind}^G_H(N)_G\) is \([f]\), where \(f\in\operatorname{Ind}^G_H(N)\) satisfies \(f(1_G)=y\) and \(\operatorname{Supp}(f)\subset H\). Thus the image in \(N^H\) of \(\nu^Gf:x\mapsto\sum_{g\in G}f(xg)\) is \((\nu^Gf)(1_G)=\sum_gf(g)\). But this also equals \(\sum_{h\in H}f(h)=\sum_hhf(1_G)=\nu^Hy\). This proves the assertion.

The argument can be strengthened to show that the canonical isomorphism is compatible with the long exact sequences on both sides.

Corollary. Let \(G\) be a finite group. For every \(\Bbbk\)-module \(N\), \[\ensuremath{\hat{\mathrm{H}}}^n\left(G, \operatorname{Ind}^G_{\{1\}}(N)\right) = 0, \quad n \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}.\]

Proof. Clearly \(\ensuremath{\hat{\mathrm{H}}}^n(\{1\},N)=0\) for every \(n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\).

Example. Let \(E|F\) be a finite Galois extension of fields, with Galois group \(\operatorname{Gal}(E|F)\) acting on \(E\). Take the coefficient ring to be \(\Bbbk=F\) or \(\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\). The Normal Basis Theorem [Li1] is equivalent to the statement \(E\simeq\operatorname{Ind}^{\operatorname{Gal}(E|F)}_{\{1\}}(F)\), so Corollary reference implies \[\ensuremath{\hat{\mathrm{H}}}^n(\operatorname{Gal}(E|F), E) = 0, \quad n \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}};\] therefore \(n\geq1\implies\operatorname{H}^n(\operatorname{Gal}(E|F),E)=0\). If \(E|F\) is cyclic and \(n=-1\), this gives another proof of the additive version of Hilbert’s Theorem 90 mentioned in [Li1]. For the multiplicative version, see Example reference.

For a general \(H\subset G\) and a \(G\)-module \(M\), the left and right adjoints of restriction give canonical morphisms \[\epsilon_M: \operatorname{ind}^G_H(\operatorname{Res}^G_H(M)) \to M, \quad \eta_M: M \to \operatorname{Ind}^G_H(\operatorname{Res}^G_H(M)).\] From the concrete description of the adjoint pairs (Proposition reference), \(\epsilon_M(g\otimes x)=gx\), while \(\eta_M(x)=[g\mapsto gx]\). Thus \(\epsilon_M\) is surjective and \(\eta_M\) is injective. Returning to the case of finite groups, we have \(\operatorname{ind}^G_{\{1\}}=\operatorname{Ind}^G_{\{1\}}\). Using \(\epsilon_M\) and \(\eta_M\), the vanishing in Corollary reference shows that each \(\ensuremath{\hat{\mathrm{H}}}^n(G,\cdot)\) is both erasable and coerasable (Definition reference). Consequently, the dimension-shifting technique of Proposition reference has the following simplified form.

Corollary (Dimension shifting). For every \(G\)-module \(M\), as usual write \(M\) as an abbreviation for \(\operatorname{Res}^G_{\{1\}}M\), and consider the short exact sequences \[\begin{gather*} 0 \to M' \to \operatorname{Ind}^G_{\{1\}}(M) \xrightarrow{\epsilon_M} M \to 0, \\ 0 \to M \xrightarrow{\eta_M} \operatorname{Ind}^G_{\{1\}}(M) \to M'' \to 0. \end{gather*}\] The corresponding connecting homomorphisms in the long exact sequences give canonical isomorphisms \[\ensuremath{\hat{\mathrm{H}}}^{n-1}(G, M'') \ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}\ensuremath{\hat{\mathrm{H}}}^n(G, M) \ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}\ensuremath{\hat{\mathrm{H}}}^{n+1}(G, M'), \quad n \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}.\]

Proof. Combine the long exact sequence (Theorem reference) with the vanishing in Corollary reference.

Many properties of Tate cohomology can be reduced by dimension shifting to the case \(n=0\). Return to the definition. Choose an arbitrary projective resolution \(P\to M\) and injective resolution \(M\to I\) of the \(G\)-module \(M\), regard both as complexes, and then consider the morphism of complexes \(P_G\to I^G\), shown in the diagram \[\text{Diagram chapter6-unit-083-d005}\] Here \(\Omega\) is the composite \(P_{0,G}\twoheadrightarrow M_G\xrightarrow{\nu}M^G\hookrightarrow I^{0,G}\); commutativity is clear. Take the mapping cone \(\operatorname{Cone}\left[P_G\to I^G\right]\), or equivalently the total complex of the diagram above (placing \(P_G\) in vertical coordinate \(-1\)). The reader is asked to verify that \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:Tate-cone-1}{} \operatorname{H}^n\left( \operatorname{Cone}\left[P_G \to I^G\right] \right) = \ensuremath{\hat{\mathrm{H}}}^n(G, M). \end{equation}\] The equation above in fact shows how to define a canonical morphism \(\Bbbk \ensuremath{\underset{{\Bbbk[G]}}{\overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes}}} M \to \operatorname{RHom}_G(\Bbbk, M)\) in the derived category \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}(G)\) of \(G\)-modules. Complete this morphism to a distinguished triangle in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}(G)\), \[\Bbbk \ensuremath{\underset{{\Bbbk[G]}}{\overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes}}} M \to \operatorname{RHom}_G(\Bbbk, M) \to \mathrm{Tate}(G, M) \xrightarrow{+1},\] so that \(\operatorname{H}^n(\mathrm{Tate}(G,M))\simeq\ensuremath{\hat{\mathrm{H}}}^n(G,M)\). The difficulty with this construction is that different choices for \(\mathrm{Tate}(G,M)\) in the distinguished triangle are isomorphic, but the isomorphisms are not canonical. This is a conspicuous defect of the theory of derived categories; see Corollary reference and the explanation following it. Nevertheless, suppose that \(\Bbbk \ensuremath{\underset{{\Bbbk[G]}}{\overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes}}} M\) (respectively, \(\operatorname{RHom}_G(\Bbbk,M)\)) is represented by a chosen complex concentrated in nonpositive (respectively, nonnegative) degrees, including but not limited to \(P_G\) (respectively, \(I^G\)) in equation. We can still define the morphism \(\Omega\), take its mapping cone as \(\mathrm{Tate}(G,M)\), and interpret it as the homotopy cokernel in the sense of Remark reference.2 The exercises will explain how to use the standard resolution of \(\Bbbk\) instead, providing further tools for computing Tate cohomology. We now discuss the special case of finite cyclic groups in greater detail.

Example. Let \(m\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}_{\geq1}\) and let \(C_m\) be the cyclic group of order \(m\); choose any generator \(\sigma\) of \(C_m\). For every \(C_m\)-module \(A\), we claim that \(\ensuremath{\hat{\mathrm{H}}}^n(C_m,A)\) is the \(\operatorname{H}^n\) of the following complex (\(n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\)): \[\cdots \xrightarrow{\sigma-1} A \xrightarrow{\nu} \underbracket{A}_{\text{degree-zero term}} \xrightarrow{\sigma-1} A \xrightarrow{\nu} A \xrightarrow{\sigma-1} \to \cdots\] This complex repeats with period \(2\). Indeed, the proof of Proposition reference explicitly wrote down the complexes computing homology and cohomology; splicing them by \(\nu\) yields the mapping cone \(\mathrm{Tate}(G,M)\) mentioned above, in precisely the form displayed. We immediately obtain canonical isomorphisms \[\ensuremath{\hat{\mathrm{H}}}^n(C_m, A) \simeq \begin{cases} A^{\nu=0} / (\sigma-1) A, & n\;\text{odd} \\ A^{\sigma=1} / \nu A, & n\;\text{even}. \end{cases}\]

Periodicity shows that if \(0\to A'\to A\to A''\to0\) is a short exact sequence of \(C_m\)-modules, then the long exact sequence of Theorem reference fits into the exact hexagon \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:Herbrand-hexagon}{} \text{Diagram chapter6-unit-083-d006} \end{equation}\]

Definition. Let \(A\) be a \(C_m\)-module (\(m\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}_{\geq1}\)). Assuming that \(\ensuremath{\hat{\mathrm{H}}}^n(C_m,A)\) is finite for every \(n\), define the positive rational number

\[h(C_m, A) := \frac{\left|\ensuremath{\hat{\mathrm{H}}}^{\text{even}}(C_m, A)\right|}{\left|\ensuremath{\hat{\mathrm{H}}}^{\text{odd}}(C_m, A)\right|},\] called the Herbrand quotient of \(A\).

If \(A\) is finite, then \(\ensuremath{\hat{\mathrm{H}}}^n(C_m,A)\) is clearly finite. Note that the number of its elements is independent of the choice of coefficient ring \(\Bbbk\); we may take \(\Bbbk=\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\). In algebraic number theory, the following theorem of Herbrand is a fundamental and important result.

Theorem (J. Herbrand). Let \(m\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}_{\geq1}\) and let \(C_m\) be the cyclic group of order \(m\).

  1. Let \(0\to A'\to A\to A''\to0\) be a short exact sequence of \(C_m\)-modules. If two of \(h(C_m,A')\), \(h(C_m,A)\), and \(h(C_m,A'')\) are defined, then the third is automatically defined; in that case, \[h(C_m, A) = h(C_m, A') h(C_m, A'').\]

  2. If \(A\) is a finite \(C_m\)-module, then \(h(C_m,A)=1\).

Proof. For (i), consider the exact hexagon equation. Write \(n_i:=|\operatorname{im}(f_i)|\). In the sense of multiplication of cardinalities, the cardinalities of the six terms are, respectively,

Diagram chapter6-unit-083-d007

The three Herbrand quotients correspond to the quotients of opposite terms in the diagram above. Thus assertion (i) is equivalent to the following observations:

  • if the cardinalities at both ends of two diagonals are finite, then the same holds at both ends of the remaining diagonal;

  • the product of the terms in square-cornered boxes equals the product of the terms in round-cornered boxes.

For (ii), there are short exact sequences of finite \(\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\)-modules \[0 \to A^{\sigma=1} \to A \xrightarrow{\sigma-1} \mathfrak{I} A \to 0, \quad 0 \to A^{\nu=0} \to A \xrightarrow{\nu} \nu A \to 0;\] here \((\sigma-1)A=\mathfrak{I}A\) follows from Lemma reference. Therefore, \[|A^{\sigma=1}| \cdot |\mathfrak{I} A| = |A^{\nu=0}| \cdot |\nu A|,\] which rearranges to \(|\ensuremath{\hat{\mathrm{H}}}^0(C_m,A)|=|\ensuremath{\hat{\mathrm{H}}}^{-1}(C_m,A)|\). This proves the assertion.

  1. From the topological point of view: in the homotopical sense.↩︎

  2. Taking the homotopy kernel of \(\Bbbk \ensuremath{\underset{{\Bbbk[G]}}{\overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes}}} M \to \operatorname{RHom}_G(\Bbbk, M)\) produces no new structure; it differs from the homotopy cokernel only by a shift.↩︎

Cohomology of Profinite Groups

This section presupposes the basic definitions and results on profinite groups from §reference. Let \(G\) be a profinite group and \(M\) a \(G\)-module. It is not difficult to verify that the following conditions are equivalent:

  1. \(M=\bigcup_KM^K\), where \(K\) ranges over the open normal subgroups of \(G\);

  2. for every \(x\in M\), the stabilizer subgroup \(\operatorname{Stab}_G(x)\) is open;

  3. the action map \(G\times M\to M\) is continuous when \(M\) is given the discrete topology.

Definition. Let \(G\) be a profinite group. If any of the conditions above holds, the \(G\)-module \(M\) is called smooth1. All smooth \(G\)-modules form a full subcategory \(G\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}^\infty\) of \(G\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\).

Although the condition on \(G\) itself is topological, characterization (i) or  (ii) of a smooth \(G\)-module is entirely algebraic: smoothness is a property of a \(G\)-module, not additional structure. It follows readily that \(G\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}^\infty\) is an abelian subcategory of \(G\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\). The operations of Definition reference have natural analogues here.

Definition–Proposition. Let \(\varphi:H\to G\) be a continuous homomorphism of profinite groups and let \(M\) be a smooth \(G\)-module. Then the \(H\)-module \(\varphi^*M\) is still smooth. This gives a functor \[\varphi^*:G\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}^\infty\to H\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}^\infty.\]

Proof. For every open normal subgroup \(K\lhd G\), its inverse image \(\varphi^{-1}(K)\lhd H\) is again open and normal. If \(x\in M^K\), then \(x\in(\varphi^*M)^{\varphi^{-1}K}\). Thus \[\varphi^*M= \bigcup_{L\lhd H:\,\text{open}}(\varphi^*M)^L,\] which proves that \(\varphi^*M\) is smooth.

Note that the functor \(\varphi^*\) is always exact. We single out two special cases:

  • Restriction.If \(H\) is a closed subgroup of \(G\), take \(\varphi\) to be the inclusion homomorphism \(H\hookrightarrow G\). The corresponding functor is denoted by \[\operatorname{Res}^G_H:G\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}^\infty\to H\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}^\infty.\]

  • Inflation.For a closed normal subgroup \(H\lhd G\), take \(\varphi\) to be the quotient homomorphism \(G\twoheadrightarrow G/H\). The corresponding functor is denoted by \[\mathrm{Infl}^G_{G/H}:G/H\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}^\infty \to G\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}^\infty.\]

    The groups \(H\) and \(G/H\) mentioned above are automatically profinite, so these definitions make sense.

Definition–Proposition. For every \(G\)-module \(M\), define \(M^\infty:=\bigcup_KM^K\), where \(K\) ranges over the open normal subgroups of \(G\). This is a smooth \(G\)-module, and \(M\) is smooth if and only if \(M=M^\infty\).

For every smooth \(G\)-module \(M'\), we have \[\operatorname{Hom}_G(M',M)=\operatorname{Hom}_G(M',M^\infty).\] In other words, \(\text{inclusion}:G\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}^\infty \leftrightarrows G\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}:(\cdot)^\infty\) is an adjoint pair.

Proof. Clear.

The elements of \(M^\infty\) are also called the smooth elements of \(M\). Since \((\cdot)^\infty\) is the right adjoint of an exact functor, it preserves injective objects (Proposition reference).

Corollary. The abelian category \(G\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}^\infty\) has enough injective objects.

Proof. Let \(M\) be a smooth \(G\)-module and embed it in an injective \(G\)-module \(I\). Then \(M=M^\infty\hookrightarrow I^\infty\), while \(I^\infty\) is an injective smooth \(G\)-module.
