Remark. In general, \(G\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}^\infty\) does not have enough projective objects. This is the principal reason why this section studies cohomology rather than homology.

Since \(G\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}^\infty\) has enough injective objects, we can discuss the right derived functors of the invariants functor \((\cdot)^G\). Our approach is first to give a direct definition that reduces to the case of finite groups, and then to identify it with the right derived functors in Proposition reference. For now we use only classical language and do not invoke derived categories. First take a profinite group \(G\) and an open normal subgroup \(K\). For every smooth \(G\)-module \(M\), the submodule of \(K\)-invariants \(M^K=(\operatorname{Res}^G_KM)^K\) naturally becomes a \(G/K\)-module. This gives a functor \((\cdot)^K:G\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}^\infty\to G/K\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\) and the evident adjoint pair \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:invariant-adjunction-profinite}{} \text{Diagram chapter6-unit-084-d001} \end{equation}\] If open normal subgroups \(K,K'\) of \(G\) satisfy \(K'\supset K\), then the inclusion \(M^{K'}\hookrightarrow M^K\) is equivariant with respect to the oppositely directed quotient homomorphism \(G/K'\twoheadleftarrow G/K\) (Definition reference). Hence for every \(n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}_{\geq0}\) there is a canonical homomorphism \[\rho^{K'}_K:\operatorname{H}^n(G/K',M^{K'})\to\operatorname{H}^n(G/K,M^K).\] If \(K_1\subset K_2\subset K_3\) are open normal subgroups of \(G\), then \(\rho^{K_2}_{K_1}\rho^{K_3}_{K_2}=\rho^{K_3}_{K_1}\). Thus the following definition makes sense.

Definition. Let \(G\) be a profinite group and \(M\) a smooth \(G\)-module. For every \(n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}_{\geq0}\), define \[\operatorname{H}^n(G,M):=\varinjlim_K\operatorname{H}^n(G/K,M^K),\] where \(K\) ranges over the open normal subgroups of \(G\), and \(\varinjlim\) is taken with respect to the partial order \(K'\preceq K\iff K\subset K'\) and the morphisms \(\rho^{K'}_K\).

All open normal subgroups form a filtered partially ordered set: they are closed under finite intersections. If \(G\) is finite, then \(\{1\}\) is its unique maximal element, and \(\operatorname{H}^n(G,M)\) reduces to the original version in §reference. In general, \[\operatorname{H}^0(G,M)=\varinjlim_K(M^K)^{G/K}=M^G.\] Let \(f:M_1\to M_2\) be a homomorphism of smooth \(G\)-modules. For every open normal subgroup \(K\), it restricts to \(f_K:M_1^K\to M_2^K\). Clearly, \(K'\supset K\) implies \(\operatorname{H}^n(f_K)\rho^{K'}_K=\rho^{K'}_K\operatorname{H}^n(f_{K'})\), so for every \(n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}_{\geq0}\) there is a homomorphism \[\operatorname{H}^n(f):\operatorname{H}^n(G,M_1)\to\operatorname{H}^n(G,M_2).\]

Example. Let \(E|F\) be a Galois extension of fields. Since \(E=\bigcup_{L|F}E^{\operatorname{Gal}(E|L)}=\bigcup_{L|F}L\), where \(L|F\) ranges over the finite Galois subextensions, the action of \(\operatorname{Gal}(E|F)\) on \(E\) is smooth. Applying Example reference to every \(L|F\) gives \[n\geq1\implies\operatorname{H}^n(\operatorname{Gal}(E|F),E) =\varinjlim_{L|F}\operatorname{H}^n(\operatorname{Gal}(L|F),L)=0.\]

Just as in Proposition reference and Remark reference for groups without topology, the cohomology of a profinite group can be computed by the standard complex or its normalized version; the difference lies in the continuity condition.

Definition. For a smooth \(G\)-module \(M\), give \(M\) the discrete topology and define its standard complex \(C(G,M)=(C^n(G,M))_n\) by \[C^n(G,M):=\{\text{continuous maps }f:G^n\to M\}, \qquad n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}_{\geq0}.\] Terms of negative degree are defined to be \(0\), while \(d^n:C^n(G,M)\to C^{n+1}(G,M)\) is given by \[\begin{multline*} (d^nf)(g_1,\ldots,g_{n+1}) =g_1f(g_2,\ldots,g_{n+1})\\ +\sum_{k=1}^n(-1)^kf(\ldots,g_kg_{k+1},\ldots) +(-1)^{n+1}f(g_1,\ldots,g_n). \end{multline*}\]

Define the normalized standard complex to be the following subcomplex \(\overline{C}(G,M)\) of \(C(G,M)\) (see Remark reference): \[\overline{C}^n(G,M)=\left\{\begin{array}{r|l} f\in C^n(G,M)&\exists 1\leq k\leq n,\; g_k=1_G\\ &\implies f(g_1,\ldots,g_n)=0 \end{array}\right\}.\]

For every open normal subgroup \(K\lhd G\), there are evident inclusions of complexes \(C(G/K,M^K)\hookrightarrow C(G,M)\) and \(\overline{C}(G/K,M^K)\hookrightarrow\overline{C}(G,M)\). Since \(M\) is discrete, a map \(f:G^n\to M\) is continuous if and only if it is locally constant. Compactness of \(G\) then gives an open normal subgroup \(K_1\lhd G\) such that \(f\) factors through \((G/K_1)^n\to M\). In particular, \(f\) assumes only finitely many values; smoothness gives an open normal subgroup \(K_2\lhd G\) such that the values of \(f\) lie in \(M^{K_2}\). Set \(K:=K_1\cap K_2\). It follows that \[C^n(G,M)\simeq\varinjlim_{K\lhd G\;\text{open}}C^n(G/K,M^K),\qquad \overline{C}^n(G,M)\simeq \varinjlim_{K\lhd G\;\text{open}}\overline{C}^n(G/K,M^K).\] As \(n\) varies, these give isomorphisms of complexes. As before, define the submodules of \(C^n(G,M)\) \[Z^n(G,M):=\operatorname{ker}(d^n),\qquad B^n(G,M):=\operatorname{im}(d^{n-1}),\] with \(B^0(G,M):=\{0\}\). Then \(\operatorname{H}^n(C(G,M))=Z^n(G,M)/B^n(G,M)\). Define the normalized versions \(\overline{Z}^n(G,M)\) and \(\overline{B}^n(G,M)\) similarly.

Theorem. Let \(G\) be a profinite group. For all \(n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}_{\geq0}\) and every smooth \(G\)-module \(M\), there are canonical isomorphisms \[\operatorname{H}^n(C(G,M))\simeq\operatorname{H}^n(G,M) \simeq\operatorname{H}^n(\overline{C}(G,M)).\]

Proof. Cohomology takes values in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ab}}\), or in \(\Bbbk\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\) if a coefficient ring \(\Bbbk\) has been specified. Filtered colimits are exact in these categories [Li1]. Hence \[Z^n(G,M)=\varinjlim_KZ^n(G/K,M^K),\qquad B^n(G,M)=\varinjlim_KB^n(G/K,M^K),\] and therefore \[\begin{multline*} \operatorname{H}^n(C(G,M)) =\dfrac{\varinjlim_KZ^n(G/K,M^K)} {\varinjlim_KB^n(G/K,M^K)}\simeq\\ \varinjlim_K\frac{Z^n(G/K,M^K)}{B^n(G/K,M^K)} =\varinjlim_K\operatorname{H}^n(C(G/K,M^K)). \end{multline*}\] Apply Proposition reference to the last term to obtain \(\varinjlim_K\operatorname{H}^n(G/K,M^K)\), namely \(\operatorname{H}^n(G,M)\).

The case of \(\overline{C}(G,M)\) is similar.

  1. In view of (iii), many sources call it discrete.↩︎

Theorem. Let \(G\) be a profinite group and let \(0\to M'\xrightarrow{f}M\xrightarrow{f'}M''\to0\) be a short exact sequence of smooth \(G\)-modules. There is an associated long exact sequence \[\begin{multline*} \cdots\to\operatorname{H}^{n-1}(G,M'')\xrightarrow{\delta^{n-1}} \operatorname{H}^n(G,M')\xrightarrow{\operatorname{H}^n(f)}\operatorname{H}^n(G,M)\\ \xrightarrow{\operatorname{H}^n(f')}\operatorname{H}^n(G,M'')\xrightarrow{\delta^n} \operatorname{H}^{n+1}(G,M')\to\cdots, \end{multline*}\]

with the convention that \(\operatorname{H}^n(G,\cdot)=0\) for \(n<0\). The connecting homomorphisms \(\delta^n\) are natural with respect to morphisms of short exact sequences; in other words, they form a cohomological \(\delta\)-functor.

Proof. We work with the standard complex; the argument for the normalized version is similar. By Proposition reference, it suffices to prove that \[0\to C^n(G,M')\to C^n(G,M)\to C^n(G,M'')\to0\] is a short exact sequence. The only point that is not immediate is the surjectivity of \(C^n(G,M)\to C^n(G,M'')\). Let \(u:G^n\to M''\) be continuous. As above, there is an open normal subgroup \(K\lhd G\) such that \(u\) is constant on each coset of \(K^n\lhd G^n\). On every coset, choose an arbitrary inverse image in \(M\) of this constant value.

Let \(M\) be a smooth \(G\)-module with the discrete topology. The low-degree terms of the complex \(C(G,M)\) or \(\overline{C}(G,M)\) still have direct interpretations.

  • (\(n=0\)).Clearly \(C^0(G,M)=M\) and \(\operatorname{H}^0(G,M)=Z^0(G,M)=M^G\). The normalized standard complex gives the same result.

  • (\(n=1\)).The elements of \(Z^1(G,M)=\overline{Z}^1(G,M)\) are continuous crossed homomorphisms \(G\to M\). Equivalently, they are continuous homomorphisms \(\sigma:G\to M\rtimes G\) satisfying \(\pi\sigma=\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_G\), as in Proposition reference. Here \(\pi:M\rtimes G\to G\) is the projection and \(M\rtimes G\) carries the product topology. On the other hand, the elements of \(B^1(G,M)\) are generated by the crossed homomorphisms \(f_m:g\mapsto gm-m\); these are automatically continuous.

  • (\(n=2\)).Suppose that \(M\) is finite. The elements of \[\operatorname{H}^2(G,M)\simeq\frac{Z^2(G,M)}{B^2(G,M)} \simeq\frac{\overline{Z}^2(G,M)}{\overline{B}^2(G,M)}\] correspond bijectively to equivalence classes of extensions of profinite groups \[1\to M\to E\xrightarrow{\pi}G\to1 \qquad\text{(short exact sequence of groups)},\]

    where the conjugation action of \(G\) on \(M\) comes from the \(G\)-module structure on \(M\). Compared with the version in Definition reference and equation, a “profinite group extension” and its classification must additionally satisfy:

    • \(E\) is a profinite group, \(\pi\) is continuous, and \(M\) is embedded as a closed subgroup of \(E\);

    • equivalences, or isomorphisms, of extensions are defined by continuous group homomorphisms \(E\to E'\), and the splitting of an extension is likewise defined topologically.

    Moreover, the automorphism group of an extension is isomorphic to \(\overline{Z}^1(G,M)\). The proofs are not difficult, but require some topological language and are therefore left as exercises for this chapter; the finiteness of \(M\) is essential.

We now return to the right derived functors \((\mathrm{R}^n(\cdot)^G)_{n\geq0}\). One could study their values on arbitrary bounded-below complexes1, or even their operation in the derived category. This section, however, discusses only smooth \(G\)-modules; the rest is left to the exercises.

Proposition. There is an isomorphism of cohomological \(\delta\)-functors \[(\operatorname{H}^n(G,\cdot))_{n\geq0} \simeq(\mathrm{R}^n(\cdot)^G)_{n\geq0}.\]

Proof. Theorem reference shows that both sides are cohomological \(\delta\)-functors, and at \(n=0\) both are the invariants functor \((\cdot)^G\). By Proposition reference, it is enough to show that \(\operatorname{H}^n(G,\cdot)\) is erasable for \(n>0\) in the sense of Definition reference. Let \(M\) be a smooth \(G\)-module and embed it in an injective smooth \(G\)-module \(I\). For every open normal subgroup \(K\lhd G\), the adjunction equation shows that \((\cdot)^K\) preserves injective objects. Hence \(I^K\) is an injective \(G/K\)-module, and \[n>0\implies\operatorname{H}^n(G,I) =\varinjlim_K\operatorname{H}^n(G/K,I^K)=0.\] This proves erasability.

By Proposition reference, the method of §reference applies directly to a continuous homomorphism \(\varphi:H\to G\) of profinite groups and defines a cohomological “pullback” operation \[\operatorname{H}^n(G,M)\to\operatorname{H}^n(H,\varphi^*M),\qquad M:\text{ a smooth $G$-module},\quad n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}_{\geq0}.\] These operations are compatible with long exact sequences. As usual, exactness of \(\varphi^*\) and the universal property of cohomological \(\delta\)-functors reduce the matter to the evident inclusion at \(n=0\), \(M^G\hookrightarrow(\varphi^*M)^H\). As a special case, for all \(n\) and all closed subgroups \(H\) there are restriction maps \(\mathrm{res}^n:\operatorname{H}^n(G,M)\to\operatorname{H}^n(H,M)\); here \(\operatorname{Res}^G_HM\) is abbreviated to \(M\). The homomorphisms above may also be constructed from the homomorphisms \[\begin{align*} \operatorname{H}^n(G/K,M^K)&\xrightarrow{\href{#eqn:change-of-group-coh}{equation}} \operatorname{H}^n(H/\varphi^{-1}(K),\varphi_K^*(M^K))\\ &\xrightarrow{M^K\subset(\varphi^*M)^{\varphi^{-1}K}} \operatorname{H}^n(H/\varphi^{-1}(K),(\varphi^*M)^{\varphi^{-1}K}), \end{align*}\] where \(K\) ranges over the open normal subgroups of \(G\). Reducing to the case of finite groups shows that the homomorphism on the standard complex is computed by the formula of Proposition reference. To prove that this map is indeed the same as the one constructed earlier by the universal property, it is enough to compare them at \(n=0\) and show compatibility with long exact sequences. The standard complex suffices for both tasks. Similarly, the corestriction homomorphism of Definition–Proposition reference extends to profinite groups. Let \(H\) be an open subgroup of \(G\). It is then automatically closed and \((G:H)\) is finite (see §reference). Define homomorphisms \[\mathrm{cor}^n:\operatorname{H}^n(H,M)\to\operatorname{H}^n(G,M),\qquad M:\text{ a smooth $G$-module},\quad n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}_{\geq0},\] which are compatible with long exact sequences and at \(n=0\) give \(\nu^{G|H}:M^H\to M^G\). The construction again uses the universal property of cohomological \(\delta\)-functors, but here we need to know that \(\operatorname{Res}^G_H:G\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}^\infty\to H\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}^\infty\) preserves injective objects; this is the content of Corollary reference. Once this fact is granted, Proposition reference still has an analogue: for every \(n\), \[\mathrm{cor}^n\circ\mathrm{res}^n =(G:H)\cdot\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{\operatorname{H}^n(G,M)}.\] As before, the proof reduces to the case \(n=0\). We now discuss induced modules in the profinite case. Henceforth \(G\) is always a profinite group. To distinguish the two settings, denote the induction functor without topology (Definition reference) by \(\operatorname{Ind}^{G,\mathrm{alg}}_H\); following Lemma reference, we realize it as a mapping space.

Definition. For a closed subgroup \(H\) of \(G\) and a smooth \(H\)-module \(N\), equip the mapping space \(\mathrm{Maps}(G,N):=\{f:G\to N\}\) with pointwise addition and scalar multiplication, together with the left \(G\)-action \[(gf)(x)=f(xg),\qquad g,x\in G.\] Define the smooth \(G\)-module \[\begin{align*} \operatorname{Ind}^G_H(N)&:=\{f\in\mathrm{Maps}(G,N)^\infty: \forall h\in H,\ \forall x\in G,\ f(hx)=hf(x)\}\\ &=(\operatorname{Ind}^{G,\mathrm{alg}}_H(N))^\infty. \end{align*}\] The notation \((\cdot)^\infty\) is from Definition–Proposition reference. This is called the \(G\)-module induced from \(N\).

Since \(G\) is compact, smoothness of \(f\in\operatorname{Ind}^{G,\mathrm{alg}}_H(N)\) is equivalent to its continuity as a map \(G\to N\), where \(N\) carries the discrete topology.

Proposition. For every closed subgroup \(H\) of \(G\), there is an adjoint pair \[\operatorname{Res}^G_H:G\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}^\infty \leftrightarrows H\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}^\infty:\operatorname{Ind}^G_H.\] Consequently, \(\operatorname{Ind}^G_H\) preserves injective objects.

If \(H\) is an open subgroup of \(G\), there is also an adjoint pair \[\operatorname{Ind}^G_H:H\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}^\infty \leftrightarrows G\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}^\infty:\operatorname{Res}^G_H.\] In this case \(\operatorname{Ind}^G_H\) also preserves projective objects.

Proof. By the adjunction in the setting without topology and Definition–Proposition reference, for every smooth \(G\)-module \(M\) and smooth \(H\)-module \(N\) there are canonical isomorphisms \[\begin{multline*} \operatorname{Hom}_H(\operatorname{Res}^G_H(M),N) \simeq\operatorname{Hom}_G(M,\operatorname{Ind}^{G,\mathrm{alg}}_H(N))\\ =\operatorname{Hom}_G(M,\operatorname{Ind}^{G,\mathrm{alg}}_H(N)^\infty) =\operatorname{Hom}_G(M,\operatorname{Ind}^G_H(N)). \end{multline*}\]

Now suppose that \(H\) is open, so that \((G:H)\) is finite. From Corollary reference we obtain the adjunction without topology \[\operatorname{Hom}_H(N,\operatorname{Res}^G_H(M)) \simeq\operatorname{Hom}_G(\operatorname{Ind}^{G,\mathrm{alg}}_H(N),M).\] We claim that \(\operatorname{Ind}^{G,\mathrm{alg}}_H(N)=\operatorname{Ind}^G_H(N)\). Take \(f\in\operatorname{Ind}^{G,\mathrm{alg}}_H(N)\) and \(x\in G\), and choose an open subgroup \(K_0\subset H\) such that \(f(x)\in N^{K_0}\). Set \(K:=x^{-1}K_0x\), which is an open subgroup of \(G\). Then \[g\in K\implies xg=xgx^{-1}x\in K_0x \implies f(xg)=f(x).\] Since \(x\) was arbitrary, the map \(f:G\to N\) is locally constant, so \(f\in\operatorname{Ind}^G_H(N)\). This proves the second adjunction.

Finally, the claims about preserving injective or projective objects follow from exactness of \(\operatorname{Res}^G_H\) and Proposition reference.

Lemma. If \(H\) is a closed subgroup of \(G\), then \(\operatorname{Ind}^G_H:H\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}^\infty\to G\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}^\infty\) is exact.

Proof. We already know that \(\operatorname{Ind}^G_H\) has a left adjoint, so it is left exact. It remains to prove that \(N_1\twoheadrightarrow N_2\) implies \(\operatorname{Ind}^G_H(N_1)\twoheadrightarrow\operatorname{Ind}^G_H(N_2)\). By Lemma reference, the quotient homomorphism \(\pi:G\to H\backslash G\) has a continuous section \(s\). For every smooth \(H\)-module \(N\), there is a \(\Bbbk\)-module isomorphism \[\text{Diagram chapter6-unit-085-d001}\] where \(x\in H\backslash G\) and \(h\in H\). Although this isomorphism does not preserve the \(G\)-action, it is natural in \(N\).

Since continuous maps \(H\backslash G\to N\) are always locally constant, working on the right-hand side immediately shows that \(\operatorname{Ind}^G_H(N_1)\to\operatorname{Ind}^G_H(N_2)\) is surjective.

Corollary. If \(H\) is an open subgroup of \(G\), then \(\operatorname{Res}^G_H:G\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}^\infty\to H\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}^\infty\) preserves injective objects.

Proof. By the preceding two results, it has the exact left adjoint \(\operatorname{Ind}^G_H\).

We now obtain the profinite version of Theorem reference.

Proposition. Let \(H\) be a closed subgroup of a profinite group \(G\) and let \(N\) be a smooth \(H\)-module. There are isomorphisms \[\operatorname{H}^n(G,\operatorname{Ind}^G_H(N))\simeq\operatorname{H}^n(H,N), \qquad n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}_{\geq0}.\]

Proof. Because \(\operatorname{Ind}^G_H\) is exact and preserves injective objects (Lemma reference and Proposition reference), the argument in Theorem reference using erasable cohomological \(\delta\)-functors applies unchanged. Recall that the heart of that argument is the case \(n=0\), namely \[\operatorname{Ind}^G_H(N)^G =(\operatorname{Ind}^{G,\mathrm{alg}}_H(N)^\infty)^G =(\operatorname{Ind}^{G,\mathrm{alg}}_H(N))^G\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}N^H.\] The first equality is the definition, the second is immediate, and the last isomorphism comes from Corollary reference.

In addition:

  • the cohomological Lyndon–Hochschild–Serre spectral sequence (see §reference) extends to the case where \(G\) is a profinite group and \(H\) is a closed normal subgroup;

  • the cup product (see §reference) also extends to profinite groups by using the direct definition on the standard complex; see Definition–Proposition reference.

The statements are unchanged, so we do not repeat them.

  1. In other words, study the hypercohomology of profinite groups.↩︎

Nonabelian Cohomology

Let \(G\) be a group. The cohomology \(\operatorname{H}^n(G,M)\) discussed previously always requires its “coefficients” \(M\) to have a module structure, or at least to be a \(\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\)-module, that is, an abelian group. This section studies the case in which the coefficients form a nonabelian group. From now on we use the symbol \(A\) in place of \(M\).

Definition. Let \(A\) be a group, with its binary operation written multiplicatively and its identity element denoted by \(1\). Suppose that \(A\) is equipped with a left action of the group \(G\), written \[G \times A \to A, \quad (g, a) \mapsto {}^g a .\] If the group action is compatible with the multiplicative structure of \(A\), \[{}^g (a_1 a_2) = {}^g a_1 {}^g a_2, \quad {}^g 1 = 1,\] then \(A\) is called a group with a \(G\)-action, or simply a \(G\)-group. A homomorphism of \(G\)-groups is defined to be a group homomorphism that preserves the \(G\)-action. The resulting category is denoted by \(G\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Grp}}\).

We will soon see that, for a \(G\)-group \(A\), without additional structure or commutativity only \(\operatorname{H}^0\) and \(\operatorname{H}^1\) can be defined in a reasonable and useful way. In this setting \(\operatorname{H}^1\) need not be a group; it is instead a pointed set.

Definition. A pointed set is data \((X,x_0)\), where \(X\) is a set and \(x_0\in X\) is its basepoint. A morphism from \((X,x_0)\) to \((Y,y_0)\) is a map \(f:X\to Y\) satisfying \(f(x_0)=y_0\). These data form the category \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Set}}_\bullet\).

Let \((X,x_0)\) be a pointed set. If a group \(G\) acts on \(X\) from the left, written \((g,x)\mapsto{}^gx\), and \({}^gx_0=x_0\) always holds, we say that \(G\) acts on \((X,x_0)\). In that case we can define the pointed subset of invariants \[(X, x_0)^G := \left\{ x \in X: \forall g \in G, \; gx = x \right\}, \quad \text{basepoint} = x_0.\] All pointed sets with a \(G\)-action, together with morphisms compatible with that action, form the category denoted by \(G\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Set}}_\bullet\).

When no confusion can arise, we often write an object \((X,x_0)\) of \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Set}}_\bullet\) simply as \(X\), and in \(G\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Set}}_\bullet\) write \((X,x_0)^G\) as \(X^G\). Every group becomes a pointed set by choosing its identity element as the basepoint. This gives the evident functor \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Grp}}\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{Set}}_\bullet\); similarly, there is a functor \(G\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Grp}}\to G\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Set}}_\bullet\). Note that the invariant subset \(A^G\) of a \(G\)-group \(A\) is a subgroup.

Definition. Let \((X,x_0)\xrightarrow{f}(Y,y_0)\xrightarrow{g}(Z,z_0)\) be morphisms in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Set}}_\bullet\) (or \(G\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Set}}_\bullet\)). This sequence of morphisms is called exact if \(g^{-1}(z_0)=\operatorname{im}(f)\). In this way, exact sequences in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Set}}_\bullet\) (or \(G\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Set}}_\bullet\)) are defined.

For abelian groups this recovers the familiar notion of exactness. We can now define \(\operatorname{H}^0\) and \(\operatorname{H}^1\) for every \(G\)-group \(A\).

Definition. Let \(A\) be an object of \(G\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Set}}_\bullet\). Define the pointed set \[\operatorname{H}^0(G, A) = Z^0(G, A) := A^G.\]

If \(A\) is a \(G\)-group, then \(\operatorname{H}^0(G,A)\) is a group. In this case, further define \[\begin{align*} Z^1(G, A) & := \left\{\begin{array}{r|l} c: G \to A & \forall g_1, g_2 \in G, \\ & c(g_1 g_2) = c(g_1) \cdot {}^{g_1} c(g_2) \end{array}\right\}, \\ \operatorname{H}^1(G, A) & := Z^1(G, A) / \sim , \end{align*}\] where the equivalence relation \(c\sim c'\) means that there is an \(a\in A\) such that, for every \(g\in G\), \[c'(g) = a^{-1} \cdot c(g) \cdot {}^g a .\] It is easy to see that this is indeed an equivalence relation—it comes from a right \(A\)-action—and \(\operatorname{H}^1(G,A)\) naturally becomes a pointed set. Its basepoint is the equivalence class determined by the constant map \(c(g)=1\).

Note that substituting \(g_1=g_2=1_G\) into the condition defining \(Z^1(G,A)\) gives \(c(1_G)=1\). Henceforth \([c]\) denotes the equivalence class of \(c\in Z^1(G,A)\).

Remark (\(\operatorname{H}^1\) as conjugacy classes of sections). Form the semidirect product \(A\rtimes G\) from the \(G\)-group \(A\), and let \(\pi\) denote the projection homomorphism \(A\rtimes G\to G\). The elements of \(Z^1(G,A)\) correspond bijectively to group homomorphisms \(\sigma:G\to A\rtimes G\) satisfying \(\pi\sigma=\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_G\) (that is, “sections” of \(\pi\)), via the map sending \(c\in Z^1(G,A)\) to \(\sigma(g)=(c(g),g)\). Moreover, \([c']=[c]\) if and only if there is an \(a\in A\) such that \(\sigma'=a^{-1}\sigma a\), where \(A\) is embedded as a subgroup of \(A\rtimes G\) and conjugation is performed pointwise.

If \(A\) is an abelian group, these constructions reduce to the descriptions of \(\operatorname{H}^0\) and \(\operatorname{H}^1\) using the standard cochain complex (Proposition reference). In the nonabelian case, the constructions remain functorial, as follows.

  • Every morphism \(f:A_1\to A_2\) induces \[\begin{gather*} \operatorname{H}^0(f): \operatorname{H}^0(G, A_1) \to \operatorname{H}^0(G, A_2), \quad \operatorname{H}^1(f): \operatorname{H}^1(G, A_1) \to \operatorname{H}^1(G, A_2); \end{gather*}\] the first map is evident, while the second is given by \(\operatorname{H}^1(f)([c])=[f\circ c]\).

  • Let \(\varphi:H\to G\) be a group homomorphism. Pull the \(G\)-action on the \(G\)-group \(A\) back to \(H\), giving the \(H\)-group \(\varphi^*A\).

    • Define the canonical morphism \(\operatorname{H}^0(G,A)\to\operatorname{H}^0(H,\varphi^*A)\) to be the evident inclusion \(A^G\hookrightarrow A^{\varphi(H)}=(\varphi^*A)^H\).

    • Define the canonical morphism of pointed sets \[\operatorname{H}^1(G, A) \to \operatorname{H}^1(H, \varphi^* A).\] It is given by \([c]\mapsto[c\circ\varphi]\).

These canonical maps have the various properties seen in §reference. They can also be summarized as follows. Given \(\varphi:H\to G\), let \(A_1\) be an object of \(G\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Set}}_\bullet\) (or \(G\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Grp}}\)), let \(A_2\) be an object of \(H\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Set}}_\bullet\) (or \(H\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Grp}}\)), and let the morphism \(f:A_1\to A_2\) be equivariant with respect to \(\varphi\), as in Definition reference. There are corresponding maps \(\operatorname{H}^i(f):\operatorname{H}^i(G,A_1)\to\operatorname{H}^i(H,A_2)\), and the analogue of Proposition reference takes the form:

  • \(\operatorname{H}^0(f)\) is the restriction of \(f\) to \(A_1^G\to A_2^H\);

  • \(\operatorname{H}^1(f)\) maps \([c]\) to \([f\circ c\circ\varphi]\).

Convention. Write \(1\) for the zero object in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Set}}_\bullet\) or \(G\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Set}}_\bullet\) determined by the singleton set.

We now come to the main subject. Henceforth consider a short exact sequence in \(G\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Set}}_\bullet\) (Definition reference) \[1 \to A \xrightarrow{u} B \xrightarrow{v} C \to 1,\] where \(A\) and \(B\) are assumed to be \(G\)-groups and \(u\) is a group homomorphism. Exactness therefore implies that \(u\) is injective and \(v\) is surjective. We further require: \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:pointed-ses-condition}{} \begin{gathered} \forall b, b' \in B, \; \left[ v(b) = v(b') \iff \exists a \in A, \; b' = b u(a) \right], \\ \text{in other words: $C$ is identified with $B/u(A)$, basepoint $= 1 \cdot u(A)$.} \end{gathered} \end{equation}\] If \(C\) is a group and \(v\) is a group homomorphism, considering \(b^{-1}b'\in v^{-1}(1)=\operatorname{im}(u)\) shows that equation holds automatically, and in this case \(u(A)\lhd B\). Many applications, however, do not fall into this case. Our present goal is to construct from these data an exact sequence that is “as long as possible,” together with the corresponding connecting morphisms. Without further comment, we identify \(A\) with its image as a subgroup of \(B\) and omit the symbol \(u\). The degree-zero case. First define the connecting morphism \(\delta^0:\operatorname{H}^0(G,C)\to\operatorname{H}^1(G,A)\). Let \(c\in C^G\). Choose any \(b\in v^{-1}(c)\). Since \(v\) preserves the \(G\)-action, equation shows that, for every \(g\in G\), there is a unique \(a(g)\in A\) such that \({}^gb=ba(g)\). Hence \(g\mapsto a(g)\) gives an element \(a\) of \(Z^1(G,A)\), because

\[a(g_1 g_2) = b^{-1} \cdot {}^{g_1 g_2} b = b^{-1} \cdot {}^{g_1} b \cdot {}^{g_1} (b^{-1} \cdot {}^{g_2} b) = a(g_1) \cdot {}^{g_1} a(g_2).\] If \(b',b\in v^{-1}(c)\), there is an \(\alpha\in A\) such that \(b'=b\alpha\), and hence \[(b')^{-1} \cdot {}^g b' = \alpha^{-1} \cdot b^{-1} \cdot {}^g b \cdot {}^g \alpha.\] This shows that the class \([a]\in\operatorname{H}^1(G,A)\) is determined solely by \(c\). If \(c\) is the basepoint of \(C\), we may take \(b=1\in B\). We have therefore obtained a morphism in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Set}}_\bullet\), \(\delta^0:\operatorname{H}^0(G,C)\to\operatorname{H}^1(G,A)\). The degree-zero case: a central subgroup. Suppose that \(C\) is a group, \(v\) is a group homomorphism, and \(A\) is contained in the center \(Z_B\) of the group \(B\); in particular, \(A\) is abelian. In this case \(\operatorname{H}^0(G,C)=C^G\) and \(\operatorname{H}^1(G,A)\) are both groups. From the definition of \(\delta^0\) and the condition \(A\subset Z_B\), it is easy to check that \(\delta^0\) is a group homomorphism. The degree-one case. Continue to suppose that \(C\) is a group, \(v\) is a group homomorphism, and \(A\subset Z_B\); then \(\operatorname{H}^2(G,A)\) can be described using the standard cochain complex. We define \(\delta^1:\operatorname{H}^1(G,C)\to\operatorname{H}^2(G,A)\). Let \(c\in Z^1(G,C)\). For every \(g\in G\), choose \(b(g)\in v^{-1}(c(g))\). Since equation always holds and \(v\) preserves the \(G\)-action, there is a unique map \(a:G^2\to A\) satisfying \[b(g_1) \cdot {}^{g_1} b(g_2) = a(g_1, g_2) b(g_1 g_2).\] We now check that \(a\in Z^2(G,A)\). This is equivalent to \[a(g_1, g_2)^{-1} \cdot a(g_1, g_2 g_3) \cdot a(g_1 g_2, g_3)^{-1} \cdot {}^{g_1} a(g_2, g_3) = 1.\] Expand the left-hand side as an expression in \(B\): \[\begin{multline*} \underbracket{b(g_1 g_2) \cdot {}^{g_1} b(g_2)^{-1} \cdot b(g_1)^{-1}}_{a(g_1, g_2)^{-1}} \cdot \underbracket{b(g_1) \cdot {}^{g_1} b(g_2 g_3) b(g_1 g_2 g_3)^{-1}}_{a(g_1, g_2 g_3)} \\ \underbracket{b(g_1 g_2 g_3) \cdot {}^{g_1 g_2} b(g_3)^{-1} \cdot b(g_1 g_2)^{-1}}_{a(g_1 g_2, g_3)^{-1}} \; \cdot \; {}^{g_1} a(g_2, g_3), \end{multline*}\] and then use \(A\subset Z_B\) to simplify it to \[\begin{multline*} b(g_1 g_2) \cdot {}^{g_1} b(g_2)^{-1} \cdot {}^{g_1} b(g_2 g_3) \cdot {}^{g_1 g_2} b(g_3)^{-1} b(g_1 g_2)^{-1} \cdot {}^{g_1} a(g_2, g_3) \\ = b(g_1 g_2) \cdot {}^{g_1} b(g_2)^{-1} \cdot \underbracket{{}^{g_1} b(g_2) \cdot {}^{g_1 g_2} b(g_3) \cdot {}^{g_1} b(g_2 g_3)^{-1}}_{{}^{g_1} a(g_2, g_3)} \cdot {}^{g_1} b(g_2 g_3) \cdot {}^{g_1 g_2} b(g_3)^{-1} b(g_1 g_2)^{-1} . \end{multline*}\] The last expression is visibly equal to \(1\), so \(a\in Z^2(G,A)\). If the choice of every \(b(g)\) is changed and written \(b'(g)=\alpha(g)b(g)\), where \(\alpha:G\to A\) is any map, then the corresponding \(a'(g_1,g_2)\) is \[\begin{align*} a'(g_1, g_2) & = \alpha(g_1) \cdot b(g_1) \cdot {}^{g_1} \alpha(g_2) \cdot {}^{g_1} b(g_2) b(g_1 g_2)^{-1} \alpha(g_1 g_2)^{-1} \\ & = \alpha(g_1) \cdot {}^{g_1} \alpha(g_2) \cdot \alpha(g_1 g_2)^{-1} \cdot a(g_1, g_2) \quad (\because\; A \subset Z_B). \end{align*}\] Thus \(a,a'\in Z^2(G,A)\) differ only by a factor belonging to \(B^2(G,A)\). Finally, consider the case in which \(c\) is replaced by \(c'(g)=\gamma^{-1}\cdot c(g)\cdot{}^g\gamma\), with \(\gamma\in C\). Choose any \(\beta\in v^{-1}(\gamma)\). For the \(b'\) corresponding to \(c'\), we may take \(b'(g)=\beta^{-1}\cdot b(g)\cdot{}^g\beta\). The map \(a':G^2\to A\) constructed from \(b'\) is \[\begin{align*} a'(g_1, g_2) & = \left( \beta^{-1} \cdot b(g_1) \cdot {}^{g_1} \beta \right) \cdot {}^{g_1} \left( \beta^{-1} \cdot b(g_2) \cdot {}^{g_2} \beta \right) \cdot \left( {}^{g_1 g_2} \beta^{-1} \cdot b(g_1 g_2)^{-1} \cdot \beta \right) \\ & = \beta^{-1} \cdot \underbracket{b(g_1) \cdot {}^{g_1} b(g_2) \cdot b(g_1 g_2)^{-1}}_{= a(g_1, g_2)} \cdot \beta \\ & = a(g_1, g_2). \end{align*}\] Thus the class of \(a\) in \(\operatorname{H}^2(G,A)\) is determined by \([c]\in\operatorname{H}^1(G,C)\). If \(c\) is the constant map with value \(1\), then \(b\) may also be chosen to be constantly \(1\), and likewise for \(a\). We have thus obtained a morphism in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Set}}_\bullet\), \(\delta^1:\operatorname{H}^1(G,C)\to\operatorname{H}^2(G,A)\).

Theorem. Let \(1\to A\xrightarrow{u}B\xrightarrow{v}C\to1\) be a short exact sequence in \(G\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Set}}_\bullet\), where \(A\) and \(B\) are \(G\)-groups and \(u\) is a group homomorphism.

  1. If condition equation holds, there is an exact sequence in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Set}}_\bullet\) \[\begin{equation*} \text{Diagram chapter6-unit-086-d001} \end{equation*}\]

  2. In addition to the assumptions above, suppose that \(C\) is also a group and \(v\) is a group homomorphism; this automatically implies equation. The exact sequence then extends to \[\begin{equation*} \text{Diagram chapter6-unit-086-d002} \end{equation*}\]

  3. If we further require that \(u(A)\) be contained in the center \(Z_B\) of \(B\), then \(\delta^0\) is a group homomorphism and the exact sequence extends to \[\begin{equation*} \text{Diagram chapter6-unit-086-d003} \end{equation*}\]

The connecting morphisms \(\delta^0\) and \(\delta^1\) are defined as above. Both are canonical, meaning that they are compatible with morphisms of short exact sequences.

Proof. The detailed constructions of \(\delta^0\) and \(\delta^1\) above already show that both are canonical; in case (iii), they also showed that \(\delta^0\) is a group homomorphism. We now check exactness. Henceforth regard \(A\) as a subgroup of \(B\) and omit \(u\).

In case (i), exactness at \(\operatorname{H}^0(G,A)\) and \(\operatorname{H}^0(G,B)\) is clear. At \(\operatorname{H}^0(G,C)\), let \(c\in C^G\). By definition, \(c\) maps to the basepoint of \(\operatorname{H}^1(G,A)\) if and only if there are \(\alpha\in A\) and \(b\in B\) such that \[v(b) = c, \quad \forall g \in G,\; b^{-1} \cdot {}^g b = \alpha^{-1} \cdot {}^g \alpha.\] But this is equivalent to the existence of \(\alpha\in A\) and \(b\in B\) such that \(v(b)=c\) and \(b\alpha^{-1}\in B^G\), which is in turn equivalent to \(c\in\operatorname{im}(\operatorname{H}^0(u))\).

At \(\operatorname{H}^1(G,A)\), let \(a\in Z^1(G,A)\). The class \([a]\in\operatorname{H}^1(G,A)\) maps to the basepoint if and only if there is a \(b\in B\) such that \(b^{-1}\cdot a(g)\cdot{}^gb=1\) for every \(g\). If this holds, set \(c:=v(b^{-1})\). Applying \(v\) to \({}^gb^{-1}=b^{-1}\cdot a(g)\) shows that \(c\in C^G\) and \([a]=\delta^0([c])\). The converse argument is similar.

In case (ii), what remains is exactness at \(\operatorname{H}^1(G,B)\). Let \(b\in Z^1(G,B)\). Its class \([b]\) maps to the basepoint if and only if there is a \(\beta\in B\) such that \(\beta^{-1}\cdot b(g)\cdot{}^g\beta\in A\) for every \(g\). Clearly, this is the same as saying that, up to \(\sim\), the class comes from \(Z^1(G,A)\).

Consider case (iii). Let \(c\in Z^1(G,C)\). Its class \([c]\) maps to the basepoint if and only if there are maps \(b:G\to B\) and \(\alpha:G\to A\) such that \(v\circ b=c\) and \[b(g_1) \cdot {}^{g_1} b(g_2) = \alpha(g_1) \cdot {}^{g_1} \alpha(g_2) \cdot \alpha(g_1 g_2)^{-1} \cdot b(g_1 g_2).\] Since \(A\subset Z_B\), if \(\alpha^{-1}b:G\to B\) is defined by pointwise multiplication, the equation above is also equivalent to \[(\alpha^{-1} b)(g_1) \cdot {}^{g_1} (\alpha^{-1} b)(g_2) = (\alpha^{-1} b)(g_1 g_2),\] that is, \(\alpha^{-1}b\in Z^1(G,B)\). Clearly this is equivalent to saying that \([c]\) comes from \(\operatorname{H}^1(G,B)\). This proves exactness.

If \(A\) and \(B\) are further required to be abelian, then \(C\simeq B/u(A)\) is an abelian group, and we recover the familiar version with coefficients in an abelian group. Note that the exact sequence in Theorem reference (i) describes the inverse image of the basepoint under \(\operatorname{H}^1(u)\), but in general it cannot determine whether two elements of \(\operatorname{H}^1(G,A)\) have the same image under \(\operatorname{H}^1(u)\). The “twisting” construction introduced in the exercises for this chapter helps address this problem.

Example. Let \(B\) be a \(G\)-group and \(A\) a subgroup stable under the \(G\)-action. Equip the set \(B/A\) with the basepoint \(1\cdot A\) and a left \(G\)-action. This gives a short exact sequence in \(G\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Set}}_\bullet\) \[1 \to A \xrightarrow{\text{inclusion}} B \xrightarrow{\text{quotient}} B/A \to 1.\] Condition equation clearly holds. Hence Theorem reference (i) gives an exact sequence in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Set}}_\bullet\) \[1 \to A^G \to B^G \to (B/A)^G \xrightarrow{\delta^0} \operatorname{H}^1(G, A) \to \operatorname{H}^1(G, B).\]

The evident map \(B^G/A^G\hookrightarrow(B/A)^G\) is injective, but it is often not bijective: a coset stable under the \(G\)-action need not contain a \(G\)-fixed point; the exercises will give an example. Nevertheless, the exact sequence identifies the cohomological obstruction. For a morphism \(f\) in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Set}}_\bullet\), define \(\operatorname{ker}(f)\) to be the inverse image of the basepoint. Then \[\begin{align*} \text{the coset}\; bA \in (B/A)^G \;\text{comes from}\; B^G & \iff bA \in \operatorname{ker}(\delta^0), \\ (B/A)^G = B^G/A^G & \iff \operatorname{ker}[\operatorname{H}^1(G, A) \to \operatorname{H}^1(G, B)] = 1. \end{align*}\]

We close this section with the nonabelian version of Shapiro’s Lemma (Theorem reference). As preparation, first define a nonabelian version of induced modules using a mapping space; compare Lemma reference. The construction applies to objects of \(H\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Grp}}\) or \(H\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Set}}_\bullet\), where \(H\) is a subgroup of \(G\); the group action is written \((h,a)\mapsto{}^ha\).

Definition. Let \(H\) be a subgroup of \(G\) and let \(A\) be an object of \(H\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Grp}}\) (or \(H\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Set}}_\bullet\)). Define the object \(\operatorname{Ind}^G_H(A)\) of \(G\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Grp}}\) (or \(G\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Set}}_\bullet\)) as follows. As an object of \(G\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Set}}\), it is \[\begin{gather*} \operatorname{Ind}^G_H(A) := \left\{\begin{array}{r|l} f: G \to A & \forall h \in H, \; \forall x \in G \\ & f(hx) = {}^h f(x). \end{array}\right\}, \\ ({}^g f)(x) := f(xg), \quad f \in \operatorname{Ind}^G_H(A), \; x, g \in G, \end{gather*}\] with the group operation (respectively, basepoint) defined pointwise on maps (respectively, by the constant map to the basepoint). We call \(A\mapsto\operatorname{Ind}^G_H(A)\) induction.

The induction construction gives compatible functors \(H\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Grp}}\to G\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Grp}}\) and \(H\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Set}}_\bullet\to G\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Set}}_\bullet\).

Theorem. Let \(H\) be a subgroup of \(G\) and let \(A\) be an object of \(H\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Set}}_\bullet\) or \(H\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Grp}}\). There are canonical isomorphisms in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Set}}_\bullet\) \[\operatorname{H}^i\left(G, \operatorname{Ind}^G_H(A)\right) \ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}\operatorname{H}^i(H, A),\] with \(i=0\) if \(A\) comes from \(H\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Set}}_\bullet\), or \(i=0,1\) if \(A\) comes from \(H\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Grp}}\). The maps are as follows.

  • (\(i=0\)).Take the map \(f\mapsto f(1_G)\), which defines \(Z^0\left(G,\operatorname{Ind}^G_H(A)\right)=\operatorname{Ind}^G_H(A)^G\to A^H=Z^0(H,A)\).

  • (\(i=1\)).Take the map \(Z^1\left(G,\operatorname{Ind}^G_H(A)\right)\to Z^1(H,A)\) sending \(c:G\to\operatorname{Ind}^G_H(A)\) to \[\begin{align*} (c|_H)(\cdot)(1_G): H & \to A \\ h & \mapsto c(h)(1_G). \end{align*}\]

Both induce morphisms on \(\operatorname{H}^i\). If \(A\) comes from \(H\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Grp}}\), the isomorphism for \(i=0\) is also an isomorphism of groups.

Proof. Routine arguments show that the maps in both cases are well-defined and preserve the basepoint or group structure; details are left to the reader.

For \(i=0\), it is easy to see that \(\operatorname{Ind}^G_H(A)^G\to A^H\) is indeed a bijection and gives an isomorphism of groups if \(A\) is an \(H\)-group. We now focus on the case where \(A\) is an object of \(H\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Grp}}\) and \(i=1\).

Suppose that \(r,s\in Z^1(G,\operatorname{Ind}^G_H(A))\) have the same image in \(\operatorname{H}^1(H,A)\). We prove that \(r\sim s\). This assumption is equivalent to the existence of an \(\alpha\in A\) such that \[r(h)(1_G) = \alpha^{-1} \cdot s(h)(1_G) \cdot {}^h \alpha\] for every \(h\in H\). There is a \(\zeta\in\operatorname{Ind}^G_H(A)\) with \(\zeta(1_G)=\alpha\). Adjusting \(s\) by \(\zeta\) within its equivalence class, we may ensure that \(r(h)(1_G)=s(h)(1_G)\) for every \(h\).

The definition of \(Z^1(G,\operatorname{Ind}^G_H(A))\) implies the identities in \(A\) \[\begin{gather*} r(g_1 g_2)(x) =r(g_1)(x) \cdot r(g_2)(xg_1), \quad s(g_1 g_2)(x) = s(g_1)(x) \cdot s(g_2)(xg_1) \end{gather*}\] for all \(x,g_1,g_2\in G\). On the one hand, substituting \(g_1=g\in G\) and \(g_2=g^{-1}x^{-1}\) and rearranging gives \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:Shapiro-noncommutative-aux0}{} \begin{aligned} r(g)(x) & = r(x^{-1})(x) \cdot r(g^{-1} x^{-1})(xg)^{-1}, \\ s(g)(x) & = s(x^{-1})(x) \cdot s(g^{-1} x^{-1})(xg)^{-1}. \end{aligned} \end{equation}\] On the other hand, substituting \(g_1=x^{-1}\) and \(g_2=h\in H\) gives \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:Shapiro-noncommutative-aux1}{} s(x^{-1} h)(x) \cdot r(x^{-1} h)(x)^{-1} = s(x^{-1})(x) \cdot r(x^{-1})(x)^{-1}. \end{equation}\]

For every \(x\in G\), define \(t(x):=s(x^{-1})(x)\cdot r(x^{-1})(x)^{-1}\). We claim that \(t:G\to A\) belongs to \(\operatorname{Ind}^G_H(A)\). Indeed, if \(h\in H\) and \(x\in G\), then \[\begin{multline*} t(hx) = s(x^{-1} h^{-1})(hx) \cdot r(x^{-1} h^{-1})(hx)^{-1} \\ = {}^h \left( s(x^{-1}h^{-1})(x) \cdot r(x^{-1} h^{-1})(x)^{-1} \right) \\ \xlongequal{\text{\href{#eqn:Shapiro-noncommutative-aux1}{equation}}} {}^h \left( s(x^{-1})(x) \cdot r(x^{-1})(x)^{-1} \right) = {}^h t(x). \end{multline*}\]

To prove \(r\sim s\), it is enough to check the identity in \(\operatorname{Ind}^G_H(A)\) given by \(t^{-1}\cdot s(g)\cdot{}^gt=r(g)\). The value of the left-hand side at \(x\in G\) is \[r(x^{-1})(x) \cdot s(x^{-1})(x)^{-1} \cdot s(g)(x) \cdot s(g^{-1} x^{-1})(xg) \cdot r(g^{-1} x^{-1})(xg)^{-1};\] expanding \(s(g)(x)\) and \(r(g)(x)\) using equation, this expression is visibly equal to \(r(g)(x)\). This proves injectivity.

Finally, prove surjectivity. Let \(s^\flat\in Z^1(H,A)\). Write \(\pi\) for the quotient map \(G\twoheadrightarrow H\backslash G\), and choose any map \(\sigma:H\backslash G\to G\) satisfying \(\pi\sigma=\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}\). Without loss of generality, assume \(\sigma(H\cdot1_G)=1_G\). Every \(g\in G\) has a unique representation \[g = \tau(g) \sigma(Hg), \quad \tau(g) \in H.\]

Note that \(\tau(1_G)=1_G\). For every \(g,x\in G\), define \[s(g)(x) := {}^{\tau(x)} s^\flat\left( \tau(\sigma(Hx)g) \right) \; \in A.\] If \(h\in H\), then \(\tau(hx)=h\tau(x)\) immediately gives \(s(g)(hx)={}^hs(g)(x)\), so \(s(g)\in\operatorname{Ind}^G_H(A)\). The next step is to show that \(s\in Z^1(G,\operatorname{Ind}^G_H(A))\). The reader is first asked to verify \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:Shapiro-noncommutative-aux2}{} \tau(uv) = \tau(u) \tau(\sigma(Hu)v), \quad u, v \in G. \end{equation}\]

We need to prove that \(s(g_1g_2)(x)=s(g_1)(x)\cdot s(g_2)(xg_1)\) for all \(g_1,g_2,x\in G\). By the definition of \(Z^1(H,A)\), the left-hand side equals \[\begin{multline*} {}^{\tau(x)} s^\flat\left( \tau(\sigma(Hx)g_1 g_2) \right) \xlongequal{\text{\href{#eqn:Shapiro-noncommutative-aux2}{equation}}} {}^{\tau(x)} s^\flat\left( \tau(\sigma(Hx)g_1) \tau(\sigma(Hx g_1)g_2) \right) \\ = {}^{\tau(x)} s^\flat\left( \tau(\sigma(Hx)g_1) \right) \cdot {}^{\tau(x)\tau(\sigma(Hx)g_1)} s^\flat\left( \tau(\sigma(Hxg_1)g_2) \right) \\ \xlongequal{\text{\href{#eqn:Shapiro-noncommutative-aux2}{equation}}} {}^{\tau(x)} s^\flat\left( \tau(\sigma(Hx)g_1) \right) \cdot {}^{\tau(xg_1)} s^\flat\left( \tau(\sigma(Hxg_1)g_2) \right), \end{multline*}\] which is the right-hand side.

Moreover, if \(h\in H\), then \(s(h)(1_G)=s^\flat(h)\), so \(s\) maps to \(s^\flat\). This proves surjectivity.

Clearly the isomorphism in Theorem reference, when

\(A\) is an abelian \(H\)-group, reduces to the special case of Proposition reference. Moreover, a direct computation shows that these isomorphisms are compatible with the connecting morphisms in Theorem reference; the details are left as an exercise.

Remark (Nonabelian cohomology of profinite groups). Let \(G\) be a profinite group. An object \(A\) of \(G\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Set}}_\bullet\) or \(G\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Grp}}\) is called smooth if \(A=\bigcup_KA^K\), where \(K\) ranges over the open normal subgroups of \(G\); in this case \(A\) is given the discrete topology. Since all arguments in this section are based on analogies with the standard cochain complex, all the preceding results apply to a profinite group \(G\) and smooth \(A\). The only difference is that \(c\in Z^i(G,A)\), as a map from \(G\) to \(A\), must be continuous, that is, locally constant. Thus \(\operatorname{H}^i(G,A)\) and the various canonical morphisms can be defined for \(i=0,1\), and \[\begin{align*} Z^i(G, A) & = \varinjlim_K Z^i(G/K, A^K), \\ \operatorname{H}^i(G, A) & = \varinjlim_K \operatorname{H}^i(G/K, A^K), \quad i = 0, 1. \end{align*}\]

In addition, the definition of \(\operatorname{Ind}^G_H(A)\) must require \(f:G\to A\) to be locally constant. The proof of Theorem reference also requires Lemma reference to ensure that the \(\zeta:G\to A\) in the injectivity part can be chosen locally constant and that the \(\sigma:H\backslash G\to G\) in the surjectivity part is continuous.

Finally, Remark reference remains valid for profinite groups \(G\): \(Z^1(G,A)\) corresponds to the set of continuous sections of the projection homomorphism \(\pi:A\rtimes G\to G\), while \(\operatorname{H}^1(G,A)\) is the quotient of the set of continuous sections by the conjugation action of \(A\).

Exercises

Let \(\Bbbk\) be a commutative ring and \(t\in\Bbbk\). For every \(\Bbbk\)-module, write \(m_t\) for the endomorphism given by multiplication by \(t\). Let \(M\) be a \(G\)-module. Show that the endomorphisms induced by \(m_t\in\operatorname{End}_G(M)\) on \(\operatorname{H}^n(G,M)\) and \(\operatorname{H}_n(G,M)\) are again precisely \(m_t\).

Hint. For cohomology, either write down the induced endomorphism on the standard complex, or take an injective resolution \(0\to M\to I^0\to\cdots\) and show that the induced endomorphism comes from the diagram \[\text{Diagram chapter6-unit-087-d001}\]

Let the \(G\)-module \(M\) be projective as a \(\Bbbk\)-module. Prove that \(\mathsf{L}\otimes M\to\Bbbk\otimes M\simeq M\) gives a projective resolution of the \(G\)-module \(M\); the same statement holds with \(\overline{\mathsf{L}}\) in place of \(\mathsf{L}\).

Hint. Apply Proposition reference.

Prove Proposition reference using the universal coefficient theorem for the cohomology of chain complexes.

Let \(p\) be a prime, \(G\) a \(p\)-group, and \(M\) a \(G\)-module satisfying \(pM=0\). Prove that the following properties are equivalent:

Hint. To prove (ii) \(\implies\) (i), take \(x\in M\smallsetminus\{0\}\) and consider the \(\ensuremath{\mathbb{F}}_p\)-vector subspace \(E\) of \(M\) generated by \(\{gx:g\in G\}\). Use \(|E^G|\equiv|E|\pmod p\) to show that \(M^G\neq0\).

To prove (iii) \(\implies\) (i), take \(M^\vee:=\operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathbb{F}}_p}(M,\ensuremath{\mathbb{F}}_p)\) with its natural \(G\)-module structure. Observe that \((M^\vee)^G\simeq\operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathbb{F}}_p}(M_G,\ensuremath{\mathbb{F}}_p)\), and deduce \(M_G=0\implies M^\vee=0\implies M=0\).

Let \(F\) be a field. A representation of a group \(G\) is data \((\rho,V)\), where \(V\) is an \(F\)-vector space, \(\operatorname{GL}(V)\) is its group of linear automorphisms, and \(\rho:G\to\operatorname{GL}(V)\) is a group homomorphism. Clearly, this is the same as a \(G\)-module with coefficients in \(F\). A projective representation is data \((\pi,V)\) with a homomorphism \(\pi:G\to\operatorname{PGL}(V):=\operatorname{GL}(V)/F^\times\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}\). Isomorphisms of representations or projective representations are defined in the evident way. Henceforth identify \(F^\times\) with \(F^\times\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}\).

  1. For a projective representation \((\pi,V)\) of \(G\), suppose that for every \(g\in G\) an inverse image \(\widetilde\pi(g)\in\operatorname{GL}(V)\) of \(\pi(g)\) has been chosen. Verify that \[\widetilde\pi(g_1)\widetilde\pi(g_2) =c(g_1,g_2)\widetilde\pi(g_1g_2)\] defines \(c\in Z^2(G,F^\times)\), where \(G\) acts trivially on \(F^\times\). If \(\widetilde\pi(1_G)=\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_V\), then \(c\in\overline{Z}^2(G,F^\times)\).

  2. Prove that the image of \(c\) in \(\operatorname{H}^2(G,F^\times)\) depends only on the isomorphism class of \((\pi,V)\) and not on any of the choices.

  3. Consider the central extension of groups \(1\to F^\times\to\widetilde G\to G\to1\) (Definition reference), where \[\widetilde G:=\{(g,\widetilde\pi)\in G\times\operatorname{GL}(V): \pi(g)=\widetilde\pi\bmod F^\times\}.\] The first homomorphism maps \(t\in F^\times\) to \((1_G,t)\) and the second is projection. Show that this extension is isomorphic to the central extension determined by the cohomology class in (ii).

  4. Give a bijection \[\{\text{representations }(\sigma,V)\text{ lifting }(\pi,V)\} \xleftrightarrow{1:1} \{\text{splittings of the central extension }\widetilde G\}.\] Show also that \((\pi,V)\) lifts to a representation if and only if the cohomology class in (ii) is trivial.

  5. Explicitly give a group \(G\) and a projective representation \((\pi,V)\) that cannot be lifted to a representation. Try to find an example with nontrivial \(\pi:G\to\operatorname{PGL}(V)\).

For subgroups \(G_1\subset G_2\subset G_3\), prove the canonical isomorphisms of functors \(\operatorname{Ind}^{G_3}_{G_2}\operatorname{Ind}^{G_2}_{G_1}\simeq\operatorname{Ind}^{G_3}_{G_1}\) and \(\operatorname{ind}^{G_3}_{G_2}\operatorname{ind}^{G_2}_{G_1}\simeq\operatorname{ind}^{G_3}_{G_1}\). Describe these isomorphisms as explicitly as possible.

Prove that if \(H\) is a subgroup of \(G\), then \(\mathrm{cd}(H)\leq\mathrm{cd}(G)\) and \(\mathrm{hd}(H)\leq\mathrm{hd}(G)\); see Definition reference. Hint. Apply Theorem reference.

Show that for \(m\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}_{\geq1}\), \(\mathrm{cd}(C_m)=\mathrm{hd}(C_m)=\infty\). Prove that \(\mathrm{cd}(G)<\infty\) implies that \(G\) is torsion-free, and that \(\mathrm{cd}(G)=0\) if and only if \(G\) is the trivial group. Hint. For the first part, apply Proposition reference with \(A=\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}/m\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\). For the other parts, consider the cyclic subgroups of \(G\).

Try to prove Corollary reference directly by operations on the standard complex.

Let \(U,V\) be subgroups of \(G\) and suppose that \((G:V)\) is finite. Write the cohomological restriction map as \(\mathrm{res}^G_U\) and the corestriction map as \(\mathrm{cor}^V_G\), and so on; the cohomological degree \(n\) is omitted from the notation. Choose a double-coset decomposition \[G=\bigsqcup_{\sigma\in S}U\sigma V,\] where the finite set \(S\subset G\) consists of representatives of the double cosets. Let \(M\) be a \(G\)-module.

  1. For every \(\sigma\in G\) and \(n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}_{\geq0}\), define in a natural way \[\mathcal{T}_\sigma: \operatorname{H}^n(V\cap\sigma^{-1}U\sigma,M) \to\operatorname{H}^n(U\cap\sigma V\sigma^{-1},M)\] so that for \(n=0\) it becomes \[M^{V\cap\sigma^{-1}U\sigma}\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}} M^{U\cap\sigma V\sigma^{-1}},\qquad x\mapsto\sigma x.\]

  2. Prove that \[\mathrm{res}^G_U\circ\mathrm{cor}^V_G =\sum_{\sigma\in S} \mathrm{cor}^{U\cap\sigma V\sigma^{-1}}_U \circ\mathcal{T}_\sigma \circ\mathrm{res}^V_{V\cap\sigma^{-1}U\sigma}.\]

  3. Describe the action of \(\mathrm{res}^G_U\circ\mathrm{cor}^U_G\) when \(U=V\lhd G\).

Let \(G\) be an abelian group, regarded as a \(\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\)-module. Define \(G\wedge G\) as the quotient of \(G\ensuremath{\underset{\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}}{\otimes}}G\) by the submodule generated by \(\{g\otimes g:g\in G\}\), and write \(x\wedge y\) for the image of \(x\otimes y\). Prove that \(\operatorname{H}_2(G,\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}})\simeq G\wedge G\).

Hint. Once a presentation \(G=F/R\) of the group has been fixed, the Hopf formula (Corollary reference) gives \(\operatorname{H}_2(G,\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}})\simeq[F,F]/[F,R]\). Since \(G\) is abelian, \([F,F]\subset R\). From the identity \([xy,z]=x[y,z]x^{-1}\cdot[x,z]\), the map \[\psi_0:G\times G\to[F,F]/[F,R],\qquad (f_1R,f_2R)\mapsto[f_1,f_2]\bmod[F,R]\] is \(\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\)-bilinear and induces a surjective homomorphism \(\psi:G\wedge G\to[F,F]/[F,R]\). Choose a basis \(\{x_i\}_{i\in I}\) of \(F\) and give \(I\) a total order. We need the following group-theoretic fact: \(H:=[F,F]/[[F,F],F]\) is a free abelian group with basis the cosets of \([x_i,x_j]\) for \(i<j\). We may therefore define \(\phi_0:H\to G\wedge G\) by mapping the coset of \([x_i,x_j]\) to \(x_iR\wedge x_jR\). Show that \[f_1,f_2\in F\implies \phi_0(\text{the coset of }[f_1,f_2])=f_1R\wedge f_2R.\] From this, descend \(\phi_0\) to a homomorphism \(\phi:[F,F]/[F,R]\to G\wedge G\), and then show that \(\phi\) and \(\psi\) are inverse to one another.

The group-theoretic fact above for finite \(I\) appears in [Ha76]; the general case follows from it.

Let \(H\lhd G\) and let \(M\) be a \(G\)-module. Give the standard complex \(C(H,M^H)\) its natural \(G/H\)-action, inducing a canonical \(G/H\)-action on every \(\operatorname{H}^n(H,M^H)\) (see the discussion preceding Lemma reference).

For the filtration in Remark reference, describe the \(E_2\) page of its spectral sequence and show that the properties in Theorem reference continue to hold. Explain the compatibility of the spectral sequence with the cup product as fully as possible.

Consider the finite cyclic group \(C_m\) of order \(m\). For every \(C_m\)-module \(A\) and \(n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}_{\geq1}\), prove that the periodicity isomorphism \(\operatorname{H}^n(C_m,A)\to\operatorname{H}^{n+2}(C_m,A)\) in Proposition reference equals the composite of the two connecting homomorphisms from the canonical short exact sequences in Example reference: \[\begin{gather*} 0\to\mathfrak{I}\otimes A\to\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}[C_m]\otimes A\to A\to0,\\ 0\to A\xrightarrow{\nu\otimes\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}}\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}[C_m]\otimes A \xrightarrow{(\sigma-1)\otimes\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}}\mathfrak{I}\otimes A\to0. \end{gather*}\]

Hint. Compute cohomology with the periodic complex \(A\xrightarrow{\sigma-1}A\xrightarrow{\nu}A\to\cdots\) from the proof of Proposition reference, starting in degree zero, and use it to describe the connecting homomorphisms. Treat the odd and even cases separately; some computation is required.

Let \(\Bbbk\) be any commutative ring and \(m\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}_{\geq1}\). Determine the structure of the cohomology algebra \(\operatorname{H}^\bullet(C_m,\Bbbk)\) as a graded \(\Bbbk\)-algebra.

For the cap product introduced in Remark reference, prove the following adjunction relation with the cup product:

\[\ensuremath{\left\langle \alpha\cup\beta,x \right\rangle} =\ensuremath{\left\langle \alpha,\beta\cap x \right\rangle}\in(M_1\otimes M_2\otimes M_3)_G,\] where \(M_1,M_2,M_3\) are \(G\)-modules, \(\alpha\in\operatorname{H}^p(G,M_1)\), \(\beta\in\operatorname{H}^q(G,M_2)\), and \(x\in\operatorname{H}_{p+q}(G,M_3)\).

In this problem \(G\) is a finite group, the coefficient ring in cohomology and homology is \(\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\), and a free \(G\)-module means a free \(\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}[G]\)-module. Write the contragredient module of a \(G\)-module \(M\) as \(M^*:=\operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}}(M,\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}})\).

  1. Take a free resolution \(\epsilon:P\to\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\) of the trivial \(G\)-module, where \(P:=[\cdots\to P_n\to P_{n-1}\to\cdots]\) and every \(P_n\) is finitely generated. Define \(P^*:=[\cdots\to P_n^*\to P_{n+1}^*\to\cdots]\). Show that \(\epsilon^*:\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\to P^*\) is a quasi-isomorphism. Hint. Every \(P_n\) is a free \(\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\)-module. If the chain complex of free \(\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\)-modules \((C_n,\partial_n)_{n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}}\) is exact and \(Z_n:=\operatorname{ker}(\partial_n)\), then the short exact sequence \(0\to Z_{n+1}\to C_{n+1}\xrightarrow{\partial_n}Z_n\to0\) splits for every \(n\).

  2. Prove that every \(P_n^*\) is a finitely generated projective \(G\)-module. Hint. It is enough to show that \(\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}[G]^*\simeq\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}[G]\).

  3. Let \(Q\) be a finitely generated projective \(G\)-module. For every \(G\)-module \(M\), prove that the canonical morphism \(\nu:(Q\otimes M)_G\to(Q\otimes M)^G\) from equation is an isomorphism. Hint. Use a direct-sum decomposition to reduce to the case \(Q=\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}[G]\), and then verify it directly. For greater simplicity, the automorphism \[\left(\sum_{g\in G}a_gg\right)\otimes x \mapsto\sum_{g\in G}a_g(g\otimes g^{-1}x)\] turns the diagonal \(G\)-action on \(\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}[G]\otimes M\) into left multiplication.

  4. Define \(P_{-n}:=P^*_{n-1}\) and splice \(P\) and \(P^*\) into the chain complex \[\mathcal{P}:=[\cdots\to P_1\to P_0 \xrightarrow{\epsilon^*\epsilon}P_{-1}\to P_{-2}\to\cdots].\] Prove that for every \(G\)-module \(M\) there is a canonical isomorphism \[\operatorname{H}^n\operatorname{Hom}_G(\mathcal{P},M) \simeq\text{Tate cohomology }\ensuremath{\hat{\mathrm{H}}}^n(G,M),\qquad n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}.\]

    Hint. For \(n\geq1\) the statement is clear. For \(n\leq-2\), use the following property: if \(Q\) is a finitely generated projective \(G\)-module, then \(Q\otimes M\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}\operatorname{Hom}(Q^*,M)\). Deduce that \[(Q\otimes M)_G\xrightarrow[\nu]{\sim}(Q\otimes M)^G \ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}\operatorname{Hom}(Q^*,M)^G=\operatorname{Hom}_G(Q^*,M).\] For \(n=0,-1\), identify \(\operatorname{Hom}_G(P_{-1},M)\to\operatorname{Hom}_G(P_0,M)\) by means of the isomorphism above with \[(P_0\otimes M)_G\xrightarrow{(\epsilon\otimes\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}})_G}M_G \xrightarrow{\nu}M^G\xrightarrow{\epsilon^*}\operatorname{Hom}_G(P_0,M).\]

  5. Use this result to prove the long exact sequence in Tate cohomology directly.

  6. Take the free resolution \(\epsilon:P\to\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\) from Proposition reference, choose its natural basis for every \(P_n\), and then explicitly describe the chain complex \(\mathcal{P}\) from (iv).

Based on (vi), a cup product on Tate cohomology can be defined as in Lemma reference, by appropriately defining \(\Delta:\mathcal{P}\to\mathcal{P}\otimes\mathcal{P}\). For explicit formulas, see [CF67].

Let \(G\) be a finite group and \(H\) a subgroup. For a \(G\)-module \(M\), use dimension shifting (Corollary reference) to extend the canonical morphisms from §reference, \(\mathrm{res}^n:\ensuremath{\hat{\mathrm{H}}}^n(G,M)\to\ensuremath{\hat{\mathrm{H}}}^n(H,M)\) and \(\mathrm{res}_n:\ensuremath{\hat{\mathrm{H}}}^{-n-1}(H,M)\to\ensuremath{\hat{\mathrm{H}}}^{-n-1}(G,M)\), from the case \(n\geq1\) to all \(n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\). For the moment, denote the former by \(\mathrm{res}_+\) and the latter by \(\mathrm{res}_-\).

  1. Describe the action of \(\mathrm{res}_+\) on \(\ensuremath{\hat{\mathrm{H}}}^0\) and the action of \(\mathrm{res}_-\) on \(\ensuremath{\hat{\mathrm{H}}}^{-1}\).

  2. Prove that \(\mathrm{res}_+\) on \(\ensuremath{\hat{\mathrm{H}}}^{-1}\) is induced by \(\nu_{G|H}:M_G\to M_H\) (Definition reference), and on \(\ensuremath{\hat{\mathrm{H}}}^{<-1}\) equals \(\mathrm{cor}_n\) (Definition–Proposition reference).

  3. Prove that \(\mathrm{res}_-\) on \(\ensuremath{\hat{\mathrm{H}}}^0\) is induced by \(\nu^{G|H}:M^H\to M^G\), and on \(\ensuremath{\hat{\mathrm{H}}}^{>0}\) equals \(\mathrm{cor}^n\).

For a group \(G\) and a bounded-below complex of \(G\)-modules \(M=[\cdots\to M^p\to M^{p+1}\to\cdots]\), let \(p\) vary in the standard complexes \(C(G,M^p)\) to form a double complex. Denote its total complex by \(C(G,M):=\operatorname{tot}((C^q(G,M^p))_{p,q})\). Prove the canonical isomorphism \[\operatorname{H}^n(C(G,M))\simeq \operatorname{H}^n(G,[\cdots\to M^p\to M^{p+1}\to\cdots]),\qquad n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}},\] where the right-hand side is defined as in §reference and is also called group hypercohomology.

Hint. By definition, the right-hand side is obtained by taking an injective resolution \(M\to I\) (recall that \(I\) is a bounded-below complex, every \(I^q\) is an injective \(G\)-module, and \(M\to I\) is a quasi-isomorphism) and then taking the cohomology determined by the \(\operatorname{Hom}\) complex \(\operatorname{Hom}^\bullet_G(\Bbbk,I)\). Show that the same cohomology can be computed by \(\operatorname{Hom}^\bullet_G(\mathsf{L},M)\).

Prove the corresponding result when \(G\) is a profinite group, requiring every \(M^p\) to be a smooth \(G\)-module and using the continuous standard complexes \(C(G,M^p)\).

Hint. Define a functor \(C(G,\cdot)\) from \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}^+(G\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}^\infty)\) to \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}^+(\Bbbk\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}})\). Show that it induces a triangulated functor at the level of \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}^+(\cdots)\) and preserves acyclic objects, and hence induces a triangulated functor at the level of \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^+(\cdots)\), still denoted by \(C(G,\cdot)\). The natural transformation \((\cdot)^G\to C(G,\cdot)\) and the universal property of right derived functors give a morphism of triangulated functors \(\mathrm{R}(\cdot)^G\to C(G,\cdot)\). To prove that this is an isomorphism, use the way-out lemma (Proposition reference) to reduce to the case handled by Theorem reference.

For a profinite group \(G\) and a finite \(G\)-module \(M\), give a complete proof of the bijective correspondence mentioned in §reference between equivalence classes of profinite group extensions and \(\operatorname{H}^2(G,M)\).

Hint. Follow the argument in §reference. In the profinite case the required observations are: (i) the group structure defined by every \(f\in\overline{Z}^2(G,M)\) on the product space \(M\times G\) makes it a profinite group; (ii) for a profinite group extension \(E\), there is an isomorphism of topological groups \(E/M\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}G\); (iii) in this situation, Lemma reference gives a continuous

section \(s:G\to E\) that can be adjusted to be normalized.

For any field \(F\), define \(\operatorname{GL}(n,F)\) to be the group of invertible \(n\times n\) matrices over \(F\), and \(\operatorname{SL}(n,F)\) to be the subgroup cut out by \(\det=1\). Observe that \(G:=\operatorname{Gal}(\ensuremath{\mathbb{C}}|\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}})\) acts on \(\operatorname{GL}(n,\ensuremath{\mathbb{C}})\) and \(\operatorname{SL}(n,\ensuremath{\mathbb{C}})\), with fixed points \(\operatorname{GL}(n,\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}})\) and \(\operatorname{SL}(n,\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}})\), respectively.

  1. Take \(n=2\). Let \(B:=\operatorname{SL}(2,\ensuremath{\mathbb{C}})\) act by conjugation on the space of all \(2\times2\) matrices, and define \(A:=\operatorname{Stab}(\begin{smallmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{smallmatrix})\). Show that this subgroup is invariant under the \(G\)-action and describe \(A^G\).

  2. Show that \(B/A\) (respectively, \(B^G/A^G\)) is naturally identified with the orbit of \(\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)\) under conjugation by \(\operatorname{SL}(2,\ensuremath{\mathbb{C}})\) (respectively, \(\operatorname{SL}(2,\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}})\)). For \(B/A\), explain how the \(G\)-action is reflected on the orbit.

  3. Show that \((B/A)^G\neq B^G/A^G\). In other words, there is a real \(2\times2\) matrix that is conjugate to \(\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)\) by \(\operatorname{SL}(2,\ensuremath{\mathbb{C}})\) but not by \(\operatorname{SL}(2,\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}})\).

  4. Show that the phenomenon above does not occur if \(\operatorname{SL}\) is replaced by \(\operatorname{GL}\).

State and prove the compatibility between the isomorphisms in Theorem reference and the connecting homomorphisms in Theorem reference.

(“Twisting” group cohomology) Use the notation of §reference. Let \(A\) be a \(G\)-group.

  1. For \(c\in Z^1(G,A)\), define a new group action \(G\times A\to A\) by \[{}^{c,g}a:=c(g)\cdot{}^ga\cdot c(g)^{-1}, \qquad g\in G,\ a\in A.\] Show that this indeed gives a \(G\)-group, denoted by \({}^cA\). Prove also that if \(c\sim c'\), there is an isomorphism of \(G\)-groups \({}^{c'}A\simeq{}^cA\); describe it explicitly.

  2. Prove that every \(c\in Z^1(G,A)\) induces a bijection \[\begin{align*} \nu_c:Z^1(G,{}^cA)&\xrightarrow{1:1}Z^1(G,A),\\ c'&\longmapsto c'c\quad\text{(pointwise multiplication)}, \end{align*}\] which induces a bijection \({\bm\nu}_c:\operatorname{H}^1(G,{}^cA)\xrightarrow{1:1}\operatorname{H}^1(G,A)\) that maps the basepoint to \([c]\). Give a simplified description when \(A\) is abelian.

  3. Suppose there is a short exact sequence \(1\to A\to B\to B/A\to1\) as in Theorem reference (i). For \(c\in Z^1(G,A)\), prove that the following diagram commutes: \[\text{Diagram chapter6-unit-087-d002}\] Use this to describe all fibers of the map \(\operatorname{H}^1(G,A)\to\operatorname{H}^1(G,B)\).

  4. State the modifications required when \(G\) is a profinite group.

Monad Theory

The starting point of this chapter, §reference, is the notion of an algebra over a monoidal category \((\mathcal{V},\otimes)\). This means an object \(A\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{V})\) equipped with a multiplication \(\mu:A\otimes A\to A\) and a unit morphism \(\eta:\mathbf{1}\to A\), satisfying the associative and unit laws. The concept is modeled on that of a monoid, while algebras over a commutative ring \(\Bbbk\) are the typical examples. These algebras form a category \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Alg}}(\mathcal{V})\). When \((\mathcal{V},\otimes)\) has stronger commutativity properties, \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Alg}}(\mathcal{V})\) acquires additional structure and properties. The best situation is when \(\mathcal{V}\) is a symmetric monoidal category; then \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Alg}}(\mathcal{V})\) is itself a symmetric monoidal category. For an algebra \(A\), a left \(A\)-module is an object \(M\) of \(\mathcal{V}\) together with a scalar-multiplication morphism \(\mu_M:A\otimes M\to M\) satisfying the associative and unit laws; right modules and bimodules are defined similarly. Since complexes are the principal objects of this book, a natural step is to take an abelian category \(\mathcal{A}\) with countable coproducts and a right-exact additive bifunctor \(\otimes:\mathcal{A}\times\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{A}\), extend \(\otimes\) to complexes by taking total complexes, and then consider the monoidal category \((\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A}),\otimes)\), usually endowed with the Koszul braiding equation. Differential graded algebras and modules thus arise naturally as a continuation of the theory; “dg” abbreviates “differential graded.” These are the subject of §reference. We also know that the \(\operatorname{Hom}\) sets in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})\) can be upgraded to \(\operatorname{Hom}\) complexes, and that composition can likewise be lifted to the level of \(\operatorname{Hom}\) complexes. In particular, the endomorphism complex \(\operatorname{End}^\bullet(X)\) of an object \(X\) becomes a dg-algebra. Generalizing these observations leads to the notion of a dg-category (Definition reference), and one can speak of dg-functors between dg-categories. After a brief introduction to closed monoidal categories in §reference, we shall explain in §reference that the category \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{dgCat}}\) of all small dg-categories is closed. Equivalently, all dg-functors between two small dg-categories \(\mathcal{C}\) and \(\mathcal{D}\) themselves form a dg-category \(\ensuremath{\EuScript{H}\mathrm{om}}(\mathcal{C},\mathcal{D})\). The various dg-structures arise naturally and are important tools in linear algebra. This chapter gives only a brief introduction, however, and §reference turns instead to coalgebras and comodules over a monoidal category \(\mathcal{V}\). These are simply algebras and modules over the opposite monoidal category \(\mathcal{V}^{\operatorname{op}}\). More concretely, a coalgebra \(C\) is equipped with a comultiplication \(\Delta:C\to C\otimes C\) and a counit morphism \(\epsilon:C\to\ensuremath{\bm{1}}\), while a left comodule \(M\) is equipped with a scalar-comultiplication morphism \(\rho:M\to C\otimes M\); their associative and unit laws are obtained by reversing all the arrows. If \(\mathcal{V}\) is a braided monoidal category, mutually compatible algebra and coalgebra structures \((A,\mu,\eta,\Delta,\epsilon)\) on an object \(A\) are called a bialgebra, and a bialgebra equipped with an antipode is called a Hopf algebra (Definition reference). In the concrete case \(\mathcal{V}=\Bbbk\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\), these concepts are inspired by geometry and topology. For example, the cohomology of a Lie group, or more generally of an H-group, naturally becomes a Hopf algebra; quantum groups form another important class of examples. Moreover, the group algebra \(\Bbbk[G]\) of any group \(G\) is also a Hopf algebra. We now introduce the protagonist of §reference, which also gives this chapter its title: the monad. For any category \(\mathcal{C}\), the endofunctor category \(\mathcal{C}^{\mathcal{C}}\) is a strict monoidal category under composition, and a monad is simply an algebra in \(\mathcal{C}^{\mathcal{C}}\); a comonad is its dual version. Simple though it is, this concept plays a major role in algebra, geometry, and computer science. One notable use of monads is to explain the various “standard resolutions” of homological algebra, such as \(\mathsf{B}R\) from §reference or \(\mathsf{L}\) from §reference. We shall investigate this aspect in §reference. Monads and comonads arise chiefly from adjoint pairs \[\text{Diagram chapter7-unit-088-d001}\] Such a pair determines a monad \(T\) on \(\mathcal{C}\) and a comonad \(L\) on \(\mathcal{D}\), expressed in terms of the unit \(\eta\) and counit \(\varepsilon\) of the adjunction as \[\begin{array}{|c|c|}\hline \text{monad} & \text{comonad} \\ \hline T := GF & L := FG \\ \mu := \left[ T^2 \xrightarrow{G\varepsilon F} T \right] & \delta := \left[ L \xrightarrow{F\eta G} L^2 \right] \\ \eta : \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{\mathcal{C}} \to T & \varepsilon: L \to \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{\mathcal{D}} \\ \hline \end{array}\] The adjoint pair naturally induces a functor \(\mathbb{K}:\mathcal{D}\to\mathcal{C}^T\) (or \(\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{D}^L\)), where \(\mathcal{C}^T\) (or \(\mathcal{D}^L\)) denotes the category of modules under the action of the monad (or its comonadic counterpart). If \(\mathbb{K}\) is an equivalence, the adjoint pair is called monadic (or comonadic). This means that the information in \(\mathcal{D}\) (or \(\mathcal{C}\)) can be reconstructed from the action of the monad (or comonad) on the other side. Beck’s Theorem reference gives a practical characterization of monadicity. The next step is Morita theory in §reference, a classical theme in ring theory. The first part considers functors between categories of left or right modules that preserve small \(\varinjlim\) (or \(\varprojlim\)). Theorem reference states that they all arise by taking the tensor product (or \(\operatorname{Hom}\)) with a bimodule \(P\). This also confirms the special position of bimodules in ring and module theory: they provide enough means to “change rings.” One thereby obtains a module-theoretic characterization of equivalences between the categories of left modules \(A\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\) and \(B\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\), called Morita equivalences (Definition–Proposition reference); the characterizations for left and right modules are entirely parallel. For the adjoint pair determined by an \((A,B)\)-bimodule \(P\), the second part examines the associated monad and comonad and their modules. Assuming that \(P\) is a finitely generated projective \(B\)-module, Proposition reference explicitly presents them as an algebra in the monoidal category \((A,A)\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\) and a coalgebra in \((B,B)\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\), respectively. From this foundation one readily obtains a refinement of Morita equivalence (Theorem reference, Corollary reference). Morita theory concerns given module categories. As a complement, in §reference we study when an abelian category \(\mathcal{A}\) is equivalent to the category of right modules over a ring \(R\). The answer involves a compact projective generator of \(\mathcal{A}\) (Theorem reference). We shall also give a sufficient condition for the finitely generated version (Theorem reference). Returning to Beck’s monadicity theorem, the first half of §reference gives a simple application in module theory, called faithfully flat descent for modules. For a homomorphism of commutative rings \(K\to L\), it explains how to reconstruct a \(K\)-module from an \(L\)-module carrying an action of the change-of-rings comonad \(\mathbf{L}\). Descent techniques are widely used in geometry, and the second half of §reference reformulates the condition of carrying an \(\mathbf{L}\)-action in the form customarily used in geometry. All of this rests on the preparation in §reference. As a special case of faithfully flat descent, §reference takes \(L|K\) to be a Galois extension of fields and reformulates the preceding result in terms of the action of the Galois group \(\operatorname{Gal}(L|K)\). This technique is called Galois descent. Its main result, Theorem reference, says that the category of \(K\)-vector spaces is equivalent to the category of \(L\)-vector spaces equipped with a smooth semilinear action of \(\operatorname{Gal}(L|K)\). The exercises give another direct proof. On the basis of faithfully flat descent, or its special case of Galois descent, one can further descend various structures such as algebras and modules. In §reference we consider a kind of data expressed in terms of vector spaces and their tensor powers. Galois descent and group cohomology then reduce the classification of such data to nonabelian group cohomology \(\operatorname{H}^1\). Although the purpose is only to illustrate the technique, it already helps clarify several basic questions in algebra, such as the classification of nondegenerate quadratic forms.

Reading Guide. This chapter falls roughly into three parts. The first (§§reference—reference) introduces algebras over monoidal categories, dg-structures, and Hopf algebras; these topics occupy a natural and important place in algebra. The second (§§reference—reference) centers on monads and the related Morita theory. The third (§§reference—reference) discusses descent. The three parts are arranged more or less sequentially, although the dg-structures and dg-categories are not needed for what follows. and of this book use several results from the second part. Further material appears in the exercises for this chapter.

Algebras over Monoidal Categories

For a fixed commutative ring \(\Bbbk\), we know that a \(\Bbbk\)-algebra is a multiplicative structure superimposed on a \(\Bbbk\)-module. Its definition can be expressed using the tensor-product bifunctor \(\otimes=\otimes_{\Bbbk}\) on \(\Bbbk\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\) and commutative diagrams. The essential point is that \((\Bbbk\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}},\otimes)\) is a monoidal category with unit \(\ensuremath{\bm{1}}:=\Bbbk\). When discussing commutative \(\Bbbk\)-algebras and their variants, the central role is played by the braiding \(c(X,Y):X\otimes Y\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}Y\otimes X\) on this monoidal category, which has the symmetry property \(c(Y,X)c(X,Y)=\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}\). See [Li1]. Once formulated in the appropriate language, this theory encompasses general monoidal categories and symmetric monoidal categories. Following [Li1], the convention in this section1 defines a monoidal category to be data \((\mathcal{V},\otimes,a,\ensuremath{\bm{1}},\iota)\), often abbreviated to \(\mathcal{V}\) or \((\mathcal{V},\otimes)\), where

  • \(\otimes: \mathcal{V} \times \mathcal{V} \to \mathcal{V}\) is a bifunctor;

  • \(a(X, Y, Z): (X \otimes Y) \otimes Z \ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}X \otimes (Y \otimes Z)\) is a canonical morphism called the associativity constraint (\(X, Y, Z \in \operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{V})\)), and it satisfies the pentagon axiom;

  • \(\ensuremath{\bm{1}}= \ensuremath{\bm{1}}_{\mathcal{V}} \in \operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{V})\) is the unit;

  • \(\iota: \ensuremath{\bm{1}}\otimes \ensuremath{\bm{1}}\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}\ensuremath{\bm{1}}\).

This gives a family of canonical isomorphisms \(\ensuremath{\bm{1}}\otimes X \xrightarrow[\sim]{\lambda_X} X \xleftarrow[\sim]{\rho_X} X \otimes \ensuremath{\bm{1}}\); by [Li1], these isomorphisms satisfy \(\lambda_{\ensuremath{\bm{1}}}=\iota=\rho_{\ensuremath{\bm{1}}}\). They are all called unit constraints and will no longer be displayed explicitly. A braiding on a monoidal category is an isomorphism of bifunctors, written \[c = \left( c(X, Y): X \otimes Y \ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}Y \otimes X\right)_{X, Y \in \operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{V})},\] required to be compatible with the associativity and unit constraints; see [Li1]. A monoidal category equipped with a specified braiding is called a braided monoidal category. If \(c(Y,X)c(X,Y)=\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{X\otimes Y}\) always holds, the data are called a symmetric monoidal category.

Definition (Algebra). An algebra over a monoidal category \(\mathcal{V}\) means data \((A,\mu,\eta)\), where \[A \in \operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{V}), \quad \mu = \mu_A: A \otimes A \to A, \quad \eta = \eta_A: \ensuremath{\bm{1}}\to A,\] such that the following diagrams commute: \[\begin{equation*} \begin{gathered} \text{Diagram chapter7-unit-088-d002} \quad \text{Diagram chapter7-unit-088-d003} \end{gathered} \end{equation*}\] Thus \(\mu\) may be viewed as a multiplication on \(A\), and \(\eta\) as its unit morphism.

A morphism from an algebra \((A,\mu,\eta)\) to \((A',\mu',\eta')\) is defined to be a morphism \(\phi:A\to A'\) in \(\mathcal{V}\) that makes the following diagrams commute: \[\text{Diagram chapter7-unit-088-d004} \quad \text{Diagram chapter7-unit-088-d005}\]

We often abbreviate \((A,\mu,\eta)\) to \(A\). In some sources an algebra is also called a ring or a monoid in \(\mathcal{V}\), and it is sometimes called an associative algebra to emphasize the associative law displayed by the second commutative diagram. The concept of a module admits a similar generalization.

Definition (Module). Let \((A,\mu,\eta)\) be an algebra over \(\mathcal{V}\). A left \(A\)-module is defined to be data \((M,\mu_M)\), where \[M \in \operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{V}), \quad \mu_M: A \otimes M \to M,\] that make the following diagrams commute: \[\text{Diagram chapter7-unit-088-d006} \quad \text{Diagram chapter7-unit-088-d007}\] Thus \(\mu_M\) may be viewed as scalar multiplication on the module.
