As usual, the module \((M,\mu_M)\) is abbreviated to \(M\). A morphism from \(M\) to \(M'\) is defined to be a morphism \(\psi:M\to M'\) in \(\mathcal{V}\) that makes the following diagram commute: \[\text{Diagram chapter7-unit-088-d008}\]

Right \(A\)-modules are defined similarly. If \(M\) carries both a left \(A\)-module structure and a right \(B\)-module structure that make the following diagram commute, \[\text{Diagram chapter7-unit-088-d009}\] then \(M\) is called an \((A,B)\)-bimodule. A morphism between two such bimodules is a morphism \(\psi:M\to M'\) that is simultaneously a morphism of left \(A\)-modules and of right \(B\)-modules.

If \(M\) is a left \(A\)-module and \(N\) a right \(B\)-module, then \(M\otimes N\) naturally becomes an \((A,B)\)-bimodule.

Remark (The unit as an algebra). For example, \(\ensuremath{\bm{1}}\) becomes an algebra with \(\mu_{\ensuremath{\bm{1}}}:=\iota\) and \(\eta_{\ensuremath{\bm{1}}}:=\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{\ensuremath{\bm{1}}}\). The required commutative diagrams follow from the standard properties of \(\ensuremath{\bm{1}}\) and \(\iota:\ensuremath{\bm{1}}\otimes\ensuremath{\bm{1}}\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}\ensuremath{\bm{1}}\); see [Li1]. For every algebra \(A\) there is exactly one morphism \(\ensuremath{\bm{1}}\to A\), and it must be \(\eta_A\).

Similarly, it is easy to see that every \(M\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{V})\) has exactly one left (or right) \(\ensuremath{\bm{1}}\)-module structure, obtained by taking \(\mu_M:\ensuremath{\bm{1}}\otimes M\to M\) to be the unit constraint of \(\mathcal{V}\).

Our next goal is to discuss

The two are closely related, and both require a braiding on \(\mathcal{V}\). We begin with commutativity.

Definition. The natural properties of the braiding show that, if \(A\) is an algebra over a braided monoidal category \(\mathcal{V}\), then replacing \(\mu\) by \(\mu\circ c(A,A)\) while leaving all other data unchanged again gives an algebra over \(\mathcal{V}\). This algebra is defined to be the opposite algebra \(A^{\operatorname{op}}\) of \(A\). The verification is lengthy but not difficult, and is left as an exercise for this chapter.

By functoriality of the braiding, if \(\phi:A_1\to A_2\) is a morphism, then it is also a morphism from \(A_1^{\operatorname{op}}\) to \(A_2^{\operatorname{op}}\).

Definition. Let \(A\) be an algebra over a braided monoidal category \(\mathcal{V}\). It is called a commutative algebra if the following diagram commutes in \(\mathcal{V}\): \[\text{Diagram chapter7-unit-088-d010}\] In other words, we require the multiplication \(\mu_A\) to satisfy the commutative law. Equivalently, \(A=A^{\operatorname{op}}\).

The algebra \(\ensuremath{\bm{1}}\) of Remark reference is a simple example of a commutative algebra. The required commutative diagram follows from the compatibility of the braiding \(c\) with the unit constraints. Continue to suppose that \(\mathcal{V}\) is a braided monoidal category. Just as over a commutative ring, for any two algebras \(A\) and \(B\) the braiding \(c\) gives a canonical algebra structure on \(A\otimes B\):

  • The multiplication \(\mu_{A \otimes B}\) is the composite \[\begin{multline*} (A \otimes B) \otimes (A \otimes B) \ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}(A \otimes (B \otimes A)) \otimes B \\ \xrightarrow{(\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_A \otimes c(B, A)) \otimes \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_B} (A \otimes (A \otimes B)) \otimes B \\ \ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}(A \otimes A) \otimes (B \otimes B) \xrightarrow{\mu_A \otimes \mu_B} A \otimes B , \end{multline*}\] where all unlabeled arrows come from associativity constraints. In braid diagram notation this composite is depicted as follows:

    Diagram chapter7-unit-088-d011

  • The unit \(\eta_{A \otimes B}\) is the composite \[\ensuremath{\bm{1}}\xrightarrow[\sim]{\iota^{-1}} \ensuremath{\bm{1}}\otimes \ensuremath{\bm{1}}\xrightarrow{\eta_A \otimes \eta_B} A \otimes B.\]

To verify that this is indeed an algebra, the conditions of Definition reference can be reduced to the corresponding properties of \((A,\mu_A,\eta_A)\) and \((B,\mu_B,\eta_B)\) using only \(c\) (to interchange the order of \(\otimes\)), \(\iota\) (to duplicate the unit), and the associativity constraints (to change the placement of parentheses). If \(M\) is a left \(A\)-module and \(N\) a left \(B\)-module, then \(M\otimes N\) naturally becomes a left \((A\otimes B)\)-module. Its construction and verification are the same as in the preceding paragraph, using \(c\) to interchange positions. The case of right modules is similar. For the algebra \(\ensuremath{\bm{1}}\) defined in Remark reference, it is clear that \(\ensuremath{\bm{1}}\otimes A\simeq A\simeq A\otimes\ensuremath{\bm{1}}\), with the isomorphisms given by the unit constraints of \(\mathcal{V}\).

Remark. The construction above is functorial in \(A\) and \(B\): if \(A\to A'\) and \(B\to B'\) are morphisms of algebras, then so is the corresponding morphism \(A\otimes B\to A'\otimes B'\). Another lengthy but straightforward fact is that, when \(A,B,C\) are all algebras, the associativity constraint \((A\otimes B)\otimes C\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}A\otimes(B\otimes C)\) is a morphism of algebras.

Lemma. Let \(A\) be an algebra over a braided monoidal category \(\mathcal{V}\). Then \(A\) is commutative if and only if its multiplication \(\mu_A:A\otimes A\to A\) is a morphism of algebras.

Proof. For \(\mu_A\) to be a morphism of algebras, two conditions are required. The condition concerning the unit is equivalent to commutativity of \[\text{Diagram chapter7-unit-088-d012}\] and this holds automatically because \(A\) is an algebra. The remaining condition is commutativity of \[\begin{equation*} \text{Diagram chapter7-unit-088-d013} \end{equation*}\] Identify the upper-left corner with \(A\otimes(A\otimes A)\otimes A\) by the associativity constraints. By associativity of \(\mu_A\), composition in the diagram along

Diagram chapter7-unit-088-d014

equals \[A \otimes (A \otimes A) \otimes A \xrightarrow{\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}\otimes \mu_A \otimes \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}} A \otimes A \otimes A \xrightarrow{\text{multiplication}} A .\] On the other hand, the definition of \(\mu_{A\otimes A}\) and the associativity of \(\mu_A\) show that composition in the diagram along

Diagram chapter7-unit-088-d015

equals \[A \otimes (A \otimes A) \otimes A \xrightarrow{\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}\otimes (\mu_A c(A,A) ) \otimes \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}} A \otimes A \otimes A \xrightarrow{\text{multiplication}} A .\] Thus \(\mu_Ac(A,A)=\mu_A\) implies that the original diagram commutes, or equivalently that \(\mu_A\) is a morphism of algebras.

Conversely, let \(f\in\left\{\mu_A,\mu_Ac(A,A)\right\}\). We have the elementary commutative diagram \[\text{Diagram chapter7-unit-088-d016}\] If \(\mu_A\) is a morphism of algebras, the preceding discussion shows that the first row gives the same composite for the two choices of \(f\). Considering the second row then yields \(\mu_A=\mu_Ac(A,A)\).

Lemma. Let \(A\) and \(B\) be algebras over a symmetric monoidal category \(\mathcal{V}\). Then \(c(A,B):A\otimes B\to B\otimes A\) is an isomorphism of algebras.

Proof. Two commutative diagrams must be verified for \(c(A,B)\). The first is \[\text{Diagram chapter7-unit-088-d017}\] Commutativity on the right follows from functoriality of \(c\), while that on the left follows from compatibility of \(c\) with the unit constraints [Li1]. For the second diagram, which says that \(c(A,B)\) preserves multiplication, the argument is based on symmetry of the braiding and is exactly the same as at the end of [Li1].

Proposition. Let \(A\) and \(B\) be commutative algebras over a symmetric monoidal category \(\mathcal{V}\). Then \(A\otimes B\) is also commutative.

Proof. It is enough to show that the multiplication \(\mu_{A\otimes B}\) is a morphism of algebras. Recall the definition of \(\mu_{A\otimes B}\) and apply Lemma reference to \(c(B,A)\), the commutativity assumptions on \(A,B\) together with Lemma reference to \(\mu_A,\mu_B\), and Remark reference on the functoriality of \(\otimes\). Every part of the composite is then a morphism of algebras.

We have defined algebras, modules, and their morphisms. All these structures form categories, with notation

structure algebra commutative algebra left \(A\)-module right \(B\)-module \((A,B)\)-bimodule
category \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Alg}}(\mathcal{V})\) \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{CAlg}}(\mathcal{V})\) \(A\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\) \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}\text{-}}B\) \((A,B)\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\)
condition \(\mathcal{V}\): monoidal category \(\mathcal{V}\): braided monoidal category \(A\): algebra \(B\): algebra \(A, B\): algebras

The preceding discussion also shows that \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Alg}}(\mathcal{V})\) and \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{CAlg}}(\mathcal{V})\) generally have less structure than \(\mathcal{V}\). Labeling the levels of structure by numbers, the situation can be represented schematically as \[\text{Diagram chapter7-unit-088-d018}\] Moreover, whenever \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Alg}}(\mathcal{V})\) or \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{CAlg}}(\mathcal{V})\) becomes a monoidal category under \(\otimes\), its unit is always \(\ensuremath{\bm{1}}\). Recall that Lemma reference says that a commutative algebra over a braided monoidal category \(\mathcal{V}\) automatically gives an algebra over the monoidal category \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Alg}}(\mathcal{V})\), by taking the multiplication \(A\otimes A\to A\) to be that of \(A\). In fact, this is the only possible choice. This leads to a simple, interesting, and important observation: there is an equivalence of categories \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:AlgAlg-CAlg}{} \ensuremath{\mathsf{Alg}}\left(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Alg}}(\mathcal{V}) \right) \simeq \ensuremath{\mathsf{CAlg}}(\mathcal{V}), \quad \mathcal{V}:\;\text{braided monoidal category}. \end{equation}\] These facts rest on the so-called Eckmann–Hilton argument; their proof is deliberately left as an exercise for this chapter, supplied with a hint.

Example. Let the category \(\mathcal{C}\) have finite products. In particular, it has an empty product, namely a terminal object, denoted by \(\ensuremath{\bm{1}}\). For every two objects \(X,Y\) there is a canonical isomorphism \(c(X,Y):X\times Y\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}Y\times X\). These data make \((\mathcal{C},\times)\) a symmetric monoidal category with unit \(\ensuremath{\bm{1}}\). We may discuss algebras over \(\mathcal{C}\), also called monoid objects in \(\mathcal{C}\)2, together with their commutative versions.

  • If \(\mathcal{C}=\ensuremath{\mathsf{Set}}\), the one-point set is the unit \(\ensuremath{\bm{1}}\). The corresponding algebras are monoids, and the corresponding commutative algebras are commutative monoids.

  • If \(\mathcal{C}=\ensuremath{\mathsf{Top}}\), the corresponding algebras are topological monoids, and the corresponding commutative algebras are commutative topological monoids.

On the other hand, let \(\Bbbk\) be a commutative ring and give \(\Bbbk\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\) the structure of a symmetric monoidal category through \(\otimes=\otimes_{\Bbbk}\), with \(\Bbbk\) as the unit \(\ensuremath{\bm{1}}\) and the braiding determined by \(x\otimes y\mapsto y\otimes x\). The corresponding algebras (or commutative algebras) are precisely algebras (or commutative algebras) in the usual algebraic sense; see [Li1].

In these concrete situations, the multiplication of an algebra \(A\) is often written directly as multiplication of elements \(xy=x\cdot y\), and the unit is directly identified with the element \(1_A\), so that the notation \(\mu_A,\eta_A\) can be omitted.

Example (Graded modules and graded algebras). Fix an abelian category \(\mathcal{A}\) and a nonempty set \(I\). An object of \(\mathcal{A}^I\) is called an \(I\)-graded object and is written \(M=(M^i)_{i\in I}\), while a morphism is written \((f^i:M^i\to N^i)_{i\in I}\). The object \(M^i\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{A})\) (or the morphism \(f^i\in\operatorname{Mor}(\mathcal{A})\)) is customarily called the degree-\(i\) component of \(M\) (or \(f\)). The special cases \(I=\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\) and \(\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}^n\) have already been discussed repeatedly in §reference, §reference, §reference, and elsewhere.

For concreteness, take for the moment \(\mathcal{A}:=\Bbbk\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\), where \(\Bbbk\) is a commutative ring. An \(I\)-graded object in \(\mathcal{A}\) is also called an \(I\)-graded module. Suppose further that \(I\) is a monoid. Define a bifunctor \(\otimes\) on the category \(\mathcal{A}^I\) by \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:graded-module}{} (M \otimes N)^i := \bigoplus_{jk=i} M^j \otimes N^k, \quad (f \otimes g)^i := \bigoplus_{jk=i} f^j \otimes g^k . \end{equation}\] Also define \(\ensuremath{\bm{1}}\) to be \(\Bbbk\) concentrated in the component \(i=1_I\) (the unit of \(I\)). These data make \(\mathcal{A}^I\) a monoidal category. The unit condition \(\eta_A:\ensuremath{\bm{1}}=\Bbbk\to A\) automatically

ensures that \(1_A:=\eta_A(1)\in A^{1_I}\).

In the special case where \(I\) is commutative, this recovers the \(I\)-graded modules and \(I\)-graded algebras introduced in [Li1].

Continue to take \(\mathcal{A}=\Bbbk\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\) and require \((I,+)\) to be a commutative monoid. Every additive homomorphism \(\epsilon:I\to\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}/2\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\) makes \(\Bbbk\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}^I\) a symmetric monoidal category with the Koszul braiding characterized by \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:Koszul-braiding}{}\begin{aligned} M^a \otimes N^b & \to N^b \otimes M^a \\ x \otimes y & \mapsto (-1)^{\epsilon(a)\epsilon(b)} y \otimes x , \end{aligned} \end{equation}\] where \(a,b\in I\). The corresponding commutative algebras are precisely the \(\epsilon\)-commutative algebras of [Li1]. The various equations and definitions that result are collectively called the Koszul sign rule. Whenever tensor positions are interchanged, the sign must be changed according to this rule.

For example, the condition for \(A\) to be a commutative algebra is written explicitly as \[x y = (-1)^{\epsilon(a) \epsilon(b)} yx, \quad x \in A^a, \; y \in A^b.\]

The typical situation is \[I \in \{\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}, \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}_{\geq 0} \}, \quad \epsilon(a) := a \;\bmod 2 ,\] where the corresponding \(\epsilon\)-commutative algebras are called anticommutative graded algebras in the source cited above. Since this braiding appears everywhere in the study of \(\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\)-graded objects, the term graded commutative is more apt.

Now return to a general abelian category \(\mathcal{A}\) and \((I,+,\epsilon)\) as above. To generalize the preceding construction, we need to extend \(\mathcal{A}\) to a symmetric monoidal category \((\mathcal{A},\otimes)\) such that

  • \(\mathcal{A}\) is an abelian category, and coproducts (that is, direct sums) of the form in equation exist;

  • \(\otimes:\mathcal{A}\times\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{A}\) is additive in each variable and preserves these coproducts.

Under these conditions, \(\otimes\) and the Koszul braiding on \(\mathcal{A}^I\) can still be defined in the same way, making \((\mathcal{A}^I,\otimes)\) a symmetric monoidal category. Its unit is still the unit \(\ensuremath{\bm{1}}\) of \(\mathcal{A}\), viewed as an \(I\)-graded object concentrated in degree zero.

For general \((\mathcal{A},\otimes)\), all verifications are the same as in the case of \(\Bbbk\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\). The only difference is that “elements” of an object no longer have meaning in the general case.

Convention. In the special case \(\mathcal{A}=\Bbbk\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\), the usual convention is to regard an \(I\)-graded module \((M^i)_{i\in I}\) as a module equipped with a direct-sum decomposition \(M=\bigoplus_{i\in I}M^i\), and to require morphisms to preserve the direct-sum components.

Example. In the construction above (\(\mathcal{A}=\Bbbk\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\)), let \(\Bbbk\) be a field with \(\mathrm{char}(\Bbbk)\neq2\), take \(I=\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}/2\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}=\{0,1\}\), and set \(\epsilon=\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}/2\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}}\). The corresponding symmetric monoidal category is denoted by \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Vect}}^-_{\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}/2\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}}(\Bbbk)\). Its objects can be viewed as \(\Bbbk\)-vector spaces equipped with a direct-sum decomposition \(V=V_0\oplus V_1\), and are also called super vector spaces. This is the source of terminology common in linear algebra and mathematical physics, such as superalgebra and commutative superalgebra.

Finally, we discuss the effect of lax monoidal functors on algebras.

Definition. Let \(\mathcal{V}\) and \(\mathcal{V}'\) be monoidal categories. According to [Li1], a right lax monoidal functor from \(\mathcal{V}\) to \(\mathcal{V}'\), abbreviated here to a lax monoidal functor, means data \((F,\xi_F,\varphi_F)\), where

\(F:\mathcal{V}\to\mathcal{V}'\) is a functor and \[\xi_F: F(\cdot) \otimes F(\cdot) \to F(\cdot \otimes \cdot), \quad \varphi_F: \ensuremath{\bm{1}}_{\mathcal{V}'} \to F\left( \ensuremath{\bm{1}}_{\mathcal{V}} \right),\] are morphisms subject to a collection of compatibility conditions with the monoidal structures. The data \((F,\xi_F,\varphi_F)\) are often abbreviated to \(F\).

If \(\mathcal{V}\) and \(\mathcal{V}'\) are both braided (or symmetric) monoidal categories, and \(F\) also makes the following diagram commute, then \(F\) is called a braided functor, or is said to be compatible with the braidings: \[\text{Diagram chapter7-unit-088-d019}\]

If \(\xi_F\) and \(\varphi_F\) in the data of a lax monoidal functor are both isomorphisms, the functor is called a monoidal functor.

We may of course also discuss morphisms between lax monoidal functors, also called natural transformations: \[\theta = (\theta_X)_{X \in \operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{V})}: F \to G, \quad F, G: \mathcal{V} \to \mathcal{V}' .\] In addition to the conditions for a natural transformation, we require \(\theta\) to make the following diagrams commute: \[\text{Diagram chapter7-unit-088-d020} \quad \text{Diagram chapter7-unit-088-d021}\]

If \(F\) and \(G\) are monoidal functors, this definition is in fact equivalent to [Li1], where \(\varphi_F\) and \(\varphi_G\) are called “standard” isomorphisms. We may therefore discuss equivalences between monoidal categories or braided monoidal categories.

Proposition. A lax monoidal functor \(F\) induces a functor \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Alg}}(\mathcal{V})\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{Alg}}(\mathcal{V}')\). If \(A\) is an algebra over \(\mathcal{V}\), then \(F\) induces \(A\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\to F(A)\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\), and similarly for the other module categories.

If, in addition, \(\mathcal{V}\) and \(\mathcal{V}'\) are braided monoidal categories and \(F\) is a braided functor, then \(F\) also induces \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{CAlg}}(\mathcal{V})\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{CAlg}}(\mathcal{V}')\), while \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Alg}}(\mathcal{V})\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{Alg}}(\mathcal{V}')\) is a lax monoidal functor. If, moreover, \(\mathcal{V}\) and \(\mathcal{V}'\) are both symmetric, then the same holds for \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{CAlg}}(\mathcal{V})\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{CAlg}}(\mathcal{V}')\).

Proof. Let \(A\) be an algebra over \(\mathcal{V}\). Define the multiplication \(\mu_{FA}\) as \(FA\otimes FA\to F(A\otimes A)\xrightarrow{F\mu_A}FA\), and the unit \(\eta_{FA}\) as \(\ensuremath{\bm{1}}_{\mathcal{V}'}\to F(\ensuremath{\bm{1}}_{\mathcal{V}})\xrightarrow{F\eta_A}FA\). The remaining verifications are routine.

Example. Consider the symmetric monoidal abelian category \(\mathcal{A}\) and the category \(\mathcal{A}^I\) from Example reference. Define the functor \[\mathrm{ev}_0: \mathcal{A}^I \to \mathcal{A}, \quad \left(M^i\right)_{i \in I} \mapsto M^0.\] This functor is exact and symmetric lax monoidal: simply take \[\xi_{\mathrm{ev}_0}(M, N): M^0 \otimes N^0 \to (M \otimes N)^0 := \bigoplus_{i+j=0} M^i \otimes N^j\] to be the evident morphism, and \(\varphi_{\mathrm{ev}_0}:\ensuremath{\bm{1}}\to\ensuremath{\bm{1}}\) to be the identity. Thus \(A\mapsto A^0\) induces lax monoidal functors \[\ensuremath{\mathsf{Alg}}(\mathcal{A}^I) \to \ensuremath{\mathsf{Alg}}(\mathcal{A}), \quad \ensuremath{\mathsf{CAlg}}(\mathcal{A}^I) \to \ensuremath{\mathsf{CAlg}}(\mathcal{A}).\]

The following remark concerns algebras over a general monoidal category \(\mathcal{V}\). Recall that finite ordinals correspond bijectively to \(\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}_{\geq0}\); the finite ordinal \(\mathbf{n}\) corresponding to \(n\) is identified with the totally ordered \(n\)-element set \(\{0,\ldots,n-1\}\), with \(0\leq1\leq2\leq\cdots\).

Remark (The walking algebra). A map \(f:A\to B\) between partially ordered sets is called order-preserving if \(a\leq a'\implies f(a)\leq f(a')\). Write \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{FinOrd}}\) for the category of finite ordinals whose morphisms are order-preserving maps between ordinals. This is a strict monoidal category under \(\mathbf{n}\otimes\mathbf{m}:=\mathbf{n}+\mathbf{m}\). A morphism \(f\otimes g:\mathbf{n}\otimes\mathbf{m}\to\mathbf{n}'\otimes\mathbf{m}'\) maps the first \(n\) elements (or the last \(m\) elements) by \(f\) (or \(g\)), and the object \(\mathbf{0}\) is the unit3. Make \(\mathbf{1}\) into an algebra over \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{FinOrd}}\): take its unit to be \(\emptyset=\mathbf{0}\hookrightarrow\mathbf{1}\) and its multiplication to be \(\mathbf{1}\otimes\mathbf{1}=\mathbf{2}\twoheadrightarrow\mathbf{1}\). The associated commutative diagrams are entirely straightforward to verify.

The ordinal \(\mathbf{1}\) (or \(\mathbf{2}\)) may be viewed as the “walking” object (or morphism). Indeed, for any category \(\mathcal{C}\), specifying a functor \(\mathbf{1}\to\mathcal{C}\) (or \(\mathbf{2}\to\mathcal{C}\)) is equivalent to specifying an object (or a morphism) in \(\mathcal{C}\). Now consider a monoidal category \(\mathcal{V}\). We claim that there is an isomorphism of categories \[\left\{ \mathcal{V}\;\text{-algebras}\; A \right\} \simeq \left\{ \text{monoidal functors}\; F: \ensuremath{\mathsf{FinOrd}} \to \mathcal{V} \right\},\] which also means that \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{FinOrd}}\) is the “walking algebra.” First, for a monoidal functor \(F:\ensuremath{\mathsf{FinOrd}}\to\mathcal{V}\), define \(A:=F(\mathbf{1})\). As a simple special case of Proposition reference, \(A\) naturally becomes an algebra over \(\mathcal{V}\): the multiplication \(\mu:A\otimes A\to A\) is \(F(\mathbf{2}\twoheadrightarrow\mathbf{1})\), while the unit \(\eta:\ensuremath{\bm{1}}_{\mathcal{V}}\to A\) is \(F(\mathbf{0}\hookrightarrow\mathbf{1})\).

Conversely, from an algebra \((A,\mu,\eta)\) over \(\mathcal{V}\) define a monoidal functor \(F:\ensuremath{\mathsf{FinOrd}}\to\mathcal{V}\) by \[F(\mathbf{n}) = A^{\otimes n} := \underbracket{A \otimes (A \otimes (\cdots))}_{n\;\text{copies of}\; A}, \quad A^{\otimes 0} := \ensuremath{\bm{1}}_{\mathcal{V}},\] For \(f:\mathbf{n}\to\mathbf{m}\), if \(f\) is injective, then \(F(f):A^{\otimes n}\to A^{\otimes m}\) is obtained by inserting \(\eta:\ensuremath{\bm{1}}_{\mathcal{V}}\to A\) outside the image of \(f\); if \(f\) is surjective, \(F(f)\) is obtained by using \(\mu:A\otimes A\to A\) to successively combine the factors in each fiber. The associativity constraints and other properties of a monoidal category ensure that these operations are well defined. A general map \(f\) has a unique surjective–injective factorization, and this defines \(F\) on morphisms. Functoriality is clear. It is not difficult to verify that the two constructions are mutually inverse.

  1. Definitions in other sources may differ slightly, but the resulting concepts of a monoidal category are equivalent.↩︎

  2. For categories of this kind, [Li1] also discusses group objects, but the inverse property cannot be formulated in an arbitrary monoidal category.↩︎

  3. Here \(\mathbf{1}\) always denotes an ordinal; the unit of the monoidal category \(\mathcal{V}\) is denoted separately by \(\ensuremath{\bm{1}}_{\mathcal{V}}\).↩︎

Example: Differential Graded Structures

Continuing the discussion in Example reference, consider a symmetric monoidal abelian category \((\mathcal{A}, \otimes)\) that admits countable coproducts. Throughout this section we also assume that \(\otimes\) is right exact in each variable. The standard example is, of course, \(\mathcal{A}=\Bbbk\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\). We previously discussed \(\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\)-graded algebras over \(\mathcal{A}\), or, equivalently, algebras over the monoidal category \((\mathcal{A}^{\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}},\otimes)\). More precisely, in the setting of Example reference, this means taking \(I=\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\) and the Koszul braiding equation corresponding to \(\epsilon(a)=a\bmod\;2\). Henceforth, “graded” always means “\(\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\)-graded.” The aim of this section is to add a “differential” structure; part of the discussion overlaps with §reference. Define the shift functor \(T:\mathcal{A}^{\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}}\to\mathcal{A}^{\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}}\) by \((TM)^n=M^{n+1}\) and \((Tf)^n=f^{n+1}\). Thus \(\left(\mathcal{A}^{\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}},T\right)\) is an abelian category with translation, and a differential object over it (Definition reference) is called a differential graded object over \(\mathcal{A}\). In fact, the abelian category \(\left(\mathcal{A}^{\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}},T\right)_d\) of differential graded objects is canonically isomorphic to the category of complexes \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})\). This has already been observed in §reference. Accordingly, from now on we identify differential graded objects over \(\mathcal{A}\) with complexes, without distinguishing between the two. We next equip \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})\) with a symmetric monoidal structure. For any complexes \(M\) and \(N\), the bifunctor \(\otimes:\mathcal{A}\times\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{A}\) gives the double complex \(M^\bullet\otimes N^\bullet\); totalization by direct sums gives \[M \otimes N := \operatorname{tot}_{\oplus}\left( M^\bullet \otimes N^\bullet \right), \quad (M \otimes N)^n = \bigoplus_{a+b=n} M^a \otimes N^b.\] In the example \(\mathcal{A}=\Bbbk\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\), the differential \(d=d_{M\otimes N}\) on the complex (or, equivalently, on the differential object) can be written elementwise as \[\begin{equation*} d(x \otimes y) = (d_M x) \otimes y + (-1)^a x \otimes (d_N y), \quad x \in M^a, \; y \in N^b. \end{equation*}\] With these definitions, the Koszul braiding equation is a morphism of complexes. The reader may verify this directly or deduce it from Proposition reference. Moreover, the unit object \(\ensuremath{\bm{1}}\) of \((\mathcal{A},\otimes)\), viewed as a complex concentrated in degree zero, is clearly the unit object of the monoidal category \((\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A}),\otimes)\). The following fact is immediate: for every \(X=(X^n,d_X^n)_n\in\operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A}))\), \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:unit-map-into-cplx}{} \operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})}(\ensuremath{\bm{1}}, X) \simeq \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{A}}\left( \ensuremath{\bm{1}}, \operatorname{ker}\left(d_X^0 \right) \right). \end{equation}\]

Definition. With respect to the symmetric monoidal structure above, the objects of \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Alg}}\left(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})\right)\) are called differential graded algebras over \(\mathcal{A}\), abbreviated dg algebras; the objects of \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{CAlg}}\left(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})\right)\) are called commutative differential graded algebras over \(\mathcal{A}\), abbreviated commutative dg algebras.

For a differential graded algebra \(A\), one can therefore also speak of left (or right) \(A\)-modules \(M\), and even of bimodules; each forms an abelian category. In this setting \(M\) is also called a differential graded module over \(A\), abbreviated a dg module. This notion combines the theory of complexes with module theory and is extremely useful. The exercises in this chapter give a further introduction; the reader may also consult monographs such as [Yek20]. To emphasize the differential graded structure, we write the category of dg modules as \(A\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{dgMod}}\), and use analogous notation for its variants. The forgetful functor \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})\to\mathcal{A}^{\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}}\) preserves \(\otimes\), so Proposition reference shows that it preserves algebra (or commutative algebra) structures. When \(\mathcal{A}=\Bbbk\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\), to say that \(A\) is a dg algebra is precisely to say that \(A\) is a graded algebra equipped with a differential \(d\) whose multiplication satisfies the Leibniz rule \[d(xy) = (dx)y + (-1)^a x (dy), \quad x \in A^a, \; y \in A^b.\] Substituting \(x=1_A=y\) gives \(d(1_A)=0\). The opposite algebra \(A^{\operatorname{op}}\) is obtained by replacing the multiplication with \(x\mathbin{\cdot^{\operatorname{op}}}y:=(-1)^{ab}yx\). Similarly, when \(\mathcal{A}=\Bbbk\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\), a left \(A\)-module \(M\) is equivalently a graded \(\Bbbk\)-module \(M\) with a scalar-multiplication morphism \(A\otimes M\to M\) satisfying associativity and the other module axioms, and equipped with a differential \(d\) satisfying the Leibniz rule \[d(tm) = (dt)m + (-1)^a t (dm), \quad t \in A^a, \; m \in M^b;\] for a right \(A\)-module \(M\), the Leibniz rule becomes \[d(mt) = (dm)t + (-1)^b m (dt), \quad t \in A^a, \; m \in M^b.\] For a general \((\mathcal{A},\otimes)\), all these properties can be formulated without elements. For example, the unit of an algebra \(A\) corresponds to a morphism \(\ensuremath{\bm{1}}\to\operatorname{ker}\left(d_A^0\right)\) in \(\mathcal{A}\); see equation. Taking cohomology gives an additive functor \(\operatorname{H}=(\operatorname{H}^n)_{n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}}:\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})\to\mathcal{A}^{\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}}\). The next result says that multiplication of complexes induces multiplication on cohomology.

Proposition. The functor \(\operatorname{H}\) induces \[\ensuremath{\mathsf{Alg}}\left(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})\right) \to \ensuremath{\mathsf{Alg}}\left(\mathcal{A}^{\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}}\right), \quad \ensuremath{\mathsf{CAlg}}\left(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})\right) \to \ensuremath{\mathsf{CAlg}}\left(\mathcal{A}^{\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}}\right).\] If \(A\) is a dg algebra and \(M\) is a left \(A\)-module (or a right module, or a bimodule), then \(\operatorname{H}(M)\) is respectively a left \(\operatorname{H}(A)\)-module (or a right module, or a bimodule).

Proof. By Proposition reference, it suffices to prove that \(\operatorname{H}\) is a lax monoidal functor. The required canonical morphism \[\xi_{\operatorname{H}}(M, N): \operatorname{H}(M) \otimes \operatorname{H}(N) \to \operatorname{H}(M \otimes N),\] is nearly tautological: it is the morphism \(\kappa\) discussed in Theorem reference or Proposition reference. On the other hand, take \[\varphi_{\operatorname{H}}: \ensuremath{\bm{1}}\to \operatorname{H}(\ensuremath{\bm{1}}) = \ensuremath{\bm{1}}\quad \text{(concentrated in degree zero)}\] to be \(\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}\).

We may also take the lax monoidal functor \(\mathrm{ev}_0:\mathcal{A}^{\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}}\to\mathcal{A}\) of Example reference. Again, Proposition reference shows that it sends graded algebras (or graded commutative algebras) to algebras (or commutative algebras), and modules to modules. Observe that \(\mathrm{ev}_0\operatorname{H}=\operatorname{H}^0\). In applications, each stage of the composite \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})\xrightarrow{\operatorname{H}}\mathcal{A}^{\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{ev}_0}\mathcal{A}\) discards information; the richest structure remains on the dg algebra itself.

Example. Let \(\Bbbk\) be a commutative ring. For any \(\Bbbk\)-linear category \(\mathcal{A}\), consider the multiplication on the Hom complexes from equation: \[\operatorname{Hom}^a(Y, Z) \times \operatorname{Hom}^b(X, Y) \to \operatorname{Hom}^{a+b}(X, Z), \quad X, Y, Z \in \operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})).\]

Because this multiplication satisfies the Leibniz rule (Lemma reference), it determines a morphism in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\Bbbk\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}})\) \[\operatorname{Hom}^\bullet(Y, Z) \otimes \operatorname{Hom}^\bullet(X, Y) \to \operatorname{Hom}^\bullet(X, Z).\] Moreover, the multiplication is associative, so \(\operatorname{End}^\bullet(X):=\operatorname{Hom}^\bullet(X,X)\) is an algebra over \((\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\Bbbk\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}),\otimes)\) with unit \(\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_X\in\operatorname{End}^0(X)\). Furthermore, \(\operatorname{Hom}^\bullet(X,Y)\) is an \((\operatorname{End}^\bullet(Y),\operatorname{End}^\bullet(X))\)-bimodule.

Taking the cohomology \(\operatorname{H}=(\operatorname{H}^n)_n\) of \(\operatorname{Hom}^\bullet(X,Y)\) gives only \[\bigoplus_{n \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}} \operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{A})}(X, Y[n]);\] whereas applying equation to \(\operatorname{Hom}^\bullet(X,Y)\) shows that \(\operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})}\) can be reconstructed as \[\operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\Bbbk\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}})}\left( \Bbbk, \operatorname{Hom}^\bullet(X, Y) \right) \simeq \operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})}(X, Y)\] with \(\Bbbk\) serving as the unit object of \((\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\Bbbk\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}),\otimes)\).

Thus the sets \(\operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})}\) and composition of morphisms in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})\) are merely shadows of the Hom complexes and their multiplication, obtained by applying \(\operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\Bbbk\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}})}(\Bbbk,\mathord\cdot)\).

Starting from the example \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})\), we are naturally led to the concept of a differential graded category. This concept involves the \(\mathcal{V}\)-enriched categories introduced in [Li1]. Briefly, for any monoidal category \(\mathcal{V}\), a \(\mathcal{V}\)-enriched category \(\mathcal{C}\) still has objects and morphisms, but the Hom sets are replaced by Hom objects in \(\mathcal{V}\), written \(\ensuremath{\EuScript{H}\mathrm{om}}=\ensuremath{\EuScript{H}\mathrm{om}}_{\mathcal{C}}\) to distinguish them. Composition of morphisms is replaced by a morphism in \(\mathcal{V}\) \[\ensuremath{\EuScript{H}\mathrm{om}}(Y, Z) \otimes \ensuremath{\EuScript{H}\mathrm{om}}(X, Y) \to \ensuremath{\EuScript{H}\mathrm{om}}(X, Z),\] while an identity morphism \(\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_X\in\operatorname{Hom}(X,X)\) is replaced by \(\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_X:\ensuremath{\bm{1}}\to\ensuremath{\EuScript{H}\mathrm{om}}(X,X)\). These are all morphisms in \(\mathcal{V}\), and their properties are expressed by commutative diagrams in \(\mathcal{V}\). For enriched versions of functors and morphisms between them, see [Li1]. They are defined in the expected way; in brief, an enriched functor lifts maps between Hom sets to morphisms between \(\ensuremath{\EuScript{H}\mathrm{om}}\) objects. For example, a \(\Bbbk\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\)-category is precisely a category enriched over \((\Bbbk\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}},\otimes)\). Conversely, let us temporarily call a category without enrichment an ordinary category. If set-theoretic size issues are ignored, an ordinary category is the same thing as a category enriched over \((\ensuremath{\mathsf{Set}},\times)\).

Definition. Let \(\Bbbk\) be a commutative ring, and consider the corresponding symmetric monoidal category \((\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\Bbbk\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}),\otimes)\). A category enriched over \((\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\Bbbk\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}),\otimes)\) is called a differential graded category over \(\Bbbk\), abbreviated a dg category over \(\Bbbk\). Functors between such categories and morphisms between those functors are defined as for enriched categories.1

By definition, an object \(X\) of a dg category gives a dg algebra \(\operatorname{End}^\bullet(X)\).

Example. Example reference says that \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})\) naturally becomes a dg category over \(\Bbbk\) for any \(\Bbbk\)-linear category \(\mathcal{A}\). For example, for every \(\Bbbk\)-algebra \(R\), the category of complexes of left (or right) \(R\)-modules is automatically a dg category over \(\Bbbk\).

Example. Let \(\Bbbk\) be a commutative ring and let \(A\) be a dg algebra over \(\mathcal{A}:=\Bbbk\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\). For left \(A\)-modules \(M\) and \(N\), define the following subcomplex of \(\operatorname{Hom}^\bullet_{\Bbbk}(M,N)\): \[\operatorname{Hom}^p_A(M, N) := \left\{\begin{array}{r|l} f \in \operatorname{Hom}^p_{\Bbbk}(M, N) & \forall m \in M, \; \forall k \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}, \; \forall t \in A^k, \\ & f(tm) = (-1)^{pk} tf(m) \end{array}\right\}.\] For left \(A\)-modules \(L\), \(M\), and \(N\), composition on the Hom complexes \(\operatorname{Hom}^\bullet_{\Bbbk}\) induces a morphism of complexes \[\operatorname{Hom}^p_A(M, N) \otimes \operatorname{Hom}^q_A(L, M) \to \operatorname{Hom}^{p+q}_A(L, N).\] Thus the category \(A\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{dgMod}}\) of left \(A\)-modules is enriched to a dg category. For right \(A\)-modules, the condition in the definition of \(\operatorname{Hom}^p_A(M,N)\) must be replaced by \(f(mt)=f(m)t\) (think about why). Bimodules are handled similarly.

The definition above can also be formulated without reference to elements, and therefore extends to a general \(\mathcal{A}\).

More precisely, a dg category enriches every Hom set of the underlying ordinary category to a Hom complex \(\operatorname{Hom}^\bullet\), while dg versions of functors and their morphisms must be formulated inside \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\Bbbk\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}})\). Explicitly:

  • A dg functor \(F:\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{D}\) between dg categories consists of a map of object sets \(F:\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{C})\to\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{D})\) and morphisms of Hom complexes \(\operatorname{Hom}^\bullet_{\mathcal{C}}(X,Y)\to \operatorname{Hom}^\bullet_{\mathcal{D}}(FX,FY)\). The latter are morphisms in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\Bbbk\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}})\) and are required to make both diagrams below commute: \[\begin{equation*} \begin{gathered} \text{Diagram chapter7-unit-089-d001} \\ \text{Diagram chapter7-unit-089-d002} \end{gathered} \end{equation*}\]

  • In the classical sense, a morphism, or natural transformation, \(\phi\) between dg functors \(F,G:\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{D}\) is a family of elements \[\begin{multline*} \phi_X \in \operatorname{ker}\left[ \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{D}}^0(FX, GX) \to \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{D}}^1(FX, GX) \right] \\ \xlongequal{\text{\href{#eqn:unit-map-into-cplx}{equation}}} \operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\Bbbk\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}})}\left(\Bbbk, \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{D}}^\bullet(FX, GX) \right) , \end{multline*}\] indexed by \(X\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{C})\), such that for every \(m\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\) and \(f\in\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}}^m(X,Y)\), \[(Gf) \phi_X = \phi_Y (Ff) \; \in \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{D}}^m(FX, GY),\] where multiplication means multiplication in the Hom complex.

Thus one may speak of isomorphisms, equivalences, adjunctions, and other notions for dg categories. An element of \(\operatorname{Hom}^n_{\mathcal{C}}(X,Y)\) is sometimes called a morphism of degree \(n\) from \(X\) to \(Y\). For a general monoidal category \(\mathcal{V}\), one may view \(\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{V}}(\ensuremath{\bm{1}},M)\) as the set of “elements” of \(M\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{V})\); this is at least natural when \(\mathcal{V}=\ensuremath{\mathsf{Set}}\) or \(\Bbbk\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\). Following this idea, every \(\mathcal{V}\)-enriched category \(\mathcal{C}\) has an underlying ordinary category defined by \[\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}}(X, Y) := \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{V}}\left( \ensuremath{\bm{1}}, \ensuremath{\EuScript{H}\mathrm{om}}_{\mathcal{C}}(X, Y) \right),\] and we continue to denote that ordinary category by \(\mathcal{C}\); see [Li1] for details. In the example of the dg category \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})\), the resulting ordinary category is the ordinary category of complexes \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})\). Thus our notation is consistent. Another operation comes from lax monoidal functors. Here is the general statement.

Proposition. Let \(F:\mathcal{V}\to\mathcal{V}'\) be a lax monoidal functor between monoidal categories. For every \(\mathcal{V}\)-enriched category \(\mathcal{C}\), define a \(\mathcal{V}'\)-enriched category \(F(\mathcal{C})\) as follows: set \(\operatorname{Ob}(F(\mathcal{C}))=\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{C})\), and for every pair of objects \(X,Y\), set \[\begin{gather*} \ensuremath{\EuScript{H}\mathrm{om}}_{F(\mathcal{C})}(X, Y) := F\ensuremath{\EuScript{H}\mathrm{om}}_{\mathcal{C}}(X, Y), \\ \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_X: \ensuremath{\bm{1}}_{\mathcal{V}'} \xrightarrow{\varphi_F} F(\ensuremath{\bm{1}}_{\mathcal{V}}) \to F\ensuremath{\EuScript{H}\mathrm{om}}_{\mathcal{C}}(X, X). \end{gather*}\] Composition is defined by \[\begin{multline*} F\ensuremath{\EuScript{H}\mathrm{om}}_{\mathcal{C}}(Y, Z) \otimes F\ensuremath{\EuScript{H}\mathrm{om}}_{\mathcal{C}}(X, Y) \\ \xrightarrow{\xi_F} F\left( \ensuremath{\EuScript{H}\mathrm{om}}_{\mathcal{C}}(Y, Z) \otimes \ensuremath{\EuScript{H}\mathrm{om}}_{\mathcal{C}}(X, Y) \right) \to F\ensuremath{\EuScript{H}\mathrm{om}}_{\mathcal{C}}(X, Z), \end{multline*}\] and on the corresponding ordinary categories this construction gives an ordinary functor \(\mathcal{C}\to F(\mathcal{C})\).

Proof. The lax monoidal structure \((F,\xi_F,\varphi_F)\) supplies all properties required of composition. On the level of ordinary categories, the functor is the identity on objects and sends a morphism \(f:\ensuremath{\bm{1}}_{\mathcal{V}}\to\ensuremath{\EuScript{H}\mathrm{om}}_{\mathcal{C}}(X,Y)\) to the composite \(\ensuremath{\bm{1}}_{\mathcal{V}'}\xrightarrow{\varphi_F}F(\ensuremath{\bm{1}}_{\mathcal{V}}) \xrightarrow{Ff}F\ensuremath{\EuScript{H}\mathrm{om}}_{\mathcal{C}}(X,Y)\).

Comparing this construction with that of Proposition reference, we see that

\(\ensuremath{\EuScript{H}\mathrm{om}}_{F(\mathcal{C})}(X,X)\), as an object of \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Alg}}(\mathcal{V}')\), is induced from \(\ensuremath{\EuScript{H}\mathrm{om}}_{\mathcal{C}}(X,X)\); the same applies to the bimodule structures on \(\ensuremath{\EuScript{H}\mathrm{om}}\).

Remark. Proposition reference gives another way to pass from a dg category to an ordinary category. Apply the lax monoidal functor \(\operatorname{H}\) of Proposition reference to any dg category \(\mathcal{C}\) over \(\Bbbk\). The result is a category \(\operatorname{H}(\mathcal{C})\) enriched over \((\Bbbk\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}^{\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}},\otimes)\), satisfying \[\operatorname{Ob}(\operatorname{H}(\mathcal{C})) = \operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{C}), \quad \ensuremath{\EuScript{H}\mathrm{om}}_{\operatorname{H}(\mathcal{C})}(X, Y) = \left( \operatorname{H}^n \operatorname{Hom}^\bullet(X, Y) \right)_{n \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}}.\] Taking the degree-\(0\) part, or equivalently applying the lax monoidal functor \(\operatorname{H}^0\) to \(\mathcal{C}\), produces an ordinary \(\Bbbk\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\)-category called the homotopy category \(\mathrm{h}(\mathcal{C})\) of \(\mathcal{C}\). It satisfies \[\operatorname{Ob}(\mathrm{h}\mathcal{C}) = \operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{C}), \quad \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathrm{h}\mathcal{C}}(X, Y) = \operatorname{H}^0 \operatorname{Hom}^\bullet(X, Y).\] In the special case \(\mathcal{C}=\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})\), substituting Definition reference immediately gives \[\mathrm{h}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})) = \ensuremath{\mathsf{K}}(\mathcal{A}).\]

As seen above, the world of dg categories supports many homotopy-flavored operations. Their meaning ultimately has to be explained through applications and also involves the abstract language of model categories. We give only a brief outline of some elementary notions, without developing them further.

Definition. Let \(F:\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{D}\) be a dg functor between dg categories. If \[\operatorname{Hom}^\bullet_{\mathcal{C}}(X, Y) \to \operatorname{Hom}^\bullet_{\mathcal{D}}(FX, FY)\] is a quasi-isomorphism for all \(X,Y\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{C})\), then \(F\) is called quasi-fully faithful. If the induced functor \(\mathrm{h}F:\mathrm{h}\mathcal{C}\to\mathrm{h}\mathcal{D}\) is essentially surjective, then \(F\) is called quasi-essentially surjective. A dg functor that is both quasi-fully faithful and quasi-essentially surjective is called a quasi-equivalence.

Thus quasi-equivalent dg categories \(\mathcal{C}\) and \(\mathcal{D}\) have equivalent homotopy categories. We continue this brief discussion of dg categories in §reference.

  1. Much of the literature on infinity categories uses the term DG-category, as well as the notation \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{DGCat}}\) for the category they form, and this notation may overlap with that of this book. Although those DG-categories are closely related to the dg categories discussed here, the two are not the same notion.↩︎

Closed Monoidal Categories

Let \(\Bbbk\) be a commutative ring. Then \(\Bbbk\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\) is a symmetric monoidal category under \(\otimes:=\otimes_{\Bbbk}\). It has the following closedness properties.

  • It is enriched over itself: the set of homomorphisms \(\operatorname{Hom}(X,Y)\) naturally has the structure of a \(\Bbbk\)-module;

  • the basic properties of the tensor product give a canonical isomorphism in \(\Bbbk\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\) \[\operatorname{Hom}(X \otimes Y, Z) \simeq \operatorname{Hom}(X, \operatorname{Hom}(Y, Z)).\]

Extending these properties to general monoidal categories leads to the following concept.

Definition. Let \(\mathcal{C}\) be a monoidal category. The category \(\mathcal{C}\) is called right closed (or left closed) if, for every object \(Y\), the functor \((\cdot)\otimes Y:\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{C}\) (or \(Y\otimes(\cdot):\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{C}\)) is equipped with a specified right adjoint. A monoidal category that is both left closed and right closed is called a closed monoidal category.

All monoidal categories considered below are braided monoidal categories, so we shall no longer distinguish left closed from right closed. In this situation, the right adjoint of \((\cdot)\otimes Y\) is denoted by \([Y,\cdot]:\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{C}\). Recall that if a category \(\mathcal{C}\) has finite products, then \(\mathcal{C}\) is a symmetric monoidal category under \(\times\), with the terminal object as its unit \(\ensuremath{\bm{1}}\) (Example reference).

Definition. Let \(\mathcal{C}\) be a category with finite products. If \((\mathcal{C},\times)\) is a closed monoidal category, then \(\mathcal{C}\) is called a Cartesian closed category.

More generally, for any two pairs of adjoint functors \((F,G)\) and \((F',G')\) between categories \(\mathcal{C}_1\) and \(\mathcal{C}_2\), every \(\varphi:F\to F'\) naturally induces \(\psi:G'\to G\); conversely, every \(\psi:G'\to G\) naturally induces \(\varphi:F\to F'\). In either case, the induced morphism is characterized by the commutative diagram \[\text{Diagram chapter7-unit-090-d001}\] This is simply an application of the Yoneda lemma. The reader may also try to write down these induced morphisms using the unit and counit of the adjoint pairs. As an application, every morphism \(Y\to Y'\) in a closed monoidal category induces \([Y',\cdot]\to[Y,\cdot]\). Thus, being a closed monoidal category is equivalent to the existence of a bifunctor \([\cdot,\cdot]:\mathcal{C}^{\operatorname{op}}\times\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{C}\) and a family of canonical bijections \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:closed-monoidal-adj0}{} \operatorname{Hom}(X \otimes Y, Z) \simeq \operatorname{Hom}(X, [Y, Z]), \end{equation}\] functorial in all three variables. The bifunctor \([\cdot,\cdot]\) is also called the internal \(\operatorname{Hom}\) of the closed monoidal category \(\mathcal{C}\). The definition also yields the following conclusions.

  • From \(\operatorname{Hom}(X,Z)\simeq\operatorname{Hom}(X\otimes\ensuremath{\bm{1}},Z)\simeq\operatorname{Hom}(X,[\ensuremath{\bm{1}},Z])\) and the Yoneda lemma, one obtains \(Z\simeq[\ensuremath{\bm{1}},Z]\);

  • the unit morphism of the adjoint pair gives \(\mathrm{coev}_{X,Y}:X\to[Y,X\otimes Y]\), while the counit morphism gives \(\mathrm{ev}_{Y,X}:[Y,X]\otimes Y\to X\);

  • from the composite \[[Y, Z] \otimes ([X, Y] \otimes X) \xrightarrow{\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}\otimes \mathrm{ev}_{X, Y}} [Y, Z] \otimes Y \xrightarrow{\mathrm{ev}_{Y, Z}} Z\] and the adjunction together with the associativity constraint, one obtains \[[Y, Z] \otimes [X, Y] \to [X, Z];\]

  • taking \(\mathrm{coev}_{\ensuremath{\bm{1}},X}\) gives a morphism \(\ensuremath{\bm{1}}\to[X,X]\).

The term internal \(\operatorname{Hom}\) and the preceding properties make clear that a closed monoidal category is enriched over itself. We first show how to recover the ordinary \(\operatorname{Hom}\) from the internal \(\operatorname{Hom}\).

Proposition. Let \(\mathcal{C}\) be a closed monoidal category. There is a family of canonical bijections \[\operatorname{Hom}(X, Y) \simeq \operatorname{Hom}(\ensuremath{\bm{1}}, [X, Y]), \quad X, Y \in \operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{C}).\]

Proof. By equation, \(\operatorname{Hom}(\ensuremath{\bm{1}},[X,Y])\simeq\operatorname{Hom}(\ensuremath{\bm{1}}\otimes X,Y)\simeq\operatorname{Hom}(X,Y)\).

To show that \(\mathcal{C}\) is enriched over itself, one must still prove that \([Y,Z]\otimes[X,Z]\to[Y,Z]\) and \(\ensuremath{\bm{1}}\to[X,X]\) satisfy axioms such as associativity. This can be checked using the standard properties of the unit and counit. Since the details are rather tedious, the proof is left as an exercise for this chapter. We next show that the adjunction equation is itself automatically internalized in \(\mathcal{C}\).

Proposition. Let \(\mathcal{C}\) be a closed monoidal category. There is a family of canonical isomorphisms \[[X \otimes Y, Z] \simeq [X, [Y, Z]];\] more precisely, this is an isomorphism between functors from \(\mathcal{C}^{\operatorname{op}}\times\mathcal{C}^{\operatorname{op}}\times\mathcal{C}\) to \(\mathcal{C}\).

Proof. Fix \(X\), \(Y\), and \(Z\). For every object \(T\), equation and the associativity constraint of \(\mathcal{C}\) give natural bijections \[\begin{multline*} \operatorname{Hom}(T, [X \otimes Y, Z]) \simeq \operatorname{Hom}(T \otimes (X \otimes Y), Z) \simeq \operatorname{Hom}((T \otimes X) \otimes Y, Z) \\ \simeq \operatorname{Hom}(T \otimes X, [Y, Z]) \simeq \operatorname{Hom}(T, [X, [Y, Z]]). \end{multline*}\] Since \(T\) is arbitrary, the Yoneda lemma gives the desired isomorphism.

The following basic examples involve the symmetric monoidal categories introduced in §reference.

  • The category of sets \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Set}}\) is Cartesian closed: take \([X,Y]\) to be the set of maps \(Y^X=\left\{\text{maps}\;X\to Y\right\}\). Then equation, or its internalized version in Proposition reference, gives the natural bijection \(Z^{X\times Y}\xrightarrow{1:1}(Z^X)^Y\). In computer science, such a bijection, or its generalization to an arbitrary closed monoidal category, is often called currying.

  • All small categories and the functors between them form the category \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Cat}}\). Its products are the products of categories \(\mathcal{C}_1\times\cdots\times\mathcal{C}_2\), and its empty product is the category \(\mathbf{1}\). The category \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Cat}}\) is Cartesian closed; this is equivalent to the following simple statement: specifying a bifunctor \(\mathcal{A}\times\mathcal{B}\to\mathcal{C}\) is equivalent to specifying a functor \(\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{B}^{\mathcal{C}}\), and is also equivalent to specifying \(\mathcal{B}\to\mathcal{C}^{\mathcal{A}}\).

  • Although the category of topological spaces \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Top}}\) has many good properties and is a symmetric monoidal category under the product \(\times\), it is not Cartesian closed; see the discussion at the end of [Kel05]. Since mapping spaces \(X^Y\) occur everywhere in topology, the cost of giving up closedness is too high. A convenient replacement is the category of compactly generated Hausdorff spaces1 \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{CGHaus}}\). It is a full subcategory of \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Top}}\) and is itself Cartesian closed. One can prove that there is an adjoint pair \(\text{Diagram chapter7-unit-090-diagram-002}\), where the inclusion functor preserves \(\varinjlim\) but not products.

  • Let \(G\) be a group and \(\Bbbk\) a commutative ring. The symmetric monoidal category \(G\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\) introduced in Proposition reference is closed: its internal \(\operatorname{Hom}\) is precisely the \(\operatorname{Hom}\) module introduced in §reference, and the required adjunction is exactly equation.

  • Again let \(\Bbbk\) be a commutative ring, and set \(\mathcal{A}:=\Bbbk\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\). As seen in §reference, the category of complexes \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})\) is a symmetric monoidal category. It is closed, with internal \(\operatorname{Hom}\) given by the \(\operatorname{Hom}\) complex. The adjunction required in equation is the adjunction between \(\operatorname{Hom}\) and \(\otimes\) at the level of complexes. Concretely, it is a corollary of Proposition reference in the case \(A=R=B=\Bbbk\). The corresponding unit and counit morphisms are \[\text{Diagram chapter7-unit-090-d002}\]

The last example shows that Definition reference of the \(\operatorname{Hom}\) complex is entirely natural, provided that \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})\) is given the symmetric monoidal structure described above.

  1. A compactly generated Hausdorff space is a Hausdorff space \(X\) with the following property: if the intersection of a subset \(A\subset X\) with every compact subset \(K\subset X\) is closed, then \(A\) is closed.↩︎

Case Study: The Closed Structure on dg-Categories

We previously discussed the closed monoidal structure on \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Cat}}\), where \(\otimes\) comes from the ordinary product of categories \(\mathcal{C}_1\times\mathcal{C}_2\). On the other hand, relative to a fixed commutative ring \(\Bbbk\), Definition reference introduced dg-categories, namely categories enriched over \((\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\Bbbk\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}),\otimes)\). The aim of this section is to show that all small dg-categories themselves form a closed monoidal category \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{dgCat}}_{\Bbbk}\). This category can be regarded as both a linearized and a complex-enriched version of \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Cat}}\), and it arises naturally and usefully in many situations. All that is needed is a sequence of lengthy but straightforward constructions. The first step is to upgrade the ordinary product of categories to a tensor product of dg-categories. This involves the symmetric braiding on \((\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\Bbbk\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}),\otimes)\).

Definition. Let \(\mathcal{C}_1\) and \(\mathcal{C}_2\) be dg-categories over \(\Bbbk\). Define a new dg-category \(\mathcal{C}_1\otimes\mathcal{C}_2\) by \[\begin{align*} \operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{C}_1 \otimes \mathcal{C}_2) & := \operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{C}_1) \times \operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{C}_2), \\ \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}_1 \otimes \mathcal{C}_2}^\bullet((X, X'), (Y, Y')) & := \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}_1}^\bullet(X, Y) \otimes \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}_2}^\bullet(X', Y'), \end{align*}\] and take \(\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_X\otimes\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{X'}\) as the unit of \(\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}_1\otimes\mathcal{C}_2}^\bullet((X,X'),(X,X'))\). Composition of morphisms is defined by \[\text{Diagram chapter7-unit-091-d001}\] where the isomorphism comes from the Koszul braiding and the associativity constraint.

The symmetry of the braiding shows that \(\mathcal{C}_1\otimes\mathcal{C}_2\) is naturally equivalent to \(\mathcal{C}_2\otimes\mathcal{C}_1\). Write \(\Bbbk\) for the dg-category with one object and endomorphism complex \(\Bbbk\). It is easy to prove that \(\Bbbk\otimes\mathcal{C}\) is equivalent to \(\mathcal{C}\otimes\Bbbk\).

Definition. Let \(\Bbbk\) be a commutative ring. Write \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{dgCat}}_{\Bbbk}\) for the category of all small dg-categories over \(\Bbbk\). This is a symmetric monoidal category with unit \(\Bbbk\).

The restriction to small categories is, of course, meant to avoid set-theoretic difficulties. Its chief benefit is that all functors between two given small categories \(\mathcal{C}\) and \(\mathcal{D}\) form a small set. The second step is to enrich the \(\operatorname{Hom}\) set between dg-functors into a complex.

Definition. Let \(F,G:\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{D}\) be dg-functors between dg-categories. For every \(n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\), a morphism of degree \(n\) from \(F\) to \(G\) is defined to be data \[\phi = \left( \phi_X \right)_{X \in \operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{C})}, \quad \phi_X \in \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{D}}^n(FX, GX),\] such that, for all \(m\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\), \(X,Y\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{C})\), and \(f\in\operatorname{Hom}^m_{\mathcal{C}}(X,Y)\), the following equality holds in \(\operatorname{Hom}^{n+m}_{\mathcal{D}}(FX,GY)\): \[(Gf) \phi_X = (-1)^{nm} \phi_Y (Ff);\] here composition in this formula is understood as the morphisms in \(\Bbbk\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\) \[\begin{gather*} \operatorname{Hom}^m_{\mathcal{D}}(GX, GY) \otimes \operatorname{Hom}^n_{\mathcal{D}}(FX, GX) \to \operatorname{Hom}^{m+n}_{\mathcal{D}}(FX, GY), \\ \operatorname{Hom}^n_{\mathcal{D}}(FY, GY) \otimes \operatorname{Hom}^m_{\mathcal{D}}(FX, FY) \to \operatorname{Hom}^{m+n}_{\mathcal{D}}(FX, GY). \end{gather*}\] The \(\Bbbk\)-module of all degree-\(n\) morphisms \(\phi:F\to G\) is denoted by \(\ensuremath{\EuScript{H}\mathrm{om}}^n(F,G)\).

The condition above may be viewed as saying that the diagram of graded morphisms \[\text{Diagram chapter7-unit-091-d002} \quad \begin{array}{cc} \phi: \text{degree }n \\ f: \text{degree }m \end{array}\] commutes up to the sign \((-1)^{nm}\) required by the Koszul sign rule. Strictly speaking, these “graded morphisms” are not morphisms, but must be understood as elements of a \(\operatorname{Hom}\) complex.

Definition–Proposition. For dg-functors \(F,G:\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{D}\) and every \(n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\), one can define a homomorphism \[d^n = d^n_{\ensuremath{\EuScript{H}\mathrm{om}}^\bullet(F, G)}: \ensuremath{\EuScript{H}\mathrm{om}}^n(F, G) \to \ensuremath{\EuScript{H}\mathrm{om}}^{n+1}(F, G).\]

For every \(\phi=(\phi_X)_{X\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{C})}\), set \[(d^n \phi)_X := d^n_{\operatorname{Hom}^\bullet(FX, GX)}(\phi_X).\] This makes \(\left(\ensuremath{\EuScript{H}\mathrm{om}}^n(F,G),d^n\right)_{n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}}\) into a complex \(\ensuremath{\EuScript{H}\mathrm{om}}^\bullet(F,G)\).

Proof. First check that \(d^n\phi\) does indeed belong to \(\ensuremath{\EuScript{H}\mathrm{om}}^{n+1}(F,G)\). Let \(f\in\operatorname{Hom}^m_{\mathcal{C}}(X,Y)\). Apply \(d^{m+n}\) to both sides of \((Gf)\phi_X=(-1)^{nm}\phi_Y(Ff)\) (suppressing the subscript \(\operatorname{Hom}^\bullet(FX,GY)\)). This gives \[\begin{align*} d^{m+n}((Gf) \phi_X) & = (d^m Gf) \phi_X + (-1)^m (Gf) (d^n \phi_X) \\ & = G (d^m f) \phi_X + (-1)^m (Gf) (d^n \phi)_X \\ & = (-1)^{n(m+1)} \phi_Y F(d^m f) + (-1)^m (Gf) (d^n \phi)_X, \\ (-1)^{nm} d^{m+n}(\phi_Y (Ff)) & = (-1)^{nm} (d^n \phi_Y) Ff + (-1)^{nm+n} \phi_Y d^n(Ff) \\ & = (-1)^{nm} (d^n \phi)_Y Ff + (-1)^{nm+n} \phi_Y F(d^m f). \end{align*}\] Equality of these two expressions immediately yields \((Gf)(d^n\phi)_X=(-1)^{(n+1)m}(d^n\phi)_YFf\).

Second, since \(\operatorname{Hom}^\bullet(FX,GX)\) is a complex, \[\begin{align*} (d^{n+1} d^n \phi)_X & = d^{n+1}_{\operatorname{Hom}^\bullet(FX, GX)}((d^n \phi)_X) \\ & = d^{n+1}_{\operatorname{Hom}^\bullet(FX, GX)} d^n_{\operatorname{Hom}^\bullet(FX, GX)} \phi_X = 0. \end{align*}\] Thus we obtain the complex \(\ensuremath{\EuScript{H}\mathrm{om}}^\bullet(F,G)\).

For three dg-functors \(F,G,H:\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{D}\), there is a composition operation \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:dgfct-iHom}{}\begin{aligned} \ensuremath{\EuScript{H}\mathrm{om}}^a(G, H) \otimes \ensuremath{\EuScript{H}\mathrm{om}}^b(F, G) & \to \ensuremath{\EuScript{H}\mathrm{om}}^{a+b}(F, H) \\ \psi \otimes \phi & \mapsto \psi\phi := \left( \psi_X \phi_X \right)_{X \in \operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{C})}, \end{aligned} \end{equation}\] where \(a,b\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\). This operation is associative and satisfies \(d^{a+b}(\psi\phi)=(d^a\psi)\phi+(-1)^a\psi(d^b\phi)\). By definition, everything reduces to a verification in \(\operatorname{Hom}^\bullet_{\mathcal{D}}\). This composition should be understood as vertical composition of graded morphisms, depicted as \[\text{Diagram chapter7-unit-091-d003} \quad \text{composed to give} \quad \text{Diagram chapter7-unit-091-d004}\] Consider the special case \(n=0\). The condition on \(\phi=(\phi_X)_X\in\ensuremath{\EuScript{H}\mathrm{om}}^0(F,G)\) says precisely that \((Gf)\phi_X=\phi_Y(Ff)\) for every \(f\in\operatorname{Hom}^m(X,Y)\), while the condition \(d^0\phi=0\) says precisely that \(\phi_X\in\operatorname{ker}\left(d^0_{\operatorname{Hom}^\bullet(FX,GX)}\right)\) for every \(X\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{C})\). Hence the elements of the \(\Bbbk\)-module \[\operatorname{ker}\left[ \ensuremath{\EuScript{H}\mathrm{om}}^0(F, G) \xrightarrow{d^0} \ensuremath{\EuScript{H}\mathrm{om}}^1(F, G) \right]\] are exactly the morphisms \(\phi:F\to G\) between the dg-functors \(F\) and \(G\) in the ordinary sense. The next step is to enrich the functor category between dg-categories into a dg-category.

Definition. For arbitrary dg-categories \(\mathcal{C}\) and \(\mathcal{D}\), define the dg-category \(\ensuremath{\EuScript{H}\mathrm{om}}(\mathcal{C},\mathcal{D})\) as follows.

  • Its objects are all dg-functors \(F:\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{D}\).

  • For any dg-functors \(F,G:\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{D}\), their \(\operatorname{Hom}\) complex is the complex \(\ensuremath{\EuScript{H}\mathrm{om}}^\bullet(F,G)\) defined above.

  • The composition operation \(\ensuremath{\EuScript{H}\mathrm{om}}^\bullet(G,H)\otimes\ensuremath{\EuScript{H}\mathrm{om}}^\bullet(F,G)\to \ensuremath{\EuScript{H}\mathrm{om}}^\bullet(F,H)\) is defined as in equation; it is called vertical composition.

If \(\mathcal{C}\) and \(\mathcal{D}\) are both small dg-categories, then \(\ensuremath{\EuScript{H}\mathrm{om}}(\mathcal{C},\mathcal{D})\) is also small: its set of objects is a small set. In Definition reference we defined the tensor product of two dg-categories, making the category \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{dgCat}}_{\Bbbk}\) of Definition reference a symmetric monoidal category under \(\otimes\). The relation between \(\otimes\) and \(\ensuremath{\EuScript{H}\mathrm{om}}\) can now be stated clearly as follows.

Proposition. The symmetric monoidal category \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{dgCat}}_{\Bbbk}\) is closed. Its internal Hom is given by \(\ensuremath{\EuScript{H}\mathrm{om}}(\mathcal{C},\mathcal{D})\) as defined above, where \(\mathcal{C}\) and \(\mathcal{D}\) range over all small dg-categories.

Proof. The key is to give a canonical isomorphism \[\operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{dgCat}}_{\Bbbk}}(\mathcal{C} \otimes \mathcal{D}, \mathcal{E}) \simeq \operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{dgCat}}_{\Bbbk}}(\mathcal{C}, \ensuremath{\EuScript{H}\mathrm{om}}(\mathcal{D}, \mathcal{E}) ).\]

If the dg-structure is ignored, the matter is simple: specifying \(F:\mathcal{C}\times\mathcal{D}\to\mathcal{E}\) is equivalent to specifying a functor \(\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{E}^{\mathcal{D}}\) that maps an object \(X\) to the functor \(F(X,\mathord\cdot):\mathcal{D}\to\mathcal{E}\). The essential issue is the condition at the level of \(\operatorname{Hom}\) that makes a functor a dg-functor.

By definition, making \(F\) into a dg-functor is equivalent to upgrading the maps on \(\operatorname{Hom}\) sets to morphisms of complexes \[F_{X, Y, Z, W}: \operatorname{Hom}^\bullet_{\mathcal{C}}(X, Y) \otimes \operatorname{Hom}^\bullet_{\mathcal{D}}(Z, W) \to \operatorname{Hom}^\bullet_{\mathcal{E}}(F(X, Z), F(Y, W)),\] functorial in all four variables. Treating the two variables of \(F\) separately, these data can be split into two parts:

  • for every \(X\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{C})\), the functor \(F(X,\mathord\cdot)\) is upgraded to a dg-functor;

  • there is a family of morphisms \(F_{X,Y,Z}:\operatorname{Hom}^\bullet_{\mathcal{C}}(X,Y)\to \operatorname{Hom}^\bullet_{\mathcal{E}}(F(X,Z),F(Y,Z))\), functorial in all three variables.

For illustration, \(F_{X,Y,Z,W}(f\otimes g)\) is obtained from \(F_{X,Y,Z}(f)\) by using \(g\in\operatorname{Hom}^b_{\mathcal{D}}(Z,W)\) through \(F(Y,\mathord\cdot)\). The data in the second item are equivalent to a family of morphisms \[\operatorname{Hom}^\bullet_{\mathcal{C}}(X, Y) \to \ensuremath{\EuScript{H}\mathrm{om}}^\bullet(F(X, \cdot), F(Y, \cdot)),\] functorial in \(X\) and \(Y\). In conclusion, specifying the dg-functor \(F\) is equivalent to specifying a dg-functor from \(\mathcal{C}\) to \(\ensuremath{\EuScript{H}\mathrm{om}}(\mathcal{D},\mathcal{E})\).

Together with the theory in §reference, the preceding discussion shows that \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{dgCat}}_{\Bbbk}\) is enriched over itself: for any small dg-categories \(\mathcal{C}\) and \(\mathcal{D}\), their \(\ensuremath{\EuScript{H}\mathrm{om}}\) object is again a dg-category. Since \(\otimes\) and \(\ensuremath{\EuScript{H}\mathrm{om}}\) determine each other through the adjunction equation, once either the definition of \(\otimes\) or that of \(\ensuremath{\EuScript{H}\mathrm{om}}\) is accepted, the other definition is at least equally natural.

Remark. With Proposition reference in hand, the general properties of closed monoidal categories show that for any three small dg-categories \(\mathcal{C}\), \(\mathcal{D}\), and \(\mathcal{E}\), composition of functors can be upgraded to a dg-functor \[\ensuremath{\EuScript{H}\mathrm{om}}(\mathcal{D}, \mathcal{E}) \otimes \ensuremath{\EuScript{H}\mathrm{om}}(\mathcal{C}, \mathcal{D}) \to \ensuremath{\EuScript{H}\mathrm{om}}(\mathcal{C}, \mathcal{E}).\] On objects, this functor maps \((G,F)\) to \(GF\); on \(\operatorname{Hom}\) complexes, it is written \[\begin{equation} \begin{gathered}\hypertarget{eqn:dgCat-fct-compose}{} \text{Diagram chapter7-unit-091-d005} \\ F_i: \mathcal{C} \to \mathcal{D}, \quad G_i: \mathcal{D} \to \mathcal{E}, \quad i = 1, 2 . \end{gathered} \end{equation}\]

The operation above may be pictured as horizontal composition of morphisms between dg-functors, with diagram \[\text{Diagram chapter7-unit-091-d006} \quad \text{composed to give} \quad \text{Diagram chapter7-unit-091-d007}\] Because this gives a functor, equation must

But the operation in (b) is precisely the vertical composition introduced in equation. Thus, we see that the order of vertical and horizontal composition can be interchanged.

For functors between ordinary categories, morphisms between the functors likewise have commuting vertical and horizontal compositions. This can be understood as a property of the Cartesian closed category \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Cat}}\) (or by regarding it as a \(2\)-category; see [Li1]). The property of \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{dgCat}}_{\Bbbk}\) above is its dg version, or its linear algebra version.

From Coalgebras to Hopf Algebras

The first aim of this section is to dualize Definition reference of an algebra. To this end, first note that the definition of a monoidal category is self-dual. Let \(\mathcal{V}\) be a monoidal category. On \(\mathcal{V}^{\operatorname{op}}\), one can retain the original bifunctor \(\otimes\) and unit object \(\ensuremath{\bm{1}}\), but replace the associativity constraint \(a\) and \(\iota:\ensuremath{\bm{1}}\otimes\ensuremath{\bm{1}}\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}\ensuremath{\bm{1}}\) in [Li1] by their inverses. In this way, \(\mathcal{V}^{\operatorname{op}}\) becomes a monoidal category. Similarly, if \(\mathcal{V}\) has a braiding \(c\) as in [Li1], taking inverses gives the corresponding braiding on \(\mathcal{V}^{\operatorname{op}}\). Under this correspondence, \(\mathcal{V}\) is a symmetric monoidal category if and only if \(\mathcal{V}^{\operatorname{op}}\) is one.

Definition (Coalgebra). Let \(\mathcal{V}\) be a monoidal category. An algebra over \(\mathcal{V}^{\operatorname{op}}\) is called a coalgebra over \(\mathcal{V}\). In other words, a coalgebra is data \((C,\Delta,\epsilon)\), where \[C \in \operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{V}), \quad \Delta = \Delta_C: C \to C \otimes C, \quad \epsilon = \epsilon_C: C \to \ensuremath{\bm{1}},\] satisfying the commutative diagrams dual to those in Definition reference: \[\text{Diagram chapter7-unit-092-d001} \quad \text{Diagram chapter7-unit-092-d002}\]

The map \(\Delta\) is customarily called the comultiplication on \(C\), and \(\epsilon\) the counit of \(C\).

A morphism from a coalgebra \((C,\Delta,\epsilon)\) to \((C',\Delta',\epsilon')\) is defined dually to Definition reference: it is a morphism \(\phi:C\to C'\) for which the following diagrams commute: \[\text{Diagram chapter7-unit-092-d003} \quad \text{Diagram chapter7-unit-092-d004}\]

If \(\mathcal{V}\) is equipped with a braiding \(c\) and \(c\Delta=\Delta\), then \((C,\Delta,\epsilon)\) is called cocommutative.

The following definition is simply the dual of Definition reference.

Definition (Comodule). Let \((C,\Delta,\epsilon)\) be a coalgebra over \(\mathcal{V}\). A left \(C\)-comodule is defined to be data \((M,\rho)\), where \[M \in \operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{V}), \quad \rho = \rho_M : M \to C \otimes M,\] and \(\rho\) may be viewed as scalar comultiplication on the left comodule. The condition is that the following diagrams commute: \[\text{Diagram chapter7-unit-092-d005} \quad \text{Diagram chapter7-unit-092-d006}\] A homomorphism from a left comodule \((M,\rho)\) to \((M',\rho')\) is a morphism \(f:M\to M'\) satisfying \((\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}\otimes f)\rho=\rho'f\). Right \(C\)-comodules, bicomodules, and homomorphisms between them are defined similarly.

An elementary but important example is \(C\) itself: with \(\rho_C:=\Delta:C\to C\otimes C\), it becomes both a left and a right comodule. Although the definition of a comodule may seem contrary to one’s usual intuition, working with comodules need not be more complicated than working with modules. For example, take \(\mathcal{V}=\Bbbk\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\), where \(\Bbbk\) is a commutative ring. Let \(M\) be a free \(\Bbbk\)-module with basis \((v_i)_{i\in I}\). Specifying \(\rho:M\to M\ensuremath{\underset{\Bbbk}{\otimes}}C\) is equivalent to specifying a family of elements \((t_{ij})_{(i,j)\in I^2}\) of \(C\) such that, for each \(i\in I\), \[\begin{equation*} \rho(v_i) = \sum_{j \in I} v_j \otimes t_{ji} \quad \text{(finite sum)}, \end{equation*}\] and the comodule conditions are expressed, for every \(i\), by \[\begin{equation*} v_i = \sum_j \epsilon(t_{ji}) v_j, \quad \sum_j v_j \otimes \Delta(t_{ji}) = \sum_{j, k} v_k \otimes t_{kj} \otimes t_{ji}. \end{equation*}\] Renaming the indices appropriately, these conditions simplify further, for all \(i,j\), to \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:comodule-matrix}{} \begin{aligned} \epsilon(t_{ji}) & = \delta_{j, i}, \\ \Delta(t_{ji}) & = \sum_k t_{jk} \otimes t_{ki}; \end{aligned} \end{equation}\] here \(\delta_{j,i}\) is the Kronecker delta, defined to be \(1\) when \(j=i\) and \(0\) otherwise. Continuing the preceding discussion, express a \(\Bbbk\)-linear map \(f:M\to M'\) between right comodules relative to the chosen bases as \(f(v_i)=\sum_jr_{ji}v'_j\), that is, as a matrix with \(r_{ji}\in\Bbbk\). A similar argument proves that \(f\) is a comodule homomorphism if and only if, for all \(i,k\), \[\begin{equation*} \begin{gathered} \sum_j r_{kj} t_{ji} = \sum_j r_{ji} t'_{kj}, \end{gathered} \end{equation*}\] where \(\Bbbk\) acts on \(C\) from the left by scalar multiplication. The version for left comodules is, of course, similar. We shall continue the discussion of several aspects of comodule theory in §reference.

Remark. If \((C,\Delta,\epsilon)\) is a coalgebra over \(\mathcal{V}\) and \((A,\mu,\eta)\) is an algebra over \(\mathcal{V}\), then \(\operatorname{Hom}(C,A)\) is equipped with a binary operation \(\star\), called convolution, as follows: \[f \star g := \mu (f \otimes g) \Delta, \quad f, g \in \operatorname{Hom}(C, A).\] The properties of \(\Delta\) and \(\mu\) readily show that \(\star\) is associative, and the following commutative diagram suffices to show that \((\operatorname{Hom}(C,A),\star)\) is a monoid with unit \(\eta\epsilon\in\operatorname{Hom}(C,A)\): \[\text{Diagram chapter7-unit-092-d007}\] A standard argument shows that if \(\varphi:C'\to C\) is a coalgebra morphism and \(\psi:A\to A'\) an algebra morphism, then \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:convolution-functorial}{} \operatorname{Hom}(C, A) \to \operatorname{Hom}(C', A'), \quad f \mapsto \psi f \varphi \end{equation}\] is a homomorphism between the convolution monoids.

From now on, let \(\mathcal{V}\) be a braided monoidal category, and write its braiding in the usual form \[c(X, Y): X \otimes Y \to Y \otimes X.\] By §reference, the category of algebras \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Alg}}(\mathcal{V})\) (or the category of coalgebras \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Alg}}(\mathcal{V}^{\operatorname{op}})^{\operatorname{op}}\)) has a monoidal structure with unit \(\ensuremath{\bm{1}}\). We may therefore consider coalgebras in the category of algebras (or algebras in the category of coalgebras). A simple but interesting observation is that both lead to the same data \((A,\mu,\eta,\Delta,\epsilon)\), with \(A\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{V})\). The conditions required of the morphisms \(A\xrightarrow{\Delta}A\otimes A\xrightarrow{\mu}A\) and \(\ensuremath{\bm{1}}\xrightarrow{\eta}A\xrightarrow{\epsilon}\ensuremath{\bm{1}}\) in \(\mathcal{V}\) are:

  1. \((A,\mu,\eta)\) is an algebra;

  2. \((A,\Delta,\epsilon)\) is a coalgebra;

  3. the comultiplication \(\Delta:A\to A\otimes A\) and counit \(\epsilon:A\to\ensuremath{\bm{1}}\) are algebra morphisms;

  4. the multiplication \(\mu:A\otimes A\to A\) and unit \(\eta:\ensuremath{\bm{1}}\to A\) are coalgebra morphisms.

Once (i) and (ii) are assumed, (iii) and (iv) are equivalent, so it is enough to check either one. Both state the compatibility of \((\Delta,\epsilon)\) and \((\mu,\eta)\) through four commutative diagrams, one for each possible pair; in formulas, \[\begin{equation*} \begin{gathered} \Delta \mu = (\mu \otimes \mu)(\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_A \otimes c(A, A) \otimes \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_A) (\Delta \otimes \Delta), \\ \Delta \eta = \eta \otimes \eta, \quad \epsilon \mu = \epsilon \otimes \epsilon, \quad \epsilon \eta = \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{\ensuremath{\bm{1}}}. \end{gathered} \end{equation*}\]

Definition (Bialgebra). Let \(\mathcal{V}\) be a braided monoidal category. If \(A\) is an algebra in the category of coalgebras over \(\mathcal{V}\), or equivalently a coalgebra in the category of algebras over \(\mathcal{V}\), then \(A\) is called a bialgebra over \(\mathcal{V}\). Concretely, a bialgebra consists of the data \((A,\mu,\eta,\Delta,\epsilon)\).

If \(A\) and \(A'\) are both bialgebras and \(\phi:A\to A'\) is simultaneously an algebra morphism and a coalgebra morphism, then \(\phi\) is called a morphism from the bialgebra \(A\) to the bialgebra \(A'\).

The full data of a bialgebra are often abbreviated simply as \(A\). If \(\Bbbk\) is a commutative ring and \(\mathcal{V}=\Bbbk\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\), then algebras, coalgebras, and bialgebras over \(\mathcal{V}\) are also called \(\Bbbk\)-algebras, \(\Bbbk\)-coalgebras, and \(\Bbbk\)-bialgebras, respectively, and so forth.

Example. Let \(M\) be a monoid and \(\Bbbk\) a commutative ring. Form the monoid algebra \(\Bbbk[M]\) over \(\Bbbk\); see [Li1]. Define the \(\Bbbk\)-module homomorphism \[\begin{align*} \Delta: \Bbbk[M] & \to \Bbbk[M] \ensuremath{\underset{\Bbbk}{\otimes}} \Bbbk[M] \\ m & \mapsto m \otimes m, \quad m \in M \end{align*}\] and \(\epsilon:\Bbbk[M]\to\Bbbk\) by mapping every \(m\in M\) to \(1\). Let us verify that these data give a \(\Bbbk\)-bialgebra.

First, \((\Bbbk[M],\Delta,\epsilon)\) is a coalgebra, since for every \(m\in M\), \[\begin{gather*} (\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}\otimes \epsilon)(\Delta(m)) = m = (\epsilon \otimes \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}})(\Delta(m)), \\ (\Delta \otimes \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}})(\Delta(m)) = m \otimes m \otimes m = (\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}\otimes \Delta)(\Delta(m)). \end{gather*}\] Note that \(\Bbbk[M]\) is always cocommutative, whereas \(\Bbbk[M]\) is commutative if and only if \(M\) is commutative.

Second, check that \(\epsilon\) and \(\Delta\) are both homomorphisms of \(\Bbbk\)-algebras. It is enough to verify, for every \(m,m'\in M\), that \[\begin{gather*} \epsilon(mm') = 1 = \epsilon(m)\epsilon(m'), \quad \epsilon(1) = 1, \\ \Delta(mm') = mm' \otimes mm' = (m \otimes m)(m' \otimes m') = \Delta(m) \Delta(m'), \\ \Delta(1) = 1 \otimes 1. \end{gather*}\]

For an algebra \(A\) over \(\mathcal{V}\), Definition reference describes left \(A\)-modules. If \(A\) is a bialgebra, we can go further as follows.

  1. On the unit object \(\ensuremath{\bm{1}}\), define a left \(A\)-module structure by taking \(\mu_{\ensuremath{\bm{1}}}:A\otimes\ensuremath{\bm{1}}\to\ensuremath{\bm{1}}\) to be the composite \(A\otimes\ensuremath{\bm{1}}\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}A\xrightarrow{\epsilon}\ensuremath{\bm{1}}\).

  2. For left \(A\)-modules \(M_i\), denote the corresponding scalar multiplication morphisms by \(\mu_i\) (\(i=1,2\)). Define the morphism \(\mu_{M_1\otimes M_2}:A\otimes(M_1\otimes M_2)\to M_1\otimes M_2\) to be the composite \[\begin{multline*} A \otimes M_1 \otimes M_2 \xrightarrow{\Delta \otimes \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{M_1 \otimes M_2}} A \otimes A \otimes M_1 \otimes M_2 \\ \xrightarrow{\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_A \otimes c(A, M_1) \otimes \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{M_2}} A \otimes M_1 \otimes A \otimes M_2 \xrightarrow{\mu_1 \otimes \mu_2} M_1 \otimes M_2. \end{multline*}\] Here, to simplify notation, parentheses in \(\otimes\) operations and the associativity constraints have been suppressed; in other words, \(\mathcal{V}\) is treated as a strict monoidal category.

These definitions are intended to give the objects \(\ensuremath{\bm{1}}\) and \(M_1\otimes M_2\) of \(\mathcal{V}\) left \(A\)-module structures. The case of right \(A\)-modules is, of course, similar.

Proposition. Let \(A\) be a bialgebra over a braided monoidal category \(\mathcal{V}\).
