The definitions above make the category of left \(A\)-modules \(A\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\) a monoidal category with unit \((\ensuremath{\bm{1}},\mu_{\ensuremath{\bm{1}}})\). The same holds for the category of right \(A\)-modules \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}\text{-}}A\).

Dually, the multiplication and unit of \(A\) make the category of left \(A\)-comodules \(A\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Comod}}\) and the category of right \(A\)-comodules \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Comod}\text{-}}A\) into monoidal categories.

For all four categories above, the forgetful functor to \(\mathcal{V}\) is always a monoidal functor.

Proof. By duality, it is enough to prove the first assertion. The verification is lengthy but straightforward; we outline it. First, one must check that scalar multiplication satisfies the commutative diagrams in Definition reference. For \((\ensuremath{\bm{1}},\mu_{\ensuremath{\bm{1}}})\), these properties follow from the fact that \(\epsilon:A\to\ensuremath{\bm{1}}\) is an algebra morphism. For the module structure on \(M_1\otimes M_2\), the diagram for scalar multiplication by the unit follows from the fact that \(\Delta:A\to A\otimes A\) is an algebra morphism, in particular from its compatibility with \(\eta\) and \(\eta\otimes\eta\).

For associativity of scalar multiplication, after expanding the definition, the issue is to prove that two maps from \(A\otimes A\otimes M_1\otimes M_2\) to \(M_1\otimes M_2\) are equal:

  1. first apply \(\Delta\otimes\Delta\otimes\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{M_1}\otimes\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{M_2}\), then, taking the braiding into account, successively let the first and third (or second and fourth) copies of \(A\) in \(A\otimes A\otimes(A\otimes A\otimes M_1\otimes M_2)\) act from the left on \(M_1\) (or \(M_2\));

  2. first apply \(\mu:A\otimes A\to A\) in the first two positions, then apply \(\mu_{M_1\otimes M_2}\). Since \[\Delta\mu = (\mu \otimes \mu) (\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}\otimes c(A, A) \otimes \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}})(\Delta \otimes \Delta),\] this map is the composite \[\begin{multline*} A \otimes A \otimes M_1 \otimes M_2 \xrightarrow{\Delta \otimes \Delta \otimes \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{M_1} \otimes \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{M_2}} A \otimes A \otimes A \otimes A \otimes M_1 \otimes M_2 \\ \xrightarrow{\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_A \otimes c(A, A) \otimes \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_A \otimes \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{M_1} \otimes \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{M_2}} \boxed{A \otimes A \otimes A \otimes A} \otimes M_1 \otimes M_2 \\ \xrightarrow{\mu \otimes \mu \otimes \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{M_1} \otimes \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{M_2}} A \otimes A \otimes M_1 \otimes M_2 \\ \xrightarrow{\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_A \otimes c(A, M_1) \otimes \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{M_2}} A \otimes M_1 \otimes A \otimes M_2 \xrightarrow{\mu_1 \otimes \mu_2} M_1 \otimes M_2. \end{multline*}\] The scalar multiplications \(\mu_1\) and \(\mu_2\) are each associative and \(c\) is functorial. Thus, taking the braiding into account, the last three arrows in this composite may also be regarded as first letting the first and second (or third and fourth) copies of \(A\) in the boxed part act successively from the left on \(M_1\) (or \(M_2\)).

Braid diagrams help explain this, as at the end of [Li1]. To prove that (a) equals (b), it is enough to verify the following equality1

Diagram chapter7-unit-092-d008

=

Diagram chapter7-unit-092-d009

which is immediately apparent.

To show that \(A\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\) is a monoidal category, one must still prove that the associativity and unit constraints for \(\otimes\) are all morphisms of left \(A\)-modules. The first assertion is straightforward. The second requires the coalgebra property \((\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}\otimes\epsilon)\Delta=\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_A= (\epsilon\otimes\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}})\Delta\), after identifying \(A\otimes\ensuremath{\bm{1}}\simeq A\simeq\ensuremath{\bm{1}}\otimes A\).

  1. There is one harmless minor difference: in the cited reference, morphisms are composed from bottom to top, whereas here they are composed in the opposite direction.↩︎

For a bialgebra \(A\), one can still ask whether the monoidal category \(A\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\) has a braiding and whether that braiding is symmetric. A natural first idea is to use the braiding \(c(M_1,M_2)\) of \(\mathcal{V}\), but in general this is not a morphism in \(A\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\). Even in the special case \(\mathcal{V}=\Bbbk\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\), the answer already involves the concept of a quasitriangular bialgebra, which cannot be explained briefly. We give only the following example, which is so simple as to be somewhat misleading.

Proposition. Let \(\mathcal{V}\) be a symmetric monoidal category.

  1. If \(A\) is a cocommutative bialgebra over \(\mathcal{V}\), then the monoidal categories \(A\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\) and \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}\text{-}}A\) become symmetric monoidal categories with respect to \(c(M_1,M_2):M_1\otimes M_2\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}M_2\otimes M_1\).

  2. Dually, if \(A\) is a commutative bialgebra over \(\mathcal{V}\), then \(A\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Comod}}\) and \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Comod}\text{-}}A\) are symmetric monoidal categories.

Proof. It is enough to treat the cocommutative case. Using the preceding notation, the assertion that \(c(M_1,M_2)\) is a morphism in \(A\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\) is equivalent to proving that the outer boundary of the following diagram commutes: \[\text{Diagram chapter7-unit-093-d001}\]

The square on the left commutes because \(A\) is cocommutative, while the square on the right commutes by functoriality of \(c\). Drawing the braid diagram shows that \[\begin{multline*} c(A \otimes M_1, A \otimes M_2) = \\ (\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_A \otimes c(A, M_2) \otimes \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{M_1}) (c(A, A) \otimes c(M_1, M_2)) (\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_A \otimes c(A, M_1) \otimes \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{M_2}), \end{multline*}\] and since \(\mathcal{V}\) is a symmetric monoidal category, the middle square also commutes. All other properties of the symmetric monoidal structure on \(A\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\) reduce to verifications in \(\mathcal{V}\).

We now introduce the concept of a Hopf algebra. Let \(\mathcal{V}\) be a braided monoidal category.

Definition. Let the data \((A,\mu,\eta,\Delta,\epsilon)\) form a bialgebra \(A\) over \(\mathcal{V}\). If an isomorphism \(S:A\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}A\) in \(\mathcal{V}\) makes the following diagram commute, \[\text{Diagram chapter7-unit-093-d002}\] that is, \[\mu (\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_A \otimes S) \Delta = \eta\epsilon = \mu (S \otimes \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_A) \Delta,\] then \(S\) is called an antipode of \(A\). A bialgebra equipped with an antipode is called a Hopf algebra. Morphisms between Hopf algebras are defined to be morphisms between their underlying bialgebras.

For example, \(\ensuremath{\bm{1}}\) is a Hopf algebra with antipode \(\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{\ensuremath{\bm{1}}}\). Interpreted using the convolution in Remark reference, an antipode \(S\) is precisely a two-sided inverse of \(\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_A\in\operatorname{End}(A)\) with respect to \(\star\). The antipode in the definition of a Hopf algebra, if it exists, is unique. This follows immediately by applying the next result to \(f=\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_A\); the result also shows that morphisms always preserve antipodes.

Proposition. Let \(A\) and \(A'\) be Hopf algebras over \(\mathcal{V}\) with antipodes \(S\) and \(S'\), respectively. For every Hopf algebra morphism \(f:A\to A'\), one has \(S'f=fS\).

Proof. By the functoriality of convolution \(\star\) in equation, both maps \[\text{Diagram chapter7-unit-093-d003}, \quad \text{Diagram chapter7-unit-093-d004}\] are homomorphisms of convolution monoids. Thus \(S'f\) and \(fS\) are both convolution inverses of \(f\in\operatorname{Hom}(A,A')\).

Because the braiding on \(\mathcal{V}\) gives a braiding on \(\mathcal{V}^{\operatorname{op}}\), the concept of a bialgebra is plainly self-dual. The next result shows that the definition of an antipode is self-dual as well.

Proposition. If \((A,\mu,\eta,\Delta,\epsilon)\) is a bialgebra over \(\mathcal{V}\), then \((A,\eta,\mu,\epsilon,\Delta)\) is a bialgebra over \(\mathcal{V}^{\operatorname{op}}\). If the Hopf algebra \((A,\mu,\eta,\Delta,\epsilon)\) has antipode \(S\), then \(S^{-1}\) is an antipode of \((A,\eta,\mu,\epsilon,\Delta)\) as a bialgebra over \(\mathcal{V}^{\operatorname{op}}\); in particular, the latter object is a Hopf algebra over \(\mathcal{V}^{\operatorname{op}}\).

Proof. The diagram in Definition reference is self-dual, but the direction of \(S\) is reversed.

Proposition. For a bialgebra \(A\), in accordance with Definition reference,

  • reversing the multiplication of \(A\) using the braiding \(c(A,A)\) produces an algebra \(A^{\mathrm{op}}\);

  • reversing the comultiplication of \(A\) using \(c(A,A)^{-1}\) produces a coalgebra \(A_{\mathrm{cop}}\).

Together, these two operations produce a bialgebra \(A^{\mathrm{op}}_{\mathrm{cop}}\). If \(A\) has an antipode \(S\), then \(S\) is also an antipode of \(A^{\mathrm{op}}_{\mathrm{cop}}\), and in this case \(S:A\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}A^{\mathrm{op}}_{\mathrm{cop}}\) is an isomorphism of bialgebras.

Proof. A routine verification shows that \(A^{\mathrm{op}}_{\mathrm{cop}}\) is indeed a bialgebra with antipode \(S\); we omit the details. The remaining assertion has two parts. First, \(S\) preserves the unit and counit. This is easy: in Proposition reference, take \(A=\ensuremath{\bm{1}}\) and \(A'=\ensuremath{\bm{1}}\), respectively.

Second, \(S\) preserves the multiplication and comultiplication. The proof in general is more involved; see [JS91] or [AM10]. Here we only sketch the special case \(\mathcal{V}=\Bbbk\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\), \(\otimes=\otimes_{\Bbbk}\) with its standard braiding. This is the only case that will be needed later.

Recall from §reference that \(A\otimes A\) is naturally a coalgebra. Equip \(\operatorname{Hom}(A\otimes A,A)\) with the convolution from Remark reference, denoted by \(\ast\), and consider the elements \[f := \mu, \quad g := \mu c(A, A) (S \otimes S), \quad h := S \mu.\] It is enough to prove that \(h\ast f=\eta_A\epsilon_{A\otimes A}=f\ast g\). This equality will show that \(f\) is invertible in the monoid \((\operatorname{Hom}(A\otimes A,A),\ast)\), and hence that \(h=g\). Let \(a,b\in A\) and write the expansions \[\begin{gather*} \Delta(a) = \sum_i a_i^{(1)} \otimes a_i^{(2)}, \quad \Delta(b) = \sum_j b_j^{(1)} \otimes b_j^{(2)}. \end{gather*}\] Write \(\mu\) simply as multiplication. From the standard braiding on \(\Bbbk\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\), one obtains \[\begin{align*} (h \ast f)(a \otimes b) & = \sum_{i, j} h\left(a^{(1)}_i \otimes b^{(1)}_j\right) f\left(a^{(2)}_i \otimes b^{(2)}_j\right) \\ & = \sum_{i, j} S\left( a^{(1)}_i b^{(1)}_j \right) a^{(2)}_i b^{(2)}_j \\ & = (\underbracket{S \star \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_A}_{\text{convolution on }\operatorname{End}(A)})(ab) = \eta_A \epsilon_A (ab), \\ (f \ast g)(a \otimes b) & = \cdots = \sum_{i, j} a^{(1)}_i b^{(1)}_j S\left( b^{(2)}_j \right) S\left( a^{(2)}_i \right) \\ & = \sum_i a^{(1)}_i \eta_A \epsilon_A(b) S\left( a^{(2)}_i \right) \\ & = \eta_A \epsilon_A (a) \cdot \eta_A \epsilon_A (b) = \eta_A \epsilon_A(ab), \\ \eta_A \epsilon_{A \otimes A}(a \otimes b) & = \eta_A\left( \epsilon_A(a)\epsilon_A(b) \right) = \eta_A \epsilon_A(ab), \end{align*}\] as claimed. Thus \(S\) preserves the multiplication of the bialgebra. A similar argument shows that \(S\) preserves the comultiplication.

In particular, if \(\mathcal{V}\) is a symmetric monoidal category, then \(S^2\) is an automorphism of \(A\).

Corollary. Let the Hopf algebra \(A\) have antipode \(S\). If \(A\) is commutative or cocommutative, then \(S^2=\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}\).

Proof. With respect to the convolution \(\star\) on \(\operatorname{End}(A)\) (Remark reference), we have \[S \star S^2 = \mu (S \otimes S^2) \Delta = \mu (S \otimes S)(\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}\otimes S) \Delta.\]

If \(A\) is commutative, then \(\mu c(A,A)=\mu\), and Proposition reference transforms the right-hand side above into \[\mu c(A, A) (S \otimes S) (\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}\otimes S)\Delta = S\mu (\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}\otimes S)\Delta = S(\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}\star S).\] The definition of an antipode says that \(\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}\star S=\eta\epsilon\), while the same proposition gives \(S\eta=\eta\); the result is \(\eta\epsilon\).

If \(A\) is cocommutative, then \(c(A,A)\Delta=\Delta\), and functoriality of the braiding transforms \(S\star S^2\) into \[\mu (S \otimes S)(\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}\otimes S) c(A, A) \Delta = \mu c(A, A) (S \otimes S)(S \otimes \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}})\Delta,\] which the same argument then transforms into \(S(S\star\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}})=\eta\epsilon\).

Thus \(S^2\) is a convolution inverse of \(S\), so \(S^2=\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}\).

All the following examples take \(\mathcal{V}=\Bbbk\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\) and \(\otimes=\otimes_{\Bbbk}\), where \(\Bbbk\) is a commutative ring.

Example. Let \(G\) be a group. Form the group \(\Bbbk\)-algebra \(\Bbbk[G]\). Example reference gives \(\Bbbk[G]\) a bialgebra structure. Define the \(\Bbbk\)-module automorphism \(S:\Bbbk[G]\to\Bbbk[G]\) by \[S(g) = g^{-1}, \quad g \in G.\] It is easy to verify that \(S\) satisfies the commutative diagram required of an antipode. Thus \(\Bbbk[G]\) is a Hopf algebra.

Example (H. Hopf). Write \(\{\mathrm{pt}\}\) for a one-point set. Let a topological space \(X\) be equipped with continuous maps \(m:X\times X\to X\) (multiplication) and \(e:\{\mathrm{pt}\}\to X\) (equivalently, a choice of an element of \(X\), the unit, also denoted by \(e\)), such that the two maps satisfy, up to homotopy, the properties required for associativity of multiplication and for a unit. Then \((X,m,e)\) is called an H-space. If a continuous map \(i:X\to X\) (taking inverses) is also chosen and satisfies, up to homotopy, the properties required of inverses, then \((X,m,e,i)\) is called an H-group.

A topological monoid (or topological group) is of course an H-space (or H-group), but the H-space and H-group conditions are much weaker. A natural example is a loop space. For a topological space \(M\) with a chosen base point \(x_0\in M\), a continuous map \(\gamma:[0,1]\to M\) satisfying \(\gamma(0)=x_0=\gamma(1)\) is called a loop in \(M\). All loops naturally form a topological space \(\Omega(M,x_0)\). If \(m\) is taken to be end-to-start concatenation of two loops, \(e\) the constant map at \(x_0\), and \(i\) reversal of the direction of a loop, then intuitively \(\Omega(M,x_0)\) forms an H-group. The key point is that associativity and the inverse properties hold only up to homotopy.

Next, consider the full subcategory \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{S}}\) of \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Top}}\) consisting of all CW complexes1; it contains spaces commonly encountered in geometry, such as manifolds. Let \(\Bbbk\) be a field. The cohomology functor with coefficients in \(\Bbbk\), namely \(\operatorname{H}^\bullet\), is a functor from \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{S}}^{\operatorname{op}}\) to the category of graded \(\Bbbk\)-vector spaces \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Vect}}(\Bbbk)^{\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}_{\geq0}}\). Equip \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Vect}}(\Bbbk)^{\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}_{\geq0}}\) with the braiding determined by the Koszul sign rule equation (in the notation there, take \(\epsilon(a)=a\bmod\;2\)). The cup product \(\mu:=\cup\) on cohomology makes the functor \(\operatorname{H}^\bullet\) factor through \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{CAlg}}\left(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Vect}}(\Bbbk)^{\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}_{\geq0}}\right)\); in short, cohomology is a commutative algebra over \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Vect}}(\Bbbk)^{\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}_{\geq0}}\).

On the other hand, give \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{S}}\) the monoidal structure determined by the product of spaces, with \(\{\mathrm{pt}\}\) as unit. The Künneth formula in topology shows that \(\operatorname{H}^\bullet\) is a monoidal functor. Moreover, homotopic maps induce the same map on cohomology. Consequently, if \(X\in\operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{S}})\) is an H-space, then \(\operatorname{H}^\bullet(X)\) is also a coalgebra over \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Vect}}(\Bbbk)^{\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}_{\geq0}}\).

Readers familiar with algebraic topology will readily conclude that the algebra and coalgebra structures on \(\operatorname{H}^\bullet(X)\) are compatible and hence give a bialgebra over \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Vect}}(\Bbbk)^{\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}_{\geq0}}\). If, in addition, \(X\) is an H-group and the automorphism induced by the map \(i\) is denoted by \(S\in\operatorname{Aut}(\operatorname{H}^\bullet(X))\), then \(\operatorname{H}^\bullet(X)\) becomes a Hopf algebra.

In fact, the multiplication (cup product) on \(\operatorname{H}^\bullet(X)\) is precisely the image of the diagonal embedding \(\mathrm{diag}:X\to X\times X\) under the Künneth formula, while its unit is the image of \(X\to\{\mathrm{pt}\}\). Thus all the properties required of the bialgebra and antipode can be verified at the level of topological spaces, up to homotopy. For example, the antipode identity \(\mu(S\otimes\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}})\Delta=\eta\epsilon\) comes from \[\left[ X \xrightarrow{\mathrm{diag}} X \times X \xrightarrow{(i, \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}})} X \times X \xrightarrow{m} X\right] \;\text{being homotopy equivalent to}\; \left[ X \to \{\mathrm{pt}\} \xrightarrow{e} X \right].\]

Thus the cohomology of an H-group is naturally a commutative Hopf algebra with a rich structure. This was Hopf’s original motivation for studying such algebras.

The exercises will provide more examples of Hopf algebras. Most are commutative or cocommutative, but there are also many Hopf algebras having neither property. The most important class among them is that of quantum groups. The relevant discussion requires a foundation in Lie theory and is not treated in this book.

  1. This is a topological term, somewhat different from the complexes defined in linear algebra.↩︎

Beck’s Monadicity Theorem

Let \(\mathcal{C}\) be a category. Consider the functor category \(\mathcal{C}^{\mathcal{C}}\), whose objects are all endofunctors \(T:\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{C}\) and whose morphisms are morphisms between endofunctors. This category is naturally monoidal: the multiplication \(\otimes\) is composition of functors, and the unit object \(\ensuremath{\bm{1}}\) is the identity functor. Since composition of functors is strictly associative, this is also a strict monoidal category.

Definition (Monad and comonad). Let \(\mathcal{C}\) be a category. An algebra in the monoidal category \(\mathcal{C}^{\mathcal{C}}\) (Definition reference) is called a monad on \(\mathcal{C}\). Dually, a monad on \(\mathcal{C}^{\operatorname{op}}\) is called a comonad on \(\mathcal{C}\).

Expanding Definition reference in the category of endofunctors \(\mathcal{C}^{\mathcal{C}}\), we find that a monad is data \((T,\mu,\eta)\), where \(T:\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{C}\) is a functor and \(\mu:T^2\to T\) and \(\eta:\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{\mathcal{C}}\to T\) are morphisms such that the following diagrams commute: \[\begin{equation*} \begin{gathered} \text{Diagram chapter7-unit-094-d001} \quad \text{Diagram chapter7-unit-094-d002} \end{gathered} \end{equation*}\] Compared with the original definition, associativity constraints are no longer needed here, while \(\eta\otimes\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}\) (or \(\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}\otimes\eta\)) becomes \(\eta T\) (or \(T\eta\)), and so on. Dually, a comonad \((L,\delta,\epsilon)\) consists of a functor \(L:\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{C}\) and morphisms \(\delta:L\to L^2\) and \(\epsilon:L\to\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{\mathcal{C}}\), subject to the commutativity of the following diagrams. \[\begin{equation*} \begin{gathered} \text{Diagram chapter7-unit-094-d003} \quad \text{Diagram chapter7-unit-094-d004} \end{gathered} \end{equation*}\] The data \((T,\mu,\eta)\) (or \((L,\delta,\epsilon)\)) are customarily abbreviated simply as \(T\) (or \(L\)). The principal source of monads and comonads is adjoint pairs.

Example (An adjoint pair determines a monad). Consider a pair of adjoint functors \[\text{Diagram chapter7-unit-094-d005}\] with the corresponding unit \(\eta:\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{\mathcal{C}}\to GF\) and counit \(\varepsilon:FG\to\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{\mathcal{D}}\). Define a monad \((T,\mu,\eta)\) on \(\mathcal{C}\) and a comonad \((L,\delta,\varepsilon)\) on \(\mathcal{D}\) as follows. \[\begin{array}{|c|c|}\hline T := GF & L := FG \\ \mu := \left[ GFGF \xrightarrow{G\varepsilon F} GF \right] & \delta := \left[ FG \xrightarrow{F\eta G} FGFG \right] \\ \eta : \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{\mathcal{C}} \to GF & \varepsilon: FG \to \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{\mathcal{D}} \\ \hline \end{array}\]

By duality, it is enough to check the monad axioms in the case \((T,\mu,\eta)\). First, the unit diagram is \[\text{Diagram chapter7-unit-094-d006}\] which commutes by the triangle identities \((G\varepsilon)(\eta G)=\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_G\) and \((\varepsilon F)(F\eta)=\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_F\). The associativity diagram is \[\text{Diagram chapter7-unit-094-d007}\] and it commutes: both composites are depicted by \[\text{Diagram chapter7-unit-094-d008}\] with only the order of composition of the two curved regions differing; the result is the same. This is a special case of the interchange law for vertical and horizontal composition of morphisms [Li1].

Since endofunctors act on \(\mathcal{C}\), we wish to discuss “modules” in \(\mathcal{C}\) under the action of a monad \(T\). For historical reasons, such a structure is also called a \(T\)-algebra.

Definition (S. Eilenberg, J. C. Moore). Let \((T,\mu,\eta)\) be a monad on \(\mathcal{C}\). A \(T\)-module is data \((M,a)\), where \(M\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{C})\) and \(a\) is a morphism \(T(M)\to M\) in \(\mathcal{C}\), such that the following diagrams commute: \[\text{Diagram chapter7-unit-094-d009} \quad \text{Diagram chapter7-unit-094-d010}\]

All \(T\)-modules form a category \(\mathcal{C}^T\). A morphism from \((M,a)\) to \((M',a')\) is defined to be a morphism \(f:M\to M'\) in \(\mathcal{C}\) that makes the following diagram commute: \[\text{Diagram chapter7-unit-094-d011}\]

Dually, let \((L,\delta,\epsilon)\) be a comonad on \(\mathcal{C}\). An \(L\)-comodule is data \((N,b)\), where \(b:N\to L(N)\) is a morphism, subject to the commutative diagrams dual to those above. The category of \(L\)-comodules is denoted by \(\mathcal{C}^L\).

The two commutative diagrams for a \(T\)-module should be viewed as the associativity and unit laws for the action of \(T\), respectively. The examples and properties below are stated mainly for monads and modules over them; the versions for comonads and comodules are entirely dual.

Example. Write \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Mon}}\) for the category of monoids, conventionally taken to be realized on small sets, and consider the adjoint pair \[\text{Diagram chapter7-unit-094-d012}\] where \(\mathbf{M}\) maps a set \(X\) to the free monoid \(\mathbf{M}(X)\), whose definition and construction are given in [Li1], and \(U\) is the forgetful functor. Thus, \[T := U\mathbf{M}: \ensuremath{\mathsf{Set}} \to \ensuremath{\mathsf{Set}}, \quad T(X) = \bigsqcup_{n \geq 0} X^n.\] In other words, an element of \(T(X)\) is a “word” \((x_1,\ldots,x_n)\) with \(n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}_{\geq0}\). The unit of the adjoint pair \(\eta_X:X\to U\mathbf{M}(X)\) maps \(x\in X\) to the word of length \(1\), \((x)\). For a monoid \(A\), the counit \(\varepsilon_A:\mathbf{M}U(A)\to A\) maps the word \((a_1,\ldots,a_n)\) to the product \(a_1\cdots a_n\in A\). Since multiplication in \(\mathbf{M}(X)\) is concatenation of words, the map \(\mu_X=U\varepsilon\mathbf{M}:T^2(X)\to T(X)\) corresponding to the monad \(T\) (or, viewed as a map \(\mathbf{M}(\mathbf{M}(X))\to\mathbf{M}(X)\)) flattens a “word of words,” that is, it concatenates a sequence of lists, as in \[\left( (x_1, \ldots, x_n), (y_1, \ldots, y_m), \ldots \right) \mapsto \left( x_1, \ldots, x_n, y_1, \ldots, y_m, \ldots \right).\]

Specifying a \(T\)-module \((M,a)\) for \(T=U\mathbf{M}\) is equivalent to specifying \(m_1\cdots m_n:=a(m_1,\ldots,m_n)\) for every word \((m_1,\ldots,m_n)\) in the set \(M\), such that \(a(m)=m\) and the associativity law \[a\left( a(x_1, \ldots, x_n), a(y_1, \ldots, y_m), \ldots \right) = a\left( x_1, \ldots, x_n, y_1, \ldots, y_m, \ldots \right)\] holds. In short, a \(T\)-module is precisely a monoid, with the image under \(a\) of the empty word (\(n=0\)) as its unit. It is easy to check that morphisms of \(T\)-modules are precisely monoid homomorphisms.

The case of the category of groups \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Grp}}\) is entirely similar; the key is to replace \(\mathbf{M}\) by the free-group functor \(\mathbf{F}\). The corresponding \(T\)-modules are precisely groups.

Example. Let \(R\) be a ring and consider the adjoint pair \[\text{Diagram chapter7-unit-094-d013}\] where \(\mathbf{F}\) maps \(X\) to the free left \(R\)-module \(R^{\oplus X}\) and \(U\) is the forgetful functor. This gives a monad \((T,\mu,\eta)\) on \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Set}}\). As in Example reference, \(T=U\mathbf{F}\) maps a set \(X\) to \(R^{\oplus X}\) regarded as a set; its elements are finite formal \(R\)-linear combinations of elements of \(X\), \(\text{“} r_1x_1+\cdots+r_nx_n \text{”}\). The unit \(\eta_X\) maps \(x\in X\) to \(\text{“}x\text{”}\), while \(\mu_X:R^{\oplus(R^{\oplus}X)}\to R^{\oplus X}\) flattens a two-level linear combination, namely, \[\begin{multline*} \text{“} \alpha (\text{“} r_1 x_1 + \cdots + r_n x_n \text{”}) + \beta (\text{“} s_1 y_1 + \cdots + s_m y_m \text{”}) + \cdots \text{”} \\ \mapsto \text{“} (\alpha r_1) x_1 + \cdots + (\alpha r_n) x_n + (\beta s_1) y_1 + \cdots + (\beta s_m) y_m + \cdots \text{”} . \end{multline*}\] Specifying a \(T\)-module \((M,a)\) is equivalent to specifying a set \(M\) together with a rule that maps formal linear combinations to elements of \(M\), maps \(\text{“}x\text{”}\) to \(x\), is associative with respect to addition and scalar multiplication, and makes scalar multiplication by \(1\in R\) the identity map. In short, \(T\)-modules are precisely left \(R\)-modules. It is clear that morphisms of \(T\)-modules are precisely module homomorphisms.

Return to the general theory. There is a forgetful functor \(U^T:\mathcal{C}^T\to\mathcal{C}\) mapping an object \((M,a)\) to \(M\). We now give its left adjoint: the free construction.

Definition–Proposition (Free \(T\)-module). Let \((T,\mu,\eta)\) be a monad on \(\mathcal{C}\). Define a functor \[\mathrm{Free}^T: \mathcal{C} \to \mathcal{C}^T , \quad \begin{array}{rl} (\text{object } M) & \mapsto (TM, \mu_M: T^2 M \to TM), \\ (\text{morphism } f: M \to M') & \mapsto Tf: TM \to TM'. \end{array}\] This gives an adjoint pair \[\text{Diagram chapter7-unit-094-d014}\] and the monad on \(\mathcal{C}\) determined by this adjoint pair is precisely \((T,\mu,\eta)\).

Proof. To check that \((TM,\mu_M)\) is a \(T\)-module, one must show that the following two diagrams commute: \[\text{Diagram chapter7-unit-094-d015} \quad \text{Diagram chapter7-unit-094-d016}\] But these diagrams are obtained by evaluating the functor diagrams in Definition reference at the object \(M\). Functoriality is clear.

Next, note that \(U^T\mathrm{Free}^T=T\). Take \(\eta:\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{\mathcal{C}}\to T\) from the data of \(T\), and define \[\epsilon: \mathrm{Free}^T U^T \to \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{\mathcal{C}^T}, \quad \epsilon_{(M, a)}: (TM, \mu_M) \xrightarrow{a} (M, a) \in \operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{C}^T).\] The left diagram in Definition reference shows that \(\epsilon_{(M,a)}\) is a morphism in \(\mathcal{C}^T\). Its functoriality is also clear.

A routine verification shows that \((\mathrm{Free}^T,U^T)\) is an adjoint pair with unit \(\eta\) and counit \(\epsilon\); we omit the details. Moreover, \[\begin{equation*} \begin{aligned} \left(U^T \epsilon \mathrm{Free}^T\right)_M & = U^T \epsilon_{(TM, \mu_M)} \\ & = \left[ \mu_M: T^2(M) \to T(M)\right], \end{aligned} \end{equation*}\] which shows that the monad on \(\mathcal{C}\) determined by the adjoint pair \((\mathrm{Free}^T,U^T)\) is \((T,\mu,\eta)\).

For the monads in Examples reference and reference, the functor \(\mathrm{Free}^T\) corresponds, respectively, to the constructions of the free monoid and the free module. Dually, a comonad \(L\) on a category \(\mathcal{D}\) also gives a free–forgetful adjoint pair; there is no need to discuss it further.

Lemma. Consider the monad \(T\) and comonad \(L\) arising from an adjoint pair \((F,G)\). Let \(N\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{D})\). The data \[M:=G(N)\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{C}), \quad a:T(M)=GFG(N)\xrightarrow{G\varepsilon_N}G(N)=M\] give \((M,a)\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{C}^T)\). We thereby obtain a functor \(\mathbb{K}:\mathcal{D}\to\mathcal{C}^T\) satisfying \(G=U^T\mathbb{K}\).

Dually, \(F\) also has a canonical factorization \(\mathcal{C}\xrightarrow{\mathbb{K}}\mathcal{D}^L\to\mathcal{D}\), which will henceforth be written \(F=U^L\mathbb{K}\), where \(U^L\) is the forgetful functor1.

Proof. It is enough to treat the case of \(T\). In this case, the two diagrams in Definition reference become \[\text{Diagram chapter7-unit-095-d001} \quad \text{Diagram chapter7-unit-095-d002}\] Their commutativity is verified exactly as in Example reference, so it need not be repeated; the functoriality of \(N\mapsto(M,a)\) is also immediate.

For a given adjoint pair \((F,G)\), applying a functor is a process that forgets structure. Lemma reference factors \(G\) (or \(F\)) as \(U^T\mathbb{K}\) (or \(U^L\mathbb{K}\)). We want to know whether structure is lost only at the second step, when the forgetful functor \(U^T\) is applied. If so, the information lost in the process can be reconstructed with the aid of the monad \(T\) (or comonad \(L\)). This consideration motivates the following concept.

Definition. Consider a pair of adjoint functors \(\text{Diagram chapter7-unit-095-diagram-003}\), which determines a monad \(T\) on \(\mathcal{C}\) and a comonad \(L\) on \(\mathcal{D}\).

  • If the functor \(\mathbb{K}:\mathcal{D}\to\mathcal{C}^T\) in Lemma reference is an equivalence of categories, the adjoint pair is called monadic.

  • If its dual version \(\mathbb{K}:\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{D}^L\) is an equivalence of categories, the adjoint pair is called comonadic.

For example, the free–forgetful adjoint pairs in Examples reference and reference are both monadic; a direct check even shows that \(\mathbb{K}\) is an isomorphism of categories in both examples. Beck’s theorem below, also called the monadicity theorem or the Barr–Beck theorem, characterizes monadicity. We need some preparation.

Definition–Proposition. Consider a diagram in a category \(\mathcal{C}\) \[\begin{equation*} \hypertarget{eqn:split-coeq}{}\text{Diagram chapter7-unit-095-d003} \end{equation*}\] such that the solid part commutes, that is, \(hu=hv\), and \(h\) and \(v\) have sections (that is, right inverses) \(s\) and \(t\), respectively, as indicated by the dashed arrows, with \(sh=ut\in\operatorname{End}(B)\). The solid part of a diagram with these properties is called a split fork. The diagram automatically gives a coequalizer of \(u\) and \(v\) in \(\mathcal{C}\).

Proof. Consider the following diagram: \[\text{Diagram chapter7-unit-095-d004} \qquad \begin{array}{ll} W \in \operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{C}) \\ ku = kv. \end{array}\] If there is a \(\varphi:Z\to W\) with \(\varphi h=k\), then \(\varphi=\varphi hs=ks\). Conversely, \(\varphi:=ks\) does satisfy \(\varphi h=ksh=kut=kvt=k\). This proves the required universal property.

Unlike coequalizers in general, split forks are “absolute”: their images under arbitrary functors are still split forks.

Example. Let \((T,\mu,\eta)\) be a monad on \(\mathcal{C}\). Every \((M,a)\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{C}^T)\) gives a split fork in \(\mathcal{C}\): \[\begin{equation*} \text{Diagram chapter7-unit-095-d005} \quad \begin{array}{ll} a (Ta) = a \mu_M , & \eta_M a = (Ta) \eta_{TM}, \\ a \eta_M = \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_M , & \mu_M \eta_{TM} = \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{TM}. \end{array} \end{equation*}\] The equalities on the right are part of Definitions reference and reference; for example, \(\eta_Ma=(Ta)\eta_{TM}\) follows from the naturality of \(\eta:\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{\mathcal{C}}\to T\). In particular, the diagram above realizes \(M\) as the coequalizer of \(Ta\) and \(\mu_M\).

Definition. Consider a functor \(G:\mathcal{D}\to\mathcal{C}\) and a pair of morphisms \(f,g:X\rightrightarrows Y\) in \(\mathcal{D}\). If there is a morphism \(h:G(Y)\to Z\) such that the diagram \[\begin{equation*} \text{Diagram chapter7-unit-095-d006} \end{equation*}\] is a split fork in \(\mathcal{C}\), then \((f,g)\) is called a \(G\)-split pair in \(\mathcal{D}\).

Let \((f,g)\) be a \(G\)-split pair. Since \((Gf,Gg)\) has a coequalizer, it is natural to ask whether that coequalizer can be lifted to a coequalizer of \((f,g)\) in \(\mathcal{D}\), and whether the lift is unique. A coequalizer is a special case of a \(\varinjlim\); the concepts of a functor creating or preserving \(\varinjlim\) in Definition reference provide the right terminology for this question. Note that the forgetful functor \(U^T:\mathcal{C}^T\to\mathcal{C}\) is conservative in the sense of Definition reference.

Lemma. Let \((T,\mu,\eta)\) be a monad on \(\mathcal{C}\). The functor \(U^T\) creates the coequalizer of every \(U^T\)-split pair.

Proof. Suppose we are given a pair of morphisms in \(\mathcal{C}^T\), \(u,v:(M,a)\rightrightarrows(M',a')\), and a split fork in \(\mathcal{C}\): \[\begin{equation*} \text{Diagram chapter7-unit-095-d007} \end{equation*}\] Since this diagram gives a coequalizer in \(\mathcal{C}\), it is enough to extend \(M''\) uniquely to an object \((M'',a'')\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{C}^T)\) such that \(h\) is a morphism in \(\mathcal{C}^T\), and then to show that this construction gives the coequalizer of \(u\) and \(v\) in \(\mathcal{C}^T\).

The image of a split fork under any functor remains a split fork. Hence, in the following diagram, whose solid part is commutative, \[\text{Diagram chapter7-unit-095-d008}\] both rows are coequalizers in \(\mathcal{C}\). The universal property therefore gives exactly one \(a''\) that makes the whole diagram commute. If \((M'',a'')\) is shown to be a \(T\)-algebra, then commutativity of the right-hand part of this diagram says precisely that \(h\) is a morphism in \(\mathcal{C}^T\).

For this, it remains to verify that the following two diagrams commute.2 \[\text{Diagram chapter7-unit-095-d009} \quad \text{Diagram chapter7-unit-095-d010}\] The coequalizer diagrams show that \(h\) and \(Th\) are epimorphisms (as is \(T^2h\)). The commutativity of the two diagrams above therefore follows immediately from that of the corresponding diagrams for \(M\) and \(M'\).

Finally, we show that \(h\) gives the coequalizer of \(u\) and \(v\) in \(\mathcal{C}^T\). Suppose there is a morphism in \(\mathcal{C}^T\) \(k:(M',a')\to(W,b)\) with \(ku=kv\).3 In \(\mathcal{C}\), there is a unique morphism \(\varphi:M''\to W\) with \(\varphi h=k\). It remains to prove that \(\varphi\) is actually a morphism in \(\mathcal{C}^T\). Consider the diagram \[\text{Diagram chapter7-unit-095-d011}\] The composites of the top and bottom rows are \(Tk\) and \(k\), respectively. Since \(h\) and \(k\) are morphisms in \(\mathcal{C}^T\), the outer boundary and the left square commute. Thus the right square commutes after composition with \(Th\). Since \(Th\) is an epimorphism, the right square itself commutes. This shows that \(\varphi\) is a morphism in \(\mathcal{C}^T\).

Lemma. Let \(G:\mathcal{D}\to\mathcal{C}\) be a functor with left adjoint \(F\), and suppose \(G\) creates the corresponding coequalizers for all \(G\)-split pairs \(f,g:X\rightrightarrows Y\) (Definition reference). Then the following diagram is a coequalizer: \[\begin{equation*} \text{Diagram chapter7-unit-095-d012} \end{equation*}\] where \(N\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{D})\).

Proof. Applying \(G\) to this diagram gives the split fork of Example reference for \((M,a):=(G(N),G\varepsilon_N)=\mathbb{K}(N)\). Since \(G\) creates the corresponding coequalizer, the original diagram is a coequalizer.

Theorem (J. M. Beck). Let \(G:\mathcal{D}\to\mathcal{C}\) be a functor with left adjoint \(F\). The following statements are equivalent:

  1. the adjoint pair \((F,G)\) is monadic (Definition reference);

  2. \(G\) creates the corresponding coequalizer for every \(G\)-split pair \(f,g:X\rightrightarrows Y\);

  3. \(G\) is conservative (Definition reference), every \(G\)-split pair \(f,g:X\rightrightarrows Y\) has a coequalizer \(X\rightrightarrows Y\to Z\) in \(\mathcal{D}\), and the image of that coequalizer under \(G\) is a coequalizer of \((Gf,Gg)\).

If any of the conditions above holds, a quasi-inverse functor \(\mathbb{L}\) to \(\mathbb{K}:\mathcal{D}\to\mathcal{C}^T\) can be described as follows. For \((M,a)\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{C}^T)\), there is a coequalizer diagram \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:Beck-aux1}{}\text{Diagram chapter7-unit-095-d013} \end{equation}\]

For the comonad determined by \((F,G)\), the criterion is entirely dual.

Proof. First, we prove (i) \(\implies\) (ii). Suppose \(\mathbb{K}:\mathcal{D}\to\mathcal{C}^T\) has a quasi-inverse functor \(\mathbb{L}\). The properties of being a split pair, being a split fork, and creating \(\varinjlim\) are invariant under equivalences of categories. Since \(G=U^T\mathbb{K}\), it is enough to prove that \(U^T:\mathcal{C}^T\to\mathcal{C}\) creates the corresponding coequalizer for every \(U^T\)-split pair. This is precisely the content of Lemma reference.

Next, (i) \(\implies\) (iii). Since (i) \(\implies\) (ii) is already known, it remains only to show that \(G\) is conservative when \(G\) is monadic. But \(G=U^T\mathbb{K}\), where \(\mathbb{K}\) is an equivalence of categories and \(U^T\) is plainly conservative. Hence \(G\) is conservative as well.

We now prove (ii) \(\implies\) (i) by constructing a quasi-inverse functor \(\mathbb{L}\) to \(\mathbb{K}\). For \((M,a)\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{C}^T)\), consider the pair of morphisms in \(\mathcal{D}\) \(\text{Diagram chapter7-unit-095-diagram-015}\) Its image under \(G\) is \(\text{Diagram chapter7-unit-095-diagram-016}\), which can be extended to a split fork by Example reference. Thus \((Fa,\varepsilon_{FM})\) is a \(G\)-split pair, and the original diagram can be extended to a coequalizer diagram in \(\mathcal{D}\), namely equation.

By equation and the universal property of coequalizers, a morphism \((M,a)\xrightarrow{\varphi}(M',a')\) in \(\mathcal{C}^T\) gives a unique morphism \(\mathbb{L}(M,a)\to\mathbb{L}(M',a')\) making the following diagram commute: \[\begin{equation*} \text{Diagram chapter7-unit-095-diagram-017} \end{equation*}\] Thus \((M,a)\mapsto\mathbb{L}(M,a)\) becomes a functor \(\mathbb{L}:\mathcal{C}^T\to\mathcal{D}\).

We next prove \(\mathbb{L}\mathbb{K}\simeq\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{\mathcal{D}}\).4 For every \(N\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{D})\), the construction above gives a coequalizer diagram \[\begin{equation*} \text{Diagram chapter7-unit-095-d014} \end{equation*}\]

Comparing this with the coequalizer diagram in Lemma reference immediately gives the canonical isomorphism \(\mathbb{L}\mathbb{K}\simeq\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{\mathcal{D}}\).

Next, we verify \(\mathbb{K}\mathbb{L}\simeq\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{\mathcal{C}^T}\). Clearly \(\mathbb{K}F=\mathrm{Free}^T\); both send an object \(M\) to \((GF(M),G\varepsilon_{FM})\). By definition and \(\mu:=G\varepsilon F\), applying \(\mathbb{K}\) to equation gives \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:Beck-aux3}{} \text{Diagram chapter7-unit-095-d015} \end{equation}\]

Applying the forgetful functor \(U^T\) to the two terms on the left of equation gives \(\text{Diagram chapter7-unit-095-d016}\). Example reference extends this diagram to a split fork with coequalizer \(M\). On the other hand, \(U^T\) creates this coequalizer (Lemma reference). Recalling Definition reference, it follows that equation is also a coequalizer diagram.

On the other hand, apply Lemma reference to the adjoint pair \((\mathrm{Free}^T,U^T)\) and the object \(N=(M,a)\). Carefully expanding the description of this adjoint pair gives the coequalizer diagram \[\text{Diagram chapter7-unit-095-diagram-021}\] Comparison with the preceding paragraph immediately gives \(\mathbb{K}\mathbb{L}\simeq\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{\mathcal{C}^T}\).

Finally, we prove (iii) \(\implies\) (ii). The second part of (iii) says precisely that all \(G\)-split pairs have coequalizers and that \(G\) preserves those coequalizers. Since \(G\) is conservative, Remark reference shows that (ii) holds.

Reversing all morphisms while retaining the direction of the functors, that is, replacing \(\mathcal{C}\) and \(\mathcal{D}\) by \(\mathcal{C}^{\operatorname{op}}\) and \(\mathcal{D}^{\operatorname{op}}\), gives the characterization of comonadicity. We omit the details.

Corollary. Consider a pair of adjoint functors \(\text{Diagram chapter7-unit-095-d017}\) with corresponding unit \(\eta\) and counit \(\varepsilon\). If this adjoint pair is monadic, then the diagram \[\text{Diagram chapter7-unit-095-d018}\] is a coequalizer for every \(N\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{D})\).

Proof. Combine Lemma reference with Theorem reference (ii).

In practice, a linear version of Beck’s theorem is often needed. More precisely, let \(\Bbbk\) be a commutative ring and \((F,G)\) an adjoint pair between \(\Bbbk\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\)-categories, with both functors \(\Bbbk\)-linear; see Definition reference and Proposition reference. It is easy to see that \(\mathcal{C}^T\) naturally becomes a \(\Bbbk\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\)-category and that, by definition, both functors in \(\mathcal{D}\xrightarrow{\mathbb{K}}\mathcal{C}^T\xrightarrow{U^T}\mathcal{C}\) are \(\Bbbk\)-linear. If condition (ii) or (iii) of Beck’s Theorem reference is satisfied, the description by the diagram equation immediately shows that the quasi-inverse functor \(\mathbb{L}\) to \(\mathbb{K}\) is also \(\Bbbk\)-linear. We therefore obtain a \(\Bbbk\)-linear equivalence \(\mathbb{K}:\mathcal{D}\to\mathcal{C}^T\).

  1. Using the same symbol \(\mathbb{K}\) will cause little confusion, since this book will not discuss monads and comonads simultaneously.↩︎

  2. Translator’s note: the lower-right node of the first diagram is printed as \(T(M'')\) in the source. The unit law for a \(T\)-algebra requires that node to be \(M''\); the target is corrected here.↩︎

  3. Translator’s note: the source prints the domain of \(k\) as \((M'',a'')\), which makes \(ku\), \(kv\), and \(\varphi h=k\) undefined. The correct domain is \((M',a')\).↩︎

  4. Translator’s note: the source prints \(\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{\mathcal{C}}\) here and in the comparison sentence below. Since \(\mathbb{L}\mathbb{K}\) is an endofunctor of \(\mathcal{D}\), the correct subscript is \(\mathcal{D}\).↩︎

Morita Theory

Throughout this section, fix a Grothendieck universe \(\mathcal{U}\) and a commutative ring \(\Bbbk\). Relative to \(\mathcal{U}\), all rings are understood to be small by default. Functors between \(\Bbbk\)-linear categories are also understood to be \(\Bbbk\)-linear unless otherwise stated, as in Definitions reference and reference. When \(\Bbbk=\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\), \(\Bbbk\)-linearity is the same as additivity. For \(\Bbbk\)-linear categories \(\mathcal{C}\) and \(\mathcal{D}\), the notation \(\mathrm{Fct}(\mathcal{C},\mathcal{D})\) or \(\mathcal{D}^{\mathcal{C}}\) denotes the category of all functors \(F:\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{D}\). Although \(\mathrm{Fct}(\mathcal{C},\mathcal{D})\) need not be a \(\mathcal{U}\)-category, this causes no difficulty below because we shall not form limits or similar constructions within it.

Definition. Let \(\mathcal{C}\) and \(\mathcal{D}\) be \(\Bbbk\)-linear categories.

  • If \(\mathcal{C}\) and \(\mathcal{D}\) are cocomplete, define the full subcategory \(\mathrm{Fct}^c(\mathcal{C},\mathcal{D})\) of \(\mathrm{Fct}(\mathcal{C},\mathcal{D})\) to consist of all functors that preserve small \(\varinjlim\).

  • If \(\mathcal{C}\) and \(\mathcal{D}\) are complete, define the full subcategory \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Fct}}_c(\mathcal{C},\mathcal{D})\) of \(\mathrm{Fct}(\mathcal{C},\mathcal{D})\) to consist of all functors that preserve small \(\varprojlim\).

In some of the literature, objects of \(\mathrm{Fct}_c\) (or \(\mathrm{Fct}^c\)) are called continuous (or cocontinuous) functors.

We use the notation of §reference. For arbitrary \(\Bbbk\)-algebras \(A\) and \(B\), define \[\begin{align*} (A, B)\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}} & := \text{the category of $(A,B)$-bimodules}, \\ A\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}} & := \text{the category of left $A$-modules} \simeq (A, \Bbbk)\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}, \\ \ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}\text{-}}B & := \text{the category of right $B$-modules} \simeq (\Bbbk, B)\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}. \end{align*}\] These are elementary examples of \(\Bbbk\)-linear categories. Recall the following basic facts from module theory. Every \((A,B)\)-bimodule \(P\) canonically induces functors preserving small \(\varinjlim\), \[P \ensuremath{\underset{B}{\otimes}} (\cdot): B\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}} \to A\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}, \quad (\cdot) \ensuremath{\underset{A}{\otimes}} P : \ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}\text{-}}A \to \ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}\text{-}}B,\] while every \((B,A)\)-bimodule \(Q\) canonically induces functors preserving small \(\varprojlim\), \[\operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}\text{-}}B}(Q, \cdot): B\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}} \to A\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}, \quad \operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}\text{-}}A}(Q, \cdot): \ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}\text{-}}A \to \ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}\text{-}}B.\] If instead one takes the functor \(\operatorname{Hom}(\mathord\cdot,R)\), where \(R\) is a \((B,A)\)-bimodule, its domain must be replaced by an opposite category such as \((B\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}})^{\operatorname{op}}\) in order for the functor still to preserve small \(\varprojlim\).

Theorem (S. Eilenberg, C. E. Watts). For arbitrary \(\Bbbk\)-algebras \(A\) and \(B\), there are equivalences \[\text{Diagram chapter7-unit-096-d001}\]

For the first and second equivalences, composition of functors corresponds to tensor product of bimodules; when \(A=B\), the identity functor comes from \(A\) as an \((A,A)\)-bimodule, up to isomorphism.

Proof. The arguments for the various equivalences are similar. We discuss only \[(A, B)\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}} \to \mathrm{Fct}^c(B\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}, A\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}).\] The discussion preceding the theorem has shown that \(P\ensuremath{\underset{B}{\otimes}}(\mathord\cdot)\) is indeed an object of \(\mathrm{Fct}^c(B\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}},A\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}})\), and a bimodule homomorphism \(P\to P'\) plainly induces a morphism of functors \(P\ensuremath{\underset{B}{\otimes}}(\mathord\cdot)\to P'\ensuremath{\underset{B}{\otimes}}(\mathord\cdot)\). We now construct a quasi-inverse functor.

For an object \(F\) of \(\mathrm{Fct}^c(B\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}},A\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}})\), regard \(B\) as a left \(B\)-module and define \(P:=F(B)\). Since \(B\) also acts on itself on the right by multiplication and \(F\) is a \(\Bbbk\)-linear functor, \(P\) naturally acquires the structure of an \((A,B)\)-bimodule. The canonical isomorphism \(P\ensuremath{\underset{B}{\otimes}}B\simeq P\) shows that \[(A, B)\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}} \to \mathrm{Fct}^c\left(B\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}, A\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}} \right) \xrightarrow{F \mapsto P} (A, B)\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}} \;\text{has composite}\; \simeq \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}.\]

For the composite in the other direction, take a functor \(F\) as above and set \(P:=F(B)\). For any left \(B\)-module \(M\), there is a canonical surjective homomorphism \[\bigoplus_{\varphi \in \operatorname{Hom}(B, M)} B \twoheadrightarrow M.\] Notice that \(\bigoplus_\varphi\) is “small.” Repeating the construction for the kernel of this surjective homomorphism gives a canonical exact sequence for \(M\), \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:Morita-aux0}{} \bigoplus_\psi B \to \bigoplus_\varphi B \to M \to 0, \end{equation}\] whose first map may be regarded as right multiplication by an infinite matrix with entries in \(B=\operatorname{End}_{B\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}}(B)\). Since \(F\) and \(P\ensuremath{\underset{B}{\otimes}}(\mathord\cdot)\) both preserve small \(\varinjlim\), applying them to equation gives exact sequences in \(A\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\), \[\begin{gather*} \bigoplus_\psi P \to \bigoplus_\varphi P \to F(M) \to 0, \\ \bigoplus_\psi P \to \bigoplus_\varphi P \to P \ensuremath{\underset{B}{\otimes}} M \to 0. \end{gather*}\] In both rows, the map \(\bigoplus_\psi P\to\bigoplus_\varphi P\) comes from the same matrix (with entries in \(B\)), and hence there is a canonical isomorphism \(F(M)\simeq P\ensuremath{\underset{B}{\otimes}}M\).

By the associativity constraint for tensor products, the first equivalence \((A,B)\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\to\mathrm{Fct}^c(B\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}},A\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}})\) sends tensor products of bimodules to composition of functors, up to isomorphism. For the second equivalence, the corresponding statement follows from the adjunction between tensor product and \(\operatorname{Hom}\); see [Li1]. In both cases, it is easy to see that the \((A,A)\)-bimodule \(A\) corresponds to the identity functor, up to isomorphism.

The sizes of these functor categories are now easy to control.

Corollary. For arbitrary \(\Bbbk\)-algebras \(A\) and \(B\), all the functor categories \(\mathrm{Fct}^c(\cdots)\) and \(\mathrm{Fct}_c(\cdots)\) appearing in Theorem reference are \(\mathcal{U}\)-categories.

Proof. Indeed, \((A,B)\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\) and \((B,A)\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\) are both \(\mathcal{U}\)-categories.

Definition–Proposition. For arbitrary \(\Bbbk\)-algebras \(A\) and \(B\), the following statements are equivalent.

  1. \(A\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\) and \(B\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\) are equivalent.

  2. There are an \((A,B)\)-bimodule \(P\) and a \((B,A)\)-bimodule \(Q\) together with

    • an isomorphism of \((A,A)\)-bimodules \(P\ensuremath{\underset{B}{\otimes}}Q\simeq A\);

    • an isomorphism of \((B,B)\)-bimodules \(Q\ensuremath{\underset{A}{\otimes}}P\simeq B\).

  3. \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}\text{-}}A\) and \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}\text{-}}B\) are equivalent.

When one of these conditions holds, \(A\) and \(B\) are called Morita equivalent.

Proof. Equivalences necessarily preserve \(\varinjlim\) and \(\varprojlim\). Theorem reference gives (i) \(\iff\) (ii) and (iii) \(\iff\) (ii).

Condition (ii) is concise but not yet sufficiently explicit. It will be refined by Theorem reference at the end of this section. Before that, we introduce several examples and related results.

Example. For commutative \(\Bbbk\)-algebras, Morita equivalence is the same as isomorphism of algebras. This rests on the canonical isomorphism \(Z(A\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}})\simeq Z(A)\), where the left-hand side is the center of the abelian category and the right-hand side is the center of the \(\Bbbk\)-algebra.

Example. Let \(n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}_{\geq1}\). Every \(\Bbbk\)-algebra \(A\) is Morita equivalent to the \(n\times n\) matrix algebra \(\mathrm{M}_n(A)\). To see this, use matrix operations to define \[\begin{align*} P & := \text{the $(A,\mathrm{M}_{n \times n}(A))$-bimodule } A^n \quad \text{(row vectors)}, \\ Q & := \text{the $(\mathrm{M}_{n \times n}(A),A)$-bimodule } A^n \quad \text{(column vectors)}. \end{align*}\] Matrix multiplication gives the required isomorphisms, \[\begin{gather*} P \ensuremath{\underset{\mathrm{M}_{n \times n}(A)}{\otimes}} Q \ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}A \quad \text{(as an $(A,A)$-bimodule)}, \\ Q \ensuremath{\underset{A}{\otimes}} P \ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}\mathrm{M}_{n \times n}(A) \quad \text{(as an $(\mathrm{M}_{n \times n}(A), \mathrm{M}_{n \times n}(A))$-bimodule)}. \end{gather*}\]

Return to the general setting. For any \((A,B)\)-bimodule \(P\), a basic fact of module theory [Li1] gives an adjoint pair \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:AB-adjunction}{}\text{Diagram chapter7-unit-096-d002} \end{equation}\] Theorem reference shows that, up to isomorphism, the functors on the left and right exhaust the objects of \(\mathrm{Fct}^c(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}\text{-}}A,\ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}\text{-}}B)\) and \(\mathrm{Fct}_c(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}\text{-}}B,\ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}\text{-}}A)\), respectively. By Example reference, the adjoint pair equation determines a monad \(T\) on \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}\text{-}}A\) and a comonad \(L\) on \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}\text{-}}B\). Their general description is as follows. Consider a right \(A\)-module \(N\) and a right \(B\)-module \(M\): \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:bimod-adjunction}{} \begin{array}{|c|c|} \hline \text{unit } \eta_N & \text{counit } \epsilon_M \\ \hline N \to \operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}\text{-}}B}\left( P, N \ensuremath{\underset{A}{\otimes}} P \right) & \operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}\text{-}}B}(P, M) \ensuremath{\underset{A}{\otimes}} P \to M \\ x \mapsto \left[ p \mapsto x \otimes p \right] & \varphi \otimes p \mapsto \varphi(p) \\ \hline \end{array} \end{equation}\] Recall the definition of an exact functor in Definition reference.

Proposition. Let \(P\) be an \((A,B)\)-bimodule. If \((\mathord\cdot)\ensuremath{\underset{A}{\otimes}}P\) (or \(\operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}\text{-}}B}(P,\mathord\cdot)\)) is a faithful exact functor, then the adjoint pair equation is comonadic (or monadic); see Definition reference and its dual version.

Proof. We give the proof for \((\mathord\cdot)\ensuremath{\underset{A}{\otimes}}P\); the argument for the other side is exactly the same.

We have already shown that \((\mathord\cdot)\ensuremath{\underset{A}{\otimes}}P\) has a right adjoint. It remains to verify the dual of condition (iii) in Theorem reference. First, we prove that \((\mathord\cdot)\ensuremath{\underset{A}{\otimes}}P\) is conservative. For a homomorphism of right \(A\)-modules \(f:N\to N'\), the required conservativity follows from \[\begin{multline*} f \;\text{is an isomorphism} \iff 0 \to N \xrightarrow{f} N' \to 0 \;\text{is exact} \\ \stackrel{\text{Proposition \href{#prop:faithful-exact}{reference} (iii)}}{\iff} 0 \to N \ensuremath{\underset{A}{\otimes}} P \xrightarrow{\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}\otimes f} N' \ensuremath{\underset{A}{\otimes}} P \to 0 \;\text{is exact} \iff \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}\otimes f \;\text{is an isomorphism}. \end{multline*}\]

Next, every pair of morphisms in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}\text{-}}A\) and \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}\text{-}}B\) has an equalizer, and the faithful exactness hypothesis ensures that \((\mathord\cdot)\ensuremath{\underset{A}{\otimes}}P\) preserves equalizers. Thus all the conditions of Theorem reference (iii) are satisfied.

This is only an abstract result. To apply it, the corresponding monad \(T\) and comonad \(L\) must be described explicitly in certain special cases. We begin with change of rings.

Example (Change of rings). Fix a homomorphism of \(\Bbbk\)-algebras \(f:A\to B\). In the preceding framework, take \(P:=B\), regarded through \(f\) as an \((A,B)\)-bimodule. In this case, the right adjoint \(\operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}\text{-}}B}(B,\mathord\cdot)\) of \((\mathord\cdot)\ensuremath{\underset{A}{\otimes}}B\) is isomorphic, via \(\varphi\mapsto\varphi(1)\), to the forgetful functor \(\mathcal{F}_{B|A}:\ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}\text{-}}B\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}\text{-}}A\), and \[\begin{array}{|c|c|} \hline \text{unit morphism }\; \eta_N & \text{counit morphism }\; \epsilon_M \\ \hline N \to \mathcal{F}_{B|A}(N \ensuremath{\underset{A}{\otimes}} B) & \mathcal{F}_{B|A}(M) \ensuremath{\underset{A}{\otimes}} B \to M \\ x \mapsto x \otimes 1 & y \otimes b \mapsto yb \\ \hline \end{array} \quad \begin{array}{c} N: \;\text{a right $A$-module,} \\ M: \;\text{a right $B$-module.} \end{array}\]

In discussions of change of rings, \(\mathcal{F}_{B|A}\) is usually omitted from the notation for simplicity. Thus the monad \(T\) and comonad \(L\) may respectively be written as \[\begin{array}{|c|c|c|} \hline T & \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}\to T & T^2 \to T \\ \hline N \mapsto N \ensuremath{\underset{A}{\otimes}} B & N \to N \ensuremath{\underset{A}{\otimes}} B & (N \ensuremath{\underset{A}{\otimes}} B) \ensuremath{\underset{A}{\otimes}} B \to N \ensuremath{\underset{A}{\otimes}} B \\ & x \mapsto x \otimes 1 & (x \otimes b) \otimes b' \mapsto x \otimes bb' \\ \hline\hline L & L \to \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}& L \to L^2 \\ \hline M \mapsto M \ensuremath{\underset{A}{\otimes}} B & M \ensuremath{\underset{A}{\otimes}} B \to M & M \ensuremath{\underset{A}{\otimes}} B \to (M \ensuremath{\underset{A}{\otimes}} B) \ensuremath{\underset{A}{\otimes}} B \\ & y \otimes b \mapsto yb & y \otimes b \mapsto (y \otimes 1) \otimes b \\ \hline \end{array}\] The required verifications are routine.

We next consider a slightly more general situation. First, for arbitrary right \(B\)-modules \(P\) and \(X\), regard \(B\) as a \((B,B)\)-bimodule in order to define the left \(B\)-module \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:P-vee}{} P^\vee := \operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}\text{-}}B}(P, B) \end{equation}\] and the canonical homomorphism of \(\Bbbk\)-modules \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:dual-Hom-X}{}\begin{aligned} X \ensuremath{\underset{B}{\otimes}} P^\vee & \to \operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}\text{-}}B}(P, X) \\ x \otimes \lambda & \mapsto x \lambda(\cdot). \end{aligned} \end{equation}\] If \(P\) is an \((A,B)\)-bimodule, then \(P^\vee\) has the structure of a \((B,A)\)-bimodule, \(\operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}\text{-}}B}(P,X)\) has the structure of a right \(A\)-module, and equation is a homomorphism of right \(A\)-modules. The same construction naturally has a version with left and right interchanged. Consequently, \(P^{\vee\vee}\) is defined, and there is also a canonical homomorphism of right \(B\)-modules \(P\to P^{\vee\vee}\).

Lemma. Let \(P\) be an \((A,B)\)-bimodule which, as a right \(B\)-module, is finitely generated and projective. Then \(P^\vee\), as a left \(B\)-module, is also finitely generated and projective, and in this situation:

  • for every \(X\), equation gives a canonical isomorphism of right \(A\)-modules;

  • \(P\to P^{\vee\vee}\) is an isomorphism.

Proof. As a right \(B\)-module, write \(P\) as a direct summand of \(B^{\oplus n}\) for some \(n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}_{\geq0}\). Then \(P^\vee\) is naturally a direct summand of \(B^{\oplus n}\). It is clear that replacing \(P\) by \(B^{\oplus n}\) in equation gives an isomorphism of \(\Bbbk\)-modules. Restricting to the direct summand \(P\) therefore still gives an isomorphism of \(\Bbbk\)-modules, hence an isomorphism of right \(A\)-modules. The assertion \(P\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}P^{\vee\vee}\) is proved in the same way: it is enough to check it for \(B^{\oplus n}\).

Under the preceding hypothesis, the adjoint pair equation can therefore be rewritten as \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:AB-adjunction-2}{}\text{Diagram chapter7-unit-097-d001} \end{equation}\]

Definition. Let \(P\) be an \((A,B)\)-bimodule which, as a right \(B\)-module, is finitely generated and projective. Define the homomorphism of \((B,B)\)-bimodules \[\text{Diagram chapter7-unit-097-d002}\] and the homomorphism of \((A,A)\)-bimodules \[\text{Diagram chapter7-unit-097-d003}\]

It is easy to check that both maps are well defined. Combining equation with Lemma reference, for every right \(A\)-module \(N\) and right \(B\)-module \(M\), the unit morphism \(\eta_N\) and counit morphism \(\epsilon_M\) of the adjoint pair equation satisfy \[\text{Diagram chapter7-unit-097-d004}\] Thus we may identify \[\begin{align*} \eta_N = \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_N \otimes \mathrm{coev}: \; & N \to N \ensuremath{\underset{A}{\otimes}} P \ensuremath{\underset{B}{\otimes}} P^\vee , \\ \epsilon_M = \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_M \otimes \mathrm{ev}: \; & M \ensuremath{\underset{B}{\otimes}} P^\vee \ensuremath{\underset{A}{\otimes}} P \to M. \end{align*}\] The preceding constructions take place at the level of the bimodules \(P\) and \(P^\vee\) and do not depend on \(M\) or \(N\) at all.

Definition. For an arbitrary \(\Bbbk\)-algebra \(A\), the category \((A,A)\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\) is monoidal under \(\otimes:=\ensuremath{\underset{A}{\otimes}}\). Hence §reference and §reference define what is meant by an algebra \(E\) (or coalgebra \(C\)) in \((A,A)\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\), as well as by left and right \(E\)-modules (or left and right \(C\)-comodules). Since the definition of a module (or comodule) involves \(\otimes\) on only one side, the following slight generalization is needed.

  • A left \(E\)-module means the following data: an \(M\in\operatorname{Ob}(A\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}})\) together with a morphism in \(A\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\), \(\mu_M:E\otimes M\to M\), such that the diagrams in Definition reference commute in \(A\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\).

  • A left \(C\)-comodule means the following data: an \(M\in\operatorname{Ob}(A\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}})\) together with a morphism in \(A\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\), \(\rho_M:M\to C\otimes M\), such that the diagrams in Definition reference commute in \(A\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\).

Right \(E\)-modules and right \(C\)-comodules are defined similarly, and morphisms between modules or comodules are defined in the standard way.

Applying the preceding sequence of results to describe the monad and comonad determined by the adjoint pair equation immediately gives the following result.

Proposition. Let \(P\) be an \((A,B)\)-bimodule which, as a right \(B\)-module, is finitely generated and projective, and define the \((B,A)\)-bimodule \(P^\vee\) as above. Then:

  • \(P\ensuremath{\underset{B}{\otimes}}P^\vee\) is an algebra in the monoidal category \((A,A)\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\). Its multiplication is given by \[\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_P \otimes \mathrm{ev} \otimes \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{P^\vee}: P \ensuremath{\underset{B}{\otimes}} P^\vee \ensuremath{\underset{A}{\otimes}} P \ensuremath{\underset{B}{\otimes}} P^\vee \to P \ensuremath{\underset{B}{\otimes}} P^\vee\] and its unit comes from \(\mathrm{coev}:A\to P\ensuremath{\underset{B}{\otimes}}P^\vee\);

  • \(P^\vee\ensuremath{\underset{A}{\otimes}}P\) is a coalgebra in the monoidal category \((B,B)\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\). Its comultiplication is given by \[\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{P^\vee} \otimes \mathrm{coev} \otimes \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_P: P^\vee \ensuremath{\underset{A}{\otimes}} P \to P^\vee \ensuremath{\underset{A}{\otimes}} P \ensuremath{\underset{B}{\otimes}} P^\vee \ensuremath{\underset{A}{\otimes}} P\] and its counit comes from \(\mathrm{ev}:P^\vee\ensuremath{\underset{A}{\otimes}}P\to B\).

Next, consider the monad \(T\) on \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}\text{-}}A\) determined by the adjoint pair equation, and the comonad \(L\) on \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}\text{-}}B\) determined by it. Use Definition reference when discussing modules and comodules.

  • Specifying a \(T\)-module is equivalent to specifying a right \(A\)-module \(N\) together with a homomorphism satisfying the usual properties such as associativity and unitality, \[N \ensuremath{\underset{A}{\otimes}} (P \ensuremath{\underset{B}{\otimes}} P^\vee) \to N;\] in other words, it is equivalent to making \(N\) a \((P\ensuremath{\underset{B}{\otimes}}P^\vee)\)-module.

  • Specifying an \(L\)-comodule is equivalent to specifying a right \(B\)-module \(M\) together with a homomorphism satisfying the usual properties such as coassociativity and counitality, \[M \to M \ensuremath{\underset{B}{\otimes}} (P^\vee \ensuremath{\underset{A}{\otimes}} P);\] in other words, it is equivalent to making \(M\) a \((P^\vee\ensuremath{\underset{A}{\otimes}}P)\)-comodule.

Proof. The proof is easier than the statement.

As a ring, \(P\ensuremath{\underset{B}{\otimes}}P^\vee\) is simply \(\operatorname{End}_{B\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}}(P)\). By contrast, the coalgebra structure on \(P^\vee\ensuremath{\underset{A}{\otimes}}P\) looks cumbersome, but it is often more convenient in applications. Nevertheless, comodules do not have an absolute advantage: for example, the coalgebra must be flat for its comodule category to be abelian. We give only an outline of a simple proof; the exercises at the end of the chapter provide more.

Proposition. Let \(C\) be a coalgebra in \((B,B)\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\). Write the category of right (or left) \(C\)-comodules as \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Comod}\text{-}}C\) (or \(C\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Comod}}\)), and write its forgetful functor to \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}\text{-}}B\) (or \(B\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\)) as \(U\). If \(C\), as a left (or right) \(B\)-module, is flat [Li1], then \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Comod}\text{-}}C\) (or \(C\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Comod}}\)) is an abelian category and \(U\) is faithful and exact.

Proof. It is enough to discuss the version for \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Comod}\text{-}}C\). Let \(f:M\to N\) be a homomorphism of right \(C\)-comodules and denote its cokernel at the level of \(B\)-modules by \(\operatorname{coker}(Uf)\). Then there is a commutative diagram in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}\text{-}}B\) with exact rows, \[\text{Diagram chapter7-unit-097-d005}\] where the dashed arrow is uniquely determined by functoriality of the cokernel. It is easy to prove that this dashed arrow gives \(\operatorname{coker}(Uf)\) a comodule structure; we denote this object by \(\operatorname{coker}(f)\), and it is the cokernel of \(f\). The reader may check the details if desired.

We wish to lift \(\operatorname{ker}(Uf)\) to a comodule in the same way. The key is to ensure that \[0 \to \operatorname{ker}(Uf) \ensuremath{\underset{B}{\otimes}} C \to M \ensuremath{\underset{B}{\otimes}} C \xrightarrow{Uf \otimes \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}} N \ensuremath{\underset{B}{\otimes}} C\] is exact in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}\text{-}}B\). This is where the flatness of \(C\) as a left \(B\)-module is needed; the remaining routine verification is similar to the cokernel case.

To prove that \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Comod}\text{-}}C\) is an abelian category, it remains to show that the canonical morphism \[\operatorname{coim}(f) = \operatorname{coker}[\operatorname{ker}(f) \hookrightarrow M] \to \operatorname{ker}[N \twoheadrightarrow \operatorname{coker}(f)] = \operatorname{im}(f)\] is an isomorphism, but this need only be checked at the level of \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}\text{-}}B\).

By construction, \(U\) preserves kernels and cokernels and is therefore exact; it is plainly faithful as well.

Returning to the main discussion, we continue the study of the functor \((\mathord\cdot)\ensuremath{\underset{A}{\otimes}}P\).

Proposition. Let \(P\) be an \((A,B)\)-bimodule which, as a right \(B\)-module, is finitely generated and projective, and suppose that \((\mathord\cdot)\ensuremath{\underset{A}{\otimes}}P\) is a faithful exact functor. A right \(A\)-module \(N\) is finitely generated if and only if the right \(B\)-module \(N\ensuremath{\underset{A}{\otimes}}P\) is finitely generated.

Proof. For the “only if” direction, suppose there are \(n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}_{\geq0}\) and a surjective homomorphism \(A^{\oplus n}\twoheadrightarrow N\). Applying the functor gives a surjective homomorphism \(P^{\oplus n}\twoheadrightarrow N\ensuremath{\underset{A}{\otimes}}P\), while \(P\), as a right \(B\)-module, is finitely generated.

For the “if” direction, take a finitely generated submodule \(N'\) of \(N\) such that the image of \(N'\ensuremath{\underset{A}{\otimes}}P\) contains a set of generators of \(N\ensuremath{\underset{A}{\otimes}}P\) as a \(B\)-module. Since \((\mathord\cdot)\ensuremath{\underset{A}{\otimes}}P\) is faithful and exact, we in fact have \(N'\ensuremath{\underset{A}{\otimes}}P\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}N\ensuremath{\underset{A}{\otimes}}P\), and hence \(N'=N\).

In fact, the property that a module is finitely generated admits an entirely categorical characterization, as follows.

Lemma. Let \(R\) be a ring and \(N\) a right \(R\)-module. Then \(N\) is finitely generated if and only if the following property holds: for every family \((N_i)_{i \in I}\) of subobjects of \(N\), if \(\sum_{i \in I}N_i=N\), then there is a finite subset \(I_0\subset I\) such that \(\sum_{i \in I_0}N_i=N\).

Proof. For the “only if” direction, let \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\) be a set of generators for \(N\). Each \(x_j\) belongs to some \(\sum_{i\in I_j}N_i\), where \(I_j\subset I\) is finite; it is enough to take \(I_0=\bigcup_{j=1}^n I_j\). For the “if” direction, consider \(N=\sum_{x\in N}xR\).

We now return to the Morita equivalences introduced in Definition–Proposition reference. We discuss only the case of right modules.

Theorem (Kiiti Morita). Let \(A\) and \(B\) be \(\Bbbk\)-algebras. Let \(\mathrm{Equiv}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}\text{-}}A,\ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}\text{-}}B)\) be the category whose objects are all equivalences \(F:\ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}\text{-}}A\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}\text{-}}B\) and whose morphisms are isomorphisms between these equivalences. On the other hand, define a category \(\mathcal{P}(A,B)\) whose objects are the \((A,B)\)-bimodules \(P\) satisfying the following conditions:

  • as a right \(B\)-module, \(P\) is a finitely generated projective generator of \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}\text{-}}B\);

  • left multiplication induces an isomorphism \(A\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}\operatorname{End}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}\text{-}}B}(P)\).

Its morphisms are defined to be bimodule isomorphisms. There are quasi-inverse functors \[\text{Diagram chapter7-unit-098-d001}\]

Proof. First, we show that \(F\mapsto F(A)\) is well defined. Observe that \(A\) is a finitely generated projective generator of \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}\text{-}}A\). Both the property of being a projective generator and the property of being finitely generated have categorical characterizations (Lemma reference), so the same holds for \(F(A)\). Moreover, abstract considerations give \[F:\operatorname{End}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}\text{-}}A}(A)\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}} \operatorname{End}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}\text{-}}B}(F(A)).\] It is easy to check that this is exactly the homomorphism \(A\to\operatorname{End}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}\text{-}}B}(F(A))\) given by left multiplication by \(A\) on \(F(A)\).

If the functor from right to left is also well defined, then Theorem reference implies that the two functors are quasi-inverse. It therefore suffices to prove the following assertion: if \(P\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{P}(A,B))\), then \(F:=(\cdot)\ensuremath{\underset{A}{\otimes}}P\) is an equivalence of categories.

Take \(P\) as above. In equation, we showed that the right adjoint of \((\cdot)\ensuremath{\underset{A}{\otimes}}P\) is \((\cdot)\ensuremath{\underset{B}{\otimes}}P^\vee\), where \(P^\vee:=\operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}\text{-}}B}(P,B)\). We seek to show that these functors are quasi-inverse. Taking \(Q=P^\vee\) in Definition–Proposition reference (ii), it is enough to prove that the bimodule homomorphisms in Definition reference, \[\mathrm{ev}:P^\vee\ensuremath{\underset{A}{\otimes}}P\to B,\qquad \mathrm{coev}:A\to P\ensuremath{\underset{B}{\otimes}}P^\vee \simeq\operatorname{End}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}\text{-}}B}(P),\] are both isomorphisms.

First consider \(\mathrm{ev}\). Since \(P\) is a generator of \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}\text{-}}B\), there is a surjective homomorphism \(P^{\oplus I}\twoheadrightarrow B\). In particular, there are \(q_1,\ldots,q_n\in P^\vee\) and \(p_1,\ldots,p_n\in P\) such that \(\sum_{i=1}^n q_i(p_i)=1_B\), or equivalently \(\mathrm{ev}(\sum_i q_i\otimes p_i)=1_B\). Thus surjectivity is proved.

Next, define an operation \(P\times P^\vee\to A\), written as multiplication. It is characterized by the following associativity-like identity in \(P\), for all \(p,p'\in P\) and \(q\in P^\vee\): \[\underbracket{(pq)}_{\in A}p' = p\underbracket{(qp')}_{\in B}.\] Here \(qp':=q(p')\). Indeed, for fixed \(p\) and \(q\), the right-hand side is an element of \(\operatorname{End}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}\text{-}}B}(P)\), while left multiplication induces \(A\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}\operatorname{End}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}\text{-}}B}(P)\); thus \(pq\in A\) is uniquely defined. The identity above also gives a second form of associativity, namely the following identity in \(P^\vee\): \[\underbracket{(qp)}_{\in B}q' = q\underbracket{(pq')}_{\in A}.\] It is enough to check that the two sides take the same value on every \(p'\in P\); this direct verification is left to the reader.

We can now prove the injectivity of \(\mathrm{ev}\). Choose \(p_i\) and \(q_i\) as in the preceding step. If \(\mathrm{ev}(\sum_{j=1}^m q'_j\otimes p'_j)=0\), then the two forms of associativity above give \[\begin{multline*} \sum_j q'_j \otimes p'_j = \sum_{i,j}(q_i p_i)q'_j\otimes p'_j = \sum_{i,j}q_i\underbracket{(p_iq'_j)}_{\in A}\otimes p'_j \\ = \sum_{i,j}q_i\otimes(p_iq'_j)p'_j = \sum_{i,j}q_i\otimes p_i\underbracket{(q'_jp'_j)}_{\in B} = \sum_i q_i\otimes p_i\sum_j q'_jp'_j=0. \end{multline*}\]

Finally, the assertion that \(\mathrm{coev}\) is an isomorphism is precisely the second condition in the definition of \(\mathcal{P}(A,B)\).

Consequently, \(A\) and \(B\) are Morita equivalent if and only if \(\mathcal{P}(A,B)\) is nonempty, while studying the category \(\mathcal{P}(A,B)\) is an entirely concrete problem in module theory. Conversely, Morita equivalence may also be used to rewrite the definition of \(\mathcal{P}(A,B)\) in a more symmetric form.

Corollary. An \((A,B)\)-bimodule \(P\) is an object of the category \(\mathcal{P}(A,B)\) in Theorem reference if and only if the following conditions hold:

  • as a left \(A\)-module, \(P\) is a finitely generated projective generator of \(A\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\), and as a right \(B\)-module, \(P\) is a finitely generated projective generator of \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}\text{-}}B\);

  • left multiplication induces an isomorphism \(A\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}\operatorname{End}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}\text{-}}B}(P)\), while right multiplication induces an isomorphism \(B^{\operatorname{op}}\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}\operatorname{End}_{A\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}}(P)\).

Proof. It is enough to prove the “only if” direction. Suppose \(P\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{P}(A,B))\). The bimodule isomorphisms already proved, \[P\ensuremath{\underset{B}{\otimes}}P^\vee\simeq A,\qquad P^\vee\ensuremath{\underset{A}{\otimes}}P\simeq B,\] not only show that \((\cdot)\ensuremath{\underset{A}{\otimes}}P:\ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}\text{-}}A\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}\text{-}}B\) is an equivalence, but also imply that \(P\ensuremath{\underset{B}{\otimes}}(\cdot):B\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\to A\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\) is an equivalence. Therefore the left-module version of Theorem reference shows that \(P\), as a left \(A\)-module, is a finitely generated projective generator, and that right multiplication induces \(B^{\operatorname{op}}\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}\operatorname{End}_{A\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}}(P)\). In fact, it is enough to repeat the first paragraph of the proof of Theorem reference for left modules.

Recognizing Module Categories

Throughout this section, continue to fix a commutative ring \(\Bbbk\). All abelian categories and functors are understood to be \(\Bbbk\)-linear unless otherwise stated. Categories of the form \(R\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\) or \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}\text{-}}R\), where \(R\) is a \(\Bbbk\)-algebra, are collectively called module categories. In §reference, we specifically studied module categories and functors between them. It is also natural to ask which categories are equivalent to module categories and how such equivalences can be described concretely. This section presents several concise, practical results about these questions. Let \(\mathcal{A}\) be an abelian category. Our approach is to consider a functor of the form \(\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{A}}(s,\mathord\cdot)\), which naturally lifts to a functor \(\mathcal{A}\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}\text{-}}R\) with \(R:=\operatorname{End}_{\mathcal{A}}(s)\). The question is when \(\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{A}}(s,\mathord\cdot)\) is an equivalence.

Recall Definition reference of a compact object. Suppose \(\mathcal{A}\) has all small filtered \(\varinjlim\) and \(X\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{A})\). The object \(X\) is called compact if, for every small filtered category \(I\) and functor \(\alpha:I\to\mathcal{A}\), the following canonical morphism is an isomorphism: \[\varinjlim_i \operatorname{Hom}\left( X, \alpha(i) \right) \to \operatorname{Hom}\left( X, \varinjlim \alpha \right).\]

Lemma. Let \(X\) be a projective object in a cocomplete abelian category \(\mathcal{A}\). Then \(X\) is compact if and only if \(\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{A}}(X,\mathord\cdot)\) preserves all small direct sums; that is, for every small set \(I\) and family of objects \((Y_i)_{i\in I}\), \(\bigoplus_{i\in I}\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{A}}(X,Y_i)\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}} \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{A}}(X,\bigoplus_{i\in I}Y_i)\). When this condition holds, \(\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{A}}(X,\mathord\cdot)\) in fact preserves all small \(\varinjlim\).

Proof. Suppose \(X\) is compact. A direct sum indexed by a small set \(I\) is the filtered \(\varinjlim\) of the finite direct sums (take all finite subsets of \(I\), ordered by inclusion). Since \(\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{A}}(X,\mathord\cdot)\) is known to preserve finite direct sums, it also preserves small direct sums.

Conversely, projectivity is equivalent to \(\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{A}}(X,\mathord\cdot)\) preserving cokernels, while a general small \(\varinjlim\) can be constructed from small direct sums and cokernels. Hence \(\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{A}}(X,\mathord\cdot)\) preserves all small \(\varinjlim\).

Example. Let \(R\) be a \(\Bbbk\)-algebra and \(M\) a projective right \(R\)-module. Then \(M\) is compact if and only if \(M\) is finitely generated.

  • Necessity: there are a small set \(I\) and homomorphisms \(i:M\to R^{\oplus I}\) and \(p:R^{\oplus I}\to M\) with \(pi=\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_M\). Compactness implies that the image of \(i\) is contained in \(R^{\oplus I_0}\) for some finite subset \(I_0\subset I\).
