Take \(p':=p|_{R^{\oplus I_0}}\); then \(p'i=\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_M\) still holds. Thus \(M\) can be realized as a direct summand of a finite-rank free module.

  • Sufficiency: apply the criterion of Lemma reference. Every homomorphism \(M\to\bigoplus_{i\in I}Y_i\) must land in \(\bigoplus_{i\in I_0}Y_i\) for some finite subset \(I_0\subset I\) (it is enough to check the images of the generators). Hence \(M\) is compact.

Proposition. Let \(\mathcal{A}\) be a cocomplete abelian category. Then \(s\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{A})\) is a compact projective generator if and only if \(\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{A}}(s,\mathord\cdot): \mathcal{A}\to\Bbbk\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\) is a faithful exact functor preserving all small \(\varinjlim\).

Proof. By Proposition reference, being a projective generator is equivalent to \(\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{A}}(s,\mathord\cdot)\) being faithful and exact. By Lemma reference, under the projectivity assumption, compactness is equivalent to \(\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{A}}(s,\mathord\cdot)\) preserving all small \(\varinjlim\).

Theorem (P. Gabriel). Let \(s\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{A})\) and set \(R:=\operatorname{End}_{\mathcal{A}}(s)\). Then \[\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{A}}(s, \cdot): \mathcal{A} \to \ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}\text{-}}R\] is an equivalence if and only if \(s\) is a compact projective generator of \(\mathcal{A}\).

Proof. For brevity, write \(G:=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{A}}(s,\mathord\cdot):\mathcal{A}\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}\text{-}}R\). First prove necessity. Since \(G\) is an equivalence and \(G(s)=R\), it is enough to check that \(R\) is a compact projective generator of \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}\text{-}}R\), which is immediate.

We now prove sufficiency. Suppose \(s\) is a compact projective generator. Proposition reference implies that \(G\) is a faithful exact functor preserving all small \(\varinjlim\), because its composite with the forgetful functor \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}\text{-}}R\to\Bbbk\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\) has these properties. Since faithfulness is already known, it is enough to prove that:

  • for all \(X,Y\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{A})\), the corresponding map \(\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{A}}(X,Y)\to\operatorname{Hom}_R(GX,GY)\) is surjective;

  • \(G\) is essentially surjective.

First, for every \(X\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{A})\), define a morphism \(\phi_X:s^{\oplus\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{A}}(s,X)}\to X\) whose restriction to the direct summand corresponding to \(f:s\to X\) is \(f\). We show that \(\phi_X\) is surjective. Otherwise, suppose that \(\operatorname{coker}(\phi_X)\neq0\). The generator property gives a nonzero morphism \(s\to\operatorname{coker}(\phi_X)\) (Proposition reference), while projectivity makes this morphism factor as \(s\xrightarrow{g}X\to\operatorname{coker}(\phi_X)\). It follows that the composite \(s^{\oplus\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{A}}(s,X)}\xrightarrow{\phi_X}X \to\operatorname{coker}(\phi_X)\) is nonzero on the direct summand corresponding to \(g\), a contradiction.

Apply the same construction to the kernel \(\operatorname{ker}(\phi_X)\). Thus every \(X\) fits into an exact sequence \[s^{\oplus J} \to s^{\oplus I} \to X \to 0, \quad I = I_X, \; J = J_X: \text{small sets}.\] Since \(G\) preserves all small \(\varinjlim\), this gives an exact sequence of right \(R\)-modules \[R^{\oplus J} \to R^{\oplus I} \to GX \to 0.\] The first morphism in each sequence may be regarded as an \(I\times J\) matrix over \(R\) acting by left multiplication; the two are in fact the same matrix.

Now consider a homomorphism of right \(R\)-modules \(f:GX\to GY\). Choose exact sequences of the preceding form for \(X\) and \(Y\). It is easy to see that \(f\) lifts to a commutative diagram with exact rows \[\text{Diagram chapter7-unit-099-d001}\] The four arrows in the left square, however, can all be expressed as matrices over \(R\). Those four matrices give the solid part of a commutative diagram with exact rows \[\text{Diagram chapter7-unit-099-d002}\] and the dashed part is uniquely determined by functoriality of the cokernel. Since \(G\) is exact, necessarily \(G(X\dashrightarrow Y)=f\).

A similar argument shows that \(G\) is essentially surjective. For a given right \(R\)-module \(M\), there is an exact sequence \[R^{\oplus L} \to R^{\oplus K} \to M \to 0,\] where the first morphism is regarded as a \(K\times L\) matrix over \(R\). The same matrix gives a cokernel exact sequence in \(\mathcal{A}\), \[s^{\oplus L} \to s^{\oplus K} \to X \to 0.\] Since \(G\) preserves all small \(\varinjlim\), necessarily \(GX\simeq M\). This completes the proof.

Another related problem is to recognize categories of finitely generated modules. Write \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}_{\mathrm{fg}}\text{-}}R\) for the category of finitely generated right \(R\)-modules. If \(R\) is a right Noetherian ring, \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}_{\mathrm{fg}}\text{-}}R\) remains an abelian category; see [Li1].

Theorem. Let \(\mathcal{A}\) be an abelian category and \(s\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{A})\). Suppose that:

  • every \(X\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{A})\) is a Noetherian object (Definition reference);

  • \(R:=\operatorname{End}_{\mathcal{A}}(s)\) is a right Noetherian ring;

  • \(s\) is a projective generator of \(\mathcal{A}\).

Then the functor \(\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{A}}(s,\mathord\cdot): \mathcal{A}\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}\text{-}}R\) factors as \[\mathcal{A} \xrightarrow{\text{equivalence}} \ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}_{\mathrm{fg}}\text{-}}R \subset \ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}\text{-}}R.\]

Proof. First show that every \(X\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{A})\) can be placed in an exact sequence \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:identify-ModR-fg-aux}{} s^{\oplus m} \to s^{\oplus n} \to X \to 0, \quad n, m \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}_{\geq 0}. \end{equation}\]

Indeed, since \(s\) is a generator, for every \(X\neq0\) there is a nonzero morphism \(\phi_1:s\to X\). If \(\phi_1\) is not surjective, there is a nonzero morphism \(s\to\operatorname{coker}(\phi_1)\); the projectivity of \(s\) ensures that this morphism factors as \(s\xrightarrow{\psi_1}X\to\operatorname{coker}(\phi_1)\). We thereby obtain \(\phi_2:=(\phi_1,\psi_1):s^{\oplus2}\to X\) with \(\operatorname{im}(\phi_2)\supsetneq\operatorname{im}(\phi_1)\). If \(\phi_2\) is not yet surjective, repeat the same procedure. Since \(X\) is a Noetherian object, this process must terminate after finitely many steps and yield a surjective morphism \(\phi_X:s^{\oplus n}\twoheadrightarrow X\). Apply the same procedure to \(\operatorname{ker}(\phi_X)\) to obtain equation.

Recall that \(s\) is a projective generator if and only if \(G:=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{A}}(s,\mathord\cdot)\) is faithful and exact. Applying \(G\) to equation gives an exact sequence \(R^{\oplus m}\to R^{\oplus n}\to GX\to0\), showing that the image of \(G\) lies in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}_{\mathrm{fg}}\text{-}}R\).

On the other hand, since \(R\) is right Noetherian, every \(M\in\operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}_{\mathrm{fg}}\text{-}}R)\) can also be placed in an exact sequence \[R^{\oplus q} \to R^{\oplus p} \to M \to 0, \quad p, q \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}_{\geq 0}.\]

The rest of the proof follows the same idea as the proof of sufficiency in Theorem reference. In that argument, the compactness of \(s\) was used only to handle infinite direct sums; here only finite direct sums occur, and every additive functor preserves them. The remainder of the argument is identical and is not repeated.

Application: Descent of Modules

In geometry, given an adjoint pair \(\text{Diagram chapter7-unit-100-diagram-001}\), the process of reconstructing information on \(\mathcal{C}\) from comodules on \(\mathcal{D}\) under the coaction of the corresponding comonad is usually called descent. This section explains the case of module theory. Consider a homomorphism of commutative rings \(K\to L\). The corresponding forgetful functor \(\mathcal{F}_{L|K}:L\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\to K\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\) fits into the adjoint pair \[\text{Diagram chapter7-unit-100-d001}\] We apply the results from the second half of §reference to study the corresponding comonad on \(L\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\). More precisely, take \(\Bbbk=K\) and apply the “change of rings” construction of Example reference. Apart from notation, we use left rather than right modules here. Since only commutative rings are considered, this makes no substantive difference. Following the description in Example reference, denote the comonad determined on \(L\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\) by the adjoint pair by \((\mathbf{L},\delta,\epsilon)\), where \[\mathbf{L} = L \ensuremath{\underset{K}{\otimes}} \mathcal{F}_{L|K}(\cdot), \quad \delta: \mathbf{L} \to \mathbf{L}^2, \quad \epsilon: \mathbf{L} \to \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}.\] From now on, as usual, the forgetful functor \(\mathcal{F}_{L|K}\) will be omitted from formulas to simplify the notation. A comodule over the comonad \(\mathbf{L}\) is a datum \((M,a)\), where \(M\) is an \(L\)-module and \(a:M\to L\ensuremath{\underset{K}{\otimes}}M\) is an \(L\)-module homomorphism, subject to the requirement that the following diagrams commute: \[\text{Diagram chapter7-unit-100-d002} \quad \text{Diagram chapter7-unit-100-d003}\] All comodules \((M,a)\) over the comonad \(\mathbf{L}\) form a category \(L\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}^{\mathbf{L}}\). The dual of Lemma reference gives the factorization \[L \ensuremath{\underset{K}{\otimes}} (\cdot) = \left[ K\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}} \xrightarrow{\mathbb{K}} L\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}^{\mathbf{L}} \xrightarrow{U^{\mathbf{L}}} L\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}} \right] \; \text{as a composite}.\] The functor \(U^{\mathbf{L}}\) forgets the coaction, \((M,a)\mapsto M\), while \(\mathbb{K}\) maps an object \(N\) to \((L\ensuremath{\underset{K}{\otimes}}N,a)\), where \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:N-comonad-action}{} \begin{aligned} a: L \ensuremath{\underset{K}{\otimes}} N & \to L \ensuremath{\underset{K}{\otimes}} (L \ensuremath{\underset{K}{\otimes}} N) \quad \text{($L$-module homomorphism)} \\ \ell \otimes x & \mapsto \ell \otimes 1 \otimes x. \end{aligned} \end{equation}\] The central question is whether the adjoint pair is comonadic; equivalently, is \(\mathbb{K}\) an equivalence?

Definition. Given a homomorphism of commutative rings \(K\to L\), if \(L\ensuremath{\underset{K}{\otimes}}(\mathord\cdot):K\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\to L\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\) is a faithful exact functor, then \(L\), as a commutative \(K\)-algebra, is called faithfully flat.

Theorem (Flat descent). Let \(L\) be a faithfully flat commutative \(K\)-algebra. Then the adjoint pair \(\left(L\ensuremath{\underset{K}{\otimes}}(\mathord\cdot),\mathcal{F}_{L|K}\right)\) is comonadic. In this case, a quasi-inverse \(\mathbb{L}\) to \(K\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\xrightarrow{\mathbb{K}}L\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}^{\mathbf{L}}\) is described by the following equalizer diagram in \(K\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\): \[\text{Diagram chapter7-unit-100-d004} \quad (M, a) \in \operatorname{Ob}\left(L\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}^{\mathbf{L}}\right).\]

Proof. Proposition reference establishes comonadicity, while the dual of Theorem reference already contains the description of the quasi-inverse functor.

Remark. It must be emphasized that at the level of the derived categories \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}(K\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}})\) and \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}(L\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}})\), although the adjoint pair in question also has a derived version as in Example reference and Example reference, there is no corresponding descent theorem.

The proof of flat descent is surprisingly simple. In practice, however, the comonad or the descent data must be described in a usable form; this is the theme of §reference. In the remainder of this section we recast the definition of \(L\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}^{\mathbf{L}}\) in another form for easy comparison with the literature. In essence, this is a concrete rewriting of Proposition reference (in its left-module version, with \(P=L=P^\vee\)), though the procedure is somewhat circuitous. For \(i=1,2\), write \(\iota_i:L\to L\ensuremath{\underset{K}{\otimes}}L\) for the homomorphism that inserts an element into the \(i\)th tensor slot. For every \(L\)-module \(M\) there is a canonical isomorphism of \(L\)-modules \[\begin{align*} L \ensuremath{\underset{K}{\otimes}} M & \ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}(L \ensuremath{\underset{K}{\otimes}} L) \ensuremath{\underset{L, \iota_2}{\otimes}} M \\ \ell \otimes m & \mapsto \ell \otimes 1 \otimes m, \end{align*}\] where the right-hand side is made an \(L\)-module through \(\iota_1\). By the standard adjunction in module theory, specifying an \(L\)-module homomorphism \(a:M\to L\ensuremath{\underset{K}{\otimes}}M\) is therefore equivalent to specifying an \(L\ensuremath{\underset{K}{\otimes}}L\)-module homomorphism \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:flat-descent-map-aux}{}\begin{aligned} \tilde{a}: (L \ensuremath{\underset{K}{\otimes}} L) \ensuremath{\underset{L, \iota_1}{\otimes}} M & \to (L \ensuremath{\underset{K}{\otimes}} L) \ensuremath{\underset{L, \iota_2}{\otimes}} M \\ 1 \otimes 1 \otimes m & \mapsto \sum_{i=1}^n \ell_i \otimes 1 \otimes m_i ; \end{aligned} \end{equation}\] here \(a(m)=\sum_{i=1}^n\ell_i\otimes m_i\). Since \(\iota_1|_K=\iota_2|_K\), when \(M\) comes from a \(K\)-module \(N\), careful substitution from equation shows that \(\tilde a\) becomes \(\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}:L\ensuremath{\underset{K}{\otimes}}L\ensuremath{\underset{K}{\otimes}}N\to L\ensuremath{\underset{K}{\otimes}}L\ensuremath{\underset{K}{\otimes}}N\). For brevity, write \(L^{\otimes n}:=L\ensuremath{\underset{K}{\otimes}}\cdots\ensuremath{\underset{K}{\otimes}}L\) (with \(n\) factors). Temporarily forget \(L\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}^{\mathbf{L}}\) and consider an arbitrary \(\tilde a:L^{\otimes2}\ensuremath{\underset{L,\iota_1}{\otimes}}M\to L^{\otimes2}\ensuremath{\underset{L,\iota_2}{\otimes}}M\). By the universal property of the tensor product [Li1], specifying a pair of homomorphisms of commutative \(K\)-algebras \(f,g:L\to E\) is equivalent to specifying a homomorphism \(f\otimes g:L\ensuremath{\underset{K}{\otimes}}L\to E\). Thus \(\tilde a\) defines the following \(E\)-module homomorphism: \[\begin{equation*} \tilde{a}_{gf} := E \ensuremath{\underset{f \otimes g}{\otimes}} \tilde{a}: E \ensuremath{\underset{L, f}{\otimes}} M \to E \ensuremath{\underset{L, g}{\otimes}} M. \end{equation*}\] As \((E,f,g)\) varies, we want to analyze the compatibility among these homomorphisms. The formula above shows that \((E,f,g):=(L\ensuremath{\underset{K}{\otimes}}L,\iota_1,\iota_2)\) is “universal” for this problem and corresponds to \(\tilde a\), while a general \((E,f,g)\) is obtained by applying \(E\ensuremath{\underset{f\otimes g}{\otimes}}(\mathord\cdot)\) to it. To analyze the “universal” case, for \(1\leq i\neq j\leq3\) write:

\(\iota^3_{ij}: L^{\otimes 2} \to L^{\otimes 3}\) insertion into tensor slots \((i,j)\)
\(\iota^3_i: L \to L^{\otimes 3}\) insertion into the \(i\)th tensor slot

Using equation, define the \(L^{\otimes3}\)-module homomorphism \[\tilde{a}_{ji} := L^{\otimes 3} \ensuremath{\underset{L, \iota^3_{ij}}{\otimes}}\tilde{a} : \; L^{\otimes 3} \ensuremath{\underset{L, \iota^3_i}{\otimes}} M \to L^{\otimes 3} \ensuremath{\underset{L, \iota^3_j}{\otimes}} M.\] Here we use \(\iota^3_{ij}\iota_1=\iota^3_i\) and \(\iota^3_{ij}\iota_2=\iota^3_j\). When \(M\) comes from a \(K\)-module, we may identify \[\tilde{a} \;\text{with}\; \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{L^{\otimes 2} \ensuremath{\underset{K}{\otimes}} N}, \quad \tilde{a}_{ji} \;\text{with}\; \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{L^{\otimes 3} \ensuremath{\underset{K}{\otimes}} N}.\] Then \(\tilde a_{31}=\tilde a_{32}\tilde a_{21}\) is clear. This is the desired compatibility condition. Its important consequence is \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:cocycle-condition-descent}{} \tilde{a}_{31} = \tilde{a}_{32} \tilde{a}_{21} \implies \begin{array}{l} \forall f, g, h: L \xrightarrow{K\text{-algebra}} E, \\ \tilde{a}_{hf} = \tilde{a}_{hg} \tilde{a}_{gf}; \end{array} \end{equation}\] the left-hand side is the “universal version” of the right-hand side.

Definition (Descent datum). Define \(\mathrm{Desc}_{K\to L}\) to be the following category. Its objects are data \((M,\tilde a)\), where \(M\) is an \(L\)-module and \(\tilde a:L^{\otimes2}\ensuremath{\underset{L,\iota_1}{\otimes}}M\to L^{\otimes2}\ensuremath{\underset{L,\iota_2}{\otimes}}M\) satisfies

  • Isomorphism condition.\(\tilde a\) is an isomorphism of \(L^{\otimes2}\)-modules;

  • Cocycle condition.\(\tilde a_{31}=\tilde a_{32}\tilde a_{21}\).

A morphism from \((M,\tilde a)\) to \((M',\tilde a')\) is an \(L\)-module homomorphism \(f:M\to M'\) satisfying \((\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}^{\otimes2}\otimes f)\tilde a= \tilde a'(\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}^{\otimes2}\otimes f)\). Such data \((M,\tilde a)\) are called descent data.

The discussion before equation shows that \(L\ensuremath{\underset{K}{\otimes}}(\mathord\cdot)\) gives a functor \(K\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\to\mathrm{Desc}_{K\to L}\). We now relate descent data to \(L\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}^{\mathbf{L}}\).

Lemma. There is an isomorphism of categories from \(L\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}^{\mathbf{L}}\) to \(\mathrm{Desc}_{K\to L}\), given on objects by \((M,a)\leftrightarrow(M,\tilde a)\) and defined on morphisms in the standard way.

Moreover, the isomorphism condition in the definition of \(\mathrm{Desc}_{K\to L}\) may be replaced by the following condition: define \(m:L^{\otimes2}\to L\) by \(m(\ell\otimes\ell')=\ell\ell'\). The endomorphism \(M\to M\) given by \(L\ensuremath{\underset{L^{\otimes 2},m}{\otimes}}\tilde a\) is \(\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_M\).

Proof. Specifying \(\tilde a\) is known to be equivalent to specifying \(a:M\to L\ensuremath{\underset{K}{\otimes}}M\). The issue is to match the conditions on the descent datum \(\tilde a\) with the conditions on \(a\) that make \((M,a)\) a comodule. This is where the second assertion will be used.

The comodule conditions are the coassociativity and counit laws. For the first, the equivalence of \(\tilde a_{31}=\tilde a_{32}\tilde a_{21}\) with coassociativity is a mechanical verification left to the reader. For the second, write \(\varphi\) for the composite \(M\xrightarrow{a}L\ensuremath{\underset{K}{\otimes}}M\xrightarrow{\epsilon_M}M\). The counit law is equivalent to \(\varphi=\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}\). Recalling that \(\epsilon_M(\ell\otimes m)=\ell m\), a similar direct verification gives \[\varphi = L \ensuremath{\underset{L^{\otimes 2}, m}{\otimes}} \tilde{a}.\] We next show that, under the assumption \(\tilde a_{31}=\tilde a_{32}\tilde a_{21}\), the map \(\tilde a\) is an isomorphism if and only if \(\varphi=\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_M\). This will complete the proof.

Suppose \(\tilde a\) is an isomorphism. Then \(\varphi\) is also an isomorphism. In equation, take \(E=L\) and \(f=g=h=\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_L\). The right-hand side readily becomes \(\varphi=\varphi^2\), and hence \(\varphi=\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_M\).

Conversely, suppose \(\varphi=\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_M\). For every homomorphism of \(K\)-algebras \(f:L\to E\), change scalars on \(\tilde a\) along the two paths of the commutative diagram \[\text{Diagram chapter7-unit-100-d005}\] This shows that \(\tilde a_{ff}=\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}\). Together with equation, it follows that \(\tilde a_{fg}^{-1}=\tilde a_{gf}\) for every \((E,f,g)\). In particular, the “universal version” \(\tilde a\) is also an isomorphism. This proves the lemma.

Theorem (Second form of flat descent). Let \(L\) be a faithfully flat commutative \(K\)-algebra. Then \[L \ensuremath{\underset{K}{\otimes}} (\cdot): K\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}} \to \mathrm{Desc}_{K \to L}\] is an equivalence of categories. One of its quasi-inverses, \(\tilde{\mathbb{L}}\), may be taken to be the equalizer \[\text{Diagram chapter7-unit-100-d006}\] where \(a\) is the map corresponding to \(\tilde a\) under equation.

Proof. By Lemma reference, this is merely a reformulation of the flat descent Theorem reference.

Theorem reference is the usual formulation of flat descent in algebraic geometry. There a faithfully flat homomorphism \(K\to L\) corresponds, in a certain sense, to a covering of a geometric object. The datum \(\tilde a\), or the corresponding \(a\), is sometimes also expressed as a homomorphism of left \(L\ensuremath{\underset{K}{\otimes}}L\)-modules, that is, of \((L,L)\)-bimodules, \[\begin{align*} \overline{a}: M \ensuremath{\underset{K}{\otimes}} L & \to L \ensuremath{\underset{K}{\otimes}} M \\ m \otimes \ell & \mapsto \sum_{i=1}^n \ell_i \otimes \ell m_i, \end{align*}\] still assuming \(a(m)=\sum_{i=1}^n\ell_i\otimes m_i\). This is obtained by contracting the tensor products in equation in the appropriate way and has the advantage of a more compact form. A contracted version for \(\tilde a_{ji}\) is obtained similarly.

Remark (Flat descent for algebras and modules). We can go on to discuss how \(L\)-algebras, or modules over those algebras, descend to \(K\). Concretely, suppose \((M,a),(M',a')\in\operatorname{Ob}(L\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}^{\mathbf{L}})\) are the images of \(N,N'\in\operatorname{Ob}(K\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}})\). Recall that \(L\ensuremath{\underset{K}{\otimes}}(\mathord\cdot):K\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\to L\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\) is a monoidal functor [Li1]; that is, there are canonical isomorphisms such as \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:change-of-ring-monoidal}{}\begin{aligned} (L \ensuremath{\underset{K}{\otimes}} N_1) \ensuremath{\underset{L}{\otimes}} (L \ensuremath{\underset{K}{\otimes}} N_2) & \ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}L \ensuremath{\underset{K}{\otimes}} (N_1 \ensuremath{\underset{K}{\otimes}} N_2) \\ (\ell_1 \otimes x) \otimes (\ell_2 \otimes y) & \mapsto \ell_1 \ell_2 \otimes (x \otimes y). \end{aligned} \end{equation}\] Use this to give \(M\ensuremath{\underset{L}{\otimes}}M'\) the \(\mathbf{L}\)-comodule structure coming from \(N\ensuremath{\underset{K}{\otimes}}N'\). Now take \(N'=N\). Giving \(N\) a \(K\)-algebra structure is equivalent to giving \(M\) an \(L\)-algebra structure such that the multiplication \(M\ensuremath{\underset{L}{\otimes}}M\to M\) and unit \(L\to M\) are both morphisms in \(L\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}^{\mathbf{L}}\); all properties such as associativity required of a \(K\)-algebra come from \(M\). The descent of \(M\)-modules to \(N\)-modules should be understood in the same way. For this purpose, descent data of the form equation may be more convenient than comodules over \(\mathbf{L}\), because all the functors involved are monoidal on \(M\), whereas \(\mathbf{L}\) itself is not a monoidal functor.

Application: Galois Descent

In what follows, \(L|K\) is a Galois extension of fields. This is a useful special case of flat descent from §reference, called Galois descent. Our strategy is to describe the corresponding comonad directly. The only tools required are the form of flat descent in Theorem reference and its preliminaries; the deeper discussion in the second half of §reference is not needed. From now on, assume that \(K\) and \(L\) are fields and that \(L|K\) is a Galois extension. The modules considered above become vector spaces. Write \[\Gamma := \operatorname{Gal}(L|K), \quad \text{equipped with the Krull topology}.\] Background on the Krull topology can be found in [Li1]; when \(L|K\) is finite, this is just the discrete topology. In fact, \(\Gamma\) is a profinite group as introduced in §reference. A map \(f:\Gamma\to X\) is called smooth if, for every \(\sigma\in\Gamma\), there is an open subgroup \(\Gamma_0\) such that \(\sigma_0\in\Gamma_0\implies f(\sigma\sigma_0)=f(\sigma)\). Write \[\mathrm{Maps}(\Gamma, X)^\infty := \left\{ \text{smooth maps } f: \Gamma \to X \right\}.\]

Lemma. If \(f\in\mathrm{Maps}(\Gamma,X)^\infty\), there is an open normal subgroup \(\Gamma'\) such that \(f\) factors through \(\Gamma/\Gamma'\). In particular, \(f\) takes only finitely many values.

Proof. For every \(\sigma\in\Gamma\), there is an open subgroup \(\Gamma_0\), depending on \(\sigma\), such that \(f\) is constant on \(\sigma\Gamma_0\). These cosets form an open cover of \(\Gamma\). Since \(\Gamma\) is compact, there is a finite subcover \(\sigma_1\Gamma_{0,1},\ldots,\sigma_r\Gamma_{0,r}\). Now choose an open normal subgroup \(\Gamma'\) contained in \(\bigcap_{i=1}^r\Gamma_{0,i}\).

We use this to describe concretely the comonad \(\mathbf{L}:M\mapsto L\ensuremath{\underset{K}{\otimes}}M\) determined by \(L|K\) on \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Vect}}(L)\).

Lemma. For every \(L\)-vector space \(M\), give \(\mathrm{Maps}(\Gamma,M)^\infty\) the following \(L\)-vector space structure: if \(\ell\in L\), then \((\ell f)(\sigma)=\sigma(\ell)f(\sigma)\) for every \(\sigma\in\Gamma\). There is an isomorphism of \(L\)-vector spaces \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:comonad-smMap}{} \text{Diagram chapter7-unit-101-d001} \end{equation}\]

Proof. It is clear that \(\Phi(M)\) is well-defined (\(\operatorname{Stab}_\Gamma(\ell)\) is always open, so \(f\) is smooth), and it is \(L\)-linear by definition. It also commutes with arbitrary direct sums: \(\Phi(\bigoplus_iM_i)=\bigoplus_i\Phi(M_i)\) (every \(f\) takes only finitely many values, so \(\mathrm{Maps}(\Gamma,\mathord\cdot)^\infty\) commutes with arbitrary direct sums). Choosing a basis of \(M\), the verification of equation reduces to the special case \(M=L\), \[\text{Diagram chapter7-unit-101-d002}\]

For every finite Galois subextension \(L'|K\) of \(L|K\), write \(\Gamma':=\operatorname{Gal}(L|L')\). We claim that the same map as above gives \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:comonad-smMap-aux}{} L' \ensuremath{\underset{K}{\otimes}} L' \ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}\mathrm{Maps}(\Gamma/\Gamma', L') := \left\{\text{maps } f: \Gamma/\Gamma' \to L' \right\}. \end{equation}\] Once this is granted, since \(\mathrm{Maps}(\Gamma,L)^\infty= \bigcup_{L'|K}\mathrm{Maps}(\Gamma/\Gamma',L')\) (apply Lemma reference; enlarging \(L'\) amounts to shrinking \(\Gamma'\)), taking the union of both sides of equation over all \(L'|K\) shows that \(\Phi(L)\) is an isomorphism.

Choose \(\alpha\) such that \(L'=K(\alpha)\). Its minimal polynomial \(p\in K[X]\) splits over \(L'\) as \(\prod_{i=1}^d(X-\alpha_i)\), with \(\alpha_1=\alpha\) and no repeated roots. The group \(\Gamma/\Gamma'=\operatorname{Gal}(L'|K)\) is in bijection with \(\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_d\) by \(\sigma\mapsto\sigma(\alpha)\). Write \(\ell\in L'\) as \(g(\alpha)\) with \(g\in K[X]\). Then \[\text{Diagram chapter7-unit-101-d003}\] This proves equation.

Lemma. Under the canonical isomorphism of Lemma reference, the comonad \((\mathbf{L},\delta,\epsilon)\) is described by the following commutative diagram, where \(M\) is any \(L\)-vector space: \[\text{Diagram chapter7-unit-101-d004}\] where \(1:=1_\Gamma\).

Proof. The counit \(\epsilon_M:L\ensuremath{\underset{K}{\otimes}}M\to M\) is \(\ell\otimes m\mapsto\ell m\), which clearly corresponds under equation to \(f\mapsto f(1)\). The comultiplication \(\delta_M:L\ensuremath{\underset{K}{\otimes}}M\to L\ensuremath{\underset{K}{\otimes}}L\ensuremath{\underset{K}{\otimes}}M\) requires a little work. If \(f\in\mathrm{Maps}(\Gamma,M)^\infty\) corresponds to \(\ell\otimes m\), then the image of the latter under \(\delta_M\), namely \(\ell\otimes(1\otimes m)\), corresponds to the map \[\Gamma \ni \sigma \mapsto \sigma(\ell) \cdot \underbracket{\left[ \tau \mapsto m \right]}_{\in \mathrm{Maps}(\Gamma, M)^\infty} = \left[ \tau \mapsto \tau(\sigma(\ell))m \xlongequal{\text{\href{#eqn:comonad-smMap}{equation}}} f(\tau\sigma) \right].\] This proves the claim.

Definition. Suppose that the group \(\Gamma=\operatorname{Gal}(L|K)\) acts on the left on an \(L\)-vector space \(M\). The action is called semilinear if \(\sigma(m+m')=\sigma(m)+\sigma(m')\) and \(\sigma(tm)=\sigma(t)\sigma(m)\) for all \(\sigma\in\Gamma\), \(t\in L\), and \(m,m'\in M\). Define the category \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Vect}}^{\Gamma,\infty}(L)\) as follows.

  • Objects: \(L\)-vector spaces \(M\) with a smooth semilinear \(\Gamma\)-action. Smoothness means that \(\operatorname{Stab}_\Gamma(m)\) is an open subgroup of \(\Gamma\) for every \(m\in M\).

  • Morphisms: \(L\)-linear maps \(\varphi\) satisfying \(\varphi(\sigma m)=\sigma(\varphi(m))\), also called \(\Gamma\)-equivariant linear maps.

Return to the comonad \(\mathbf{L}\) determined by the Galois extension \(L|K\). Its category of comodules is denoted \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Vect}}(L)^{\mathbf{L}}\).

Lemma. With the notation above, there is an isomorphism of categories \[\ensuremath{\mathsf{Vect}}(L)^{\mathbf{L}} \simeq \ensuremath{\mathsf{Vect}}^{\Gamma, \infty}(L).\] If \(M\) is an object of \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Vect}}^{\Gamma,\infty}(L)\), the corresponding object in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Vect}}(L)^{\mathbf{L}}\) is \((M,a)\), where \(a\) is characterized by the fact that the composite \[M \xrightarrow{a} L \ensuremath{\underset{K}{\otimes}} M \xrightarrow[\sim]{\Phi(M)} \mathrm{Maps}(\Gamma, M)^\infty\] maps \(m\in M\) to the map \([\sigma\mapsto\sigma m]\) from \(\Gamma\) to \(M\).

Proof. First observe that \(\mathrm{Maps}(\Gamma,\mathord\cdot)^\infty\) is a functor: every map \(\varphi:M_1\to M_2\) induces \(\mathrm{Maps}(\Gamma,M_1)^\infty\to \mathrm{Maps}(\Gamma,M_2)^\infty\), mapping \(f\) to \(\varphi f\).

Next, use Lemma reference to rewrite and combine the two commutative diagrams defining a comodule into \[\text{Diagram chapter7-unit-101-d005}\] where \(a'\) corresponds to \(a\). Specifying an \(L\)-linear map \(a':M\to\mathrm{Maps}(\Gamma,M)^\infty\) is equivalent to specifying a map \(\beta:\Gamma\times M\to M\) such that

  • \(\beta(\sigma,m+m')=\beta(\sigma,m)+\beta(\sigma,m')\) and \(\beta(\sigma,tm)=\sigma(t)\beta(\sigma,m)\), with \(t\in L\);

  • for every \(m\in M\) and \(\sigma\in\Gamma\), there is an open subgroup \(\Gamma_0\) such that \(\sigma_0\in\Gamma_0\implies \beta(\sigma\sigma_0,m)=\beta(\sigma,m)\).

The concrete correspondence is, of course, \(\beta(\sigma,m)=a'(m)(\sigma)\). The commutative diagram above then translates into \[\beta(\tau\sigma, m) = \beta(\tau, \beta(\sigma, m)), \quad \beta(1, m) = m.\]

At the level of objects, these conditions are precisely those of a smooth semilinear action of \(\Gamma\). The verification on morphisms is immediate.

Lemma. If \((M,a)\in\operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Vect}}(L)^{\mathbf{L}})\) comes from a \(K\)-vector space \(N\), then the corresponding object of \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Vect}}^{\Gamma,\infty}(L)\) is \(L\ensuremath{\underset{K}{\otimes}}N\) with the smooth semilinear action \[\sigma (\ell \otimes x) = \sigma(\ell) \otimes x, \quad \ell \in L, \; x \in N, \quad \sigma \in \Gamma.\]

Proof. We have \(M=L\ensuremath{\underset{K}{\otimes}}N\). By equation, the homomorphism \(a\) maps \(\ell\otimes x\) to \(\ell\otimes1\otimes x\). The characterization of the semilinear action therefore gives \[\sigma (\ell \otimes x) = \Phi(M)(\ell \otimes (1 \otimes x))(\sigma) = \sigma(\ell) (1 \otimes x) = \sigma(\ell) \otimes x,\] for arbitrary \(\ell\in L\) and \(x\in N\). This proves the lemma.

Take \((M,a)\in\operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Vect}}(L)^{\mathbf{L}})\). Since \(\Phi(M)(1\otimes m)(\sigma)=\sigma(1)m=m\), the description of \(a\) in Lemma reference extends to the following commutative diagram in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Vect}}(K)\): \[\text{Diagram chapter7-unit-101-d006}\] Thus the equalizer in Theorem reference is the operation of taking \(\Gamma\)-invariants, \[M^\Gamma := \left\{ m \in M: \forall \sigma \in \Gamma, \; \sigma m = m \right\}.\] Notice that \(M\mapsto M^\Gamma\) gives a \(K\)-linear functor between \(K\)-linear categories, \[(\cdot)^{\Gamma}: \ensuremath{\mathsf{Vect}}^{\Gamma, \infty}(L) \to \ensuremath{\mathsf{Vect}}(K).\]

Theorem (Galois descent). Let \(L|K\) be a Galois extension of fields and let \(\Gamma=\operatorname{Gal}(L|K)\). Then the functor \[\text{Diagram chapter7-unit-101-d007}\] is an equivalence of categories. A quasi-inverse may be taken to be \((\mathord\cdot)^\Gamma:\ensuremath{\mathsf{Vect}}^{\Gamma,\infty}(L) \to\ensuremath{\mathsf{Vect}}(K)\).

Proof. Clearly \(L\) is a faithfully flat \(K\)-algebra. Lemma reference and the preceding description of the equalizer reduce the assertion to the flat descent Theorem reference.

Let us view Theorem reference from another angle. For every \(M\in\operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Vect}}^{\Gamma,\infty}(L))\), define \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:Galois-descent-iotaM}{} \iota_M: L \ensuremath{\underset{K}{\otimes}} (M^{\Gamma}) \to M, \quad \ell \otimes x \mapsto \ell x . \end{equation}\] This is clearly a \(\Gamma\)-equivariant linear map. There is a simple adjoint pair \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:Galois-descent-adjunction}{} \text{Diagram chapter7-unit-101-d008} \end{equation}\]

  • It is easy to see that the unit of the adjunction \(N\to(L\ensuremath{\underset{K}{\otimes}}N)^\Gamma\) maps \(x\) to \(1\otimes x\). This is an isomorphism: choose a basis \(B\) of \(N\). An element \(\sum_{b\in B}\ell_b\otimes b\) (a finite sum) of \(L\ensuremath{\underset{K}{\otimes}}N\) is \(\Gamma\)-invariant if and only if each \(\ell_b\) is invariant; equivalently, \(\sum_b\ell_b\otimes b=1\otimes\sum_b\ell_b b\in N\).

  • The counit morphism is precisely the previously defined \(\iota_M\).

    If \(M=L\ensuremath{\underset{K}{\otimes}}N\), the preceding item gives \(L\ensuremath{\underset{K}{\otimes}}(M^\Gamma)=L\ensuremath{\underset{K}{\otimes}}(1\otimes N)\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}} L\ensuremath{\underset{K}{\otimes}}N=M\), so \(\iota_M\) is an isomorphism in this case.

Once Theorem reference is accepted, every \(M\) comes from some \(N\), so the discussion above shows that \((L\ensuremath{\underset{K}{\otimes}}(\mathord\cdot),(\mathord\cdot)^\Gamma)\) is an adjoint equivalence. Conversely, if \(\iota_M\) can be shown to be an isomorphism for every \(M\), the Galois descent Theorem reference follows anew. Although the proof by flat descent has a natural conceptual flow, it is admittedly indirect. The exercises will give a direct method for proving that \(\iota_M\) is an isomorphism; the technique is also useful elsewhere.

Remark (Galois descent for algebras and modules). Let \(N_1,N_2\in\operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Vect}}(K))\). Under equation, the natural semilinear \(\Gamma\)-action on \(L\ensuremath{\underset{K}{\otimes}}(N_1\ensuremath{\underset{K}{\otimes}}N_2)\) becomes the “diagonal action” on \((L\ensuremath{\underset{K}{\otimes}}N_1)\ensuremath{\underset{L}{\otimes}}(L\ensuremath{\underset{K}{\otimes}}N_2)\), namely the simultaneous action on both tensor slots. Specifying a \(K\)-algebra \(N\) is equivalent to specifying an \(L\)-algebra structure on \(M:=L\ensuremath{\underset{K}{\otimes}}N\) such that its algebra operations are compatible with the semilinear \(\Gamma\)-action: \[\sigma(1_M) = 1_M , \quad \sigma (xy) = \sigma(x) \sigma(y).\] Modules over \(K\)-algebras should be understood in the same way. This is analogous to the idea of Remark reference.

The Relation between Galois Descent and \(\operatorname{H}^1\)

Descent is a powerful method for classifying various algebraic or geometric objects; its general formulation requires the language of algebraic geometry. For ease of exposition, we make two simplifying assumptions in this section.

  1. We use only Galois descent (Theorem reference and the discussion following it), rather than flat descent or more general techniques.

  2. As far as possible, this book uses algebraic language, especially that of linear algebra, to explain the examples. We must therefore narrow the scope of the classification problem. In fact, we shall consider only a certain class of tensors in finite-dimensional vector spaces.

This viewpoint naturally leads to the nonabelian cohomology \(\operatorname{H}^1\) of the Galois group. The discussion below draws on the tools of §reference and §reference. Since we need to allow infinite Galois extensions, we shall also continue to use the language of profinite groups; see §reference. We first introduce the necessary notation.

Convention. Throughout this section, fix a field \(K\) and write \(\otimes:=\otimes_K\). For a finite-dimensional \(K\)-vector space \(V\), write \(V^\vee\) for its dual space. For each \((p,q)\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}_{\geq0}^2\), introduce the notation \[T^{p,q}V:=V^{\otimes p}\otimes(V^\vee)^{\otimes q}.\] Following the convention of differential geometry, the elements of \(T^{p,q}V\) are called tensors of type \((p,q)\) on \(V\).

Every isomorphism \(g:V\to V'\) between finite-dimensional \(K\)-vector spaces naturally induces an isomorphism \(T^{p,q}V\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}T^{p,q}V'\); for convenience, this induced isomorphism is still denoted by \(g\). Moreover, finite dimensionality gives a canonical isomorphism \((V_1\otimes V_2)^\vee\simeq V_1^\vee\otimes V_2^\vee\). In the classification problems considered in this section, the principal objects are data of the following form, defined over the field \(K\): \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:tensor-data}{} \mathbf{t}=(V,I,(t_i,p_i,q_i)_{i\in I}), \end{equation}\] where

  • \(V\) is a finite-dimensional \(K\)-vector space;

  • \(I\) is a set (which may be empty);

  • \((p_i,q_i)\) is a family of pairs of nonnegative integers, indexed by \(i\in I\);

  • \(t_i\in T^{p_i,q_i}V\) is a family of tensors, indexed by \(i\in I\).

In other words, we study a family of tensors of specified types in a finite-dimensional vector space. Given another datum \[\mathbf{t}'=(V',I,(t'_i,p_i,q_i)_{i\in I}),\] if there is an isomorphism of \(K\)-vector spaces \(g:V\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}V'\) such that \(gt_i=t'_i\) for every \(i\), then \(g\) is called an isomorphism between the two data, and we write \[g\mathbf{t}=\mathbf{t}'\quad\text{or}\quad g:\mathbf{t}\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}\mathbf{t}'.\] We wish to classify such data \(\mathbf{t}\) up to isomorphism, or more specifically to classify those \(\mathbf{t}\) satisfying additional conditions. These conditions must be algebraically expressible and preserved by isomorphisms. Although the theoretical framework is confined to linear algebra, its range of applications is already quite broad. Here are several special cases.

  1. Consider data \((V,b)\), where \(b\in(V^\vee)^{\otimes2}\) is a tensor of type \((0,2)\). Classifying these data is equivalent to classifying bilinear forms on \(V\). We may also impose conditions such as symmetry, antisymmetry, or nondegeneracy on \(b\); all of these are “algebraic” conditions. Multilinear forms may be treated similarly.

  2. We may also classify \((V,\varphi_1,\ldots,\varphi_n)\), where \(\varphi_i\in V\otimes V^\vee\) is a tensor of type \((1,1)\). Since \(V\otimes V^\vee\simeq\operatorname{End}_K(V)\), this amounts to classifying \(V\) together with a family of linear endomorphisms. Various algebraic relations may be imposed, such as commutativity among the endomorphisms.

  3. Next consider data \((V,\mu)\), where \(\mu\in V\otimes(V^\vee)^{\otimes2}\) is a tensor of type \((1,2)\), which may also be regarded as an element of \(\operatorname{Hom}_K(V\otimes V,V)\). This amounts to classifying \(V\) together with a bilinear “multiplication” \(V\times V\to V\). If the operation is required to be associative and to have a unit (the latter may be regarded as a tensor of type \((1,0)\)), these conditions make \(V\) into a \(K\)-algebra. Other conditions may be imposed on \(\mu\) in order to study structures such as Lie algebras and Jordan algebras.

More generally, equation can be extended in a natural way to treat the classification of a family of vector subspaces, or at least lines, in \(T^{p,q}V\). We shall not pursue this because of space constraints.

Definition. For a finite-dimensional \(K\)-vector space \(V\), write \(\operatorname{GL}(V)\) for its group of linear automorphisms. For data \(\mathbf{t}\) as in equation, define the subgroup of \(\operatorname{GL}(V)\) \[G(\mathbf{t}):=\{g\in\operatorname{GL}(V):g\mathbf{t}=\mathbf{t}\}.\]

Choose a basis for \(V\) and write the conditions \(gt_i=t_i\) in coordinates for every \(i\in I\). Thus \(G(\mathbf{t})\) is cut out inside \(\operatorname{GL}(V)\) by a family of polynomial equations. In the examples above, if \(\mathbf{t}\) corresponds to a nondegenerate symmetric (respectively, antisymmetric) bilinear form \(b:V\times V\to K\), then the corresponding \(G(\mathbf{t})\) is the orthogonal group \(\mathrm{O}(V,b)\) (respectively, the symplectic group \(\mathrm{Sp}(V,b)\)). If \(\mathbf{t}\) is the tensor of type \((0,\dim V)\) given by the determinant, then the corresponding group is the special linear group \(\operatorname{SL}(V):=\{g:\det g=1\}\).

Definition. For every field extension \(L|K\) and \(K\)-vector space \(V\), write \(V_L:=L\ensuremath{\underset{K}{\otimes}}V\), regarded as an \(L\)-vector space. Through the canonical isomorphism of \(L\)-vector spaces \[(T^{p,q}V)_L\simeq T^{p,q}(V_L),\] every datum \(\mathbf{t}\) on \(V\) of the form equation induces a datum \(\mathbf{t}_L\) on \(V_L\), defined over the extension field \(L\).

Field extension does not change the numerical part of the data, \((\dim V,I,(p_i,q_i)_i)\). Recall that when \(L|K\) is a Galois extension, \(\operatorname{Gal}(L|K)\) acts smoothly and semilinearly on \(V_L\) (Lemma reference); we write the action on the left. In fact, it acts smoothly and semilinearly on every \(T^{p,q}(V_L)\) (Definition reference), “diagonally” on tensor products and by \(\check v\mapsto\check v\sigma^{-1}\) on the dual space \(V^\vee\) (the contragredient action, or “inverse step”). Relative to the isomorphism above, its invariant subspace is \[T^{p,q}(V_L)^{\operatorname{Gal}(L|K)}=T^{p,q}V.\] This is precisely Galois descent at the level of objects. At the level of morphisms, it is expressed by the following result.

Lemma. Let \(V\) and \(W\) be finite-dimensional \(K\)-vector spaces. For every \(h\in\operatorname{Hom}_L(V_L,W_L)\) and \(\sigma\in\operatorname{Gal}(L|K)\), define \[{}^\sigma h:=\sigma h\sigma^{-1}:V_L\to W_L.\] This map is again \(L\)-linear. The formula gives a smooth semilinear action of \(\operatorname{Gal}(L|K)\) on the \(L\)-vector space \(\operatorname{Hom}_L(V_L,W_L)\). This action is compatible with composition of linear maps, and \[\operatorname{Hom}_L(V_L,W_L)^{\operatorname{Gal}(L|K)}=\operatorname{Hom}_K(V,W).\] Here \(\operatorname{Hom}_K(V,W)\) is embedded in \(\operatorname{Hom}_L(V_L,W_L)\) by \(f\mapsto f_L:=\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_L\otimes f\).

Proof. The reader may check directly that \({}^\sigma h\) is indeed \(L\)-linear. For smoothness, choose bases of \(V\) and \(W\) and identify the elements of \(\operatorname{Hom}_L(V_L,W_L)\) with matrices. Then \(\operatorname{Gal}(L|K)\) acts in the standard way on every matrix entry. Since \(h\) involves only finitely many matrix entries, they are all contained in some finite subextension \(E|K\) of \(L|K\). Hence the open subgroup \(\operatorname{Gal}(L|E)\) fixes \(h\). The remaining assertions about the action \((\sigma,h)\mapsto{}^\sigma h\) are readily verified.

The equality \(\operatorname{Hom}_L(V_L,W_L)^{\operatorname{Gal}(L|K)}=\operatorname{Hom}_K(V,W)\) follows directly from Galois descent and is also easy to see directly from matrices.

Taking the special case \(V=W\), we see that \(\operatorname{Gal}(L|K)\) acts on \(\operatorname{GL}(V_L)\) by \((\sigma,g)\mapsto{}^\sigma g\), and that \(\operatorname{GL}(V_L)^{\operatorname{Gal}(L|K)}=\operatorname{GL}(V)\).

Lemma. For data \(\mathbf{t}\) of the form equation, the smooth action of \(\operatorname{Gal}(L|K)\) on \(\operatorname{GL}(V_L)\) preserves \(G(\mathbf{t}_L)\). Thus \(G(\mathbf{t}_L)\) becomes a smooth \(\operatorname{Gal}(L|K)\)-group in the sense of Remark reference; its invariant subgroup satisfies \[G(\mathbf{t}_L)^{\operatorname{Gal}(L|K)}=G(\mathbf{t}).\]

Proof. Let \(g\in G(\mathbf{t}_L)\) and \(\sigma\in\operatorname{Gal}(L|K)\). Then \[({}^\sigma g)\mathbf{t}_L =({}^\sigma g)(\sigma\mathbf{t}_L) =\sigma g\sigma^{-1}(\sigma\mathbf{t}_L) =\sigma(g\mathbf{t}_L) =\sigma(\mathbf{t}_L) =\mathbf{t}_L.\] Thus the action of \(\operatorname{Gal}(L|K)\) preserves \(G(\mathbf{t}_L)\). The remaining assertions follow immediately.

In practice, the classification of data equation usually becomes simpler after extending scalars to a sufficiently large field \(L\). For example, the isomorphism class of a nondegenerate quadratic form over an algebraically closed field is completely determined by its dimension, whereas the situation is more complicated over a general field such as \(\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}\), \(\ensuremath{\mathbb{Q}}_p\), or \(\ensuremath{\mathbb{Q}}\). Conditions imposed in the classification problems above, such as nondegeneracy or associativity of multiplication, can usually be checked after any field extension. The problem therefore splits into two parts:

  1. Over a sufficiently large field \(L\), classify data of the form equation satisfying the desired conditions; a typical choice is to take \(L\) to be a separably closed field.

  2. Choose data \(\mathbf{t}_0\) defined over \(K\), take a sufficiently large Galois extension \(L|K\), and study the data \(\mathbf{t}\) satisfying \(\mathbf{t}_L\simeq\mathbf{t}_{0,L}\).

The first part may be called geometric, while the second is arithmetic. This section focuses on the arithmetic part, which motivates the following definition.

Definition. Let \(\mathbf{t}_0\) be data of the form equation defined over the field \(K\), and let \(L|K\) be a Galois extension. Set \[\mathcal{T}(\mathbf{t}_0):= \left\{ \begin{array}{r|l} \mathbf{t}:\text{ data of the form \href{#eqn:tensor-data}{equation}} & \text{there exists an isomorphism }h:\mathbf{t}_{0,L}\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}\mathbf{t}_L \\ \text{defined over the field $K$}& \end{array} \right\}.\] Also write \(\mathscr{T}(\mathbf{t}_0):=\mathcal{T}(\mathbf{t}_0)/\simeq\).

This definition requires only the existence of an isomorphism \(h\), without specifying a choice; any two choices differ by right multiplication by an element of \(G(\mathbf{t}_{0,L})\). Write \[\Gamma:=\operatorname{Gal}(L|K),\qquad\text{equipped with the Krull topology}.\] If \(\sigma\in\Gamma\) and \(h:\mathbf{t}_{0,L}\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}\mathbf{t}_L\) (that is, \(h(\mathbf{t}_{0,L})=\mathbf{t}_L\)), then \[{}^\sigma h(\mathbf{t}_{0,L}) ={}^\sigma h(\sigma\mathbf{t}_{0,L}) =\sigma(h(\mathbf{t}_{0,L})) =\sigma(\mathbf{t}_L) =\mathbf{t}_L.\] Consequently, there is a unique map \(c:\Gamma\to G(\mathbf{t}_{0,L})\) such that \[{}^\sigma h=hc(\sigma),\qquad \sigma\in\operatorname{Gal}(L|K).\] From \({}^{\sigma\tau}h={}^\sigma(hc(\tau))={}^\sigma h\cdot {}^\sigma c(\tau)=h\cdot c(\sigma)\cdot{}^\sigma c(\tau)\), we obtain \[c(\sigma\tau)=c(\sigma)\cdot{}^\sigma c(\tau), \qquad \sigma,\tau\in\Gamma.\] Without loss of generality, suppose that \(\mathbf{t}_0\) and \(\mathbf{t}\) are realized on spaces \(V\) and \(W\), respectively, so that \(h\in\operatorname{Hom}_L(V_L,W_L)\). Since the action of \(\Gamma\) is smooth, there is an open subgroup \(\Gamma_0\subset\Gamma\) that fixes \(h\); consequently, \(c\) factors through \(\Gamma/\Gamma_0\). If the choice of \(h\) is changed to \(h'=ha\), where \(a\in G(\mathbf{t}_{0,L})\), then the corresponding \(c'\) satisfies \[c'(\sigma)=(h')^{-1}\cdot{}^\sigma h' =a^{-1}\cdot h^{-1}\cdot{}^\sigma h\cdot{}^\sigma a =a^{-1}\cdot c(\sigma)\cdot{}^\sigma a.\] Comparing these observations one by one with Definition reference of nonabelian \(\operatorname{H}^1\), and using Remark reference for the profinite version, we obtain a map \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:Galois-H1-prep}{} \begin{aligned} \mathcal{T}(\mathbf{t}_0)&\longrightarrow \operatorname{H}^1\left(\Gamma,G(\mathbf{t}_{0,L})\right),\\ \mathbf{t}&\longmapsto[c]:=\text{the equivalence class of }c. \end{aligned} \end{equation}\] This map is canonical and independent of all auxiliary choices. Recall also that \(\operatorname{H}^1\left(\Gamma,G(\mathbf{t}_{0,L})\right)\) is generally not a group, but a pointed set whose base point is represented by the constant map \(\Gamma\to G(\mathbf{t}_{0,L})\) with value the identity automorphism \(1\). On the other hand, \(\mathcal{T}(\mathbf{t}_0)\) has the obvious base point \(\mathbf{t}_0\), as does its quotient \(\mathscr{T}(\mathbf{t}_0)\). The map equation clearly preserves base points, as one sees by taking \(h=\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}\).

Theorem. For data \(\mathbf{t}_0\) and a Galois extension \(L|K\) as above, with \(\Gamma:=\operatorname{Gal}(L|K)\), the map equation induces a base-point-preserving bijection \[\mathscr{T}(\mathbf{t}_0)\;\xrightarrow{1:1}\; \operatorname{H}^1\left(\Gamma,G(\mathbf{t}_{0,L})\right).\]

Proof. First we show that equation factors through \(\mathscr{T}(\mathbf{t}_0)\). Let \(f:\mathbf{t}\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}\mathbf{t}'\), so that \(f_L:\mathbf{t}_L\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}\mathbf{t}'_L\). From \(h:\mathbf{t}_{0,L}\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}\mathbf{t}_L\) we obtain \(f_Lh:\mathbf{t}_{0,L}\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}\mathbf{t}'_L\). Since \({}^\sigma f_L=f_L\), we have \((f_Lh)^{-1}\cdot{}^\sigma(f_Lh)=h^{-1}\cdot{}^\sigma h\), and hence the corresponding \(c\) is unchanged.

Next we show that \(\mathscr{T}(\mathbf{t}_0)\to \operatorname{H}^1\left(\Gamma,G(\mathbf{t}_{0,L})\right)\) is injective. Suppose that data \(\mathbf{t}\) and \(\mathbf{t}'\) and isomorphisms \[\mathbf{t}'_L\xleftarrow[\sim]{h'}\mathbf{t}_{0,L} \xrightarrow[\sim]{h}\mathbf{t}_L,\] are given, and that there is an \(a\in G(\mathbf{t}_{0,L})\) satisfying \[(h')^{-1}\cdot{}^\sigma h' =a^{-1}\cdot h^{-1}\cdot{}^\sigma h\cdot{}^\sigma a, \qquad\sigma\in\Gamma.\] Consequently, \[ha(h')^{-1} ={}^\sigma h\cdot{}^\sigma a\cdot{}^\sigma(h')^{-1}, \qquad\sigma\in\Gamma.\] In other words, \(ha(h')^{-1}:\mathbf{t}'_L\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}\mathbf{t}_L\) is invariant under the \(\Gamma\)-action and therefore descends to an isomorphism \(\mathbf{t}'\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}\mathbf{t}\).

Finally, we show that \(\mathscr{T}(\mathbf{t}_0)\to \operatorname{H}^1\left(\Gamma,G(\mathbf{t}_{0,L})\right)\) is surjective. Take \(c\in Z^1(\Gamma,G(\mathbf{t}_{0,L}))\). Since \(c(\sigma)\in\operatorname{GL}(V_L)\), we may use it to define a new \(\Gamma\)-action, denoted by \(\odot\), on \(V_L\): \[\sigma\odot v:=c(\sigma)(\sigma v), \qquad\sigma\in\Gamma,\quad v\in V_L.\]

From \(c(\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}})=1\) and \[\sigma\odot(\tau\odot v) =c(\sigma)\sigma(c(\tau)(\tau v)) =c(\sigma)\bigl({}^\sigma c(\tau)(\sigma\tau v)\bigr) =(\sigma\tau)\odot v,\] it follows that \(\odot\) is indeed a \(\Gamma\)-action, while the smoothness of \(c\) ensures that \(\odot\) is still a smooth semilinear action. Define the \(K\)-vector space \(W:=(V_L)^{\Gamma,\;\odot\text{-action}}\). By Galois descent, we obtain an isomorphism of \(L\)-vector spaces that preserves the semilinear \(\Gamma\)-actions, \[\begin{gather*} h:(V_L,\;\odot\text{-action})\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}} (W_L,\;\text{natural action}),\\ w\in W\implies h(w)=1\otimes w. \end{gather*}\]

On the other hand, \(\Gamma\) also acts semilinearly through \(\odot\) on each \(T^{p,q}(V_L)\) (see the discussion following Definition reference), and because \(c(\sigma)\in G(\mathbf{t}_{0,L})\), we have \[\sigma\odot\mathbf{t}_{0,L} =c(\sigma)(\sigma\mathbf{t}_{0,L}) =c(\sigma)\mathbf{t}_{0,L} =\mathbf{t}_{0,L}.\] Thus, relative to \(\odot\), the datum \(\mathbf{t}_{0,L}\) descends to a datum \(\mathbf{t}\) on \(W\), characterized by \(h(\mathbf{t}_{0,L})=\mathbf{t}_L\).

It follows that \(\mathbf{t}\in\mathcal{T}(\mathbf{t}_0)\). The corresponding isomorphism \(h\) satisfies \(\sigma(h(v))=h(\sigma\odot v)=(hc(\sigma)\sigma)(v)\), that is, the identity \(\sigma h=hc(\sigma)\sigma\). Rewriting this as \(h^{-1}\cdot{}^\sigma h=c(\sigma)\) shows that \(\mathbf{t}\) maps to \([c]\) under equation. This proves the assertion.

The simplest and most direct application is the following. It follows from the general fact that every finite-dimensional vector space has a basis, so that dimension determines the isomorphism class of a finite-dimensional vector space.

Theorem (Hilbert’s Theorem 90: the \(\operatorname{GL}\) version). Let \(V\) be a finite-dimensional \(K\)-vector space and let \(L|K\) be a Galois extension. Thus \(\Gamma:=\operatorname{Gal}(L|K)\) acts smoothly on the group \(\operatorname{GL}(V_L)\). Then \[\operatorname{H}^1(\Gamma,\operatorname{GL}(V_L))=1.\]

Proof. Apply Theorem reference, but take data \(\mathbf{t}_0\) with \(I=\emptyset\). In other words, the data specify only a finite-dimensional \(K\)-vector space \(V\), with no tensors. In this case, the elements of \(\mathscr{T}(\mathbf{t}_0)\) correspond bijectively to the isomorphism classes of \(K\)-vector spaces \(W\) satisfying \(W_L\simeq V_L\), equivalently \(\dim W=\dim V\). Clearly, there is only one such isomorphism class.

Similarly, over a field of characteristic \(\neq2\), the general fact that every symplectic space \((V,\omega)\) has a symplectic basis leads to the following result.

Theorem. Let \(\mathrm{char}(K)\neq2\), let \(V\) be a \(K\)-vector space, and let \(\omega:V\times V\to K\) be a nondegenerate antisymmetric bilinear form (also called a symplectic form, while the datum \((V,\omega)\) is called a symplectic space). The corresponding symplectic group is defined by \[\begin{align*} \operatorname{Sp}(V)&=\operatorname{Sp}(V,\omega)\\ &:=\{g\in\operatorname{GL}(V):\forall v_1,v_2\in V,\; \omega(gv_1,gv_2)=\omega(v_1,v_2)\}. \end{align*}\]

Let \(L|K\) be a Galois extension. Define the group \(\operatorname{Sp}(V_L)\) and the action of \(\Gamma:=\operatorname{Gal}(L|K)\) on it similarly; this action is smooth. Then \[\operatorname{H}^1(\Gamma,\operatorname{Sp}(V_L))=1.\]

Proof. The data \(\mathbf{t}_0\) under consideration consist of the space \(V\) and the tensor \(\omega\) of type \((0,2)\). The nondegeneracy and antisymmetry of a bilinear form can be checked after any field extension. Therefore the elements of \(\mathscr{T}(\mathbf{t}_0)\) correspond bijectively to the isomorphism classes of symplectic spaces \((W,\eta)\) over \(K\) satisfying \((W_L,\eta_L)\simeq(V_L,\omega_L)\). By the structure theorem for symplectic spaces—namely, that their dimension determines their isomorphism class—such data \((W,\eta)\) form a single isomorphism class.

Example. Take \(\dim V=1\) in Theorem reference. Since \(\operatorname{GL}(V_L)\simeq L^\times\) with the standard \(\Gamma\)-action, we obtain \[\operatorname{H}^1(\Gamma,L^\times)=0.\] Since \(L^\times\) is abelian, additive notation is used in this equation. If \(L|K\) is finite, it can be written in terms of the Tate cohomology of Definition reference as \(\ensuremath{\hat{\mathrm{H}}}^1(\Gamma,L^\times)=0\).

If \(L|K\) is further assumed to be cyclic, the periodicity stated in Example reference gives \[\ensuremath{\hat{\mathrm{H}}}^{-1}(\Gamma,L^\times) \simeq\ensuremath{\hat{\mathrm{H}}}^1(\Gamma,L^\times)=0.\] Thus we naturally recover the multiplicative version of Hilbert’s Theorem 90; see [Li1].

In general, directly computing \(\operatorname{H}^1\) in order to classify mathematical objects may be rather difficult. Its value lies in the new perspective that it provides, as well as in the availability of cohomological tools such as the long exact sequence (Theorem reference) for studying classification problems.

Exercises

Complete the argument omitted from Definition reference, and prove that for an algebra \(A\) over a symmetric monoidal category \(\mathcal{V}\), a left \(A\)-module is the same thing as a right \(A^{\operatorname{op}}\)-module.

Let \(\mathcal{V}\) be a braided monoidal category and let \((A,\mu_A,\eta_A)\) be an algebra over it. Prove that if there are morphisms \(\mu':A\otimes A\to A\) and \(\eta':\ensuremath{\bm{1}}\to A\) in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Alg}}(\mathcal{V})\) that make \(A\) into an algebra over \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Alg}}(\mathcal{V})\), then necessarily \(\eta'=\eta_A\) and \(\mu'=\mu_A\). In particular, Lemma reference then shows that \(A\) is commutative. Deduce equation. Hint. It is easy to show that \(\eta'=\eta_A\). For \(\mu'=\mu_A\), write \(\mu_{A\otimes A}\) for the multiplication on \(A\otimes A\). The assumption gives the commutative diagram \[\text{Diagram chapter7-unit-103-d001}\] If the four copies of \(A\) are placed in a \(2\times2\) array, this commutative diagram can be visualized as the interchange law between horizontal and vertical multiplication:

Vertical: multiply using \(\mu_A\)

The argument for \(\mu'=\mu_A\) can now be pictured as

Try also to translate this picture into the corresponding commutative diagram or equation.

Consider a dg-algebra \(A\) over \(\mathcal{A}\) (Definition reference). Verify that when \(A=\ensuremath{\bm{1}}\) (the unit object), both left and right \(A\)-modules reduce to complexes over \(\mathcal{A}\).

Fix a commutative ring \(\Bbbk\). Let \(A\) be a dg-algebra over \(\Bbbk\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\) and let \(M\) be a complex. Prove that giving \(M\) the structure of a left \(A\)-module is equivalent to specifying a homomorphism of dg-algebras \(A\to\operatorname{End}^\bullet(M):=\operatorname{Hom}^\bullet(M,M)\).

Let \(\Bbbk\) be a commutative ring and \(R\) a dg-algebra over \(\Bbbk\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\). For a right \(R\)-module \(X\) and a left \(R\)-module \(Y\), identify \(R\) and \(X,Y\), respectively, with a \(\Bbbk\)-algebra and \(\Bbbk\)-modules equipped with direct-sum decompositions \[R = \bigoplus_n R^n, \quad X = \bigoplus_n X^n, \quad Y = \bigoplus_n Y^n\] and degree-\(1\) endomorphisms \(d\) satisfying \(d^2=0\). Thus \(X\ensuremath{\underset{R}{\otimes}}Y\) is already defined as a \(\Bbbk\)-module.

  1. Recall that \(X\otimes Y=\bigoplus_n(\bigoplus_{p+q=n}X^p\otimes Y^q)\) is both a \(\Bbbk\)-module and a complex. For the evident \(\Bbbk\)-module homomorphism \(\pi:X\otimes Y\twoheadrightarrow X\ensuremath{\underset{R}{\otimes}}Y\), verify that \(\operatorname{ker}(\pi)\) is a subcomplex, so that \(X\ensuremath{\underset{R}{\otimes}}Y\) has a canonical complex structure.

  2. Prove that if \(X\) is an \((A,R)\)-bimodule and \(Y\) is an \((R,B)\)-bimodule, where \(A\) and \(B\) are also dg-algebras, then \(X\ensuremath{\underset{R}{\otimes}}Y\) is naturally an \((A,B)\)-bimodule. Use this to extend the adjunction of Proposition reference to dg-modules. Here \(\operatorname{Hom}^\bullet(Y_B,Z_B)\) and \(\operatorname{Hom}^\bullet({}_AX,{}_AZ)\) are defined as complexes as in Example reference, but the signs must be handled carefully when assigning the \((A,R)\)- and \((R,B)\)-bimodule structures.

Fix a dg-algebra \(A\) over \(\mathcal{A}\). It is called non-positive if \(p>0\implies A^p=0\). For a left (or right) \(A\)-module \(M\) and \(n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\), take the truncation subcomplex \(\tau^{\leq n}M\) as in Definition reference. Prove that if \(A\) is non-positive, then:

  1. every \(d_M^p:M^p\to M^{p+1}\) is \(A^0\)-linear;

  2. there is a short exact sequence of \(A\)-modules \(0\to\tau^{\leq n}M\to M\to\tilde\tau^{\geq n+1}M\to0\).

Fix a dg-algebra \(A\) over \(\mathcal{A}\). Recall that all left \(A\)-modules form the dg-category \(A\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{dgMod}}\) (Example reference); Remark reference then gives the homotopy category \(\mathrm{h}(A\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{dgMod}})\). A left \(A\)-module \(M\) is called acyclic if it is acyclic as a complex; a morphism of \(A\)-modules \(f:M\to N\) is called a quasi-isomorphism if it is a quasi-isomorphism of complexes.

  1. Let \(M\) be a left \(A\)-module whose structure is determined by a family of morphisms in \(\mathcal{A}\), \(\alpha_{A,M}^{p,q}:A^p\otimes M^q\to M^{p+q}\) (\(p,q\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\)). Show that the formula \[\alpha_{A, M[1]}^{p, q} := (-1)^p \alpha_{A, M}^{p, q+1} .\] gives the complex \(M[1]\) a left \(A\)-module structure. Then show that \(M\mapsto M[1]\) defines a dg-functor from \(A\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{dgMod}}\) to itself.

  2. For every morphism \(f:M\to N\) in \(A\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{dgMod}}\), show that the mapping cone \(\operatorname{Cone}(f)\) has a canonical left \(A\)-module structure, given in the notation above by \[\alpha_{A, \operatorname{Cone}(f)}^{p, q} = \alpha_{A, M[1]}^{p, q} \oplus \alpha_{A, N}^{p, q}.\]

  3. Following the construction of §reference, use mapping cones to make \(\mathrm{h}(A\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{dgMod}})\) a triangulated category. Next perform Verdier localization at the acyclic \(A\)-modules, or equivalently adjoin inverses to the quasi-isomorphisms, to obtain the derived category \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}(A\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{dgMod}})\). Define the corresponding \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^{\star}(A\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{dgMod}})\) for \(\star\in\{+,-,\ensuremath{\mathrm{b}}\}\).

  4. Assuming that \(A\) is non-positive, extend Proposition reference to \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}(A\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{dgMod}})\) and \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}^{\star}(A\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{dgMod}})\) for \(\star\in\{+,-,\ensuremath{\mathrm{b}}\}\). Hint. Use the truncation functors.

  5. Following §reference, define K-injective and K-projective \(A\)-modules and use them to describe the morphisms in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{D}}(A\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{dgMod}})\). Place this discussion in the framework of §reference to study their relation to derived functors.

  6. For a right \(A\)-module \(M\), show that the complex \(M[1]\) has the right \(A\)-module structure \(\alpha_{M[1],A}^{p,q}=\alpha_{M,A}^{p,q+1}\) and that all the preceding properties remain valid.

Let \(\mathcal{C}\) be a dg-category over \(\Bbbk\). Define \(\mathcal{C}^{\operatorname{op}}\) by \(\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{C}^{\operatorname{op}})=\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{C})\) and, for all \(X,Y\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{C}^{\operatorname{op}})\), \(\operatorname{Hom}^\bullet_{\mathcal{C}^{\operatorname{op}}}(X,Y):= \operatorname{Hom}^\bullet_{\mathcal{C}}(Y,X)\). Define composition by \[\begin{align*} \operatorname{Hom}^p_{\mathcal{C}^{\operatorname{op}}}(Y, Z) \ensuremath{\underset{\Bbbk}{\otimes}} \operatorname{Hom}^q_{\mathcal{C}^{\operatorname{op}}}(X, Y) & \to \operatorname{Hom}^{p+q}_{\mathcal{C}^{\operatorname{op}}}(X, Z) \quad p, q \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\\ f \otimes g & \mapsto (-1)^{pq} \underbracket{f \circ g}_{\text{composition in }\operatorname{Hom}^\bullet_{\mathcal{C}}}. \end{align*}\] Verify that this indeed defines a dg-category \(\mathcal{C}^{\operatorname{op}}\), called the opposite dg-category of \(\mathcal{C}\).

Fix a commutative ring \(\Bbbk\), a dg-algebra \(R\) over \(\Bbbk\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\), a right \(R\)-module \(X\), and a left \(R\)-module \(Y\). Prove that the previously introduced functors \[X \ensuremath{\underset{R}{\otimes}} (\cdot): R\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{dgMod}} \to \ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\Bbbk), \quad (\cdot) \ensuremath{\underset{R}{\otimes}} Y: \ensuremath{\mathsf{dgMod}\text{-}}R \to \ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\Bbbk),\] upgrade naturally to dg-functors. Outline the corresponding statements when \(X\) or \(Y\) also has a bimodule structure. Hint. The key is to define the morphisms between the \(\operatorname{Hom}\) complexes. For \(X\ensuremath{\underset{R}{\otimes}}(\mathord\cdot)\), let \(M\) and \(N\) be left \(R\)-modules. The Koszul sign rule requires the image of \(f\in\operatorname{Hom}^n_R(M,N)\), namely \(\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_X\otimes f\in \operatorname{Hom}^n(X\ensuremath{\underset{R}{\otimes}}M,X\ensuremath{\underset{R}{\otimes}}N)\), to be defined by \[(\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_X \otimes f)(x \otimes m) = (-1)^{pn} x \otimes f(m), \quad x \in X^p, \; m \in M^q.\] One must verify that \(\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_X\otimes d_{\operatorname{Hom}^\bullet}(f)= d_{\operatorname{Hom}^\bullet}(\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_X\otimes f)\).

The case \((\mathord\cdot)\ensuremath{\underset{R}{\otimes}}Y\) is simpler: take \((f\otimes\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_Y)(m\otimes y)=f(m)\otimes y\).

Let \(\mathcal{C}\) be a dg-category over a commutative ring \(\Bbbk\) and let \(M\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{C})\).

  1. Upgrade \(\operatorname{Hom}^\bullet(M,\mathord\cdot):\mathcal{C}\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\Bbbk)\) to a dg-functor. Hint. Let \(X,Y\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{C})\) and \(f\in\operatorname{Hom}^n(X,Y)\). Set \(\mathcal{H}_X=\operatorname{Hom}^\bullet(M,X)\). The image of \(f\) should be \[\left[ f_*: g \xmapsto{\text{morphism of degree }n} fg \right] \in \operatorname{Hom}^n(\mathcal{H}_X, \mathcal{H}_Y).\] Use the definition of the \(\operatorname{Hom}\) complex to verify that \((d_{\operatorname{Hom}^\bullet(X,Y)}f)_*= d_{\operatorname{Hom}^\bullet(\mathcal{H}_X,\mathcal{H}_Y)}(f_*)\).

  2. Upgrade \(\operatorname{Hom}^\bullet(\mathord\cdot,M):\mathcal{C}\to \ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\Bbbk)^{\operatorname{op}}\) to a dg-functor. Hint. Set \(\mathcal{K}_X=\operatorname{Hom}^\bullet(X,M)\). The Koszul sign rule requires the image of \(f\in\operatorname{Hom}^n(X,Y)\) to be \[\left[\begin{array}{c} f^*: g \xmapsto{\text{morphism of degree }n} (-1)^{np} gf \\ \forall p \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}, \; \forall\; g \in \operatorname{Hom}^p(Y, M) \end{array}\right] \in \operatorname{Hom}^n(\mathcal{K}_Y, \mathcal{K}_X).\] Verify carefully that

    • \((d_{\operatorname{Hom}^\bullet(X,Y)}f)^*= d_{\operatorname{Hom}^\bullet(\mathcal{K}_Y,\mathcal{K}_X)}(f^*)\);

    • \((fh)^*\) equals the composite of \(h^*\) and \(f^*\) in \(\operatorname{Hom}^\bullet_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\Bbbk)}\).

Prove that the canonical morphisms \([Y,Z]\otimes[X,Y]\to[X,Z]\) and \(\ensuremath{\bm{1}}\to[X,X]\) defined for a closed monoidal category in §reference satisfy associativity and unit laws. Thus a closed monoidal category is enriched over itself with respect to its internal \(\operatorname{Hom}\). Hint. Verify this directly, or consult [Kel05].

Consider the polynomial algebra \(\Bbbk[t]\) over a commutative ring \(\Bbbk\). Define \(\Delta\), \(\epsilon\), and \(S\), respectively, by \[\Delta(t^n) = \sum_{k=0}^n \binom{n}{k} t^k \otimes t^{n-k}, \quad \epsilon(t^n) = \begin{cases} 1, & n = 0 \\ 0, & n \neq 0 \end{cases}, \quad S(t^n) = (-1)^n t^n,\] where \(n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}_{\geq0}\). Verify that these data define a commutative and cocommutative Hopf \(\Bbbk\)-algebra.

Let \(A\) be a Hopf algebra over a commutative ring. An ideal \(I\) of \(A\) is called a Hopf ideal if \(\Delta(I)\subset I\otimes A+A\otimes I\), \(\epsilon(I)=0\), and \(S(I)\subset I\). Show that quotienting by a Hopf ideal gives a Hopf algebra \(A/I\).

Let \(\Bbbk\) be a commutative ring and \(V\) a \(\Bbbk\)-module. On the tensor algebra \(T(V)\) (see [Li1]) one can define \(\Bbbk\)-algebra homomorphisms \(\Delta:T(V)\to T(V)\otimes T(V)\) and \(\epsilon:T(V)\to\Bbbk\) such that, for every \(v\in V\), \[\begin{gather*} \Delta(v) = v \otimes 1 + 1 \otimes v, \quad \epsilon(v) = 0; \end{gather*}\] here the algebra structure on \(T(V)\otimes T(V)\) is defined by the trivial braiding \(x\otimes y\mapsto y\otimes x\).

  1. Verify that this makes \(T(V)\) a bialgebra.

  2. Show how to define a \(\Bbbk\)-module automorphism \(S:T(V)\to T(V)\) such that \(S(v)=-v\) and \(S\) is a bialgebra antiautomorphism (Proposition reference); more explicitly, \[S(v_1 \cdots v_n) = (-1)^n v_n \cdots v_1, \quad n \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}_{\geq 0}, \quad v_1, \ldots, v_n \in V.\] Verify that this makes \(T(V)\) a Hopf algebra.

  3. Show that the symmetric algebra \(\operatorname{Sym}(V)\) has the analogous properties; in fact it is a quotient of \(T(V)\) by a Hopf ideal.

  4. Treat the version for the exterior algebra \(\bigwedge(V)\), but define the multiplication on \(\bigwedge(V)\otimes\bigwedge(V)\) using the Koszul braiding equation (take \(\epsilon(a)=a\bmod\;2\) there), so that homogeneous elements \(x,y,z,w\in\bigwedge(V)\) satisfy \((x\otimes y)(z\otimes w)=(-1)^{\deg y\deg z}xz\otimes yw\). This ensures that \((1\otimes v+v\otimes1)^2\) is the zero element of \(\bigwedge(V)\otimes\bigwedge(V)\) for every \(v\in V\).

(E. Taft) Let \(q\) be a primitive \(n\)th root of unity in a field \(\Bbbk\), where \(n\geq2\). Consider the \(\Bbbk\)-algebra \(H\) defined by generators \(g\), \(x\), and relations \[g^n = 1, \quad x^n = 0, \quad gxg^{-1} = qx.\] Show that one can define \(\Delta:H\to H\ensuremath{\underset{\Bbbk}{\otimes}}H\) and \(\epsilon:H\to\Bbbk\) satisfying \[\begin{gather*} \Delta(g) = g \otimes g, \quad \Delta(x) = 1 \otimes x + x \otimes g, \\ \epsilon(g) = 1, \quad \epsilon(x) = 0, \end{gather*}\] and making \(H\) a Hopf \(\Bbbk\)-algebra with antipode \[S:H\to H, \quad S(g)=g^{-1}, \quad S(x)=-g^{-1}x.\]

Show that \(H\) is neither commutative nor cocommutative. When \(n=2\), the corresponding Hopf algebra is also called Sweedler’s Hopf algebra.

Let \((A,\Delta,\epsilon)\) be a coalgebra over a commutative ring \(\Bbbk\). If \(x\in A\) satisfies \(\Delta(x)=1\otimes x+x\otimes1\), then \(x\) is called primitive.

  1. Prove that \(\epsilon(x)=0\) for every primitive element \(x\).

  2. Let \((A,\mu,\eta,\Delta,\epsilon)\) be a bialgebra and write \(\mu\) as multiplication, so \(xy=\mu(x\otimes y)\). Prove that if \(x,y\in A\) are primitive, then \(xy-yx\) is primitive as well.

  3. Still taking \(A\) to be a bialgebra, let \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\in A\) be primitive elements and let \(V\) be the free \(\Bbbk\)-module with basis \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\). This gives a \(\Bbbk\)-algebra homomorphism \(\phi:T(V)\to A\). Prove that \(\phi\) is also a bialgebra homomorphism.

Let \((A,\Delta,\epsilon)\) be a coalgebra over a commutative ring \(\Bbbk\), with \(A\neq\{0\}\) and \(A\) torsion-free as a \(\Bbbk\)-module. A nonzero element \(x\in A\) satisfying \(\Delta(x)=x\otimes x\) is called group-like. Denote the set of all group-like elements by \(\mathcal{G}(A)\).

  1. Prove that \(x\in\mathcal{G}(A)\) implies \(\epsilon(x)=1\).

  2. Prove that if \((A,\mu,\eta,\Delta,\epsilon)\) is a bialgebra, then \(\mathcal{G}(A)\) is a monoid under the multiplication \(\mu\) of \(A\), with unit \(1_A:=\eta(1)\).

  3. For a monoid \(M\) and the corresponding bialgebra \(\Bbbk[M]\) (Example reference), prove that \(\mathcal{G}(\Bbbk[M])=M\).

  4. Let \(A\) be a Hopf algebra with antipode \(S\). Prove that \(\mathcal{G}(A)\) is a group and that the inverse of \(x\in\mathcal{G}(A)\) is \(S(x)\).

Let \((A,\Delta,\epsilon)\) be a nonzero coalgebra over a field \(\Bbbk\). Prove that \(\mathcal{G}(A)\) is a linearly independent subset of \(A\). Hint. Suppose otherwise, and choose a shortest nontrivial linear relation among these elements. Without loss of generality, write \(x_1=\sum_{i=2}^n a_i x_i\), where \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\in\mathcal{G}(A)\) are pairwise distinct and \(a_i\in\Bbbk\). Then \(x_2,\ldots,x_n\) are linearly independent, while \(x_1\otimes x_1=\sum_{i=2}^n a_i x_i\otimes x_i\).

Write \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{TopCMon}}\) for the category of commutative topological monoids, \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Top}}_\bullet\) for the category of pointed topological spaces, and \(U:\ensuremath{\mathsf{TopCMon}}\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{Top}}_\bullet\) for the forgetful functor (the base point corresponds to the unit). Construct a left adjoint \(\operatorname{Sym}:\ensuremath{\mathsf{Top}}_\bullet\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{TopCMon}}\) to \(U\). For a pointed topological space \((X,x)\), the object \(\operatorname{Sym}(X,x)\) is also called the infinite symmetric product of \((X,x)\); explain this terminology. The Dold–Thom theorem in algebraic topology is based on this construction.

Let the \((A,B)\)-bimodule \(P\) be finitely generated projective as a right \(B\)-module, and suppose that \((\mathord\cdot)\ensuremath{\underset{A}{\otimes}}P\) is a faithful exact functor. Prove that a right \(A\)-module \(N\) is finitely presented (Example reference) if and only if \(N\ensuremath{\underset{A}{\otimes}}P\) is finitely presented as a right \(B\)-module. This complements Proposition reference.

Consider a commutative ring \(\Bbbk\) and a homomorphism of \(\Bbbk\)-algebras \(f:A\to B\). We have an adjoint pair \[\text{Diagram chapter7-unit-104-d001}\] where, for every right \(A\)-module \(N\), \(\operatorname{Hom}_A(B,N)\) is given the right \(B\)-module structure \((\phi b)(x)=\phi(bx)\). More precisely,

  • the unit morphism \(M\to\operatorname{Hom}_A(B,M)\) maps \(m\) to \([b\mapsto mb]\);

  • the counit morphism \(\operatorname{Hom}_A(B,N)\to N\) maps \(\phi\) to \(\phi(1)\).

See [Li1]. As a complement to Example reference, determine explicitly the corresponding monad and comonad.

Let \(R\) be a commutative ring. Write \(R\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Alg}}\) for the category of \(R\)-algebras. Consider the adjoint pair \(\text{Diagram chapter7-unit-104-diagram-002}\), where \(T(\mathord\cdot)\) is the tensor-algebra functor and \(U\) is the forgetful functor.

  1. Prove directly that modules under the corresponding monad on \(R\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\) are \(R\)-algebras, and hence that the adjoint pair is monadic.

  2. Replace \(T(\mathord\cdot)\) by \(\operatorname{Sym}(\mathord\cdot)\) and \(\bigwedge(\mathord\cdot)\), then state and prove the corresponding results; see [Li1].

Complete the argument of Proposition reference, and then prove the following stronger version. Let \(C\) be a coalgebra in \((B,B)\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\). Prove that:

  1. the forgetful functor \(U:\ensuremath{\mathsf{Comod}\text{-}}C\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}\text{-}}B\) has a right adjoint; Hint. Write \(\Delta\) for the comultiplication of \(C\) and \(\epsilon\) for its counit. For a right \(B\)-module \(N\), make \(N\ensuremath{\underset{B}{\otimes}}C\) a right \(C\)-comodule via \(\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_N\otimes\Delta\). For every right \(C\)-comodule \(M\), verify that \[\text{Diagram chapter7-unit-104-d002}\] are mutually inverse, where \(\rho:M\to M\ensuremath{\underset{B}{\otimes}}C\) specifies the comodule structure of \(M\).

  2. the forgetful functor \(U\) creates all small \(\varinjlim\); hence \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Comod}\text{-}}C\) is cocomplete;

  3. the category \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Comod}\text{-}}C\) has a cogenerator (Definition reference); Hint. Take a cogenerator of the Grothendieck category \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}\text{-}}B\), then take its image under the right adjoint of \(U\).

  4. if \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Comod}\text{-}}C\) is an abelian category and \(U\) is exact, then \(C\) is flat as a left \(B\)-module. Hint. Let \(g:M\to N\) be a monomorphism of right \(B\)-modules. Use the exactness of \(U\) and the fact that a right adjoint preserves kernels to show that \(g\otimes\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_C:M\ensuremath{\underset{B}{\otimes}}C\to N\ensuremath{\underset{B}{\otimes}}C\) remains injective.

As in the preceding exercise, continue to let \(C\) be a coalgebra in \((B,B)\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\) and let \(M\) be a right \(C\)-comodule. Prove that if a quotient \(B\)-module \(M''\) of \(M\) (or a \(B\)-submodule \(M'\) of \(M\)) has a comodule structure making \(M\twoheadrightarrow M''\) (or \(M'\hookrightarrow M\)) a comodule homomorphism, then that comodule structure is unique. In the submodule case, additionally assume that \(C\) is flat as a left \(B\)-module.

Following the explanation at the end of §reference, give a direct proof of the Galois descent Theorem reference by the following steps. Use the notation from that section: let \(M\in\operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Vect}}^{\Gamma,\infty}(L))\) and define the canonical map \(\iota_M\) by equation.

  1. Let \(M'\) be a \(\Gamma\)-invariant subspace of \(L\ensuremath{\underset{K}{\otimes}}(M^\Gamma)\), that is, \(\Gamma M'\subset M'\). Prove that if \(M'\cap(1\otimes M^\Gamma)=\{0\}\), then \(M'=\{0\}\). Hint. Choose a basis \((y_i)_{i\in I}\) of \(M^\Gamma\). If \(M'\neq\{0\}\), choose in it a nonzero expression with the fewest possible terms, \(\sum_{i\in I}\ell_i\otimes y_i\) (a finite sum). After a suitable normalization, it may be assumed to have the form \[m' = 1 \otimes y_{i_0} + \ell_1 \otimes y_{i_1} + \cdots, \quad \ell_1 \notin K.\] Choose \(\sigma\in\Gamma\) such that \(\sigma(\ell_1)\neq\ell_1\), and consider \(m'-\sigma(m')\) to obtain a contradiction.

  2. Prove that \(\iota_M:L\ensuremath{\underset{K}{\otimes}}(M^\Gamma)\to M\) is injective. Hint. Consider \(M':=\operatorname{ker}(\iota_M)\).

  3. Prove that \(\iota_M\) is surjective. Hint. Consider a finite Galois subextension \(E|K\) of \(L|K\). Take \(a_1,\ldots,a_n\) as a basis of \(E\) as a vector space over \(K\), and choose representatives \(\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}=\sigma_1,\ldots,\sigma_n\in\Gamma\) for the elements of \(\operatorname{Gal}(E|K)\). Field theory shows that \((\sigma_i(a_j))_{1\leq i,j\leq n}\) is an invertible matrix over \(E\); write its inverse as \((b_{ij})_{1\leq i,j\leq n}\). For \(m\in M^{\operatorname{Gal}(L|E)}\), derive \[m = \sum_{i=1}^n b_{i1} \sum_{j=1}^n \sigma_j(a_i m) \; \in \operatorname{im}(\iota_M).\]

  4. Use the preceding results to show that equation is an adjoint equivalence, thus giving a direct proof of Theorem reference.

Let \(G\) be a group and \(L|K\) a Galois extension of fields. Write \(G\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\) (or \(G\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}_L\)) for the category of \(G\)-modules with coefficients in \(K\) (or \(L\)); see Definition reference. Use the Galois descent methods of §§reference—reference to describe \(G\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\) in terms of objects of \(G\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}_L\) equipped with an appropriate \(\operatorname{Gal}(L|K)\)-action.

Use the notation of §reference. Let \(c\in Z^1(\Gamma,G(\mathbf{t}_{0,L}))\). Recall from the proof of Theorem reference that, through Galois descent, \(c\) defines a \(K\)-vector space \(W\) with data \(\mathbf{t}\) on it, as well as an isomorphism \(h:\mathbf{t}_{0,L}\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}\mathbf{t}_L\).

  1. Show that \(g\mapsto h^{-1}gh\) gives a group isomorphism \(\nu:G(\mathbf{t}_L)\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}G(\mathbf{t}_{0,L})\). Show that \(f \xmapsto{\sigma \in \Gamma} c(\sigma)({}^\sigma f)c(\sigma)^{-1}\) gives a new \(\Gamma\)-action on \(G(\mathbf{t}_{0,L})\). Denote this structure by \({}^cG(\mathbf{t}_{0,L})\), and show that \(\nu:G(\mathbf{t}_L)\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}{}^cG(\mathbf{t}_{0,L})\) is \(\Gamma\)-equivariant.

  2. Show that the following formula gives a well-defined map: \[\begin{align*} Z^1(\Gamma, G(\mathbf{t}_L)) & \to Z^1(\Gamma, G(\mathbf{t}_{0, L})) \\ \tilde{c} & \mapsto \left[\sigma \mapsto \nu(\tilde{c}(\sigma)) c(\sigma) \right]. \end{align*}\] It induces a bijection \(\operatorname{H}^1(\Gamma,G(\mathbf{t}_L))\to \operatorname{H}^1(\Gamma,G(\mathbf{t}_{0,L}))\) that maps the base point to \([c]\). Hint. Compare the “twisting” construction in the exercises for .
