  3. Show that, under the correspondence in Theorem reference, this bijection corresponds to the equality \(\mathscr{T}(\mathbf{t})=\mathscr{T}(\mathbf{t}_0)\).

Let \(K\) be a field with \(\mathrm{char}(K)\neq2\). A nondegenerate symmetric bilinear form \(q:V\times V\to K\) on a finite-dimensional \(K\)-vector space \(V\) will simply be called a nondegenerate quadratic form. In the orthogonal group \(\mathrm{O}(q)=\mathrm{O}(V,q)\), write \(\operatorname{SO}(q)=\operatorname{SO}(V,q)\) for the subgroup cut out by \(\det=1\). For every Galois extension \(L|K\), there is a nondegenerate quadratic form \((V_L,q_L)\) and the corresponding groups, all equipped with a smooth action of \(\Gamma:=\operatorname{Gal}(L|K)\).

  1. Write \(\mu_2:=\{\pm1\}\subset K^\times\). Show that \(\mathrm{O}(q)/\operatorname{SO}(q)\simeq\mu_2\). For the version \(\mathrm{O}(q_L)/\operatorname{SO}(q_L)\), explain the relation between this isomorphism and the \(\Gamma\)-action.

  2. Using the tools of §reference, show that the elements of \(\operatorname{H}^1(\Gamma,\mathrm{O}(q_L))\) correspond bijectively to the isomorphism classes of nondegenerate quadratic forms \((V',q')\) over \(K\) with \(\dim V'=\dim V\), where the base point corresponds to \((V,q)\).

  3. Apply Theorem reference to obtain the exact sequence of pointed sets \[\mathrm{O}(q) \xrightarrow{\det} \mu_2 \to \operatorname{H}^1(\Gamma, \operatorname{SO}(q_L)) \xrightarrow{\varphi} \operatorname{H}^1(\Gamma, \mathrm{O}(q_L)) \xrightarrow{\psi} \operatorname{H}^1(\Gamma, \mu_2).\] Try to show that \(\varphi\) is injective. Hint. Surjectivity of \(\det\) only shows that \(\varphi^{-1}(\text{base point})=\{\text{base point}\}\). To prove injectivity, one must vary \((V,q)\) and apply the twisting technique from the preceding exercise.

  4. Show that \(\operatorname{H}^1(\Gamma,\mu_2)\simeq K^\times/K^{\times,2}\). Also show that \(\psi\) is the map \[\left[ (V', q'):\; \text{nondegenerate quadratic form} \right] \mapsto \mathrm{disc}(q') / \mathrm{disc}(q),\] where one chooses any basis of \(V'\), identifies \(q'\) with a symmetric matrix, and defines \[\mathrm{disc}(q') := (-1)^n \det(q') \bmod K^{\times 2}, \quad \dim V = 2n \;\text{or}\; 2n+1.\]

  5. Show that the elements of \(\operatorname{H}^1(\Gamma,\operatorname{SO}(q_L))\) correspond bijectively to the isomorphism classes of nondegenerate quadratic forms \((V',q')\) over \(K\) satisfying \(\dim V'=\dim V\) and \(\mathrm{disc}(q')=\mathrm{disc}(q)\), with the base point corresponding to \((V,q)\).

Simplicial Methods

Let \(\ensuremath{\bm\Delta}\) be the category of nonempty finite ordinals. By definition, a simplicial object in a category \(\mathcal{C}\) is a functor \(X:\ensuremath{\bm\Delta}^{\operatorname{op}}\to\mathcal{C}\). Equivalently, it can be described as a sequence of objects \(X_0,X_1,\ldots\) together with morphisms \(d_i:X_n\to X_{n-1}\) (faces) and \(s_j:X_n\to X_{n+1}\) (degeneracies), for \(0\leq i,j\leq n\), satisfying the family of identities equation. Such functors form the category \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{s}}\mathcal{C}\). In the special case \(\mathcal{C}=\ensuremath{\mathsf{Set}}\), these objects are also called simplicial sets. Their basic theory is discussed in §§reference–reference. Write \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{FinOrd}}\) for the category of finite ordinals. If the functor underlying a simplicial object \(X\) extends to a functor \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{FinOrd}}\to\mathcal{C}\), then \(X\) is called an augmented simplicial object. This is equivalent to adding a term \(X_{-1}\) in degree \(-1\) to the data \((X_n,d_i,s_j)_{n,i,j}\). Simplicial sets originate in topology. The basic idea is to decompose a space as a gluing of simplices; the intuitive picture of simplices (a point, a line segment, a triangle, a tetrahedron, and so forth) is

\(0\) dimensions \(1\) dimension \(2\) dimensions \(3\) dimensions \(\cdots\)
Diagram chapter8-unit-106-diagram-001 Diagram chapter8-unit-106-diagram-002 Diagram chapter8-unit-106-diagram-003 Diagram chapter8-unit-106-diagram-004 \(\cdots\)

Such a decomposition gives a concrete, combinatorial way to understand homology, homotopy, and other questions about spaces. The rigorous formulation used here was introduced by S. Eilenberg and J. A. Zilber in 1950. The language of simplicial sets has a broad reach and is not confined to classical topological questions. For example, it can describe a category through the construction called its “nerve”, introduced in §reference. Category theory concerns objects in diagrams (shown as zero-dimensional points), morphisms (shown as one-dimensional arrows), and commutativity (associated with two-dimensional pieces such as triangles or squares). It is therefore unsurprising that categories and spaces can be united within the same mathematical structure. After introducing nerves and classifying spaces as basic examples of simplicial sets, §reference returns to the geometric intuition and defines the geometric realization \(|X|\) of a simplicial set \(X\). Theorem reference shows that geometric realization and the singular-set functor \(\mathrm{Sing}\) familiar from topology form an adjoint pair \[\text{Diagram chapter8-unit-106-d001}\] If \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Top}}\) is replaced by the category \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{CGHaus}}\) of compactly generated Hausdorff spaces, customary in homotopy theory, geometric realization also satisfies \(|X\times Y|\simeq|X|\times|Y|\). The product on the left is formed degreewise from the two simplicial sets. The proof is related to triangulating products and involves some nontrivial combinatorial details; since this is not a topology textbook, we shall not pursue them. For the subject of this book, simplicial objects in an abelian category \(\mathcal{A}\) are more important. In this situation, \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{s}}\mathcal{A}\) is also an abelian category; for example, simplicial abelian groups form the abelian category \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{sAb}}\). The fundamental result is the Dold–Kan correspondence in §reference (Theorem reference), which, for an abelian category \(\mathcal{A}\), gives an adjoint pair of equivalences \[\text{Diagram chapter8-unit-106-d002}\] where \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ch}}_{\geq0}(\mathcal{A})\) denotes the abelian category of nonnegatively graded chain complexes over \(\mathcal{A}\). The functor \(\mathrm{N}\) maps a simplicial object \(X\) to the corresponding normalized chain complex \(\mathrm{N}X\). More precisely, define the unnormalized chain complex of \(X\in\operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{s}}\mathcal{A})\) by \[\mathrm{C}X := \left( X_n, \partial_n\right)_{n \geq 0}, \quad \partial_n := \sum_{i=0}^n (-1)^i d_i : X_n \to X_{n-1}.\] Then \(\mathrm{N}X\) may be taken as the chain subcomplex of \(\mathrm{C}X\) given by \((\mathrm{N}X)_n:=\bigcap_{i=1}^n\operatorname{ker}(d_i)\), or regarded as the quotient of \(\mathrm{C}X\) by its degenerate part. The isomorphism between these two forms is the content of Proposition reference. Moreover, Theorem reference shows that the inclusion morphism \(u:\mathrm{N}X\to\mathrm{C}X\) is a quasi-isomorphism of chain complexes. The Dold–Kan correspondence makes simplicial theory one of the sources of homological algebra, not only historically but also conceptually and technically. Simplicial methods can explain and enrich the basic operations on complexes or chain complexes; for example, homotopy and contractibility have simplicial versions and thereby acquire topological interpretations. This is discussed in §reference. Another application connects simplicial methods with the theory of monads from §reference. In this way, an object of a category can be canonically expanded into an augmented simplicial object or an augmented cosimplicial object. Because these techniques are related to the operation of “adding a bar” in Hochschild homology, they are collectively called bar constructions and form the subject of §reference. Through the Dold–Kan correspondence and some observations about contractibility, bar constructions explain the standard resolutions in Hochschild theory (see §reference) and group cohomology (see §reference); they all turn out to arise from a single idea at a higher level. The Exercises contain another extension of the bar construction. By definition, the bisimplicial objects discussed in §reference are simply functors \(\ensuremath{\bm\Delta}^{\operatorname{op}}\times\ensuremath{\bm\Delta}^{\operatorname{op}}\to\mathcal{C}\); they form the category \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{s}}^2\mathcal{C}\). If \(\mathcal{A}\) is an abelian category, the Eilenberg–Zilber Theorem reference, which directly concerns \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{s}}^2\mathcal{A}\), is a fundamental construction in algebraic topology. From the viewpoint of pure category theory, if \(\mathcal{A}\) is a monoidal category (for example, \(\mathcal{A}=\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ab}}\)), the theorem gives two canonical monoidal structures, in opposite directions, on the functor \(\mathrm{N}:\ensuremath{\mathsf{s}}\mathcal{A}\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ch}}_{\geq0}(\mathcal{A})\). The applications of bisimplicial objects are not limited to this, however. The last two sections of this chapter, §reference and §reference, discuss \(\operatorname{Hom}\) objects and mapping cones for simplicial sets, respectively. On the one hand, they correspond to mapping spaces and cones in the topological intuition. On the other hand, in the case of abelian groups, the Dold–Kan correspondence gives the familiar \(\operatorname{Hom}\) chain complexes and mapping cones. Thus the related constructions on complexes or chain complexes receive a transparent explanation, while for topologists all of this is already familiar.

Simplicial Objects

In Remark reference, we recalled monotone maps between partially ordered sets and used them to define the category \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{FinOrd}}\) of finite ordinals. This chapter focuses on its full subcategory \(\ensuremath{\bm\Delta}\) consisting of the nonempty ordinals.

Definition. Let \(\ensuremath{\bm\Delta}\) be the category of all nonempty finite ordinals and monotone maps between them. In other words, its objects are the totally ordered sets \([n]:=\{0,\ldots,n\}\) for \(n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}_{\geq0}\), and its morphisms are monotone maps.

Note that \([n]\) should not be confused with \(\mathbf{n}\), which in this book denotes the totally ordered set \(\{0,\ldots,n-1\}\) or the corresponding category. Every morphism \([l]\to[n]\) in \(\ensuremath{\bm\Delta}\) has a unique factorization as a surjective monotone map followed by an injective monotone map, \[[l] \twoheadrightarrow [m] \hookrightarrow [n], \quad n \geq m \leq l.\] An injective (respectively, surjective) map of this kind can be decomposed further into pieces that at each step omit exactly one element (respectively, identify exactly two elements). In other words, every morphism can be factored as a composite of the following two kinds of morphisms.

Coface \(\mathrm{d}^i = \mathrm{d}^{n, i}: [n-1] \hookrightarrow [n]\) \(0 \leq i \leq n\) monotone injection omitting only \(i\in[n]\)
Codegeneracy \(\mathrm{s}^j = \mathrm{s}^{n, j}: [n+1] \twoheadrightarrow [n]\) \(0 \leq j \leq n\) monotone surjection taking the value \(j\in[n]\) twice

An injective (respectively, surjective) monotone map can be decomposed into cofaces (respectively, codegeneracies) in several ways, depending on the order in which the elements are omitted (respectively, identified). The following cosimplicial identities are easy to verify: \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:cosimplicial-identity}{}\begin{array}{ll} \mathrm{d}^j \mathrm{d}^i = \mathrm{d}^i \mathrm{d}^{j-1}, & i < j, \\ \mathrm{s}^j \mathrm{d}^i = \mathrm{d}^i \mathrm{s}^{j-1} & i < j, \\ \mathrm{s}^j \mathrm{d}^j = \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}= \mathrm{s}^j \mathrm{d}^{j+1}, & \forall j, \\ \mathrm{s}^j \mathrm{d}^i = \mathrm{d}^{i-1} \mathrm{s}^j, & i > j+1, \\ \mathrm{s}^j \mathrm{s}^i = \mathrm{s}^i \mathrm{s}^{j+1}, & i \leq j. \end{array} \end{equation}\] Examining how one passes between the various decompositions of an injective (respectively, surjective) monotone map shows that the cofaces, codegeneracies, and equation give a complete system of generators and relations for the morphisms of \(\ensuremath{\bm\Delta}\). Viewed in \(\ensuremath{\bm\Delta}^{\operatorname{op}}\), these give the corresponding morphisms

Face \(\mathrm{d}_i = \mathrm{d}^n_i: [n] \xrightarrow{\operatorname{op}} [n-1]\) \(0 \leq i \leq n\)
Degeneracy \(\mathrm{s}_j = \mathrm{s}^n_j: [n] \xrightarrow{\operatorname{op}} [n+1]\) \(0 \leq j \leq n\)

The symbol \(\xrightarrow{\operatorname{op}}\) merely reminds us that the arrow lies in the opposite category \(\ensuremath{\bm\Delta}^{\operatorname{op}}\). Reversing equation gives the simplicial identities \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:simplicial-identity}{}\begin{array}{ll} \mathrm{d}_i \mathrm{d}_j = \mathrm{d}_{j-1} \mathrm{d}_i, & i < j \\ \mathrm{d}_i \mathrm{s}_j = \mathrm{s}_{j-1} \mathrm{d}_i & i < j \\ \mathrm{d}_j \mathrm{s}_j = \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}= \mathrm{d}_{j+1} \mathrm{s}_j, & \forall j \\ \mathrm{d}_i \mathrm{s}_j = \mathrm{s}_j \mathrm{d}_{i-1}, & i > j+1 \\ \mathrm{s}_i \mathrm{s}_j = \mathrm{s}_{j+1} \mathrm{s}_i, & i \leq j. \end{array} \end{equation}\]

Definition. For a category \(\mathcal{C}\),

  • a simplicial object in it means a functor \(\ensuremath{\bm\Delta}^{\operatorname{op}}\to\mathcal{C}\); all simplicial objects form the category \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{s}}\mathcal{C}:=\mathcal{C}^{\ensuremath{\bm\Delta}^{\operatorname{op}}}\);

  • a cosimplicial object in it means a functor \(\ensuremath{\bm\Delta}\to\mathcal{C}\); all cosimplicial objects form the category \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{cs}}\mathcal{C}:=\mathcal{C}^{\ensuremath{\bm\Delta}}\).

Consequently, \((\ensuremath{\mathsf{cs}}\mathcal{C})^{\operatorname{op}}\simeq\ensuremath{\mathsf{s}}(\mathcal{C}^{\operatorname{op}})\). If the functor underlying a simplicial (respectively, cosimplicial) object has an extension to \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{FinOrd}}^{\operatorname{op}}\) (respectively, \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{FinOrd}}\)), then the object is called augmented.

By the preceding discussion, giving a simplicial object \(X\) is equivalent to giving a family of objects \((X_n)_{n\geq0}\) in \(\mathcal{C}\) together with a family of morphisms satisfying equation, \[d_i = d^n_i: X_n \to X_{n-1} \; \text{(face)}, \quad s_j = s^n_j: X_n \to X_{n+1} \; \text{(degeneracy)}, \quad 0 \leq i, j \leq n.\] The object \(X_n\) is called the degree-\(n\) term of \(X\). A morphism from a simplicial object \(X\) to \(Y\) is equivalently a family of morphisms \((f_n:X_n\to Y_n)_{n\geq0}\) in \(\mathcal{C}\) satisfying, for every \(n\geq0\), the compatibility conditions \[d^{n+1}_i f_{n+1} = f_n d^{n+1}_i, \quad s^n_j f_n = f_{n+1} s^n_j .\] Dually, giving a cosimplicial object \(X\) is equivalent to giving a family of objects \((X^n)_{n\geq0}\) in \(\mathcal{C}\) together with a family of morphisms satisfying equation, \[d^i = d^{n, i}: X^{n-1} \to X^n \; \text{(coface)}, \quad s^j = s^{n, j}: X^{n+1} \to X^n \; \text{(codegeneracy)}, \quad 0 \leq i, j \leq n.\] Its morphisms are families of morphisms \(f^n:X^n\to Y^n\) compatible with all \(d^i\) and \(s^j\). An augmentation of a simplicial (respectively, cosimplicial) object \(X\) is equivalently the addition to the data of a morphism \(X_0\to X_{-1}\) (respectively, \(X^{-1}\to X^0\)) and a commutative diagram \(\text{Diagram chapter8-unit-106-diagram-007}\) (respectively, its dual). This morphism is called the augmentation morphism.

Convention. For a morphism \(\phi:[m]\to[n]\) in \(\ensuremath{\bm\Delta}\) and a simplicial (respectively, cosimplicial) object \(X\) in a category \(\mathcal{C}\), denote the corresponding morphism by \(\phi^*:X_n\to X_m\) (respectively, \(\phi_*:X^m\to X^n\)).

Remark. All nonempty ordinals and the injective monotone maps between them form a category \(\ensuremath{\bm\Delta}_+\). A functor of the form \(\ensuremath{\bm\Delta}_+^{\operatorname{op}}\to\mathcal{C}\) is called a semisimplicial object in \(\mathcal{C}\). This is equivalent to deleting the degeneracy morphisms \(s_j\) and the associated conditions from the definition of a simplicial object. Every simplicial object gives a corresponding semisimplicial object. Augmented semisimplicial objects may be defined similarly. The case of cosemisimplicial objects is entirely dual.

Example. Let \(C\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{C})\). The corresponding constant simplicial object \(\mathrm{const}(C)\) is determined by \(\mathrm{const}(C)_n=C\) and \(s_j=\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_C=d_i\) for all \(n,i,j\). As a simple exercise, check that \[\left\{ \text{augmentations of }X\right\} \xleftrightarrow{1:1} \left\{ (C, \varphi): C \in \operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{C}), \; \varphi: X \to \mathrm{const}(C) \right\}.\] Concretely, for a given augmentation of \(X\), take \(C=X_{-1}\) and let \(\varphi_n\) be the composite \(X_n\xrightarrow{\iota_k^*}X_0\to X_{-1}\), where \(\iota_k:[0]\to[n]\) sends \(0\) to any \(k\) with \(0\leq k\leq n\). The case of constant cosimplicial objects is entirely similar.

Example. Let \(B\to A\) be a morphism in a category \(\mathcal{C}\). If the following fiber products exist, \[X_n := \underbracket{B \ensuremath{\underset{A}{\times}} \cdots \ensuremath{\underset{A}{\times}} B}_{n+1 \;\text{factors}}, \quad n \geq 0,\] each morphism \(f:[m]\to[n]\) induces a morphism \(X_n\to X_m\) whose \(i\)th component is the projection \(B\ensuremath{\underset{A}{\times}}\cdots\ensuremath{\underset{A}{\times}}B\xrightarrow{\mathrm{pr}_{f(i)}}B\). This gives a simplicial object \(X\) in \(\mathcal{C}\). It is augmented by taking \(B\to A\) as the morphism \(X_0\to X_{-1}\).

Remark (Order-reversal duality). For each \(n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}_{\geq0}\), define a bijection \(w_n\) of \(\{0,\ldots,n\}\) with itself by \(w_n(i)=n-i\). Define an autoisomorphism \(w\) of the category \(\ensuremath{\bm\Delta}\) that preserves the objects \([n]\) and maps a morphism \(f:[n]\to[m]\) to \(wf:=w_mfw_n\). Note that \[w^2 = \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{\ensuremath{\bm\Delta}}, \quad w \mathrm{d}^{n, i} = \mathrm{d}^{n, n-i}, \quad w \mathrm{s}^{n, j} = \mathrm{s}^{n, n-j}.\] A more intrinsic viewpoint is that \(w\) maps \([n]\) to the poset with the reversed order \([n]^{\operatorname{op}}\), or, when regarded as a category, to its opposite category. This category is still uniquely isomorphic to \([n]\). The action of \(w\) on morphisms is expressed by the commutative diagram \[\text{Diagram chapter8-unit-106-d003} \quad f^{\operatorname{op}} \xlongequal{\text{as a map}} f.\] For every category \(\mathcal{C}\), this gives an autoisomorphism \(X\mapsto X\circ w\) of \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{s}}\mathcal{C}\) (respectively, \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{cs}}\mathcal{C}\)).

Finally, we outline the relation between monoidal structures and simplicial objects.

Definition. Every functor \(F:\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{D}\) induces a functor \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{s}}\mathcal{C}\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{s}}\mathcal{D}\) that maps the data \((X_n,d_i,s_j)_{n,i,j}\) to \((FX_n,Fd_i,Fs_j)_{n,i,j}\). Moreover, there is a direct relation \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{s}}(\mathcal{C}_1\times\mathcal{C}_2)\simeq \ensuremath{\mathsf{s}}\mathcal{C}_1\times\ensuremath{\mathsf{s}}\mathcal{C}_2\).

Apply this observation to a monoidal category \(\mathcal{C}\) and the bifunctor \(\otimes:\mathcal{C}\times\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{C}\). For every \(X,Y\in\operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{s}}\mathcal{C})\), define \(X\otimes Y\in\operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{s}}\mathcal{C})\) so that its degree-\(n\) term is \(X_n\otimes Y_n\), while its face and degeneracy morphisms have the forms \(d_i\otimes d_i\) and \(s_j\otimes s_j\), respectively.

Thus, if \(\mathcal{C}\) is a monoidal category, then \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{s}}\mathcal{C}\) also has a corresponding monoidal structure, with the constant simplicial object \(\mathrm{const}(\ensuremath{\bm{1}})\) as its unit. The analogous statement holds for cosimplicial objects.

Simplicial Sets

The simplicial objects of Definition reference in the case \(\mathcal{C}=\ensuremath{\mathsf{Set}}\) are called simplicial sets. Relative to a fixed Grothendieck universe, the precise meaning of \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Set}}\) in this book is the category of all small sets; these details do not affect the content of this section.

Definition. A simplicial object in the category of sets \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Set}}\) is called a simplicial set; a cosimplicial object in it is called a cosimplicial set.

By Definition reference, all simplicial sets (or cosimplicial sets) form the category \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{sSet}}:=\ensuremath{\mathsf{Set}}^{\ensuremath{\bm\Delta}^{\operatorname{op}}}\) (or \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{csSet}}:=\ensuremath{\mathsf{Set}}^{\ensuremath{\bm\Delta}}\)).

Definition. For every \(n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}_{\geq0}\), write \(\Delta^n\) for the simplicial set determined by \(\operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\bm\Delta}}(\mathord\cdot,[n]): \ensuremath{\bm\Delta}^{\operatorname{op}}\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{Set}}\). It is called the standard \(n\)-simplex.

Thus \((\Delta^n)_m=\operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\bm\Delta}}([m],[n])\) is the set of all order-preserving maps \([m]\to[n]\). The map \((\Delta^n)_{m'}\to(\Delta^n)_m\) induced by an order-preserving map \(\phi:[m]\to[m']\) is precisely pullback of maps, \(\phi^*:f\mapsto f\phi\).

Example. We introduce two common subobjects of the standard \(n\)-simplex \(\Delta^n\).

  • Boundary.Define the subfunctor \(\partial\Delta^n\) of \(\Delta^n\) by \[(\partial \Delta^n)_m := \left\{ f: [m] \to [n] \; \text{order-preserving}, \operatorname{im}(f) \neq [n] \right\}, \quad m \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}_{\geq 0}.\] If \(m<n\), then \((\partial\Delta^n)_m=(\Delta^n)_m\); if \(m\geq n\), the elements of \((\partial\Delta^n)_m\) are obtained by repeated degeneracies from \((\Delta^n)_h\) for \(0\leq h<n\).

  • Horn.For \(0\leq k\leq n\), define the subfunctor \(\Lambda^n_k\) of \(\Delta^n\) by \[(\Lambda^n_k)_m := \left\{ f: [m] \to [n] \;\text{order-preserving}, \operatorname{im}(f) \not\supset [n] \smallsetminus \{k\} \right\}, \quad m \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}_{\geq 0}.\] We call \(k\) the vertex of the horn.

Every pullback \(\phi^*:f\mapsto f\phi\) clearly preserves the conditions above, so both are subfunctors. The exercises in this chapter will show how \(\Lambda^n_i\) (or \(\partial\Delta^n\)) can be expressed precisely as a gluing of \(n\) (or \(n+1\)) copies of \(\Delta^{n-1}\).

The constant simplicial set given by the empty set, \(\mathrm{const}(\emptyset)\), is abbreviated to \(\emptyset\). Thus \(\partial\Delta^0=\emptyset\). In §reference we will give an intuitive interpretation of simplicial sets. In particular, we will depict the geometric images of \(\Delta^n\supset\Lambda^n_i\supset\partial\Delta^n\). The Yoneda lemma (Theorem reference) immediately gives the following canonical isomorphism, where \(n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}_{\geq0}\) and \(X\in\operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{sSet}})\): \[\begin{equation} \begin{gathered} \text{Diagram chapter8-unit-107-d001} \\ \phi([n]): \operatorname{End}([n]) = \Delta^n([n]) \to X([n]) =: X_n. \end{gathered} \end{equation}\]

Definition. An element of \(X_n\) is called an \(n\)-simplex of the simplicial set \(X\). If \(x\in X_n\) lies in the image of some \(s_j\), it is called degenerate; otherwise it is called non-degenerate.

As a simple exercise, verify that the non-degenerate \(m\)-simplices of \(\Delta^n\) correspond to the order-preserving injections \([m]\hookrightarrow[n]\); there are \(\binom{n+1}{m+1}\) of them. Furthermore, the Yoneda lemma ensures that \(h_{\ensuremath{\bm\Delta}}:[n]\mapsto\Delta^n\) defines a fully faithful functor \(\ensuremath{\bm\Delta}\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{sSet}}\). Every morphism \(f:[m]\to[n]\) in \(\ensuremath{\bm\Delta}\) induces \(f:\Delta^m\to\Delta^n\). Specifying an \((m+1)\)-element subset \(\{k_0,\ldots,k_m\}\subset[n]\) is equivalent to specifying an order-preserving injection \([m]\hookrightarrow[n]\). The corresponding morphism between standard simplices is also written \[\Delta^m \xrightarrow{\{k_0, \ldots, k_m\}} \Delta^n .\] The intuitive meaning of simplicial sets will be explained by geometric realization in §reference. Before that, we introduce a series of abstract constructions, beginning with the join and the left and right cones of simplicial sets. Write \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{FinLin}}_+\) for the full subcategory of the category of finite totally ordered sets (also called finite linearly ordered sets) \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{FinLin}}\) obtained by removing the empty set; its morphisms are order-preserving maps. Since \(\ensuremath{\bm\Delta}\) is a skeleton of \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{FinLin}}_+\), a simplicial set can equivalently be viewed as a functor \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{FinLin}}_+^{\operatorname{op}}\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{Set}}\).

Convention. Let \(J\) be an object of \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{FinLin}}_+\). Every subset \(I\subset J\) is automatically a finite totally ordered set. If it also satisfies \[\forall (i, j) \in I \times J, \quad j \leq i \implies j \in I,\] then \(I\) is called an initial segment of \(J\), written \(I\sqsubset J\).

Definition. The join \(X\star X'\) of simplicial sets \(X\) and \(X'\) is defined as the following functor \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{FinLin}}_+^{\operatorname{op}}\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{Set}}\): \[(X \star X')(J) = \bigsqcup_{I \sqsubset J} X(I) \times X'(J \smallsetminus I).\] Here (and only here), \(X(\emptyset)\) and \(X'(\emptyset)\) are defined to be one-point sets. For every order-preserving map \(f:J_1\to J\) and \(I\sqsubset J\), set \(I_1:=f^{-1}(I)\). Then \(I_1\sqsubset J_1\) and there is a map \[X(I) \times X'(J \smallsetminus I) \to X(I_1) \times X'(J_1 \smallsetminus I_1).\] This yields an induced morphism \(f^*:(X\star X')(J)\to(X\star X')(J_1)\), which determines the simplicial structure on \(X\star X'\).

There are canonical morphisms \(X\to X\star Y\leftarrow Y\). The definition can also be written in the earlier notation as \[(X \star Y)_n = X_n \sqcup Y_n \sqcup \bigsqcup_{j+k = n-1} X_j \times Y_k .\] The morphisms \(d_i\) and \(s_i\) are obtained directly from the corresponding morphisms on \(X\) and \(Y\). For example, for \(d_i:(X\star Y)_n\to(X\star Y)_{n-1}\), its restrictions to the subsets \(X_n\) and \(Y_n\) are the original \(d_i\), while on \(X_j\times Y_k\) it is given by \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:join-formulas}{}\begin{gathered} d_i(x, y) = \begin{cases} (d_i x, y), & i \leq j, \; j \neq 0 \\ (x, d_{i-j-1} y), & i > j, \; k \neq 0, \end{cases} \\ j=0 \implies d_0(x, y) = y \in Y_{n-1}, \\ k=0 \implies d_n(x, y) = x \in X_{n-1}. \end{gathered} \end{equation}\]

Proposition. Write \(X_n^{\mathrm{nd}}\subset X_n\) for the subset of non-degenerate \(n\)-simplices of the simplicial set \(X\) (Definition reference). For all \(X\) and \(Y\), \[(X \star Y)^{\mathrm{nd}}_n = X^{\mathrm{nd}}_n \sqcup Y^{\mathrm{nd}}_n \sqcup \bigsqcup_{j+k=n-1} X^{\mathrm{nd}}_j \times Y^{\mathrm{nd}}_k.\]

Proof. Let \(Z\) be a simplicial set. For every nonempty finite totally ordered set \(J\), an element \(x\in Z(J)\) is degenerate if and only if there is an order-preserving surjection that is not injective, \(f:J\twoheadrightarrow J_0\), such that \(x\in\operatorname{im}[f^*:Z(J_0)\to Z(J)]\). The rest follows immediately from this observation.

Definition. The left cone with base a simplicial set \(X\) is \(X^{\lhd}:=\Delta^0\star X\), while the right cone is \(X^{\rhd}:=X\star\Delta^0\).

An intuitive interpretation of cones is given in Example reference. The exercises will examine further properties of the join operation.

Example: Nerves of Categories

This section introduces the nerves of categories and, through them, the classifying spaces of groups. Both are important examples of simplicial sets.

Example (Nerve of a category). Let \(\mathcal{C}\) be a small category. Define the functor \[\ensuremath{\bm\Delta}^{\operatorname{op}} \to \ensuremath{\mathsf{Set}}, \quad [n] \mapsto \left\{ \text{all functors } [n] \to \mathcal{C} \right\}.\] As a simplicial set it is denoted by \(\mathrm{N}\mathcal{C}\) and called the nerve of \(\mathcal{C}\). Specifying an element of \(\mathrm{N}\mathcal{C}_n\) is equivalent to specifying a functor \([n]\to\mathcal{C}\), that is, a chain of morphisms in \(\mathcal{C}\) \[(f_1, \ldots, f_n): C_0 \xrightarrow{f_1} C_1 \xrightarrow{f_2} \cdots \xrightarrow{f_n} C_n.\] Thus \(\mathrm{N}\mathcal{C}_0\) may be identified with \(\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{C})\), and \(\mathrm{N}\mathcal{C}_1\) with \(\operatorname{Mor}(\mathcal{C})\).

The face morphisms \(d_i:\mathrm{N}\mathcal{C}_n\to \mathrm{N}\mathcal{C}_{n-1}\) and degeneracy morphisms \(s_j:\mathrm{N}\mathcal{C}_n\to\mathrm{N}\mathcal{C}_{n+1}\) are given by \[\begin{align*} d_i(f_1, \ldots, f_n) & = \begin{cases} (f_2, \cdots, f_n), & i = 0 \\ (\ldots, f_{i+1} f_i, \ldots), & 0 < i < n, \\ (f_1, \ldots, f_{n-1}), & i = n, \end{cases} \\ s_j(f_1, \ldots, f_n) & = \begin{cases} \left( \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{C_0}, f_1, \ldots, f_n \right), & j = 0 \\ (\ldots, f_j, \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{C_j}, f_{j+1}, \ldots ), & 0 < j < n \\ (f_1, \ldots, f_n, \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{C_n}), & j = n. \end{cases} \end{align*}\]

Remark. Unfolding the definitions shows that the simplicial sets \(\mathrm{N}(\mathcal{C}^{\operatorname{op}})\) and \(\mathrm{N}\mathcal{C}\) are related by the order-reversing duality of Remark reference. The details are left to the reader.

The nerve realizes a category concretely through combinatorial/topological data and contains all the information of the original category. This is the content of Proposition reference, which will soon be proved. We first characterize which simplicial sets are nerves; the argument is instructive.

Proposition (Characterization of nerves). Let \(X\) be a simplicial set. The following statements are equivalent.

  1. There is a small category \(\mathcal{C}\) such that \(\mathrm{N}\mathcal{C}\simeq X\).

  2. \(X\) has the unique inner horn-filling property: for every integer \(0<i<n\) and every morphism \(\sigma':\Lambda^n_i\to X\) in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{sSet}}\) (such a \(\Lambda^n_i\) is called an inner horn), there is a unique \(\sigma:\Delta^n\to X\) extending \(\sigma'\).

Proof. First prove (i) \(\implies\) (ii). Let \(X=\mathrm{N}\mathcal{C}\) and \(0<i<n\); we wish to extend \(\sigma':\Lambda^n_i\to X\) to \(\Delta^n\). For every \(0\leq k\leq n\) (or \(0<k\leq n\)), the morphism \(\Delta^0\xrightarrow{\{k\}}\Delta^n\) (or \(\Delta^1\xrightarrow{\{k-1,k\}}\Delta^n\)) factors through \(\Lambda^n_i\). Denote its image under \(\sigma'\) by \(C_k\in X_0=\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{C})\) (or \([g_k:C_{k-1}\to C_k]\in X_1=\operatorname{Mor}(\mathcal{C})\)). This gives an element of \(X_n\), \[C_0 \xrightarrow{g_1} C_1 \xrightarrow{g_2} \cdots \xrightarrow{g_n} C_n.\] Write \(\sigma\) for the corresponding morphism \(\Delta^n\to X\). The construction also shows that \(\sigma\) is the only possible extension of \(\sigma'\). Since \(\Lambda^n_i=\bigcup_{j\neq i}\operatorname{im}[\mathrm{d}^j: \Delta^{n-1}\to\Delta^n]\), it remains to verify \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:inner-horn-filling-aux0}{} \sigma \circ \mathrm{d}^j = \sigma' \circ \mathrm{d}^j : \Delta^{n-1} \to X, \quad j \neq i . \end{equation}\]

By the definition of the nerve, proving equation reduces to the following verification. For each \(j\neq i\) and each pair of adjacent elements \(h<k\) in the sequence \(0,\ldots,\widehat{j},\ldots,n\) (where \(\widehat{j}\) means that \(j\) is omitted), the pullbacks of \(\sigma\) and \(\sigma'\) along \(\Delta^1\xrightarrow{\{h,k\}}\Lambda^n_i\subset\Delta^n\) must agree.

  • If \(k=h+1\), this is guaranteed by the construction of \(\sigma\). In particular, equation always holds when \(j\in\{0,n\}\).

  • Suppose \((h,k)=(j-1,j+1)\). If \(n=2\), this case cannot occur. If \(n>2\), then either \(j-1>0\) or \(j+1<n\). When \(j-1>0\), \(\{j-1,j+1\}\) factors as \[\Delta^1 \xrightarrow{\{j-2, j\}} \Delta^{n-1} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{d}^0 = \{1, \ldots, n\}} \Lambda^n_i \subset \Delta^n.\] By the already known \(j=0\) case of equation, the two pullbacks agree. Similarly, when \(j+1<n\), the issue reduces to the known case \(j=n\).

Now prove (ii) \(\implies\) (i). Define a category \(\mathcal{C}\) by \(\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{C}):=X_0\) and, for all \(C,C'\in X_0\), \[\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}}(C, C') := \left\{ f \in X_1: d_1(f) = C, \; d_0(f) = C' \right\}.\] Use the degeneracy map \(s_0:X_0\to X_1\) to define the identity morphism \(\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_C\) as \(s_0(C)\). We also depict a morphism \(f\) as \(0\xrightarrow{f}1\) to emphasize that it corresponds to a \(1\)-simplex \([1]=\{0,1\}\to X\).

If \(d_0(f)=d_1(g)\), define the composite by \(gf:=d_1(\sigma)\), where \(\sigma:\Delta^2\to X\) is the unique extension of \[\text{Diagram chapter8-unit-108-d001}: \Lambda^2_1 \to X \quad \text{that is,}\quad d^0(\sigma) = g, \quad d^2(\sigma) = f.\]

The laws \(f\circ\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_C=f\) and \(\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{C'}\circ f=f\) are witnessed, respectively, by the following elements of \(X_2\). \[\text{Diagram chapter8-unit-108-d002} \quad \text{Diagram chapter8-unit-108-d003}\]

For associativity \(h(gf)=(hg)f\), construct \(\sigma':\Lambda^3_2\to X\) whose three faces are, respectively, \[\text{Diagram chapter8-unit-108-d004} \quad \text{Diagram chapter8-unit-108-d005} \quad \text{Diagram chapter8-unit-108-d006}\] This horn has a unique extension \(\sigma:\Delta^3\to X\) such that \(d^2(\sigma)\in X_2\) has the form \[\text{Diagram chapter8-unit-108-d007}\] By construction, however, this \(2\)-simplex also determines the composite of \(f\) and \(hg\), proving \((hg)f=h(gf)\).

Thus \(\mathcal{C}\) is a category. There is a canonical morphism \(X\to\mathrm{N}\mathcal{C}\): from a given \(\Delta^n\to X\), pull back along each \(\Delta^1\xrightarrow{\{j,j+1\}}\Delta^n\) to obtain a chain of morphisms. By construction, \(X_n\to\mathrm{N}\mathcal{C}_n\) is clearly a bijection for \(n=0,1\). If \(n\geq2\), choose \(0<i<n\) and consider the commutative diagram \[\text{Diagram chapter8-unit-108-d008}\] By the assumption and the unique inner horn-filling property, both vertical arrows are bijections. Moreover, \(\Lambda^n_i\) can be expressed as the \(\varinjlim\) of a family of \(\Delta^{n-1}\) and \(\Delta^{n-2}\) (that is, the gluing of \(n\) faces), so induction shows that the arrow in the second row is also a bijection. This proves the result.

Notice also that in the argument (ii) \(\implies\) (i), if there is a small category \(\mathcal{C}_0\) with \(X=\mathrm{N}(\mathcal{C}_0)\), then the category \(\mathcal{C}\) constructed in the proof is exactly \(\mathcal{C}_0\). Write \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Cat}}\) for the category of all small categories, with functors as morphisms. Every functor \(F:\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{C}'\) induces a morphism \(\mathrm{N}F:\mathrm{N}\mathcal{C}\to\mathrm{N}\mathcal{C}'\) in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{sSet}}\), mapping \((f_1,\ldots,f_n)\) to \((Ff_1,\ldots,Ff_n)\). This gives the nerve functor \(\mathrm{N}:\ensuremath{\mathsf{Cat}}\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{sSet}}\).

Proposition. The nerve functor \(\mathrm{N}:\ensuremath{\mathsf{Cat}}\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{sSet}}\) is fully faithful.

Proof. The proof of Proposition reference has already shown how to reconstruct morphisms and their composition from the nerve of a category. Hence a morphism \(\mathrm{N}(\mathcal{C})\to\mathrm{N}(\mathcal{C}')\) naturally induces a functor \(\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{C}'\). It is easy to see that this construction and the construction induced by \(\mathrm{N}\) are mutually inverse.

Example (Classifying space). Let \(\Gamma\) be a monoid. Define the categories \(\mathcal{B}\Gamma\) and \(\mathcal{E}\Gamma\) as follows:

Category Object set Morphisms Composition of morphisms
\(\mathcal{B}\Gamma\) \(\{\star\}\) \(\operatorname{End}_{\mathcal{B}\Gamma}(\star)=\Gamma\) multiplication in \(\Gamma\)
\(\mathcal{E}\Gamma\) \(\Gamma\) \(\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{E}\Gamma}(g,g')=\{h\in\Gamma:hg=g'\}\) multiplication in \(\Gamma\)

Define the nerves \(\mathrm{B}\Gamma:=\mathrm{N}((\mathcal{B}\Gamma)^{\operatorname{op}})\) and \(\mathrm{E}\Gamma:=\mathrm{N}((\mathcal{E}\Gamma)^{\operatorname{op}})\). The simplicial set \(\mathrm{B}\Gamma\) is called the classifying space of \(\Gamma\). Taking \((\cdots)^{\operatorname{op}}\) amounts to reversing the arrows in the definition of the nerve without changing their labels. Thus \[\begin{equation*} \begin{array}{|c|c|c|} \hline \text{Set} & \text{Element} & \text{Corresponding chain of morphisms in }\mathcal{B}\Gamma\text{ or }\mathcal{E}\Gamma \\ \hline (\mathrm{B}\Gamma)_n = \Gamma^n & (g_1, \ldots, g_n) & \star \xleftarrow{g_1} \cdots \leftarrow \star \xleftarrow{g_n} \star \\ \hline (\mathrm{E}\Gamma)_n = \Gamma^{n+1} & (g_1, \ldots, g_{n+1}) & g_1 \cdots g_{n+1} \xleftarrow{g_1} \cdots \leftarrow g_n g_{n+1} \xleftarrow{g_n} g_{n+1} \\ \hline \end{array} \end{equation*}\] Substitution into the definitions gives, for every \(n\geq0\), \[\begin{equation*} \mathrm{B}\Gamma: \qquad \begin{aligned} d_i(g_1, \ldots, g_n) & = \begin{cases} (g_2, \ldots, g_n), & i = 0 \\ (\ldots, g_i g_{i+1} , \ldots), & 0 < i < n \\ (g_1, \ldots, g_{n-1}), & i = n, \end{cases} \\ s_j(g_1, \ldots, g_n) & = \begin{cases} (1, g_1, \ldots, g_n), & j = 0 \\ (\ldots, g_j, 1, g_{j+1}, \ldots), & 0 < j < n \\ (g_1, \ldots, g_n, 1), & j = n, \end{cases} \end{aligned} \end{equation*}\] and \[\begin{equation*} \mathrm{E}\Gamma: \qquad \begin{aligned} d_i(g_1, \ldots, g_{n+1}) & = \begin{cases} (g_2, \ldots, g_{n+1}), & i = 0 \\ (g_1, \ldots, g_i g_{i+1} , \ldots), & 0 < i \leq n, \end{cases} \\ s_j(g_1, \ldots, g_{n+1}) & = \begin{cases} (1, g_1, \ldots, g_{n+1}), & j = 0 \\ (\ldots, g_j, 1, g_{j+1}, \ldots), & 0 < j \leq n. \end{cases} \end{aligned} \end{equation*}\]

There is a natural functor \((\mathcal{E}\Gamma)^{\operatorname{op}}\to(\mathcal{B}\Gamma)^{\operatorname{op}}\) mapping all objects to \(\star\) and every morphism \(h\in\Gamma\) to \(h\). The induced morphism \(\mathrm{E}\Gamma\to\mathrm{B}\Gamma\) simply maps \((g_1,\ldots,g_{n+1})\) to \((g_1,\ldots,g_n)\). The right multiplication action of \(\Gamma\) on \((\mathrm{E}\Gamma)_n\) acts along its fibers, or in other words changes the datum \(g_{n+1}\): \[(g_1, \ldots, g_n, g_{n+1})g = (g_1, \ldots, g_n, g_{n+1}g).\] These actions clearly commute with \(d_i\) and \(s_j\). If \(\Gamma\) is a group, the action is also free.

In topology, \(\mathrm{B}\Gamma\) (or its geometric realization \(|\mathrm{B}\Gamma|\); see §reference) serves to classify \(\Gamma\)-torsors over spaces, while \(\mathrm{E}\Gamma\to\mathrm{B}\Gamma\) gives the universal torsor. Example reference will show that \(\mathrm{E}\Gamma\) is “right-contractible.”

The Geometric-Realization Functor

We now begin to build a geometric picture of the simplicial sets introduced in §reference. We start with the standard \(n\)-simplex, where \(n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}_{\geq0}\). Write the standard ordered basis of \(\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^{n+1}\) as \(e_0,\ldots,e_n\). Define \[|\Delta^n| := \left\{ (x_0, \ldots, x_n) \in (\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}_{\geq 0})^{n+1} : \sum_{i=0}^n x_i = 1 \right\} \quad \par\textbf{Diagram chapter8-unit-109-d001}\par\] Its vertices are labeled \(0,\ldots,n\) by \(i\leftrightarrow e_i\). Its interior is given the standard orientation for which \(e_1-e_0,\ldots,e_n-e_{n-1}\) is a positively oriented basis at every point. Every monotone map \(f:[m]\to[n]\) induces a map \[\text{Diagram chapter8-unit-109-d002}\] If \(f\) is not surjective, the image of \(|f|\) lies in the boundary. The embedding \(|\mathrm{d}^i|:|\Delta^{n-1}|\to|\Delta^n|\) may be used to compare the orientation on the interior of \(|\Delta^{n-1}|\) with the orientation induced on the boundary by \(|\Delta^n|\). A standard determinant calculation shows that they differ by a factor of \((-1)^i\). The following figure illustrates the case \(n=2\).

Diagram chapter8-unit-109-d003

Summarizing the discussion above, we obtain a functor \[\begin{equation*} |\cdot|: \ensuremath{\bm\Delta}\to \ensuremath{\mathsf{Top}} \quad \left\{\begin{array}{ll} \text{objects} & [n] \mapsto |\Delta^n| \\ \text{morphisms} & f \mapsto |f| . \end{array}\right. \end{equation*}\] We wish to extend it to a functor \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{sSet}}\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{Top}}\). Recall that \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Top}}\) is cocomplete.

Definition (Geometric-realization functor). The functor \(|\cdot|:\ensuremath{\mathsf{sSet}}\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{Top}}\) is defined as follows. If \(X\) is a simplicial set, then \[|X| := \varinjlim_{n, x} |\Delta^n|,\] where \(n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}_{\geq0}\) and \(x\in X_n\), or equivalently, where \(x\) is a morphism \(\Delta^n\to X\). Such pairs \((n,x)\) form a category. A morphism from \((n,x)\) to \((m,y)\) is precisely an \(f\in\operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\bm\Delta}}([n],[m])\) for which the diagram \[\text{Diagram chapter8-unit-109-d004}\] commutes; equivalently, \(f^*:X_m\to X_n\) must satisfy \(f^*(y)=x\).

For fixed \(m\geq0\), the category of data \((n,x:\Delta^n\to\Delta^m)\) has the terminal object \((m,\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{\Delta^m})\). Therefore the geometric realization of \(\Delta^m\) is canonically identified with the previously defined \(|\Delta^m|\). Thus the notation is consistent.

Remark. For every simplicial set \(X\), there is a canonical isomorphism \(\varinjlim_{n,x}\Delta^n\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}X\). This follows directly by applying the Density Theorem reference to the category \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{sSet}}=\ensuremath{\bm\Delta}^{\wedge}\); the reader is invited to check it.

Remark. By Theorem reference, geometric realization is the left Kan extension of the functor \(|\cdot|:\ensuremath{\bm\Delta}\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{Top}}\) along \(\ensuremath{\bm\Delta}\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{sSet}}\); see Definition reference. Thus the construction is entirely natural.

By the construction above, for each \(n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}_{\geq0}\) and \(x\in X_n\), the universal property of \(\varinjlim\) gives a canonical map \(i_{n,x}:|\Delta^n|\to|X|\), compatible as \((n,x)\) varies. Taking \(\varinjlim\) in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Top}}\) is simply the operation of gluing topological spaces. More concretely, the geometric realization can be written as the quotient space \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:geom-realization-quotient}{} |X| = \dfrac{\displaystyle\bigsqcup_{n \geq 0} X_n \times |\Delta^n| }{(f^*(y), t) \sim (y, |f|(t)) }, \quad \text{Diagram chapter8-unit-109-d005} \end{equation}\] In keeping with the geometric intuition, a simplicial set \(X\) may be viewed as a model of a space. The sets \(X_0,X_1,\ldots\) are the collections of building blocks of the model: each element of \(X_n\) corresponds to, and labels, one copy of \(|\Delta^n|\). The various maps \(f^*:X_m\to X_n\) serve as assembly instructions that determine how these copies of \(|\Delta^n|\) are glued together. Since the morphisms in \(\ensuremath{\bm\Delta}\) have already been described explicitly, the equivalence relation in equation can be generated by two special kinds of \(f\).

  • Take \(\mathrm{d}^i:[n-1]\hookrightarrow[n]\). Then \(|\mathrm{d}^i|\) embeds \(\{d_i(x)\}\times|\Delta^{n-1}|\) into \(\{x\}\times|\Delta^n|\). Thus the face map \(d_i:X_n\to X_{n-1}\) labels the \(i\)th face of the \(n\)-dimensional component corresponding to \(x\) by \(d_i(x)\), and the gluing is then performed according to these labels.

  • Take \(\mathrm{s}^j:[n+1]\twoheadrightarrow[n]\). Then \(|\mathrm{s}^j|\) “collapses” \(\{s_j(x)\}\times|\Delta^{n+1}|\) onto \(\{x\}\times|\Delta^n|\). Thus the degeneracy map \(s_j:X_n\to X_{n+1}\) determines how an \(n\)-dimensional component corresponding to \(x\) gives rise to a “degenerate” \((n+1)\)-dimensional component, labeled \(s_j(x)\), which is collapsed onto its \(j\)th face during the gluing process.

Consequently, degenerate \(n\)-simplices (Definition reference) may be omitted from the gluing process, but the degeneracy data still cannot be ignored. For example, a face map \(d_i:X_n\to X_{n-1}\) may well map a nondegenerate simplex to a degenerate simplex.

Example. As an illustration, \(\partial\Delta^n\) in Example reference realizes the boundary of the standard \(n\)-simplex in the intuitive sense, while the horn \(\Lambda^n_k\) is obtained by removing from \(\partial\Delta^n\) the face opposite its \(k\)th vertex. Here is one illustration:

Diagram chapter8-unit-109-d006

Example. For every topological space \(\mathcal{X}\), define the cone over it, \(\operatorname{Cone}_{\mathrm{top}}(\mathcal{X})\), to be the space obtained by contracting the closed subset \(\mathcal{X}\times\{0\}\) of \(\mathcal{X}\times[0,1]\) to a single point. Visually, \[\operatorname{Cone}_{\mathrm{top}}(\mathcal{X}) = \; \par\textbf{Diagram chapter8-unit-109-d007}\par\] As a simple exercise, check that \(|X^{\lhd}|\simeq\operatorname{Cone}_{\mathrm{top}}(|X|)\simeq|X^{\rhd}|\). This shows that the cones in Definition reference are aptly named; the only difference between the left and right cones is their orientation.

By presenting a triangulation of a space as a simplicial set, one can extract many important topological properties. This approach is aptly called “combinatorial topology”. Further discussion and examples may be found in [You].

Definition (Singular-set functor). For every topological space \(E\), define the simplicial set \(\mathrm{Sing}(E)\) by \[\mathrm{Sing}(E)_n := \operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{Top}}}(|\Delta^n|, E), \quad n \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}_{\geq 0},\] where \(d_i:\mathrm{Sing}(E)_n\to\mathrm{Sing}(E)_{n-1}\) (respectively, \(s_j:\mathrm{Sing}(E)_n\to\mathrm{Sing}(E)_{n+1}\)) is given by pullback along \(|\mathrm{d}^i|:|\Delta^{n-1}|\to|\Delta^n|\) (respectively, \(|\mathrm{s}^j|:|\Delta^{n+1}|\to|\Delta^n|\)). This is called the (simplicial) singular set associated with \(E\). The construction gives a functor \[\mathrm{Sing}: \ensuremath{\mathsf{Top}} \to \ensuremath{\mathsf{sSet}}.\]

Theorem. The geometric-realization functor is left adjoint to the singular-set functor. In other words, there is a natural bijection \[\text{Diagram chapter8-unit-109-d008}\] where \(X\in\operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{sSet}})\) and \(E\in\operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Top}})\).

Proof. Recall that \(|X|=\varinjlim_{n,x}|\Delta^n|\). There are canonical isomorphisms \[\begin{align*} \operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{Top}}}\left( \varinjlim_{n, x} |\Delta^n| , E \right) & \ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}\varprojlim_{n, x} \operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{Top}}}(|\Delta^n|, E) = \varprojlim_{n, x} \mathrm{Sing}(E)_n \\ & \ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}\varprojlim_{n, x} \operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{sSet}}}\left( \Delta^n, \mathrm{Sing}(E) \right) \\ \varphi & \mapsto \left( \psi_n(x) := \varphi \circ i_{n, x} \right)_{n, x}. \end{align*}\]

Every family of morphisms \((\psi_n(x))_{n,x}\) determined by a morphism \(\psi:X\to\mathrm{Sing}(E)\) satisfies the compatibility conditions, and thus is an element of the inverse limit on the right-hand side above. To complete the proof, it remains to show that giving a morphism \(\psi\) is equivalent to giving a compatible family of morphisms; this is exactly what Remark reference guarantees.

Remark. For homotopy theory, the category \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{CGHaus}}\) mentioned in §reference may be more convenient than \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Top}}\). Since the inclusion functor \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{CGHaus}}\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{Top}}\) has a right adjoint \(k\), it preserves \(\varinjlim\). Moreover, \(|\Delta^n|\) is a compactly generated Hausdorff space. Consequently, the gluing (respectively, the formation of \(\operatorname{Hom}\)) in geometric realization (respectively, the singular set) may be carried out within \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{CGHaus}}\)1. Thus the adjoint pair of Theorem reference factors into two adjunctions, written with the same notation as \[\text{Diagram chapter8-unit-109-d009}\]

For any two simplicial sets \(X\) and \(Y\), their product is defined degreewise: \[\begin{gather*} (X \times Y)_n = X_n \times Y_n, \\ d_i(x, y) = (d_i(x), d_i(y)), \\ s_j(x, y) = (s_j(x), s_j(y)). \end{gather*}\] This is both the categorical product in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{sSet}}=\ensuremath{\mathsf{Set}}^{\ensuremath{\bm\Delta}^{\operatorname{op}}}\) and the construction of Definition reference applied to the monoidal category \((\ensuremath{\mathsf{Set}},\times)\). Although both definitions arise from category theory, the following fundamental result shows that they also have geometric meaning.

Theorem. For simplicial sets \(X\) and \(Y\), there is a canonical isomorphism in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{CGHaus}}\) \[|X \times Y| \simeq |X| \times |Y|.\] More generally, the \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{CGHaus}}\)-valued version of \(|\cdot|\) preserves finite limits. If either \(X\) or \(Y\) has only finitely many nondegenerate simplices, then \(|X\times Y|\simeq|X|\times|Y|\) also holds in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Top}}\).

The proof in the general case is rather involved; see [GZ67] or [Dri03]. The isomorphism does not hold in general for the \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Top}}\)-valued version of geometric realization. Notice also that the condition stated in the theorem for the \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Top}}\)-valued version is not optimal.

Corollary. Write \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Grp}}\) for the category of groups. If a simplicial set \(X\) can be promoted to an object of \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{sGrp}}\), then \(|X|\) naturally has the structure of a topological group. Analogous results hold for other algebraic structures.

In view of Theorem reference, it is natural to define a homotopy from \(g\) to \(f\), for morphisms \(f,g:X\rightrightarrows Y\) in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{sSet}}\), as a morphism \(H:X\times\Delta^1\to Y\) making the following diagram commute: \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:simplicial-homotopy-prep}{} \text{Diagram chapter8-unit-109-d010} \end{equation}\] As a special case, the composite \(X\times\Delta^1\xrightarrow{\text{projection}}X\xrightarrow{f}Y\) gives a constant homotopy from \(f\) to itself. Homotopy as defined here is not, however, an equivalence relation: a simple example already shows that it need not be symmetric. In homotopy theory one usually imposes an additional condition on \(Y\), for example that it be a Kan complex. The homotopy relation then has the expected properties, allowing homotopy groups, weak equivalences, and related notions to be studied combinatorially. Although this book does not prove Theorem reference, it is useful to say a little more about the simple special case \(X=\Delta^p\) and \(Y=\Delta^q\). For example, how can the nondegenerate simplices of \(\Delta^p\times\Delta^q\) be classified? The answer not only helps explain the geometric realization of a product; the related construction will also be needed later. First, the product of two partially ordered sets \(S_1\) and \(S_2\) becomes a partially ordered set under \((a_1,a_2)\leq(b_1,b_2)\) if and only if \(a_1\leq b_1\) and \(a_2\leq b_2\). This is also the product of the corresponding categories.

Definition. Let \(p,q\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}_{\geq0}\). A \((p,q)\)-shuffle is an injective monotone map \(\sigma:[p+q]\to[p]\times[q]\).

For every \(n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}_{\geq0}\), specifying a monotone map \(\sigma:[n]\to[p]\times[q]\) is equivalent to specifying a pair of monotone maps \(\sigma_-:[n]\to[p]\) and \(\sigma_+:[n]\to[q]\). It is also equivalent to specifying an \(n\)-simplex of \(\Delta^p\times\Delta^q\). The condition that \(\sigma\) be injective says precisely that the path \(i\mapsto(\sigma_-(i),\sigma_+(i))\) never remains stationary, for \(i=0,\ldots,n\). When \(n=p+q\), the situation may be pictured as follows: \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:pq-shuffle-diag}{} \par\textbf{Diagram chapter8-unit-109-d011}\par \quad \text{exactly $p+q$ steps.} \end{equation}\] Thus, for a \((p,q)\)-shuffle \(\sigma\), define \[\begin{align*} I_\pm & := \left\{ 1 \leq i \leq p+q : \sigma_\pm(i-1) < \sigma_\pm(i) \right\} \\ & = \left\{ 1 \leq i \leq p+q : \sigma_\pm(i-1) = \sigma_\pm(i) - 1 \right\} \\ & = \left\{ 1 \leq i \leq p+q: \sigma_\mp(i-1) = \sigma_\mp(i) \right\}, \end{align*}\] so that \(I_+\sqcup I_-=\{1,\ldots,p+q\}\). The subsets \(I_+\) and \(I_-\) correspond, respectively, to the upward and rightward portions of the path in equation. Thus a \((p,q)\)-shuffle may also be viewed as an ordering of \(p\) symbols \(\rightarrow\) and \(q\) symbols \(\uparrow\); there are \(\binom{p+q}{p}\) such orderings. These observations also show that \(\sigma_+\) and \(\sigma_-\) are surjective monotone maps for every \((p,q)\)-shuffle.

Proposition. Let \(p,q\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}_{\geq0}\). Consider an \(n\)-simplex of \(\Delta^p\times\Delta^q\), that is, a monotone map \(\sigma:[n]\to[p]\times[q]\). Set \((p_i,q_i):=\sigma(i)\) and \((p',q'):=(p_n-p_0,q_n-q_0)\). Then \(\sigma\) is nondegenerate if and only if the following conditions hold:

  • \(p'+q'=n\);

  • \(\sigma\) factors as a \((p',q')\)-shuffle \(\sigma':[n]\to[p']\times[q']\) followed by a monotone injection \([p']\times[q']\hookrightarrow[p]\times[q]\) of the form \(f\times g\).

Proof. Identify \(\sigma\) with the pair of monotone maps \((\sigma_-,\sigma_+)\). Consider the path \(i\mapsto(p_i,q_i)\) as in equation. The condition that \(\sigma\) be nondegenerate is equivalent to the condition that this path never remains stationary. The rest is clear.

Using this description of the nondegenerate simplices, the reader may visualize the isomorphism \(|\Delta^p\times\Delta^q|\simeq|\Delta^p|\times|\Delta^q|\) in the cases \((p,q)=(1,1)\) and \((2,1)\). For example, the following figure shows the triangulation of \(|\Delta^2|\times|\Delta^1|\) into three tetrahedra, corresponding to the \(3=\binom{3}{2}\) \((2,1)\)-shuffles.

Diagram chapter8-unit-109-d012

Definition. Let \(\sigma\) be a \((p,q)\)-shuffle. Its sign is defined by \[\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma) := (-1)^{|I_\sigma|}, \quad I_\sigma := \left\{ (i, j) \in I_- \times I_+ : i > j \right\}.\]

If \(\sigma\) is viewed as an ordering of \(p\) symbols \(\rightarrow\) and \(q\) symbols \(\uparrow\), then \(I_\sigma\) is precisely the set of pairs \((j,i)\), with \(j<i\), that occur in the reversed order \((\uparrow,\rightarrow)\). A simple combinatorial exercise shows that there is a unique \(\tau\in\mathfrak{S}_{p+q}\) that rearranges the word into the form \(\rightarrow\cdots\rightarrow\uparrow\cdots\uparrow\) without changing the internal order within either \(I_+\) or \(I_-\). Thus Definition reference is equivalent to \(\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)=\operatorname{sgn}(\tau)\). For a \((p,q)\)-shuffle \(\sigma\), exchanging the roles of \(\sigma_-\) and \(\sigma_+\) gives a \((q,p)\)-shuffle \(\sigma'\). The interpretation above and a basic combinatorial argument give \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:shuffle-sign-0}{} \operatorname{sgn}(\sigma) = (-1)^{pq} \operatorname{sgn}(\sigma'). \end{equation}\] In the same spirit, define a \((p,q,r)\)-shuffle to be an injective monotone map \(\sigma=(\sigma_-,\sigma_0,\sigma_+):[p+q+r]\to[p]\times[q]\times[r]\), or, equivalently, regard it as an ordering of the symbols \(\rightarrow\), \(\nearrow\), and \(\uparrow\). Define \(\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma):=(-1)^{|I_\sigma|}\), where \(I_\sigma\) consists of all triples of indices \(k>j>i\) corresponding to odd permutations of \((\rightarrow,\nearrow,\uparrow)\). The same standard combinatorial exercise shows that if the \((p,q,r)\)-shuffle \(\sigma\) has a factorization \[[p+q+r] \xrightarrow{\sigma_1} [p+q] \times [r] \xrightarrow{\sigma_2 \times \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{[r]}} [p] \times [q] \times [r],\] then \(\sigma_1\) is a \((p+q,r)\)-shuffle, \(\sigma_2\) is a \((p,q)\)-shuffle, and \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:shuffle-sign-1}{} \operatorname{sgn}(\sigma) = \operatorname{sgn}(\sigma_1) \operatorname{sgn}(\sigma_2). \end{equation}\] There is, of course, a corresponding statement for a factorization \([p+q+r]\to[p]\times[q+r]\to[p]\times[q]\times[r]\). Equations equation and equation are entirely combinatorial in nature; their detailed verification is left to the exercises for this chapter. These observations will be used in §reference.

  1. It must be explained that the \(\varinjlim\) in question does indeed exist in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{CGHaus}}\). This is a topological issue; see [GZ67].↩︎

The Dold–Kan Correspondence

Following the conventions of algebraic topology, for an additive category \(\mathcal{A}\) we consider the category of chain complexes over it (Definition reference), denoted by \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ch}}(\mathcal{A})\), together with its subcategory \[\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ch}}_{\geq 0}(\mathcal{A}) := \left\{ A = (A_n, \partial_n)_{n \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}} : \text{chain complex}, \; \forall n < 0, \; A_n = 0 \right\},\] where \(\partial_n=\partial_n^A:A_n\to A_{n-1}\). For an object of \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ch}}_{\geq0}(\mathcal{A})\), it plainly suffices to specify the data \((A_n)_{n\geq0}\) and \((\partial_n)_{n\geq1}\). The category \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ch}}_{\geq m}(\mathcal{A})\) is defined similarly; compare the cochain complex version in Definition reference. By enlarging the chosen Grothendieck universe if necessary, we may assume that \(\mathcal{A}\) is a small additive category; see [Li1]. From \(\mathcal{A}\) one can define the category \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{s}}\mathcal{A}\) of simplicial objects; the constant simplicial object corresponding to \(0\) is still denoted by \(0\in\operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{s}}\mathcal{A})\). This section aims to give a first account of the relationships among these categories. More precisely, we shall define three functors \[\text{Diagram chapter8-unit-110-d001}\] where \(\mathrm{N}\) is defined only when \(\mathcal{A}\) is an abelian category. Both \(\mathrm{C}\) and \(\mathrm{N}\) extend to the semisimplicial objects of Remark reference; in other words, neither of them involves the degeneracy morphisms. Our treatment follows [LuHA]. We begin by making the relevant definitions explicit.

Definition (Unnormalized chain complex). For a semisimplicial object \(X\) in \(\mathcal{A}\) and every \(n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}_{\geq1}\), define \[\partial_n := \sum_{i=0}^n (-1)^i d_i: X_n \to X_{n-1}.\] The objects \((X_n)_{n\geq0}\) together with \((\partial_n)_n\) form an object \(\mathrm{C}X\) of \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ch}}_{\geq0}(\mathcal{A})\), called the unnormalized chain complex, or Moore chain complex, given by \(X\). Thus \((\mathrm{C}X)_n=X_n\).

We must show that \(\partial_{n-1}\partial_n=0\) when \(n>1\). Indeed, the identity \(i<j\implies d_id_j=d_{j-1}d_i\) in equation gives \[\begin{multline*} \partial_{n-1} \partial_n = \sum_{i=0}^{n-1} \sum_{j=0}^n (-1)^{i+j} d_i d_j \\ = \sum_{0 \leq i < j \leq n} (-1)^{i+j} d_{j-1} d_i + \sum_{n-1 \geq i \geq j \geq 0} (-1)^{i+j} d_i d_j = 0. \end{multline*}\] This construction is plainly canonical in \(X\) and gives the functor \(\mathrm{C}\).

Example. Let \(\Bbbk\) be a commutative ring and \(\mathcal{A}=\Bbbk\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\). For a group \(\Gamma\), Example reference gives the corresponding simplicial set \(\mathrm{E}\Gamma\). Define a simplicial object \(\Bbbk\mathrm{E}\Gamma\) in \(\Bbbk\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\) whose term in degree \(n\) is the free \(\Bbbk\)-module with basis \((\mathrm{E}\Gamma)_n\), and whose \(d_i\) and \(s_i\) are extended linearly. We claim that \(\mathrm{C}(\Bbbk\mathrm{E}\Gamma)\) is precisely the chain complex \(\mathsf{L}:=(\mathsf{L}_n,\partial'_n)_n\) introduced in Definition reference. First, \(\mathsf{L}_n\) is by definition the free \(\Bbbk\)-module with basis \(\Gamma^{n+1}\). Take the map from \((\mathrm{E}\Gamma)_n=\Gamma^{n+1}\) to \(\mathsf{L}_n\) \[\left( g_1, \ldots, g_{n+1} \right) \mapsto \left(g_1 \cdots g_{n+1}, \; \ldots , \; g_n g_{n+1}, \; g_{n+1}\right).\] Extend it linearly to \((\Bbbk\mathrm{E}\Gamma)_n\). The reader may verify that \(\sum_i(-1)^id_i\) thereby corresponds to \(\partial'_n:\mathsf{L}_n\to\mathsf{L}_{n-1}\), giving the asserted isomorphism.

Moreover, \(\Gamma\) acts on the right on each \((\mathrm{E}\Gamma)_n\) by \((g_1,\ldots,g_{n+1})\xmapsto{g}(g_1,\ldots,g_n,g_{n+1}g)\). In the basis coordinates of \(\mathsf{L}_n\), this action becomes \((g_0,\ldots,g_n)\xmapsto{g}(g_0g,\ldots,g_ng)\). Thus we recover the right \(\Gamma\)-action on \(\mathsf{L}\) from Definition reference. Consequently, the complexes obtained by taking degreewise \(\Gamma\)-coinvariants of the chain complexes \(\mathrm{C}(\Bbbk\mathrm{E}\Gamma)\) and \(\mathsf{L}\) are also isomorphic. On the \(\mathrm{C}(\Bbbk\mathrm{E}\Gamma)\) side, this amounts to taking the degreewise quotient of \(\mathrm{E}\Gamma\) and then the free \(\Bbbk\)-module. It follows that \[\mathrm{C}(\Bbbk\mathrm{B}\Gamma) \simeq \mathsf{L} \ensuremath{\underset{\Bbbk[\Gamma]}{\otimes}} \Bbbk,\] where the tensor product involves the augmentation homomorphism \(\Bbbk[\Gamma]\to\Bbbk\). As a consequence, group homology (Definition reference) is interpreted as \[\operatorname{H}_n(\mathrm{B}\Gamma; \Bbbk) := \operatorname{H}_n \mathrm{C}(\Bbbk\mathrm{B}\Gamma) \simeq \operatorname{H}_n(\Gamma, \Bbbk), \quad n \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}_{\geq 0}.\]

The left-hand side features the homology of a simplicial set, a general construction to be introduced in Definition reference. The exercises in this chapter will give a similar isomorphism for the normalized version \(\overline{\mathsf{L}}\) of \(\mathsf{L}\), corresponding to the normalized chain complex \(\mathrm{N}(\Bbbk\mathrm{E}\Gamma)\) to be discussed in Definition reference.

Definition. Let \((A_n,\partial_n)_{n\geq0}\) be an object of \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ch}}_{\geq0}(\mathcal{A})\). Define an object \(\Gamma(A)\) of \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{s}}\mathcal{A}\) as follows: \[(\Gamma A)_n := \bigoplus_{t: [n] \twoheadrightarrow [k]} A_k.\]

For every morphism \(f:[m]\to[n]\) in \(\ensuremath{\bm\Delta}\), the corresponding morphism \(f^*:(\Gamma A)_n\to(\Gamma A)_m\) is represented, with respect to the direct-sum decomposition above, by the matrix \[\left( \Phi_{u, t} : A_k \to A_l \right)_{\substack{ u: [m] \twoheadrightarrow [l] \\ t: [n] \twoheadrightarrow [k] }}.\] This matrix is determined as follows. Given \(t:[n]\twoheadrightarrow[k]\), take the surjection–injection factorization of \(tf\), \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:Dold-Kan-epi-mono}{}\text{Diagram chapter8-unit-110-d002} \end{equation}\]

  • if \(l=k\), set \(\Phi_{u,t}=\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}\);

  • if \(l=k-1\) and \(v=\mathrm{d}^0\) (the order-preserving injection omitting \(0\)), set \(\Phi_{u,t}=\partial_k:A_k\to A_{k-1}\);

  • in all other cases, set \(\Phi_{u,t}=0\).

Notice that once \(f\) and \(t\) are given, there is at most one \(u\) for which \(\Phi_{u,t}\neq0\).

The verification that \(\Gamma A\in\operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{s}}\mathcal{A})\) is somewhat tedious and is omitted. The heart of the construction lies in the direct summand \(A_n\) of \((\Gamma A)_n\) and its behavior under order-preserving injections. All lower-degree direct summands \(A_k\) arise from degeneracies induced by surjections \([n]\twoheadrightarrow[k]\); the definition of \(f^*\) in the general case merely implements this idea. The construction above is canonical and gives a functor \(\Gamma:\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ch}}_{\geq0}(\mathcal{A})\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{s}}\mathcal{A}\).

Definition. Let \(\mathcal{A}\) be an abelian category. For a semisimplicial object \(X\) in \(\mathcal{A}\) and every \(n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}_{\geq0}\), define \[\begin{align*} (\mathrm{N} X)_n & := \bigcap_{i=1}^n \operatorname{ker}\left[ d_i: X_n \to X_{n-1} \right], \quad n \geq 1, \\ (\mathrm{N} X)_0 & := X_0. \end{align*}\]

The morphisms \(\mathrm{N}X_n\to\mathrm{N}X_{n-1}\) induced by \(X_n\xrightarrow{d_0}X_{n-1}\) (verify this using equation) are henceforth denoted by \(\partial_n\). Together with these objects, they form an object \(\mathrm{N}X\) of \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ch}}_{\geq0}(\mathcal{A})\), called the normalized chain complex corresponding to \(X\).

Proposition. For \(X\) as above and every \(n\geq0\), write \(u_n:(\mathrm{N}X)_n\hookrightarrow X_n\) for the natural inclusion. Then \((u_n)_{n\geq0}\) forms a monomorphism \(u:\mathrm{N}X\to\mathrm{C}X\) in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ch}}_{\geq0}(\mathcal{A})\); this construction is functorial in \(X\).

Proof. This follows directly from the definitions of \(\mathrm{N}X\) and \(\mathrm{C}X\).

The next few results are preparations for the Dold–Kan theorem, Theorem reference.

Lemma. Let \(\mathcal{A}\) be an abelian category. For every \(A\in\operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ch}}_{\geq0}(\mathcal{A}))\) and \(n\geq0\), we have \(\mathrm{N}\Gamma(A)_n=A_n\). These identifications give an isomorphism of functors \(\eta:\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ch}}_{\geq0}(\mathcal{A})}\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}} \mathrm{N}\Gamma\).

Proof. Given \(t:[n]\twoheadrightarrow[k]\) with \(k<n\), one can always choose \(1\leq i\leq n\) such that \(t^{-1}(t(i))\) has at least two elements. Consequently \(t\mathrm{d}^i\) is surjective, and the following diagram commutes: \[\text{Diagram chapter8-unit-110-d003}\] Definition reference then shows that \(\mathrm{N}\Gamma(A)_n\) is contained in the direct summand \(A_n\) corresponding to \(\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}:[n]\to[n]\). The same definition readily gives \(\mathrm{N}\Gamma(A)_n=A_n\) and shows that \(\mathrm{N}\Gamma(A)_{n+1}\to\mathrm{N}\Gamma(A)_n\) is precisely \(\partial_{n+1}:A_{n+1}\to A_n\). This proves the result.

Lemma. Let \(\mathcal{A}\) be an abelian category. The functors above form an adjunction \[\text{Diagram chapter8-unit-110-d004}\]

  • Its unit morphism is the isomorphism \(\eta\) of Lemma reference.

  • Its counit morphism \(\epsilon:\Gamma\mathrm{N}\to\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{s}}\mathcal{A}}\) is described as follows. For \(t:[n]\twoheadrightarrow[k]\), on the corresponding direct summand \((\mathrm{N}X)_k\) of \(\Gamma\mathrm{N}(X)_n\), the map \(\epsilon_{X,n}\) is the composite \((\mathrm{N}X)_k\subset X_k\xrightarrow{t^*}X_n\).

Proof. For \(A\in\operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ch}}_{\geq0}(\mathcal{A}))\) and \(X\in\operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{s}}\mathcal{A})\), we first prove that the composite \[\operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{s}}\mathcal{A}}(\Gamma(A), X) \xrightarrow{\mathrm{N}} \operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ch}}_{\geq 0}(\mathcal{A})}(\mathrm{N}\Gamma(A), \mathrm{N}(X)) \xrightarrow{\eta_A^*} \operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ch}}_{\geq 0}(\mathcal{A})}(A, \mathrm{N}(X))\] is a bijection. Its inverse is defined concretely as follows. Given \(\phi=(\phi_n)_{n\geq0}:A\to\mathrm{N}(X)\), define a morphism \[\Phi_n: (\Gamma A)_n = \bigoplus_{t: [n] \twoheadrightarrow [k]} A_k \to X_n\] whose restriction to the direct summand corresponding to \(t:[n]\twoheadrightarrow[k]\) is the composite \[A_k \xrightarrow{\phi_k} (\mathrm{N}X)_k \subset X_k \xrightarrow{t^*} X_n.\] For such a \(t\) and an arbitrary \(f:[m]\to[n]\), take the surjection–injection factorization of \(tf\) as in equation, and consider the following diagram in \(\mathcal{A}\) (see Definition reference): \[\text{Diagram chapter8-unit-110-d005}\] The left square commutes by the definition of the normalized chain complex \(\mathrm{N}X\), the middle square plainly commutes, and the right square commutes because \(tf=vu\). Thus \(\Phi=(\Phi_n)_n\) is a morphism in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{s}}\mathcal{A}\).

The verification that \(\eta_A^*\mathrm{N}\) and \(\phi\mapsto\Phi\) are mutually inverse is routine. In the description of \(\phi\mapsto\Phi\), take \(\phi=\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{\mathrm{N}X}\); the result is exactly the asserted \(\epsilon\).

Lemma. Take \(\mathcal{A}=\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ab}}\). Then \(\Gamma\) is an equivalence; more precisely, the adjunction \(\text{Diagram chapter8-unit-110-diagram-006}\) is an adjoint equivalence in the sense of [Li1].

Proof. It suffices to prove that the counit morphism \(\epsilon\) of Lemma reference is an isomorphism. Let \(X\in\operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{s}}\mathcal{A})\). We claim that \(\epsilon_{X,n}:\Gamma(\mathrm{N}X)_n\to X_n\) is injective for every \(n\geq0\). Let \(x=(x_t)_t\) be an element of its domain, where \(t\) ranges over all order-preserving surjections \([n]\twoheadrightarrow[k]\). For a given \(t\), define the order-preserving injection \[\begin{align*} s = s_t : [k] & \hookrightarrow [n] \\ i & \mapsto \min t^{-1}(i), \end{align*}\] which satisfies \(ts=\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{[k]}\). Suppose that \(x\neq0\), and write \[S := \left\{t: x_t \neq 0 \right\} \neq \emptyset.\] Choose the smallest \(k\) for which there is a \(t:[n]\twoheadrightarrow[k]\) in \(S\), then choose such a \(t\) minimizing \(\sum_{i=0}^k\min t^{-1}(i)\), and construct \(s\). We shall prove that \(s^*(\epsilon_{X,n}(x))=x_t\in X_k\), which shows that \(\epsilon_{X,n}(x)\neq0\).

By the concrete description of \(\epsilon_{X,n}\), it is enough to show that for every \(t':[n]\twoheadrightarrow[k']\), \(s^*(t')^*(x_{t'})\neq0\) implies \(t=t'\). Set \(u:=t's:[k]\to[k']\). If \(t'\notin S\), then \(x_{t'}=0\). Thus it remains to consider \(t'\in S\) satisfying \(s^*(t')^*(x_{t'})=u^*(x_{t'})\neq0\).

Since \(t\) is order-preserving and surjective, \(\min t^{-1}(0)=0\), and the same holds for \(t'\), so \(u(0)=0\). Moreover, \(x_{t'}\in(\mathrm{N}X)_{k'}\) implies that \(u^*(x_{t'})\neq0\) is possible only if \(\operatorname{im}(u)\supset\{1,\ldots,k'\}\). Hence we may assume that \(u\) is surjective. The minimality of \(k\) then forces \(k'=k\) and \(u=\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}\).

Consequently, \(t'(\min t^{-1}(i))=i\) for \(i=0,\ldots,k\), and hence \(\min(t')^{-1}(i)\leq\min t^{-1}(i)\). By the choice of \(t\), we obtain \(\min(t')^{-1}(i)=\min t^{-1}(i)\) for every \(0\leq i\leq k\). An order-preserving surjection is determined by the initial points of its fibers, so this is equivalent to \(t=t'\). Thus \(\epsilon_{X,n}\) is injective.

We now prove by induction on \(n\) that \(\epsilon_{X,n}\) is surjective. We claim that, for every \(0\leq i\leq n\), \[\operatorname{im}\left( \epsilon_{X, n} \right) \supset X(i)_n := \bigcap_{i < j \leq n} \operatorname{ker}(d_j) \subset X_n.\]

For \(i=0\), we have \(X(i)_n=(\mathrm{N}X)_n\), and the inclusion above follows readily from the concrete description of \(\epsilon_{X,n}\). Our goal is the case \(i=n\). Let \(n\geq i\geq1\) and \(y\in X(i)_n\). The induction hypothesis for \(n-1\) and the description of \(\epsilon_{X,n}\) give \[s_{i-1} d_i(y) \in s_{i-1}\left( \operatorname{im}\left(\epsilon_{X, n-1}\right) \right) \subset \operatorname{im}\left( \epsilon_{X, n} \right).\]

On the other hand, the simplicial identities equation give \[\begin{gather*} d_i s_{i-1} d_i = d_i, \\ j > i \implies d_j s_{i-1} d_i = s_{i-1} d_{j-1} d_i = s_{i-1} d_i d_j. \end{gather*}\] Thus \(y-s_{i-1}d_i(y)\in X(i-1)_n\), and the induction hypothesis for \(i-1\) shows that this element lies in \(\operatorname{im}(\epsilon_{X,n})\). Therefore \(y\in\operatorname{im}(\epsilon_{X,n})\), as required.

Theorem (A. Dold, D. Kan). For every additive category \(\mathcal{A}\), the functor \(\Gamma:\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ch}}_{\geq0}(\mathcal{A})\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{s}}\mathcal{A}\) is fully faithful.

  • If \(\mathcal{A}\) is also a Karoubi category as mentioned in §reference, meaning that every idempotent has a kernel, then \(\Gamma\) is an equivalence of categories.

  • If, in addition, \(\mathcal{A}\) is an abelian category (and hence also a Karoubi category), then \(\mathrm{N}\) is a quasi-inverse functor to \(\Gamma\), and \(\text{Diagram chapter8-unit-111-diagram-001}\) is an adjoint equivalence. The unit and counit morphisms of the adjunction are described in Lemma reference.

Proof. Consider the functor \[\tilde{h}_{\mathcal{A}}: \mathcal{A} \to \tilde{\mathcal{A}}^\wedge := \ensuremath{\mathsf{Ab}}^{(\mathcal{A}^{\operatorname{op}})}, \quad Y \mapsto \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{A}}(\cdot, Y).\] Its composite with the forgetful functor \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ab}}\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{Set}}\) is the Yoneda embedding \(h_{\mathcal{A}}:\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{A}^\wedge\) recalled in §reference. The functor \(\tilde{h}_{\mathcal{A}}\) is fully faithful. This is simply the \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ab}}\)-enriched version of the Yoneda lemma, but it can also be deduced from the original version. For every \(Y_1,Y_2\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{A})\), the composite map \[\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{A}}(Y_1, Y_2) \to \operatorname{Hom}_{\tilde{\mathcal{A}}^\wedge}\left(\tilde{h}_{\mathcal{A}}(Y_1), \tilde{h}_{\mathcal{A}}(Y_2) \right) \to \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{A}^\wedge}\left( h_{\mathcal{A}}(Y_1), h_{\mathcal{A}}(Y_2)\right)\] is known to be bijective, while the second map is plainly injective. Therefore both maps are bijective.

Proposition reference shows that \(\tilde{\mathcal{A}}^\wedge\) is naturally an abelian category. Use the same symbol \(\tilde{h}_{\mathcal{A}}\) for the induced functors on chain complexes and simplicial objects, and consider the diagram \[\begin{equation*} \text{Diagram chapter8-unit-111-d001} \end{equation*}\] This diagram commutes up to a canonical isomorphism. The observation in the preceding paragraph shows that both vertical arrows are fully faithful, while applying Lemma reference objectwise shows that the second row is an equivalence of categories. Hence \(\Gamma\) in the first row is fully faithful.

For any functor \(F:\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{C}'\), an object \(X'\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{C}')\) is said to lie in the essential image of \(F\) if there is an \(X\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{C})\) such that \(X'\simeq FX\). Together with the description in Lemma reference of the quasi-inverse to \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ch}}_{\geq0}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ab}})\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{s}}\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ab}}\), this yields the following conclusion: \(X\in\operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{s}}\mathcal{A})\) lies in the essential image of \(\Gamma\) if and only if \((\mathrm{N}\tilde{h}_{\mathcal{A}}(X))_n\) lies in the essential image of \(\tilde{h}_{\mathcal{A}}:\mathcal{A}\to \tilde{\mathcal{A}}^\wedge\) for every \(n\geq0\).

Notice that \(\tilde{h}_{\mathcal{A}}:\mathcal{A}\to\tilde{\mathcal{A}}^\wedge\) preserves finite direct sums. If \(\mathcal{A}\) is a Karoubi category, the essential image of \(\mathcal{A}\to\tilde{\mathcal{A}}^\wedge\) is therefore closed under taking direct summands. Since \((\mathrm{N}\tilde{h}_{\mathcal{A}}(X))_n\) is a direct summand of \((\Gamma\mathrm{N}\tilde{h}_{\mathcal{A}}(X))_n\simeq \tilde{h}_{\mathcal{A}}(X)_n\),1 in this case \(\Gamma\) is fully faithful and essentially surjective, hence an equivalence.

Finally, the adjoint equivalence theorem [Li1] ensures that a quasi-inverse to \(\Gamma:\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ch}}_{\geq0}(\mathcal{A})\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{s}}\mathcal{A}\) can always be made into its right adjoint. If \(\mathcal{A}\) is an abelian category, Lemma reference has already shown that \(\mathrm{N}\) is the right adjoint of \(\Gamma\), and hence is also its quasi-inverse. This proves the result.

Convention. In view of this result, if \(\mathcal{A}\) is a Karoubi category, we may choose a quasi-inverse functor to \(\Gamma:\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ch}}_{\geq0}(\mathcal{A})\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{s}}\mathcal{A}\) and naturally denote it by \(\mathrm{N}\).

Although \(\mathrm{N}X\) was initially defined as a subobject of \(\mathrm{C}X\), it can also be understood as a quotient object; the latter viewpoint is often more convenient. We now explain this. Let \(\mathcal{A}\) be a Karoubi category and \(X\in\operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{s}}\mathcal{A})\). For every \(n\geq0\), define the morphism \(\Psi_n\) in \(\mathcal{A}\) as the one characterized by the commutativity of the following diagram for every \(0\leq j<n\): \[\text{Diagram chapter8-unit-111-d002}\] Thus taking \(\operatorname{coker}(\Psi_n)\) (that is, the coequalizer of \(\Psi_n\) and \(0\)) intuitively removes every degenerate part from \(X_n\), at least when \(\mathcal{A}\) is an abelian category. The next result not only guarantees that \(\operatorname{coker}(\Psi_n)\) exists, but also identifies it with \((\mathrm{N}X)_n\) via the natural embedding \(u:\mathrm{N}X\to\mathrm{C}X\) in Proposition reference. This gives another perspective on \(\mathrm{N}X\).

Proposition. In the situation above, \(\operatorname{coker}(\Psi_n)\) exists and is canonically isomorphic to \((\mathrm{N}X)_n\). Consider the corresponding composite \(v_n:X_n\twoheadrightarrow\operatorname{coker}(\Psi_n)\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}(\mathrm{N}X)_n\). Then \((v_n)_n\) gives a morphism \(v:\mathrm{C}X\to\mathrm{N}X\) satisfying \(vu=\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{\mathrm{N}X}\) for the natural embedding \(u:\mathrm{N}X\hookrightarrow\mathrm{C}X\); this construction is functorial in \(X\).

Proof. By Theorem reference, we may assume that \(X=\Gamma A\), where \(A\in\operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ch}}_{\geq0}(\mathcal{A}))\). In this case, \(\Psi_n\) can be written as \[\bigoplus_{0 \leq i < n} \bigoplus_{t: [n-1] \twoheadrightarrow [k]} A_k \to \bigoplus_{t': [n] \twoheadrightarrow [k] } A_k.\] From Definition reference of the functor \(\Gamma\), we see that \(\Psi_n\) acts on the \((i,t)\)-summand on the left as follows. Form the composite \([n]\xrightarrow{\mathrm{s}^i}[n-1]\xrightarrow{t}[k]\), which is still an order-preserving surjection, and denote it by \(t'\); then \(A_k\) is mapped identically to the \(A_k\)-summand on the right corresponding to \(t'\).

Observe that \(t':[n]\twoheadrightarrow[k]\) arises from such a pair \((i,t)\) if and only if \(k<n\). Using the \(\eta\) of Lemma reference, define \(v_n\) to be the composite \((\Gamma A)_n\xrightarrow{\text{projection}}A_n \xrightarrow[\sim]{\eta}(\mathrm{N}\Gamma A)_n\). The discussion above shows that \[[\text{quotient}: (\Gamma A)_n \to \operatorname{coker}\Psi_n] \simeq [v_n: (\Gamma A)_n \twoheadrightarrow (\mathrm{N}\Gamma A)_n ] .\]

Expanding the definitions immediately gives \(v_nu_n=\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{(\mathrm{N}\Gamma A)_n}\). We next show that \((v_n)_n\) gives a morphism \(v\) in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ch}}_{\geq0}(\mathcal{A})\). This is equivalent to saying that the outer rectangle of the following diagram commutes: \[\text{Diagram chapter8-unit-111-d003}\] The lower part commutes because \(\eta\) is a morphism, while the commutativity of the upper part follows by directly applying the definition of \(d_i^{\Gamma A}\) (take \(f=\mathrm{d}^i\) in Definition reference). Finally, the functoriality of \(v\) in \(X\) is clear.

Our next goal is to compare \(\mathrm{C}\) and \(\mathrm{N}\) more precisely in the case of an abelian category. There is a notion of homotopy for morphisms between chain complexes; see Definition reference and Remark reference. A morphism of chain complexes is called a quasi-isomorphism if it induces isomorphisms on homology.
