Theorem. Let \(\mathcal{A}\) be an abelian category and \(X\in\operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{s}}\mathcal{A})\). Then \(u:\mathrm{N}X\to\mathrm{C}X\) from Lemma reference and \(v:\mathrm{C}X\to\mathrm{N}X\) from Proposition reference are both quasi-isomorphisms.

Proof. We know that \(vu=\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{\mathrm{N}X}\), so it is enough to prove that \(v\) is a quasi-isomorphism. Since \(v\) has a right inverse, it is an epimorphism. The long exact sequence of chain complexes (Proposition reference) reduces the problem to proving that \(\operatorname{ker}(v)\) is acyclic. By Theorem reference, we may henceforth assume that \(X=\Gamma A\), where \(A\in\operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ch}}_{\geq0}(\mathcal{A}))\). Therefore \[\begin{gather*} (\mathrm{C}X)_n = \bigoplus_{t: [n] \twoheadrightarrow [k]} A_k, \\ \partial_n : (\mathrm{C}X)_n \to (\mathrm{C}X)_{n-1}. \end{gather*}\]

For \(n\geq0\) and \(i\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\), let \((\mathrm{C}^{\leq i}X)_n\) denote the subobject of \((\mathrm{C}X)_n\) cut out by the direct summands satisfying \[\exists \; j, \quad \max\{n-i, 1\} \leq j \leq n, \quad t(j) = t(j-1).\] We have \(i\leq i'\implies(\mathrm{C}^{\leq i}X)_n\subset (\mathrm{C}^{\leq i'}X)_n\).

Since \(v_n\) is simply the projection onto the summand \(t=\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{[n]}\), if \(i\geq n-1\) then \((\mathrm{C}^{\leq i}X)_n=\operatorname{ker}(v_n)\). We now show that \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:Dold-Kan-N-C-aux0}{} \left( (\mathrm{C}^{\leq i} X)_n \right)_{n \geq 0} \;\text{forms a chain subcomplex of}\; \mathrm{C}X \;\text{denoted by}\; \mathrm{C}^{\leq i} X. \end{equation}\]

To prove this, fix a map \(t:[n]\twoheadrightarrow[k]\) and an index \(\max\{n-i,1\}\leq j\leq n\) satisfying the condition above. From now on write \(d_i=d_i^X\) and \(s_j=s_j^X\). For every \(0\leq h\leq n\), take \(m=n-1\) and \(f=\mathrm{d}^h:[n-1]\hookrightarrow[n]\) in the diagram equation.

  • Suppose \(h\notin\{j-1,j\}\) and set \(j':=(\mathrm{d}^h)^{-1}(j)\). Then \(u:[n-1]\twoheadrightarrow[l]\) satisfies \(u(j')=u(j'-1)\), and it is easy to see that \(n-1-i\leq j'\leq n-1\). In this case, \((-1)^hd_h:X_n\to X_{n-1}\) maps \(A_k\) to the direct summand of \((\mathrm{C}^{\leq i}X)_{n-1}\) determined by \(u\).

  • In the situation of the preceding item, if also \(h\geq n-i-1\), the range of \(j'\) can be sharpened to \(n-i\leq j'\leq n-1\). In other words, the image of \(A_k\) then lies in \((\mathrm{C}^{\leq i-1}X)_{n-1}\).

  • For \(h\in\{j-1,j\}\), verify that \(t\mathrm{d}^{j-1}=t\mathrm{d}^j\). It follows that \(d_{j-1},d_j:X_n\rightrightarrows X_{n-1}\) agree on the direct summand \(A_k\) corresponding to \(t\), so \((-1)^{j-1}d_{j-1}\) and \((-1)^jd_j\) cancel on that summand.

This proves equation. The second and third items also give the congruence \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:Dold-Kan-N-C-aux}{} \sum_{h=0}^n (-1)^h d_h \equiv \sum_{h=0}^{n-i-2} (-1)^h d_h \pmod{ \mathrm{C}^{\leq i-1} X }. \end{equation}\]

Thus it is enough to prove that \(\mathrm{C}^{\leq i}X\) is acyclic. Set \[D:=\mathrm{C}^{\leq i}X/\mathrm{C}^{\leq i-1}X.\] Notice that \(\mathrm{C}^{<-1}X=0\). The long exact sequence of chain complexes then reduces the problem to proving inductively that \(D\) is acyclic, for \(i\geq0\).

To prove that \(D\) is acyclic, consider the family of morphisms \[\begin{gather*} (-1)^{n-i-1}s_{n-i-1}:X_n\to X_{n+1}, \quad n\geq i+1. \end{gather*}\] A direct verification shows that these morphisms preserve both \((\mathrm{C}^{\leq i-1}X)_\bullet\) and \((\mathrm{C}^{\leq i}X)_\bullet\) (this choice of bounds is optimal), and therefore induce \[h_n:D_n\to D_{n+1}.\]

Extend the definition of \(s_k\) by zero to every \(k\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\), and thereby extend the definition of \(h_n\) by zero to the case \(n\leq i\). Notice that \(n\leq i\implies D_n=0\), so this is the only reasonable choice. We claim that \[\partial^D_{n+1}h_n+h_{n-1}\partial^D_n=\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{D_n}, \quad n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}.\] This will show that \(D\) is acyclic. First, applying equation gives \[\partial^D_n = \sum_{j=0}^{n-i-2} (-1)^j d_j \;\bmod\; \mathrm{C}^{\leq i-1}(X)_{n-1}.\] Together with equation, this gives, for \(n\geq i+1\), \[\begin{align*} \partial^D_{n+1} h_n & = (-1)^{n-i-1} \sum_{j=0}^{n-i-1} (-1)^j d_j s_{n-i-1} \; \bmod\; \mathrm{C}^{\leq i-1}(X)_n \\ & = (-1)^{n-i-1} \sum_{j=0}^{n-i-2} (-1)^j s_{n-i-2} d_j + \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{\mathrm{C}^{\leq i}(X)_n} \; \bmod\; \mathrm{C}^{\leq i-1}(X)_n \\ & = -h_{n-1} \partial^D_n + \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{D_n}. \end{align*}\] The identity also holds trivially for \(n\leq i\). This proves the claim.

Remark. Naturally, one may ask for corresponding versions of the various theorems in this section, particularly the Dold–Kan correspondence, for the category of complexes \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})\) or its subcategories \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}_{\leq0}(\mathcal{A})\) and \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}_{\geq0}(\mathcal{A})\). There are at least two simple approaches: reflection, and reversal or duality.

  1. As explained in Remark reference, \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}(\mathcal{A})\) and \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ch}}(\mathcal{A})\) correspond by \(X^n=X_{-n}\) and \(d^n=\partial_{-n}\). All the results in this section can be transported to complexes through this correspondence. For example, the reflected version of Theorem reference is an adjoint equivalence between \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}_{\leq0}(\mathcal{A})\) and \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{s}}\mathcal{A}\).

  2. Another approach is to consider the category of cosimplicial objects \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{cs}}\mathcal{A}\). There are equivalences of categories \[\ensuremath{\mathsf{cs}}\mathcal{A} \simeq \ensuremath{\mathsf{s}}\left(\mathcal{A}^{\operatorname{op}}\right)^{\operatorname{op}} \simeq \ensuremath{\mathsf{Ch}}_{\geq 0}(\mathcal{A}^{\operatorname{op}})^{\operatorname{op}} \simeq \ensuremath{\mathsf{C}}_{\geq 0}(\mathcal{A}),\] where the final step comes from reversing the arrows, as in Remark reference.

Operations such as taking the normalized complex can likewise be translated into the category of complexes.

  1. Translator’s note: the final term is printed as \(h_{\mathcal{A}}(X)_n\) in the source. The other objects in this isomorphism are \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ab}}\)-valued presheaves, so the correctly typed term is \(\tilde{h}_{\mathcal{A}}(X)_n\).↩︎

Homology Computation

A classical application of the functors \(\mathrm{C}\) and \(\mathrm{N}\) is the definition of the homology of a simplicial set, which is closely connected to the study of algebraic topology.

Definition. For every \(K\in\operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{sSet}})\), define \(\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}K\in\operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{sAb}})\) by taking \((\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}K)_n\) to be the free \(\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\)-module with basis \(K_n\), with the maps \(d_i,s_j\) induced by the corresponding maps on \(K\). This construction gives a functor \(\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}(\cdot):\ensuremath{\mathsf{sSet}}\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{sAb}}\).

Proposition. There is a natural adjunction \(\text{Diagram chapter8-unit-112-diagram-001}\).

Proof. Both \(\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}(\cdot)\) and the forgetful functor are defined degreewise. The entire assertion follows directly from the free–forgetful adjunction \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Set}}\leftrightarrows\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ab}}\).

Consequently, for every \(X\in\operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{sAb}})\), specifying a morphism \(\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\Delta^n\to X\) is equivalent to specifying an element of \(X_n\). Moreover, \(\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}(X\times Y)\simeq\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}X\otimes\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}Y\), where the tensor product on the right is formed degreewise, with \(n\)-th term \(\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}X_n\ensuremath{\underset{\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}}{\otimes}}\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}Y_n\).

Definition. For a simplicial set \(K\) and every \(n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}_{\geq0}\), write \(\operatorname{H}_n(K;\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}):=\operatorname{H}_n\bigl(\mathrm{C}(\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}K)\bigr)\); this group is called the \(n\)-th homology group of \(K\). The construction gives a family of functors \(\operatorname{H}_n(\cdot;\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}):\ensuremath{\mathsf{sSet}}\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ab}}\).

  • More generally, for a \(\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\)-module \(M\), homology with coefficients in \(M\) is defined by \(\operatorname{H}_n(K;M):=\operatorname{H}_n\bigl(\mathrm{C}(\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}K)\otimes M\bigr)\), where \(\mathord\cdot\otimes M\) means taking \(\mathord\cdot\ensuremath{\underset{\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}}{\otimes}}M\) in every term of the chain complex.

  • Cohomology with coefficients in \(M\) is defined by \(\operatorname{H}^n(K;M):=\operatorname{H}^n\bigl(\operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}}(\mathrm{C}(\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}K),M)\bigr)\), with the expression in parentheses regarded as a complex. By the universal property of \(\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}(\cdot)\), the \(n\)-th term of this complex can also be identified with \[\mathrm{Maps}(K_n,M):=\{\text{maps }K_n\to M\}.\] This set becomes a \(\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\)-module under pointwise operations, and its differential homomorphism is identified with \(\sum_i(-1)^i(d_i)^*\).

If \(\mathrm{C}(\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}K)\) in the definition above is replaced by \(\mathrm{N}(\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}K)\), the resulting homology (or cohomology) groups are canonically isomorphic; this is a consequence of Theorem reference. Using \(\mathrm{N}(\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}K)\) is sometimes simpler, because Proposition reference gives \[\mathrm{N}(\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}K)_n=\bigoplus_{x\in K_n^{\mathrm{nd}}}\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}x.\] Here \(K_n^{\mathrm{nd}}\subset K_n\) is the subset of nondegenerate \(n\)-simplices, while the map \(\mathrm{N}(\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}K)_n\to\mathrm{N}(\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}K)_{n-1}\) is obtained by first taking \(\sum_{i=0}^n(-1)^id_i\) and then projecting to the \(K_{n-1}^{\mathrm{nd}}\) part. For example, \[\begin{align*} \mathrm{N}(\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\Delta^0)&=\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\;\text{placed in degree $0$},\\ \mathrm{C}(\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\Delta^0)&= \left[\cdots\xrightarrow{1}\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\xrightarrow{0}\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}} \xrightarrow{1}\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\xrightarrow{0}\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\right]. \end{align*}\]

Example. As a useful special case, let \((Q,\leq)\) be a nonempty small poset with a least element \(e\). This gives order-preserving maps \[[0]\xrightarrow{0\mapsto e}Q\longrightarrow[0].\] Regard \(Q\) as a category and take the nerve \(S:=\mathrm{N}(Q)\) from Example reference. By the original definition of the nerve, we also have \(\mathrm{N}([n])=\Delta^n\). We thus obtain morphisms in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{sSet}}\) \[\Delta^0\xrightarrow{i}S\xrightarrow{q}\Delta^0, \qquad qi=\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{\Delta^0}.\] It follows that we have \[\begin{gather*} \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}=\mathrm{N}(\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\Delta^0) \xrightarrow{\mathrm{N}i}\mathrm{N}(\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}S) \xrightarrow{\mathrm{N}q}\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}, \end{gather*}\] where \(\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\) is regarded as a chain complex placed in degree \(0\). We claim that \(\mathrm{N}i\) and \(\mathrm{N}q\) are mutually inverse in the homotopy category of chain complexes. In particular, \(\operatorname{H}_0(Q;M)\simeq M\), while \(\operatorname{H}_n(Q;M)=\{0\}\) for \(n\neq0\).

Since \(qi=\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}\), it remains only to construct a homotopy from \(\mathrm{N}i\mathrm{N}q\) to \(\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}\). For every \(n\geq0\), observe that the elements of \(S_n^{\mathrm{nd}}\) are the chains in \(Q\) of the form \(q_0<\cdots<q_n\). Define \[\begin{align*} h_n:S_n^{\mathrm{nd}}&\longrightarrow S_{n+1}^{\mathrm{nd}}\cup\{0\},\qquad n\geq0,\\ q_0<\cdots<q_n&\longmapsto \begin{cases} e<q_0<\cdots<q_n,&q_0\neq e,\\ 0,&q_0=e. \end{cases} \end{align*}\] Extend this map linearly to \(\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}S_n^{\mathrm{nd}}\simeq\mathrm{N}(\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}S)_n\). It readily satisfies the conditions for a homotopy; the details are left to the reader as an exercise.

The computation of homology is inseparable from homotopy. Under the Dold–Kan correspondence, homotopies of chain complexes reflect homotopies of simplicial objects, and the latter can be defined combinatorially.

Definition (Simplicial homotopy). Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be simplicial objects in a category \(\mathcal{C}\), and let \(f,g:X\rightrightarrows Y\) be a pair of morphisms. A simplicial homotopy from \(g\) to \(f\) is a family of morphisms \[h_i=h_i^n:X_n\to Y_{n+1},\qquad0\leq i\leq n,\] briefly denoted by \(h\), satisfying \[\begin{align*} d_0h_0&=f_n,\\ d_{n+1}h_n&=g_n,\\ d_ih_j&= \begin{cases} h_{j-1}d_i,&0\leq i<j,\\ d_ih_{i-1},&1\leq i=j,\\ h_jd_{i-1},&i>j+1, \end{cases}\\ s_ih_j&= \begin{cases} h_{j+1}s_i,&i\leq j,\\ h_js_{i-1},&i>j. \end{cases} \end{align*}\]

The definition above is combinatorial. When \(\mathcal{C}=\ensuremath{\mathsf{Set}}\), however, it is the same as equation, which is based on topological intuition. Why is this so? For every \(n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}_{\geq0}\), write \((\Delta^1)_n=\{\alpha_{-1},\ldots,\alpha_n\}\) explicitly, where \(\alpha_i:[n]\to[1]\) maps the numbers \(\leq i\) to \(0\) and all the others to \(1\). Then specifying \(H_n:(X\times\Delta^1)_n\to Y_n\) is equivalent to specifying \(H_{-1}^n,\ldots,H_n^n:X_n\to Y_n\).

  • Given the data \((h_i^n)_{i,n}\) of a simplicial homotopy, define \(H_{-1}^n=g\), \(H_n^n=f\), and \(H_i^n=d_{n+1}h_i^n\) for \(0\leq i\leq n-1\).

  • Given the data \(H\) of the commutative diagram equation, define \(h_i^n:=H_i^{n+1}s_i:X_n\to Y_{n+1}\).

A routine verification shows that the two maps are well defined and mutually inverse. For the case \(\mathcal{C}=\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ab}}\), simply replace \(X\times\Delta^1\) in equation by \(X\otimes\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\Delta^1\) and work in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{sAb}}\); the same argument applies without change. The following result is therefore entirely unsurprising.

Proposition. Consider a pair of morphisms \(f,g:X\rightrightarrows Y\) in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{s}}\mathcal{A}\). If \(h\) is a simplicial homotopy from \(g\) to \(f\), then \(\bigl(\sum_{j=0}^n(-1)^jh_j^n\bigr)_{n\geq0}\) defines a homotopy between \(\mathrm{C}f,\mathrm{C}g:\mathrm{C}X\rightrightarrows \mathrm{C}Y\).

Proof. As usual, denote all face morphisms of \(X\) and \(Y\) uniformly by \(d_i\), and omit the superscripts on \(h_j\); this creates no ambiguity. We have the following equality in \(\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{A}}(X_n,Y_n)\): \[\begin{multline*} \sum_{i=0}^{n+1}(-1)^id_i\sum_{j=0}^n(-1)^jh_j +\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}(-1)^jh_j\sum_{i=0}^n(-1)^id_i\\ =f_n-g_n +\sum_{\substack{0\leq i\leq n+1\\0\leq j\leq n\\ (i,j)\neq(0,0),(n+1,n)}}(-1)^{i+j}d_ih_j +\sum_{\substack{0\leq i\leq n\\0\leq j\leq n-1}} (-1)^{i+j}h_jd_i. \end{multline*}\] The first sum on the last line can be rewritten as \[\begin{align*} &\sum_{\substack{0\leq i\leq n+1\\i<j\leq n}} (-1)^{i+j}h_{j-1}d_i +\sum_{i=1}^nd_ih_i-\sum_{i=1}^nd_ih_{i-1} +\sum_{\substack{1\leq i\leq n+1\\0\leq j<i-1}} (-1)^{i+j}h_jd_{i-1}\\ &\qquad=-\sum_{\substack{0\leq i\leq n\\i\leq j\leq n-1}} (-1)^{i+j}h_jd_i -\sum_{\substack{0\leq i\leq n\\0\leq j<i}} (-1)^{i+j}h_jd_i. \end{align*}\] Here we used \(1\leq i\leq n\implies d_ih_i=d_ih_{i-1}\). This expression cancels the second sum and leaves only \(f_n-g_n\).

We next consider augmented semisimplicial objects (Remark reference) and their corresponding chain complexes; these results will be used in §reference. Unless stated otherwise, the augmentation morphism of an augmented semisimplicial object \(X\) will always be denoted by \(\epsilon:X_0\to X_{-1}\).

Definition. For an augmented semisimplicial object \(X\) in an additive category \(\mathcal{A}\), the corresponding complex \(\mathrm{C}X\) can be extended to the chain complex \[\begin{equation*} \begin{gathered} \mathrm{C}^{\mathrm{aug}}X:= \left[\cdots\xrightarrow{\partial_3}X_2 \xrightarrow{\partial_2}X_1 \xrightarrow{\partial_1}X_0 \xrightarrow{\partial_0:=\epsilon}X_{-1} \to0\to\cdots\right],\\ \partial_n:=\sum_{i=0}^n(-1)^id_i:X_n\to X_{n-1}, \qquad n\geq1. \end{gathered} \end{equation*}\]

The equality \(\epsilon d_0=\epsilon d_1\) shows that \(\mathrm{C}^{\mathrm{aug}}X\) is indeed an object of \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ch}}_{\geq-1}(\mathcal{A})\). It can also be regarded as the following morphism in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ch}}_{\geq0}(\mathcal{A})\): \[\epsilon:\mathrm{C}X\to \underbracket{X_{-1}}_{\text{placed in degree $0$}}, \qquad\text{$\epsilon$ in degree $0$, and $0$ in every other degree}.\]

Definition. Let \(X\) be an augmented semisimplicial object in an arbitrary category \(\mathcal{C}\). If there is a family of morphisms \(k_n:X_n\to X_{n+1}\), with \(n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}_{\geq-1}\), call \(X\) left contractible or right contractible, according to which column of conditions below is satisfied:

Left contractible Right contractible
\(\epsilon k_{-1}=\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{X_{-1}}\) \(\epsilon k_{-1}=\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{X_{-1}}\)
\(d_0k_n=\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{X_n}\) \(d_{n+1}k_n=\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{X_n}\)
\(d_ik_n=k_{n-1}d_{i-1}\;(1\leq i\leq n+1,\;n\geq1)\) \(d_ik_n=k_{n-1}d_i\;(0\leq i\leq n,\;n\geq1)\)
\(d_1k_0=k_{-1}\epsilon\) \(d_0k_0=k_{-1}\epsilon\)

The reader may verify that left and right contractibility are order-reversal duals in the sense of Remark reference. Moreover, both are “absolute” properties: if \(X\) is left (or right) contractible, with corresponding data \((k_n)_{n\geq-1}\), then for every functor \(F:\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{D}\) the data \((Fk_n)_{n\geq-1}\) make \(F(X)\) left (or right) contractible.

Example. For any monoid \(\Gamma\), make the \(\mathrm{E}\Gamma\) of Example reference into an augmented simplicial set by taking \((\mathrm{E}\Gamma)_{-1}=\{1\}\) and the augmentation morphism \(\epsilon:(\mathrm{E}\Gamma)_0\to(\mathrm{E}\Gamma)_{-1}\) to be the constant map. This object is right contractible: for \(n\geq-1\), define \(k_n:(\mathrm{E}\Gamma)_n\to(\mathrm{E}\Gamma)_{n+1}\) by \((g_1,\ldots,g_{n+1})\mapsto(g_1,\ldots,g_{n+1},1)\). This map plainly satisfies \(\epsilon k_{-1}=\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}\); after expanding the definitions, the verifications that \(d_{n+1}k_n=\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}\), \(d_ik_n=k_{n-1}d_i\) for \(0\leq i\leq n\), \(n\geq1\), and \(d_0k_0=k_{-1}\epsilon\) are also immediate.

If \(\Bbbk\) is a commutative ring, identify the chain complex \(\mathrm{C}(\Bbbk\mathrm{E}\Gamma)\) with the chain complex \(\mathsf{L}=(\mathsf{L}_n,\partial'_n)_n\) from Definition reference, as in Example reference. The augmentation \(\mathsf{L}\to\Bbbk\) is precisely the augmentation of the resolution in Proposition reference. In view of the next proposition, the contractibility of \(\mathrm{E}\Gamma\) (and hence of \(\Bbbk\mathrm{E}\Gamma\)) gives a topological explanation for the fact that \(\mathsf{L}\to\Bbbk\) is a quasi-isomorphism.

Proposition. Let \(\mathcal{A}\) be an additive category and let \(X\) be a left or right contractible augmented semisimplicial object in \(\mathcal{A}\). Then the identity morphism from \(\mathrm{C}^{\mathrm{aug}}X\) to itself is null-homotopic.

Proof. First consider the left-contractible case, and take the family of morphisms \(k_n:X_n\to X_{n+1}\) from its definition. Define \(k_n=0\) for \(n<-1\) (or \(\partial_n=0\) for \(n<0\)), and also define \(\partial_0=\epsilon\). We want to use \((k_n)_n\) as a witness to the null homotopy, that is, to prove \[\partial_{n+1}k_n+k_{n-1}\partial_n=\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{X_n}.\]

For \(n<-1\), both sides equal \(0\). For \(n=-1\), the left-hand side is \(\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{X_{-1}}\). For \(n=0\), the left-hand side is \(d_0k_0-d_1k_0+k_{-1}\epsilon=\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{X_0}\). For \(n\geq1\), computing the left-hand side gives \[\begin{multline*} \sum_{i=0}^{n+1}(-1)^id_ik_n +\sum_{i=0}^n(-1)^ik_{n-1}d_i\\ =\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{X_n} +\sum_{i=1}^{n+1}(-1)^ik_{n-1}d_{i-1} +\sum_{i=0}^n(-1)^ik_{n-1}d_i =\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{X_n}. \end{multline*}\]

For the right-contractible case, use \(\bigl((-1)^{n+1}k_n\bigr)_n\) instead.

The Bar Construction

Definition reference explains what is meant by a monad on a category \(\mathcal{C}\), as well as its dual notion, a comonad. The starting point of this section is a way to produce an augmented cosimplicial (respectively, simplicial) object in \(\operatorname{End}(\mathcal{C})\) from a monad (respectively, a comonad). In this way, many basic constructions in homological algebra can be explained naturally, including Hochschild homology and cohomology, which will be revisited at the end of the section (Example reference).

Example. Let \((T,\mu,\eta)\) be a monad on a category \(\mathcal{C}\), that is, an algebra in the category of endofunctors \(\operatorname{End}(\mathcal{C})=\mathcal{C}^{\mathcal{C}}\). The “walking algebra” construction of Remark reference gives the corresponding monoidal functor \[\ensuremath{\mathsf{FinOrd}} \to \operatorname{End}(\mathcal{C}), \quad \mathbf{n} \mapsto T^n ,\] that is, an augmented cosimplicial object in \(\operatorname{End}(\mathcal{C})\). Dually, a comonad \((L,\delta,\epsilon)\) on a category \(\mathcal{D}\) gives an augmented simplicial object in \(\operatorname{End}(\mathcal{D})\); here \(\delta:L\to L^2\) and \(\epsilon:L\to\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{\mathcal{D}}\).

  • In this section we shall mainly consider the augmented simplicial object on \(\mathcal{D}\) given by the comonad. Explicitly, its term in degree \(n\) is \(L^{n+1}\), while its face and degeneracy morphisms are readily written as \[\begin{align*} d_i := L^i \epsilon L^{n-i}: L^{n+1} & \to L^n, \\ s_j := L^j \delta L^{n-j}: L^{n+1} & \to L^{n+2}, \quad 0 \leq i, j \leq n ; \end{align*}\] the term in degree \(-1\) of the augmented object is the identity functor. Notice that the formula for \(d_0\) still makes sense when \(n=0\) and gives the augmentation morphism \(\epsilon:L\to\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{\mathcal{D}}\).

  • Correspondingly, the augmented cosimplicial object on \(\mathcal{C}\) has \(T^{n+1}\) as its term in degree \(n\), and \[\begin{align*} d^i & : = T^i \eta T^{n-i}: T^n \to T^{n+1}, \\ s^j & := T^j \mu T^{n-j}: T^{n+2} \to T^{n+1}, \quad 0 \leq i, j \leq n ; \end{align*}\] when \(n=0\), \(d^0\) becomes the augmentation morphism \(\eta:\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{\mathcal{C}}\to T\).

An important source of monads and comonads is adjoint pairs of functors. In view of their origins in classical theory (see §reference), constructions of this kind are collectively called bar constructions.

Example (Bar construction: an adjoint pair). Suppose we are given an adjoint pair \[\text{Diagram chapter8-unit-113-d001} \quad \begin{array}{ll} \eta: \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{\mathcal{C}} \to GF & \text{unit} \\ \epsilon: FG \to \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{\mathcal{D}} & \text{counit} \end{array}\] By Example reference, this gives

  • the monad \((T,\mu,\eta):=(GF,G\epsilon F,\eta)\) on \(\mathcal{C}\), whose corresponding augmented cosimplicial object is denoted by \[\mathrm{Cobar}(F, G): \ensuremath{\mathsf{FinOrd}} \to \operatorname{End}(\mathcal{C});\]

  • the comonad \((L,\delta,\varepsilon):=(FG,F\eta G,\epsilon)\) on \(\mathcal{D}\), whose corresponding augmented simplicial object is denoted by \[\mathrm{Bar}(F, G): \ensuremath{\mathsf{FinOrd}}^{\operatorname{op}} \to \operatorname{End}(\mathcal{D}).\]

The corresponding face and degeneracy morphisms (and their dual versions) have been described in Example reference.

Since \(\mathrm{Bar}(F,G)\) (respectively, \(\mathrm{Cobar}(F,G)\)) takes values in the functor category \(\operatorname{End}(\mathcal{D})\) (respectively, \(\operatorname{End}(\mathcal{C})\)), we can compose each of its terms with \(G\) on the left (respectively, on the right). The former composition produces an augmented simplicial object \(G\mathrm{Bar}(F,G):\ensuremath{\mathsf{FinOrd}}^{\operatorname{op}}\to \mathcal{C}^{\mathcal{D}}\), whose general term is the functor \[\begin{align*} G\mathrm{Bar}(F, G)_n & = GL^{n+1} = (GF)^{n+1} G \\ & = T^{n+1}G: \mathcal{D} \to \mathcal{C}, \quad n \geq -1. \end{align*}\]

The face morphism \(d_i:T^{n+1}G\to T^nG\) (understood as the augmentation morphism when \(i=n=0\)) is \[d_i = \left\{\begin{array}{rll} G L^i \epsilon L^{n-i} & = T^i G \epsilon F T^{n-i-1} G & \\ & = T^i \mu T^{n-i-1} G, & \text{if}\; 0 \leq i < n, \\ G L^n \epsilon & = T^n G \epsilon , & \text{if}\; i = n. \end{array}\right.\]

The degeneracy morphism with source the term in degree \(n\geq0\), \(s_j:T^{n+1}G\to T^{n+2}G\), is given by \[\begin{align*} s_j = G L^j \delta L^{n-j} & = G L^j F \eta G L^{n-j} \\ & = T^{j+1} \eta T^{n-j} G, \quad 0 \leq j \leq n. \end{align*}\]

The augmented cosimplicial object \(\mathrm{Cobar}(F,G)G\) has a corresponding description: its term in degree \(n\) is again \(T^{n+1}G=GL^{n+1}\), while \[\begin{gather*} \left[ d^i: GL^n \to GL^{n+1} \right] = \begin{cases} GL^{i-1} \delta L^{n-i}, & 0 \leq i < n \\ \eta GL^n , & i = n, \end{cases} \\ \left[ s^j: GL^{n+2} \to GL^{n+1} \right] = GL^j \epsilon L^{n-j+1}, \quad 0 \leq j \leq n. \end{gather*}\] 1 Likewise, when \(i=n=0\), \(d^0\) is to be understood as the augmentation morphism \(\eta G:G\to GFG=GL\).

Readers new to the subject are advised to pause here. For a homomorphism \(f:A\to B\) of \(\Bbbk\)-algebras and the adjoint pair \[\text{Diagram chapter8-unit-113-d002}\] describe the value of \(\mathrm{Bar}\) (respectively, \(\mathrm{Cobar}\)) at a left \(B\)-module \(M\) (respectively, a left \(A\)-module \(N\)), and then use the functor \(\mathrm{C}\) of Definition reference to write down the corresponding chain complex. For the right-module version, the corresponding comonad (respectively, monad) was described completely in Example reference.

Example (Bar construction: free and forgetful). Let \((T,\mu,\eta)\) be a monad on a category \(\mathcal{C}\). Definition–Proposition reference gives an adjoint pair \[\text{Diagram chapter8-unit-113-d003}\] and its induced monad is precisely \((T,\mu,\eta)\). Substituting this into Example reference produces the augmented simplicial object \[\mathrm{Bar}(T) := \mathrm{Bar}(\mathrm{Free}^T, U^T): \ensuremath{\mathsf{FinOrd}}^{\operatorname{op}} \to \operatorname{End}(\mathcal{C}^T).\]

Evaluation at \((M,a)\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{C}^T)\) is a functor from \(\operatorname{End}(\mathcal{C}^T)\) to \(\mathcal{C}^T\). Evaluating every term of \(\mathrm{Bar}(T)\) gives the augmented simplicial object \[\mathrm{Bar}(M, a): \ensuremath{\mathsf{FinOrd}}^{\operatorname{op}} \to \mathcal{C}^T .\]

Now consider \(U^T\mathrm{Bar}(M,a):\ensuremath{\mathsf{FinOrd}}^{\operatorname{op}}\to \mathcal{C}\); this is also the result of evaluating \(U^T\mathrm{Bar}(T)\) at \((M,a)\).

  • Substitution into Example reference shows that the general term of \(U^T\mathrm{Bar}(M,a)\) is \[U^T \mathrm{Bar}(M, a)_n = T^{n+1} U^T (M, a) = T^{n+1} M, \quad n \geq -1.\]

  • Again denote the counit of \((\mathrm{Free}^T,U^T)\) by \(\epsilon\). The proof of Definition–Proposition reference has shown that \[\left[ \epsilon_{(M, a)} : \mathrm{Free}^T U^T (M, a) = (TM, \mu_M) \to (M, a) \right] = a,\] so the face morphisms of \(U^T\mathrm{Bar}(M,a)\) are \[\begin{equation*} \left[ d_i: T^{n+1}M \to T^n M \right] = \begin{cases} T^i \mu_{T^{n-i-1} M}, & 0 \leq i < n \\ T^n a, & i = n. \end{cases} \end{equation*}\] This formula also makes sense when \(i=n=0\) and gives the augmentation morphism, namely \(a:TM\to M\).

  • Its degeneracy morphisms are \[\left[ s_j: T^{n+1} M \to T^{n+2} M \right] = T^{j+1} \eta_{T^{n-j} M}, \quad 0 \leq j \leq n .\]

Thus \(U^T\mathrm{Bar}(M,a)\) can be written concisely as \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:bar-simplicial-resolution}{} \text{Diagram chapter8-unit-113-d004} \end{equation}\]

We have already explained abstractly that these arrows satisfy the simplicial identities equation, although a direct verification also presents no essential difficulty. Moreover, Example reference shows that the right end of the diagram realizes \(a:TM\to M\) as a coequalizer.

  1. Translator’s note: in the printed case distinction for \(d^i\), the boundary conditions are interchanged. Consistently with \(d^i=T^i\eta T^{n-i}\), the first line applies for \(1\leq i\leq n\), while the second applies for \(i=0\).↩︎

The augmented simplicial object in equation given by the bar construction can be viewed heuristically as a replacement for \(M\). To clarify this idea, consider the following question. Let \(\Gamma\) be a group, and equip the one-point set \(\{\mathrm{pt}\}\) with the trivial right \(\Gamma\)-action. How should we understand \[\text{the ``quotient space''}\; \{\mathrm{pt}\} / \Gamma ?\] With the naive definition of a quotient set or topological space, the answer is of course uninteresting; in general, taking the quotient by a nonfree action erases information from the original space. Various needs arising in practice, however, prompt us to seek a more refined definition of a quotient by a nonfree action. To this end, write \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Set}\text{-}}\Gamma\) for the category of all small right \(\Gamma\)-sets, and consider the free–forgetful adjunction \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Set}}\leftrightarrows\ensuremath{\mathsf{Set}\text{-}}\Gamma\). From the one-point right \(\Gamma\)-set \(\{\mathrm{pt}\}\), the bar construction produces a simplicial object in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Set}\text{-}}\Gamma\); this is precisely the simplicial set \(\mathrm{E}\Gamma\) introduced in Example reference. The detailed verification is left as an exercise in this chapter. Once this fact is understood and the bar construction is accepted as a replacement for \(\{\mathrm{pt}\}\) in this setting, it is reasonable to define \(\{\mathrm{pt}\}/\Gamma\) as \((\mathrm{E}\Gamma)/\Gamma\simeq\mathrm{B}\Gamma\). This is a quotient by a free action and gives the classifying space of \(\Gamma\); it is more natural, and usually more useful, than the naive quotient set. In what sense can the augmented simplicial objects in Examples reference and reference be said to provide a kind of replacement, or “resolution”, of the original object? The idea comes from topology, and its precise meaning involves the contractibility of Definition reference. One related result is the following.

Proposition. In the setting of Example reference, suppose we are given an adjoint pair \[\text{Diagram chapter8-unit-114-d001} \quad \begin{array}{ll} \eta: \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{\mathcal{C}} \to GF & \text{unit} \\ \epsilon: FG \to \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{\mathcal{D}} & \text{counit} \end{array}\] and form the augmented simplicial object \(\mathrm{Bar}(F,G)\) in \(\operatorname{End}(\mathcal{D})\). Then \(G\mathrm{Bar}(F,G)\) is left contractible.

Proof. Use the notation of Example reference, such as \(T=GF\) and \(\mu:T^2\to T\). Recall that \(G\mathrm{Bar}(F,G)_n=T^{n+1}G\). For every \(n\geq-1\), define \[k_n := \eta T^{n+1}G: T^{n+1}G \to T^{n+2}G .\] Recall also that the face morphism \(d_i:T^{n+1}G\to T^nG\) of \(G\mathrm{Bar}(F,G)\) is \(T^i\mu T^{n-i-1}G\) if \(0\leq i<n\), and \(T^nG\epsilon\) if \(i=n\); its augmentation morphism is \(G\epsilon:TG\to G\) (note that this notation differs from that in Definition reference). We now verify the conditions for left contractibility one by one.

First, the triangle identity for the adjunction gives \((G\epsilon)k_{-1}=(G\epsilon)(\eta G)=\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_G\).

Second, \((T,\mu,\eta)\) is a monad, so \(\mu(\eta T)=\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_T\). If \(n\geq0\), composing both sides on the right with \(T^nG\) gives \(d_0k_n=\mu T^nG\cdot\eta T^{n+1}G=\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{T^{n+1}G}\).

Finally, by the naturality of \(\eta\), the following diagram commutes when \(1\leq i\leq n+1\): \[\text{Diagram chapter8-unit-114-d002} \quad \varphi := \begin{cases} T^{i-1} \mu T^{n-i} G, & 1 \leq i \leq n \\ T^n G\epsilon, & i = n+1. \end{cases}\] This gives \(d_1k_0=k_{-1}(G\epsilon)\) when \(i=1\) and \(n=0\), and \(d_ik_n=k_{n-1}d_{i-1}\) when \(n\geq1\). The result follows.

Although the contractibility of \(G\mathrm{Bar}(F,G)\) does not necessarily imply that \(\mathrm{Bar}(F,G)\) is contractible, Proposition reference is already sufficient for the applications below. The exercises in this chapter will introduce further results concerning contractibility. For additive categories, the meaning of “resolution” can also be carried to the level of chain complexes and thus understood through linear algebra. First, by Definition reference, an augmented simplicial object \(X\) in an additive category gives an augmentation \(\mathrm{C}^{\mathrm{aug}}X\) of the chain complex \(\mathrm{C}X\). If the identity morphism of a chain complex is null-homotopic, the chain complex itself is called null-homotopic.

Theorem. Let \(\mathcal{A}\) be an additive category, suppose an adjoint pair is given, \[\text{Diagram chapter8-unit-114-d003}\] and form the augmented simplicial object \(\mathrm{Bar}(F,G)\) in \(\operatorname{End}(\mathcal{B})\) (respectively, \(G\mathrm{Bar}(F,G)\) in \(\mathcal{A}^{\mathcal{B}}\)).

  • Notice that \(\mathcal{A}^{\mathcal{B}}\) is an additive category (see the first part of §reference). The chain complex \(\mathrm{C}^{\mathrm{aug}}\bigl(G\mathrm{Bar}(F,G)\bigr)\) from Definition reference is null-homotopic.

  • For every \(Y\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{B})\), evaluate \(\mathrm{Bar}(F,G)\) (respectively, \(G\mathrm{Bar}(F,G)\)) at \(Y\) degreewise. This produces an augmented simplicial object \(\mathrm{Bar}(Y)\) in \(\mathcal{B}\) (respectively, \(G\mathrm{Bar}(Y)\) in \(\mathcal{A}\)), and the chain complex \(\mathrm{C}^{\mathrm{aug}}\bigl(G\mathrm{Bar}(Y)\bigr)\) in \(\mathcal{A}\) is null-homotopic.

Proof. Proposition reference shows that \(G\mathrm{Bar}(F,G)\) is left contractible. Since contractibility is an absolute condition, \(G\mathrm{Bar}(Y)\) obtained through the evaluation functor \(\mathrm{ev}_Y:\mathcal{A}^{\mathcal{B}}\to\mathcal{A}\) is naturally left contractible as well. Apply Proposition reference to both objects.

Now suppose that \(\mathcal{A}\) and \(\mathcal{B}\) are both additive categories. For an adjoint pair as in Theorem reference and \(Y\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{B})\), since \(\mathrm{Bar}(Y)_{-1}=Y\), flattening \(\mathrm{C}^{\mathrm{aug}}(\mathrm{Bar}(Y))\) gives a morphism in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ch}}_{\geq0}(\mathcal{B})\) \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:bar-resolution}{} \epsilon_Y: \mathrm{C}(\mathrm{Bar}(Y)) \to Y; \end{equation}\] it is canonical in \(Y\), and its degree-zero part is precisely the augmentation morphism \(\epsilon_Y:FG(Y)\to Y\) of \(\mathrm{Bar}(Y)\), so the notation is appropriate.

Corollary. Suppose an adjoint pair of abelian categories is given1 \(\text{Diagram chapter8-unit-114-diagram-004}\) and let \(Y\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{B})\). The morphism obtained by applying \(G\) degreewise to equation, namely \[G\epsilon_Y: \mathrm{C}(G\mathrm{Bar}(Y)) \to GY ,\] is a quasi-isomorphism in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ch}}(\mathcal{A})\).

Proof. Theorem reference implies that \(\mathrm{C}^{\mathrm{aug}}(G\mathrm{Bar}(Y))\) is acyclic, and the result follows immediately.

Example (The bar resolution of a module and Hochschild homology/cohomology). Let \(\Bbbk\) be a commutative ring and \(R\) a \(\Bbbk\)-algebra. Write \(\otimes:=\otimes_{\Bbbk}\). By Example reference, the comonad determined by the adjoint pair \[\text{Diagram chapter8-unit-114-d004}\] is the endofunctor \(L:M\mapsto R\otimes M\) on \(R\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\). There is a corresponding version for right \(R\)-modules, which we shall not repeat.

Now apply the bar construction. For every left \(R\)-module \(M\), we have a canonical morphism in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ch}}_{\geq0}(R\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}})\) \[\epsilon_M: \mathrm{C}(\mathrm{Bar}(M)) \to M;\] this is a quasi-isomorphism because Corollary reference ensures that \(\epsilon_M\) is a quasi-isomorphism at the level of \(\Bbbk\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\). Explicitly, \[\mathrm{C}(\mathrm{Bar}(M))_n = L^{n+1}(M) = R^{\otimes (n+1)} \otimes M.\] According to Example reference and the description of \(L\to\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}\) in Example reference (namely, “multiplying in”), the map \(L^{n+1}(M)\to L^n(M)\) is \[\begin{multline*} \partial_n: r_0 \otimes \cdots \otimes r_n \otimes x \mapsto \\ \sum_{k=0}^{n-1} (-1)^k \cdots \otimes r_k r_{k+1} \otimes \cdots \otimes x + (-1)^n r_0 \otimes \cdots \otimes r_{n-1} \otimes r_n x, \end{multline*}\] where \(x\in M\) and \(r_i\in R\). This formula still makes sense when \(n=0\) (\(r_0\otimes x\mapsto r_0x\)), and thus gives the augmented version \(\epsilon:\mathrm{C}(\mathrm{Bar}(M))\to M\), namely \(\mathrm{C}^{\mathrm{aug}}(\mathrm{Bar}(M))\).

Now consider the special case \(M=R\). In this case \[\begin{align*} \mathrm{C}(\mathrm{Bar}(R))_n & = R^{\otimes (n+2)} = R \otimes R^{\otimes n} \otimes R, \\ \partial_n(r_0 \otimes \cdots \otimes r_{n+1}) & = \sum_{k=0}^n (-1)^k \cdots \otimes r_k r_{k+1} \otimes \cdots. \end{align*}\]

Although \(\mathrm{C}(\mathrm{Bar}(R))\) and its augmentation \(\mathrm{C}^{\mathrm{aug}}(\mathrm{Bar}(R))\) are, by definition, chain complexes of left \(R\)-modules, the description above upgrades both to chain complexes of \((R,R)\)-bimodules: \(R\) acts by left multiplication on the first factor and by right multiplication on the last factor of \(R\otimes R^{\otimes n}\otimes R\). This upgrade of structure is no coincidence. Since \(\mathrm{C}^{\mathrm{aug}}(\mathrm{Bar}(\mathord\cdot))\) is a functor, every endomorphism of \(R\) as a left \(R\)-module (for example, right multiplication) lifts naturally to the entire bar construction.

Comparison with Definition reference shows immediately that these are precisely the chain complexes used to define Hochschild homology and cohomology: \[\mathrm{C}(\mathrm{Bar}(R)) = \mathsf{B} R, \quad \mathrm{C}^{\mathrm{aug}}(\mathrm{Bar}(R)) = \mathsf{B}' R.\] Notice also that Lemma reference is just a special case of Theorem reference.

Write \(R^e:=R\otimes R^{\operatorname{op}}\) and, according to Convention reference, identify left \(R^e\)-modules, \((R,R)\)-bimodules, and right \(R^e\)-modules. From this viewpoint, the Hochschild homology \(\operatorname{HH}_\bullet(M)\) (respectively, cohomology \(\operatorname{HH}^\bullet(M)\)) of a bimodule \(M\) is a derived version of \(M\ensuremath{\underset{R^e}{\otimes}}R\) (respectively, \(\operatorname{Hom}_{R^e}(R,M)\)): the bimodule \(R\) is replaced by its bar resolution \(\mathrm{C}(\mathrm{Bar}(R))\), after which homology (respectively, cohomology) is computed.

This idea of replacement pervades the study of derived functors and derived categories, but the situation here is slightly different. In the framework of and , \(R\) should be replaced by its flat resolution (respectively, projective resolution) as a bimodule. This yields \(\operatorname{Tor}^{R^e}_\bullet(M,R)\) (respectively, \(\operatorname{Ext}^\bullet_{R^e}(R,M)\)), or the corresponding object in the derived category. Example reference (respectively, Example reference) shows that if \(R\) is flat (respectively, projective) as a \(\Bbbk\)-module, these objects are naturally isomorphic to \(\operatorname{HH}_\bullet(M)\) (respectively, \(\operatorname{HH}^\bullet(M)\)); this need not hold in general.

Example (The bar resolution and group homology). Let \(\Gamma\) be a group. Continue the discussion of Example reference for the group algebra \(R:=\Bbbk[\Gamma]\); in this case, \(M\) is the same as a left \(\Gamma\)-module in the sense of §reference. Recall that \((\mathord\cdot)_{\Gamma}:\Gamma\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\to\Bbbk\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\) is the coinvariants functor. We claim that \(\epsilon_M:\mathrm{C}(\mathrm{Bar}(M))\to M\) is a \((\mathord\cdot)_{\Gamma}\)-acyclic resolution in \(\Gamma\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\) (Convention reference). Its quasi-isomorphism property is already known. To see that every \(\mathrm{Bar}(M)_n=\Bbbk[\Gamma]^{\otimes(n+1)}\otimes M\) is \((\mathord\cdot)_{\Gamma}\)-acyclic, first use Shapiro’s lemma (Theorem reference), which gives, for every \(\Bbbk\)-module \(P\), \[\operatorname{H}_k(\Gamma, \Bbbk[\Gamma] \otimes P ) = \operatorname{H}_k\left( \Gamma, \operatorname{ind}^{\Gamma}_{\{1\}}(P) \right) \simeq \operatorname{H}_k(\{1\}, P),\] and the right-hand side is always \(0\) when \(k>0\). Apply this with \(P=\Bbbk[\Gamma]^{\otimes n}\otimes M\) to obtain the claim.

Consequently, Corollary reference implies \(\operatorname{H}_n(\Gamma,M)\simeq \operatorname{H}_n\bigl(\mathrm{C}((\mathrm{Bar}(M)_{\Gamma}))\bigr)\); here the functor \((\mathord\cdot)_{\Gamma}\) may be applied either to the simplicial object or, equivalently, to the corresponding chain complex. This interprets group homology as comonad homology in the sense of the exercises in this chapter. More precisely, taking \(\Gamma\)-coinvariants of \(\mathrm{Bar}(M)_n\) amounts to removing the first tensor factor in \(\Bbbk[\Gamma]^{\otimes(n+1)}\otimes M\) via \(\Bbbk[\Gamma]\twoheadrightarrow\Bbbk\), giving \(\Bbbk[\Gamma]^{\otimes n}\otimes M\). Under this identification, \(\mathrm{Bar}(M)_{n,\Gamma}\to\mathrm{Bar}(M)_{n-1,\Gamma}\) is given by \[\begin{multline*} g_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes g_n \otimes x \mapsto g_2 \otimes \cdots \otimes g_n \otimes x + \sum_{k=1}^{n-1} (-1)^k \cdots \otimes g_k g_{k+1} \otimes \cdots \otimes x \\ + (-1)^n g_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes g_{n-1} \otimes g_n x, \end{multline*}\] where \(g_i\in\Gamma\) and \(x\in M\). Comparison with Proposition reference shows immediately that \(\mathrm{C}(\mathrm{Bar}(M))_{\Gamma}\) is precisely the standard chain complex computing \(\operatorname{H}_n(\Gamma,M)\).

  1. Here \(F\) and \(G\) are necessarily additive functors; see Corollary reference.↩︎

Bisimplicial Objects

We begin with some general definitions. For objects \([m_1],\ldots,[m_n]\) of \(\ensuremath{\bm\Delta}\), from now on we shall also write the object \(([m_1],\ldots,[m_n])\) of \((\ensuremath{\bm\Delta})^n\) as \([m_1]\times\cdots\times[m_n]\) for typographical convenience.

Definition. Let \(\mathcal{C}\) be an arbitrary category and \(n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}_{\geq1}\). A functor of the form \(X:(\ensuremath{\bm\Delta}^{\operatorname{op}})^n\to\mathcal{C}\) (respectively, \(\ensuremath{\bm\Delta}^n\to\mathcal{C}\)) is called an \(n\)-fold simplicial object (respectively, an \(n\)-fold cosimplicial object) in \(\mathcal{C}\); its morphisms are morphisms of such functors. When \(n=2\), the corresponding objects are called bisimplicial (respectively, bicosimplicial) objects. The value of an \(n\)-fold simplicial (respectively, cosimplicial) object \(X\) at \([m_1]\times\cdots\times[m_n]\) is denoted by \(X_{m_1,\ldots,m_n}\) (respectively, \(X^{m_1,\ldots,m_n}\)).

Thus an \(n\)-fold simplicial object is determined by a family of objects \(X_{m_1,\ldots,m_n}\), where \(m_1,\ldots,m_n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}_{\geq0}\), together with its face morphisms \[{}^k d_i: X_{m_1, \ldots, m_n} \to X_{\ldots, m_k - 1, \ldots}, \quad 1 \leq k \leq n, \quad 0 \leq i \leq m_k\] and its degeneracy morphisms \[{}^k s_j: X_{m_1, \ldots, m_n} \to X_{\ldots, m_k + 1, \ldots}, \quad 1 \leq k \leq n, \quad 0 \leq j \leq m_k .\] These morphisms are required to satisfy equation for each \(k\), and morphisms corresponding to different values of \(k\) must commute. This is simply the multivariable version of Definition reference. More generally, for every morphism in \(\ensuremath{\bm\Delta}^n\) \[f:[m_1]\times\cdots\times[m_n]\to[m'_1]\times\cdots\times[m'_n],\] there is a corresponding pullback \(f^*:X_{m'_1,\ldots,m'_n}\to X_{m_1,\ldots,m_n}\). The case of \(n\)-fold cosimplicial objects is dual.

Example. Take \(\mathcal{C}=\ensuremath{\mathsf{Set}}\). As in Definition reference, we can define the standard \(n\)-fold simplicial set \[\Delta^{p_1, \ldots, p_n} := \operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\bm\Delta}^n}\left(\cdot, [p_1] \times \cdots \times [p_n] \right).\] Next take \(\mathcal{C}=\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ab}}\). Imitating Definition reference, for every \(n\)-fold simplicial set \(K\) we can define an \(n\)-fold simplicial object \(\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}K\) in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ab}}\). Specifying a morphism \(\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\Delta^{p_1,\ldots,p_n}\to X\) is equivalent to specifying an element of \(X_{p_1,\ldots,p_n}\).

If \(\mathcal{C}\) is a small category, the category of all \(n\)-fold simplicial objects is denoted by \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{s}}^n\mathcal{C}\). Thus \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{s}}^1\mathcal{C}=\ensuremath{\mathsf{s}}\mathcal{C}\), while, if \(n>1\), \[\ensuremath{\mathsf{s}}^n\mathcal{C}=\ensuremath{\mathsf{s}}\bigl(\ensuremath{\mathsf{s}}^{n-1}\mathcal{C}\bigr) =\ensuremath{\mathsf{s}}^{n-1}\bigl(\ensuremath{\mathsf{s}}\mathcal{C}\bigr),\] and so on. The case of \(n\)-fold cosimplicial objects is analogous. The semisimplicial objects of Remark reference plainly have an \(n\)-fold version, obtained by removing the degeneracy morphisms and the related conditions from the definition above.

Definition. With the notation above, the diagonal functor \(d:\ensuremath{\mathsf{s}}^n\mathcal{C}\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{s}}\mathcal{C}\) maps an \(n\)-fold simplicial object \(X\) to the simplicial object \[d(X)_n := X_{n, \ldots, n},\] whose face and degeneracy morphisms are defined respectively by \(d_i=\prod_k{}^kd_i\) and \(s_j=\prod_k{}^ks_j\). On morphisms, the functor is defined in the evident way. Equivalently, \(d(X)\) is the composite of \(X\) with the diagonal embedding \(\ensuremath{\bm\Delta}^{\operatorname{op}}\to(\ensuremath{\bm\Delta}^{\operatorname{op}})^n\). The cosimplicial case is entirely dual.

Example. Let \((\mathcal{C},\otimes)\) be a monoidal category, for example \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Set}}\) with the product \(\times\). For \(X_1,\ldots,X_n\in\operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{s}}\mathcal{C})\), we obtain an object of \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{s}}^n\mathcal{C}\) whose \((m_1,\ldots,m_n)\)-term is \(X_{1,m_1}\otimes\cdots\otimes X_{n,m_n}\). This \(n\)-fold simplicial object is denoted by \[X_1 \boxtimes \cdots \boxtimes X_n \in \operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{s}}^n \mathcal{C}).\]

This should not be confused with \(X_1\otimes\cdots\otimes X_n\in\operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{s}}\mathcal{C})\) from Definition reference; the two are related by \[X_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes X_n = d(X_1 \boxtimes \cdots \boxtimes X_n).\] A basic example is obtained from the monoidal category \((\ensuremath{\mathsf{Set}},\times)\). In this case \(\Delta^{p_1}\boxtimes\cdots\boxtimes\Delta^{p_n} =\Delta^{p_1,\ldots,p_n}\), while \(\Delta^{p_1}\otimes\cdots\otimes\Delta^{p_n} =\Delta^{p_1}\times\cdots\times\Delta^{p_n}\), the simplicial set obtained by taking the product degreewise.

General \(n\)-fold simplicial objects play an indispensable role in homotopy theory and its applications. This section is mainly concerned with abelian categories, focusing on the special case \(n=2\). The first step is to introduce a variant of Definition reference. Recall the definition of a double complex in Definition reference, or more precisely its chain-complex version. The category of double chain complexes is denoted by \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ch}}^2(\cdots)\), and \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ch}}^2_{\geq0}(\cdots)\) is defined similarly. For a bisemisimplicial object, we also introduce the notation \[\ensuremath{{}^\vartriangleright d}_i := {}^1 d_i , \quad \ensuremath{{}^\vartriangle d}_i := {}^2 d_i,\] for the face morphisms in the “horizontal” and “vertical” directions. For a bisimplicial object, the degeneracy morphisms are similarly denoted by \(\ensuremath{{}^\vartriangleright s}_j={}^1s_j\) and \(\ensuremath{{}^\vartriangle s}_j={}^2s_j\).

Definition. Let \(\mathcal{A}\) be an additive category and \(X\) a bisemisimplicial object in \(\mathcal{A}\). The corresponding unnormalized double chain complex (or Moore double chain complex) consists of \(\bigl(X_{p,q}\bigr)_{p,q\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}_{\geq0}}\) together with the data \[\begin{align*} \ensuremath{{}^\vartriangleright \partial}_{p, q} & := \sum_{i=0}^p (-1)^i \ensuremath{{}^\vartriangleright d}_i: X_{p, q} \to X_{p-1, q}, \\ \ensuremath{{}^\vartriangle \partial}_{p, q} & := \sum_{i=0}^q (-1)^i \ensuremath{{}^\vartriangle d}_i: X_{p, q} \to X_{p, q-1}. \end{align*}\] By convention, \(X_{p,q}:=0\) when \((p,q)\notin\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}_{\geq0}^2\). The resulting double chain complex is denoted by \(\mathrm{C}^2X\in\operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ch}}^2(\mathcal{A}))\).

To show that this really is a double chain complex, we must verify \(\ensuremath{{}^\vartriangleright \partial}_{p-1,q}\ensuremath{{}^\vartriangleright \partial}_{p,q}=0\), \(\ensuremath{{}^\vartriangle \partial}_{p,q-1}\ensuremath{{}^\vartriangle \partial}_{p,q}=0\), and \(\ensuremath{{}^\vartriangle \partial}_{p-1,q}\ensuremath{{}^\vartriangleright \partial}_{p,q}=\ensuremath{{}^\vartriangleright \partial}_{p,q-1}\ensuremath{{}^\vartriangle \partial}_{p,q}\). The first two identities are exactly as in Definition reference; the last follows directly from the commutativity of \(\ensuremath{{}^\vartriangleright d}_i\) and \(\ensuremath{{}^\vartriangle d}_j\). We thus obtain an additive functor \[\mathrm{C}^2: \ensuremath{\mathsf{s}}^2 \mathcal{A} \to \ensuremath{\mathsf{Ch}}^2(\mathcal{A}).\] Since \((p,q)\notin\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}_{\geq0}^2\) implies \(X_{p,q}=0\), we may now naturally define its total chain complex by \[(\operatorname{tot}X)_n := \bigoplus_{p+q = n} X_{p, q}, \quad \text{Diagram chapter8-unit-115-d001}\] The same argument as in Definition reference shows that \(\operatorname{tot}X\) really is a chain complex. Thus the composite functor \(\operatorname{tot}\circ\mathrm{C}^2:\ensuremath{\mathsf{s}}^2\mathcal{A}\to \ensuremath{\mathsf{Ch}}_{\geq0}(\mathcal{A})\) is defined. The same construction can be applied to \(n\)-fold simplicial objects over \(\mathcal{A}\) to obtain a functor \(\mathrm{C}^n:\ensuremath{\mathsf{s}}^n\mathcal{A}\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ch}}^n(\mathcal{A})\) and the corresponding total chain complex; see Remark reference.

Example. Suppose \(\mathcal{A}\) has the structure of a monoidal category such that the bifunctor \(\otimes:\mathcal{A}\times\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{A}\) is additive in each variable. If \(C_1,C_2\in\operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ch}}_{\geq0}(\mathcal{A}))\), we naturally obtain a double chain complex \(C_1\boxtimes C_2\) whose \((p,q)\)-term is \(C_{1,p}\otimes C_{2,q}\) and whose \(\ensuremath{{}^\vartriangleright \partial}\) and \(\ensuremath{{}^\vartriangle \partial}\) come from \(C_1\) and \(C_2\), respectively. If \(A,B\in\operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{s}}\mathcal{A})\), there is a simple relation between the double chain complex \(\mathrm{C}A\boxtimes\mathrm{C}B\) and the bisimplicial object \(A\boxtimes B\) of Example reference: \[\mathrm{C}^2 (A \boxtimes B) = \mathrm{C}A \boxtimes \mathrm{C}B.\] Moreover, \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ch}}_{\geq0}(\mathcal{A})\) becomes a monoidal category with \[C_1 \otimes C_2 := \operatorname{tot}(C_1 \boxtimes C_2),\] and its unit is plainly \(\ensuremath{\bm{1}}\) placed in degree zero.

Definition reference gives an additive functor \(d:\ensuremath{\mathsf{s}}^2\mathcal{A}\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{s}}\mathcal{A}\). The aim of this section is to explain, under the assumption that \(\mathcal{A}\) is an abelian category, the relationship between the functors \[\operatorname{tot}\circ \mathrm{C}^2 , \; \mathrm{C} \circ d: \; \ensuremath{\mathsf{s}}^2 \mathcal{A} \rightrightarrows \ensuremath{\mathsf{Ch}}_{\geq 0}(\mathcal{A}).\] This relationship involves the \((p,q)\)-shuffle \(\sigma\) of Definition reference and its sign \(\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)\) from Definition reference.

Definition. Let \(\mathcal{A}\) be an additive category and \(X\) a bisimplicial object in \(\mathcal{A}\). For a fixed \((p,q)\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}_{\geq0}^2\), write \(n:=p+q\).

  1. Define \(\overline{\mathrm{EZ}}_{p,q}:X_{p,q}\to X_{n,n}\) by \[\overline{\mathrm{EZ}}_{p, q} := \sum_{\sigma: (p,q)\text{-shuffle}} \operatorname{sgn}(\sigma) \left( \sigma_- \times \sigma_+ : [n] \times [n] \to [p] \times [q] \right)^*.\] A lengthy but straightforward argument, omitted here, shows that these maps combine to form a morphism of chain complexes called the shuffle morphism, or Eilenberg–Zilber morphism: \[\overline{\mathrm{EZ}}: \operatorname{tot}(\mathrm{C}^2 X) \to \mathrm{C}(dX).\]

  2. Define \(\overline{\mathrm{AW}}_n:=\sum_{p+q=n}\overline{\mathrm{AW}}_{p,q}: \mathrm{C}(dX)_n\to\operatorname{tot}(\mathrm{C}^2X)_n\), where \(\overline{\mathrm{AW}}_{p,q}:X_{n,n}\to X_{p,q}\) is defined as \((\lambda^n_p\times\rho^n_q)^*\), with \[\begin{array}{rl} \lambda^n_p: [p] \hookrightarrow [n], & i \mapsto i, \\ \rho^n_q: [q] \hookrightarrow [n], & i \mapsto n - q + i. \end{array}\] Similarly, these maps combine to form a morphism of chain complexes \(\overline{\mathrm{AW}}:\mathrm{C}(dX)\to\operatorname{tot}(\mathrm{C}^2X)\), called the Alexander–Whitney morphism.

These morphisms are functorial not only in \(X\), but also in the category \(\mathcal{A}\) and in functors between such categories. They were originally introduced in topology in connection with the homology of product spaces. We next introduce the normalized versions of \(\overline{\mathrm{EZ}}\) and \(\overline{\mathrm{AW}}\). Let \(\mathcal{A}\) be a monoidal abelian category such that \(\otimes:\mathcal{A}\times\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{A}\) is additive in each variable. Take \(A,B\in\operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{s}}\mathcal{A})\). Since \(\mathrm{C}^2(A\boxtimes B)=\mathrm{C}A\boxtimes\mathrm{C}B\), we have \[\mathrm{C}A \otimes \mathrm{C}B := \operatorname{tot}\left( \mathrm{C}A \boxtimes \mathrm{C}B \right) = \operatorname{tot}\, \mathrm{C}^2 (A \boxtimes B).\] We also use the simplified notation \[\begin{gather*} A \otimes B := d(A \boxtimes B), \\ \mathrm{N}A \otimes \mathrm{N}B := \operatorname{tot}\left( \mathrm{N}A \boxtimes \mathrm{N}B \right). \end{gather*}\]

Lemma. Consider the monoidal abelian category \(\mathcal{A}\) above. Recall that, for every \(Y\in\operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{s}}(\mathcal{A}))\), Proposition reference identifies \(\mathrm{N}Y\) with \(\mathrm{C}Y/\text{degenerate part}\). Under this identification, the morphisms \(\overline{\mathrm{AW}}\) and \(\overline{\mathrm{EZ}}\) each factor uniquely through the following commutative diagram: \[\text{Diagram chapter8-unit-116-d001}\]

Proof. For \(\mathrm{AW}\), it is enough to verify, for all \(p,q\geq0\) and \(n:=p+q\), the following equalities of morphisms in \(\ensuremath{\bm\Delta}\): \[\begin{align*} \lambda^n_p \circ \mathrm{s}^j & = \mathrm{s}^j \circ \lambda^{n+1}_{p+1}, \\ \rho^n_q \circ \mathrm{s}^j & = \mathrm{s}^{j+n-q} \circ \rho^{n+1}_{q+1}, \end{align*}\] where the respective conditions on \(j\) are \(0\leq j\leq p\) and \(0\leq j\leq q\). This verification is immediate.

For \(\mathrm{EZ}\), let \(\sigma\) be a \((p,q)\)-shuffle and let \(0\leq j\leq p-1\). Consider the restriction of \(\overline{\mathrm{EZ}}_{p,q}\) to \(\operatorname{im}(s_j)\otimes B_q\). The earlier discussion of \((p,q)\)-shuffles shows that there is a unique \(0\leq k<n:=p+q\) such that \(\sigma_-(k)=j\) and \(\sigma_-(k+1)=j+1\); at the same time, \(\sigma_+(k+1)=\sigma_+(k)\). This gives the equalities in \(\ensuremath{\bm\Delta}\) \[\begin{align*} \mathrm{s}^j \sigma_- \underbracket{\mathrm{d}^k \mathrm{s}^k}_{[n] \leftarrow [n]} & = \mathrm{s}^j \sigma_- : [n] \to [p-1] , \\ \sigma_+ \mathrm{d}^k \mathrm{s}^k & = \sigma_+ : [n] \to [q] . \end{align*}\]

Pulling back along these equalities, we see that \(\overline{\mathrm{EZ}}_{p,q}|_{\operatorname{im}(s_j)\otimes B_q}\) is contained in the part degenerate through \(s_k\). The case \(0\leq j\leq q-1\) and \(\overline{\mathrm{EZ}}_{p,q}|_{A_p\otimes\operatorname{im}(s_j)}\) is handled in the same way.

The following result is also called the generalized Eilenberg–Zilber theorem.

Theorem (S. Eilenberg, J. A. Zilber, P. Cartier). Let \(\mathcal{A}\) be an abelian category and \(X\in\operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{s}}^2\mathcal{A})\). The canonical morphisms defined above, \(\text{Diagram chapter8-unit-116-diagram-002}\) are mutually inverse on homology; in particular, both are quasi-isomorphisms.

Proof.

Since \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{s}}^2\mathcal{A}\simeq\ensuremath{\mathsf{s}}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{s}}\mathcal{A})\) and \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ch}}^2_{\geq0}(\mathcal{A})\simeq \ensuremath{\mathsf{Ch}}_{\geq0}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ch}}_{\geq0}(\mathcal{A}))\), the Dold–Kan correspondence has a double version, which we continue to denote by the equivalence of categories \(\Gamma:\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ch}}^2_{\geq0}(\mathcal{A})\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{s}}^2\mathcal{A}\). We may therefore assume that \(X=\Gamma A\) for \(A\in\operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ch}}^2_{\geq0}(\mathcal{A}))\). If \(p+q>n\) implies \(A_{p,q}=0\), we say that \(A\) has degree \(\leq n\).

First suppose that \(\mathcal{A}=\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ab}}\), with the monoidal structure from the tensor product \(\otimes=\otimes_{\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}}\). Observe that \(\operatorname{tot}\), \(\mathrm{C}^2\), \(\mathrm{C}\), and \(d\) are all right-exact additive functors and preserve arbitrary direct sums. The canonical morphisms \(\overline{\mathrm{EZ}}\) and \(\overline{\mathrm{AW}}\) are likewise compatible with arbitrary direct sums. Write \(A\) as a filtered union of bounded subobjects. Since the filtered colimit \(\varinjlim\) preserves homology, the problem reduces to the case where \(A\) has degree \(\leq n\) for a fixed \(n\geq0\). We argue by induction on \(n\).

Brutal truncation of \(A\) gives a short exact sequence \(0\to A'\to A\to A''\to0\), where

  • \(A'\) has degree \(\leq n-1\);

  • all nonzero terms of \(A''\) lie in the part \(p+q=n\);

  • the short exact sequence splits in every bidegree \((p,q)\).

The description of the functor \(\Gamma\) shows that \(0\to\Gamma A'\to\Gamma A\to\Gamma A''\to0\) is likewise a degreewise split short exact sequence in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{s}}^2\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ab}}\). Strictly speaking, the double version of \(\Gamma\) is needed here, but its form is analogous.

We therefore obtain a commutative diagram of chain complexes with exact rows: \[\text{Diagram chapter8-unit-116-d002}\] This diagram inductively reduces the problem to the case of \(A''\). In other words, under the induction hypothesis, the original problem depends only on \((A_{p,q})_{p+q=n}\).

It therefore suffices to handle the case in which \(A\) is a direct sum of several copies of \(C\otimes(\mathrm{N}(\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\Delta^p)\boxtimes \mathrm{N}(\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\Delta^q))\), with \(p+q=n\) and \(C\in\operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ab}})\). We can further reduce to a single copy for one pair \((p,q)\), and then factor \(\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_C\) out of all the maps to reduce to the special case \(C=\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\). Notice that the part of \(\mathrm{N}(\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\Delta^p)\) in degrees below \(p\) does not affect the problem; the same holds with \(q\) in place of \(p\). Correspondingly, \(X=\Gamma A\simeq\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}(\Delta^p\times\Delta^q)\). By Theorem reference and Lemma reference, it suffices to prove that \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:Eilenberg-Zilber-aux}{} \text{Diagram chapter8-unit-116-d003} \; \text{are mutually inverse on homology.} \end{equation}\]

The posets \([p]\), \([q]\), and \([p]\times[q]\) each have a least element, \(0\) or \((0,0)\), so the homotopy equivalences \(\mathrm{N}i\) and \(\mathrm{N}q\) from Example reference apply. It is easy to verify that the following diagram commutes: \[\begin{equation*} \text{Diagram chapter8-unit-116-d004} \end{equation*}\] The first row is concentrated in degree zero, and the standard isomorphism \(\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\otimes\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\simeq\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\) maps \(1\otimes1\) to \(1\). The verification of commutativity involves only the degree-zero terms of \(\mathrm{EZ}\) and \(\mathrm{AW}\), and is therefore immediate. This proves equation.

We now return to a general category \(\mathcal{A}\). Suppose there is a faithful exact functor (Proposition reference) \(F:\mathcal{A}\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ab}}\). By definition, \(\operatorname{tot}\), \(\mathrm{C}^2\), \(\mathrm{C}\), and \(d\) commute with \(F\), while \(\overline{\mathrm{EZ}}\) and \(\overline{\mathrm{AW}}\) are plainly compatible with \(F\). Faithfulness and exactness then reduce the problem to the known case \(\mathcal{A}=\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ab}}\).

If \(\mathcal{A}\) has a projective generator, for example \(\mathcal{A}=\ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}\text{-}}R\) for a ring \(R\), there is always a faithful exact functor to \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ab}}\). For a general abelian category \(\mathcal{A}\), the existence of \(F\) is guaranteed by the Freyd–Mitchell theorem reference; for this purpose, the Grothendieck universe may be enlarged as necessary to make \(\mathcal{A}\) a small category.

Remark (Monoidal structures). Let \(\mathcal{A}\) be a monoidal category and suppose that \(\otimes\) is additive in each variable. Lemma reference has already given canonical morphisms of the form \[\text{Diagram chapter8-unit-116-d005}\] for \(A,B\in\operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{s}}\mathcal{A})\). The special case of the generalized Eilenberg–Zilber theorem with \(X=A\boxtimes B\) states that these morphisms are mutually inverse on homology. Recall that \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ch}}_{\geq0}(\mathcal{A})\) is also a monoidal category (Example reference), and there are the evident morphisms \[\text{Diagram chapter8-unit-116-d006}\]

From an abstract viewpoint, the shuffle morphism (respectively, the Alexander–Whitney morphism) equips \(\mathrm{C}\) and \(\mathrm{N}\) with the structure of right-lax (respectively, left-lax) monoidal functors; see [Li1]. For the shuffle morphism, this roughly means that \(\overline{\mathrm{EZ}}_{p,q}\) and \(\mathrm{EZ}_{p,q}\) are associative and compatible with the unit; the case of \(\overline{\mathrm{AW}}\) and \(\mathrm{AW}\) is dual. These assertions can also be verified directly, though at length. For example, associativity of the shuffle morphism involves equation, while the case of the Alexander–Whitney morphism is simpler.

If \(\mathcal{A}\) is a symmetric monoidal category, \(\overline{\mathrm{EZ}}\) and \(\mathrm{EZ}\) also preserve the Koszul braiding introduced in equation. For \(\overline{\mathrm{EZ}}\), this is equivalent to the commutativity of the following diagram in \(\mathcal{A}\): \[\text{Diagram chapter8-unit-116-d007}\] Here \(p,q\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}_{\geq0}\). The maps \(\mathrm{swap}\) in the two columns come from the braiding \(c(X,Y):X\otimes Y\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}Y\otimes X\) on \(\mathcal{A}\) and its induced degreewise action on simplicial objects; the maps themselves involve no sign. The proof follows directly from the definition and equation. By contrast, \(\overline{\mathrm{AW}}\) and \(\mathrm{AW}\) need not be compatible with the braiding.

Broadly speaking, the Dold–Kan correspondence functor \(\mathrm{N}\) of Theorem reference, together with its unnormalized version \(\mathrm{C}\), is monoidal in both the right-lax and left-lax senses. The required data are supplied respectively by the shuffle morphism and the Alexander–Whitney morphism. If \(\mathcal{A}\) is symmetric monoidal, the right-lax monoidal functor structure is also symmetric. The concept of a bilax monoidal functor [AM10] gives a more precise formulation of these structures.

Closed Structures

The aim of this section is to explain the closed structures on \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{sSet}}\) and \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{sAb}}\). For \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{sSet}}\), this is the Cartesian closed structure of Definition reference; for \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{sAb}}\), it is the monoidal structure given by the tensor product that is closed. In other words, we seek to promote the \(\operatorname{Hom}\) sets to suitable simplicial objects. We first discuss the category \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{sSet}}\) of simplicial sets, then its version for \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{sAb}}\) and its comparison, via the Dold–Kan correspondence, with the \(\operatorname{Hom}\) complex. The last step requires the results of §reference.

Definition. For \(X,Y\in\operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{sSet}})\), define \(\ensuremath{\EuScript{H}\mathrm{om}}(X,Y)=\ensuremath{\EuScript{H}\mathrm{om}}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{sSet}}}(X,Y)\in\operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{sSet}})\) as follows: \[\ensuremath{\EuScript{H}\mathrm{om}}(X,Y)_n:=\operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{sSet}}}(X\times\Delta^n,Y), \qquad n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}_{\geq0}.\] For every morphism \(f:[m]\to[n]\) in \(\ensuremath{\bm\Delta}\), define \(f^*:\ensuremath{\EuScript{H}\mathrm{om}}(X,Y)_n\to\ensuremath{\EuScript{H}\mathrm{om}}(X,Y)_m\) by pullback, that is, by precomposition, along \[\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_X\times f:X\times\Delta^m\to X\times\Delta^n.\] Also define the evaluation morphism \[\mathrm{ev}_{X,Y}:\ensuremath{\EuScript{H}\mathrm{om}}(X,Y)\times X\to Y\] as follows: the image of \((\varphi,x)\in\operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{sSet}}}(X\times\Delta^n,Y)\times X_n\) is \(\mathrm{ev}_{X,Y,n}(\varphi,x):=\varphi(x,\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{[n]})\in Y_n\). Recall that \((\Delta^n)_n=\operatorname{End}_{\ensuremath{\bm\Delta}}([n])\).

We must check that \(\mathrm{ev}_{X,Y}\) is indeed a morphism in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{sSet}}\). This is immediate: for \(f:[m]\to[n]\) and \((\varphi,x)\in\ensuremath{\EuScript{H}\mathrm{om}}(X,Y)_n\times X_n\), we have \[\begin{align*} \mathrm{ev}_{X,Y,m}\bigl(f^*(\varphi),f^*(x)\bigr) &=((\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_X\times f)^*\varphi) \bigl(f^*(x),\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{[m]}\bigr)\\ &=\varphi\bigl( \underbracket{f^*(x),\;f}_{\in X_m\times(\Delta^n)_m}\bigr) =\varphi\bigl(f^*(x),f^*\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{[n]}\bigr)\\ &=f^*\bigl(\varphi(x,\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{[n]})\bigr) =f^*\bigl(\mathrm{ev}_{X,Y,n}(\varphi,x)\bigr). \end{align*}\] As \(X,Y\) vary, this construction gives a functor \(\ensuremath{\EuScript{H}\mathrm{om}}:\ensuremath{\mathsf{sSet}}^{\operatorname{op}}\times\ensuremath{\mathsf{sSet}}\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{sSet}}\), while \(\mathrm{ev}\) is natural in \(X\) and \(Y\).

Proposition. For every \(X,Y,Z\in\operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{sSet}})\), there is a canonical bijection \[\text{Diagram chapter8-unit-117-d001}\] It sends \(g:X\to\ensuremath{\EuScript{H}\mathrm{om}}(Y,Z)\) to the composite \[X\times Y\xrightarrow{g\times\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_Y} \ensuremath{\EuScript{H}\mathrm{om}}(Y,Z)\times Y\xrightarrow{\mathrm{ev}_{Y,Z}}Z.\] Conversely, it sends \(h:X\times Y\to Z\) to the following morphism. For \(n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}_{\geq0}\) and \(x\in X_n\), let \(\iota_x:\Delta^n\to X\) be the morphism corresponding to \(x\). The image of \(x\) is the composite \[Y\times\Delta^n\xrightarrow{\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_Y\times\iota_x}Y\times X \xrightarrow[\sim]{\text{swap}}X\times Y\xrightarrow{h}Z.\]

Proof. A routine verification.

Corollary. The bijection in Proposition reference makes \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{sSet}}\) a Cartesian closed category in the sense of Definition reference, with bifunctor \(\ensuremath{\EuScript{H}\mathrm{om}}\).

Proof. Recall that the product in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{sSet}}\) is simply the product \(X\times Y\) of simplicial sets, and similarly for the other products. It remains to compare equation with the canonical bijection in Proposition reference.

The general theory of closed monoidal categories (see §reference) gives a canonical morphism \(\ensuremath{\EuScript{H}\mathrm{om}}(X,Y)\times X\to Y\): it is the image of \(\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}\) under \[\operatorname{End}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{sSet}}}\bigl(\ensuremath{\EuScript{H}\mathrm{om}}(X,Y)\bigr)\xrightarrow{1:1} \operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{sSet}}}\bigl(\ensuremath{\EuScript{H}\mathrm{om}}(X,Y)\times X,Y\bigr).\] Unwinding the definitions shows that this morphism is precisely the \(\mathrm{ev}_{X,Y}\) defined above.

Example. Proposition reference says that the nerve functor \(\mathrm{N}\) embeds \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Cat}}\) fully faithfully into \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{sSet}}\). How is \(\ensuremath{\EuScript{H}\mathrm{om}}\) reflected at the level of categories? The answer is simple: for any small categories \(\mathcal{C}\) and \(\mathcal{D}\), there is a canonical isomorphism \[\ensuremath{\EuScript{H}\mathrm{om}}(\mathrm{N}\mathcal{C},\mathrm{N}\mathcal{D}) \simeq\mathrm{N}(\mathcal{D}^{\mathcal{C}}).\] Indeed, \(\mathrm{N}\) takes products of categories to products of simplicial sets, and \(\mathrm{N}([n])=\Delta^n\). Since \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Cat}}\) is also Cartesian closed, we obtain \[\begin{multline*} \operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{sSet}}}(\mathrm{N}\mathcal{C}\times\Delta^n, \mathrm{N}\mathcal{D}) =\operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{sSet}}}(\mathrm{N}(\mathcal{C}\times[n]), \mathrm{N}\mathcal{D})\\ \simeq\operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{Cat}}}(\mathcal{C}\times[n],\mathcal{D}) \simeq\operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{Cat}}}([n],\mathcal{D}^{\mathcal{C}}) =\mathrm{N}(\mathcal{D}^{\mathcal{C}})_n. \end{multline*}\] It is easy to check that the pullbacks on both sides correspond for every morphism \(f:[m]\to[n]\) in \(\ensuremath{\bm\Delta}\).

Now consider \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{sAb}}\). Recall that it has the symmetric monoidal structure arising from \(\otimes:=\otimes_{\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}}\), namely the degreewise tensor product. For \(X\in\operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{sAb}})\) and \(K\in\operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{sSet}})\), define \[X\otimes K:=X\otimes\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}K\in\operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{sAb}}).\] In particular, \(X\otimes\Delta^n\) is defined. This construction gives a bifunctor \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{sAb}}\times\ensuremath{\mathsf{sSet}}\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{sAb}}\).

Definition. For \(X,Y\in\operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{sAb}})\), define \(\ensuremath{\EuScript{H}\mathrm{om}}(X,Y)=\ensuremath{\EuScript{H}\mathrm{om}}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{sAb}}}(X,Y)\in\operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{sAb}})\) by \(\ensuremath{\EuScript{H}\mathrm{om}}(X,Y)_n:=\operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{sAb}}}(X\otimes\Delta^n,Y)\). The pullback morphisms are defined as in Definition reference.

Proposition. For every \(X,Y,Z\in\operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{sAb}})\), there is a canonical commutative diagram \[\text{Diagram chapter8-unit-117-d002}\]

Proof. The first row is Proposition reference. The vertical arrow on the right embeds \(\operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{sAb}}}(X\otimes Y,Z)\) as the bilinear part of \(\operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{sSet}}}(X\times Y,Z)\). The image of the embedding on the left consists of all \(\varphi:X\to\ensuremath{\EuScript{H}\mathrm{om}}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{sSet}}}(Y,Z)\) for which the family of morphisms \[\varphi_n:X_n\to\operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{sSet}}}(Y\times\Delta^n,Z)\] satisfies, for every \(n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}_{\geq0}\),

  • \(\varphi_n(x):Y\times\Delta^n\to Z\) is additive in the \(Y\) variable for every \(x\in X_n\), or equivalently factors through \(\operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{sAb}}}(Y\otimes\Delta^n,Z)\);

  • the resulting map \(\varphi_n:X_n\to\operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{sAb}}}(Y\otimes\Delta^n,Z)\) is additive.

Unwinding the definitions immediately shows that these two descriptions correspond.

In fact, \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{sAb}}\) is an additive category, and the bijection \(\operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{sAb}}}\bigl(X,\ensuremath{\EuScript{H}\mathrm{om}}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{sAb}}}(Y,Z)\bigr) \simeq\operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{sAb}}}(X\otimes Y,Z)\) is an isomorphism of \(\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\)-modules.

Corollary. Let \(X,Y\in\operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{sAb}})\) and \(K\in\operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{sSet}})\). There are canonical isomorphisms of \(\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\)-modules \[\begin{align*} \operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{sAb}}}(X\otimes K,Y) &\simeq\operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{sSet}}} \bigl(K,\ensuremath{\EuScript{H}\mathrm{om}}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{sAb}}}(X,Y)\bigr)\\ &\simeq\operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{sAb}}} \bigl(X,\ensuremath{\EuScript{H}\mathrm{om}}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{sSet}}}(K,Y)\bigr). \end{align*}\] By the universal property, the underlying simplicial set of \(\ensuremath{\EuScript{H}\mathrm{om}}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{sSet}}}(K,Y)\) in the last term is naturally identified with the underlying simplicial set of \(\ensuremath{\EuScript{H}\mathrm{om}}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{sAb}}}(\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}K,Y)\), and thus acquires the structure of an object of \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{sAb}}\).

Proof. Proposition reference gives \[\begin{align*} \operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{sAb}}}(X\otimes K,Y) &\simeq\operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{sAb}}}(\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}K\otimes X,Y)\\ &\simeq\operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{sAb}}} \bigl(\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}K,\ensuremath{\EuScript{H}\mathrm{om}}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{sAb}}}(X,Y)\bigr). \end{align*}\] The adjunction property of \(\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}(\cdot)\) shows that the last term is \(\operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{sSet}}}(K,\ensuremath{\EuScript{H}\mathrm{om}}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{sAb}}}(X,Y))\). Similarly, \(\operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{sAb}}}(X\otimes K,Y)\simeq \operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{sAb}}}(X,\ensuremath{\EuScript{H}\mathrm{om}}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{sAb}}}(\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}K,Y))\).

Corollary. The canonical bijection in Proposition reference makes \((\ensuremath{\mathsf{sAb}},\otimes)\) a closed monoidal category in the sense of Definition reference, with bifunctor \(\ensuremath{\EuScript{H}\mathrm{om}}\).

As for simplicial sets, the general theory of closed monoidal categories gives a canonical evaluation morphism \[\mathrm{ev}_{X,Y}:\ensuremath{\EuScript{H}\mathrm{om}}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{sAb}}}(X,Y)\otimes X\to Y.\] This morphism has a concrete description similar to Definition reference, obtained simply by unwinding the definitions. We now study the relationship between \(\ensuremath{\EuScript{H}\mathrm{om}}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{sAb}}}\) and the \(\operatorname{Hom}\) complex from the perspective of the Dold–Kan correspondence (Theorem reference). They are the internal \(\operatorname{Hom}\) objects of the closed monoidal categories \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{sAb}}\) and \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ch}}_{\geq0}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ab}})\), respectively. Although the normalized chain complex functor \(\mathrm{N}:\ensuremath{\mathsf{sAb}}\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ch}}_{\geq0}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ab}})\) is an equivalence, it is not a monoidal functor. We therefore cannot directly deduce an isomorphism between \(\mathrm{N}\ensuremath{\EuScript{H}\mathrm{om}}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{sAb}}}(X,Y)\) and \(\operatorname{Hom}^\bullet(\mathrm{N}X,\mathrm{N}Y)\). Nevertheless, the results of §reference still provide a pair of canonical morphisms \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:Hom-N}{} \text{Diagram chapter8-unit-117-d003} \end{equation}\]

  • By the closed monoidal structure on \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ch}}_{\geq0}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ab}})\), giving a morphism from left to right is equivalent to giving a morphism \[\mathrm{N}\ensuremath{\EuScript{H}\mathrm{om}}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{sAb}}}(X,Y)\otimes\mathrm{N}X \longrightarrow\mathrm{N}Y.\] Take this morphism to be the composite \[\mathrm{N}\ensuremath{\EuScript{H}\mathrm{om}}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{sAb}}}(X,Y)\otimes\mathrm{N}X \xrightarrow{\mathrm{EZ}} \mathrm{N}\bigl(\ensuremath{\EuScript{H}\mathrm{om}}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{sAb}}}(X,Y)\otimes X\bigr) \xrightarrow{\mathrm{N}(\mathrm{ev}_{X,Y})}\mathrm{N}Y.\]

  • Apply the left adjoint \(\Gamma\) of \(\mathrm{N}\), which is also its quasi-inverse. Giving a morphism from right to left is equivalent to giving a morphism \[\Gamma\operatorname{Hom}^\bullet(\mathrm{N}X,\mathrm{N}Y) \longrightarrow\ensuremath{\EuScript{H}\mathrm{om}}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{sAb}}}(X,Y).\] By the closed monoidal structure on \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{sAb}}\), this is also equivalent to giving a morphism \(\Gamma\operatorname{Hom}^\bullet(\mathrm{N}X,\mathrm{N}Y)\otimes X\to Y\). Concretely, choose this morphism so that its image under \(\mathrm{N}\) is the composite \[\begin{multline*} \mathrm{N}\bigl(\Gamma\operatorname{Hom}^\bullet(\mathrm{N}X,\mathrm{N}Y) \otimes X\bigr) \xrightarrow{\mathrm{AW}} \mathrm{N}\Gamma\operatorname{Hom}^\bullet(\mathrm{N}X,\mathrm{N}Y) \otimes\mathrm{N}X\\ \simeq\operatorname{Hom}^\bullet(\mathrm{N}X,\mathrm{N}Y)\otimes\mathrm{N}X \xrightarrow{\text{evaluation}}\mathrm{N}Y. \end{multline*}\]

The point of the construction above is that \(\mathrm{N}\) is both a right lax and a left lax monoidal functor. If \(\mathrm{N}\) were monoidal, or equivalently if \(\mathrm{EZ}\) and \(\mathrm{AW}\) were both isomorphisms, an abstract argument would show that the two morphisms in equation are mutually inverse; in reality, they are not. However, the general Eilenberg–Zilber theorem, Theorem reference, states that \(\mathrm{EZ}\) and \(\mathrm{AW}\) are mutually inverse on homology. This gives the following relationship between the \(\operatorname{Hom}\) complex and \(\ensuremath{\EuScript{H}\mathrm{om}}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{sAb}}}\).

Proposition. For every \(X,Y\in\operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{sAb}})\), the pair of morphisms in equation are mutually inverse on homology.

If \(\Bbbk\) is a commutative ring, an analogous result holds after replacing \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ab}}\) by the symmetric monoidal category \(\Bbbk\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\) and considering simplicial objects in it.

Remark. The definition of \(\ensuremath{\EuScript{H}\mathrm{om}}\) can be extended to an arbitrary additive category \(\mathcal{A}\). Indeed, in the description of \(\ensuremath{\EuScript{H}\mathrm{om}}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{sAb}}}(X,Y)_n\), we have \[(X\otimes\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\Delta^n)_k =X_k\otimes\left(\bigoplus_{u:[k]\to[n]}\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\right) \simeq\bigoplus_{u:[k]\to[n]}X_k.\] The last term involves only finite direct sums and no elements; the maps \(d_i,s_j\), and so forth also have simple descriptions in this direct-sum presentation. We can therefore define a bifunctor \[\ensuremath{\EuScript{H}\mathrm{om}}_{\mathcal{A}}:(\ensuremath{\mathsf{s}}\mathcal{A})^{\operatorname{op}} \times\ensuremath{\mathsf{s}}\mathcal{A}\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{s}}\mathcal{A},\] which is additive in each variable.

The Mapping Cone Revisited

As we saw in §reference and §reference, the mapping cone \(\operatorname{Cone}(f)\) plays an important role in the theory of complexes and in the study of derived categories. The aim of this section is to interpret it through the Dold–Kan correspondence and to explain why a mapping cone really is a “cone.” More precisely, we shall study the chain complex version of the mapping cone; see Remark reference. We begin with mapping cones and mapping cylinders in topology. Consider a continuous map \(F:\mathcal{X}\to\mathcal{Y}\) with \(\mathcal{X}\neq\emptyset\).
