Its mapping cylinder is the quotient space \[\begin{equation*} \operatorname{Cyl}_{\mathrm{top}}(F) := \dfrac{(\mathcal{X} \times [0, 1]) \sqcup \mathcal{Y}}{\forall x \in \mathcal{X}, \; (x, 1) \sim F(x)}, \end{equation*}\] where \(\times\) (respectively, \(\sqcup\)) denotes the product (respectively, disjoint union) of topological spaces. The mapping cone is defined by \[\begin{equation*} \begin{aligned} \operatorname{Cone}_{\mathrm{top}}(F) & := \dfrac{(\mathcal{X} \times [0, 1]) \sqcup \mathcal{Y}}{\forall x \in \mathcal{X}, \; (x, 1) \sim F(x), \; (x, 0) \sim (\star, 0)} \\ & \simeq \dfrac{\operatorname{Cyl}_{\mathrm{top}}(F)}{\forall x \in \mathcal{X}, \; (x, 0) \sim (\star, 0)}, \end{aligned} \end{equation*}\] where \(\star\in\mathcal{X}\) is an arbitrary point. Intuitively, \(\mathcal{X}\times[0,1]\) may be pictured as a tube with cross-section \(\mathcal{X}\). The cylinder \(\operatorname{Cyl}_{\mathrm{top}}(F)\) is obtained by gluing the end \(\mathcal{X}\times\{1\}\) of the tube to \(\mathcal{Y}\) via \(F\), while \(\operatorname{Cone}_{\mathrm{top}}(F)\) further contracts the end \(\mathcal{X}\times\{0\}\) to a single point. Schematically: \[\operatorname{Cyl}_{\mathrm{top}}(F) = \par\textbf{Diagram chapter8-unit-118-d001}\par \quad \operatorname{Cone}_{\mathrm{top}}(F) = \par\textbf{Diagram chapter8-unit-118-d002}\par\] Simplicial sets provide a concrete way to describe topological spaces. More precisely, Theorem reference gives an adjoint pair \[\text{Diagram chapter8-unit-118-d003}\] and the two categories model equivalent homotopy theories in a precise sense. The same construction works with \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Top}}\) replaced by \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{CGHaus}}\). We now translate the preceding discussion into \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{sSet}}\). We may assume that \[\mathcal{X} = |X|, \quad \mathcal{Y} = |Y|, \quad F = |f|: |X| \to |Y|,\] where \(f:X\to Y\) is a morphism in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{sSet}}\). From the viewpoint of simplicial sets, the mapping cone is easier to describe than the mapping cylinder. We begin with the cone on \(\mathcal{X}\), \(\operatorname{Cone}_{\mathrm{top}}(\mathcal{X}):= \operatorname{Cone}_{\mathrm{top}}(\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{\mathcal{X}})\). If \(\mathcal{X}=|X|\), then \(\operatorname{Cone}_{\mathrm{top}}(\mathcal{X})\simeq|X^{\lhd}|\simeq|X^{\rhd}|\) (Example reference). Below we focus on the left cone \(X^{\lhd}=\Delta^0\star X\) and its corresponding chain complex. For every simplicial set \(Z\), write \(Z_n^{\mathrm{nd}}\) for the set of all nondegenerate \(n\)-simplices in it, and write \(\{\mathrm{pt}\}=(\Delta^0)_0=(\Delta^0)_0^{\mathrm{nd}}\). Proposition reference, or topological intuition, gives \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:Cone-X-aux1}{} (\Delta^0 \star X)^{\mathrm{nd}}_n = \begin{cases} X^{\mathrm{nd}}_n \sqcup \left( \{ \mathrm{pt} \} \times X^{\mathrm{nd}}_{n-1} \right), & n > 0 \\ \{\mathrm{pt}\} \sqcup X_0, & n = 0. \end{cases} \end{equation}\] Substituting equation and the general formulas discussed above it shows that, for \(n\geq1\), the restrictions of \(d_i:(\Delta^0\star X)_n\to(\Delta^0\star X)_{n-1}\) to \(\{\mathrm{pt}\}\times X_{n-1}\) and \(X_n\) are as follows: \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:Cone-X-aux2}{}\begin{gathered} \text{Diagram chapter8-unit-118-d004} \quad \text{Diagram chapter8-unit-118-d005} \end{gathered} \end{equation}\] If \(n=1\), the term \(\{\mathrm{pt}\}\times X_{n-2}\) in this formula is to be understood as \(\{\mathrm{pt}\}\). Since our goal is a chain complex, the next step is to linearize the problem using the functor \(\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}(\mathord\cdot)\) of Definition reference, and then pass to chain complexes via the Dold–Kan correspondence: \[\begin{equation*} \mathrm{N}(\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}X^{\lhd}) \simeq \mathrm{C}(\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}X^{\lhd}) \big/ \text{degenerate part} \quad \text{(Proposition \href{#prop:Dold-Kan-v}{reference})}. \end{equation*}\] To simplify notation in the rest of this section, write \(\mathrm{N}X:=\mathrm{N}(\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}X)\) and \(\mathrm{N}f:=\mathrm{N}(\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}f)\). The chain-complex structure on \(\mathrm{C}(\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}X^{\lhd})\) comes from \(\partial_n:=\sum_{i=0}^n(-1)^id_i\). Combining equation, equation, and the description of \(\operatorname{Cone}(\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{\mathrm{N}X})\) in Remark reference, we obtain a short exact sequence of chain complexes \[0 \to \underbracket{\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\{\mathrm{pt}\}}_{\text{degree zero}} \to \mathrm{N}(\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}X^{\lhd}) \to \operatorname{Cone}(\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{\mathrm{N}X}) \to 0.\] Next, the functors \(|\mathord\cdot|\) and \(\mathrm{N}\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}(\mathord\cdot)\) preserve pushout diagrams: the former is a left adjoint, while the latter is the composite of a left adjoint with an equivalence; in topology, a pushout diagram means gluing. Therefore, for \(f:X\to Y\) define \[\begin{equation*} \operatorname{Cone}_{\mathrm{s}}(f) := X^{\lhd} \ensuremath{\underset{X, f}{\sqcup}} Y. \end{equation*}\] We then obtain \[\text{Diagram chapter8-unit-118-d006} \xleftarrow{|\cdot|} \text{Diagram chapter8-unit-118-d007} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{N}} \text{Diagram chapter8-unit-118-d008}\] This chain of constructions shows that the linear-algebraic counterpart of \(\operatorname{Cone}_{\mathrm{top}}(F)\) should be \(\mathrm{N}\operatorname{Cone}_{\mathrm{s}}(f)\).

Proposition. With the notation above, there is a canonical short exact sequence of chain complexes \[0 \to \underbracket{\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\{\mathrm{pt}\}}_{\text{degree zero}} \to \mathrm{N}\operatorname{Cone}_{\mathrm{s}}(f) \to \operatorname{Cone}(\mathrm{N}f) \to 0.\]

Proof. The pushout does not affect the chain subcomplex \(\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\{\mathrm{pt}\}\) of \(\mathrm{N}X^{\lhd}\) corresponding to the cone point. In degree \(n\), it replaces every \(X_n\) by \(Y_n\) and replaces the projection \(\mathrm{pr}_2\) in equation by \(f_{n-1}\mathrm{pr}_2\). Thus, on the quotient \(\operatorname{Cone}(\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{\mathrm{N}X})\), the resulting pushout is precisely \(\operatorname{Cone}(\mathrm{N}f)\); see Remark reference.

Remark. The mapping cylinder \(\operatorname{Cyl}_{\mathrm{top}}(F)\) and its chain-complex version can be compared similarly; here there is no need to quotient out the contribution of the cone point. However, the mapping cylinder involves products of simplicial sets, whereas \(\mathrm{N}\) is not a monoidal functor. Topological accounts therefore usually use CW complexes rather than simplicial sets, since products are easier to handle in the world of CW complexes.

In short, the mapping cone of chain complexes is the quotient of the mapping cone arising from simplicial sets (or topology) by a copy of \(\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\) coming from the cone point \(\mathrm{pt}\). In the study of chain complexes, the main role of the mapping cone is that every map \(\phi:A\to B\) extends to a sequence \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:cofiber-comparison-A}{} A \xrightarrow{\phi} B \to \operatorname{Cone}(\phi) \to A[-1] \xrightarrow{-\phi[-1]} B[-1] \to \cdots . \end{equation}\] In the topological setting, the map corresponding to \(\operatorname{Cone}(\phi)\to A[-1]\) is obtained by contracting the base \(\mathcal{Y}\) of \(\operatorname{Cone}_{\mathrm{top}}(F)\) to a point. The result is denoted by \(S\mathcal{X}\); it is independent of \(\mathcal{Y}\) (see the figure below) and defines a functor \(S\). The corresponding sequence of maps is \[\begin{equation*} \par\textbf{Diagram chapter8-unit-118-d009}\par \xrightarrow{F} \par\textbf{Diagram chapter8-unit-118-d010}\par \xrightarrow{\text{inclusion}} \par\textbf{Diagram chapter8-unit-118-d011}\par \xrightarrow{\text{collapse}} \par\textbf{Diagram chapter8-unit-118-d012}\par \to \cdots . \end{equation*}\] This sequence is called the cofiber sequence generated by \(f\) (more precisely, the unpointed version). If we work in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{sSet}}\) and take the chain complexes of the corresponding sequence, the result is roughly equation. The qualification “roughly” is needed because:

  • The map \(S\mathcal{X}\to S\mathcal{Y}\) cannot simply be defined as \(S(F)\); the vertical coordinate must be reversed appropriately. At the level of linear algebra, this corresponds to \(-\phi[-1]\) in equation; see a topology textbook for details.

  • As Proposition reference shows, the various chain complexes contain one extra copy of \(\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\) corresponding to the cone point of spaces such as \(\operatorname{Cone}_{\mathrm{top}}(F)\) and \(S\mathcal{X}\). In topology, this issue is avoided by using pointed spaces and, in the topological cone construction, contracting the part associated with the base point.

If we set all details aside for the moment, the theory of derived categories constructed in §reference, with \(\mathcal{A}=\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ab}}\), may also be viewed in broad outline as a somewhat coarse “linearization” of homotopy theory1. As the related questions increasingly involve topological ideas and methods, we stop here so as not to stray too far afield.

  1. More precisely, stable homotopy theory, since chain complexes allow terms in negative degrees.↩︎

begin

Prove that, for every category \(\mathcal{C}\), the construction \(C\mapsto\mathrm{const}(C)\) of Example reference gives a fully faithful functor \(\mathcal{C}\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{s}}\mathcal{C}\).

Let \(X\) be a simplicial set and \(x\in X_n\). Prove that there is a sequence of indices \(j_1<\cdots<j_h\) and a nondegenerate simplex \(y\) such that \(x=s_{j_h}\cdots s_{j_1}(y)\), and that \(y\) is unique. Hint. The difficulty lies in uniqueness. Suppose that \(Sy=x=S'y'\), where \(S\) and \(S'\) are both of the form in the statement. We can choose a composite \(D\) of a sequence of face morphisms such that \(y=DSy=DS'y'\). Rewrite \(DS'\) in the form \(\widetilde{S}'\widetilde{D}\) (the meaning of the notation is clear). Since \(y\) is nondegenerate, we must have \(\widetilde{S}'=\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}\), and hence \(y=\widetilde{D}y'\). Use symmetry to conclude that \(y=y'\) and \(\widetilde{D}=\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}\).

Show that the following diagram exists in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{sSet}}\), with both the upper and lower parts commutative, for \(0\leq i<j\leq n\): \[\text{Diagram chapter8-unit-119-d001}\] Here \(\bigsqcup\) is taken degreewise in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{sSet}}=\ensuremath{\mathsf{Set}}^{\ensuremath{\bm\Delta}^{\operatorname{op}}}\), while \(\iota_{i<j}\) (respectively, \(\iota_i\)) denotes the embedding into the \(i<j\) term (respectively, the \(i\)th term). All arrows in the middle row are characterized by this commutativity. Show, moreover, that the middle row is a coequalizer.

Similarly, show that for every \(0\leq k\leq n\) there is also a diagram \[\text{Diagram chapter8-unit-119-d002}\] whose middle row is a coequalizer and where \(i,j\neq k\). Try to explain the topological meaning of these coequalizers.

Verify the following properties of the join operation \(\star\) in Definition reference.

  1. Simplicial sets naturally form a monoidal category under \(\star\), with the constant empty simplicial set \(\emptyset\) as unit object.

  2. The order-reversal duality of Remark reference gives an automorphism of \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{sSet}}\), provisionally denoted by \(X\mapsto\hat{X}\). Show that \((X\star Y)^{\wedge}\simeq\hat{Y}\star\hat{X}\).

  3. Verify that \(\Delta^p\star\Delta^q\simeq\Delta^{p+q+1}\).

Show that taking the order-reversal dual of a simplicial set does not change its geometric realization, up to canonical homeomorphism. Hint. Begin with the case of \(\Delta^n\).

Verify the assertion of Example reference.

Let \(\mathcal{C}\) and \(\mathcal{C}'\) be categories. Define the category \(\mathcal{C}\star\mathcal{C}'\) as follows: \[\begin{align*} \operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{C} \star \mathcal{C}') & := \operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{C}) \sqcup \operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{C}'), \\ \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{C} \star \mathcal{C}'}(X, Y) & := \begin{cases} \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}}(X, Y), & X, Y \in \operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{C}) \\ \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}'}(X, Y), & X, Y \in \operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{C}'), \\ \text{one-point set}, & X \in \operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{C}), \; Y \in \operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{C}'), \\ \emptyset, & X \in \operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{C}'), \; Y \in \operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{C}). \end{cases} \end{align*}\] Composition and identity morphisms are defined in the evident way. Prove that the join operation \(\star\) on simplicial sets and the nerve functor of Example reference are related by \[\mathrm{N}(\mathcal{C}) \star \mathrm{N}(\mathcal{C}') \simeq \mathrm{N}(\mathcal{C} \star \mathcal{C}').\]

Give a more detailed proof of Equations equation and equation.

For a simplicial object \(X\) in an arbitrary category, define the simplicial objects called the decalages \(\mathrm{Déc}_0X\) and \(\mathrm{Déc}^0X\) by \((\mathrm{Déc}_0X)_n=(\mathrm{Déc}^0X)_n=X_{n+1}\) and \[\begin{gather*} d^{\mathrm{Déc}_0 X, n}_i = d^{X, n+1}_i, \quad s^{\mathrm{Déc}_0 X, n}_j = s^{X, n+1}_j, \\ d^{\mathrm{Déc}^0 X, n}_i = d^{X, n+1}_{i+1}, \quad s^{\mathrm{Déc}^0 X, n}_j = s^{X, n+1}_{j+1}. \end{gather*}\] Show that both are well-defined and are related by the order-reversal duality (Remark reference). Also show that for an additive category, \(\mathrm{C}(\mathrm{Déc}^0X)=\mathrm{C}(X)[1]\); see Remark reference.

Continuing the preceding exercise, show that \(d_0:X_1\to X_0\) (respectively, \(d_1:X_1\to X_0\)) gives an augmentation of \(\mathrm{Déc}_0X\) (respectively, \(\mathrm{Déc}^0X\)), with \(X_0\) as the term of degree \(-1\). Show further that, after augmentation, \(\mathrm{Déc}_0X\) is right contractible and \(\mathrm{Déc}^0X\) is left contractible; see Definition reference. Hint. It suffices to treat \(\mathrm{Déc}_0X\). Take \(k_{n-1}:=s_n:X_n\to X_{n+1}\).

Prove that a small category \(\mathcal{C}\) is a groupoid (that is, all its morphisms are invertible) if and only if \(\mathrm{N}\mathcal{C}\) satisfies the following condition: for every \(n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}_{\geq1}\) and \(0\leq i\leq n\), every morphism \(\Lambda^n_i\to\mathrm{N}\mathcal{C}\) can be extended to \(\Delta^n\to\mathrm{N}\mathcal{C}\), without requiring uniqueness. A simplicial set satisfying this extension condition is called a Kan complex.

Continue the discussion of Example reference. Show that the normalized complex \(\overline{\mathsf{L}}\), after being reversed into a chain complex, is isomorphic to \(\mathrm{N}(\Bbbk\mathrm{E}\Gamma)\). Hint. First use Proposition reference to identify \(\mathrm{N}(X)\) with a quotient of \(\mathrm{C}(X)\).

Let \(\Gamma\) be a monoid. Write \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Set}\text{-}}\Gamma\) for the category of all small sets with a right \(\Gamma\)-action.

  1. Describe explicitly the free–forgetful adjoint pair \[\text{Diagram chapter8-unit-119-d003}\] together with its unit and counit morphisms. Show that the corresponding monad \(T\) gives an equivalence \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Set}\text{-}}\Gamma\simeq\ensuremath{\mathsf{Set}}^T\). Hint. The functor \(\mathrm{F}\) sends a set \(X\) to \(X\times\Gamma\), with \(\Gamma\) acting by right multiplication on the second component. The unit morphism is \(x\mapsto(x,1)\), while the counit morphism is the action map.

  2. For every right \(\Gamma\)-set \(X\), describe the corresponding simplicial object \(\mathrm{Bar}(X)\) in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Set}\text{-}}\Gamma\); see Examples reference and reference.

  3. Take the one-point set \(X=\{\mathrm{pt}\}\) with trivial right \(\Gamma\)-action. Show that the corresponding simplicial object is isomorphic to \(\mathrm{E}\Gamma\) of Example reference; it becomes a simplicial object in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Set}\text{-}}\Gamma\) via the right \(\Gamma\)-action on each \((\mathrm{E}\Gamma)_n\).

Fix a group \(\Gamma\). In Example reference, take the group algebra \(R=\Bbbk[\Gamma]\) and take \(M\) to be the trivial \(\Gamma\)-module \(\Bbbk\); see Example reference. Show that the corresponding \(\epsilon_{\Bbbk}:\mathrm{C}(\mathrm{Bar}(\Bbbk))\to\Bbbk\) is isomorphic to the resolution \(\mathsf{L}=(\mathsf{L}_n,\partial'_n)_n\to\Bbbk\) of Proposition reference. Hint. Use equation.

Let \(\Bbbk\) be a commutative ring and \(\mathcal{A}=\Bbbk\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\), with \(\otimes=\otimes_{\Bbbk}\). Let \(\Gamma\) be a group. Consider the simplicial object \(\Bbbk\mathrm{E}\Gamma\) of Example reference. Apply Definition reference of the Alexander–Whitney morphism to \(X:=\Bbbk\mathrm{E}\Gamma\boxtimes\Bbbk\mathrm{E}\Gamma\), and then consider the morphism \[\mathrm{C}(\Bbbk\mathrm{E}\Gamma) \to \mathrm{C}(\underbracket{\Bbbk\mathrm{E}\Gamma \otimes \Bbbk\mathrm{E}\Gamma}_{\simeq \Bbbk(\mathrm{E}\Gamma \times \mathrm{E}\Gamma)}) \xrightarrow{\overline{\mathrm{AW}}} \mathrm{C}(\Bbbk\mathrm{E}\Gamma) \otimes \mathrm{C}(\Bbbk\mathrm{E}\Gamma).\] The first arrow is induced by the diagonal embedding of simplicial sets \(\mathrm{E}\Gamma\to\mathrm{E}\Gamma\times\mathrm{E}\Gamma\). In view of Example reference, the composite can also be regarded as a morphism of chain complexes \[\mathsf{L} \to \mathsf{L} \otimes \mathsf{L}.\] Use this to interpret the morphism \(\Delta:\mathsf{L}\to\mathsf{L}\otimes\mathsf{L}\) used in the definition of the cup product in group cohomology; see Lemma reference (ii). Hint. Substitution of the definition of \(\overline{\mathrm{AW}}\) shows that the \((p,q)\) component of the composite morphism differs from that in Lemma reference (ii) by a factor \((-1)^{pq}\). This difference arises because the discussion there uses \((\mathsf{L}_n,\partial_n)_n\), whereas Example reference uses \((\mathsf{L}_n,\partial'_n)_n\). At the level of the simplicial set \(\mathrm{E}\Gamma\), the two differ by order reversal (Remark reference). Observe that order-reversal duality interchanges the roles of \(\lambda^n_p\) and \(\rho^n_q\) in \(\overline{\mathrm{AW}}\), or equivalently interchanges the two copies of \(\mathrm{C}(\Bbbk\mathrm{E}\Gamma)\).

Consider a comonad \((L,\delta,\epsilon)\) on a category \(\mathcal{D}\). For every \(\mathcal{M}\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{D})\), if \(\epsilon_{\mathcal{M}}:L\mathcal{M}\to\mathcal{M}\) has a right inverse \(f:\mathcal{M}\to L\mathcal{M}\), then \(\mathcal{M}\) is called an \(L\)-projective object. Dually, from a monad \((T,\mu,\eta)\) on a category \(\mathcal{C}\), we define a \(T\)-injective object in \(\mathcal{C}\).

By duality, the following discussion focuses mainly on the concept of \(L\)-projectivity. By the method of Example reference, we obtain in \(\operatorname{End}(\mathcal{D})\) an augmented simplicial object \((L^{n+1})_{n\geq-1}\); the data \(d_i\), \(s_j\), and so forth are omitted from the notation. For an \(L\)-projective object \(\mathcal{M}\) and a corresponding \(f\), define \[k_n := L^{n+1} f : L^{n+1} \mathcal{M} \to L^{n+2} \mathcal{M}, \quad n \geq -1.\] Prove that this makes the augmented simplicial object \((L^{n+1}\mathcal{M})_{n\geq-1}\) right contractible (Definition reference). Hint. We know that \(\epsilon_{\mathcal{M}}k_{-1}=\epsilon_{\mathcal{M}}f =\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{\mathcal{M}}\). Applying \(L^{n+1}\) to both sides gives \(d_{n+1}k_n=\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{L^{n+1}\mathcal{M}}\), while naturality ensures that \[\text{Diagram chapter8-unit-120-d001} \quad\text{commutes, that is,}\; d_0 k_0 = f\epsilon_{\mathcal{M}} = k_{-1} \epsilon_{\mathcal{M}}.\] Replace \(f\) by \(L^{n-i}f\), and then apply \(L^i\) to the corresponding diagram. The same method gives \(d_ik_n=k_{n-1}d_i\) for \(0\leq i\leq n\).

For a ring \(R\), the free–forgetful adjoint pair \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Set}}\leftrightarrows R\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\) determines a comonad \(L\) on \(R\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\). Prove that a left \(R\)-module is \(L\)-projective if and only if it is a projective module.

Consider an adjoint pair \(\text{Diagram chapter8-unit-120-diagram-002}\) and the corresponding comonad \((L,\delta,\epsilon)=(FG,F\eta G,\epsilon)\) on \(\mathcal{D}\) (Example reference). Prove that every object of the form \(F\mathcal{N}\), for \(\mathcal{N}\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{C})\), is \(L\)-projective. Consequently, for every \(\mathcal{M}\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{D})\), every term of the simplicial object \((L^{n+1}\mathcal{M})_{n\geq0}\) is \(L\)-projective. Hint. Take \(f=F\eta_{\mathcal{N}}:F(\mathcal{N})\to FGF(\mathcal{N}) =L(F(\mathcal{N}))\). Then \(\epsilon_{F(\mathcal{N})}f=\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{F(\mathcal{N})}\) is precisely one of the triangle identities of the adjunction.

Continue to consider the comonad \(L\) arising from the adjoint pair \((F,G)\). Show that \(\mathcal{P}\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{D})\) is \(L\)-projective if and only if it has the following lifting property. For every pair of morphisms \(\alpha:\mathcal{M}_1\to\mathcal{M}_2\) and \(\phi:\mathcal{P}\to\mathcal{M}_2\) in \(\mathcal{D}\), if \(G\alpha\) has a right inverse, then there is a morphism \(\beta:\mathcal{P}\to\mathcal{M}_1\) such that \(\phi=\alpha\beta\). Hint. For the “if” direction, apply the lifting property to \(\alpha:=\epsilon_{\mathcal{P}}:FG(\mathcal{P})\to\mathcal{P}\) and \(\phi:=\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}\). For the “only if” direction, first explain why \(\mathcal{P}\) in the lifting property can be replaced by \(FG(\mathcal{P})\), and then use the adjunction to show that \[\alpha_*:\operatorname{Hom}(FG(\mathcal{P}),\mathcal{M}_1)\to \operatorname{Hom}(FG(\mathcal{P}),\mathcal{M}_2)\] is surjective.

For an arbitrary commutative ring \(\Bbbk\) and a homomorphism of \(\Bbbk\)-algebras \(S\to R\), consider the adjoint pairs \[\begin{equation*} \text{Diagram chapter8-unit-120-d002} \end{equation*}\] which give a comonad \(L\) and a monad \(T\), respectively, on \(R\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\). Use the lifting property above, or its dual, to determine necessary and sufficient conditions for a left \(R\)-module \(M\) to be an \(L\)-projective (respectively, \(T\)-injective) object, and compare these conditions with projectivity (respectively, injectivity) of modules.

On this basis one can construct a theory called relative homological algebra; see [Ho56]. Its distinguishing feature is that it considers only those exact sequences of \(R\)-modules that are split exact over \(S\). The next exercise examines relative versions of the \(\operatorname{Tor}\) and \(\operatorname{Ext}\) functors.

Consider an adjoint pair between abelian categories \(\text{Diagram chapter8-unit-120-diagram-004}\). Prove for every \(\mathcal{M}\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{D})\) that:

  1. There is an object \(\mathcal{P}_\bullet\) of \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ch}}_{\geq0}(\mathcal{D})\) together with a morphism \(\epsilon:\mathcal{P}_\bullet\to\mathcal{M}\) such that

    • each \(\mathcal{P}_n\) is \(L\)-projective for \(n\geq0\);

    • the identity morphism on \(\cdots\to G\mathcal{P}_1\to G\mathcal{P}_0\to G\mathcal{M}\to0\) is null-homotopic; in other words, this is a split exact complex.

    Hint. Apply Proposition reference.

  2. For any two morphisms \(\epsilon:\mathcal{P}_\bullet\to\mathcal{M}\) and \(\epsilon':\mathcal{P}'_\bullet\to\mathcal{M}\) satisfying the conditions above, there is a homotopy equivalence \(f:\mathcal{P}\to\mathcal{P}'\) such that \(\epsilon'f=\epsilon\). Hint. Use the lifting property introduced above.

(M. Barr, J. M. Beck) Let \(L\) be a comonad on a category \(\mathcal{D}\). Write \(\mathrm{Bar}(\mathcal{M})\) for the simplicial object obtained by evaluating the construction of Example reference at \(\mathcal{M}\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{D})\). For every abelian category \(\mathcal{A}\) and functor \(E:\mathcal{D}\to\mathcal{A}\), define the comonad homology of \((L,E)\) to be the family of objects in \(\mathcal{A}\) \[\operatorname{H}^L_n(E; \mathcal{M}) := \operatorname{H}_n\left( \mathrm{C}(E\mathrm{Bar}(\mathcal{M})) \right), \quad n \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}_{\geq 0},\] where \(E\mathrm{Bar}(\mathcal{M})\) means that \(E\) is applied to every term of \(\mathrm{Bar}(\mathcal{M})\). Dually, if \(T\) is a monad on a category \(\mathcal{C}\) and \(F:\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{A}\) is a functor to an abelian category, one can similarly define the value of the monad cohomology \((T,F)\) at \(\mathcal{N}\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{C})\); we omit the details.

  1. Write down the natural morphism \(\operatorname{H}^L_0(E;\mathcal{M})\to E\mathcal{M}\) and show that it is an isomorphism if \(\mathcal{M}\) is \(L\)-projective.

  2. Suppose that \(L\) arises from an adjoint pair \((F,G)\) between abelian categories and that \(E\) is an additive functor. Prove that if \(\mathcal{P}_\bullet\to\mathcal{M}\) is a morphism in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ch}}_{\geq0}(\mathcal{D})\) satisfying

    • every \(\mathcal{P}_n\) is \(L\)-projective for \(n\geq0\);

    • the identity morphism on \(\cdots\to G\mathcal{P}_1\to G\mathcal{P}_0\to G\mathcal{M}\to0\) is null-homotopic,

    then \(\operatorname{H}^L_n(E;\mathcal{M})\simeq\operatorname{H}_n(E\mathcal{P}_\bullet)\). Thus comonad homology can be computed using such \(L\)-projective resolutions.

  3. Continue under the assumptions above. A pair of morphisms \(\mathcal{M}'\to\mathcal{M}\to\mathcal{M}''\) in \(\mathcal{D}\) is called a \(G\)-split short exact sequence if, after applying \(G\), it becomes a split short exact sequence in \(\mathcal{C}\). Prove that a \(G\)-split short exact sequence naturally induces a long exact sequence for \(\operatorname{H}^L_n(E;\mathord\cdot)\).

(G. Hochschild [Ho56]) For an arbitrary commutative ring \(\Bbbk\) and a homomorphism of \(\Bbbk\)-algebras \(S\to R\), consider the comonad \(L\) on \(R\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\) determined by the adjoint pair \[\text{Diagram chapter8-unit-120-d003}\] For a right \(R\)-module \(A\) and left \(R\)-modules \(B,N\), define the \(\Bbbk\)-modules \[\begin{align*} \operatorname{Tor}^{R|S}_n(A, N) & := \operatorname{H}^L_n\left( A \ensuremath{\underset{R}{\otimes}}(\cdot) ; N \right), \\ \operatorname{Ext}_{R|S}^n(N, B) & := \operatorname{H}^L_n\left( \operatorname{Hom}_R(\cdot, B) ; N \right), \end{align*}\] where \(\operatorname{Hom}_R(\mathord\cdot,B)\) is regarded as a functor \(R\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\to S\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}^{\operatorname{op}}\). These are called the relative \(\operatorname{Tor}\) and relative \(\operatorname{Ext}\) functors.

  1. Show that both are functorial in every variable. Describe the corresponding chain complexes explicitly, and show that \[\operatorname{Tor}^{R|S}_0(A, N) \simeq A \ensuremath{\underset{R}{\otimes}} N, \quad \operatorname{Ext}_{R|S}^0(N, B) \simeq \operatorname{Hom}_R(N, B).\]

  2. Show that the bifunctor \(\operatorname{Tor}^{R|S}_n\) has a “balanced” property analogous to Theorem reference.1

  3. Prove that if \(I\) is a two-sided ideal of \(S\) and \(R=S/I\), then for \(n>0\), \(\operatorname{Tor}_n^{R|S}=0=\operatorname{Ext}^n_{R|S}\). Thus relative \(\operatorname{Tor}\) and relative \(\operatorname{Ext}\) differ from their absolute versions in §reference. Hint. In this case \(L=\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{R\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}}\).

  4. Write \(R^e=R\ensuremath{\underset{\Bbbk}{\otimes}}R^{\operatorname{op}}\). Prove that \(\operatorname{HH}_n(M)\simeq\operatorname{Tor}^{R^e|\Bbbk}_n(M,R)\) and \(\operatorname{HH}^n(M)\simeq\operatorname{Ext}_{R^e|\Bbbk}^n(R,M)\); see Example reference. Hint. Reduce the problem to the assertion that \(\mathrm{C}(\mathrm{Bar}(R))_n=R\otimes R^{\otimes n}\otimes R\) is an \(L\)-projective \(R^e\)-module.

end

  1. The \(\operatorname{Ext}_{R|S}^n\) case is not discussed because it involves the notion of monad cohomology, which we have not developed here; see the references for details.↩︎

Duality

The notion of duality originates in the theory of vector spaces. Let \(\Bbbk\) be a field, and denote the dual space of a \(\Bbbk\)-vector space \(V\) by \(V^\vee:=\operatorname{Hom}_{\Bbbk}(V,\Bbbk)\). There are

  • the evaluation map \(\mathrm{ev}:V\otimes V^\vee\to\Bbbk\), which sends \(v\otimes\lambda\) to \(\lambda(v)\);

  • if \(V\) is finite-dimensional, also the coevaluation map \(\mathrm{coev}:\Bbbk\to V^\vee\otimes V\), which sends \(1\) to \(\sum_{i=1}^n\check{v}_i\otimes v_i\), where \((v_i)_{i=1}^n\) is any basis of \(V\) and \((\check{v}_i)_{i=1}^n\) its dual basis.

In the finite-dimensional case, they satisfy the fundamental identities \[(\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{V^\vee} \otimes \mathrm{ev})(\mathrm{coev} \otimes \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{V^\vee}) = \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{V^\vee}, \quad (\mathrm{ev} \otimes \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_V) (\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_V \otimes \mathrm{coev}) = \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_V.\] In a general monoidal category, the duality data defined in §reference directly generalize the situation above: they consist of a pair of objects \((L,R)\) together with morphisms \(\mathrm{ev}:L\otimes R\to\ensuremath{\bm{1}}\) and \(\mathrm{coev}:\ensuremath{\bm{1}}\to R\otimes L\) satisfying the preceding fundamental identities. In this situation, \(R\) is called a right dual of \(L\), while \(L\) is called a left dual of \(R\). A monoidal category in which every object has a left dual (respectively, a right dual) is called left rigid (respectively, right rigid). For braided monoidal categories, §reference will explain how the two kinds of dual are related. Thus, if an object \(X\) has a dual, we can define the trace \(\operatorname{Tr}(f)\) of \(f\in\operatorname{End}(X)\) and subsequently its dimension \(\dim X:=\operatorname{Tr}(\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_X)\). Both are elements of \(\operatorname{End}(\ensuremath{\bm{1}})\). Strictly speaking, each has a left and a right version, but the two need not be distinguished in a symmetric monoidal category. This book mainly discusses abelian categories equipped with symmetric monoidal structures, such as categories of modules over commutative rings (see Proposition reference). As long as the reader understands the usefulness of dual vector spaces, the value of this generalization will be self-evident. Duality becomes still more powerful in the setting of \(2\)-categories, but that lies beyond the scope of this book. Examples of duality are the subject of §reference. The examples closest to algebra are the category \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}_{\mathrm{f}}\text{-}}A\) of finite-dimensional right \(A\)-modules for a \(\Bbbk\)-Hopf algebra \(A\), and its comodule counterpart \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Comod}_{\mathrm{f}}\text{-}}A\) (Proposition reference). In both cases, duality reflects properties of the antipode \(S:A\to A\). Examples involving Hopf algebras are important in the study of quantum groups and also prepare the way for the theory of Tannakian categories. The material in §§reference—reference of this chapter concerns the coalgebra reconstruction problem. For every coalgebra \(L\), the abelian category \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Comod}_{\mathrm{f}}\text{-}}L\) is locally finite (Definition reference) and comes equipped with a faithful exact forgetful functor \(U:\ensuremath{\mathsf{Comod}_{\mathrm{f}}\text{-}}L\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{Vect}}_{\mathrm{f}}(\Bbbk)\). The reconstruction problem asks for a converse:

How can one construct a coalgebra \(L\) from a locally finite \(\Bbbk\)-linear abelian category \(\mathcal{A}\) and a faithful exact functor \(\omega:\mathcal{A}\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{Vect}}_{\mathrm{f}}(\Bbbk)\) in such a way that \((\mathcal{A},\omega)\) is naturally equivalent to \((\ensuremath{\mathsf{Comod}_{\mathrm{f}}\text{-}}L,U)\)?

The approach taken in this chapter uses the coendomorphism coalgebra \(\operatorname{coE}(\omega)=\operatorname{coE}_{\Bbbk}(\omega)\) of the functor \(\omega\) (Definition–Proposition reference). This coalgebra coacts on each \(\omega(X)\) and is “universal” with respect to these coactions. The proof of the coalgebra reconstruction theorem, Theorem reference, involves the theory of comonads from §reference, basic Morita theory from §reference, a technical result about locally finite abelian categories from §reference, and the Ind-ization introduced in §reference. If \((\mathcal{A},\omega)\) is equipped with a monoidal structure, then \(\operatorname{coE}(\omega)\) also becomes a bialgebra. If \(\mathcal{A}\) is both left and right rigid, then \(\operatorname{coE}(\omega)\) is even a Hopf algebra (Theorem reference). The presentation in this part mainly follows [Del90]. After all these preparations, §reference will introduce the precise definition of a Tannakian category. These are symmetric monoidal categories \(\mathcal{T}\) with special properties. The formal definition is due to N. Saavedra Rivano and P. Deligne, while its motivation goes back to work of Tadao Tannaka and his successors. Among the conditions in Definition reference, the most prominent is the existence of a nonzero commutative \(\Bbbk\)-algebra \(B\) and a right exact monoidal functor \(\omega:\mathcal{T}\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}\text{-}}B\) compatible with the braiding; this is called a fiber functor for \(\mathcal{T}\) over \(B\). The setting of algebraic geometry requires that \(B\) be allowed to be general, but many elementary applications involve only neutral fiber functors. In that case, \(\omega\) is a faithful exact functor with values in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Vect}}_{\mathrm{f}}(\Bbbk)\). The corresponding neutral Tannakian reconstruction theorem, Theorem reference, is simply an application of the preceding results: it states that \(\operatorname{coE}(\omega)\) is a commutative Hopf algebra and identifies \((\mathcal{T},\omega)\) with \((\ensuremath{\mathsf{Comod}_{\mathrm{f}}\text{-}}\operatorname{coE}(\omega),U)\). 1 Many properties of \((\mathcal{T},\omega)\) are thereby translated into properties of this Hopf algebra. For a general fiber functor, Corollary reference relates the commutative Hopf algebra \(\operatorname{coE}_B(\omega)\) over \(B\) to the group \(\operatorname{Aut}^\otimes(\omega)\) of \(\otimes\)-automorphisms of \(\omega\). All the information about \(\operatorname{coE}_B(\omega)\) is contained in \(\operatorname{Aut}^\otimes\), provided the latter is understood as a group functor \(B\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{CAlg}}\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{Grp}}\) rather than merely as a single group. This viewpoint is entirely natural in algebraic geometry. Finally, §reference returns to the historical origins of Tannakian categories. Using the preceding theory, it explains how to reconstruct a finite group \(G\) from the category \(G\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}_{\mathrm{f}}\) of finite-dimensional \(G\)-modules (Definition reference), together with the forgetful functor \(\omega\) to \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Vect}}_{\mathrm{f}}(\Bbbk)\). Since in abstract harmonic analysis \(G\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}_{\mathrm{f}}\) is in some sense a “dual” of \(G\), this result is also called the finite-group version of the Tannaka–Krein duality theorem. In fact, once it is known that \(G\)-modules are the same as right comodules over the function space \(C(G)\), the desired isomorphism \(G\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}\operatorname{Aut}^\otimes(\omega)\) has a shorter proof. The detour through the reconstruction theorem is taken only to explain the origin of Tannakian categories.

Duality in Monoidal Categories

We first introduce a notion that applies to all monoidal categories and then refine it step by step.

Definition. Let \(\mathcal{C}\) be a monoidal category and \(L,R\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{C})\). If there are morphisms \[\mathrm{ev}: L \otimes R \to \ensuremath{\bm{1}}, \quad \mathrm{coev}: \ensuremath{\bm{1}}\to R \otimes L\] such that the following two composites are \(\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_R\) and \(\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_L\), respectively, then \(L\) is called a left dual of \(R\), while \(R\) is called a right dual of \(L\): \[\begin{gather*} R \simeq \ensuremath{\bm{1}}\otimes R \xrightarrow{\mathrm{coev} \otimes \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_R} (R \otimes L) \otimes R \simeq R \otimes (L \otimes R) \xrightarrow{\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_R \otimes \mathrm{ev}} R \otimes \ensuremath{\bm{1}}\simeq R, \\ L \simeq L \otimes \ensuremath{\bm{1}}\xrightarrow{\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_L \otimes \mathrm{coev}} L \otimes (R \otimes L) \simeq (L \otimes R) \otimes L \xrightarrow{\mathrm{ev} \otimes \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_L} \ensuremath{\bm{1}}\otimes L \simeq L. \end{gather*}\] The quadruple \((L,R,\mathrm{ev},\mathrm{coev})\) is called duality data.

The morphisms \(\mathrm{ev}\) and \(\mathrm{coev}\) in duality data should be understood as “evaluation” and its dual. The unit constraints, associativity constraints, and placement of parentheses involved in the definition cause no difficulty and will often be suppressed from now on. Definition reference may remind the reader of the unit and counit morphisms of adjoint functors. Duality does indeed encompass the theory of adjoint functors, but to see this one must work in \(2\)-categories or more general structures; that lies beyond the scope of this book.

Proposition. Let \(F:\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{D}\) be a monoidal functor between monoidal categories. Every duality datum \((L,R,\mathrm{ev},\mathrm{coev})\) in \(\mathcal{C}\) canonically induces the duality datum \((FL,FR,F\mathrm{ev},F\mathrm{coev})\) in \(\mathcal{D}\).

Proof. To interpret \((FL,FR,F\mathrm{ev},F\mathrm{coev})\) as duality data, it suffices to consider the commutative diagram \[\text{Diagram chapter9-unit-121-d001}\] The vertical arrows come from the monoidal-functor structure. The required property is therefore reduced to the corresponding property in \(\mathcal{C}\).

Definition–Proposition. Let \(\mathcal{C}\) be a monoidal category and \(X\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{C})\). If \(X\) has a right dual (respectively, a left dual), write its duality data as \((X,X^*,\mathrm{ev},\mathrm{coev})\) (respectively, \(({}^*X,X,\mathrm{ev},\mathrm{coev})\)). Then these data are unique up to unique isomorphism.

Thus, without ambiguity, we may speak of the right dual \(X^*\) (respectively, the left dual \({}^*X\)) of \(X\).

Proof. Reversing the order of \(\otimes\) turns left duals into right duals and vice versa, so it suffices to treat the case of \(X^*\). Suppose that the data \((X_i^*,\mathrm{ev}_i,\mathrm{coev}_i)\) give right duals of \(X\), for \(i=1,2\). First we prove uniqueness of the isomorphism. If \(\alpha:X_1^*\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}X_2^*\) is compatible with the duality morphisms \(\mathrm{ev}_i\) and \(\mathrm{coev}_i\), then the following diagram commutes: \[\text{Diagram chapter9-unit-121-d002}\] By the definition of a right dual, the composite along the lower path is \((\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}\otimes\mathrm{ev}_2)(\mathrm{coev}_2\otimes\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}) =\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{X_2^*}\). The corresponding statement also holds for the inverse morphism \(\beta:X_2^*\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}X_1^*\). Hence the desired morphisms \(\alpha:X_1^*\to X_2^*\) and \(\beta:X_2^*\to X_1^*\) can only be the composites \[\begin{gather*} X_1^* \xrightarrow{\mathrm{coev}_2 \otimes \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{X_1^*}} X_2^* \otimes X \otimes X_1^* \xrightarrow{\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{X_2^*} \otimes \mathrm{ev}_1} X_2^* , \\ X_2^* \xrightarrow{\mathrm{coev}_1 \otimes \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{X_2^*}} X_1^* \otimes X \otimes X_2^* \xrightarrow{\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{X_1^*} \otimes \mathrm{ev}_2} X_1^* . \end{gather*}\]

We now show that the \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) defined above are indeed compatible with the duality morphisms. By symmetry, it suffices to consider \(\alpha\). The definition of a right dual gives the commutative diagrams \[\text{Diagram chapter9-unit-121-d003} \quad \text{Diagram chapter9-unit-121-d004}\] Their vertical composites are \(\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}\otimes\alpha\) and \(\alpha\otimes\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}\), respectively, proving the required compatibility.

Next we prove that \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) are mutually inverse. Again, it suffices to prove \(\beta\alpha=\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}\). Consider the diagram \[\text{Diagram chapter9-unit-121-d005}\] The three squares plainly commute, while the triangle commutes by the definition of a right dual. Hence the entire diagram commutes. The composite along \(\par\textbf{Diagram chapter9-unit-121-diagram-006}\par\) is \(\beta\alpha\), while the composite along \(\par\textbf{Diagram chapter9-unit-121-diagram-007}\par\) is \(\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{X_1^*}\). This completes the proof.

The relationship between left and right duals can be written as \({}^*(X^*)=X\) and \(({}^*X)^*=X\). Although duality data are often chosen in an argument or exposition, duality is fundamentally a property of an object, not additional structure.

Example. In every monoidal category, \[\ensuremath{\bm{1}}^* = \ensuremath{\bm{1}}= {}^* \ensuremath{\bm{1}},\] and the required morphisms \(\mathrm{ev}\) and \(\mathrm{coev}\) both arise from the unit constraint \(\ensuremath{\bm{1}}\otimes\ensuremath{\bm{1}}\simeq\ensuremath{\bm{1}}\).

Definition (N. Saavedra Rivano). If every object in a monoidal category \(\mathcal{C}\) has a left dual (respectively, a right dual), then \(\mathcal{C}\) is called a left rigid (respectively, right rigid) category.

The idea behind the proof of Definition–Proposition reference is actually simple, but its execution produces many formulas and commutative diagrams. In arguments involving duality, a visualization technique called a string diagram is very useful; compare §reference or [Li1]. More precisely, objects are drawn as vertices and morphisms as arrows, with composition read from top to bottom. For example, \(\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_X\), \(f:X\to Y\), \(g:Y\to Z\), and \(gf\) are drawn, respectively, as

Diagram chapter9-unit-121-d006

Thus, pre- or postcomposing a morphism with \(\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}\) amounts to extending its arrow. The \(\otimes\)-product of morphisms is represented by placing their arrows side by side; for example, \(f\otimes g\) is drawn as

Diagram chapter9-unit-121-d007

Since \(X\otimes\ensuremath{\bm{1}}\simeq X\simeq\ensuremath{\bm{1}}\otimes X\), the unit \(\ensuremath{\bm{1}}\) can be omitted from a string diagram; in other words, the string has no end at that point. If the dual exists, the morphisms \(\mathrm{ev}:X\otimes X^*\to\ensuremath{\bm{1}}\) and \(\mathrm{coev}:\ensuremath{\bm{1}}\to X^*\otimes X\) are therefore drawn, respectively, as

Diagram chapter9-unit-121-d008

Under the same assumptions, the identities in Definition reference, \[(\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_X \otimes \mathrm{ev}) (\mathrm{coev} \otimes \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_X ) = \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_X = (\mathrm{ev} \otimes \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_X) (\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_X \otimes \mathrm{coev})\] are represented by \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:Zorro}{} \par\textbf{Diagram chapter9-unit-121-d009}\par \quad = \quad \par\textbf{Diagram chapter9-unit-121-d010}\par \quad = \quad \par\textbf{Diagram chapter9-unit-121-d011}\par \end{equation}\] provided, of course, that the duals in question exist. These diagrams give Definition reference the operational flavor of “straightening a string.” In some of the literature, the diagrams above are drawn after a rotation by \(\frac{\pi}{2}\) and are therefore also called the Z identities. By the correspondence between algebraic identities and operations on string diagrams, basic algebraic identities involving duality can be found simply by following the diagrams, or even proved directly from them. As an exercise, the reader may try to rewrite the proof of Definition–Proposition reference as a simple diagram. The following result shows that duality naturally reverses the order of \(\otimes\).

Proposition. Let \(\mathcal{C}\) be a monoidal category and \(X,Y\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{C})\).

  1. If \(X\) and \(Y\) have left duals \({}^*X\) and \({}^*Y\), respectively, then \({}^*Y\otimes{}^*X\) is a left dual of \(X\otimes Y\). The corresponding data can be depicted in terms of the duality data of \(X\) and \(Y\) as \[\begin{equation*} \mathrm{ev}_{X \otimes Y} = \left[ \text{Diagram chapter9-unit-121-d012}\right], \quad \mathrm{coev}_{X \otimes Y} = \left[ \text{Diagram chapter9-unit-121-d013}\right]. \end{equation*}\]

  2. If \(X\) and \(Y\) have right duals \(X^*\) and \(Y^*\), respectively, then \(Y^*\otimes X^*\) is a right dual of \(X\otimes Y\). The corresponding data can be depicted in terms of the duality data of \(X\) and \(Y\) as \[\begin{equation*} \mathrm{ev}_{X \otimes Y} = \left[ \text{Diagram chapter9-unit-121-d014}\right], \quad \mathrm{coev}_{X \otimes Y} = \left[ \text{Diagram chapter9-unit-121-d015}\right]. \end{equation*}\]

Proof. We must verify the identities in Definition reference, namely the Z identities equation. Equivalently, we must check that \[\begin{align*} \text{Diagram chapter9-unit-121-d016} & = \text{Diagram chapter9-unit-121-d017}, \\ \text{Diagram chapter9-unit-121-d018} & = \text{Diagram chapter9-unit-121-d019} \end{align*}\] Strictly speaking, the diagrams on the left should be stretched in the vertical direction as in equation: insert several copies of \(\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}\), shift them horizontally as appropriate, and then straighten them. The identities above are then clear. The corresponding formal verification is based on the various naturality properties of the unit constraints; the details are left to the interested reader.

Definition. Let \(f:X\to Y\) be a morphism in a monoidal category \(\mathcal{C}\). Suppose that \(X\) and \(Y\) both have left duals \({}^*X\) and \({}^*Y\) (respectively, right duals \(X^*\) and \(Y^*\)). The left dual morphism \({}^*f:{}^*Y\to{}^*X\) (respectively, the right dual morphism \(f^*:Y^*\to X^*\)) of \(f\) is defined as follows: \[\begin{equation*} \begin{aligned} \hypertarget{o014.aljabr2.chapter9.duality-a.q008}{} {}^* f := (\mathrm{ev}_Y \otimes \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}) (\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}\otimes f \otimes \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}) (\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}\otimes \mathrm{coev}_X) \; & \par\textbf{Diagram chapter9-unit-121-d020}\par, \\ \hypertarget{o014.aljabr2.chapter9.duality-a.q009}{} f^* := (\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}\otimes \mathrm{ev}_Y) (\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}\otimes f \otimes \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}) (\mathrm{coev}_X \otimes \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}) \; & \par\textbf{Diagram chapter9-unit-121-d021}\par. \end{aligned} \end{equation*}\]

  1. Translator’s note: the source prints the second pair as \((\operatorname{coE}(\omega),U)\). Since the first component of that pair must be a category carrying the forgetful functor \(U\), the well-typed expression is \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Comod}_{\mathrm{f}}\text{-}}\operatorname{coE}(\omega)\).↩︎

From the relationship between left and right duals and Definition–Proposition reference, one checks that \({}^* (f^*) = f = ({}^* f)^*\); this is immediately apparent upon drawing a “diagram within a diagram”. Moreover, \({}^* (\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_X) = \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{{}^* X}\) and \((\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_X)^* = \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{X^*}\) follow directly from the definitions. Here are two useful sets of identities concerning the left and right duals of \(f: X \to Y\); once again, the diagrams provide the proof. \[\begin{gather} \hypertarget{eqn:f-dual-coev}{} \par\textbf{Diagram chapter9-unit-122-d001}\par = \par\textbf{Diagram chapter9-unit-122-d002}\par \qquad \par\textbf{Diagram chapter9-unit-122-d003}\par = \par\textbf{Diagram chapter9-unit-122-d004}\par \\ \hypertarget{o014.aljabr2.chapter9.duality-rigidity-b.eq002}{} \hypertarget{eqn:f-dual-ev}{} \par\textbf{Diagram chapter9-unit-122-d005}\par \; = \; \par\textbf{Diagram chapter9-unit-122-d006}\par \qquad \par\textbf{Diagram chapter9-unit-122-d007}\par \; = \; \par\textbf{Diagram chapter9-unit-122-d008}\par \end{gather}\]

Proposition. Let \(X \xrightarrow{f} Y \xrightarrow{g} Z\) be morphisms in a monoidal category \(\mathcal{C}\). If all these objects have left duals (respectively, right duals), then \({}^* (gf) = {}^* f \; {}^* g\) (respectively, \((gf)^* = f^* g^*\)).

Proof. Apply the Zorro identity equation; one picture is worth a thousand words.

Corollary. Let \(\mathcal{C}\) be a left rigid (respectively, right rigid) category, and equip \(\mathcal{C}^{\operatorname{op}}\) with the monoidal structure that reverses both the arrows and the order of the arguments of \(\otimes\). Then there is a monoidal functor \(\mathcal{C} \to \mathcal{C}^{\operatorname{op}}\) sending an object \(X\) to \({}^* X\) (respectively, \(X^*\)) and a morphism \(f\) to \({}^* f\) (respectively, \(f^*\)).

Somewhat surprisingly, every morphism between monoidal functors whose source is a left or right rigid category must be an isomorphism. This helps explain the meaning of the term “rigid”.

Proposition. Let \(F, G: \mathcal{C} \rightrightarrows \mathcal{D}\) be monoidal functors between monoidal categories. If \(\mathcal{C}\) is left rigid (respectively, right rigid), then every morphism \(\varphi: F \to G\) of monoidal functors is an isomorphism. In fact, \((\varphi_X)^{-1} = \left(\varphi_{{}^* X}\right)^*\) (respectively, \({}^* \left( \varphi_{X^*} \right)\)).

Proof. It suffices to consider the left rigid case. Fix \(X \in \operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{C})\), together with its left dual \({}^* X\) and the data \(\mathrm{ev}\) and \(\mathrm{coev}\). We have the commutative diagrams \[\begin{equation*} \begin{gathered} \text{Diagram chapter9-unit-122-d009} \\ \text{Diagram chapter9-unit-122-d010} \end{gathered} \end{equation*}\] Moreover, Proposition reference shows that composition along the two rows makes \(F({}^* X)\) and \(G({}^* X)\) into left duals of \(F(X)\) and \(G(X)\), respectively. Thus \((\varphi_{{}^* X})^*: G(X) \to F(X)\) is defined. We thereby obtain the following diagrammatic identities: \[\begin{equation*} \begin{aligned} \par\textbf{Diagram chapter9-unit-122-d011}\par & = \par\textbf{Diagram chapter9-unit-122-d012}\par, \\ \par\textbf{Diagram chapter9-unit-122-d013}\par & = \par\textbf{Diagram chapter9-unit-122-d014}\par, \end{aligned} \end{equation*}\] By equation, the two right-hand sides are \(\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{GX}\) and \(\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{FX}\), respectively. This proves that \(\left(\varphi_{{}^* X}\right)^*\) is indeed the inverse of \(\varphi_X\).

Proposition. Let \(\mathcal{C}\) be a monoidal category and let \(X, Y \in \operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{C})\).

  1. If \(X\) has a left dual \({}^* X\), there are mutually inverse bijections \(\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}}(X, Y) \xleftrightarrow{1:1} \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}}(\ensuremath{\bm{1}}, Y \otimes {}^* X)\) as follows. \[\begin{equation*} \begin{aligned} \par\textbf{Diagram chapter9-unit-122-d015}\par & \; \longmapsto \; \par\textbf{Diagram chapter9-unit-122-d016}\par \\ \par\textbf{Diagram chapter9-unit-122-d017}\par & \; \longmapsfrom \; \par\textbf{Diagram chapter9-unit-122-d018}\par \end{aligned} \end{equation*}\]

  2. If \(X\) has a right dual \(X^*\), there are mutually inverse bijections \(\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}}(X, Y) \xleftrightarrow{1:1} \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}}(\ensuremath{\bm{1}}, X^* \otimes Y)\) as follows. \[\begin{equation*} \begin{aligned} \par\textbf{Diagram chapter9-unit-122-d019}\par & \; \longmapsto \; \par\textbf{Diagram chapter9-unit-122-d020}\par \\ \par\textbf{Diagram chapter9-unit-122-d021}\par & \; \longmapsfrom \; \par\textbf{Diagram chapter9-unit-122-d022}\par \end{aligned} \end{equation*}\]

  3. More generally, whenever the duals in question exist, there are canonical bijections \[\text{Diagram chapter9-unit-122-d023}\] and \[\text{Diagram chapter9-unit-122-d024}\]

Proof. For (i) and (ii), checking that the displayed maps are mutually inverse is merely an application of equation. The same idea, expressed by a slightly more awkward diagram, also proves (iii).

In the settings of (i) and (ii), it is easy to describe composition of morphisms on the element \(\varphi\) on the right-hand side of the bijection (hint: apply the morphism \(\mathrm{ev}\)). These canonical operations lead to the following result.

Corollary. Let \(\mathcal{C}\) be a left rigid (respectively, right rigid) category in the sense of Definition reference. Defining the internal \(\operatorname{Hom}\) by \(\ensuremath{\EuScript{H}\mathrm{om}}_{\text{left}}(X, Y) := Y \otimes {}^* X\) (respectively, \(\ensuremath{\EuScript{H}\mathrm{om}}_{\text{right}}(X, Y) := X^* \otimes Y\)) makes \(\mathcal{C}\) a right closed (respectively, left closed) monoidal category in the sense of Definition reference.

Proof. Apply Proposition reference (iii) to Definition reference; the remaining verifications are routine.

Corollary. Let \(X \in \operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{C})\).

  • If \(X\) has a left dual \({}^* X\), then \((\cdot) \otimes X\) preserves all small \(\varinjlim\), while \(X \otimes (\cdot)\) preserves all small \(\varprojlim\).

  • If \(X\) has a right dual \(X^*\), then \((\cdot) \otimes X\) preserves all small \(\varprojlim\), while \(X \otimes (\cdot)\) preserves all small \(\varinjlim\).

Proof. Consider the case in which \(X\) has a left dual \({}^* X\). Proposition reference (iii) implies that the functor \((\cdot) \otimes X\) has right adjoint \((\cdot) \otimes {}^* X\), whereas the functor \(X \otimes (\cdot) \simeq ({}^* X)^* \otimes (\cdot)\) has left adjoint \({}^* X \otimes (\cdot)\).

Reversing the order of \(\otimes\) in the preceding argument gives the case in which \(X\) has a right dual \(X^*\).

Duality: Trace and Dimension

In §reference we introduced several concepts related to duality. Each comes in left and right versions, depending on the position of the object in \(\otimes\). In many applications the monoidal category under consideration is symmetric, so there is no need to distinguish the two. We begin with the case of a braided monoidal category. As usual, its braiding is written in the form \[c(X,Y): X \otimes Y \ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}Y \otimes X\] The braiding is symmetric precisely when \(c(X,Y)^{-1}=c(Y,X)\). Braid diagrams may be used together with the string-diagram techniques introduced in §reference.

Lemma. Let \(\mathcal{C}\) be a braided monoidal category. If \(X^*\) is a right dual of \(X\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{C})\), then \(X^*\) is also a left dual of \(X\). More precisely, define \[\begin{align*} \mathrm{ev}' & := \mathrm{ev} \circ c(X, X^*)^{-1}: X^* \otimes X \to \ensuremath{\bm{1}}, \\ \mathrm{coev}' & := c(X^*, X) \circ \mathrm{coev}: \ensuremath{\bm{1}}\to X \otimes X^* , \end{align*}\] Then \((X^*,X,\mathrm{ev}',\mathrm{coev}')\) is duality data. The case of a left dual \({}^*X\) is similar. If \(\mathcal{C}\) is symmetric monoidal, then \(\mathrm{ev}''=\mathrm{ev}\) and \(\mathrm{coev}''=\mathrm{coev}\) as well.

Proof. This is an application of the axioms of a braiding. For example, \((\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}\otimes\mathrm{ev}')(\mathrm{coev}'\otimes\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}) =\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}\) reduces to the commutativity of the following diagram: \[\text{Diagram chapter9-unit-123-d001}\] The small square commutes by functoriality of the braiding, whereas the large square on the right is a standard braid-diagram argument; compare §reference.

Thus an object \(X\) in a braided monoidal category has a left dual if and only if it has a right dual. In a symmetric monoidal category we may identify the two versions and uniformly denote dual objects and dual morphisms by \(X^*\) and \(f^*\). The most typical example is, of course, the category of modules over a commutative ring. With the tensor product of modules it is a symmetric monoidal category, and duality in it has a simple characterization.

Proposition. Let \(R\) be a commutative ring, and make \(R\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\) into a symmetric monoidal category via \(\otimes_R\). An \(R\)-module \(M\) has a dual \(M^*\) if and only if \(M\) is finitely generated and projective. In that case one may take \(M^*:=\operatorname{Hom}_R(M,R)\), with \(\mathrm{ev}_M\) and \(\mathrm{coev}_M\) as in Definition reference (take \(A=B=\Bbbk=R\) and \(P=M\); the present \(M^*\) is denoted there by \(M^\vee\)), up to possibly reversing the order of the tensor factors.

Proof. The “if” direction is easier, since the choice of \((M^*,\mathrm{ev}_M,\mathrm{coev}_M)\) is explicit. In the special case \(M=R\), we may identify \(M^*\) with \(R\), and then \(\mathrm{ev}_M(x\otimes y)=xy\) and \(\mathrm{coev}_M(1)=1\otimes1\); all required identities are immediate.

The construction of \((M^*,\mathrm{ev}_M,\mathrm{coev}_M)\) is plainly compatible with direct sums, giving the case \(M=R^{\oplus n}\). Every finitely generated projective module \(M\) is a direct summand of some \(R^{\oplus n}\); hence \(M\) has a dual.

Now consider the “only if” direction. Suppose the \(R\)-module \(M\) has a dual \(M^*\). By Proposition reference (ii), for every \(R\)-module \(M'\) there is an isomorphism of \(R\)-modules \[\text{Diagram chapter9-unit-123-d002}\]

Taking \(M'=R\), we obtain \(\operatorname{Hom}_R(M,R)\simeq\operatorname{Hom}_R(R,M^*)\simeq M^*\). This isomorphism sends \(\lambda\in M^*\) to the following homomorphism: \[\text{Diagram chapter9-unit-123-d003}\] Thus \(M^*\) may be identified with \(\operatorname{Hom}_R(M,R)\) and \(\mathrm{ev}_M\) with evaluation.

Consider the identity \((\mathrm{ev}_M\otimes\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_M) (\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_M\otimes\mathrm{coev}_M)=\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_M\). Write \(\mathrm{coev}_M(1)=\sum_{i=1}^n\lambda_i\otimes m_i\). This identity is equivalent to \(\sum_i\lambda_i(m)m_i=m\) for every \(m\), that is, \(\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_M\) factors as \[M \xrightarrow{(\lambda_1, \ldots, \lambda_n)} R^{\oplus n} \xrightarrow{(m_1, \ldots, m_n)} M,\] This shows that \(M\) is a direct summand of \(R^{\oplus n}\).

Definition. For a braided monoidal category, left rigidity and right rigidity in Definition reference are equivalent. A braided monoidal category satisfying either condition is called a rigid category.

Once an abelian category structure is added, the unit object of a rigid braided monoidal category displays a special property. We first prove that \(\otimes\) is automatically additive in each variable.

Proposition. Let \(\mathcal{C}\) be a rigid braided monoidal category. If \(\mathcal{C}\) is also an additive category, then \(\otimes\) is an additive bifunctor.

Proof. Fix \(X\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{C})\). Proposition reference (iii) implies that the functor \(X\otimes(\cdot)\) has right adjoint \(X^*\otimes(\cdot)\). Thus Corollary reference (v) ensures that \(X\otimes(\cdot)\) is additive. By the braiding, the same holds for \((\cdot)\otimes X\).

Proposition. Let \(\mathcal{C}\) be both a rigid braided monoidal category and an abelian category. If \(\iota:U\hookrightarrow\ensuremath{\bm{1}}\) is a subobject, then \(\ensuremath{\bm{1}}=U\oplus\operatorname{ker}(\iota^*)\). Consequently:

  1. the object \(\ensuremath{\bm{1}}\) is split (Definition reference);

  2. if \(\operatorname{End}_{\mathcal{C}}(\ensuremath{\bm{1}})\) is a field, then \(\ensuremath{\bm{1}}\) is a simple object.

Proof. Set \(V:=\operatorname{coker}(\iota)\). We know that \(\otimes\) is an exact additive functor in each variable (Corollary reference and Proposition reference). We therefore obtain the following commutative diagram, whose solid-line rows are exact: \[\text{Diagram chapter9-unit-123-d004}\] The composite represented by the dashed arrow is \(0\). Hence \(U\otimes V=0\) and \(U\otimes U\simeq U\).

For every object \(T\), the same argument gives a monomorphism \(\iota\otimes\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_T:U\otimes T\hookrightarrow T\). Thus \(U\otimes T=0\) if and only if \(\iota\otimes\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_T=0\). In turn, this is equivalent to the vanishing of the corresponding morphism \(T\to U^*\otimes T\) under Proposition reference (iii). It is not hard to show that the latter morphism is precisely \(\iota^*\otimes\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_T\) (exercise in this chapter). Therefore, for every object \(X\), the largest subobject \(T\subset X\) satisfying \(U\otimes T=0\) is the largest subobject for which \(T\to U^*\otimes T\hookrightarrow U^*\otimes X\) vanishes, and this is also \[\operatorname{ker}\left[ \iota^* \otimes \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_X: X \to U^* \otimes X \right] \simeq \operatorname{ker}(\iota^*) \otimes X.\]

  • Apply this to \(X=V\) and use \(U\otimes V=0\); we obtain \(\operatorname{ker}(\iota^*)\otimes V\simeq V\).

  • Apply this to \(X=U\). Since every subobject \(T\) of \(U\) is also a subobject of \(\ensuremath{\bm{1}}\), we have \(U\otimes T\supset T\otimes T\simeq T\). Consequently, \(\operatorname{ker}(\iota^*)\otimes U=0\).

Substituting these two results into the short exact sequence \[0 \to \operatorname{ker}(\iota^*) \otimes U \to \operatorname{ker}(\iota^*) \to \operatorname{ker}(\iota^*) \otimes V \to 0,\] immediately gives \(\ensuremath{\bm{1}}\supset\operatorname{ker}(\iota^*)\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}V\). This splits the sequence \(0\to U\to\ensuremath{\bm{1}}\to V\to0\). Since \(U\) was an arbitrary subobject, this is precisely the assertion that \(\ensuremath{\bm{1}}\) is split.

Finally, Corollary reference implies that if \(\operatorname{End}_{\mathcal{C}}(\ensuremath{\bm{1}})\) is a field, then \(\ensuremath{\bm{1}}\) is indecomposable; hence \(\ensuremath{\bm{1}}\) is simple.

In any monoidal category \(\mathcal{C}\), \(\operatorname{End}(\ensuremath{\bm{1}})\) is a monoid, and it is easy to prove that it is commutative; see [Li1]. The unit constraint \(X\simeq\ensuremath{\bm{1}}\otimes X\) makes every element of \(\operatorname{End}(\ensuremath{\bm{1}})\) act on each \(X\) by an endomorphism. These endomorphisms determine a monoid homomorphism \(\operatorname{End}(\ensuremath{\bm{1}})\to Z(\mathcal{C})\), where \(Z(\mathcal{C})\) denotes the center of the category \(\mathcal{C}\). By the general properties of the center, composition of morphisms is bilinear with respect to the action of \(\operatorname{End}(\ensuremath{\bm{1}})\): \[(z f) g = z(f g) = f (z g), \quad X \xrightarrow{g} Y \xrightarrow{f} Z, \quad z \in \operatorname{End}(\ensuremath{\bm{1}}).\] Moreover, the axioms of \(\otimes\) (see [Li1]) readily imply that \(\otimes\) is bilinear as well: \[(zf_1) \otimes f_2 = z(f_1 \otimes f_2) = f_1 \otimes (z f_2), \quad f_i \in \operatorname{Hom}(X_i, Y_i), \quad z \in \operatorname{End}(\ensuremath{\bm{1}}).\] Thus \(\operatorname{End}(\ensuremath{\bm{1}})\) may be regarded as providing a kind of “scalars” for the monoidal category \(\mathcal{C}\).

Definition. Let \(f\in\operatorname{End}(X)\) be an endomorphism in a braided monoidal category \(\mathcal{C}\), and suppose \(X\) has a dual. Define the left trace of \(f\) (abbreviated simply to trace) by \[\operatorname{Tr}(f) = \operatorname{Tr}_{\text{left}}(f) := \mathrm{ev}_X \left( f \otimes \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{X^*} \right) \mathrm{coev}'_X \; \in \operatorname{End}(\ensuremath{\bm{1}}),\] and define its right trace by \[\operatorname{Tr}_{\text{right}}(f) := \mathrm{ev}'_X \left( \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{X^*} \otimes f \right) \mathrm{coev}_X,\] where \(\mathrm{coev}'_X\) and \(\mathrm{ev}'_X\) are as in Lemma reference. By Definition–Proposition reference, neither trace depends on the choice of duality data.

Definition. Let \(X\) be an object of a braided monoidal category \(\mathcal{C}\), and suppose \(X\) has a dual. Its left dimension (abbreviated simply to dimension) is defined by \[\dim X = \dim_{\text{left}} X := \operatorname{Tr}(\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_X) \; \in \operatorname{End}(\ensuremath{\bm{1}}),\] and its right dimension is defined by \(\dim_{\text{right}}X:=\operatorname{Tr}_{\text{right}}(\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_X)\).

The left and right traces are depicted, respectively, as follows: \[\operatorname{Tr}_{\text{left}}(f) = \par\textbf{Diagram chapter9-unit-123-d005}\par \xlongequal{\text{abbrev.}}\; \par\textbf{Diagram chapter9-unit-123-d006}\par \qquad \operatorname{Tr}_{\text{right}}(f) \xlongequal{\text{abbrev.}}\; \par\textbf{Diagram chapter9-unit-123-d007}\par\] If \(\mathcal{C}\) is a symmetric monoidal category, the left and right versions of both trace and dimension always agree. This is the principal setting for later applications. When the role of the category \(\mathcal{C}\) needs to be emphasized, we use notation such as \(\operatorname{Tr}_{\mathcal{C}}\) and \(\dim_{\mathcal{C}}\). Some authors also call these the quantum trace and quantum dimension. Example reference will explain their relation to the classical versions.

Proposition. Let \(F:\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{D}\) be a monoidal functor between braided monoidal categories that preserves the braiding. For every endomorphism \(f\in\operatorname{End}(X)\) in \(\mathcal{C}\), provided \(X\) has a dual, we have \(F\left(\operatorname{Tr}_{\mathcal{C}}(f)\right)=\operatorname{Tr}_{\mathcal{D}}(Ff)\); the same holds for the right trace. In particular, \(F\left(\dim_{\mathcal{C}}X\right)=\dim_{\mathcal{D}}(FX)\).

Proof. The proof is exactly the same as that of Proposition reference.

The trace defined above has properties analogous to those of the trace of a linear map.

Proposition. Let \(\mathcal{C}\) be a braided monoidal category. In the following statements, whenever an endomorphism \(f\in\operatorname{End}(X)\) is considered, it is understood that \(X\) has a dual.

  1. We have \(\operatorname{Tr}_{\text{left}}(f)=\operatorname{Tr}_{\text{right}}({}^*f)\) and \(\operatorname{Tr}_{\text{right}}(f)=\operatorname{Tr}_{\text{left}}(f^*)\).

  2. Suppose \(X\) and \(Y\) both have duals. For every \(\text{Diagram chapter9-unit-123-diagram-008}\), we have \(\operatorname{Tr}_{\text{left}}(gf)=\operatorname{Tr}_{\text{left}}(({}^{**}f)g)\) and \(\operatorname{Tr}_{\text{right}}(gf)=\operatorname{Tr}_{\text{right}}((f^{**})g)\). Observe that if \(\mathcal{C}\) is symmetric monoidal, then \({}^{**}f=f=f^{**}\).

  3. For every \(f\in\operatorname{End}(X)\) and \(g\in\operatorname{End}(Y)\), we have \(\operatorname{Tr}(f\otimes g)=\operatorname{Tr}(f)\operatorname{Tr}(g)\).

  4. If \(a\in\operatorname{End}(\ensuremath{\bm{1}})\), then \(\operatorname{Tr}(af)=a\operatorname{Tr}(f)\).

  5. Suppose \(\mathcal{C}\) is an \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ab}}\)-category and \(\otimes\) is additive in the first (respectively, second) variable. Then for every \(f,g\in\operatorname{End}(X)\) we have \(\operatorname{Tr}_{\text{left}}(f+g)=\operatorname{Tr}_{\text{left}}(f)+\operatorname{Tr}_{\text{left}}(g)\) (respectively, \(\operatorname{Tr}_{\text{right}}(f+g)=\operatorname{Tr}_{\text{right}}(f)+\operatorname{Tr}_{\text{right}}(g)\)).

In (iii) and (iv), \(\operatorname{Tr}\) may mean either the left trace or the right trace.

Proof. As usual, the proof relies chiefly on pictures. By symmetry it suffices to consider the left trace. First, in the trace diagrams, closing off the bottom of every term in equation immediately gives (i). Similarly, (ii) is depicted using equation as follows. \[\par\textbf{Diagram chapter9-unit-123-d008}\par = \par\textbf{Diagram chapter9-unit-123-d009}\par = \par\textbf{Diagram chapter9-unit-123-d010}\par\]

For (iii), the key is the intuitive identity \[\par\textbf{Diagram chapter9-unit-123-d011}\par \; = \; \par\textbf{Diagram chapter9-unit-123-d012}\par \; = \; \par\textbf{Diagram chapter9-unit-123-d013}\par\] Its formal proof is based on the various naturality properties of the unit object.

Assertion (iv) follows from the bilinearity of morphism composition and \(\otimes\) with respect to \(\operatorname{End}(\ensuremath{\bm{1}})\). Assertion (v) follows directly from the written definitions of the left and right traces, without recourse to diagrams.

Proposition reference (iv) and (v) may be understood as the linearity properties of the trace. As a special case of (iii), we also have \(\dim(X\otimes Y)=\dim X\,\dim Y\).

Examples of Duality

We next examine some basic examples of duality theory.

Example. Consider the category \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Vect}}(\Bbbk)\) of vector spaces over a field \(\Bbbk\), with its standard symmetric monoidal structure and unit \(\ensuremath{\bm{1}}:=\Bbbk\). This is the basic model for duality. Proposition reference implies that for every \(\Bbbk\)-vector space \(V\), \[V \;\text{has a dual} \iff V \;\text{is finite-dimensional}.\] More concretely, for an \(n\)-dimensional \(\Bbbk\)-vector space, its dual (with no need to distinguish left from right) is taken to be \[V^* := \operatorname{Hom}_{\Bbbk}(V, \Bbbk),\] with the corresponding morphisms \[\text{Diagram chapter9-unit-124-d001} \quad \text{Diagram chapter9-unit-124-d002}\] Here \(v_1,\ldots,v_n\) is any basis of \(V\), while \(\check v_1,\ldots,\check v_n\) is its dual basis. These definitions are a special case of Proposition reference, and can also be verified directly without difficulty.

Finite-dimensional \(\Bbbk\)-vector spaces form a rigid category under \(\otimes\), denoted by \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Vect}}_{\mathrm f}(\Bbbk)\). All operations involving duals reduce to the following elementary facts.

  • The isomorphism \(V^*\otimes W\simeq\operatorname{Hom}(\Bbbk,V^*\otimes W)\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}\operatorname{Hom}(V,W)\) sends \(\sum_i\check v_i\otimes w_i\) to the linear map \(\sum_i\check v_i(\mathord\cdot)w_i\).

  • The dual \(f^*:W^*\to V^*\) of a morphism \(f:V\to W\) is precisely the transpose of the linear map; the diagrammatic identity equation says it all.

  • Trace and dimension take values in \(\operatorname{End}(\Bbbk)\simeq\Bbbk\). Since \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Vect}}_{\mathrm f}(\Bbbk)\) is symmetric, there is no need to distinguish left from right.

  • Upon identifying \(\operatorname{End}(V)\) with \(V^*\otimes V\), \[\operatorname{Tr}\left(\sum_i\check v_i\otimes v_i\right)= \sum_i\check v_i(v_i)\] is precisely the classical trace. Likewise, \(\dim V\) is the image of the classical dimension under the homomorphism \(\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\to\Bbbk\).

Example. Consider the symmetric monoidal category \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Vect}}^-_{\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}/2\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}}(\Bbbk)\) from Example reference. Its objects and morphisms are written, respectively, as \(V=V_0\oplus V_1\) and \(f=(f_0,f_1)\), with \(\Bbbk=\Bbbk\oplus\{0\}\) as the unit. As in Example reference, an object \(V\) has a dual if and only if it is finite-dimensional as a \(\Bbbk\)-vector space; all such objects form the full subcategory \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Vect}}^-_{\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}/2\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}, f}(\Bbbk)\). If \(V\) is finite-dimensional, its dual may be taken to be \[V^* = V^*_0 \oplus V^*_1, \quad V^*_i := \operatorname{Hom}_{\Bbbk}(V_i, \Bbbk),\] with \[\text{Diagram chapter9-unit-124-d003}\] Here \(v_{0,1},\ldots,v_{0,n_0}\) (respectively, \(v_{1,1},\ldots,v_{1,n_1}\)) is any basis of \(V_0\) (respectively, \(V_1\)), while \(\check v_{0,1},\ldots,\check v_{0,n_0}\) (respectively, \(\check v_{1,1},\ldots,\check v_{1,n_1}\)) is the dual basis. The conditions of Definition reference can be checked directly.

  • The isomorphism \((V^*\otimes W)_0\simeq\operatorname{Hom}(\Bbbk,V^*\otimes W) \ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}\operatorname{Hom}(V,W)\) sends \(\sum_i\check v_i\otimes w_i\) to the linear map \(\sum_i\check v_i(\mathord\cdot)w_i\), where either \(\check v_i\in V_0^*\) and \(w_i\in W_0\), or \(\check v_i\in V_1^*\) and \(w_i\in W_1\).

  • The dual \(f^*:W^*\to V^*\) of a morphism \(f:V\to W\) is again the transpose of the linear map, applied separately to each direct summand.

  • Trace and dimension again take values in \(\operatorname{End}(\Bbbk)\simeq\Bbbk\), with no distinction between left and right. The trace of an endomorphism \(f=(f_0,f_1)\in\operatorname{End}(V)\) is \(\operatorname{Tr}(f_0)-\operatorname{Tr}(f_1)\) and is called the supertrace. Correspondingly, the superdimension \(\dim V\) is the image of \(\dim V_0-\dim V_1\) under \(\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\to\Bbbk\).

A similar description applies to the more general category \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Vect}}^{\epsilon}_I(\Bbbk)\) of graded \(\Bbbk\)-vector spaces, where \(I\) is a commutative monoid and \(\epsilon:I\to\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}/2\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\); see Example reference. Objects and morphisms of this symmetric monoidal category still have the forms \(\bigoplus_{i\in I}V_i\) and \((f_i)_{i\in I}\), while the signs depend on \(\epsilon(i)\).

Observe that \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Vect}}(\Bbbk)\) embeds into \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Vect}}^-_{\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}/2\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}}(\Bbbk)\) via \(V\mapsto(V_0,V_1):=(V,\{0\})\). Thus Example reference subsumes the classical theory of Example reference. Furthermore, when \(\Bbbk\in\{\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}},\ensuremath{\mathbb{C}}\}\), \(\Bbbk\)-super vector spaces may be generalized to super vector bundles over a topological manifold \(M\). Supertrace and superdimension extend accordingly to super vector bundles; the sole difference is that they take values in the endomorphism monoid of the trivial super vector bundle \(M\times(\Bbbk\oplus\{0\})\), namely in \(\{\text{continuous functions }M\to\Bbbk\}\). Next come two nonlinear examples.

Example (Correspondences). Let \(\mathrm{Corr}\) be the following category. Its objects are all small sets, and a morphism from \(X\) to \(Y\) is defined to be an isomorphism class of diagrams \([X\xleftarrow{u}A\xrightarrow{v}Y]\), where \(A\) is any small set and \(u,v\) are arbitrary maps; isomorphism is understood in the evident way. Such a diagram is called a “correspondence” from \(X\) to \(Y\) and generalizes the notion of a map.1 Composition of \([Y\leftarrow B\rightarrow Z]\) with \([X\leftarrow A\rightarrow Y]\) is defined by the fiber product: \[\text{Diagram chapter9-unit-124-d004}\] The identity morphism of an object \(X\) is \(X\xleftarrow{\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}}X\xrightarrow{\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}}X\), or any diagram isomorphic to it. Special cases of composition are \[\begin{gather*} [Y = Y \xrightarrow{w} Z] \circ [X \xleftarrow{u} A \xrightarrow{v} Y] = [X \xleftarrow{u} A \xrightarrow{wv} Z ], \\ [Y \xleftarrow{z} B \xrightarrow{w} Z] \circ [X \xleftarrow{u} Y = Y] = [X \xleftarrow{uz} B \xrightarrow{w} Z]. \end{gather*}\] Abstract sets are used here purely for pedagogical reasons. In applications, \(X\), \(Y\), and so forth are usually taken to be suitable geometric objects, such as topological spaces or schemes.

Now equip \(\mathrm{Corr}\) with a monoidal structure: define \(X\otimes Y:=X\times Y\), with the one-point set \(\mathrm{pt}\) as the unit \(\ensuremath{\bm{1}}\). This category is naturally symmetric monoidal and is also rigid: for every \(X\), take \(X^*=X\) together with \[\mathrm{coev}_X := \left[\text{Diagram chapter9-unit-124-d005}\right], \quad \mathrm{ev}_X := \left[\text{Diagram chapter9-unit-124-d006}\right]\] The reader is invited to verify carefully the conditions of Definition reference.

  • Once the definitions are expanded, the isomorphism \(\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathrm{Corr}}(X,Y)\simeq \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathrm{Corr}}(\ensuremath{\bm{1}},X^*\otimes Y)\) becomes a tautology.

  • The dual of the morphism \(f=[X\xleftarrow{u}A\xrightarrow{v}Y]\) is \(f^*=[Y\xleftarrow{v}A\xrightarrow{u}X]\). This follows immediately by working through the definitions; the details are left to the reader.

  • Trace and dimension take values in \(\operatorname{End}_{\mathrm{Corr}}(\ensuremath{\bm{1}})\). The elements of this set are isomorphism classes of diagrams \([\mathrm{pt}\leftarrow A\rightarrow\mathrm{pt}]\) and are completely determined by the cardinality \(|A|\).

  • For an arbitrary map \(u:A\to X\), write \(\Gamma_u:=\{(a,u(a)):a\in A\}\subset A\times X\) for its graph. The trace of the endomorphism \(f=[X\xleftarrow{u}A\xrightarrow{v}X]\) is described by the diagram \[\text{Diagram chapter9-unit-124-d007}\] Each diamond is a pullback square. Observe that \(\Gamma_u\cap\Gamma_v\simeq\{a\in A:u(a)=v(a)\}\).

    Write \(\Delta:=\Gamma_{\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_X}\subset X\times X\) for the diagonal subset. In the special case \(A=X\) and \(u=\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_X\), the vertex of the diagram is the fixed-point set \(\Gamma_v\cap\Delta=\{x\in X:v(x)=x\}\). Thus \(\operatorname{Tr}(f)\) does nothing but count fixed points.

  • In the special case \(u=v=\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_X\), we see that \(\dim X\) is the self-intersection \(\Delta\cap\Delta\) of the diagonal. In the present setting of sets, \(\Delta\cap\Delta\) is simply \(X\), so \(\dim X\in\operatorname{End}_{\mathrm{Corr}}(\ensuremath{\bm{1}})\) merely records \(|X|\). In more refined geometric or topological settings, together with a suitable “derived” framework, the self-intersection of the diagonal can yield more subtle and important information.

Example (Cobordisms). Consider the monoidal category \(n\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Cob}}\) from [Li1]. Its objects are compact closed oriented \((n-1)\)-manifolds, where \(n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}_{\geq1}\), while its morphisms are equivalence classes of “cobordisms” represented by oriented \(n\)-manifolds with boundary; equivalence means a diffeomorphism preserving the boundary. The monoidal structure comes from disjoint union of oriented manifolds, with the empty manifold \(\emptyset\) as unit. Concrete depictions of cobordisms, commonly called “pairs of pants”, may be found in the cited reference. To respect the string-diagram convention of §reference, however, cobordisms should be drawn from top to bottom, rather than from left to right as in that reference.

Diffeomorphic closed manifolds are also isomorphic in \(n\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Cob}}\), so the monoidal structure is symmetric. This category is also rigid: for every object \(X\), reversing orientation gives \(X^*\). More precisely, the morphisms \(\mathrm{ev}_X:X\sqcup X^*\to\emptyset\) and \(\mathrm{coev}_X:\emptyset\to X\sqcup X^*\) make the manifold with boundary \(X\times[0,1]\) into a cobordism in two different ways, which may be understood as products of oriented manifolds: \[\begin{gather*} \mathrm{ev}_X := X \times \par\textbf{Diagram chapter9-unit-124-d008}\par \; , \quad \mathrm{coev}_X := X \times \par\textbf{Diagram chapter9-unit-124-d009}\par \; . \end{gather*}\]

  • As in the reference above, the definition of \(n\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Cob}}\) already incorporates the bijection \[\begin{align*} \operatorname{Hom}_{n\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Cob}}}(X, Y) & \xleftrightarrow{1:1} \operatorname{Hom}_{n\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Cob}}}\left( \emptyset, X^* \sqcup Y\right) \\ & = \left\{ W: \text{oriented with boundary, together with data}\; \partial W \ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}X^* \sqcup Y \right\} / \sim . \end{align*}\]

  • The dual of a morphism, that is, of a cobordism, simply reverses \(\partial W\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}X^*\sqcup Y\) to \(\partial W\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}(Y^*)^*\sqcup X^*\).

  • Trace and dimension take values in \[\operatorname{End}_{n\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Cob}}}(\emptyset)= \{\text{compact closed manifolds of dimension }n\}/\sim .\]

  • By the description of \(\mathrm{ev}_X\) and \(\mathrm{coev}_X\) above, taking the trace of \(f\in\operatorname{End}_{n\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Cob}}}(X)\) amounts to gluing together the two \(X\)-ends of the cobordism \(f\).
