Since the identity morphism \(\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_X\) corresponds to the trivial cobordism \(X\times[0,1]\), we obtain \[\dim X = X \times \par\textbf{Diagram chapter9-unit-124-d010}\par \; .\]

For \(n\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Cob}}\), the various diagrams introduced in §reference acquire literal meaning. Here the method and the objects share the same geometric substance.

  1. If \(f:X\to Y\) is a map, take \(A\) to be the graph of \(f\).↩︎

Finally, we discuss how duality appears for modules and comodules over Hopf algebras; see §reference. Let \(\Bbbk\) be a field and let \((A,\mu,\eta,\Delta,\epsilon)\) be a \(\Bbbk\)-bialgebra, that is, a bialgebra in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Vect}}(\Bbbk)\). Proposition reference explained how the algebra and coalgebra structures are used together to equip the categories \[A\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}, \quad \ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}\text{-}}A, \quad A\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Comod}}, \quad \ensuremath{\mathsf{Comod}\text{-}}A\] with natural monoidal structures. We wish to characterize duality in them. Only the cases of right modules and right comodules are described below. Since the forgetful functor from \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}\text{-}}A\) (respectively, \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Comod}\text{-}}A\)) to \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Vect}}(\Bbbk)\) is monoidal, if a right \(A\)-module (respectively, right \(A\)-comodule) \(M\) has a left or right dual, then:

  • \(\dim_{\Bbbk}M<\infty\);

  • both the left and right dual must be realized on the dual vector space \(M^\vee:=\operatorname{Hom}_{\Bbbk}(M,\Bbbk)\);

  • at the level of \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Vect}}_{\mathrm f}(\Bbbk)\), the morphisms \(\mathrm{ev}\) and \(\mathrm{coev}\) are determined, up to isomorphism, as in Example reference.

An \(A\)-module (respectively, \(A\)-comodule) is called finite-dimensional if it is finite-dimensional as a \(\Bbbk\)-vector space. We henceforth focus on finite-dimensional \(M\); the corresponding categories are denoted by \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}_{\mathrm f}\text{-}}A\), and so forth.1 Readers familiar with commutative ring theory will have no difficulty generalizing the following results to an arbitrary commutative ring \(\Bbbk\), provided \(M\) is required to be a finitely generated projective \(\Bbbk\)-module. The key is to equip \(M^\vee\) with a suitable right \(A\)-module (respectively, right \(A\)-comodule) structure. Write \(\otimes:=\otimes_{\Bbbk}\). The dual functor in the finite-dimensional case extends to \[(\cdot)^\vee := \operatorname{Hom}_{\Bbbk}(\cdot, \Bbbk): \ensuremath{\mathsf{Vect}}(\Bbbk)^{\operatorname{op}} \to \ensuremath{\mathsf{Vect}}(\Bbbk).\] This functor is only right lax monoidal: there is a canonical morphism \(N^\vee\otimes M^\vee\to(M\otimes N)^\vee\). We also have the family of evaluation morphisms \[\mathrm{ev}_M: M \otimes M^\vee \to \Bbbk.\] First suppose \(M\) is a right \(A\)-module, with scalar multiplication given by \(a:M\otimes A\to M\). Since \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Vect}}(\Bbbk)\) is a concrete category, the language of elements and maps is more direct. Take the following transpose \({}^ta:A\otimes M^\vee\to M^\vee\), which makes \(M^\vee\) a left \(A\)-module: \[\mathrm{ev}\left(m, {}^t a(t \otimes \lambda)\right) = \mathrm{ev}\left( a(m \otimes t), \lambda \right),\] where \(m\in M\), \(\lambda\in M^\vee\), and \(t\in A\). For a right \(A\)-comodule \(M\), choose a basis \(v_1,\ldots,v_n\) of \(M\) and the dual basis \(\check v_1,\ldots,\check v_n\) of \(M^\vee\). Its comodule structure may be written as \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:comodule-basis}{} \rho(v_i) = \sum_{j=1}^n v_j \otimes t_{ji}, \quad t_{ji} \in A, \quad 1 \leq i \leq n. \end{equation}\] The preceding transpose operation has a dual version for \(\rho\): define \[{}^t \rho: M^\vee \to A \otimes M^\vee, \quad \check{v}_i \mapsto \sum_{j=1}^n t_{ij} \otimes \check{v}_j.\] It follows from equation and its left-comodule version that \({}^t\rho\) makes \(M^\vee\) a left \(A\)-comodule; one can also check that this structure is independent of the choice of basis. The question is how to return to right \(A\)-modules and right \(A\)-comodules. This can be done canonically when \(A\) is a Hopf algebra, as follows.

Proposition. Let \(\Bbbk\) be a field and let \(A\) be a Hopf \(\Bbbk\)-algebra with antipode \(S\) (Definition reference), with data \((A,\mu,\eta,\Delta,\epsilon)\). If \(M\) is a finite-dimensional right \(A\)-module (respectively, right \(A\)-comodule), then \(M\) has both a left dual and a right dual, both realized on the dual vector space \(M^\vee\), as follows.

  • Suppose the right \(A\)-module structure on \(M\) is given by \(a:M\otimes A\to M\). Then:

    Left dual Right dual
    \({}^\vee a: M^\vee \otimes A \to M^\vee\) \(a^\vee: M^\vee \otimes A \to M^\vee\)
    \({}^\vee a(\lambda \otimes t) = {}^t a\left( S^{-1} t \otimes \lambda\right)\) \(a^\vee(\lambda \otimes t) = {}^t a\left(St \otimes \lambda \right)\)

    where \({}^ta\) is the transpose defined above, \(\lambda\in M^\vee\), and \(t\in A\).

  • Suppose the right \(A\)-comodule structure on \(M\) is given by \(\rho:M\to M\otimes A\) and, after choosing a basis, is described as in equation. Then:

    Left dual Right dual
    \({}^\vee \rho: M^\vee \to M^\vee \otimes A\) \(\rho^\vee: M^\vee \to M^\vee \otimes A\)
    \({}^\vee \rho (\check{v}_i) = \sum_j \check{v}_j \otimes St_{ij}\) \(\rho^\vee (\check{v}_i) = \sum_j \check{v}_j \otimes S^{-1} t_{ij}\)

Consequently, the category \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}_{\mathrm f}\text{-}}A\) of finite-dimensional right \(A\)-modules (respectively, the category \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Comod}_{\mathrm f}\text{-}}A\) of finite-dimensional right \(A\)-comodules) is both left and right rigid. The cases of left \(A\)-modules or comodules are entirely similar, with left and right interchanged.

Proof. First consider a right \(A\)-module \(M\). With the notation above, since \(S\) gives a homomorphism \(A\to A^{\mathrm{op}}_{\mathrm{cop}}\) (Proposition reference) and the braiding of \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Vect}}(\Bbbk)\) is symmetric, both constructions in the table make \(M^\vee\) a right \(A\)-module. We claim that, for the right \(A\)-module structure on \(M^\vee\) given by \(a^\vee\), \(\mathrm{ev}:M\otimes M^\vee\to\Bbbk\) is a homomorphism of right \(A\)-modules.

Write \(a\) and \(a^\vee\) directly as right multiplication, as is customary in ring theory; also write \(\mu:A\otimes A\to A\) as multiplication and omit \(\eta:\Bbbk\to A\) from the notation. Let \(\Delta(t)=\sum_i t_i^{(1)}\otimes t_i^{(2)}\). Right-multiplying \(m\otimes\lambda\in M\otimes M^\vee\) by \(t\) and then evaluating gives \[\mathrm{ev}\left( \sum_i m t_i^{(1)}, \lambda t_i^{(2)} \right) = \mathrm{ev}\left( \sum_i m t_i^{(1)} S\left(t_i^{(2)}\right), \lambda \right).\] The definition of the antipode gives \(\sum_i t_i^{(1)}S(t_i^{(2)})=\epsilon(t)\), so this expression becomes \(\epsilon(t)\mathrm{ev}(m\otimes\lambda)\). Since the \(A\)-module structure on \(\Bbbk\) is induced by \(\epsilon\), this proves that \(\mathrm{ev}\) is a homomorphism of right \(A\)-modules.

Next, check that \(\mathrm{coev}:\Bbbk\to M^\vee\otimes M\) is a homomorphism of right \(A\)-modules, still using the structure \(a^\vee\) on \(M^\vee\). Identify \(M^\vee\otimes M\) with \(\operatorname{End}_{\Bbbk}(M)\); then \(\mathrm{coev}(1)=\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_M\). It suffices to check that for every \(t\in A\), \[\epsilon(t) \cdot \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_M = \sum_i \left( t_i^{(2)} \;\text{acting on the right} \right) \circ \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_M \circ \left( S t_i^{(1)} \;\text{acting on the right} \right).\] This is equivalent to proving \(\epsilon(t)=\sum_iS(t_i^{(1)})t_i^{(2)}\), which again follows directly from the definition of the antipode.

Thus \(M^\vee\), with the structure \(a^\vee\), gives the right dual of \(M\) and is denoted by \(M^*\). The left dual can be handled similarly, or reduced to the following simple observation. Equip \(M^\vee\) with the right \(A\)-module structure \({}^\vee a\) and denote the result by \({}^*M\). It is easy to see that \(({}^*M)^*\), as given by the preceding construction, returns to \(M\); hence \({}^*M\) is a left dual of \(M\).

For a finite-dimensional right \(A\)-comodule \(M\), we use the method of undetermined coefficients. Suppose \(M^\vee\) has a right comodule structure determined by an \(n\times n\) matrix over \(A\), \(U=(u_{ij})_{i,j}\), via \[\check{v}_i \mapsto \sum_{j=1}^n \check{v}_j \otimes u_{ji}, \quad 1 \leq i \leq n.\] The necessary and sufficient conditions for \(U\) to define a right comodule structure were listed in equation.

Recall that \(\mathrm{ev}(v_i,\check v_j)=\delta_{i,j}\), where \(\delta\) is the Kronecker symbol, and \(\mathrm{coev}(1)=\sum_i\check v_i\otimes v_i\). The condition that \(\mathrm{ev}\) and \(\mathrm{coev}\) be homomorphisms of right \(A\)-comodules can then be written as \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:Hopf-module-dual-aux}{} \sum_k t_{ki} u_{kj} = \delta_{i, j} = \sum_k u_{ik} t_{jk}. \end{equation}\] Write \(T=(t_{ij})_{i,j}\) and let \({}^tT\) denote its transpose. In matrix language the preceding condition becomes \[({}^t T) U = 1_{n \times n} = U ({}^t T).\] Thus finding a right dual of \(M\) amounts to finding \(({}^tT)^{-1}\). Similarly, finding a left dual of \(M\) amounts to finding \({}^t(T^{-1})\). The assertions about the right and left duals reduce, respectively, to checking \[\begin{align*} \sum_k t_{ki} S^{-1}(t_{jk}) & = \delta_{i, j} = \sum_k S^{-1} (t_{ki}) t_{jk}, \\ \sum_k t_{ik} S(t_{kj}) & = \delta_{i, j} = \sum_k S(t_{ik}) t_{kj}. \end{align*}\]

This is immediate. Since \(\Delta(t_{ij})=\sum_k t_{ik}\otimes t_{kj}\), the definition of the antipode shows that both sides in the second line equal \(\epsilon(t_{ij})=\delta_{i,j}\). Apply \(S^{-1}\) to both equalities in the second line and use the fact that \(S\) preserves the unit and reverses the order of multiplication; rearranging yields the first line. This proves the assertion.

If \(A\) is noncommutative, \({}^t(T^{-1})\) and \(({}^tT)^{-1}\) need not be equal. Thus the argument above also shows that left and right duals do not in general coincide. In fact, Corollary reference below will show conversely how the rigidity of the category of finite-dimensional comodules determines a Hopf structure on a bialgebra. A sequence of theoretical preparations will be needed first.

  1. Do not confuse this with \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}_{\mathrm{fg}}\text{-}}A\) in Theorem reference, the category of finitely generated right \(A\)-modules.↩︎

The Endomorphism Coalgebra

Beginning with this section, we lay a series of foundations for the theory of Tannakian categories (see §reference); some of the tools and ideas involved have broader applications. The principal reference is [Del90]. Let \(\Bbbk\) be a commutative ring. For any category \(\mathcal{A}\) and functor \(\xi:\mathcal{A}\to\Bbbk\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\), we may consider the \(\Bbbk\)-algebra \(\operatorname{End}(\xi)\) of endomorphisms of the functor. It gives a family of \(\Bbbk\)-linear maps \[\operatorname{End}(\xi) \ensuremath{\underset{\Bbbk}{\otimes}} \xi(X) \to \xi(X), \quad X \in \operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{A}),\] functorial in \(X\), or briefly \(\operatorname{End}(\xi)\ensuremath{\underset{\Bbbk}{\otimes}}\xi\to\xi\). Moreover, \(\operatorname{End}(\xi)\) is universal for such actions: tautologically, giving an action of a \(\Bbbk\)-algebra \(E\) on \(\xi\) is equivalent to giving an algebra homomorphism \(E\to\operatorname{End}(\xi)\). The multiplication on \(\operatorname{End}(\xi)\) can be derived abstractly from this universal property. For the problems we shall address, the dual version of this construction is both more useful and simpler. We must, however, consider functors taking values in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}\text{-}}B\), where \(B\) is a \(\Bbbk\)-algebra, assumed nonzero by convention. This construction is closely related to the abstract categorical construction called a coend; an exercise in this chapter gives further details.

Definition. Let \(\Bbbk\) be a commutative ring, \(B\) a \(\Bbbk\)-algebra, and \(\omega_1,\omega_2:\mathcal{A}\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}\text{-}}B\) functors. Consider a \((B,B)\)-bimodule \(L\) together with a natural transformation \(a:\omega_2\to\omega_1\ensuremath{\underset{B}{\otimes}}L\), that is, a family of right \(B\)-module homomorphisms \[a_X: \omega_2(X) \to \omega_1(X) \ensuremath{\underset{B}{\otimes}} L, \quad X \in \operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{A}),\] such that the following diagram commutes for every \(f\in\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{A}}(X,Y)\): \[\text{Diagram chapter9-unit-126-d001}\]

A morphism from the data \((L,a)\) to \((L',a')\) is defined to be a bimodule homomorphism \(t:L\to L'\) that makes the following diagram commute for all \(X\): \[\text{Diagram chapter9-unit-126-d002}\] Conversely, data \((L,a)\) and a bimodule homomorphism \(t:L\to L'\) determine \(a'\) by this diagram, together with a morphism \(t:(L,a)\to(L',a')\).

If the category of all such data \((L,a)\) and morphisms has an initial object, denote the corresponding \((B,B)\)-bimodule by \[\operatorname{coH}(\omega_1, \omega_2) = \operatorname{coH}_{\Bbbk}(\omega_1, \omega_2),\] and denote the corresponding morphism by \(\lambda:\omega_2\to\omega_1\ensuremath{\underset{B}{\otimes}}L\). We also write \[\operatorname{coE}(\omega) = \operatorname{coE}_{\Bbbk}(\omega) := \operatorname{coH}(\omega, \omega).\]

The symbols \(\operatorname{coH}\) and \(\operatorname{coE}\) stand for \(\operatorname{coHom}\) and \(\operatorname{coEnd}\), respectively; they should be viewed as dual to \(\operatorname{Hom}\) and \(\operatorname{End}\), and the abbreviations are merely typographical. Note that the notion of a \((B,B)\)-bimodule depends not only on the ring structure of \(B\), but also on \(\Bbbk\).

Remark. The equality \(\operatorname{coH}(\omega_1,\omega_2)=0\) means that every morphism \(\omega_2\to\omega_1\ensuremath{\underset{B}{\otimes}}L\) is zero; the definition does not exclude this possibility. By contrast, if \(\operatorname{coE}(\omega)\) exists and \(\omega\) is not the constant zero functor, then \(\operatorname{coE}(\omega)\neq0\), since \(\omega\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}\omega\ensuremath{\underset{B}{\otimes}}B\).

If \(\operatorname{coE}(\omega)\) exists, applying the universal property to \(\omega\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}\omega\ensuremath{\underset{B}{\otimes}}B\) gives a bimodule homomorphism \[\epsilon: \operatorname{coE}(\omega) \to B.\] On the other hand, assuming the relevant \(\operatorname{coH}\) objects exist, successive application to \(\omega_1,\omega_2,\omega_3\) yields the morphism \[\begin{equation*} \omega_3 \to \omega_2 \ensuremath{\underset{B}{\otimes}} \operatorname{coH}(\omega_2, \omega_3) \to \omega_1 \ensuremath{\underset{B}{\otimes}} \operatorname{coH}(\omega_1, \omega_2) \ensuremath{\underset{B}{\otimes}} \operatorname{coH}(\omega_2, \omega_3). \end{equation*}\] The universal property then gives a canonical bimodule homomorphism \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:L-comult-prep}{} \operatorname{coH}(\omega_1, \omega_3) \to \operatorname{coH}(\omega_1, \omega_2) \ensuremath{\underset{B}{\otimes}} \operatorname{coH}(\omega_2, \omega_3). \end{equation}\] A routine check with the functors \(\omega_1,\ldots,\omega_4\) shows that equation satisfies coassociativity. Thus \(\operatorname{coE}(\omega)\) becomes a coalgebra in \((B,B)\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\), with \(\epsilon:\operatorname{coE}(\omega)\to B\) as counit, while every \(\omega(X)\) becomes a \(\operatorname{coE}(\omega)\)-comodule via the canonical morphism \(\lambda\). This discussion is summarized as follows.

Definition–Proposition (Endomorphism coalgebra). Let \(\omega:\mathcal{A}\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}\text{-}}B\) be a functor and suppose \(\operatorname{coE}(\omega)\) exists.

  • As an object of the monoidal category \((B,B)\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\), \(\operatorname{coE}(\omega)\) has a canonical coalgebra structure such that every \(\omega(X)\) becomes a \(\operatorname{coE}(\omega)\)-comodule via the canonical morphism, and morphisms in \(\mathcal{A}\) induce comodule homomorphisms. We call \(\operatorname{coE}(\omega)\) the endomorphism coalgebra of \(\omega\).1

  • For every coalgebra \(L\) in \((B,B)\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\), compatibly giving all \(\omega(X)\) an \(L\)-comodule structure is equivalent to giving a coalgebra homomorphism \(\operatorname{coE}(\omega)\to L\).

Remark. Given a functor \(T:\mathcal{A}'\to\mathcal{A}\) and \(\omega_1,\omega_2:\mathcal{A}\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}\text{-}}B\), assuming the relevant \(\operatorname{coH}\) objects exist, the canonical morphism \(\omega_2(TX)\to\omega_1(TX)\ensuremath{\underset{B}{\otimes}}\operatorname{coH}(\omega_1,\omega_2)\) together with the universal property naturally induces a homomorphism \[\operatorname{coH}(\omega_1 T, \omega_2 T) \to \operatorname{coH}(\omega_1, \omega_2),\] compatible with all the structures above. In particular, taking \(\omega_1=\omega=\omega_2\) gives a coalgebra homomorphism \(\operatorname{coE}(\omega T)\to\operatorname{coE}(\omega)\).

Proposition. Let \(\omega_1,\omega_2:\mathcal{A}\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}\text{-}}B\) be functors. Suppose \(\mathcal{A}\) is the union of a family of subcategories, each denoted by \(\mathcal{A}'\), and write \(\omega_i':=\omega_i|_{\mathcal{A}'}\). If \(\operatorname{coH}(\omega_1',\omega_2')\) exists for every \(\mathcal{A}'\), then \(\operatorname{coH}(\omega_1,\omega_2)\) exists and there is a canonical isomorphism \[\varinjlim_{\mathcal{A}'} \operatorname{coH}(\omega'_1, \omega'_2) \ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}\operatorname{coH}(\omega_1, \omega_2).\] The colimit on the left is ordered by inclusion; its transition homomorphisms are given as in Remark reference. The isomorphism is compatible with equation.

Proof. For every \((B,B)\)-bimodule \(L\), giving a morphism \(\omega_2\to\omega_1\ensuremath{\underset{B}{\otimes}}L\) is equivalent to compatibly giving \(\omega_2'\to\omega_1'\ensuremath{\underset{B}{\otimes}}L\) for every \(\mathcal{A}'\); this in turn is equivalent to giving a compatible family of homomorphisms \(\operatorname{coH}(\omega_1',\omega_2')\to L\).

The issue is how to ensure the existence of \(\operatorname{coH}(\omega_1,\omega_2)\), which is not automatic. We must first control the size of the category. Fix a Grothendieck universe \(\mathcal{U}\), relative to which we may speak of small sets and small categories. A category is called essentially small if the isomorphism classes of its objects form a small set (Definition reference).

Convention. Let \(\Bbbk\) be a commutative ring and \(B\) a \(\Bbbk\)-algebra. We shall need the following notation.

  • Consider the full subcategories \[\underbracket{\ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}_{\mathrm{pfg}}\text{-}}B}_{\text{projective + finitely generated}} \subset \underbracket{\ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}_{\mathrm{fg}}\text{-}}B}_{\text{finitely generated}} \subset \ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}\text{-}}B.\]

  • For every right \(B\)-module \(P\), define the left \(B\)-module \(P^\vee\) according to equation. Every homomorphism \(\varphi:P\to Q\) induces the dual homomorphism \(\varphi^\vee:Q^\vee\to P^\vee\).

Following this book’s convention for algebraic structures, \(\Bbbk\) and \(B\) are assumed to be realized on small sets. Finite generation ensures that \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}_{\mathrm{fg}}\text{-}}B\) and \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Vect}}_{\mathrm f}(\Bbbk)\) are essentially small categories; they are also \(\Bbbk\)-linear. The essentially small category \(\mathcal{A}\) considered in this section, however, need not have a \(\Bbbk\)-linear structure.

For every \(P_1,P_2\in\operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}_{\mathrm{pfg}}\text{-}}B)\), there is a canonical isomorphism \[\begin{equation*} \begin{aligned} \operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}\text{-}}B}\left( P_2, P_1 \ensuremath{\underset{B}{\otimes}} L \right) & \ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}\operatorname{Hom}_{(B, B)\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}}\left( P_1^\vee \ensuremath{\underset{\Bbbk}{\otimes}} P_2, L \right) \\ \varphi & \mapsto \left[ \check{p}_1 \otimes p_2 \mapsto (\check{p}_1 \otimes \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_L)(\varphi(p_2)) \right] . \end{aligned} \end{equation*}\] This is easily reduced to the case in which \(P_1\) and \(P_2\) are finite-rank free modules. Therefore, when \(\omega_1,\omega_2:\mathcal{A}\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}\text{-}}B\) take values in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}_{\mathrm{pfg}}\text{-}}B\), giving data \(a=(a_X)_X\) as in Definition reference is equivalent to giving a family of homomorphisms \[\alpha_X: \omega_1(X)^\vee \ensuremath{\underset{\Bbbk}{\otimes}} \omega_2(X) \to L, \quad X \in \operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{A}),\] whose functoriality in \(X\) translates into commutativity of the following diagram for every \(f\in\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{A}}(X,Y)\): \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:cogebra-L}{}\text{Diagram chapter9-unit-126-d003} \end{equation}\]

Proposition. Let \(\mathcal{A}\) be an essentially small category and let \(\omega_1,\omega_2:\mathcal{A}\to \ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}_{\mathrm{pfg}}\text{-}}B\) be arbitrary functors. Then \(\operatorname{coH}(\omega_1,\omega_2)\) of Definition reference exists.

Proof. The only point to prove is the existence of an initial object. Use the commutative diagram equation. Let \(L_0\) be the direct sum of all \(\omega_1(X)^\vee\ensuremath{\underset{\Bbbk}{\otimes}}\omega_2(X)\), where \(X\) ranges over a set of representatives for \(\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{A})/\simeq\); this is where essential smallness is needed. For every \(f:X\to Y\), define \[\delta_f := \omega_1(f)^\vee \otimes \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}- \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}\otimes \omega_2(f) : \omega_1(Y)^\vee \ensuremath{\underset{\Bbbk}{\otimes}} \omega_2(X) \to L_0.\] Then \(\operatorname{coH}(\omega_1,\omega_2):=L_0/\sum_f\operatorname{im}(\delta_f)\) is the desired object.

Convention. The following concrete notation will be useful. For \(t\in\omega_1(X)^\vee\ensuremath{\underset{\Bbbk}{\otimes}}\omega_2(X)\), write \([t]\) for its image in \(\operatorname{coH}(\omega_1,\omega_2)\); these images generate \(\operatorname{coH}(\omega_1,\omega_2)\). In the universal property of Definition reference, the image in \(L\) of \([\phi\otimes x]\in\operatorname{coE}(\omega)\) is obtained by first mapping \(x\in\omega(X)\) through \(\omega(X)\to\omega(X)\ensuremath{\underset{B}{\otimes}}L\) and then contracting with \(\phi\in\omega(X)^\vee\).

  1. Perhaps “coendomorphism coalgebra” would be a more accurate name.↩︎

For a functor \(\omega: \mathcal{A} \to \ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}_{\mathrm{pfg}}\text{-}}B\), the evaluation homomorphism \(\mathrm{ev}_{\omega(X)}: \omega(X)^\vee \ensuremath{\underset{\Bbbk}{\otimes}} \omega(X) \to B\) is a homomorphism of \((B, B)\)-bimodules. The canonical homomorphism that it determines is precisely the previously defined homomorphism \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:L-counit}{} \begin{aligned} \epsilon: \operatorname{coE}(\omega) & \to B \\ [t] & \mapsto \mathrm{ev}_{\omega(X)}(t). \end{aligned} \end{equation}\] If \(\omega_1(X)\) is free, choose a \(B\)-basis \((v_i)_{i=1}^n\) and its dual basis \((\check{v}_i)_{i=1}^n\). Then \(\lambda_X: \omega_2(X) \to \omega_1(X) \ensuremath{\underset{B}{\otimes}} \operatorname{coH}(\omega_1, \omega_2)\) may be written as \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:L-coaction}{}\begin{aligned} w & \mapsto \sum_{i=1}^n v_i \otimes [\check{v}_i \otimes w]; \end{aligned} \end{equation}\] It follows that for arbitrary \(\omega_1, \omega_2, \omega_3\), if \(\omega_1(X)\) and \(\omega_2(X)\) are free, \(\lambda \in \omega_1(X)^\vee\), and \(w \in \omega_3(X)\), then \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:L-comult}{}\begin{aligned} \operatorname{coH}(\omega_1, \omega_3) & \to \operatorname{coH}(\omega_1, \omega_2) \ensuremath{\underset{B}{\otimes}} \operatorname{coH}(\omega_2, \omega_3) \\ [\lambda \otimes w] & \mapsto \sum_i [\lambda \otimes v_i] \otimes [\check{v}_i \otimes w]. \end{aligned} \end{equation}\] The next step is to introduce a monoidal structure. For this, \(B\) must be commutative and we must take \(\Bbbk = B\) in the preceding construction. Then \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}\text{-}}B\) and \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}_{\mathrm{pfg}}\text{-}}B\) are both symmetric monoidal categories under \(\otimes_B\), with \(B\) as unit. To emphasize this setting, we denote the corresponding \(\operatorname{coH}\) and \(\operatorname{coE}\) by \(\operatorname{coH}_B\) and \(\operatorname{coE}_B\); in this case, a \((B, B)\)-bimodule is the same thing as a \(B\)-module. Let \(\mathcal{A}\), \(\mathcal{A}'\), and so forth be arbitrary categories. First take functors \[\omega_i: \mathcal{A} \to \ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}\text{-}}B, \quad \omega'_i: \mathcal{A}' \to \ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}\text{-}}B, \quad i =1, 2.\] Define \(\omega_i \boxtimes \omega'_i: \mathcal{A} \times \mathcal{A}' \to \ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}\text{-}}B\) by sending an object \((X, X')\) to \(\omega_i(X) \ensuremath{\underset{B}{\otimes}} \omega'_i(X')\). Assuming that the relevant \(\operatorname{coH}\) objects exist, apply the universal property to the family of morphisms \[\begin{align*} \omega_2(X) \ensuremath{\underset{B}{\otimes}} \omega'_2(X') & \to \omega_1(X) \ensuremath{\underset{B}{\otimes}} \operatorname{coH}_B(\omega_1, \omega_2) \ensuremath{\underset{B}{\otimes}} \omega'_1(X') \ensuremath{\underset{B}{\otimes}} \operatorname{coH}_B(\omega'_1, \omega'_2) \\ & \simeq \omega_1(X) \ensuremath{\underset{B}{\otimes}} \omega'_1(X') \ensuremath{\underset{B}{\otimes}} \operatorname{coH}_B(\omega_1, \omega_2) \ensuremath{\underset{B}{\otimes}} \operatorname{coH}_B(\omega'_1, \omega'_2) \end{align*}\] to obtain a canonical morphism \[\nu: \operatorname{coH}_B(\omega_1 \boxtimes \omega'_1, \omega_2 \boxtimes \omega'_2) \to \operatorname{coH}_B(\omega_1, \omega_2) \ensuremath{\underset{B}{\otimes}} \operatorname{coH}_B(\omega'_1, \omega'_2),\] that makes the following diagram commute for every \((X, X') \in \operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{A} \times \mathcal{A}')\): \[\par\textbf{Diagram chapter9-unit-127-d001}\par\]

Lemma. With the notation above, suppose in addition that all \(\omega_i\) and \(\omega'_i\) take values in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}_{\mathrm{pfg}}\text{-}}B\). Then \(\omega_i \boxtimes \omega'_i\) also takes values there and, in this setting, \(\nu\) is an isomorphism. Following Convention reference, it can be described explicitly by \[\begin{equation*} \nu: \left[ (\phi \otimes \phi') \otimes (x \otimes x') \right] \mapsto [\phi \otimes x] \otimes [\phi' \otimes x']. \end{equation*}\]

Proof. Since \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}_{\mathrm{pfg}}\text{-}}B\) is closed under \(\otimes_B\), the functor \(\omega \boxtimes \omega'\) takes values there. Returning to the construction in equation and Proposition reference immediately gives the explicit description of \(\nu\).

Next we show that \(\nu\) is an isomorphism. By the construction in Proposition reference, \(\operatorname{coH}_B(\omega_1, \omega_2)\) may suitably be expressed as \(\varinjlim_{X, Y} \omega_1(Y)^\vee \ensuremath{\underset{B}{\otimes}} \omega_2(X)\), with the relevant morphisms coming from equation; the same is of course true for the other \(\operatorname{coH}_B\) objects involved in \(\nu\). Thus the assertion that \(\nu\) is an isomorphism is equivalent to saying that the evident morphism \[\begin{multline*} \varinjlim_{X, X', Y, Y'} \omega_1(Y)^\vee \ensuremath{\underset{B}{\otimes}} \omega'_1(Y')^\vee \ensuremath{\underset{B}{\otimes}} \omega_2(X) \ensuremath{\underset{B}{\otimes}} \omega'_2(X') \\ \to \varinjlim_{X, Y} \left( \omega_1(Y)^\vee \ensuremath{\underset{B}{\otimes}} \omega_2(X) \right) \ensuremath{\underset{B}{\otimes}} \varinjlim_{X', Y'} \left( \omega'_1(Y')^\vee \ensuremath{\underset{B}{\otimes}} \omega'_2(X') \right) \end{multline*}\] is an isomorphism. This in turn reduces to the standard fact from module theory that \(\ensuremath{\underset{B}{\otimes}}\) preserves all small \(\varinjlim\) [Li1].

We continue the preceding discussion. Consider the functors \[\begin{gather*} \otimes: \mathcal{A} \times \mathcal{A}' \to \mathcal{A}'' , \\ \omega_i: \mathcal{A} \to \ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}_{\mathrm{pfg}}\text{-}}B, \quad \omega'_i: \mathcal{A}' \to \ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}_{\mathrm{pfg}}\text{-}}B, \quad \omega''_i: \mathcal{A}'' \to \ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}_{\mathrm{pfg}}\text{-}}B \quad i =1, 2, \end{gather*}\] together with isomorphisms \(\theta_i: \omega_i \boxtimes \omega'_i \ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}\omega''_i \circ \otimes\), whose dual versions are denoted by \(\theta_i^\vee\). The preceding preparations give a \(B\)-linear homomorphism \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:L-tensor}{} \text{Diagram chapter9-unit-127-d002} \end{equation}\] The preceding commutative diagram for \(\nu\) implies that the following diagram commutes; the details are left to the reader. \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:L-bialgebra-prod}{} \text{Diagram chapter9-unit-127-d003} \end{equation}\] Now suppose further that \(\mathcal{A} = \mathcal{A}' = \mathcal{A}''\) is a monoidal category, \(\otimes\) is its product, and \(\omega''_i = \omega'_i = \omega_i\) are monoidal functors (\(i=1,2\)). Write \(\mathcal{A}_0\) for the category with just one object and one morphism (the identity), and define \(\iota: \mathcal{A}_0 \to \mathcal{A}\) by sending its unique object to \(\ensuremath{\bm{1}}\). A direct manipulation of the definitions gives \[\operatorname{coH}_B(\omega_1 \iota, \omega_2 \iota) \simeq B \ensuremath{\underset{B}{\otimes}} B \simeq B.\] Functoriality in Remark reference then gives the canonical map \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:L-bialgebra-unit}{} B \simeq \operatorname{coH}_B(\omega_1 \iota, \omega_2 \iota) \to \operatorname{coH}_B(\omega_1, \omega_2), \quad b \mapsto [b \otimes 1] = [1 \otimes b]. \end{equation}\]

Proposition. In the setting above, suppose \(\mathcal{A} = \mathcal{A}' = \mathcal{A}''\) is a monoidal category, \(\omega_1\) and \(\omega_2\) are monoidal functors, and \(\omega''_i = \omega'_i = \omega_i\).

  1. The corresponding homomorphism \(\operatorname{coH}_B(\omega_1, \omega_2) \ensuremath{\underset{B}{\otimes}} \operatorname{coH}_B(\omega_1, \omega_2) \to \operatorname{coH}_B(\omega_1, \omega_2)\) makes \(\operatorname{coH}_B(\omega_1, \omega_2)\) a \(B\)-algebra, with equation as its unit.

  2. In the special case \(\omega_1 = \omega = \omega_2\), this structure makes \(\operatorname{coE}_B(\omega)\) a bialgebra.

  3. If \(\mathcal{A}\) is a symmetric monoidal category and \(\omega_1\), \(\omega_2\) are compatible with the braiding, then \(\operatorname{coH}_B(\omega_1, \omega_2)\) is a commutative \(B\)-algebra.

Proof. Since the multiplication on \(\operatorname{coH}_B(\omega_1, \omega_2)\) has a natural characterization through equation and equation, all the remaining assertions merely reflect the monoidal structure and require only formal arguments; the details are omitted.

The Reconstruction Theorem

Throughout this section, \(\Bbbk\) is a fixed commutative ring. Unless stated otherwise, all categories and functors considered below are \(\Bbbk\)-linear; in particular, the bifunctor \(\otimes\) of a monoidal category is understood to be \(\Bbbk\)-linear in each variable. For a \(\Bbbk\)-algebra \(B\), Convention reference defined the essentially small categories \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}_{\mathrm{pfg}}\text{-}}B\subset \ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}_{\mathrm{fg}}\text{-}}B\). If \(C\) is a coalgebra in the monoidal category \((B,B)\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\), write \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Comod}\text{-}}C\) for the category of right \(C\)-comodules; these comodule structures are superimposed on structures in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}\text{-}}B\), as explained after Definition reference. Imposing projectivity and finiteness conditions as right \(B\)-modules gives the full subcategories \[\underbracket{\ensuremath{\mathsf{Comod}_{\mathrm{pf}}\text{-}}C}_{\text{projective + finitely generated}} \subset \underbracket{\ensuremath{\mathsf{Comod}_{\mathrm{f}}\text{-}}C}_{\text{finitely generated}} \subset \ensuremath{\mathsf{Comod}\text{-}}C.\] Finite generation ensures that \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Comod}_{\mathrm f}\text{-}}C\) is also an essentially small category in the sense of Definition reference. To gain a more concrete understanding of \(\operatorname{coE}(\omega)=\operatorname{coE}_{\Bbbk}(\omega)\) from §reference, consider the setting of Proposition reference. Take \(\Bbbk\)-algebras \(A,B\), not necessarily commutative, and an \((A,B)\)-bimodule \(P\). Suppose \(P\) is finitely generated and projective as a right \(B\)-module. Let \(\mathcal{A}\) be a full subcategory of \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}\text{-}}A\) satisfying

  • \(A\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{A})\);

  • \(\omega:=(\mathord\cdot)\ensuremath{\underset{A}{\otimes}}P\) defines a functor \(\mathcal{A}\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}_{\mathrm{pfg}}\text{-}}B\).

Proposition reference asserts that the \((B,B)\)-bimodule \(P^\vee\ensuremath{\underset{A}{\otimes}}P\) is the coalgebra corresponding to the comonad determined by the adjoint pair \[\begin{equation*} \text{Diagram chapter9-unit-128-d001} \end{equation*}\] The coalgebra \(P^\vee\ensuremath{\underset{A}{\otimes}}P\) naturally coacts on every \(\omega(N)=N\ensuremath{\underset{A}{\otimes}}P\). Explicitly, the coaction is \[N \ensuremath{\underset{A}{\otimes}} P \xrightarrow{\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_N \otimes \mathrm{coev} \otimes \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_P} N \ensuremath{\underset{A}{\otimes}} P \ensuremath{\underset{B}{\otimes}} P^\vee \ensuremath{\underset{A}{\otimes}} P, \quad N \in \operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}\text{-}}A).\] Definition–Proposition reference then gives a canonical coalgebra homomorphism \[\operatorname{coE}(\omega) \to P^\vee \ensuremath{\underset{A}{\otimes}} P.\]

Proposition. In the setting above, the homomorphism \(\operatorname{coE}(\omega)\to P^\vee\ensuremath{\underset{A}{\otimes}}P\) is an isomorphism.

Proof. Let \(\mathcal{A}^\flat\) be the full subcategory of \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}\text{-}}A\) with \(\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{A}^\flat)=\{A\}\), and write \(i\) for the inclusion functor. Remark reference gives the commutative diagram \[\text{Diagram chapter9-unit-128-d002}\] The reader can check directly that \(\operatorname{coE}(\omega i)\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}P^\vee\ensuremath{\underset{A}{\otimes}}P\). Hence \(\operatorname{coE}(\omega i)\to\operatorname{coE}(\omega)\) has a left inverse. If this morphism is surjective, then \(\operatorname{coE}(\omega i)\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}\operatorname{coE}(\omega)\), and consequently \(\operatorname{coE}(\omega)\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}P^\vee\ensuremath{\underset{A}{\otimes}}P\).

By the concrete constructions of \(\operatorname{coE}(\omega)\) and \(\operatorname{coE}(\omega i)\), it remains to prove, for every \(Y\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{A})\), that \[\operatorname{im}\left[ \omega(Y)^\vee \ensuremath{\underset{\Bbbk}{\otimes}} \omega(Y) \to \operatorname{coE}(\omega) \right] \subset \operatorname{im}\left[ \omega(A)^\vee \ensuremath{\underset{\Bbbk}{\otimes}} \omega(A) \to \operatorname{coE}(\omega) \right].\]

Write \(t\in\omega(Y)^\vee\ensuremath{\underset{\Bbbk}{\otimes}}\omega(Y)\) as a finite sum \(\sum_i\lambda_i\otimes o_i\). By the concrete form of \(\omega\), each \(o_i\in\omega(Y)\) is a finite linear combination of elements of the form \(\omega(f)(x)\), where \(x\in\omega(A)\) and \(f\in\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{A}}(A,Y)\). Thus the problem further reduces to the case \(t=\lambda\otimes\omega(f)(x)\). This follows by considering the image of \(\lambda\otimes x\in\omega(Y)^\vee\ensuremath{\underset{\Bbbk}{\otimes}}\omega(A)\) in the commutative diagram \[\text{Diagram chapter9-unit-128-d003}\]

For any essentially small category \(\mathcal{A}\) and any functor \(\omega:\mathcal{A}\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}_{\mathrm{pfg}}\text{-}}B\), Definition–Proposition reference canonically factors \(\omega\) as \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:L-canonical-decomp}{} \mathcal{A} \xrightarrow{\overline{\omega}} \ensuremath{\mathsf{Comod}_{\mathrm{pf}}\text{-}}\operatorname{coE}(\omega) \xrightarrow{U} \ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}_{\mathrm{pfg}}\text{-}}B, \end{equation}\] where \(U\) is the forgetful functor. We wish to determine when \(\overline\omega\) is an equivalence. The following lemma underlies the various reconstruction theorems below. The core of its proof uses Beck’s Monadicity Theorem reference. We will also need the characterization of faithful exact functors from Proposition reference, the notion of a locally finite abelian category from Definition reference, and some Ind-completion techniques from .

Lemma. Let \(\Bbbk\) be a field, let \(\mathcal{A}\) be a locally finite abelian category, and let \(s\) be a projective generator of \(\mathcal{A}\). Consider a faithful exact functor \[\omega: \mathcal{A} \to \ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}\text{-}}B,\] and suppose that it takes values in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}_{\mathrm{pfg}}\text{-}}B\).

  1. The coalgebra \(\operatorname{coE}(\omega)\) can be written concretely as \(P^\vee\ensuremath{\underset{A}{\otimes}}P\), where \(A=\operatorname{End}_{\mathcal{A}}(s)\) and \(P=\omega(s)\).

  2. The functor \(\overline\omega\) in the canonical factorization equation is an equivalence of categories.

  3. We have \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Comod}_{\mathrm{pf}}\text{-}}\operatorname{coE}(\omega)= \ensuremath{\mathsf{Comod}_{\mathrm f}\text{-}}\operatorname{coE}(\omega)\).

Proof. Observe that \(A\) is a finite-dimensional \(\Bbbk\)-algebra. All the hypotheses of Theorem reference hold, and \(\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{A}}(s,\mathord\cdot)\) gives an equivalence \(\mathcal{A}\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}_{\mathrm{fg}}\text{-}}A\). Thus the problem reduces to the case \(\mathcal{A}=\ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}_{\mathrm{fg}}\text{-}}A\) and \(s=A\). The first observation is that \(\omega\) now extends canonically to a functor \[\Omega: \ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}\text{-}}A \to \ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}\text{-}}B,\] by the following construction.

  • On objects.Take the small filtered colimit \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:Tannaka-tilde-omega}{} \Omega(N) = \varinjlim_{\substack{N' \subset N \\ \text{finitely generated}}} \omega(N'). \end{equation}\]

  • On morphisms.For a homomorphism of right \(A\)-modules \(f:N_1\to N_2\), take \[\begin{align*} \Omega(f) & = \varprojlim_{N'_1 \subset N_1} \varinjlim_{\substack{N'_2 \subset N_2 \\ N'_2 \supset \operatorname{im}(f|_{N'_1}) }} \left[ \omega(f|_{N'_1}): \omega(N'_1) \to \omega(N'_2) \right] \\ & \in \varprojlim_{N'_1 \subset N_1} \varinjlim_{N'_2 \subset N_2} \operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}\text{-}}B}\left( \omega(N'_1), \omega(N'_2)\right). \end{align*}\] The right-hand side determines a homomorphism \(\Omega(N_1)\to\Omega(N_2)\) in the evident way.

For readers using the theory of Ind-completion from §§reference–reference, this construction merely identifies \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}\text{-}}A\) with \(\operatorname{Ind}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}_{\mathrm{fg}}\text{-}}A)\) and then uses the cocompleteness of \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}\text{-}}B\) to extend \(\omega\) to \(\operatorname{Ind}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}_{\mathrm{fg}}\text{-}}A)\) by filtered colimits; see Definition–Proposition reference.

The following properties are general facts about Ind-completion and can also be checked directly from the construction of \(\Omega\).

  • The restriction of \(\Omega\) to \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}_{\mathrm{fg}}\text{-}}A\) is isomorphic to \(\omega\).

  • \(\Omega\) is an exact \(\Bbbk\)-linear functor; see Proposition reference(ii) and the preceding discussion, which use the exactness of \(\omega\) and the fact that \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}\text{-}}B\) is a Grothendieck category.

  • \(\Omega\) preserves all small colimits; see Proposition reference(iii), which uses the fact that \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}_{\mathrm{fg}}\text{-}}A\) is essentially small.

Moreover, since \(\omega\) is left exact, for all finitely generated submodules \(N'\subset N''\) of \(N\), the transition homomorphism \(\omega(N')\to\omega(N'')\) in equation is monic. The elementary construction of filtered colimits in the category of modules then gives \[\Omega(N) = 0 \iff \forall N', \; \omega(N') = 0 \stackrel{\because \;\omega\;\text{faithful}}{\iff} \; \forall N', \; N' = 0 \iff N = 0.\] Thus \(\Omega\) is faithful and exact.

We may now apply Theorem reference to \(\Omega\) to obtain \[\Omega \simeq (\cdot) \ensuremath{\underset{A}{\otimes}} P, \quad P := \Omega(A) = \omega(A) \in \operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}_{\mathrm{pfg}}\text{-}}B).\] Its restriction to \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}_{\mathrm{fg}}\text{-}}A\) gives the original functor \(\omega\). Together with Proposition reference, this also gives the description of \(\operatorname{coE}(\omega)\) in (i).

Since \(\Omega\) is faithful and exact, Proposition reference shows that the adjoint pair \[\begin{equation*} \text{Diagram chapter9-unit-128-d004} \end{equation*}\] is comonadic, with corresponding coalgebra \(P^\vee\ensuremath{\underset{A}{\otimes}}P\). Thus \(\Omega\) factors canonically as an equivalence followed by the forgetful functor: \[\ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}\text{-}}A \xrightarrow[\sim]{\overline{\Omega}} \ensuremath{\mathsf{Comod}\text{-}}\left(P^\vee \ensuremath{\underset{A}{\otimes}} P\right) \xrightarrow{U} \ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}\text{-}}B.\]

By Proposition reference, this factorization restricts to the commutative diagram \[\text{Diagram chapter9-unit-128-d005}\] The composite of the first row is \(\omega\), which is known to take values in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}_{\mathrm{pfg}}\text{-}}B\); this proves (iii). The curved arrow in the diagram is therefore \(\overline\omega\), and (ii) follows.

The relation between the preceding result and abelian subcategories is also easy to describe.

Lemma. Suppose that \(\mathcal{A}\) and \(\omega\) satisfy the hypotheses of Lemma reference. Every abelian subcategory \(\mathcal{A}'\), together with \(\omega|_{\mathcal{A}'}\), also satisfies these hypotheses. Moreover, the canonical homomorphism \(\operatorname{coE}(\omega|_{\mathcal{A}'})\to\operatorname{coE}(\omega)\) from Remark reference is monic.

Proof. It is clear that \(\mathcal{A}'\) is locally finite. Without loss of generality, we may suppose that \(\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{A}')\subset\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{A})\) is closed under isomorphisms. We use the following general properties; their proofs are not difficult and can be found in the exercises of .

  • Choose a projective generator \(s\) of \(\mathcal{A}\). It has a largest quotient object lying in \(\mathcal{A}'\), denoted by \(s'\), and \(s'\) is a projective generator of \(\mathcal{A}'\).

  • Write \(A:=\operatorname{End}(s)\) and \(A':=\operatorname{End}(s')\simeq\operatorname{Hom}(s,s')\). There is a two-sided ideal \(\mathfrak a\) such that \(A\to A'\) induces \(A/\mathfrak a\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}A'\). More explicitly, if \(t:=\operatorname{ker}[s\twoheadrightarrow s']\subset s\), then \(\mathfrak a=\operatorname{Hom}(s,t)\subset A\).

  • After identifying \(\mathcal{A}\) with \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}_{\mathrm{fg}}\text{-}}A\), the category \(\mathcal{A}'\) is identified with the full subcategory consisting of modules annihilated by \(\mathfrak a\).

Choose a basis \(\phi_1,\ldots,\phi_m\) of the \(\Bbbk\)-vector space \(\operatorname{Hom}(s,t)\). The generator property gives an exact sequence \[s^{\oplus m} \xrightarrow{(\phi_i)_i} s \to s' \to 0.\] Write \(P:=\omega(s)\) and \(P':=\omega(s')\). The algebra \(A\) acts on \(P\) from the left through \(\omega\), and the corresponding exact sequence \[P^{\oplus m} \xrightarrow{(\omega(\phi_i))_i} P \to P' \to 0\] shows that \(P'\simeq P/\mathfrak aP\).

The proof of Lemma reference showed that \((\mathord\cdot)\ensuremath{\underset{A}{\otimes}}P:\ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}\text{-}}A\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}\text{-}}B\) is exact. Together with the description above, this gives \[\begin{align*} (P')^\vee \ensuremath{\underset{A/\mathfrak{a}}{\otimes}} P' & \simeq (A/\mathfrak{a} \ensuremath{\underset{A}{\otimes}} P)^\vee \ensuremath{\underset{A/\mathfrak{a}}{\otimes}} ( A/\mathfrak{a} \ensuremath{\underset{A}{\otimes}} P) \\ & \simeq (A/\mathfrak{a} \ensuremath{\underset{A}{\otimes}} P)^\vee \ensuremath{\underset{A}{\otimes}} P \\ & \hookrightarrow P^\vee \ensuremath{\underset{A}{\otimes}} P. \end{align*}\] It is not difficult to check that this is precisely the canonical homomorphism \(\operatorname{coE}(\omega|_{\mathcal{A}'})\to\operatorname{coE}(\omega)\).

Example. Here are some initial applications of Lemma reference for \(B=\Bbbk\); recall that \(\Bbbk\) is assumed to be a field. For a nonempty set \(I\), define \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Vect}}_I(\Bbbk)\) to be the category of \(I\)-graded \(\Bbbk\)-vector spaces (Example reference, with trivial \(\epsilon\)). The objects \((M^i)_{i\in I}\) satisfying \(\sum_i\dim_{\Bbbk}M^i<\infty\) form the full subcategory \(\mathcal{A}:=\ensuremath{\mathsf{Vect}}_{I,\mathrm f}(\Bbbk)\). Write \(\Bbbk[I]\) for the \(\Bbbk\)-vector space with basis \(I\); the following structure makes it a cocommutative coalgebra: \[\epsilon(i) = 1, \quad \Delta(i) = i \otimes i, \quad i \in I.\] Define a functor \(\omega_I:\mathcal{A}\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{Vect}}_{\mathrm f}(\Bbbk)\) by sending \((M^i)_{i\in I}\) to \(\bigoplus_iM^i\).

  1. The simplest case \(|I|=1\) amounts to taking \(\mathcal{A}=\ensuremath{\mathsf{Vect}}_{\mathrm f}(\Bbbk)\) and \(\omega_I=\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}\); the projective generator \(s\) may be taken to be \(\Bbbk\). A direct calculation from the definition, or Lemma reference(i), gives \[\operatorname{coE}(\omega_I) \simeq \Bbbk, \quad \epsilon(1) = 1, \quad \Delta(1) = 1 \otimes 1.\] Thus, when \(|I|=1\), we have \(\operatorname{coE}(\omega_I)\simeq\Bbbk\simeq\Bbbk[I]\).

  2. Next, if \(I\) is finite, then \(\operatorname{coE}(\omega_I)\simeq\Bbbk[I]\). This can be deduced from the preceding case or understood by applying Lemma reference(i), taking as projective generator \(s\) the object defined by \(M^i=\Bbbk\) for every \(i\).

    Observe that if \(I\subset J\), the embedding \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Vect}}_{I,\mathrm f}(\Bbbk)\subset \ensuremath{\mathsf{Vect}}_{J,\mathrm f}(\Bbbk)\) induces \(\Bbbk[I]\to\Bbbk[J]\), namely the coalgebra embedding induced by \(I\hookrightarrow J\).

  3. For every nonempty set \(I\), we likewise have \(\operatorname{coE}(\omega_I)\simeq\Bbbk[I]\). More precisely, if \(x\in M^i\) and \(\phi\in(M^i)^\vee\) satisfy \(\phi(x)=1\), then \([\phi\otimes x]\in\operatorname{coE}(\omega_I)\) corresponds to \(i\in\Bbbk[I]\).

    The set \(I\) is the filtered union of its finite subsets, and both the category \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Vect}}_{I,\mathrm f}(\Bbbk)\) and the coalgebra \(\Bbbk[I]\) reduce to the finite case in the same way. Since the case of finite \(I\) is known, Proposition reference immediately gives \[\operatorname{coE}(\omega_I) \simeq \varinjlim_{J \subset I, |J| < \infty} \operatorname{coE}(\omega_J).\] Taking colimits is a key technique that will reappear in the next proof.

The following theorem is the main intermediate result so far, and its proof depends on the technical results of §reference. Recall that if \((L,\mu,\eta,\Delta,\epsilon)\) is a \(B\)-bialgebra, Proposition reference equips \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Comod}\text{-}}L\) with a natural monoidal structure: the operation \(\otimes\) comes from \(\mu\), and the unit is \(B\) with the coaction given by \(\eta:B\to B\ensuremath{\underset{B}{\otimes}}L\simeq L\). Observe that \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Comod}_{\mathrm{pf}}\text{-}}L\) is a monoidal subcategory.

Theorem. Let \(\Bbbk\) be a field, let \(B\) be a \(\Bbbk\)-algebra, let \(\mathcal{A}\) be a locally finite abelian category, and let \(\omega:\mathcal{A}\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}\text{-}}B\) be a faithful exact functor taking values in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}_{\mathrm{pfg}}\text{-}}B\).

  1. The functor \(\overline\omega\) in the canonical factorization equation is an equivalence of categories. Moreover, there is a family of abelian subcategories \(\mathcal{A}'\) of \(\mathcal{A}\) such that

    • \(\bigcup_{\mathcal{A}'}\mathcal{A}'=\mathcal{A}\) is a filtered union of subcategories;

    • every \(\mathcal{A}'\) has a projective generator,

    and for this family there is an isomorphism of coalgebras \[\operatorname{coE}(\omega) \simeq \varinjlim_{\mathcal{A}'} \operatorname{coE}(\omega'), \quad \omega' := \omega|_{\mathcal{A}'}.\] The transition homomorphisms on the right come from Remark reference, and all of them are coalgebra embeddings. In this situation, \[\ensuremath{\mathsf{Comod}_{\mathrm f}\text{-}}\operatorname{coE}(\omega)= \ensuremath{\mathsf{Comod}_{\mathrm{pf}}\text{-}}\operatorname{coE}(\omega).\]

  2. If \(\mathcal{A}\) has a monoidal-category structure, \(B=\Bbbk\), and \(\omega\) is a monoidal functor, then with respect to the \(\Bbbk\)-bialgebra structure on \(\operatorname{coE}(\omega)\) from Proposition reference, both \(\overline\omega\) and \(U\) are monoidal functors.

  3. Under the same assumptions, if in addition \(\mathcal{A}\) is a symmetric monoidal category and \(\omega\) is compatible with the braidings, then \(\operatorname{coE}(\omega)\) is commutative as an algebra, while \(\overline\omega\) and \(U\) are also compatible with the braidings.

Proof. Proposition reference writes \(\mathcal{A}\) as the filtered union of abelian subcategories \(\mathcal{A}'\) having projective generators; for example, we may take \(\mathcal{A}'=\ensuremath{\left\langle X \right\rangle}\) for \(X\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{A})\). Proposition reference shows that \(\operatorname{coE}(\omega)\simeq\varinjlim_{\mathcal{A}'}\operatorname{coE}(\omega')\), and Lemma reference shows that all the transition homomorphisms are coalgebra embeddings. The canonical factorization equation is obtained by taking the filtered union of \[\text{Diagram chapter9-unit-129-d001}\] Lemma reference states that every \(\overline{\omega'}\) is an equivalence, so \(\overline\omega\) is also an equivalence. Moreover, \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Comod}_{\mathrm{pf}}\text{-}}\operatorname{coE}(\omega')= \ensuremath{\mathsf{Comod}_{\mathrm f}\text{-}}\operatorname{coE}(\omega')\); the same process simultaneously gives this equality for \(\operatorname{coE}(\omega)\). This proves (i).

If \(\mathcal{A}\) is monoidal and \(B=\Bbbk\), the forgetful functor \(U\) is always monoidal for the structure on \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Comod}\text{-}}\operatorname{coE}(\omega)\) coming from the bialgebra \(\operatorname{coE}(\omega)\). The commutative diagram equation, with all of \(\omega_i,\omega_i',\omega_i''\) replaced by \(\omega\), shows that \(\overline\omega\) is also monoidal. This proves (ii), and a similar argument proves (iii).

Example. Let \(\Gamma\) be a monoid and let \(B=\Bbbk\) be a field, so that \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}_{\mathrm{pfg}}\text{-}}B=\ensuremath{\mathsf{Vect}}_{\mathrm f}(\Bbbk)\). Example reference shows that the coalgebra corresponding to \[\omega_\Gamma: \ensuremath{\mathsf{Vect}}_{\Gamma, \mathrm{f}}(\Bbbk) \to \ensuremath{\mathsf{Vect}}_{\mathrm{f}}(\Bbbk), \quad (M^\gamma)_{\gamma \in \Gamma} \to \bigoplus_\gamma M^\gamma\] is \(\Bbbk[\Gamma]\). Moreover, \(\Bbbk[\Gamma]\) carries a bialgebra structure (Example reference). On the other hand, \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Vect}}_{\Gamma,\mathrm f}(\Bbbk)\) is a monoidal category and \(\omega_\Gamma\) is a monoidal functor (Example reference); this also equips \(\Bbbk[\Gamma]\) with a bialgebra structure. The two structures coincide, as one checks by comparing the description of multiplication in equation with Example reference; the details are left to the reader.

Reconstruction of Hopf Algebras

This section continues the discussion of §reference. Theorem reference constructs the coalgebra \(\operatorname{coE}(\omega)\) from the data \((\mathcal{A}, \omega)\) and identifies \(\mathcal{A}\) with \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Comod}_{\mathrm{f}}\text{-}}\operatorname{coE}(\omega)\). The most basic situation is when \(B = \Bbbk\) is a field. For a \(\Bbbk\)-coalgebra \(L\), take \[\begin{gather*} \mathcal{A} := \ensuremath{\mathsf{Comod}_{\mathrm{f}}\text{-}}L , \\ \omega := U: \ensuremath{\mathsf{Comod}_{\mathrm{f}}\text{-}}L \xrightarrow{\text{forget}} \ensuremath{\mathsf{Vect}}_{\mathrm{f}}(\Bbbk). \end{gather*}\]

Since \(\Bbbk\) is a field, Proposition reference with \(B = \Bbbk\) shows that \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Comod}\text{-}}L\) is an abelian category, while \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Comod}_{\mathrm{f}}\text{-}}L\), formed by the finite-dimensional comodules, is clearly a locally finite abelian subcategory. It is now natural to ask: does the corresponding \(\operatorname{coE}(\omega)\) reconstruct the original datum \(L\), or does it instead produce a new coalgebra? As expected, the answer is “reconstruction”, but a little argument is required.

The first step is to make clear how to compare \(\operatorname{coE}(\omega)\) and \(L\). Since \(L\) coacts from the right on every \(\omega(X)\), the universal property induces a coalgebra homomorphism \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:u-comparison}{} u: \operatorname{coE}(\omega) \to L. \end{equation}\] The original question is equivalent to asking whether \(u\) is an isomorphism. We first prove a simple result.

Lemma. Let \(\Bbbk\) be a field and let \(L\) be a \(\Bbbk\)-coalgebra, with the comultiplication homomorphism denoted by \(\Delta\) and the counit homomorphism by \(\epsilon\). Every right \(L\)-comodule \(V\) is a union of finite-dimensional subcomodules.

Proof. Suppose that the comodule structure is given by \(\rho: V \to V \ensuremath{\underset{\Bbbk}{\otimes}} L\). For each \(x \in V \ensuremath{\underset{\Bbbk}{\otimes}} L\), define the subspace \[V(x) := \ensuremath{\left\langle (\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}\otimes \lambda)(x) : \lambda \in \operatorname{Hom}_{\Bbbk}(L, \Bbbk) \right\rangle} \; \subset V ;\] if \(x\) is written concretely as \(\sum_{i=1}^n v_i \otimes \ell_i\), with \(\ell_1, \ldots, \ell_n\) linearly independent, then clearly \(V(x) = \ensuremath{\left\langle v_1, \ldots, v_n \right\rangle}\), and hence \(x \in V(x) \ensuremath{\underset{\Bbbk}{\otimes}} L\).

Take \(v \in V\). Setting \(x = \rho(v)\) and \(\lambda = \epsilon\) gives \(v \in V(\rho(v))\). We next show that \(\rho(V(\rho(v))) \subset V(\rho(v)) \ensuremath{\underset{\Bbbk}{\otimes}} L\). Write again \(\rho(v) = \sum_i v_i \otimes \ell_i\); the equation \((\rho \otimes \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}})\rho(v) = (\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}\otimes \Delta)\rho(v)\) in the definition of a comodule can be written as the following equation in \(V \ensuremath{\underset{\Bbbk}{\otimes}} L \ensuremath{\underset{\Bbbk}{\otimes}} L\): \[\sum_i \rho(v_i) \otimes \ell_i = \sum_i v_i \otimes \Delta(\ell_i).\]

Extend \(\ell_1, \ldots, \ell_n\) to a basis and contract with the dual basis. This gives \(\rho(v_i) \in V(\rho(v)) \ensuremath{\underset{\Bbbk}{\otimes}} L\) for \(i = 1, \ldots, n\).

Thus every finite-dimensional subspace \(\ensuremath{\left\langle v_1, \ldots, v_m \right\rangle}\) of \(V\) is contained in the subcomodule \(\sum_{i=1}^m V(\rho(v_i))\), which is clearly finite-dimensional.

Lemma. With the notation above, \(u: \operatorname{coE}(\omega) \to L\) in equation is an isomorphism of coalgebras.

Proof. We show that all right \(L\)-comodules \(V\), together with all homomorphisms between them, lift naturally to right \(\operatorname{coE}(\omega)\)-comodules. For \(\dim_{\Bbbk} V < \infty\), this is by definition—apply Definition–Proposition reference to \(\mathcal{A} = \ensuremath{\mathsf{Comod}_{\mathrm{f}}\text{-}}L\) and \(\omega = U\); the general case then follows from Lemma reference.

Now take \(V=L\) with the right \(L\)-comodule structure determined by \(\Delta\). The lifted \(\operatorname{coE}(\omega)\)-comodule structure corresponds to \(\tilde{\Delta}: L \to L \ensuremath{\underset{\Bbbk}{\otimes}} \operatorname{coE}(\omega)\). This is the same as saying that the triangular part of the following diagram commutes: \[\text{Diagram chapter9-unit-130-d001}\] and its square part clearly commutes as well. Denote the composite of the first row by \(\gamma\); then \(u\gamma = \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_L\). It remains only to prove that \(\gamma\) is surjective.

Let \(\rho: V \to V \ensuremath{\underset{\Bbbk}{\otimes}} L\) be a finite-dimensional right \(L\)-comodule. The commutative diagram in the definition \[\text{Diagram chapter9-unit-130-d002}\] is also equivalent to saying that \(\rho\) is a homomorphism of \(L\)-comodules, provided that \(V \ensuremath{\underset{\Bbbk}{\otimes}} L\) is equipped with the comodule structure coming from \(L\) and \(\Delta\). Now lift \(V\) naturally to a \(\operatorname{coE}(\omega)\)-comodule, corresponding to \(\tilde{\rho}: V \to V \ensuremath{\underset{\Bbbk}{\otimes}} \operatorname{coE}(\omega)\); if the comodule \(V \ensuremath{\underset{\Bbbk}{\otimes}} L\) is lifted similarly, its structure corresponds to \(\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}\otimes \tilde{\Delta}: V \ensuremath{\underset{\Bbbk}{\otimes}} L \to V \ensuremath{\underset{\Bbbk}{\otimes}} L \ensuremath{\underset{\Bbbk}{\otimes}} \operatorname{coE}(\omega)\). The comodule homomorphism \(\rho\) also lifts to the \(\operatorname{coE}(\omega)\) level, which is the same as saying that the square in the following diagram commutes: \[\text{Diagram chapter9-unit-130-d003}\] Since the composite of the second row is \(\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}\), we obtain \(\tilde{\rho} = (\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_V \otimes \gamma)\rho\). One checks that the map \(\alpha_V: V^\vee \ensuremath{\underset{\Bbbk}{\otimes}} V \to \operatorname{coE}(\omega)\) induced by \(\tilde{\rho}\) therefore factors as \[V^\vee \ensuremath{\underset{\Bbbk}{\otimes}} V \xrightarrow{\text{induced by $\rho$}} L \xrightarrow{\gamma} \operatorname{coE}(\omega).\]

Recalling the construction of \(\operatorname{coE}(\omega)\), as \(V\) varies, the images \(\operatorname{im}(\alpha_V)\) generate all of \(\operatorname{coE}(\omega)\). Thus \(\gamma\) is surjective.

As one might expect, if \(L\) is a bialgebra, then equation is also an isomorphism of bialgebras. The required argument is entirely routine and need not be spelled out.

Definition. For the chosen field \(\Bbbk\), define the category \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Fib}}(\Bbbk)\) as follows.

  • Its objects are data \((\mathcal{A}, \omega)\), where \(\mathcal{A}\) is a locally finite abelian category (and hence essentially small), and \(\omega: \mathcal{A} \to \ensuremath{\mathsf{Vect}}_{\mathrm{f}}(\Bbbk)\) is a faithful exact functor.

  • A morphism from \((\mathcal{A}, \omega)\) to \((\mathcal{A}', \omega')\) is a datum \((F, \alpha)\), where \(F: \mathcal{A} \to \mathcal{A}'\) is a functor and \(\alpha: \omega \ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}\omega' F\) is an isomorphism of functors. Identities and composition are defined in the evident way.

Similarly, define the category \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Fib}}^{\otimes}(\Bbbk)\), with the following additional conditions:

  • \(\mathcal{A}\) in an object \((\mathcal{A}, \omega)\) must be equipped with a monoidal structure, and \(\omega\) must be a monoidal functor;

  • \(F\) in a morphism must also be a monoidal functor, and \(\alpha\) must be an isomorphism of monoidal functors.

Observe that if \((\mathcal{A}, \omega)\) is an object of \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Fib}}^{\otimes}(\Bbbk)\), faithfulness and exactness imply that \(\operatorname{End}_{\mathcal{A}}(\ensuremath{\bm{1}}) \to \Bbbk\) is a monomorphism of \(\Bbbk\)-algebras; thus in this case \(\operatorname{End}_{\mathcal{A}}(\ensuremath{\bm{1}}) \ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}\Bbbk\).

On the other hand, denote the category of \(\Bbbk\)-coalgebras (respectively, \(\Bbbk\)-bialgebras) and their homomorphisms by \(\Bbbk\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{coAlg}}\) (respectively, \(\Bbbk\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{biAlg}}\)).

  • There are evident functors \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Fib}}(\Bbbk) \to \Bbbk\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{coAlg}}\) and \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Fib}}^{\otimes}(\Bbbk) \to \Bbbk\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{biAlg}}\). Both send an object \((\mathcal{A}, \omega)\) to \(\operatorname{coE}(\omega)\), while a morphism \((\mathcal{A}, \omega) \to (\mathcal{A}', \omega')\) induces a coalgebra or bialgebra homomorphism \(\operatorname{coE}(\omega) \simeq \operatorname{coE}(\omega' F) \to \operatorname{coE}(\omega')\).

  • There are also functors in the opposite direction: for a coalgebra or bialgebra \(L\), take the corresponding datum \(\left(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Comod}_{\mathrm{f}}\text{-}}L, U \right)\); on morphisms, for a homomorphism \(\phi: L \to L'\), a right \(L\)-comodule \((M, \rho)\) becomes a right \(L'\)-comodule through \(M \xrightarrow{(\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}\otimes \phi) \rho} M \otimes L'\). This gives \(\left(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Comod}_{\mathrm{f}}\text{-}}L, U \right) \to \left(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Comod}_{\mathrm{f}}\text{-}}L', U' \right)\).

Theorem. Let \(\Bbbk\) be a field. The constructions above give two pairs of mutually quasi-inverse functors \[\text{Diagram chapter9-unit-130-d004}\]

Proof. Write the functors in the two directions as \(Z: \star \leftrightarrows \star :Y\). For the first pair, the isomorphism \(u\) in Lemma reference gives \(ZY \ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}\), while the equivalence \(\overline{\omega}\) in Theorem reference (i) gives \(\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}YZ\).

For the second pair, since it is already known that when \(L\) is a bialgebra, \(u\) in equation is also an isomorphism of bialgebras, we still have \(ZY \ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}\) in the monoidal setting; meanwhile, \(\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}YZ\) is now the content of Theorem reference (ii).

We now add the duality introduced in §reference to the framework of Reconstruction Theorem reference. As usual, we consider only the simple situation in which \(B = \Bbbk\) is a field.

Theorem. Under the assumptions of Theorem reference, suppose further that \((\mathcal{A}, \omega)\) is an object of \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Fib}}^{\otimes}(\Bbbk)\) and that \(\mathcal{A}\) is both left and right rigid. Then \(\operatorname{coE}(\omega)\) is a Hopf algebra.

Proof. It suffices to show that the bialgebra \(\operatorname{coE}(\omega)\) has an antipode. Use the left rigidity of \(\mathcal{A}\) to define the functor \(X \mapsto {}^* X\). For each \(X \in \operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{A})\), since monoidal functors preserve duals, we obtain \(\omega({}^* X) \simeq \omega(X)^\vee\); since the monoidal structure on \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Vect}}_{\mathrm{f}}(\Bbbk)\) is symmetric, we also obtain \(\omega(X) \simeq \omega({}^* X)^\vee\). Now consider \[\phi \in \omega(X)^\vee \simeq \omega({}^* X), \quad x \in \omega(X) \simeq \omega({}^* X)^\vee ,\] where \(X \in \operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{A})\) is arbitrary. In the notation of Convention reference, both \([\phi \otimes x]\) and \([x \otimes \phi]\) are therefore elements of \(\operatorname{coE}(\omega)\). We claim that \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:Tannaka-aux2}{} \text{there is a linear map}\; S: \operatorname{coE}(\omega) \to \operatorname{coE}(\omega), \;\text{characterized by}\; S[\phi \otimes x] = [x \otimes \phi]. \end{equation}\]

For this, observe that for every morphism \(f: X \to Y\) in \(\mathcal{A}\), there are commutative diagrams \[\text{Diagram chapter9-unit-130-d005} \quad \text{Diagram chapter9-unit-130-d006}\] where all the vertical arrows come from the isomorphisms in the preceding paragraph. For \(\psi \in \omega(Y)^\vee\) and \(x \in \omega(X)\), there are corresponding elements \(\psi' \in \omega({}^* Y)\) and \(x' \in \omega({}^* X)^\vee\) such that, respectively, \[\omega(f)^\vee (\psi) \leftrightarrow \omega({}^* f)(\psi'), \quad \omega(f)(x) \leftrightarrow \omega({}^* f)^\vee(x').\] Substituting this into the construction and description of \(\operatorname{coE}(\omega)\) in the proof of Proposition reference, we see that \(\delta_f\) there corresponds to \(\delta_{{}^* f}\). Thus

\([\phi \otimes x] \mapsto [x \otimes \phi]\) indeed defines a unique linear map \(S\), proving equation.

Our goal is to prove that \(S\) is an antipode. The construction in the preceding paragraph can also be carried out with \(X^*\) in place of \({}^* X\), yielding a linear map \(T: \operatorname{coE}(\omega) \to \operatorname{coE}(\omega)\); this map is likewise written in the form \([\phi \otimes x] \mapsto [x \otimes \phi]\). From \({}^* (X^*) = X = ({}^* X)^*\), it is easy to see that \(ST = \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}= TS\); in particular, \(S\) is an isomorphism. This is the first requirement for an antipode.

Next, denote the multiplication, comultiplication, unit, and counit homomorphisms of \(\operatorname{coE}(\omega)\) by \(\mu\), \(\Delta\), \(\eta\), and \(\epsilon\), respectively. Choose an object \(X\) and a basis \(v_1, \ldots, v_n\) of the \(\Bbbk\)-vector space \(\omega(X)\). Denote the dual basis of \(\omega(X)^\vee\) by \(\check{v}_1, \ldots, \check{v}_n\). Denote the morphisms for the left dual of \(X\) by \[\mathrm{ev}_X: {}^* X \otimes X \to \ensuremath{\bm{1}}, \quad \mathrm{coev}_X: \ensuremath{\bm{1}}\to X \otimes {}^* X.\] Their images under \(\omega\) realize the duality between \(\omega(X)\) and \(\omega({}^* X)\). Recall that \((\cdot)^\vee\) is the dual in the symmetric monoidal category \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Vect}}_{\mathrm{f}}(\Bbbk)\), with no distinction between left and right; henceforth we may identify \[\begin{equation*} \omega(\ensuremath{\bm{1}}) \simeq \omega(\ensuremath{\bm{1}})^\vee, \quad \omega(X \otimes {}^* X) \simeq \omega({}^* X \otimes X)^\vee, \end{equation*}\] and correspondingly identify \(\omega(\mathrm{coev}_X)\) with \(\omega(\mathrm{ev}_X)^\vee\).

For every \(\phi \in \omega(X)^\vee\) and \(x \in \omega(X)\), the description of \(\Delta\) (respectively, \(\mu\)) in equation (respectively, equation) gives \[\begin{align*} \Delta([\phi \otimes x]) & = \sum_{i=1}^n [\phi \otimes v_i] \otimes [\check{v}_i \otimes x], \\ \mu(S \otimes \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}})\Delta([\phi \otimes x]) & = \sum_{i=1}^n \mu\left( [v_i \otimes \phi] \otimes [\check{v}_i \otimes x] \right) \\ & = \sum_{i=1}^n \left[ (v_i \otimes \check{v}_i) \otimes (\phi \otimes x) \right] \\ & = \left[ \mathrm{coev}_{\omega(X)}(1) \otimes (\phi \otimes x) \right] \\ & = \left[ \omega(\mathrm{coev}_X)(1) \otimes (\phi \otimes x) \right]. \end{align*}\] However, equation implies that the following diagram commutes: \[\text{Diagram chapter9-unit-130-d007}\] Therefore, \[\begin{gather*} \left[ \omega(\mathrm{coev}_X)(1) \otimes (\phi \otimes x) \right] = \eta\left( \omega(\mathrm{ev}_X)(\phi \otimes x) \right) \xlongequal{\text{\href{#eqn:L-counit}{equation}}} \eta\epsilon\left( \phi \otimes x \right), \end{gather*}\] which proves \(\mu(S \otimes \ensuremath{\mathrm{id}})\Delta = \eta\epsilon\). Similarly, \(\mu(\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}\otimes S)\Delta = \eta\epsilon\). Thus \(S\) is an antipode.

Corollary. Under the bijection given by Theorem reference, \[\text{Diagram chapter9-unit-130-d008}\] the category \(\mathcal{A}\) in an object \((\mathcal{A}, \omega)\) on the left is both left and right rigid if and only if the object \(L\) on the right is a Hopf algebra.

Proof. The “only if” direction follows from Theorem reference, whereas the “if” direction was explained in Proposition reference.

In the proof of Theorem reference, the left rigidity of \(\mathcal{A}\) plays the principal role; right rigidity is used only to ensure that \(S\) is an isomorphism. If the definition of a Hopf algebra allows a noninvertible \(S\), then the category of right comodules \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Comod}_{\mathrm{f}}\text{-}}L\) is only left rigid; see the formulas in Proposition reference.

Tannakian Categories

The theory of Tannakian categories is a thorough reformulation, due to Saavedra Rivano and Deligne [Sa72,Del90], of the work of Tadao Tannaka [Ta38] and M. Krein [Kr49] on representations of compact groups; its guiding ideas originate with Grothendieck. Related ideas were later developed far more broadly in Lurie and Bhatt’s work on derived algebraic geometry. We shall broadly follow Deligne’s treatment. Unless stated otherwise, throughout this section we retain the assumptions of §reference, with a fixed field \(\Bbbk\).

Definition. Let \(\mathcal{T}\) be an essentially small abelian category (Definition reference) equipped with a symmetric monoidal structure for which \(\otimes\) is \(\Bbbk\)-linear in each variable. The category \(\mathcal{T}\) is called a Tannakian category over the field \(\Bbbk\) if it has the following properties.

  • If \(\ensuremath{\bm{1}}\) denotes the unit of \(\mathcal{T}\), then \(\operatorname{End}_{\mathcal{T}}(\ensuremath{\bm{1}})=\Bbbk\).

  • As a symmetric monoidal category, \(\mathcal{T}\) is rigid (Definition reference).

  • There exist a commutative \(\Bbbk\)-algebra \(B\), taken by convention to be nonzero, and a right-exact monoidal functor compatible with the braiding \[\omega: \mathcal{T} \to \ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}\text{-}}B.\] Such a functor is called a fiber functor for \(\mathcal{T}\) over \(B\).1

A fiber functor over \(\Bbbk\) is called neutral. If a Tannakian category \(\mathcal{T}\) has a neutral fiber functor, then \(\mathcal{T}\) is called a neutral Tannakian category.

By the definition of the dual of a morphism in Definition reference, the duality functor \((\mathord\cdot)^*\) of a Tannakian category is necessarily \(\Bbbk\)-linear. The preceding definition is quite flexible. If \(\omega\) is a fiber functor over \(B\) and \(B\to B'\) is a homomorphism of commutative \(\Bbbk\)-algebras, then \(\omega\ensuremath{\underset{B}{\otimes}}B'\) is a fiber functor over \(B'\). These axioms have several nontrivial consequences, in which duality plays a key role.

Lemma. Let \(\mathcal{T}\) be a Tannakian category.

  1. For every commutative \(\Bbbk\)-algebra \(B\), every fiber functor \(\omega\) over \(B\) takes values in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}_{\mathrm{pfg}}\text{-}}B\) and is automatically faithful and exact.

  2. There exist a field extension \(\Bbbk'|\Bbbk\) and a fiber functor over \(\Bbbk'\).

  3. If \(\omega\) is a fiber functor over \(B\), the canonical map \[\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{T}}(X,Y)\ensuremath{\underset{\Bbbk}{\otimes}}B\to \operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}\text{-}}B}(\omega(X),\omega(Y))\] is injective.

  4. The category \(\mathcal{T}\) is locally finite (Definition reference).

Proof. For (i), since \(\omega\) is monoidal and \(\mathcal{T}\) is rigid, Proposition reference shows that \(\omega\) takes values in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}_{\mathrm{pfg}}\text{-}}B\). We next prove that \(\omega\) is left exact. Consider any exact sequence in \(\mathcal{T}\) \[0 \to X \to Y \to Z.\] Its dual is also exact, so applying \(\omega\) gives an exact sequence in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}\text{-}}B\) \[\omega(Z)^\vee \to \omega(Y)^\vee \to \omega(X)^\vee \to 0.\] Apply \((\mathord\cdot)^\vee=\operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}\text{-}}B}(\mathord\cdot,B)\) once more. Together with Proposition reference and \(\omega(\mathord\cdot)^{\vee\vee}\simeq\omega(\mathord\cdot)\), this yields the exact sequence \[0 \to \omega(X) \to \omega(Y) \to \omega(Z).\]

For faithfulness, the definition of duality shows that \(X\neq0\) if and only if \(\mathrm{ev}_X:X\otimes X^*\to\ensuremath{\bm{1}}\) is nonzero. Meanwhile, Proposition reference and \(\operatorname{End}_{\mathcal{T}}(\ensuremath{\bm{1}})=\Bbbk\) show that this is equivalent to \(\mathrm{ev}_X\) being an epimorphism. Since \(\omega\) is both monoidal and exact, \(X\neq0\) therefore gives an epimorphism \(\omega(X)\ensuremath{\underset{B}{\otimes}}\omega(X)^\vee\twoheadrightarrow B\), and hence \(\omega(X)\neq0\).

For (ii), choose a fiber functor \(\omega\) over \(B\) and a maximal ideal \(\mathfrak m\) of \(B\), and put \(\Bbbk':=B/\mathfrak m\). Then \(\omega\ensuremath{\underset{B}{\otimes}}\Bbbk'\) is a fiber functor over \(\Bbbk'\).

For (iii), take linearly independent elements \(f_1,\ldots,f_n\in\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{T}}(X,Y)\). In the notation of Corollary reference, they define a morphism \(\Phi:\ensuremath{\bm{1}}^{\oplus n}\to\ensuremath{\EuScript{H}\mathrm{om}}(X,Y)\). We claim that \(\Phi\) is a monomorphism. Indeed, \(\ensuremath{\bm{1}}\) is simple (Proposition reference), so \(\operatorname{ker}(\Phi)\) has finite length. If \(\operatorname{ker}(\Phi)\neq0\), all its composition factors are \(\ensuremath{\bm{1}}\); see §reference. In particular there is a monomorphism \(\ensuremath{\bm{1}}\hookrightarrow\operatorname{ker}(\Phi)\hookrightarrow\ensuremath{\bm{1}}^{\oplus n}\). Since \(\operatorname{End}_{\mathcal{T}}(\ensuremath{\bm{1}})=\Bbbk\), composing with \(\Phi\) gives a morphism \(\ensuremath{\bm{1}}\to\ensuremath{\EuScript{H}\mathrm{om}}(X,Y)\) that is zero on the one hand, but on the other hand corresponds to \(\sum_{i=1}^na_if_i\in\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{T}}(X,Y)\) for some \(a_1,\ldots,a_n\in\Bbbk\) not all zero. This contradicts linear independence.

Applying the exact monoidal functor \(\omega\) to \(\Phi\) gives a monomorphism of \(B\)-modules \(B^{\oplus n}\hookrightarrow \operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}\text{-}}B}(\omega(X),\omega(Y))\). This is precisely the restriction of the canonical map under consideration to \(\bigoplus_{i=1}^n\Bbbk f_i\ensuremath{\underset{\Bbbk}{\otimes}}B\).

For (iv), first use (ii) to obtain a fiber functor \(\omega\) over a field extension \(\Bbbk'\). The faithful exactness in (i) already implies that every \(X\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{T})\) has finite length. Next, (iii) gives a \(\Bbbk'\)-linear embedding \[\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{T}}(X,Y)\ensuremath{\underset{\Bbbk}{\otimes}}\Bbbk' \hookrightarrow\operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{Vect}}_{\mathrm f}(\Bbbk')} (\omega(X),\omega(Y)).\] The right-hand side is finite-dimensional, and hence \(\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{T}}(X,Y)\) is a finite-dimensional \(\Bbbk\)-vector space.

By Lemma reference, the theoretical framework of §reference applies to every Tannakian category \(\mathcal{T}\) and every fiber functor \(\omega:\mathcal{T}\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}_{\mathrm{pfg}}\text{-}}B\) over a commutative \(\Bbbk\)-algebra \(B\). From the viewpoint of algebraic geometry, \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}_{\mathrm{pfg}}\text{-}}B\) corresponds to the category of vector bundles on the affine scheme \(\operatorname{Spec}B\). It is therefore necessary to consider general \(B\), although doing so also requires additional theoretical tools. The reconstruction theorem below treats only the case \(B=\Bbbk\).

Theorem. Let \(\mathcal{T}\) be a neutral Tannakian category and let \(\omega:\mathcal{T}\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{Vect}}_{\mathrm f}(\Bbbk)\) be a neutral fiber functor. Then \(\omega\) factors canonically as \[\mathcal{T} \xrightarrow{\overline{\omega}} \ensuremath{\mathsf{Comod}_{\mathrm{f}}\text{-}}\operatorname{coE}(\omega) \xrightarrow{U} \ensuremath{\mathsf{Vect}}_{\mathrm{f}}(\Bbbk),\] where \(\operatorname{coE}(\omega)\) carries a canonical commutative Hopf algebra structure, and \(\overline\omega\) is an equivalence of symmetric monoidal categories.

Proof. Since \(\mathcal{T}\) is now known to be locally finite, the assertion follows immediately from Theorems reference and reference.

Example. Let \(H\) be a commutative Hopf \(\Bbbk\)-algebra. Proposition reference shows that the category of finite-dimensional comodules \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Comod}_{\mathrm f}\text{-}}H\) is naturally a neutral Tannakian category, with the forgetful functor as its standard neutral fiber functor: \[\omega: \ensuremath{\mathsf{Comod}_{\mathrm{f}}\text{-}}H \to \ensuremath{\mathsf{Vect}}_{\mathrm{f}}(\Bbbk), \quad M \mapsto (M\;\text{as a vector space}).\] Theorem reference says that, up to equivalence, this family of examples exhausts all neutral Tannakian categories.

Example. Let \((\Gamma,+)\) be an abelian group and put \(\mathcal{T}=\ensuremath{\mathsf{Vect}}_{\Gamma,\mathrm f}(\Bbbk)\), in the notation of Examples reference and reference. Equip \(\mathcal{T}\) with the standard braiding \[\begin{align*} c(M, N): M \otimes N & \ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}N \otimes M \\ x \otimes y & \mapsto y \otimes x, \quad x \in M^\gamma, \; y \in N^\eta. \end{align*}\] This makes \(\mathcal{T}\) a neutral Tannakian category, with \(\omega_\Gamma:(M^\gamma)_{\gamma\in\Gamma}\mapsto \bigoplus_\gamma M^\gamma\) as neutral fiber functor. The key point is rigidity, which is precisely the multivariable version of Example reference. The corresponding endomorphism coalgebra is already known: it is the Hopf algebra \(\Bbbk[\Gamma]\).

Although \(\Gamma=\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\) and \(\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}/2\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\) are both allowed, the braiding here does not involve the Koszul sign rule equation; if it did, \(\omega_\Gamma\) would not preserve the braiding. The theory of Tannakian categories therefore cannot be applied directly to categories such as the category of super vector spaces \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Vect}}^-_{\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}/2\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}},\mathrm f}(\Bbbk)\), because it has no fiber functor to \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Vect}}_{\mathrm f}(\Bbbk)\).

Remark. Some assertions of linear algebra—that is, assertions about fiber functors—can be translated into the language of Hopf algebras by Theorem reference. As a simple and useful example, for a neutral fiber functor \(\omega\) and an abelian group \((\Gamma,+)\), consider the following three kinds of data.

  1. Equip each \(\omega(X)\) with a \(\Gamma\)-grading; that is, specify a family of isomorphisms \[\alpha_X: \omega(X) \ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}\omega_\Gamma(FX), \quad FX \in \operatorname{Ob}\left( \ensuremath{\mathsf{Vect}}_{\Gamma, \mathrm{f}}(\Bbbk) \right),\] with \(FX\) and \(\alpha_X\) functorial in \(X\), and such that \(\omega(\ensuremath{\bm{1}})\simeq\Bbbk\) and \(\omega(X\otimes X')\simeq\omega(X)\otimes\omega(X')\) both lift to the level of \(\Gamma\)-graded vector spaces.

  2. Specify a monoidal functor \(F:\mathcal{T}\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{Vect}}_{\Gamma,\mathrm f}(\Bbbk)\) together with an isomorphism of monoidal functors \(\alpha:\omega\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}\omega_\Gamma F\).

  3. Specify a homomorphism of \(\Bbbk\)-bialgebras \(\operatorname{coE}(\omega)\to\Bbbk[\Gamma]\).

Data (i) and (ii) differ only in wording. In the language of Definition reference, (ii) is the same as specifying the morphism in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Fib}}^{\otimes}(\Bbbk)\) \((F,\alpha):(\mathcal{T},\omega)\to (\ensuremath{\mathsf{Vect}}_{\Gamma,\mathrm f}(\Bbbk),\omega_\Gamma)\). Hence the Reconstruction Theorem reference ensures that (ii) and (iii) are equivalent.

For example, for the most common grading \(\Gamma=\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\), data (iii) amount to giving a homomorphism of Hopf algebras \(\operatorname{coE}(\omega)\to\Bbbk[T,T^{-1}]\), where \(T\) is an indeterminate.
