  1. The term comes from the Grothendieck school and is rooted in an analogy with the theory of covering spaces.↩︎

Finally, we briefly discuss the relationship between fiber functors. Unlike the preceding discussion, this part does not involve the reconstruction theorem. Let \(\mathcal{T}\) be a Tannakian category, and let \(\omega_1,\omega_2\) be fiber functors over a commutative \(\Bbbk\)-algebra \(B\). For every commutative \(B\)-algebra \(B'\), define the set \[\begin{equation*} \ensuremath{\EuScript{H}\mathrm{om}}^\otimes_B(\omega_2, \omega_1)(B') := \operatorname{Hom}_{\text{monoidal functors}}\left( \omega_2 \ensuremath{\underset{B}{\otimes}} B', \omega_1 \ensuremath{\underset{B}{\otimes}} B' \right). \end{equation*}\] As \(B'\) varies, this defines a functor \(B\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{CAlg}}\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{Set}}\). Recall that Proposition reference (iii) equips \(\operatorname{coH}_B(\omega_1,\omega_2)\) with the structure of a commutative \(B\)-algebra.

Proposition. For a Tannakian category \(\mathcal{T}\) and fiber functors \(\omega_1,\omega_2:\mathcal{T}\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}\text{-}}B\), there is an isomorphism of functors \[\ensuremath{\EuScript{H}\mathrm{om}}^\otimes_B(\omega_2, \omega_1) \simeq \operatorname{Hom}_{B\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{CAlg}}}\left( \operatorname{coH}_B(\omega_1, \omega_2) , \; \cdot \; \right).\] Composition of homomorphisms on the right is induced by equation.

Proof. To simplify notation, write \(\operatorname{coH}_B(\omega_1,\omega_2)\) as \(\operatorname{coH}\) from now on. Specifying a morphism, without regard to the monoidal structure, \[\tilde{\varphi}: \omega_2 \ensuremath{\underset{B}{\otimes}} B' \to \omega_1 \ensuremath{\underset{B}{\otimes}} B' \quad (\text{both valued in }\ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}\text{-}}B')\] is equivalent to specifying a morphism \[\varphi: \omega_2 \to \omega_1 \ensuremath{\underset{B}{\otimes}} B' \quad (\text{both valued in }\ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}\text{-}}B),\] which, by the universal property of \(\operatorname{coH}\), is in turn equivalent to specifying a homomorphism of \(B\)-modules \[\psi: \operatorname{coH}\to B'.\] It remains to prove that \(\tilde{\varphi}\) preserves the monoidal structure if and only if \(\psi\) is a homomorphism of \(B\)-algebras. The argument is formal, although spelling it out is somewhat lengthy.

Write the multiplication morphisms as \(m:B'\ensuremath{\underset{B}{\otimes}}B'\to B'\) and \(\mu:\operatorname{coH}\ensuremath{\underset{B}{\otimes}}\operatorname{coH}\to\operatorname{coH}\). It is immediate that \(\tilde{\varphi}\) preserves the unit, respectively \(\otimes\), if and only if the left-hand, respectively right-hand, diagram below always commutes: \[\text{Diagram chapter9-unit-132-d001} \quad \text{Diagram chapter9-unit-132-d002}\]

First consider the left-hand diagram. Its first row factors as \(\omega_2(\ensuremath{\bm{1}})\to\omega_1(\ensuremath{\bm{1}})\ensuremath{\underset{B}{\otimes}}\operatorname{coH} \xrightarrow{\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}\otimes\psi}\omega_1(\ensuremath{\bm{1}})\ensuremath{\underset{B}{\otimes}}B'\). After identifying every \(\omega_i(\ensuremath{\bm{1}})\) with \(B\), commutativity of the left-hand diagram is equivalent to commutativity of \(\text{Diagram chapter9-unit-132-d003}\), which in turn is equivalent to \(\psi\) preserving the unit.

We now show that commutativity of the right-hand diagram is equivalent to \(\psi\) preserving multiplication. Consider \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:Isom-Tannakian-aux0}{} \text{Diagram chapter9-unit-132-d004} \end{equation}\] The upper and lower curved regions always commute, while commutativity of the square on the left reduces to the characterization of \(\mu\) in equation.

Define \(\eta:=\omega_1^\vee\ensuremath{\underset{B}{\otimes}}\omega_2\), which is a monoidal functor \(\mathcal{T}\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}\text{-}}B\). The square portion of equation can be rearranged as \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:Isom-Tannakian-aux}{} \text{Diagram chapter9-unit-132-diagram-005} \end{equation}\] The left-hand square still commutes, while \(\psi\) preserves multiplication if and only if the right-hand square commutes.

If \(\tilde{\varphi}\) preserves \(\otimes\), then the large outer frame in equation commutes, and hence so does the outer frame of its square portion. Thus the outer frame of equation commutes. This shows that the right-hand square commutes after precomposition with \(\eta(X)\ensuremath{\underset{B}{\otimes}}\eta(Y)\to\operatorname{coH}\ensuremath{\underset{B}{\otimes}}\operatorname{coH}\). Since \(X\) and \(Y\) are arbitrary, the universal property of \(\operatorname{coH}\), or its concrete construction in Proposition reference, suffices to show that the right-hand square in equation commutes.

Conversely, suppose the right-hand square in equation commutes. Then the entire diagram equation commutes, so the large outer frame in equation commutes; hence \(\tilde{\varphi}\) preserves \(\otimes\). This completes the verification.

The rigidity of \(\mathcal{T}\) implies that every element of \(\ensuremath{\EuScript{H}\mathrm{om}}^\otimes_B(\omega_2,\omega_1)(B')\) is an isomorphism; this is an application of Proposition reference. The next result is therefore immediate.

Corollary. For a Tannakian category \(\mathcal{T}\), a commutative \(\Bbbk\)-algebra \(B\), and a fiber functor \(\omega:\mathcal{T}\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}\text{-}}B\), write \(\operatorname{Aut}^{\otimes}(\omega)\) for the group of monoidal automorphisms of \(\omega\). Then, for every commutative \(B\)-algebra \(B'\), there is a canonical isomorphism \[\operatorname{Aut}^{\otimes}\left( \omega \ensuremath{\underset{B}{\otimes}} B' \right) \simeq \operatorname{Hom}_{B\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{CAlg}}}\left(\operatorname{coE}_B(\omega), B' \right),\] where multiplication in the group on the right is reflected by the comultiplication of \(\operatorname{coE}_B(\omega)\).

One can further show that the identity element and inversion in the automorphism group arise respectively from the counit morphism and the antipode of \(\operatorname{coE}_B(\omega)\). The verification is simple and formal, so it is left as an exercise for this chapter. Considering the Yoneda embedding of \(B\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{CAlg}}\) gives the following conclusion: \[\text{Diagram chapter9-unit-132-d005}\] Thus, once \(\operatorname{Aut}^{\otimes}\) is viewed functorially, the entire long story of the endomorphism coalgebra ultimately returns to the group of \(\otimes\)-automorphisms of the fiber functor.

In the situation of Proposition reference, Deligne proved in [Del90] that \(\operatorname{coH}_B(\omega_1,\omega_2)\) is faithfully flat as a \(B\)-module; in particular, \(\operatorname{coH}_B(\omega_1,\omega_2)\neq0\). We shall not give the detailed proof, but its importance in algebraic geometry is worth mentioning. It guarantees the existence of a faithfully flat \(B\)-algebra \(B'\) and an isomorphism \(\omega_1\ensuremath{\underset{B}{\otimes}}B'\simeq\omega_2\ensuremath{\underset{B}{\otimes}}B'\); for example, one may take \(B'=\operatorname{coH}_B(\omega_1,\omega_2)\). Thus fiber functors are unique up to faithfully flat change of rings, while properties over the original ring \(B\) can in principle be reconstructed from descent data as in §reference. This is the principal benefit of faithful flatness.

The Tannaka–Krein Theorem for Finite Groups

Classical Tannaka–Krein theory [Ta38, Kr49] is chiefly concerned with the following question: given a compact topological group \(G\), how can \(G\) be reconstructed from its category of representations? The answer is closely tied to the tensor-product structure and duality; see [FL14]. This section gives a concise interpretation of the Tannaka–Krein reconstruction theorem based on the preceding results, but treats only finite groups rather than compact groups.

Let \(G\) be a group and \(\Bbbk\) a field. Henceforth write \(\otimes := \otimes_{\Bbbk}\), and denote the identity element of \(G\) by \(1_G\).

The principal objects of interest are the \(G\)-modules introduced in Definition reference, which in many contexts are also called representations of \(G\). In brief, they are \(\Bbbk\)-vector spaces \(V\) equipped with a linear left \(G\)-action \(G \times V \to V\), written as left multiplication \((g,v)\mapsto gv\). All \(G\)-modules form a \(\Bbbk\)-linear Abelian category \(G\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\), whose \(\operatorname{Hom}\) is denoted by \(\operatorname{Hom}_G\). The forgetful functor \[\omega: G\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}} \to \ensuremath{\mathsf{Vect}}(\Bbbk)\] of course sends a \(G\)-module \(V\) to its underlying \(\Bbbk\)-vector space \(V\).

Write the group algebra of \(G\) as \(\Bbbk[G]\); by Example reference, it is a Hopf algebra. As stated in Proposition reference, \(G\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\) is isomorphic to \(\Bbbk[G]\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\), and we shall switch between these two viewpoints without further comment.

Convention. The dimension of a \(G\)-module means its dimension as a \(\Bbbk\)-vector space. Write \(G\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}_{\mathrm{f}}\) for the full subcategory of \(G\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\) consisting of finite-dimensional \(G\)-modules.

The field \(\Bbbk\) endowed with the trivial \(G\)-action is called the trivial \(G\)-module (Example reference). For \(G\)-modules \(V\) and \(W\), the spaces \(V\otimes W\) and \(\operatorname{Hom}(V,W):=\operatorname{Hom}_{\Bbbk}(V,W)\) carry canonical \(G\)-module structures. The special case \(\operatorname{Hom}(V,\Bbbk)\) of the latter is called the contragredient \(G\)-module of \(V\), and is also denoted by \(V^*\) to distinguish it from the vector-space dual. These operations were described in detail after Definition reference.

Proposition. The tensor-product operation above, \((V,W)\mapsto V\otimes W\), gives \(G\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\) a symmetric monoidal structure whose unit is the trivial \(G\)-module \(\Bbbk\), and makes the forgetful functor \(G\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{Vect}}(\Bbbk)\) monoidal. The full subcategory \(G\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}_{\mathrm{f}}\) is then a neutral Tannakian category, and the forgetful functor \(\omega:G\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}_{\mathrm{f}}\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{Vect}}_{\mathrm{f}}(\Bbbk)\) is its fiber functor.

Proof. The symmetric monoidal structure on \(G\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\) can be checked directly from the definition of the tensor product. Readers who prefer a big-picture account may instead reason as follows.

  • Since \(\Bbbk[G]\) is a Hopf algebra, Proposition reference equips \(\Bbbk[G]\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\) with a monoidal structure for which the forgetful functor is monoidal. Because the comultiplication on \(\Bbbk[G]\) is \(g\mapsto g\otimes g\), carefully expanding the definitions shows that this is precisely the tensor-product operation defined above.

  • Since \(\Bbbk[G]\) is cocommutative, Proposition reference (i) further implies that \(\Bbbk[G]\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\) is a symmetric monoidal category.

Clearly \(G\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}_{\mathrm{f}}\) is a monoidal subcategory of \(G\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\) and is also an Abelian category. For every \(n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}_{\geq 0}\), all \(G\)-module structures that can be placed on \(\Bbbk^n\) form a small set; hence \(G\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}_{\mathrm{f}}\) is essentially small. Plainly, \[\operatorname{End}_G\left(\Bbbk:\; \text{the trivial $G$-module}\right) = \Bbbk.\]

Checking the definition of duality in §reference step by step shows that the contragredient operation \(V\mapsto V^*\) makes \(G\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}_{\mathrm{f}}\) rigid. Its duality data come from the familiar morphisms \[\text{Diagram chapter9-unit-133-d001} \quad \text{Diagram chapter9-unit-133-d002}\] where \((v_i)_i\) is any basis of \(V\) as a vector space and \((\check v_i)_i\) is its dual basis; both are morphisms in \(G\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\). From the viewpoint of the Hopf algebra \(\Bbbk[G]\), rigidity also follows from Proposition reference and the fact that the antipode of \(\Bbbk[G]\) is \(g\mapsto g^{-1}\).

The constructions above also show that the forgetful functor \(\omega:G\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}_{\mathrm{f}}\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{Vect}}_{\mathrm{f}}(\Bbbk)\) is monoidal, compatible with the symmetric monoidal structures on both sides, and plainly exact. Thus \(\omega\) is a neutral fiber functor on the neutral Tannakian category \(G\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}_{\mathrm{f}}\).

From now on suppose that \(G\) is finite. The central question of this section is:

How can the group \(G\) be reconstructed from the data \(\left(G\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}_{\mathrm{f}},\omega\right)\)?

The results obtained in §reference already bring us close to an answer, but the machinery still requires some adjustment. First we must interpret \(G\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}_{\mathrm{f}}\) as a comodule category.

Definition. Continue to assume that \(G\) is finite. Define the \(\Bbbk\)-vector space \[C(G) := \left\{\text{maps}\; f: G \to \Bbbk \right\},\] with vector-space structure given by pointwise operations. There is moreover a canonical isomorphism \[\text{Diagram chapter9-unit-133-d003}\]

Identifying \(C(G)\otimes C(G)\) with \(C(G\times G)\), the space \(C(G)\) has the following structure:

Multiplication Comultiplication \(\Delta\) Unit Counit \(\epsilon\) Antipode \(S\)
Pointwise multiplication \(f \mapsto \left[ (g_1, g_2) \mapsto f(g_1 g_2) \right]\) Constant function \(1\) \(f \mapsto f(1_G)\) \((Sf)(g) = f(g^{-1})\)

The reader is invited to give a brief verification that this is a commutative Hopf algebra. Consequently, Proposition reference (ii) ensures that \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Comod}\text{-}}C(G)\) is a symmetric monoidal category, while Proposition reference makes \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Comod}_{\mathrm{f}}\text{-}}C(G)\) a rigid symmetric monoidal category; compare the big-picture part of the preceding proof.

For every \(g\in G\), let \(\mathbf{1}_g\in C(G)\) be the element equal to \(1\) at \(g\) and \(0\) elsewhere. These elements form a basis of \(C(G)\), and multiplication and comultiplication are respectively determined by \(\mathbf{1}_{g_1}\mathbf{1}_{g_2}=\delta_{g_1,g_2}\mathbf{1}_{g_1}\) (with \(\delta\) the Kronecker symbol) and \(\Delta(\mathbf{1}_g)=\sum_{xy=g}\mathbf{1}_x\otimes\mathbf{1}_y\).

Proposition. There is an isomorphism of categories \(G\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\simeq\ensuremath{\mathsf{Comod}\text{-}}C(G)\). The right \(C(G)\)-comodule corresponding to a \(G\)-module \(V\) is \(V\) equipped with the linear map \[\text{Diagram chapter9-unit-133-d004}\] while the \(G\)-module corresponding to a right \(C(G)\)-comodule \((V,\rho)\) is \(V\) equipped with the map \[\begin{align*} G \times V & \to V \\ (g, v) & \mapsto \underbracket{\rho(v)}_{\text{map}\; G \to V}(g). \end{align*}\]

Furthermore, the symmetric monoidal structures on \(G\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\) and \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Comod}\text{-}}C(G)\) correspond under this isomorphism. All these isomorphisms preserve the forgetful functors to \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Vect}}(\Bbbk)\), as expressed by the commutative diagram \[\text{Diagram chapter9-unit-133-d005}\]

In particular, \(G\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}_{\mathrm{f}}\) and \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Comod}_{\mathrm{f}}\text{-}}C(G)\) are likewise isomorphic, and the isomorphism preserves their forgetful functors to \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Vect}}_{\mathrm{f}}(\Bbbk)\).

Proof. Unwind the definitions.

Lemma. There is a bijection \(G\xrightarrow{1:1}\operatorname{Hom}_{\Bbbk\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{CAlg}}}(C(G),\Bbbk)\) sending \(g\) to the evaluation homomorphism \(f\mapsto f(g)\). Endow the right-hand side with the binary operation induced by \(\Delta:C(G)\to C(G\times G)\simeq C(G)\otimes C(G)\), which sends \((\varphi_1,\varphi_2)\) to \((\varphi_1\otimes\varphi_2)\circ\Delta\). Then this bijection is an isomorphism of groups.

Proof. Every \(\Bbbk\)-algebra homomorphism \(\varphi:C(G)\to\Bbbk\) is surjective, so \(\operatorname{ker}(\varphi)\) is a maximal ideal. As a \(\Bbbk\)-algebra, however, \(C(G)\) is the direct product of \(G\) copies of \(\Bbbk\), via the map \(f\mapsto(f(g))_{g\in G}\). It is easy to show that the maximal ideals of \(\prod_{g\in G}\Bbbk\) correspond bijectively to the elements of \(G\) through \[g \in G \quad \leftrightarrow \quad \Bbbk \times \cdots \times \underbracket{\{0\}}_{\text{$g$-component}} \times \cdots \times \Bbbk\] See [Li1], or prove this directly. The required bijection follows at once.

To see how group multiplication is reflected on \(\operatorname{Hom}_{\Bbbk\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{CAlg}}}(C(G),\Bbbk)\), it suffices to verify that \[\text{Diagram chapter9-unit-133-d006}\] is commutative. This presents no essential difficulty.

We can now answer the reconstruction question posed above. The answer involves the group \(\operatorname{Aut}^{\otimes}(\omega)\) introduced in Corollary reference; the point is to describe the isomorphism explicitly.

Theorem (T. Tannaka, M. Krein). Let \(\Bbbk\) be a field and \(G\) a finite group. Consider the forgetful functor \(\omega:G\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}_{\mathrm{f}}\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{Vect}}_{\mathrm{f}}(\Bbbk)\). There is an isomorphism of groups \[A: G \ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}\operatorname{Aut}^\otimes(\omega),\] described explicitly as follows: for \(g\in G\) and a finite-dimensional \(G\)-module \(V\), the map \(A(g)_V:V\to V\) is the \(\Bbbk\)-linear map \(v\mapsto gv\).

Proof. We know that \(\omega\) is a neutral fiber functor on the Tannakian category \(G\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}_{\mathrm{f}}\) (Proposition reference), and therefore it has an associated commutative Hopf algebra \(\operatorname{coE}(\omega)\). Taking \(B=B'=\Bbbk\) in Corollary reference gives an isomorphism of groups \[\operatorname{Aut}^{\otimes}(\omega) \simeq \operatorname{Hom}_{\Bbbk\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{CAlg}}}\left(\operatorname{coE}(\omega), \Bbbk \right).\]

The commutative diagram in Proposition reference implies \[\operatorname{coE}(\omega) \simeq \operatorname{coE}\left(\omega_{C(G)}: \ensuremath{\mathsf{Comod}_{\mathrm{f}}\text{-}}C(G) \to \ensuremath{\mathsf{Vect}}_{\mathrm{f}}(\Bbbk) \right),\] while Lemma reference, together with the explanation following it, further gives \[\operatorname{coE}\left( \omega_{C(G)} \right) \simeq C(G);\] all of these are canonical isomorphisms of bialgebras. Substituting Lemma reference, we obtain isomorphisms of groups \[\text{Diagram chapter9-unit-133-d007}\] The image \(B(g)\) under the first isomorphism is the evaluation homomorphism \(f\mapsto f(g)\). On the other hand, by the universal property of \(\operatorname{coE}(\omega)=\operatorname{coH}(\omega,\omega)\simeq C(G)\) in Definition reference (with \(L=\Bbbk\)), the second isomorphism in fact extends to \[\operatorname{Hom}_{\Bbbk}(C(G), \Bbbk) \ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}\operatorname{Hom}_{\Bbbk}(\omega, \omega),\] and that universal property shows that the correspondence between \(A\) and \(B\) is characterized by the following commutative diagram in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Vect}}_{\mathrm{f}}(\Bbbk)\): \[\text{Diagram chapter9-unit-133-d008}\] where \(V\) ranges over the finite-dimensional \(G\)-modules and \(\rho\) is defined as in Proposition reference. Substituting \(B(g)(f)=f(g)\) immediately gives \(A(g)_V(v)=gv\), as required.

Under suitable conditions on \(\Bbbk\), one can go further and characterize those commutative Hopf algebras isomorphic to \(C(G)\) for some finite group \(G\). Such questions belong to elementary algebraic geometry or commutative ring theory, and we shall not pursue them here.

Finally, there is another method that does not depend on a fiber functor and reconstructs a compact group solely from its category of \(G\)-modules. It is called the Doplicher–Roberts reconstruction theorem and has its origins in quantum field theory. Interested readers may consult the survey [Mu07].

Exercises

Let \(\Bbbk\) be a field and let \(V,W\) be \(\Bbbk\)-vector spaces; as usual, set \(V^\vee:=\operatorname{Hom}_{\Bbbk}(V,\Bbbk)\), and so on. Write down the canonical linear map \(V^\vee\ensuremath{\underset{\Bbbk}{\otimes}}W^\vee\to(V\ensuremath{\underset{\Bbbk}{\otimes}}W)^\vee\). Show that it is always injective, but is not surjective when both \(V\) and \(W\) are infinite-dimensional.

Let \(T\) be any object of a monoidal category \(\mathcal{C}\), and let \(\iota:U\to\ensuremath{\bm{1}}\) be a morphism. Assuming that the left dual of \(U\) (respectively the right dual \(U^*\)) exists, prove that the bijection in Proposition reference(iii) \[\operatorname{Hom}(T\otimes U,T)\to\operatorname{Hom}(T,T\otimes{}^*U)\] (respectively \(\operatorname{Hom}(U\otimes T,T)\to\operatorname{Hom}(T,U^*\otimes T)\)) sends \(\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_T\otimes\iota\) to \(\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_T\otimes{}^*\iota\) (respectively sends \(\iota\otimes\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_T\) to \(\iota^*\otimes\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_T\)).

Suppose that the monoidal category \(\mathcal{C}\) is also additive, with zero object \(0\), and that \(\otimes\) is an additive bifunctor. Show that \(X\otimes0=0=0\otimes X\) for every \(X\).

Let \(\mathcal{C}\) be a rigid braided monoidal category that is also Abelian, and suppose that \(\operatorname{End}_{\mathcal{C}}(\ensuremath{\bm{1}})\) is a field. Given \(X\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{C})\) and its right dual \(X^*\), prove that \(X\neq0\) is equivalent to \(X\otimes X^*\neq0\), and also to \(X^*\otimes X\neq0\). Hint. Observe that \(X\neq0\) is equivalent to \(\mathrm{ev}_X\neq0\), and also to \(\mathrm{coev}_X\neq0\); apply Proposition reference.

Let \(\mathcal{C}\) and \(\mathcal{C}'\) be rigid symmetric monoidal categories, both of which are also Abelian, with \(\operatorname{End}_{\mathcal{C}}(\ensuremath{\bm{1}})\) a field and \(\ensuremath{\bm{1}}'\neq0\). Prove that every exact monoidal functor compatible with the braidings, \(F:\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{C}'\), satisfies \(X\neq0\iff F(X)\neq0\). Hint. Repeat the argument of Lemma reference(i), or use the method of the preceding exercise.

(Nobuo Yoneda) Let \(\mathcal{C},\mathcal{D}\) be categories and let \(F:\mathcal{C}^{\operatorname{op}}\times\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{D}\) be a functor. A wedge for \(F\) means data \(\left(W,(e_X)_{X\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{C})}\right)\), also written \(e:W\xrightarrow{\bullet}F\), consisting of

  • an object \(W\) of \(\mathcal{D}\);

  • a morphism \(e_X:W\to F(X,X)\) in \(\mathcal{D}\),

such that the following diagram commutes for every \(f:X\to Y\) in \(\mathcal{C}\): \[\text{Diagram chapter9-unit-134-d001}\]

Dually, define a cowedge to be data \((M,(f_X)_X)\), written \(f:F\xrightarrow{\bullet}M\), subject to the commutativity of \[\text{Diagram chapter9-unit-134-d002}\]

  1. Explain how all wedges (respectively cowedges) for \(F\) form a category. If the category of wedges (respectively cowedges) has a terminal (respectively initial) object, that object is called the end (respectively coend) of \(F\), and is denoted by \[\text{end}\;=\int_{X\in\mathcal{C}}F(X,X),\qquad \text{coend}\;=\int^{X\in\mathcal{C}}F(X,X).\] Here the integral is only notation, but it is not unmotivated.

  2. Interpret equation and the construction of \(\operatorname{coH}(\omega_1,\omega_2)\) in Proposition reference as a special case of a coend.

  3. Suppose that \(\mathcal{C}\) is essentially small relative to the chosen Grothendieck universe (Definition reference), and that \(\mathcal{D}\) is complete (respectively cocomplete). Prove that every \(F\) has an end (respectively coend).

  4. For two functors \(F,G:\mathcal{C}^{\operatorname{op}}\times\mathcal{C}\rightrightarrows\mathcal{D}\), define a dinatural transformation \(\alpha:F\xrightarrow{\bullet}G\) to be data \((\alpha_X)_{X\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{C})}\), where \(\alpha_X:F(X,X)\to G(X,X)\), such that the following diagram commutes for every \(f:X\to Y\) in \(\mathcal{C}\): \[\text{Diagram chapter9-unit-134-d003}\] Show that the wedges and cowedges above are special cases of dinatural transformations. Also show that natural transformations, that is, morphisms between functors \(\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{D}\) or \(\mathcal{C}^{\operatorname{op}}\to\mathcal{D}\), are special cases as well.

A detailed account of ends and coends can be found in the monograph [Lor21].

Consider two functors \(F,G:\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{D}\), where \(\mathcal{C}\) is essentially small. Prove that the set of morphisms between them can be interpreted as the end \[\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{D}^{\mathcal{C}}}(F,G)\simeq \int_{X\in\mathcal{C}}\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{D}}(FX,GX).\] Use this to interpret the center \(Z(\mathcal{C})\) of the category \(\mathcal{C}\) as an end determined by \(\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}}\).

Let \(\Bbbk\) be a field. Prove that the coend of the functor \(\operatorname{Hom}_{\Bbbk}:\ensuremath{\mathsf{Vect}}_{\mathrm f}(\Bbbk)^{\operatorname{op}}\times \ensuremath{\mathsf{Vect}}_{\mathrm f}(\Bbbk)\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{Vect}}_{\mathrm f}(\Bbbk)\) can be identified with \(\Bbbk\) together with the trace maps \[\operatorname{Tr}_V:\operatorname{End}_{\Bbbk}(V)\to\Bbbk,\qquad V:\;\text{a finite-dimensional $\Bbbk$-vector space}.\]

In general, an end resembles an operation of taking invariants, whereas a coend resembles gluing. For readers familiar with simplicial sets, interpret the geometric realization functor \(|\mathord\cdot|\) discussed in §reference as the coend

\[|X|\simeq\int^{[n]\in\ensuremath{\bm\Delta}}X_n\times|\Delta^n|,\qquad X\in\operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{sSet}}).\]

For a small category \(\mathcal{C}\), define the functor category \(\mathcal{C}^\wedge:=\ensuremath{\mathsf{Set}}^{\mathcal{C}^{\operatorname{op}}}\). Prove that for every \(\mathcal{F}\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{C}^\wedge)\) there is a canonical isomorphism in \(\mathcal{C}^\wedge\) \[\int^{X\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{C})}\mathcal{F}(X)\times \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}}(\cdot,X)\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}\mathcal{F}.\] This coend comes from the functor \[\mathcal{C}^{\operatorname{op}}\times\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{C}^\wedge, \quad(X,Y)\mapsto\mathcal{F}(X)\times\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}}(\cdot,Y).\] Hint. See §reference, especially the density theorem reference.

Let \(\mathcal{T}\) be a Tannakian category, let \(\omega:\mathcal{T}\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}\text{-}}B\) be a fiber functor, and let \(B'\) be a commutative \(B\)-algebra. Show that, under the isomorphism of Corollary reference, the identity element and inversion in the group \(\operatorname{Aut}^{\otimes}(\omega\ensuremath{\underset{B}{\otimes}}B')\) arise respectively from the counit and antipode of \(\operatorname{coE}_B(\omega)\) through the functor \(\operatorname{Hom}_{B\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{CAlg}}}(\mathord\cdot,B')\). Hint. The identity and inverse in a group are uniquely determined by multiplication. Multiplication is already known to correspond to the comultiplication of \(\operatorname{coE}(\omega)\).

Let \(G\) be a group, let \(G\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Set}}\) denote the category of all small sets with a left \(G\)-action, and let \(U:G\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Set}}\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{Set}}\) be the forgetful functor. Give a natural isomorphism of groups \[G\simeq\operatorname{Aut}(U).\] Explain how this may be viewed as a simple prototype of the Tannaka–Krein theorem reference. Hint. Apply the Yoneda lemma to \(U\simeq\operatorname{Hom}_{G\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Set}}}(G,\mathord\cdot)\) to obtain an isomorphism of monoids \(G\simeq\operatorname{End}(U)\).

Further Material on Abelian Categories

This appendix is a collection of topics related, directly or indirectly, to Abelian categories; it is almost a miscellaneous stew. In principle, the prerequisites extend no further than the first half of and a small part of . Section reference begins with a brief review of the Yoneda embedding. Its density theorem, Theorem reference, is standard knowledge in category theory, yet is often omitted from textbooks. These tools will be used frequently in §reference. Although the compact objects and presentable categories introduced in §reference are not absolutely necessary elsewhere in this book, they provide a convenient and common language. The discussion of regular cardinals there also paves the way for §reference. The next two sections are directly related to Abelian categories. The Gabriel–Popescu theorem in §reference explains the structure of Grothendieck categories, while the locally finite Abelian categories discussed in §reference are needed in §reference. The focus of the latter section is Proposition reference, due to O. Gabber, whose proof requires some ingenuity.

Density of the Yoneda Embedding

We first recall the theoretical framework surrounding the Yoneda embedding. For any category \(\mathcal{C}\), define the functor categories \[\mathcal{C}^\wedge := \ensuremath{\mathsf{Set}}^{\mathcal{C}^{\operatorname{op}}}, \quad \mathcal{C}^\vee := \left(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Set}}^{\operatorname{op}}\right)^{\mathcal{C}^{\operatorname{op}}} = \left( \ensuremath{\mathsf{Set}}^{\mathcal{C}} \right)^{\operatorname{op}}.\] They are dual to each other: \((\mathcal{C}^\vee)^{\operatorname{op}}=(\mathcal{C}^{\operatorname{op}})^\wedge\). Relative to a previously chosen Grothendieck universe \(\mathcal{U}\), the categories \(\mathcal{C}^\wedge\) and \(\mathcal{C}^\vee\) are generally large unless \(\mathcal{C}\) is small. The Yoneda embeddings are the following functors: \[\begin{align*} h_{\mathcal{C}}: \mathcal{C} & \longrightarrow \mathcal{C}^\wedge & k_{\mathcal{C}}: \mathcal{C} & \longrightarrow \mathcal{C}^\vee \\ S & \longmapsto \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}}(\cdot, S), & S & \longmapsto \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}}(S, \cdot). \end{align*}\] The following restates [Li1].

Theorem (Nobuo Yoneda). For every \(S\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{C})\), \(A\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{C}^\wedge)\), and \(B\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{C}^\vee)\), the canonical maps \[\text{Diagram appendix1-unit-135-d001} \quad \text{Diagram appendix1-unit-135-d002}\] are bijections. Consequently, \(h_{\mathcal{C}}\) and \(k_{\mathcal{C}}\) are both fully faithful functors.

Definition. A functor \(\mathcal{C}^{\operatorname{op}}\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{Set}}\) (respectively \(\mathcal{C}\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{Set}}\)) that, up to isomorphism, lies in the image of \(h_{\mathcal{C}}\) (respectively \(k_{\mathcal{C}}\)) is called a representable functor.

Although \(\mathcal{C}^\wedge\) (respectively \(\mathcal{C}^\vee\)) is much larger than \(\mathcal{C}\), each of its objects can be written canonically as a \(\varinjlim\) (respectively \(\varprojlim\)) of representable functors. Before stating this density theorem, we need a few definitions.

  • For each \(A\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{C}^\wedge)\), define the category \((h_{\mathcal{C}}/A)\) as in Definition reference. Its objects are data \(\underline S:=\left(S,h_{\mathcal{C}}(S)\xrightarrow{\phi_{\underline S}}A\right)\). A morphism from \(\underline S\) to \(\underline S'\) is an \(f\in\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}}(S,S')\) satisfying \(\phi_{\underline S}=\phi_{\underline S'}h_{\mathcal{C}}(f)\).

  • Dually, for \(B\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{C}^\vee)\) there is a category \((B/k_{\mathcal{C}})\). Its objects are data \(\overline S:=\left(S,B\xrightarrow{\psi_{\overline S}}k_{\mathcal{C}}(S)\right)\), where \(\psi_{\overline S}\) is regarded as a morphism in \(\mathcal{C}^\vee\); morphisms \(\overline S\to\overline S'\) are defined similarly.

Theorem (Density). For every \(A\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{C}^\wedge)\) and \(B\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{C}^\vee)\), the families of morphisms \(\phi_{\underline S}\) and \(\psi_{\overline S}\) above respectively give canonical isomorphisms in \(\mathcal{C}^\wedge\) and \(\mathcal{C}^\vee\) \[\varinjlim_{\underline{S}} h_{\mathcal{C}}(S) \ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}A, \quad B \ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}\varprojlim_{\overline{S}} k_{\mathcal{C}}(S).\]

Proof. It suffices to prove the first assertion. For any \(A'\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{C}^\wedge)\), there is a map \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:Yoneda-density-aux}{} \begin{aligned} \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}^\wedge}(A, A') & \longrightarrow \left\{\begin{array}{l} \text{compatible families of morphisms}\; a'_{\underline{S}}: h_{\mathcal{C}}(S) \to A' , \\ \text{where}\; \underline{S} = (S, \phi_{\underline{S}}) \in \operatorname{Ob}((h_{\mathcal{C}}/A)) \end{array}\right\} \\ \varphi & \longmapsto \left( a'_{\underline{S}} := \varphi \phi_{\underline{S}}\right)_{\underline{S}} . \end{aligned} \end{equation}\]

Define the reverse map as follows. Given data \((a'_{\underline S})_{\underline S}\), for every \(S\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{C})\) and \(a_S\in A(S)\) take, by Theorem reference, the corresponding morphism \(\phi:h_{\mathcal{C}}(S)\to A\), thereby determining \(\underline S:=(S,\phi)\in\operatorname{Ob}((h_{\mathcal{C}}/A))\). The assignment \(a_S\mapsto a'_{\underline S}\) then gives a map \(A(S)\to A'(S)\). We claim:

  • as \(S\) varies, the maps \(A(S)\to A'(S)\) give a morphism \(\varphi:A\to A'\) in \(\mathcal{C}^\wedge\);

  • the map \((a'_{\underline S})_{\underline S}\mapsto\varphi\) and the map in equation are mutually inverse.

As with many results concerning the Yoneda embedding, the detailed verification is nearly tautological and is omitted.

Thus equation is a bijection. In the special case \(A'=A\), it sends \(\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_A\) to \((a'_{\underline S}=\phi_{\underline S})_{\underline S}\). This verifies precisely that \(A\), together with the morphisms \(\phi_{\underline S}:h_{\mathcal{C}}(S)\to A\), has the universal property of the colimit.

The reader may also consult the treatment in [ML98].

Remark. The isomorphism involving \(B\) can also be restated in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Set}}^{\mathcal{C}}\) as \(\varinjlim_{\overline S}\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}}(S,\mathord\cdot)\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}B\), where \(\overline S\) ranges over data \((S,\psi'_{\overline S})\) with \(S\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{C})\) and \(\psi'_{\overline S}:\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}}(S,\mathord\cdot)\to B(\mathord\cdot)\) a morphism in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Set}}^{\mathcal{C}}\).

One application of Theorem reference is the extension of functors defined on a small category. We state only the version for \(\mathcal{C}^\wedge\). Let \(\mathcal{C}\) be a small category, let \(\mathcal{D}\) be a cocomplete category, possibly large but required to have all small colimits, and let \(F:\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{D}\) be a functor. Define \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:Yoneda-F-tilde}{}\begin{aligned} \tilde{F}: \mathcal{C}^\wedge & \to \mathcal{D} \\ X & \mapsto \varinjlim_{\underline{S}} F(S), \end{aligned} \end{equation}\] where \(\underline S=(S,\phi_{\underline S}:h_{\mathcal{C}}(S)\to X)\) ranges over the small category \((h_{\mathcal{C}}/X)\). If \(X\) comes from an object \(T\) of \(\mathcal{C}\), then \((h_{\mathcal{C}}/X)\) has the terminal object \((T,h_{\mathcal{C}}(T)\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}X)\). Thus the meaning of extension is that the following diagram commutes up to canonical isomorphism: \[\text{Diagram appendix1-unit-135-d003}\] We now show that \(\tilde F\) always has a right adjoint and therefore preserves all small colimits. This fact will be used in §reference.

Proposition. Let \(\mathcal{C}\) be a small category and \(\mathcal{D}\) a cocomplete category, possibly large. For a functor \(F:\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{D}\), take the canonical extension \(\tilde F:\mathcal{C}^\wedge\to\mathcal{D}\) defined in equation. Then \(\tilde F\) has the right adjoint \[\ensuremath{\EuScript{H}\mathrm{om}}(F, \cdot): \mathcal{D} \to \mathcal{C}^\wedge ,\] defined by:

  • \(\ensuremath{\EuScript{H}\mathrm{om}}(F,Y)(S)=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{D}}(FS,Y)\) for every \(S\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{C})\) and \(Y\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{D})\);

  • a morphism \(f:Y\to Y'\) induces a morphism \(f_*:\operatorname{Hom}(F(\mathord\cdot),Y)\to\operatorname{Hom}(F(\mathord\cdot),Y')\) in \(\mathcal{C}^\wedge\).

Consequently, \(\tilde F\) preserves all small colimits.

Proof. For \(X\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{C}^\wedge)\) and \(Y\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{D})\), the equality \(X=\varinjlim_{\underline S}h_{\mathcal{C}}(S)\) and the universal property of the colimit give canonical bijections \[\begin{multline*} \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}^\wedge}(X, \ensuremath{\EuScript{H}\mathrm{om}}(F, Y)) \simeq \varprojlim_{\underline{S}} \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}^\wedge}(h_{\mathcal{C}}(S), \ensuremath{\EuScript{H}\mathrm{om}}(F, Y)) \simeq \varprojlim_{\underline{S}} \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{D}}(FS, Y) \\ \simeq \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{D}}(\varinjlim_{\underline{S}} FS, Y ) = \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{D}}(\tilde{F}X, Y). \end{multline*}\] Thus \(\ensuremath{\EuScript{H}\mathrm{om}}(F,\mathord\cdot)\) is indeed right adjoint to \(\tilde F:\mathcal{C}^\wedge\to\mathcal{D}\).

Compact Objects and Presentable Categories

Compactness in category theory is a common refinement of many finiteness conditions in algebra, geometry, and algebraic geometry. Throughout this section we fix a category \(\mathcal{C}\); unless stated otherwise, we always assume that \(\mathcal{C}\) has all small filtered \(\varinjlim\).

Consider a small filtered category \(I\) and a functor \(\alpha:I\to\mathcal{C}\). For \(X\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{C})\), the canonical family of morphisms \(\iota_i:\alpha(i)\to\varinjlim\alpha\) induces a family \((\iota_i)_*:\operatorname{Hom}(X,\alpha(i))\to\operatorname{Hom}\left(X,\varinjlim\alpha\right)\), with \(i\in\operatorname{Ob}(I)\), and hence a canonical map \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:I-small-gen}{} \varinjlim_{i \in \operatorname{Ob}(I)} \operatorname{Hom}\left( X, \alpha(i) \right) \to \operatorname{Hom}\left( X, \varinjlim \alpha \right). \end{equation}\]

Definition. Let \((P,\leq)\) be a nonempty partially ordered set and let \(\kappa\) be an infinite cardinal. If every subset \(P_0\) satisfying \(|P_0|<\kappa\) has an upper bound in \(P\), then \((P,\leq)\) is called \(\kappa\)-filtered.

If \(\kappa\leq\kappa'\), then \(\kappa'\)-filtered implies \(\kappa\)-filtered. Taking \(\kappa:=\aleph_0=\omega\) recovers the filtered partially ordered sets introduced in Example reference.

Definition. If \(X\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{C})\) is such that equation is an isomorphism for every small filtered category \(I\) and every \(\alpha:I\to\mathcal{C}\), then \(X\) is called a compact object of \(\mathcal{C}\).

Given a small cardinal \(\kappa\), if \(I\) is further restricted to small \(\kappa\)-filtered partially ordered sets, then an \(X\) satisfying the corresponding condition is called a \(\kappa\)-compact object.

In the terminology of Definition reference, \(X\) is compact if and only if \(\operatorname{Hom}(X,\cdot):\mathcal{C}\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{Set}}\) preserves small filtered \(\varinjlim\). If \(\kappa\leq\kappa'\), then \(\kappa\)-compactness implies \(\kappa'\)-compactness.

Remark. At first glance the definitions of compact and \(\aleph_0\)-compact objects appear different: the former involves all small filtered categories, whereas the latter permits only small filtered partially ordered sets. There is, however, a nontrivial fact [AR94]:

For every small filtered category \(I\), there is a small filtered partially ordered set \((\mathcal{P},\leq)\) together with a cofinal functor \(\mathcal{P}\to I\).

It follows that compactness is equivalent to \(\aleph_0\)-compactness. A proof will be sketched in the exercises.

Using the definition of a filtered category and the concrete description of filtered \(\varinjlim\) in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Set}}\) (Proposition reference), we see that

  • the map equation is surjective \(\iff\) every \(f:X\to\varinjlim\alpha\) factors as \(X\xrightarrow{f_i}\alpha(i)\xrightarrow{\iota_i}\varinjlim\alpha\);1

  • the map equation is injective \(\iff\) for every \(i\in\operatorname{Ob}(I)\) and every \(f,g\in\operatorname{Hom}(X,\alpha(i))\) satisfying \(\iota_i f=\iota_i g\), there is a morphism \(i\to j\) in \(I\) such that the images of \(f\) and \(g\) in \(\operatorname{Hom}(X,\alpha(j))\) are equal.

Example. For \(\mathcal{C}=\ensuremath{\mathsf{Set}}\), an object \(X\) is compact if and only if \(X\) is a finite set. The if direction follows immediately from the preceding discussion and the concrete description of \(\varinjlim\alpha\). For the only-if direction, express \(X\) as the filtered \(\varinjlim\) of its finite subsets and consider \(\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_X\).

Example. Let \(R\) be a ring. For \(\mathcal{C}=R\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\), an object \(X\) is compact if and only if it is finitely presented; in other words, there exist \(a,b\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}_{\geq0}\) and an exact sequence of \(R\)-modules \[R^{\oplus b} \to R^{\oplus a} \xrightarrow{p} X \to 0 .\] For filtered \(\varinjlim\) in \(R\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\), see the explanation in [Li1]. The only-if direction is left as an exercise. We sketch the if direction. Take the images of the standard basis of \(R^{\oplus a}\) to obtain generators \(x_1,\ldots,x_a\) of \(X\). First we prove that equation is injective. Suppose that \(f,g\in\operatorname{Hom}(X,\alpha(i))\) satisfy \(\iota_i f=\iota_i g\). For every \(x\in\{x_1,\ldots,x_a\}\), there is an \(i\to j_x\) such that the images of \(f(x)\) and \(g(x)\) in \(\alpha(j_x)\) are equal. The filteredness of \(I\) then gives the desired \(i\to j\), for which the images of \(f\) and \(g\) in \(\operatorname{Hom}(X,\alpha(j))\) are equal.

Next we prove that equation is surjective. Consider \(f:X\to\varinjlim\alpha\). For every \(x\in\{x_1,\ldots,x_a\}\), there are \(j_x\) and \(m_x\in\alpha(j_x)\) such that \(f(x)=\iota_{j_x}(m_x)\). Again, filteredness ensures that the \(j_x\) may be chosen independently of \(x\); denote the common choice by \(j\). This determines a morphism \(m:R^{\oplus a}\to\alpha(j)\) such that \(fp=\iota_jm\). Since \(b\) is finite, by passing sufficiently far along a morphism \(j\to i\) and then replacing \(j\) by \(i\), we may also arrange for \(m\) to vanish identically on the image of \(R^{\oplus b}\). This gives the required \(f_i\).

For compact objects determined by various kinds of algebraic structure, [AR94] gives a more complete discussion. For instance, the compact objects in the category of groups \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Grp}}\) are precisely the finitely presented groups.

Another important class of compact objects comes from the Yoneda embedding \(h_{\mathcal{D}}:\mathcal{D}\to\mathcal{D}^\wedge\) recalled in §reference.

Proposition. Let \(\mathcal{D}\) be any category and \(X\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{D})\). Then \(h_{\mathcal{D}}(X)\) is compact in \(\mathcal{D}^\wedge\).

Proof. Given a small filtered category \(I\) and a functor \(\alpha:I\to\mathcal{D}^\wedge\), Theorem reference and the pointwise construction of \(\varinjlim\) in \(\mathcal{D}^\wedge\) (see [Li1], where it is denoted by \(\ensuremath{\text{“}\varinjlim\text{”}}\)) give \[\begin{align*} \varinjlim_i \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{D}^{\wedge}}(h_{\mathcal{D}}(X), \alpha(i)) & \simeq \varinjlim_i \left(\alpha(i)(X)\right) \\ & = (\varinjlim \alpha)(X) \\ & \simeq \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{D}^\wedge}(h_{\mathcal{D}}(X), \varinjlim \alpha). \end{align*}\] A routine verification shows that this is the canonical map in equation. Thus compactness follows.

By further restricting the filtered category \(I\) in equation, one obtains various versions of compactness. We first focus on the regular cardinals introduced in [Li1]; a more careful treatment is useful here.2 First let \(\alpha>0\) be any infinite ordinal. Consider a limit ordinal \(\theta>0\) and a strictly increasing sequence of ordinals \((a_\beta)_{\substack{\beta:\text{ordinal}\\\beta<\theta}}\). If \(\sup_{\beta<\theta}a_\beta=\alpha\), the sequence is called cofinal in \(\alpha\). If \(\alpha\) is a limit ordinal, define \[\mathrm{cf}(\alpha) := \inf\left\{ \theta > 0: \text{limit ordinal}, \; \exists (a_\beta)_{\beta < \theta}\; \text{as above, cofinal in $\alpha$} \right\};\] this \(\inf\) is well-defined and is attained by some \(\theta\) of the indicated kind; for \(\sup\) and \(\inf\) of ordinals, see [Li1]. Taking \(a_\beta:=\beta\) immediately gives \(\mathrm{cf}(\alpha)\leq\alpha\).

Note that every infinite cardinal, viewed as an ordinal, is necessarily a limit ordinal; see the discussion following [Li1].

Definition. An infinite cardinal \(\kappa\) is called a regular cardinal if, viewed as an ordinal, it satisfies \(\mathrm{cf}(\kappa)=\kappa\).

Proposition. Let \(\alpha>0\) be a limit ordinal.

  1. \(\mathrm{cf}(\mathrm{cf}(\alpha)) = \mathrm{cf}(\alpha)\);

  2. if a nonempty subset \(S\subset\alpha\) satisfies \(\sup S=\alpha\), then \(|S|\geq\mathrm{cf}(\alpha)\) as ordinals;

  3. \(\mathrm{cf}(\alpha)\) is a regular cardinal.

Proof. For (i), the key is to prove \(\mathrm{cf}(\alpha)\leq\mathrm{cf}(\mathrm{cf}(\alpha))\). Suppose that \((a_\beta)_{\beta<\theta}\) is cofinal in \(\alpha\) and \((b(\gamma))_{\gamma<\psi}\) is cofinal in \(\theta\). Then \(\left(a_{b(\gamma)}\right)_{\gamma<\psi}\) is cofinal in \(\alpha\). Hence \(\mathrm{cf}(\alpha)\leq\mathrm{cf}(\theta)\). Now take \(\theta=\mathrm{cf}(\alpha)\).

For (ii), choose any bijection \(f:|S|\to S\). Recall that \(|S|\) is an ordinal, while \(\alpha\notin S\). We claim that there are a limit ordinal \(\theta\) and an order-preserving embedding \(i:\theta\hookrightarrow|S|\) (hence \(\theta\leq|S|\)) such that the sequence of ordinals \(\left(f(i(\beta))\right)_{\beta<\theta}\) in \(S\) is strictly increasing and \(\sup_{\beta<\theta}f(i(\beta))=\sup S=\alpha\).

Indeed, this is an application of transfinite recursion. More explicitly, take \[\begin{align*} i(0) & := \inf |S| = 0, \\ i(n+1) & := \inf\left\{ t \in |S|: f(t) > f(i(n)) \right\}, \quad n \in \omega := \{0, 1, 2, \ldots\}, \\ i(\omega) & := \inf\left\{ t \in |S|: \forall k < \omega, \; f(t) > f(i(k)) \right\}, \end{align*}\] and continue transfinitely in this manner until stopping at \(\theta\). This proves the claim, and immediately yields \(|S|\geq\theta\geq\mathrm{cf}(\alpha)\).

For (iii), in view of (i), it remains only to show that \(\mathrm{cf}(\alpha)\) is a cardinal. If \(\beta>0\) is a limit ordinal, then (ii) implies \(\beta\geq|\beta|\geq\mathrm{cf}(\beta)\). Substituting \(\beta=\mathrm{cf}(\alpha)\) and using (i), we obtain \(\mathrm{cf}(\alpha)=|\mathrm{cf}(\alpha)|\), so \(\mathrm{cf}(\alpha)\) is a cardinal.

Proposition (See [Je03).] Let \(\lambda\) be an infinite cardinal. Then \(\mathrm{cf}(2^\lambda)>\lambda\).

Proof. This is a standard result in set theory. Let \(0<\alpha\leq\lambda\) be a limit ordinal and let \((a_\beta)_{\beta<\alpha}\) be a sequence of ordinals satisfying \(a_\beta<2^\lambda\). Write \(\kappa_\beta:=|a_\beta|<2^\lambda\). By the definitions of the supremum of ordinals and cardinal arithmetic, \[\left| \sup_{\beta < \alpha} a_\beta \right| = \left| \bigcup_{\beta < \alpha} a_\beta \right| \leq \sum_{\beta < \alpha} \kappa_\beta.\] König’s lemma for cardinal arithmetic (see [Li1], or [Je03]) gives \[\begin{align*} \sum_{\beta < \alpha} \kappa_\beta & < \prod_{\beta < \alpha} 2^\lambda = (2^\lambda)^{|\alpha|} \\ & = 2^{\lambda \cdot |\alpha|} \leq 2^{\lambda \cdot \lambda} = 2^\lambda ; \end{align*}\] the last step uses [Li1]. Thus \(\lambda\geq\mathrm{cf}(2^\lambda)\) is impossible.

Lemma. Let \(T\) be a small set. Then there is a small regular cardinal \(\mu\) such that \(\mu>|T|\).

Proof. Recall that a Grothendieck universe \(\mathcal{U}\) has already been fixed. The question depends only on \(|T|\), so we may assume without loss of generality that \(T\in\mathcal{U}\) is infinite. Its power set \(P(T)\) then belongs to \(\mathcal{U}\). Write \(\lambda:=|T|\). Proposition reference says that \(\mathrm{cf}(2^\lambda)>\lambda\). Since \(\mathrm{cf}(2^\lambda)\) is both a regular cardinal (Proposition reference (iii)) and embeddable as a subset of \(2^\lambda=|P(T)|\), the choice \(\mu:=\mathrm{cf}(2^\lambda)\) has the required properties.

We now return to the main line of category theory. The following notion originates in [GU71]; a textbook reference is [AR94].

Definition (P. Gabriel, F. Ulmer). Let \(\mathcal{C}\) be a category as above and let \(\kappa\) be a small regular cardinal.

  1. The category \(\mathcal{C}\) is called \(\kappa\)-accessible if it satisfies the following conditions:

    • \(\mathcal{C}\) has all small \(\kappa\)-filtered \(\varinjlim\) (Definition reference);

    • there is a small subset \(S\subset\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{C})\) consisting of \(\kappa\)-compact objects (Definition reference) such that every \(X\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{C})\) can be expressed as a small \(\kappa\)-filtered \(\varinjlim\) of elements of \(S\).

  2. A functor between \(\kappa\)-accessible categories is called \(\kappa\)-accessible if it preserves small \(\kappa\)-filtered \(\varinjlim\).

  3. A cocomplete \(\kappa\)-accessible category is called a \(\kappa\)-presentable category.3

When \(\kappa'\) is sufficiently large relative to \(\kappa\), the corresponding conditions are weaker than those for \(\kappa\). A category that is \(\kappa\)-accessible (respectively \(\kappa\)-presentable) for some small regular cardinal \(\kappa\) is called accessible (respectively presentable). Similarly, a functor between presentable categories is called accessible if it is \(\kappa\)-accessible for some small regular cardinal \(\kappa\).

One can verify that the categories \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Set}}\) and \(R\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\) discussed in Examples reference and reference are both presentable; in fact, they are \(\aleph_0\)-presentable. See also the exercises.

For the following important result we can give only part of the proof here.

Theorem (P. Gabriel, F. Ulmer). Let \(\kappa\) be a small regular cardinal and let \(F:\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{D}\) be a functor between presentable categories. Then:

  1. \(F\) has a right adjoint if and only if it preserves small \(\varinjlim\);

  2. \(F\) has a left adjoint if and only if it is accessible and preserves small \(\varprojlim\).

Proof. The only-if direction of (i) is well known. The converse follows from the special adjoint functor theorem reference and the following facts. First, Lemma reference implies that the set \(S\) in Definition reference is a generating family for \(\mathcal{C}\); second, every presentable category is co-well-powered, by [AR94].

Assertion (ii) follows from Freyd’s adjoint functor theorem reference; see [AR94] for details.

  1. Translator’s note: the source prints the target of the last arrow as \(X\). Since \(\iota_i\) is the canonical morphism to the colimit, the type-correct target is \(\varinjlim\alpha\).↩︎

  2. Readers uninterested in set theory may skip the following discussion.↩︎

  3. Gabriel once called these algebraic categories; the literature [AR94, GU71] calls them locally presentable categories, while here the terminology is changed following [Lu09].↩︎

The Gabriel–Popescu Theorem

This section continues and supplements §reference. Fix a Grothendieck category \(\mathcal{A}\), and abbreviate \(\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{A}}\) to \(\operatorname{Hom}\). Write \(X^{\oplus I}\) for the direct sum in \(\mathcal{A}\) of \(I\) copies of an object \(X\), where \(I\) is a small set.

The Gabriel–Popescu theorem will show that \(\mathcal{A}\) can always be realized as a reflective localization (Remark reference) of a category of right modules \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}\text{-}}R\) for some ring \(R\). The ring \(R\) and the functors involved depend on a generator \(s\). We follow L. Kuhn’s proof [Ku94]; one of its steps requires the classical theory of derived functors, for which see §reference.

Choose \(s\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{A})\), put \(R:=\operatorname{End}(s)\), and consider the functor \[\begin{align*} G: \mathcal{A} & \to \ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}\text{-}}R \\ X & \mapsto \operatorname{Hom}(s, X), \end{align*}\] where \(R\) acts on the right of \(\operatorname{Hom}(s,X)\) by composition of morphisms. It is easy to see that \(G\) is an additive functor between Abelian categories and preserves all small \(\varprojlim\). Henceforth write \(\operatorname{Hom}_R:=\operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}\text{-}}R}\) to distinguish it from \(\operatorname{Hom}:=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{A}}\).

For every \(r\in R\), define \(\lambda_r:x\mapsto rx\) in \(\operatorname{End}_R(R)\). Notice that \(G(s)=R\), and that \(\lambda_r:R\to R\) is precisely the image under \(G\) of the morphism \(r:s\to s\).

Lemma. The functor \(G:\mathcal{A}\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}\text{-}}R\) above has a left adjoint \(P:\ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}\text{-}}R\to\mathcal{A}\). The counit \(\varepsilon:PG\to\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}\) of this adjunction makes \(\varepsilon_s:PG(s)=P(R)\to s\) an isomorphism, and the following diagram commutes: \[\text{Diagram appendix1-unit-137-d001}\]

Proof. The existence of the left adjoint \(P\) follows from the special adjoint functor theorem reference and Corollary reference. We next claim that, for every \(Y\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{A})\), the following diagram commutes: \[\text{Diagram appendix1-unit-137-d002}\]

  • Commutativity of the upper part is a general property of the adjunction \((P,G)\). Given \(f\in\operatorname{Hom}(s,Y)\), the morphism \(f\varepsilon_s:PGs\to Y\) corresponds to \(G(f\varepsilon_s)\circ\eta_{Gs}:Gs\to GY\); see [Li1]. By the triangle identity for the adjunction, the latter equals \((Gf)\circ\left((G\varepsilon_s)\eta_{Gs}\right)=Gf\).

  • Commutativity of the lower part follows directly from the definition of \(G\).

Thus \(\varepsilon_s^*\) is an isomorphism. Taking \(Y\) to be the injective cogenerator supplied by Corollary reference then shows that \(\varepsilon_s\) is an isomorphism. Finally, the assertion about the first diagram is equivalent to the commutativity of \[\text{Diagram appendix1-unit-137-d003} \quad (r \in R)\] But \(R=Gs\) and \(\lambda_r=Gr\), so this follows from the naturality of \(\varepsilon\).

How can \(P\) be described? For every right \(R\)-module \(M\), there are small sets \(I,J\) and an exact sequence \[R^{\oplus J} \to R^{\oplus I} \to M \to 0;\] Since \(P\) preserves small \(\varinjlim\), it follows that \(PM\simeq\operatorname{coker}\left[s^{\oplus J}\to s^{\oplus I}\right]\).

The following result is stated in terms of the Serre quotient of an Abelian category; see Theorem reference for details. A Serre quotient is a special case of a localization.

Theorem (P. Gabriel, N. Popescu, L. Kuhn). Let \(s\) be a generator of the Grothendieck category \(\mathcal{A}\). Then:

  • the functor \(G=\operatorname{Hom}(s,\cdot):\mathcal{A}\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}\text{-}}R\) has an exact left adjoint \(P\);

  • \(G\) is fully faithful, and the counit of the adjunction gives an isomorphism \(\varepsilon:PG\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{\mathcal{A}}\);1

  • \(P\) induces an equivalence of categories \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}\text{-}}R/\operatorname{ker}(P)\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}\mathcal{A}\).

Proof. Lemma reference has shown that \(G\) has a left adjoint \(P\). We claim that if \(u:M\to GX\) is a monomorphism in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}\text{-}}R\), then the corresponding morphism \(v:=\varepsilon_X\circ Pu:PM\to X\) (see [Li1]) is a monomorphism in \(\mathcal{A}\). Express \(M\) as the filtered \(\varinjlim\) of its finitely generated \(R\)-submodules. Since \(P\) preserves \(\varinjlim\) and filtered \(\varinjlim\) in \(\mathcal{A}\) are exact, the problem reduces to the case where \(M\) is finitely generated.

Identify \(s\) with \(P(R)\) via \(\varepsilon_s\). Choose a finite set \(I\) and a surjection \(R^{\oplus I}\twoheadrightarrow M\). This gives \(e:s^{\oplus I}\twoheadrightarrow PM\). To conclude that \(v\) is a monomorphism, it suffices to prove \(\operatorname{ker}(ve)=\operatorname{ker}(e)\). By the generator property (for instance, Proposition reference), the problem further reduces to showing that any morphism \(f:s\to s^{\oplus I}\) satisfying \(vef=0\) also satisfies \(ef=0\). Make two observations:

  • By construction, \(e\) is the image under \(P\) of a morphism. Since \(I\) is finite, write \(f\) as an element of \(R^{\oplus I}\) and inspect its components one by one; the commutative diagram in Lemma reference ensures that \(f\) is also in the image of \(P\).

  • If a morphism \(\psi:N\to M\) in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}\text{-}}R\) satisfies \(v\circ P\psi=0\), then \(\psi=0\). This follows from the monicity of \(u\) and the commutative diagram in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ab}}\) \[\text{Diagram appendix1-unit-137-d004}\]

Thus \(ef:s\to PM\) is always in the image of \(P\), while \(vef=0\) implies \(ef=0\). This proves the claim.

The counit \(\varepsilon\) of an adjunction is an isomorphism if and only if the right adjoint \(G\) is fully faithful; this general fact is an exercise in . We now prove that \(\varepsilon\) is an isomorphism. Let \(X\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{A})\). Since \(\varepsilon_X:PG(X)\hookrightarrow X\) corresponds to \(\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{GX}\), taking \(u=\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{GX}\) in the preceding step shows that \(\varepsilon_X\) is a monomorphism. For surjectivity, Proposition reference reduces the problem to proving that every \(\alpha:s\to X\) factors through \(\varepsilon_X:PG(X)\hookrightarrow X\), and the required factorization is supplied by the diagram \[\text{Diagram appendix1-unit-137-d005}\]

Next we prove that \(P\) is exact. It is already right exact, so it suffices to show that the left derived functor \(\mathrm{L}_1P=0\). For any right \(R\)-module \(M\), take a short exact sequence \[0 \to K \xrightarrow{u} F \to M \to 0, \quad F: \text{a free module}.\] By dimension shifting (Proposition reference), \[\mathrm{L}_1 P (M) \simeq \operatorname{ker}[Pu: P(K) \to P(F)].\] The problem therefore reduces to proving that \(Pu\) is monic. Express \(F\) as the filtered \(\varinjlim\) of its finite-rank free submodules \(F'\) (or as their increasing union), and correspondingly write \(K=\varinjlim_{F'}(F'\cap K)\). Since \(P\) preserves \(\varinjlim\) and filtered \(\varinjlim\) in \(\mathcal{A}\) are exact, the problem reduces to the case \(F=R^{\oplus I}\simeq G(s^{\oplus I})\) for a finite set \(I\). But at the start of the proof we showed that if \(u:K\to G(s^{\oplus I})\) is monic, then \(v=\varepsilon_{s^{\oplus I}}\circ Pu:P(K)\to s^{\oplus I}\) is monic; hence \(Pu\) is monic. Exactness follows.

Finally, applying the universal property in Theorem reference to \(P\) factors it through a faithful additive functor \(\overline P:\ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}\text{-}}R/\operatorname{ker}(P)\to\mathcal{A}\). Let \(\overline G\) be the composite \(\mathcal{A}\xrightarrow{G}\ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}\text{-}}R\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}\text{-}}R/\operatorname{ker}(P)\). Then \(\overline P\circ\overline G\simeq P\circ G\simeq\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{\mathcal{A}}\). It follows that \(\overline P\) is also full and essentially surjective, with \(\overline G\) as a quasi-inverse, as desired.

Remark. The Gabriel–Popescu theorem reference implies that a Grothendieck category is presentable in the sense of Definition reference. Indeed, \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}\text{-}}R\simeq R^{\operatorname{op}}\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\) is known to be presentable, and [AR94] reflects this property to \(\mathcal{A}\).

  1. Translator’s note: the source prints \(\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}\text{-}}R}\). Since \(PG\) is an endofunctor of \(\mathcal{A}\), the type-correct target of the counit is \(\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{\mathcal{A}}\).↩︎

Locally Finite Abelian Categories

The aim of this section is to introduce a finiteness condition on Abelian categories that supplies the technical support needed in §reference. Readers are advised first to learn the statements of Definition reference, Definition reference, and Proposition reference, while skipping the subsequent lemmas and proofs. We fix a Grothendieck universe \(\mathcal{U}\) in order to discuss what is meant by small sets and small categories.

Definition. A category \(\mathcal{C}\) is called essentially small if it is equivalent to a small category, or equivalently if \(\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{C})/\simeq\) is a small set.

Fix a field \(\Bbbk\). All Abelian categories \(\mathcal{A}\) considered below are understood to be \(\Bbbk\)-linear.

Definition. Relative to the fixed field \(\Bbbk\), an essentially small Abelian category \(\mathcal{A}\) (Definition reference) is called locally finite if it has the following properties: \[\begin{equation*} \forall X, Y \in \operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{A}) \quad \left\{\begin{array}{l} X\; \text{is an object of finite length (Definition \href{#def:finite-length-object}{reference})}, \\ \dim_{\Bbbk} \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{A}}(X, Y) < \infty. \end{array}\right. \end{equation*}\]

Convention. For an Abelian category \(\mathcal{A}\) and \(X\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{A})\), define the Abelian subcategory \(\ensuremath{\left\langle X \right\rangle}\) of \(\mathcal{A}\) by \[Y \in \operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\left\langle X \right\rangle}) \iff \exists n \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}_{\geq 0} \; \text{such that}\; Y \;\text{is a subquotient of}\; X^{\oplus n}.\]

It is easy to see that \(\mathcal{A}\) is the union of all the subcategories \(\ensuremath{\left\langle X \right\rangle}\). Moreover, \(\ensuremath{\left\langle X \right\rangle}\subset\ensuremath{\left\langle X\oplus Y \right\rangle}\supset\ensuremath{\left\langle Y \right\rangle}\) shows that this union is filtered. We are interested in locally finite Abelian categories of the form \(\ensuremath{\left\langle X \right\rangle}\).

Proposition (O. Gabber). Let \(\mathcal{A}\) be a locally finite Abelian category, and suppose there is an \(X\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{A})\) such that \(\mathcal{A}=\ensuremath{\left\langle X \right\rangle}\). Then \(\mathcal{A}\) has a projective generator.

The proof requires some preparation.

Definition. In any Abelian category, let \(\alpha:E\twoheadrightarrow Y\) be an epimorphism. If there is no proper subobject \(E'\) of \(E\) for which \(\alpha|_{E'}\) is still epic, then \(\alpha\) is called an essential extension.

Lemma. Let \(S\) be a simple object in any Abelian category, and let \(\alpha:E\twoheadrightarrow S\) be an essential extension. Then, for every simple object \(T\), pullback along \(\alpha\) gives an isomorphism \(\alpha^*:\operatorname{Hom}(S,T)\to\operatorname{Hom}(E,T)\).

Proof. Pullback along the epimorphism \(\alpha\) is always injective; we prove surjectivity. Let \(\phi\in\operatorname{Hom}(E,T)\smallsetminus\{0\}\). Since \(\alpha|_{\operatorname{ker}(\phi)}\) is not epic, simplicity of \(S\) implies \(\operatorname{ker}(\phi)\subset\operatorname{ker}(\alpha)\). The induced morphism \(T\simeq E/\operatorname{ker}(\phi)\twoheadrightarrow E/\operatorname{ker}(\alpha)\simeq S\) must be an isomorphism, so \(\operatorname{ker}(\phi)=\operatorname{ker}(\alpha)\). Hence there is a \(\phi'\in\operatorname{Hom}(S,T)\) such that \(\phi=\phi'\alpha=\alpha^*(\phi')\).

For an object \(Y\) of finite length in an Abelian category, write \(\mathrm{JH}(Y)\) for the multiset of its composition factors, counted with multiplicity (Definition–Theorem reference).

Lemma. Let \(\mathcal{A}\) be an Abelian category and \(X\) an object of finite length. Consider a simple object \(S\) of \(\ensuremath{\left\langle X \right\rangle}\) and an essential extension \(\alpha:E\twoheadrightarrow S\). For every \(Y\in\operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\left\langle X \right\rangle})\), let \(\ell_S(Y)\) be the number, counted with multiplicity, of composition factors in \(\mathrm{JH}(Y)\) isomorphic to \(S\). Then \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:essential-ext-aux}{} \dim_{\Bbbk} \operatorname{Hom}(E, Y) \leq \ell_S(Y) \dim_{\Bbbk} \operatorname{End}(S); \end{equation}\] if \(Y\) is simple, equality holds.

In addition, the following statements are equivalent:

  1. \(E\) is a projective object of \(\ensuremath{\left\langle X \right\rangle}\);

  2. equality holds in equation for every \(Y\in\operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\left\langle X \right\rangle})\);

  3. equality holds in equation for \(Y=X\).

Proof. As a function of \(Y\), the right-hand side of equation is additive on short exact sequences \(0\to Y'\to Y\to Y''\to0\). On the other hand, \(\operatorname{Hom}(E,\cdot)\) is left exact, so the left-hand side of equation is subadditive: \[\dim_{\Bbbk} \operatorname{Hom}(E, Y) \leq \dim_{\Bbbk} \operatorname{Hom}(E, Y') + \dim_{\Bbbk} \operatorname{Hom}(E, Y'').\] Equality in this formula holds for every short exact sequence if and only if \(E\) is projective in \(\ensuremath{\left\langle X \right\rangle}\).

If \(Y\) is simple, Lemma reference implies that the left-hand side of equation is \(\dim_{\Bbbk}\operatorname{End}(S)\) when \(Y\simeq S\), and is \(0\) otherwise. The right-hand side has the same property, so equality in equation holds in this case. For general \(Y\), consider a composition series and apply the first paragraph. This proves both the inequality equation and (i) \(\implies\) (ii). Conversely, equality in equation makes \(\dim_{\Bbbk}\operatorname{Hom}(E,\cdot)\) additive, proving (ii) \(\implies\) (i).

Clearly (ii) \(\implies\) (iii). We prove (iii) \(\implies\) (ii). Since the inequality equation has already been established, the first paragraph shows that if equality holds for \(Y\), it also holds for \(Y'\) and \(Y''\). By assumption it holds for \(X\), hence for every \(X^{\oplus n}\) and all its subquotients. This gives (ii).

We now return to the goal of this section.

Proof (Proposition reference). We may assume that \(X\neq0\). First suppose that, for every element \(S\) of \(\mathrm{JH}(X)\) without multiplicities, there is an epimorphism \(P_S\twoheadrightarrow S\) such that \(P_S\) is projective in \(\ensuremath{\left\langle X \right\rangle}\). We show that the direct sum \(P\) of all these \(P_S\) is a projective generator of \(\ensuremath{\left\langle X \right\rangle}\).

Indeed, \(P\) is automatically projective in \(\ensuremath{\left\langle X \right\rangle}\). By Proposition reference, it remains to show that \(Y\neq0\implies\operatorname{Hom}(P,Y)\neq0\) for every \(Y\in\operatorname{Ob}(\ensuremath{\left\langle X \right\rangle})\). Choose a simple quotient \(Y\twoheadrightarrow S\). Projectivity of \(P_S\) factors \(P_S\twoheadrightarrow S\) as \(P_S\to Y\twoheadrightarrow S\), and this gives a nonzero morphism \(P\xrightarrow{\text{projection}}P_S\to Y\).

Now fix a simple object \(S\) of \(\ensuremath{\left\langle X \right\rangle}\) and construct \(P_S\twoheadrightarrow S\). Choose a composition series of \(X\) \[X = X_0 \supsetneq \cdots \supsetneq X_r = 0, \quad r \geq 1.\] For \(i=1,\ldots,r\), we shall recursively construct a sequence of essential extensions \(P_i\twoheadrightarrow S\) such that \[\dim_{\Bbbk} \operatorname{Hom}(P_i, X/X_i) = \ell_S(X/X_i) \dim_{\Bbbk} \operatorname{End}(S).\] Once this is proved, Lemma reference shows that \(P_r\) is projective in \(\ensuremath{\left\langle X \right\rangle}\), and \(P_S:=P_r\twoheadrightarrow S\) is the desired morphism.

Take \(P_1=S\); Lemma reference shows that the equality holds. Now let \(1\leq i<r\) and suppose \(P_i\) has been constructed. Choose a \(\Bbbk\)-basis \(\phi_1,\ldots,\phi_n\) of \(\operatorname{Hom}(P_i,X/X_i)\). Form the fiber products \[\text{Diagram appendix1-unit-138-d001} \quad 1 \leq j \leq n.\] Notice that \(Q_j\twoheadrightarrow P_i\) (Proposition reference). Let \(Q\) be the fiber product of \(Q_1,\ldots,Q_n\) over \(P_i\). Since fiber products may be formed one step at a time, the same reasoning shows that \(Q\to P_i\) is epic. Choose a subobject \(P_{i+1}\) of \(Q\) such that the composite \(P_{i+1}\hookrightarrow Q\to P_i\), denoted \(p^{i+1}_i\), is epic, and such that \(P_{i+1}\) is minimal with this property. By construction, the composite \(P_{i+1}\xrightarrow{p^{i+1}_i}P_i\twoheadrightarrow S\) is an essential extension. Also write \(t_j\) for the composite \(P_{i+1}\hookrightarrow Q\xrightarrow{\text{projection}}Q_j\).

We claim that \((p^{i+1}_i)^*:\operatorname{Hom}(P_i,X/X_i)\to\operatorname{Hom}(P_{i+1},X/X_i)\) is an isomorphism. It is injective, and the dimension of the left-hand side is known to be \(\ell_S(X/X_i)\dim_{\Bbbk}\operatorname{End}(S)\), while Lemma reference bounds the dimension of the right-hand side by the same number. This proves the claim.

Denote the map \(\operatorname{Hom}(P_{i+1},X/X_{i+1})\to\operatorname{Hom}(P_{i+1},X/X_i)\) by \(\Phi_i\). By the claim, we can define a reverse \(\Bbbk\)-linear map \(\Psi_i\) by sending \(\phi_jp^{i+1}_i\) to \(\psi_jt_j\), for \(1\leq j\leq n\). We verify that \(\Phi_i\Psi_i=\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}\). On each \(\phi_jp^{i+1}_i\), this follows immediately from the commutative diagram \[\text{Diagram appendix1-unit-138-d002}\] which says precisely that \(\Phi_i(\psi_jt_j)=\phi_jp^{i+1}_i\).

We therefore have a split short exact sequence \[\text{Diagram appendix1-unit-138-d003}\] Lemma reference and the induction hypothesis show that the dimensions of the terms at the left and right are respectively \[\ell_S(X_i/X_{i+1}) \dim_{\Bbbk} \operatorname{End}(S), \quad \ell_S(X/X_i) \dim_{\Bbbk} \operatorname{End}(S).\] By additivity of \(\ell_S(\cdot)\), the middle term therefore has the required dimension. This completes the proof.

Exercises

In the discussion of §reference, fix a commutative ring \(\Bbbk\), require \(\mathcal{C}\) to be a \(\Bbbk\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\)-category (Definition reference), replace \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Set}}\) by \(\Bbbk\ensuremath{\text{-}\mathsf{Mod}}\) in the definitions of \(\mathcal{C}^\wedge\) and \(\mathcal{C}^\vee\), and require the functors to be \(\Bbbk\)-linear. Formulate the corresponding \(\Bbbk\)-linear versions of Theorems reference and reference.

Complete the only-if part of Example reference. Hint. Every \(R\)-module can be written as a filtered \(\varinjlim\) of finitely presented \(R\)-modules, not necessarily its submodules; for simplicity, write \(X=\varinjlim\alpha\). Consider a preimage of \(\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_X\) under equation. This gives \(f_i\in\operatorname{Hom}(X,\alpha(i))\) such that \(\iota_i f_i=\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_X\), and hence a decomposition \(\alpha(i)\simeq X\oplus N\). Since \(N\) is isomorphic to a quotient of \(\alpha(i)\), it is a finitely generated \(R\)-module. The problem reduces to the fact that the quotient of a finitely presented \(R\)-module by a finitely generated submodule is still finitely presented.

Explain the relation between the cofinal ordinal sequences introduced in §reference and the cofinal subcategories of Definition reference.

(J. Adámek, J. Rosický) Prove the fact mentioned in Remark reference as follows: for every small filtered category \(I\), there is a small filtered partially ordered set \((\mathcal{P},\leq)\) together with a cofinal functor \(\mathcal{P}\to I\).

  1. Suppose that the small filtered category \(I\) has the following property: every finite subcategory \(\mathcal{A}\) is contained in a finite subcategory \(\mathcal{A}'\) having a unique terminal object. Note that a subcategory need not be full, and that a finite category means one with finite sets of objects and morphisms. Let \(\mathcal{I}\) be the set of all subcategories having a unique terminal object, partially ordered by inclusion \(\subset\). Show that one can define a functor \[H: \mathcal{I} \to I,\] sending an object \(\mathcal{A}\) to its unique terminal object \(H\mathcal{A}\) and an inclusion \(\mathcal{A}_1\subset\mathcal{A}_2\) to the unique morphism \(H\mathcal{A}_1\to H\mathcal{A}_2\) in \(\mathcal{A}_2\).

  2. In the notation above, show that \((\mathcal{I},\subset)\) is a small filtered partially ordered set and that \(H\) is cofinal.

  3. Now let \(I\) be any small filtered category. Show that the product category \(I\times\omega\) has the property assumed in (i), and that the projection functor \(I\times\omega\to I\) is cofinal. Here \(\omega\) is the totally ordered set of nonnegative integers.

    Hint. Clearly \(I\times\omega\) is filtered. Given a finite subcategory \(\mathcal{A}\) of \(I\times\omega\), show that there are an object \((i,n)\) of \(I\times\omega\) and a cone whose base is the inclusion functor \(\mathcal{A}\to I\times\omega\) and whose vertex is \((i,n)\) (Convention reference). Adjoin to \(\mathcal{A}\) the object \((i,n+1)\), its identity morphism, and all composites of the morphisms \((j,k)\to(i,n)\) in the cone with the canonical morphism \((i,n)\to(i,n+1)\). This produces a finite subcategory \(\mathcal{A}'\) having the unique terminal object \((i,n+1)\).

  4. Use (iii) to prove the existence of the required cofinal functor \(\mathcal{P}\to I\).

Let \(\mathcal{C}\) be an accessible category.

  1. Choose a small subset \(S\subset\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{C})\) as in Definition reference, and let \(\mathcal{S}\) be the full subcategory it generates. Prove that the Yoneda embedding restricts to a fully faithful functor \(\mathcal{C}\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{Set}}^{\mathcal{S}^{\operatorname{op}}}\).

  2. Prove that \(\mathcal{C}\) is well-powered (Definition reference). Hint. For every object \(F\) of \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Set}}^{\mathcal{S}^{\operatorname{op}}}\) and every \(X\in S\), the set \(FX\) and its power set are both small. Use this to show that \(\mathrm{Sub}_F\) is a small set.

Fix a field \(\Bbbk\). Let \(\mathcal{A}\) be a locally finite \(\Bbbk\)-linear Abelian category, let \(\mathcal{A}'\) be an Abelian subcategory, and write its inclusion functor as \(i:\mathcal{A}'\to\mathcal{A}\). Assume that the subset \(\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{A}')\subset\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{A})\) is closed under isomorphism.

  1. Show that for every \(X\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{A})\), the intersection of the partially ordered set of quotient objects \(\mathrm{Quot}_X\) (respectively the partially ordered set of subobjects \(\mathrm{Sub}_X\)) with \(\mathcal{A}'\) has a unique greatest element, denoted \(i^*(X)\) (respectively \(i^!(X)\)), and that \(i^*\) (respectively \(i^!\)) gives a left (respectively right) adjoint to \(i\).

  2. Suppose that \(\mathcal{A}\) has a projective generator \(s\). Prove that \(s':=i^*(s)\) is a projective generator of \(\mathcal{A}'\).

  3. For \(s,s'\) as above, put \(A:=\operatorname{End}(s)\) and \(A':=\operatorname{End}(s')\). Prove that \[A = \operatorname{Hom}(s, s) \to \operatorname{Hom}(s, s') \ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\leftarrow}}\operatorname{Hom}(s', s') = A'\] makes \(A'\) a quotient ring of \(A\), written \(A'=A/\mathfrak{a}\). Prove that \(\mathcal{A}\) and \(s\) satisfy the hypotheses of Theorem reference, so that \(\mathcal{A}\) is equivalent to \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}_{\mathrm{fg}}\text{-}}A\), while \(\mathcal{A}'\) is equivalent to the full subcategory consisting of modules annihilated by the two-sided ideal \(\mathfrak{a}\).

Introduction to Ind-Objects and Pro-Objects

Given a category \(\mathcal{C}\), what is an ind-object over it? Through the Yoneda embedding \(\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{C}^{\wedge}\), an ind-object can be defined rigorously as an object of \(\mathcal{C}^\wedge\) of the form \(X=\ensuremath{\text{“}\varinjlim\text{”}}X_i\), where \(i\) ranges over a small filtered category \(I\) and \(X_i\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{C})\). The symbol \(\ensuremath{\text{“}\varinjlim\text{”}}\) distinguishes \(\varinjlim\) in \(\mathcal{C}^{\wedge}\) from \(\varinjlim\) in \(\mathcal{C}\). One can prove that \[\operatorname{Hom}(X, Y) = \varprojlim_i \varinjlim_j \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}}(X_i, Y_j), \quad X = \ensuremath{\text{“}\varinjlim\text{”}}X_i, \; Y = \ensuremath{\text{“}\varinjlim\text{”}}Y_j.\] Thus, roughly speaking, an ind-object \(X\) may be imagined as a filtered system represented by a family of objects \(X_i\) of \(\mathcal{C}\) together with a compatible family of morphisms \(X_i\to X_j\), as \(i\to j\) ranges over \(\operatorname{Mor}(I)\). The choice of \((X_i)_i\) representing \(X\), however, is not unique. There is also a dual notion, called a pro-object over \(\mathcal{C}\). The presentation here follows [KS06].

As a source of examples, §reference begins with profinite groups. These are both a special class of topological groups and, equivalently, filtered \(\varprojlim\) of finite groups in the category of topological groups (Remark reference). On this basis, Example reference will later show that profinite groups are precisely the pro-objects over the category of finite groups, and so can be handled by algebraic methods. This class of topological groups occurs especially often in mathematics and is also background knowledge for several chapters of this book.

Section reference gives the formal definitions of ind-objects and pro-objects, a description of their morphisms, and some preliminary examples. The subsequent discussion focuses on ind-objects. Section reference studies the category \(\operatorname{Ind}\mathcal{C}\) of all ind-objects over \(\mathcal{C}\), also called the Ind-completion of \(\mathcal{C}\); it contains \(\mathcal{C}\) as a full subcategory. We shall study how to recognize ind-objects inside \(\mathcal{C}^{\wedge}\) (Proposition reference), that is, how to characterize when a functor \(\mathcal{C}^{\operatorname{op}}\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{Set}}\) is ind-representable, and then discuss the interaction between \(\mathcal{C}\to\operatorname{Ind}\mathcal{C}\) and limits. In particular, we shall show that \(\operatorname{Ind}\mathcal{C}\) has all small filtered \(\varinjlim\).

Dually, \(\mathcal{C}\) also has a Pro-completion: all pro-objects form the category \(\operatorname{Pro}\mathcal{C}=\operatorname{Ind}\left(\mathcal{C}^{\operatorname{op}}\right)^{\operatorname{op}}\).

The Ind-extension of functors is the subject of §reference. The results include how to extend a functor \(\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{D}\) to \(\operatorname{Ind}\mathcal{C}\) (Definition–Proposition reference), and how to recognize whether a category \(\mathcal{C}\) is the Ind-completion of a full subcategory \(\mathcal{C}'\) (Proposition reference).

In §reference, these results are applied to an Abelian category \(\mathcal{C}\) to show that both embeddings \(\mathcal{C}\to\operatorname{Ind}\mathcal{C}\) and \(\mathcal{C}\to\operatorname{Pro}\mathcal{C}\) are fully faithful exact functors between Abelian categories (Theorem reference). That section also discusses exactness of functor extensions for Abelian categories (Proposition reference). Furthermore, Theorem reference shows that the Ind-completion of a small Abelian category is a Grothendieck category.
