Using the preceding results and the basic fact that Grothendieck categories have injective cogenerators, §reference proves the Freyd–Mitchell embedding theorem: every small Abelian category admits a fully faithful exact embedding into \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}\text{-}}R\), where \(R\) is a ring realized on a small set. The route through Ind-completion is neither the most elementary nor the shortest; compared with the Freyd–Mitchell theorem itself, however, Ind-completion may be a more valuable technique.

Prelude: Profinite Groups

We first define profinite groups from the topological viewpoint: they are topological groups with specified properties. On the few occasions when set size must be distinguished, the topological groups under consideration are understood to be realized on small sets; otherwise we shall not mention this point again.

Definition. A profinite group is a topological group \(G\) satisfying:

  • \(G\) is a compact Hausdorff group;

  • \(G\) has a neighborhood basis at the identity \(1_G\) consisting of normal subgroups.

Let \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{TopGrp}}\) denote the category of all topological groups, with continuous homomorphisms as morphisms. The profinite groups form a full subcategory of \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{TopGrp}}\).

If \(G\) is profinite, a neighborhood basis at \(1_G\) may be taken to consist of all open normal subgroups \(K\lhd G\). For a detailed discussion, see [FL14] or [Li1].

Remark. Another characterization is that a topological group \(G\) is profinite if and only if it is a totally disconnected compact group; see [FL14]. The following related fact is also useful: a Hausdorff topological space \(E\) is locally compact and totally disconnected if and only if every \(e\in E\) has a neighborhood basis consisting of compact open subsets.

If \(H\) is an open subgroup of \(G\), choose a representative \(g\) for each coset \(\bar g\in G/H\). The decomposition \(G=\bigsqcup_{\bar g\in G/H}gH\), together with compactness, implies that \((G:H)\) is finite. Moreover, \(H=G\smallsetminus\bigcup_{\bar g\neq H}gH\) shows that \(H\) is closed.

We record a few more basic properties.

Lemma. Let \(G\) be a topological group and \(H\) a subgroup. Then:

  1. the quotient map \(\pi:G\to G/H\) is open with respect to the quotient topology on \(G/H\);

  2. \(G/H\) with the quotient topology is Hausdorff if and only if \(H\) is closed;

  3. the quotient topology on \(G/H\) is discrete if and only if \(H\) is open.

The same assertions of course hold for \(H\backslash G\).

Proof. For (i), if \(U\) is an open subset of \(G\),1 then \(\pi^{-1}(\pi(U))=\bigcup_{h\in H}Uh\) is open. Hence \(\pi(U)\) is open by the definition of the quotient topology.

The only-if direction of (ii) follows from \(H=\pi^{-1}(1_G\cdot H)\). For the if direction, given distinct cosets \(xH\neq yH\), choose an open subset \(V\ni1_G\) of \(G\) such that \(Vx\cap yH=\emptyset\), and then choose an open subset \(U\ni1_G\) such that \(U^{-1}U\subset V\). This ensures \(UxH\cap UyH=\emptyset\), while (i) shows that \(\pi(Ux)\) and \(\pi(Uy)\) are both open.

The only-if direction of (iii) again follows from \(H=\pi^{-1}(1_G\cdot H)\). Now suppose that \(H\) is open. By (i), \(\{1_G\cdot H\}=\pi(H)\) is open; translation shows that every singleton in \(G/H\) is open. This proves the if direction.

Proposition. Let \(G\) be a profinite group.

  1. If \(H\) is a closed subgroup of \(G\), then \(H\) is profinite.

  2. If \(H\) is a closed normal subgroup of \(G\), then \(G/H\) is profinite with the quotient topology.

Proof. For (i), the closed subgroup \(H\) is of course compact and Hausdorff. A neighborhood basis at \(1_G\) is given by all \(K\cap H\), where \(K\) ranges over the open normal subgroups of \(G\).

For (ii), closedness of \(H\) implies that \(G/H\) is Hausdorff, and compactness of \(G\) implies that \(G/H\) is compact. A neighborhood basis of \(G/H\) at \(1_G\cdot H\) is given by all \(KH/H\), where \(K\) ranges over the open normal subgroups of \(G\); each \(KH/H\) is an open normal subgroup of \(G/H\).

It is easy to prove that the product of a family of profinite groups \((G_i)_i\), indexed by a small set, is again profinite. For any small category \(I\) and functor \(\beta:I^{\operatorname{op}}\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{TopGrp}}\), abbreviated as \((G_i)_{i\in\operatorname{Ob}(I)}\) with \(G_i:=\beta(i)\), give \[\left( \varprojlim_i G_i := \varprojlim \beta \right) \hookrightarrow \prod_i G_i\] the topology inherited from the product space on the right, making it a closed subgroup. This gives the \(\varprojlim\) in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{TopGrp}}\). Hence if every \(G_i\) is profinite, then \(\varprojlim_iG_i\) is profinite. It follows that the category of profinite groups is complete.

Example. The simplest example is a finite group \(G\); in this case there is only one Hausdorff topology, namely the discrete topology. The following examples are also common.

  • Let \(G:=\operatorname{Gal}(E|F)\) be the Galois group of a Galois extension \(E|F\), endowed with the Krull topology [Li1]. The corresponding neighborhood basis consists of the subgroups \(\operatorname{Gal}(E|L)\), where \(L|F\) ranges over the finite Galois subextensions of \(E|F\).

  • For a prime \(p\), let \(\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}_p\) be the ring of \(p\)-adic integers, and let \(\operatorname{SL}(n,\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}_p)\) be the group of \(n\times n\) matrices over it with determinant \(1\). Endowed with the topology inherited from the space \(\mathrm{M}_n(\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}_p)\) of \(n\times n\) matrices, this too is a profinite group.

  • For any group \(G\), its profinite completion is defined by \[\hat{G} := \varprojlim_{\substack{N \lhd G \\ (G:N) < \infty}} G/N,\] where each \(G/N\) is given the discrete topology. As the name suggests, this is a profinite group.

Remark. The preceding discussion shows that if finite groups are given the discrete topology, then their small \(\varprojlim\) are profinite. Conversely, every profinite group \(G\) can be written as \(\varprojlim_iG_i\), where \((I,\leq)\) is a small filtered partially ordered set and every \(G_i\) is finite; see [Li1]. Concretely, one may choose a neighborhood basis \((K_i)_{i\in I}\) at \(1_G\) consisting of open normal subgroups, order the index set by reverse inclusion, and put \(G_i:=G/K_i\).

For a Galois-group example, \(\operatorname{Gal}(E|F)=\varprojlim_{L|F}\operatorname{Gal}(L|F)\), where \(L|F\) ranges over the finite Galois subextensions of \(E|F\).

Consider profinite groups \(G=\varprojlim_iG_i\) and \(H=\varprojlim_jH_j\) presented as above. Since the subgroups \(\operatorname{ker}[G\to G_i]\) form a neighborhood basis at \(1_G\), there are canonical isomorphisms \[\begin{align*} \operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{TopGrp}}}(G, H) & = \operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{TopGrp}}}\left(\varprojlim_i G_i, \varprojlim_j H_j \right) \\ & \simeq \varprojlim_j \operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{TopGrp}}}\left( \varprojlim_i G_i, H_j \right) \quad \text{($\because\; \varprojlim$ has its universal property)} \\ & \simeq \varprojlim_j \varinjlim_i \operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{Grp}}}(G_i, H_j) \quad \text{($\because$\; every continuous homomorphism factors through some $G_i$)}; \end{align*}\] Thus profinite groups can also be handled algebraically; see Example reference below.

Definition. Let \(p\) be a prime. A profinite group \(G\) is called a pro-\(p\) group if, for every sufficiently small open normal subgroup \(K\lhd G\), the quotient \(G/K\) is a \(p\)-group. Equivalently, \(G\) can be written as \(\varprojlim_iG_i\), where \((I,\leq)\) is a filtered partially ordered set and every \(G_i\) is a \(p\)-group.

Such groups occur frequently in number theory. The exercises contain further discussion of pro-\(p\) groups.

The following result shows that quotient maps of profinite groups by closed subgroups have particularly simple topological behavior, quite unlike the usual situation for Lie groups.

Lemma. Let \(H\) and \(H'\) be closed subgroups of a profinite group \(G\), with \(H'\subset H\). Then the quotient map \(\pi:G/H'\twoheadrightarrow G/H\) has a continuous section \(s:G/H\to G/H'\); in other words, \(s\) is continuous and satisfies \(\pi s=\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{G/H}\).2

An analogous assertion holds for the quotient map \(H'\backslash G\twoheadrightarrow H\backslash G\).

Proof. First consider the case in which \((H:H')\) is finite. Then \(H\) is the disjoint union of \(H'\) and finitely many of its left translates, so \(H'\) is open in \(H\). There is an open normal subgroup \(U\lhd G\) such that \(U\cap H\subset H'\). The restriction of \(\pi\) is therefore a bijection \(UH'/H'\to UH/H\); by compactness it is a homeomorphism, and its inverse gives a continuous section on the open subset \(UH/H\) of \(G/H\). Finally, translate this section to extend it over all of \(G/H\).

In the general case, the reader is asked to reduce the problem to \(H'=\{1_G\}\). In that case, consider all data \((T,t)\), where \(T\subset H\) is a closed subgroup and \(t\) is a continuous section of \(G/T\twoheadrightarrow G/H\). Partially order these data by declaring \((T_1,t_1)\preceq(T_2,t_2)\) if \(T_2\subset T_1\) and \(t_1\) factors as \(G/H\xrightarrow{t_2}G/T_2\twoheadrightarrow G/T_1\). Zorn’s lemma ensures the existence of a maximal element. The key point is that if \(((S_i,s_i))_i\) is a chain for \(\preceq\) and \(S':=\bigcap_iS_i\), then the canonical map \(G/S'\to\varprojlim_iG/S_i\) is continuous and injective with dense image; compactness therefore makes it a homeomorphism. We may consequently define \(s':=\varprojlim_i s_i:G/H\to G/S'\), obtaining an upper bound \((S',s')\) for the chain.

Let \((S,s)\) be a maximal element of this partially ordered set. If \(S=\{1\}\), we are done. If \(S\neq\{1\}\), choose an open normal subgroup \(U\) of \(G\) such that \(S\cap U\neq S\). Since \((S:S\cap U)\) is finite, the first step of the proof gives a continuous section of \(G/(S\cap U)\to G/S\). Composing it with \(s\) gives a continuous section of \(G/(S\cap U)\to G/H\), contradicting the maximality of \((S,s)\).

The version for \(H'\backslash G\twoheadrightarrow H\backslash G\) is identical.

The most important special case is \(H'=\{1_G\}\). Then a continuous section \(s\) induces a homeomorphism of topological spaces \((G/H)\times H\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}G\), sending \((x,h)\) to \(s(x)h\). The conclusion for \(G\twoheadrightarrow H\backslash G\) is of course analogous.

  1. Translator’s note: the source says that \(U\) is an open subset of \(G/H\), but the expressions \(\pi(U)\) and \(\bigcup_{h\in H}Uh\) require \(U\subset G\).↩︎

  2. Translator’s note: the source has the undefined subscript \(G/H_2\) on this identity; the codomain of \(\pi\) makes \(G/H\) the type-correct subscript.↩︎

Ind-Objects and Pro-Objects

From this section onward, fix a Grothendieck universe \(\mathcal{U}\); the terms small category and small set refer to this choice. Unless stated otherwise, an unqualified category is understood to be a \(\mathcal{U}\)-category; otherwise it is called a large category. Recall that \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Set}}\) denotes the category of small sets.

Let \(\mathcal{C}\) be a category. In §reference we recalled the two Yoneda embeddings \[h_{\mathcal{C}}: \mathcal{C}\to \mathcal{C}^\wedge, \quad k_{\mathcal{C}}: \mathcal{C} \to \mathcal{C}^\vee.\] They are of course dual to each other. Note that unless \(\mathcal{C}\) is small, \(\mathcal{C}^\wedge\) and \(\mathcal{C}^\vee\) are generally large categories. When no confusion can arise, we shall often omit the functors \(h_{\mathcal{C}}\) and \(k_{\mathcal{C}}\) from the notation.

Recall the lessons of [Li1]:

  • \(\mathcal{C}^\wedge\) has all small \(\varinjlim\) and small \(\varprojlim\), constructed pointwise in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Set}}\);

  • in general, the Yoneda embedding \(\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{C}^\wedge\) preserves \(\varprojlim\) but not \(\varinjlim\).

Following the convention there,1 in this section the \(\varinjlim\) of \(\alpha:I\to\mathcal{C}^\wedge\) will be written separately as \[\ensuremath{\text{“}\varinjlim\text{”}}\alpha \;\text{or}\; \ensuremath{\text{“}\varinjlim\text{”}}\alpha(i),\] where \(i\) ranges over \(\operatorname{Ob}(I)\). This distinguishes it from \(\varinjlim\) in \(\mathcal{C}\).

Dually, we write \(\ensuremath{\text{“}\varprojlim\text{”}}\) for the \(\varprojlim\) in \(\mathcal{C}^\vee\) obtained by the pointwise construction, since in general \(\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{C}^\vee\) preserves \(\varinjlim\) but not \(\varprojlim\).

The density theorem reference says that every object of \(\mathcal{C}^\wedge\) can be expressed as a \(\ensuremath{\text{“}\varinjlim\text{”}}\) of objects of \(\mathcal{C}\). The ind-objects are those which can be so expressed using a filtered \(\ensuremath{\text{“}\varinjlim\text{”}}\); the dual objects in \(\mathcal{C}^\vee\) are called pro-objects.

Definition. Let \(\mathcal{C}\) be a category.

  • If \(X\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{C}^\wedge)\) can be written as \(\ensuremath{\text{“}\varinjlim\text{”}}X_i\), where the index ranges over a small filtered category \(I\) and \(X_i\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{C})\) (equivalently, the data define a functor \(I\to\mathcal{C}\)), then \(X\) is called an ind-object over \(\mathcal{C}\).

  • If \(X\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{C}^\vee)\) can be written as \(\ensuremath{\text{“}\varprojlim\text{”}}X_i\), where the index ranges over a small filtered category \(I\) and \(X_i\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{C})\) (equivalently, the data define a functor \(I^{\operatorname{op}}\to\mathcal{C}\)), then \(X\) is called a pro-object over \(\mathcal{C}\).

All ind-objects form a category \(\operatorname{Ind}\mathcal{C}\) and all pro-objects form a category \(\operatorname{Pro}\mathcal{C}\); they are respectively full subcategories of \(\mathcal{C}^\wedge\) and \(\mathcal{C}^\vee\).

We therefore have fully faithful functors \(\mathcal{C}\to\operatorname{Ind}\mathcal{C}\) and \(\mathcal{C}\to\operatorname{Pro}\mathcal{C}\). Corollary reference will control the sizes of \(\operatorname{Ind}\mathcal{C}\) and \(\operatorname{Pro}\mathcal{C}\) and show that they are not large categories.

It is immediate from the definition that \((\operatorname{Ind}\mathcal{C})^{\operatorname{op}}\simeq\operatorname{Pro}(\mathcal{C}^{\operatorname{op}})\). Henceforth we write ind-objects (respectively pro-objects) as \(\ensuremath{\text{“}\varinjlim\text{”}}X_i\) (respectively \(\ensuremath{\text{“}\varprojlim\text{”}}Y_i\)) without further comment; remember that such presentations are not unique.

Proposition. Let \(X=\ensuremath{\text{“}\varinjlim\text{”}}X_i\) and \(Y=\ensuremath{\text{“}\varinjlim\text{”}}Y_j\) be ind-objects over \(\mathcal{C}\). There is a canonical bijection \[\operatorname{Hom}_{\operatorname{Ind}\mathcal{C}}(X, Y) \simeq \varprojlim_i \varinjlim_j \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}}(X_i, Y_j).\] Similarly, for pro-objects \(X=\ensuremath{\text{“}\varprojlim\text{”}}X_i\) and \(Y=\ensuremath{\text{“}\varprojlim\text{”}}Y_j\), there is a canonical bijection \[\operatorname{Hom}_{\operatorname{Pro}\mathcal{C}}(X, Y) \simeq \varprojlim_j \varinjlim_i \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}}(X_i, Y_j).\] The limits on the right are all understood to be taken in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Set}}\).

Proof. For ind-objects, \[\begin{align*} \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}^\wedge}\left(\ensuremath{\text{“}\varinjlim\text{”}}X_i, \ensuremath{\text{“}\varinjlim\text{”}}Y_j \right) & = \varprojlim_i \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}^\wedge}\left( X_i, \ensuremath{\text{“}\varinjlim\text{”}}Y_j \right) & (\because\; \varinjlim \; \text{in $\mathcal{C}^{\wedge}$}) \\ & = \varprojlim_i \left[ \left( \ensuremath{\text{“}\varinjlim\text{”}}Y_j \right)(X_i) \right] & (\because\; \text{Theorem \href{#prop:Yoneda}{reference}}) \\ & = \varprojlim_i \varinjlim_j \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}}(X_i, Y_j) & (\because\; \text{the construction of }\ensuremath{\text{“}\varinjlim\text{”}}). \end{align*}\] The last two equalities can also be viewed as an expression of the compactness of \(X_i\) in \(\mathcal{C}^\wedge\) (Proposition reference). The pro-object case is dual.

Corollary. The categories \(\operatorname{Ind}\mathcal{C}\) and \(\operatorname{Pro}\mathcal{C}\) constructed above are \(\mathcal{U}\)-categories, just as \(\mathcal{C}\) is.

Proof. Every \(\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}}(X_i,Y_j)\) in Proposition reference is a \(\mathcal{U}\)-small set, and the \(\varprojlim\) and \(\varinjlim\) are also taken over small categories.

Notice that the definitions of \(\operatorname{Ind}\mathcal{C}\) and \(\operatorname{Pro}\mathcal{C}\) depend on the choice of universe \(\mathcal{U}\). For their precise relation to \(\mathcal{U}\), see [KS06]; we shall not pursue this point here.

All algebraic structures in the following examples are understood to be realized on small sets.

Example. Let \(\Bbbk\) be a field. Denote the category of finite-dimensional \(\Bbbk\)-vector spaces by \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Vect}}_{\mathrm{f}}(\Bbbk)\) and the category of all \(\Bbbk\)-vector spaces by \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Vect}}(\Bbbk)\). We shall show that \[\operatorname{Ind}\ensuremath{\mathsf{Vect}}_{\mathrm{f}}(\Bbbk) \;\text{is equivalent to}\; \ensuremath{\mathsf{Vect}}(\Bbbk).\]

Define a functor \(\operatorname{Ind}\ensuremath{\mathsf{Vect}}_{\mathrm{f}}(\Bbbk)\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{Vect}}(\Bbbk)\) by sending \(\ensuremath{\text{“}\varinjlim\text{”}}V_i\) to \(V:=\varinjlim_iV_i\) in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Vect}}(\Bbbk)\). The key to showing that it is fully faithful is \[\operatorname{Hom}_{\Bbbk}(V, W) \simeq \varprojlim_i \varinjlim_j \operatorname{Hom}_{\Bbbk}(V_i, W_j).\] Indeed, specifying a linear map \(f:V\to W\) is equivalent to specifying a compatible family of linear maps \(f_i:V_i\to W\), while the concrete description of filtered \(\varinjlim\) in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Vect}}(\Bbbk)\) shows that each \(f_i\) factors through some \(W_j\).

The functor \(\operatorname{Ind}\ensuremath{\mathsf{Vect}}_{\mathrm{f}}(\Bbbk)\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{Vect}}(\Bbbk)\) is also essentially surjective. For any \(\Bbbk\)-vector space \(V\), its finite-dimensional subspaces \(V^\flat\) form a filtered partially ordered set under inclusion, and there is a canonical isomorphism \(\varinjlim V^\flat\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}V\) in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Vect}}(\Bbbk)\).

A similar and even simpler argument shows that \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Set}}\) is equivalent to \(\operatorname{Ind}\ensuremath{\mathsf{FinSet}}\), where \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{FinSet}}\) denotes the category of finite small sets. Observe that \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{FinSet}}\) and \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Vect}}_{\mathrm{f}}(\Bbbk)\) are both essentially small: the isomorphism classes of their objects form a small set. Thus ind-objects are a construction that obtains the large from the small.

There is no shortage of such examples; Proposition reference will give a unified criterion for recognizing the Ind-completion of a category.

Example. Let \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{FinGrp}}\) denote the category of finite groups and let \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{proFinGrp}}\) denote the category of profinite groups from Definition reference. We shall show that \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{proFinGrp}}\) is equivalent to \(\operatorname{Pro}\ensuremath{\mathsf{FinGrp}}\).

Define a functor \(\operatorname{Pro}\ensuremath{\mathsf{FinGrp}}\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{proFinGrp}}\) by sending \(\ensuremath{\text{“}\varprojlim\text{”}}G_i\) to \(G:=\varprojlim_iG_i\) in the category \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{TopGrp}}\) of topological groups, giving each \(G_i\) the discrete topology. By definition, the data \((G_i)_i\) come from a functor \(I^{\operatorname{op}}\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{TopGrp}}\), where \(I\) is a small filtered category; Remark reference shows, however, that \(I\) may also be taken to be a filtered partially ordered set. As in Example reference, the equivalence reduces to proving that

  • the group \(G\) above is profinite;

  • \(\operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{TopGrp}}}(G,H)\simeq\varprojlim_j\varinjlim_i\operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{FinGrp}}}(G_i,H_j)\);

  • every profinite group can be expressed as a small filtered \(\varprojlim\) of finite groups.

But these are precisely the contents of Remark reference.

When \(\mathcal{C}\) itself already has small filtered \(\varinjlim\), there is also a relation in the reverse direction between \(\operatorname{Ind}\mathcal{C}\) and \(\mathcal{C}\). We give the dual statement for pro-objects at the same time.

Proposition. Suppose that for every small filtered category \(I\) and every functor \(\alpha:I\to\mathcal{C}\) (respectively \(\beta:I^{\operatorname{op}}\to\mathcal{C}\)), the object \(\varinjlim\alpha\) (respectively \(\varprojlim\beta\)) always exists. Then the embedding \(\iota:\mathcal{C}\to\operatorname{Ind}\mathcal{C}\) (respectively \(\mathcal{C}\to\operatorname{Pro}\mathcal{C}\)) has a left adjoint \(\sigma:\operatorname{Ind}\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{C}\) (respectively a right adjoint \(\tau:\operatorname{Pro}\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{C}\)), with \(\sigma\iota\simeq\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{\mathcal{C}}\) (respectively \(\tau\iota\simeq\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}_{\mathcal{C}}\)).

More concretely, if \(X=\ensuremath{\text{“}\varinjlim\text{”}}X_i\) (respectively \(X=\ensuremath{\text{“}\varprojlim\text{”}}X_i\)), then there is a canonical isomorphism \(\sigma(X)\simeq\varinjlim_iX_i\) (respectively \(\tau(X)\simeq\varprojlim_iX_i\)).

Proof. It suffices to treat the ind-version. By [Li1], the existence of a left adjoint \(\sigma\) is equivalent to the representability, for every ind-object \(X\), of the functor \[\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}^\wedge}(X, \cdot): \mathcal{C} \to \ensuremath{\mathsf{Set}}\] Write \(X=\ensuremath{\text{“}\varinjlim\text{”}}X_i\). This functor is isomorphic to \[\varprojlim_i \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}}(X_i, \cdot) \simeq \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}}\left( \varinjlim_i X_i, \cdot\right).\] This proves both the existence of the left adjoint \(\sigma\) and the asserted description.

For theoretical purposes, we often wish to align morphisms in \(\operatorname{Ind}\mathcal{C}\) or \(\operatorname{Pro}\mathcal{C}\). The following result does this.

Lemma. Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be ind-objects (respectively pro-objects) over \(\mathcal{C}\).

  1. There are a small filtered category \(K\) and functors \(\gamma,\delta:K\to\mathcal{C}\) (respectively \(K^{\operatorname{op}}\to\mathcal{C}\)) such that \(X=\ensuremath{\text{“}\varinjlim\text{”}}\gamma\) and \(Y=\ensuremath{\text{“}\varinjlim\text{”}}\delta\) (respectively \(X=\ensuremath{\text{“}\varprojlim\text{”}}\gamma\) and \(Y=\ensuremath{\text{“}\varprojlim\text{”}}\delta\)).

  2. Given a morphism \(f:X\to Y\), the data in (i) may be chosen together with a morphism of functors \(\varphi:\gamma\to\delta\) such that \(f\) equals \(\ensuremath{\text{“}\varinjlim\text{”}}\varphi\) (respectively \(\ensuremath{\text{“}\varprojlim\text{”}}\varphi\)).

  3. More generally, given two morphisms \(f,g:X\rightrightarrows Y\), the data may be chosen so that they are represented by the \(\ensuremath{\text{“}\varinjlim\text{”}}\) (respectively \(\ensuremath{\text{“}\varprojlim\text{”}}\)) of two morphisms \(\varphi,\psi:\gamma\to\delta\).

Proof. It suffices to treat the ind-version. For (i), first suppose that \(X\) and \(Y\) arise respectively from functors \(\alpha:I\to\mathcal{C}\) and \(\beta:J\to\mathcal{C}\). Define \(K\) to be the product category \(I\times J\); recall that its objects are pairs \((i,j)\in\operatorname{Ob}(I)\times\operatorname{Ob}(J)\) and that \(\operatorname{Hom}_K((i,j),(i',j')):=\operatorname{Hom}_I(i,i')\times\operatorname{Hom}_J(j,j')\). It is easy to see that \(K\) is small and filtered, and that both projection functors \[I \leftarrow K \rightarrow J, \quad i \mapsfrom (i, j) \mapsto j\] are cofinal (Definition reference); this follows by expanding the definitions. Define \(\gamma\) and \(\delta\) by composing these projections with \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\), respectively. Proposition reference then gives \(\ensuremath{\text{“}\varinjlim\text{”}}\alpha=\ensuremath{\text{“}\varinjlim\text{”}}\gamma\) and \(\ensuremath{\text{“}\varinjlim\text{”}}\beta=\ensuremath{\text{“}\varinjlim\text{”}}\delta\).

For (ii), modify the construction as follows. This time, let \(K\) be the category whose objects are triples \((i,j,t)\) forming a commutative diagram \[\text{Diagram appendix2-unit-141-d001}\] with morphisms defined by the evident commutative triangular diagrams. There are functors \(I\leftarrow K\rightarrow J\) given on objects by \(i\mapsfrom(i,j,t)\mapsto j\). Again define \(\gamma\) and \(\delta\) by composing these functors with \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\). The reader is asked to verify that

  • \(K\) is a small filtered category;

  • both functors \(I\leftarrow K\rightarrow J\) are cofinal;

  • the data \(t\) define a morphism \(\varphi:\gamma\to\delta\).

These facts give the required commutative diagram \[\text{Diagram appendix2-unit-141-d002}\]

For the pair of morphisms \(f,g:X\rightrightarrows Y\) in (iii), the argument is similar: define the objects of \(K\) to be quadruples \((i,j,s,t)\) with \(s,t:\alpha(i)\rightrightarrows\beta(j)\).2 The details are left to the reader.

The result above generalizes naturally to any finite collection of morphisms \(f,g,\ldots\in\operatorname{Hom}_{\operatorname{Ind}\mathcal{C}}(X,Y)\).

  1. This notation was introduced by P. Deligne.↩︎

  2. Translator’s note: the source prints \(\alpha(j)\) as the target, but \(j\) indexes \(\beta\) and the maps represent morphisms to \(Y\); the type-correct target is \(\beta(j)\).↩︎

Ind-Completion of Categories

Continuing the discussion of §reference, we now focus on ind-objects. The passage from \(\mathcal{C}\) to \(\operatorname{Ind}\mathcal{C}\) is an important technique, often called the Ind-completion of \(\mathcal{C}\).

Definition. Let \(I\) be a category. If there is a small category \(J\) together with a cofinal functor \(J\to I\) (Definition reference), then \(I\) is called cofinally small.

Lemma. A category \(I\) is cofinally small if and only if it has a full subcategory \(I'\) such that the inclusion functor \(I'\to I\) is cofinal and \(I'\) is small. If \(I\) is filtered, then \(I'\) is filtered as well.

Proof. It suffices to explain the only-if direction and the final assertion. Take a cofinal functor \(H:J\to I\) as in the definition. Let \(I'\) be the full subcategory consisting of all objects \(H(j)\), for \(j\in\operatorname{Ob}(J)\); it is plainly small. Factor \(H\) as \[J \xrightarrow{H'} I' \xrightarrow{G: \text{inclusion functor}} I.\] To prove that \(G:I'\to I\) is cofinal is equivalent to proving that the comma category \((i/G)\) is connected for every \(i\in\operatorname{Ob}(I)\); see Definition reference. This follows easily from the connectedness of \((i/H)\), and the verification is left to the reader.

For the filteredness of the cofinal full subcategory \(I'\), see Proposition reference.

Proposition (Recognizing ind-objects). Let \(X\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{C}^\wedge)\). The following statements are equivalent:

  1. \(X\) is an ind-object over \(\mathcal{C}\);

  2. the category \((h_{\mathcal{C}}/X)\) appearing in Theorem reference is filtered and cofinally small.

Proof. We first prove (i) \(\implies\) (ii). For filteredness, suppose that \(X=\ensuremath{\text{“}\varinjlim\text{”}}X_i\), where \(i\) ranges over the objects of a small filtered category \(I\) and \(X_i\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{C})\). Let \(\phi:S\to X\) and \(\phi':S'\to X\) be any two objects of \((h_{\mathcal{C}}/X)\). Proposition reference shows that there is an \(i\) (respectively, an \(i'\)) such that \(\phi\) (respectively, \(\phi'\)) factors through \(X_i\) (respectively, \(X_{i'}\)). Since \(I\) is filtered, we may assume without loss of generality that \(i=i'\). Thus both \(\phi\) and \(\phi'\) factor through the object \(X_i\to X\) of \((h_{\mathcal{C}}/X)\). This is the first condition for a filtered category.

The same argument also shows that the family of canonical morphisms \((X_i\to X)_i\) defines a cofinal functor \(I\to(h_{\mathcal{C}}/X)\). Hence \((h_{\mathcal{C}}/X)\) is cofinally small.

Next, consider two morphisms in \((h_{\mathcal{C}}/X)\) of the form \[\text{Diagram appendix2-unit-142-d001}\] We know that \(\phi'\) factors through some \(\phi'_i:S'\to X_i\). The equality \(\phi'f=\phi'g\) implies that there is a morphism \(\alpha:i\to j\) in \(I\) such that \(X(\alpha)\phi'_if=X(\alpha)\phi'_ig\), where \(X(\alpha):X_i\to X_j\). Equivalently, \(f\) and \(g\) are equalized by the following diagram: \[\text{Diagram appendix2-unit-142-d002}\] This proves that \((h_{\mathcal{C}}/X)\) is filtered.

We now prove (ii) \(\implies\) (i). Theorem reference shows that \(X\) is the \(\ensuremath{\text{“}\varinjlim\text{”}}\) of the functor \((h_{\mathcal{C}}/X)\to\mathcal{C}^\wedge\) that sends \(\phi:S\to X\) to \(S\). By Lemma reference, choose a cofinal full subcategory \(I\) of \((h_{\mathcal{C}}/X)\) such that \(I\) is a small filtered category. We may therefore write \(X\) as the ind-object \(\ensuremath{\text{“}\varinjlim\text{”}}X_i\).

A functor \(X:\mathcal{C}^{\operatorname{op}}\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{Set}}\) that lies in \(\operatorname{Ind}\mathcal{C}\) is also called ind-representable. Proposition reference is equivalently a criterion for ind-representability. Dually, one may speak of pro-representable functors and give an analogous criterion.

The following results use the terminology of Definition reference.

Proposition. The fully faithful functor \(\operatorname{Ind}\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{C}^\wedge\) creates small filtered \(\varinjlim\). In particular, \(\operatorname{Ind}\mathcal{C}\) has all small filtered \(\varinjlim\).

Proof. Take a small filtered category \(I\) and a functor \(\alpha:I\to\operatorname{Ind}\mathcal{C}\), and write \(X:=\ensuremath{\text{“}\varinjlim\text{”}}\alpha\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{C}^\wedge)\). Our goal is to prove that \(X\) lies in \(\operatorname{Ind}\mathcal{C}\). By Proposition reference, it suffices to prove that \((h_{\mathcal{C}}/X)\) is filtered and cofinally small.

For the first condition of filteredness, take \(\phi:S\to X\) and \(\phi':S'\to X\). Proposition reference implies that there are \(i,i'\in\operatorname{Ob}(I)\) such that these morphisms factor respectively through \(\phi_i:S\to X_i\) and \(\phi'_{i'}:S'\to X_{i'}\);1 without loss of generality, we may assume that \(i=i'\). Since \(X_i\) is an ind-object, write it as \(\ensuremath{\text{“}\varinjlim\text{”}}X_{ij}\). Applying Proposition reference once more, we may assume that both \(\phi_i\) and \(\phi'_i\) factor through some \(X_{ij}\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{C})\); the canonical morphism \(X_{ij}\to X\) makes it an object of \((h_{\mathcal{C}}/X)\).

The second condition, concerning the equalization of morphisms, is handled in the same way.

We now check that \((h_{\mathcal{C}}/X)\) is cofinally small. By Lemma reference, for each \(i\) there is a small subset \(S_i\) of \(\operatorname{Ob}((h_{\mathcal{C}}/X_i))\) such that every object of \((h_{\mathcal{C}}/X_i)\) has a morphism to an object of \(S_i\). Write \(F_i:(h_{\mathcal{C}}/X_i)\to(h_{\mathcal{C}}/X)\) for the evident functor, and set \[S:=\bigcup_i F_i(S_i)\;\subset\operatorname{Ob}((h_{\mathcal{C}}/X)).\] Then \(S\) is a small set, and the preceding argument in fact shows that every object of \((h_{\mathcal{C}}/X)\) has a morphism to an object of \(S\). Thus \(S\) determines a cofinal full subcategory of \((h_{\mathcal{C}}/X)\) (apply Proposition reference); consequently, \((h_{\mathcal{C}}/X)\) is cofinally small.

Lemma. Suppose that \(\mathcal{C}\) has finite \(\varprojlim\). Then the functor \(\operatorname{Ind}\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{C}^\wedge\) creates finite \(\varprojlim\), while \(\mathcal{C}\to\operatorname{Ind}\mathcal{C}\) preserves finite \(\varprojlim\). In particular, \(\operatorname{Ind}\mathcal{C}\) has finite \(\varprojlim\).

Under these hypotheses, finite \(\varprojlim\) in \(\operatorname{Ind}\mathcal{C}\) commute with small filtered \(\varinjlim\).

Proof. It is known that the embedding \(\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{C}^\wedge\) preserves small \(\varprojlim\). The assertion in the first paragraph therefore reduces to proving that \(\operatorname{Ind}\mathcal{C}\) is closed under finite \(\varprojlim\) in \(\mathcal{C}^\wedge\).

Since \(\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{C}^\wedge\) preserves small \(\varprojlim\), it sends a terminal object to a terminal object. The problem thus reduces further to proving that \(\operatorname{Ind}\mathcal{C}\) is closed under finite products and equalizers in \(\mathcal{C}^\wedge\). For the product of two ind-objects \(X\) and \(Y\), use Lemma reference (i) to choose a filtered category \(K\) and present them as \(X=\ensuremath{\text{“}\varinjlim\text{”}}X_k\) and \(Y=\ensuremath{\text{“}\varinjlim\text{”}}Y_k\). We claim that \(\ensuremath{\text{“}\varinjlim\text{”}}(X_k\times Y_k)\) gives \(X\times Y\) in \(\mathcal{C}^\wedge\). Indeed, for every \(S\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{C})\), \[\begin{multline*} \left(\ensuremath{\text{“}\varinjlim\text{”}}(X_k \times Y_k)\right)(S) = \varinjlim_k \left((X_k \times Y_k)(S)\right) = \varinjlim_k (X_k(S) \times Y_k(S)) \\ \simeq \varinjlim_k X_k(S) \times \varinjlim_k Y_k(S) = X(S) \times Y(S); \end{multline*}\] the canonical isomorphism on the second line uses the fact that small filtered \(\varinjlim\) commute with finite \(\varprojlim\) in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Set}}\) (Proposition reference).

Next we handle equalizers. Consider morphisms \(f,g:X\rightrightarrows Y\) between ind-objects. By Lemma reference (iii), we may assume that \(X=\ensuremath{\text{“}\varinjlim\text{”}}X_i\), \(Y=\ensuremath{\text{“}\varinjlim\text{”}}Y_i\), and that \(f,g\) arise respectively from two families of morphisms \(f_i,g_i:X_i\rightrightarrows Y_i\). Take \(\operatorname{ker}(f_i,g_i)\) in \(\mathcal{C}\). For every \(S\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{C})\) and every \(i\), we obtain an equalizer diagram in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Set}}\): \[\text{Diagram appendix2-unit-142-d003}\] Take \(\varinjlim\) over \(i\) and apply once again the fact that small filtered \(\varinjlim\) commute with finite \(\varprojlim\) in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Set}}\). This gives an equalizer diagram \[\text{Diagram appendix2-unit-142-d004}\] As \(S\) varies, this shows that the ind-object \(\ensuremath{\text{“}\varinjlim\text{”}}\operatorname{ker}(f_i,g_i)\) gives \(\operatorname{ker}(f,g)\) in \(\mathcal{C}^\wedge\).

In fact, the argument shows that small filtered \(\varinjlim\) commute with finite \(\varprojlim\) in \(\mathcal{C}^\wedge\); this is checked by reducing to \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Set}}\). Since \(\operatorname{Ind}\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{C}^\wedge\) creates small filtered \(\varinjlim\) (Proposition reference) and finite \(\varprojlim\), the commutation property continues to hold in \(\operatorname{Ind}\mathcal{C}\).

Lemma. Suppose that \(\mathcal{C}\) has finite \(\varinjlim\). Then \(\operatorname{Ind}\mathcal{C}\) also has finite \(\varinjlim\), and \(\mathcal{C}\to\operatorname{Ind}\mathcal{C}\) preserves them.

Under these hypotheses, \(\operatorname{Ind}\mathcal{C}\) is cocomplete.

Proof. Decompose finite \(\varinjlim\) into three cases: an initial object, coproducts of two objects, and coequalizers.

Suppose that \(X\) is an initial object of \(\mathcal{C}\). Then, for every ind-object \(Y=\ensuremath{\text{“}\varinjlim\text{”}}Y_j\), we have \(\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}^\wedge}(X,Y)\simeq\varinjlim_j\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}}(X,Y_j)\), which is plainly a singleton. Thus \(X\) is an initial object of \(\operatorname{Ind}\mathcal{C}\).

Next consider the coproduct of ind-objects \(X\) and \(Y\). Use Lemma reference (i) to choose a filtered category \(K\) and present both objects as \(X=\ensuremath{\text{“}\varinjlim\text{”}}X_k\) and \(Y=\ensuremath{\text{“}\varinjlim\text{”}}Y_k\). We claim that their coproduct is given by the ind-object \(\ensuremath{\text{“}\varinjlim\text{”}}(X_k\sqcup Y_k)\). For every ind-object \(S=\ensuremath{\text{“}\varinjlim\text{”}}S_h\), \[\begin{multline*} \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}^\wedge}(\ensuremath{\text{“}\varinjlim\text{”}}(X_k \sqcup Y_k), S) \simeq \varprojlim_k \varinjlim_h \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}}(X_k \sqcup Y_k, S_h) \\ \simeq \varprojlim_k \varinjlim_h \left( \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}}(X_k, S_h) \times \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}}(Y_k, S_h) \right) \\ \simeq \varprojlim_k \varinjlim_h \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}}(X_k, S_h) \times \varprojlim_k \varinjlim_h \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}}(Y_k, S_h), \end{multline*}\] where the last step uses the commutation of \(\varprojlim\) with \(\varprojlim\), as well as the commutation of small filtered \(\varinjlim\) with finite \(\varprojlim\) in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Set}}\). The final result is \(\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}^\wedge}(X,S)\times\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}^\wedge}(Y,S)\), and all the isomorphisms are canonical.

Now consider the coequalizer case. Let \(f,g:X\rightrightarrows Y\) be morphisms between ind-objects. By Lemma reference (iii), we may assume that \(X=\ensuremath{\text{“}\varinjlim\text{”}}X_i\), \(Y=\ensuremath{\text{“}\varinjlim\text{”}}Y_i\), and that \(f,g\) arise from two families of morphisms \(f_i,g_i:X_i\rightrightarrows Y_i\). For every \(S\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{C})\) and every \(i\), we have an equalizer diagram in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Set}}\): \[\text{Diagram appendix2-unit-142-d005}\]

If, via the Yoneda embedding, \(\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}}\) is rewritten as \(\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}^\wedge}\) and the object \(S\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{C})\) above is enlarged to an ind-object \(S=\ensuremath{\text{“}\varinjlim\text{”}}S_j\), the diagram remains an equalizer. Indeed, by Proposition reference, this merely amounts to replacing \(S\) by \(S_j\) in the formula above and then applying one additional \(\varinjlim_j\); an equalizer is a finite \(\varprojlim\), however, and hence is preserved by \(\varinjlim_j\).

Take \(\varprojlim_i\) of the resulting equalizer diagram, and then move \(\varprojlim_i\) into the first argument of \(\operatorname{Hom}\), where it becomes \(\ensuremath{\text{“}\varinjlim\text{”}}\). The result is an equalizer diagram in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Set}}\): \[\text{Diagram appendix2-unit-142-d006}\] Thus we have verified that \(\ensuremath{\text{“}\varinjlim\text{”}}\operatorname{coker}(f_i,g_i)\) has the universal property required of \(\operatorname{coker}(f,g)\) in \(\operatorname{Ind}\mathcal{C}\).

Finally, to prove that \(\operatorname{Ind}\mathcal{C}\) is cocomplete, it suffices to show that it has small coproducts. But an arbitrary small coproduct can be expressed as a filtered \(\varinjlim\) of finite coproducts. Apply Proposition reference. This proves the assertion.

  1. Translator’s note: the source prints the domain of \(\phi'_{i'}\) as \(S\). Since \(\phi'\) has domain \(S'\), the type-correct domain is \(S'\).↩︎

Ind-Completion and Extension of Functors

We continue the discussion of the preceding section, but shift the focus to functors.

Definition–Proposition (Ind-completion of a functor). Let \(F:\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{D}\) be a functor. There is a canonical functor \(\operatorname{Ind}F:\operatorname{Ind}\mathcal{C}\to\operatorname{Ind}\mathcal{D}\) such that the following diagram commutes up to canonical isomorphism: \[\text{Diagram appendix2-unit-143-d001}\] For every ind-object \(X=\ensuremath{\text{“}\varinjlim\text{”}}X_i\) over \(\mathcal{C}\), there is a canonical isomorphism \((\operatorname{Ind}F)(X)\simeq\ensuremath{\text{“}\varinjlim\text{”}}F(X_i)\).

Proof. The density theorem for the Yoneda embedding, Theorem reference, canonically presents every \(X\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{C}^\wedge)\) as \[X \simeq \ensuremath{\text{“}\varinjlim\text{”}}_{\phi: S \to X} S,\] where the data on the right are indexed by the category \((h_{\mathcal{C}}/X)\). For an ind-object \(X\), we wish to define \[(\operatorname{Ind}F)(X) := \ensuremath{\text{“}\varinjlim\text{”}}_{\phi: S \to X} F(S),\] which is plainly canonical; the issue is to show that the right-hand side is an ind-object over \(\mathcal{D}\). By Proposition reference, \((h_{\mathcal{C}}/X)\) is a filtered, cofinally small category. By Lemma reference, choose a cofinal full subcategory \(I\) that is small and filtered. Thus \((\operatorname{Ind}F)(X)\) is presented as a small filtered colimit indexed by \(I\), and hence is indeed an ind-object.

For a given ind-object \(X=\ensuremath{\text{“}\varinjlim\text{”}}X_i\), the proof of Proposition reference showed that the family of canonical morphisms \((X_i\to X)_i\) gives a cofinal functor \(I\to(h_{\mathcal{C}}/X)\). It follows immediately that \((\operatorname{Ind}F)(X)\simeq\ensuremath{\text{“}\varinjlim\text{”}}F(X_i)\). Taking \(X\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{C})\) and taking \(I\) to be the filtered poset with a single object gives the desired commutative diagram, up to canonical isomorphism.

Lemma. Let \(F:\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{D}\) be a functor. If \(\mathcal{C}\) and \(\mathcal{D}\) have finite \(\varinjlim\) (respectively, finite \(\varprojlim\)), and if \(F\) preserves them, then the functor \(\operatorname{Ind}F:\operatorname{Ind}\mathcal{C}\to\operatorname{Ind}\mathcal{D}\) constructed in Definition–Proposition reference also preserves them.

Proof. The existence of finite \(\varinjlim\) (respectively, finite \(\varprojlim\)) in \(\operatorname{Ind}\mathcal{C}\) and \(\operatorname{Ind}\mathcal{D}\) is guaranteed by Lemma reference (respectively, Lemma reference). Reviewing their proofs, one sees that all the \(\varinjlim\) (respectively, \(\varprojlim\)) considered there are described “index by index,” once the ind-objects and morphisms in question have been suitably aligned; meanwhile, \(\operatorname{Ind}F\) has the corresponding description. The issue therefore reduces to the assumption that \(F:\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{D}\) preserves finite \(\varinjlim\) (respectively, finite \(\varprojlim\)).

Lemma. Let \(F:\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{D}\) be a functor, and suppose that \(\mathcal{C}\) is small. Write \(F^\wedge:\mathcal{C}^\wedge\to\mathcal{D}^\wedge\) for the functor obtained by applying equation to the composite \(\mathcal{C}\xrightarrow{F}\mathcal{D}\xrightarrow{h_{\mathcal{D}}}\mathcal{D}^\wedge\). Up to isomorphism, the following diagram commutes: \[\text{Diagram appendix2-unit-143-d002}\] where both vertical functors are the evident embeddings.

Consequently, \(\operatorname{Ind}F\) preserves small filtered \(\varinjlim\).

Proof. Recall that \(\mathcal{D}^\wedge\) is cocomplete, so \(F^\wedge\) is indeed defined. For the first assertion, take an ind-object \(X=\ensuremath{\text{“}\varinjlim\text{”}}X_i\) over \(\mathcal{C}\), where \(i\) ranges over a small filtered category \(I\), or more generally over a cofinally small filtered category; the latter can canonically be taken to be \((h_{\mathcal{C}}/X)\). By the construction in equation, its image under \(F^\wedge\) is \(\ensuremath{\text{“}\varinjlim\text{”}}F(X_i)\) in \(\mathcal{D}^\wedge\). By the proof of Definition–Proposition reference, this is also precisely the image of \((\operatorname{Ind}F)(X)\) in \(\mathcal{D}^\wedge\).

For the second assertion, Proposition reference states that \(F^\wedge\) preserves small \(\varinjlim\). Since the vertical functors in the diagram create small filtered \(\varinjlim\) (Proposition reference), it follows immediately that \(\operatorname{Ind}F\) preserves small filtered \(\varinjlim\).

Definition–Proposition. Let \(F:\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{D}\) be a functor, and suppose that \(\mathcal{D}\) has small filtered \(\varinjlim\). Define \(\hat{F}:\operatorname{Ind}\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{D}\) to be the composite functor \[\operatorname{Ind}\mathcal{C} \xrightarrow{\operatorname{Ind}F} \operatorname{Ind}\mathcal{D} \xrightarrow[\text{Proposition \href{#prop:Ind-adjunction}{reference}}]{\sigma} \mathcal{D};\] if \(X=\ensuremath{\text{“}\varinjlim\text{”}}X_i\) is an ind-object over \(\mathcal{C}\), then there is a canonical isomorphism \(\hat{F}(X)\simeq\varinjlim_i F(X_i)\). In particular, the composite of \(\hat{F}\) with the embedding \(\mathcal{C}\to\operatorname{Ind}\mathcal{C}\) is isomorphic to \(F\).

If, in addition, \(\mathcal{C}\) and \(\mathcal{D}\) have finite \(\varinjlim\), and \(F\) preserves them, then \(\hat{F}\) preserves them as well.

Proof. The first assertion merely combines the relevant statements in Proposition reference and Definition–Proposition reference.

For the second assertion, Lemma reference shows that \(\operatorname{Ind}F\) preserves finite \(\varinjlim\). On the other hand, since \(\sigma\) has a right adjoint, it too preserves \(\varinjlim\).

When \(\mathcal{C}\) is a small category, Definition–Proposition reference can be strengthened further.

Proposition. Let \(F:\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{D}\) be a functor, suppose that \(\mathcal{C}\) is small, and suppose that \(\mathcal{D}\) has small filtered \(\varinjlim\). Then \(\hat{F}:\operatorname{Ind}\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{D}\) preserves all small filtered \(\varinjlim\).

Proof. Lemma reference shows that \(\operatorname{Ind}F\) preserves small filtered \(\varinjlim\), while \(\sigma\) has a right adjoint.

Proposition (Recognizing an Ind-completion). Suppose that \(\mathcal{C}\) has small filtered \(\varinjlim\) and that \(\mathcal{C}'\) is a full subcategory of \(\mathcal{C}\). The embedding functor \(\iota:\mathcal{C}'\to\mathcal{C}\) induces a functor \(\hat{\iota}:\operatorname{Ind}(\mathcal{C}')\to\mathcal{C}\) by the construction of Definition–Proposition reference. Suppose that \(\mathcal{C}'\) satisfies the following conditions:

  • every object of \(\mathcal{C}'\) is compact in \(\mathcal{C}\) (Definition reference);

  • every object of \(\mathcal{C}\) can be presented as a small filtered \(\varinjlim\) of objects in \(\mathcal{C}'\).

Then \(\hat{\iota}\) is an equivalence.

Proof. By construction, \(\hat{\iota}\) sends an ind-object \(\ensuremath{\text{“}\varinjlim\text{”}}X_i\) over \(\mathcal{C}'\) to \(\varinjlim X_i\) in \(\mathcal{C}\); here \(I\to\mathcal{C}'\) is the given functor and \(I\) is small and filtered. By assumption, every object of \(\mathcal{C}\) can be presented in this form, so \(\hat{\iota}\) is essentially surjective.

We next prove that \(\hat{\iota}\) is fully faithful. Consider ind-objects \(\ensuremath{\text{“}\varinjlim\text{”}}X_i\) and \(\ensuremath{\text{“}\varinjlim\text{”}}Y_j\) over \(\mathcal{C}'\). By compactness of the objects of \(\mathcal{C}'\) in \(\mathcal{C}\), an argument similar to that of Proposition reference gives \[\begin{gather*} \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}}\left( \varinjlim_i X_i, \; \varinjlim_j Y_j\right) \simeq \varprojlim_i \varinjlim_j \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}'}(X_i, Y_j). \end{gather*}\] This is a canonical bijection, proving the assertion.

Conversely, if \(\mathcal{C}=\operatorname{Ind}(\mathcal{C}')\), then \(\mathcal{C}'\) embeds as a full subcategory of \(\mathcal{C}\) and satisfies all the conditions above.

Ind-Completion of Abelian Categories

This section continues the discussion and standing assumptions of §§reference—reference.

Theorem. If \(\mathcal{C}\) is an Abelian category, then \(\operatorname{Ind}\mathcal{C}\) is also Abelian and \(\mathcal{C}\to\operatorname{Ind}\mathcal{C}\) is a fully faithful exact functor.

Dually, if \(\mathcal{C}\) is an Abelian category, then \(\mathcal{C}\to\operatorname{Pro}\mathcal{C}\) is likewise a fully faithful exact functor between Abelian categories.

Proof. We first treat the assertion about \(\operatorname{Ind}\mathcal{C}\). Below, write \(\operatorname{Hom}:=\operatorname{Hom}_{\operatorname{Ind}\mathcal{C}}\). Since \(\mathcal{C}\to\operatorname{Ind}\mathcal{C}\) preserves finite \(\varinjlim\) (Lemma reference) and finite \(\varprojlim\) (Lemma reference), it sends a zero object to a zero object. This also shows that \(\operatorname{Ind}\mathcal{C}\) has finite \(\varinjlim\) and finite \(\varprojlim\).

Next, the canonical morphism in equation, \[\delta: Y \sqcup Y \to Y \times Y, \quad Y \in \operatorname{Ob}(\operatorname{Ind}\mathcal{C}),\] is always an isomorphism: by the “index-by-index” construction of products and coproducts of ind-objects, verification reduces immediately to the case \(X,Y\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{C})\). Following the method of Proposition reference, we may therefore define addition on \(\operatorname{Hom}(X,Y)\) by taking \(f+g\) to be the composite \[X \to X \times X \xrightarrow{f \times g} Y \times Y \xrightarrow{\delta^{-1}} Y \sqcup Y \to Y.\] The reader may check that under \[\operatorname{Hom}(X,Y)\simeq\varprojlim_i\varinjlim_j\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}}(X_i,Y_j),\] this operation becomes the addition on \(\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}}\) characterized in the same way (recall that \(\varinjlim_j\) is filtered). Thus this operation indeed makes \(\operatorname{Ind}\mathcal{C}\) an \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ab}}\)-category, then an additive category, and makes \(\mathcal{C}\to\operatorname{Ind}\mathcal{C}\) an additive functor.

Consider any morphism \(f:X\to Y\) in \(\operatorname{Ind}\mathcal{C}\). We claim that the canonical morphism \(\operatorname{coim}(f)\to\operatorname{im}(f)\) is always an isomorphism. By Lemma reference (ii), we may assume that \(f\) is induced by a family of morphisms \(f_i:X_i\to Y_i\) in \(\mathcal{C}\). In an additive category, images and coimages are described by kernels and cokernels (Proposition reference); recall also the properties established in the preceding proof, such as \(\operatorname{ker}(f)=\ensuremath{\text{“}\varinjlim\text{”}}\operatorname{ker}(f_i)\). The assertion therefore reduces immediately to \(\operatorname{coim}(f_i)\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}\operatorname{im}(f_i)\). Hence \(\operatorname{Ind}\mathcal{C}\) is Abelian.

Finally, exactness of \(\mathcal{C}\to\operatorname{Ind}\mathcal{C}\) follows because this functor preserves finite \(\varinjlim\) and finite \(\varprojlim\).

The concept of an Abelian category is self-dual (Proposition reference), and \(\operatorname{Pro}\mathcal{C}\simeq\operatorname{Ind}(\mathcal{C}^{\operatorname{op}})^{\operatorname{op}}\). The dual assertion about \(\operatorname{Pro}\mathcal{C}\) follows at once.

Recall that an Abelian category is a special kind of additive category, and additivity is a property of a category, not additional structure; see the discussion following Corollary reference.

Remark. If \(\mathcal{C}\) is further assumed to be a \(\Bbbk\)-linear Abelian category, where \(\Bbbk\) is a commutative ring, then the same is true of \(\operatorname{Ind}\mathcal{C}\), and \(\mathcal{C}\to\operatorname{Ind}\mathcal{C}\) is a \(\Bbbk\)-linear functor. The key is to define canonically a \(\Bbbk\)-module structure on every \(\operatorname{Hom}(X,Y)\) such that, on the right-hand side of the bijection \[\operatorname{Hom}(X, Y) \simeq \varprojlim_i \varinjlim_j \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}}(X_i, Y_j),\] it is reflected by the \(\Bbbk\)-module structure on each \(\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}}(X_i,Y_j)\). This condition can be taken as the definition, but one must show that it depends only on \(X\) and \(Y\), not on the choices of \((X_i)_i\) and \((Y_j)_j\). The verification presents no essential difficulty; the details are left as an exercise.

Lemma. Let \(F:\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{D}\) be a functor between Abelian categories. The functor \(\operatorname{Ind}F:\operatorname{Ind}\mathcal{C}\to\operatorname{Ind}\mathcal{D}\) of Definition–Proposition reference is also additive.

Proof. Consider ind-objects \(X=\ensuremath{\text{“}\varinjlim\text{”}}X_i\) and \(Y=\ensuremath{\text{“}\varinjlim\text{”}}Y_j\) over \(\mathcal{C}\). By construction, the map induced by \(\operatorname{Ind}F\) on morphisms is \[\varprojlim_i \varinjlim_j \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}}(X_i, Y_j) \xrightarrow{\text{induced by $F$}} \varprojlim_i \varinjlim_j \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{D}}(FX_i, FY_j).\] In view of the addition on the \(\operatorname{Hom}\)-sets of \(\operatorname{Ind}\mathcal{C}\) and \(\operatorname{Ind}\mathcal{D}\) (see the proof of Theorem reference), this map is a homomorphism of additive groups.

Lemma. If the Abelian category \(\mathcal{C}\) has small filtered \(\varinjlim\), then the functor \(\sigma:\operatorname{Ind}\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{C}\) of Proposition reference is additive.

Proof. This can be verified directly as above, or deduced from the following fact: \(\sigma\) is left adjoint to \(\operatorname{Ind}\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{C}\), so Corollary reference (v) implies its additivity.

If \(\mathcal{C}\) and \(\mathcal{D}\) are \(\Bbbk\)-linear, where \(\Bbbk\) is a commutative ring, and \(F\) is also \(\Bbbk\)-linear, the preceding results have evident generalizations.

The following result is used in §reference.

Proposition. Let \(F:\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{D}\) be a right-exact functor between Abelian categories. Suppose that \(\mathcal{D}\) has small filtered \(\varinjlim\).

  1. The extension \(\hat{F}:\operatorname{Ind}\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{D}\) given by Definition–Proposition reference is right exact.

  2. If, in addition, \(F\) is exact and small filtered \(\varinjlim\) are exact in \(\mathcal{D}\), then \(\hat{F}\) is exact.

  3. Under the hypotheses of (i), if \(\mathcal{C}\) is also assumed to be small, then \(\hat{F}\) preserves all small \(\varinjlim\).

Proof. The preceding two lemmas show that \(\hat{F}\) is additive, while Definition–Proposition reference shows that \(\hat{F}\) preserves finite \(\varinjlim\). This proves (i).

Now assume the hypotheses of (ii). It suffices to prove that \(\hat{F}\) preserves \(\operatorname{ker}\). Let \(f:X\to Y\) be a morphism in \(\operatorname{Ind}\mathcal{C}\). By Lemma reference (ii), we may assume that \(X=\ensuremath{\text{“}\varinjlim\text{”}}X_i\), \(Y=\ensuremath{\text{“}\varinjlim\text{”}}Y_i\), and \(f=\ensuremath{\text{“}\varinjlim\text{”}}f_i\), where the morphisms \(f_i:X_i\to Y_i\) satisfy the compatibility conditions. First apply \(F\) and then \(\varinjlim_i\) to the exact sequence \[0 \to \operatorname{ker}(f_i) \to X_i \xrightarrow{f_i} Y_i.\] The result is the exact sequence \[0 \to \varinjlim_i F\operatorname{ker}(f_i) \to \varinjlim_i FX_i \to \varinjlim_i FY_i.\]

By the proof of Lemma reference, \(\ensuremath{\text{“}\varinjlim\text{”}}\operatorname{ker}(f_i)=\ensuremath{\text{“}\varinjlim\text{”}}\operatorname{ker}(f_i,0)\) gives \(\operatorname{ker}(f)=\operatorname{ker}(f,0)\); hence the first term of this sequence is identified with \(\hat{F}(\operatorname{ker}(f))\). On the other hand, the morphism in the second part is identified with \(\hat{F}f:\hat{F}X\to\hat{F}Y\). This proves (ii).

Now consider (iii). Proposition reference states that \(\hat{F}\) preserves all small filtered \(\varinjlim\).1 Together with right exactness, this implies that \(\hat{F}\) preserves all small \(\varinjlim\).

We continue by focusing on the Ind-completion of a small category. We shall need the theory of Grothendieck categories from §reference.

Lemma. If \(\mathcal{C}\) is a small category with finite \(\varinjlim\), then \(\operatorname{Ind}\mathcal{C}\) has a generator.

Proof. We know that \(\operatorname{Ind}\mathcal{C}\) is cocomplete (Lemma reference) and that \(\mathcal{C}\) is small. Thus, in \(\operatorname{Ind}\mathcal{C}\) we may form \[s := \coprod_{X \in \operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{C})} X.\]

We show that \(s\) is a generator. For a pair of morphisms \(f,g:X\rightrightarrows Y\) in \(\operatorname{Ind}\mathcal{C}\), write \(X=\ensuremath{\text{“}\varinjlim\text{”}}X_i\). By the construction of \(s\), for each \(i\) one may choose \(\epsilon_i\) such that the composite \[X_i \xrightarrow{\text{canonical coproduct morphism}} s \xrightarrow{\epsilon_i} X\] is the canonical morphism \(X_i\to X\). If \(f\epsilon=g\epsilon\) for every morphism \(\epsilon:s\to X\), then taking \(\epsilon=\epsilon_i\) shows that the restrictions of \(f\) and \(g\) to every \(X_i\) agree; hence \(f=g\).

Theorem. If \(\mathcal{C}\) is a small Abelian category, then \(\operatorname{Ind}\mathcal{C}\) is a Grothendieck category.

Proof. Theorem reference states that \(\operatorname{Ind}\mathcal{C}\) is Abelian. We verify the conditions for a Grothendieck category one by one.

  • Cocompleteness.This is contained in Lemma reference.

  • Generator.Its existence is guaranteed by Lemma reference.

  • Exactness of small filtered \(\varinjlim\).Let \(I\) be a small filtered category, let \(\alpha,\beta,\gamma:I\to\operatorname{Ind}\mathcal{C}\) be functors, and let \(\alpha\to\beta\to\gamma\) be morphisms such that \[0 \to \alpha(i) \to \beta(i) \to \gamma(i) \to 0\] is a short exact sequence for every \(i\in\operatorname{Ob}(I)\). We wish to prove that \[0 \to \varinjlim \alpha \to \varinjlim \beta \to \varinjlim \gamma \to 0\] is also exact. As explained in Example reference, \(\varinjlim\) always preserves \(\operatorname{coker}\); the point is to prove that it preserves \(\operatorname{ker}\). But \(\operatorname{ker}\) is a finite \(\varprojlim\), so this follows from the second assertion of Lemma reference.

This proves the theorem.

  1. Translator’s note: the source adds the pointer “(ii),” although Proposition reference is not divided into numbered parts.↩︎

The Freyd–Mitchell Embedding Theorem

We continue to fix a Grothendieck universe \(\mathcal{U}\) in order to distinguish categories (which by default mean \(\mathcal{U}\)-categories) from small categories. By convention, all groups, rings, and modules mentioned below are by default realized on small sets (that is, \(\mathcal{U}\)-sets).

Lemma. Let \(\mathcal{C}\) be a cocomplete Abelian category with a projective generator, and let \(O\) be a small subset of \(\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{C})\). Then \(\mathcal{C}\) has a projective generator \(S\) such that every \(X\in O\) is a quotient of \(S\).

Proof. Choose any projective generator \(s\) of \(\mathcal{C}\). Since \(\mathcal{C}\) is cocomplete, form the direct sum \[S := \bigoplus_{X \in O} s^{\oplus \operatorname{Hom}(s, X)}.\] This object remains projective. For each \(X\in O\), define the canonical morphism \(S\twoheadrightarrow X\) whose restriction to the direct-summand copy of \(s\) corresponding to \(f\in\operatorname{Hom}(s,X)\) is \(f\), and whose restriction to every other direct-summand copy is \(0\). The generator property readily shows that this is an epimorphism; see the proof of Theorem reference for details.

The following result is a simple variation on Theorem reference.

Lemma. Let \(S\) be a projective generator of an Abelian category \(\mathcal{C}\). Define \(R:=\operatorname{End}_{\mathcal{C}}(S)\), thereby obtaining a faithful exact functor (Proposition reference) \[G := \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}}(S, \cdot): \mathcal{C} \to \ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}\text{-}}R.\] If \(X\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{C})\) is a quotient of a direct sum of finitely many copies of \(S\), then the map induced by \(G\), \[\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}}(X, Y) \to \operatorname{Hom}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}\text{-}}R}(GX, GY)\] is bijective for every \(Y\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{C})\).

Proof. Take \(m\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}_{\geq 0}\) and a short exact sequence in \(\mathcal{C}\) \[0 \to X' \to S^{\oplus m} \to X \to 0.\] Applying \(G\) gives a short exact sequence in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}\text{-}}R\). Consider the following commutative diagram with exact rows in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ab}}\): \[\begin{equation} \hypertarget{eqn:FM-prep-2}{}\text{Diagram appendix2-unit-145-d001} \end{equation}\] where all vertical arrows arise from the faithful functor \(G\) and hence are injective. Observe that the composite \[\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}}(S, Y) \xrightarrow{\ensuremath{\mathrm{id}}} GY \xleftarrow[\psi(1_R) \mapsfrom \psi]{\sim} \operatorname{Hom}_R(R, GY) = \operatorname{Hom}_R(GS, GY)\] is the same as the map on \(\operatorname{Hom}\) induced by \(G\). This is of course nearly a tautology, and was checked in the proof of Lemma reference. Since \(G\) is additive, the middle vertical arrow in equation is an isomorphism. A straightforward diagram chase in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ab}}\) shows that the left vertical arrow is also an isomorphism.

Theorem (P. Freyd, B. Mitchell [Fr03).] Let \(\mathcal{A}\) be a small Abelian category. Then there are a ring \(R\) and a fully faithful exact functor \(F:\mathcal{A}\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}\text{-}}R\).

Proof. The following argument is taken from [KS06]. Since \(\mathcal{A}^{\operatorname{op}}\) is again a small Abelian category, Theorem reference shows that \(\operatorname{Ind}(\mathcal{A}^{\operatorname{op}})\) is a Grothendieck category. Corollary reference therefore guarantees that it has an injective cogenerator. Recalling that \[\operatorname{Pro}(\mathcal{A}) \simeq \operatorname{Ind}(\mathcal{A}^{\operatorname{op}})^{\operatorname{op}},\] we conclude that \(\operatorname{Pro}(\mathcal{A})\) has a projective generator. Moreover, \(\mathcal{A}\to\operatorname{Pro}(\mathcal{A})\) is a fully faithful exact functor between Abelian categories (Theorem reference).

Regard \(\mathcal{A}\) as a full subcategory of \(\operatorname{Pro}(\mathcal{A})\). Applying Lemma reference, with \(O=\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{A})\), gives a projective generator \(S\) of \(\operatorname{Pro}(\mathcal{A})\) such that every object of \(\mathcal{A}\) is a quotient of \(S\). Now consider the functor \[\mathcal{A} \to \operatorname{Pro}(\mathcal{A}) \xrightarrow{G} \ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}\text{-}}R , \quad G := \operatorname{Hom}_{\operatorname{Pro}(\mathcal{A})}(S, \cdot), \; R := \operatorname{End}_{\operatorname{Pro}(\mathcal{A})}(S).\]1 Write the composite as \(F\). Since each factor is exact, \(F\) is exact. Lemma reference shows that \(G\) is fully faithful; therefore \(F\) is fully faithful. This proves the theorem.

Corollary. Let \(\mathcal{A}\) be a small Abelian category. Then there is a faithful exact functor \(E:\mathcal{A}\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ab}}\).

The Freyd–Mitchell theorem allows many commutative-diagram arguments about general Abelian categories to be reduced to the case of \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Mod}\text{-}}R\), or even of \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Ab}}\). Since these two categories are concrete, their objects have elements, and diagram-chasing techniques [Li1] greatly simplify many problems. Under suitable set-theoretic assumptions, the requirement that the category be small can be met by enlarging the Grothendieck universe.

  1. Translator’s note: the source prints the endomorphism-ring subscript as \(\operatorname{Pro}\mathcal{C}\). Here \(S\) is an object of \(\operatorname{Pro}(\mathcal{A})\), so the type-correct subscript is \(\operatorname{Pro}(\mathcal{A})\).↩︎

Exercises

Let \(E\) be a Hausdorff topological group, let \(M\) be a finite normal subgroup of \(E\), and suppose that \(E/M\) is a profinite group with respect to the quotient topology. Prove that \(E\) is also profinite.

Define \(\hat{\mathbb{N}}\) to be the set of all maps \(n:\{\text{primes}\}\to\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}_{\geq 0}\sqcup\{+\infty\}\); its elements may be written formally as products \(\prod_{p:\text{prime}}p^{n_p}\). Via prime factorization, \(\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}_{\geq 1}\) embeds as a subset of \(\hat{\mathbb{N}}\). Multiplication, greatest common divisors, least common multiples, and the notion of being relatively prime are defined for these expressions in the evident way. Let \(H\) be a closed subgroup of a profinite group \(G\). Define \[(G:H) := \text{the least common multiple of all}\; (G/K : H/(H \cap K)) \;\text{in $\hat{\mathbb{N}}$},\] where \(K\) ranges over the open normal subgroups of \(G\).

  1. Prove that \((G:H)\) is also the least common multiple of all \((G:L)\), where \(L\) ranges over the open subgroups containing \(H\). Hint. Every such \(L\) must contain an open subgroup of the form \(HK\), with \(K\) as above.

  2. Prove that if \(H_2\subset H_1\subset G\), then \((G:H_2)=(G:H_1)(H_1:H_2)\).

    Hint. Set \(G_K=G/K\) and \(H_{i,K}=H_i/H_i\cap K\). It is known that \((G_K:H_{2,K})=(G_K:H_{1,K})(H_{1,K}:H_{2,K})\); take least common multiples on both sides of the equality.

  3. Let \(H_1\supset H_2\supset\cdots\) be a descending sequence of closed subgroups, and put \(H:=\bigcap_iH_i\). Prove that \((G:H)\) is the least common multiple of all \((G:H_i)\).

  4. Prove that \(H\) is open if and only if \((G:H)\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}_{\geq 1}\).

Let \(p\) be a prime and let \(G\) be a profinite group. A closed subgroup \(P\) satisfying

is called a pro-\(p\) Sylow subgroup of \(G\).

  1. Prove that \(G\) always has a pro-\(p\) Sylow subgroup. Hint. Every \(G/K\) has a Sylow \(p\)-subgroup \(P_K\). Apply the fact that a filtered \(\varprojlim\) of nonempty finite sets is nonempty (the next exercise) to choose \(P_K\) compatibly for every \(G/K\), and then consider \(\varprojlim_KP_K\hookrightarrow G\).

  2. For the profinite completion \(\hat{\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}}:=\varprojlim_{n\geq 1}\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}/n\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\) of \(\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\), verify that the additive group of the ring of \(p\)-adic integers \(\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}_p\) is a pro-\(p\) Sylow subgroup of \(\hat{\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}}\).

  3. Prove that any two pro-\(p\) Sylow subgroups are conjugate. Hint. As in the argument for (i), reduce to the case of finite groups.

  4. Prove that every pro-\(p\) subgroup of \(G\) is contained in a pro-\(p\) Sylow subgroup.1

(N. Bourbaki [BouE]) Let \((I,\leq)\) be a nonempty filtered partially ordered set, and let a functor \(X:I^{\operatorname{op}}\to\ensuremath{\mathsf{Set}}\) be given, written as \((X_i)_{i\in\operatorname{Ob}(I)}\); denote the map corresponding to \(i\leq j\) by \(f_{ij}:X_j\to X_i\). By the following method, prove that if every \(X_i\) is a nonempty finite set, then \(\varprojlim_iX_i\neq\emptyset\).

  1. Consider families of sets \((A_i)_{i\in\operatorname{Ob}(I)}\) satisfying \[\emptyset \neq A_i \subset X_i, \quad i \leq j \implies f_{ij}(A_j) \subset A_i .\] These families form a set \(\Sigma\). Give it the partial order \(\preceq\) defined as follows: \((A_i)_i\preceq(A'_i)_i\) means that \(A'_i\subset A_i\) for every \(i\). Use Zorn’s lemma to show that \((\Sigma,\preceq)\) has a maximal element.

    Hint. Clearly \(\Sigma\) is nonempty. For a chain in \((\Sigma,\preceq)\), check that taking intersections at each index \(i\) still gives an element of \(\Sigma\), and hence gives an upper bound for the chain. Nonemptiness requires the hypothesis that the sets are finite.

  2. Prove that if \((A_i)_i\) is a maximal element of \((\Sigma,\preceq)\), then \(f_{ij}(A_j)=A_i\) for every \(i\leq j\).

    Hint. Set \(A'_i:=\bigcap_{i\leq j}f_{ij}(A_j)\subset A_i\). It suffices to prove that \((A'_i)_i\in\Sigma\). Nonemptiness follows from the finiteness hypothesis; the only other point to prove is that \(f_{ij}(A'_j)\subset A'_i\). First observe that \(f_{ij}(A'_j)\subset\bigcap_{j\leq k}f_{ik}(A_k)\). Then use filteredness to show that \(\bigcap_{j\leq k}f_{ik}(A_k)=\bigcap_{i\leq h}f_{ih}(A_h)=A'_i\).

  3. Continuing from the preceding parts, prove that every \(A_i\) in a maximal element \((A_i)_i\) is a singleton, and thereby prove that \(\varprojlim_iX_i\neq\emptyset\).

    Hint. Choose \(i\in\operatorname{Ob}(I)\) and \(x_i\in A_i\). For each \(j\), define \[B_j := \begin{cases} A_j \cap f_{ij}^{-1}(x_i), & i \leq j \\ A_j, & \text{otherwise}. \end{cases}\] Prove that \((B_j)_j\in\Sigma\), so that \(A_j=B_j\) always, including when \(i=j\).

Observe that the case \((I,\leq)=(\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}_{\geq 0},\leq)\) can be handled by Lemma reference.

Form the category \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{ext}}_{\mathrm{alg}}(F)\) (respectively, \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{ext}}_{\mathrm{f}}(F)\)) of all algebraic extensions (respectively, finite extensions) of a field \(F\). Show that \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{ext}}_{\mathrm{alg}}(F)\) is equivalent to \(\operatorname{Ind}\left(\ensuremath{\mathsf{ext}}_{\mathrm{f}}(F)\right)\).

Let \(A\) be a coalgebra over a field \(\Bbbk\), that is, a coalgebra in the monoidal category \(\left(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Vect}}(\Bbbk),\otimes_{\Bbbk}\right)\) (Definition reference). Write \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Comod}\text{-}}A\) for the category of right \(A\)-comodules (Definition reference), and write \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Comod}_{\mathrm{f}}\text{-}}A\) for its full subcategory consisting of finite-dimensional right \(A\)-comodules. Prove that \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Comod}\text{-}}A\) is equivalent to \(\operatorname{Ind}\left(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Comod}_{\mathrm{f}}\text{-}}A\right)\).

Hint. As in the case of vector spaces in Example reference, apply Lemma reference.

Consider a full subcategory \(\mathcal{C}'\subset\mathcal{C}\) and a functor \(F':\mathcal{C}'\to\mathcal{D}\). Assume that

  • \(\mathcal{C}'\) is small, and all its objects are compact in \(\mathcal{C}\);

  • every object of \(\mathcal{C}\) can be written as a small filtered \(\varinjlim\) of objects of \(\mathcal{C}'\);

  • \(\mathcal{D}\) has small filtered \(\varinjlim\).

Prove that under these hypotheses \(F'\) extends to a functor \(F:\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{D}\) that preserves small filtered \(\varinjlim\); up to isomorphism, \(F\) is unique.

Hint. First extend \(F'\) to \(\widehat{F'}:\operatorname{Ind}(\mathcal{C}')\to\mathcal{D}\) (Definition–Proposition reference), and then obtain \(F:\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{D}\) via the equivalence in Proposition reference. We also need Proposition reference.

For uniqueness, observe that if an object \(X\) of \(\mathcal{C}\) is written as \(\varinjlim_iX_i\), where \(I\to\mathcal{C}'\) is a functor and \(I\) is a small filtered category, then necessarily \(F(X)\simeq\varinjlim_iF'(X_i)\).

Suppose that the category \(\mathcal{C}\) has finite \(\varinjlim\). Prove that \(\operatorname{Ind}\mathcal{C}\) is an \(\aleph_0\)-presentable category in the sense of Definition reference.

A compact Hausdorff totally disconnected topological space is called a Stone space; by convention, topological spaces are by default realized on small sets. Write \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Stone}}\) for the category of all Stone spaces, and \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{FinSet}}\) for the category of all finite small sets.

  1. Prove that the Cantor set and \(\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}_p\) are Stone spaces, for any prime \(p\).

  2. Prove that \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Stone}}\) is equivalent to \(\operatorname{Pro}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{FinSet}})\); thus Stone spaces may be regarded as profinite sets.

  3. Prove that profinite groups are precisely the group objects in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Stone}}\).

  4. Prove that the category of locally compact Hausdorff totally disconnected topological spaces is equivalent to \(\operatorname{Ind}\operatorname{Pro}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{FinSet}})\); prove that \(\ensuremath{\mathbb{Q}}_p\) is such a space.

Check the details of Remark reference.

Show that \(\operatorname{Ind}\mathcal{C}\) can be characterized by the following property: for every category \(\mathcal{D}\) with small filtered \(\varinjlim\), the functor induced by \(\mathcal{C}\to\operatorname{Ind}\mathcal{C}\), \[\mathrm{Fct}^0(\operatorname{Ind}\mathcal{C}, \mathcal{D}) \to \mathrm{Fct}(\mathcal{C}, \mathcal{D})\] is an equivalence. Here \(\mathrm{Fct}(\cdots)\) denotes a functor category, while the superscript \(0\) denotes the full subcategory consisting of functors that preserve small filtered \(\varinjlim\).

  1. Translator’s note: in this item the source says “Sylow \(p\)-subgroup,” whereas the object defined and discussed here is a pro-\(p\) Sylow subgroup.↩︎

Mastery Bridge 001: Diagram Chasing

Status and attribution. This unit is independent instructional material prepared to accompany this book. It is not part of Wen-Wei Li’s source text and must not be attributed to him. Production provenance: OpenAI Codex gpt-5.6-sol, Ultra. This material is available under the Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International license (CC BY 4.0; https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/), and is therefore compatible with the license of the source text.

Prerequisite map

This unit can be read after mastering the following short chain of prerequisites.

  • Kernels, cokernels, and their functoriality: §reference, especially equation.

  • Images, coimages, and epi–mono factorization: §reference.

  • Abelian categories and the stability of epimorphisms and monomorphisms under pullback and pushout: §reference and Proposition reference.

  • Complexes, cohomology, and exactness: §reference, especially Definition reference.

  • The categorical construction of connecting morphisms and the Snake Lemma: §reference, Remark reference, and Theorem reference.

Conceptually, the progression is \[\text{kernels/cokernels} \Longrightarrow \text{images and exactness} \Longrightarrow \text{lift--map--descend} \Longrightarrow \text{connecting morphisms}.\]

Working method: start with the obstruction

For element chasing in a module category, use the following discipline.

  1. State precisely what must be proved: membership in a kernel or image, or equality of two cokernel classes.

  2. Start with the element that measures the obstruction, usually a kernel element or a cokernel class.

  3. Lift an element only along an arrow known to be surjective. Map an element forward along any available arrow.

  4. Use commutativity to move an equation to the other side of the diagram, then use exactness to replace a statement of “being zero” by “coming from the preceding image.”

  5. If a choice is required, prove that the difference between any two choices vanishes in the final target.

In a general abelian category, an “element” can be replaced by a morphism from a test object. When a lift is not directly available, use an epimorphic cover as in Lemma reference. In this way, the element chases below are not merely heuristic: they are concrete models for arguments with kernels, cokernels, and factorizations.

As a worked example, consider the commutative diagram of \(R\)-modules \[\text{Diagram mastery-bridge-001-diagram-chasing-diagram-001}\] with both rows exact. Suppose that \(a'\) and \(a''\) are injective. To prove that \(a\) is injective, start with the obstruction \(x\in\operatorname{ker}(a)\). Commutativity gives \(a''p(x)=qa(x)=0\), so the injectivity of \(a''\) gives \(p(x)=0\). Exactness of the top row gives \(x=i(x')\) for some \(x'\in A'\). Next, \[0=a(x)=a i(x')=j a'(x').\] Because \(j\) and \(a'\) are injective, \(x'=0\), and hence \(x=0\). Notice the recurring pattern: start in a kernel, move right, use injectivity, return to the left by exactness, and then use injectivity once more.

Exercises and complete solutions

Exercise 1 — Functoriality of kernels, cokernels, and images

Let \[\text{Diagram mastery-bridge-001-diagram-chasing-diagram-002} \qquad (ga=bf)\] be a commutative square of \(R\)-modules.

  1. Construct the natural homomorphisms \(\overline a:\operatorname{ker}(f)\to\operatorname{ker}(g)\) and \(\overline b:\operatorname{coker}(f)\to\operatorname{coker}(g)\).

  2. Prove that \(b(\operatorname{im}(f))\subset\operatorname{im}(g)\), with equality if \(a\) is surjective.

  3. Prove that \(\operatorname{ker}(f)=a^{-1}(\operatorname{ker}(g))\) if \(b\) is injective.

Solution.

If \(x\in\operatorname{ker}(f)\), then \(g(a(x))=b(f(x))=0\), so \(a(x)\in\operatorname{ker}(g)\). Restricting \(a\) gives \(\overline a:\operatorname{ker}(f)\to\operatorname{ker}(g)\). For cokernels, define \[\overline b([y])=[b(y)], \qquad [y]\in B/\operatorname{im}(f).\] If \(y\) is replaced by \(y+f(x)\), then \(b(y+f(x))=b(y)+g(a(x))\), which determines the same class modulo \(\operatorname{im}(g)\). Thus \(\overline b\) is well defined. These two constructions are precisely those in equation.

Next, \[b(\operatorname{im}(f))=b(f(A))=g(a(A))\subset g(A')=\operatorname{im}(g).\] If \(a\) is surjective, then \(a(A)=A'\), so the inclusion is an equality. Finally, \(x\in\operatorname{ker}(f)\) always implies \(a(x)\in\operatorname{ker}(g)\). Conversely, if \(a(x)\in\operatorname{ker}(g)\), then \(0=g(a(x))=b(f(x))\); injectivity of \(b\) gives \(f(x)=0\). Thus \(x\in\operatorname{ker}(f)\), and consequently \(\operatorname{ker}(f)=a^{-1}(\operatorname{ker}(g))\).

Exercise 2 — Intersections, sums, and the isomorphism theorem

Let \(U\) and \(V\) be submodules of an \(R\)-module \(M\). Define \[r:U\cap V\longrightarrow U\oplus V,\quad r(w)=(w,-w), \qquad s:U\oplus V\longrightarrow U+V,\quad s(u,v)=u+v.\] Prove that \[0\longrightarrow U\cap V\xrightarrow{r}U\oplus V \xrightarrow{s}U+V\longrightarrow0\] is exact. Use a kernel-and-image chase to obtain the canonical isomorphism \[U/(U\cap V)\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}(U+V)/V.\]

Solution.

If \(r(w)=0\), then the first component gives \(w=0\), so \(r\) is injective. Moreover, \(s(r(w))=w-w=0\), and hence \(\operatorname{im}(r)\subset\operatorname{ker}(s)\). If \((u,v)\in\operatorname{ker}(s)\), then \(u+v=0\). Thus \(u=-v\) belongs to both \(U\) and \(V\), and \[(u,v)=(u,-u)=r(u).\] Consequently \(\operatorname{ker}(s)=\operatorname{im}(r)\). Every element of \(U+V\) has the form \(u+v\), so \(s\) is surjective. The sequence is exact.

Now consider the homomorphism \[\theta:U\longrightarrow (U+V)/V,\qquad u\longmapsto u+V.\] This map is surjective because \((u+v)+V=u+V\). Its kernel consists of all \(u\in U\) that also belong to \(V\), namely \(U\cap V\). Epi–mono factorization, or the Isomorphism Theorem reference, gives the canonical isomorphism \(U/(U\cap V)\ensuremath{\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}}(U+V)/V\).

Exercise 3 — Short Five Lemma

In the commutative diagram \[\text{Diagram mastery-bridge-001-diagram-chasing-diagram-003}\] suppose that both rows are exact.

  1. If \(a'\) and \(a''\) are injective, prove that \(a\) is injective.

  2. If \(a'\) and \(a''\) are surjective, prove that \(a\) is surjective.

  3. Conclude that if \(a'\) and \(a''\) are isomorphisms, then \(a\) is also an isomorphism.

Solution.

For (i), take \(x\in A\) with \(a(x)=0\). Then \(a''p(x)=qa(x)=0\). Since \(a''\) is injective, \(p(x)=0\); exactness of the top row gives \(x=i(x')\). Next, \(0=a i(x')=j a'(x')\). Since \(j\) and \(a'\) are injective, \(x'=0\), and hence \(x=0\).

For (ii), take \(y\in B\) and set \(y''=q(y)\). Surjectivity of \(a''\) gives \(x''\in A''\) with \(a''(x'')=y''\). Since \(p\) is surjective, choose \(x\in A\) with \(p(x)=x''\). Now \[q(y-a(x))=y''-a''p(x)=0.\] Exactness of the bottom row gives \(y-a(x)=j(y')\) for some \(y'\in B'\). Surjectivity of \(a'\) gives \(x'\in A'\) with \(a'(x')=y'\). Therefore \[y=a(x)+j(a'(x'))=a(x+i(x')).\] Thus \(a\) is surjective. If the two outer morphisms are isomorphisms, (i) and (ii) show that \(a\) is both injective and surjective, and therefore an isomorphism.

Exercise 4 — Nine Lemma

Consider the commutative diagram of \(R\)-modules \[\text{Diagram mastery-bridge-001-diagram-chasing-diagram-004}\] with all three columns exact. Suppose that the top and middle rows are exact. Prove that the bottom row is also exact.

Solution.

First we prove that \(f''\) is injective. Take \(a''\in A''\) with \(f''(a'')=0\), and lift \(a''\) to \(a\in A\).
